## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with those possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a single glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which places in their works, commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture.**

**An edition surpassing all others and easily preferable to them all, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reissued works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, uniform throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; one thousand three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 850

## Ebbo, or Ebo, Bishop of Rheims

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice Concerning Ebbo

*(Flodoard, Ecclesiastical History of Rheims)*

[Col. 0009A] Vulfarius was succeeded by Ebbo, an energetic man, educated in the liberal disciplines, a Transrhenish and German by birth, and, as is reported, the foster-brother and fellow student of the emperor Louis. He took great care to equip the Church with many resources, especially with craftsmen, whom he gathered from every quarter, established in residences, and rewarded with benefices.

He restored to ecclesiastical ownership certain slaves or tenants who had deserted the Church, having recovered and secured them by law before the public judges, both through his own efforts and through Radulfus, the vicedominus and advocate of the Church. He also exchanged certain properties and slaves belonging to the Church with various persons for the advantage of the parties involved. He likewise obtained imperial decrees concerning these exchanges.

From the emperor Louis he also secured letters to Count Robert for the defense of ecclesiastical property, which certain people were attempting to seize. He organized several estates of the Church by having their tenants and their services recorded by capable men.

[Col. 0009B] At the urging of this bishop, Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, composed six little books on remedies for sins and on the order and judgments of penance.

This Bishop Ebbo received Pope Stephen at Rheims together with King Louis.

Finally, when discord arose between father and son—namely, the emperor Louis and Lothair—he favored the son’s party. Together with the other bishops, he rebuked the emperor Louis for certain faults alleged against him, when his sons seized him and Lothair brought his father with him to the palace at Compiègne. There he had him confined with the bishops and several other leading men, who ordered him to go into a monastery and remain there all the days of his life.

Louis refused this and did not consent to their will. Then all the bishops who were present are said to have treated him harshly, reproaching him for his sins, taking the sword from his side, and clothing him in sackcloth.

[Col. 0009C] Therefore, after Louis was restored by his son of the same name [Col. 0010A] to his kingdom and his honor, Ebbo was deposed from the episcopate for disloyalty to the emperor.

After this deposition, Ebbo is said to have lived in the regions of Cisalpine Gaul until the death of the emperor Louis, which occurred in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 840. After the emperor’s death, Lothair came from Italy into Francia. Ebbo met him at Worms, and after several days Lothair restored to him, by an imperial decree, the see and diocese of Rheims.

A synod held at Soissons opposed this restoration, asserting that one condemned by that synod and by forty-three bishops could not be restored by a smaller number. Ebbo brought this decree to Rheims with him, circulated it there among many people of different professions and orders, and had it publicly read in the church of Rheims.

Thus, at the time when Lothair expelled Charles from the kingdom and drove him beyond the Seine, Ebbo received the see of Rheims six years after [Col. 0010B] his deposition and began to exercise the episcopal ministry. Celebrating ordinations, he ordained certain clerics, and held this bishopric for approximately a year, until Charles, having regained his strength, returned to Belgica.

When Ebbo heard this, he abandoned the see of Rheims, went to Lothair, and remained in his familiar service until he went to Rome together with Drogo, bishop of Metz. There he asked Pope Sergius to reconcile him and grant him the pallium. The same pope, however, granted him communion only and refused to give him the pallium.

When Ebbo returned from Rome, he possessed the abbey of Saint Columbanus in Italy, granted by the emperor Lothair, until he refused to carry out a mission to Greece entrusted to him by that emperor. Consequently, after the properties given to him by the emperor had been taken away, he moved to King Louis of Germany. From him he obtained a bishopric in the region of Saxony, where thereafter he performed the episcopal ministry.

[Col. 0009]

## Confession of Ebbo

*(In Flodoard, in the same place)*

[Col. 0009D] I, Ebbo, an unworthy bishop, recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, appointed as judges of my offenses my witnesses and confessors—namely, Archbishop Aiulfus, Bishop Badaradus, and also Bishop Modoinus—and I gave them a sincere confession, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the episcopal office and ministry, for which I recognize myself to be unworthy, and make myself a stranger to it on account of my crimes, in which I have secretly confessed to them that I sinned.

I did this in such a way that they might be witnesses of another person succeeding me, being consecrated, and being appointed in my place, one who could worthily preside over and benefit the Church, over which until now I have presided unworthily.

And so that thereafter I might be unable, by canonical authority, to make any claim or appeal, I confirmed it by subscribing with my own hand.

I, Ebbo, formerly bishop, have subscribed.

# Apologia of Ebbo

*(In Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. 3)*

[Col. 0011]

[Col. 0011A] Of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, legate of the holy apostolic see for the conversion of the pagans and the redemption of captives, dispatched with the consent of Louis Caesar and of all the dignitaries of his palace; afterward, during the time of persecution, expelled from the church of Rheims after many bishops and other noble laymen had suffered exile, and subjected to seven years of confinement; then, upon the succession of Lothair Augustus, recalled and restored publicly and with ecclesiastical authority, with the great officials assisting or deciding together with the holy Catholic bishops subscribed below:

Drogo, archiepiscopal prelate of the palace; and with holy unanimity all these agreeing with him: Autgarius, archbishop; Amalwinus, archbishop; Audax, archbishop; Hetti, archbishop; Joseph, bishop; Adalulfus, bishop; David, bishop; Hrodingus, bishop; Gislebertus, bishop; Herminus, bishop; Frotharius, bishop; Badaratus, bishop; Hagano, bishop; Hrotgarius, bishop; Ado, [Col. 0011C] bishop; Samuel, bishop; Provocatus, bishop; Hrambertus, bishop; Rataldus [lacuna]; Amalricus, called bishop; together with very many other priests and deacons assisting in the public palace at Ingelenheim.

After these matters had been completed—canonical restoration, the chief palatine affairs, and the solemn reception by the bishops of the province—this was confirmed on the eighth day before the Ides of December in the principal church and holy see of Rheims. All the bishops of the diocese, or their representatives, came to meet him there, together with distinguished fellow citizens advanced by ecclesiastical or public necessity or usefulness, except those prevented solely by inability to come. Rejoicing together in a general assembly, they issued this public subscription with unanimous agreement, having been reasonably instructed by the examples of the ancient Fathers.

[Col. 0011D] By writing these things, all the bishops listed below unanimously established and confirmed them.

Since it is not unknown, and appears to have been ascertained by many, how this great Church of Gaul, under the rule of the Franks, is in these times shaken and afflicted by various disturbances and by violent indignation arising from the discord of princes, many bishops have consequently been forcibly expelled from their own sees, or, abandoning their flocks through fear, have been driven into exile in different regions.

Among them was Ebbo, archbishop of the church of Rheims, who was torn from his own see and led into a violent exile by the indignation of the princes. Therefore, after he had been brought back under guard in order to escape danger and calm the fury of his persecutors, and to buy time so that he might reserve himself for a better moment, he withdrew from the episcopal ministry with the consent of the bishops. In the midst of terrors and discord, reason does not permit victims to be offered, as the Lord says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there,” and so forth (Matthew 5:23).

After God had restored more peaceful times to his Church, it pleased the princes and ecclesiastical magistrates that this same shepherd should return to his rightful fold and once again receive for protection the sheep whom he had been compelled to abandon.

To these ecclesiastical and proper proceedings I, Theoderic, bishop of Cambrai, gave canonical assent. Just as I previously grieved in sympathy over his departure, so now I rejoice over his return; and, confirming these decisions of the elders and brothers, I have subscribed, because I have read that such things often occurred in other ecclesiastical records.

Hrodhadus, bishop of Soissons, have likewise confirmed these things.

Hildemannus, bishop of Beauvais, likewise. Symeon, bishop of Laon, likewise. Erpwinus, bishop of Senlis, likewise. Raginharius, bishop of Amiens, likewise. Emmo, bishop of Noyon, likewise. Folcwinus, bishop of Thérouanne, likewise.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Most High God, with Louis Caesar reigning gloriously—although the first period of his reign shone very brightly with prosperity, its final period, shaken by excessive adversity, suffered what was almost divine indignation, the force of which the Gospel always greatly dreads concerning the last times, saying: “Brother will hand over brother to death, and father his son, and children will rise against their parents” (Matthew 10:21).

Many powerful men were consequently expelled from their homeland; bishops of God and other ministers likewise suffered confinement and exile. Certain noble laymen of both sexes were even compelled to assume the monastic habit, so that, at least chastened by these scourges and swiftly corrected, they might receive remedies for salvation. For those whom gentle prosperity had corrupted needed harsh adversity to cleanse them, lest the divine majesty should itself rage against them and bring them to punishment in hell.

Having recognized these evident dangers, I, Ebbo of Rheims, an unworthy bishop, afflicted along with the other anxious persons by three pressures—namely, stripped of all my possessions, oppressed by the prince’s anger and confinement, and additionally wearied by bodily illness—did not blush to say with the holy Psalmist: “I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Psalm 37:19).

If, warned by divine scourges, I had neglected the law of the Lord in prosperity, I ought to flee to it in adversity. Thus, if I had once unjustly injured anyone through power, I resolved here in my distress to bear patiently the person injuring me. If I had unjustly taken anything from anyone, I did not resist when everything was taken from me; rather, to the one taking my tunic I also left my cloak.

If at some time I had neglected to love even one enemy, I learned here to pray for my persecutors. Thus, accusing myself in humble satisfaction, I decided to calm the fury of my persecutors rather than litigate, instructed by holy Abraham, who, amid dangers, divesting himself of authority over his wife, chose humbly to yield to those using force rather than damnably resist.

The holy Apostle likewise taught the same thing when he said: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Romans 12:19).

Amid divine scourges, blessed Job preferred not to murmur but to pray and confess his sins. In his anxiety, among his many other laments, he said: “I have sinned: what shall I do to you, O guardian of men?” (Job 7:20).

Encouraged by these manifold examples of the Fathers, driven by the same worldly force, I was compelled to appear before the palace tribunal—not before a synodal assembly of holy men, to which a bishop may not be forcibly dragged, but which ought rather to be canonically convened freely.

It happened, nevertheless, that I stood amid a multitude of holy brothers who had long been afflicted there by the hardships of winter. Refreshed by their pious consolation, that divinely inspired sentence of charity came before me: “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

With their counsel assisting me, I chose three of them as my most trusted helpers: namely, Archbishop Aiulfus and Bishops Badaradus and Modoinus. With them I carefully discussed the teaching of our Savior and the remission of sins, mindful of the Gospel command: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar” (Matthew 5:23).

Seeing by this authority that my brother—and all the more my prince—was angry against me, I left the gift of my offering before the altar. Yielding with complete satisfaction to the consent of the confessors and brothers mentioned above, and because I hoped to recover concord, I patiently accepted all the injuries inflicted upon me. Through the purity of confession I believed that I would receive remission and pardon of sins, not condemnation.

I judged pride in myself to be a diabolical death, vain glory, and perpetual ruin. I condemned in myself the harmful friendship of this world—that is, of those who love the world—which, according to divine testimony, belongs to enmity against God, and I regarded it as a punishment of hell, since Holy Scripture says: “Whoever is a friend of this age will be counted an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

I regarded an insult against a brother, as a foolish utterance, as a punishment of Gehenna according to the Gospel law. I abhorred lying and hatred no less than homicide, as the Apostle testifies: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

In the same way I rejected lying as the worst crime, concerning which it has been divinely decreed: “You will destroy all who speak a lie” (Psalm 5:7). By this crime God is offended, one’s neighbor is deceived, and the deceitful person himself perishes through his own necessity.

Terrified and pierced by these and other similar, most fearful plagues, I groaned—not falsely but devoutly—as the Lord chastised me; for “those whom he loves, he rebukes and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). The holy Apostle cries out: “When we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32).

[Col. 0014B] Therefore, lest those raging against me sin further, I employed the example of escape given by our Savior, who hid himself among the hands of his persecutors and went out from the temple. Nor, when dangers threatened, did I delay leaving the temple and withdrawing from the pontifical office, since I had already been forcibly excluded for three years from the place where I was bound to offer sacrifice.

At the time of the Passion, the apostles too, frightened, sought not the ritual of sacrifice but only hidden places of prayer, with prudent vigilance, in order to conceal themselves. For fear together with fraternal discord does not rightly celebrate divine gifts; nor does a time of mourning call for solemn rites, but rather for remedies of escape, as the Psalm says: “I will confess my injustices against myself, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin. For this every holy person will pray to you at the fitting time” (Psalm 32:6).

If the saints labor for the remission of sins at this fitting time, sinners must certainly not delay running to the remedies of confession.

Therefore, the public inscription of my confession should in no way be considered harmful, but rather extremely beneficial. Through it it is shown that remission of sins can certainly be achieved, since the law of penitents, which begins in sorrow, rightly rises to joy, as the divine sentence says: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm 126:6).

For the Lord is read not to despise or condemn, but rather to heal and raise up, those contrite in heart. In my distress, therefore, I issued my subscription not under the title of condemnation but rather of deliverance. I endured it not because I had been convicted, but because I was under severe constraint.

I judged it better to insert it here in a public record as a testimony of truth, lest it later be stained by the lies of some rival through addition or subtraction. What was then done privately as an argument for deliverance may now be discussed publicly everywhere by all in the spirit of true charity; and, since no definite crime of condemnation is there established, he may in no way thereafter suffer any risk of disgrace.

Such a subscription must therefore be regarded not as harmful but as greatly beneficial. It calmed the fury of my persecutors, alleviated the anxious winter hardships endured by the brothers, and rescued me from the anger of my persecutors. Moreover, according to the authority of the Holy Scriptures, it offers remission of sins to me who confess, if I persevere, divinely chastised, in certain amendment of conduct.

I wrote it in a condition in which I did not fall before God but rather grew stronger through humble satisfaction. I offered these words, having issued them under compulsion to those using force, because I am certain and know whom I have believed, saying: “I, Ebbo, an unworthy bishop,” and so forth. See the confession above.

If anyone should decide that I must be condemned on the basis of this salutary written formula, discovered amid distress, he could likewise oppress me in all my writings, in which I never justify myself but everywhere declare myself by subscribing as an unworthy bishop.

Yet no one will be able to detect me in this same subscription as either a violator or a liar, because no one afterward presided there more usefully. For nearly seven years, during which remission is customarily granted in the holy Church to penitents for their sins, I waited patiently and impeded no one’s dignity of consecration there.

“Do not condemn,” says our Lord God, “and you will not be condemned; for in the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Luke 6:37).

This document, therefore, composed in response to various necessities—namely, on account of offenses and persecutors—if it still creates a scruple for someone who takes offense, let him examine the meaning of all the words written there. If he finds a definite crime from which canonical condemnation rightly follows, I ask that he judge justly and not with malice.

While he considers himself to be standing, let him beware lest he fall; for the malicious judge who looks for a speck in another’s eye does not feel the beam in his own.

Canonical authority shines more brightly than daylight: just as a bishop is never canonically deposed without a definite crime, so a bishop may not withdraw from office by spontaneous absolution—much less under the custody imposed by another through violence—without the concordant presence or consent of the citizens subject to him.

Ecclesiastical restoration therefore rightly prevails in all these matters over every other violent invention or arbitrary act of those who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ.

All acts that were not supported on every side by canonical authority are therefore justly judged null. Finally, trusting in so many and such great ecclesiastical safeguards and statutes, I sought remedies both present and eternal. I reproved myself among other harmful contagions for remaining too silent when it was time to speak and speaking too much when it was time to be silent.

I implored the divine majesty to set a guard over my mouth and a door of restraint around my lips: “Let not my heart incline to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins; but let the righteous rebuke me always in mercy” (Psalm 141:3, 6).

Since divine power permits even the righteous to rebuke only in mercy, how could a sinner lawfully condemn a sinner without divine vengeance? The Lord of lords permitted no one to condemn the adulterous woman, deserving of legal penalties, except one without sin (John 8:3).

Pierced in heart by this example of mercy, he showed that he desired not to kill but rather to have mercy than sacrifice (Hosea 6:6). He did not condemn the publican accusing himself (Luke 18:13), but rather justified him; he did not crush him but raised him up, since he did not say, “Whoever humbles himself will be condemned,” but, “He will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Likewise, he did not reject the man lying half-dead, but entrusted him for care to the holy innkeepers, who possessed the power of binding and loosing. In addition to the divinely received gift of the coins for the man's restoration, he urged them compassionately to show concern for the gain of eternal reward, saying: “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:30–35).

David’s momentary contrition likewise merited not his deposition but his restoration. The holy apostles, rebuked after the resurrection for their promised and feigned perseverance during the Passion, and for their folly, unbelief, and hardness of heart—and Peter, whose denial was cleansed through contrition of heart—are not celebrated as condemned, but rather as corrected and restored to their former dignities.

The holy Church of God everywhere rejoices in imitation of the restoration of the fallen. It is likewise clear that laymen of both sexes, compelled by recent authority of the palace in their distress to assume the monastic habit of penitents, returned to their former worldly condition when peace was restored.

By the same practice, it is evident that there is no disgrace if an offended cleric, after humble satisfaction, recovers his proper clerical status.

Since such evident examples of divine benefits from the New and Old Testaments have been shown to us, I devotedly offered myself to the humble satisfaction commonly known and mentioned above, because from the beginning humble satisfaction has always merited restoration rather than condemnation.

After the persecution, when Lothair Caesar, the glorious heir of the offended prince, succeeded him, ecclesiastical concord was immediately restored to me. Finding the Church vacant, which I had once lost by violence, I received it back after nearly seven years—not presumptuously, but duly, at the request of the holy orders there, after my satisfaction.

Many magnificent bishops assisted together with the prince. By their authority I was recalled by all. It pleased me that this annotation should be made known throughout the universal Catholic Church of God in these written records, to be read in future times, and that the sinister opinions of false brothers should be erased by this certain truth.

It was fitting to satisfy the holy and true brothers in all these matters and to rejoice more over the grace of restoration than to grieve over the wickedness of condemnation. This festive restoration, as was proper to suggest, will provide worthy descendants for God.

# Account of the Clergy of Rheims

[Col. 0017] How Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, because he had conspired against the Emperor Louis the Pious, was deposed by the bishops in the year 835; after Louis’s death was restored to his see; and then deposed again.

*(Duchesne, Writers of the History of the Franks)*

[Col. 0017A] When all the people abandoned the emperor Louis and went over to his son Lothair, Bishop Ebbo also went with them to Lothair.

Lothair, traveling through the imperial palaces, brought his father with him as far as Soissons, to the monastery of Saint Medard. There, at the urging and command of the other bishops, or of the leading men of the kingdom, Ebbo was compelled—because Soissons was in his diocese—to impose public penance upon him. For this he incurred Louis’s excessive and perpetual hostility.

Afterward, a very large part of the nobles and people once again turned to the aforesaid emperor, abandoning his son Lothair, and restored him to the empire at the monastery of Saint-Denis.

At that time Bishop Ebbo was staying in the monastery of Saint Basolus, [Col. 0017B] within the parish of Rheims. He was lame in both feet and afflicted by an excessive illness.

Fearing that he could neither leave with Lothair nor soften the emperor’s mind toward him in any way, and fearing that—as commonly happens in such a storm of fury—he might be killed by frivolous and undisciplined men, supposedly for loyalty to the lord emperor, he ordered himself to be carried to a nearby river called the Marne. He was put into a boat and taken to Paris, to the cell of a certain recluse.

He hoped that he could remain there safely until he might somehow appease the emperor’s mind or, having recovered his health, be able to follow Lothair.

When the lord emperor heard that he had fled there, he sent orders that Ebbo be taken under guard to the monastery of Saint Boniface at Voldas, [Col. 0017C] kept there, and brought after two years to Thionville, in the parish of Metz, where the emperor’s public assembly was being held.

Presented before the council of bishops, he was accused by the emperor and for a long time tormented by extreme terrors. Finally, after deliberation with his fellow bishops and brothers, they reasoned that, since neither a bishop nor an archbishop could be stripped of all his possessions, held under guard, and separated from his church, and since he could not be condemned in a synod that had not been convened by apostolic authority or confirmed by its legation, in accordance with the decrees of the holy Fathers, nor be tortured any longer in such circumstances—and that, even while physically sound, he should in some way avoid the anger of the greatest prince—he was compelled to write this document:

“I, Ebbo, formerly an unworthy bishop, recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, appointed as judges of my offenses my witnesses and confessors—namely, Archbishop Aiulfus, Bishop Bradaradus, and also Bishop Modoinus—and gave them a sincere confession, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the episcopal office and ministry, for which I recognize myself to be unworthy, and make myself a stranger to it on account of my crimes, in which I have secretly confessed to them that I sinned.

“I did this in such a way that they might be witnesses of another person succeeding me, being consecrated, and being appointed in my place, one who could worthily preside over and benefit the Church, over which until now I have presided unworthily. And so that thereafter I might be unable, by canonical authority, to make any claim or appeal, I confirmed it by subscribing with my own hand.”

No one ever afterward sought the testimony of these witnesses or confessors concerning the succession or the consecration of another, although one of them—namely Badaratus—was present at Ebbo’s restoration.

[Col. 0018B] When the council had ended, he was returned under strict custody to the same place, namely the monastery of Saint Boniface. After some time, he was likewise entrusted for safekeeping to Freculf, bishop of Lisieux, and from there to Boso the abbot, in the monastery of Saint Benedict. Under Boso’s authority he was living in exile when the lord emperor entered upon the way of all flesh.

After the emperor’s death, the aforesaid abbot Boso brought him back to Lothair, and he met him at Ingelheim. There, when a synod had been assembled by apostolic authority and at the command of the emperor Lothair, he was restored before that assembly by these bishops: Drogo; Bishop Hecti; Archbishop Othgar; Archbishop David; Archbishop Amalwin; Archbishop Joseph; Archbishop Andaux; [Col. 0018C] Bishop Adalulf; Bishop Erminius; Bishop Badaradus; Bishop Agano; Bishop Samuel; Bishop Roding; Bishop Frothar; Bishop Gislebert; Bishop Ado; Bishop Hrampert; Bishop Ratulf, called a bishop; Bishop Harcarrus, called a bishop; Bishop Amalric, called a bishop; and Boso, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, together with many other abbots, priests, and deacons.

The aforesaid emperor Lothair, or rather the council just mentioned, sent him back to his own see, namely the church of Rheims. Arriving there on the eighth day before the Ides of December, he was received by his suffragan bishops, Bishop Rothad, Bishop Simeon, Bishop Lupus, and Bishop Erpuinus, together with representatives of all the other bishops of the diocese of Rheims. Since those bishops were detained by various illnesses and were unable to be present there bodily, they nevertheless presented their presence to him through ecclesiastical envoys and letters of excuse.

Moreover, he was received by the canons and monks, and by letters from the neighboring districts of the entire diocese, together with an immense multitude [Col. 0018D] of both sexes. All of them, carrying palm branches and burning candles and proclaiming praises to God from the depths of their hearts and with the loftiest voices, went a long way out from the church to meet him; and, singing psalms without interruption, they led him as far as the church. [Col. 0019A]

When the prayer had been completed and silence imposed, Bishop Rothad ascended the ambo, taking with him the monk Ingobert. He first addressed the rejoicing people concerning the desired return of their own shepherd, and explained how he had been restored by the holy council, or by the emperor Lothair, and sent back to them. He then ordered the monk Ingobert to read aloud the document of Ebbo’s restoration.

In the presence of the entire church, the envoys of the bishops also gave, each one, the written assent of his own bishop and people. All these documents were publicly read aloud by the monk Ingobert. Finally, the chorepiscopus Jutaus [Vitaus], vicar of Bishop Theodoric, gave the assent written below. We have inserted it here before the others so that, through it, the events may be understood more clearly, although they are briefly summarized, and so that the agreement of those who could not be present at his restoration may be more plainly recognized.

> “Since it is not unknown, but seems to have been ascertained by many, how this greatest Church of Gaul, under the rule of the Franks, has in these times been shaken and afflicted by various disturbances and conflicts, through the violent indignation of princes, many bishops have been driven from their own sees or, having abandoned their flocks through fear, have been exiled in different regions. Among them was Ebbo, archbishop [Col. 0019C] of the church of Rheims, who was seized from his own see and, through the violent indignation of the princes, led into exile.
>
> “Having therefore been brought back under custody, so that he might escape the danger threatening him and calm the fury of his persecutors, buying time in order to reserve himself for a better season, he withdrew from the episcopal ministry with the consent of the bishops. For amid terrors and conflicts reason does not permit one to offer sacrifices, as the Lord says: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there,’ and so forth.
>
> “But after God had restored calmer times to His Church, it pleased the princes and ecclesiastical authorities that this same shepherd should return to the flock owed to him, and that he should again receive for protection the sheep whom he had been compelled to abandon. [Col. 0019D] Accordingly, in these ecclesiastical matters, I, Theodoric, bishop of Cambrai, giving canonical assent, just as I formerly grieved in compassion over his departure, so now rejoice over his return; and, strengthening the decrees of the elders and brethren, I have subscribed to them. For I have read in other ecclesiastical records that such things have often occurred.”

When these matters had been completed, the bells again resounding and the entire Church crying out, “We praise You, O God,” the often-mentioned Bishop Ebbo was led into the vestry. He was clothed in episcopal vestments, as were the other bishops, and they proceeded with him to celebrate Mass.

For Bishop Rothad supported him with his right hand, while on his own side he had Lupus, bishop of the church of Châlons, and Hirminfred, a priest who later became bishop of the church of Beauvais. Bishop Simeon supported him with his left hand, and on his own side he likewise had Bishop Erpuinus and Vitaus [Jutaus], chorepiscopus of the church of Cambrai. Thus they proceeded with him to the holy altar, led him to his own seat, and, all sitting with him, shared with him in the entire episcopal office on that day.

During the long period of his exile, three bishops had been ordained in his absence: Bishop Simeon, Bishop Lupus, and Bishop Erpuinus. Such ordinations are altogether prohibited by the most holy canons. After the consecration and the solemn celebration of the sacrifice had been completed with the whole Church present, they entreated him to establish and confirm their ordination by his authority. He most graciously heard their prayers and publicly gave them, before the most holy altar, rings and staffs as tokens of his authority, in confirmation of their ordination. He also addressed the entire Church concerning them, so that everyone might know that he consented, in the charity that comes from God, to their ordination, without reserve.

Afterward, receiving the assistance and embassy of the often-mentioned emperor Lothair, he went to the thresholds of the blessed apostles. He was not satisfied with his restoration without the authority of the apostolic see, given the consent of so many bishops and other good men. There he was most graciously received by the most devout and spiritual father Gregory, namely the lord apostolic, and was fully restored by apostolic authority, as we have in our possession. [Col. 0020C]

Finally, after he had peacefully discharged all the episcopal offices for more than two years, the often-mentioned mother, the church of Rheims, summoned us to the ecclesiastical ranks. God knows that we did not undertake these offices presumptuously; rather, we were advanced by the election of the Church’s ministers, by the acclamation of our teachers, and even by the offering of the entire Church.

After this, when they divided their paternal kingdoms among themselves, the emperor Lothair and our lord, the most glorious king Charles, the aforesaid mother of ours, the church of Rheims, fell into the portion and dominion of the most glorious King Charles. With him was the most influential and greatly favored Fulcho, the abbot who had previously held that church as a priest under the emperor lord Louis and, through the favor of that same king with whom he was, had obtained it again.

Fearing the attack and fury of Fulcho, the aforesaid Bishop Ebbo—who was not yet reconciled with that king, since he had remained with Lothair, to whom he had first attached himself—withdrew and stayed with him. Since he feared that he could not peacefully regain his own see, he obtained, by apostolic authority and with the consent of the bishops, and also by a grant from Louis, king of Germany, the vacant see of Hildesheim for the time being, while always aspiring to his own see.

It is established by the testimony of many that he sought to recover that see from King Charles, although he was burdened by a severe illness of the feet. Compelled by necessity, he returned to the aforesaid see of Hildesheim and, in accordance with the restoration by the apostolic see, is shown to have discharged the episcopal office immutably until the end of his life. There, among many other good works, he also performed various ordinations, which all who love God gladly embrace, without ever reproaching them in any way.

Meanwhile, each of us peacefully ministered in his own order and shared communion with all who came together at that same mother Church, both bishops and kings, as well as all the powerful—until King Charles, mentioned above, later entrusted the same church to the governance of the venerable Hincmar.

Immediately after his ordination, Hincmar, hostile toward us, prohibited us from ministering. When we humbly questioned him, seeking to learn our fault and the reason for our deposition, he did not wish to allege any fault against us; nevertheless, he ordered us to cease from our own offices. Those among us who did not wish to withdraw from the church of Rheims because of this same prohibition afterward continued to minister without any opposition.

It would be lengthy to set down in writing how many quarrels and disputes arose between him and our ordainer, the often-mentioned Ebbo, because Hincmar was unable to obtain what he desired. At last he prevailed upon the most devout Pope Leo to give him judges for his case: Bishop Drogo, Archbishop Otgar, Archbishop Hecti, and Archbishop Gunbald.

Accordingly, by sending letters to the aforesaid Hincmar, he ordered him to appear at Trier before those judges, who had received authority to hear his case, in order to answer the charges against Ebbo. This was never brought to completion, because various circumstances intervened.

The matters contained between these two signs we heard from the monk himself and from those who were present; we ourselves, however, did not see them.

> “Likewise, as is reported, when the same Hincmar requested the pallium from apostolic authority, he was unable to obtain it until a certain Ermenard, a monk of Orbais, had confirmed under oath to that holy Roman see that Ebbo had already departed this world. Yet Ebbo was still alive, although weighed down by old age and various illnesses, and was peacefully directing and governing the see of Hildesheim.
>
> “Nevertheless, in the very letters of apostolic authority by which the use of the pallium was granted to Hincmar, this was cautiously inserted, as it can be found in the archives of the holy mother Roman Church: ‘We grant you the use of the pallium, provided that the dispute which exists between you and Ebbo remains unaffected.’
>
> “To bring this dispute to an end, the same Ebbo was never able to appear, neither under any command nor by any order of authority. While they were thus contending, we always bore our shameful deposition humbly and peacefully.”

After our aforesaid ordainer died in the month of March, our lord Hincmar immediately obtained from King Charles that a synod be summoned at Soissons, at the monastery of Saint Medard. He ordered us—nearly fourteen priests and deacons at that time—to go there, promising that he would treat us mercifully.

When we refused and humbly pleaded that he should not make us go there to our greater confusion and deposition, he did not listen. Rather, he ordered our masters to compel us by every means to go there; and they did so.

When we arrived, he ordered us to submit a written statement of accusation. We were entirely unwilling to do this, since we already knew in part, and afterward came to know more clearly, what was being plotted against us. Nevertheless, although compelled, all of us except one submitted it.

That one had been handed over, before Ebbo was removed, by canonical letters to Liutard, bishop of Vincennes, and afterward, with Liutard’s permission and at his request, had been ordained together with us. He was with King Charles and did not come to the synod at all, since his own bishop was not there. Nor had he, like us, come to the synod after being canonically summoned. Therefore he did not send his name there in writing, although it is said that he wrote it in the statement which we had been forced to sign and sent it there through Sigloard, Leuto, and Isaac. He did no such thing.

After the statement had been submitted, our lord Archbishop Hincmar rose and chose judges for himself: Wenilo, archbishop; Amalric, archbishop; and Pardulus, his suffragan bishop, entrusting his own place to him as well.

He then ordered us to choose judges, although we had already been excommunicated by him alone—if it is permissible to say so—not canonically. Remaining in this extreme distress, we feared that if we did not choose judges, this would be attributed to pride and arrogance; but if we did choose them, we knew that it would in no way benefit us, since everything was being violently extorted from us. For we were not allowed to speak at all, whether because of the prejudice of condemnation or because our summons to the synod was unlawful.

The judges whom we were to choose also had to be selected without any intervening period of time, under the pressure of sudden necessity, whereas according to the provisions of the laws judges ought to be chosen after a sufficient interval, so that they may be carefully instructed about the matters on which they are to pronounce judgment.

[Col. 0021]

## THE LITTLE POEMS OF EBBO

*(Flodoard, Ecclesiastical History of Rheims)*

[Col. 0021]

### I. Inscription that Ebbo placed before the church of Saint Peter

Louis, made Caesar while Stephen the great pope crowned him

[Col. 0022D] in this see, then Ebbo the bishop

renewed all the foundations of this place;

the bishop, subjecting the city’s rights to himself, enlarged everything.

### II. Epitaph of Ebbo’s mother

If you ask about the beginnings of my life,

know that they fell at the beginning of Charles’s reign:

while Louis was triumphing, my final day passed.

The Rhine first washed my character, the German river;

the Loire, the Gallic river, nourished it in its second stage;

the Seine cherished my youth (*juventam*, evidently corrupted in the printed text as *jumentam*), while the foul Vidula was filthy.

My only son was bishop of this city;

he took me as his companion in his labors,

desiring to renew the place next to ruin.

For nearly ten years we spent our time together here:

Ebbo was the ruler; I, humble Himiltrudis, was his mother.

Together we raised the foundations of the holy see,

while the bishop performed the labor owed to God.

Weary, I sought rest. Behold, beneath this mound,

on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, death carried me away.

O traveler, always beware of excesses.

I confess that I did not profit as I ought while I could;

speak a word of pardon; grant, O God, forgiveness to sinners.

**In the year of the Lord 850. Hartmann, monk of Saint Gall.**

[Col. 0023]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON HARTMANN

*(Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature)*

[Col. 0023B] Hartmann, monk of Saint Gall, whom Ekkehard testifies in chapter 15 of the *Life of Notker* to have flourished in the time of Abbot Grimald and Harmot—that is, around the year 850 [Note: Canisius, vol. III, Basnage edition, part II, p. 562; add vol. III, part III, p. 187]—was a man of great counsel. That holy man composed a litany in humble prayer and made its melody.

Canisius published that litany among Hartmann’s other sacred hymns in volume 5 of the *Ancient Lessons*, part 2 (in the new edition, volume 2, part 3, p. 192); it was reprinted from there in the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 27, pp. 509 ff. Compare the material drawn from a manuscript of the Helmstedt Library and published by Polycarp Leyser in his *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 263.

Ekkehard there distinguishes from this Hartmann a younger Hartmann, whose melodies, he says, together with those of Waltmann, “do not conceal what they themselves were like”; for many works of theirs are renowned throughout the Church.

[Col. 0023B]

## POEMS OF HARTMANN

*(See Patrologia, volume LXXXVII, column 30 and following.)*

**In the year of the Lord 850. Ermenric, monk of Reichenau.**

[Col. 0023]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ERMENRIC

*(Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature)*

[Col. 0023C] Ermenric, or Ermanric, a disciple of Walahfrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau, and himself a monk of Reichenau, wrote, after Walahfrid’s death in 849, a book on grammar for Grimold, archchaplain. Mabillon published from it fragments containing much material about the distinguished men of Saint Gall in volume 4 [Col. 0024C] of his *Analecta*, p. 329 (in the new edition, folio edition, pp. 420–422).

No one has yet brought to light the short work which, as Ermenric testifies, he sent to Bishop Gozbald concerning the beginning of the monastery of Reichenau and the life of the brothers serving God there.

[Col. 0025]

## FRAGMENTS FROM ERMANRIC’S BOOK ON GRAMMAR

[Note: [Col. 0025C] In the library of Saint Gall there is a little book, from which we give the fragments, bearing this title: “Here begins the letter of Ermenric, bishop, to Lord Grimold, abbot and archchaplain.” The codex was written in the author’s lifetime, that is, more than eight hundred years ago, at the time when Grimold governed the monastery of Saint Gall; according to Ekkehard, he assumed control of that monastery in the year 841. The title of the little book was written by the primary hand, except for the name of the bishop, which was added by a secondary but ancient hand. This Ermenric was a monk of Reichenau, distinct from Ermenric, the monk of Ellwangen. From these fragments we also learn, among other things, that Walahfrid, abbot of Reichenau, whose death is assigned to the year 849 by Hepidanus [Col. 0025D] and Hermann, died while on an embassy which, at the command of Louis, king of Germany, he had undertaken to Charles, his brother, surnamed the Bald. In the aforesaid codex [Col. 0026C] the little book is missing which Ermenric said near the end of the preceding fragments that he had written concerning the beginning of the monastery of Reichenau and the life of the monks of that place. The poet Homer, who is mentioned near the end, is Master Grimald, to whom Walahfrid Strabo addresses a certain poem, *To Master Grimald*, whom he afterward calls Homer in these words:

> Although beneath the offices of kings you lead your life,
>
> I do not pass you by—will you hide in caves, Homer?
>
> For I know that the Sicilian caverns please you,
>
> where alone you may enjoy the Muses and their love.

[Col. 0026D] Thus this Homer was distinct from Angilbert, abbot of Centula, to whom that name is assigned; and likewise distinct from Grimald the archchaplain.]

### TO GRIMOLD, ARCHCHAPLAIN

*Containing much about the distinguished men of Saint Gall*

*(Mabillon, Old Analecta)*

[Col. 0025]

[Col. 0025A] After I had long pondered, most learned of teachers, how I might first begin the foundation of winning your beloved friendship, two great lights presented themselves to my mind amid many thoughts: the greater light, by which we are enlightened so that God may be loved, and the lesser light, by which we love our neighbor. The other commandments depend upon these, just as all the remaining parts depend mutually upon the noun and the verb, in which we hold the person and the action.

For I am well aware that you are exceedingly careful both in poetry and in every art of the ancients, to such a degree that at times you proceed magnificently clothed in comic buskins, and at other times in the sevenfold garment which Wisdom had woven for herself with her own hands. In addition, adorned with the jewels of every virtue, you are distinguished by humility, temperate in justice, serene in fortitude, cautious in prudence, modest in temperance, ardent in zeal for God, gentle in patience, most cheerful in adversity, and humblest in prosperity.

Nor is it without reason that you surpass others on these wings of virtue: for, in the first flower of your youth, you were nurtured among the courtiers of the blessed Augusti in the most becoming manners, and from them you learned both the doctrine of every discipline and the rule of right living—from men who, throughout their empire, were supreme with God.

Even to this day you cling to that most delightful stream, resplendent in every lineage of virtue and flowing from the chief fountains of all Europe—namely, our most beloved King Louis. Although he rules within a narrower boundary of lands, he surpasses in virtue Hercules ruling the centaurs and in agility Ulysses. Ask the Slavs [Col. 0025C] all around, and you will not marvel at my brief account.

Finally, we, his poor fosterlings, have in that same stream greater resources, with Scythian Canai [reading uncertain] and forms themselves preferred to the Nile. We give thanks to Him who has granted us so clear and wholesome a fountain of every good, from which we always draw all that is peaceful and useful, and which He Himself offers inexhaustibly to all who hasten toward Him and desires to be drawn from.

But alas! This same unstable fountain, so that it might not flow openly, is often blocked at the expense of both private persons and pagan or foreign men by the contrivances of certain people. A wilderness appears, and beasts speak, until, dammed up within itself and not without danger to its own being, it patiently consumed itself, while, with God protecting it, it defended the commonwealth with weapons.

In whose household you yourself lived like a faithful Iolaus, watching his right flank; and through you we learned better than through the laws of other peoples how incomparable his piety, virtue, and intelligence are—since he possesses power in God alone, and the abundance of his riches is the glory of wisdom.

For although he is inferior to others in wisdom, as has been said, he was judged by his grandfather alone to possess a portion of it. So long as that grandfather survives, you have someone by whom to sharpen your talent, already wearied by extreme old age; and if you keep the excellent Charles before your eyes, you will have nothing either to grieve over or to fear. But more of this elsewhere.

Moreover, my dearest teacher, lest you accuse me of having strayed too far from the road I began, I return at last to the point toward which all virtues look: namely, that first we should love God and our Lord with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind. He is eternal beauty, eternal sweetness, eternal delight, eternal fragrance, eternal joy, everlasting honor, and unfailing happiness. Then we should love our neighbors [Col. 0026C] as ourselves.

The author then treats of the soul and reason; afterward he adds:

> I have set forth these matters concerning the state or substance of the soul at such length so that readers who profess to love God may know that they ought to love Him as you do: namely, with the whole soul, that is, with reason and with all its senses, with firm faith, certain hope, and perfect charity; believing in Him, hoping in Him, and loving Him from whom all good things are, in whom all things are, and through whom all good things exist and endure.

Because of this love, although you remain attached in bodily appearance to the world, in spirit you despise the present age, desiring to depart and be with Christ. You undertake earthly and temporal matters more from obligation than from intention; you devote yourself to works of mercy; you are outstanding in hospitality; you are intent upon the service of God; and you diligently honor everything belonging to the worship or religious observance of divine piety, which the Greeks call θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*, “reverence for God”).

You love the priests of Christ and restore the vessels of sacred buildings; you visit monasteries [Col. 0027B] and, after visiting them, arrange their affairs with paternal affection; and, if anything irregular exists in them, you correct it equitably and lead it back to a condition of fairness.

And for whom, or for what reason, do you do these things, if not for God, whom you love, and for your neighbor, whom you love as yourself—and sometimes more than yourself? When you deprive yourself of food or clothing and give it to someone in need, do you not honor your needy neighbor more than yourself?

And to impress this upon you with something familiar: behold how many prayers you offer, how many vigils you endure, how many journeys you undertake, and how much you expend here and there among the common people for our unconquered king, after God our head, for his most beloved side-rib, and for all the offspring proceeding from it together.

You walk, you run, crawling over mountains and swimming in rivers; you cross forests and fly across the fields. Yet these labors are no longer burdensome to the diligent spirit, because labor produces patience, patience produces endurance, and endurance produces perseverance, while perseverance brings about charity.

He then adduces much concerning love of neighbor, and afterward concerning the four cardinal and intellectual virtues. Later he descends to grammatical matters, and finally returns to moral subjects—love, the soul, and redemption. Then, in praise of Grimoald, he adds the following:

> And lest you think me hypocritical in these praises, I shall tell you without any mask of pretense—for, as you know, while my most blessed teacher Walahfrid was traveling to Charles, his brother, to deliver a reply from our lord the king, and died there, while you were expecting him to return safely from that place, you ordered me to go from the monastery of Reichenau to the monastery of Saint Gall in order to reside and study there. You instructed me to remain there for some time, having been honorably received by the brothers; and I did so according to your gracious command.
>
> “I boarded a ship and, with every favorable circumstance, reached that place under God’s guidance. I saw such virtues in those same brothers that I scarcely think even Pythagoras of Samos, let alone myself, could express them.
>
> “One is found to be more humble and patient than another; there is no bitter zeal among them, nor the venom of envy. Only charity presides there, and justice reigns. Thus charity is the mother of the virtues, concord her daughter, and simplicity their attendant; it unquestionably has its own dwelling there. Although from time to time it may have sojourned elsewhere and shown itself there in fragments, here it always remains whole, together with its daughter and servant.
>
> “No guest who arrives is left without these three coming to meet him. They are continually together and inseparable, like a threefold cord; scattered among all, yet remaining entire, they provide one ministry to everyone.
>
> “From the breasts of this charity the lord Engilpert drew generosity, and the most ingenious Herimod drew kindness. Both are supremely worthy before God and men, and wholly faithful to you, their beloved lord; like golden lampstands, they shine in your house before God.
>
> “It does no harm if the light of one burns somewhat more intensely, while the other burns more gently and therefore longer. Both are pleasing: the cluster that ripens sooner in the sun’s heat and the one that ripens late; the swift horse and the one that walks cautiously are equally praised by those who at one time or another use the usefulness of this one or that one, as circumstances permit.
>
> “It would indeed be a long task to go through individually by name the many and excellent servants of God whom I saw there, adorned with every art and every form of virtue. Nor have I rarely found anywhere men so industrious in constructing buildings from every material, just as one can clearly see in a nest what sort of birds inhabit it. Look upon the basilica and the cloister of the monastery, and you will not marvel at what I report.
>
> “And, not to remain silent about everyone: what is Uvinihartus except a Daedalus himself? Or who is Isenric except a second Bezalel? In whose hand the adze is always at work, except when he stands at the service of the holy altar.
>
> “There is such humility in them that men so perfect do not disdain to perform rustic labor with their own hands, mindful of the saying: ‘By humility heaven is entered, and by charity one reaches the everlasting kingdom.’
>
> “What shall I say of the lord Amalger, prudent in counsel and distinguished by the excellence of his entire character? How devout he is in divine worship is attested by the golden altar, before which he sits diligently in prayer and does not lie prostrate.
>
> “I say nothing of the lord Radger, a man of the greatest simplicity, until I have reached the point at which I can explain more fully how the entire community labored throughout the whole day on one of those columns which stand around the basilica itself. At last, when everyone was already weary and withdrawing, he alone did not abandon the work he had begun. Yet he was sweating in vain until he burst into these words: ‘Saint Gall, split it!’ And, wonderfully, at these simply spoken words the immense mass of the rock appeared, of its own accord, split open at the place where the entire multitude had labored before. Thus it was plainly shown that it was not human labor but the merit of Saint Gall that could split it, since at the simple invocation of his name it appeared so easily cleft. And because that same brother was a pillar of the spiritual building, he was most fittingly glorified by such a miracle.
>
> “Finally, it would be a long undertaking to gather into so brief a discourse all the good deeds of those brothers, in which they excel through the merit of Saint Gall, since they are all one, and they themselves are in Christ and Christ in them. Nothing is impossible for God, the head, who loves His members; nor will anything be difficult for His members to obtain, since they are so closely joined to their head.
>
> “I confess that I saw every praiseworthy quality in them, and especially laughing charity, while I saw one who murmured either nowhere or scarcely anywhere. In them is fulfilled what God once promised through His prophet, saying: ‘I shall come and dwell with them, and they with me; I shall walk among them and be their God, and they shall be my people.’ And in accordance with the Psalmist’s exhortation, the old men there always praise the name of the Lord together with the young.”

Therefore, my most beloved Father, lord Grimold, I now feel that the intention long hidden in my mind ought to be disclosed. Since by God’s grace I have seen good things in you and in your household, I have thought, as a kind of kiss returned for your charity, to commend in writing what I know about your goodness and consider most worthy.

Why should we not entrust to memory the deeds of men who live with Christ, when we read with such zeal the deeds of wicked men who are dead and buried with the devil in hell? For what were Jupiter or Mars except very wicked men? And what, on the other hand, were Saint Columbanus and Saint Gall except very good men? Their household, although separated by such great distances of land, is nevertheless one; and it is so great that by God’s grace it performs signs.

But since it would take too long to mention everything, or to recount the life of Saint Gall, whose shepherd you are, possessing his hut most excellently and ruling his household, let me, for love’s sake, pluck a few little flowers from his virtues and arrange them in metrical melodies, like a floral crown, upon your head. Thus, if I said above that you were jeweled with every ornament of virtue, the sun will not see you star-studded but lacking only a crown.

The aforesaid teacher of mine, the lord Walahfrid—well known to you, a man of the simplest and altogether most upright life—wrote the life of that confessor of Christ. You yourself, as a learned teacher, nurtured him as a learned sophist, and, so that he might shine more brightly in the house of God, you raised him, already preceded by God’s light, upon the lampstand.

But alas, for grief! Bitter death, which knows how to spare no one, suddenly took him from us; yet it did not claim that soul for itself, for Christ took possession of it. He wished to adorn the deeds of the most blessed Gall with the poet’s buskin, but, overtaken by death, he brought his life to an end in the midst of life.

For this reason certain brothers, and especially the most devout Gozpert—not, as you might say, the Bald, but bald in the head as far as the ears and nevertheless full of every holy benevolence, the nephew of the most fortunate abbot Gozpert—requested me, being driven by a certain force, to complete as a client and follower what the devoted master had not completed. I affirm that the reward of the beginner is the same as that of the one who completes the work.

I would, I confess, have satisfied their wishes in this matter if our beloved friend had shown some patience in making this request. For he is so eager in his zeal that in one and the same hour he wishes both to milk the cow and to press the cheese, although Rome was not built in a day, nor is wheat harvested on the same day on which it is sown.

Moreover, he did not think that his thirst could be quenched from a single spring. He ran to the sea, invoking—I know not what new Homer for this purpose—on this side of the Rhine: one who, after the manner of Flaccus, does not run in poetry but flows.

Furthermore, the Alps philosophize about the man; beneath them Radpert possesses Mount Sambutinus in lyrical sound. If he knew the caves of the Muses, he would be such as Cynthian Apollo. When his poetry sometimes alternates in the ancient manner, Hartmodus pulls at his ears, recasting it to conform to propriety.

For he too possesses the art of philosophizing, like Aristotle directing the pen toward the mind. And since the miracles of Saint Gall are many, he ought to have many supporters and manifold praisers.

And lest I alone remain silent in his praise, I have myself experienced his immense benefits, both in the clarity of my voice and in the consolation of my grief, so that at night, before the ringing of the bell, he would sing this verse before me:

> O fosterling, restrain your grief.

I poured this grief before God in the crypt of that same saint, so that, for the sake of enduring concord, it might never be changed there on my account.

Therefore, although I am lower than the poets named above and sufficiently despised because of their witty elegance—since I do not claim to be a poet, or even more unskilled than a poet (*ἀμυσώτερον*, “more unversed in the Muses”)—nevertheless, at your command and under your authority, since you delight in words, I pluck small things from great ones, and so forth.

Among these matters I also fear the missiles of a certain Scottish pouch [Col. 0030C], or those shot from its side, which now gathers in the regions of Ausonia *puttoni Littonias*, or some other unknown food. Although it appears with a brow worn bare, it will appear when the *putto* tastes of it. [The wording and foreign terms in this corrupt passage are uncertain.]

A third fear presses upon me: the Bald, already mentioned, favors these regions, but your privilege is always preserved. One thing consoles me concerning him: such a Bald will never be safe—or rather, he will be safe if he has been properly made bald.

And perhaps he had experienced this shuddering at the Cumentian bridge, when he returned from the monastery of Bobbio carrying with him the relics of Saint Columbanus. Through some negligence, as he was leaving the ship, he struck the prow and fell into the sea. Then, having been brought out by those who came to his aid, he was thought by the sailors to be Paul. But because, like Jacob of old, he limped, he was recognized by those leading him as the man who had previously walked in this manner by himself. Yet the danger was exceedingly great—and God is to be praised, for He delivered him by His miracle. I leave these matters to be related elsewhere, in their proper place.

Moreover, my most beloved master and lord, at the end of this letter I earnestly beseech Your Holiness to receive these trifles of my eloquence as I confidently trust you will, in accordance with your fatherly goodness.

I have also appended to this work a brief little treatise which I composed concerning the foundation of our monastery and the life of the brothers serving God there; I commended the statements themselves to the most learned man in every respect, the lord Bishop Gotbald, for approval or refutation. And because he judged them pleasing to himself, I have sent them to be examined by your not-unfavorable judgment. Know also that I did not set these down on wax or on a tablet, but sent them to you just as they were dictated in the schools at hand: so that, if perhaps they should not please when read aloud, there would be no grief that something had perished which was evidently of little value. In the former work I imitated Anicius Boethius; in this one, I have partly followed the manner of our Prosper. But you, most discerning teacher, using lynx-like eyes in such matters, assist me with your prayers, so that one day you may hear me, safely carried to the harbor of rest, singing the *celeuma* from the heights among the most joyful. May the holy and inseparable Trinity grant you and all your flock good health, remembering me forever. Amen.

O fortunate elder poet, worthy of that name,

[Col. 0031B] We ask that Christ grant you the help you desire, etc. Indeed, before I touch upon anything concerning the Life of Saint Gall, I shall say a few words about the essence or substance of the Holy Trinity, etc.

First, before we touch upon the Life of Saint Gall, we have rightly decided that a brief account should be given of the situation of this homeland and its rivers, namely the Rhine and the Danube.

Now, first touching upon the places along the river Rhine,

where the most worthy hero dwelt, etc.

These peoples Europe holds beneath its ancient name,

whom the Danube retains together with the divisions of the Rhine.

And enough has now been said of this; I shall presently celebrate the famous river.

[Col. 0032A] The Rhine, descending from the lofty Ausonian mountains,

seems to spread into the sea of Brigantium.

The sea is so called from the ancient name of the river,

which is now called the Podamic gulf in its familiar channel.

And as it stretches around through long courses,

in its fertility it remains unequalled by any rivers,

surpassing them in its abundance of fish-bearing life.

From here it cuts across the middle of the water and embraces a city,

which is called Constance by the name of its own ruler,

whom now the most illustrious bishop Solomon adorns,

a man gracious in his doctrine, piety, and worship of God.

Then, proceeding onward, it produces the bright Auvia from its soil,

an island which alone, Augia, is superior to the others.

For by doctrine it enriches the unlearned with a learned life,

and, fertile in trees, is everywhere enclosed by vines.

[Col. 0032B] There flowers always bloom, and lilies breathe their fragrance.

It nourishes me joyfully, and with holy nourishment;

may the people praise it [lacuna] from here as far as the Britons,

whose guardian is Folcwin, the candid abbot.

May he remain safe and dear for a long time, as I gladly pray,

and enjoy tranquil peace for many years.

May he possess without end the joys of new life, ever new, etc.

Rather, dismissing all the Pelasgians from my lips,

I turn entirely to the blessed Gaul whom I celebrate in song,

Gaul, I say, the Lord’s own, holy and gracious in piety,

for whose love we desire to write something.

But do not cut these things apart with your gentle hand, Homer.

Rather, grant great things to great masters;

but give our small odes of song to the small.

## In the Year of Our Lord 853. Erchambert, Bishop of Freising

[Col. 0031]

## Historical Notice Concerning Erchambert

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

[Col. 0031C] A fragment of Erchambert, taken from the *Brief Chronicle of the Frankish Kings and Mayors of the Palace*, from Chlodhar to Theodoric, son of the younger Dagobert, that is, from the year 613 to 727, appears in Freher, volume I of the *Writers of Frankish History*, p. 167; in André du Chesne, volume I of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, pp. 780–781; and in Ruinart’s edition of Gregory of Tours, p. 1352. See also Charles Le Cointe, volume IV of the *Annals*, p. 176.

## Letter of Erchambert to His People Concerning the Body of the Apostle Saint Bartholomew, Allegedly Brought into Bavaria

*(Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, volume VI.)*

[Col. 0031D] Erchambert, by the gift of God’s grace a humble bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the brothers serving Christ.

Finally, let your benevolence know that a certain man named Felix sent word through his messenger to our lord king, saying that he had brought with him into our regions the body of the Apostle Saint Bartholomew and the bodies of other saints. We heard this with joy and willing hearts, praising God. But we were still uncertain whether we ought to regard it as credible, or whether it had happened that the faithful men of our lord had come together in his presence; and we began to reflect upon the matter.

Then, when we had considered it, we gathered together in this way: we undertook to observe a three-day fast, so that we might deserve to have almighty God show us by some signs whether the aforesaid Felix was speaking the truth or otherwise, and so that the devil, by deceiving us, might not lead us astray.

We ask and command those who are willing voluntarily to observe this fast to abstain from wine, meat, mead, *melscada*, beer, milk, and eggs, and to follow the cross at the ninth hour on the twelfth day before the Kalends, on the eleventh day before the Kalends, and on the tenth day before the Kalends; and we ask that you not neglect to transmit this notice to others thereafter.

## Fragment of Erchambert, from the *Brief Chronicle of the Frankish Kings and Mayors of the Palace*

[Col. 0033B] King Chlodhar of Austrasia, after Kings Theodoric and Theodebert, brothers, had died, took possession of their kingdom with the counsel and assistance of Pippin the Elder, who at that time was mayor of the palace. The aforesaid king obtained the monarchy of the three kingdoms for sixteen years, just as Abbot Saint Columbanus had previously foretold to him in a prophetic spirit—for King Theodoric, instigated by his grandmother Brunhilda, had expelled him from his monastery. As soon as Chlodhar captured her, he caused her to end her life dishonorably. At that time Gundoland was mayor of the palace, an outstanding man.

Not long afterward, the king sent the aforesaid Pippin into Austrasia with his already grown son Dagobert, to establish him there as king; he appointed Pippin as Dagobert’s mayor of the palace and tutor.

King Dagobert reigned for sixteen years after his father’s death. He was a magnificent giver and distributor of gifts to the churches of God. His mayor of the palace was Erchanoldus [Erchanbaldus], an illustrious man. Meanwhile Pippin was duke in Austrasia, and died not long after King Dagobert’s death.

King Chlodoveus, Dagobert’s son, reigned for sixteen years. He was devoted to every kind of impurity. The mayor of the palace was the same as above.

King Chlodhar, son of Chlodoveus, died while still in the youthful age of childhood and reigned for four years. His mayor of the palace was Ebroin.

King Theodoric, son of Chlodoveus and brother of Chlodhar, reigned for nineteen years. His mayor of the palace was Berthar. After Berthar was killed, Pippin the Younger, son of Ansegisil [Ansgisus], came from Austrasia and succeeded to the office of mayor of the palace.

[Col. 0033D] From then on the kings began to have the name but not the authority. Nevertheless, wherever they were established, abundant provisions were supplied to them, and constant guardianship was maintained over them so that they could not exercise anything by right of royal power. At that time and afterward, Duke Gotefrid of the Alamanni and the other dukes in the surrounding regions refused to obey the dukes of the Franks, since they were unable to serve the Merovingian kings as they had previously been accustomed to do. Therefore each of them kept to himself, until at last, after the death of Duke Gotefrid, Carlus and the other princes of the Franks gradually endeavored by whatever methods they could to bring them back under their authority.

They established Chlodoveus, still a child and son of Theodoric, as king; he reigned for only two years. His mayor of the palace was the aforesaid Pippin.

They established Childebert, son of Theodoric and brother of Chlodoveus, as king; he reigned for seventeen years. Grimoald, Pippin’s son, was appointed mayor of the palace, because Pippin himself had begun to fall ill; he died of that illness, while Grimoald was killed in the meantime.

They established Dagobert, son of Childebert, as king; he reigned for five years. His mayor of the palace was Thedoaldus, son of Grimoald, followed by Regnifredus [Raginfredus].

[Col. 0034C] At that time Carlus, Pippin’s son by a concubine, was being held in custody by Plectrude, the wife of that same Pippin. With the Lord’s help he barely escaped.

They established as king a former cleric named Danihel, whose hair was growing out, and called him Chilperic. Since the royal line had failed, they appointed the man whom they could find who was closest to the Merovingians; for the Merovingians, as they say, like the ancient Nazirite, wore their head hair without having it cut. He reigned for six years.

Meanwhile the aforesaid prince Carlus fled to Austrasia, to his paternal seats, and there seized the principate. He established as his king a man named Chlodhar and fought many battles with King Chilperic and his mayor of the palace, Reganfredus. He defeated them as he wished and recovered his father’s treasure from Plectrude. His king Chlodhar died not long afterward.

They established as king of the Franks Theodoric, son of the younger Dagobert, who had been raised in the monastery of Cala; he reigned for six years. His mayor of the palace and prince was Carolus, who, governing both kingdoms vigorously and continually waging and winning wars against the neighboring kings and dukes, eventually overcame all those who appeared likely to oppose him.

## In the Year of Our Lord 853. Nithard, Abbot of Saint-Riquier

[Col. 0035]

## Historical Notice Concerning Nithard

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

[Col. 0035A] Nithard, son of Saint Angilbert and grandson of Charlemagne through his daughter Bertha, was abbot of Saint-Riquier of the Benedictine order in Gaul, in the diocese of Amiens; he was killed in battle against the Danes in the year 853. See the Sammarthani, volume IV, p. 787, where they discuss Angilbert, and p. 788; Paul Petau’s *Syntagma on Nithard*, published at Paris in 1616, quarto, and volume II of André du Chesne’s *On Frankish Affairs*, p. 351; Vossius II, 34; Baluze on Lupus’s Letter 55; and Caspar Barthius XLVI, 9, *Adversaria*. In Barthius’s judgment, Nithard was “a thoughtful and prudent writer, and remarkably eloquent for those times, as indeed befitted a man born of so great a family and supported by such extensive experience of affairs; for Nithard served as an envoy between the sons of Louis the Pious and commanded several companies on the side of Charles the Bald. In other respects he is sufficiently praised, if only he had indulged his hatred of Lothar less.”

He wrote, apparently to Lothar’s brother Charles the Bald, four books on the disputes of the sons of Louis the Pious, from the year 814, when Charlemagne died, up to the year 843. They were first published by Pierre Pithou among the twelve contemporary writers, Paris, 1588; Frankfurt, 1594, octavo, pp. 433, 488. They then appeared in volume II of André du Chesne’s *On Frankish Affairs*, p. 359, in more corrected form from the manuscript of Alexandre Petau; and finally in the writers of German history assembled by Johann Georg Kulpis, which he appended to Aeneas Sylvius’s *On the Affairs of Frederick III*, Strasbourg, 1685 and 1702, folio, p. 83.

Bonaventure Vulcanius’s excerpts from the third book of Nithard’s histories, in his collection *On the Letters and Language of the Goths*, Leiden, 1597, octavo, p. 67, contain the formula of the treaty between Louis, son of Louis the Pious, and Charles the Bald, repeated from Nithard in both languages, Theodisc and Romance; I discussed that formula above, volume IV, p. 287.

The authors of the *Literary History of Gaul*, volume V, p. 204, believe that this distinguished Gallic writer never practiced the monastic profession. Former Gallic writers had persuaded themselves that he had been a monk only on the basis of the conjecture that his corpse had received the same burial as his father Angilbert, abbot of Saint-Riquier.
