Since, however, it is certain that he died from a wound received in battle, those same authors of the *Literary History of Gaul*, volume V, p. 205, much more plausibly suspect that he served as a soldier and died at the time when the Normans were making hostile incursions through Neustria and the district of Amiens, in the year 858 or 859.

## On Nithard, Grandson of Charlemagne, and the Entire Lineage of That Same Nithard: A Brief Summary

*From the two-month leisure of Paul Petau, Counselor in the Court of France, concerning postponed matters.*

[Col. 0035B] Nithard—whom some of our countrymen called Vitaldus, others Withardus, and others Guithardus—was born to Angilbert as his father and Bertha, daughter of Charlemagne, as his mother.

[Note: Author of the manuscript Life of Lord Angilbert.]

Angilbert, illustrious by the nobility of his family and outstanding in ability and integrity of character, presided over palace and royal affairs under King Pippin, son of Charles Martel. Alcuin expressed this in more fitting and explicit language when he said that Angilbert was first officer of the palace of King Pippin.

For, in interpreting Alcuin’s statement as referring to Pippin the Pious of France, not to Pippin, king of Italy and his grandson, both the preceding circumstances and many other considerations led me to do so. Nor should anyone be troubled by the sequence and connection of Alcuin’s letters, which, like most collections of others, were piled together carelessly and never arranged.

[Note: The letter of Alcuin which is number 51 in Canisius’s printed edition is number 42 in the manuscript, and was addressed to Angilbert, first officer of King Pippin’s palace.]

[Note: Nor were they even brought together into a single corpus, as can be observed from the various written books; Trithemius also gave warning of this.]

Although that position at the palace was one of the highest dignities, it was nevertheless given to Angilbert while he was still of lesser age. The author of Angilbert’s Life indicates this when he reports that, while Pippin was alive, Charles and Carloman treated Angilbert as a son or brother.

To this should also be applied what Pope Hadrian of Rome later wrote in reply to King Charlemagne:

[Note: This letter was published at Rome among the letters of the supreme pontiffs, volume II, p. 714, and in part I of volume III of the Councils, 1606, p. 263.]

“From your exalted royal power,” he says, “your faithful familiar, Angilbert, abbot and minister of the chapel, has been sent to us. He was nurtured in your palace from almost the very beginnings of childhood and has been admitted to all your counsels.”

Moreover, Angilbert’s grandfather and great-grandfathers were all illustrious, dear to the Frankish kings, foremost in rank, and connected by marriage or kinship with the nobility.

[Note: From the Life of the lord Angilbert.]

Angilbert himself, pleasing to everyone by the elegance of his stature and the beauty of his face, and thoroughly educated in the liberal studies, was, at the urging of his parents and with the consent of the princes, marked with the title of cleric. He provided the palace with a great example of devout conduct.

After Pippin’s death, Charles held Angilbert closer than anyone else, made him privy to all his secrets, and appointed him chief of the chaplains. He also made him his keeper of silence, so that he might order the whole kingdom according to Angilbert’s counsel, and gave him his daughter Bertha as wife. To increase his honor at court, he entrusted him with the dukedom of the entire coastal region. From this union our Nithard and Harnidus were born.

After some time, when Angilbert, afflicted by a serious illness, had vowed to God that he would undertake the monastic order, he recovered his health and first placed his wife Bertha, consecrated under the sacred veil, in a suitable place within the monastery of Centula, where she could devote herself to vigils and fasts. Soon afterward, in the same place, he received the monastic habit from Symphorian, abbot of that place.

When that abbot died within a short time, Angilbert was chosen as his successor by the votes of all, with King Charles’s approval. He resolved to restore the monastery of Centula—which is situated in Ponthieu, in the diocese of Amiens, and dedicated to Saint Riquier—and to enlarge it in its buildings, resources, and number of monks.

I have not yet discovered the year in which Symphorian died and Angilbert began that abbatial office. It is certain, however, that in the year 792 the bishop Felix of Urgel, led by Abbot Angilbert into the presence of Pope Hadrian, condemned his heresy after making a confession.

[Note: In the corruptly printed books of Ado of Vienne, he is called Aurelian.]

[Note: The Mainz Annals—which we first owe to P. Pithou and which Marquard Freher, counselor to the Palatine, later published anew together with the continuing work of the monk of Fulda—call Angilbert “abbot.”]

Perhaps Letter 28 [manuscript 63] of Alcuin to Pope Hadrian belongs to that same year. In written books Alcuin speaks of Angilbert as follows:

“Because the most chosen envoy of my lord king, my dearest son Angilbert, is being sent to the most blessed fatherhood of Your Holiness, of supreme authority, I have not thought it necessary to set down in writing what that faithful and prudent man will be able, in person and in accordance with my lord king’s command, to communicate better to the ears of Your Excellency,” etc.

Alcuin calls him the secretary of the king’s will and declares him exceptionally faithful to all his friends.

Yet I am not unaware that this same letter of Alcuin could conveniently be assigned to the year 794, when Pope Hadrian wrote to King Charles himself to say that Charlemagne’s capitulary against the synod which the Greeks wished to call the Seventh had been sent to him through Angilbert.

[Note: We mentioned these letters above.]

But I have this difficulty here: in a written manuscript—from which Elias Philiras, that is, John Tilius, the famous Briocensian of the age of the Fathers and later bishop of Meaux, published in 1549 [Note: Saint John the Baptist is called the other Elias; and φίλυρα is the linden tree, called *tillet* among us.] that work of Charlemagne, completed in four books against the Greek synod concerning the veneration of images—the following words appear at the end:

“Abbot Ingelrannus wrote this book at the command of Charlemagne and carried it to Pope Hadrian.”

How these statements can agree with Hadrian’s aforementioned letter, I do not see.

[Note: The manuscript of that letter contains no other name than Angilbert.]

Nor can this Ingelrannus be the archbishop of Metz, who under Charlemagne was first officer of the holy chapel. For he had died in the year 791.

[Note: The Frankish Annals, in Canisius, volume III, p. 215, where he is nevertheless corruptly called Angiltranus, through an error in the writing.]

But while I mention Engilramnus, another matter that had nearly slipped from my memory returns to it: how could it be that, although Angilbert was archchaplain under Charlemagne—as the author of his Life and the aforementioned letter of Hadrian indicate—Adalhardus, abbot of Corbie Major, nevertheless states so precisely under Charlemagne that only these three, namely Fulrad, Engelramnus, and Hildibald, were *apocrisiarii*?

[Note: Anastasius calls Hildibald “Hildivaldus” in his Life of Leo III.]

Nor is an archchaplain different from an *apocrisiarius*. For Adalhardus himself says that our countrymen call an *apocrisiarius* a chaplain.

[Note: They had governors and prefects of certain provinces among their soldiers assigned to responses, or *apocrisiarii*. *Novellae* 24, chapter 4, and 25, chapter 1.]

Hence Alcuin too calls this Engilramnus first officer of the holy chapel.

[Note: Letter 25 in Canisius, which is number 79 in the written book.]

The chronicle of the bishops of Metz likewise calls him archchaplain of the palace. But I shall discuss these matters elsewhere.

I return to Angilbert. In the year 796, when Pope Leo, ordained after Hadrian, had sent to King Charles, together with other gifts, the keys of the confession of Saint Peter—or, as the Saxon Poet says, “the keys by which the confession of the holy Peter is preserved”—and the banner of the city of Rome, and had asked him to send one of his nobles to confirm the Roman people to him by oath:

[Note: That is, to Charlemagne. See Theganus under the year 816, p. 109, and Aventinus, book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*.]

“Abbot Angilbert of the monastery of Saint Riquier was sent for this purpose. Through him he also sent a large part of the treasure which Duke Henry of Friuli, after the royal city of the Huns—called the Ring—had been plundered, had brought to the king from Pannonia in that same year,” etc.

At that time Angilbert also carried letters from Alcuin to Leo III and to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.

[Note: These are numbers 27 and 59 in the printed editions, but numbers 72 and 73 in the manuscript of excellent quality.]

Meanwhile the buildings of Saint Riquier, or the monastery of Centula, rose up, and at last three churches erected there were dedicated by twelve venerable bishops: Meginhard, bishop of Rouen; George; Absalon; Gerfrid; Pleon; Hildigard; Theodoin; Ydelmar; Benedict; Kellan; and John and Passivus, legates of the holy Roman Church.

This occurred shortly before Charlemagne obtained the imperial dignity. Someone might perhaps infer that Charlemagne had attended this dedication from what Nibelungus, the published Annals, Regino, Ademar in the Life of Charlemagne, the Saxon Poet, and others have recorded: that in the year of our Lord 800 Charles celebrated Holy Easter at Saint Riquier.

[Note: In Regino’s Chronicle it is corruptly read today as “at Saint Richard.”]

But this cannot stand, since at Centula the solemnity of the church’s dedication is celebrated on the Kalends of January, according to an old book.

What adornment he gave his church, and with what relics of the saints he enriched it, could neither be nor ought to be compressed into this brief work; nor did it seem appropriate to add, with the same intention, some of his verses collected here and there in various places.

Angilbert also accompanied Charlemagne, who was soon to become emperor, to Rome, and obtained from Pope Leo III a privilege by which the abbot alone would have ecclesiastical jurisdiction over the entire estate of Centula, and the bishop of the see of Amiens would not be able to appoint churches or clergy there.

[Note: This privilege was written, examined, and subscribed by Zacharias, regional deacon and librarian of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the indiction.]

The privilege states that this had come about through the “petition” of “our brother and fellow bishop Jesse, bishop of the Amiens, together with Abbot Angilbert. They communicated this petition to us in the presence of our glorious and most excellent son Charles, whom, with God as author, we have today consecrated Augustus for the defense and advancement of the holy universal Church,” etc.

It also mentions the monastery of Centula as “recently restored and brought back to a noble condition.”

[Note: From the Life of the lord Angilbert.]

Angilbert summoned Master Alcuin to him and arranged for a little book on the Life of Saint Riquier, composed in a rough style, to be rewritten and copied in a more polished and lucid form. Alcuin also composed nocturnal and diurnal hymns and antiphons concerning the saint’s life.

[Note: Published in Surius, volume II, p. 981.]

At the end, Angilbert was present when Charles was making his testament, as Eginhard testifies. He died at almost the same time as Charlemagne, namely on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March in the year 814, while the fifth day before the Kalends of February of that same year had been the last day of Charlemagne’s life.

[Note: The author is Hariulf, born in Ponthieu, who completed in four books, in the year 1088, the history of his monastery of Centula, begun many years earlier by Lord Saxovallus. He was also the third abbot of Aldenburg, and Aubert Miraeus attributes to him, in the *Origins of the Belgian Monasteries*, the Life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, which is attributed to Lisiardus in Surius, volume IV, p. 174.]

Angilbert wished his body to be buried before the gate of Saint Salvator and the church of Saint Riquier. It may perhaps not be burdensome to add something about the enclosure of that place, taken from the author of his Life, who says that he borrowed it from Angilbert’s own testament:

[Note: The dedication of the oratory of Saint Gabriel took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, while that of the chapel of Saint Michael took place on the third day before the Kalends of October. Note that altar, oratory, and chapel mean the same thing.]

“The very walls,” he says, “which are called Paradise—the *parvis*—rising with towered mass, were consecrated with three altars: namely, at the western gate, the altar of Saint Michael; at the southern gate, the altar of Saint Gabriel, which the venerable Bishop Hildivard consecrated; and at the northern gate, the altar of Saint Raphael, which Jesse, the religious bishop of the Amiens, dedicated on the second day before the Nones of September,” etc.

Twenty-eight years after Angilbert’s death, on the Nones of November, he was lifted from that place, and his body was found intact and without spices.

[Note: That is, in the year 842.]

[Note: Nithard, book IV, p. 372.]

Abbot Ribbodo transferred him inside the church and placed him at the entrance to the choir, on the western side of the same larger church, since Abbot Ribbodo no longer wished the relics of so great a man to be trampled under the feet of those entering the church.

[Col. 0039C] Soon he became renowned for many miracles, was made a companion of the saints, and enlarged the Gallican litany.

[Note: At that time the litanies were divided: there was a Gallican, an Italian, and a Roman litany, which our older writers mention separately.]

The abbot of that same monastery, Anscherus, sent several of his miracles, contained in three books, to Radulfus, archbishop of Reims, after many years.

[Note: Radulfus occupied the see of Reims in the year 1107, according to a manuscript catalogue of the archbishops of Reims; or, as is commonly believed, in 1114.]

Nevertheless, you will search in vain for Angilbert—as for countless other saints who are our protectors—among modern collections of the saints. These things have been said concerning Nithard’s father.

His mother was Bertha, the daughter of Charlemagne and Hildegard.

Concerning Charles I consider this one detail less well known: he also bore the name David. Alcuin and others of that age frequently addressed him by this name in their letters. That this was his proper name, not an assumed one, is confirmed by these words of Alcuin addressed to him:

[Note: In the letter beginning, “To the lord David, beloved in the Lord of lords, most dear king, Flaccus, faithful envoy. As I was returning from Uvicus,” etc. It is number 12 in one manuscript and number 13 in another; it has not yet been published.]

“May,” he says, “abundant blessing upon the sons of your noble family increase through your benefactions, just as, through the holiness of your most beloved namesake, King David, the power of the royal throne was preserved for all his grandchildren, as we read,” etc.

Alcuin would not have called him a namesake if he had intended to give Charles the name merely because of his likeness to and imitation of David.

Perhaps the name was changed for him when he was baptized or anointed king. The same thing was done, after all, with Pippin, king of Italy, his son.

[Note: The same happened to Leo III, whose baptismal name was Conon. *Historia Miscella*, book XXI.]

I am surprised that, among so many authors who wrote of Charlemagne’s deeds, so few observed this.

We owe this information to Nibelungus, son of Count Childebrand, maternal uncle of Pippin, king of the Franks, and to Gervase of Tilbury, marshal of the kingdom of Arles and kinsman of Otto IV.

[Col. 0040B] Nibelungus’s words under the year 781 are certainly these:

“King Charles went to Rome, and his son, who was called Carloman, was baptized there. Pope Hadrian, changing his name, called him Pippin, and anointed him king over Italy, and his brother Louis king over Aquitaine. And there Rotrude, the king’s daughter, was betrothed to Emperor Constantine.”

[Note: Gervase reads *Francis* for *ei*—“to him”—in the book entitled *Otia Imperialia*, in the chapter on the Kingdom of the Franks and its origin.]

[Note: Gervase incorrectly calls him Urbanus.]

[Note: Elsewhere she is called Ruodtrudis.]

That is what he says. I shall add nothing further about Charles.

His wife Hildegard, or Hildegardis, mother of Bertha and a woman of the foremost nobility of the Swabians, had as her parents Esnerius, lord of Campidonum, and Regard, a Bavarian by nationality; her brother was Uldalricus.

[Note: Eginhard.]

She herself was the founder of the monastery of Campidonum, called Kempten by the Germans today. It is still one of the four monasteries of the Roman Empire. Some say that she was buried there in the year 783; nevertheless, the author of the Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz says that she was buried in the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Metz, while the *Life of Louis the Pious* more correctly asserts that she rests in the Basilica of Saint Arnulf, together with her son, the Emperor Louis, and the archbishop Drogo.

[Note: Munster, book III of the *Cosmography*, p. 562; but Caspar Bruschius, *On the German Monasteries*, p. 25, names her father Hildebrand; Vasseburg of Verdun, *History*, book III, folio 143, names him Godefrid.]

[Note: A monk of Saint Gall, in his *Deeds of Charlemagne*, in Canisius, volume I, p. 371; the learned François Pithou hesitantly suspects that he should be called Clement Scotus.]

As for the name given to Nithard’s mother Bertha, it came from her grandmother, namely Charlemagne’s mother. Although a foreigner, that grandmother nevertheless bore a name long used among the Franks, indeed one plainly Frankish in origin, if the ancient author of the Life of Saint Bertha is to be trusted.

[Note: She built the monastery of Blangy around the year 682; it is today in the diocese of Boulogne in Gaul.]

“Bertha,” he says, “is a Frankish name which in Latin speech means ‘shining’ or ‘bright.’”

With these matters concerning Nithard’s birth and ancestry established in advance, it is easy to learn from reading his History what he did and where he was active while the storm of war raged among the brothers Lothar, Louis, and Charles. That History was directed to Charles and was written at his command.

For Nithard served under Charles, as heir through his father to the duchy or county of the maritime region of France. Since other possessions that had come to him by hereditary right lay on both sides of the Meuse—which was the boundary between the kingdoms of Lothar and Charles—and although the weariness of the long war made him seek leisure everywhere, he believed that it could be found nowhere, since, as he himself says at the beginning of book IV, fortune had joined him to all affairs on every side.

[Note: Nithard, book I, p. 312.]

Although he belonged among those to whom, in the year 842, when Lothar was thought to have fled from the kingdom, the division of that kingdom between Louis and Charles was entrusted and assigned, he was nevertheless always eager to establish peace between the brothers.

[Note: Nithard, book IV, p. 360.]

But as the brothers’ hatreds nowhere subsided, he finally resolved to withdraw from public affairs altogether, as he himself declares at the beginning of book IV.

Thus, when he ceased writing history, it was the year of our Lord 844. At that time, after the recent translation of Saint Angilbert by Abbot Ribbodo, he developed an even greater innate desire for withdrawal and the solitary life.

That same year Abbot Ribbodo died at Centula. After Ribbodo’s death he was succeeded by Hludovicus, a man of royal descent, as the author of the Life of Saint Angilbert says; another monk of that place, whose name is still unknown to us, calls him “born from royal seed.”

[Note: He wrote three books in verse on the miracles of Saint Riquier some 550 years ago, and a fourth on the translation of the saint by Hugh Capet, then duke of the Franks.]

This is the same man whom Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, notes as having stayed in the monastery of Ferrières itself and as having been educated not far from it. Later, Lupus records that he held a correspondence office at the palace of Charles the Bald.

[Note: Namely, in the monastery of Saint Peter the Living at Sens, as many considerations have persuaded me; and I believe that he was also buried there.]

Finally, Lupus calls him “the highest” of abbots and “most illustrious.”

King Charles too, in a diploma of his own issued at the royal palace of Compiègne on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth year of his reign and the seventh indiction, calls him “his venerable and beloved kinsman.”

Therefore Nithard too, at that very time abandoning the world, devoted himself to God. But I cannot assert with sufficient certainty to which monastery he first betook himself. The fact that he went to Centula, together with the memory of his father Saint Angilbert [Col. 0041C] and his kinship with Abbot Hludovicus, might easily persuade one of this. Yet what I read in Lupus of Ferrières, in his fifty-fifth letter to Marcuvardus [Note: Marcuvardus was his name, not Marcuvadus, and he was abbot of Prüm in 829. He died in 853; so says Regino.] the third abbot of Prüm, leaves me doubtful and uncertain:

“Nithard’s arrival at Silvacum,” he says, “greatly gladdened me [Note: This place is mentioned in several passages of Hincmar of Reims, in his controversy with Hincmar, bishop of Laon, and elsewhere. Perhaps Saulnoy, an abbey near Laon (près Laon)], where the needs of the monastery had drawn me. His presence brought it about that these letters were delivered to your fatherhood, since it showed that you were safe and that our common son Egilo [Note: He was first a monk of Ferrières, then of Prüm—not also of Saint Peter Alive at Sens—and afterwards succeeded Marcuvard at Prüm in 853. Later Charles the Bald made him abbot of Flavigny, and finally he became archbishop of Sens; he rests in the monastery of Saint Peter Alive. Lupus mentions him in various places, as do Regino and Jacques Tavellus, a man both discerning and learned in history, in his account of the archbishops of Sens.] had recovered from a very serious illness, through the assistance of divine favor,” and so forth.

Moreover, Marcuvard, abbot of Prüm, wrote to Dido [Col. 0042A] [Note: This letter of Marcuvard was written in 848. At that time Dido was abbot of Saint Peter Alive at Sens, over which he presided for a few years. The author is Gaufridus, in his history of that monastery.] the abbot, a highly skilled physician, in his seventy-second letter:

“The exceptional expertise of your art,” so I read it, “made widely known by the report of many, became known to us especially through the report of Brother Nithard. From him also we learned that you open access everywhere to those in need,” and so forth.

These passages therefore suggest that Nithard was rather a monk of Prüm than of Centula. Be that as it may, it is certain from Hariulf and from other sources that he became abbot of Centula. But Hariulf, the historian of Centula, was misled by a slight failure of memory when he said that Nithard succeeded his father; and likewise the author of the *Life of Lord Angilbert* was mistaken in placing him after Abbot Ribbodo. For after Angilbert came Hericus; after Hericus, Helysachar [Note: It will be helpful to note, if you read Agobard, that Helysachar was abbot of Centula; Agobard mentions him on pp. 94, 260, and elsewhere. He too is said to have been head of the monastery of Jumièges. Hariulf, Book III, chapter 4.]; after him, Ribbodo; after Ribbodo, Hludovicus; then Nithard; and afterwards Hruodulfus, the maternal uncle of Charles the Bald, namely, the brother of the empress Judith, and so on.

This was pointed out to me by the following brief note, written long ago in the margin of a manuscript of Hariulf:

“After Lord Hludovicus,” it says, “Lord Nithardus is said to have been placed in charge; and because at that time a severe persecution by the pagans was pressing upon them, he also assumed the government of the maritime region.”

Thus after Hludovicus Nithard was both abbot and count, as his father Angilbert had been; and the same dignity remained with several of the successors of the archimandrites of that monastery [Note: Hariulf, Book III of the *History of Centula*, chapter 10].

Since this countship of maritime France is also indiscriminately called a duchy by Hariulf and by authors of that period, I shall insert here, in passing, the following observation. I have never attached much weight to what I once read in both the *History of the Lords of Amboise* [Note: It begins: “You have very often requested that the history of the lords of Amboise …”] and the deeds of the counts of Anjou [Note: Their author was a monk of Marmoutier; they begin: “The history, or deeds, of the counts of Anjou …”]: namely, that Hugh, duke of Burgundy, was appointed guardian of Charles the Simple, still a small child, and that the power he received—then called *abbacomitatus*—was changed by his successors into the more presumptuous term *ducamen*, “ducal authority.”

Nithard, however, presided over the monastery of Centula for only a very few days. He was killed in battle in the year 853, as I infer from many indications, while the Danes [Note: These words are found in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus* at Angers, and also in the *History of the Emperors, Kings of the Franks, and Counts of Anjou*, which begins “Ada” and ends with Louis the Fat.] and the Suevi—whom the Germans call *Nortman*, that is, “Northerners”—had left the borders of their homeland and for twenty years had been ravaging the entire coast with fires, plunder, and every kind of cruelty [Col. 0042C].

He himself was buried in the very place where Angilbert had first rested: at the entrance, or portico, of the larger church, which was dedicated to the holy Savior and Saint Richarius. Hariulf [Note: Book IV, chapter 32.] related this in the following account, and in still fuller words:

“In the time of Gervinus,” he says, “the first of that name among the abbots of Centula [Note: This Gervinus died on 3 March 1074, according to Hariulf], the tomb of Lord and Saint Angilbert was unknown, and therefore received no earthly honor, although his most celebrated memory shone on the lips of all the Franks and Ponthievins, as well as in the sight of the splendid church once founded by him.

“When the venerable Gervinus had once gone to the monastery of Gorze, situated on the boundary of the territory of Metz, he borrowed from the brothers of that place a codex containing certain matters concerning the deeds of that holy man and of other abbots of our monastery, and brought it to Centula. In it he found that the holy Abbot Angilbert had passed to glory on 18 February.

“The monks of Centula were greatly delighted by this, since from the time when the monastery had been burned under the pagan Guaramundus down to the present day, the date of his passing had been unknown to them. Gervinus—who may rightly be called a man of desires—therefore began to search at the church doors, where he had learned that Angilbert had first been buried. He did not find his body there, however; but in the same sarcophagus in which Angilbert had once rested, he found a leather-covered wooden bier containing the body of Lord Nithard, his son, abbot and count, sprinkled with salt. On his head could be seen the wound by which he had been killed in battle.

“Having therefore closed the same tomb again, he resolved to search elsewhere for the holy bodily remains of Angilbert,” and so forth.

I shall not delay you, reader, any longer; and, with my hurried pen, many things have slipped in which I had not intended to weave into the beginning. I shall add only this concerning the title of Nithard’s book. Although in the manuscript book from which P. Pithaeus, an honor of his age, published it, there is no title naming either the book or its author [Note: This book once belonged to the monastery of Saint Maglorius in Paris, perhaps, if I conjecture correctly, through the generosity of Hugh the Great, father of Hugh Capet, king of the Franks. He was the first to build it.];

and although, from a manuscript of the *History of Centula* [Note: Two copies survive, entirely unlike each other. The author of the one under discussion here is Hariulf.], it appears that it ought to be called a “Chronicle” or “Deeds of the Franks,” nevertheless it is not unreasonable that the work should be called by its author a “History of the Discord,” or “of the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious.”

That this was the title of Nithard’s little work will be made clear by an author of unknown name [Note: The beginning of this preface is: “When I observed that very many, and almost all, were uncertain about the deeds of the kings of the Franks …” But Book I begins: “Among those years in which the people of the Hebrews …”], who in 1214 wrote a history of the Franks in three books in Latin. Fifty years later another man, born in Aquitaine, translated it into French and dedicated it to Alfonso, count of Poitiers and Toulouse, brother of Saint Louis, king of France. From his preface we have copied the following:

“These materials,” he says, “were taken from the deeds of Saints Remigius, Lupus, and Indicellus [Al., Vind.]; also from the *Life of Saint Lambert*, which begins: ‘The glorious man Lambert, accepted by the eternal King as a martyr,’ and so forth; from the chronicles of Hugh of Fleury [Note: Fleury, a village on the Loire, was famous for the monastery of Saint Benedict. I am surprised that the old French translator failed to know this.], and of Robert of Auxerre [Note: He was a monk of Saint-Marien, whose *Chronicle* Nicolas Camusat, canon of Troyes, wished to publish in 1608; it is well known to every learned person]; some, too, from the book of Isidore called the *Etymologies*; from the chronicles of Saint Peter Alive at Sens [Note: Their author was Gaufridus de Collono, a monk of that same place; they end in the year 1294]; from the history of the Lombards; from the book of Guertinus, who admits that he was a pupil of Charlemagne; from a certain history entitled in the name of Turpin; from a certain little book dealing with the deeds of the kings of the Franks, which is found at Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; also from the book of Nithard, which deals with the discord of the sons of Louis the Pious; from the chronicles of La Charité; from the history of Jerusalem; and some material from the *Deeds of Louis the Pious* and of Philip, who now reigns,” and so forth.

That is what he says. I have written out the whole passage here so that, reader, several as yet unpublished writers of French history might become known to you, and so that I might either instill in you some desire to illuminate our Gaul—for which all Catholic kings and princes owe their Christianity—or, as I would rather hope, increase that desire to some extent.

## ADDITION

[Col. 0044A]

Page 4, line 12, concerning the words, “He appointed him *silentiarius*, so that he might order the whole kingdom according to his counsel,” the following had been added in the inner margin.

The exact words of the ancient narrator of the *Life of Saint Angilbert* are these:

“Charles appointed that same man his *silentiarius*, so that, having recognized the depth of his prudence, he might arrange the welfare of the whole kingdom according to his counsel.”

To this I add the following. I have set down the ancient author’s very words so that, if you should wish to investigate the office of this *silentiarius*, you may not accuse me of having altered anything in the wording. For my part, I find it difficult to determine with certainty what his duties were.

Nor should I be led to believe that he was one of the school of *silentiarii* mentioned in title 16 of Book XII of the *Code of Justinian*. Those men, keeping watch at the threshold of the sacred consistory, commanded nothing but quiet and silence. Zonaras rightly assigns this function to that college; and, when he records that Anastasius Dicorus had been a *silentiarius* before he obtained the imperial power, he adds: *chamaizēlōn touto einai axiōmatōn*—“that this belongs among the lower dignities.” For the work was servile. There were also *silentiarii* among the slaves.

Salvianus, in Book IV *On Providence*, makes a fitting observation when he wishes to show that masters may be charged with far worse things than slaves:

“Not only misery,” he says, “but punishments as well drive slaves to flight. The stewards tremble, the *silentiarii* tremble, the procurators tremble—so that, among them all, scarcely any are less slaves than their own masters,” and so forth.

For this reason I refer only reluctantly to that class what is said of Anastasius—and what is confirmed by Cedrenus [p. 291], the *Suda*, and others—namely, that before the imperial power was conferred upon him he had been a *silentiarius*. The same applies to what Procopius records in Book IV *On the Buildings of Justinian*: that Theodore was Justinian’s *silentiarius*.

I distinguish the prince’s *silentiarius* from those who belonged to the school of *silentiarii*. This is shown by the following words of this ancient author concerning Charles:

“He appointed him his *silentiarius*” [Col. 0044C].

Moreover, since he was concerned with the welfare of the whole kingdom, and since that dignity was added to Angilbert after he had already held the highest honors, shortly before he took Bertha, the king’s daughter, as his wife, no one will deny that the king’s *silentiarius* was far removed from a mere watchman.

Perhaps, then, this *silentiarius* was the man who presided over the *silentium*. For in that age the *silentium* meant an assembly of a few men who, separately from the people, deliberated among themselves on more serious matters. Among them the emperor sat elevated on a platform or tribunal; it was his task to pursue in speech the matters that were to be discussed in council. Perhaps the *silentiarius* performed this function in the emperor’s place.

For this discussion was also called *dialexis*—“conference”—and *selention*, as Zonaras, Nicetas, and others testify. The assembly itself was also called the *silentium*, or, to use Zonaras’s words, “the senate council” (*ē tēn synklēton boulēn*). The author of the *Miscellaneous History* has shown this. In Book XXI he says:

“Impious Leo held a *silentium* against the holy and venerable icons,” in the tribunal of nineteen cubits, “with the patriarch Germanus also summoned,” and so forth.

Here he means nothing other than what he related in Book XXII concerning Constantine Copronymus, the son of that Leo III:

“Impious Constantine,” he says, “assembled an unjust council of thirty-eight bishops against the holy and venerable images.”

And again:

“When they had assembled at Blachernae, the emperor Constantine ascended the platform, holding Constantine, bishop of Syleion. After he had prayed, he proclaimed in a loud voice, saying: ‘To Constantine, universal patriarch, many years,’” and so forth.

Do not suppose, reader, that I am asserting all this as fully true. Rather, if you are versed in this field of learning—which is certainly very useful to those who labor in the forensic arena, and plainly necessary to those engaged in public affairs—and if something better than these explanations should occur to you, you have found me ready to proclaim your learning and follow your lead.

Meanwhile, enjoy life, and live.

*A little is sufficient for the wise.*

[Col. 0045A]

# THE FOUR BOOKS OF NITHARD, SON OF ANGILBERT, GRANDSON THROUGH HIS DAUGHTER BERTHA OF CHARLEMAGNE THE EMPEROR, ON THE DISSENSIONS OF THE SONS OF LOUIS THE PIOUS

Up to the year 843. Addressed to Charles the Bald, king of the Franks. Recently purged of countless errors and corruptions, partly with the aid of a very ancient manuscript preserved in the library of Monsieur Alexandre Petau, S.P., and partly through conjectures drawn from the sense of the history.

[Col. 0045]

# BOOK ONE

## PREFACE

[Col. 0045B]

Since, as you know very well, my lord, you and your people had by no means deserved the persecution inflicted by your brother and had endured it for nearly two years, before we entered the city of Châlons you instructed me to commit to writing, by the service of my pen, the events that had taken place in your time.

I confess that the command was timely and agreeable, if leisure had been granted to carry out so great a task with fitting dignity. But if you find anything inserted in this work that is less polished or less carefully composed than the magnitude of the subject required, you and your people owe me forgiveness all the more readily, since you know that, while I was carrying out this work, I was being driven by the same storm as you.

I had intended to pass over the events that occurred during the time of your pious father [Col. 0045C], but the truth of your disputes will be more readily apparent to anyone who reads them if I first briefly touch upon certain matters that we know occurred in their proper time. Nor does it seem right to omit entirely the venerable memory of your grandfather. Therefore let the text begin here.

Charles, of blessed memory and deservedly called “the Great,” emperor by all nations, died in good old age at about the third hour of the day, and left all Europe filled with every kind of goodness. He was a man of every wisdom and every virtue, so far surpassing the human race of his time that he appeared terrible, lovable, and admirable alike to all who inhabited the world; and thus, as became manifest to everyone, he made the whole empire honorable and useful in every respect.

For, beyond everything that I admit was worthy of admiration, he alone restrained the ferocity and iron hearts of the Franks and barbarians—which Roman power had been unable to tame—with such measured terror that they plainly dared to undertake nothing in the empire except what accorded with the public good [Col. 0046B]. He reigned successfully for thirty-two years and likewise held the reins of the empire with complete success for fourteen years.

The heir to so great a dignity was Louis, the youngest of his sons born in lawful marriage. When the others had died, Louis succeeded him. As soon as he learned with certainty that his father had died (815), he came directly from Aquitaine to Aachen. There he brought under his authority, without any hindrance, the people who came to him from every direction, intending to deliberate about the others who appeared to trust him.

At the beginning of his reign he ordered the great amount of money left by his father to be divided into three parts. He spent one part on the funeral, and divided the other two between himself and his sisters born to their father in lawful marriage; he also urgently ordered the sisters to leave the palace for their own monasteries.

He made his brothers, still of tender age—Drogo, Hugh, and Theoderic—participants at his table. He ordered them to be brought up with him in the palace, and granted the kingdom of Italy to his nephew Bernard, son of Pippin (818). Because Bernard soon afterwards rebelled against him, he was captured and deprived both of his eyesight and of his life by Bertmund, prefect of the province of Lyon.

Fearing, then, that the brothers just mentioned might, after stirring up the people, do the same thing, he ordered them to come to a public assembly, had them tonsured, and entrusted them to monasteries under free custody (819).

After this had been done, he joined his sons in lawful marriage and divided the entire empire among them in such a way (821) that Pippin would have Aquitaine, Louis Bavaria, and Lothar the whole empire after Louis’s departure. He also granted Lothar the right to bear the imperial title together with himself.

Meanwhile Queen Irmengard, their mother, died, and shortly afterwards the emperor Louis took Judith as his wife (823), by whom Charles was born.

After Charles had been born, the father did not know what to do for him, since he had divided the whole empire among his other sons. While the anxious father pleaded with his sons on behalf of the child, Lothar finally consented and confirmed by oath that the father might give Charles whatever portion of the kingdom he wished. He also swore that in the future he would be Charles’s guardian and defender against all his enemies.

But at the instigation of Hugh, whose daughter Lothar had married (829), and of Matfrid and the others, he soon regretted having done this and sought a way to annul what he had done. This did not escape the notice of either father or mother. Accordingly, Lothar secretly tried in one way and another to destroy what his father had established, though not openly.

For this reason the father took a certain Bernard, duke of Septimania, as his assistant, appointed him chamberlain, entrusted Charles to him, and placed him second to himself in the empire. But Bernard, by using the state unwisely, completely overturned what he ought to have strengthened. At about the same time Alamannia was assigned to Charles by decree.

Then Lothar, as though he had found a legitimate grievance, began to encourage both his brothers and the whole people as though they were restoring the condition of the state. Accordingly, they came together with all the people to meet their father at Compiègne (830). They veiled the queen, tonsured her brothers Conrad and Rudolf, and entrusted them to Pippin to be kept in Aquitaine.

Bernard too escaped by flight and withdrew to Septimania. His brother Eribert was captured, deprived of his eyesight, and handed over to be kept in Italy.

Lothar, having obtained control of the state on these terms, kept his father and Charles under free custody (831). He had ordered monks to remain with them, to introduce Louis to the monastic life and persuade him to undertake it.

But the state was growing worse day by day, since everyone, enticed by greed, sought his own advantage. Therefore both the monks mentioned above and the others who grieved over what had been done began to ask Louis whether, if the state were restored to him, he wished to raise it up and support it to the best of his ability—especially divine worship, by which the whole order of things is sustained and governed.

Because he readily confessed that he did, they quickly agreed to its restoration. They took with them a certain monk named Guntbald and secretly sent him on this business to Pippin and Louis, the emperor’s sons, under the pretext of religion. He promised that, if they were willing to join him and those who desired this in restoring their father, he would enlarge the kingdom of both brothers.

They therefore obeyed very readily and eagerly. When an assembly had been arranged, the queen and her brothers were restored to him, and the entire people submitted themselves to his authority.

Those who had taken Lothar’s side were then brought before the council. Lothar himself sentenced them to death, or, sparing their lives, thrust them into exile. He allowed Lothar, content with Italy alone, to depart on the condition that he would not thereafter attempt anything in the kingdom against his father’s will.

When these matters had been settled and the state seemed to be breathing again for a little while, the monk Guntbald, whom we mentioned above, wanted to be second in the empire because he had worked so hard for its restoration. Bernard, however, as stated earlier, had formerly held that position and strove with the greatest effort to recover it.

Pippin and Louis too, although their kingdoms had been enlarged as promised, were each working to become first in the empire after their father. But those who then administered the state resisted their wishes.

At about this time (833), Aquitaine was taken from Pippin and given to Charles, and the leading men of the people who supported his father swore allegiance in Charles’s service. Those whom we mentioned above took this badly. They spread the report that the state was being administered uselessly and stirred up the people as though toward legitimate government.

They released Wala, Elisachar, Matfrid, and the others who had been driven into exile from custody, and compelled Lothar to invade the state. Moreover, they brought in Gregory, pope of the Roman see, with fervent entreaties and under the same pretext, so that with his authority they might more freely accomplish what they desired.

Accordingly, the emperor, together with everything that belonged to his empire, and his three sons, who came against him with a huge army, as well as Pope Gregory with his entire Roman retinue, converged at Elisach [Col. 0048B]. They pitched their camps near Mount Siguuald, and the sons, by various emotional appeals, compelled the people to defect from their father.

Finally, when some had escaped by flight, the father was captured with only a very few supporters. His wife was taken from him and sent into exile in Lombardy, while Charles was kept under strict custody together with his father.

Pope Gregory, overcome by regret for his journey, returned to Rome more slowly than he wished. Lothar had once again obtained the empire on terms that were unjust, and what he had so easily acquired unjustly he lost again still more easily and justly (834).

For Pippin and Louis were deeply troubled when they saw that Lothar wished to claim the whole empire for himself and reduce them to an inferior position. Moreover, while Lambert and Matfrid were disputing which of them should be second to Lothar in the empire, they began to quarrel.

Since each sought his own advantage, they utterly neglected the state. The people, seeing this, were displeased. The sons were also overcome by shame and regret because they had twice deprived their father of his honor; and the whole people felt the same because they had twice abandoned their emperor. Therefore all sides agreed to restore him and hastened from everywhere to Saint-Denis, where Lothar was then keeping their father and Charles.

Seeing that this determination exceeded his strength, Lothar took up arms before they could assemble, released his father and Charles, and set out for Vienne.

The considerable crowd that was present nevertheless wished again and again to use force against Lothar on behalf of his father. Once the king had been recovered, they gathered with the bishops and all the clergy at the basilica of Saint-Denis, offered devout praises to God, placed the crown and weapons upon their king, and hastened to deliberate about the remaining matters.

The father postponed pursuing Lothar, but sent messengers after him to order him to hasten beyond the Alps. He received Pippin, who came to him, kindly and thanked him for having worked toward his restoration. He allowed Pippin, as he had requested, to return to Aquitaine.

From every direction the faithful who had escaped and had been accustomed to govern the state came together. With them he set out for Aachen to winter there, and at last he received Louis, who had arrived, with gratitude. He ordered Louis to remain with him as a support.

Meanwhile those who were guarding Judith in Italy, hearing that Lothar had fled and that the father was governing the empire, seized Judith and set out in flight. They reached Aachen safely and brought the emperor a welcome gift. Nevertheless she was not received back into the royal bed until, because no accuser was present, she had cleared herself by oath, together with her relatives, before the people of the charges brought against her.

At about this time (835), Matfrid and Lambert and the others on Lothar’s side were staying near the Breton March. Vodo and all those dwelling between the Seine and the Loire were sent against them.

They gathered together from both directions with a strong force. Their small numbers, and therefore their extreme necessity, made them united. But the very large number of Vodo’s followers made them careless, divided, and disordered. Consequently, when battle was joined, they fled [Col. 0049C].

Vodo fell, as did Odo, Vivianus, Fulbertus, and an innumerable multitude of common people. The victors promptly sent word of this to Lothar, instructing him to meet them with an army as quickly as possible.

He readily complied. Gathering a strong force, he came to Chalon, surrounded the city with a siege, besieged it by fighting for three days, and finally, after capturing the city, burned it together with its churches.

He ordered Gerberga to be drowned in the Arar according to the custom used for sorcerers. He punished Gozhelm and Senila [Gauzlin and Sanila] by beheading. He spared Warin’s life, but bound him by oath to assist him thereafter to the best of his ability.

Lothar and his followers, made confident by the successful outcome of two battles, hoped that they could easily invade the whole empire. They therefore went to Orléans to deliberate about the remaining matters.

When the father heard this, he gathered a strong force in Francia. He also summoned his son Louis, with all those who lived beyond the Rhine, to assist him, and set out to punish the enormous crime committed by his son against the empire.

Lothar, encouraged by the same hope with which he had been accustomed to lead the Franks away, thought it right to go out to meet him. Accordingly, both sides converged and pitched their camps above the river, near a village called Calviac.

But the Franks, overcome by regret because they had twice abandoned the emperor and judging it shameful to commit such an act again, refused to be driven into defection. Therefore, since he saw no opportunity either for flight or for battle, Lothar finally ended the conflict on the following terms: he was to depart beyond the Alps within the appointed number of days; thereafter he was not to presume to enter the borders of Francia without his father’s order; and he was not to attempt anything further within his father’s empire against his father’s will.

Both he and his followers confirmed by oath that they would observe these terms for themselves and their people.

When these matters had been settled (838), the father governed the empire as he had been accustomed to do, with the men who had usually assisted him. But when he saw that the people in no way wished to abandon him during his lifetime, as they had been accustomed to do, he called an assembly at Aachen in winter and assigned Charles a portion of the kingdom marked out by these boundaries:

from the sea through the borders of Saxony as far as the borders of the Rhinelanders; all Frisia; and, through the borders of the Rhinelanders, the counties of Moilla, Halt, Trahammolant, and Masagobbi [Masagouvi].

Then whatever lies between the Meuse and the Seine as far as Burgundy, together with Verdun; and from Burgundy, Toul, Odorn, Bed, Blois, Parthenay, both Barrois districts, Brienne, Troyes, Auxerre, Sens, the Gâtinais, Melun, Étampes, Château-Thierry, and Paris; and thereafter along the Seine to the Ocean Sea, and by the sea itself as far as Frisia.

He gave to his aforesaid son Charles all the bishoprics, abbeys, counties, royal estates, and everything situated within the boundaries specified above, together with everything belonging to them, wherever it might be located and whatever appeared to be under his jurisdiction. He gave it with divine and paternal authority and implored the mercy of almighty God that it might remain secure.

Hilduin, abbot of the church of Saint-Denis, Gerard, count of the city of Paris, and all the others inhabiting the aforesaid territories assembled and confirmed their allegiance to Charles by oath.

When Lothar and Louis heard this, they were deeply troubled and therefore called a conference. They came to it, but when they saw that they could not openly object to any of these arrangements, they craftily concealed their intention to undertake anything against their father’s will and withdrew.

Nevertheless, a considerable disturbance arose because of that conference, though it quickly subsided.

From there the father came to Quierzy in mid-September. He likewise very easily suppressed a certain disturbance, gave the aforesaid Charles arms and a crown, as well as a certain portion of the kingdom between the Seine and the Loire, and seemed to make Pippin and Charles united. He then graciously permitted Pippin to depart for Aquitaine, while he sent Charles to the portion of the kingdom he had given him.

When Charles arrived there, all those inhabiting those territories came to him and, having pledged themselves, confirmed their allegiance to him by oath.

At the same time it was reported that Louis had rebelled against his father and wished to claim for himself everything that belonged to the kingdom beyond the Rhine. When his father heard this, he called an assembly, came to Mainz, crossed the army over the river, and compelled Louis to flee into Bavaria.

He returned joyfully to Aachen, since wherever he had turned he had been victorious by divine command.

Nevertheless, because old age was advancing and, owing to various afflictions, almost decrepitude was impending, his mother and the leading men of the people who had worked for Charles in accordance with his father’s will feared that, if he died before these matters were completed, the brothers’ hatred might rise against them to the point of destruction.

They therefore judged it appropriate that the father should take one of his sons as an assistant; and, if the others were unwilling to remain united after his departure, at least these two, made allies, might be able to resist the faction of the envious.

As necessity pressed and they were therefore occupied with constant deliberation over this choice, everyone agreed that, if Lothar were willing to show himself reliable in this matter, an alliance ought to be made with him.

For, as stated above, Lothar had once sworn to his father, mother, and Charles that whatever portion of the kingdom his father wished to give Charles, he would accept it, and that throughout all the days of his life he ought to consent to and protect it against all Charles’s enemies.

Therefore they chose envoys and sent them to Lothar in Italy. They promised that, if he were willing thereafter to preserve his father’s will concerning Charles, everything he had hitherto done wrong against him would be forgiven, and that the entire kingdom, except Bavaria, would be divided between Lothar and Charles.

Since these terms seemed acceptable to Lothar and his followers, both sides swore that they desired this arrangement and would carry it out.

Therefore they assembled at the city of the Vangiones, where a meeting had been proclaimed (839). There Lodharius fell most humbly at his father’s feet before everyone, saying: “I know that I have sinned before God and before you, lord father. I ask not for a kingdom, but for pardon, and that I may merit your favor.” The father, as a pious and merciful man, both pardoned the one who asked forgiveness for his offenses and granted favor to the one who begged for it [Col. 0051C]—on this express condition, namely, that henceforth he should in no way act against his father’s will, either against Karolus or anywhere in the kingdom. Then he received him kindly, and, kissing him, gave thanks to God for the son whom He had reconciled after his estrangement.

They then turned to the midday meal, intending on the following day to deliberate about the other matters which their men had sworn. On the next day they held a council. Then the father, desiring to fulfill what his men had sworn, said: “Behold, son: as I promised, the whole kingdom lies before you; divide it as you please. If you divide it, the choice of the portions will belong to Karolus. But if we divide it, the choice of the portions will likewise belong to you.”

When he had tried for three days to divide it but could not do so at all, Lodharius sent Josippus and Richard to his father, begging him and his men to divide the kingdom [Col. 0051D] and to grant him the choice of the portions. Moreover, they testified, in accordance with the oath they had sworn to him, that they delayed carrying this out for no other reason than their ignorance of the regions. Accordingly, the father, as fairly as he could, divided the whole kingdom with his men, excluding Bavaria; and Lodharius, with his men, chose—and indeed received—the southern portion from the Meuse. He agreed that the western portion should be given to Karolus [Col. 0052A], and together with his father he announced before all the people that this was his will.

Then the father, insofar as he could, made the brothers united, asking and imploring them to love one another, exhorting them to protect one another, entreating them, and expressing his desire that this should be done. After these matters had been completed, he sent Lodharius kindly and peacefully back to Italy, enriched by the gift of pardon and by royal gifts. He recalled to his memory the oaths he had often sworn, the occasions on which he had offended him, and the occasions on which he had pardoned his offenses; and, with fatherly affection, he warned and charged him not to allow, in any way, even that latest arrangement which they had just made and which he had confirmed before everyone as his will, to be rendered fruitless.

At the same time, the father had received news that Pippinus had died [Col. 0052B]. One part of the people was awaiting what the grandfather would order concerning the kingdom or his grandsons; another part, having taken up his son Pippinus, because he was the eldest, was exercising tyranny. Therefore, after completing with Lodharius the matters described above, the father gathered a strong force and set out through Cavillonum and Claromontium, together with Karolus and his mother. He kindly received there the portion of the people that had been awaiting him. Since he had formerly granted the kingdom of Aquitaine to Karolus, he urged and instructed the people to commend themselves to him. They all, having placed themselves under his protection, confirmed their loyalty to him by oath. After this, he set about restraining the tyrants.

At the same time Ludhowicus, as was his custom, left Bavaria and invaded Alamannia, together with certain Thuringians and Saxons whom he had enticed [Col. 0052C] (840). Therefore his father, recalled from Aquitaine—leaving Karolus, together with his mother, at Poitiers—celebrated Holy Easter at Aachen, and then by one and the same route proceeded toward Thuringia. After driving his son Lodhuwicus from it, and redeeming his route through the Slavs, he forced him to flee into Bavaria.

When this had been accomplished, on the Kalends of July he proclaimed a meeting at the city of the Vangiones, and ordered his son Lodharius to come from Italy, intending to deliberate with him and with the others who trusted him about Lodhuwicus. While matters stood thus—with Lodharius in Italy, Lodhuwicus beyond the Rhine, and Karolus in Aquitaine—Lodhuwicus the emperor, their father, died on an island near Mainz on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. His brother Drogo, bishop and archchaplain, buried him with fitting honor, together with the bishops, abbots, and counts, in the city of Metz, at the church of Saint Arnulf [Col. 0052D]. He lived sixty-four years. He ruled Aquitaine for thirty-seven years. He held the imperial title for twenty-seven years and six months.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0051]

### PREFACE

[Col. 0051D]

Having for the present, according to my strength, set forth the beginnings of your dissensions [Col. 0052D]—from which every reader who wishes to know why, after the death of your father, Lodharius [Col. 0053A] decided to persecute you and your brother may judge, gather the facts, and recognize whether he acted justly—I shall now endeavor to record, insofar as memory and strength permit, with what courage and skill he carried this out. I ask you, however, to consider the difficulties arising from this same distress that have impeded my own weakness. And if I neglect anything in this work, I ask you to forgive me.

When Lodharius heard that his father had died, he immediately sent messengers everywhere, especially throughout all Francia, to announce that he would come to take possession of the empire that had once been assigned to him. He promised each person that he would grant the honors bestowed by his father and would increase them. He also ordered those whose loyalty was doubtful to be confirmed by oath. Moreover, he commanded them to advance to meet him as quickly as they could [Col. 0053B]. To those unwilling to do so, he ordered that the death penalty be proclaimed.

He himself advanced slowly, wishing to learn how matters would turn out before he crossed the Alps. Thus, enticed from every side by greed and fear, they flocked to him. Seeing this, and becoming confident in hope and strength, he began to deliberate by what means he might more freely seize the entire empire. He considered it settled that he should first send a force against Lodhuwicus, whom he perceived to be near his route; and, in order to destroy him by force, he applied every effort.

Meanwhile, he craftily sent envoys to Karolus in Aquitaine, announcing that he was well-disposed toward him, as his father had determined and as was proper toward his godson. Nevertheless, he begged Karolus to spare his nephew, Pippinus’s son, until he could speak with him [Col. 0053C]. Having arranged these matters, he directed his journey toward the city of the Vangiones.

At that time Lodhuwicus had left part of his army there for the purpose of guarding it, while he had gone to meet those Saxons whom he had enticed. Therefore Lodharius, after a small engagement, forced the guards to flee. Crossing the Rhine with his entire army, he proceeded toward Frankfurt. There, unexpectedly, Lodharius and Lodhuwicus came together from opposite directions. Having arranged a peace during the night, one of them established his camp there, while the other camped where the Main flows into the Rhine, without fraternal affection.

Since Lodhuwicus was resisting bravely, and Lodharius did not trust that he could subdue him without battle, he hoped that Karolus could be overcome more easily. He therefore ended the conflict by an agreement that they should meet again at the same place on the third day before the Ides of November [Col. 0053D]; and, if no agreement intervened according to the terms set, they should decide by arms what was owed to each. Having set these matters aside, he attempted to subdue Karolus.

At that time Karolus had come to Bourges for the assembly at which Pippinus’s men had sworn that Pippinus would appear. When he received news from everyone, he chose envoys—namely Nithardus and Adelgarius—and sent them to Lodharius as quickly as he could. He instructed and begged him to remember the oaths they had sworn to one another and to preserve what their father had established between them.

He further asked him to remember their relationship as brothers and godfather and godson: let him keep what was his, and let him permit him, without conflict, to possess what their father, with Lodharius’s consent, had granted him (840). He promised that, if Lodharius did this, he wished to remain his faithful and subject servant, as was proper for a younger brother toward the firstborn.

Moreover, he promised from his heart to pardon whatever he had hitherto done against him, and begged him not to incite his men further or disturb the kingdom entrusted to him by God. He instructed him to yield everywhere to peace and concord, and announced that he regarded this as settled on behalf of himself and his men and therefore wished to preserve it. Even if the other did not believe that matters stood thus, he promised to make him certain of it in whatever way he wished.

Lodharius pretended to receive these words kindly, but allowed the envoys to return only after greeting him, replying through his men that he would answer the other matters. Moreover, because they had refused to turn to him after their pledged loyalty had been frustrated, he deprived them of the honors their father had given them [Col. 0054A]. Thus, unwillingly, he gave an indication of what he was planning to do to his brother.

Meanwhile all those living between the Meuse and the Seine sent to Karolus, instructing him to come before Lodharius could occupy the region, and promising that they would await his arrival. Accordingly Karolus hastened this journey with very few men, coming from Aquitaine to Carisiacum; and he kindly received those who came to him from the Carbonaria and the regions below it. But beyond that point Herenfridus, Gislebertus, Bovo, and the others, deceived by Odulfus and neglecting the loyalty they had confirmed, defected.

At the same time a messenger came from Aquitaine, announcing that Pippinus intended to attack Karolus’s mother together with those who favored his party. Therefore Karolus, leaving the Franks there, instructed them that, if his brother wished to oppress those men before his return, they should advance to meet him [Col. 0054B].

He also sent messengers to Lodharius, Hugo, Adelhardus, Gerardus, and Hegilo, repeating everything that he had recently instructed Lodharius. He further begged them, for God’s sake, not to deprive him of his men and thus further dissipate the kingdom which God and their father had given him with Lodharius’s consent. Having arranged these matters, he hurried to Aquitaine, attacked Pippinus and his men, and forced them to flee.

At the same time, while Lodharius was returning from Lodhuwicus and everyone from this side of the Carbonaria was coming to him, he crossed the Meuse and decided to proceed as far as the Seine. As he was making his way there, Hilduinus, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Gerardus, count of the city of Paris, having defected from Karolus and broken faith, came to him.

When Pippinus, son of Bernard, king of the Lombards, and the others saw this [Col. 0054C], they preferred, in the manner of slaves, to abandon their loyalty and despise their oaths rather than relinquish their possessions for even a short time. Thus, abandoning their faith, they followed those whom we have mentioned above and surrendered themselves to Lodharius.

Lodharius, now emboldened, crossed the Seine. As was his custom, he sent ahead men who would draw away those living between the Seine and the Loire, some by threats and some by flatteries. He himself followed at a slow pace, as he was accustomed to do, and proceeded toward the city of Caremtena. When he learned that Theodericus, Ericus, and those who had decided to follow him were going to come to him, he relied on the hope of his multitude and resolved to advance as far as the Loire.

Karolus, meanwhile, having returned from the flight in which he had scattered Pippinus and his men, and having no secure place where he could leave his mother, was likewise hurrying toward the regions of Francia.

In the meantime Karolus heard that all those whom we have mentioned above had defected from him, and that Lodharius had decided to persecute him to the death with a huge army. On one side Pippinus was hostile, and on the other the Bretons. They therefore summoned and held a council to deliberate easily about all these matters, and an exceedingly easy course of action was found.

Since they had nothing left except their lives and bodies, they preferred to die nobly rather than abandon their betrayed king. Accordingly they went to meet Lodharius, and advanced toward the city of Orléans from opposite directions, pitching their camps about six leagues apart [Col. 0055A]. They sent envoys to one another.

Karolus sought peace solely on the grounds of justice; Lodharius, however, was striving to determine by what trick he could deceive and overcome him without a battle. When, because the other side was resisting stoutly, he despaired of carrying this out, he hoped that his forces, which had begun to increase daily, would grow stronger and that he would then be able more easily to subjugate Karolus, with whom they had decided to fight.

Deceived in this hope, he ended the battle by an agreement that Aquitaine, Septimania, Provence, and ten counties between the Loire and the Seine should be ceded to Karolus. The arrangement was that Karolus should remain content with these territories for the time being, until they met at Attigny on the eighth day before the Ides of May; there, he promised, they would jointly consider and establish what was advantageous to both sides.

The leading men of Karolus’s party, seeing that the matter exceeded their strength, and fearing above all that, if battle were joined, they might be unable to save their king with so few men—for everyone had considerable hope in his character [Col. 0055B]—agreed to the terms on this condition: that henceforth Lodharius should be as faithful a friend to Karolus as a brother ought by justice to be toward his brother; that he should ensure that Karolus held peacefully the kingdoms assigned to him; and that, in the meantime, he should permit Karolus to proceed hostilely against Lodhuwicus. Otherwise, they were to be released from the oath they had sworn.

By this stratagem they both rescued their king from danger and soon released themselves from their oath. For before those who had sworn these things left the place, Lodharius attempted to draw some of those present away from Karolus; and on the following day he received some of his own men. Moreover, he immediately sent men into the kingdoms assigned to Karolus and disturbed them as much as he could, so that they would not submit to him. He proceeded to receive those coming to him from Provence, and considered how he might overcome Lodhuwicus by deceit or by force.

Meanwhile Karolus came to the city of Orléans and gladly and kindly received Teotbaldus and Warinus, together with certain men from Burgundy who came to him. From there he went to meet Bernardus, as he had ordered, and proceeded toward the city of Nevers.

Bernardus, however, as was his custom, delayed coming to him, saying that he had confirmed by oath with Pippinus and his men that neither of them should enter into any agreement with anyone without the consent of the other. Therefore he declared that he wished to go to them, and promised that, if he could arrange for his men to come over together with him, all would be well; but if not, once the oath had been dissolved, he would return to Karolus within fifteen days and commit himself to his authority.

Accordingly Karolus again came to Bourges to meet him. When Bernardus came there but did nothing of the kind, Karolus took the deceptions he had practiced against his father and was still practicing against him very seriously. Fearing that he might otherwise be unable to capture him, he suddenly resolved to attack him.

Bernardus sensed this, though late, and fled, barely escaping. Karolus struck down some of his men, left others wounded and half-dead, and captured others unharmed, ordering them to be guarded in the manner of prisoners. He permitted all their equipment to be plundered.

Thereupon Bernardus, having been humbled, came shortly afterward as a suppliant to Karolus, saying that he had been faithful to him and had wished to be faithful then also, if permitted; and that, although he had suffered this insult, he did not doubt that he would remain faithful in the future. He promised that, if anyone wished to say otherwise, he would repel the charge by arms.

Karolus, persuaded by these words, received him into the fellowship of friendship, enriched with gifts and favor, and sent him out to attempt, as he had promised, to bring Pippinus and his men into subjection. Having arranged these matters, he went to the city of Le Mans to receive Lantbertus, Ericus, and the others with them.

When he received them there with great courtesy, he immediately sent to Nomenoius, duke of the Bretons, wishing to know whether he was willing to submit to his authority. Nomenoius, following the counsel of many, sent gifts to Karolus and confirmed by oath that he would thereafter preserve his loyalty to him [Col. 0056A].

When these matters had been completed, and the time of the assembly that they had appointed at Attigny seemed to be approaching, Karolus was anxious about what he and his men ought to do with prudence and firm loyalty. He therefore summoned those who shared his counsels, repeated the matter known to everyone, and asked them to disclose how they thought he and his men could most suitably be freed from so great a calamity. He declared that he wished in everything to obey the public interest and that, if necessary, he would not hesitate to undergo death for it.

When they saw that their strength seemed to be increasing on every side, they recalled the ambushes that Lodharius had sought to lay in the time of his father against their father and Karolus, and those that, after their father’s death, he had been preparing without respite against his brothers [Col. 0056B]. They also remembered the oaths that he had recently violated. They said that they willingly wished to obtain all justice from him, but that these indications gave them no hope of anything good. Therefore it seemed advisable to them all that Karolus should not delay coming to the appointed assembly by whatever means he could.

If his brother wished, as he had promised, to seek and establish the common good, this pleased them all and it would be fitting that he should be received gladly. If not, then, trusting in justice and therefore in divine assistance, as well as in his faithful men, Karolus should not neglect to obtain by every effort whatever kingdom his father had granted him with the consent of both brothers and their faithful followers.

Therefore he ordered all the Aquitanians who favored his party to follow him, together with his mother. He did the same with anyone from Burgundy and with those between the Loire and the Seine who wished to belong to his jurisdiction [Col. 0056C]. He himself, together with those who were then present, undertook the aforesaid journey, although it seemed difficult.

When he reached the Seine, he found Guntboldus, Warnarius, Arnulfus, Gerardus, and all the counts, abbots, and bishops from the Carbonaria and below it. Lodharius had left them there for the specific purpose of preventing Karolus from crossing without his consent. In addition, the flooding river had denied them fords everywhere. The guards of the river had either destroyed all the boats or certainly sunk them. Gerardus had also destroyed every bridge he found.

Thus the crossing had become extraordinarily difficult and caused no small trouble to those wishing to pass [Col. 0056D]. While their minds were being harassed in many ways by so many difficulties, they were eventually informed, through the advice of merchants, that boats had been brought away from the mouth where the Seine flows into the sea by a strong current and had been put ashore near the city of Rouen.

Coming there, Karolus filled twenty-eight of them with armed soldiers and, having boarded them himself, sent men ahead to announce that he was coming. He offered pardon to everyone who wished it, but instructed those unwilling to accept it to depart and leave him the kingdom given to him by God.

When they despised this offer and the fleet seemed to be approaching, as soon as they recognized the cross by which they had sworn and recognized Karolus, they abandoned the shore and immediately fled. Since he could not overtake them—the horses had delayed while crossing—he directed his journey toward Saint-Denis for the sake of praise and prayer.

When he came there, he learned that those whom the flight had scattered had gathered together with Arnulfus, Gerardus, and the others, and intended to attack Teutbaldus, Warinus, Otbertus, and the rest, who, as had been ordered, were coming to Karolus.

Therefore he proceeded to Saint-Germain for the sake of prayer. Traveling throughout the night, at dawn he received Warinus and his companions safely at the place where the Luva flows into the Seine. He then proceeded by the same route to the city of Sens.

From there he rose during the night and traveled by way of Utta, hoping that, as had been reported to him, those whom we have mentioned above were stationed in the same forest. For he had arranged to attack them wherever and however he could.

He would certainly have done so, had not the danger of death, threatening at the very door, been announced to those who were anxiously awaiting him. Therefore almost all of them, exceedingly terrified and anxious for their lives, took flight by whatever route they could [Col. 0057A]. Since Karolus could not overtake them, and his companions and horses were exhausted, after the Lord’s Supper he allowed them to rest, and on the following day went to the city of Troyes.

At the same time, while Karolus was carrying out the matters described above, Lodharius, as has been stated, was considering with all his mind how he might subdue Lodhuwicus by deceit or by force—or, what he preferred, destroy him. For this business he suitably summoned Otgarius, bishop of the see of Mainz, and Adhelbertus, count of Metz. Both of them hated Lodhuwicus to the point of death.

Adhelbertus had now recovered from the illness that had confined him for almost a year, as though he had revived for the purpose of fratricide [Col. 0057B]. At that time he was so prudent in counsel that no one wished to alter a judgment pronounced by him.

At his instigation Lodharius gathered an immense multitude from every side and crossed the Rhine, sending ahead, as was his custom, men who attempted to draw away the wavering populace by threats and flatteries. The people who were with Lodhuwicus feared that they would be unable to withstand so great an army. Some, having lost heart, went over to Lodharius; others took flight and abandoned Lodhuwicus.

Since all other support was lacking on every side, Lodhuwicus departed with very few men and withdrew into Bavaria. When this happened to Lodhuwicus, Lodharius no longer thought that Lodhuwicus could prevail in any way. Therefore he left the duke Adhelbertus, whom we have just mentioned, there for the purpose of binding the people to himself by oaths and preventing Lodhuwicus from going to Karolus, should he wish to do so [Col. 0058A].

Lodharius himself, having learned that Karolus had crossed the Seine, prepared to go to meet him. He quickly sent men ahead to learn the truth of the matter—where Karolus was and with whom—since Lodharius intended to celebrate Easter at Aachen.

A remarkable event, and one deserving to be noted, happened to Karolus on that same Holy Saturday.
