Neither he nor anyone in his company possessed anything except what they were wearing, and their weapons and horses. When he was leaving the bath and preparing to put on the same garments that he had removed, suddenly messengers from Aquitaine appeared at the door, carrying the crown and all the royal ornaments, as well as everything pertaining to divine worship [Col. 0058B] (842).

Who would not marvel that a few and almost unknown men were able to carry unharmed across so many stretches of land, while everyone everywhere was intent on plunder, so many talents of gold and an immeasurable quantity of jewels? And, what I confess is even more astonishing, how could they have arrived at the appointed place, or certainly on the appointed day and hour, when Karolus himself did not know where he ought to be with his men?

This event could not have seemed to occur in any other way than by divine gift and command. It therefore inspired wonder in his fellow soldiers and raised them all to the greatest hope of salvation. Then Karolus and the entire rejoicing company turned to celebrate the festivals.

When he had completed what he had begun, he kindly received Lodharius’s envoys and ordered them to dine with him. He also instructed them to return on the following day, promising that through his own men he would answer what his brother had sent him.

In Lodharius’s embassy it was complained that Karolus had exceeded, without Lodharius’s consent, the boundaries that he had assigned to him. Since he had done so, Lodharius instructed his envoys to find him wherever he was and to tell him to remain there for the time being, until he should be informed whether he ought to come to the appointed place or to another location that seemed more suitable to Lodharius [Col. 0058C].

Karolus replied through his men that he had exceeded the appointed boundaries for this reason: Lodharius had allowed nothing to remain secure of all the benefits promised and confirmed by oath on his behalf. He had added to his jurisdiction some of Karolus’s men whom he had enticed beyond what had been agreed, and had deprived others of life.

Moreover, he had disturbed, as far as he could, the kingdoms which he was supposed to bring into subjection to Karolus. Most importantly, he had attacked his brother hostilely and had forced him to seek assistance from pagans.

Nevertheless, although matters stood thus, Karolus announced that he wished to come to the assembly which they had established by common agreement. If Lodharius wished, as he had promised, to seek and establish the common good, this would please him; but if not, Karolus declared that, regarding the kingdom which God and his father had given him with the consent of his men, he would in everything obey the counsels of his faithful followers according to the will of God.

Having arranged these matters, he undertook the same journey and reached the aforesaid place a day before Lodharius arrived. Lodharius, however, as though deliberately, delayed coming [Col. 0058D]. Nevertheless, he frequently sent envoys filled with various complaints, and took precautions lest Karolus should unexpectedly attack him.

Meanwhile envoys had come from Lodhuwicus, announcing that, if he knew how it could be done, Lodhuwicus wished to come to Karolus’s aid. Karolus replied that he needed this assistance, gave suitable thanks for his willingness, and immediately sent the aforesaid envoys back to urge him to hasten.

After waiting there four days or more for Lodharius’s arrival, while Lodharius continued to delay coming, Karolus summoned an assembly and held a council to deliberate what seemed most advisable for him to do thereafter.

Some said that, since his mother was coming together with the Aquitanians, he ought to go to meet her. But most advised either that he should set out to meet Lodharius or that he should await his arrival wherever Karolus wished. They argued especially that, if Karolus began to turn his journey elsewhere, everyone would claim that he had taken flight; as a result Lodharius and his men would become bolder. They also hoped that all those who, out of fear, had not yet joined either side would flock to Karolus—and this did happen.

Although it was difficult, the earlier opinion prevailed. Therefore Karolus went to the city of Cadhellonum. There he received his mother together with the Aquitanians, and suddenly it was announced that Lodhuwicus had defeated Adhelbertus, duke of the Austrasians, in battle, had crossed the Rhine, and was coming as quickly as possible to Karolus’s aid.

When this became known throughout the entire camp, everyone urged that they should go out cheerfully to meet him [Col. 0059A]. Lodharius, too, when he discovered that matters stood thus, announced to the surrounding populace that Karolus had taken flight and that he wished to pursue him as quickly as possible.

By this report he made those faithful to him more eager, instilled courage to join him in those who were doubtful, and made his own party stronger. When Karolus learned that Lodharius was pursuing him, and since they had pitched their camp in a difficult place surrounded by waters and marshes, he immediately proceeded to meet him, so that they could engage without any difficulty if Lodharius wished.

When this was reported to Lodharius, he pitched his camp and, as though the horses were exhausted, gave them two days’ rest [Col. 0059B]. When they had done the same thing again, and frequently sent envoys to one another but could reach no useful decision, Lodhuwicus and Karolus at last approached and met.

At the same assembly they sorrowfully discussed all the things which Lodharius, without any restraint, was inflicting upon them and their men. They decided to deliberate on the following day about what would be most expedient to do thereafter.

At dawn they assembled and held a council, in which they greatly lamented so great a calamity [conquirunt: “they investigate/inquire”]. When each had finished recounting what things, how many, and of what kind they had suffered at the hands of their brother, it seemed good to everyone, unanimously and with equal agreement, both to the sacred order of bishops and to the laymen, to choose noble, prudent, and benevolent men [Col. 0059C].

Through these men they would communicate what their father had established between them and what they had suffered from Lodharius after their father’s death. They would also implore him to remember almighty God and to grant peace to his brothers and to the whole Church of God; to yield to each person what was justly owed by the consent of their father and brothers.

Moreover, they offered him whatever in the entire army they appeared to possess apart from horses and weapons, asking him to accept their just petitions. If he wished to heed these admonitions and supplications, they said that this would please them. If not, they said that, by divine favor, they could undoubtedly hope for assistance, provided that they wished to do everything just and humbly strove to offer this to their brother.

Since these proposals rightly seemed acceptable, they were immediately carried out.

But Lothair despised these proposals as though they were nothing. Through his men he declared that he wanted nothing except battle, and immediately set out to meet Pepin, who was coming to him from Aquitaine. When Louis and his men learned this as quickly as possible, they took the matter exceedingly hard—for they had been gravely worn down on every side, both by the length of the journey and by battles and various hardships, and especially by the lack of horses. Nevertheless, although matters stood thus, they feared that, if one brother should abandon the other’s assistance, they would leave an unworthy memory to their descendants. To prevent this, they chose rather to endure every deprivation, even death if necessary, than to lose their undefeated name. Therefore, oppressed by sorrow but strengthened by the same magnanimity, they encouraged one another and proceeded joyfully and swiftly, so that they might overtake Lothair as soon as possible.

When, unexpectedly, the two armies became visible to one another near the city of Alciodorus, Lothair immediately feared that his brothers might wish to fall upon him without delay, and he went out from the camp a short distance under arms. When his brothers learned that he had done this, they took some armed men with them and advanced to meet him without delay. They sent messengers to one another and arranged peace during the night. Their camps were about three leagues apart, more or less, with a small marsh and wooded ground between them; consequently, access from one to the other was difficult.

Therefore, at dawn, Louis and Charles sent to Lothair and declared that they were greatly displeased that he had denied them peace without battle [Col. 0061A]. They added that they desired peace and, if it could be achieved, without any deceit. First, they should invoke God by fasts and vows. Then, if Lothair wished to cross over to them, they promised to provide him with a place of crossing, so that, once every obstacle had been removed on their side and that of their men, they could meet without any hidden deception. They ordered him to confirm this by oath, if he wished. If he did not wish to do so, they nevertheless asked and begged him to grant and confirm the same terms to them.

Lothair, however, promised that he would reply through his own men, as was his custom. As soon as the envoys had returned, he immediately set out to meet them and sought the place where he would establish his camp, Fontaneum. On that same day, however, his brothers, hastening after Lothair, passed him and encamped near a village called Tauriacus.

On the following day, the armies, prepared for battle, advanced a short distance beyond their camps. Louis and Charles sent word ahead to Lothair that he should remember the condition of brotherhood; that he should allow the Church of God and the entire Christian people to have peace; that he should grant them the kingdoms which their father had assigned to them with his consent; and that he should retain what was his, not by merit but solely by the mercy left to him by their father. As a gift, they offered him whatever they appeared to possess in the entire army apart from arms and horses. If he refused this, each of them would yield him a portion of the kingdom: one as far as Carbonaria, the other as far as the Rhine. If he rejected that proposal as well, they would divide the whole of Francia equally, and whichever of these arrangements he preferred would be under his authority.

To this Lothair replied, as usual, through his men that he would note whatever pleased him [Col. 0061C]. At that moment he sent Drogo, Hugh, and Hegibert, declaring that they had never before communicated anything of this kind to him and that he wished to have time to consider it. In reality, Pepin had not yet arrived, and he wanted to await him during this delay. Nevertheless, he ordered Ricuinus, Hirmenald, and Frederick to confirm by oath that he was asking for this truce for no other reason than that he wished to seek the common welfare both of them and of the entire people, as justice between brothers and the people of Christ required.

Louis and Charles, made credulous by this oath, agreed to peace for that day, the following day, and even until the second hour of the third day—namely, 25 June [VII Kalends of July]. With the peace confirmed by oath on both sides, they returned to their camps, intending to celebrate the Mass of Saint John on the following day.

On that same day, after Lothair had also received Pepin as a reinforcement, he sent word to his brothers that they knew the imperial name had been bestowed upon him with great authority, and that they should consider how he might fulfill the magnificent office of that name. He added that he was by no means willingly seeking the welfare of either of them. When they were asked whether he wished to accept any of the proposals they had conveyed, or whether he had sent them any definitive answer, they replied that none of these matters had been entrusted to them.

Therefore, when every hope of justice and peace on his part seemed to have disappeared, they sent him word [Col. 0062B] that, if he had found no better course, he should either accept one of the proposals they had made or know that on the following day—on 25 June, as stated above, at the second hour of the day—they would come to the judgment of almighty God over the matter he had imposed upon them against their will.

Lothair contemptuously rejected this in his usual manner and replied that they would see what he ought to do.

While I was writing these things as I remained beside the Loire near Saint-Eluduald, a solar eclipse occurred at the first hour, on the first day of the week, 18 October, with the Sun in Scorpio.

Leaving these matters aside, Louis and Charles rose at dawn, occupied the summit of a mountain adjoining Lothair’s camp with, as it appeared, one-third of their army, and awaited his arrival and the second hour, as their men had sworn. When both the appointed time and Lothair were present, they joined battle over the Riuda [Rivolus] of the Burgundians, with great violence.

Louis and Lothair fought bravely at a place called Brittas. When Lothair was defeated there, he turned his back and fled. The part of the army which Charles encountered at the place commonly called Fagit immediately fled. But the part which attacked Adalard at Solennat, together with the others—whom, with the Lord’s help, I had supplied with no small reinforcement—fought bravely. Both sides were victorious there. Finally, however, all those on Lothair’s side fled.

Thus Lothair brought the first engagement to an end; let the second book also end here.

# BOOK THREE

## PREFACE

Since I am ashamed to hear anything unfortunate about our family, and especially since I am exceedingly reluctant to report it, I have therefore resolved—without at all contemptuously rejecting the command—to bring this work entirely to an end when the desired conclusion of the second book had arrived. But lest anyone, deceived in any way, should presume to recount the events of our time otherwise than they occurred, I agreed to add a third little book from matters in which I myself took part.

After the battle had been fought bravely, as stated above, Louis and Charles began to deliberate on what should be done with those who had fled. Some, having been seized with anger, urged them to pursue the enemy. Others, however, and especially the kings, took pity on their brother and the people, and wished that, chastened by God’s judgment and by this blow, they might recover from their wicked ambition and, by God’s gift, thereafter become united in true justice. In this matter they advised waiting for the mercy of almighty God.

The rest of the multitude agreed with them [Col. 0063A]. They withdrew from battle and plunder and returned to the camps around midday, to deliberate on what seemed wisest to do next.

There had indeed been an enormous amount of plunder and an enormous slaughter. Yet there was also a mercy worthy of admiration—or rather, rightly deserving notice—both on the part of the kings and of everyone else. For they decided to spend the Sunday there on various grounds. After Mass had been celebrated, they entrusted friends and enemies alike, the faithful and the unbelieving alike, to burial. Those who had been struck down and were half alive they likewise restored with all their strength and heartfelt care.

Afterward they sent after those who had escaped by flight, offering to forgive all their offenses if they wished to return in good faith. Then the kings and the people, grieving over their brother and the Christian people, began to ask the bishops what they ought to do about this matter [Col. 0063B].

Accordingly, all the bishops gathered unanimously in council. It was established in the public assembly that they had fought solely for justice and equity, and that this had been made manifest by God’s judgment. Therefore every minister of God ought to be regarded as free from guilt in this affair, whether as adviser or as agent.

But whoever was conscious that he had advised or undertaken anything in this expedition out of anger, hatred, vainglory, or any other vice was to confess it secretly; a secret offense was to be judged according to the measure of the fault. Nevertheless, in honor and praise of so great a declaration of justice, they asked for help in obtaining remission for the offenses of their dead brothers—for they knew that, being imperfect and with sins intervening, they had sinned in many ways, willingly and unwillingly—and that through this assistance they might be stripped of and freed from those sins [Col. 0063C]. They further prayed that, just as God had until then shown himself their helper and protector in justice, so he might continue to be so everywhere thereafter. For all these matters a three-day fast was imposed, and it was indeed willingly and solemnly observed.

When these matters had been completed, Louis resolved to make for the Rhine. Charles, however, for various reasons, and especially because of Pepin, judged that he should go to Aquitaine in an effort to bring him under his authority. Bernard, duke of Septimania, although he had been about three leagues distant from the site of the aforementioned battle, had supplied neither side with reinforcements.

When Bernard learned that Charles had won the victory, he sent his son William to him. He ordered William to commend himself to Charles if Charles wished to grant him the honors he had held in Burgundy [Col. 0063D]. He also boasted and declared that he could and would bring Pepin, together with his men, into a treaty by which Charles might subdue him.

Charles received this embassy kindly and granted everything that William had requested, warning him to do everything in his power to ensure that the promise concerning Pepin and his men was fulfilled. When it seemed that adversity had been driven away on every side and that the hope of prosperity favored everyone here and there, Louis and his men made for the Rhine, while Charles, together with his mother, went to the Loire.

The administration of the state was abandoned more carelessly than was proper; each man departed very readily wherever his inclination carried him. When Pepin heard this, he delayed entering into the treaty with Charles which he had shortly before desired. Bernard came to Charles, but did not agree to commend himself to him. Some nevertheless defected from Pepin, and this expedition benefited Charles only in that respect: he received those men as his allies.

Meanwhile Adalard and the others whom Charles had sent to the Franks, wishing to know whether they wanted to return to him, came to Carisiacum, where Charles had ordered them to send envoys. They encountered very few men, who said that, if Charles himself were present, they would certainly not delay coming to him. Otherwise, they said, they did not know whether he was alive or not.

For those who supported Lothair’s party had boasted that Charles had fallen in battle, that Louis had been wounded, and that he had fled. Therefore they declared that it would be ill-advised to enter into any treaty with anyone in uncertain circumstances [Col. 0064B].

Guntbold and the others who had gathered together pretended that they were about to attack the aforementioned envoys of Charles; and they certainly would have done so if they had dared. Therefore Adalard and the others sent to Charles, declaring that he should hasten to come as quickly as he could, so that he might provide them assistance and might learn whether, as they claimed, the Franks wished to come to him.

They themselves went to the city of Paris to await Charles’s arrival. When this was reported to Charles, he immediately directed his journey into those regions. When he reached the Seine, he encountered Adalard and the others at Spedonna.

Although he was anxious because the appointed meeting with his brother in the city of Langres on 1 September was now imminent, he resolved at least to hasten through the city of Beauvais, then by way of Compiègne and Soissons, and from there through Rheims and Châlons to Langres, so that he might strive to observe what he had arranged with his brother and might also be able to receive any of the Franks who wished to come to him.

The Franks, despising the same small force which the Aquitanians had despised, delayed submitting to him for the present by means of various fabrications. When Charles learned this, he began to hasten along the route mentioned above.

As he was making for Soissons, the monks of Saint-Medard came to meet him, begging him to transfer the bodies of the saints Medard, Sebastian, Gregory, Tiburtius, Peter and Marcellinus, Marius, Martha, Audifax and Abachuc, Onesimus, Meresina and Leocadia, Marianus, Pelagius, and Maurus, Florianus with his six brothers, Gildardus, Serenus, and the lord Remigius, archbishop of Rouen, into the basilica where they now rest and which was already then largely built [Col. 0064D].

Charles agreed to their request, remained there, and, as they had asked, carried the bodies of the blessed saints on his own shoulders with every mark of reverence. He also added, by decree, the estate called Barnacha to the property of that church.

When these matters had been completed, he made for Rheims. On arriving there, he received word that Louis could not come to the meeting which they had arranged in Langres because Lothair intended to invade his kingdom with a hostile force. His uncle and Count Gislebert of the Mansuarians [Mausuarians] had also sent word that, if Charles went into those regions, they would come to him together with the others [Col. 0065A].

Therefore, both to assist his brother and to be able to receive those men if they wished to come to him, Charles directed his journey toward Saint-Quentin. There he encountered Hugh, as had been announced, and from there proceeded toward the region of Utrecht.

When Lothair heard this, he abandoned Louis, whom he had shortly before decided to pursue, and set out from Worms for the meeting which he had summoned at the estate of Theodonis; he began considering how he might attack Charles.

When Charles learned this at Wasiticum, he sent Hugh, Adalard, Gislebert, and the others to bind them to him by whatever treaty they could make. He also sent Rabanus to Louis, declaring how he was situated in those regions for his assistance [Col. 0065B].

When Lothair heard this, he abandoned that plan and prepared to advance against Louis with all his forces. He sent to Pepin, warning and begging him to strive, as usual, to provide assistance as quickly as he could.

Charles also sent the venerable Bishop Exemeno to Lothair. In his customary humble manner, he ordered him to ask and entreat Lothair to remember that he was his brother and godson; to remember what their father had established between them and what both Lothair and his men had sworn among themselves; to remember that, most recently, his will had been declared by God’s judgment between them.

If he did not wish to remember all these things, he should cease persecuting the holy Church of God; he should take pity on the poor, widows, and orphans; and he should abandon his attempt to enter the kingdom granted to him by his father’s consent, lest he once again compel the Christian people to gather for mutual slaughter.

When these matters had been arranged, Charles himself went to the city of Paris to await both the arrival of his brother Louis and the other faithful men whom he had summoned from every direction.

When Lothair learned this, he directed his journey toward the same city. He had with him a considerable part of the Saxons and Austrasians, as well as of the Alamanni, and relying especially on their aid, he came to Saint-Denis.

He had found about twenty ships there. Moreover, the Seine was low, as it usually is in September, and offered an extremely easy crossing. Therefore his men boasted that they could cross easily and pretended that this was precisely what they most wanted to do [Col. 0065D].

Charles therefore ordered some men to guard Paris and Melun; he stationed others wherever he knew that fords or boats existed. He himself established his camp opposite Saint-Denis, near Saint-Fluduald, in the middle of the region, so that, if necessary, he could prevent Lothair from crossing or come to the aid of his men if Lothair attempted to attack them somewhere.

To make it readily apparent where assistance ought to be provided, he stationed signals and guards at suitable places according to military custom.

Then, marvelously, although at that time we knew of no rain anywhere in the region for two months, the Seine suddenly began to swell under a clear sky and of its own accord blocked all the fords in those places [Col. 0066A].

When matters stood thus, Lothair, seeing that every crossing there was blocked to him, sent word that he wished to make peace with Charles on the condition that Charles abandon the treaty which he had confirmed by oaths with his brother Louis. Lothair, for his part, would abandon the treaty which he had likewise confirmed by oaths with his nephew Pepin. Charles would retain the western part beyond the Seine, excluding Provence and Septimania, and they would be joined as though by perpetual peace.

In reality, Lothair thought that by this arrangement he could deceive both men more easily and hoped by this stratagem to seize the whole empire.

Charles replied that he did not wish to violate the treaty which necessity had compelled him to make with his brother. Moreover, it did not at all seem proper that he should abandon the kingdom which his father had given him from the Meuse to the Seine, especially since so much nobility from those regions had followed him and ought not to be deceived in its loyalty [Col. 0066B].

Therefore, since winter was approaching, he sent word that each man should retain the honors which their father had given them, if Lothair wished, until spring, when they could all meet either with a few men or with their entire retinue; and if they did not reach agreement on the arrangements already established or those yet to be established, they should decide by arms what was owed to each.

Lothair rejected this in his customary manner and, leaving Saint-Denis to meet Pepin, who was coming to him from Aquitaine, directed his journey toward Sens. Charles, on the other hand, considered how he might receive Louis as his ally.

Meanwhile Charles was informed that his sister Hildegard was holding a certain Adelgar, one of his men, as a prisoner and had ordered him to be kept with her in the city of Laon. For this reason Charles selected men equipped for the task and, as the day was already ending, hastened into those regions.

The city was about thirty leagues distant. He traveled throughout the night, despite severe frost. At about the third hour of the day, Hildegard and the citizens unexpectedly received sudden word that Charles had arrived with an innumerable multitude and that the entire city was surrounded by soldiers.

Terrified by this news, since they had no hope either of escape or of defending the walls, they sought peace that same night. They immediately returned Adelgar and promised with complete submission to surrender themselves and the city to him on the following day without a conflict.

While this was taking place, the soldiers, greatly resenting the delay, and stirred by weariness from the labor they had endured during the preceding night, began rushing from every side toward the destruction of the city [Col. 0066D]. It would undoubtedly have immediately been given over to flames and plunder had Charles not, moved by pity for the churches of God, his sister, and the Christian people, striven with the utmost effort to restrain their spirit by threats and kindness.

After he had made them withdraw, he granted Hildegard what she had requested and departed from the city for Salmonsiacum. On the following day Hildegard came under his protection, as she had promised, and restored the city unharmed and without conflict to his authority.

Charles received his sister kindly and forgave her everything she had hitherto done against him. He addressed her gently with many words and, if she thereafter wished to be well disposed toward him, promised her with the utmost humanity every kindness which a brother owes a sister. He allowed her to depart wherever she wished.

He restored the city’s rights and, when these matters had been completed, returned to his men whom he had left near Paris.

At Sens, after receiving Pepin, Lothair was anxious about what he ought to do. Charles had led part of his army across the Seine and directed it into the forest commonly called Perche. Lothair feared that either he or his men might hinder them and therefore decided first to pursue them. By doing so he hoped both to make them surrender easily and, through that terror, to subjugate the rest to himself; above all, he hoped to bring Nomenoius, duke of the Bretons, under his dominion.

But he undertook all this in vain, accomplishing none of it. Charles’s entire army escaped from him safely [Col. 0067B], he recovered none of his own men, and Nomenoius insolently rejected everything he had commanded him.

While matters stood thus, Lothair suddenly received word that Louis and Charles, together with a vast army, were endeavoring to reach one another. Seeing himself surrounded on every side by adverse circumstances, and having completed a great but fruitless circuit, he began to return from Tours and, with his army exhausted, finally reached Francia.

Pepin, seized by remorse because he had joined Lothair, withdrew to Aquitaine.

Meanwhile Charles heard that Otgar, bishop of the see of Mainz, together with the others, had prevented his brother Louis from crossing over to him. He hastened his journey through the city of Toul and entered Alsace [Elizata], at Zabern. When Otgar learned this, he abandoned the riverbank with the others [Col. 0067C], and each of them hid himself as quickly as he could.

Therefore, on 14 February [XVI Kalends of March], Louis and Charles met in the city formerly called Argentaria and now commonly called Strasbourg. Louis swore the oaths written below in the Romance language, while Charles swore them in the Germanic language. Before the oaths, they addressed the assembled people, one in the Germanic language and the other in the Romance language.

Louis, being the elder, began first as follows:

“Many times you have seen how Lothair, by pursuing me and this brother of mine after the death of our father, has tried to destroy us even unto annihilation. When neither brotherhood, nor Christianity, nor any human ingenuity could, while preserving justice, help to establish peace between us, we were finally compelled to bring the matter to the judgment of almighty God, so that, by his will, we might be content with whatever was due to each of us. In this, as you know, by God’s mercy we proved victorious. He, having been defeated, withdrew with his men wherever he could.

“Then, moved by brotherly love and by compassion for the Christian people, we did not wish to pursue and destroy them. Instead, as before, we sent word that at least thereafter each man should be granted his rightful due. But he, no longer content with divine judgment, continues once again to pursue both me and this brother of mine with a hostile army. Moreover, he devastates our people with fires, plunder, and killings.

“Therefore, compelled by necessity, we have now met. And because we believe that you doubt the steadfastness of our loyalty and the firmness of our brotherhood, we have decided to swear this oath between us in your presence. We do not do this because we have been enticed by any wicked ambition, but so that, if God grants us peace through your assistance, we may be more certain of the common welfare. But if—and may it not happen—I should presume to violate the oath which I shall swear to my brother, I release each one of you from my authority and from the oath which you have sworn to me.”

When Charles had delivered the same speech in the Romance language, Louis, since he was the elder, first testified that he would observe the following:

> “For the love of God, for the Christian people, and for our common salvation, from this day forward, insofar as God grants me knowledge and power, I shall save this brother of mine Charles, and aid him in every matter, as one ought to save his brother according to justice, provided that he does the same for me. And I shall never make any agreement which, to the harm of this brother of mine Charles, would be made by my will.”

When Louis had completed this, Charles testified to the same words in the Germanic language:

> “In God’s love, for the Christian people and for our common salvation, from this day forward, insofar as God grants me knowledge and power, I shall hold to my brother Louis as a man ought, according to justice, provided that he does the same for me. And I shall never make any agreement which, by my will, would be to the harm of this brother of mine Louis.”

The oath which the people of both men likewise testified to, each in his own language, is as follows in the Romance language:

> “If Louis keeps the oath which he has sworn to his brother Charles, and Charles, my lord, does not keep what he has sworn to him, if I cannot turn him back, neither I nor anyone whom I can turn back will give Louis any aid against Charles.”

In the Germanic language:

> “If Charles keeps the oath which he has sworn to his brother Louis, and Louis, my lord, breaks what he has sworn to him, if I cannot prevent him, neither I nor anyone whom I can turn back will go against Charles in his service.”

When these matters had been completed, Louis directed his journey along the Rhine by way of Speyer, while Charles proceeded beside the Vosges by way of Wissembourg toward Worms.

The summer in which the aforementioned battle was fought was extremely cold, and all the crops were gathered very late. Autumn and winter, however, followed their natural course. On the same day on which the aforementioned brothers and the leading men of the people made the aforesaid pact, much snow fell with the ensuing frost.

A comet appeared in December, January, and February, until the aforementioned meeting. It rose through the center of Pisces and disappeared after the council had been completed, between the constellation called by some Lyra and by others Andromeda, and the dimmer Arcturus.

Having briefly touched upon the sequence of the seasons and the stars, let us return to the course of the history. When they had come to Worms, they selected envoys and immediately sent them to Lothair and to Aquitaine [Saxony]. They arranged to await the arrival of these men and of Carloman between Worms and Mainz.

Here, too, it is not at all beside the point to relate a few things, since they appear pleasant and deservedly worthy of notice, about the character of these kings and the unanimity with which they lived meanwhile.

Both were of medium stature, beautiful with every grace, and suited to every exercise. Both were bold, generous, equally prudent and eloquent, and their holy and venerable harmony exceeded all the nobility previously mentioned among brothers.

Their banquets were nearly constant, and whatever valuables either possessed, he gave to the other with the utmost kindness. They had one house for dining and one for sleeping. They managed public and private affairs with equal agreement. Neither asked anything of the other except what he judged useful and fitting for him.

They also often attended athletic games in this manner for the sake of exercise. They assembled wherever a suitable spectacle seemed likely, and while the entire multitude stood on either side, first equal numbers of Saxons, Gascons, Austrasians, and Britons from each side charged rapidly against one another as though they intended to be adversaries.

Then one side, turning its back and protected by shields, pretended that it wished to escape to its pursuing companions. In turn, however, they attempted to pursue those whom they had been fleeing, until at last both kings, together with all the young men, sprang forward with a tremendous shout, their horses released and their spears brandished, pursuing now one side and now the other as they turned their backs.

It was a spectacle worthy of such nobility and restraint. No one amid so great a multitude and diversity of peoples dared to inflict any injury or insult on another—as often happens among a very few familiar people.

While matters stood thus, Carloman came to his father in Mainz with a vast army of Bavarians and Alamanni. Bardo, who had been sent to Saxony, did likewise, reporting that the Saxons had rejected Lothair’s commands and were willing to do whatever Louis and Charles ordered them.

Lothair also unwisely delayed listening to the envoys who had been sent to him. Both Louis and Charles, as well as the entire army, took this badly, and they considered how they might reach him.

Accordingly, on 17 March [XVI Kalends of April], they set out along the road in those regions. Charles entered upon the difficult route through the Vosges; Louis traveled by land and along the Rhine through Bingen; and Carloman went by way of the Einrich. On the following day, at about the sixth hour, they came to Conflans and immediately proceeded to Saint Castor for prayer.

They heard Mass, and afterward the same kings, under arms, boarded ships and quickly crossed the Moselle. When Otgar, bishop of the see of Mainz, Count Hatto, Heriold, and the others saw this—for Lothair had left them there to prevent the crossing—they were terrified, abandoned the riverbank, and fled.

When Lothair learned at Sinzig that his brothers had crossed the Moselle, he too immediately did not cease departing from both kingdom and residence until he reached the bank of the Rhône with the few who had decided to follow him, leaving the rest behind.

Thus Lothair brought the second engagement to an end; let the third book end here.

# BOOK FOUR

## PREFACE

As I have already said, I am pleased not only to rest from this work of narration, but also to withdraw entirely from public affairs. My mind, filled with various complaints and made anxious by continual meditation, is tossed about. Yet because fortune has bound me to all these matters here and there and carries me, mourning, through powerful storms, I do not know where—or rather, I do not know at all—toward what harbor it is carrying me.

Meanwhile, if I find some free time, what harm will there be if, as I have been ordered, I take care to entrust the deeds of our princes and nobles to the memory of writing? Therefore I shall undertake—or assist in—this fourth work of history; and if I cannot be useful in other matters yet to come, at least through my own labor I shall clear away for posterity some small cloud of error concerning these events.

When Louis and Charles learned by reliable indications that Lothair had departed from his kingdom, they made for Aachen, which was then the principal residence of Francia, intending on the following day to deliberate on what seemed wiser to do concerning the people and kingdom left behind by their brother.

First, it seemed proper to refer the matter to the bishops and priests, most of whom were present, so that through their counsel, as though by divine inspiration, the beginning and authority of these affairs might emerge [Col. 0070C]. This was entrusted to them, since it rightly appeared sound.

As they considered Lothair’s conduct from the beginning—how he had driven his father from the kingdom; how often his ambition had made the Christian people forswear themselves; how often he himself had frustrated what he had sworn to his father and brothers; how often after his father’s death he had attempted to disinherit and destroy his brothers; how many murders, adulteries, arsons, and crimes of every kind the universal Church had suffered through his most abominable ambition; and how, in addition, he possessed neither the knowledge required to govern the state nor any trace of good will which anyone could discover in his government—they declared that, for these reasons, not undeservedly but by the just judgment of almighty God, he had first fled from battle and then from his own kingdom [Col. 0070D].

Therefore all unanimously judged and agreed that, because of his wickedness, God’s vengeance had expelled him and had justly entrusted the kingdom to his better brothers to govern.

Nevertheless, they did not grant them this authority until they had openly asked them whether they wished to govern it by following the example of their expelled brother or according to God’s will. When they replied that, insofar as God granted them knowledge and ability, they wished to govern and rule themselves and their people according to his will, the bishops said:

> “By divine authority we admonish, exhort, and command you to undertake it and govern it according to God’s will.”

Each of them then selected twelve men from among his own people for this task. They formed a single body, and, as seemed fitting to them, they agreed that the kingdom should be divided between them.

In this division, they adjusted not so much to the fertility or equal proportion of the kingdom as to the kinship and suitability of each man’s share.

Louis received all Frisia [Note: [Col. 0071D] Thus the old manuscript; recently someone attempted to supplement it as follows: “And the eastern kingdoms fell to him, namely all Germany as far as the waters of the Rhine, together with certain cities beyond the Rhine and the neighboring districts.”] . . . [lacuna]

But Charles [Note: [Col. 0072D] Thus the old manuscript; the same person recently attempted to supplement it as follows: “But Charles received the western kingdoms from the British Ocean to the river Meuse, in which region the name of Francia has remained from that time until the present.”] . . . [lacuna]

When these matters had been completed, each of them received from the people who had followed him, and bound them by oath to remain faithful thereafter. Charles, for his part, crossed the Meuse in order to organize his kingdom; Louis, however, went to Cologne on account of the Saxons. Since I perceive that their circumstances are of the greatest importance, I think they must by no means be passed over.

The Saxons, as is clear to all who dwell throughout Europe, were converted by the emperor Charles the Great—rightly called so by all nations—from their varied worship of idols to the true and Christian religion through much and diverse labor. From the beginning they were outstanding both in nobility and in readiness for war, as they repeatedly demonstrated by many signs. This people as a whole is divided into three orders. Among them there are those whom in their language they call Edhilingi, those whom they call Frilingi, and those whom they call Lazzi. In Latin these mean: nobles, freeborn, and servile.

But the part of them that was regarded as noble was divided into two factions during the dispute between Lothair and his brothers: one followed Lothair, the other Louis. Matters being thus situated, Lothair, seeing that after his brothers’ victory the people who had been with him were inclined to abandon him, sought assistance wherever and however he could, constrained by various necessities. On one side he distributed public property for private uses; on another he granted liberty to some and promised others that he would grant it after the victory. He also sent to Saxony, promising the Frilingi and Lazzi, whose multitude is infinite, that if they supported him, he would allow them thereafter to have the same law that their ancestors had possessed in the time when they were worshipers of idols. Excessively eager for this, they gave themselves a new name, namely Stellinga; and, gathered into one body, with their lords almost driven from the kingdom, they lived according to the ancient custom, each under whatever law he wished.

Moreover, Lothair had brought in the Northmen for assistance and had subjected part of the Christians to them; he also gave them permission to plunder the other Christians. Therefore Louis feared that these same Northmen, as well as the Slavs, because of their kinship with the Saxons who had called themselves Stellinga, might join with them, invade the kingdom in order to claim it for themselves, and abolish the Christian religion in those regions. For this reason, as we have stated, he went especially to [Cologne] and, insofar as he was able, took precautions against the other disorders in his kingdom as well, lest this most abominable evil befall the holy Church of God.

When these matters had been completed, Louis approached the city of Verdun by way of the village of Teutonia, while Charles came by way of Reims, intending to deliberate about what ought next to be done.

At the same time the Northmen plundered Cotuuig; crossing the sea there, they likewise devastated Hamuuig and Nodhunnuuig. Lothair, however, having withdrawn above the bank of the Rhône, settled there, relying on a vessel on that river, and drew to himself from every side as many men as he could for assistance. Nevertheless, he sent an envoy to his brothers, declaring that, if he knew how it could be done, he wished to send his leading men to them to deliberate about peace. The reply was that he should send whomever he wished: anyone could easily know where that course would lead them.

They themselves, however, went by one and the same route through the city of the Tricasini and the city of Cadhellon. When they had reached Miliciacum, Iosippus, Eberhard, Egbert, together with the others on Lothair’s side, came to them, saying that Lothair had recognized that he had sinned against God and against them, and no longer wished there to be strife between them and the Christian people. If they wished, they should increase his share beyond a third of the kingdom on account of the imperial title which their father had granted him, and on account of the dignity of the empire which their grandfather had added to the Frankish kingdom. Otherwise, they should grant him only a third of the whole, excluding Lombardy, Bavaria, and Aquitaine; and, with God’s favor, each of them should govern his portion of the kingdom as best he could. Each should enjoy the assistance and goodwill of the other; they should grant peace and laws, each to the other’s subjects; and, with God as author, an enduring peace should be established between them.

When Louis and Charles heard this, and it was highly pleasing to them and to the whole people, they gathered together with their leading men and discussed with joyful hearts what they should do about such matters. They said that this was what they had wanted at the beginning of the dispute, and that, although because of intervening sins it could not have been productive, they had often sent this message to him. Nevertheless, they gave thanks to almighty God, by whose aid they had finally deserved that their brother, who had always rejected peace and concord, should then, by God’s generosity, seek them.

Yet, according to their customary practice, they referred the matter to the bishops and priests, so that, wherever divine authority wished to direct it, they might be ready with willing hearts to obey its command. Since it seemed best to all of them that peace should be made between the brothers, they agreed, summoned envoys, and granted the requests.

When they had spent four days or more in dividing the kingdom, it was finally decided that all the bishoprics, abbeys, counties, and royal estates situated between the Rhine and the Meuse, up to the source of the Meuse, and then to the source of the Saugonna, and likewise along the Saugonna to its confluence with the Rhône, and thereafter along the Rhône to the Tyrrhenian Sea—all, that is, lying on this side of the Alps, except [lacuna]—should be offered to him as a third part of the kingdom. If he refused to accept this, they should decide by arms what was owed to each. Although this was judged by some to be beyond what was just and appropriate, it was conveyed through Conrad, Abbo [Cobbo], Adalhard, and the others.

Meanwhile, until those who had been sent returned, they decided to remain in the same place, awaiting Lothair’s response. When they came to Lothair, they found him somewhat less animated than usual. He said that he was not satisfied with what his brothers had sent him, because it was not an equal portion; and he further pleaded the case of his followers, because in the part being offered to him he would have no means of restoring to them what they were losing.

For this reason—though I do not know by what deception they were misled—those who had been sent increased his share beyond the defined portion as far as the Carbonaria. Moreover, if he accepted this until a time mutually agreed upon, they swore to him that then his brothers would divide the whole kingdom, excluding Lombardy, Bavaria, and Aquitaine, into three parts by oath, as fairly as they could; that the choice of the portions of that kingdom would belong to Lothair; and that whichever portion he chose, they would grant and preserve to him for all the days of his life, provided that he did the same for them. If he did not otherwise believe this, they promised by oath that they would act accordingly.

Lothair also swore that this was his wish and that he would fulfill it on his side, provided that his brothers carried out what their envoys had then sworn to him.

Accordingly, in the middle of June, on the Thursday, near the city of Mâcon, on an island called Ansilla, Lothair, Louis, and Charles met with an equal number of leading men, and swore this oath to one another: namely, that from that day onward they would preserve peace among themselves; and that, at the assembly which their faithful men would establish there, they would divide the whole kingdom, excluding Lombardy, Bavaria, and Aquitaine, into three parts by oath, as fairly as they could. The choice of the portions of that kingdom would belong to Lothair; and each of them would preserve for the others, throughout their lives, whichever portion each received, provided that his brother acted similarly toward him and his followers.

When this had been completed, and words of peace had been exchanged, they departed peacefully and returned to their camps, intending to deliberate about the remaining matters on the following day. Although with difficulty, it was nevertheless achieved that, until the assembly they had appointed for the first day of October, each should remain peacefully in whatever portion he wished.

Louis went to Saxony to organize it, while Charles went to Aquitaine. Lothair, now feeling secure about the choice of the portions of the kingdom, went hunting in the Ardennes and deprived of their offices all the leading men of the people in his portion who, when he had left the kingdom, had been compelled by necessity to defect from him.

Louis, for his part, nobly—but by a lawful slaughter—suppressed in Saxony the rebels who, as stated above, had called themselves Stellinga. Charles drove Pippin into Aquitaine. While Pippin remained concealed, Charles could accomplish nothing else of note, except that he left behind a certain duke Warin and others who seemed faithful to him, to guard that country. Moreover, Count Egfrid of Toulouse captured some of Pippin’s associates in ambush—men who had been sent to destroy him—and struck down others.

Charles himself set out for the assembly which he had arranged with his brother Louis at Worms. When he arrived at Metz on the day before the Kalends of October, he found Lothair at the village of Teutonia, where he had come before the appointed assembly and was staying otherwise than he had arranged. For this reason, those who on behalf of Louis and Charles were supposed to remain at Metz for the division of the kingdom considered it by no means safe to divide the kingdom there while their lords were at Worms and Lothair at the village of Teutonia. Worms is about seventy leagues, more or less, from Metz; the village of Teutonia about eight.

It also occurred to them that Lothair had often proved exceedingly ready and willing to deceive his brothers. Therefore they did not dare entrust their safety to him without some security. Charles, consequently, taking thought for their safety, sent to Lothair and announced that, since he had come and was staying there otherwise than had been agreed, if he wished his brother’s envoys and Charles’s own to remain there together with his men, he should give him hostages, so that Charles might be confident of their safety. Otherwise, he should send his envoys to them at Worms, and they should give him whatever hostages he wished. If not, they should withdraw from Metz by an equal distance. If he did not want this either, their envoys should meet in whatever place he wished midway between them.

For Charles said that he ought not to neglect the safety of so many noble men. There were eighty chosen men, outstanding among the entire multitude in nobility; if their destruction were not prevented, he said, it could inflict the greatest loss upon himself and his brother.

At last, for the convenience of everyone, it was decided that their envoys—one hundred and ten in number—should meet at the confluence without hostages and divide the kingdom there as fairly as they could.

Accordingly, when they met there on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, lest some scandal should arise among their men for any reason, those who had come from Louis and Charles took up the eastern bank of the Rhine, while those who had come from Lothair took up the western bank; and every day they went to Saint Castor for their common conference.

When those who had been sent by Louis and Charles approached the division of the kingdom with various complaints, it was asked whether any of them possessed a complete and exact knowledge of the whole empire. Since no one could be found who did, it was asked why their envoys had not traversed it in the intervening time and made a written survey of it. When they discovered that Lothair did not want this done either, they said that it was impossible for anyone who was ignorant of something to divide it equally.

Finally, since they were required by oath to divide it as fairly and well as they could and knew how, it was asked whether they could sincerely swear to do this, knowing that no one could carry it out properly in ignorance. This matter too was entrusted to the bishops for deliberation.

They gathered on both sides in the basilica of Saint Castor. Those on Lothair’s side said that if anyone had violated his oath, he could atone for it, and that it would therefore be better for them to do this than for the Church of God to suffer so many robberies, burnings, murders, and adulteries any longer.

But those who were on the side of Louis and Charles replied that, since neither course was necessary, why should they sin against God? It would be better to confirm peace between them, send men jointly throughout the empire, and make a written survey of it; then, at last, they could swear to what was certain without danger and divide it equally. In this way, they maintained, they could avoid perjury and other crimes, unless blind greed stood in the way. Thus they declared that they neither wished to injure themselves by an oath nor to grant anyone permission to do so.

Disagreeing on these matters, each group withdrew to its own people by the route through which it had come. Then they all assembled in the same house. Those on Lothair’s side said that they were ready both to take the oath and to make the division, as had been sworn. Those on the side of Louis and Charles likewise said that they wished to do so, if they could.

Finally, since neither side dared agree to what the other wanted without the authority of their lords, they decided that peace should prevail between them until they could learn what their lords wished to accept concerning these matters. It seemed that this could take place on the Nones of November. They therefore departed after setting a period for the peace.

On that day a great earthquake occurred throughout almost all this Gaul. On the same day the memorable man Angilbert was transferred to Centula; in the twenty-eighth [twenty-ninth] year after his death, his body was found intact and undissolved, without spices. This man was born at that time into a family of no little distinction. Madhelgaud, Richard, and he were of one lineage, and they were rightly held in high regard by Charles the Great. By Berchta, the daughter of that great king, he fathered Harnid, my brother, and me, Nithard.

At Centula he built a magnificent work in honor of almighty God and Saint Richarius, and governed the household entrusted to him with great distinction. Thus, after completing his life in every happiness at Centula, he rested in peace.

Having briefly touched upon my origin, I now wish to return to the sequence of the history.

When, as stated above, each of those who had returned reported to his king what he had discovered, they agreed—because of scarcity on one side, the approach of winter on another, and also because the leading men of the people, having once experienced the danger, did not want to fight a second battle—that peace should be maintained between them until the twentieth day after the feast of Saint John.

To establish it, the leading men of the people from both sides gathered at the village of Teutonia. They swore that the kings themselves should meanwhile preserve mutual peace; and that nothing should in any way be omitted: at that same assembly they were to divide the whole kingdom as fairly as they could, and, as had been sworn, the choice of the portions of that kingdom was to belong to Lothair.

Then each departed in whatever direction he wished. Lothair went to Aachen to winter, Louis to Bavaria, while Charles came to Quierzy to take a wife. At the same time, the Moors, brought in by Sigenulf, the brother of Sigihard, for the purpose of assistance, invaded Benevento. At the same time also, the Stellinga rebelled again in Saxony against their lords; but when battle was joined, they were struck down in a great slaughter. Thus, by authority, that which had presumed to rise without authority perished.

Charles, as stated above, took Hirmentrude in marriage, the daughter of Wodon and Ingeltrude and the granddaughter of Adalhard. In his own time, his father had loved this Adalhard so greatly that whatever Adalhard wished throughout the empire, his father would do. Adalhard, however, giving little thought to the public good, aimed to please everyone. On one side he urged the distribution of liberties, on another of public resources, for private uses; and when he brought about whatever each person requested, he utterly destroyed the commonwealth. In this way it came about that, in the present crisis, he could easily turn the people wherever he wished.

For this reason Charles entered the marriage mentioned above, chiefly because he thought that through her he could claim the greatest part of the common people for himself. After the wedding had been completed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord solemnly at Saint-Quentin. He also made arrangements at Valenciennes for those of his faithful men who were to remain between the Meuse and the Seine for the purpose of guarding the region.

Then, together with his wife, he set out for the regions of Aquitaine in the winter of the year 843 of the Incarnation of the Lord. That winter was exceedingly cold and prolonged, and also abounded in illnesses; it was highly unfavorable to agriculture, cattle, and bees.

Let everyone here consider with what madness he neglects the public good and rages according to private and personal desires, while by both he so greatly offends the Creator that he even makes all the elements hostile to his madness. I shall proceed to prove this very readily by examples still almost universally known.

In the time of Charles the Great, of blessed memory, who died nearly thirty years ago, this people followed one and the same straight way—and therefore the public way of the Lord—and so peace and concord existed everywhere among them. But now, by contrast, since each person follows the path he desires, dissensions and quarrels are openly found everywhere. Then abundance and joy flourished everywhere; now scarcity and sorrow prevail everywhere. Then the elements themselves were favorable to each king; now they are hostile everywhere to all, as Scripture, produced by divine gift, testifies: “And the world will fight against the senseless” (Wisdom III).

At that time there was an eclipse of the moon on the thirteenth [variant: fifteenth] day before the Kalends of April. Moreover, much snow fell that same night and, as stated above, brought sorrow upon everyone by the just judgment of God. This happened, I say, because on every side robberies and every kind of evil were insinuating themselves everywhere, while elsewhere the disorder of the atmosphere was taking away everyone’s hope of good.

## In the Year of the Lord 853. Amulo, Bishop of Lyons

[Col. 0077]

[Col. 0077]

## Historical Notice

*(In Galland’s* Library of the Ancient Fathers, *volume XIII.)*

[Col. 0077A] Our author is called by different names in the books of the ancients: he is known as Amulo, Hamulus, or even Hamularius. He was a Gaul by nationality, succeeded Agobard, and held the see of Lyons from the year 841 until 852 and beyond. Concerning him, in addition to the bibliographers, Cointius [Note: Volume VIII, page 650] and Dominic de Colonia [Note: *Literary History of Lyons*, volume II, page 127] will provide further information for the curious. Cavaeus carefully reviewed his writings. From Baluze’s edition of Agobard, we have selected as especially important two letters: one to Theobald concerning certain counterfeit relics of saints, and the other to Gottschalk for refuting his doctrine and morals. In addition, there are two short works addressed to the same Gottschalk concerning foreknowledge, predestination, and free will, etc., drawn from a certain manuscript codex at Trier. Sirmond was the first to publish these at Paris in the year 1649.

[Col. 0077A]

## Letters of Amulo

[Col. 0077]

### First Letter. To Theobald, Bishop of Langres

[Col. 0077B]

**I.** To the most reverend Theobald, worthy of honor for the pure affection of love [Note: He is also called Teotbald or Teutbold; he became bishop in the year 844], bishop of the Church of Langres, Amulo, humble bishop of the Church of Lyons, eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Through your beloved brother, your chorepiscopus [Note: This was Ingelrannus, acting as the bishop’s representative at the castle of Dijon], you recently informed us that at the castle of Dijon, in the church of the blessed martyr Benignus, certain things had begun to occur among those who appeared to be gathering from every place for the sake of prayer and veneration—especially, indeed, as some maintain, only among women. This had disturbed your mind with a certain uncertainty, and you judged that our counsel—that is, fraternal counsel—was necessary and should be sought.

For he said that in the previous year two men who claimed to be monks had brought to the aforesaid basilica of the holy martyr what appeared to be the bones of some saint. They asserted that they had taken them either from the city of Rome or from some regions of Italy—I do not know which. Yet, with astonishing shamelessness, they said that they had forgotten the saint’s name.

As though they could truly have loved and venerated him so greatly, if they had known him to be a saint, that they would have labored so earnestly to carry him across so great a distance—unless his name had been familiar and widely known in the places from which, they claimed, he had been taken, and had been so made known to and impressed upon these men that they desired and sought him, or even stole him, in order to place him within the borders of their own region and commend him to the veneration of the faithful.

Or could they perhaps have recognized someone as worthy of such great veneration, desired to transfer him with such great love, and themselves carried him continually over so long a journey, yet forgotten his name even for a single hour? Could they have failed to pray that he whom they loved and venerated so greatly would be present to them through continual desire and prayer, for the protection of their salvation and to obtain divine mercy, with devout and unceasing remembrance? Or could they have been so utterly lazy and stupid that they did not even take care to record his name in writing as a reminder to themselves?

**II.** Therefore, as our aforesaid brother reported, you acted prudently and religiously in judging that such relics—whose authority was entirely absent and whose very name was unknown—should neither be accepted nor wholly despised, provided that those who had brought them could, as they promised, clearly demonstrate under careful examination that certainty concerning the matter had been brought from those same regions.

He told us that one of the aforesaid monks, who had remained at Dijon, has now died, while the other, who had gone to investigate and report back, has by no means returned.

Nevertheless, while those bones—brought by such contemptible persons, confirmed by no assertion of truth, and introduced into the Church through so foolish an account—are reverently preserved as though for the sake of honor beside the tomb of the aforesaid glorious martyr, certain things resembling miracles have begun to occur in the same basilica. They are not acts of healing and cures by which any signs of divine mercy and favor might be shown, but blows and collisions by which wretched little women suddenly appear to fall and strike themselves in the very house of prayer, and as though to be tormented, although no injuries appear on any part of their bodies and they seem to display no trace of any wound.

For this reason such a crowd of people, as though filled with wonder, has rushed there that, as we have learned not only from the brother whom you sent but also from some others, there are now said to be three hundred or four hundred persons, or even more. They are said to fall and strike themselves in the manner described and then, after recovering their senses for a short while, to be healed, yet to be wholly unable to leave the place. For, if they attempt to return to their homes, they are immediately struck by some new and unknown blow and compelled to return to the church from which they had gone out.

Among them, it is said, are not only girls but also younger married women and women of more mature age, both more respectable and more humble.

**III.** You have informed us that such things have begun to occur not only in the church of Saint Benignus but also in another church within the same castle and in several others throughout your parishes. For we have learned through a reliable report that similar things—or rather, things being feigned—have begun to occur in the territory of Augustodunum, in a place called Sedelocus, at the church in which the holy martyrs Andochius, Thyrsus, and Felix are buried.

We waited several days, hoping that, as we requested through your aforesaid chorepiscopus, you would explain more carefully in your letters both the manner and the course of this affair. Thus, instructed more precisely and clearly, we might, with the grace of God assisting, be found all the more ready to reply.

But since you wrote nothing afterward, it seemed better to us not to delay in fulfilling toward your affection the duty of a response, according to what we could learn or infer from his report. Therefore, to answer all these matters briefly, insofar as Christ deigns to grant us the ability, and to remove the uncertainty of the case together with your affection, it seems to us first of all that those bones—which are said, with no reason and no authority, to belong to some unknown saint, and from which this first itch of curiosity appears to have arisen—should be removed entirely from the sacred sanctuary and the celebrated site.

They should by no means remain inside the church, but should be buried outside, in the courtyard, or certainly beneath a wall, or near it; or, as we consider more useful, near another secluded place, suitable and clean, under the knowledge of only a few. Thus, since they are said to be holy, some reverence may be shown them; but since it is entirely unknown whether they are so, they will not become an occasion of error and superstition for the ignorant people.

Nor should we fear that we might perhaps incur some offense through such care. Almighty God wishes us to be cautious and discerning in matters that concern him, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.” And again: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.”

Therefore the Lord also warns us, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.”

In this matter we have a great and venerable example of piety in the acts of Saint Martin, so that we may by no means rashly place faith in uncertain things. That blessed and glorious confessor and bishop of Christ, when he found a certain place consecrated by his predecessors under the title of an altar and frequented by crowds of people, but found neither the name of the martyr who was said to be buried there nor the time of his passion, entirely abstained from that place and would not in any way lend his authority to the opinion of the common people [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, book 8], until the truth of the matter had been divinely revealed to him. Then he also freed the people from the error of that superstition. [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 8.]

**IV.** We also find in the decrees of blessed Pope Gelasius bishops gravely censured and described as almost alien to the spirit of Christianity because they rashly presume to establish with sacred rites churches built in the name of any deceased persons whatsoever, perhaps not even of the faithful [Note: Gelasius’s *Decrees*, chapter 25].

We also know that the bodies of certain highly venerable saints lay for many years either among the graves of fields or in a corner of a church, until they manifested themselves through worthy revelations.

Therefore, in accordance with apostolic and evangelical authority and the venerable examples and institutions of the holy Fathers, let the object from which so great an opportunity for superstition has sprung—and from which no salutary benefit is proved to arise—be removed from among them and dealt with in an appropriate manner.

Even if one, or at most two or three, signs of healing or cures were truly and credibly celebrated in that same church of the blessed martyr Benignus during the very time when such things are occurring, these must certainly be referred, with all joy, veneration, and due thanksgiving, to the glory of God and to the merits of the most blessed and glorious martyr.

This does not, however, make the other things said to occur either in that martyr’s church or in many others worthy of approval. For, insofar as the sequence of what happened itself shows, it may have been that this first arose from a vain opinion: an opportunity may have presented itself when the recently brought body of a saint was being shown and commended to the crowds of people who, as is customary in many places, perhaps gathered there for prayer during the days of Lent; and someone who was entirely unknown was needlessly pressed upon them as worthy of veneration.

Then, when the solemnity of Easter subsequently arrived—the time when these events are said to have begun—worthless and wicked little men, taking advantage of the opportunity, whether driven by the necessity of hunger or stirred by the desire for profit, may have begun to invent and display such apparent blows, collisions, and derangements, followed again by healings, whether the performers were men or women.

**V.** When the people, deceived by a needless opinion, began to regard this with wonder or fear, they began bringing such large numbers of people there and administering to those who seemed afflicted, as though out of compassion, that those who appeared to suffer such things not only refused to leave the place but pretended that they were entirely unable to withdraw, as though struck by a new affliction and debility.

For when have such signs ever multiplied in the Churches of God, in the shrines of the most blessed martyrs—signs by which the sick were not healed, but the healthy were struck down and driven mad? When has the prayer of the saints obtained such healings from the Lord, by which simple and innocent girls are restored unharmed in God’s sanctuary, but, if they wish to bring joy over their safety to their parents, are immediately struck again and prevented from returning to their parents’ homes?

When, moreover, have holy martyrs restored married Christian women to health in their sanctuaries in such a way that they separated them from their husbands and struck them with the punishment of sudden calamity so that they could not return to their husbands’ homes?

Who does not see that these things have been contrived either by the deceptions of the most wicked men or by the tricks and mockeries of demons? They easily oppress or even seize those who are dull in understanding, empty of faith, full of curiosity, and astonished by vanity, so that, with God justly permitting it and their own wickedness raging, such things may even be genuinely carried out in them.

Thus, as though from a single place through the cunning of men and the wickedness of the worst demons—who gladly mock human salvation—this plague of superstition and illusion appears to have spread through one place after another. Even in sacred places and the basilicas of holy martyrs there are some who, for the sake of shameful profit, not only fail to prohibit these things or instruct the erring people in sincere and pure religious observance, but even incite them to pursue such practices, proclaiming them as though they were religious people and tripping them up with their flatteries, solely so that they may fill their own purses with the people’s vows and gifts or devote themselves to feasts and drinking.

Of such men the Prophet rightly says: “They feed on the sins of my people and lift up their souls toward their iniquity.”

We would not speak in the course of this response about the fabrication of such illusions and the insane greed of certain people, if, during the time of our pious father and predecessor, we had not experienced such things with absolute certainty within our own parish in certain little men, both men and women, so that we are not permitted to doubt them in any way.

**VI.** We have indeed several times seen before him people who pretended to be demoniacs and persons afflicted by demons. But when they were subjected to many blows and beatings, they immediately confessed their most wretched deception and publicly explained the necessities and poverty by which they had displayed such behavior in order to supply themselves. They then appeared unharmed by every demonic assault, just as they in fact were.

We also know of a certain city not far from our borders, called Ucetia, situated in the province of Narbonne. There, during the time of our predecessor of pious memory, when such blows and collisions began to occur at the tomb of Saint Firminus, the bishop, certain marks of punishment were found on the limbs of those who fell, as though sulfur had burned there. The common people became terrified and astonished and began thronging to the church in groups with many vows and gifts.

Acting on the counsel of that same father of ours, the Narbonese bishop who still survives, Bartholomew, preached and commanded them not to frequent any longer in such a manner that place which they had begun to visit superstitiously, but rather to spend whatever they had been accustomed to bring there on the needs of the poor and works of mercy.

When this had been done, the entire deception immediately ceased, both there and in the other places where it had likewise begun to occur. The faithful people breathed again in the desired safety and tranquility.

## VII

Therefore, it seems entirely right to us, as reason itself dictates and the examples of good men instruct us, that you should take up a pious zeal and priestly sincerity [Col. 0082B] and severity; and, lest the house of the Lord—which ought to be a house of prayer—become a house of commerce and a den of thieves, you should purge it of this sort of diabolical invention and fabrication, by which such a multitude of unhappy people, and especially women—something deeply to be lamented and shameful—is held bound, as though captive and deprived of reason.

Announce and solemnly urge all people faithfully that, abandoning this sort of vain and destructive thronging, from which no salvation of the soul, no bodily safety, and no benefit to life is known to result, each people should remain quietly in the parishes and churches to which it has been assigned: where it receives holy baptism; where it partakes of the body and blood of the Lord; where it is accustomed to hear the solemn celebration of Mass; where it receives from its priest penance for guilt, visitation [Col. 0082C] in illness, and burial in death; where it is also commanded to offer its tithes and firstfruits; where it rejoices that its children are initiated through the grace of baptism; where it constantly hears the word of God and learns what ought and ought not to be done.

There, I say, let each people gladly bring its vows and offerings; there let it pour out its prayers and supplications before the Lord; there let it seek the intercession of all the saints, who, as it is written, “Follow the Lamb wherever he goes,” and therefore are present everywhere to those who faithfully invoke them. Through them and in them, moreover, the almighty God—who promises his people, saying, “In every place where the memory of my name shall be, I will come to you and bless you”—is present.

There, therefore, let each people distribute alms to orphans and widows, to the poor and to strangers, from the modest resources that God has granted; let it provide the services of hospitality; and whatever it was accustomed to consume in feasting, drunkenness, and the profit-seeking of frivolous people, let it spend on these beneficial works for itself and for its neighbor. For this is the legitimate and ecclesiastical form of religion; this is the ancient custom of the faithful, through which both the vanity of innovations is cut away and the old and upright path of evangelical and apostolic instruction is preserved.
