But if some illnesses and weaknesses occur, each person has at hand, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic command, the means by which he may “summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person” (James 5:14).

[Col. 0083A] **VIII.** When these things have been faithfully and persistently announced and observed, with the Lord granting you success, we trust in his goodness that, when the empty and superfluous distribution of gifts and vows has ceased, that multitude of pretenders and the pretended attacks and derangements will also cease. Each person will then be compelled to seek—not to display vain and false phenomena—but what is necessary for sustaining his little body, or even to beg for it.

Thus, if some should wish to appear more obstinate in such conduct, they will seem to us to have to be restrained by severe beatings and compelled to confess the truth. For even if it were true that those attempting to depart from those places were immediately seized by some new kind of illness, then, the more clearly this happened through the devil’s assault, the more confidently they ought to depart, with the Lord showing mercy and protecting them; and, faithfully despising the enemy’s terrors, they ought to implore that mercy in the legitimate places, according to ecclesiastical custom.

For no envy should be suspected there among the holy martyrs and the spirits and souls of the righteous who already reign with the Lord; rather, there is complete unity of charity and fellowship in goodness. Therefore, if sick persons offered to them are faithfully led to the shrines of other saints in order to avoid temptation, those saints should be believed not to become indignant, but rather to favor them, rejoice, and offer congratulations.

One of these saints in particular, namely the great apostle Paul, says to the other saints because of this unity of spirit: “If you forgive anyone anything, I forgive it also. For if I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake in the person of Christ.”

[Col. 0083C] But if it is the vow and desire of faithful peoples humbly to frequent the shrines of different martyrs and other saints, there are fixed and legitimate days on which it is appropriate to do this devoutly, according to the ancient observance of the Church: namely, during the general Rogation days; during the litanies appointed for various tribulations and needs; during the forty-day fasts; and also during the vigils and feast days of the martyrs.

**IX.** All these practices derive from the law of the universal Church, are commended by the preaching and proclamation of priests, and ought to be observed with the greatest attentiveness through the obedience and devotion of all the faithful. Nevertheless, on other days also, sacred places may reasonably be visited in silence and with pure devotion, not with display and tumult.

But how absurd it is that these practices, so legitimate and so constantly proclaimed, should be neglected by most common people either carelessly or only barely and unwillingly observed, while they are extremely ready to pursue those things which no one preaches or teaches—and which people pursue merely because of the vanity of their minds, even when others oppose them. To such people the words of the blessed apostle Paul must often be impressed: “Brothers, do not become childish in your understanding; but be infants in malice, so that you may be mature in understanding.”

And likewise the words of blessed James: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation [Col. 0084A], and to keep oneself undefiled by this world.”

Attending to these and similar apostolic exhortations, therefore, both priests and peoples should serve the Lord devoutly, earnestly, and faithfully in their own places, and should pursue purity of mind and the fruits of mercy rather than vanity or display.

For even if some of those deceitful people who deceive others were truly possessed and afflicted by demons, they ought to have been treated quietly, according to ecclesiastical custom, either in their own places by their own priests or at the shrines of whatever martyrs by relatives and friends, and, with God’s grace assisting, cleansed—not pointlessly pursued amid crowds and tumult.

I have diligently endeavored, insofar as the Lord granted me ability, to answer your question in accordance with divine authority and paternal instruction. [Col. 0084B] Receive these things willingly; and if God has inspired you with anything better, carry it out with ready intention and watchful care, so that the Lord’s flock entrusted to your governance may, with the same Lord’s help, avoid the stumbling-block of error and attain an increase of religion and sincerity.

We have also sent you a copy of the letter of the aforementioned pious father and our nourisher to the aforesaid bishop of Narbonne, so that anyone who wishes to know more subtly and fully about such matters may be instructed more abundantly and deeply by reading it.

May almighty God graciously protect and preserve your reverend charity continually for the building up of his Church.

# LETTER II. TO GOTTSCHALK

[Col. 0084C] **Amulo, humble bishop of the Church of Lyon, sends greetings to his most beloved brother Gottschalk** [Note: [Col. 0083D] Monk of Orbais, learned indeed but a disturber of the Church; condemned at the Synod of Quierzy, already at Mainz, and beaten with rods in the year 849 because of his obstinacy.].

That I call you “brother” at the beginning of this letter, although I know that you oppose fraternal unity, I do through that charity which God grants us and which Scripture commanded us, saying: “Say to those who hate you: You are our brothers.” For even if brotherhood perishes on the part of those who are such, the affection of brotherhood ought not therefore to grow cold or perish in us also.

But when I call you not only “brother” but also “most beloved,” the Lord knows that I love you faithfully, wishing for you what I wish for myself. Therefore I sincerely wish you salvation, both present and future, through that devotion to divine worship which, as the Apostle testifies, “is useful for all things, holding the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come.”

After hearing and recognizing what you sent in your writings, and what you very urgently demanded that I learn through one of our brothers, I hesitated for a long time whether I ought to answer you: a man long accused of new presumptions against the Church and of no small errors, and, as I hear, condemned by the authority of an episcopal council because of his obstinacy.

For I thought it might seem presumptuous and shameless if I undertook on my own to say or answer anything about a matter that had been determined through the investigation, judgment, and sentence of our prudent and reverend brothers. Yet, on the other hand, to disregard and pass over in silence your great entreaty and supplication did not seem consistent with Christian devotion and charity, through which especially the law of Christ is fulfilled in us, as the Apostle testifies and commends it: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

Accordingly, after he had said of himself, “I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak; I became all things to all people, so that I might save all,” and afterward, “not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved,” he immediately added, in order to instruct and form us according to his example and thereby according to Christ’s example: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

For he is that true and pious Samaritan who mercifully took pity on the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, robbed by bandits along the road, wounded, and left half-dead; he bound up his wounds and treated them by pouring in wine and oil. Wishing us to be imitators of such mercy and goodness, at the end of this parable he says to each one of us: “Go, and you do likewise.”

He clearly shows that the one who is truly a neighbor to his brother, and truly his imitator, is the one who comes to the needs and weaknesses of his brother with ready devotion and compassion.

Provoked, therefore, by this consideration, and trusting in the most sincere charity of our venerable brothers and fellow priests—for through it we are one in the Lord and ought to share with one another the burdens and duties of the ministry entrusted to us, so that their good may, through the spirit of unanimity, be ours, and ours, if by God’s mercy we have any, may be theirs—I judged it better and more salutary to write something back to your brotherhood than, through useless silence, to seem both to distrust them and to offer no counsel to you, so distressed, afflicted, anxious, and troubled.

Therefore I pray the most abundant and unfailing grace of almighty Lord and Savior to grant us useful and truthful consolation and instruction, and to prepare and calm your speech and mind, so that you may receive what we are about to say with pious gentleness and humility; and, setting aside hostility and the desire for contention, may willingly hear what is true; and may obediently receive not our words, but the words of God and of the holy Fathers, submitting your mind and understanding to them with sincere devotion.

For, as truthful Scripture truthfully says: “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their end leads to death.” And: “Whoever trusts in his own thoughts acts impiously.” Therefore the same Scripture elsewhere warns, saying: “And do not rely on your own prudence.”

How greatly this evil must be avoided by a human being was also shown by blessed Ephrem, a father of admirable holiness and most illustrious teaching. At the hour of his departure, he earnestly warned one of his disciples who stood beside him, a man of great, sharp, and excessively inquisitive intellect, saying: “Beware, Pauline, lest you ever submit yourself to your own thoughts.”

[Col. 0086A] How great a good obedience is, and how great an evil contention and obstinacy are, divine speech teaches us again, where it says through the prophet Samuel: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry.”

Therefore, if you wish to be a good, useful, and peaceful son of the Church, do not entrust yourself to your own judgment. Rather, readily yield to the judgments and sentence of your superiors—indeed, to divine and ecclesiastical authorities—gladly accept them, and submit obediently, so that the Spirit of God may dwell in you. For the Lord says through the Prophet: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

[Col. 0086B] We certainly see the last and most dangerous times foretold long ago by the Apostle, full of ignorance and weakness of mind. In them we must always remember and fear the Lord’s terrifying saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be plunged into the depths of the sea.”

And again: “Woe to the world because of scandals! For it is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to that person through whom the scandal comes!”

We must also beware of itching ears and tongues, lest we be ready and eager either to hear or to speak novelties. For the Apostle condemns both itching ears and profane novelties of speech; and, warning that the oppositions of falsely named knowledge must be avoided, he immediately adds concerning that falsely named knowledge: “Professing it, they fell away from the faith.”

While you were still in the regions of the German kingdom, we first heard a distressing report about your name: namely, that you were sowing novelties and airing foolish and undisciplined questions.

Then a certain writing of yours was also brought to us through the efforts of ecclesiastical men. In it you set out at great length and with complete clarity—indeed, as it seemed to you, also with testimonies from Scripture or the holy Fathers—what you thought or taught, explaining it in many ways.

Now we have also received other substantial writings of yours, which you appear to have written or issued to the bishops—or against the bishops—who were present at the council [Col. 0086D] of your condemnation.

In these writings you carefully attempted, with all the force you could bring to bear, to explain what you held concerning one question alone, namely divine predestination. Thus it has happened that, from both your writings—that which we received through others and that which we received from you—we seem to have learned fully in what dangerous questions your understanding is wavering, or, what is most grievous, being shipwrecked.

Therefore, it seems possible and useful for us to proceed briefly by arranging, from the whole sequence of your writings, those matters that appear most contrary to the Catholic faith into short and distinct chapters, adding or appending to each one what Holy Scripture teaches in opposition, what the Church of God most firmly holds, and what it everywhere teaches faithfully and beneficially.

You must submit to this doctrine and these judgments irrefragably, as a devoted and pious son, if you wish to be found a living and sound member within the unity of her body, rather than, by the judgment of righteous severity, to deserve amputation along with the rotten and dead members.

We have directed this form of our discourse, preserving in all things the legitimate order and ecclesiastical authority, not to you, who through an unhappy and pitiable fall have incurred excommunication from the Church, but principally to our most reverend and beloved metropolitan bishop, your superior. We trust in the Lord’s mercy that, when he reads these things and recognizes our compassionate affection toward you, he will be moved not by any indignation against you but by the heart of a good father and pious shepherd.

Then, when these matters have been read through appropriately and considered calmly with you, if you are willing to submit to the truth with divine grace inspiring you, you will no longer wander from the fold. Rather, carried back upon the shoulders of the good and supreme Shepherd, you will be happily restored to the unity of the sheep that has been found and redeemed, amid the rejoicing of heavenly and earthly beings.

These, then, are the matters in your writings that we have rightly marked as deserving reproof, and reproved, as enemies of the true Catholic faith; and we have briefly indicated how they must be corrected according to the rule of truth.

First, we are greatly displeased that you say and assert that no one redeemed by Christ’s blood can perish.

This statement is opposed to the Catholic faith in two ways. If you affirm that no one from among the number of Christians can perish after once being baptized in Christ and made a participant in Christ’s redemption, you plainly contradict the Apostle, who preaches and solemnly declares: “The unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God.”

For those who have committed this or that crime will not attain the kingdom of God and have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. Among these are also those who deny Christ, concerning whom he himself gives this terrifying testimony: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.”

The same applies to those of fruitless faith, concerning whom he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

It also applies to the foolish virgins who did not take oil in their vessels with their lamps, to whom, when the door of the kingdom has been shut, he will say: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you.”

Or, if you do not believe that all who are regenerated through the grace of baptism with true faith and devotion are redeemed by Christ’s blood—indeed, baptized into Christ’s death and blood—although many of them afterward perish through heresies or various other crimes, this is manifestly contrary to the blessed apostle Paul, who says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

It is likewise contrary to blessed John, who testifies concerning the same Lord: “He loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

It is also contrary to blessed Peter, who speaks of the most wicked heretics who departed from the Church after Christ’s redemption in baptism, saying: “They deny the Lord who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.”

And the Lord himself says through the Prophet concerning those same heretics: “I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me.”

Therefore, according to the Catholic, apostolic, prophetic, and evangelical faith, all these people who faithfully approach Christ’s baptism have certainly been redeemed—not by any other price, but by Christ’s blood. But since many of them have made that same grace ineffectual in themselves and therefore perish eternally, in what sense is it true that no one redeemed by Christ’s blood can perish?

Second, we are greatly displeased that you affirm that the truest and holiest sacraments of the Church—namely, exorcisms, baptism, chrism, the Eucharist, and the laying on of hands—are given perfunctorily and ineffectually to all who perish after receiving them, since you deny that they were redeemed by Christ’s blood, without which the mysteries themselves would have to be regarded as empty and meaningless mockeries.

On the contrary, the Apostle teaches that both the reality of Christ’s redemption and the true effect of the divine mysteries are conferred even upon those who perish irreparably, when he says: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God, etc.”

And again: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified to be polluted [Col. 0088C], and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

And elsewhere: “And the weak brother,” he says, “will perish through your conscience, for whom Christ died!”

Thus the truth of the mysteries accomplishes its power when they are received faithfully, even in those who do not remain in the truth of those same mysteries.

You must also understand correctly that, in that rule for interpreting the Scriptures concerning the true and counterfeit body of Christ—which you attempt to use as though it confirmed this error—the term “counterfeit” refers to life and conduct, not, God forbid, to the divine mysteries and sacraments.

Third, we are greatly displeased that you misuse the testimonies of divine Scripture and the most sincere sayings of the holy Fathers so perversely that you try in many ways to assert from them, though they are wrongly understood, all these points that you argue most clearly against divine truth and the faith of the Fathers.

You go so far as to affirm that those who perish from among the number of the faithful were not incorporated into Christ and the Church—not even when they were first offered by others in infancy, or when, having reached maturity, they themselves faithfully approached to receive the mysteries of regeneration and the Lord’s offering—and that they did not become members of the sheep that was sought and saved; consequently, you say, they were never Christians.

For how is someone a Christian who does not belong to the body of Christ, who is not a member of Christ? On the contrary, the Apostle says that even those who can commit grave sins and perish in that same grave sin are members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit, so long as they act faithfully and innocently.

“Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not.”

And again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him,” and so forth.

Fourth, we are greatly displeased that you think and speak so harshly, undisciplinedly, and savagely about divine predestination in the condemnation of the reprobate that you say all those who will be placed on the left on the day of judgment and condemned with the devil and his angels to eternal fire for their evil merits have been divinely predestined to destruction in such a way that absolutely none of them ever could have been saved and none can be saved.

What else is it to think and say this than to blaspheme God gravely and horribly, if his predestination imposed upon them irrevocably the necessity that they could not at all do anything conducive to their salvation?

But far be it from us to accept this, lest the fault for their condemnation belong to God, who made them such, rather than to them, who could not be otherwise.

Scripture resists this error—or rather, this most savage impiety—when it says of him: “He commanded no one to act impiously, and he gave no one permission to sin.”

And the judge of the living and the dead himself destroys this insane falsehood. He foretold that on that day of judgment he would say to those who stand on the left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

So that he might immediately make perfectly clear why they deserve to depart inseparably from him, why they are accursed, and why they are joined with the devil and his angels in eternal punishment—not because of a prior sentence of predestination, but because of the merit of their wickedness—he adds: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” and so forth.

Here it is plainly shown that they are not condemned because they were unable to perform works of salvation, but because they were unwilling to perform them.

Therefore the Psalmist says of this same righteous and eternal Judge: “For you will repay each person according to his works.” He does not say, “according to his prior sentences,” as this insane and frenzied doctrine attempts to assert, for no other purpose than the subversion of its hearers.

On the contrary, the Catholic faith most firmly holds that not even the devil and his angels were ever predestined to be such. Rather, because they wished through their own fault to be such, the punishments of eternal fire were prepared for them.

For almighty God is not the author of evil merits, nor of evil human beings, nor of evil angels. They themselves are the authors of the evil which they committed by their own will. God, however, is the righteous avenger and judge in those things which they will suffer through his equity.

He therefore eternally foreknew their future evil merits, but his foreknowledge did not impose upon them the necessity of being unable to be otherwise; it merely foresaw that they would not wish to be otherwise.

He predestined perpetual punishments for those wicked angels and reprobate human beings—not because he himself makes them wicked and reprobate, but because he foresaw that they would become wicked and reprobate through their own fault. And if he foresaw that they would become such through their own fault, what wonder is it if, by his just judgment, he predestined them to eternal punishments and fires, so that those who sinned willingly might be punished unwillingly?

Almighty God therefore did not predestine in them the wicked things they were going to do by their own evil will, but the things that he himself was going to ordain concerning them by his most equitable judgment.

For he predestined nothing unjust, but only what was just. He foreknew unjust deeds as God, as future; he predestined them as a just judge to be condemned.

Nor did he impose upon any evil human being or angel, through either his foreknowledge or his predestination, a necessity of acting wickedly, but only the necessity of enduring eternal punishments for evil deeds.

Therefore Scripture most truthfully says to him: “Eternal God, who knows hidden things, who knows all things before they come to be.”

And again concerning him: “For all things were known to the Lord God before they were created; likewise, after completion, he regards all things.”

And elsewhere: “From age to age,” it says, “he regards, and nothing is new in his sight.”

There are indeed some among the evil and those destined for condemnation who could not have been otherwise, such as newborn infants who died under the guilt of original sin, for whom no help could be provided through Christ’s baptism; and likewise those who were ignorant of God, who could not invoke one in whom they had not believed, nor hear without a preacher, nor have a preacher sent to them, because they had merited that none be sent to them.

Yet even in these cases there is no injustice with God, because original sin dragged the former to death, while original sin together with actual sin dragged the latter.

Nevertheless, the Judge himself is just everywhere. From the entire mass of the human race, justly condemned on account of the merit of the first transgression, he makes some vessels of mercy by gratuitous grace, while he permits others to be vessels of wrath by a just judgment.

But if the question is where Scripture speaks of predestination in a negative sense, the actual word itself may perhaps not easily be found used in this sense; nevertheless, the meaning of the word clearly appears in many passages.

Thus, first, concerning the fallen angels, the blessed apostle Jude says: “The angels who did not preserve their principality, but abandoned their dwelling, he has handed over, condemned, to prisons of darkness, to be held for judgment and punishment.”

And the apostle Paul says concerning Antichrist: “And the man of sin, the son of perdition, will be revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

And shortly afterward: “The Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming.”

Concerning Judas the betrayer, the Lord himself, when praying for the apostles, says: “None of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.”

The apostles also say to the Lord, praying about the election of his successor Matthias: “Show which of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas transgressed, so that he might go to his own place.”

There is also the saying spoken through Solomon: “The Lord has made everything for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.”

And what is written in the book of Job: “For the wicked is kept for the day of destruction and is led to the day of wrath.”

And in the Book of Wisdom concerning the Egyptians: “For a necessity worthy of them was leading them to this end.”

And in Jeremiah concerning certain people: “Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and consecrate them for the day of slaughter.”

To such people the prophet Amos also says: “You who are set apart for the day of evil and draw near to the throne of iniquity.”

Likewise, concerning the wicked and sacrilegious sons of Eli, it is said: “They did not listen to the voice of their father, because the Lord wished to kill them.”

And to Amaziah, the transgressing and impious king, the prophet says: “I know,” he says, “that God has determined to kill you, because you have done this evil and, in addition, have not obeyed my counsel.”

All these passages must be weighed faithfully, so that in them the wickedness of evil beings—whether angels or human beings—and the undefiled justice of God who avenges may be recognized.

He preordained and handed over the evil angels to be kept for judgment and punishment, but this was required by their impiety, because they did not preserve the order and honor that they could have had under God and with God.

Judas was foreknown and foretold as the son of perdition, but because of the merit of his impious betrayal he went to his own place—that is, the place destined and prepared for him in punishment—because he had transgressed from the place of ministry [Col. 0091C] and apostleship.

Thus it is no wonder that, because Antichrist was foreknown as the man of sin, he was also foreknown and foretold as the son of perdition.

The evil and impious person is prepared for the evil day and kept for the day of destruction and wrath, but because he will exist as evil and impious of his own accord.

The necessity of divine judgment was also leading the Egyptians to the ruin and destruction prepared for them, but it was a fitting necessity, since it was just on account of their impieties and obstinacy.

Likewise, those who wished to devote themselves like sheep to eternal death—since by their impious hands and words they summoned it—are gathered like a flock of perdition and consecrated, that is, in a certain sense separated, for the evil day and the day of slaughter.

The impious sons of Eli and that impious king Amaziah were also judged unworthy to receive the counsel of their salvation, and God prepared them for slaughter and destruction. But this was just, on account of the merits of the impieties that Scripture first records concerning them: they deserved both to be blinded and to perish.

Scripture also says: “And whoever transgresses from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword.”

He therefore prepared and preordained such a transgressor for the sword—that is, for death and destruction—but justly, because he had voluntarily transgressed from righteousness to sin.

According to this understanding of divine authority, therefore, almighty God by his just judgment predestines punishments for the wicked and predestines the wicked for punishments; yet he predestines no one to be wicked, because the good God is the author not of evil but of good, the just avenger of evil deeds, and, if those who commit evil turn to him, the merciful forgiver.

It should nevertheless be understood that, just as the word “predestination” is less commonly used in Scripture in a negative sense, so it is also used more rarely by the teachers. For this reason, one should by no means contend about it with excessive insistence.

Fifthly, we detest and abhor no less the fact that you have so fiercely risen up against those who are worthy of eternal destruction that you have said they have been predestined to destruction just as irrevocably and immutably as God himself is immutable and unchangeable. You even exhort the bishops to whom you write, as though compassionately, to preach this to the people: since they can no longer escape their condemnation, they should at least supplicate and humble themselves before God to some extent, so that he may mitigate and lighten, however little, the punishments decreed for them. I ask you: where have you ever read this in the sacred Scriptures? Where have you found it among the holy and catholic doctors of the Church? Why do you not similarly exhort the devil and his angels to pray and entreat the Lord now, since they could not escape their appointed condemnation, so that their eternal punishments may become milder and more bearable? Or what more do you leave to these people, whom you assert have likewise been condemned by an irrevocable sentence?

The faith of the Church contradicts this atrocious impiety. It believes that the devil and his angels have fallen irreparably; but it is entirely certain that, even for impious human beings, if they acknowledge their sins, mourn them, confess them, and implore divine mercy, the door of forgiveness is opened. Thus the prophet teaches and exhorts, saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the impious man abandon his way, and the wicked man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is rich in forgiveness.” And again: “Who will walk in darkness, and there is no light for him? Let him hope in the name of the Lord and rely upon his God.” And the Lord himself says: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts.” And elsewhere: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your apostasies.” And again: “The impiety of the impious man will not harm him on whatever day he turns away from his impiety.”

This is the faith and piety of the Church: it knows that the devil will remain in his evils without repentance and will receive no forgiveness; but that, through God’s ineffable goodness, the remedy of repentance is granted to human beings who turn to God, and that access to salvation is not denied them. I ask you: what has the human race done against you? What has the Church done against you? What have so many of your neighbors and brothers within the Church done against you, that you should try to block and bar from them so great and so manifest a door of God’s mercy? What faithful ecclesiastical man has ever preached in such a way that you are not ashamed to insist upon and affirm these things so earnestly and obstinately?

Truly, this harshness is not Christian but pagan—indeed, devilish. If you could properly consider and recognize it, you would certainly seal your heart and put your hand over your mouth. We do indeed read in the Gospel that the blessed John the Evangelist said of the Jews: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart.”

But, as the blessed Augustine faithfully and catholically explains in the fifty-third treatise on this same evangelist [Note: [Col. 0093D] Treatise 53 on John]: “It is said, ‘They could not,’ where it must be understood that they were unwilling, just as it is said of the Lord our God: ‘If we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.’ Of the Almighty it is said, ‘He cannot.’ Therefore, just as the statement that the Lord cannot deny himself is praise of the divine will, so the statement that they could not believe is blame of the human will.” It is not that human beings cannot be changed for the better, but that, as long as they think arrogantly, they cannot believe.

[Col. 0093B] God foreknew this concerning the Jews, who were blinded and hardened, and the prophet spoke of it by God’s Spirit. Therefore, according to the understanding of that most faithful teacher, they could not believe because God truly foresaw their future inability—that is, their proud impiety, by which they despised the Lord’s humility—and the prophet truly foretold it through God’s Spirit.

Let us therefore close our ears against this unheard-of harshness and these words of rashness, and let us hear the aforesaid teacher praying sweetly and arguing sweetly against the profane empty talk of vanity:

“Some,” he says, “have been lifted up into pride by excessive confidence in their own will, while others have been cast down into negligence by excessive distrust of their own will. The former say: Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, when that lies within our power? The latter say: Why do we strive to live well, when that lies within God’s power? O Lord! O Father who are in heaven! Do not lead us into either of these temptations, but deliver us from evil.

“Let us hear the Lord saying: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail,’ lest we suppose that our faith lies within free will in such a way that it does not need divine help. Let us also hear the evangelist saying: ‘He gave them power to become children of God,’ lest we suppose altogether that what we believe is not within our power. Nevertheless, let us recognize his benefits in both matters. For thanks must be given because power has been granted, and prayer must be offered lest weakness succumb.”

Sixthly, we likewise detested the fact that you repeatedly say that God and his saints will exult and rejoice in the destruction of those whom you assert have been predestined to eternal condemnation, whereas Scripture most clearly says the contrary: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.” And elsewhere: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the impious, but that he should turn and live.” And again: “Is the death of the impious my desire, says the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his evil way and live?”

How, then, does he rejoice in the death and condemnation of the impious, when he himself swears that this is not his desire? Or how does he rejoice at anyone’s ruin, when he needs neither anyone’s good nor anyone’s evil in order to become, as it were, more powerful or more blessed? You did indeed produce testimonies from Scripture, as though to fortify your position, but you did so incongruently and not in the sense in which they were placed there.

Such is the statement: “I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you.” And there is the passage which concerns not the general destruction of the impious, as you have presented it, but specifically the misery and calamity of the unbelieving Jews in Deuteronomy: “And just as the Lord rejoiced over you, doing you good and multiplying you, so he will rejoice in destroying and overthrowing you.”

Yet great and devout consideration is needed before one can in any way understand God’s laughter and mockery at the destruction of the lost, and his joy or exultation—not only in the advancement of the upright but also in the overthrow of the wicked. As was shown above, he does not rejoice in anyone’s death or anyone’s destruction, and who swears that he does not will anyone to perish, since he does not desire the destruction of his creature as an enemy of that creature. Rather, in those who perish he loves only the end of wickedness and the order and retribution of justice.

Thus he will laugh and mock at the destruction of the impious and wicked when, humbling and condemning their pride and contempt with a punishment they deserve, he shows that all the vanity and arrogance of the creature against the Creator are worthy of derision and mockery. For this reason the same divine words were put in that form: he did not say “because of your destruction,” but “at your destruction”—that is, not because of those who perished through their own fault, but because, in their just destruction and in the contemplation of rational and blessed creation, the praise and glory of the Creator will increase, with every elect creature exulting—not in the torments of the wretched, but in the equity and truth of the divine judgments.

This is also granted in the present age to the souls of the saints, as the Psalmist says: “The daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord.” It is therefore not because of anyone’s destruction, but because of the justice of divine equity. In this sense the statement can also be understood: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” And the saying in Solomon: “And in the destruction of the impious there will be praise.”

Almighty God rejoices either by doing good to the righteous or by repaying evil to the wicked. This does not mean that he himself is changed and varied by different emotions, for his rejoicing, like his being, is eternal and immutable; with him there is “no change or shadow of alteration.” But just as the Spirit of the Father is said to speak in those whom he makes speak, whom he instructs and forms for the testimony of truth—and is also said to petition for the saints, to groan, and to desire, because he inspires those whom he fills with the disposition to petition, groan, and desire—so he himself rejoices in the saints in whom he deigns to dwell, because he undoubtedly makes them rejoice, whether in the gifts of grace that he bestows upon the godly or in the judgments and acts of equity by which he punishes the impious.

Although, on their account, they are saddened with human feeling, as the Apostle says of himself and as human beings are, nevertheless, under the direction and illumination of the divine Spirit, they do not cease to praise and glorify God’s just judgments. Since, then, the divine words require such great—and ineffably greater—care if they are to be understood at all, they should not easily be brought forward by anyone as though they supported his own case, lest perhaps, when properly examined, they be found to stand against him.

Seventhly, two exceedingly grave evils in your conduct greatly displeased us. The first is that you tear the priests of God and the rulers of the Churches with such insults, reproaches, and curses, and trample them underfoot with such contempt and defiance—having been pitiably deceived by a spirit of error and pride—that you appear to possess absolutely nothing of Christian patience or Christian reverence.

Among other things, you do not fear to call all who resist the zeal of your insane opinions in defense of the faith heretics, and you dare to name them “Rhabbanics,” after the good, learned, and catholic bishop. Nor do you fear God, although through a vain instability of mind and body, and an even vainer curiosity and arrogance, you have fallen into such great snares of the devil. Nor are you ashamed that you have been detected and refuted by everyone everywhere in so many errors and lies. Nor do you grieve that, behold, for so many years you have remained cut off from the body of the Church by a condemnation of just severity and deprived of all fellowship and consolation among the good, like a useless shoot and a dry branch destined for the fire.

Yet, in addition, your mouth is still full of cursing and bitterness. Having been turned into a crooked bow, you shoot—not against the Lord, as you suppose, but against the Church your mother and her prelates, your fathers—contemptuously assailing the Lord with sacrilegious boldness.

The second evil in your conduct is that, in everything you say and think, as your writing makes clear, you never at all entreat anyone, in the manner of good people, piously and humbly; you submit yourself to no one’s judgment or authority. You do not say what piety often does and ought to say:

“I beg you, good man or good brother: if I am in any respect mistaken in what I say, bear with my weakness and instruct my ignorance. You will thereby test my obedience, for I shall be ready willingly to accept whatever Truth deigns to make clear.”

Instead, you trust your own judgment so completely and glory in gazing upon and contemplating truth itself that in your writings you do not even entreat God to reveal to you what is better.

Therefore, I strongly exhort and admonish your fraternity, and persuade you with paternal piety and fraternal charity, to return to yourself, to turn back to your heart, to shake far from you this vain error and this fruitless and destructive labor, and to restore yourself to the holy mother Church; restore yourself to obedience to the Lord and to your priests and fathers; restore yourself to the fraternal charity of all.

Then, although you now lie like a discarded vessel, with God’s grace cooperating you may become in his house a useful vessel, prepared for every good work. Do not be terrified by consideration either of the error into which you have fallen or of the injuries you have inflicted upon God’s priests, lest on this account you find them, as it were, implacable.

We will all pray for you, and they themselves, willingly, for the love of Christ, will forget themselves. Among everyone, both your past errors will be consigned to oblivion and the present good of your conversion will become a cause for joy and exultation. Only do not doubt or delay, but rescue yourself like a doe from the hand and like a bird from the snare of the bird-catcher, lest, overtaken by sudden death in such a condemnation, you leave to the mother Church—whom you now cause continual sorrow—an everlasting mourning, God forbid.

Believe without doubt that I say these things to you out of true and sincere love for you and solely out of concern for your salvation. Do not suppose at all that when I treated certain matters above somewhat more harshly and severely, I did so for your shame or condemnation. Know with absolute certainty that I said them only so that I might place them before your eyes, like a mirror, to be judged truthfully and, with God’s grace assisting, corrected as quickly and diligently as possible. For, as you yourself know well, “the wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.”

Finally, I briefly inform your charity that, within Gaul, nearly in the time of the blessed Pope Leo—or Agapitus—a venerable council highly useful to the Church of God was held by numerous bishops, presided over by the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, a man of admirable holiness and virtues and miracles. There, it is established that a careful definition was made concerning the grace of God and human free will, and concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination: how these matters ought to be understood, held, and taught with the greatest moderation.

Therefore I append these very few words for the instruction of your prudence. They say:

“We also believe, according to the catholic faith, that after receiving the grace of baptism, all who have been baptized can and ought, with Christ’s help and cooperation, to fulfill whatever pertains to the salvation of the soul, if they are willing to labor faithfully. But we not only do not believe that anyone has been predestined to evil by divine power; if there are people who wish to believe such a great evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete detestation.”

[Col. 0097]

TWO SHORT WORKS OF AMULO ON THE SAME SUBJECT, appended to Amulo’s letter to Gottschalk in the Trier manuscript.

FIRST SHORT WORK. A response to someone’s question concerning divine foreknowledge or predestination and free will.

[Col. 0097A] Almighty God, because he is most truly the true and only God, foresaw everything in his eternal and immutable knowledge, before it came to be, as Scripture testifies, saying: “Eternal God, who are the knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be.”

Therefore he undoubtedly foresaw both the good things that the good would do and the evil things that the wicked would commit. In the case of the good, however, he himself acted by his grace so that they would be good; in the case of the wicked, he did not himself make them wicked—God forbid—but merely foresaw that they would become such through their own fault.

For God’s foreknowledge did not impose necessity upon them, so that they could not be otherwise; it merely foresaw, in his omnipotent majesty as God, what they would become by their own will. Thus Scripture, making known to us the unblemished justice of God, says of him: “He commanded no one to act impiously, and he gave no one opportunity to sin.”

Therefore, the impious and wicked are themselves responsible for the impious things they do and for turning the period of this present life, which God gave them for doing good, in the opposite direction toward practicing evil. Consequently, they are rightly condemned by his justice.

The same almighty God also foresaw their eternal condemnation, but on account of the merit of those whom he foresaw would persevere in their own wickedness—not on account of any injustice on his part, God forbid. He has established nothing unjustly, and he repays each person according to his works: eternal good things to those who do good and everlasting evil to those who do evil.

Therefore he entirely foresaw the good, both that they would become good through his grace and that through the same grace they would receive eternal rewards—that is, that they would live well in the present age and be happily rewarded in the age to come. Yet both are gifts of God’s mercy.

For this reason the Apostle calls them vessels of mercy, saying: “That he might show the riches of his grace in vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.”

Conversely, in the case of the wicked, he foresaw both that they would become wicked through their own wickedness and that, through his justice, they would be condemned to eternal punishment. He foresaw this concerning Judas the betrayer, that he would betray him, as the Gospel says: “Though he was one of the twelve”; and he also foresaw his eternal condemnation when he said: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

So also, concerning the impious Jews, he undoubtedly foresaw their future impiety, of which he foretold in the Psalm: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” He also foresaw their subsequent condemnation, concerning which he added in the same Psalm: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.”

But in these people, and in all the wicked, the first belongs to their own depravity, while the second proceeds from divine equity.

The same way must be understood concerning God’s predestination: in the case of the good, he predestined both their future goodness, which he granted through his grace, and their eternal reward for that same goodness, so that by his gift they would become good and by his gift they would be rewarded. Thus the Apostle says: “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him.”

And elsewhere: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.”

He certainly predestined his elect so that, in the present, they might be received through the grace of baptism into the adoption of God’s children, and in the future might be made conformed to the image of the Son of God, renewed and glorified according to his image by that same grace of God.

He predestined them entirely so that they would be good—not from themselves, but from him—and blessed—not through themselves, but through him. In both respects, therefore, he foreknew and predestined the good things that would come to be in them and through them.

In the case of the wicked and impious, however, almighty God did not predestine wickedness and impiety—that is, he did not predestine them to be wicked and impious, unable to be anything else. Rather, those whom he foreknew and foresaw would become wicked and impious through their own fault, he predestined to eternal condemnation by a just judgment.

This was not because they could not be otherwise, but because they did not wish to be otherwise. They themselves therefore became the cause of their own destruction; God, however, is the just judge and the just disposer of that condemnation. He did not predestine anything unjust, but something just.

Yet he predestines crowns for the righteous and punishments for the unjust, because both are just. Commending this justice of his to us, the Apostle says: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? By no means.”

And because he now grants patience to all, so that they may turn to repentance, while those who perish perish through their own contempt and hardness, because they despised such great patience of God, he says again elsewhere: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?”

But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.

Another Scripture also testifies to this, saying: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living; but the impious summon it upon themselves by their hands and words, and, considering it a friend, they turned aside and made agreements with it, because they are worthy to belong to its company.”

Almighty God therefore does not become the cause of death or destruction for any human being. Rather, the impious themselves summon death and destruction upon themselves by their hands and words: by acting wickedly and persuading others to act even more wickedly, they bring condemnation upon themselves and others; by loving the way of iniquity and destruction, they turn aside from the straight path and hasten toward eternal condemnation as though, having given one another their right hands, they were bound by a common agreement in wickedness, as if by a vow and pledge—confederates of death and enemies of eternal life.

According to their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath. On that day of God’s just judgment, since each person receives according to his works, no one is condemned by any prejudgment of God, but according to the merit of his own iniquity.

He did not predestine anyone to be wicked; rather, he truly predestined every wicked person not to remain unpunished. For just as every just law does not command a crime, lest it be unjust, yet punishes the criminal so that it may truly be just, so God predestines punishment for the wicked, not wickedness itself.

Therefore, whoever says that those who perish have been predestined to destruction, so that it could not happen otherwise, must likewise say of the righteous that they are saved because they were predestined to salvation and could not be otherwise.

Whoever says these things so confusedly and foolishly takes away from the former the merit of their condemnation and from the latter the merit of their salvation. What else does he thereby accomplish than to impose upon those who perish a necessity of destruction and upon those who are saved a necessity of salvation? Thus the former would not be justly condemned, since they could not be righteous, nor would the latter be justly rewarded, since they could not be anything other than righteous. In both cases, therefore, destruction and salvation would result not from the judgment of one’s own action but from the prejudgment of divine preordination.

And where would be the statement: “He will repay each person according to his works”? And again: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? By no means.”

For if God predestined those who perish to destruction in such a way that they could not be otherwise, the cause of their destruction is plainly attributed to God. To think or say this is horrible blasphemy.

But the faith of the catholic Church, whose children and followers we ought to be, instructs us to hold firmly what we briefly set out above according to the authority of Holy Scripture: namely, that almighty God foresaw the wickedness of the wicked because it comes from them; he did not predestine it because it does not come from him. He both foresaw their punishment because he is God and predestined it because he is just, so that in them there would be the merit of their condemnation, while in him there would be the power and judgment of a just condemnation.

[Col. 0100A] For God predestines only what he himself will do; but he foreknows many things that he himself will not do, such as all evils, which the wicked certainly do, not he.

The wicked themselves do not perish because they could not be good, but because they did not wish to be good. Through their own fault they have persisted as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and have remained in the mass of condemnation, whether by original or actual merit.

In the case of the good, as has been sufficiently shown above, almighty God both foresaw and predestined that they would be good in the present life through his grace and blessed in the future. For he is the author of both their goods—that is, of their present and future good—and therefore undoubtedly the foreknower and predestiner of both.

Consequently, they themselves not only could have been otherwise, but actually were otherwise before they were made righteous from among the impious by him who justifies the impious.

Whether among those who are saved or among those who perish, it is one’s own will that is rewarded and one’s own will that is condemned. In the former, because it has been healed by the grace of the Lord Savior so that it changed from evil and crooked to good and upright, it is undoubtedly crowned most deservedly. In the latter, because it refuses to receive healing through the Savior, it will most justly receive eternal condemnation from the same judge.

This, in brief, is the whole doctrine concerning free will that must be held according to the truth of the catholic faith: namely, that God created every human being with free will. But because through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned, free will in the whole human race was so vitiated and corrupted by the merit of that transgression, and so blinded and weakened, that it is sufficient for human beings to do evil—that is, to fall into iniquity—and can be free only for that purpose. It cannot rise toward good action—that is, toward the practice of virtue and the fruit of good works—or grow strong in it in any way, unless it is restored, illuminated, and healed through faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, and through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

As the Savior himself promises in the Gospel, saying: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.” And the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

Through this grace of Christ and the Spirit of Christ, human free will, illuminated and healed, may gratefully utter the Psalmist’s words: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

Whoever, then, desires to receive this grace of freedom, so as to become truly free for living well and piously, should not presume upon his own powers, but faithfully entrust himself to him to be healed and strengthened. Of him the same Psalmist says: “The steps of a man will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way.” Let him pray and entreat him, saying: “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.” And again: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth,” and other similar passages.

SECOND SHORT WORK. [Col. 0101] On the grace and foreknowledge of God, and on predestination and free will; also on hope and confidence in salvation, and on the judgment of Saint Augustine.

(This short work follows Amulo’s letter in an old manuscript, without a title and, as it appears, without a beginning.)

[Col. 0101A] We must therefore believe in the grace of God, by which the human race, with no preceding good merits of its own, is saved solely by God’s gratuitous goodness and mercy through the one mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ.

The Lord himself commends this grace in the Gospel, saying: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.” The Apostle also proclaims it, saying: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” And elsewhere: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ.”

He signifies this grace when he says to the faithful: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves. For it is the gift of God.” That is, both things: that you have been saved and that you have been saved through faith; both your salvation and your faith.

Through this grace—that is, through his gratuitous gift—God the Father draws whomever he wishes to his Son. He draws them not by necessity, but by a will and love that delight in him, just as the Son himself said: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

The Son himself also draws these same people to himself, as he says: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.”

Those regenerated in baptism, both infants and adults, receive this grace, as do the faithful every day in every good thought, work, and word. It exhorts by inspiring what is good; it confirms what it has inspired by preserving it. For there is no good in a human being that is not a gift of God.

Through this grace, our daily sins are also forgiven when we humbly confess and implore forgiveness, as the blessed apostle John testifies, saying: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.”

We must also believe in the foreknowledge of God, by which he foresaw everything in his eternal knowledge, and by which all things that are going to happen were foreknown to him—not only the good things that he himself does and rewards in his own people, but also the evil things that he himself does not do, but merely judges and condemns in others.

Therefore Scripture says: “You who know all things before they come to be.” Thus, in that eternal foreknowledge, everything was eternally and immutably foreknown to him exactly as it was entirely going to happen. And because he foresaw it most truly and certainly, it will happen exactly as he foresaw it.

Concerning this foreknowledge the Apostle says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.”

He foreknew those who would believe and those who would not believe; he foreknew those who would persevere in faith and those who would not persevere; he foreknew those who would be in eternal life and those who would burn in eternal fire. Therefore he also foreknew the definite number of his saints.

Thus it is sung mystically in the Psalm: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.” And the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his.”

We must also believe in the predestination and election of the saints: for those whom he foreknew would be saved and liberated by his grace, he predestined—that is, preordained—and elected—that is, separated them from the mass of perdition and the fellowship of the reprobate—so that by his grace they might become vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.

He did not predestine and elect them because he foresaw that they would become righteous through themselves. Rather, he foreknew and predestined them for this purpose: that he might freely justify them by his grace. The Apostle testifies to the whole matter in this way, saying: “For those whom he foreknew and predestined,” and so forth.

God’s foreknowledge and predestination therefore provided this for them: that they would become what they were not—that is, that they would become conformed to the image of his Son—and that they would be called with a calling not merely of an external voice, but also of grace inspiring and assisting inwardly.

This predestination of God is sometimes called God’s purpose, as the Apostle says: “For we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called saints according to his purpose.”

Concerning this purpose and grace, promised and given to the saints before the foundation of the world and before eternal times, he says again: “In hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times, but manifested his word at its proper times.”

And elsewhere: “According to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been manifested through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ.”

Concerning this calling it was said: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance”—that is, without change.

Therefore we must believe that the good of perseverance belongs to the saints not only as a gift, but as a great and especially necessary gift of God. For what benefit is it to have begun to possess these goods and then to lose them before the end of life or at the end of life?

We must also believe that free and upright freedom of the will, naturally implanted in human beings by God from the beginning, was, through the merit of the first transgression, so vitiated, weakened, and corrupted that it cannot rise toward the love of truth and justice unless it is awakened, healed, strengthened, and freed from the defect of its own depravity by Christ’s gift.

For this reason Scripture says: “God created man upright, but he himself became involved in countless questions.” And after this fall of human depravity, the same Scripture says what followed: “For the sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil.”

This weakness of free will, by which the human sense and thought, through the defect of a condemned origin, are inclined and directed toward evil, and by which free will itself is held captive, is healed by that physician alone. He alone liberates, and the liberator restores freedom—the one who says of himself: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”

And again: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

He restores free will by his grace, so that, just as it was inclined and ready toward evil, it may become much more eagerly and delightfully inclined and ready toward good. Concerning this freedom the Apostle says: “But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

Therefore this grace, foreknowledge, predestination, election, and calling, as well as the casting down and restoration of free will, so clearly proclaimed in the Scriptures, must be held by us with the utmost fidelity and firmness. These things are not proclaimed in order to cast the faithful person down from hope and confidence in salvation, or to break him, but so that, with all human pride humbled and every presumption regarding one’s own powers laid aside, each person may submit himself faithfully to God and commend himself to him to be governed, protected by his power, aided by his goodness, and preserved and perfected by his grace. This grace is nothing other than the mercy and kindness of the Redeemer: by his death we are made alive, by his blood we are redeemed, by his righteousness we are acquitted, and by his cross we are saved. Thus there may be accomplished in us, not for despair but for salvation, what the Apostle says: “But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.” And elsewhere: “But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.” Thus he himself may be everything for us, and we may wholly belong to him—not trusting partly in ourselves and partly in him—and each one of us may faithfully say to him with the Psalmist: “I am yours; save me.”

For what does he mean by thinking that he should commend himself to God in such an intimate way as to say, “I am yours,” unless he wished it to be understood that he had wanted to belong to himself to his own harm—which is the first and greatest evil of disobedience? Therefore, as though saying, “I wanted to be mine, and I destroyed myself,” he says, “I am yours; save me.” Indeed, every faithful person, trust firmly in Christ and commit yourself wholly to him, as far as you can. Do not wish to be as though you belonged to yourself and were under your own control; rather, confess that you are the servant of that most merciful and most beneficial Lord. For in this way he will never cease to raise you up to himself, and he will permit nothing to happen to you except what benefits you, even if you do not know it.

For this is the wisdom of God, which speaks and admonishes, saying (Ecclesiasticus 24:24 ff.): “I am the mother of beautiful love and of fear, and of knowledge and of holy hope. In me is all grace of the way and of truth; in me is all hope of life and of virtue. Come to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my offspring. For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Whoever listens to me will not be confounded, and those who work in me will not sin.” For her, the wise man prays, saying (Wisdom 9:10): “Send her from your holy heavens, and from the seat of your greatness, so that she may be with me and labor with me, and that I may know what is acceptable to you.”

Nor should it be thought contradictory that it is sometimes found in the writings of Saint Augustine, and perhaps also of other Catholic teachers, that the impious too were predestined either to eternal condemnation or to eternal destruction. For almighty God did not, by his divine power—as though prejudging them—predestine to evil those whom he foresaw would perish in their sin, whether original or actual, and in their impiety, so that by this very predestination he would compel them to be evil and to arrive at the endurance of eternal evils. Rather, those whom, as the one who foresees all things, he foresaw would become liable to perpetual condemnation, whether through the origin justly condemned in Adam or through their own impiety, he ordained by a just judgment for eternal destruction; and by ordaining them, he certainly predestined them.

But let us now hear blessed Augustine, how he too, after the Apostle the foremost preacher of predestination and grace, urges the faithful to works of piety and perseverance in prayer, so that they may deserve to receive the reward of their calling.

> [Note: [Col. 0103D] Treatise 40 on John, at the end.]
>
> “O, if only the heart were somehow sighing for that ineffable glory! O, if only we felt our pilgrimage in groaning, and did not love the world, and with a devout mind continually knocked at him who called us! Desire is the bosom of the heart: we shall receive, if we extend desire as far as we can. The divine Scripture says this with us; the gathering of peoples says this; the celebration of the sacraments says this; holy baptism says this; the songs of praise to God say this; this discussion of ours says this: that this desire may not merely be sown and sprout, but may also be increased to the measure of such capacity that it may be fit to receive what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.
>
> “But love with me. The person who loves God does not love money very much. I too have felt our weakness. I did not dare to say, ‘He does not love money,’ but, ‘He does not love money very much’—as though money should be loved, but not very much.” O, if only we loved God worthily! We would not love money at all.
>
> “‘Money will be for you an instrument of pilgrimage, not an incitement to greed: something you use for necessity, not something you enjoy for pleasure. Love God, if what you hear and praise has accomplished anything in you. Use the world; do not let the world capture you. You have entered upon a journey. You came to depart, not to remain. You are traveling; this life is an inn. Use money as a traveler at an inn uses a table, a cup, a pitcher, and a bed: he will depart, not remain.
>
> “‘If you are such people, lift up your heart, you who can, and listen to me. If you are such people, you will come to his promises. For the one who called you has a great hand, and it is no great thing for you. He called; let him be invoked. Say to him: “You called us; we invoke you.” Behold, we have heard you calling; hear us invoking you. Lead us to what you promised; complete what you began. Do not abandon your gifts; do not abandon your field. Let your shoots enter the granary.
>
> “‘Temptations abound in the world, but greater is he who made the world. Temptations abound, but the one who places his hope in him in whom there is no failure does not fail.’”

[Col. 0105A]

### The Sayings of Augustine on Predestination and the Grace of God, and on Human Free Will, Collected by Amulo, Bishop of Lyon

*(Bibliotheca veterum Patrum.)* (G)*

[Col. 0105]

### Preface of Jacques Sirmond

[Col. 0105B] This collection of sayings was brought to us by the same old manuscript that recently brought Amulo’s letter to Gottschalk; and, unless our conjecture deceives us, Amulo himself—the author of the letter—is also the author of this Collection. You will immediately recognize, reader, with your customary discernment, the work’s twofold value. First, concerning many and very important matters now under dispute, it will reveal what Augustine thought and taught in Augustine’s own words, as was to be desired. Second, it will draw from Augustine’s words their true and useful meaning, so that we may not listen to bad interpreters.

There are indeed, as there once were, people who ensnare the unwary under Augustine’s name. For Augustine could not have been more cautious or more fortunate than the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, whose words heretics have at times misused to defend their errors. For the rest, let those who wish follow such men—whether they fail to understand Augustine, as did the monks of Hadrumetum, or falsely attribute things to him, as do the predestinarians. We, with Amulo as our guide, shall understand Augustine’s sayings in the sense that most agrees with the Church’s judgments, builds up our faith and confidence, and gives us wholly to God and to divine providence. We reject those who, although far removed from Augustine, nevertheless glory in Augustine’s name and, together with Gottschalk, are not ashamed to call Augustine their own.

### A Second Preface by the Same Sirmond: On How Highly the Sayings of Saint Augustine Ought Properly to Be Valued

[Col. 0105]

[Col. 0105C] Although no one can doubt that the sayings of Saint Augustine ought to be held in great esteem and honor, as the fruit of admirable teaching and of a most wise and illustrious master of the churches of Christ, as Facundus says, nevertheless two kinds of caution must be exercised in their regard, lest deception intrude. First, we must take care lest they deceive us because they have perhaps been wrongly explained; second, we must observe moderation in praising their author.

In former times the monks of Hadrumetum had misunderstood Augustine’s letter to Xystus, and were led almost to believe that he denied human free will—unless Augustine had warned them of their error and disclosed his mind to them in his book *On Grace and Free Will*. Again, when Augustine had written that certain people were predestined to destruction, some interpreted this as though he were saying that they had been predestined to sin. In opposition, Fulgentius, in the first book addressed to Monimus, taught that predestination must be understood as predestination not to iniquity but to punishment.

Our first concern, therefore, must be to investigate in what sense Augustine’s words ought to be understood. The next concern is this: when Augustine’s authority is at issue, we should love Augustine in such a way that we do not listen to those who strive to exalt him beyond what is proper. In doing so, they fail to notice that they will have as their opponent the very man whom they indulge in praising, since, in writing to Saint Jerome in Letter 28, Augustine knew to grant this honor to the writers of the canonical books alone: that he believed they had nowhere erred.

As for himself, he was so far from claiming the same privilege for himself that, in Letter 143 to Marcellinus, he severely rebuked certain admirers of his who thought otherwise about him:

> “But you,” he says, “who love me greatly, if you assert me against those whose malice, ignorance, or understanding finds fault with me, so that you say I have nowhere erred in my writings, you labor in vain. You have undertaken a bad cause, and with me as judge you are easily defeated in it, because it does not please me when my dearest friends consider me to be what I am not.”

### Preface of Amulo

[Col. 0105]

[Col. 0105D] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let every faithful person faithfully read the following sayings of blessed Augustine. We have diligently collected them from his books and, with the help of the same Lord, salutarily arranged them; in this little book we eagerly offer them to be tasted and sweetly chewed over. Thus the devout and simple reader, so as not to be wearied by the great and manifold discussions of the aforesaid Father, or frightened and disturbed by the depth and perplexity of such great questions, may learn in a brief compendium where to build his faith faithfully and how to shape his conduct beneficially.

Let him receive these things as nourishment for salvation and use them as ointments of sweetness, so that through the practice of piety and devout supplication he may increasingly experience each day how truly Scripture speaks to all who faithfully seek and invoke God: “Seek God, and your soul shall live” (Psalm 68). And again: “Seek good, and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord of hosts will be with you, as you have said” (Amos 5). And elsewhere: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (1 Chronicles 16). “Seek the Lord, and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Psalm 104).

Likewise, the Lord himself says elsewhere: “You shall go and pray to me, and I will hear you. You shall seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart, and I shall be found by you, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 29). For, as the Psalmist says, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144).

Far be it from us to think that a teacher of piety drives anyone to hesitation or distrust because, in accordance with the teaching of holy Scripture, he teaches and urges everyone to place hope not in themselves but in God, since it is written: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17); and shortly afterward: “He shall be like a tamarisk in the desert, and he shall not see when good comes” (ibid.).

On the contrary: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence. He shall be like a tree transplanted beside waters, which sends its roots toward moisture” (ibid.), and so forth. Hence it is also sung in the Psalm: “But for me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm 72).

Let us therefore listen faithfully and learn with the greatest diligence, from these very brief and very sweet sayings of the most blessed Father, what ought to be thought and held, according to the most certain rule of the Catholic faith, concerning original sin transmitted from Adam into the whole human race; concerning free will corrupted in Adam and to be healed through Christ; concerning the grace of God by which the human race is saved; concerning the measure of the righteousness of the faithful in this life; concerning the usefulness of correction and exhortation; concerning the predestination, election, and calling of the saints; and concerning the gift of perseverance to the end, by which one reaches the good that has no end.
