We shall also learn how much the life of the faithful is aided before God, progresses, and is strengthened by prayers, almsgiving, and other practices of piety, so that the fallen may be lifted up, the wounded healed, and the crushed raised; so that by asking one may receive, by seeking one may find, and by knocking one may enter; and so that, with God’s grace cooperating, the good fight may be fought, the course completed, the faith kept, the Lord’s coming loved, and the one who has fought lawfully crowned.

Thus, through these things and from these things—which so great a Father necessarily and faithfully teaches concerning such great matters—may the building up of our faith progress, so that the confidence of our hope may grow warm and be kindled, the devotion of our prayer may be stirred, and the discipline of our conduct shaped. For before the almighty Lord, the author of truth and piety, faith does not hinder devotion; rather, devotion is directed and built up by faith, so that the more faithfully someone thinks about him and, by thinking, venerates him, the more readily and effectively he may obtain his grace. Holy Scripture says: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who trust in him” (Wisdom 1).

## The Book Begins

[Col. 0107]

### Chapter One

[Col. 0107C] From the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, addressed to the bishops Eutropius and Paul

[Col. 0107D] **Saying I.** (Chapter 3.) “We have been saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what does a person hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8). Therefore righteousness will be complete when health is complete; health will be complete when love is complete, for love is the fullness of the law. Love, however, will be complete when we see him as he is. For nothing will be added to love when faith has reached vision.

**II.** (Chapter 4.) Through freedom of the will it came about that man was with sin; but the punitive corruption that followed made necessity arise from freedom. Hence the faithful person cries out to God: “Bring me out of my necessities” (Psalm 24). When placed under these necessities, we either cannot understand what we want, or, having understood it, neither wish nor have the strength to accomplish it.

For freedom itself is also promised to believers by the Liberator: “If the Son,” he says, “sets you free, then you shall truly be free” (John 8). For when the will was overcome by the fault into which it had fallen, nature lost its freedom. Hence another Scripture says: “By whatever a person is overcome, by this he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2).

Therefore, just as the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill, so the free do not need a liberator, but slaves do, so that gratitude for freedom may say to him: “You have saved my soul from necessities.” For true freedom is health itself; it would not have been lost if the good will had remained.

But because the will sinned, the harsh necessity of possessing sin followed the sinning will, until the whole infirmity is healed and complete freedom is received. In that freedom, just as the will to live happily must necessarily remain, so there must also be a voluntary and blessed necessity of living well and never sinning.

**III.** (Chapter 5.) The Lord, who completed and abridged his word upon the earth, said that the law and the prophets hang upon two commandments, so that we might understand that whatever else has been divinely commanded finds its end in these two and must be referred to them: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments,” he says, “hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22).

Whatever, therefore, we are forbidden by God’s law to do, and whatever we are commanded to do, we are forbidden and commanded for this purpose: that we may fulfill these two commandments. Perhaps the general prohibition is, “You shall not covet”; and the general command is, “You shall love.”

Hence the Apostle Paul briefly embraced both in one passage. The prohibition is: “Do not be conformed to this age”; the command is: “But be transformed in the newness of your mind” (Romans 12). The former belongs to not coveting, the latter to loving; the former to self-restraint, the latter to righteousness; the former to turning away from evil, the latter to doing good.

By not coveting, we strip off the old nature; by loving, we put on the new. Yet no one can be self-controlled unless God grants it; and the love of God is poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

This takes place day by day in those who progress by willing, believing, and invoking, and who, forgetting what lies behind, stretch forward to what lies ahead. For the law gives this command so that, when a person fails in fulfilling these things, he may not, swollen with pride, exalt himself, but, wearied, flee to grace. Thus the law, terrifying him, may lead him to love Christ in the role of a tutor.

**IV.** (Chapter 8.) Let us run so that we may obtain the prize. For all who run rightly will obtain it—not as in a theatrical contest, where all indeed run but one receives the palm. Let us run by believing, hoping, and desiring. Let us run by chastising the body, and by cheerfully and wholeheartedly giving alms in doing good and forgiving evils; and let us pray that the strength of those who run may be aided. Thus let us hear the commandments of perfection, lest we neglect to run toward the fullness of love.

[Col. 0109D] **V.** (Chapter 10.) Who does not know that, since love is the general command, because love is the end of the commandment and the fullness of the law, what is done by loving rather than by fearing is not burdensome? Those who try to fulfill God’s commandments through fear labor under them. But perfect love casts out fear and makes the burden of the commandment light—not merely failing to press us down with the weight of burdens, but even lifting us up like wings.

Yet, in order to possess this love, even as much as can be possessed in this body of death, the freedom of our will is insufficient unless the grace of God aids us through Jesus Christ our Lord. This love, as must often be said, is poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

Scripture mentions that the divine commandments are not burdensome for no other reason than this: the soul that feels them to be burdensome should understand that it has not yet received the strength by which the Lord’s commandments become what they are commended as being—light and sweet—and it should pray with a groaning of the will to obtain the gift of ease.

For the person who says, “Make my heart blameless,” and, “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118); and, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”; and, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6); and other such prayers, which it would be lengthy to enumerate, is certainly praying that he may do God’s commandments.

They would neither be commanded if our will accomplished nothing in them, nor be prayed for if the will alone were sufficient. They are therefore commended as not burdensome so that the person to whom they are burdensome may understand that he has not yet received the gift by which they are not burdensome, and may not suppose that he fulfills them because he acts in such a way that they are burdensome. For God loves a cheerful giver.

Nevertheless, when he feels them to be burdensome, he should not be broken by despair, but should be compelled to seek, ask, and knock.

**VI.** (Chapter 11.) It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life was said of the Only-Begotten alone; it is another thing to be without complaint, which could be said of many righteous people even in this life. For there is a certain manner of good life concerning which no just complaint can be made even in this human society.

Who could justly complain about a person who wishes evil to no one, faithfully gives counsel to those whom he can help, and, despite another’s injuries, does not retain a desire for vengeance, so that he can truthfully say, “As we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6)? And yet, by the very fact that he truly says, “Forgive as we also forgive,” he declares that he is not without sin.

**VII.** (Ibid.) The person who guards God’s ways does not deviate from them in such a way as to abandon them, but progresses by running in them, even if at times, as a weak person, he stumbles or falters. He progresses by diminishing his sins until he reaches the place where he is without sin. For he cannot otherwise progress in this way except by guarding his ways.

The apostate turns away from the Lord’s commandments and departs from them—not the person who, even though he has sin, does not abandon perseverance in struggling against it, until he reaches the place where no struggle with death remains.

[Col. 0110D] **VIII.** (Chapter 12.) A person keeps himself from every evil thing if he either never consents at all to sin—which is never entirely absent—or, if he is sometimes hard pressed by it, is not overcome by it. He is like a stronger wrestler: even if he is sometimes held, he does not thereby lose the position in which he is found superior.

A person is indeed read of as being without crime; he is read of as being without complaint; but no one is read of as being without sin except the Son of Man, who is also the one and only Son of God.

**IX.** (Chapter 13.) A person will then possess many good things most truly when he has withdrawn from every sin. For then there will be no evils, so that he will not need to say, “Deliver us from evil.”

Nevertheless, even now everyone who progresses while progressing with right intention withdraws from every sin, and is farther from it the nearer he comes to the fullness and perfection of righteousness. For concupiscence itself—which is sin dwelling in our flesh—even though it still remains in mortal members, does not cease to diminish in those who progress.

It is one thing, therefore, to withdraw from every sin that is now present in action; it is another thing to have withdrawn from every sin, which will occur in that perfection then.

**X.** (Chapter 13.) How was it said, “There is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13), unless because that psalm censures a certain people among whom there was no one who did good, since they wished to remain sons of man and not be sons of God, whose grace makes a person good so that he may do good?

Here we must understand that “good” of which it says there: “God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God.” Thus there was no one to do this good—which is to seek God—not even one, among that class of human beings which was predestined to destruction. For upon them God’s foreknowledge looked and pronounced sentence.

**XI.** (Chapter 14.) “No one is good except one, God.” This may be because, although God made all created things very good, compared with the Creator they are not good—in comparison with him they do not even truly exist.

For in the highest and proper sense he said of himself, “I am who I am.” Thus it was said, “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10), just as it was said of John, “He was not the light” (John 1), although the Lord says that he was a lamp, as he says of the disciples to whom he said, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5).

But in comparison with that light which is the true light illuminating every person coming into this world, John was not the light.

Or it may be because even the sons of God, when compared with themselves as they will be in that eternal perfection, are so good that they are still also evil—something I would not dare to say of them. For who would dare to say that those whose father is God are evil, unless the Lord himself said, “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more…” (Matthew 7), and what follows?

When he said, “your father,” he showed that those people were already sons of God, although he did not fail to say that they were still evil. Hence the man who had asked what good he should do was admonished to seek the one by whose grace he was good, for to be good—that is, to be what he is—is proper to the one who is unchangeably good and cannot be evil at all.

**XII.** (Chapter 15.) “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him” (1 John 3). This is accomplished by the will: by believing, hoping, and loving; by chastising the body; by giving alms; by forgiving injuries; by praying insistently; and by asking for the strength to progress, while truthfully saying, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” and, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

This is precisely what is done so that the heart may be cleansed, every sin removed, and whatever the just Judge finds hidden and insufficiently purified when he sits upon the throne may be forgiven by his mercy, so that through living for God it may be restored wholly healthy and clean.

“For judgment without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy.” But mercy triumphs over judgment. If this were not so, what hope would there be? For when the just King sits upon the throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin?

Then, therefore, through his mercy, the righteous, fully and perfectly cleansed, will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun.

**XIII.** (Ibid.) Christ now cleanses the Church by the washing of water in the word, washing away past sins and driving away from her the dominion of evil angels. Then, perfecting her healings, he makes her come to that glorious state in which she has neither spot nor wrinkle.

“For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.” I think this mystery is signified by the saying: “Behold, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13)—that is, I am brought to completion.

He said this in the person of his body, which is the Church, arranging according to distinct and ordered times what he signified by his resurrection in the three-day period.

**XIV.** (Ibid.) A person turns away from sin when, by progressing, he departs from it and is renewed day by day; he should turn himself toward the work of mercy and cleanse his heart from every offense. Let him show mercy, so that what remains may be forgiven.

This is rightly understood, without vain and empty boasting, in what Saint John said: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before the Lord, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him” (1 John 2).

In this passage he seems to have admonished us not to let our heart condemn us during prayer and petition—that is, lest, when we begin to say, “Forgive us as we also forgive,” we should be pierced by remorse because we do not do what we say, or even dare not say what we do not do, and so lose confidence in asking.

**XV.** (Chapter 18.) How is it true that “Everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him” (1 John 3), when, according to the vision and knowledge that will exist in direct sight, no one sees or knows him in this life; but, according to the vision and knowledge that exists in faith, there are many who sin—certainly the apostates themselves, who nevertheless once believed in him—so that it could not be said of any of them, according to the vision and knowledge that still exists in faith, “He has neither seen him nor known him”?

I think it must be understood in this way: the renewal that is to be perfected sees and knows him; but the infirmity that is to be removed neither sees nor knows him. If, amid whatever remnants of this infirmity remain within us, we say, “We have no sin,” we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

**XVI.** (Ibid.) Although through the grace of renewal we are sons of God, nevertheless, because of the remnants of infirmity, what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

Then there will be no sin, because no infirmity, either inward or outward, will remain. Everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy. He sanctifies himself not through himself, but by believing in and invoking the one who sanctifies his saints.

The perfection of this sanctification, which is now progressing and growing day by day, will remove all remnants of infirmity.

**XVII.** (Chapter 19.) We wish to obtain God’s grace or mercy when we say, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” or, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” Why do we ask for these things in prayer with such great groaning if it belongs to the one who wills and runs, rather than to God who shows mercy?

This does not mean that the matter occurs without our will, but that the will does not accomplish what it undertakes unless it is divinely aided. This is the health of faith, which makes us pray, seek so that we may find, ask so that we may receive, and knock so that it may be opened to us.

Whoever argues against this closes the door of God’s mercy against himself. I do not wish to say more about so great a matter, because I entrust it more suitably to the groanings of the faithful than to my own words.

**XVIII.** (Ibid.) Our willing is good when God works in us both to will and to work according to his good will. In Deuteronomy it is written: “He set life and death before man, good and evil, and admonished him to choose life” (Deuteronomy 30).

But this admonition itself comes from mercy, and choosing life would be of no benefit unless God inspired the love by which it is chosen and granted that the chosen life be possessed. Of this it is said: “For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his will” (Psalm 29). It is also said: “If you are willing to keep the commandments, they shall preserve you” (Ecclesiasticus 15).

But he ought to give thanks to God that he willed the commandments, since one abandoned by every light of truth could not will these things. When fire and water are placed before a person, he extends his hand toward whichever he wishes; but the one who calls is higher, and calls more loftily than every human thought.

**XIX.** (Ibid.) The law was established because of transgression until the offspring came to whom the promise had been made. Hence it entered in so that sin might abound; and where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.

That is, the purpose was that man should receive commandments while proudly trusting in his own powers; then, failing in those commandments and becoming a transgressor as well, he would seek a liberator and savior. Thus the fear of the law, having humbled him, would lead him to faith and grace as a tutor.

Thus, after infirmities had multiplied, matters thereafter advanced more rapidly, and Christ came at the fitting time to heal them. The ancient righteous also believed in his grace, aided by that same grace, so that they might rejoice in foreknowing him; and some even foretold that he would come. This occurred either among the people of Israel, as with Moses, Joshua son of Nun, Samuel, and others of that kind; or outside that people, as with Job; or before that people, as with Abraham, Noah, and all the others whom divine Scripture either mentions or leaves unmentioned.

For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, without whose grace no one is freed from condemnation—whether from the condemnation he drew from the one in whom all sinned, or from the condemnation he later added by his own iniquities.

**XX.** It is said, “Be my helper; do not abandon me,” not, of course, for acquiring bodily goods and avoiding bodily evils, but for carrying out and perfecting righteousness. For this reason we say, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

No one is helped unless he himself also does something. He is helped if he invokes, if he believes, if he has been called according to the purpose. This is in accordance with the saying: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

We therefore run as we progress, while our health runs forward in those who progress. A scar too is said to run when a wound is treated well and carefully, so that we may be perfected in every respect and be entirely without any infirmity of sin. God not only wills this, but also brings it about and assists it.

The grace of God through Christ Jesus our Lord accomplishes this with us—not only through commandments, sacraments, and examples, but also through the Holy Spirit, by whom love is secretly poured into our hearts. He intercedes with unutterable groanings until health is perfected in us and God is shown to us as he is to be seen in eternal truth.

**XXI.** Whoever thinks that any human being, or any human beings, has been or is in this life—apart from the one mediator between God and human beings—for whom the remission of sins was not necessary, contradicts divine Scripture, where the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5).

Such a person must also assert through impious contention that there can be human beings who, without Christ the mediator liberating and saving them, are free and saved from sin, although he said: “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9; Luke 12).

XXII. (The same.) Whoever says that, after receiving forgiveness of sins, any human being has lived, or is living, so justly in this flesh that he has no sin whatsoever, contradicts the apostle John, who says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). For he does not say, “We had,” but “We have.” If anyone asserts that this was said of the sin which dwells in our mortal flesh, according to the defect contracted through the will of the first man who sinned, and whose desires the apostle Paul commands us not to obey, but that one does not sin who gives no consent whatever to that same sin dwelling in the flesh, to any evil work, whether in deed, word, or thought, although concupiscence itself is stirred—which has received the name “sin” in another sense because consenting to it is sin, while it is stirred in us against our will—he indeed makes subtle distinctions. But let him consider what is done in the Lord’s Prayer, where we say: “Forgive us our debts.” Unless I am mistaken, there would be no need to say this if we never consented even slightly to the desires of that same sin, whether through a slip of the tongue or through taking pleasure in a thought. In that case we would need to say only: “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” Nor would the apostle James say: “We all offend in many things” (James 3). No one offends unless an evil desire, contrary to the rule of justice, persuades him—whether by deception or by prevailing over him—to desire or avoid something that he ought not to do, say, or think. But plainly, whoever denies that we ought to pray not to enter into temptation—and he denies it who maintains that a human being does not need the help of God’s grace in order not to sin, but that the human will, once it has received the law alone, is sufficient—I have no doubt must be removed from the hearing of all and anathematized by the mouth of all.

## CHAPTER II. From the book *On Nature and Grace*, addressed to Timasius and James

### SENTENCE I. (Chapter 1)

Whoever understands that the righteousness of God is established not in the commandment of the law, by which fear is instilled, but in the help of Christ’s grace, to which alone the fear of the law, like that of a pedagogue, leads beneficially, understands why he is a Christian. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing. [Col. 0115C] But if he did not die for nothing, the ungodly person is justified in him alone, when faith in him who justifies the ungodly is reckoned as righteousness. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his blood.

### II. (Chapter 3)

Human nature was originally created blameless and without any defect. But this human nature, in which each person is born from Adam, already needs a physician, because it is not sound. All the good things it possesses in its formation, life, senses, and mind it has from God Most High, its Creator and Maker. But the defect that darkens and weakens these natural goods, so that it needs illumination and healing, was not contracted from a blameless Maker; rather, it comes from original sin, which was committed through free will. Consequently, this penal nature belongs to the most just punishment.

### III. (The same)

For although we are already a new creation in Christ, we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others were. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in trespasses, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace we have been saved. (Chapter 4.) This grace of Christ, without which neither infants nor adults can be saved, is not paid out according to merits but given freely; for that reason it is called grace. “Being justified,” he says, “freely by his blood” (Romans 3). Therefore those who are not delivered by him—whether because they have not yet been able to hear, because they were unwilling to obey, or because, while they were unable by reason of age to hear, they did not receive the bath of regeneration, which they could have received and through which they would have been saved—are justly condemned, because they are not without sin: either the sin they have drawn from their origin, or the sin they have added through evil conduct. For all have sinned, whether in Adam or in themselves, and lack the glory of God. (Chapter 5.) Therefore the entire mass owes punishment; and if the punishment of condemnation owed by all were repaid to all, it would unquestionably be repaid justly. Those, then, who are delivered from it by grace are called not vessels of their merits but vessels of mercy. And whose mercy is it, if not that of the one who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified? Who, then, could be so utterly and insanely mad as not to give ineffable thanks for the mercy that delivers those whom he willed to deliver, when in no way could he rightly blame the justice that condemns all without exception?

### IV. (Chapter 6)

If we understand the Scriptures, we are not compelled to argue against Christian grace and to say things by which we attempt to show that human nature does not need a physician in infants, because it is sound, and that, in adults, it can be sufficient for itself unto righteousness if it wishes. These things indeed appear to be stated cleverly, but they belong to the wisdom of speech by which the cross of Christ is made void; nor is this the wisdom that descends from above.

### V. (Chapter 12)

In the writings of the New Testament we learn that this is the purpose of the law when it rebukes: that, because of the things done wrongly, one should flee to the grace of the merciful Lord, as though a pedagogue were confining us within the same faith that was afterward revealed. Through that grace, wrongs are forgiven, and with the help of that same grace they are not committed.

### VI. (Chapter 15)

How great is the evil of the human tongue, since it can be tamed by no human being, while even beasts are tamed by human beings? The Apostle did not say this so that we should negligently allow this evil to continue ruling over us, but so that we might ask for the help of divine grace to tame the tongue. For he did not say, “No one can tame the tongue,” but “No human being” (James 3), so that when it is tamed by God’s mercy, God’s help, and God’s grace, we might acknowledge that this is accomplished. Let the soul therefore attempt to tame the tongue, and while attempting it, let it ask for help; let the tongue pray that the tongue may be tamed, with the gift of him who said to his own: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). Thus, by the commandment we are urged to do what, while attempting it and unable by our own strength, we should pray for divine help to accomplish.

### VII. (Chapter 16)

“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, without doubting” (James 1). This is the faith to which the commandments compel us: the law commands, faith obtains.

### VIII. (Chapter 18)

The Lord’s Prayer reminds us that both things must be requested: that our debts be forgiven us, and that we not be brought into temptation. The former is so that past sins may be expiated; the latter so that future sins may be avoided. Although this cannot happen unless the will is present, the will alone is nevertheless not sufficient for it to happen. Therefore prayer is offered to the Lord for this purpose, neither superfluously nor shamelessly. For what is more foolish than to pray that you may not do what lies within your power?

### IX. (Chapter 22)

The light of truth rightly abandons the transgressor of the law; once abandoned, he is blind, and must necessarily offend more, be tormented by falling, and, after being tormented, fail to rise. Thus he hears the voice of the law only so that he may be admonished to implore the grace of the Savior.

### X. (Chapter 23)

The life of the righteous, exercised by troubles, shone more brilliantly; and by overcoming them through patience it obtained greater glory—but with the help of God’s grace, with the help of God’s Spirit, with the help of God’s mercy. It did not exalt itself through proud will, but earned strength through humble confession. For it knew how to say to God: “For you are my patience” (Psalm 70).

### XI. (Chapter 25)

Would that there had been no misery, so that this mercy would not have been necessary! But the sin of iniquity—so much graver because the human being could more easily have avoided sin, since no weakness yet held him—was followed by a most just punishment, so that he might receive within himself the reciprocal payment for his sin, losing the obedience of his body, placed beneath him in a certain sense, which he himself had contemptuously refused to render in the first place to his own Lord. And because we are now born with that same law of sin, which fights against the law of our mind, we ought neither to murmur against God nor argue against a matter that is perfectly evident, but seek and pray for mercy on account of that punishment.

### XII. (Chapter 26)

Just as, for example, a person who limps because of a wound is treated so that, once the previous injury has been healed, his future walking may be straight, so the heavenly physician heals our evils not only so that they may no longer exist, but so that thereafter we may be able to walk rightly. Yet even when sound, we shall be able to do this only with his help.

### XIII. (The same)

When a human physician has healed a person, he leaves him thereafter to be sustained by bodily elements and nourishment, so that the same health may grow strong and persist through suitable support—leaving this to God, who provides these things to those living in the flesh, since even the things the physician applied while treating him belonged to God. For a physician does not heal anyone with things he himself has created, but with the resources of the one who creates everything necessary for the healthy and the diseased. But when God, through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, heals a spiritually sick person or gives life to one who is dead—that is, justifies the ungodly—and brings him to perfect health, that is, to perfect life and righteousness, he does not abandon him, provided that he is not abandoned, so that he may always live piously and justly. For just as the bodily eye, even when entirely sound, cannot see unless aided by the brightness of light, so a human being, even when perfectly justified, cannot live rightly unless divinely aided by eternal light.

### XIV. (Chapter 27)

Because of our will, without which we cannot act well, it can quickly creep into the human mind that whatever it does well is entirely its own, and it may say in its abundance: “I shall never be moved” (Psalm 29). Therefore he who in his favor had bestowed strength upon his beauty turned his face away for a little while, so that the one who had said this might become troubled, because that very pride is to be healed through pains. (Chapter 28.) It is not therefore said to a human being, “You must sin, lest you sin”; rather, it is said: “God withdraws from you for a little the thing over which you are proud, so that you may know that it is not yours but his, and learn not to be proud.”

### XV. (Chapter 30)

The defect through which sin is committed has not yet been healed in every respect. It grew from health that was not rightly used. From this defect, now in poor condition, a person commits many things, whether through weakness or blindness. For this defect we must pray that it may be healed, so that thereafter we may live in perpetual health; we must not be proud, as though a human being were healed by the same power by which he was corrupted.

### XVI. (Chapter 31)

God does not quickly heal pride itself, which lies in wait for the human mind even in right actions. For its healing, the pious soul pleads with tears and great groans that he extend his right hand to those who strive to overcome it, to trample it down, and in a certain sense to crush it; for, as I think, its final shadow will be swallowed up at that noonday. That midday is promised in Scripture: “He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday,” if what was written above is fulfilled: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act” (Psalm 36).

### XVII. (The same)

We too work, but we cooperate with God as he works, because his mercy goes before us. It goes before us so that we may be healed, and follows after us so that, once healed, we may also be strengthened. It goes before us so that we may be called, and follows after us so that we may be glorified. It goes before us so that we may live piously, and follows after us so that we may always live with him; for without him we can do nothing. Both things are written: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58), and: “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 22).

### XVIII. (The same)

Let us reveal our way to the Lord by confession; let us not extol it in self-defense. For if it is not his way but ours, it is unquestionably not straight. Let us reveal it by confessing, because it is not hidden from him, even if we try to conceal it. (Chapter 32.) It is good to confess to the Lord. In this way he will give us what pleases him, if what displeases him in us also displeases us. “He will turn,” as it is written, “our paths away from his way,” and he will make ours what is his, because it is supplied by him to those who believe in him and hope in him, so that he himself may accomplish it.

### XIX. (Chapter 34)

We must not praise the Creator in such a way that we are forced—or, rather, truly compelled—to call the Savior superfluous. Let us therefore honor human nature with worthy praises, and refer those praises to the glory of the Creator. But because he created us, let us be grateful in such a way that, because he heals us, we are not ungrateful. As for our defects, which he heals, let us attribute them not to the divine work but to the human will and to his just punishment. But just as we confess that it was within our power not to approach them, so let us acknowledge that their healing belongs more to his mercy than to our power.

### XX. (Chapter 35)

The examples of certain people whom we read to have sinned were not written, says the person who understands soundly, so that they might lead us to despair of not sinning or somehow provide us with security in sinning. Rather, they were written so that we might learn either the humility of repentance or that salvation should not be despaired of even in such falls. For some, having fallen into sins, perish more completely through despair. They not only neglect the medicine of repentance but become slaves of lust and criminal desires, to fulfill their shameful and wicked longings, as though they would perish if they did not do what lust urges, even though certain condemnation already awaits them. Against this disease, which is exceedingly dangerous and destructive, the recollection of sins is effective—even sins into which righteous and holy people have fallen.

### XXI. (The same)

It is not without reason that even the righteous say in prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6). And after the Lord Christ had explained this same prayer by teaching it, he most truthfully added: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6). Through this daily, spiritual incense, as it were, which is offered before God upon the altar of the heart—a heart that we are admonished to have above—even if one does not live here without sin, one may die without sin, while forgiveness repeatedly wipes away what is repeatedly committed through ignorance or weakness.

### XXII. (Chapter 43)

God, being as good as he is just, made the human being such that he would be capable of being without sin, if he wished. For who does not know that he was made sound and blameless, and established with free will and free power to live justly? But now the subject is the man whom robbers left half-dead on the road. Severely wounded and pierced by grievous injuries, he cannot ascend to the height of righteousness in the way he was able to descend from it; and even if he is already in the inn, he is still being treated. God therefore does not command the impossible; rather, by commanding, he admonishes you both to do what you can and to ask for what you cannot.

### XXIII. (Chapter 44)

The faith that healed the righteous of ancient times is the faith that heals us also: faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Faith in his blood, faith in his death, and faith in his resurrection. “Therefore, having the same spirit of faith, we also believe, and therefore we speak” (1 Corinthians 4).

### XXIV. (Chapter 55)

Leave the man alone; let him cry out what he was crying out. For he desires not merely to be exempt from punishment for past sins through pardon, but also thereafter to be strong and vigorous enough not to sin. In the inner person he delights in the law of God. Yet he sees another law in his members fighting against the law of his mind. He sees that it is present; he does not remember that it was present. He is pressed by what is present, not recalling what is past. Nor does he merely see it fighting against him; he sees it also taking him captive in the law of sin that is in his members—not the law that was there in the past. Hence he cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7). Let him be permitted to pray; let him be permitted to implore the help of the most powerful physician. Why is he opposed? Why is he obstructed? Why is the wretched man forbidden to seek the mercy of Christ?

### XXV. (Chapter 67)

We ask for help when we say: “Do not bring us into temptation.” We would not ask for this help if we believed that resistance were in no way possible. Sin can be avoided, but only with the aid of him who cannot be deceived. For this very thing also belongs to avoiding sin, if we truthfully say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” In the body, too, the harm of disease is guarded against in two ways: so that it does not occur, and so that, if it occurs, it may be healed quickly. To prevent it from occurring, let us guard against it by saying: “Do not bring us into temptation”; to ensure that it is healed quickly, let us guard against it by saying: “Forgive us our debts.”

### XXVI. (The same)

Perhaps people would rightly complain if no human being ever existed who conquered error and lust. But since the one who is present everywhere calls out in many ways through creation serving its Lord, teaches the believer, consoles the one who hopes, exhorts the one who loves, helps the one who strives, and hears the one who pleads, you are not charged with guilt for what you unknowingly fail to know against your will, but for neglecting to seek what you do not know; nor for failing to bind up wounded members, but for despising the one who wishes to heal.

### XXVII. (Chapter 69)

The commandments are very good, if we use them lawfully. For precisely because we firmly believe that God is just and good and could not have commanded the impossible, we are thereby admonished both what we should do in easy matters and what we should ask in difficult ones. For love makes everything easy; to love alone Christ’s burden is light—or love itself is the one burden that is light. In accordance with this it is said: “His commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5). Whoever finds them burdensome should consider that the statement “they are not burdensome” could not have been spoken divinely unless there could be an affection of heart for which they are not burdensome; and he should ask for what he lacks, so that he may fulfill what is commanded.

[Col. 0120D] XXVIII. (The same)

How is it said, “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Psalm 16), unless both statements are true? (Chapter 70.) They are hard for fear, light for love. Thus beginning love is beginning righteousness; advanced love is advanced righteousness; great love is great righteousness; perfect love is perfect righteousness. But love arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith is greatest in this life when life itself is despised for its sake.

## CHAPTER III. From the letters and the book *On Grace and Free Will*, addressed to the monk Valentinus

### SENTENCE I. (Letter 1)

First, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him (John 3). Later, however, as the apostle Paul writes, God will judge the world, when he comes, as the whole Church confesses in the Creed, to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4). If, then, God’s grace does not exist, how does he save the world? And if free will does not exist, how does he judge the world?

### II. (Letter 2)

Only infants, who do not yet have works of their own, whether good or evil, will be condemned on account of original sin alone if the grace of the Savior does not come to their aid through the bath of regeneration. But all the others, who already use free will and have added their own sins to original sin, if they are not rescued by God’s grace from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Christ, will receive judgment according to the merits not only of their origin but also of their own will. The good, too, will obtain a reward according to the merits of their good will; yet they have attained even that good will through God’s grace. Thus what is written will be fulfilled: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (Romans 2).

### III. (The same)

The Catholic faith certainly does not deny free will, whether toward an evil life or toward a good one. Nor does it attribute so much to free will that it can accomplish anything without God’s grace—whether turning from evil to good, making progress in good with perseverance, or reaching eternal good, where it will no longer fear falling away.

### IV. (The same)

Understand what has been commanded to you: “Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways” (Hebrews 12). Understand that, when you do this, the Lord God grants you the ability to do it. You will not turn aside to the right, although you walk in right-hand ways, if you do not trust in your own strength; and he himself will be your strength, making your paths straight and leading your journeys forward in peace. Therefore, whoever says, “My will is sufficient for me to perform good works,” turns aside to the right. But those who think that a good life must be abandoned when they hear God’s grace preached in such a way that it is believed and understood that grace itself makes human wills good when they are evil, and itself also preserves the wills that have become good, turn aside to the left.

### From the book *On Grace and Free Will*

### V. (Chapter 2)

Human pride is accustomed to say: “If I had known, I would have done it; I did not do it because I did not know,” or, “If I knew, I would do it; I do not do it because I do not know.” This excuse is removed from them when a commandment is given or knowledge of how not to sin is made clear. But there are people who even try to excuse themselves on God’s account. To them the apostle James says: “Let no one say when he is tempted, ‘I am being tempted by God.’ For God is not a tempter of evils. Rather, each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence. Then, when concupiscence has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin has been completed, it produces death” (James 1). Likewise, to those wishing to excuse themselves on God’s account, the Book of Solomon’s Proverbs replies: “The folly of a man subverts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Proverbs 19). And the Book of Ecclesiasticus says: “Do not say, ‘It was because of the Lord that I departed,’ for you must not do what he hates. Do not say, ‘He himself led me astray.’ For he has no need of a sinful man. The Lord hates every abomination, and it is not lovable to those who fear him. He himself made him from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel. If you wish, you will keep the commandments and the good faith of the covenant” (Ecclesiasticus 15).

[Col. 0122B] VI. (The same)

No one should blame God in his heart; each person should blame himself when he sins. Nor, when he does anything according to God, should he remove it from his own will. For when he does something willingly, then it should be called a good work; then he should hope for the reward of a good work from him of whom it is said: “He will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2).

### VII. (Chapter 3)

A person who knows sins more seriously than one who does not know. Yet one must not therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance in order to seek an excuse there. It is one thing not to have known, another to have been unwilling to know. For the will is accused in the case of the one of whom it is said: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good” (Psalm 35). But even that ignorance which belongs not to those who are unwilling to know but to those who simply do not know excuses no one so completely that he will not burn in eternal fire, if he did not believe because he had not heard at all what he was to believe—although perhaps he will burn more mildly. For it was not said without reason: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you” (Psalm 78), and what the Apostle says: “When he comes in a flame of fire to inflict vengeance upon those who do not know God” (2 Thessalonians 2).

### VIII. (Chapter 4)

We must beware lest the divine testimonies, when understood in defense of free will, be interpreted in such a way that no place is left for God’s help and grace toward a pious life and good conduct, for which an eternal reward is owed. Otherwise the wretched human being, when living and acting well—or, rather, when he thinks he is living and acting well—may dare to glory in himself rather than in the Lord and place his hope of living rightly in himself, thereby bringing upon himself the curse of the prophet Jeremiah, who says: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, who makes flesh the support of his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17). Since the prophet did not say, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in himself,” someone might think that “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” was said so that no one should place his hope in another human being, but in himself. Therefore, to show that he had admonished a person not to place hope even in himself, after saying, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man,” he immediately added, “who makes flesh the support of his arm.” “Arm” signifies the power to act; by “flesh” human weakness is to be understood. Accordingly, the one who makes flesh the support of his arm is the one who thinks that a fragile and feeble power—that is, a human power—is sufficient for him to act well, and who does not hope for help from the Lord. For this reason he added, “and his heart departs from the Lord.” Let us therefore not place our hope for acting well in a human being, making flesh the support of our arm. Let our heart not depart from the Lord, but let it say to him: “Be my helper; do not forsake me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Psalm 26).

### IX. (Chapter 4)

“Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15). Therefore the victory by which sin is conquered is nothing other than God’s gift, in this struggle helping free will.

### X. (The same)

Let the heavenly teacher say: “Watch and pray that you do not enter into temptation” (Matthew 24). Therefore, each person who fights against his own concupiscence should pray not to enter into temptation—that is, not to be drawn away and enticed by it. He does not enter into temptation if he overcomes evil concupiscence by a good will. Yet the choice of the human will is not sufficient unless victory is granted by the Lord to the one praying not to enter into temptation. What could display God’s grace more clearly than that the thing prayed for is received? For if our Savior had said, “Watch, so that you do not enter into temptation,” he would seem merely to have admonished us. But when he added, “and pray,” it is shown that God helps us not to enter into temptation.

[Col. 0123C] XI. (Chapter 5)

Unless our very turning toward God were also God’s gift, it would not be said to him: “God of hosts, restore us” (Psalm 79); and: “O God, you who turn us, give us life” (Psalm 84); and: “Restore us, O God of our salvation” (Psalm 84); along with other passages of this kind, which it would take too long to enumerate. For what else is coming to Christ than turning toward him by believing? Yet he says: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6).

### XII. (Chapter 6)

God’s grace is shown not to be given according to our merits, since we see it given not only when no good merits precede but even when many evil merits precede—and we see it given every day. But plainly, once it has been given, our good merits also begin to exist, although through it. For if it withdraws itself, a human being falls, not raised upright but hurled headlong by free will. Therefore, even when a person has begun to possess good merits, he ought not to attribute them to himself but to God, to whom it is said: “Be my helper; do not forsake me” (Psalm 26).

### XIII. (The same)

It is necessary for a human being that God’s grace not only justify the ungodly—that is, make the ungodly righteous, when good things are repaid to him for evil things—but also that, once he has been justified by faith, grace should walk with him and that he should lean upon it, lest he fall. For this reason it is written in the Song of Songs concerning the Church herself: “Who is this who ascends, made white, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song of Songs 8). She has been made white, for she could not be white through herself. And by whom has she been made white, if not by the one who says through the prophet: “Though your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isaiah 1)? Once she has been made white, she walks well; but only if she perseveringly leans upon the one by whom she was made white. For this reason Jesus himself, upon whom the whitened one leans, said to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

### XIV. (The same)

God crowns his own gifts, not your merits, if your merits come from yourself and not from him. For if they are such, they are evil, and God does not crown them. But if they are good, they are God’s gifts, because, as the apostle James says: “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1). Hence John, the forerunner of our Lord, says: “A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3). From heaven, certainly—from where the Spirit also came when Jesus ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings.

### XV. (Chapter 8)

Our good life is nothing other than God’s grace. Without doubt, eternal life, which is given in return for a good life, is also God’s grace. It too is given freely, because the good life to which it is given was itself given freely. But that life to which eternal life is given is grace alone. The eternal life given to it, because it is its reward, is grace for grace, as a reward for righteousness.

### XVI. (Chapter 11)

“When by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live”: glorify him, praise him, and give thanks to him, by whose Spirit you are moved so that you are able to do these things and show yourselves to be children of God. (Chapter 12.) For as many as are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Therefore, as many as are led by their own spirit, trusting in their own strength, with only the help of the law added and without the help of grace, are not sons of God.

### XVII. (Chapter 14)

Neither knowledge of the divine law, nor nature, nor the mere forgiveness of sins is that grace which is given through Jesus Christ our Lord. Rather, grace itself makes the law fulfilled and nature liberated, so that sin may not rule.

### XVIII. (The same)

We cannot do what the law commands unless, by asking through faith, we obtain the ability to do it. For if faith belongs only to free will and is not given by God, why do we pray for those who are unwilling to believe, that they may believe? We would certainly do this in vain unless we most rightly believed that almighty God can turn even perverse wills, contrary to faith, toward believing.

### XIX. (Chapter 15)

Let us remember God saying: “Turn and you will live,” while it is said to him: “Turn us, O God.” Let us remember God saying: “Cast all your ungodlinesses away from you,” while he himself justifies the ungodly. Let us remember him himself saying: “Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit,” while he says: “I will give you a new heart, and I will give you a new spirit” (Psalm 84; Ezekiel 18, 36). How, then, does what he says—“Make yourselves”—also mean, “I will give you”? Why does he command, if he himself is going to give? Why does he give, if a human being is going to make? It is because he gives what he commands, while helping the one to whom he commands so that he may do it.

### XX. (Chapter 15)

Free will is always in us, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil, or free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But God’s grace is always good, and through it a person becomes one of good will who was previously of evil will. Through it also the good will itself, which has already begun to exist, is increased and becomes so great that it can fulfill the divine commandments that it wills to fulfill, when it wills them very strongly and perfectly. For this purpose the statement was written: “If you wish, you will keep the commandments” (Ecclesiasticus 15): so that a person who wishes but cannot may recognize that he does not yet truly wish, and may pray to possess as much will as is sufficient to fulfill the commandments. For in this way he is helped to do what is commanded.

### XXI. (Chapter 16)

Who does not know that God would not command what he knew could not be done by a human being? But he commands certain things that we cannot do so that we may learn what we ought to ask of him. This is faith itself: by praying, it obtains what the law commands.

### XXII. (The same)

It is certain that we will keep the commandments if we wish. But because the will is prepared by the Lord, we must ask him to make us will as much as is sufficient for us to do through willing. It is certain that we will when we will. But he makes us will the good, concerning whom I quoted shortly before that the will is prepared by the Lord; concerning him it is said: “The steps of a human being will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Psalm 36); and it is said: “God, who works in you both to will” (Philippians 2). It is certain that we do when we do. But he makes us do, supplying the will with the most effective strength—he who said: “I will cause you to walk in my justifications, and to observe and do my judgments” (Ezekiel 36). When he says, “I will cause you to do,” what else does he say than: “I will take away from you the heart of stone, from which you did not do, and I will give you a heart of flesh, from which you will do”? And what is this except: “I will take away the hard heart, from which you did not do, and I will give you an obedient heart, from which you will do”? He makes us do, to whom a human being says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth” (Psalm 140). For this means: “Cause me to set a guard over my mouth.” The one who said, “I have set a guard over my mouth” (Psalm 38), had already obtained this benefit from God.

XXIII. (Chapter 17.) Almighty God completes by cooperating what he begins by working, since he himself works so that we may will, initiating the process, and then cooperates with those who will, bringing it to completion. Therefore the Apostle says: “I am confident that he who has begun a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.” Thus, in order that we may will, he works without us; but when we will—and will in such a way that we act—he cooperates with us. Nevertheless, without him, whether working so that we may will or cooperating when we will, we can accomplish nothing in the works of piety.

[Col. 0126A] XXIV. (Chapter 18.) Why was it said, “Let us love one another, because love is from God” (1 John IV), unless free will is admonished by the commandment to seek God’s gift? It would indeed be admonished altogether without result unless it first received some measure of love, so that it might seek an addition to itself from which to fulfill what it was commanded. When it says, “Let us love one another,” there is law; when it says, “because love is from God,” there is grace. For the wisdom of God carries law and mercy upon its tongue. Hence it is written in the psalm: “For he who gave the law will also give blessing” (Psalm LXXXIII).

XXV. (Chapter 21.) What is more senseless, and more alien to the very holiness of love, than to confess that knowledge—which, without love, puffs up—is from God, while love—which prevents knowledge from puffing up—is from ourselves? Again, when the Apostle says, “the love of Christ surpassing knowledge” (Ephesians III), what is more insane than to suppose that knowledge, which must be subjected to love, is from God, while love, which surpasses knowledge, is from human beings? True faith and sound doctrine, however, say that both are from God, because it is written: “From his face proceed knowledge and understanding,” and it is written: “Love is from God”; and we read of the spirit of knowledge and piety, and we read of the spirit of power, love, and self-control. Yet the gift of love is greater than that of knowledge. For when knowledge is in a person, love is necessary lest he be puffed up. But love does not envy, does not act wrongly, and is not puffed up.

[Col. 0126C] XXVI. (Chapter 20.) The grace of God does not take away human will; rather, it changes it from evil into good, and, once it has become good, assists it.

XXVII. (Chapter 21.) This must be fixed and immovable in your hearts: there is no injustice with God. Accordingly, when you read in the writings of truth that human beings are led astray by God, or that their minds are blunted or their hearts hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise we shall fall into that saying of Solomon: “The folly of a man perverts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Proverbs XIX).

XXVIII. (Ibid.) Grace is not given according to the merits of human beings; otherwise grace would no longer be grace, because it is called grace precisely because it is given freely.

[Col. 0126D] XXIX. (Chapter 22.) “The law entered in so that the trespass might abound; but where the trespass abounded, grace abounded all the more.” Yet grace brings this about: that those who did evil now do good, not that they persist in evil and suppose that good things ought to be rendered to them. Therefore they should not say, “Let us do evil so that good may come”; rather: “We did evil, and good came; now let us do good, so that in the age to come we may receive good for good, since in this age we have received good for evil.”

XXX. (Chapter 23.) When you hear the Lord saying, “I, the Lord, led that prophet astray” (Ezekiel XIV), and the Apostle saying, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Romans IX), believe that, in the one whom he permits to be led astray or hardened, there were evil merits; but in the one on whom he has mercy, faithfully and without hesitation recognize the grace of God—not rendering evil for evil, but good for evil. Nor should you therefore take free will away from Pharaoh, because in many places God says, “I hardened Pharaoh,” or “I have hardened,” or “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.” For that reason Pharaoh himself did not fail to harden his own heart. This too is read about him, when the dog-fly was removed from Egypt, for Scripture says: “And Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also, and he would not let the people go” (Exodus VIII). Thus God hardened him through just judgment, and Pharaoh himself through free will.

XXXI. (Chapter 23.) Be certain that your labor will not be in vain if, progressing in a good purpose, you persevere to the end. For God, who now does not repay those whom he liberates according to their works, will then repay each person according to his works. God will certainly repay evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good; and good for good, because he is both good and just. He will not repay evil for good, because he is not unjust. Thus he will repay evil for evil—punishment for injustice; he repays good for evil—grace for injustice; and he will repay good for good—grace for grace.

# CHAPTER IV

From the book *On Correction and Grace*, addressed to the aforementioned Valentinus.

## Sentence I. (Chapter 1.)

The Lord not only showed us what evil we should avoid and what good we should do—which is all that the letter of the law can do—but also helps us to avoid evil and do good, which no one can do without the Spirit of grace. If grace is absent, the law is present for the purpose of making people guilty and killing them. Therefore the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” Whoever therefore uses the law properly declares in it what is good and evil; and, not trusting in his own strength, he flees to the grace of God, by whose assistance he avoids evil and does good. But who flees to grace unless the Lord directs a person’s steps and he wills his way? Accordingly, even the desire for the help of grace is the beginning of grace, concerning which that man says: “And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High’” (Psalm LXXVI).

II. (Ibid.) We must confess that we possess free will both for doing evil and for doing good. But in doing evil, each person is free from righteousness and a slave to sin; in doing good, no one can be free unless he has been liberated by the one who said: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VII). Yet this does not mean that, once someone has been freed from the domination of sin, he no longer needs the help of his liberator. Rather, hearing him say, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV), let him himself also say to him: “Be my helper; do not abandon me” (Psalm XXVI), and so forth.

[Col. 0128A] III. (Chapter 2.) Let those who say, “Why are we preached to and commanded to avoid evil and do good, if we do not do this ourselves, but God works in us both the willing and the doing?” not deceive themselves. Rather, if they are children of God, let them understand that they are led by the Spirit of God, so that they may do what must be done; and when they have done it, let them give thanks to the one by whom they are led. For they are led so that they may act, not so that they themselves may do nothing. To this end they are shown what they ought to do: so that, when they do it as it ought to be done—that is, with love and delight in righteousness—they may rejoice that they have received the sweetness the Lord gave, so that his land might yield its fruit. But when they do not act, whether by failing to do anything at all or by acting without love, let them pray to receive what they do not yet possess. For what will they have that they will not receive, or what do they have that they have not received?

IV. (Chapter 3.) The apostles, teachers of the churches, did and commanded everything that ought to be done, rebuked what was not done, and prayed that it might be done. The Apostle commanded, saying: “Let everything you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians XVI). He rebukes them, saying: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded? But you do injustice and defraud, and this against your brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?” (1 Corinthians VI.) Let us also hear him praying: “May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all” (1 Thessalonians III). He commands that love be possessed, rebukes because love is not possessed, and prays that love may abound. O human being, in the commandment recognize what you ought to have; in the rebuke recognize that you do not have it through your own fault; in the prayer recognize from whom you are to receive what you wish to have.

V. (Chapter 5.) What the person who does not wish to be rebuked wants to be done on his behalf, when he says, “Pray for me instead,” is precisely why he must be rebuked: so that he too may act on his own behalf. For that pain by which he is displeased with himself when he feels the sting of correction arouses him to a greater desire for prayer, so that, with God showing mercy and love increasing to assist him, he may cease doing shameful and grievous things and may do things worthy of praise and thanksgiving.

VI. (Ibid.) The usefulness of correction—which is beneficially applied now more, now less, according to the diversity of sins—is beneficial when the heavenly physician looks upon the person. For it accomplishes nothing unless it makes each person repent of his sin. And who gives this except the one who looked upon the apostle Peter while he was denying him and made him weep?

VII. (Ibid.) God can correct whomever he wishes even without anyone’s rebuke, and by the hidden and powerful medicine of his power can bring that person to the salutary grief of repentance. Just as we must not cease praying for those whom we wish to correct—even though, when no human being was praying for Peter, the Lord looked upon him and made him weep over his sin—so correction must not be neglected, although God makes those whom he wishes correct even without being corrected. A person benefits from correction when the one who makes those whom he wishes progress even without correction shows mercy and gives help.

[Col. 0129A] VIII. (Chapter 6.) Let the condemnable [origin] be rebuked, so that from the pain of correction the will for renewal may arise—provided that the person being rebuked is a child of promise. Thus, while the sound of correction resounds and lashes him externally, God works within him by a hidden inspiration, both the willing and the doing. But if someone who has already been renewed and justified falls back by his own will into an evil life, he certainly cannot say, “I did not receive it,” since he lost the grace of God that he had received through his own free will turned toward evil. If, pierced by correction, he groans with salutary remorse and turns to similar good works or even to better ones, then the usefulness of correction is clearly revealed in him. Yet correction through a human being—whether it proceeds from love or not—benefits the person corrected only through God.

IX. (Ibid.) If we say that perseverance, so praiseworthy and blessed, belongs to a human being in such a way that it is not from God, then first of all we nullify what the Lord said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII). For what did he pray for him except perseverance to the end? If this came from one human being to another, it would not need to be requested from God. Furthermore, when the Apostle says, “But we pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians XIII), without doubt he prays to God for their perseverance. For the person who abandons the good does evil; and the person who, instead of turning away from evil, inclines toward it by failing to persevere in the good, certainly does not do nothing evil.

X. (Chapter 7.) Those are elect who have been called according to the purpose—not their own purpose, but God’s, of which he says elsewhere: “That the purpose of God according to election might remain, not from works but from him who calls, it was said to him, ‘The elder will serve the younger’” (Romans IX); and elsewhere: “Not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace” (2 Timothy I).

XI. (Ibid.) “Many are called, but few are elect.” For all who are elect are certainly also called, but not all who are called are consequently elect. Those, therefore, are elect—as has often been said—who are called according to the purpose, and who have also been predestined and foreknown.

XII. (Chapter 12.) If we have been able to learn from the Holy Scriptures that no holy angels will now fall, how much more sublimely have they themselves learned this truth revealed to them? For a blessed life without end and equality with the angels have been promised to us. From this promise we are certain that, when we have entered that life after the judgment, we shall not fall from it. But if the angels themselves do not know this about themselves, we shall be not equal but more blessed than they. The truth, however, promised us equality with them. It is therefore certain that they know by direct vision what we know by faith: namely, that no holy angel will ever fall.

XIII. (Chapter 11.) The only-begotten Son of God, equal and coeternal with the Father, became human for us and was crucified by sinful human beings, without any original or personal sin. Although he rose on the third day, never to die again, he nevertheless endured death for mortals—the one who granted life to the dead—so that, redeemed by his blood and having received so great and such a pledge, they might say: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, how will he not also give us everything with him?” (Romans I.)

XIV. (Ibid.) Christ assumed our nature—that is, the rational soul and human flesh—in a uniquely marvelous, or marvelously unique, assumption, so that, without any preceding merits of his righteousness, the Son of God would be such from the beginning at which he began to be human that he and the Word, who is without beginning, would be one person. No one is so blind through ignorance of so great a matter and of the faith as to dare say that, although the Son of Man was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, he nevertheless merited through free will—by living well and performing good works without sin—to become the Son of God, in opposition to the Gospel, which says: “The Word became flesh” (John I). For where did this occur except in the virgin’s womb, from which Christ’s humanity had its beginning? Likewise, when the Virgin asked how what was announced to her by the angel would happen, the angel answered: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I). “Therefore,” he says—not because of works, which obviously did not yet exist, since he had not yet been born, but because the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her; therefore the holy one who would be born from her would be called the Son of God.

This birth, wholly gratuitous, certainly joined human nature to God and flesh to the Word in the unity of one person. Good works followed this birth; good works did not merit it. Nor was there any fear that, in this ineffable manner, once human nature had been assumed by God the Word into the unity of one person, it might sin through free will, since the assumption itself was such that the human nature assumed by God could admit no movement of an evil will within itself. Through this mediator, God showed that those whom he redeems by his blood he makes thereafter eternally good from evil. He assumed him in such a way that he was never evil, nor was he made good out of evil.

[Col. 0130D] XV. (Ibid.) God did not even will that the first man should exist without his grace, although he left him to his free will, because free will is sufficient for evil but insufficient for good unless it is assisted by the omnipotent Good. If that man had not abandoned this assistance through free will, he would always have been good. This is the first grace given to the first Adam; but the grace in the second Adam is more powerful. The first grace is that by which a person is made capable of possessing righteousness, if he wills. The second therefore has greater power: by it a person is also made to will, and to will so greatly, and to love with such ardor, that the will of the spirit conquers the will of the flesh, which desires contrary things.

Nor was the first grace small, since it also displayed the power of free will: the first man was assisted in such a way that without this assistance he would not remain good, but, if he wished, he could abandon this assistance. The second grace, however, is so much greater that it is little merely for a person to recover through it the liberty he lost; indeed, it is little merely not to be able without it either to grasp the good or to remain in the good, even if he wishes, unless he is also made to will.

Thus God had given the human being a good will—for he had made him in the one who made him upright—and had given him assistance, without which he could not remain in that good will if he wished; but whether he would wish, he left to his free will. Since he did not wish to remain, the fault is certainly his, just as the merit would have been his had he wished to remain. So acted the holy angels: when others fell through free will, they themselves stood by that same free will and merited to receive the fitting reward of this steadfastness, namely, such a fullness of blessedness that they are absolutely certain they will always remain in it.

But if this assistance had been lacking to either an angel or a human being when they were first made—since their nature had not been made such that it could remain without divine assistance, even if it wished—then they would not have fallen through their own fault. The assistance without which they could not remain would have been lacking. Now, however, for those to whom such assistance is lacking, this is already the punishment of sin; while for those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace, not according to debt. Through Jesus Christ our Lord it is given all the more abundantly to those to whom God has been pleased to give it, so that it may not merely be present, without which we cannot remain even if we wish, but may also be so great and of such a kind that we do will.

Through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding to it perseveringly, there comes about in us not only the ability to do what we will, but also the willing of what we are able to do.

XVI. (Chapter 12.) The first freedom of the will was the ability not to sin; the final freedom will be much greater: the inability to sin. The first immortality was the ability not to die; the final immortality will be much greater: the inability to die. The first was the power of perseverance—the ability not to abandon the good; the final will be the blessedness of perseverance—the inability to abandon the good. Surely, because the final goods will be more powerful and better, the first were neither nothing nor insignificant?

XVII. (Chapter 14.) When human beings come or return to the way of righteousness through correction, who works salvation in their hearts except the one who, while one person plants, another waters, and another works in fields or among little trees, gives the growth—God?

XVIII. (Chapter 16.) Grace does not prohibit correction, nor does correction deny grace. Therefore righteousness must be commanded in such a way that the grace of God—by which what is commanded may be done—is sought in faithful prayer. Both must be done in such a way that righteous correction is not neglected. Let all these things be done with love, because love does not commit sin and covers a multitude of sins.

XIX. No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. But if a person possesses any truth or righteousness, it comes from that source for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled as it were by drops from it, we may not fail along the way.

# CHAPTER V

From Sermon 51, an exposition of the Gospel according to John.

## Sentence I.

The Lord, who foreknew the future, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews; he foretold it, however, without causing it.
