For God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows the future sins of human beings. He foreknew their sins—not his own, nor anyone else’s, but theirs. Therefore, if the things he foreknew as theirs are not theirs, he did not truly foreknow them. But because his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, without doubt it is not someone else but those whom God foreknew would sin who commit the sins. The Jews therefore committed the sin: the one who does not delight in sin did not compel them to commit it, but the one from whom nothing is hidden foretold that they would commit it. And so, if they had wished to do not evil but good, they would not have been prevented, and they would have been foreseen as going to do this by the one who knows what each person will do and what will be repaid to him for his work.

II. God foresaw the evil will of the Jews, and the one from whom the future cannot be hidden announced it beforehand through the prophet. “But,” you say, “the prophet gives another cause, not their will.” What cause does the prophet give? “Because God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear; and he blinded their eyes and hardened their heart” (Romans XI). I answer that their will also merited this. For God blinds and hardens in this way by abandoning and not assisting; he can do this by a hidden judgment, though he cannot do it unjustly. Religious piety must preserve this conviction wholly firm and inviolate.

When the Apostle was treating this same exceedingly difficult question, he said: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not!” (Romans IX.) Let it therefore be far from us that there should be injustice with God. Whether he assists, he acts mercifully; or whether he does not assist, he acts justly, because he does everything not rashly but by judgment.

III. If the judgments of the saints are just, how much more just are those of God, who justifies and sanctifies? They are therefore just, but hidden. Accordingly, when questions of this kind arise—why one person is this way and another that way; why one is blinded when God abandons him, while another is enlightened when God assists him—let us not arrogate to ourselves judgment concerning the judgment of so great a judge. Rather, trembling, let us exclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans XI.) Hence it is also said in the psalm: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV).

IV. Let us hear Scripture admonishing and saying: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiasticus III). This is not because these things have been denied to us, since God our teacher says: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Luke VIII). But if, as the Apostle says, we “walk in what we have attained” (Philippians III), God has revealed to us not only what we do not know and ought to know, but also, if we think anything otherwise, that very thing.

We have attained the way of faith; let us hold to it with the greatest perseverance. It leads to the king’s chamber, “in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” We must walk, advance, and grow, so that our hearts may become capable of those things that we cannot now contain. And if the last day finds us advancing, there we shall learn what we could not learn here.

V. No one should defend free will in such a way as to attempt to take away from us the prayer in which we say, “Do not lead us into temptation.” Nor should anyone again deny the freedom of the will and dare to excuse sin. Rather, let us hear the Lord both commanding and assisting: commanding what we ought to do and helping us to fulfill it.

VI. Excessive confidence in their own will lifted some people into pride, while excessive distrust of their own will cast others down into negligence. The former say: “Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, since this lies within our power?” The latter say: “Why do we try to live well, since this lies within God’s power?” O Lord, O Father who are in heaven, do not lead us into either of these temptations, but deliver us from evil.

Let us hear the Lord saying: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII), lest we suppose that our faith lies within free will in such a way that it does not need divine assistance. Let us also hear the evangelist saying: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John III), lest we suppose altogether that what we believe is not within our power. Nevertheless, let us recognize his benefits in both matters. We must give thanks because power has been given, and we must pray lest weakness succumb. This is the faith that works through love, according to the measure the Lord has apportioned to each person, so that whoever boasts may boast not in himself but in the Lord.

VII. All those who think so proudly that they believe so much must be attributed to the powers of their own will that they deny the necessity of divine assistance for living well cannot believe in Christ. The syllables of Christ’s name and the sacraments of Christ accomplish nothing where Christ’s faith is resisted. The faith of Christ is to believe in the one who justifies the ungodly; to believe in the mediator, without whom we are not reconciled to God; to believe in the Savior, who came to seek and save what had perished; to believe in the one who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

Whoever, therefore, ignorant of the righteousness of God by which the ungodly are justified, wishes to establish his own righteousness—by which the proud person is convicted—cannot believe in this righteousness. This is not because human beings cannot be changed for the better, but because, so long as they think such things, they cannot believe. For this reason they are blinded and hardened: because, by denying divine assistance, they are not assisted.

# CHAPTER VI

From the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and likewise *On the Gift of Perseverance*, addressed to Prosper and Hilary.

## Sentence I. (Chapter 10.)

The only difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation for grace, while grace is the gift itself. Thus what the Apostle says—“not from works, lest anyone should boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians II)—is grace. But what follows—“which God prepared so that we might walk in them”—is predestination. Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew the things that he himself was going to do. Hence it is said: “He made the things that are to be” (Isaiah XLV).

He can also foreknow things that he does not do, such as all sins. For although there are some sins that are also punishments of sinners—whence it is said, “God handed them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper” (Romans I)—the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment. Consequently, the predestination of God, which is directed toward the good, is, as I have said, the preparation for grace; while grace is the effect of predestination itself.

II. (Chapter 11.) When the Apostle says, “Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace” (Romans IV), it is astonishing that people prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise. “But,” you say, “God’s will concerning me is uncertain to me.” What then? Is your own will concerning yourself certain to you, and are you not afraid? “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians X). Since both are uncertain, why does a person not entrust his faith, hope, and love to the firmer one?

III. (Chapter 15.) The Savior himself, the mediator himself between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, is also the most glorious light of predestination and grace. For in order that this human being, assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into the unity of person, might be the only-begotten Son of God, what did he merit? What good of his, however small, preceded him so that he might attain this ineffable excellence? By the Word acting and assuming him, the human being, from the moment he began to exist, began to be the only Son of God. That woman conceived the only Son of God by grace. The only Son of God was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary—not through the desire of the flesh, but solely through God’s gift.

Free will existed in him, and existed all the more because he could not serve sin. Thus the very fountain of grace appears to us in our Head, from which, according to the measure of each person, grace spreads through all his members. By that grace every Christian becomes a human being from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that human being became Christ from his beginning; here too, born again from the same Spirit from whom he was born. By the same Spirit forgiveness of sins is effected in us by whom it was effected that he had no sin. God certainly foreknew that he would accomplish these things. This, therefore, is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most clearly in the Holy One of holy ones.

## On the Gift of Perseverance

[Col. 0135A]

IV. (Chapter 1.) Perseverance is a gift of God: by it one perseveres in Christ to the end, the end being the point at which this present life concludes, in which alone there is danger of falling. Therefore, whether a person has received this gift is uncertain so long as he lives this life. For if he falls before he dies, he is certainly said not to have persevered—and this is said most truly. How then can someone who did not persevere be said to have received or possessed perseverance?

V. (Ibid.) If someone possesses self-control and falls from it and becomes uncontrolled, or likewise possesses righteousness, patience, or faith itself, he is rightly said to have had these things and not to have them. For he was self-controlled, righteous, patient, or faithful for as long as he was so; but when he ceased to be so, he is no longer what he was. But how could the person who did not persevere have been persevering, since each person demonstrates that he is persevering by persevering? This person did not do so.

[Col. 0135B] VI. The perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end must in no way be said to have been possessed by someone who did not persevere to the end. Rather, a faithful person of one year—and, if one may imagine anything shorter, one who lived faithfully until he died—possessed this gift more than a person of many years who departed from the stability of faith a short time before death.

VII. (Chapter 2.) When it is prayed by the saints, the prayer called the Lord’s Prayer, because the Lord taught it, is understood to ask for scarcely anything other than perseverance.

[We say: “Hallowed be your name,” not because we wish God to be made holy by our prayers, but because we ask him that his name may be hallowed in us. For by whom is God made holy, when he himself sanctifies? But because he himself said, “Be holy, because I too am holy,” we ask and pray that we who have been sanctified in baptism may persevere in what we began to be. We therefore pray that this sanctification may remain in us. And because our Lord and judge threatens the one whom he has healed and brought to life not to sin, lest something worse happen to him, we make this petition in continual prayers and ask for it day and night: that the sanctification and vivification received from God’s grace may be preserved by his protection.]

When we say, “Your kingdom come,” do we ask anything else except that what we do not doubt will come to all the saints may also come to us? Therefore those who are already holy—what do they pray for except that they may persevere in the holiness given to them? For the kingdom of God will not come in any other way; it is certain that it will come not to others but to those who persevere to the end.

(Chapter 3.) “Your will be done in heaven and on earth,” or, as it is read in most manuscripts and used more frequently by those praying, “as in heaven and on earth.” Most understand this to mean: “As the holy angels do your will, so may we do it”—so that earth may imitate heaven, that is, the human being may imitate the angel, or the unbeliever the believer. However great the holiness with which human beings excel, they are not yet equal to the angels of God; therefore God’s will is not yet done in them as it is in heaven.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” (Chapter 4.) We ask that this bread be given to us daily, lest we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as food for salvation, if some more serious offense intervenes and we are kept from the heavenly bread by being excluded from communion, be separated from the body of Christ.

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” (Chapter 5.) How necessarily, how providently, and how beneficially we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for our sins! While forgiveness is sought from God, the mind of the conscience recalls its own condition. So that no one may please himself as though innocent and perish by exalting himself, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded to pray daily for sins. Thus John too, placing this in his epistle, said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

But when the saints say, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil,” what else do they pray for except that they may persevere in holiness? For once this gift of God has been granted to them—and that it is God’s gift is clearly shown when it is requested from him—no saint fails to hold perseverance in holiness to the end. No one ceases to persevere in the Christian purpose unless he is first led into temptation. If therefore what he asks is granted to him, namely, that he not be led into temptation, then, by God’s gift, he persists in the sanctification he received, also by God’s gift.

VIII. (Chapter 6.) Let people not say that perseverance has been given to anyone until the end has itself arrived and the person to whom it was given has been found to have persevered to the end. We call someone chaste whom we know to be chaste, whether or not he will remain in that chastity; and if he possesses some other divine gift that can be retained and lost, we say that he has it for as long as he has it, and if he loses it, we say that he had it. But perseverance to the end—since no one possesses it except the one who perseveres to the end—many may possess, but no one can lose.

For there is no need to fear that, when a person has persevered to the end, some evil will may arise in him so that he does not persevere to the end. This gift of God can indeed be earnestly sought, but once it has been given, it cannot be lost through obstinate defiance. For when a person perseveres to the end, he can lose neither this gift nor any of the other things that could have been lost before the end.

IX. God commanded that his saints say to him in prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation” (ibid.). Therefore, whoever is heard when asking this is not led into the temptation of defiance, through which he might, or might deserve to, lose the perseverance of holiness. But someone abandons God by his own will, so that he is deservedly abandoned by God—who would deny this? Yet for that very reason we ask not to be led into temptation, so that this may not happen. And if we are heard, it certainly does not happen, because God does not permit it to happen [Col. 0137A]. For he is powerful both to turn wills from evil toward good and to convert and direct those inclined to fall into a course pleasing to him. It is not without reason that one says to him: “God, you will turn us and give us life” (Ps. LXXXIV); it is not without reason that one says: “Do not give me over to moving my foot” (Ps. CXX); it is not without reason that one says: “Do not hand me over, Lord, to the desire of the sinner” (Ps. CXXXIX); and, finally, it is not without reason that one says: “Do not lead us into temptation.” For whoever is not led into temptation is certainly not led into the temptation of his evil will; and whoever is not led into the temptation of his evil will is not led into any temptation at all.

X. (Chapter 6.) We live more securely if we give everything to God, rather than entrusting ourselves partly to him and partly to ourselves. [Col. 0137B] For when we ask not to come into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and frailty. By praying in this way, no one should exalt himself insolently, no one should arrogate anything to himself proudly or presumptuously, and no one should claim as his own the glory either of confession or of suffering, since the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). Thus, when humble and submissive confession comes first, and everything that is humbly requested with fear of God is given wholly to God, it is granted through his own mercy.

XI. (Chapter 7.) After the fall of humanity, God willed that a person’s approach to him belong solely to his grace; nor did he will that a person’s not departing from him belong to anything other than his grace. [Col. 0137C] He placed this grace in the one in whom we obtained our portion, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes all things. Thus, just as he works so that we may approach, so he works so that we may not depart.

XII. (Ibid.) In this matter the Church should by no means seek laborious debates, but should attend to her daily prayers. She prays that unbelievers may believe; therefore God turns them to faith. She prays that believers may persevere; therefore God grants perseverance to the end. God foreknew that he would do these things. This is the predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world.

XIII. (Chapter 16.) Since it is clear that God gives some things even to those who do not pray, such as the beginning of faith, while he has prepared other things only for those who pray, such as perseverance to the end, whoever thinks that he possesses this perseverance from himself does not pray to possess it. We must therefore take care lest, while fearing that exhortation may grow lukewarm, prayer be extinguished and pride kindled.

XIV. (Chapter 17.) God undoubtedly foreknew that he would give his gifts to those to whom he gives them, and prepared them in his foreknowledge. Therefore those whom he predestined, he also called—with that calling which I am often not reluctant to mention, of which it is said: “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. XI). For to arrange in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—the works he would accomplish in the future: this, and nothing else, is to predestine.

[Col. 0138A] XV. (Chapter 21.) It matters how much one errs, in what matters one errs, how readily one corrects oneself, and with what obstinacy one attempts to defend one’s error. A person is a cause for good hope if the final day of this life finds him progressing in such a way that what was lacking to his progress may be added to him, and he may be judged more in need of completion than of punishment.

XVI. (Ibid.) Whoever, as a faithful Catholic, recoils from saying that God’s grace is given according to our merits should not therefore remove faith itself from God’s grace, on the grounds that he obtained mercy so as to become faithful. Accordingly, he should also attribute perseverance to the end to God’s grace, because he obtains the mercy that he daily asks for, namely, not to be led into temptation. Between the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance [Col. 0138B] lie those things by which we live rightly. God therefore foreknew that he would bestow all these things—namely, the beginning of faith and everything else thereafter, up to the end—as his gifts upon those whom he called.

XVII. (Chapter 22.) But should one fear that a person will then despair of himself, when he is shown that his hope must be placed in God, whereas he would not despair if, in the height of his pride and misery, he placed it in himself? (Chapter 23.) And would that those slow of heart and weak—who cannot, or do not yet know how to, understand the Scriptures or their interpretations—might hear, or not hear, our discussions on this question in such a way that they would look more closely at their prayers, which the Church has always had and will have from her beginning until this age comes to an end. For when has prayer not been offered in the Church [Col. 0138C] for unbelievers and her enemies, that they might believe? When has any believer had an unbelieving friend, neighbor, or spouse and not asked the Lord to give that person an obedient mind for the Christian faith? Who has ever failed to pray for himself, that he might remain in the Lord? Or who has ever dared to criticize—even in thought, let alone in speech—a priest invoking the Lord over the faithful when he said, “Grant them, Lord, to persevere in you to the end,” rather than responding to such a blessing with a believing heart and confessing mouth, “Amen”? For what else do the faithful pray in the Lord’s Prayer, especially when they say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” except that they may persevere in holy obedience?

Thus, just as in these prayers, the Church was born, has grown, and continues to grow in this faith: the faith by which it is believed that God’s grace is not given according to the merits of those who receive it. For the Church would not pray that faith be given to unbelievers unless it believed that God turns to himself human wills that have turned away and set themselves against him. Nor would the Church pray that anyone might persevere un deceived and unconquered in faith in Christ amid the world’s temptations unless it believed that the Lord so holds our heart under his power that, although the good which we hold is held by our own will, we nevertheless hold it only if he works in us the will to do so. But if the Church asks these things from him while thinking that they are given to her by herself, then her prayers are not genuine but perfunctory—which may this be far from us. For who would truly groan, desiring to receive [Col. 0139A] from the Lord what he prays for, if he thought that he took it from himself rather than from the Lord?

XVIII. (Chapter 23.) “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself,” says the Apostle, “intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII). What does “the Spirit himself intercedes” mean, except that he causes us to intercede with inexpressible but genuine groanings, because the Spirit is truth? For this is the one of whom he says elsewhere: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV). And here what does “crying” mean except “causing us to cry”? We understand that it is itself also God’s gift that we cry out to God with a sincere heart and spiritually. Those who think that it comes from us, rather than being given to us, so that we may ask, seek, and knock, are therefore deceived. We have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”

XIX. (Ibid.) What the Church asks from the Lord, and has asked ever since she began to exist, God foreknew that he would give to those whom he called, so that he has already given it in that very predestination. The Apostle declares this without ambiguity. Writing to Timothy, he says: “Work together for the Gospel according to the truth of God, who saves us and calls us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been revealed through the coming of our Savior Christ Jesus” (II Tim. II). Let the person who dares to say that the Church once did not possess the truth of this predestination and grace also say that she once did not pray, or did not pray sincerely, either that unbelievers should believe or that believers should persevere. If she has always prayed for these good things, she certainly always believed that they were God’s gifts; nor was it ever lawful for her to deny that they were foreknown by him. Therefore the Church of Christ has never lacked faith in this predestination.

XX. (Chapter 24.) This too is God’s commandment, and obediently to hear this commandment—namely, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I)—is likewise a gift of God. I do not hesitate to say that whoever does not possess this gift possesses whatever else he may have in vain.

XXI. (Ibid.) We pray that God may grant us to understand and confess that, after the immense and ineffable ruin in which we all fell through one person, no one is liberated except by God’s grace; and that this grace is not returned as something owed according to the merits of those who receive it [Col. 0140A], but, as true grace, is freely given without preceding merits.

XXII. (Ibid.) There is no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself. Whoever wishes, as a faithful person, to understand it well should attend to him and find himself in him. I mean the faithful person who believes and confesses that he possesses a true human nature—our nature, that is—although, in a unique manner, it was exalted by the Word of God’s assuming it into the one Son of God, so that the one who assumed it and what he assumed were one person in the Trinity. For the assumption of a human being did not produce a quaternity; rather, the Trinity remained, that assumption ineffably making the truth of one person in God and human being.

For we do not say that Christ is God alone, as the Manichaean heretics do; nor human being alone, as the Photinian heretics do; nor human in such a way that he lacks anything known to belong to human nature—whether a soul, or within the soul a rational mind, or flesh not taken from a woman but made from the Word changed and transformed into flesh. These three points gave rise to three various and distinct false and empty parties among the Apollinarian heretics. Rather, we say that Christ is true God, born from God the Father without any beginning in time, and the same true human being, born from a human mother at the fullness of a definite time. His humanity, by which he is less than the Father, does not diminish anything from his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father. These two together are one Christ, who, according to his divinity, most truly said, “I and the Father are one,” and, according to his humanity, most truly said, “The Father is greater than I” (John X; XIV).

Therefore, the one who made him a just human being from the seed of David—one who would never be unjust—without any merit of a preceding will on his part, himself makes the unjust just without any merit of a preceding will on their part, so that he may be the head and they his members. The one who made him a human being without any preceding merits of his own, without sin either inherited by origin or committed by will that could be forgiven him, himself makes those who believe in him, without any preceding merits of theirs, people whose every sin he forgives. The one who made him such that he never had, and never would have, an evil will himself makes a good will out of an evil will in his members. He therefore predestined both him and us: in him, that he should be our head; and in us, that we should be his body. He foreknew not our future merits, but his own future works.

[Col. 0141]

AMULON’S [Note: [Col. 0141D] Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius published this book under the name of Rabanus Maurus. But many critics, including highly authoritative ones and the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, judged—both from the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts [Col. 0142D] and from the difference in style—that it should be removed from Rabanus and restored to our Amulo. We follow them. See the *Histoire littéraire de la France*. EDITOR.] LETTER, OR BOOK AGAINST THE JEWS, TO KING CHARLES. (G)*

[Col. 0141]

[Col. 0141A] I. How detestable is the Jews’ faithlessness, how harmful their association among Christians is to the faithful, and how dangerous it is to the teachers of the churches is unknown to many—not only to common and plebeian people, but also to nobles and persons of rank, learned and unlearned alike—and especially to those among whom there is no residence or association of the aforementioned unbelievers. Therefore we have considered it necessary briefly to set down in this letter both the religious harm that the Christian people suffer from their intermingling and what divine authority, the venerable institutions of the holy Fathers, and the religious edicts of ancient rulers have commanded to be observed concerning them. We do so so that these matters may reach the knowledge of all who have been entrusted to us in the Lord for governance, or of anyone who may wish and be able to know them, both through us and through your unanimous fraternity and fraternal unanimity. [Col. 0141B]

II. The very necessity of pastoral office strongly compels us to undertake this task diligently, as do the losses of souls, for which, following the Apostle’s example, we ought to burn with zeal for God and, with the Lord’s help, guard them from the snares of the ancient serpent, which always attempts to corrupt the minds of the faithful with the poison of its malice. Thus the Church of the living God, the Bride of the Lamb, may be preserved pure and chaste for her own husband in the sincerity of faith and religion.

As the same Apostle says: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve [Col. 0141C] by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2–3). That this is especially to be feared by us, who in these last and dangerous times have, by the hidden judgment of God, received the governance of the Church, the same Apostle testifies elsewhere and openly announces the danger that threatens, saying: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceptive spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their own conscience seared” (I Tim. IV, 1). Therefore in the Gospel the Lord also terrifies the minds of all the faithful and warns them, saying: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8).

The prophet Isaiah too signifies this time and these most dangerous [Col. 0142A] days, in which, as iniquity abounds, the love of many grows cold, when he says: “On that day the peg that had been fastened in a secure place will be removed; it will be broken, perish, and fall, and what had hung upon it, because the Lord has spoken” (Isa. XXII, 25).

III. First, therefore, we recall this to mind, so that every faithful person may reflect and consider who and what manner of people those are of whom we now speak, and how greatly they must be avoided—namely, faithless and blasphemous Jews. For concerning them the Lord speaks in John’s Apocalypse to the angel, that is, the priest, of the church of Smyrna, saying: “I know your tribulation and your poverty, but you are rich; and you are blasphemed by those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan” [Col. 0142B] (Rev. II, 9). And again he writes to the angel of the church of Philadelphia: “Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not, but lie. Behold, I will make them come and worship before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you” (Rev. III, 9).

The blessed Apostle Paul also says concerning these people—not Jews, as they falsely claim, but a synagogue of Satan—to the Thessalonians: “For you suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, and do not please God and are hostile to all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, and thus continually filling up their sins. But the wrath of God has come upon them at last” (I Thess. II, 14–16).

The blessed John also commands the faithful concerning such people in his Letter, saying: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house and do not say ‘Hail’ to him; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John 10–11). Although some think that this was said only about heretics who have withdrawn from the Church and teach things contrary to the faith of Christ, we must nevertheless consider attentively that the Apostle made no exception, but spoke generally about all who reject Christ’s doctrine: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine,” and so forth.

IV. But if someone objects to us that this expression concerning coming—where it says, “If anyone comes to you”—is ordinarily used in Scripture, in a certain particular sense, of false teachers [Col. 0142D], concerning whom the Lord also says: [Col. 0143A] “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII, 15); and again: [Col. 0143A] “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John X, 8), let him read the book of blessed Augustine entitled *Against Five Heresies*—namely, those of pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians. He will clearly recognize that the Jews are false teachers and are reckoned among the other heretics. For this reason, in every conversation and association, meeting or procession, and kiss—through which many flatter them—they must be avoided as heretics, indeed as worse than heretics.

This is how the Catholic Church judges them to be: during the days of the Lord’s Passion, after heretics and schismatics, and nearly after pagans, she prays for them. [Col. 0143B] In this way she plainly shows that they are worse than heretics and close to pagans. For it is characteristic of heretics to hold some true and some false opinions about the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God; but it is characteristic of Jews to believe everything false about him, since they in no way believe him to be God and still suppose that he is to come merely as a human being of common nature, that is, begotten from a man and a woman. Their confession that there is one God, the creator of all things, is not even something worshipers of idols ordinarily deny.

V. Therefore the venerable Doctor mentioned above, in his book *On True Religion* (Chapter 5), commends and repeatedly emphasizes that four classes of erring people must be avoided in every way within the Christian religion, saying: “Religion is to be sought neither amid the confusion of pagans, nor amid the refuse of heretics, nor amid the languor of schismatics, nor amid the blindness of Jews [Col. 0143C], but only among those who are called Christians, Catholics, and orthodox—that is, guardians of integrity and followers of what is right.”

There, too, showing and teaching that the Church of God must deal with these four classes of people so cautiously and piously that she is not only not corrupted by them but also advances and shines forth toward what is better, he adds (Chapter 6), saying: “For this Catholic Church of God, spread strongly and broadly throughout the whole world, makes use of all who err for her own advancement and for their correction when they are willing to awaken. She uses the Gentiles as material for her work, heretics for testing her doctrine, schismatics as evidence of her stability, and Jews [Col. 0143D] as a comparison that displays her beauty. Thus she invites some and excludes others; leaves some behind and goes before others; yet grants all the power to share in God’s grace, whether they are still to be formed, reformed, gathered again, or admitted.”

And a little later he says again (Chapter 7): “Having therefore rejected all those who neither philosophize within sacred things nor are consecrated within philosophy; those who, whether through perverse opinion or through some hostility, have proudly deviated from the rule and communion of the Catholic Church; and those who have refused to possess the light of their Scriptures and the grace of the spiritual people called the New Testament—whom I have summarized as briefly as I could—we must hold to the Christian religion and communion with that Church which is Catholic, and is called Catholic not only by her own people but also by all her enemies.” [Col. 0144A]

VI. In accordance with these words of the holy Doctor and Father, all these people must be rejected, including and along with them the Jews. The Church of God must use them only in such a way that she herself may advance, they may be corrected, and she may become beautiful by comparison with them—not, God forbid, become defiled by sharing in them. They must be avoided as enemies of God and adversaries of the cross of Christ, concerning whom the Lord Christ himself says: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke II, 23).

The blessed Apostle John taught by examples as well as by words—such as those we quoted above—[Col. 0144B] how carefully the company of these people must be avoided. The blessed Irenaeus, the most ancient bishop of the church of Lyons and glorious martyr, writes in his books about himself and the blessed Polycarp, his disciple (Book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 3), saying:

“Polycarp was not only instructed by the apostles and associated with those who had seen the Lord, but was also appointed by the apostles themselves as bishop of the church of the Smyrnaeans. We too saw him in our early youth—for he lived a very long time and reached an advanced age—and he was noble in his life and still nobler in his death, since he ended his life in martyrdom. Even now there are people who heard from him that John, the Lord’s disciple, had entered a bathhouse at Ephesus to wash and, seeing Cerinthus [Col. 0144C] there, immediately leapt up and departed without bathing, saying: ‘Let us flee from here, lest the bathhouse itself collapse, since Cerinthus, the enemy of truth, is inside.’”

Likewise, when Polycarp once encountered Marcion, who said to him, “Do you recognize us?” he replied, “I recognize you, I recognize you—the firstborn of Satan.”

At that time the apostles and their disciples exercised such caution in religion that they would not tolerate even verbal association with anyone who had deviated from the truth.

If someone should perhaps say in response that Cerinthus was a heretic, not a Jew, let him know that in the time of the apostles there were no heretics except from among Jews and Samaritans, such as Simon and Menander, Ebion and Nicolaus. From the errors of the aforementioned Cerinthus [Col. 0144D] he should also recognize that everything he asserted was Jewish. He preached that our Lord Jesus Christ was merely a human being and had not risen; he said that the flesh ought to be circumcised. After the resurrection, he said, Christ’s kingdom would be earthly and would be established in Jerusalem; human beings would again live in the flesh, subject to desires and vices; the legal festivals would again be celebrated; and fleshly sacrifices would again be slaughtered.

VII. The Gospel too shows how polluted this most wicked generation is and how truly it has become a synagogue of Satan, when the Lord says: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house vacant, swept with brooms, and decorated. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the final condition of that person becomes worse than the first” (Luke XI, 24–26).

So it will happen also to this most wicked generation. Explaining these words of the Lord, blessed Jerome says:

“The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the law, and it traveled through dry places, seeking rest for itself.” Expelled, that is, from the Jews, it traveled through the wilderness of the Gentiles. When the Gentiles later believed in the Lord, the spirit, finding no place among the nations, said: “I will return [Col. 0145A] to my former house from which I came; I will have the Jews whom I had previously abandoned.” And when it came, it found the house vacant [Col. 0145B], swept with brooms. The temple of the Jews was vacant, for it did not have Christ as its guest, who said: “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV, 31). And elsewhere: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII, 35).

Because they had neither the protection of God nor that of the angels, and because they were decorated with the superfluous observances of the law and the traditions of the Pharisees, the devil returned to his former dwelling. Adding to himself a sevenfold number of demons, he inhabits his former house, and its final condition becomes worse than its first. For they are now possessed by a far greater number of demons, blaspheming Christ Jesus in their synagogues, than they had been possessed in Egypt before they knew the law.

“Concerning these blasphemies of theirs—not only against the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0145C] but also against his Church—the same Doctor, in his exposition of the prophet Amos, when explaining the words, ‘And he retained his fury and kept his indignation to the end’ (Amos I, 2), says:

“‘Holding their ancient fury and anger to this day in their synagogues, under the name of Nazarenes they blaspheme the Christian people.’

“Again, when explaining in the same prophet the words of the Lord by which he condemns the psalms and songs that they seem to sing in the synagogues of Satan—‘Take away from me the noise of your songs, and I will not hear the songs of your lyre’ (Amos V, 23)—the aforementioned Doctor, joining them with heretics, speaks as follows:

“‘The tradition of the Jews also, and the psalms they sing in their synagogues, and the composed praise of heretics, are noise [Col. 0145D] to the Lord and, so to speak, the grunting of swine and the braying of donkeys.’”

VIII. The same Doctor also teaches us by his own example with what hatred and execration such blasphemers of Christ and his Church must be abominated. In one place he says: “If it is appropriate to hate human beings and detest some nation, I turn away from circumcision with extraordinary hatred, for to this day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan.”

Elsewhere as well (Letter 151, Question 10): “The many traditions of the Pharisees, which they now call *deuterōseis* (δευτερώσεις, ‘second teachings’), and how animal-like their fables are, I cannot bring myself to recount; for many of them are so shameful that I blush to speak of them.”

In his exposition of Isaiah (on Chapter VIII) [Col. 0146A], when explaining the passage in which the Lord is foretold as “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the two houses of Israel,” he also explains in these words who the first authors of such fables and doctrines were, when they began among the Jews, and through what succession of schools they reached the final captivity:

“‘The Nazarenes, who receive Christ in such a way that they do not abandon the observances of the ancient law, interpret the two houses as Shammai and Hillel. From them arose the scribes and Pharisees. Their school was taken up by Akiba, after him by Mehir, who was succeeded by Johanan son of Zacchaeus, and after him by Eliezer, and in order by Telphon, then again by Joseph the Galilean, and finally by Joshua up to the captivity of Jerusalem.

“‘Shammai and Hillel [Col. 0146B] therefore arose in Judaea not long before the Lord was born. The former’s name means “destroyer,” and the latter’s “profane,” because through their traditions (*deuterōseis*) they destroyed and polluted the commandments of the law. These are the two houses that did not receive the Savior, who became their ruin and their scandal.’”

IX. Such were the teachers of the scribes and Pharisees, teachers of fables and superstitions. The Lord frequently rebukes them in the Gospel, especially when he destroys all their errors with one prophetic testimony, saying: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition?” (Matt. XV, 3.) And shortly afterward: [Col. 0146C] “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: ‘This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of human beings’” (ibid., verses 7–9).

Thus these blind and faithless Jews, followers of those perverse and impious teachers, have abandoned the truth of the law and the prophets and to this day observe traditions and follow errors. They are especially occupied with reading these things; they discuss them among themselves; and every Sabbath they do not cease to preach them in the synagogues of Satan. If they attempt to understand anything from the books of the divine law, they corrupt it according to their blindness and have miserably closed the door of truth against themselves. What their Lord reproaches these same teachers—or rather, destroyers—in the Gospel has been most clearly fulfilled in them: [Col. 0146D] “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke XI, 52).

X. Finally, let your religious holiness listen for a little while to how they mock and ridicule our Lord Jesus Christ and his Christian people with unspeakable and unheard-of blasphemies and insults. They impiously alter the name of the holy apostles and call them *apostates*, as though they had not been sent by God but were deserters from their own law.

The Gospel—which in Greek speech we understand to mean “good news”—they most maliciously alter in their own language and call *HAVONGALION*, which in Latin means “the revelation of iniquity.” They assert, [Col. 0147A] evidently, that not the mystery of human salvation but the iniquity by which the whole world would be sent into error had been revealed in it. In their madness they do not realize that this word, which they themselves have fabricated, is also an entirely clear testimony to their iniquity, just as it is written concerning the wicked person in the Book of Job (Chapter XX): “The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. The offspring of his house will be exposed; it will be stripped away on the day of fury.”

They have become so inflamed with hatred of the Lord Jesus Christ that from East to West, through all the regions overseas and on this side of the sea where Jews live, they sent commands that they should in no way chant in their synagogues the nineteenth psalm, which, under the appearance of a prayer, is written entirely about the most manifest coming of the Savior.

[Col. 0147B] They feared, evidently, that by saying—as it is sung there—“May the Lord answer you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you” (Ps. XIX, 2), and the other words that follow, and then adding with absolute certainty concerning him, “Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ. He will answer him from his holy heaven; salvation is in the mighty deeds of his right hand” (verse 7), and at the end of the psalm, “Lord, save the king and answer us on the day when we call upon you” (verse 10), they might appear, by saying these things, to bless and wish well to one who was present.

They therefore removed the psalm, which for so many ages had been sung daily among the others in the synagogue’s assembly, and decided that it must be silenced in every way until the coming of their Christ. In this matter too they fulfilled [Col. 0147C] in the wretched people what the Lord had reproached them for so long beforehand through the prophet Micah (Chapter II), saying: “You have turned those who passed by peaceably into war; you have driven the women of my people from their pleasant homes; from their little ones you have taken away my praise forever.”

But in doing these things and kicking, as it were, against the goad, they added to the wound of impiety in themselves.

XI. But could they abolish the prophecy of the psalm or the presence of Christ? We see him so clearly manifested among the nations that what God the Father says to the Lord Savior himself through the prophet Isaiah has been most truly fulfilled: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isa. XLIX, 6). The same prophet again says: [Col. 0147D] “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God” (ibid., LII, 10). And through the prophet Malachi the Lord testifies, saying: “For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is presented to my name” (Mal. I, 11).

Concerning this offering—which is certainly the precious passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, who loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance—in the aforementioned psalm it is said to him concerning God the Father: “May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering be made rich” (Ps. XIX, 4).

[Col. 0148A] **XII.** As time went on, and errors continually increased through the teachers of impiety, they became so blinded that they invented for themselves, from their own imagination, two messiahs—that is, two Christs. One of them, they say, exists in accordance with God’s promise, from the lineage of David. They maintain that he was born in Judea on the night when the house of God at Jerusalem was destroyed under Vespasian and Titus, and that, by some means unknown to me, he was brought to Rome; that there, down to the present day, he has been confined in hidden caves and underground chambers; and that in such a prison he is bound with iron, weighed down with chains, and wounded over his entire body.

They trust that through these wounds they possess forgiveness of sins, and that what Isaiah said (in chapter LIII) is fulfilled in them: “And in his wound there shall be healing for us.” They also have it written in their traditions that this particular messiah once showed himself to one of their great teachers, named Joshua ben Levi. He first appeared in filthy clothing. When Joshua, not knowing who he was, rebuked him for walking about so unwashed and neglected, he suddenly changed into another appearance and appeared like a handsome old man, holding in his hand a precious sapphire stone. When Joshua marvelled at this and asked who he was, he replied: “I am the messiah, who endure many sufferings for you, and I shall redeem you from captivity; and all of you shall receive a sapphire stone such as you see me holding.”

Then, he said, what is written in Isaiah would be fulfilled in them: “Poor woman, storm-tossed, without any consolation: behold, I shall set your stones in order, and lay your foundations in sapphires; and I shall make your battlements of jasper, your gates of carved stones, and all your boundaries of desirable stones” (Isa. LIV, 11–12).

They therefore hope that such a messiah will come at the end of time to gather them from captivity—for this alone, like the most wretched slaves, do they know how to long. He will come in the clouds of heaven, as though the prophet Daniel had spoken of him: “I was watching in a vision, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming” (Dan. VII, 13), and so forth. They call him the messiah Ben David, that is, the son of David.

**XIII.** But they say that the second messiah is from the tribe of Ephraim, and therefore they call him [Col. 0148D] the messiah Ben Ephraim, that is, the son of Ephraim. Their teachers dreamed this up solely from the circumstance that it is written in Jeremiah, where the Lord says: “For I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn” (Jer. XXXI, 9).

They hope that, after their return from captivity, when the fiercest nations—Gog and Magog—come against them for war, he will go out to fight them; that he will be killed in that same war and mourned bitterly by the entire Jewish people. They say that this is what is written in the prophet Zechariah: “And they shall look upon him whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with a mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn; and the families of the land shall mourn, each family separately, and their women separately” (Zach. XII, 10–12), and so forth.

Their impiety has advanced so far that they have even tried to falsify prophetic Scripture. Where we read—as it has stood in the Hebrew language from the beginning—that God speaks in the first person: “And I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer; and they shall look upon me whom they pierced” (ibid.), the Prophet immediately makes clear that the one speaking these things about himself is God, adding: “And they shall mourn for him with a mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn”—for this one is God.

**XIV. Answer of the truth against the aforementioned Jewish error** [Col. 0149B]

The one who says that he will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer—and not upon others, as these madmen deliriously claim—immediately adds, speaking of those same inhabitants of Jerusalem: “And they shall look upon me whom they pierced.” The only-begotten and firstborn of God the Father is the one of whom it is written in the Gospel: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I, 14). The Apostle also says: “So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII, 29). And it is written in the Apocalypse: “The firstborn of the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Apoc. I, 5). And in the Psalm: “And I shall make him firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 28).

[Col. 0149C] Thus, in these prophetic statements, the mystery of Christ is comprehended both briefly and completely: the one who was pierced and transfixed by the impious is shown to be God, the only-begotten, and the firstborn.

Where we, in accordance with the faith of Holy Scripture, read God speaking in the first person, “And they shall look upon me whom they pierced,” they, although they did not dare to alter the text of the book itself—restrained by divine providence—nevertheless have written externally, in the margin, as we have stated above: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” They pass this on to their disciples, so that they copy it as it stands in the text but read it as it is written outside the text. Thus, according to their madness, they may maintain that the Jews will look upon him whom Gog and Magog pierced, although this passage makes no mention whatsoever of those nations. Rather, it mentions above the inhabitants of Jerusalem, concerning whom God plainly says: “And they shall look upon me whom they pierced.” Of these same people it immediately adds: “And the families of the land shall mourn, each family separately”—that is, the families of the house of David, the house of Nathan, the house of Levi, the house of Shimei, and all the others—so that it may be understood that those who pierced him will themselves mourn for so great a crime.

This may refer either to the first coming, after the Lord’s passion, when, at the preaching of the apostles, they were pierced in heart and said sorrowfully, “Men, brothers, what shall we do?” (Acts II, 37–38), and immediately received the counsel that led to salvation, when Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ”; or to the second coming, when the Lord comes for judgment, they will see in him the wounds they inflicted and will recognize that they are to be condemned for so great an impiety.

Then will be fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Matt. XXIV, 30). Hence blessed John also testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes; amen” (Apoc. I, 7).

**XV.** Thus these wretched people, unable to endure sound doctrine but accumulating teachers for themselves according to their own desires, with itching ears, have turned away from the truth and turned to fables. While they refuse to accept the one true Christ, whose coming is shown most clearly already to have taken place from the Law and the Prophets, they have fashioned for themselves two false christs from the evil treasure of their hearts. In this way they have wholly prepared themselves for the illusions of Antichrist.

For where in the prophetic Scriptures was it ever heard that, as they say, Christ would be born at the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple? On the contrary, while the Temple and the city still stood, God promised his coming through the prophet Malachi, saying: “Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and immediately the Ruler whom you seek will come to his Temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III, 1).

And not only his coming but also his passion, which would take place before the destruction of the city and the Temple, was announced by the angel Gabriel through the prophet Daniel, saying: “And after sixty-two weeks Christ will be killed, and his people, who will deny him, will not be his. And the people, together with the leader who is to come, will destroy the city and the sanctuary. And its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed” (Dan. IX, 26).

These words clearly show that not only did Christ’s coming and passion precede the devastation of the city and the Temple, but that the overthrow itself immediately followed on account of the passion and death which they impiously inflicted upon him. They lost Christ the ruler concerning whom it had been promised through the prophet Micah: “From you a ruler will go forth, who will govern my people Israel” (Mic. V). Rightly, therefore, they are not his people, since they denied and killed him.

For this crime they were handed over to eternal captivity. Although they promise themselves liberation from it, the Prophet plainly confirms that “its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed; and desolation will continue until the consummation and the end” (Dan. IX, 27).

**XVI.** The prophet Jeremiah likewise bears witness to this. At the Lord’s command, he threw an earthen potter’s vessel before their eyes and broke it, saying: “Thus says the Lord: In this way I shall crush this city and this people, as a potter’s vessel is crushed and can no longer be restored” (Jer. XIX, 11).

The Lord also threatens them in the same way through the prophet Hosea, saying: “Because of the wickedness of their inventions, I shall drive them out of my house. I shall no longer continue to love them” (Hos. IX, 15). And again: “My people will await my return, but a yoke will be imposed upon it at once, and it will not be removed” (ibid. XI, 7).

Moreover, through the prophet Malachi, at the coming of Elijah, he promises them not a release from captivity, not a return to the land of Judea, and not a restoration of the city, the Temple, and the legal ceremonies, but salvation alone and the grace of faith alone. The Lord says: “Behold, I shall send you Elijah the Tishbite, and he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to their fathers” (Mal. IV, 5–6).

That is, the hearts of these carnal children, now separated by their unbelief from the faith of their ancient fathers, will then, when so great a prophet preaches and God turns them, be joined to the faith of their fathers. In accordance with the Apostle (Rom. XI, 24), branches broken off because of unbelief will, through the goodness of God, be grafted into their own olive tree.

Likewise, in the prophet Hosea, after all those days during which—as was foretold—the children of Israel sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an ephod, and without teraphim, only the seeking and finding of God and his Christ is promised to them for salvation. The Lord says through the same prophet: “After this the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the last days” (Hos. III, 5).

Accordingly, Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, where he speaks of their final salvation, promises them only the removal of impiety and the forgiveness of sins through the grace of the Savior, saying: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved, as it is written: The one who delivers will come from Zion, and he will turn impiety away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Rom. XI, 25–27).

**XVII.** What, then, does it profit these wretched people that they pretend their Christ has already come, that he was born in that destruction of Jerusalem, that he was confined in a prison near the city of Rome, and that down to the present day he has suffered many pains for their liberation? Through these claims they seek to nullify among their hearers the coming of the true Christ, so plainly manifested among all the nations, and to present themselves as innocent of his passion and death.

The one whom they regard as their Christ suffers such great and prolonged evils not from them but from the Romans. Yet, according to the truth of the Scriptures, no other Christ is to be received except the one whom they themselves fastened to the cross. He himself testifies through the prophet Malachi, saying: “If a man pierces God, because you pierce me, and you, the whole nation, pierce me” (Mal. III, 8).

Concerning him it is also written in Zechariah: “And it shall be said to him: What are these wounds in the midst of your hands? And he shall say: I was wounded in the house of those who loved me” (Zach. XIII, 6).

Or how, after so many centuries—when nearly a thousand years have now been completed since their devastation and dispersion—do they try to obscure the coming of the one who shone upon the world so brightly that the prophet Hosea says of him: “His going forth has been prepared like the dawn” (Hos. VI, 3)?

Habakkuk likewise says: “His brightness will be like the light; horns are in his hands, and there his strength is hidden” (Hab. III, 4). This most plainly refers to the passion of the cross.

**XVIII.** Isaiah also says: “For the sake of Zion I shall not be silent, and for the sake of Jerusalem I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness and her Savior is kindled like a lamp. And the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your glorious one” (Isa. LXII, 1–2).

Through the same prophet, the Lord promises that he will not delay for a long time but will swiftly and most speedily triumph over the devil and seize his prey and spoils. After saying, “For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX, 6), and elsewhere, “His name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14), he added: “And the Lord said to me: Call his name, ‘Hasten to seize the spoils; hurry to plunder’” (Isa. VIII, 3).

Therefore, against these hard-hearted people, who refuse to accept God’s present righteousness and thereby distance themselves from righteousness, God cries out through the same prophet, saying: “Listen to me, hard of heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near; it will not be far away, and my salvation will not delay. I shall give salvation in Zion and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. XLVI, 12–13).

“My righteous one is near; my Savior has gone forth, and my arms shall judge the peoples” (Isa. LI, 5).

What wonder, then, if such people, themselves wandering and leading others into error, invented that story about the appearance of their pseudochrist to their great teacher whom they call Joshua ben Levi? Perhaps that very man was the impious teacher whom, as we showed above, blessed Jerome says held their school until the captivity as the seventh after Shammai and Hillel (in chapter VIII of Isaiah). Perhaps he himself devised this deception to mislead the wretched people, so that they might regard such a promise as consolation amid the calamities of the captivity that had then begun.

What wonder, I ask, if either these people fabricated this story or, to strengthen their unbelief, Satan himself—transforming himself into an angel of light, as he once even cast a snare of temptation from the Scriptures before our Lord—mocked them by a just judgment of God? To the one who deserved both to be deceived and to deceive, he was permitted to appear in this way and to utter such things as though they came from prophetic words, so that they might be turned away from faith in the true Savior and miserably provoked, according to the desires of their hearts, to await false and empty things.

In them God fulfilled what he had earlier threatened terrifyingly in the Psalms, saying: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. So I let them go according to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own inventions” (Ps. LXXX, 12–13).

[Col. 0153A] **XIX.** We also read in ecclesiastical histories (Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, chapter XXXVII) that they were deceived on several occasions, either by apostate men or by the devil himself, when he transformed himself into an angel of light.

Thus Julian the emperor (the *Tripartite History*, book VI, chapter XLIII), having turned from Christianity to the worship of idols and having become in every respect an Antichrist, among his other acts of impiety permitted them to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem out of hatred for Christ, so that they might sacrifice lawful victims there.

When Jews had been gathered from all the provinces and they were laying new foundations for the Temple, an earthquake suddenly arose during the night. Stones were torn from the lowest parts of the foundations and scattered far and wide. A fiery globe also came forth from the interior of the Temple and struck many of them down with its flames. Terrified by this, some confessed Christ against their will. And so that they would not believe that this had happened by chance, on the following night the sign of the cross appeared on their garments.

In the time of Theodosius the Younger (the *Tripartite History*, book XII, chapter IX), the devil appeared to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses. He promised to lead them across the sea on dry feet to the promised land. After many had been killed, the survivors who had been saved immediately fled to the grace of Christ.

Blessed Jerome also writes in his *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, while explaining the passage where the prophet is commanded to lie upon his left side for three hundred and ninety days and bear the iniquities of the house of Israel, and likewise to lie upon his right side for forty days and bear the iniquities of the house of Judah.

[Col. 0153C] Taken together, these days amount to four hundred and thirty, and are reckoned as the same number of years, since the Lord says to the same prophet: “A day for a year, a day, I say, for a year I have given you” (Ezek. IV).

That teacher therefore writes—and in these words explains their utterly vain hope of release from the captivity in which they are now held—saying (St. Jerome, on chapter IV of Ezekiel):

“The Jews wish to reckon, from the second year of Vespasian, when Jerusalem was captured by the Romans and the Temple overturned, four hundred and thirty years during which the people would remain in tribulation, distress, and the yoke of captivity, and then return to their former condition. Thus, just as the children of Israel were in Egypt for four hundred and thirty years, so the final captivity would end after the same number. It is also written in Exodus (XL, 112): ‘Now the dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.’ And again (verse XLI): ‘After four hundred and thirty years had passed, the whole army went out during the night.’”

This number of years from the beginning of their captivity had not yet been completed in the days of blessed Jerome. Now, however, it has not only been completed but almost doubled. For from the coming of the Lord and Savior, eight hundred and forty-six years are presently reckoned.

**XX.** Their ancestors, therefore, were deceived by a vain expectation; and these people are deceived as well, with still greater blindness. Although they see that their present captivity and servitude have not been loosened after seventy years, as happened in the case of Babylon, nor after four hundred and thirty years, as in the case of Egypt, nor even after five hundred years, which have already been completed, they do not understand that they have sinned against God more grievously than ever before by crucifying the Son of God and crying out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

For this reason they have been abandoned by God and given over to oblivion, until they become ashamed of their unbelief and begin to desire not temporal but eternal freedom, which is in Christ.

The almighty God threatened this to them through Moses, saying: “I shall reduce your cities to solitude and make your sanctuaries desolate; nor shall I receive any longer the fragrance of a pleasing sacrifice. I shall lay waste your land, and your enemies will be astonished at it when its inhabitants have been removed. But I shall scatter you among the nations and draw the sword after you; your land will be desolate and your cities ruined” (Lev. XXVI, 31–33).

And again: “You shall perish among the nations, and a hostile land shall consume you. If any of them should remain even from these, they will waste away in their iniquities in the land of their enemies; and because of the sins of their fathers and their own, they will be afflicted until they confess their iniquities and those of their ancestors, by which they transgressed against me and walked contrary to me. Therefore I also shall walk against them and bring them into a hostile land, until their uncircumcised mind becomes ashamed. Then they will pray concerning their impieties, and I shall remember my covenant which I made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (verses 38–42).

If they were seeking the true salvation and freedom promised in these words of God, they could long ago have understood that their sanctuaries had been made desolate, so that—as God himself testifies—he no longer receives from them a pleasing fragrance. They would not await the restoration of those sanctuaries, which will not occur, but would humbly submit themselves to God to be restored, confessing their own iniquities and those of their ancestors and praying concerning their impieties, so that they might deserve to obtain forgiveness.

But because their uncircumcised mind is not yet ashamed, they suppose that their pseudochrist will never die or rise again, but will live forever; and that he will suddenly appear from his confinement, coming in the clouds of heaven.

[Col. 0154D] **XXI.** Likewise, some unbelieving Jews, deceived by a perverse opinion, had often heard in the Scriptures concerning Christ that his kingdom would be eternal. Thus in Isaiah it is written: “His government will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace; he will sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from this time and forever” (Isa. IX, 7). And in the Psalm: “His throne is like the days of heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 30). Again: “His throne is like the sun in my sight and like the full moon forever” (verse 37).

They therefore thought that the same Christ promised in the Law and the Prophets would never die. When the Lord Jesus Christ spoke of his passion—as it is written in the Gospel—they objected to him, saying: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” (John XII, 34).

But neither those people understood, nor do these people understand, that according to those same divine Scriptures no other Christ is to be believed in except the one who truly died and was buried for the sins of God’s people and, rising again, dies no more, so that he truly remains forever.

The Lord testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he shall give the impious for his burial and the rich for his death” (Isa. LIII, 8–9). And again: “If he makes his life an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (verse 10). And shortly afterward: “Therefore I shall allot him many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he gave his life over to death” (verse 12), and so forth.

Thus both things were prophesied, and both are true in Christ: death for a time, and after death the glory of resurrection forever.

Of what other Christ could the prophet Daniel have said: “I was watching in my night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds” (Dan. VII, 13), and so forth, except the one rejected by these people? As Daniel foretells in another vision—as we also said above—“After sixty-two weeks Christ will be killed, and his people will not be his; and the people, together with the leader who is to come, will destroy the city and the sanctuary” (ibid. IX, 26).

[Col. 0155C] **XXII.** Where did they ever read of the other pseudochrist whom they call the messiah Ben Ephraim? Which of the prophets ever foretold that a messiah would come from the tribe of Ephraim?

Did not the patriarch Jacob, in the blessings of his sons, and all the prophets thereafter testify that he would come from the tribe of Judah and the house of David? Is it not perfectly clear that obstinate and contentious blindness in impiety devised this idea so that, where the prophet Zechariah speaks most plainly of Christ, whom they crucified—“And they shall mourn for him with a mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as one grieves over the death of a firstborn” (Zach. XII, 10)—the killing not of the one who truly is Christ but of another, who was assailed by them, might be understood from the words of the Lord in Jeremiah: “For I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn” (Jer. XXXI, 9), so that, as far as they are able, the true passion of Christ may be nullified?

Let them read the books of the prophets, especially the prophet Hosea, and see that the ten tribes of the Israelite people, after they were divided from the house of David and established Jeroboam son of Nebat, from the tribe of Ephraim, as their king in Samaria, were frequently called Ephraim—and Israel—because of the royal house that began among them from Ephraim, and because they constituted the greater part of the Israelite people.

Likewise, that part of the people which remained with the house of David is called Judah because of the royal house chosen from the tribe of Judah. Hence we often read (in the Books of Kings): “Behold, these things are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah,” concerning the former; and concerning the latter: “Behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.”

Concerning these two parts of the people, divided into two kingdoms, Hosea says: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah?” (Hos. VI, 4).

To this people—Israel and Ephraim—separated from the house of David by Jeroboam son of Nebat and alienated from the Temple of God, which worshipped golden calves at Bethel and Dan until the day of its captivity, and which was then led away by the kings of the Assyrians into eternal captivity, the Lord says through Hosea: “I shall no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I shall utterly forget them” (Hos. I, 6).

To this people, I say, a great—and truly great—consolation is promised: although it does not deserve ever to be released from the yoke of temporal captivity, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, if it wishes to believe in him, it will receive such happiness that God will become a father to Israel and Ephraim will be his firstborn. In this way it will recover the glory which it formerly received when liberated from Egypt, when the Lord said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son; let him go, so that he may serve me” (Exod. IV, 22–23).

**XXIII.** Since the truth of this matter is so clear, why do they make darkness for themselves out of light? Why do they dare to say that some messiah—that is, an anointed one—will come from Ephraim?

Does being firstborn also mean being anointed? It was said generally of the entire people: “Israel is my firstborn son”; yet apart from the priestly house and the royal house, it did not receive the glory of anointing.

Let them hear the Psalm speaking against their error, even before the division of the people took place under Rehoboam son of Solomon, and plainly declaring from where the true Savior was to be expected: “He rejected the tent of Joseph, and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim; but he chose the tribe of Judah” (Ps. LXXVII, 67–68).

And shortly afterward: “He chose David his servant and took him from the flocks of sheep, from following the nursing ewes” (verses 70–71). He brought him forth to shepherd Jacob, his people, and Israel, his inheritance.

As for the nations Gog and Magog, and likewise the other prophetic promises and threats which have been set forth with great obscurity, it is exceedingly foolish to wish to dispute anything with these people while they despise matters so true, so manifest, and upon which salvation entirely depends. However those other things are to be understood and received, unless they first faithfully accept these matters, they cannot be saved.

**XXIV.** Since our discussion concerns the false and blind teachers of the Jews, concerning whom the Lord testifies, saying: “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.
