Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. If the blind guide the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. XV, 13–14), we think it necessary to give a brief warning.

Some of our people are accustomed to admire the books of Josephus and Philo excessively and take greater pleasure in reading them than in reading the divine writings. These men were learned, indeed, but they were impious Jews, and they should not be followed to any great extent. Since they were alienated from the truth, they were not free from error. By expanding and explaining the divine histories at length, they insert much that is false and superfluous from their own minds; according to their deceptive opinion, they either corrupt or weaken the sound meanings of God’s words.

Therefore the ancient teachers of the Church take from them only those matters which, in their books, are reported in agreement with our Scriptures concerning historical events; and even these are very few and rare, especially those which they themselves wrote after seeing them with their own eyes, such as the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish Temple and priesthood.

Blessed Augustine instructs and warns us about this caution in his books against Faustus the Manichaean (book XII, chapter 30), saying:

“Philo was a man of exceedingly liberal learning, one of the Jews who ridicule the passion of Christ which we have recognized. The Greeks do not hesitate to compare his eloquence with Plato’s. He attempted to interpret certain passages from the Scriptures, not to understand Christ, in whom he had not believed, but so that it might become more apparent how great the difference is between referring everything to Christ, for whose sake those things were truly spoken, and pursuing any conjectures whatsoever, with whatever acuity of mind, apart from him.

“This shows how powerful is what the Apostle says: ‘When you turn to the Lord, the veil will be taken away’ (II Cor. III, 16).

“To mention something from this same Philo: wishing to understand the ark of the flood as constructed according to the proportions of the human body, he examined everything member by member. When he consulted even the subtleties of numerical rules, everything fittingly presented itself to him, since nothing hindered him from understanding Christ: for the Savior of the human race also appeared in a human body. Yet these correspondences did not compel him, since the human body is also possessed by other human beings.

“But when he came to the door made in the side of the ark, every conjecture of human ingenuity failed. Nevertheless, in order to say something, he dared to believe, dared to say, and dared to write that the lower parts of the body, through which urine and excrement are expelled, were signified by that door. It is no wonder that, having failed to find the door, he went so far astray. If he had turned to Christ, with the veil removed he would have found the sacraments of the Church flowing from the side of that man.”

**XXV.** We have said these things about the two pseudochrists of the Jews and about their teachers—not teachers but deceivers—who abominate the true Christ, our Lord and Savior, with such hatred and pursue him with such curses and blasphemies that the ears of the faithful cannot bear them.

Before we recall their other poisonous insults, it first seems necessary—not only to refute their rage but also to confirm the truth of our faith—to set forth what both their ancestors and these people themselves, still raging today, object as a disgrace against the Lord Savior and all his faithful; and, insofar as the Lord assists us, to demonstrate how plainly it pertains both to the condemnation of their impiety and to the mystery of our redemption.

They blaspheme that we believe in one whom God’s Law calls accursed because he was hung upon a tree, and therefore ordered him to be buried on the same day on which he was hung, lest, if he remained on the gallows through the night, their land should be polluted through him.

Yet they do not even know that he was fastened with nails to the wood of the cross and suspended by that very nailing. Instead, they defame him as having been punished in the manner of the robbers who are now hanged; and, at the shouting and command of their teacher Joshua, as having been quickly taken down from the wood and thrown into a tomb in a certain garden full of cabbages, lest their land should be contaminated.

**XXVI.** It is clear where they derive this opportunity for such impious blasphemy. As we read in Deuteronomy, God’s Law says through Moses:

“When a man has committed a sin punishable by death, and, condemned to death, has been hanged on a gallows, his corpse shall not remain on the wood, but shall be buried on that same day; for he is accursed by God who hangs upon a tree. You shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God has given you as a possession” (Deut. XXI, 22–23).

We cannot deny that this passage prophesies the passion of Christ, because the Apostle also confirms it, saying: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, as it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Gal. III, 13).

The Lord also bears witness to this in the Gospel, speaking to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V, 46).

When blessed Augustine explained these words of the Lord in his books against Faustus (book XVI, chapters 22–23), he said:

“I and those who think somewhat more attentively with me about that evangelical and dominical saying—where he did not say, ‘For he wrote about me,’ so that it might be believed that he wrote other things also which do not pertain to Christ, but said, ‘For he wrote about me’—understand that the whole intention of that Scripture pertains solely to understanding the grace of Christ.”

All those things, therefore, have no correct meaning unless they are referred to as prophetic of the dispensation by which the human race is aided. We must not be ashamed of the disgrace of Christ’s cross, which, against all human reproaches, we bear upon the most prominent part of the body—that is, upon the forehead. Rather, with devotion and care, and with the help of God’s grace, we must investigate how these things are to be understood soundly in accordance with the authority of Holy Scripture and the sense of the Catholic Fathers, so that confusion may increase for them and edification for us.

### XXVII

To make this clearer and more evident, let us briefly set aside the edition of blessed Jerome, who interpreted this passage not word for word but according to its sense. It seems appropriate to present the very words as they are set down in Hebrew, and the order of the words as he himself expressed them in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, from the translation of Theodotion. Thus it is read there:

> “And because there will be in a man sin and a judgment of death, and he will die, and you will hang him on a tree. His corpse shall not sleep upon the tree, because you shall bury him by burial on that very day; for he who is hanged is a curse of God, and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you to inherit.”

Where this translator rendered “shall not sleep,” others rendered “shall not remain overnight,” or “shall not linger,” or “shall not continue.” Where he rendered “his corpse,” the others translated “his cadaver” or “his body.”

Thus, plainly and wonderfully, in these words the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ is prophesied through the likeness of those condemned to the cross and the gibbet. He, for our sins, was counted among the wicked and criminals. What was to happen in him and concerning him is confirmed and commended as though it were truly future when it is said: “And because there will be in a man sin and a judgment of death, and he will die, and you will hang him on a tree,” and so forth. The whole passage is presented not in the manner of one who doubts, but of one who prophesies.

When it says, “And because there will be in a man sin,” what is to be understood? Certainly not his own, because, as another prophet testifies, “he committed no iniquity, and there was no deceit in his mouth”; rather, it is the sin of all of us, as the same prophet says: “All we like sheep have gone astray; each has turned to his own way; and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. LIII, 6). Blessed Peter the apostle likewise says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree” (I Peter II, 24).

Accordingly, it rightly follows: “the judgment of death”—namely, our death, which was owed from the beginning because of sin and was inflicted upon the sinful human being by God’s judgment, when he said: “On whatever day you eat from it”—that is, from the forbidden tree—“you shall die the death” (Gen. II, 17). Hence the Apostle also says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings” (Rom. V, 12).

### XXVIII

This man therefore took upon himself the sin of all of us, and the judgment of our death. Scripture then adds concerning him: “And he will die, and you will hang him on a tree.”

Here it is greatly to be wondered at that it is first said, “he will die,” and afterward, “you will hang him on a tree,” since it is evident that our Lord was first hung upon the tree by the hands of unbelievers, and afterward, when every part of his passion had been completed, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit when he willed.

Yet this was spoken with profound divine wisdom: after the Law had said, “There will be in a man sin and a judgment of death,” it immediately added, “and he will die,” and then, “and you will hang him on a tree.” In this way it first demonstrated his power and afterward displayed their cruelty: for they killed him, insofar as it lay within their power, by hanging him on the tree—him who had died by his own will and power, compelled neither by human violence nor by any punishment or torture.

In the Gospel this man and Lord himself bears witness to this power over his death, saying:

> “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John X, 18).

And in the Psalm he says:

> “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5).

And again:

> “I slept” (Ps. III, 6);

that is: Let them not insult me as though I had been killed by their violence. I slept: I died of my own accord and by my own power, when I willed. Thus the power of the one who died is wonderfully commended, while the savagery of his persecutors is not excused.

Scripture continues:

> “His corpse shall not sleep upon the tree, because you shall bury him by burial on that very day.”

In this statement, through the word “sleep,” the sleep of one who will awaken—that is, rise again—is expressed. Thus he himself says of Lazarus:

> “Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep” (John XI, 11);

and of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom he was about to raise:

> “The girl is not dead, but sleeping” (Luke VIII, 52);

and concerning him, his enemies say in the Psalm:

> “The one who sleeps will not rise again” (Ps. XL, 9).

By “corpse,” however, his true death is shown, since an inanimate body is called *morticinum*, a dead body. It is likewise called a *cadaver*, from *cadere*, “to fall,” because through death it falls to the earth—not only when it dissolves into the earth, according to what was said to Adam, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III, 19), and as Ecclesiastes says, “and the dust returns to the earth from which it came” (Eccles. XII, 7), but also because what is already dead is reckoned as earth and is entrusted to the earth. Hence the Lord also says of himself:

> “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII, 24).

### XXIX

What mystery, then, is signified by the commandment in the Law and its fulfillment in the Gospel—as we read—through divine providence by the persecutors: that this man’s corpse, or cadaver, or body should not sleep, remain overnight, linger, or continue upon the tree?

For it is written that “the Jews, so that the bodies might not remain on the cross, asked Pilate that their legs should be broken” (John XIX, 31)—namely, the legs of the Lord and of the robbers who were crucified with him—“and that they should be taken away.”

Here the depth of the mystery is exceedingly great. Whether it was so that, when they hastened to take down and bury his body, three great mysteries still lacking in Christ’s passion might be fulfilled—namely, the opening of his side by the soldier’s spear; the issuing of water and blood from that opening; and the preservation of his bones intact, because he was found already dead—the Evangelist greatly and magnificently commends all these things, fulfilled on the occasion of hastening his burial, saying:

> “Then the soldiers came, and they broke the legs of the first and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. He who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you also may believe. For these things happened so that Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They will look upon him whom they pierced.’”

This was so that, through the opening of his side, the door might be opened for us by which we should enter into life, and that we might be incorporated into Christ through the water of baptism and the blood of redemption.

### XXX

Since the Law commands concerning the lamb sacrificed at Passover, “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. XII, 46), let us recognize that this is the true Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Blessed Paul the Apostle also bears witness concerning him:

> “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7).

Or, because the Lord suffered on the Parasceve—that is, on the sixth day, Friday—and because the mystery of the Sabbath, commended from the beginning of the world, had to be fulfilled in him, the Law commanded that his burial be hastened on the evening of that same Parasceve, so that, when the sacrament of his passion had been completed, he might rest in the tomb on the Sabbath and rise at the dawning of the first day of the week, as he had foretold in the Psalm:

> “I will rise at dawn” (Ps. LVI, 9; CVII, 3).

Hence the twenty-first Psalm, which was written concerning his passion and the glory of his resurrection, bears the superscription, “For the morning assumption,” or, as it is in Hebrew, “For the morning deer.”

He thus showed that what had been prefigured at the beginning of the world had been wholly fulfilled in him. There we are mystically told that God, after all the works he had made—works that were very good—rested on the Sabbath. This signified that our Lord and King, existing before the ages, after working our salvation in the midst of the earth and saying to the Father, “I have glorified you upon the earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do” (John XVII, 4), would rest in the tomb on that same day.

Thus, after the labor of his passion, through the power of the resurrection, he would enter into his rest, concerning which the Psalmist says:

> “Arise, Lord, into your rest” (Ps. CXXXI, 8).

In this way the most sacred three-day period of his passion, burial, and resurrection—which the Spirit of the Law foresaw and ordained—might remain inviolable.

### XXXI

As for that faithless people who killed Christ, the Law rightly says to them:

> “His cadaver shall not remain overnight, or remain, upon the tree, because you shall bury him by burial on that very day” (Deut. XXI, 23).

This means that they should neither mock nor scorn the disgrace of Christ’s passion and death, signified by the cadaver hanging upon the tree, as though they were despising and displaying for ridicule the crucified Son of God before their eyes. Rather, they should hasten to bury him—that is, to honor his death, which he accepted for the salvation of all, since burial is an honor paid to the dead—and they should hasten to fulfill this quickly, within that very day.

That is: they should do so in this time of redemption and salvation, in which the Lamb of God was sacrificed for our sins and of which it is said everywhere:

> “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8).

Concerning that day of the Savior’s coming, and of the salvation and redemption that he accomplished through his passion, the Psalm also sings:

> “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 24–26).

And in another Psalm the Holy Spirit says to the same Jews:

> “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8), and so forth.

Therefore, while this acceptable time and day of salvation continue—the salvation instituted for us by him who died and rose again for the salvation of all—the Law urges them to repent of their crime, or at least not to delay covering the crime they committed against him, so that they may deservedly hear:

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

They should hasten to honor Christ’s precious death, which they hold up to ridicule and mockery. For if, throughout this whole day—that is, throughout this entire saving period, for as long as the present life lasts—they neglect to fulfill this, the night of death, the night of condemnation and eternal darkness, will overtake them. Then he who was hung upon the tree for the salvation of all will spend the night and remain among them upon the tree, because after death they will be unable to amend the mockery and scorn of his passion that they maintained throughout their lives. Scripture says:

> “When a wicked man dies, there will be no further hope” (Prov. XI, 7).

Concerning this day and this night the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

> “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. The night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX, 5, 4).

### XXXII

Even now the Jews possess the dreadful night of unbelief and blindness that the Lord threatened against them through the prophet, saying:

> “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10).

Yet the day still belonged to them when the Lord suffered among them for the salvation of the whole world and rose again. For forty days afterward he confirmed the faith of his disciples, whom he had chosen from among them; and on the fortieth day, while they watched, he ascended into heaven.

After the Holy Spirit had been sent, the holy apostles began to preach among them. In one day, through their preaching and miracles, three thousand believed; on another day, five thousand; and afterward countless thousands, both in Judea and in the other regions.

But when the rest hardened themselves and did not believe, rejecting the word of God and judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, the apostles turned to the Gentiles, so that what had previously been prophesied might be fulfilled:

> “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isa. XLIX, 6).

They, however, remained in the night of their misery and blindness.

Therefore, all those among them who believed in the Lord’s passion in response to the apostles’ preaching and mighty works buried him who had been hung upon the tree, in accordance with the prophecy of the Law, on that same day. While God’s grace still shone upon them, they honored Christ’s precious death with devout remembrance; for we also call the tombs of the dead “memorials.”

But for the others, overcome by the dreadful night and mocking Christ’s venerable passion to this day, he remains and spends the night hanging upon the tree, because they refuse to offer him an honorable memorial.

So that they might not incur this great evil, while time was still being granted and an opportunity for salvation remained, the Law exhorted them figuratively, saying:

> “His cadaver shall not remain overnight upon the tree, because you shall bury him by burial on that very day” (Deut. XXI, 23).

Hence the Lord also said to those same Jews:

> “There is still a little light among you. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. Whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light” (John XII, 35–36).

### XXXIII

When the Law had commanded that he who was hanging upon the tree should not remain there, but should be buried on that same day, it added the reason why this honor was owed him, saying:

> “For he who is hanged is a curse of God”;

which means nothing other than, “Cursed by God,” as the other translators rendered it.

Therefore the passion and death of this man who was hung must be honored with devout remembrance, because “he who is hanged is a curse of God.” That is, it was not through his own fault, his own violence, or his own wicked plans that the Jews were able to do this to the Lord Jesus Christ; rather, they were permitted to do it by God’s purpose and foreknowledge.

He wished to submit to our curse so that we might become participants in his blessing. Our curse is twofold: guilt and punishment. As guilt, it is written:

> “Cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this Law, to do them” (Deut. XXVII, 26).

As punishment, it is written to the first man at the beginning:

> “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II, 17).

This curse descended from that man upon the human race. Since he deserved both curses—the curse of guilt, because he transgressed the Lord’s commandment, and the curse of punishment, because he was sentenced to death—all human beings were therefore bound by both curses.

But the true Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, came, alone without the curse of guilt, because he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth. Undeservedly he took upon himself the curse of our punishment and the curse of our death, so that he might free us from both curses. He suffered for us, not for himself: without guilt, he endured punishment, so that he might abolish both guilt and punishment.

God mercifully ordained this for our salvation before the foundation of the world. He foretold it through his prophets, and in the last days he accomplished it as it had been foretold. Blessed Peter the apostle bears witness to this concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, saying to the Jews:

> “This man, handed over according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by the hands of lawless men, after afflicting him” (Acts II, 23).

Again, while the apostles and the whole Church were praying, they said to God:

> “For truly they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of the Jews, to do whatever your hand and your plan had decreed would happen” (Acts IV, v. 2 and following).

Thus God the Father cursed this man when, for our salvation, he handed him over to our curse and our death, as he himself testifies:

> “Because of the transgression of my people I struck him” (Isa. LIII, 8).

And in the prophet Zechariah, calling the power of his passion a sword, he says:

> “Sword, awake against my shepherd and against the man who is joined to me, says the Lord. Strike the shepherd,” and so forth (Zech. XIII, 7).

Hence Isaiah says:

> “And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity” (Isa. LIII, 10).

And the Apostle, most earnestly commending to us the greatness of God’s goodness, says:

> “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

### XXXIV

Since, therefore, through such great divine kindness this man voluntarily submitted to our curse and was counted among criminals, the Law commanded that his passion be honored with devout remembrance.

For the Holy Spirit would not have given so absurd a command concerning his simple burial, ordering that it be prepared by those who crucified him, when the one who performed it—that is, Joseph of Arimathea—according to the Gospel, “had not consented to their plan and action” (Luke XXIII, 51).

The Law adds how great a pollution and defilement would come upon the Jews who refused and refuse to offer this honor to the Lord, saying:

> “And you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance” (Deut. XXI, 23).

They themselves are the land that the Lord God once gave them, so that they might be his hereditary people, as Moses says to them:

> “The Lord chose you from among all the nations, so that you might be his hereditary people” (Deut. IV, 20).

They themselves are the land to which Jeremiah cried:

> “Land, land, land, hear the word of the Lord” (Jer. XXII, 29);

and of which it is said in the Psalm:

> “The land was defiled with blood, and they were polluted by their works,”

or, as we customarily sing:

> “The land was slain with blood, and it was contaminated by their works” (Ps. CV, 38–39).

They ought therefore to have shown the honor of faith to the Lord and Savior, who suffered and died upon the wood of the cross for the salvation of the world, so that they might deserve to hear, together with the holy apostles and the others who believed from that same people, through the prophet Malachi:

> “All the nations will call you blessed, for you will be a desirable land” (Mal. III, 12).

But because they despised and continue to despise him, and to this day read these things with furious minds and savage faces while detesting the one about whom they were written, they have defiled and polluted their land—that is, themselves—and do not possess the promised blessing. Rather, the prophet Ezekiel says to them daily:

> “You are an unclean land, and not rained upon” (Ezek. XXII, 24);

and Isaiah says:

> “Your hands are full of blood.”

And again:

> “For your hands are polluted with blood, and your fingers with iniquity” (Isa. I, 15; LIX, 3).

This is because they cried out, saying:

> “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

### XXXV

They ought to have feared this contamination and pollution of their land—that is, of themselves—and not the nonexistent pollution by which they imagined that the land of their habitation would be defiled by the corpses of those hung upon the cross unless they were buried on the same day.

Blessed King and prophet David certainly did not fear this. In order to appease God’s anger, he handed over seven men from the house of Saul to the Gibeonites to be crucified. From the beginning of the barley harvest until all the crops had been harvested and rain fell upon them from heaven, he left them there and did not have any of them buried.

If they reply that these men were crucified in the land of the Gibeonites, who were not among the children of Israel, and that for this reason they were left there, let them read in the same book of Samuel that this happened not at Gibeon but at Gibeah of Benjamin. The Gibeonites themselves said to David:

> “Let us crucify them at Gibeah of Saul, once the Lord’s chosen one” (II Sam. XXI, 6).

If they say that David feared incurring God’s anger, supposing that he would have presumed to bury men once condemned and assigned to divine vengeance, let them read what happened afterward. When he was informed that Saul’s concubine, spreading sackcloth upon a stone beneath herself, had guarded them day and night from wild beasts and birds for so long a time, he not only did not rebuke her, but, as an imitator and surpasser of such piety, brought the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead. He also ordered the bones of those seven who had been crucified to be gathered. Without abhorrence, but with pious honor, he buried them in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father.

God was not offended by this. On the contrary, Scripture says:

> “They did everything that the king had commanded. And afterward God was reconciled to the land” (II Sam. XXI, 14).

Blessed David therefore was not afraid of these things, because in that chapter of the Law he understood not the punishment of some detestable man, but the mystery of the Savior.

Or, if these people so religiously, as they think, preserved their land from pollution, what is the reason that for so many centuries it has vomited them out as though they were unclean?

### XXXVI

There is scarcely any testimony among the prophetic Scriptures in which both the manner of Christ’s passion upon the wood of the cross and the reality of his death are expressed so clearly. Therefore the holy Apostle, not being ashamed of the testimony concerning Christ, chose this passage above all others to place in his writings, in order to commend the truth and grace of his passion.

Even the statement that, according to blessed Jerome’s edition, is read at the beginning of this chapter—“When a man has committed sin and a judgment of death” (Deut. XXI, 22)—must faithfully be referred to the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

The same applies to the words in which he speaks in the Psalm from the person of his body:

> “The words of my offenses” (Ps. XXI, 2);

and again:

> “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Ps. LXVIII, 6).

Because he became a participant in our nature, he transformed our voice in himself, mercifully taking upon himself our cause as well, while God laid upon him the iniquity of us all.

Scripture therefore rightly says of him:

> “When a man has committed sin and a judgment of death”;

because all who have sinned belong to the body of this man. For this reason they were justly to be punished by death, unless they were redeemed by his undeserved death, as he says:

> “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. XIII, 14).

In accordance with this sense, the vision of the prophet Nathan, in which his coming is promised from the seed of David, also rightly includes what God says concerning him:

> “If he commits any iniquity, I will reprove him with the rod of men and with the blows of the children of men; but I will not remove my mercy from him” (II Sam. VII, 14).

For they are his members and belong to his unity. As long as they live in mortality, they cannot be without sin; therefore they commit iniquity, as the blessed apostle John testifies:

> “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” (I John III, 4).

And again, speaking for all:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

God therefore reproves them with the rod of men and with the blows of the children of men, correcting and disciplining them temporally, because, as it is written:

> “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebr. XII, 6).

Yet he does not remove his mercy from him in whom and through whom he shows them mercy. At times he also exacts vengeance, as the Psalmist says concerning such people:

> “O God, you were merciful to them, and avenging all their inventions” (Ps. XCVIII, 8).

For in him who is their head, just as there could be no iniquity, so there were no chastising or purifying scourges of his own, but only those belonging to our salvation.

### XXXVII

Blessed Jerome likewise teaches that in the passage where, according to Theodotion, it is written, “For he who is hanged is a curse of God,” the Hebrew may be read as “For he who is hanged is an injury to God,” or indeed, “For God has been hanged shamefully.”

This is highly effective in exposing the impiety of the Jews, because it clearly demonstrates that the unjust hanging of this man is an injury to God the Father, who is dishonored and despised in his own Son. The Son himself confirms this in the Gospel:

> “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V, 23);

and elsewhere:

> “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (John XV, 23);

and again:

> “Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me” (Luke X, 16).

Not only is his hanging an injury to God; the man who was hung is himself evidently God—God who was hung shamefully.

The Apostle confirms this in almost the same words:

> “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

The impious crucifiers thought that he was merely a human being and a man of ordinary nature, but he himself was secretly both God and the Lord of glory.

Blessed Augustine, treating this passage against Faustus the Manichaean (book XIV, chapter 6), says among other things:

> “When it was added, ‘everyone,’ so that it might be said, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree,’ Moses certainly did not fail to foresee that the righteous would also be upon the cross. Rather, he rightly foresaw that heretics would deny the true death of the Lord. For this reason they wished to separate Christ from this curse, so that they might also separate him from the reality of death.
>
> “If that death was not real, no curse hung upon Christ crucified on the tree, because he was not truly crucified. But against the heretics who would come long afterward, Moses cries out from afar: ‘You evade the issue without cause, you who dislike the truth of Christ’s death. Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree—not this one, he says, or that one, but absolutely everyone. Christ would be outside Adam’s curse only if he were outside Adam’s death. But when he accepted death from a human being and for a human being, he did not disdain to accept from him and for him also the curse that accompanies death.’”

And later, in chapter 7:

> “The prophecy asserts this because it knew that Christ’s death would hang upon the cross, and that heretics would arise who would say: ‘He did hang upon the tree, but only in some appearance, not so that he would truly die.’ By crying out, therefore, ‘cursed,’ it cried out nothing other than that he truly died, knowing that the death of a sinful human being—which he himself accepted without sin—came from the curse expressed in the words, ‘If you touch, you will die.’
>
> “The serpent hung upon the tree also pertains to this, signifying that Christ did not feign a false death, but hung the true death upon the tree of his passion—the death into which that serpent cast humanity through evil counsel. They refuse to perceive this true death, and therefore they are not healed from the serpent’s poison, just as in the wilderness all who looked upon it were healed.”

### XXXVIII

Some inexperienced Christians also customarily say that being fastened to a tree is one thing, and hanging upon a tree another. They think the question can be resolved by saying that Judas was the one cursed by Moses because he hanged himself with a noose—as though they knew first whether he had hanged himself from wood or from stone.

But the Apostle clearly does not allow us to understand anything other than that this was foretold concerning Christ.

As for the Jews’ refusal to believe that he was fastened to the cross with nails, their blindness is astonishing, since—as we have already mentioned above—they hear him say through the prophet Zechariah:

> “They will look upon me whom they pierced” (Zech. XII, 10).

And through Malachi:

> “Will a human being pierce God, because you pierce me? And you pierce me, the whole nation” (Mal. III, 8–9).

In Solomon, concerning the same one who, although rich, became poor for our sake, it is written:

> “Do not use violence against the poor because he is poor, nor crush the needy at the gate, because the Lord will judge his case and will pierce those who pierced his soul” (Prov. XXII, 22–23).

This is the poor man of whom another prophet says:

> “Behold, your King comes to you, righteous and Savior; he himself is poor” (Zech. IX, 9), and so forth.

Thus they fashioned pseudo-Christs for themselves, turning the unhappy people away from faith in the true Christ by deceiving them with a vain expectation of their coming.

### XXXIX

For this reason, in order to make our same Lord Jesus Christ irredeemably hateful to their hearers, they call him in their own language *Ussum Hamizri*. In Latin this is said to mean “the Egyptian Dissipator.”

It was not enough for their fathers to say to him, when he was present among them in the flesh:

> “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII, 48);

or to say concerning him to Pilate:

> “We found this man subverting our nation” (Luke XXIII, 2).

These people, offspring and fosterlings of sinful men, must also defame him with new insults and curses, asserting that he is the Egyptian dissipator of his own people. I suppose this is because of that Egyptian magician and false prophet who once deceived and ruined many of them, concerning whom the tribune also speaks to Paul in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Are you not the Egyptian who, before these days, stirred up a riot and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the assassins?” (Acts XXI, 38).

The worship that the faithful offer him throughout the world they call the worship of Baal and the religion of a foreign god, as though he were the one concerning whom the Psalm commands:

> “There shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. LXXX, 10).

They assert that the heavy and most foul odor commonly perceived in the morning hours at the beginning of summer comes from the infernal torments in which he is tortured in the underworld, because he troubled their nation and deceived the whole world.

They interpret the peoples of the nations who have accepted his faith as Babylon, and understand Christ our King as the king of this Babylon. Whatever is said in that vision of Isaiah, whose title is “The Oracle concerning Babylon” (Isa. XIII, 1), about the release of God’s people from Babylonian captivity and the destruction of that king and kingdom, they impiously attempt to transfer entirely to their own deliverance from this final captivity and to Christ’s downfall, as they imagine it.

It is as though the prophet were promising them, saying:

> “And it shall be on that day, when the Lord gives you rest from your labor, from your trembling, and from the hard servitude in which you served before, that you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon and say: ‘How the exactor has ceased, how the tribute has come to rest! The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers,’” and so forth.

Then, as though they were insulting Christ himself, they say:

> “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning! You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations! You said in your heart: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne’” (Isa. XIV, 12–13), and so forth.

They assert that what follows has been fulfilled entirely in him:

> “Yet you will be brought down to the underworld, to the depths of the pit. Those who see you will bend toward you and look upon you. Is this the man who troubled the earth?” and so forth.

And shortly afterward:

> “But you have been cast out from your tomb like a useless branch, defiled and wrapped together with those who were killed by the sword and went down to the foundations of the pit. Like a rotting corpse, you will have no fellowship with them, nor will you share their burial. For you have destroyed your land; you have killed your people.”

XL. And they say that he was taken down by his elders [Col. 0169A] from the wood, and buried in a tomb, so that everyone would know that he had died and had not been resurrected; then, they say, he was taken out of the tomb again, dragged through the whole city by means of a hook, and thus cast away. For this reason, they claim, his tomb still stands empty to this day, filthy and filled with stones and refuse that they customarily throw into it.

Although the impious fathers of these impious men have always understood this passage of prophetic reading as referring to King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, in accordance with the truth of the historical account—as blessed Jerome writes in his commentaries on the same prophet, saying (in chapter XIV):

> “The Hebrews relate a story of this kind. Evil-merodach, who had previously ruled for seven years while his father Nebuchadnezzar was living among the beasts, remained in prison with Jehoiachin, king of Judah, until his father’s death, after Nebuchadnezzar had been restored to the kingdom. When his father died and Evil-merodach again succeeded to the kingdom, he was not accepted by the leading men, who feared that the man believed to be dead might still be alive. Therefore, to establish the fact of his father’s death, he opened the tomb and dragged out his corpse with a hook and ropes.”

But these men, as has been said, in the monstrous intensity of their hatred for Christ and in their frenzied blasphemy, devised such things in order to make the Lord Christ detestable to their hearers. Against them the prophet Isaiah himself cries out, saying:

> “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples—him the nations will entreat, and his tomb will be glorious” (Isa. XI, 10).

He most clearly shows that there is no other Christ than this one, who came forth from the root of Jesse; who stands as a sign for the peoples; whom the nations everywhere now entreat; and whose tomb is not, as these men blaspheme, contemptible and shameful, but altogether glorious. For it has been illumined by the glory of the resurrection and, as not only the peoples of Christians but also those of the Saracens and barbarian nations know, it is held in every form of honor and veneration.

Moreover, where we read, “His resting-place will be glorious,” the Hebrew properly says: “His rest will be glory.” These words clearly show that death was not punishment for him, as unbelievers think, but a rest in which he rested when he willed. This rest of death was not disgrace for him but glory, because his flesh, unlike that of other mortals, did not decay in the tomb but was swiftly glorified through the resurrection, as he himself had foretold in the Psalm, according to the Hebrew translation:

> “Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my glory exulted, and my flesh will dwell securely. For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 9–10).

But these men were not satisfied even with such great and heinous blasphemies. They descended into so deep an abyss of misery that they are convinced—and carefully observe the practice—that none of their prayers can be acceptable to God unless in it they curse our Lord Jesus Christ, confessing him to be impious and the son of an impious man, that is, of some pagan whom they call PANDERA. They say that the Lord’s mother committed adultery with him, and that from this union was born the one in whom we believe.

[Col. 0170A] XLI. Against such enemies of the truth, and such rabid dogs raging against Christ, let us awaken within ourselves, as far as we can, the zeal of God, remembering that saying:

> “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10);

and again:

> “My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. CXVIII, 139);

and elsewhere:

> “Do I not hate those who hate you, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21–22).

Let us also take care that, among the countless and serious evils by which we have deserved God’s anger and justly endure his continual scourges, this especially wicked and detestable crime of blasphemy may be so restrained—or, if possible, with the cooperation of divine mercy, corrected through disciplinary censure and devotion to holy preaching—that it may not be counted as a grave charge against our most illustrious rulers and against us ourselves, who preside unworthily over the governance of the Churches.

For blessed Jerome also teaches (in chapter I of Nahum):

> “Just as we ought to be patient when we suffer personal injuries, so, if we see anyone blaspheming God with a sacrilegious mouth, we ought not to preserve our patience there, but to resist the sacrilegious person and condemn the blasphemous mouth by answering with the truth.”

Let us remember the holy anger of Phinehas, the severity of Elijah, the zeal of Simon the Canaanite, the severity of Peter, who slew Ananias and Sapphira, and the steadfastness of Paul, who condemned Elymas the magician to eternal blindness because he resisted the ways of the Lord. For cruelty on behalf of God is piety.

[Col. 0170C] What is especially grievous is that through these enemies of the cross of Christ, who speak whatever they wish with unrestrained freedom and act as they wish, continual losses of souls occur among us and in the various cities of his kingdom wherever that people is dispersed. Many Christians, contrary to the authority of the Scriptures and the decrees of the sacred canons, attach themselves to them so indiscriminately that they are continually polluted by their companionship and serve them both in their houses and in their fields.

Although they are not permitted to possess Christian slaves, they do have free Christian servants serving them. Their impiety advances among these people in accordance with what the Apostle says:

> “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33),

so that they say that these Christians preach better to them than our priests. Often their male and female hired workers keep the Sabbath with them, work with them on Sunday, violate the abstinence of Lent with them, and—what is more wretched—are even debauched by them. In very many places within our parishes, shameful to say, divine sacrifices are celebrated with their wine, deliberately polluted by them in many ways, which Christians continually drink and purchase.

XLII. We have been informed by certain people who come to Christianity from their error—and through whom their other evils are also faithfully explained to us—that some of them, who are illicitly appointed tax collectors in certain cities, are accustomed in more remote places to bind poor and ignorant Christians harshly on account of the same tax. Then they persuade them to deny Christ, and afterward release them as though they were treating them more leniently.

We ourselves have learned by reliable experience that they habitually lie in wait for those who, converted from their perfidy, believe and are baptized, with such malicious cunning that they say:

> “What harm is there if you believe in Christ? Hold only to this: God has no one like him or equal to him.”

Thus, as blessed Leo says concerning the devil (Sermon 7 on the Nativity of the Lord), these ministers of his do not cease everywhere to spread the snares of deception and to persist in corrupting the faith of believers by every possible means.

We have even heard some of them say that there is a greater God and a lesser God. Since they are convicted by many testimonies of the prophets of confessing the Lord Jesus Christ as God, they assert that he is less than the Father. Hence, in their widespread perfidy, they consider Christ a mere human being.

Others among them, being refuted by the foregoing argument, say that he was loved by God to such an extent that God gave him his name, but not the reality of the name.

The extent to which their wicked association and poisonous conversation advance impiety—since, as the Apostle says, “their speech spreads like gangrene” (II Tim. II, 17)—can be observed by everyone in the case of one man whom they miserably and horribly deceived.

For something that we do not remember ever having happened before occurred: a palace deacon, nobly born, nobly raised, trained in the offices of the Church, and well regarded by the prince, was seduced by them. Drawn away and enticed by their diabolical persuasions, he abandoned the palace, abandoned his homeland and parents, and entirely abandoned the kingdom of the Christians. Now in Spain, among the Saracens and associated with Jews, he has been persuaded by the impious to deny Christ the Son of God, profane the grace of baptism, accept carnal circumcision, and change his name, so that the man formerly called Bodo is now called Eliezer. Thus, wholly transformed into a Jew in superstition and appearance, bearded and married, he blasphemes Christ and his Church daily in the synagogues of Satan with the others.

XLIII. Therefore, this present year, detesting their impiety and desiring to remove from their contagion the Christian people entrusted to us in the Lord, I publicly announced—once, twice, and three times—that, in accordance with the ecclesiastical statutes, everyone should separate himself from their association, so that Christians would not serve them either in the city or in the villages. Rather, they themselves should conduct and provide for their necessities with their pagan slaves, and no one should be contaminated by their food or drink.

I also gave certain stricter orders, wishing to eradicate this long-standing evil completely and, with the Lord’s help, desiring to imitate the good example of our pious pastor, teacher, and predecessor, [Note: [Col. 0171D] Namely Agobard, who directed a letter against the Jews to Louis the Pious. EDIT.] a proven and orthodox man. While there was still some degree of peace in this kingdom, he labored greatly to correct this evil, not only by words but also by writings.

But because the work he began was obstructed by the turmoil of the times, I now fear divine judgment if, insofar as God grants the opportunity, I neglect it, lest those who on this account are contaminated, corrupted, or even perish be charged to my negligence and guilt.

XLIV. Therefore, let the unanimity of your holiness cooperate with and support us, so that by common effort, resolve, and supplication we may obtain from our pious rulers that throughout their kingdom the institutions of the holy canons and ancient laws concerning this matter be observed.

For—as we must faithfully announce, and they must receive with Christian piety—even concerning these servants and tributaries of theirs, although they are unbelievers, they will have to render an account to the King of kings and Lord of lords: how they restrained them from their impiety; how they urged them toward salvation; how they protected the Christian people from their contamination and depravity; and how, as pious sons and rulers of the Church, they did not neglect ecclesiastical statutes for the sake of the annual taxes and gifts that are paid to them.

For, speaking with due reverence, they do not possess a broader empire or a more eminent principate than those ancient and pious rulers in whose times both those statutes were sincerely observed and similar services were paid by the Jews.

Even if some of their fiscal slaves—who are, of course, Christians—were injurious and damaging to one of their neighbors in his field, vineyard, or livestock, they would certainly wish them to be restrained by secular laws and the injured man to have restored whatever injury and damage he had suffered.

How much more ought they, by royal strength and ecclesiastical authority, to prohibit and suppress these unbelieving slaves, who frequently and grievously injure the field of the Lord Jesus Christ, which he purchased with his precious blood—that is, the Church of the faithful?

Concerning this field, of which they too have been appointed guardians and cultivators, Scripture commands that it not be harmed, saying:

> “Do not touch the boundaries of the little ones, and do not enter the field of orphans. For their near kinsman is strong, and he himself will judge their case against you” (Prov. XXIII, 10).

XLV. But how great was the concern among Christian rulers—not only Roman but also Frankish and those of other peoples—for the enemies and blasphemers of the truth, among whom the Jews themselves must especially be counted; and how much discipline they exercised against them, whether to restrain or correct them, for love of Christ and the protection of the Church of God—we can better indicate if we briefly present certain examples from the sayings, deeds, and edicts of the holy Fathers concerning this matter.

Blessed Augustine speaks as follows of such people in his treatises on the evangelist John (Treatise XI):

> “These people even dare to say that they usually suffer persecution from Catholic kings or Catholic rulers. What persecution do they endure? Bodily affliction, if indeed they have ever suffered even that. The persecution they inflict is more serious. What they suffer is bodily; what they inflict concerns the deception of the spirit.
>
> “Listen and see in the ancient events themselves all the signs and indications of future things. We find that Sarah afflicted her maidservant Hagar. Sarah is free. After the maidservant began to grow proud, Sarah afflicted her severely, and Hagar fled from her presence. Behold, the free woman afflicted the maidservant, yet the Apostle does not call this persecution.
>
> “The slave plays with his master—that is, Ishmael with Isaac—and the Apostle calls this persecution. That affliction is not called persecution, while that mockery is called persecution.
>
> “Therefore, when God wishes to stir up authorities against heretics, schismatics, destroyers of the Church, those who insult Christ, and blasphemers of baptism, let them not be surprised that God stirs them up so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah.
>
> “Let Hagar recognize herself and bow her neck. For when she departed from her mistress, an angel met her and said: ‘What is the matter, Hagar, maidservant of Sarah?’ When she complained about her mistress, what did she hear from the angel? ‘Return to your mistress’ (Gen. XVI, 9).
>
> “She is therefore afflicted so that she may return. And would that she return! Yet they are surprised that Christian authorities are moved against the detestable destroyers of the Church. Would they then not be moved? And how would they render an account to God for their rule?
>
> “Let your charity attend to what I say: this concerns the Christian kings of the world, that in their times they should desire their mother, the Church from whom they were spiritually born, to be at peace.
>
> “We read the visions of Daniel and the prophetic deeds. Three boys praised God in the fire. King Nebuchadnezzar marveled at the boys praising God and at the fire that did not harm them. When he had marveled, what did he say? He was neither a Jew nor circumcised, he who had erected his statue and compelled everyone to worship it; yet he said: ‘I issue a decree to all tribes and languages throughout the whole earth: Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to death, and his house shall be destroyed’ (Dan. III, 96).
>
> “Behold how a foreign king rages lest the God of Israel be blasphemed. If Nebuchadnezzar praised God, proclaimed him, and gave glory to him who delivered the three boys from the fire—and gave glory by sending such a decree throughout his kingdom—how much more should those kings be moved and rage who see not three boys delivered from the flame but the whole world and themselves delivered from hell, when they see Christ, by whom they were delivered, insulted among Christians? When they hear a Christian being told: ‘Say that you are not a Christian’?
>
> “They wish to do such things, and at least they do not wish to suffer such things. For they kill souls while being afflicted in body.”

XLVI. If anyone thinks from these words of blessed Augustine that such measures ought to be taken only against heretics, let him remember from what precedes that the worst of the heretics are the Jews. And if the other heretics are rightly understood in the figure of the maidservant Hagar, much more so is the unbelieving Jewish people, concerning whom the Apostle teaches that the following must be understood:

> “Cast out the maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant will not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. XXI, 10).

The same blessed Augustine writes in a certain letter about this discipline, which should be piously exercised toward such people (Letter 204):

> “By no means should those who are loved be permitted, with impunity and cruelly, to follow their evil will. For if an evil will must always be permitted its freedom, why were the Israelites, when they resisted and murmured, restrained from evil by such harsh scourges and compelled toward the promised land?
>
> “If an evil will must always be permitted its freedom, why was Paul not permitted to follow the evil will by which he persecuted the Church? Rather, he was struck down so that he might be blinded; he was blinded so that he might be changed; he was changed so that he might be sent; he was sent so that, just as he had acted in error, he might suffer such things for the truth.
>
> “If an evil will must always be permitted its freedom, why are negligent shepherds rebuked, and why is it said to them: ‘You did not bring back the wandering one; you did not seek the lost’ (Ezek. XXXIV, 4)?
>
> “Many disciples indeed withdrew from the Lord, and were permitted, according to their own choice, to depart in evil and impious fashion. But to the other twelve who remained it was said: ‘Do you also wish to go away?’ (John VI, 68).
>
> “At that time, however, the Church was first beginning to sprout with new growth, and the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled in her: ‘All the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him’ (Ps. LXXI, 11).
>
> “The more this is fulfilled, the greater authority the Church exercises, so that she not only invites but also compels people to what is good. This was what the Lord wished to signify. Although he possessed great authority, he first chose to commend humility.
>
> “He also showed this clearly in the likeness of the banquet. He sent to those who had been invited, and they did not wish to come; and the word said: ‘Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame’ (Luke XIV, 21). And again: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled’ (ibid., 23).
>
> “Of those who came first it was said: ‘Bring them in’; it was not said: ‘Compel them.’ Thus the beginnings of the Church, while she was still growing, were signified, so that she might also have the strength to compel. Therefore, because it was necessary that, once strengthened by her power and greatness, people should also be compelled to the banquet of eternal salvation, after it had been said, ‘What you commanded has been done, and there is still room,’ he said: ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter.’
>
> “One who is compelled is forced to go where he does not wish; but once he has entered, he is nourished willingly.”

XLVII. Inflamed by this zeal for religion, the most Christian emperors Theodosius and Valentinian enacted a law of the following kind (Appendix to the Theodosian Code, Book VI):

> “Since it is not fitting for religious peoples to be corrupted by any superstitions, we order that the Manichaeans, all heretics and schismatics, astrologers, and every sect hostile to the Catholic faith be expelled from the very sight of the various cities, so that the cities may not be defiled even by the contagion of their presence.
>
> “We also deny Jews and pagans the right to conduct legal actions or to serve in the army. We do not wish Christian persons to serve them, lest, under the pretext of domination, they change the practice of the venerable religion.
>
> “We therefore order that all persons belonging to this disastrous error be excluded, unless timely correction comes to their aid.”

The same Augusti, in defense of the Christian religion and to suppress the impiety of Jews, Samaritans, heretics, and pagans, thereby appeasing the anger of God, which the madness of such people provokes, issued another edict (Novel of the Theodosian Code, concerning the Jews, Book I):

> “We recognize that the chief concern of imperial majesty is the investigation of true religion. If we maintain its worship, we open a path of prosperity to human affairs. Having learned this through long experience, we have resolved to establish for posterity, by the right of perpetual duration, the holy ceremonies that we know are attacked by the Jews, Samaritans, pagans, and other monstrous classes of heretics, whose understanding is blinded.
>
> “Therefore, lest these savage sects roam too freely into the life and customs of our age through indiscriminate confusion, we enact this law, which shall endure forever: no Jew and no Samaritan may attain honors or dignities; no administration of civil service shall be open to them, nor may they serve even as defenders.
>
> “For we have believed it unlawful that those who are enemies of the heavenly majesty and of Roman laws should, under the appearance of any office, dare to harass Christians or even priests with injuries on any pretext, or presume to condemn or adjudicate anyone according to our laws.
>
> “Nor may they preside over prison custody, lest Christians, as commonly happens, sometimes confined there, should suffer a second prison through the hatred of their guards.
>
> “They may not again dare to construct any synagogue. If they do so, let them know that the building will benefit the Catholic Church, and that the authors of the construction will be fined fifty pounds of gold. They may repair only the ruins of their synagogues, and that under the permission granted.
>
> “Any Jew who transfers a slave or free person, whether unwillingly or through punishable persuasion, from the worship of the Christian religion to a detestable sect and rite shall lose his property and be punished by death, being assigned the most just penalty of blood because he attacked another’s faith through perverse doctrine.
>
> “Anyone from among them who has insinuated himself into honors shall be treated as though he had always belonged to the lowest condition, lest we seem to have granted the benefit of immunity to detestable men through an insulting pursuit of privilege.
>
> “Any pagan found anywhere celebrating the wicked rites of sacrifices shall provoke our anger against his property and his blood, so that by such a victim the revered majesty of the heavenly deity may be appeased.
>
> “Whatever has been established by ancient laws against the Manichaeans, always offensive to God; against the Eunomians, authors of heretical perversity; against the Montanists, Phrygians, Photinians, Priscillianists, Codrogi [Perhaps Ascodrogi], Hydro-phobes, Borborites, and Ophites—let it be carried out promptly, with negligence set aside.
>
> “We have decreed these things in the insatiable honor of the Catholic religion, and we wish them to be brought to the knowledge of all cities and provinces and of everyone.”

XLVIII. We recall these things to memory not because we desire the blood of any person to be shed—far be that from us—but simply to note how great was the religious concern of Christian rulers and how severe their disciplinary judgment was toward Jews and other impious people.

Constantine, the great and most religious emperor, detesting Jewish impiety with this same zeal for piety and judging it wicked if they were permitted to propagate the sacrilegious rite of their superstition among any class of people, issued the following law (Theodosian Code, “That No Christian,” Book I):

> “If any Jew purchases a Christian slave or one belonging to any other sect and circumcises him, the slave shall be removed from the power of that Jew and remain free.”

Nor is it surprising that religious rulers established these and similar measures to restrain and repel Jewish superstition, since even the jurist Julius Paulus carefully expressed the ancient observance of the Roman people on this matter in the fifth book of his Sentences, in these words (Julius Paulus, Book V, title 22):

> “Roman citizens who permit themselves or their slaves to be circumcised according to the Jewish rite shall, after the confiscation of their property, be permanently deported to an island. Physicians shall be punished by death.”

He also says:

> “If Jews circumcise slaves purchased from another nation, they shall either be deported or punished by death.”

Here the pious foresight and diligence not only of our religious rulers but also of all the priests of the Lord must be especially vigilant, so that the souls of the wretched—that is, the slaves who have been deceived by them and held bound in the snare of impious superstition—may, through the benefit of such great laws, both be restored to freedom and, incorporated into the holy Church through the grace of baptism, be saved from the judgment of Gehenna. In the Gospel the Lord terrifyingly threatens this judgment not only against deceivers of this kind but also against those deceived, saying:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matt. XXIII, 15).

Jovianus, a most courageous and religious man, was chosen by the Roman army to assume the empire after the death of Julian the Apostate, whose sacrileges had profaned that army. Unwilling to rule over impious men, he publicly declared that he could not govern them because he was a Christian. Then, they say, all replied with one voice: “We too are Christians.” He was unwilling to accept the empire until he had heard this declaration. Thus, at one and the same time, he became emperor, confessor, and dispeller of the wrongly introduced error (Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History, Book XI, chapter 1).

[Col. 0176D] XLIX. Childebert, the most pious and Christian king of the Franks, issued an edict “that Jews, from the Lord’s Supper until the first Easter, be denied permission to walk through the streets or marketplace as though for the purpose of mockery” (Council of Orléans III, canon 30; Council of Mâcon I, canon 14).

Reccared, a most religious king in Spain, brought the entire Gothic people over whom he ruled from the perversity of the Arian heresy to the true faith. He did not permit anyone to serve in his kingdom who, through heretical perfidy, was not afraid to be an enemy in the kingdom of God.

His successor, King Sisebut, converted all the Jews subject to his kingdom to faith in Christ. To the former of these kings, blessed Pope Gregory wrote a letter of congratulation and exhortation, speaking as follows (St. Gregory, Book VII of the Register, Letter 128):

> “I cannot express in words, most excellent son, how much I rejoice in your work and your life. In our own days we have heard of the power of a new miracle: through your excellence the entire Gothic people has been transferred from the error of the Arian heresy to the firmness of the true faith.
>
> “With the prophet I desire to cry out: ‘This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High’ (Ps. LXXVI, 11).
>
> “When this great work is known, whose heart, even if made of stone, would not immediately grow tender in praise of almighty God and in love for your excellence?
>
> “I confess that I often enjoy telling my sons, when we are gathered together, of what has been accomplished through you, and often marveling at it with them.
>
> “These things also frequently stir me against myself, because I, lazy and useless, then lie inert in idleness when kings labor for the gathering of souls and the gain of the heavenly homeland.
>
> “In your work and in our rejoicing, I wish to cry out with the angels: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’ (Luke II, 14).”

Since the same king had already begun to labor in his kingdom to correct the perfidy of the Jews as well, blessed Gregory adds shortly afterward:

> “Moreover, I declare that your work has increased the praises of God. When your excellence issued a certain constitution against the perfidy of the Jews, and those against whom it had been issued attempted to bend the rectitude of your mind by offering a sum of money, your excellence despised the offer, seeking to please the judgment of almighty God, and preferred innocence to gold.
>
> “In this matter the deed of King David comes to my mind. When the water he desired from the cistern of Bethlehem, which lay among enemy forces, had been brought to him by his obedient soldiers, he immediately said: ‘Far be it from me to drink the blood of just men’ (II Sam. XXIII, 16–17). Because he poured it out and refused to drink it, it is written: ‘He poured it out as a libation to the Lord.’
>
> “If, therefore, water despised by an armed king was turned into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what kind of sacrifice the king offered to almighty God who, for love of him, refused to accept not water but gold.
>
> “Therefore, most excellent son, I shall say confidently: You poured out gold as a libation to the Lord, because you did not wish to possess it against him.”

L. The same blessed Pope Gregory, writing to Theoderic and Theodebert, kings of the Franks, and to Queen Brunichild, admonishes them in these words not to allow Christians to serve Jews (Book VII of the Register, Letter 115):

> “We were astonished that in your kingdom you permit Jews to possess Christian slaves. For what are all Christians except members of Christ? We all know that you faithfully honor the head of these members. But let your excellence consider how contradictory it is to honor the head and permit his members to be trampled by his enemies.
>
> “Therefore we ask that your constitution remove this evil of wickedness from your kingdom, so that in this matter you may show yourselves more worthy worshipers of almighty God, because you free his faithful from his enemies.”

Similarly, the same pope, writing to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, teaches that Christians—and even Jews’ own sons, if they become Christians—should render them nothing except what is proper and appropriate for God’s sake, and should not remain in their houses. He writes as follows (Book VII of the Register, Letter 35):

> “It has been reported to us that Basil, a Hebrew whose sons, by God’s favor, are Christians, wishes to grant certain slaves to them by right of gift only on the condition that, under cover of this opportunity, they serve him, with only the title of lordship removed; and afterward, if they should happen to believe that they ought to flee to the Church and become Christians, they should be claimed not as free persons but as belonging to those to whom they had previously been given.
>
> “In this matter it is fitting that your Fraternity be vigilant. If he wishes to give any slaves to his sons, so that every opportunity for fraud may be removed, they must in every way become Christians and not remain in his house. But when circumstances require that he make use of their assistance, they must be ordered to prevent this. That is also what it is fitting for his own sons to provide him, and what is appropriate for God’s sake.”

### LI

In accordance with these examples and the decrees of former rulers, and with the admonitions of the most blessed father and pontiff, we must faithfully and vigilantly, with the Lord’s help, persevere, lest the peoples of the faithful be stained and corrupted by association and contact with the impious. For when faithful emperors and holy rulers of the Church established such measures, they followed the authority of divine law in every respect and commended it to us for observance. That law shows this Jewish people, because of its infidelity and impiety, to be accursed and detestable in all things, saying to it through Moses:

> “If you will not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, so as to keep and do all his commandments, all these curses will come upon you and overtake you. You shall be accursed in the city and accursed in the field; accursed shall be your granary, and accursed your stores; accursed the fruit of your womb. You shall be accursed when you enter, and accursed when you depart. The Lord will send famine upon you” (Deut. 28:15–20), and so forth.

We now plainly see all these things fulfilled in this unhappy people. Because of its iniquity, by which it denied the Son of God, it was accursed in the city of Jerusalem before the captivity, and accursed in the field of the whole world after the captivity. Not only were its granary and stores accursed, but also the fruit of its womb, that is, its children, just as those wicked fathers cursed both themselves and their children, saying:

> “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

This people is accursed when entering this life by birth and accursed when departing from it by death. The Lord sent upon it the famine that he had threatened through the prophet Amos, saying:

> “Behold, the days are coming, when I will send a famine upon the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord. They shall wander from sea to sea and from north to east, seeking the word of the Lord, and they shall not find it” (Amos 8:11–12).

For now, indeed, although they seek and meditate upon the Law and the Prophets and are scattered throughout the whole world, they do not find the Word of the Lord, that is, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ. Although knowledge of him shines throughout the whole world like the midday sun from heaven, they grope like blind people in darkness, as was said to them in those very curses of the Law:

> “May the Lord strike you with madness, blindness, and derangement of mind; and you shall grope at midday, as a blind man gropes in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways” (Deut. 28:28–29).

Through this blindness they also incur that curse which is the cause of all the others. Among the rest, as it is properly written in Hebrew, it is stated thus:

> “And your life shall hang before you; you shall fear night and day, and you shall not trust in your life” (Deut. 28:66).

What is this life of the people of God except the one who says in the Gospel:

> “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25),

and concerning whom Jeremiah says on behalf of all the elect:

> “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins; of him we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’?” (Lam. 4:20).

The Jews saw this life of theirs hanging before them on the wood of the cross. While doubting whether to believe in his presence, they feared night and day—that is, both when his majesty was hidden from them by his sufferings and when it was revealed through his miracles. Thus, while they hesitated before the former and despised the latter, they did not believe in their life.

This curse certainly remains among them to this day. For while they refuse to believe that their life, which had first been destined for them—according to the Lord’s saying, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24)—was raised from the dead, so that through this faith they might be given life and be able to say with the prophet, “After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6:3), they continue to mock their life to this day as though it were hanging on a gallows.

Hence in our edition it is rightly translated: “And your life shall be as though hanging before you,” namely because the disgrace of the cross, which passed away when Christ rose from the dead, is mocked by their impiety and blindness as though it still remained.

And because they, like natural branches, became degenerate and were broken away from the root of the patriarchs, while the wild olive of the nations was grafted into the good olive, they still hear among those very curses:

> “The foreigner who lives with you shall rise above you and become higher, while you shall descend and become lower” (Deut. 28:43–44). He shall lend to you, and you shall not lend to him. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail.

As we plainly see, the Church from the nations lends money to that people—the money of the word of God—but they have nothing with which to lend. The people of the nations is the head, possessing the Lord Jesus Christ; they are the tail, because they have fallen from the head.

This they will indeed always remain until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved—that is, all who are to be saved. For concerning those of these people who are now unbelieving, the Lord will increase the plagues, as it is written in those curses: great and lasting plagues, most evil and perpetual diseases. Another translation says, “most true plagues and true diseases.”

The Lord speaks to the prophet Haggai:

> “Ask the priests of the Law, saying: If one who is unclean in soul touches any of these things—bread, wine, oil, cooked food, or any kind of food—will it be defiled?” And the priests answered, “It will be defiled.” And the Lord said: “So is this people, and so is this nation before my face” (Hag. 2:12–15).

Hence the Apostle also confirms this, saying:

> “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15),

so that we may understand that the tables of the unclean are themselves unclean. For how could the tables of those whose granaries and storehouses are accursed not be unclean?

### LII

Therefore, according to the authority of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, the most holy and blessed fathers and rulers of the churches of God instruct and compel us, by their examples and synodal decrees, completely to avoid association and fellowship with this accursed and unclean people. We believe that these decrees should now be briefly recorded and, with priestly diligence, brought to the knowledge of all.

The life written about the blessed confessor Hilary shows how carefully he always avoided the profane associations of Jews and heretics. He so abhorred such enemies of the Church that he shared with them not only no meal but not even a greeting when they passed by. In doing this the holy man observed that apostolic command:

> “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 1:11).

### LIII

Concerning Saint Ambrose, an outstanding confessor, renowned both for his teaching and for his miracles, it is written in his deeds as follows (Paulinus, *Life of St. Ambrose*):

> “In the regions of the East, in a certain town, the synagogue of the Jews was burned by Christian men, because the Jews had insulted Christian monks. Therefore the comes of the East sent a report concerning this matter to the emperor Theodosius. When he received it, the emperor ordered that the synagogue should be rebuilt by the bishop.
>
