> “But when the substance of this order reached the ears of the venerable Bishop Ambrose, since he himself could not arrive in time, he sent a letter to the emperor (Book II, Letter 17). In it he urged him to revoke what had been decreed and demanded that the emperor grant him a hearing. If he was not worthy to be heard by the emperor, then the emperor was not worthy to be heard on his behalf, nor to entrust his prayers or vows to him. Ambrose declared himself ready to suffer death for such a matter, lest by his silence he make the emperor a transgressor, since the emperor had issued so unjust an order against the Church.
>
> “Later, when he returned to Milan, after the emperor had been seated in the church, he discussed the same matter before the people. In that discussion he introduced the person of the Lord speaking to the emperor:

> “‘I made you emperor from the lowest condition; I handed over to you the army of your enemy; I gave you the forces that he had prepared against you with his army; I reduced your enemy to your power; I established one of your offspring upon the throne of the kingdom; I made you triumph without labor. And do you grant triumphs over me to my enemies?’

> “When the emperor descended from the raised seat, he said: ‘Today, bishop, you have brought an accusation against us.’ But Ambrose replied that he had spoken not against him but for him.

> “Then the emperor said: ‘In truth, I had issued harsh orders concerning the restoration of the synagogue; but it was said that vengeance should be taken upon the monks by the counts who were present at the time.’ To them the bishop replied: ‘I am dealing with the emperor; with you I must deal differently.’

> “And so he obtained the revocation of what had been decreed. He was unwilling to approach the altar until the emperor had testified on his faith that he ought to act accordingly. The bishop said to him: ‘Then I act on your faith.’ The emperor replied: ‘Act on my faith.’ After this pledge had been repeated, the priest confidently celebrated the divine mysteries.”

### LIV

In this deed of so great a man, who could in no way tolerate that the synagogue of the Jews, although burned by Christians, should be restored by the bishop and by those same Christians, and who was prepared to suffer death for such a matter lest he make the emperor a transgressor, what else must our rulers consider, and what else must we imitate with all our strength, except first that they must beware of granting honor to the enemies of Christ against Christ, who exalted them so honorably?

Next, let us all understand equally that their synagogue—the synagogue, certainly, of Satan—is a sacrilegious house erected against the Church of God, not a house of prayer but a den of robbers. It was therefore wholly unworthy that Christians should erect their house of sacrilege and blasphemy against Christ. And if this had been done under compulsion from the emperor, the emperor would undoubtedly have become a transgressor against the Christian religion.

They have been permitted to conduct their civil affairs in secular courts, but their sacrileges must always be abominated and never shared. To prevent a Christian emperor and a Christian people from sharing in them through transgression, the holy man believed that he would receive martyrdom if he suffered death for such a cause.

### LV

Alchimus Avitus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, an outstanding and orthodox teacher; Saint Apollinaris, bishop of the Church of Valence, whose merits are still gloriously attested by his frequent miracles; Saint Gregory, bishop of the Church of Langres, whose revered memory still flourishes in the Church; and the blessed Viventiolus, bishop of the Church of Lyon, whose teaching is also attested by the writings of others about him, together with twenty other most reverend bishops, assembled in the name of the Lord for the defense and stability of the Church, decreed the following among other matters (Council of Epaon, canon 15):

> “If a cleric of superior rank attends the banquet of any heretic, he shall not have the peace of the Church for a year. If younger clerics presume to do so, they shall be flogged. Our constitution has also forbidden laymen to attend Jewish banquets. Nor shall anyone who has been defiled by a Jewish banquet eat bread with any of our clergy.”

And in the conclusion of their statutes, trusting in the Lord’s presence, as he himself says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20), they decreed as follows:

> “Accordingly, if any of the holy bishops who have confirmed these decisions by their own subscriptions, or any successors whom God may appoint to them, should depart from the integrity of this observance after these matters have been approved by common consent through heavenly inspiration, let him know that he will be guilty before the judgment both of God and of the brotherhood.”

### LVI

Saint Caesarius, bishop of the Church of Arles, whose merit and teaching are attested by his life, his written miracles, and his many distinguished works, together with thirty-five other bishops or vicars of bishops, assembled in the name of the Lord for the defense and confirmation of Catholic truth, decreed among other matters as follows (Council of Agde, canon 40):

> “Henceforth all clerics and laypeople alike shall avoid Jewish banquets, and no one shall receive them at a banquet. Since they do not use the common foods of Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to consume their food, when they judge unclean the things that we consume with the Apostle’s permission. Thus Catholics would begin to be lower than Jews: if we use what they set before us, while they despise what is offered by us.”

### LVII

Priscus, bishop of the Church of Lyon; Arthemius of Sens; Remedius of Bourges; and Saint Syagrius, bishop of the Aedui, together with many others, renewing the ecclesiastical statutes, defined as follows (First Council of Mâcon, canon 13):

> “Let Jews not be appointed judges for Christian peoples, nor be permitted to act as tax collectors, through which arrangement—God forbid—Christians might appear to be subject to them.”

**Canon 14.**

> “Let Jews be denied permission, from the Lord’s Supper until the first day of Easter, according to the edict of the late King Childebert, to walk through the streets or marketplace as though for the purpose of insulting others; and let them show reverence to all the Lord’s priests and clerics. Nor should they presume to occupy a seat before priests unless they have been ordained. If they should presume to do so, let them be restrained by the judges of the places, according to the standing of the person involved.”

**Canon 15.**

> “Let no Christian presume to participate in Jewish banquets. If any cleric or layperson should presume to do so—something impious to say—let whoever has been defiled by their impieties know that he is to be excluded from the fellowship of all Christians.”

**Canon 16.**

> “Although it was established long ago, not only by the canons but also by the benefits of the laws, what must be preserved concerning Christians who are entangled in Jewish service either through captivity or through any kind of fraud, nevertheless, because a complaint has now arisen that certain Jews residing in cities or municipalities have broken out into such insolence and arrogance that even when Christians protest, they do not allow them to be freed from their servitude, not even for a price, we therefore decree in the present council, with God as our guide, that no Christian shall henceforth serve a Jew. Rather, upon payment of twelve solidi for each able-bodied slave, any Christian shall have permission to redeem that slave either into freedom or into service.

> “For it is impious that those whom Christ the Lord redeemed by the shedding of his blood should remain entangled in the bonds of persecutors. If any Jew should refuse to comply with what we have decreed, then, for as long as he delays accepting the stipulated sum, the slave himself shall be permitted to live with Christians wherever he wishes.

> “We also specifically decree that if any Jew is convicted of persuading a Christian slave to adopt the Jewish error, he shall both lose that slave and be punished by legal condemnation.”

### LVIII

Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, together with twenty-four other bishops or vicars of bishops, likewise assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ for matters concerning his body, which is the Church. Among many other decisions they decreed the following (Third Council of Orléans, canon 30):

> “Since, by God’s favor, we live under the rule of Catholic kings, from the day of the Lord’s Supper until the second day of the week during Easter—that is, throughout those four days—Jews shall not presume to go out among Christians or to mingle with Catholic peoples in any place or on any occasion.”

In the Council of Laodicea (canons 37 and 38) it was decreed:

> “It is not permitted to receive from Jews or heretics the festive gifts that are sent, nor to celebrate festivals with them. Nor is it permitted to receive unleavened bread from Jews or to share in their impieties.”

And in another council (First Council of Clermont, canon 6):

> “If anyone is joined to Jewish depravity in a marital union—that is, if either a Christian woman is joined in carnal association with a Jew or a Jewish woman with a Christian—those who are known to have committed so great a crime shall immediately be excluded from the Christian assembly and banquet and from communion with the Church.”

### LIX

Behold, the most holy and reverend fathers of the churches of God, our predecessors in the Lord, define all these matters with the utmost clarity, even under protestation of divine judgment, and hand them down to us for observance without prejudice: the sacrilegious association of the Jews, like that of all other heretics, must be utterly detested; their profane and sacrilegious banquet must be judged such; and whoever shares with them in this manner is declared to be defiled by their impieties.

What, then, must we attempt and do in response, except that, envying them nothing in their life, salvation, peace, or wealth—but rather sincerely seeking their true salvation, for which the Church is accustomed solemnly to pray—we should preserve ecclesiastical sincerity and discipline toward them and ensure that the peoples of the faithful entrusted to us are in no way allowed to become entangled in their contaminations and sacrileges?

### LX

For we must not make people who are ruined and do not see their own ruin—that is, the Jews themselves—falsely secure through our flattery, praise, or, God forbid, defenses. We must not become deceivers of those whose correctors we ought to be.

The Lord threatens such people through the prophet, saying:

> “Those who bless this people, and those who are blessed, shall be thrown down” (Isa. 9:16).

But we must vigilantly restrain their blasphemies and frequently announce to them what the Lord himself terribly threatens them with, saying:

> “For if you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins” (John 8:24).

We should strive, insofar as we can by God’s gift, to imitate the Apostle’s compassion and kindness. Concerning them he says:

> “I speak the truth in Christ—I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit—that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, my kindred according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9:1–4).

And again:

> “Brothers, the desire of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation” (Rom. 10:1).

And elsewhere:

> “Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the nations, I will glorify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” (Rom. 11:13–15).

Finally, we must faithfully impress upon everyone that all must fear and beware lest, just as at the time of his Passion our Lord Jesus Christ—who was to reconcile all things through the blood of his cross—was sold by a false disciple and handed over by false persecutors to be mocked and crucified, so now he should in some way be purchased by the impious Jews for more freely insulting and blaspheming him.

**In the year of the Lord 853. Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt.**

---

## Historical and Bibliographical Notice

*(Fabricius, [*Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*].)*

### Haymo

Haymo, a disciple of Alcuin, together with Rabanus Maurus, who esteemed him as a friend and dedicated to him his twenty-two books *On the Universe*; teacher of Henry of Auxerre; an imitator of Bede’s studies and diligence; formerly a Benedictine monk of Fulda and, in 839, master at Hersfeld [**Note:** Trithemius, chapter 257, wrote that he had been an abbot, and others follow him. Christoph Browerus denies this in *Fuldensian Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 13, as does D. Paulus Antonius ὁ Μακαρίτης (“the Blessed”) in his dissertation *On the Life and Teaching of Haymo*, Halle in Saxony, 1700, pp. 5 ff.]; in 839, monk of Hersfeld; and from 841 to 853 [**Note:** Not 834, as Trithemius has it; nor 858, as Combefis has it in the *Concionatory Library*] bishop of Halberstadt.

He took part in the synod of Mainz in 848, at which Gottschalk was condemned. John of Winnigstedt records in his manuscript *Chronicle* [**Note:** In D. Antonius, p. 8] that Haymo enriched the cathedral church of Halberstadt with a distinguished library, collected at considerable expense, but that it perished in a disastrous fire in 1179.

Melchior Neofanius, in his *Catalogue of the Bishops of Halberstadt*, writes of Haymo:

> He was an example of piety, devoted to study,  
> and continually produced sacred books  
> in a long succession, with learned commentaries,  
> leaving the divine volumes enlarged . . .

Winnigstedt likewise testifies (p. 12) that the same Haymo

> Explains the whole Bible by his own ingenuity.

The works surviving in print from his commentaries are as follows.

### Commentary on the Psalms

A commentary which he gathered, like a spiritual little bee, from the most flourishing gardens and meadows of all the ancients—Augustine, Cassiodorus, and others. It was published at Freiburg, Antwerp, Cologne, and Paris, in 1533, octavo, through the efforts of Erasmus; see his Book XXVIII, Letter 11.

Appended to this commentary are scholia on the Song of Isaiah 12; on King Hezekiah, Isaiah 38; on Hannah, the mother of Samuel, 1 Samuel 2; on Moses, Exodus 15; on the prophet Habakkuk, chapter 3; and on Moses, Deuteronomy 32.

### On Isaiah

Three books, published by Nicholas Herborn of the Order of Friars Minor, Cologne, 1531, octavo.

### On the Twelve Prophets and the Song of Songs

An exposition, Cologne, 1533, octavo. I am surprised that Hosea is omitted by William Crovaeus, p. 165 of the *Catalogue of Writers on Scripture*, and by Jacob Longus, p. 766 of the *Sacred Library*. For in this volume the first commentary presented is on Hosea, in which, as elsewhere, Haymo willingly follows Jerome.

Those who attribute the exposition of the Song of Songs either to Cassiodorus or to Thomas Aquinas rely on a slight conjecture. Certainly all writers include a commentary on the Song of Songs among Haymo’s works, including the anonymous writer of Melk, chapter 76.

### Homilies or Popular Sermons on the Gospels

The summer and winter parts, for Sundays, weekdays, and saints’ days. Cologne, 1534, octavo, two volumes, edited by Godfrey Hittorp; and, more accurately corrected, 1540, octavo.

Some of Haymo’s homilies are also found in Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary* on the annual Gospel readings. See below under *Homiliary*. They are also included in Combefis’s *Concionatory Library*.

### Commentaries on All the Epistles of Paul

These were derived from Hilary the Deacon—who is Ambrose in this work—as well as Augustine, Origen, and others. Published in 1528, octavo, without place of publication; and Cologne, 1539, octavo.

Under the false name of Remigius of Rheims [**Note:** Rivetus, *Sacred Critics*, Book IV, chapter 27], they were published by Juan Bautista Villalpando, Rome, 1598, folio, and reprinted at Mainz, 1614, folio.

Some wished to attribute them to Remigius of Lyon [**Note:** Blondellus, p. 87 ff., *On Bishops*], others, more plausibly, to Remigius of Auxerre [**Note:** Albertinus, *On the Holy Eucharist*, p. 937]. See Richard Simon, Book III of the *Critical History of the New Testament*, chapter 26.

The editors of the new edition of the *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 42, note that a brief work by Haymo, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, was taken from his commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, found and published by Dacherus in vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 27, appended to his sermons. But in Haymo’s commentary on 1 Corinthians 11 I find nothing of the kind. If the work was written by Haymo, it would be difficult to cite any older witness or clearer advocate of μετουσίωσις—“transubstantiation”—whose confession is so explicit:

> “We believe, faithfully confess, and hold that the substance of bread and wine is substantially converted, through the operation of divine power, into another substance, that is, into flesh and blood.”

The passage from Paul the Deacon which Mabillon places before Haymo’s text in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 215 (new edition, p. 497), is likewise far from being capable of serving as such an unequivocal testimony.

### On the Apocalypse

Seven books, Paris, 1535, octavo, based on Ansbertus, Primasius, Bede, and others.

I have seen no more, although Trithemius, and after him Bale, XIII.8; Pitseus, p. 147; and others mention works by Haymo on the five books of Moses; Joshua; Judges; Ruth; the four Books of Kings; two books of Chronicles; Ezra; Nehemiah; Esther; Tobit; Judith; Job; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; the Acts of the Apostles; and the canonical Epistles, in seven books; as well as a book *On the Holy Trinity*.

Honorius, IV.7, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, also praises Haymo’s book *On the Pleasure of the World*. But I have not found the short exposition of the canons mentioned in the dissertation *On the Life and Teaching of Haymo*, p. 14, nor the four books of commentaries on the four Evangelists mentioned by Pitseus, p. 147.

### On the Memory of Christian Affairs [**Note:** This is the genuine title found in manuscripts and in Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, XII.9, as well as in Trithemius and others. In Turrianus, p. 37 of the *Apology for the Apostolic Canons*, Haymo is cited under the title *On the Memorable Events of Christian Affairs*], from the birth of Christ to the time of Theodosius the Great, in ten books: a concise abridgment of the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius and Rufinus.

It was published by Alexander Brassicanus, Hagenau, 1531, octavo; Cologne, 1531, octavo, and 1573; 1600, duodecimo; and under the care of Marcus Zuerius Boxhornius, together with elementary materials on the Christian religion written in the ancient language of the Alemanni and Saxons, Leiden, 1650, duodecimo. It was also published from the recension of Johann Joachim Mader, Helmstedt, 1671, quarto, and with the notes of Petrus Galesinius, Rome, 1564, folio, appended to works by Salvian, Maximus of Turin, Pacianus, Sulpicius Severus, and Dorotheus of Tyre.

It was also published in French, translated by Claude d’Espence, Paris, 1573. Certain emendations by Latinius are found in his *Sacred and Profane Library*, p. 166.

### On the Variety of Books, or On the Love of the Heavenly Homeland

Three books, Cologne, 1531, octavo, and Paris.*

Eucharius Cervicornus, who prepared and published the Cologne edition of Haymo’s commentary on Isaiah from 1531, warned in his preface to that work that, at the very time when the typesetters were laboring to print the book, a work of Haymo’s commentary had appeared somewhere, apparently a recension—or revision—prepared by Haymo himself.

He said that he could in no way be persuaded that Haymo had undertaken the same work twice, since Haymo himself had never mentioned such a thing and the German archives contained only a single copy of his commentary on Isaiah. He therefore judged the latter work either to be the product of another Haymo—perhaps the Haymo, an alumnus of the Franciscan family, whom Trithemius lists among ecclesiastical writers—or the fabrication of some pseudonymous author.

This new commentary of Haymo on Isaiah may perhaps be the work published by the Parisians in that same year, 1531.

When I was examining a certain codex of the library of the canons of the major church of Lucca, I found, among many excerpts from the Fathers collected by an anonymous writer, several passages copied into an exposition of the mystery of the Holy Trinity from Haymo’s commentaries on Isaiah, as the title itself stated.

When I compared these passages with the Haymian commentaries published at Cologne, I found that they differed entirely from them. Apart from a few small points of agreement, they diverged in every other respect. I therefore suspect that these fragments of the Lucca codex are remnants of that other commentary by Haymo. Since few had seen the printed Parisian work, I copied these fragments and here present one as a specimen.

As for the author, I have nothing to offer. Nevertheless, I would have preferred to attribute it to the Haymo who was archdeacon of Canterbury, a writer of the eleventh century, whom, among other works, English writers assign commentaries on Isaiah; Fabricius testifies to this.

I shall now present, by way of a specimen, a single passage from the manuscript fragments, to which I shall append a similar passage found in the Cologne editions.

> “The seraphim stood above it; each had six wings. With two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. And one cried to the other, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.’
>
> “Seraphim means ‘those who burn,’ in accordance with what we read elsewhere: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire.’ The Lord is shown in the seraphim in part and hidden in part. For they cover his face and his feet. We cannot know what came before the world or what will come after the world; they contemplate only what lies between, what was made in the six days.
>
> “Nor is it surprising to believe this about the seraphim, since the apostles likewise reveal the Savior to believers and conceal him from unbelievers. The veil was also before the ark of the covenant.
>
> “They are said to have wings because of their speed and their movement throughout all things, or because they always dwell in higher places. For the statement about the winds—‘who walks upon the wings of the winds’—does not truly testify, in accordance with the fables of poets, that the winds possess wings through the license of painters. Rather, it signifies their swift movement throughout all things.
>
> “Rather, it signifies swift movement throughout all things; and the passage concerning six wings for each, which we know only from the creation of the world, also concerns the present age [the wording is textually uncertain]. When it says, ‘one cries to the other,’ or, according to the Hebrews, ‘this one to that one,’ that is, one to another, they exhort one another to the praises of the Lord and say, ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts,’ so that they may display the mystery of the Trinity in the one divinity.
>
> “They testify that no longer is the temple of the Jews, as formerly, but the whole earth full of his glory—he who for our salvation deigned to assume a human body and descend to the earth.
>
> “Some Latin writers understand the two seraphim as the Old and New Testaments, since the text speaks only of the present age. Hence they are said to have six wings, to cover the face and feet of God, to offer testimony to the truth in rivalry with one another, and to reveal the mystery of the Trinity in everything they cry out. They marvel at one another that the Lord of hosts, being in the form of God, should rather have taken the form of a servant and humbled himself even to death, even death on a cross; and that not only the heavenly beings should know him as Father, but the earth also.”

The Cologne edition of 1531 reads as follows:

> “The seraphim stood above it. The two seraphim are understood as the two Testaments, the New and the Old. For ‘seraphim’ means ‘one who burns’ or ‘burning.’ And if we ask where this salutary burning may be found, there is no doubt that it is in the sacred volumes, from whose reading all human vices are cleansed and the inmost recesses of the heart are kindled with love of God and neighbor.”

The remainder has no connection whatsoever with the manuscript.

The work of the Homilies has never, as I believe, been sufficiently examined by writers on literary history. The very learned authors of the *Gallican Literary History*, vol. V, p. 118, observed that there are two editions of Haymo’s *Homilies*, very different from one another: one under the title:

“An excellent work of D. Haymo, bishop, etc., of Homilies—or, if you prefer, Sermons—to the People on the Gospels of the Entire Year; Winter Part. Cologne, 1531, octavo, edited by Gottfried Hittorp.” [Col. 0188C]

The other bears the title:

“Homilies of D. Haymo, bishop, etc., on the Sunday Gospels.”

They declare the former work to be genuinely Haymo’s, while they attribute the latter to an earlier Haymo at the abbey of Hirsau, who began that office in the year 1091. They say that Haymo’s work was first printed at Cologne by Cervicornus in the year 1531, in octavo. On turning the pages, I find Haymo’s winter part of the *Homilies*, printed without the printer’s name, to have been published at Cologne in 1537 at the expense of M. Gottfried Hittorp. In the dedicatory letter given by Hittorp, I read that this edition was prepared from a copy of a manuscript received from Peter Drolshagen, abbot of Heisterbach. Hittorp, however, notes that shortly before that time there had appeared a work of Haymo’s *Homilies* “perhaps by a good author, either deprived of his proper name, or, if his name was Haymo, certainly [Col. 0188D] not the one whom we now publish, namely the bishop of Halberstadt.” That letter is dated 3 August 1532.

From this I conclude that the genuine Cologne edition appeared in 1532. How, then, could those French writers have asserted that the Cologne edition edited by Hittorp belonged to the year 1531? Nor is the name of Eucharius Cervicornus, the printer, found there either. If, therefore, there was a Cologne edition of 1531, it is plainly different from the genuine edition prepared by Hittorp.

Finally, this Cologne edition of 1537 has not, so far as I have read, been mentioned by anyone. The summer part of the same *Homilies* is likewise marked by me as printed in 1537 by Cervicornus, whose name appears there. Its title is as follows:

“The summer part of the *Homilies* of D. Haymo, etc., now carefully printed for the fourth time.”

This part was enlarged by an appendix of twenty-three homilies of Haymo on the Sunday Epistles after the feast of Pentecost, which had hitherto been missing and are now printed for the first time, except for four [Col. 0189A] previously printed once. In addition to these, two other homilies were added on two readings from the Apocalypse. The first of these had previously been printed only once; the second had nowhere been printed before this date.

This final volume contains no preface. Yet the title, accurately reported in this way, clearly demonstrates that the editions of this work have not hitherto been reported and examined with sufficient accuracy by writers on literary history, as will be evident to anyone comparing what they say. The same French writers also say that they do not sufficiently understand what Crowe means when, in his *Catalogue of Writers on Sacred Scripture*, he states that an exposition on all the canonical Epistles is attached to this work.

I believe, however, that I have discovered where that English writer obtained this information. For this is what I read in the title of the previously mentioned edition of the winter *Homilies*: “Some very beautiful sermons of the same Haymo on the canonical Epistles have been added.” Yet anyone who carefully turns through that volume is nowhere able to find them.

[Col. 0189A]

## The Life of D. Haymo by John Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim

[Col. 0189B]

Haymo was the third bishop of the Church of Halberstadt in Saxony. He had previously been abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and was German by nationality. He had once been a student of the monk Alcuin, for whom Rabanus, then abbot of Fulda, composed twenty-two books *On the Universe*. Haymo was certainly a man learned in every field, a most discerning interpreter of the divine Scriptures, and a man of outstanding ability in delivering homilies to the people.

He was first a monk of the monastery of Fulda together with Rabanus; afterward he became the third abbot of Hersfeld; finally he was consecrated the third bishop of Halberstadt. He governed that same Church vigorously by word and example for thirteen years.

He wrote almost innumerable short works, among which the following are reported:

| Work | Books |
|---|---:|
| On the five books of Moses | 5 |
| On Judges | 1 |
| On Kings | 1 |
| On Tobit | 1 |
| On Judith | 1 |
| On Job | 1 |
| On the prophet Isaiah | 3 |
| On Jeremiah | 1 |
| On Ezekiel | 1 |
| On Daniel | 1 |
| On the twelve minor prophets | 12 |
| Also on the Psalms | 1 |
| Homilies on the Gospels | 2 |
| On all the Epistles of Paul | 1 |
| On the canonical Epistles | 7 |
| On the Apocalypse | 1 |
| On the variety of books | 3 |
| On the Holy Trinity | 1 |
| On the Christian … of things [uncertain] | 1 |
| On Joshua | 1 |
| On Ruth | 1 |
| On Chronicles | 1 |
| On Ezra and Nehemiah | 1 |
| On Esther | 1 |
| On the Song of Songs | 1 |
| “Isaiah the noble prophet” | |
| “And it came to pass, etc., says the blessed man” | |
| “The Word that was made” | |
| “They are called hymns, etc.” | |

| “From Corinth, the metropolitan city” | |
| On the Acts of the Apostles | 1 |
| “We read in Ecclesiastes” | |
| “Since you are one and most holy” | |

He is also said to have written many other letters, sermons, and various treatises that have not come to my notice. He died under Louis the Emperor, the son of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 834, in the twelfth indiction. He was buried in the Church of Saint Stephen at Halberstadt.

[Col. 0191]

# The First Part of the Works of Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt

## Biblical Commentaries

### A Pious, Brief, and Clear Explanation of All the Psalms

He gathered this, like a spiritual little bee, from all the most flourishing gardens and meadows of the ancients, so that an abundant supply of the most wholesome honey might be available to the simple and the occupied.

*(From the edition published at Cologne in 1561, edited by Erasmus, at the press of the heirs of Johann Quentel.)* (G)*

## Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam Sends Greetings to the Distinguished Man John Emstedius, Carthusian of Louvain

[Col. 0191A]

Although I am well aware, dearest brother, that you are not without companions who enliven your solitude and do not allow this silence to remain mute, it nevertheless seemed appropriate to add one companion who speaks piously rather than eloquently. Yet I do not see how it can be denied that what is spoken piously is also spoken eloquently.

This companion is Haymo, N., monk, abbot, and bishop, who explains the Psalms of David with remarkable brevity and remarkable simplicity and clarity. For several centuries this was the practice of learned monks: whatever the ancients had written either more subtly for the learned or more expansively for the people, they reduced to a compendium, with such transparent brevity that it could easily be understood both by the occupied and by those of limited education.

Anselm, Bede, Claudius, and this Haymo, who now comes into your embrace, belong especially to this tradition. Their industry has brought no small benefit to the Church, particularly if one considers both the times and the regions in which they lived.

It is fitting that those who, having cast aside every impediment, hasten toward that heavenly life should be as unencumbered as possible and should not be weighed down by burdens that are less than necessary. It is therefore all the more astonishing that certain people, who profess apostolic simplicity in food and clothing, embrace a doctrine that is anything but simple, but is made extremely thorny by superfluous subtleties, Averroist doctrines, and additional new fantasies.

When monks were of this character, their name was gracious to everyone, and it was honorable to be called a monk. Now, however, the evil conduct of some causes even the good to suffer the annoyance of a common reproach.

When Aristippus was exceedingly delighted by a certain perfume, he said: “May misfortune befall those catamites who have brought such a beautiful thing into disrepute.” In similar words, one might not unjustly express indignation against those who, through their own fault, have brought the name “monk” into disrepute, although in reality no name ought to be more deserving of applause.

For who would not love people who, truly dead to the world, have wholly dedicated themselves to God? Their life and speech are such that no one leaves their presence or conversation without becoming better; no one fears any harm from them—not fraud from those who regard money as refuse and distribute what they possess to the needy; not vengeance from those who, in accordance with evangelical teaching, pray for their persecutors, show love to those who hate them, and repay evil deeds with good; nor any danger to chastity from those who are incorrupt both in heart and in body.

Because of their singular humility, they place themselves above no one, envy no one, and despise no one. The closer they come to the summit of perfection, the more they consider themselves the lowest of all. Although they are truly the jewels and flowers of the Church, they themselves call themselves its dregs.

They either raise up the falls of others or interpret them charitably, while they are severe judges of themselves. They openly magnify the good deeds of others and modestly diminish their own. They flatter no one; they strike no one present with insolent words; they slander no one absent. Nothing is heard from their mouths except what is in their hearts: words of charity, words of consolation, words of friendly admonition, and words of thanksgiving.

In them there is a courtesy that is not artificial but proceeds from a good conscience. [Col. 0192C–0193A] In short, they present to us a kind of image of that heavenly city and, in a certain way, represent the angelic choirs: either because they continually sing the praises of God, or because, transformed into spirits, they have no dealings with the passions of the flesh, or because they live in complete harmony, or because, after the manner of angels, they act as intermediaries between human beings and God, commending the prayers of peoples to him and obtaining through their constant prayers many blessings from him—not for themselves alone but for the common good.

What, moreover, if the gift of prophecy is added to these virtues, so that they teach the people freely, purely, and incorruptibly, whether by their voice, through books that they write, or by both? And what if, by crucifying their flesh as far as possible through fasts, vigils, and labors, they make up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, and in a certain way offer themselves as sacrifices for the salvation of the people?

And you, layman, can you wish evil upon those who, while you lie heavily burdened by gluttony and snore deeply, keep vigil and fast for your sake? While you provoke God to anger through gambling, prostitutes, and other crimes, they intercede for you. While you speak ill of them among human beings, they speak well of you before God.

Who would not venerate such men as demigods, or love them as men divinely given for the public good—even if he himself were a wicked man? For extraordinary virtue wins even its enemies over to admiration of it. Those who do good to no one nevertheless, by natural instinct, revere those who do good to the wicked no less than to the good.

What, then, is the perversity of those who despise someone for the very reason that he is a monk? Whoever says “monk” speaks of the sum of all heroic virtues, which earn goodwill and favor from the good and extort them from the wicked.

If the word alone displeases you, let them be called, if you wish, “simple” and “solitary” instead of “monk.” But solitude is not measured by the number of one’s companions; it is measured by separation from evil affections. Otherwise, even the Carthusians would not be solitary.

Wherever this solitude is present, there is the most crowded fellowship. He is happily solitary who is not corrupted by the companionship of any wicked person, who has no inner turmoil of conflicting passions, yet is not in agreement with God.

In this sense one may be a monk even in the courts of princes, in public offices, and amid the ordinary dealings of human beings. What, then, is the perversity of hating a monk for the very reason that he is a monk? You profess to be a Christian, yet you turn away from those who most resemble Christ?

I know that many will immediately object that most people are very far from this image. We should therefore approve no way of life if, because of the bad, we hate the good as well. What, then, remains? Nothing except that we love human beings, interpret uncertain matters in the better sense, overlook lesser faults, and strive to cure more serious faults rather than aggravate them; and that we also honor the order and institution itself.

If to the civility of ordinary people there is added the industry of monks who devote themselves wholeheartedly to the things that truly belong to religion, the world’s former favor will quickly revive and the mouths of slanderers will quickly fall silent. Thus they will not only live pleasing to God and esteemed by human beings, but will also live here happily and cheerfully.

No one lives more peacefully or pleasantly than those who are truly monks; no one lives more miserably than those who are not monks in their hearts. For the former, the monastery is paradise; for the latter, it is a bakery. Yet to a great extent it lies in each person’s hands to turn his bakery into paradise.

I return to Haymo. Playing David’s harp, he will rouse your angelic company to spiritual dances, so that you may sing psalms to the Lord in hymns and songs, in your hearts. Let no one despise the simplicity of his diction; let everyone embrace the piety of his thoughts.

I give this warning because I suspect that many are like I once was: they grow nauseated by everything that lacks the seasonings and ornaments of rhetoricians. But when I was a child in Christ, I understood as a child; and would that I had now completely done away with the things belonging to childhood.

If this service of mine earns any favor with you, I ask you at some time to commend this sinner—ἁμαρτωλόν—to Christ in your prayers.

This copy was supplied by the venerable monastery of regular canons commonly called Marbach in Alsace, the remains of the most ill-omened peasant uprising. May the Lord repay them good for evil.

Freiburg im Breisgau, in the year 1533 from the birth of Christ, on the day before the Kalends of March [28 February].

# The Commentary on the Psalms Begins

[Col. 0193]

## On the First Psalm

[Col. 0193D]

Each psalm is called a hymn, for a hymn is praise of God accompanied by song. In every psalm the praise of God is found. Whether the subject is the power of the divinity, the perfection of Christ’s humanity, the holiness of his members, or the conversion of penitents, God is shown to be worthy of praise.

It is accompanied by song because the psalms were composed by the prophet with rejoicing and generate rejoicing in the minds of those who understand them rightly. For, having recognized the destruction of the whole human race on account of the disobedience of the first human being, and foreseeing through the Holy Spirit the future restoration through the obedience of the second, he announces it with great rejoicing together with the prophet.

Each psalm is called a soliloquy, because in them the Holy Spirit alone speaks without any assistance from human ingenuity. Or it is called a soliloquy not because the Psalms alone speak of Christ, but because they do so more worthily and more clearly than the other prophecies—more frequently and more openly in fewer words. Because of the dignity of this prophecy, the Church makes more frequent use of it.

When he says simply “the Prophet,” he identifies David specifically for us, just as through “the Apostle” we identify Paul. Prophecy is the same as vision. Hence, in the Book of Kings, the prophet Samuel is called “the seer,” when Saul says: “Where is the house of the seer?”

Not every vision, however, is called prophecy, but only that which is supplied by the Spirit alone. It may concern the past, as in Moses: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; or the present, as when someone sees through the Spirit things occurring in the present that he could not see by nature—for example, when Ezekiel’s spirit was transported to Jerusalem so that he might see what was happening there; or the future, as in this same prophecy.

Prophecy is inspired either through a dream, as in Joseph; through an angel, as in the case of Zechariah; through inward inspiration, as in this same work, the Psalter; or through figures, as when Noah, by means of the ark that he guided through the waters of the flood, prefigured the Church, which is to be guided by Christ through the dangers of the world.

This prophecy is called the Psalter, a name taken from a certain musical instrument with which David and the other leaders of the singing accompanied the psalms.

Prophecy is defined as follows: Prophecy is divine inspiration that demonstrates, with unchangeable truth, the outcomes of things either through visions, deeds, or the statements of certain persons.

Through visions, as in the case of Ezekiel and blessed John when they were placed in ecstasy. Through deeds, as in the case of Abraham through the sacrifice of the ram, and Jacob, who, by crossing his hands, blessed Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph. Through statements, as when it is read in Moses concerning Christ: “I will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers; listen to him as to me” (Deut. 18); or in the Psalter.

Prophecy through statements occurs in two ways: either by grace or by permission. By grace, as in Moses and the other good men. By permission, as in the prophetess Sibyl and in unbelieving philosophers, who foretold many things about Christ through divine inspiration.

Because David wished to enlarge the worship of God, and could not lead human beings to worship God through the meaning of the psalms, since they were brutish, he endeavored to stir them to worship through both the harmony of instruments and human singing.

Therefore, when he brought back the ark from Shiloh, he appointed three thousand men singing with every musical instrument, and placed one hundred and fifty over them. He also appointed four others over all of them: Ethan, Heman, Asaph, and Jeduthun. He himself, accompanying the singing with the psaltery in the tabernacle, invited the others to divine worship.

This work was called the Psalter from that instrument, with this significance: just as that instrument has ten strings and is hollow above, from which it resounds, so this prophecy resounds by always speaking of things above. For it speaks of spiritual things, not for the sake of human favor, as the philosophers of the world do, but from desire for eternal life.

The ten strings of that psaltery signify the ten commandments of the Law. Whoever carries out what is read in the Psalter fulfills all those commandments well.

Just as the psaltery, because it sounds from above, signifies the giving of life to the spirit, so the lyre, because it sounds from below, signifies the mortification of the flesh. The psaltery signifies the giving of life to the spirit because it constantly urges us to do those things in which the spirit is given life.

The melody produced by that musical instrument when its strings were struck by hand is properly called a psalm. By analogy with it, the parts of this prophecy are called psalms, because in them we are invited to a certain activity of the hands—whether of the affections or of the bodily hands—so that in this first psalm we are invited to conformity with the second parent.

Just as that melody in which only the strings sounded without a voice was called a psalm, so that in which only the voice was sung without strings was called a song. Where the melody preceded on the strings and the living voice followed, it was called “a song of a psalm”; where the living voice preceded and the melody followed, it was called “a psalm of a song.” According to these differences, certain psalms are found bearing such titles.

It must be understood, however, that David did not compose the psalms in the order in which they are arranged here. When he had sinned with Uriah’s wife, he composed “Have mercy on me, O God.” Afterward, concerning the persecution by Absalom, he published “Lord, how they have increased.” Likewise, when he was anointed king by Samuel, he composed “The Lord is my illumination.” After Saul’s death, “I will love you,” and so forth.

Ezra, moved by divine inspiration, arranged them in this order. We do not know the reason for the order, although we believe that there was one.

The common subject of this entire work is Christ, understood in three ways: according to his divinity, according to his humanity, and according to his body.

What is inserted concerning opposing forces—that is, demons and the impious—is not included because it belongs to the principal subject, but so that it may serve that principal subject; it is introduced for certain useful purposes. Thus, in the first psalm, he introduces the impious in order to deter people from resembling them through their punishment and to lead them back to conformity with Christ.

He treats this subject in the following way: he shows the power of the divinity, the perfection of Christ’s humanity, the universality of the holiness of his members, and the conversion of sinners.

The common purpose, likewise, is to make us conformable to Christ, so that “just as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear the image of the heavenly.”

Since Ezra had assigned a title to the other psalms, he assigned none to this psalm because this psalm is the title of all the others. Just as a title gives a preliminary indication of the whole subject that follows, so this psalm touches upon the subject of the work that follows.

It touches upon Christ’s humanity where it shows him to be free from every sin; upon his divinity where it says that he was planted beside streams of water; and upon Christ’s body where it shows that he was useful to us, when it says: “He will give his fruit in its season.”

Alternatively, he did not place a title on this psalm because he had read somewhere that Christ himself called this psalm “the head of the book,” where it says: “In the head of the book it is written concerning me,” and so forth. Ezra therefore did not dare to add a title when Christ, through David, had called this psalm “the head of the book” (Ps. 39).

This psalm, then, has Christ as its subject, as was stated above. It treats Christ in this way: it removes every evil from him, places in him the fullness of every virtue, and shows that he is useful to us.

It must be understood, however, that the perfections which it presents here generally concerning Christ are treated individually and in parts in the following psalms. One psalm deals with Christ’s humility, another with his patience, another with his resurrection, and so likewise in the others.

This psalm also has a common purpose: namely, that we may be conformed to the new human being. Since it intends to make us conformable to Christ, it first sets forth Christ’s dignity, and the prophet invites us in this way:

“You who mourn, oppressed by the misery of the first parent, abandon that old one and draw near to this one, for this is the blessed man, the opposite of the first.”

He speaks by comparison with an exile, who departed from his natural place and, having found a place pleasing to him, began to linger there and could no longer be recalled as readily as before, when he had first begun to depart.

If afterward he is elevated to a chair—that is, to a position of teaching—he is still less easily brought back. So Adam, placed in blessedness, departed—not locally—from the one who is present everywhere, as the Psalmist says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 8). Rather, he withdrew from God through dissimilarity, whereas one approaches God through likeness.

He departed through dissimilarity when, setting reason aside—by which he had been created like God—he obeyed Eve and the serpent’s counsel. He stood in the way of sinners when he actually ate the fruit. He sat in the chair of pestilence when, by concealing and excusing his sin, he taught his descendants by his example to make excuses; and thus he became weak, although he had been made strong by God.

For he could have remained immortal and incapable of suffering if he had wished to obey the Lord’s commands steadfastly. God had placed him in a paradise of delight, where there were fruits: one would extinguish hunger, another thirst, and others would extinguish or drive away other sufferings. There was also the tree of life. If he had eaten its fruit at the appropriate times, he would have avoided death and old age.

Against this weakness of his, Christ is called “a man of strength.” Although he was born in fragile flesh, he did not yield to temptations and did not fail under any tribulation. Against Adam’s unhappiness, Christ is called blessed:

“He did not depart,” that is, he did not withdraw from God by will, thought, or consent. To show his merit even more fully, the prophet notes that Christ had a persuader of departure, when he adds: “In the counsel of the impious.” For the devil persuaded him to worship him and give him the kingdoms of the world.

He calls those who oppose the worship of God “impious,” namely unbelievers. “Sinners” are those who live shamefully. Christ himself did not stand in the way of sinners, that is, in evil works.

We understand “standing” as an action because, just as one who is already standing in another’s land cannot be recalled as easily as one who has only begun to depart, so one who is engaged in the act of sin is not recalled as readily as one who is sinful only in the will.

He calls evil works “the way of sinners,” because sinners proceed along them toward eternal condemnation.

“In the chair of pestilence”: that is, he neither made a practice of doing evil by word or deed nor taught it. He did sit in a chair, because he was an outstanding teacher. The chair is the seat of the teacher, the throne of kings, and the tribunal of the judge.

No pestilence followed from his teaching; from him no weakness passed into others. Pestilence is a weakness that passes from one animal to many, or even to all.

By saying “he did not depart,” “he did not stand,” and “he did not sit,” he shows Christ to be free from every sin. For every sin consists either in the will, or in thought, or in consent—the will being signified by “departing”; or in action, understood by “standing”; or in teaching, understood by “sitting in the chair of pestilence.”

It may be asked why, after removing the will to sin from Christ through “he did not depart,” he also removes action and teaching, since removal of the will removes these other things as well.

We say that this was done to show that sins are removed from Christ in the same order in which they grow in others. A human being first sins in the will—that is, through consent and thought—then in action, and finally in teaching, namely, by example and word. These same three deaths of the soul are signified by the three dead whom the Lord raised.

The will to sin, the first death of the soul, is signified by the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom he raised in the house. For the one who sins only by will is still in the house; he has not yet proceeded to action.

The other death of the soul, the act of sin, is signified by the dead man whom he raised outside the gate. For by completing sins we go outside the gates of the senses, no longer remaining in mere thought.

The teaching of sin is signified by the dead man already stinking and corrupting the air, since through the stench of that teaching others too are corrupted.

### “But in the Law of the Lord”

Having removed every sin and evil from Christ, he shows him filled with every kind of virtue.

The connection is this: Christ did not depart, but his will was in the Law of the Lord—that is, he had the will to fulfill the Law of the Lord.

The Law of God is the holy commandment that consists in avoiding sins and performing good deeds. He rightly says “in the Law,” and not “under the Law,” because the latter expression implies compulsion.

Christ fulfilled the Law by spontaneous will. He not only wished to fulfill it, but fulfilled it in every respect. This is what follows: “And he will meditate on fulfilling his Law,” that is, he will be diligent in its fulfillment, considering how it may be fulfilled more perfectly.

He does not say “he will meditate” because Christ himself would be meditating, but because, just as someone who meditates fulfills something more perfectly than one who does not meditate, so Christ fulfilled the Law better than all others.

He uses the future tense—“he will meditate”—because he is speaking according to human usage. It is characteristic of human beings to speak of future things by means of future forms. When he narrates future things as though they had already happened, he is not speaking according to human usage, but because his spirit was carried up to the counsels of God, in whose providence all things are already past. Just as he read them as past in that book, so he reported them to human beings as already present.

“By day and by night”: that is, continually; or, in prosperity and adversity. Prosperity is meant when, after the miracle of the five loaves, the Jews wished to make him their king. Adversity is meant in the Passion.

### “And he will be”

Having shown Christ free from every sin and filled with every good, he adds the benefit that he has conferred upon us, since those qualities could exist without benefiting us. He says:

“And he will be like a tree.”

Here the prophet speaks about Christ by a very close comparison. Just as a tree planted in a moist place blossoms and bears fruit at the proper time, so does Christ.

He himself was planted—that is, sanctified at his conception by the Holy Spirit without the movement of lust—and remained steadfast against every assault of the devil’s temptation.

“Beside streams of water”: that is, beside flowing waters. By “waters” we understand the Holy Spirit. Hence elsewhere it is said: “From his belly will flow rivers of living water.” This was said “of himself, namely, the one whom believers in him were to receive” (John 7).

The Holy Spirit is signified by water because, just as water solidifies the earth and makes it fruitful, so through the Holy Spirit those whose necks have been loosened are strengthened by the bond of love and faith, and produce the fruit of good works. Just as water extinguishes thirst, so the Holy Spirit extinguishes the burning of sin.

He says “flowing” because no obstacle can resist the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said: “No one could resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6).

He says “beside,” because the nature of humanity was not changed into the nature of divinity, but was beside it—that is, united to it. Or by “flowing waters” he means peoples who flow together. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “The waters are many peoples.”

He says that Christ was beside the peoples because he had not sinful flesh, but flesh like that of sin.

“The tree will give its fruit”: that is, it will bear fruit in its season. So Christ also gave his fruit, namely, the restoration of the human race.

“In its season”: that is, at the appropriate time. In his Passion he redeemed souls from the power of the devil; in his resurrection he gave us hope of rising again; in his ascension he opened the heavenly entrances for us. Thus Christ was given to us as the tree of life.

Through the use of his body and the imitation of righteousness, Christ removes from us eternal death and old age, which the tree of life used to remove, as we said above.

“And its leaf”: that is, his word. It will not fall away from the truth under any circumstance; that is, it will not fall. For the Lord says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24).

The word is signified by the leaf because, just as a leaf protects and adorns the fruit, so Christ’s words adorn and protect his gifts. For the grace given in baptism could not be preserved in any way unless it were afterward maintained by the teaching of the Gospel.

These promises will be for our benefit.

“And everything that he does”: Christ’s deeds, even the humiliations that he endured, “will prosper”—that is, they will prove beneficial to us. Thus the scourges that he endured become for us an example of humility and patience.

[Col. 0200A]

### “Not so the impious, not so”

After inviting us to conformity with Christ through his goodness, he calls us to the same conformity through the terror of Christ’s adversaries.

The connection is this: Christ was such a one, but the impious are not so—neither free from sin, nor filled with righteousness, nor useful—and so on without limit. This is signified for us by the repeated adverb.

“I say, not so, but like dust”: that is, unfruitful and bound by no bond of charity, “which the wind casts away”—that is, diabolical temptation—“from the face of the earth,” namely, from the solidity of the Church.

The Church is called earth because of its solidity and fruitfulness. The “face of the earth” is not said of a place where there is dust, but where the earth is solid.

### “Therefore”

Because they are dust, removed from the face of the earth, “therefore the impious will not rise”—that is, they will not have a resurrection.

Since all do not rise in the same way, both the good and the wicked, he specifies: “in judgment.” That is, they will not rise in such a way as to be judged or to judge.

The impious—that is, unbelievers, such as Jews and gentiles—and also those who are torn away from this life and expelled from the Church will not be judged in the second resurrection, because they have already been judged here. As the Apostle says: “Those who sinned without the Law will perish without the Law” (Rom. 2).

Those who depart from the present life while remaining in the Church, concerning whose works it is uncertain whether they are good or evil, will be judged: some for life, some for death.

Those whose holiness in the Church is certain will not be judged, because they have already been led by the Church to life and judged in this life. They will judge—but not all of them, only those who hold the place of the apostles, such as bishops and others of this kind.

They will judge because, by comparison with themselves, they show that others are deserving of condemnation. For although the just and the impious are of the same nature, the impious have not imitated Christ’s life as the just have.

The impious will not rise, nor will sinners—that is, Christians who sin secretly—rise in such a way that they are in the council of the just, namely, in judgment with the just, by whom whatever is done is done with counsel and reason.

Alternatively, because the Hebrew has “in the congregation,” some read “in the council,” meaning that sinners will not be in the company of the just.

The same verse may also be read of the first resurrection of the soul through repentance, so that we say: The impious will not rise in judgment—that is, in the discernment of good and evil—in such a way that, having avoided evil, they do good; nor will sinners rise in such a way that they are numbered among the just.

This statement concerns those who have become hardened.

“Because the Lord knows.” Therefore the ungodly and sinners will not rise, because the Lord does not know their way. He places the consequence of this preceding statement: “And the way of the ungodly will perish.” “Way” means their evil deeds, which will lead them to condemnation. The proof of this is first given by contrast, where it says, “because the Lord knows”—that is, he approves the just and the way of the just.

## ON PSALM II

### Title

A Psalm of David (although no title is placed before this psalm among the Hebrews).

“Why did the nations rage?” “A Psalm of David”—that is, this treatise, which is called a psalm because, just as a sweet melody called a psalm is produced on the psaltery by the movement of the strings through the action of the hands, so this treatise moves us toward works in which a sweet melody is made for God.

“It is attributed to David”—that is, it treats of Christ, who is signified by David, because David is interpreted as “desirable to behold” or “strong of hand.” For who is stronger than Christ, who conquered the powers of the air? All the fathers who came before desired to see him, as Simeon did—for he used to say in his prayers, “When will he come? When will I see him?” All the saints still desire to see him.

In this psalm Christ the king is the subject. It treats of him in this way: it shows that all who have plotted anything against his kingdom accomplish nothing, but rather harm themselves. Then it shows him as the powerful king of the Jews and of the nations. Its purpose is to admonish us to serve Christ the king with fear and trembling. This is indicated at the end of the psalm, where it says: “Serve the Lord in fear.”

“Why did the nations rage?” Peter, speaking in the Acts of the Apostles, says that this is the first psalm: “Lord, kings have gathered together against your Son,” as David says in the preceding psalm.

He begins with those who plotted against Christ. Here the Lord speaks by way of a question, not to seek information but to reprove, saying: “Why”—that is, for what reason—“did the nations rage?” By “raged” he indicates that they are beastlike, since raging belongs to beasts. Their rage was expressed when they said: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him.”

By “the nations” he understands the Roman soldiers, who are called nations because, just as they have been born, so they remain—that is, without law and without any established rule of justice. “And the peoples” means the Jews, who are called peoples because they have been gathered together in order to live according to law through the Law.

“They plotted vain things”—namely, that Christ was not the Messiah, or that they could keep him in the tomb.

“They stood by, the kings.” The peoples did not merely plot against the Lord; kings also stood by—that is, stood against Christ, persevering in evil action against him. By “kings” he first understands Herod, who persecuted Christ by killing the children; and secondly, Herod’s nephew, with whose consent the Lord was killed.

“Kings,” I say, “of the earth”—that is, earthly kings. “And rulers”—that is, Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas, and the other rulers—“gathered together as one.” Even if they were not all present, they were all united in will, “against the Lord,” the Father, because they were against his Christ. For whoever persecutes the one who was sent also persecutes the one who sent him. Here Christ speaks of himself as though of a third person.

“Let us break apart.” They gathered together, I say, saying: “Let us break their bonds”—that is, the bonds of God the Father and Christ, or of Christ and his disciples. By “bonds” he names Christ’s preaching, miracles, and promises, by which human beings are bound to the Christian faith. Thus, having despised those bonds, “let us cast their yoke from us”—that is, their Lord.

[Col. 0202A] “He who dwells in the heavens.” They raged and stood by, but he who dwells in the heavens—that is, either materially in the heavens or in the saints, in whom God is said to dwell because he finds no offense in them—“will laugh at them.” That is, he will make them worthy of mockery, because they will appear unable to accomplish anything against the kingdom of God.

“And the Lord will mock them”—that is, he will make them objects of disgrace. Hence, throughout the world today they are held in reproach. *Sanna* is mockery made through the nose.

“Then.” This laughter and mockery occurred in this age; but then—that is, thereafter, or in the other life—he “will speak,” either through the voice of a minister or by his own voice, not a placable voice but “in anger.” This does not mean that there can be anger or any change in God; rather, it is spoken by comparison with an angry person who inflicts punishment.

For this voice will be heard at the judgment: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew XXV). Or, even if no voice were heard at the judgment, the very evidence of the matter would make the Lord appear to speak as one who is angry.

By “anger” he understands vengeance. But because anger signifies a brief vengeance, he adds: “And he will trouble them in his fury”—that is, with continual vengeance.

Up to this point he has shown that those who labored against Christ’s kingdom are ineffective and disgraced. Now he shows him as the powerful king of the Jews and of the nations, and he speaks in his own person as follows: They are troubled, “but I have been appointed king”—that is, firmly established by that God.

He calls him king because he perfectly rules his own people upon Zion. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” by which the universal Church may be understood, since it is always engaged in contemplation of eternal life and in providence, guarding against its enemies.

Nevertheless, here by Zion we understand only the Church of the Jews, because Zion was the head of the kingdom of the Jews. On account of its stability and the excellence of its virtues, he calls that Church the holy mountain.

“His”—that is, God’s. “Proclaiming” in that Church “the decree”—that is, his law.

He not only appointed me king over the Jews, but also over the nations. We have this where he says: “I will give you the nations.” To confirm this, he first sets forth the authority of the Lord himself who makes the promise, saying: “The Lord God said.”

The saying appears in the very fulfillment of the matter. After first establishing the kingdom, “to me,” on the authority of the one who promises, he shows the reason why God would subject the nations to him: namely, because he is his Son.

And he says this: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”—that is, eternally. He wished “today” to be understood as eternity because he had no suitable word by which to designate a present that never departs from eternity.

He says “I have begotten” rather than “I beget,” so that this ineffable generation would not appear to have begun recently. He joins the past tense to indicate to us that this generation both is and has been. Hence it is said: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah LIII).

And because you are my Son, therefore “ask of me”—that is, assume humanity, in which you are able to ask. According to his divinity he could not ask, since according to that nature he was equal to the Father.

“Ask,” I say, “and I will give you the nations as your inheritance”—that is, those over whom you will rule and whom you will cultivate. For one who is heir to something rules it and cultivates it more than anyone else.

And I will not give you just any nations, such as the Greeks or others, but also “the ends of the earth”—that is, the nations dwelling in the furthest regions of the world. I will give them to you “as a possession,” so that you may possess them forever.

I ought justly to subject the nations to you, because “you will rule them with an iron rod”—that is, with inflexible discipline. Those who will not receive discipline, “you will shatter”—that is, punish: some for correction, others for condemnation.

“They will be shattered like a potter’s vessel.” They are shattered easily; by this comparison he indicates that those whom the Lord will shatter are made of clay.

The Father’s words continue. “And now”—that is, after he has shown him to be such a king—“you kings,” that is, those who rule your earthly condition well, “understand” how great he is.

“And you who judge the earth”—that is, leaders of the Church who exercise judgment over others—“be instructed,” that is, cease to be unlearned, so that you may know how to judge your subjects wisely.

“And serve the Lord in fear.” Lest his kingdom appear harsh—of which it is written, “For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew XI)—he therefore adds: “and rejoice in him.”

And lest the joy and gentleness of his kingdom produce negligence, he adds, “with trembling,” subjecting the body. In this verse, in which we are admonished concerning the service of God, the purpose of the psalm is clearly indicated.

And so that you may be able to serve, “take hold of discipline”—that is, even if the Lord did not give it, seek every correction of the Lord. For the Apostle says: “If you are without discipline, then you are adulterers and not sons” (Hebrews XII).

“Take hold,” I say, “lest at any time”—that is, on the day of judgment, although he now spares—“the Lord become angry,” that is, display in you the effect of one who is angry, and thus “you perish,” removed “from the way of the just”—that is, from the works of the just.

“Take hold,” I say, “lest you perish,” and also so that you may be blessed. For all who trust—that is, who place their hope in him with a pure conscience—will be blessed.

They will indeed be blessed “when his anger”—that is, his vengeance—“has been kindled.” Just as fire does not fail while there is fuel, so Christ’s vengeance will not fail while they endure. This will be “for a short time,” since the time is short.

Or, “for a short time,” because, when judgment is imminent, sudden punishment is inflicted upon the ungodly.

It may also be read in the voice of prophecy, introducing Christ where he says: “But I have been appointed.” Join it in this way: “They gathered together against his Christ,” who says: “They will be troubled, but I have been appointed,” and so forth.

The prophet also speaks where he says: “And now, kings, understand.” Join it in this way: Christ is such a king: “And now, you kings, understand.”

## ON PSALM III

### Title

A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.

“Lord, why have they multiplied?” He touches upon the history that David endured from Absalom.

While his father was still alive, Absalom was uncertain to which of his sons he would leave the kingdom. Coveting the kingdom immoderately for himself, Absalom corrupted many of the people by crafty promises and finally caused himself to be appointed king by seizing power.

David, however, knowing that this seizure had not occurred by God’s will, and knowing that this scourge had been given to him by God for the sin of adultery and murder—concerning which sin it had been divinely said to him, “The sword will not depart from the house of David” (2 Samuel XII)—patiently endured his son’s persecution. He left the city barefoot with some of his men and fled from his son’s presence.

When some people cursed him as he departed and insulted him by throwing stones, calling him a man of blood, he did not permit his men to repay them in kind, but patiently endured the persecution, saying that one neither ought nor could resist the scourges of God.

Joab, however, paying no attention to David’s patience, pursued Absalom with the army and killed him while he was hanging from a tree by his hair. For while fleeing, Absalom was suspended over a mule, his uncut hair becoming entangled around a branch.

Through this persecution David composed this psalm. Filled with the Holy Spirit, through his own patience he represented Christ’s patience, paid the penalty, and through the wickedness of his son foreshadowed Judas’s wickedness.

For Christ is signified by David, since patience is displayed in this psalm; Judas is understood through Absalom, who is called Christ’s son because he was his disciple.

Absalom is interpreted as “the peace of the father”—not because he had peace with his father, but because his father had peace with him. So Judas did not have peace with Christ, although Christ maintained peace both with everyone else and with him.

And just as Absalom was hanged by himself, so was Judas.

The title is therefore explained as follows: This psalm is attributed to David—that is, to Christ—and treats of one of his affairs, which occurred when he fled from the face of Absalom—that is, from Judas’s inward face, not locally but in knowledge.

Before Judas had the intention of betraying the Lord, he displayed a certain obedience to the Lord, although hypocritically, and he also performed miracles. But after the devil entered his heart so that he would betray the Lord, the Lord departed from his heart—namely, from Judas’s heart, who had first been his son.

The subject of this psalm is Christ. It treats of him in this way: it touches upon his passion and glorification, but does not explain the passion part by part, as he does in certain other psalms.

Its purpose is to invite us to patience through Christ’s example, so that we may not fear every kind of insult. Hence the Apostle also says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Romans VIII).

This purpose is indicated in the psalm where it says: “I will not fear the thousands of the people”—the voice of Christ.

It begins with the passion, as he speaks to the Father in a kind of astonishment:

[Col. 0205A] “Lord God, why”—that is, for what reason—“have they multiplied?” So that my son, namely Judas, is also among “those who trouble me.”

He does not speak in astonishment because he himself is astonished, but to show us that it is astonishing that they persecuted the physician of their salvation, innocent in every respect, as though he were guilty.

“Many rise up against me”—that is, they assume power against me. They could have troubled him without presuming to exercise power over him.

“Many rise up, and many say,” whether by thought, voice, or deed, “to my soul”—that is, to my life—“there is no salvation,” that is, no bodily deliverance, “for him,” namely Christ, “who claimed to be the Son of God,” “in his God.”

This does not mean that they thought he had a God, but rather that they spoke of the one whom they made his God. Hence they insulted him, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him deliver him now, if he wants him” (Matthew XXVI). Or many say this while insulting “my soul.”

“But you, Lord, are my protector”—that is, you took my humanity under your protection, uniting it to yourself in the conception.

Here he speaks by comparison: just as a powerful guardian and advocate takes an orphan or any weak person under his protection, so divinity took humanity under its protection and preserved it free from every sin.

“You,” I say, “are my glory”—that is, the cause of my glorious resurrection—“and the one who lifts up my head”—that is, my exaltation, namely, that I, exalted and previously free from every sin, should be above every creature.

This verse treats of glorification. He sets forth a certain merit of Christ by which he shows him worthy of such exaltation.

The connection is this: You rightly exalted me because “I cried to the Lord,” at one time with an outward cry. Hence the Apostle, offering prayers and supplications to God with a loud cry and tears, cried inwardly to the Lord continually.

A cry consists in directing the mind toward God with a restrained intensity of devotion.

“I cried” with my own “voice,” I who had often cried out through the voices of the prophets. I cried “from his holy mountain”—that is, from my elevation in virtues, sanctified by him. And because I cried in holiness, he rightly “heard me.”

To hear is to grant a petition.

Or “from his holy mountain” may refer to the one who hears, as follows: God “heard me from his holy mountain”—that is, from the lofty power of his divinity—so that he made me a participant in that power, just as someone might say, “The king heard me from his treasures,” meaning that he made me a participant in them.

“He heard me,” and it was necessary, because “I slept”—that is, during the time of my passion I endured all insults as though asleep.

For just as a sleeping person, although possessing reason, power, strength, and the rest, does not exercise them and is quickly awakened from sleep, so Christ during his passion displayed no power, although he had previously shown it by performing miracles, as in the case of Lazarus and others. He was quickly awakened when he rose again.

“And I was overcome with sleep”—that is, I rested, lying in the tomb, from all tumult.

The difference between sleeping and being overcome with sleep is that in the latter there is the greatest sweetness and tranquility.

Having shown the necessity of being heard, he now sets forth the hearing itself. The connection is: “I slept and rose again”—that is, I rose outside the law common to all the dead, O princes of the kings of the earth.

Therefore “I rose again because the Lord received me”—that is, he was joined to my humanity. For if divinity had not been joined to humanity, humanity would have remained dead according to the manner of other human beings.

Because “I rose again,” I will “no longer fear” in my members. For although his own people may fear, they are not his own in this respect.

Hence it is said: “Love casts out fear” (Romans XIII).

“Thousands of the people,” however many there may be, would nevertheless appear worthy of fear because they surround me in my people. This is what it means that they surround me.

Once Christ had become incapable of suffering and immortal, he could no longer fear in himself. Those who persecute the faithful persecute not them but Christ in them.

When he says, “I will not fear,” he indicates the purpose: that we should patiently endure everything and not be afraid.

“You, Lord, arise”—that is, confer assisting grace.

The Lord is said to lie down when, after withdrawing grace, he permits his own people to yield to some temptation. He is said to rise when he makes his own people overcome every temptation.

This is understood from the fact that, while Christ slept in the boat, his disciples were in danger; when he arose, the disturbance ceased.

“Arise,” I say, “and save me” and my people, “my God.”

It is certain that you will do this, and he shows it by contrast, saying:
