“For you have struck all” who oppose me, by inward and outward condemnation, because they opposed me “without cause.”

And not only have you struck those who opposed me in their deeds, but “you have crushed the teeth of sinners”—that is, their biting accusations and slanders—meaning that you will crush them by showing them to be useless and deserving of condemnation.

Hence elsewhere: “We fools regarded their life as madness and their end as without honor. See how they are counted among the sons of God” (Wisdom V).

When he announces a future matter in the past tense, he does not speak according to the matter in itself, but as one snatched up into God’s counsel, in which all future things are as certain as past things are to us.

Here he insults the ungodly because “you have crushed sinners.” Therefore he is patient, because “salvation belongs to the Lord”—that is, giving complete salvation in this life.

“And upon your people” there “will be your blessing”—that is, everlasting blessedness. He says “upon” because they will be exalted above their merit, according to the Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII).

## ON PSALM IV

### Title

For the end: a psalm of song, of David.

“When I called, he heard me.” This treatise concerns good action, where it says: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of justice.” In this respect it is called a psalm.

It also concerns song—that is, exultation, namely eternal blessedness—where it says: “Who will show us good things?” and so forth.

It is more precise here than in any of the preceding psalms, because after presenting the doubt of certain people it shows us the certainty of eternal life, where it says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us,” and “in peace, in the same.”

Because we are to rejoice in that good, which this psalm treats of more worthily, it is called a song. And because that exultation—eternal life—is the cause of good action, it is called “a psalm of song.”

The expression “psalm of song” is drawn from musical performance, in which the living voice went before and harmony followed.

This psalm is attributed to David because David the prophet speaks here, or because any faithful soul speaks here. That soul is signified by David, that is, by the Church, since the Church is strong of hand in overcoming the devil’s temptations and desirable to behold because of the beauty of holiness. Many who are pierced in the heart desire to attain its perfection, according to the saying: “All the rich among the people will entreat your favor.”

The psalm, I say, tends “to the end”—that is, to Christ, presenting him to us as an example.

Since “end” is understood in two ways—namely, destruction, as the destruction of wood occurs through fire, and completion, that is, the completion of any thing—Christ is never called destruction but completion. In him all the things that God had promised through the prophets were completed.

Hence the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans X).

Or “end” may be understood as the time of grace, which is called the end of the ages because in it all God’s promises were completed. Hence the Apostle says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians X).

The subject of this psalm is justice. It treats of this subject by rebuking idolaters and lovers of the world, where it says: “How long will you be heavy-hearted?” It also admonishes us to justice, where it says: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of justice,” and so forth.

It makes splendid promises, promising Christ by calling him “his holy one.” Through him the prayers of the saints will be heard. It also shows the certainty of eternal good, which is the end of the other promises.

Its purpose is to admonish us to seek that good, for the sake of which both rebukes and promises are given. This purpose is indicated where it says: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of justice.”

It places the rebukes and admonitions separately, but mixes the promises together.

It begins with a promise in this way: Do not worship idols or love worldly things, but cling to justice, and your prayers will be heard. God promises this to you in my example:

“For when I called”—that is, when I called upon God to dwell in me—“God heard me,” the giver of justice. Not perfectly, but “of my justice,” such as my fragility can possess.

By saying, “When I called, he heard,” he indicates that calling and hearing occur together. When he says, “God heard me, the God of my justice,” he shows that no one is heard by God unless he possesses some justice.

He states in what way he was heard, saying: “In tribulation you enlarged me”—that is, you increased me.

Since tribulation usually brings narrowness—grief over tribulation, hatred of the one who causes it, silence about the truth, and so forth—you enlarged my heart so that I would even love my enemy and rejoice in tribulation.

Although he had previously spoken of the third person, saying “he heard,” because of his great intimacy he turns to the second person when he says, “you enlarged me.”

“You enlarged me,” and still “have mercy on me”—that is, remove from me the miseries of this world so that I may be subject to no temptations—“and hear my prayer”—that is, place in me an increase of virtues and confirmation of the good things that are in me.

After he has said “he heard,” it may seem unnecessary to add “have mercy and hear.” But it was appropriate to add this, because miseries remain after being heard; therefore preservation and increase of good things are necessary.

After the hearing he sets forth the rebuke. The connection is: “The Lord heard me,” because I was just; and therefore, “sons of men, how long”—that is, how long will you remain—“heavy-hearted”? How long will the will to idolatry or the desire for earthly things weigh you down?

In the divine Scriptures “man” is understood in two ways: according to carnality or according to earthliness. In either way the phrase may be read: “sons of men”—that is, sons of the carnal—“how long will you be like them?” Or “sons of men”—that is, of rational beings—“why do you not imitate reason?”

He shows that they sin by their will, and also that they sin through delight, when he says: “Why do you love vanity?” He also shows that they sin in action when he says: “And seek falsehood”—that is, idols.

They are vain because they are not gods. They are falsehoods because through them people expect a life that they cannot give.

Likewise, worldly things are vain because, although they are thought to be good by those who desire them, they are not good. People also labor greatly to obtain what they love—namely, worldly things—which are nevertheless falsehoods because they promise sufficiency and blessedness, which they cannot give.

“Know” that these things are falsehoods. And “know this also: the Lord has made his holy one wondrous”—that is, he has made Christ wondrous, Christ who is called the Holy of Holies. Through him “the Lord will hear me when I cry to him,” so that I may possess him.

Again, in this verse does he place a promise for us? Do not seek falsehood, but rather “be angry” at your past sins, “and” thereafter “do not sin.”

Or understand it this way: Do not seek falsehood, but “be angry.” Since this is natural, I cannot forbid it to you; I tolerate it. “And” nevertheless “do not sin”—that is, do not bring that anger into action.

And concerning “the things that you say”—that is, think—“in your hearts,” that is, in your thoughts, “be pierced with remorse.” And concerning “the things that you say in your beds”—that is, in those matters in which you consent to some bodily pleasure.

A bed is the place where wild beasts lie and roll about. In the same way our body is called the soul’s bed, insofar as our foolish soul consents to pleasures. In this verse we recognize the admonition: “Do not sin.”

And because it is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good, he adds: rather, “sacrifice the sacrifice of justice”—that is, justice, which is called a sacrifice because it is pleasing to God like a sacrifice.

[Col. 0209A] Do not offer this for human approval, like hypocrites, but sacrifice it so that it may please God.

“And” therefore “hope in the Lord”—that is, be certain of future good. Many doubt this and, still thinking carnally, say to us: “You preach those good things to us, but who will show us these good things?” That is, who has come from there and reported to us what those good things are?

They doubt, but we know the certainty of it, because “the light of your countenance has been marked upon us”—that is, in the higher part of us, in reason; this sign has been impressed upon the soul, namely, “the light of your countenance.”

This is the cross, which is called light because it is the cause through which the countenance of God—that is, God’s will—shines into our soul.

The sign of the cross is in the soul that has died to every carnal desire. Hence Paul says: “Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI).

The more a person withdraws from the desires of the flesh, the more he progresses in knowledge of God.

We are certain because “it has been marked upon us,” and also because you, Lord, “have given gladness in my heart” concerning that future good, through a pure conscience—“in my heart,” that is, a heart different from the hearts of the ungodly, concerning whom it is said: “There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord.”

Or otherwise: “The light of your countenance”—that is, your luminous countenance, namely your wisdom, which is the living image of your entire will. That light “has been marked upon us”—that is, in our soul—so that, through wisdom, namely through your Son dwelling in us, our reason may be enlightened and make us certain of eternal good.

Because “that light is upon us,” therefore “you have given gladness in my heart.”

“There is gladness in my heart,” but they “have multiplied”—that is, they have been divided in many ways according to their desire for temporal goods. This is “from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil.”

He says “their” to distinguish them from us. Our grain is the bread that descended from heaven; our wine is the inebriating cup; our oil is the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is said: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Psalm XXII).

Here “fruit” is used improperly, because we call only that a fruit which we enjoy for its own sake.

They “have multiplied,” but I “will sleep in peace” in this life, tending “toward the same”—that is, toward identity—namely, toward true peace, of which it is said: “My peace I give you.” And finally, in that true peace, “I will rest.”

He says “I will sleep” by comparison, because just as a sleeping person does not perceive external things, so a faithful person is not roused from tranquility of mind by worldly cares.

“I will rest in peace, because you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope”—that is, in a unique hope, a hope placed in you alone, because I desire nothing except you alone.

Or “uniquely”—that is, in a different manner—“from those who have multiplied,” namely, from lovers of earthly things.

## ON PSALM V

### Title

For the end: for her who receives the inheritance.

“My words.” This psalm is offered for her—that is, for the honor of the Church—which already in the present and still more in the future receives the inheritance, namely God, who feeds and sustains us.

Here he touches upon the history of the free woman and the slave woman: Sarah, who obtained the inheritance with her son, and Hagar, who was cast out with her son (Genesis XVI).

The free woman signifies the New Law; her son Isaac signifies the Christian people. The slave woman signifies the Old Law; her son Ishmael signifies the multitude of unbelievers.

The psalm, I say, tends “to the end”—that is, directs each faithful person toward Christ.

Its subject is the Church, and the Church speaks here. It treats of her as follows: it describes her asking for the inheritance and affirms that she will possess it; it shows that her rival will be excluded; it asks to be freed from her rival; it also shows that the rival, namely the slave woman, persecutes the free woman; and it sets forth the manner of blessedness.

Its purpose is to give us certainty of eternal good. Through all these things it admonishes us toward Christ, and it begins with the request for the inheritance:

“My words”—that is, vocal prayers—“receive”—that is, fulfill what I ask—“Lord.”

When it says “with your ears,” it speaks by comparison. For ears in God mean nothing other than mercy and power. Through power God fulfills; through mercy God hears.

“My cry”—that is, understand the affection of my heart. A cry is understood to be in the heart. The Apostle bears witness, saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians IV).

And because I ask with voice and affection, “pay attention”—that is, show yourself attentive; attend more intensely than usual—“to the voice of my prayer,” that is, to the voice proceeding from the affection of the heart.

This threefold request tends toward one thing: that God hear the prayer.

Just as he makes a threefold request, so he sets forth a Trinity as the one who hears: “receive,” “understand,” “pay attention.”

“My King”—that is, Christ, who is called king because he rules his own in justice—“and my God,” that is, Creator; this refers to the Father.

Christ is placed first because through him one comes to the Father.

“And you, Lord,” namely the Holy Spirit, “receive,” and so forth.

“Because I will pray to you, Lord.” This is the reason why he should pay attention: because he perseveres in prayer, which is expressed by “I will pray.”

After the three persons have been set forth, he does not say “pay attention” in the plural but “pay attention” in the singular, because Holy Church understands unity in the Trinity.

“In the morning.” I will cry out in this way, and you “will hear my voice,” both inward and outward.

“In the morning”—that is, at the beginning of my conversion. While a person is in sins, he is in night; when he rises from sins, he is in the morning, that is, at the beginning of the light.

“Morning” is taken from the Greek and signifies nothing other than light. Hence *septimana* means “seven lights.” By saying “in the morning”—that is, that he is heard at the beginning of conversion—he indicates the mercy of the one who hears.

And you will hear because “in the morning I will stand before you”—that is, I will perform such works that I may be worthy to stand in your sight—“and I will see” God.

He shows that such a person sees God by setting forth the contrary, saying: “Because you are God,” and therefore “you do not will iniquity.”

Thus “I will stand and see” this, namely, “because you are God,” and so forth.

And because you do not will “iniquity,” therefore “the malicious one”—that is, the one who is ill-disposed toward his neighbor—“will not dwell near you.”

Although God is everywhere, the malicious person is not said to be near him. To be near God is to enjoy his good things; to be far from him is not to enjoy them.

“Nor will the unjust”—that is, those who sin in their actions—“remain before your eyes.” Although all flesh will see God at the judgment, not all will remain in contemplation of God, but only the just.

“Because I will pray to you” is the only phrase that should be retained. Not “they will remain,” because you “hate all who work [Col. 0211B] iniquity.” By saying “who work,” and not “who have worked,” he shows that those who have sinned are not condemned unless they persist in the will to sin.

“You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” that is, those who persevere in falsehood. “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” because this is contrary to truth. Truth concerns what is; falsehood is neither substance nor nature, but concerns what is not. And deservedly is the one destroyed who turns away from what is toward what is not. To lie is to speak contrary to what one inwardly thinks.

Augustine: There are certain lies told for someone’s safety or advantage, not from malice but from kindness, such as the midwives who told Pharaoh a falsehood on behalf of the Hebrew children. Such lies are praised not in their deed but in their intention; [Col. 0211C] those who lie in this way may at some point deserve to be freed from every lie. There is also the lie told in jest, which does not deceive, since the person to whom it is spoken knows that it is said as a joke. These two kinds are not without fault, but the fault is not great.

For the perfect, however, it is not fitting to lie, not even for temporal life, whose loss—whether one’s own or another’s—does not destroy the soul. It is permissible for them, if they do not tell what is false, to remain silent about what is true. Thus, if someone does not wish to deliver a person to death, let him keep silent about the truth, but let him not speak falsely; and let him not kill his own soul for another’s body. It is not a fault to remain silent about the truth, as the Lord says: “I have many things to say to you” (John 16).

That, however, where there is no double heart, should not be called a lie. For example, if someone lends a sword and promises to return it to the person who asks for it, but that person later asks for it while raving mad, I ought not to return it, [Col. 0211D] lest he kill himself or someone else. Here there is no double heart, because when I promised to return it I did not know that the madman would later ask for it again.

Or let us understand “falsehood” as heresy, such as denying that Christ is God or denying the Virgin’s childbirth. It is on account of such falsehoods that he intensifies his statement by saying, “You will destroy.”

What he said—“You hate those who work iniquity”—he demonstrates in detail, saying: Truly, “you hate those who work iniquity,” because “the man of blood,” that is, the murderer, “and the deceitful man,” that is, the one who kills someone living by deceit, whether through evil persuasion or by taking away his possessions, “the Lord will abominate,” that is, he will remove him from every good. Or, “he will abominate” means that the Lord will remove him from the fellowship of rational beings.

[Col. 0212A] Since he said, “You are not a God who wills iniquity,” he indicated the exclusion of the rival; thereafter he will indicate that he himself is to possess an inheritance. These others will be excluded, but “I,” that is, the Church, “will enter into your house,” that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem. By saying “house,” he indicates a permanent dwelling.

“I will enter”—and this not according to my merits, but “in the multitude of your mercy,” that is, according to the abundance of your mercy—“and I will worship toward the temple,” that is, toward Christ, through whom one enters the heavenly house. He is called the temple because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Concerning him he himself says: “Destroy this temple.” “Holy,” that is, sanctified from his conception; “your,” that is, from you. “I will worship,” I say, “in your fear,” that is, in a fear appropriate [Col. 0212B] to you—not slavish, but filial.

And so that I may be able to enter, you, “Lord, lead me,” that is, be my guide in the present, giving me strength, “in your righteousness.” I do not ask on the basis of mercy alone, but your righteousness requires this: just as you condemn the wicked, so you should reward the righteous. “Lead me,” I say, “because of my enemies,” who wish to hinder me; and in the future “direct my way,” showing me how I may avoid my enemies. “My way” means my works, so that those works may be “in your sight,” that is, in your good pleasure, and so that I may understand that way. Here he asks to be freed from the rival; he also indicates persecution by saying, “because of my enemies.”

Therefore I say, “Direct me; lead me because of my enemies, for there is no truth in their mouth.” Nor am I surprised, because their heart is empty; hence it is said: “Out of the [Col. 0212C] abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12).

“Their throat also,” that is, their mouth—for voices are formed in the throat—“is an open tomb,” that is, like an open tomb. Just as an open tomb gives off a stench and awaits some corpse, so they emit foul words, namely heresies, and incorporate others into themselves by separating them from the body of the Church and making them like themselves.

Here he indicates the open preaching of heresy and suggests the hidden seduction of words. “They acted deceitfully with their tongues,” that is, by flattering speech they recommended deadly poisons to the hearts of their hearers. He said “they acted” so as to prove that their malice was present not only in their tongues but also in their conduct. He calls the seduction hidden when falsehood is mixed with truth; it is open where [Col. 0212D] there is falsehood alone.

And because they are such, “God, judge them,” that is, show that they are deserving of condemnation. He does not say this from a malicious wish, but he cannot fail to agree with the divine judgment.

He shows how he wishes them to be judged, saying: “Let them fall from their counsels,” that is, let the thoughts by which they hope to obtain a kingdom they do not deserve be found empty. Or, “let them fall,” that is, let them be unable to accomplish what they plan.

“And drive them out” of your kingdom, punishing them “according to the multitude of their ungodliness,” that is, so that the measure of their punishments corresponds to the measure of their offenses. “Drive them out,” I say, “because they have provoked you to anger, Lord.”

[Col. 0213A] Let these, then, be driven out, but “let all who hope in you rejoice” in soul, and also “let them exult” in body “forever,” that is, in eternal exultation—and this because you “will dwell in them.” Here he establishes the manner of blessedness when he says that it is eternal, and also that it consists in the fact that he himself will dwell in them. He also gives assurance of that blessedness by saying, “let them rejoice; they will exult,” because “you will dwell in them.”

“And” also “they will glory,” that is, they will rejoice that they are glorious on account of the crown of their merits. “All who are in you,” that is, all who are held in you, “who love your name,” that is, your fame and glory, since we cannot possess knowledge of the divine substance. By saying “all,” he indicates that even those who have a lesser share in that [Col. 0213B] blessedness are glorious.

“They will glory, because you will bless,” that is, you will give increase to virtue, “the righteous man,” namely, in this life, on account of which he will glory in the next. “They will glory,” and “you will bless,” and all these things will proceed from your good will, by which you have “crowned” them. This is what he says: “You have crowned us” in your good will. That good will will not merely be our crown and reward in the life to come; it is also, in the present life, our shield, that is, our protection.

He expresses this intransitively when he says: “With the shield of good will,” that is, with good will existing as a shield. This is expressed by comparison: just as a round shield placed before the breast is a protection, while a crown is placed above, so in this life good will is a protection because it enables one to merit; and in the other life it is reward and crown.

## PSALM VI

### Title: To the end, for the Eighth; a Psalm of David

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” Augustine: Some say that the Eighth signifies the Lord’s coming, because, as they claim, he will come after seven thousand years. But no one knows that period. Rather, it is the eighth day, because all times revolve in a cycle of seven days, whereas that day will have no variation.

Or there are two lives. One pertains to the body, which is the old man, to whom the Old Testament was also given and over whom death reigned. The other pertains to the soul, which is the new man, regenerated through Christ. The number four pertains to the body, and the number three to the soul. When both have been completed, as it were, in the number seven, the eighth day of judgment will come, when [Col. 0213D] each person will be repaid according to his merits.

Therefore, fearing this, the Church prays as follows: “To the end, for the Eighth; a Psalm of David.” That is, this psalm is attributed to the penitent David, or to any penitent person. The penitent is represented by David because he is both “strong of hand” when he overcomes sins and “desirable in appearance,” since other sinners desire to attain conformity with him.

I call it a psalm appointed for the eighth day, that is, for the day of judgment, or for fear of the future, which will come after the week of this world, which revolves through seven days. I call it a psalm directing its hearers to the end, that is, to Christ.

Its subject is any true penitent, and here too the speaker is a penitent. He treats this subject in the following way: he makes a supplication, shows satisfaction, that is, amendment, and [Col. 0214A] offers a prayer for his enemies. Its purpose is to lead us to repentance and, through all these things, to direct us to Christ.

He begins with a supplication. The prophet, conscious of his sins—or any penitent person—and terrified by fear of the punishments that he understands are to come upon sinners on the eighth day, knowing that supplication is more effective before the judge himself than excuse, beseeches him by the power of that judge, saying:

“Lord”—in this life rebuke me, that is, convict me of having sinned, while nevertheless making me repent—“do not rebuke me in your fury,” that is, in your more severe vengeance, namely the future judgment. And here correct me: “do not correct me,” that is, do not restrain me there from the evil undertaking into which I had entered, “in [Col. 0214B] your anger,” that is, in a lighter punishment, namely by giving me a punishment lighter than your fury.

Or, “in your anger” means in some punishment inflicted after death before the judgment, that is, in purgatory. By presenting God as so greatly to be feared, he indicates his power.

“Do not rebuke me; do not correct me,” but rather “have mercy on me, Lord.” And this is necessary “because” I “am weak” under the weight of sins. “I am weak”; therefore, “heal me, Lord,” that is, show by healing me the compassionate affections you have concerning my miseries, namely by removing my sins.

“For my bones,” that is, the higher power of my soul, namely the mind, “are troubled” by the multitude of sins. By “bones,” which are the stronger part of the body, the stronger part of the soul is signified according to merit. By speaking of “bones” in the plural, he understands the strengths of the mind—chastity, temperance, and other such virtues—to have been weakened.

[Col. 0214C] The higher power of the soul has been troubled, “and my soul,” that is, the whole soul, not merely according to its higher power but also according to its lower power, namely according to all the senses, so that it sins in hearing and seeing and so forth, “has been greatly troubled,” that is, by many serious sins.

When he says that he is weak and that the soul is troubled according to both its higher and lower powers, he indicates every kind of penitence. “I am greatly troubled”; and you, Lord, “how long” will you delay healing me?

Do not delay, but you who have until now been hostile while I was impenitent, “turn” toward me, who have turned toward you, as you said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1). Turn, be merciful, and rescue my soul from the bonds of sins [Col. 0214D] by which it is held. “Save me,” namely by giving me virtues.

When he sets forth his weaknesses, he beseeches him on account of his own miseries. But now, by saying “turn,” he beseeches him through the mercy of the judge himself, when he says, “because of your mercy.”

Therefore I pray that you heal, rescue, and save me quickly, “because there is no remembrance of you in death.” That is, no one placed at life’s passing will have a fruitful remembrance of you if he merely remembers you—and especially in hell. Understand “hell” as despair.

“Who will confess to you?” He does not deny every kind of confession. For it is written concerning the rich man: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me” (Luke 16), and so forth. But he denies salutary [Col. 0215A] confession.

Isaiah speaks of both in this way: “For those who are in hell will not praise you, nor will those who are dead bless you” (Isaiah 38). In this verse he makes his supplication through confession before the judge. For it is God’s custom to receive confession only in this life.

Confession in death and in hell is useless. Therefore, considering this, “I have labored” by keeping watch, fasting, and offering the other fruits of repentance, “in my groaning,” that is, in compunction of heart proceeding from remembrance of sins and fear of punishments.

A groan is called almost a “double lament,” because it is doubled over sin and over the punishment of sin. Concerning this it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5).

“I have labored,” and I will labor, namely “I will wash,” [Col. 0215B] that is, I will cleanse, “my bed,” that is, my flesh, going “through every night,” that is, through every sin. Sins are called nights because through ignorance they blind the mind.

The flesh is called a bed because the soul rests in it by consenting to its pleasures. I will not merely wash, but also “water,” that is, prepare for fruitfulness, “my couch with my tears,” both inward and outward. An inward tear is compunction.

“My couch,” that is, my flesh, which is called a couch insofar as it is placed beneath our dominion. Through the watering of tears, the body itself is made suitable for fruitfulness, just as the earth is prepared for fruitfulness by the watering of water. In this verse he shows satisfaction.

“I have labored” and “I will wash,” because “my eye,” the inward eye, [Col. 0215C] that is, reason, “has been troubled,” that is, terrified, “because of the fury,” that is, because of the cause of the fury that the Lord will exercise on the day of judgment.

And rightly has it been troubled, “because I have grown old,” that is, although I ought to have been a member of the new man, I was a member of the old man, so that I deserve to be cast away, like the Old Testament, dwelling “among all my enemies,” that is, acting together with every kind of sin, namely adultery, fornication, and so forth.

I have grown old among all my enemies; but now, “all you who work iniquity,” whoever you are, “depart from me” spiritually, because henceforth I do not wish to do evil with you, “for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping,” that is, of my compunction, because he has heard it by forgiving my sins.

[Col. 0215D] “The Lord has heard my supplication,” namely, that I might not sin thereafter, “and the Lord himself has received my prayer,” by giving me virtues. He says “Lord” twice and “God” once, and thus expresses the Trinity. By saying “depart from me,” he indicated amendment, namely that he would no longer sin.

Here he prays for his enemies. For it was just that, having obtained forgiveness, he should likewise forgive others.

The continuation is: “The Lord has heard me”; therefore, “let my enemies,” seeing me, “be ashamed” of their evil works, “and let them be greatly troubled” by fear of the future judgment, that is, so that they may repent and turn to good works, and after their conversion be ashamed [Col. 0216A] of their former sins.

That shame is beneficial, so that we may avoid sins—and this “very quickly,” that is, so that they do not wait for death or hell.

## PSALM VII

### Title: To the end, a Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush the son of Jemini

“Lord my God.” It is written (2 Samuel 16) that David sent Cush the son of Jemini, a member of his household, with Absalom, so that he might remain with him during the persecution and report Absalom’s secrets back to David. When David heard those secrets and hoped to be delivered, he composed this psalm, considering not the history itself but what the history signified.

For just as through those hidden matters he possessed hope of deliverance, so every righteous person through the incarnation [Col. 0216B] of Christ hopes to be freed from the power of the devil.

This psalm suits David, that is, the Lord’s man himself, and all righteous people, because here every righteous person speaks. He sang this psalm to the Lord, that is, with exultation, and on account of the things contained in this psalm he praised the Lord. For every righteous person praises the Lord with exultation on account of the things contained in this psalm.

“Concerning the words of Cush” means concerning the manifestation of silence, that is, of Christ’s incarnation, which is manifested here. This psalm treats of silence, that is, of the incarnation of God—a silence that was hidden at that time. It also treats of the hidden silence of judgment, namely the judgment he now exercises: that he permits the wicked to prevail over the good and afflicts them with various kinds of punishment.

For Cush is interpreted as “silence,” [Col. 0216C] specifically “the son of Jemini,” that is, generated from God’s propitiation. Jemini, in turn, is interpreted as “right hand”; by the right hand, propitiation is understood.

I call it a psalm directing its hearers to the end, that is, to Christ, through hope. Its subject is the mystery of Christ, namely divinity joined to humanity. It treats this subject as follows: it shows the exaltation of divinity, which he possessed in taking vengeance on his enemies and possessing their boundaries; and it shows how he judges every righteous person, both the Lord’s man and others, and every wicked person.

God always judges in this life that the righteous should be punished by the wicked for their perfection. This judgment of God shows that they endure it patiently and therefore pray. Then he gives a warning to the wicked, and in this way intends to establish us in hope.

Just as we said above concerning Psalm 3, “Lord, [Col. 0216D] how they have multiplied,” which was placed third because it treats of the resurrection, which took place on the third day, so we can also call this one the seventh because it treats of the hope in which we rest, just as the Lord rested on the seventh day.

The righteous person, or Christ, speaking here and enduring persecutors with patience, first offers a prayer that he may be freed from his enemies, saying:

“Lord,” who possess dominion, “God,” that is, creator of all things, who are “my” God through intimacy, “I have hoped in you.” Here we note the purpose: “and therefore save me,” so that I may not yield to the temptations of my enemies.

“Save me,” I say—me thereby delivered “from all who persecute me,” both external and internal—and “deliver me,” namely so that they may no longer rise up against me.

[Col. 0217A] Therefore I say, “save me, lest my enemy ever seize my soul,” acting like a lion. Concerning this enemy the Apostle says: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

“Since there is no one,” that is, since there is no other one “who may redeem” by giving a price, “nor anyone who may save,” rescuing the redeemed so that they do not yield to the enemy’s ambushes, except you.

You ought to save me because there is no other who can do so; and also because I have done nothing for which they should persecute me.

“And if I, Lord God, have done this,” that is, if I have deserved their persecution—namely these evils that they inflict on me—then let these evils that I am now about to mention befall me.

When he said, “If I have done this,” he specifies it by adding: “If there is iniquity [Col. 0217B] in my hands,” that is, in my works. It is clear concerning Christ that he had no iniquity. As for the other righteous, even if they are not free from sins, they commit nothing against their persecutors.

I have not deserved this because I first inflicted evil on them, nor because I repaid evil with evil. This is what he adds: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” By saying “those who repaid,” he indicates that he received evil from those to whom he had rendered the service of kindness.

Through all these statements, and especially through this one, he commends his patience.

“If I have done these things, let me deservedly fall,” that is, be overcome, “empty” before my enemies, that is, receiving no fruit of patience—which would deservedly happen to me.

Or “empty before my enemies” means frustrated, acquiring none of my enemies.

[Col. 0217C] In addition to this evil, let another also befall me: namely, “let the enemy pursue my soul,” that is, let the devil and his members attack it, “and seize my life,” that is, make me succumb to himself—my life meaning the soul by which I ought to live—“and trample it down,” that is, make me contemptible through many disgraces, so that it may be wholly “on the earth,” that is, devoted to earthly things, and thereby become food for the devil.

“And let him bring my glory,” that is, my reason—for it is called my glory because through it I am like God—“down into the dust,” that is, make it like dust: just as dust does not resist the wind, so may my reason not resist the devil.

“If I have done this,” let these evils mentioned above befall me. But because I have not done them, “arise, Lord, in your [Col. 0217D] anger,” that is, in your vengeance, so that you may rescue human beings from the devil, “and exalt yourself in the boundaries,” that is, in the possessions, “of your enemies,” that is, of the demons, by possessing those whom the devil now possesses.

The Lord is exalted in breasts when praise in confession is offered to him by those who have been converted. From this verse he begins to show the exaltation of divinity.

“Arise,” I say, so that you may possess the boundaries of your enemies, “and arise in the commandment that you have given,” that is, establish and fulfill your laws in all those who have been possessed. Thus the assembly of the peoples will surround you, attacking both Christ and the other righteous.

“And because of this,” because of its obstinacy against you, “return on high,” that is, withdraw yourself from their [Col. 0218A] knowledge, so that you may be on high. Just as you humbled yourself so that they might know you by assuming flesh, so withdraw yourself into the height in which you were.

Or, “Arise in the commandment that you have given” means: in the law you commanded us to punish the wicked; therefore arise against them in accordance with that law.

“And” thus “the assembly,” which withdrew from you because of the death and disgrace inflicted on you, “will surround you,” that is, by adhering to you it will surround you. And for the sake of confirming it, “return on high,” that is, show yourself powerful through the Ascension, so that those who had adhered to you in your humiliation may likewise look upon you, glorified, as their rewarder.

Since he said, “Arise, Lord,” he showed the exaltation of divinity. Thereafter he shows the judgment and turns to us, as though he were saying: The Lord has been exalted in this way, and the Lord himself judges the peoples. And you, “Lord, judge me according to my innocence,” that is, according to my good works, “and according to my innocence,” namely, according to the fact that I have harmed no one, “which is upon me,” that is, given to me from above.

“Judge me,” I say, and “let the iniquity of sinners be brought to an end,” that is, let it be completed in me, the righteous, so that they may torture me according to the will of their wickedness. And by this “you will direct the righteous” toward yourself.

In this verse the judgment of the righteous and the wicked is indicated. By saying that sinners should complete their iniquity, he shows the judgment of sinners. For it is just that “the one who is filthy should be filthy still” (Revelation 22).

When he says that, after the iniquity of sinners has been completed in the righteous, the righteous themselves are directed, he presents the judgment of the righteous. For God judges his own by testing them through persecution.

In Christ, the iniquity of the Jews was completed when he was crucified; the righteous one himself was directed when he rose from the dead. Decius’s iniquity was completed in Lawrence when he killed him by fire. The same applies to other righteous and wicked people.

Judge according to righteousness, I say, “you who search hearts,” that is, who see thoughts perfectly, “and reins,” that is, carnal pleasures, for the reins are the seat of lust. Or let us understand “reins” as stronger thoughts, since God alone knows the secrets of the heart.

I said, “The iniquity of sinners will be completed”; and against that iniquity let there be for me “help from the Lord,” so that it may not prevail over me, which is just according to my [Col. 0218D] patience and righteousness, “who saves the upright in heart,” because they overcome every temptation of the enemy.

And because the Lord is such, therefore you wicked people, turn to him, because “unless you turn, he will brandish his sword” against you, since he is God the judge, that is, he will repay each person according to his desert.

By this he shows that he has the power to punish. And so that they may not excuse themselves by claiming that the judge lacks power, he adds: “strong,” that is, one whose will no one can resist.

And so that they might not say, “If he were powerful, he would already have punished us,” he adds: “patient,” that is, not punishing immediately but awaiting the sinners’ repentance. He proves that he is patient by not immediately punishing sins. This is what follows: “Does he become angry every day?” [Col. 0219A] That is, does he punish every day? “No.”

And because he is judge and powerful, therefore “unless you turn to him, he will brandish his sword,” sending you to judgment. To the righteous he will show it gleaming, but to the wicked, dark. A brandished sword shows at one moment darkness and at another brightness.

In the judgment he will brandish his sword; and already “he has bent his bow,” that is, he strikes us with threats through divine Scripture. By the wood of the bow the Old Testament is understood, because, like wood, it was useless and inflexible by itself. By the cord, the New Testament is understood, by which the Old is stretched and brought back to the usefulness of understanding. “And he prepared it,” that is, through certain teachers he made it intelligible to us.

“And in it,” namely in that bow, divine Scripture, “he prepared [Col. 0219B] vessels of death,” that is, the apostles and other teachers, from whom death is offered. For whom? For those who do not receive their teaching. But for those “who burn,” that is, who desire God, he “made ready his arrows,” namely the preachers themselves, or the divine judgments that wound hearts, making them suitable to be received and understood.

Hence the Apostle says: “We are the fragrance of death leading to death for some, and the fragrance of life leading to life for others” (2 Corinthians 2).

Although God brandishes the sword in this way and prepares the bow in this way, the wicked do not cease. Behold, the wicked man “was in labor,” that is, he attempts to bring forth “injustice,” not because someone else compels him to do this, but because he himself “conceived” it through thought and will, and conceived “pain,” that is, sin, for which he ought chiefly to grieve, “and gave birth,” that is, [Col. 0219C] completed in action, to “iniquity.”

By doing these things he “opened a pit for himself,” that is, prepared for himself a precipice of sin, “and dug it out,” that is, enlarged the danger, “and fell into the pit that he had made.” By the very means through which he prepared death for others, he rather hindered himself.

Hence Augustine says: No one sins against another without first sinning against himself. Just as someone wishing to deceive others first opens the earth, then digs it out by enlarging the pit, and finally, unless he takes good care, falls into that same pit.

A pit is so called because its bottom is hidden. Sin is called a pit insofar as we do not know the end of the ruin that threatens as a result of sin.

In this life the sinner falls into the pit of sin, but finally, on the day of judgment, “his pain will return,” [Col. 0219D] that is, the sin committed here with pleasure will there inflict pain, “upon his head,” that is, upon his soul. For the soul will there be punished for everything in which it sinned here.

“And upon his crown,” that is, upon his higher part, namely reason, “his iniquity will descend,” that is, the sins to which reason consented here will there be destroyed without any blindness.

Since he said, “God is a just judge,” he presented a warning to the wicked.

And because he is such, therefore “I will confess to the Lord,” that is, I will praise the Lord. “Confession” is understood either of sins or of praise. “According to,” that is, because of, “his righteousness,” and I will sing psalms by doing good works “to the name of the Lord,” that is, to increase [Col. 0220A] the Lord’s honor, “the Most High,” whose name ought to be praised because he himself is Most High.

To sing psalms is to carry out the Lord’s commandments in one’s works and to sing hymns, psalms, and songs with voice and heart.

## PSALM VIII

### Title: To the end, a Psalm of David, for the winepresses

“Lord, our Lord.” This psalm suits the prophet David and all those of the Church that existed before Christ’s coming.

I call it a psalm dealing with the winepresses, that is, with the Church. It is understood as a winepress because in it there are both those who are to be rejected and those who are to be received. Just as wine is pressed out in a winepress and retained, while the grape-skin remains and is thrown away, so [Col. 0220B] the whole pressure of the Church occurs by Christ’s permission.

The psalm directs us to Christ, and this is what “to the end” means: it admonishes us unbelievers to submit voluntarily to God.

Its subject is Christ. It treats him as follows: it shows the excellent power of his divinity through his magnificent works; it also shows his humanity, first humbled and then exalted above every creature.

Its purpose is to admonish unbelievers to submit to such a Lord. Here the speaker is the prophet, or any member of the Church that existed before Christ’s coming. Beginning with the magnification of divinity and considering a certain exultation according to Christ’s dignity, he first says:

“Lord,” who rule over all, “our Lord” you are especially, because we have been made participants in your good things, [Col. 0220C] “how,” that is, how greatly, “your name,” your honor, fame, and glory, “is admirable,” not only in Africa, as certain heretics used to say, but “throughout the whole earth.”

Therefore I say that your name is wondrous, both because “your magnificence,” that is, your magnificent Son, “has been raised above all the heavens,” that is, above the entire angelic creation—or materially above all the heavens. This could not happen unless he were both human and God.

Your name is therefore wondrous for this reason, and also because you “perfected,” that is, made perfect, “praise from the mouth of infants and nursing children.” “Infants” refers to age; “nursing children” means the simple, who needed to be fed with simple teaching.

He calls the praise of children perfect because it does not arise from human ingenuity but solely from the operation of divinity. You perfected it, I say, “because of your enemies,” namely the Pharisees.

This prophecy is taught and expounded in the Gospel from the Lord’s mouth. When the children were being forbidden by the Jews to resound with the Lord’s praise, he replied: “Have you not read that from the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise?” (Matthew 21).

Because of your enemies, I say, “so that you may destroy the enemy,” namely the malicious one, “and the avenger,” that is, the defender of his own law who attacks the truth of the Gospel.

Therefore he says, “you will destroy,” because “I will see” in my successors “your heavens,” that is, the holy apostles, who are called heavens because they contain God’s secrets [Col. 0221A] and also rain the dew of heavenly teaching upon the faithful.

From this we may understand by “heavens” the evangelical books, which contain God’s secrets.

“Heavens,” I say, “the work of your fingers,” that is, those whom the divinity itself has made. By using “fingers” in the plural, he signifies the plurality of persons in the Godhead. Elsewhere he clearly indicates the Trinity when he says: “Who has measured the mass of the earth with three fingers?”

“I will see the moon and the stars.” By the moon he understands the lower Church under the apostles, or the universal Church, which is called the moon because of its waning and increase. By the stars he understands those who shine within the Church in themselves.

“These stars,” or “which”—namely the heavens and the moon—“you founded,” that is, established firmly, so that they cannot be moved by any temptations.

[Col. 0221B] Since you have made all these things, then “what is man?” That is, I see man to be something great, insofar as you are mindful of him. For through the sending of your Son you prepare the restoration of the human race.

“Or what is the son of man?” That is, what is the humanity of Christ? “Because you visit him,” uniting your Son to yourself.

By saying “son of man,” he indicates that Christ is truly human. By saying “of man,” not “of men,” he suggests that he did not derive his humanity from a human father but from his mother alone.

You visited the son of man, and that Son together with the visiting divinity—that is, the whole Christ—“you diminished” according to divinity. Divinity was humbled when it allowed humanity to be united to it.

Hence the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Col. 0221C] (Philippians 2).

You diminished him, I say, so that Christ, according to his humanity, was lower than the angels, because he was capable of suffering and mortal, “but only a little,” because even while he was so fragile, the angels ministered to him as to the Lord.

And after he had first been diminished in this way, “you crowned him with glory” in the resurrection “and honor,” that is, with a multitude of servants through his exaltation to heaven.

When he says “you crowned,” he indicates that some confess the glory of the crown of the whole world’s resurrection and Ascension. And thus, having honored him, “you established him over the works of your hands,” even over the angelic creation.

And because he could have established him as more worthy than all creatures without nevertheless subjecting all things to him—for one bishop may be more worthy than all the others without all being subject to him—he adds: “under [Col. 0221D] his feet,” that is, you subjected “all things” to him completely, meaning all creatures.

For just as what is under someone’s feet is wholly subject to him, so all things are subject to Christ. Although some still rebel, they do nothing except by his permission.

Or “under his feet” means under his humanity, which is called the feet because through it divinity descended to us.

He shows in detail what all things he subjected: “sheep,” that is, the simple in the Church, concerning whom the Lord says to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21); “and oxen,” that is, holy preachers who thresh the Church. Hence Moses says: “You shall not muzzle the ox that is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25).

He says “all” in the feminine form in order to signify certain [Col. 0222A] offspring in the Church.

“Moreover, the cattle of the field”: by the cattle of the field he understands those who are held under no one’s guardianship and wander widely. By saying “moreover,” he indicates their distinction from the good.

And also “the birds of the heavens,” that is, those who are lifted up in pride; “and the fish of the sea,” that is, those who seek food with curiosity and pursue worldly things anxiously.

For just as fish diligently seek their food, so some seek possessions, like merchants, while others investigate the natures of things, like philosophers, who traverse the paths of the sea.

By the sea we understand the world, which is always in motion, like the sea.

Earlier, when he said “you diminished,” he showed the humility of the human nature; from that point up to here he has spoken of the exaltation of the human nature.

Having thus shown such great dignity, he concludes, as it were, in the same admonition with which he had begun. He ends with: “O Lord, our Lord.” And a mystery is indicated there, so that just as we begin from what is good, so we may end with it.

## PSALM IX. TITLE: To the end, a psalm of David, concerning the hidden things of the Son.

“I will confess.” This psalm applies to David, who here also speaks concerning the hidden things of the Son, that is, of Christ. For in this psalm the hidden things of Christ are discussed, and it directs us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. In this psalm he intends to invite us to fear Christ. Its subject is the work of Christ at his first and second coming, concerning which he proceeds as follows. He shows that at his second coming Christ will condemn the devil together with his members. At his first coming, however, he shows what he does for his own people and what he does against the persecutors of the Church, whether against the head, Antichrist, or against his followers. Then he pronounces a curse upon the persecutors of the Church. Next, considering the evils that Antichrist will inflict upon the Church, he enumerates those evils in the form of a question. Finally, he prays for the end of the world.

Foreseeing the destruction of the enemies at the second coming, the prophet bursts into a kind of exultation, saying: “I will confess to you, O Lord,” with a confession of praise. He says “with my heart,” because no confession is effective that does not proceed from the heart; he says “my,” because it is subject to him; he says “whole,” because it is obstructed by no evil thought or anything else. “I will recount all your wonders.” He does not say this because he recounts all God’s wonders, but because whatever he says about him is wondrous.

“I will rejoice” also in spirit, “and exult” in body—not in worldly things, but “in you.” “I will sing psalms” also by doing good works, “to your name,” in order to magnify the name of that “Most High” Lord, since you are the Most High.

“I will rejoice,” I say, “and exult. When my enemy turns back,” that is, in contemplating the enemy’s conversion. Although he rules over us here in a certain manner, nevertheless on the day of judgment his dominion will be utterly destroyed. His turning back—that is, the destruction of his dominion—began through Christ’s death, but will be fully completed on the day of judgment. He and his followers “will be weakened,” that is, they will lose the power to do harm; this weakening likewise begins in the present life through Christ’s death. And they “will perish” by eternal damnation, removed “from your face,” that is, from your knowledge, according to what is said: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI).

Therefore they will perish and be weakened “because you have established my cause,” that is, made it useful to me. For there he left us an example of patience and humility. And “the judgment,” that is, the sentence of death imposed by the Jews, “you have made mine,” that is, useful to me. For through your death we have been redeemed. You can destroy the adversaries because “you sit,” that is, rest, “upon the throne,” that is, upon the royal seat, “you who judge justice,” that is, justly. By this he indicates that God wills to destroy them.

“You judge this justice,” namely: “You rebuked the nations,” that is, you will condemn those who live like pagans by rebuking them for their evil deeds. “And the ungodly,” that is, the devil, “will perish” eternally. “You will blot out their name,” that is, all their power—the power of those who live like pagans—forever. And lest we understand “forever” as extending only to the end of the world, as Moses says, “The Lord will reign forever and beyond” (Exod. XV), he adds, “and unto the age,” that is, the age succeeding this one.

The ungodly will perish because “the weapons”—that is, the temptations—“of the enemy,” that is, of the devil, “will fail at the end,” that is, after they reach the final end. “And you will destroy their cities,” that is, the gatherings of their subjects, fortified by the opinions of false teachers for the defense of their errors. And then “their memory will perish,” namely, that affection which the saints have for them while they are still living in this life. Hence the Gospel says: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke XVI), “with a sound,” that is, with the great anguish of those who perish. For just as the destruction of some city brings great grief and a great tumult, so it will be among those who perish.

“They will perish in this way, but the Lord remains forever.” He truly remains forever because “he prepared his throne for judgment,” that is, while he was being judged—or “for judgment,” so that he may judge. “And he himself will judge the world,” that is, all the good who live throughout the world, “with equity,” namely, according to their merits. “He will also judge the peoples,” namely, sinners, “with justice,” that is, according to the merits of each individual.

[Col. 0223D] Thus far he has dealt with the second coming; now he begins to discuss the first. First he shows what Christ does for his own people. At the second coming he will judge, while that same Lord, in this life, became the refuge of the poor. He rightly says “became,” because although God owed nothing to humanity—for humanity had withdrawn from him through its own guilt—he nevertheless made a mediator, through whom he would redeem humanity. He says “refuge” by way of comparison: just as combatants, when they cannot stand their ground, flee to some fortified place, so the faithful, when they cannot stand by their own strength, flee to Christ, who either supplies endurance or lessens their sufferings.

He calls him poor who, although he possesses things, has been emptied of earthly desire and longs to grow rich through heavenly generosity. He is also the helper who cooperates with us: if someone begins to fast, God lends him his hand. He is a helper, I say, in tribulation. The sweetest help is that which is supplied in need, as he says in another psalm: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will honor me” (Ps. XLIX). And he is not a helper in tribulation in just any manner, but “in times of opportunity,” that is, according to what is fitting. If someone in tribulation asks that the tribulations be removed, he is not worthy to be heard; but if he begs for endurance, he is worthy to be heard.

You help in tribulation, and you do not abandon them, that is, you do not allow them to be overcome. Although you abandon them—that is, although for a time you allow them to suffer tribulation, or even occasionally to fall—some falls are useful, such as the falls of those “who seek you, O Lord,” that is, those who strive in every way to obey your will.

And because you have not abandoned them, therefore “let all who know your name hope in you.” He understands “to know” not as inward knowledge, but as consisting solely in faith and good works. Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John I).

He does not abandon his own, but will seek their blood. Therefore, “sing psalms to the Lord,” and he specifies which Lord: the one who bodily “dwells in Zion,” that is, in Judea. For Zion is the capital of Judea, where Christ dwelt in the presence of his body. Hence he himself says: “I was sent bodily only to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel” (Matt. XV).

Alternatively, by Zion, which means “watchtower,” we may understand the Church. “Declare among the nations,” that is, among those who live like pagans, “his zealous purposes”—namely this: “For he is the one who seeks their blood,” that is, the blood of those who seek the Lord; “he has remembered,” namely, those who are afflicted and those who afflict. God seems to have forgotten his own when he permits them to suffer tribulation; he remembers them when he comes to their aid.

He calls them “zealous purposes” because God does not merely judge, but exacts vengeance with deliberate purpose. “He has remembered the afflicted, and has not forgotten the cry of the poor”—that is, the supplication of those who cannot endure tribulations. God immediately has mercy and delivers them from tribulation.

“The cry of the poor,” who say: “Have mercy on me, O Lord,” namely, in this way: “See my humility,” that is, my affliction. “See,” I say, “from my enemies,” that is, from the pride of my enemies. For if you consider the manner in which they inflict their proud attacks, you can understand how great is the affliction of those who endure them.

When he says to the Lord, “See my humility,” he speaks by comparison. Just as someone fights better if his lord sees him, so Christ’s faithful endure better if God sees them. For the Lord’s seeing is his helping.

“See my humility.” And thus “I will exult in your salvation,” that is, in your saving deliverance.

And therefore I ought to exult, because you are the one “who exalts me,” that is, by removing me “from the gates of death,” namely, from evil works through which one enters hell. Thus, exalted, I am placed “at the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the virtues which are the entrance into the Church. It is called the daughter of Zion because it was begotten in Zion, that is, in Judea, through Christ’s passion.

Alternatively, it is called the daughter of Zion, that is, the daughter of the watchtower, because there would be no Church unless it contemplated God. “I will proclaim” to all others “all your praises,” not because he says everything that can be said about God with praise, but because whatever he says will be his praise.

And because you exalt me in this way, “I will exult in your salvation.” Here he begins to say what God does to the persecutors of the Church at the first coming.

The connection is as follows: God helps his own in this way, “but the nations,” that is, those who live like pagans, “are caught in the destruction which they themselves made.” For when they kill others bodily, they kill themselves spiritually. “Caught” is said by way of comparison. Just as a nail driven into wood or mud cannot rise again by itself, so those murderers cannot by themselves rise from their wickedness. And “their foot,” that is, their desire, “has been caught in the snare,” that is, in the deceitfulness, “which they secretly laid,” that is, secretly set for others.

They do not know that this judgment of the Lord has been given against them in this life, but “the Lord will be known as he executes judgments,” because “the sinner has been caught,” in this life, “in the works of his hands,” that is, in the pleasures derived from his actions.

Because sinners persecute the Church of God in this way, therefore “let them turn back” from their purpose of persecution and be cast “into hell,” the material hell. I mean sinners, namely, “all the nations that forget God,” that is, those who either do not have faith or, if they have it, do not perform God’s works.

They will truly turn back, because the poor will be rewarded. And this is: “The forgetfulness of the poor will not be unto the end,” that is, forever. For although God seems in this life to forget the poor, nevertheless, when he comes at the end of the age, the Lord will not forget them. And if the Lord remembers the poor in a general sense, then he will much more remember the patience of the poor. Thus: “The patience of the poor,” that is, the reward of the poor’s patience, “will not perish.” Here he invokes punishment upon the persecutors.

And so that their patience may not perish, “you, O Lord, arise. Let man not be strengthened,” that is, let him not long prosper in the persecution of the saints. “Man” means Antichrist, who, although he claims to be God, is simply a man. Let him not be strengthened, and also let “the nations,” namely, his followers and accomplices, “be judged in your sight.” Even if others do not know that they have been judged, nevertheless they are judged before you.

Let them be judged in this manner: “Appoint a lawgiver over them,” namely, Antichrist, who will establish over them a law contrary to the law of Christ. And let them also be judged in this way: “Let the nations themselves know” at some point “that they are merely human,” that is, carnal.

The prophet, looking ahead to the great persecution that will come from Antichrist, complains as though God had withdrawn from his own, enumerating Antichrist’s evil deeds. The connection is as follows: I therefore pray that that man may not be strengthened, because I see such great tribulation inflicted by him upon your people that you seem to have withdrawn from them.

And therefore, “why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away,” that is, why do you permit your people to suffer such great tribulation? And why do you also “despise,” that is, just as you seem to have withdrawn, so you also seem to despise them, “in times of opportunity, in tribulation”? That is, when, amid such great tribulations, it would seem fitting for God to strengthen his own by miracles, he will seem to despise them, since he will provide neither miracles nor any such consolation. Here he wishes to enumerate the evils that Antichrist will inflict upon the faithful, and by enumerating them he shows that these evils harm those who inflict them but benefit those who endure them. The connection is as follows:

You seem to have withdrawn, because “the ungodly man is proud,” and out of pride that singular man, Antichrist, afflicts the saints. And while he is so proud, “the poor man is set on fire.” By “is set on fire” he indicates both that the poor man is afflicted and that he is purified. “The ungodly man is proud,” and he and his followers devise evil counsels against the saints, in which counsels “they are caught.” By “they are caught” he indicates that they are hindered by the very snares through which they harm others.

The ungodly man is proud, the poor man is set on fire, and the sinner is praised according to his deeds. He is praised, I say, “in the desires of his soul,” because everything he desires succeeds for him. And those who praise him say: “He could not do these things unless God were with him.” “And the ungodly man himself” is blessed, because he has wickedness by his will; that is, he is exalted, since even in evil deeds he is said to act well.

And because he is thus praised and blessed, “the sinner has provoked the Lord,” that singular man; that is, he has aroused his anger. And he has done so also because he “will not seek” God as his helper, acting “according to the abundance of his anger,” that is, in great fury.

“There is no God even before his eyes,” that is, he does not consider God capable of doing anything. And beyond all these things, “his ways,” that is, his works, “are polluted at all times,” that is, he has never done anything good.

Therefore he has provoked God, because “your judgments are removed from his sight,” that is, from his consideration. For he neither regards you as ruler of all things nor as the future judge. And this is because “he will rule over all his enemies,” since in reality he will subject all the kings of the earth.

He will truly rule, because “he said in his heart,” that is, he reasoned in his heart: “I will move from one generation,” which is subject to me, “to another generation,” which will be subjected to me, “not without evil,” that is, without inflicting evils upon them. Here he indicates the excessive wickedness of that man’s evil.

He is also one “whose mouth is full of wickedness,” that is, blasphemy against God, “and bitterness,” because he speaks bitter and shameful words to human beings, “and deceit,” because he deceives people through hidden deceptions, that is, through promises, and so forth. “Under his tongue are labor and pain,” that is, in his heart, because he thinks of nothing else except how to inflict labor and pain upon the faithful.

Alternatively, “under his tongue” means that those who hear him fear his tongue more than labor and pain.

“He sits,” that is, lingers, “in ambush with the rich,” that is, with the powerful, through whose assistance he will deceive people. He sits “in ambush,” I say, in places “hidden.” For he will secretly deceive people, turning the Scriptures of the prophets toward himself, saying: “I am the promised Messiah. In me too is fulfilled the prophecy that says: ‘All kings will adore him; all nations will serve him’” (Ps. LXXI). He sits for this purpose, “to kill the innocent,” spiritually.

“His eyes also look upon the poor,” through merciful affection. For he will say: “I will move toward you, because you are so afflicted. Abandon that foolishness and turn to me.” Outwardly he will show himself to have affection for them, but inwardly he “lies in wait.” This is what he says: “In secret, like a lion in his den.” When he compares him to a lion, he shows that he will force people to cling to him by violence. When he says “in his den,” he suggests that he acts deceitfully.

And for this purpose, namely, “he lies in wait to seize the poor man.” And lest we always understand the seizure as violent, he adds: “To seize the poor man,” I say, also “when he draws him,” that is, while he seduces him with various flatteries. By repeating “he lies in wait,” he shows that he is extremely intent upon ambushes.

He lies in wait for the poor man in order to seize him, and he will seize him because “he will humble him,” that is, bend him under his laws. “In his snare,” that is, in the snare of Antichrist. While he prepares a snare for others, he himself is caught in it. “He will bend himself,” that is, he will gradually descend toward ruin. For the more he afflicts others, the nearer he himself is to ruin. “And he will fall,” because the Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth; but he will fall only then “when he has ruled over the poor,” whom he will subject to himself.

And rightly will he fall. “For he said in his heart,” that is, he reasoned in his heart, because he believed what he said to be true: “God has forgotten his own,” and “has turned away his face,” that is, his presence, “so that he may not see” the deeds that I perform in punishing them; and not even “at the end,” that is, neither in this life nor in the future.

Seeing that people in the time of Antichrist will seek death because of their excessive tribulation, the prophet introduces their person and prays for the end and for Christ’s second coming, just as above he also made the complaint in their person. The connection is as follows:

He says that God has forgotten them, but you, “O Lord God, arise, and let your hand be exalted,” that is, your vengeance, “so that you do not forget the poor,” as that man supposes.

And rightly should you take vengeance upon him, because “the ungodly man has provoked God.” And why has he provoked him? That is, what was the principal cause of that provocation? This: “For he said in his heart,” thinking as follows: “The Lord will not seek,” that is, will not exact vengeance. This provocation was therefore especially great because his speech is directed against God himself; and this is what it means to set one’s mouth in heaven. By speaking through questions, he urges us to inquire; by responding, he satisfies those who inquire.

He says, “He will not seek,” but you, Lord, see how you “deliver him into your hands,” that is, into your vengeance. You truly see this, because the depths of his thoughts are not hidden from your sight. This is what he says: “For you consider labor and pain,” that is, his thought about inflicting pain and labor upon others. Hence it was said above: “Under his tongue are labor and pain.”

You ought rightly to deliver them into your hands, because “to you,” that is, into your keeping, “the poor man has been abandoned.” That is, he trusts in no one else except you alone. And the poor man abandoned to you will not be frustrated, because “you will be the helper of the orphan,” that is, of one whose father and mother have died: the devil is the father, and the pleasure of the flesh the mother.

The devil is called “father” because all animal human beings are both generated and born in sin. Pleasure is called “mother” because, just as a mother gives birth to a child, so the pleasure of the flesh nourishes the fool.

Because the poor man has been abandoned to you, therefore “crush,” that is, annihilate, “the arm,” that is, the strength and power, “of the sinner” in action, “and of the wicked man” in intention. It is now time for his power to be destroyed, because his wickedness has been completed and the Church has been purified by his persecution. This is what follows: “His sin will be sought”—let us understand this as meaning that an inquiry will be made as to what place his sin has in the Church—“and it will not be found.” For where nothing remains to be purified, there the ungodly man has no place.

His arm will be crushed, “but the Lord will reign forever.” And I say “forever” in such a way that it is understood as “unto the age of the age.” And lest the nations say, “We too will reign with him,” he adds: “You nations will perish from his land,” removed, namely, from the land of the living.

“Truly, nations, you will perish, because the Lord has heard the desire of the poor,” and also “the preparation of their heart,” that is, from the moment they have a will prepared either by God or by themselves, “your ear hears.” Another translation has “desire” where ours has “preparation.” Therefore let us read it in such a way that it has the same force as “desire”: “He has heard the desire and the preparation,” that is, that which they strove with all the effort of their strength to attain by prayer.

[Col. 0228D] He has heard the desire, namely, “to judge for the orphan and the humble,” that is, to judge for the honor of the orphan and the humble, “so that man may not presume,” that is, may not dare, “to magnify himself any further upon the earth,” namely, the earth of the living, which is called earth because of its solidity.

## PSALM X. TITLE: To the end, a psalm of David.

“In the Lord.” This psalm, namely, applies to David the prophet, who speaks here as well, directing his hearers toward the end, that is, toward Christ. For in this psalm he intends to admonish us to resist heretics. Its subject is Christ, concerning whom he proceeds as follows. He shows that in his judgment Christ blinds certain people, such as heretics. He also shows that he helps and protects his own, so that they do not succumb to the heresies of those people. He further shows that he punishes those ungodly people. And thus he begins against the heretics, as though he were saying: Resist heretics by my example, because “I trust in the Lord.” Therefore, “How,” that is, with what audacity, “do you say”—that is, dare to say, to the detriment of my soul—“Cross over,” that is, pass from the lowliness of scriptural understanding in which you are now to the height of our understanding? This is what he means by “to the mountain.” Then he will be like a sparrow.

There is a certain kind of sparrow which, abandoning low places, builds its nest in the mountains in order to guard itself against snares. The heretics think that those whom they join to themselves are like these sparrows. Another translation has “like a bird,” and according to this the prophet says: “If I were to cross over to you, I would be like a bird,” that is, unstable.

“I said, I trust in the Lord.” And this is necessary, “because behold,” that is, openly, “sinners have drawn,” that is, have applied to their own party, “the bow,” that is, divine Scripture. By calling them sinners, he shows that they have been blinded because of their sins. “They have prepared arrows,” that is, their own opinions; they have sought out arguments and authorities by which to make those opinions appear plausible, “in their quiver,” that is, in their poisonous heart. They have done this “in order to shoot,” that is, kill, “the upright in heart” who are “in darkness.”

The heretics shoot in darkness, that is, in simplicity. They do not attack enlightened and learned men, but the uneducated and those who are ignorant of the Scriptures. Alternatively, “in darkness” means in ambiguity, since by mixing in truth they try to conceal their falsehood. “They shoot,” I say, “the upright in heart in darkness,” that is, in simplicity, because they do not know how to defend themselves through the Scriptures.

They have drawn the bow, I say, “which they have destroyed” through evil interpretations of “what you perfected,” that is, made perfect—namely, divine Scripture. For although the prophets and others are said to have written it, they themselves did nothing; God wrote through them.

Alternatively, “which you perfected” means Christ, whom they are said to destroy by denying something concerning his truth, as if, while granting everything else, they were to deny that the Virgin gave birth.

They have destroyed him. “But what has the just man done?” That is, what has God done? By calling him just, he hints that God ought to help his own and reject his adversaries.

What has he done? Behold what he has done: “The Lord” of all is “in his holy temple.” He is “the Lord,” that is, the one who rules all his own with a kind of familiar dominion. He is “in heaven,” that is, in his secret chambers. “His throne is there,” because there he rests and judges without offense.

He dwells in the temple and sits in heaven, yet he does not abandon even the lesser ones. This is what he means by “his eyes,” that is, the affections of his mercies, “look upon the poor,” helping and sustaining them. And “his eyelids,” that is, the divine Scriptures, “question,” that is, test, “the children of men,” that is, prove the good and the evil.

The Scriptures are called eyelids because eyelids are closed and opened, and so are the divine Scriptures. When the divine Scripture is closed to a good person, it proves him: although the good person may not understand it, he does not neglect it or impose his own meaning upon it by corrupting it. When it is opened, it proves the evil person, because he attributes it not to God’s grace but to his own ingenuity and grows proud.

“They question the children of men,” because the Lord himself “questions the just and the ungodly.” The good person answers appropriately, but “he who loves iniquity,” that is, the evil person, answers in such a way that in the very answer it becomes apparent that he “hates his own soul.”
