Having said that the Lord is in his holy temple, he showed that the Lord protects his own. Now he shows how he will punish his adversaries. The connection is as follows:

The wicked man hates his own soul, and the Lord “rains snares,” that is, errors, by which they are ensnared, “upon sinners,” that is, to the detriment of sinners. He says “rains” because holy Scripture, which is fruitful rain for others, is changed for them into snares and errors.

“Fire,” that is, the heat of desire, “and sulfur,” that is, foul deeds, “and the spirit of storms,” that is, stormy actions, “are their portion,” a portion, I say, “of the cup,” that is, of God’s judgment. In this life he calls God’s judgment a cup because to some it gives life and to others death. Or the cup—that is, eternal judgment—is a portion consisting of “fire,” infernal fire; “sulfur,” the stench of hell; and “the spirit of storms,” the violence of eternal damnation.

Therefore the Lord helps his own “because the just Lord has loved justice.” And this is justice: that he should help his own. He rains snares and the other evils because “his face,” that is, his anger, which is understood through the face, “sees equity,” that is, he repays the wicked with what is just. Hence it is said: “Let the one who is filthy become filthy still.”

## PSALM XI. TITLE: To the end, a psalm of David, concerning the Eighth.

“Save me.” The one who speaks here does so “concerning the Eighth,” not merely out of fear of judgment, as above in “O Lord, not in anger,” but in order to obtain the Eighth, that is, eternal glory, which will be given on that day, to which he thinks he will happily arrive through the Savior whom he introduces. And he directs us toward the end.

For he exhorts us—his contemporaries and all others—to make Christ the end of their expectation. Its subject is Christ, concerning whom he proceeds as follows: he shows that the salvation of the human race was promised through Christ, and that Christ is capable of accomplishing it. He demonstrates this by showing that Christ is opposed to vanity, through which that salvation is lost. Seeking to be freed from this vanity, he begins as follows:

“Save me, O Lord,” so that the vanity of this age may not prevail over me. And this is necessary, “because the holy one has failed,” that is, holiness has been diminished. By saying “has failed,” he indicates that humanity was created in holiness and that among the earlier fathers there were many holy people.

It truly has failed, “because truths have been diminished,” that is, shortened, “by the children of men,” that is, by rational beings, whose reason they ought to have imitated. By saying “truths” in the plural, he indicates that every kind of truth has been diminished in many people. By saying “diminished,” he clearly indicates that God’s gifts have been corrupted by human faults.

Truth has been diminished, and vanity has entered in. Thus: “They have spoken vain things,” that is, things that do not pertain to true salvation. And not just a few, but “each one to his neighbor,” that is, to deceive his neighbor. I mean those who are “deceitful lips,” that is, talkative and loquacious people who deceive secretly.

Such people have spoken “in their heart,” that is, in multiplicity, because, in order to deceive each individual, they employ different arts according to each person’s character. Here he invokes punishment.

[Col. 0231B] They speak vain things, but “may the Lord destroy deceitful lips.” Among deceitful lips he especially curses what was most harmful when he says “the boastful tongue,” namely, that of worldly philosophers. He says “destroy” so that those who had gathered together in one perversity may perish indiscriminately.

They—namely, the philosophers—“said: We will magnify our lips,” that is, we will say great things about ourselves. And we can do this because “our lips,” that is, our speech, “are from ourselves,” that is, from our own ingenuity. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. I). “Our lips are from ourselves,” because “who is our lord?” That is, who rules over us, especially in knowledge?

They say this, but the Lord says this: “Now”—as though I had slept until now, but now, in the time of grace—“I will arise,” namely, in order to remove “the misery of the needy,” that is, of the Gentiles. They are called needy because they possessed no riches of knowledge either through the Law or through the prophets.

“And because of the groaning of the poor,” that is, of the Jews. They are called poor because, although they had the Law and the prophets, these were nevertheless insufficient for salvation. By “groaning” he indicates that some had the greatest longing for Christ’s coming. Here he begins to show the promise of salvation.

“I will arise,” and what I am going to do is “place it in the Savior,” that is, in Jesus, because through him I will save the human race. And “in him I will act confidently,” not timidly, as through servants, but with authority. This was fulfilled when he himself drove the people from the temple (Matt. XXI).

“I will act confidently in him.” And I will rightly be able to do this because “the sayings of that Lord” are “sayings,” that is, of great weight, as when it is said, “This is a man,” meaning a great man. They are “pure,” that is, without any admixture of falsehood, and they are “silver,” that is, like silver.

For just as silver rings more elegantly and clearly than the other metals, so the sayings of the Lord resound more sweetly than all others in the ears of the faithful. Silver, I say, “tested by fire.” Just as silver is proved by fire, so Christ proved his sayings to be true through his passion.

“Tested in the earth,” that is, purified from earth. The sayings of Christ are without any earthly quality, because nowhere do they move a person toward the desire for earthly things. “Purified sevenfold.” For just as silver purified seven times is exceedingly pure, so the sayings of Christ are without every stain through the sevenfold Spirit, who is called sevenfold because of the seven gifts.

He is called the Spirit “of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. II); and the final one is placed first in the quotation. Through the number seven, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit may be understood.

“You, O Lord,” who are such, “will preserve us” in eternal blessedness, which he understands by the Eighth. And you will “guard” us in this life “from this” most wicked “generation” that speaks vain things, so that their attacks do not move me away from your truth, and thus you will lead me “forever.”

You will preserve us and guard us. “But the ungodly walk,” that is, labor, “in a circle,” that is, in the desire for earthly things, in which they will never reach the true end. Just as someone walking in a circle never finds the goal.

“But you have multiplied the children of men,” that is, of rational beings who use the reason of their fathers. You have multiplied them here by virtues and finally by eternal reward, not according to their merits, but “according to your height,” that is, according to your mercy. When he says “you have multiplied,” he looks back to the promise made to Abraham (Gen. XVI and XVII). In this final verse he places a brief conclusion concerning both groups, namely, the good and the evil.

## PSALM XII. TITLE: To the end, a psalm of David.

“How long, O Lord?” This psalm applies to David the prophet, who speaks here. It is a psalm, I say, leading toward the end, that is, toward Christ. For in this psalm he intends by his example to invite us to love Christ.

Its subject is David himself and others like him, concerning whom he proceeds as follows: he presents himself as complaining about the delay of Christ’s coming; he also presents a request that Christ come quickly. Finally, he presents himself as bearing patiently the possibility that Christ may not come in his own time. He begins with a question:

“Lord, you will forget me.” God is said to have forgotten humanity before Christ’s coming because before him no one was brought into paradise; even the just, although without punishment, were held in hell. “And how long, O Lord,” will this forgetfulness last? It will last until the end of the ages, that is, until the time of grace.

I understand correctly that it will last until then. And “how long, O Lord, will you turn your face away,” that is, your Son, who is called the face and image of the Father? That is: Why do you delay sending the one whom you are going to send?

“How long shall I set plans concerning his coming in my soul?” And I will place “pain” over the delay of his coming “in my heart throughout the day,” that is, from day to day. By saying that he grieves over Christ’s coming, he indicates that he possesses great love for Christ, and thereby invites us also to the same love.

[Col. 0233A] “And how long will he be exalted,” that is, will he rule? Before Christ’s coming, the enemy rejoiced over the captivity of humanity, because he also held the just. “My enemy,” that is, the devil, “will be exalted” over me and over the other good.

Here he makes a request that God send the one whom he is going to send. The connection is as follows: The enemy has been exalted, but you, Lord, “look upon us” by sending your Son. He says “look upon,” in contrast with what he had said above, “you turn your face away.” “Hear me, O Lord my God,” by freeing me from the devil and restoring me to paradise.

Look upon us by sending your Son. And if you do not wish to send him so quickly, at least “enlighten my eyes,” namely, my inner eyes, so that I may have a true understanding of him, “lest I ever sleep in death,” through negligence arising from human weakness, and thus proceed into the death of the soul.

Also enlighten me so that I may not be deceived by the devil’s prompting. This is what he says: “Lest at any time my enemy,” that is, the devil, “say, ‘I have prevailed against him.’”

Let him not say, “I have prevailed,” because “if I am moved,” namely, from the purpose of good works, “those who afflict me will rejoice.” You must never tolerate their rejoicing, because they are your enemies. They will rejoice if I am moved, but I will not be moved, because “I have hoped in your mercy.” Here he begins, from what preceded, to speak of patience.

“And I hoped in your mercy”; and therefore, even if I do not see Christ himself with my eyes, nevertheless “my heart shall rejoice in your salvation,” that is, in your Jesus. And to such a “Lord I shall sing” in my mind, “and I shall sing psalms” through good works, “to the name of the Lord,” that is, to magnify the name of that “most high” Lord—and rightly so, because he is the one “who bestows good things upon me.” By “I shall sing” he signifies the theoretical, that is, contemplative life; by “I shall sing psalms,” the practical, that is, active life.

## ON PSALM 13

### TITLE: To the end. A psalm of David.

“He said, the fool.” This psalm suits David the prophet, or any righteous person. Some add “to David” itself, and then it suits Christ alone, directing us “to the end,” that is, to Christ. The subject is Christ the visitor, not received by the Jews; and it treats of him as follows: it rebukes the Jews because they did not receive him, describes the Jews’ wickedness, and threatens them at the end. Its purpose is to exhort us to faith. By rebuking them for unbelief and threatening them, it warns us not to be unbelieving but faithful. It is the voice of David the prophet, and he begins with a rebuke, saying:

“The fool,” that is, that Jewish people, paying no attention to the Law and the Prophets, in whom Christ had been promised to them, nor to his life free from sin, nor to the miracles that Christ performed, “said” with his mouth—and, to aggravate their wickedness still further, this was what he had “in his heart”—namely, something he had not learned from the Law and the Prophets: that this man, who is capable of suffering and mortal, hungry, and so forth, “is not God,” nor the Son of God. Hence they mocked him, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27). And he gives the reason why they said this: they were blinded on account of their sins. The continuation is:

“This is what the fool said,” and this because “they are corrupt,” that is, having departed from the reason of truth, “and have become abominable,” that is, detestable through evil deeds, “in their pursuits,” that is, they have plunged themselves with every effort into the most shameful acts, to such an extent that now “there is no one among them who does good.” And because they did certain things that appeared good, he shows that they were not good, because there is no one “who does good” until he comes “to the one,” that is, to Christ. For Christ alone is the one without whom human frailty cannot do any good; once we have reached him through faith, we can do good. Hence the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

They say that that man is not God, but they say this wrongly, because he is God. And this is what “the Lord God looked down upon,” that is, had mercy “from heaven,” that is, from his humanity. It is called heaven for this reason: the divine secrets were entrusted to it. Or because, just as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so that humanity was exalted above every creature. He looked, I say, “upon the sons of men,” and for this purpose, namely, “to see”—not because anything is hidden from him, but so that he might make others see openly—whether there is anyone “understanding” him as God; or, after understanding, “seeking” him through good works.

He looked down, but “all have turned aside,” that is, they paid no attention; and “together,” that is, from the time they began to turn aside, “they have become useless,” to such an extent that “there is no one” among them “who does good, not even one,” as above. When he says “all have turned aside,” he does not mean everyone, but those who said, “There is no God.” Thus far he has rebuked them because they did not receive their visitor; now he describes their wickedness. It should be known, however, that the prophet did not place the following three verses in this psalm. But because the Apostle, rebuking the Jews’ faith in his Epistle to the Romans (ch. 3), joined them together in this way, and because the Church, attending to his authority as well as David’s, did not alter his arrangement, they remain here.

“There is no one who does good,” but rather, “their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully,” as explained above; and “under their lips,” that is, in their heart, is “poison,” that is, hatred comparable to poison. For just as poison spreads through all the veins—hence it is called poison—so that hatred occupies the whole person and blocks all human virtues. When he says “of asps,” he indicates that this hatred is incurable, and that the Jews themselves possess the nature of an asp. For the nature of an asp is that, when it is charmed, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail, lest it hear the incantations. So too the Jews, through their desire for earthly things and their attachment to custom, block the ancient ear, lest they hear Christ’s preaching. Or otherwise: “The poison of asps is under their lips,” that is, beneath their words, because their words are more harmful than the poison of asps.

“Their mouth is full of cursing,” that is, blasphemy against God, “and bitterness,” because they spoke bitter words to him, as when they said: “Crucify him, and so forth” (Luke 23). “Their feet,” that is, their affections. Affections are called feet because, just as the body is carried by the feet, so the mind is carried in different directions by its affections, “are swift to shed the blood” of the Savior.

All these things are their ways, and in “their ways,” that is, in their deeds, there is “destruction”: their deeds deserve destruction, that is, eternal damnation. Or “destruction,” as happened to them through Titus and Vespasian in the destruction of Jerusalem, “and misery in their ways,” when they were led captive throughout the whole world. Destruction is said to be in their ways just as it is said to the thief: “In your way there is a cross.” And although afflicted in this way, “they did not know the way of peace,” that is, Christ, who truly is the way of peace. Hence he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14). “They did not know.” Hence the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2). They also committed the other evils that had been described as present in them, because “the fear of God is not before their eyes,” that is, before the eyes of their heart, since they pay no attention to him. That they did not know Christ is attested by the authoritative saying: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

Then he sets forth the threat. They did not know, but certainly they will know; and this is what follows: “Will they not finally know” the Lord—“all who work” that outstanding “iniquity,” namely, the Lord’s death—“who also devour my people,” that is, the apostles or other righteous people? If Christ is speaking, he rightly says “my people,” subject to him. If the prophet or another righteous person is speaking, he rightly says “his people,” since he is one of them. They devour them, I say, “like the food of bread,” because just as a hungry person is nourished by bread, so they are nourished by the tribulation of the righteous.

They also “did not call upon God,” because prayers cannot be heard except through Christ. “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear,” that is, the fear they held inwardly—although it ought not to have been held—they displayed outwardly in their bodies. For they said: “If we believe in him, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.” Where fear was warranted, they did not fear, when they killed the righteous man without paying attention to him. Just as it is prudence to fear at the proper time, so it is folly to fear when there should be no fear.

“Will they not know”—namely, this—“that the Lord is in the generation of the righteous,” and that he dwells in the righteous? Therefore those who persecute them ought to fear. You did not call upon God, but rather you confounded, that is, showed to be confoundable, “his plan,” insofar as it concerned you: the plan of restoring the human race. This was because that plan belonged to “the poor,” and because God is his hope, since he trusted in the Lord alone. For this reason his plan ought rather to have been received than rejected. The Apostle testifies that Christ was poor, saying: “Though he was rich, he became poor for us” (2 Cor. 8).

You “confounded their plan,” but this was foolish, because “who will come from Zion,” that is, Judea, and “give salvation,” that is, a greeting, “to Israel,” that is, to the Israelite people, unless this man? Certainly no one. And he will not merely give salvation, but “when he turns away,” in the future, “the captivity,” that is, suffering and mortality—whose captivity?—“of his people.” And when he has turned it away, Jacob will rejoice, that is, the one who struggles against sins, namely, those living actively; “and Israel will be glad,” that is, the man who sees God, by which we understand contemplatives.

## ON PSALM 14

### TITLE: A psalm of David. The voice of David the prophet.

“Lord, who will dwell?” In this psalm the subject is the righteous person and, spiritually, Christ. It treats of them as follows: it poses a question and an answer, and in the answer describes the righteous person, attributing to him ten virtues. Spiritually these belong to Christ alone, though they can in some way be applied to other righteous people. Its purpose is to warn us not to presume upon the kingdom of God, as many do who, although unjust, nevertheless presume to be sons of God. Just as a priest asks God for answers and then reports what he has heard to the people, so the prophet asks God who are the inhabitants of his tabernacle, saying:

“Lord,” I see many who say that they are in your tabernacle, but “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” That is, in your present Church, where there is a place of warfare. Tabernacles are field-houses. When he says “will dwell,” he means not only those entering but also those persevering. “Or who at last will rest on your mountain,” that is, in the security of the eternal kingdom, where there is no struggle but supreme rest? For just as those who are on a mountain are safe from enemies, so will those who are there be safe. I say “on your holy mountain,” which you have sanctified. After posing the question, he also gives the answer, as though the Lord himself were responding.

I asked who would dwell; behold who: the one “who enters” the Church of God “without blemish”—Christ, indeed, without any blemish, while the other righteous are without serious sin. Here one of the ten virtues is indicated: “and who practices righteousness” of some kind. For if he enters without blemish but does not practice righteousness, he is not righteous.

He also enters who “speaks truth in his heart,” that is, who always retains the truth and keeps silent about it before hearers who would trample upon God’s word. It is sometimes good to keep God’s word silent; hence the Gospel commands: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). To practice righteousness is the second virtue; this is the third: he “enters who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue,” that is, who, by preaching the truth, has deceived no one, neither for money nor in any similar way. This is the fourth virtue.

He will also enter who “has done no evil to his neighbor,” by striking him or taking away his possessions. This is the fifth virtue. “And has not accepted reproach against his neighbors,” that is, it was not acceptable to him to say something to his neighbors for the sake of disgracing them; and if he said anything shameful for the purpose of correction, nor was he pleased when another said such a thing to him. This is the sixth virtue.

He will enter who is such because “the malicious one,” that is, the devil, “has been reduced to nothing in his sight,” that is, has been regarded as worthless. Thus, when Christ was tempted by the devil, he said to him: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 4). He makes the malicious one worthless, but “glorifies those who fear the Lord,” that is, honors the righteous. This verse indicates the seventh virtue.

And he “who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive,” that is, speaks firmly and does not lie—just as whatever Christ told the apostles was fulfilled. This is the eighth virtue. And he “who did not give his money,” namely, earthly money, “at interest,” but entrusted his money to Judas to distribute to the poor. Spiritually, however, money is rightly commanded to be lent at interest. This is the ninth virtue. And he who “did not accept gifts against the innocent.” Christ did indeed receive gifts, but not in order to oppress the innocent. This is the tenth virtue. All these things are found spiritually in Christ.

But “whoever,” another person, insofar as human frailty permits, not only speaks but “does these things will not be moved,” that is, will not be separated from God “forever,” but will enter the tabernacle of God and rest on God’s holy mountain.

## ON PSALM 15

### TITLE: An inscription of the title to David himself.

“Preserve me.” The prophet Ezra, understanding that David had written this psalm concerning the restoration of Christ’s kingdom, and foreseeing also that during Christ’s Passion this title would be written: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews,” and that they would contradict that title, saying to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews’” (John 19), gave this psalm its title in order to confirm that title. When he says that the psalm is inscribed, he also shows that the title is inscribed, because both the title and the psalm concern the same thing, namely Christ’s kingdom.

The title is explained as follows: “This inscription of the title,” that is, this psalm, which is also the title, because it concerns the gaining of that kingdom, just as the title does during the Passion, “is inscribed,” that is, written immutably. For whoever may contradict it, he is always the King of the Jews, that is, of those who truly confess God. This inscription of the title suits David himself, that is, Christ, because David is nowhere read to have written any title about himself, nor did anyone else write a title about him.

Or the title may be explained in this way: “An inscription of the title to David himself,” that is, the action from which the psalm speaks is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ acting for his own victory. For among the ancients a title was inscribed on a triumphal arch to designate a victory.

The subject is the restored kingdom, that is, the faithful, and it treats of this as follows: it sets forth the weakness of humanity and the glory of the inheritance, that is, of Christ’s people. Then, in the form of thanksgiving, it treats of the Passion, resurrection, and ascension, through which the restoration of the kingdom was accomplished. Its purpose is to warn us not to contradict the title, but to confess that Christ is King of the Jews.

It is the voice of Christ according to his humanity. He begins with the weakness of humanity, as though, placed amid dangers, he were saying:

“Lord God, preserve me,” lest these tribulations prevail against me. Here he implies that he possesses nothing from himself, but asks God: “Preserve me.” And you ought to do so “because I have hoped in you”; I have placed my hope in you. For this reason he also said to you: “Lord, you are my God,” that is, you are very familiar to me. Therefore I say “God,” “because you have no need of my good things,” that is, I possess no good thing from myself, but rather from you. For if I possessed anything from myself, you would need it, and you would not be sufficient in yourself. When Christ says that he possesses no good thing from himself, he shows that those who think they possess some good from themselves are exceedingly presumptuous.

Here he begins to show the glory of the inheritance. The continuation is:

“I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God.’” And now this Lord has “made all my desires wonderful,” that is, has shown them to be wonderful. Christ’s desire is that all should fulfill his commandments. God has shown this desire to be wonderful to “the holy,” when he makes them understand that, if they fulfill this desire, they will become incapable of suffering and immortal. I say “to the holy who are on earth,” who are called holy because they are on earth, that is, in stability, not amid the waves of this world. I say “his earth,” namely, the earth of blessing, not of cursing, such as Adam’s earth (Gen. 3). And because some might understand the desire without having it established in themselves, he adds “in them,” so that he “made it wonderful” in such a way that it was established in them.

“Made wonderful”: formerly they were weak, and while they were weak, under the natural law, “their weaknesses,” that is, their sins, were “multiplied” through the written Law. Hence the Apostle says: “The Law entered so that the trespass might abound” (Rom. 5). “Afterward,” that is, after they recognized that they could not be saved through the Law, but rather that sins were multiplied through it, “they hastened” through it, namely, toward Christ.

“They hastened,” and therefore now “I will not gather their assemblies,” that is, their gatherings and institutions for the shedding of blood, as under the other Law. But now I will not receive blood, that is, a sacrifice involving the shedding of blood, whether of a lamb or a goat. Here the Lord openly promised liberation from the burden of the Law: “Nor will I remember their names,” that is, their infamy. Formerly some were called thieves, others idolaters, and others by similar names. Here the remission of sins is indicated: “I will not remember,” and this “through my lips,” that is, through the Old and New Testaments. These Testaments are called lips because, just as lips come together to form a word, so the two Testaments agree in the promise of the remission of sins. In the Old Testament, as in Ezekiel: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18). In the New, where Christ said to the apostles: “Whose sins you forgive…” (John 20). Or by “lips” let us understand the apostles, because God speaks through them.

“I will not remember their names,” but “the Lord will be the portion of my inheritance,” because, while others choose for themselves clothing, gold, and so forth, my inheritance makes the Lord alone its portion. “And the Lord is the portion of my cup.” By the inheritance of the faithful, possession by God is understood; by the cup, the distribution of their merits. By the cup we signify the same thing as by the inheritance, but insofar as God distributes diverse gifts to them. Or spiritually we understand by the cup those who imitate Christ’s Passion. “The Lord is the portion, and you, Lord, will restore my inheritance to me,” which I had lost through the transgression of the first parent.

And that inheritance is among glorious things. Hence: “The cords,” that is, riches, or elections, or divisions, “have fallen,” that is, have come to me. “Falling” is found elsewhere in a good sense, where it says: “The lot fell upon Matthias” (Acts 1). They fell, I say, “among glorious things.” Therefore by cords we understand elections, because just as an inheritance is divided by cords, so the righteous are separated from the reprobate by election, that is, by divine inspiration. These elections are said to fall, that is, to come about by chance, because we do not know why God chooses some and rejects others. I say that they fell “among glorious things for me,” for that inheritance of mine is glorious, although others despise it because they see it as ragged and afflicted.

Here he begins the thanksgiving. The continuation is:

The Lord will restore the glorious inheritance to me; therefore “I will bless the Lord,” that is, I will praise him. To bless the Lord is to proclaim him and to recognize concerning him the things that belong to him by nature. I ought to bless him because he is the one “who gives me understanding,” that is, true understanding concerning all things. And “in addition” I will bless him for the Passion. This is what follows: “My kidneys,” that is, my fleshly relatives. By kidneys are understood those who belong to one generation, because the seed of generation is in the kidneys; “rebuked me” with words and blows, even “until night,” that is, until death.

They rebuked me, but I “always looked ahead,” namely, to my resurrection. I looked ahead to “the Lord in my sight,” that is, in my inward sight; I was as certain of my resurrection as though I already saw it. Therefore I looked ahead, “because” during the Passion itself he “is at my right hand,” that is, in my help, “so that I may not be shaken” by any tribulation.

Because he is at my right hand, “for this reason my heart rejoiced” in the hope of resurrection, “and my tongue exulted.” For that joy is perfect which is conceived both in a glad heart and expressed in eager speech. Hence the Lord himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). “In addition,” that is, because of this, “my flesh” also, that is, my body in the tomb, “will rest in hope”—the hope that Christ himself had concerning the future resurrection. Hence the prophet says: “I will sleep and rest” (Ps. 4).

In this hope, namely, “because I will not abandon my soul in the underworld,” as the souls of the saints had previously been kept in the underworld. Christ’s soul, however, did not remain in the underworld, but led others away with him. “Nor will you give” me, “your holy one,” that is, my sanctified body, “to see,” that is, to undergo, “corruption,” that is, putrefaction. The fact that elsewhere he is said to have been corruptible is not contrary to this statement, because he is called corruptible only insofar as he could be wounded. What is said here—“nor will you give your holy one to see corruption”—could not suit David the prophet, whose corruption is certain, as Peter testifies in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 2). Through this he himself shows that the prophet had proclaimed the resurrection of Christ.

You will not give him to see corruption, but rather “you will make known to me the ways of life,” namely, the means of entering true life, which no one had possessed before Christ. “You will fill me with joy” at the assumption: I mean, placed “with your face,” that is, in your presence. And there, with me placed “at your right hand,” that is, among your greater goods, there will be “delights,” that is, ineffable beatitudes, “to the end,” that is, Christ.

## ON PSALM 16

### TITLE: A prayer of David.

“Hear, Lord.” Although prayers are contained in the other psalms, this psalm and certain following ones are called prayers because throughout their entire composition they contain prayers and instruct us to pray. “A prayer,” that is, the psalm called a prayer, is attributed to David, that is, to Christ himself. Prayer is understood in two ways: either as supplication or as any kind of speech. Here it is understood as supplication.

The subject is Christ praying, and it treats of him as follows: before the time of the Passion he prays to be restored according to righteousness, namely, that God direct his steps in his paths. He also asks to be delivered from the Jews in the imminence of the Passion. He further asks to be rewarded according to his merits, namely, with the glory of the resurrection, and for them to receive punishment according to their evil merits. Its purpose is to instruct us in prayer. In this first and second verse are contained the three prayers we have mentioned, which he later treats individually.

It is the voice of Christ speaking according to his humanity:

“Lord God, hear my righteousness,” that is, fulfill what my righteousness asks. He says “my righteousness” more expressly than “my words,” because righteousness itself cries out that his steps be directed before the Passion: “Attend to my supplication,” concerning the removal of miseries, so that he may in no way be shaken by the plots of the Jews.

“Give ear to my entreaty,” concerning the obtaining of good things, namely, the resurrection. Prayer properly concerns the obtaining of good things; supplication properly concerns the removal of evils. Although hearing, supplication, and prayer are the same in God, he uses different terms according to the analogy of human beings. “Receive my prayer,” which you ought to do, because it was not made “with deceitful lips,” since there was no evil either in his mouth or in his heart.

He carries out the first part of the prayer, namely, “Hear, Lord, my righteousness,” in this way: “Let my judgment come forth,” that is, judge me, “from your face,” that is, from your affection, according to what you see and know in me. With what confidence do I ask to be judged according to your knowledge? Because I know that there are equities in me, and “let your eyes see these equities in me,” that is, let your knowledge see them.

He unfolds these equities, saying: “You have proved,” that is, shown to be proved, “my heart,” that is, my will, because I desired nothing except equity. And by proving it, “you visited,” that is, helped it, because without your help it could not stand, “by night,” that is, in the time of adversity. “You proved my heart” in this way: “you examined,” that is, showed me to have been examined, “by fire,” that is, in burning tribulation, as when they drove him outside the city to stone him (Acts 7). And in so great an examination, “iniquity was not found in me.”

This is true to such an extent that “iniquity was not found in me,” so that “my mouth would not speak”—namely, it is unnecessary for my mouth to speak about it, because it is sufficiently evident. And as though someone might say: Since iniquity was not found in you, why are you afflicted? He replied: “Because of the words,” namely, the words of your prophets that must be fulfilled, “of your lips I have kept”—I have steadfastly endured—“hard ways,” that is, tribulations. Another translation has “the way of the robber,” and the meaning is the same. I say “ways,” which are “the works of men,” that is, works deserved by human, carnal beings.

Or otherwise: Iniquity was so completely not found in me that my mouth “would not speak the works of men,” that is, falsehood. Here he shows his greatest perfection. For the most perfect person is one who does not sin even with his tongue. He calls falsehoods “of men” because human beings have lying from themselves, not from God. Or I say in this way: “Iniquity was not found in me” to such an extent “that my mouth would not speak the works of men,” that is, that I would boast about them, as is the custom of human beings.

And because I am so perfect, “perfect,” that is, preserve “my steps” to the end, where the perfection of merits is complete. My steps are my works, by which I walk “in your paths,” that is, in your stricter commandments, so that I may not deviate in anything from your commandment. Direct my steps in such a way that even “my footprints,” that is, the apostles and my other followers, “may not be moved” from your paths. Footprints are signs of feet, and for this reason the apostles are called footprints, because in them the signs of Christ’s righteousness appear. And because they are footprints, they cannot be perfect unless the one whom they imitate is most perfect.

Here he begins to carry out the second prayer, namely, that he attend to his supplication. The continuation is:

“Perfect my steps,” and also “incline your ear to me,” that is, condescend to me. Knowing his own weakness, he could not merit such dignity; therefore he asks the divinity itself to humble itself in order to help him, like a sick person who cannot rise and asks a physician to humble himself in order to help him. “Hear my words.” I say, “incline” and “hear my words,” and I am confident because “I cried out, for you heard me.” This crying out, because one is heard, belongs only to the saints, who cry out securely from the purity of their conscience and do not fear being heard. Others are heard because they cry out, although their conscience accuses them of certain things.

“Hear my words,” and do more abundantly for me than for others. This is: “Make your mercies wonderful,” that is, make them wondrous. For God’s mercies have been made wonderful in Christ because he was free from sin and endured every persecution more patiently than all others. And you rightly should make them wonderful, since you “save those who hope in you,” lest they yield to tribulations.

I say, make them wonderful, and in this way “guard me,” so that they may not drag me into sin, “from those resisting,” that is, from the Jews who oppose “your right hand,” that is, me, your Son. The Son of God is called the right hand because through him God accomplishes all things. Guard me, I say, “as the apple of the eye,” as the apple ought to be guarded. Christ rightly compares himself to the apple of the eye. For just as the pupil is the nobler part of the eye and illuminates the whole body, so Christ is the nobler part of the Church and illuminates the whole Church.

“Guard me and protect me” so that I may not feel the heat, that is, so that I may not suffer unwillingly “from the face,” that is, from the presence, “of the ungodly.” By “face” he indicates present assault. It was therefore necessary that he be protected, “because they afflicted me.” Protect me, I say, “under the shadow of your wings,” that is, under the cooling shade of mercy and charity. Here he speaks by comparison. For just as a bird protects its young so that they do not feel the heat, so God protected Christ with the cooling shade of mercy and charity.

It was necessary that you protect me, because “enemies,” that is, the Jews, “surrounded my soul,” wishing to take away my soul, that is, my life. This occurred when they surrounded him with swords and clubs. They also “shut in their fat.” For just as some fat people enclose their fat with additional fat, so that nothing can enter them, so the Jews, fat—that is, filled with many wickednesses—enclosed their wickednesses, so that no truth could enter them, on account of the sin of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore “their mouth spoke pride,” saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us; we have no king except Caesar” (Luke 19; John 19).

They surrounded him with swords and clubs, and they also surrounded him on the cross, as though for the spectacle of crucifixion, “casting” me “out,” outside the city. “Now,” that is, whereas previously he had sent servants, now he had also sent me, the heir, to the vineyard (Matt. 21). They “set their eyes,” that is, their intentions, “to turn toward the earth,” that is, they considered only earthly things: they feared losing the Law and the nation. Or they turned their eyes toward the earth because they thought that he was not God but merely a human being.

They surrounded me with clubs and swords; they surrounded me for the spectacle of crucifixion. And this because they “received,” that is, with joy, as though receiving the greatest gift from Pilate, or from Judas who handed me over, or from God who promised me. They received “me,” prepared for my death, “like a lion and a lion’s cub ready for prey.” By the lions we should understand the greater persecutors of the Lord; by the cubs, the lesser ones, namely, the people. When he says “dwelling in secret places,” he indicates the hidden judgment of the Jews, who secretly plotted the Lord’s death.

Here he begins to pray concerning the reward of himself for good and of the persecutors for evil. The continuation is:

They plot these evils against me, but you, who until now appear to have slept, “rise up and go before him,” that is, the Jewish people. “Go before him” is spoken by comparison: when two people run, the one who gets ahead takes the prize and accomplishes his will. Thus, when God and the Jews were running toward Christ’s death, God got ahead of them by raising him whom they wanted to hold in death. “And trip him up,” that is, overthrow him, by comparison with wrestlers.

He says “go before him” in this sense: “deliver my soul from the ungodly,” that is, from the devil, by causing me to rise again. And you ought to do so because this is the “sword,” that is, the weapon by which you must conquer the enemies. “Deliver this sword from the enemies,” that is, from the Jews, who are enemies “of your hand,” that is, of your operation. God’s operation was to redeem the human race.

Trip them up in this way: “divide them, Lord, from their land during their life,” that is, while they are alive. This division took place in the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus and Vespasian, which occurred while the Jews were still living. “Divide them,” I say, removing them “from the few,” that is, from the apostles. Or by “the few” we may understand those who, at the warning of the angel announcing Jerusalem’s destruction, withdrew into Agrippa’s kingdom.

And rightly you will divide them, because “their belly,” that is, their carnality, “has been filled with your hidden things,” that is, with sins hidden from you—not hidden from your knowledge, but in their perpetration.

For this reason also you should divide them, because they are “filled,” that is, filled with wickedness in the manner of the Lord. Filled, I say, “with children,” that is, to the disadvantage of their children. In this way they “divided their remnants among the little ones,” that is, the surplus of their curse among “their little ones,” that is, their children. For when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27), they harmed not only themselves but especially their children, because they have remained blinded to the present day.

Or “they are filled with children,” that is, to the disadvantage of their children, because they “did not make themselves his remnants,” namely, those whom they ought to have made their own, of whom the prophet had said: “The remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10; Rom. 9). They did not make themselves those remnants, namely, the humble and submissive, but “divided them among their little ones,” who through humility and rejection became those remnants. Another translation has “swine-like,” that is, uncleanness.

Because Christ had displayed his weakness throughout the psalm, lest he therefore be thought a mere man, he now shows his exaltation. The continuation is:

You will divide them, “but I shall appear before your presence,” that is, before you. This was fulfilled in the Ascension. “I shall appear,” I say, “in righteousness,” that is, according to what my righteousness demands, “and your glory will finally appear,” namely, that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. This appearance will take place at the judgment, and “when the glory appears, then I shall be satisfied,” when my body has been completed. For then Christ’s body will be complete, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father.

## ON PSALM 17

### TITLE: To the end. For the servant of the Lord, David. The words of this song, which he spoke to the Lord on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. And he said:

“‘I will love you.’” David composed this psalm after Saul’s death (2 Sam. 2), rejoicing that he had been delivered from his enemies [Col. 0244C]. Yet he did not write it merely about his own rejoicing, but because he saw that Christ would be delivered from his enemies; hence he considered this a cause for the greatest rejoicing—not only Christ as an individual, but Christ together with his entire body, both before his coming and afterward.

“Words of this song,” that is, the words of this psalm, which concern spiritual matters—matters over which one ought to rejoice. It is attributed to David, that is, to Christ the child, that is, the servant of the Lord. He is aptly signified by “child,” because he served the Lord in purity and simplicity. There are, indeed, certain servants who are not called children: namely, those who serve their masters out of fear of punishment or hope of temporal reward. If he had simply said “to David the child,” it could be understood of the historical David; but Ezra, understanding through the Holy Spirit that this was spoken of the spiritual David [Col. 0244D], by adding “of this song” removes the historical interpretation. For so great a prophet would not say that one ought to rejoice over temporal matters.

“The words which he spoke,” completing them “to the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s honor, “on the day,” that is, in the time of grace, “on which the Lord God delivered him,” that is, the whole Christ, “from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of all his enemies,” both visible and invisible, “and from the hand of Saul,” that is, from the hand of death. We understand death by Saul because Saul is interpreted as “petition.” The Israelite people asked for him as their king (1 Sam. 8), against the Lord’s will. Likewise, the human being whom God had made immortal on the condition of obedience himself sought out, with hands and feet, the death that God had not made [Col. 0245A].

I say that these words are attributed to Christ together with all his members. I say that the words direct us “to the end,” that is, to Christ: for he intends to invite us to love God through the example of himself. The subject matter consists of God’s gifts or mercies: salvation, the submission of peoples, and vengeance upon enemies. He treats this subject as follows: he first sets forth rejoicing over the giver; he shows the calamity of the human race before Christ’s coming and, conversely, the remedies brought by Christ’s coming; a third section concerns Christ’s power; a fourth commends the gifts themselves. It is the voice of Christ, both according to his own person and according to his members. Continuation:

Christ spoke the words of this song and said: [Col. 0245B] “O Lord, I have loved, and I love, and ‘I will love you.’” By saying “I will love,” he indicates the perseverance of this love, because you are “my strength”: for in myself I am weak, but in you I am strong for fighting against the wicked. It is as though he said: Do you wish to know the one to whom I am speaking? He is “my firmament,” that is, the one who makes me firm so that I may not fail, “and my refuge,” namely, the one to whom I flee as to a tower. If the faithful do not know what ought to be done, they are instructed by divine counsel concerning what should be done. And because someone might be strong, firm, and knowledgeable about what should be done, yet still fail—as did certain heretics who thought that, once instructed by God, they were sufficient by their own powers—he adds, “and my deliverer,” that is, the one who delivers me from my enemies [Col. 0245C], “because,” if God were to withdraw his hand, he would immediately fail.

“God,” that is, my Creator, “my helper” in cooperating, because without him I can do nothing good; and therefore “I will hope in him,” that is, I will place all my hope in him. He is also “my protector.” For just as someone protects another in battle so that no arrow may wound him, so God protects Christ so that not even a small temptation may touch him. Here we understand Christ together with all his members. When they are wounded—as David was in adultery (2 Sam. 11)—they are not members of Christ.

“And the horn of my salvation.” He says “horn” because, just as animals drive away enemies with their horns, so God scatters Christ’s enemies and makes him safe. This horn is the cause of my salvation [Col. 0245D]. Yet he did not do the things mentioned above for me because of my own merit; rather, he received me as an orphan. Hence: “and my receiver.”

And because he did all these good things for me, therefore, “praising, I will call upon the Lord”: praising him for the benefits already received, I will call upon him for those yet to be received; and through him, when called upon, “I shall be saved from my enemies.”

Up to this point the whole Christ has spoken about rejoicing in the giver. Now, in the person of the ancient fathers, he speaks about the calamity in which they were before Christ’s coming. Continuation:

It was necessary that I be saved from my enemies, because “the pains of death,” that is, the pains arising from the power of the devil, “surrounded me,” and “torrents of iniquity,” that is [Col. 0246A], the iniquities of human beings, which are like a torrent. Just as a torrent grows through rain and becomes violent, so human iniquities increase tumultuously and violently attack the saints; “they troubled me,” that is, they made me anxious.

Moreover, “the pains of hell surrounded me,” that is, the pagans, who on account of the merit of their evil life are to be tormented in hell. Or:

“The pains of hell,” that is, infernal punishments, “surrounded me”: I am so certain of them that it is as though they had already surrounded me, unless Christ’s coming redeems me. Again, he sets forth another aspect of his calamity when he says, “the snares of death,” that is, original sin, “anticipated me,” even though I was unaware of it, because from conception itself a human being is ensnared by that sin [Col. 0246B].

“And in my great tribulation I called upon the Lord”; and from that very invocation I burst into a cry. Hence: “and I cried to my God,” that is, I asked with the full exertion of my strength.

In opposition to what he had said, “I called upon him,” he adds, “and he heard my voice from his holy temple.” We may suitably understand this either as heaven or as the Lord’s body, which is his holy temple, because it contains the secrets of God. In opposition to what he said, “I cried,” he adds, “and my cry in his sight,” that is, existing in his good pleasure, “entered into his ears,” that is, it was heard.

Having shown the calamities of the human race before Christ’s coming, he now shows the remedies God brought to the human race through Christ’s coming, and indicates that coming to us through certain mysteries [Col. 0246C]. Continuation:

He heard my cry because he sent his Son. At his coming, “the earth,” that is, earthly people, “was moved” from the security in which it had been, when it heard the new preaching and was uncertain what to hold; “and it trembled,” because it feared him as the future judge and punisher of its wickedness; “and the foundations of the mountains,” that is, the mountains founded upon them, “were shaken.” By mountains let us understand the rich or distinguished people of this world, whose foundation consists of the riches and honors in which they place their hope. These foundations were shaken when, at Christ’s coming, they learned that one ought not to hope in earthly riches.

“And it was moved,” that is, the rich themselves were moved to repentance, because the earth was moved and shaken [Col. 0246D] “because the Lord was angry with them,” that is, because they recognized that the Lord was angry with them on account of their sins. He was angry with them, and “in his anger,” that is, in the consideration of his anger, “smoke rose,” that is, repentance. We understand repentance by smoke because, just as smoke is the first indication of fire and makes the eyes shed tears, so repentance is the first indication of charity and produces most fruitful tears.

By saying “it rose,” he indicates that this repentance is directed toward God himself; “and fire,” that is, the charity that moved repentance, “was kindled from his face,” that is, it became more fervent through his illumination. By “was kindled” he indicates the appearance of charity. “Coals” also “were kindled,” that is, human beings [Col. 0247A] in whom the ardor of charity had been extinguished through the fault of the first parent; “they were kindled by him,” that is, by God’s giving the fire of charity. For just as those in whom fire has been extinguished are properly called coals, so human beings are properly called coals when charity has been extinguished in them.

Although he had shown the remedies that God provided for the human race, he had not yet shown through whom God provided them. Now he shows through whom all those things were accomplished. Continuation:

“The earth was moved,” and the other things were accomplished because God “inclined the heavens,” that is, he humbled the heavens, meaning heavenly things—namely, the divinity itself—and he inclined the angels themselves through his frequent visitation of human beings. Or, he inclined the angels through the compassion he showed for the restoration of the human race [Col. 0247B]. And God himself “descended,” uniting himself to human nature. The angels too were inclined when they approached the Lord and ministered to him (Matt. 4).

“He inclined, he descended”; and although he was thus humbled, he did not lose his power, but “darkness,” that is, the devil, is “under his feet,” that is, is wholly subjected to him, like something placed beneath the feet. We understand the devil by darkness because, just as darkness obscures the eyes, so the devil blinds sinners and makes them dark, so that they cannot recognize the light of truth.

He descended, I say, and the same one ascended above every angelic creature: in the Ascension he was exalted. By that order we understand all the others: “and he flew upon the wings of the winds,” that is, his fame was swifter than the winds [Col. 0247C]. For when he was born, he was recognized in Chaldea through the stars (Matt. 2); when he was crucified, he was known at Athens through the darkening of the sun. He describes the winds as winged because of their speed. When he says “he flew” twice, he indicates his very great swiftness.

Or, in this way:

“He ascended above the cherubim,” that is, above the whole fullness of knowledge, because no one possesses knowledge so complete that he can comprehend that secret which was penetrated in the Ascension; “and he flew upon the wings,” that is, he surpassed the agility of the understanding of the saints. By winds we understand the saints, because of their agility; by wings, the swiftness of their understanding. And although they understood something about him, “he flew,” because there was something else that they could not understand. Even if they came to understand it through some effort, again he flew, and again he flew.

Through the foregoing he had not yet said that he had assumed human nature [Col. 0247D]; now, in what follows, he plainly shows this. Continuation:

Do not believe that the one who ascended and descended is only God, but also man. Hence: “and he made darkness,” that is, human flesh, “his hiding place,” namely, the flesh in which the divinity lay hidden. Here “darkness” is understood positively. Just as we call a speech dark when it contains great depth, so “his tent is around him,” that is, those who serve him are around him—those who are close to him, possessing some knowledge and familiarity with him.

Who are these? Among those who are in the tent, some are dark [Col. 0248A] and some exceedingly bright: “but dark water,” that is, obscure teaching, is “in the clouds of the air,” that is, in the higher clouds, namely, in the prophets. For these prophets were not sent throughout the world because of the obscurity of their preaching.

“But because of the splendor, the clouds,” that is, the holy apostles—who are called “clouds” because they rain upon God’s earth and make it fruitful through spiritual teaching—are clouds “because of the splendor,” since they preach openly and are intelligible to everyone, “in his sight.” They are called “because of the splendor” because they receive present illumination from knowledge of him. Such “clouds passed” through different parts of the world to announce the word of God.

And behold, from those clouds came forth “hail,” that is, rebuke concerning sins, “and coals of fire,” that is, certain people who had been dead and who, through the fervor of charity, became inflamed [Col. 0248B].

The “clouds,” that is, the apostles, passed through, and “the Lord thundered from heaven,” that is, from those clouds which are called heaven because they contain heavenly secrets. “The Lord thundered,” that is, he rebuked through threats of judgment; and “the Most High gave his voice,” that is, evangelical teaching. And behold, “hail and coals of fire.”

The Lord himself “sent forth his arrows,” that is, the disciples of the disciples. They are called arrows because they wound human hearts with the word of God. He scatters those to whom they are sent, because he took some and rejected others. He sent forth arrows, and through the arrows he “multiplied flashes of lightning,” that is, he made many miracles.

We understand miracles by flashes of lightning because, just as people are terrified by flashes of lightning, so through miracles—and through those miracles—“he troubled them,” moving them from their sins to conversion [Col. 0248C].

Through those arrows the world gained knowledge of the truth. Hence: “and the fountains appeared,” that is, wise people became known to everyone. I say “fountains of waters,” that is, people from whom many waters flow—many teachings. Although this wisdom had previously been hidden, it then became known in them.

And through those same people “the foundations,” that is, the prophets through whom the Church was founded—foundations, I say, “of the world,” that is, of the Church, which was gathered from the whole world, that is, from every part of the earth—“were revealed,” that is, were made manifest. For the holy apostles and the other preachers [Col. 0248D] also made the Scripture of the prophets intelligible.

“The fountains appeared,” and this happened “at the rebuke” of the preachers. When they rebuked some, through that very rebuke they were recognized by others as wise; “and through the inspiration of the spirit of your anger,” that is, through the Spirit breathing your anger into them.

Having shown the mysteries of Christ’s coming, he wishes to show what those mysteries accomplish, namely, the Church. Continuation:

“He sent forth arrows”; he also sent the Holy Spirit “from on high,” that is, from the Father. By saying “he sent,” he indicates a gift; by saying “from on high,” equality. When he says “he sent,” he does not mean that the one sent is understood to be lesser than the one sending; rather, the whole Trinity sends the Holy Spirit [Col. 0249A].

“And he received me.” Christ speaks this in the person of his whole body. He “received” me, that is, he gathered me as though I were a fugitive; and this reception occurs through inspiration. “And he assumed me” into dignity through faith, baptism, and the other virtues, “from many waters,” that is, from many peoples. Hence John says: “The many waters are many peoples.” Or, “from waters,” that is, from many baptisms: for although baptism is one, it takes place among many peoples.

And having thus assumed me, “he delivered me from my strongest enemies,” that is, from demons, “and from those who hated me,” that is, from evil people. It was necessary that he deliver me because “they were strengthened against me.” For the more the faithful are afflicted, the more they are inflamed in faith, become stronger, and convert others to the faith [Col. 0249B].

“And they anticipated me,” that is, according to their own estimation they prevailed over me, “on the day of my affliction,” that is, in this life in which the saints are afflicted. In the other life they are not afflicted but crowned. And because they thought they had prevailed over me, against this he says, “the Lord became my protector,” that is, my shield, so that I might not be wounded by any persecution.

The Church protected me, and through the many tribulations that sometimes produce anguish in the weaker, “he led me out into spaciousness,” into the breadth of charity and the number of members. And why should we enumerate his good things? Through all these things “he saved me,” and this not because of my merits but because of his great grace. Hence: “because he desired me,” that is, desired to have me.

He did all these things [Col. 0249C] through his grace, according to the beginnings of salvation; but he made recompense according to merits. There are two recompenses, one for the just and one for the wicked; one in this life and one in the other life. In this life the just person receives recompense for his justice, because he receives an increase of justice, but in the future he receives a crown. In this life the wicked person receives recompense so that he may become more filthy, but in the future life he receives eternal fire. Continuation:

“He saved me” according to his will, “and the Lord will recompense me according to my justice,” that is, according to my good works, “and according to the purity of my hands,” that is, according to the innocence of my actions: that I abstained from evil and harmed no one—“he will recompense me.”

“I say, according to my justice, because I have kept” [Col. 0249D] “the ways of the Lord,” that is, the Lord’s commandments, through which we walk toward God by good works; “according to the purity of my hands,” because I “have not acted wickedly,” that is, I have not acted in such a way that I would be called wicked; I have not done evil by departing “from my God.”

“I have kept the ways and have not acted wickedly,” because “all his judgments” are in my consideration. Hence: “in my sight,” all of them, both those concerning good and those concerning evil, both in this life and in the other. Therefore, not exhausted by human weakness, “I did not cast his justifications away from me,” but perseveringly endured them.

“I did not cast them away,” and therefore “I shall be blameless with him,” namely, with God. For whoever wishes to cling to the blameless Lord must himself be blameless [Col. 0250A]. Therefore I am blameless because “I will guard myself from my iniquity,” as though it were natural to me. Hence the Apostle says: “We were born children of wrath” (Eph. 2). By saying “I will guard,” he indicates that vigilance must be applied to the preservation of the virtues.

Now he discusses the recompense of the just in the future life. Continuation:

In this life I shall be blameless, and in the future “the Lord will recompense me according to my justice and according to the purity of my hands,” which I have “in the sight of his eyes,” that is, in the good pleasure of his mercy. For just as a powerful person keeps before his eyes what he loves, while he does not wish to keep before his eyes what he does not love, so God is said to look upon what pleases him and to neglect what does not please him.

Because he had said above, “my justice,” lest justice appear to come from human beings, he shows that [Col. 0250B] no justice can exist without God. Continuation:

I said, “my justice,” and yet “with the holy one,” that is, so that a person may be holy, “you will be,” you God, who are “holy,” that is, sanctifying; “and with the innocent man,” that is, so that he may be innocent, “you will be” innocent, that is, making him innocent.

“And with the chosen one,” that is, so that someone may be chosen—separated from the lost—“you will be chosen.” He does not say “chosen” because God was in fellowship with the wicked, but “chosen,” that is, eternally removed from the wicked. “And with the perverse,” that is, with the one who perverts himself away from you, “you will pervert yourself,” by withdrawing grace; you will aid the perverse person toward greater perversity. Another translation confirms this interpretation, reading [Col. 0250C]: “You will pervert the perverse.” This is the recompense that God gives to the wicked in this life.

[Col. 0250D] Therefore I say that in this life you will act in this way toward both good and wicked people, “because” in the other life “you will save the humble people,” that is, the good, “and you will humble the eyes of the proud,” that is, afflict them. We understand pride by “eyes” because pride is marked in the eyes. Or let us read the wording in this way. Continuation remains the same:

I said, “my justice,” but you, human being, will not be holy through yourself; rather, “you will be holy with the Holy One,” that is, with Christ your helper, doing his works; and “with him who is innocent,” that is, through him who is innocent, “you will be innocent”; and with Christ, who is chosen, “you will be chosen”; and “with the perverse,” that is, with the devil, “you will pervert yourself.” Continuation:

Therefore I say that in this life the just and the wicked receive recompense according to their merits, “because you,” God, in the other life, “will save the humble people and will humble the eyes of the proud.”

Through all the foregoing we understand that God illuminates the Church. Seeing that it has been illuminated, the Church prays God to illuminate others through it by converting them. Hence:

“For you illuminate my lamp,” that is, certain people from the Church, so that they may illuminate others. They are called a lamp because the light of the Holy Spirit shines in them. He says “my” because they belong to his fellowship. “And you, Lord my God, illuminate my darkness,” that is, unbelievers and ignorant people who are in darkness because they have no knowledge of God [Col. 0251A]; “my,” that is, predestined to be mine.

I ask you to illuminate the darkness, and I ask this confidently, because “I shall be delivered,” that is, those of mine who are still darkness shall be delivered “from temptation,” from the devil, “in you,” that is, through you, “and in my God,” that is, through God’s help. In him “I shall cross the wall,” that is, the obstacle of sins. That wall, however, is not utterly destroyed; rather, the just cross over it with God’s help.

I rightly say “in my God,” because he is “my God,” and “his way,” that is, his commandments, “is undefiled,” because he commands nothing unclean to be done. “And the words of the Lord,” that is, the evangelical teaching itself, “are tested by fire,” that is, they have been uttered with careful examination, by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0251B]. The Holy Spirit is called fire because he places the ardor of charity in those in whom he dwells. And although he is so exalted, he does not abandon his own, but “is the protector of all who hope in him.”

There is no other God besides this great Lord: “for who is God besides the Lord,” that is, besides him who rules in such a way? Or, O you Gentiles, “who is God besides our God?” It is as though he said: If you do not have our Lord, you have no lord.

Here he begins to speak about Christ’s power.

There is no “God besides our God,” and this “God is the one who girded me,” that is, who prepared me, the Lord’s human being, with divine “power” to fight against the devil. This girding took place from conception itself [Col. 0251C]. He says “girded” in opposition to what he said above: “The snares of death anticipated me.” Just as original sin had anticipated the human race at conception, so the Holy Spirit signified Christ from conception itself; and through this he “made my way blameless,” that is, all the works of my entire life.

This same God also “made perfect,” that is, made “my feet” perfect—my affections—“like those of deer,” that is, similar to deer. For just as a deer avoids thorns, leaps over ditches and muddy places, and climbs a mountain, so Christ, through the holy affection of his will, leaps over the thorny and dangerous sins of the world and the pits of sinners, reaches the heights of heaven, and this is what follows: God himself “establishing me upon high places.”

[Col. 0251D] This same God also “teaches my hands,” that is, my actions, “for battle” against the devil. And you, Lord, “have made,” you who made my person your own, “my arms” into “a bronze bow,” that is, those through whom I act. If there were a bronze bow that shot arrows, it would be tireless because it was bronze. Likewise, Christ’s arms send forth arrows by which they wound human hearts, and they are tireless.

You made them, and “you gave me protection,” that is, defense, which is the cause “of your salvation,” that is, of salvation given by you; “and your right hand,” that is, your Son, “received me,” the Lord’s human being.

Because he was about to say that Christ would conquer others through his own people, he first sets forth [Col. 0252A] a certain aptitude by which he shows them suited to do this. Continuation:

“Your right hand received me, and your discipline,” that is, the justice with which you examine your own people, “corrected me,” that is, corrected my people concerning past things, up to “the end,” that is, up to completion. because something remained uncorrected, “and your discipline itself will teach me,” that is, will teach my people, so that they may not sin any further.

And through them “you enlarged my steps,” that is, you made my works known throughout the whole world, “and my footprints,” that is, those in whom signs of my justice appear, “were not weakened,” that is, they were not overcome by enemies. For it was necessary that those who were sent to teach others be irreproachable in every respect.

[Col. 0252B] Or, in this way: “Your discipline corrected” and taught my people, and thus “you enlarged” “my steps” in the virtues—that is, my disciples, who are called steps. Or this may be said of Christ, according to the Apostle, who says: “From what he suffered, he learned obedience” (Heb. 5). The disciples are called “steps” because through them God enters the world. And although they had been so enlarged, they did not become proud, but were “under me,” that is, wholly subject to me; and these same people, who are also my “footprints,” were not weakened.

And through such people I will “pursue” my enemies by reasoning, that is, those who contradict me, “and I will overtake them” in argument, because they will have no inner means by which they can resist; “and I will not turn back” from rebuking them “until they fail” [Col. 0252C] from their sect, that is, until they are converted.

Some I will pursue by reason, as has been said; others I will “break” through tribulation, “and they will not be able to stand” against me, but rather “will fall under my feet,” that is, they will be wholly subjected to me.

He has shown that Christ will subject certain people who resist him to his dominion. Now he turns to the enemies—that is, the demons—and specifically to the Jews. Continuation:

“I will pursue my enemies,” and you, Lord, “have overthrown those rising up against me,” that is, the devils who wanted to oppress me and seize the kingdom; you overthrew them “under me,” that is, under my power, because they do nothing except by Christ’s permission [Col. 0252D]. And he first sets forth the reason by which he shows Christ worthy that those demons should be subjected to him, when he says:

“You girded me with the power” of divinity “for battle” against the demons; and “my enemies,” namely the Jews, who are called Christ’s spiritual enemies, you partly “gave me as a back,” that is, made them my followers. For just as servants are called their master’s back because they follow him from behind, so Christ’s followers are called his back. And partly “you destroyed” them, namely “those who hated me,” those who had become hardened in hatred of me.

“You scattered them,” and in that scattering “they cried out” to be delivered, “and there was no one” among them “who could save,” because their leader was the devil, who could not deliver them. “They also cried to the Lord, [Col. 0253A] and he did not hear,” because they did not seek to be heard through the Son.

You scattered them, and I “will crush them,” that is, I will shatter their strength so that it cannot be gathered into power. I will make them “like dust,” that is, by withdrawing grace I will make them dissolved and unstable. Nor will I leave them, reduced to dust, in repose; rather, I will place them “before the face of the wind,” that is, I will make them such that they fail without awaiting the face of the wind, that is, the firmness of temptation: they fail at the first temptation. “And I will wipe them away,” that is, I will destroy them, “like the mud of the streets.”

Just as the mud of the streets is defiled in itself and defiles others who pass along the street, so the Jews are defiled in themselves and defile others who walk through the streets, that is, through earthly desires, by the example of their evil life [Col. 0253B]. He calls carnal desires “the street” because through them one passes without any restraint toward the devil.

And lest anyone think that, once these Jews had been destroyed, Christ would lose his kingdom, he shows that, after being withdrawn from them, he nevertheless possesses the kingdom. Continuation:

They will be destroyed, “but me,” O God, “you will deliver,” that is, withdraw, “from the contradictions of the people,” that is, from the contradicting Jewish people, which always contradicts me. And after delivering me from them, “you will establish me as head of the nations,” that is, so that I may be king of the nations.

You will therefore make me king of the nations because “the people” of the nations, “whom I did not know” through bodily habitation—I neither sent prophets nor gave the law—“served me,” that is, believed in me. For whoever believes [Col. 0253C] serves. Thus, “at the hearing of the ear,” that is, as soon as they heard, they “obeyed me.” This praise of the nations is a reproach of the Jews.

You will deliver me because those who ought to have been my “sons” became “strangers”; they lied to me, speaking falsehoods about me, denying that I was the Son of God and saying many other things. And those same “sons,” having become “strangers” when they ought to have been renewed as the new human being came, “grew old,” that is, whereas previously they had been old—sinners—they became even greater sinners. And as such they “limped,” that is, they erred, “from their paths,” that is, from the paths they had devised for themselves.

They themselves invented certain traditions, such as washing their hands before eating and avoiding contact with anything unclean. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Why do you also transgress the commandments of your fathers because of your traditions?” (Matt. 15) [Col. 0253D].

Or, in this way: “They limped,” that is, they erred, “from their paths,” that is, the paths they ought to have made their own, because in the Scriptures they possess only a literal understanding and not a spiritual one. These Scriptures are called paths because, rightly understood, they lead to life. He says that they limped by analogy: just as a lame person is firm in one foot but weak in the other, so the Jews are firm in the literal sense but weak in the spiritual, because they use allegory wrongly and rarely. Their limping was prefigured by the lame Jacob (Gen. 12).

They limped; they lied. But “the Lord lives,” that is, he is vigorous in his own people and reigns; and “my God is blessed,” that is, praised; and “may God himself be exalted” [Col. 0254A] in the multitude of believers, the giver “of my salvation.”

I rightly say, “Let him be blessed,” because you “give me vengeance,” that is, you avenge me upon my enemies. Here the commendation of the gifts begins: “and you subject peoples,” so that they become “under me,” that is, obedient to me. You are my deliverer from my enemies, even from those who are “wrathful,” that is, exceedingly fierce.

And you will “exalt me above those rising up against me,” because the more they rose up, the more Christ was exalted; and those rising up were crushed by the devil. “And you will deliver me from the wicked man,” that is, from the Jewish people, or from any wicked person.

“Therefore” I will “confess to you,” [Col. 0254B] that is, praise you, Lord, “among the nations,” that is, among different peoples; “and I will sing a psalm,” that is, perform a good work, “to your name,” that is, for your honor. When he says, “I will sing a psalm,” he makes it understood that he will not merely act well but will also be an example of good action to others.

In confessing this I say: this Lord “magnifies,” that is, makes magnificent, “the salvations of his king,” that is, those saved by their king, namely Christ. I also say this: he does everything out of mercy. Hence, “he is the one who shows mercy to David,” that is, to the one signified, “his Christ,” that is, his king, “and to his seed,” that is, to his followers. And this is not for a time only, but “forever,” that is, for as long as the world shall exist. Or: “to David, his Christ,” that is, his anointed one, “and to his seed,” that is, to Christ and his followers [Col. 0254C].

## PSALM XVIII. TITLE

“For the end; alternatively, for the victor; a psalm of David.”
