“‘The heavens declare.’” This psalm suits the prophet David, who speaks here, directing his hearers toward the end, that is, toward Christ. He intends to admonish his hearers, especially the Jews, to leave behind their old condition and pass over to the newness of Christ.

Its subject is Christ’s incarnation. He treats it by commending it through the excellence of its preaching, through its own excellence, through the goodness of the law, and through the good instruction that it brought to the world. He also commends it by praying to be cleansed from sins, so that he may be worthy to praise it. Thus he begins with the preaching:

Abandon the oldness of your mind and hear the new preaching. It ought especially to be heard because of the dignity of the preachers themselves, for “the heavens,” that is, the apostles, “declare” as a true and not fabricated matter the “glory,” that is, the divinity, “of God,” that is, of Christ; and “the firmament,” that is, the steadfast apostles who remain firm in this preaching of Christ, “announces” as an accomplished fact “the works,” that is, the miracles, “of his hands,” that is, of his works, meaning of the divinity that performs them.

He rightly calls the apostles “firmament” in the preaching of Christ’s miracles, because many people contradicted him, and many were ashamed to preach that he had suffered or died.

Or, in this way: let “work” be understood as a singular nominative in “the work of his hands.” A human being announces that the “firmament,” that is, the Church, has been established [Col. 0255A]. The Church was established, that is, made stable, by Christ himself amid the restless waves of this world. This was signified by the firmament that was made between the waters.

Or it may be said that the material heavens declare God’s glory through the star that announced to the world that God had become human (Matt. 2).

Here he commends the incarnation itself through the distinction within its preaching. Continuation:

The heavens will preach; and thus “day,” that is, the wise person, “utters the word,” that is, the Son of God, “to day,” that is, to the wise person. He says “utters” by analogy with someone who is full: just as a person who is full belches something forth from inner fullness, so the wise person speaks from abundance. “And night,” that is, the humble person, “shows knowledge to night,” that is, to another humble person [Col. 0255B]—namely, temporal matters concerning Christ, such as his passion and birth.

In this respect, too, the same reality may be called day and night: he preaches humble things to the humble and lofty things to the wise. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Among the perfect we speak wisdom, but to you I gave milk as drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 1).

After showing the distinction in preaching, he shows the magnificence of that preaching. Continuation:

“The heavens declare the glory,” and they declare it in every language. Hence: “there are no utterances,” that is, languages, “nor speeches,” that is, modes of speaking. For within the same language we speak in one way to the wise, in another way to ordinary people, and in another way to those of lower ability—“whose voices,” that is, the voices of those speeches, “are not heard.”

Again he commends this same preaching through its breadth [Col. 0255C], namely because it has been spread throughout all the lands. Continuation:

They spoke in all languages, and not merely in one land: “but their sound,” that is, their fame, “went forth into all the earth,” and not merely their sound, but also “their words” themselves—namely, that they proclaimed Christ incarnate, born, and so forth. They went forth “to the ends of the earth,” that is, to its farthest regions; and not merely to one part of the earth, but to all of it. This is what he says: “the circuit of the earth,” that is, all around. Here he commends the Incarnation in itself by demonstrating its dignity. Continuation: “The heavens declare,” and all these things take place. And why? Because the Son of God came into the world; and this is what follows:

[Col. 0255D] “He set up a tent,” that is, his flesh, in which he served God, “in the sun,” that is, openly; or in the heat of tribulation; or in the virgin, in whom he was joined to humanity. “And he himself, like a bridegroom,” that is, resembling a bridegroom—well adorned with virtues, so that his beloved, that is, the Church, might willingly receive him, as a bride receives her bridegroom—“coming forth from the bridal chamber,” that is, from the virgin’s womb, where the betrothal was made, because when the Godhead united itself to humanity, it promised itself as liberator to the other human nature. I say “from his bridal chamber,” that is, one suitable to him, because no powerful king from God ever had so good a bridal chamber.

And thus, coming forth, “he exulted to run the course,” that is, he ran the course joyfully—the course being all the works that he performed—“like a giant,” that is, comparable to a giant. For just as a giant does not fear threats, does not care for softness, and is indefatigable, so also Christ.

Because he had said, “He set up” and “he exulted,” without specifying who that person was, as though someone might ask, “Who is he?”, he shows through certain indications that he is the Son of God, saying: “His going forth,” namely, of the one who did this, “is from the highest heaven,” that is, from God the Father, than whom nothing is higher. The Son’s going forth was his manifestation: previously hidden, he manifested himself through the flesh. By saying “going forth,” he implies a distinction of persons; by saying “from the highest,” he indicates that he is in the highest, and thus equal to God the Father.

His going forth was from the Father, and he who went forth encountered him in the ascension, that is, found the Father for himself; “and his encounter was even unto his highest point,” that is, unto the Father, because he found no one besides the Father equal to himself. Hence it is said: “His going forth was from the Father, his return was to the Father.” “And there is no one who can hide himself,” that is, excuse himself, “from his heat,” that is, from the Holy Spirit, because he knows everything that is in a human being. Hence it is said: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and judgment” (John 16). We understand the Holy Spirit through “heat,” because he truly kindles the hearts of the faithful with fire. Hence the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). Here, too, he signifies the third Person through “heat.”

Here he begins to commend the Incarnation through the law and its instruction. Under the name “law” six things are included: law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear, and judgments. Continuation:

He himself went forth, and “the law of the Lord,” that is, prohibition, “is immaculate,” that is, making people immaculate, because it prohibits evil and prohibits nothing that ought to be done. It is also “converting,” not merely turning the hands away from evil works, but converting “souls,” that is, wills, so that they desire evil in no way. It does this through fear of punishment.

It is also “the testimony of the Lord,” that is, the promise of eternal good made by the Lord. Christ’s promise is therefore called testimony because, just as testimony makes us certain about something uncertain, so Christ’s promise made us certain of eternal life, which had been uncertain to us. I say “testimony” that is “faithful,” that is, credible; and this testimony “gives wisdom,” that is, knowledge of God, not to the proud but to “little ones,” that is, to the humble. For the humble person, having heard the promise of eternal good, diligently seeks knowledge of it.

“The justices” of that “Lord,” that is, those works which he teaches us to perform—visiting the sick, giving bread to the poor, and so forth—are “right,” that is, natural. Nature itself requires that we have compassion on our afflicted human nature and give what we possess in common to those in need, because these justices are “gladdening the hearts.” Whoever acts well rejoices inwardly.

“The commandment also of the Lord,” namely, the commandment concerning charity, is spiritual, “clear” in itself, “enlightening the eyes” within. For the more someone is kindled by charity, the more brightly he is illuminated by knowledge of God.

“The fear” also “of the Lord” is “holy,” that is, making people holy. There is a kind of fear that is not good, namely, fear of bodily tribulations. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10). There is another fear that is good, defined as love and reverence joined with dread. We love God because of his mercy, but we are in dread because of his judgment. This is the fear discussed here, which the Lord approves in the Gospel, saying: “Rather fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna” (ibid.).

And this fear “endures for ever and ever,” that is, for as long as age succeeds age, namely, throughout this entire life; or “for the age” that follows this “age,” that is, eternally. For even in the life to come we shall love God, and no one can fail to love him. And because of their omnipotence, “the judgments” also—that is, the aforesaid commands of the Lord, by which he commands something to be done—are “true.” They do not need external testimony, as most human judgments do, but are “justified in themselves,” because they appear just by themselves. The Lord’s commands are therefore called judgments because he makes them with discernment, and they become judgments.

These judgments are “desirable,” that is, worthy of being desired, by those who do not possess them, “above gold and precious stone”—not just any stone, but one “very precious.” Through these two things, which are the most valued of all worldly possessions, he indicates that the Lord’s commandment is both more precious and dearer than all worldly things.

They are desirable to those who do not possess them; but to those who possess them they are “sweeter than honey,” any honey, and the honeycomb—yet he means honey that is in the comb. Thus it is “above honey and the honeycomb.”

It is evident from this that they are sweeter and more worthy, because “your servant keeps them.” He does not act foolishly in this, because “in keeping them there is great reward,” namely, eternal life will be given to the one who keeps them.

Here he begins to ask that God cleanse him from sins, so that he may be able worthily to praise the Incarnation, think about it, and speak of it. Continuation:

I praise that Incarnation, and so that I may be able worthily to praise it, “cleanse me from my hidden faults.” He calls those sins hidden which arise from oneself, namely, those committed without anyone’s prompting, which are not recognized according to their own nature. I call them hidden because “who understands sins?” No one, that is: who remembers all his own sins? Hence Paul says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (2 Corinthians 4).

“And spare” me, “your servant, from alien sins,” that is, from sins committed at the persuasion of a human being or the devil. Or “from alien [sins],” that is, from human beings or demons: spare me, I say, so that they may not lead me into temptation.

And I bless you; you ought to spare me because “if the wicked do not dominate me,” once I have been cleansed from my own sins, “then I shall be immaculate” from common sins, “and I shall also be cleansed from the greatest sin,” that is, pride. It is called the greatest sin because through it angels and human beings fell, and because it reigns especially even among good things.

Even if I become such, then “the words of my mouth will be” such “as to please” you, “and the meditation of my heart,” from which the words proceed, will be “in your sight,” that is, in your good pleasure, “always.”

I speak of you, “Lord,” who are “my helper” in good things and “my redeemer” from evil things.

## Psalm XIX

### Title

“To the end,” or “for the victor,” or “for victory”: a psalm of David.

“He will hear you.” Here the Prophet speaks, directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. The subject is prosperity in the Church, which seemed destined to come only after a long time. The Prophet foresaw the Church flourishing at Christ’s coming, in the acceptance of the sacrifice, and so forth. He treats it as follows: he desires that these things happen to the Church and affirms that they will happen. By showing himself to desire them, he sets before us an example of piety, by which he strives to invite us to piety. He begins with this desire:

O Church, “may the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation,” that is, in your greatest need. He describes being heard in parts when he says, “may he protect you,” that is, may he be your shield, “the name of the God of Jacob”—that is, just as God protected Jacob, so may he protect you.

May he protect the Church as he protected Jacob, because just as Jacob supplanted the firstborn in receiving the blessing (Genesis 27), so the Church supplants the Synagogue in the name of God, that is, in the fame of God. For we understand the divine essence only through its fame; we do not yet possess the reality itself. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

And may he also “send you help” for cooperation “from the holy place,” that is, from Christ, or from heaven, “and may he defend you” against evil “from Zion,” that is, from contemplation—namely, from his divinity, through which he contemplates all things.

“May he remember,” that is, show himself mindful through some recompense, “all your sacrifice,” that is, the offering that is made daily on the altar. He says “all” because, although it is one sacrifice, the same sacrifice is performed in countless places. It is the same sacrifice that is called a “holocaust,” that is, wholly burned, because he offered himself entirely to God, in body and soul, suffering even unto death.

May such a sacrifice “be made fat,” that is, acceptable. This is drawn from the sacrifices of the ancients, whose fat sacrifice was said to be more pleasing to God.

“May he also grant you according to your heart,” that is, according to your understanding, so that just as you understand, God may confirm you in it, lest you be perverted toward some error; “and may he confirm all your counsel.” The counsel of the holy Church is that it neither be broken by adversity nor exalted by prosperity.

And rightly do I ask this, because I shall share in that good. This is what follows:

[Col. 0259A] “We shall rejoice”—I and the children of the Church, one of whom I am—“in your salvation,” that is, in your Jesus, “and we shall be magnified,” that is, made great, “in the name of the Lord our God,” that is, because in this age we shall bear his name, namely, we shall be called Christians.

Because I shall share in it, I therefore desire that the Lord fulfill not only the petitions mentioned above but “all your petitions.” By repeating these wishes so often, he displays the affection of his piety.

Here he begins to confirm that the things he had desired for the Church would truly come to it. I desire that he fulfill them, and I affirm that he will fulfill them, because “now”—that is, so long before Christ’s coming—“I have known whom the Lord,” the Father, “has saved: his Christ,” that is, his king, in the Resurrection. [Col. 0259B] Continuation:

He will save him in the Resurrection and Ascension, and he will also “hear him” crying out for us through the representation of his humanity, “from heaven,” that is, from his flesh, or from his material “holy heaven,” because “salvation belongs to his right hand,” that is, to his Son. For he himself is the giver of all salvation, and that salvation is not in weakness but “in powers,” that is, in great powers, which cannot in any way be destroyed, unlike human praise.

The salvation of this Lord is in powers; but these, not attending to it, boast “in chariots,” and those others “in horses.” Through chariots and horses he signifies the greatest honors, namely, two kinds of triumphs. “But we shall call upon” our dwelling-place “in the name of our God,” that is, because we bear only the name of God and are called Christians; or because we possess his fame without knowledge of his essence.

They are in chariots and horses, while we have hope in the Lord. Their pride turns out badly for them, whereas our humility turns out well for us. This is what follows:

“They are bound” in the bond of sins “and have fallen” from vice into vice; “but we have risen” from sins to virtues. That resurrection was not through equality, nor was it merely any kind of rising, such as from one thing to another; hence he says, “we have been raised upright.” By saying “we have risen,” he indicates freedom of choice. By saying “we have been raised upright,” he indicates assisting grace.

And do not allow this king, who makes us such people, to be held by death. Rather, you, “Lord, save” that “king” [Col. 0259D] by raising him from the dead. And through that saved one, “hear us on the day when we call,” that is, in the time of the present life, in which it is permitted to call; or especially on the day of the Resurrection, when the faithful have been rescued from the darkness of death.

## Psalm XX

### Title

“To the end,” or “for the victor,” alternatively “for victory”: a psalm of David.

“Lord, in your strength.” The subject is Christ the King, and he treats him as follows: he describes his strength and glory and desires that he do what a good king ought to do, namely, spare his subjects and subdue the proud. His purpose is to condemn the unbelief of the Jews. By showing Christ to be so glorious and powerful, he admonishes the Jews to abandon their unbelief. He also terrifies them, affirming that Christ himself will punish his enemies when he says: “You will place them like a furnace of fire.”

He begins the description of his strength by directing his prayer to God the Father and saying:

“Lord, this king,” namely Christ, “will rejoice,” not like other kings, who sometimes yield to their enemies, but “in your strength,” in the same power that you possess through the divinity joined to him. That king will also “exult” bodily “over your salvation,” that is, in the salvation that you will accomplish through him for the human race; or, directing his attention above your salvation, “exceedingly.” He rightly says this: the greater the abundance of the benefit, the greater the magnitude of the joy.

[Col. 0260B] He will exult, and rightly, because “you granted him the desire of his heart.” Christ’s spiritual desire was that through his death he might redeem the human race. Although every desire belongs to the heart, he nevertheless adds “of his heart” in order to express the desire more fully, as in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired.”

And from the spiritual “will of his lips,” that is, the will he expressed through his lips, “you did not defraud him,” that is, nothing remained unfulfilled that he spiritually requested. Or, if “will” is understood, we shall say, “you did not defraud him,” by denying him his will.

And rightly did you grant his desire, “because you anticipated him” before his birth “with blessings,” namely, by giving him blessings, making him free from sin and perfect in righteousness—righteousness that also became the cause of our blessings. These blessings are “of sweetness,” because they were sweet to Christ, since his purity of conscience always pleased him.

By saying that Christ was anticipated with blessings of sweetness, he distinguishes him from those who are anticipated with the curse of bitterness, that is, original sin.

He adds another aspect of Christ’s glory, saying: “You placed,” eternally, “upon his head,” that is, upon Christ’s own person, which is the head of the whole Christ, namely, the more exalted part within the whole Christ. The whole Christ is called both head and body. You placed upon his head “a crown,” that is, the apostles, who are called a crown because, just as a crown makes a person distinguished, it is also the reward of victory. That crown was “of precious stone.” The apostles are called stones because of their solidity and stability, and precious because of the radiance of their virtues.

He continues to unfold the glory of the same king in other respects.

“He asked you for life,” namely, eternal life. Here true humanity is indicated: it does not consider itself sufficient unto itself, but in humility asks the Lord for everlasting life. “And you granted him length of days,” not merely for a hundred years, but “for the age” that follows this “age,” that is, unto the end of the age, and also into the age that follows this age. He does not say that the length of days belongs to the future life because there are days there, but because of its duration.

[Col. 0261A] “You will also place upon him,” as upon a foundation, “glory,” namely, glorious martyrs, “and great beauty,” that is, great beauties, such as Martin and Hilary and the other confessors. You will place them upon him because “his glory is great in your salvation,” that is, in your Word united to him. The manifestation of that glory was fitting, and it was demonstrated by the fact that the apostles were founded upon him.

I rightly say, “You will place glory upon him,” because he is the blessing of all nations. This is what follows:

“For you will give him as a blessing,” in this life by giving virtues, “and for ever and ever,” that is, in the other life by giving a crown. Here he confirms the promise made to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 32; Galatians 3).

And you will also “make him joyful with the joy” that his people will have “in your presence,” that is, in your presence, when he enjoys perfect knowledge of you. Then joy will be perfect, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father.

He gives the cause of all the things mentioned above, so that we may say: God gave this king long life and the other things mentioned because this “king” “hopes,” that is, has placed everyone’s hope “in the Lord.” He does not do this out of confidence in merits, but rather “in his mercy”; “he will not be moved” from confidence in that mercy. And rightly so, because “the mercy belongs to the Most High.”

Having shown the strength and glory of that king, he passes to the second matter: he desires that the king exercise justice over the good and the wicked. Up to this point he directed his words to the Father; now he directs them to the Son.

Since you are such a king, therefore, O Lord, “let your hand be found,” that is, your operation, “by all your enemies,” that is, let all who are now enemies, diligently seeking your works, imitate them. But if some do not wish to find your works in this way, “your right hand,” that is, your power, “will find” for their condemnation “all those who hate you.”

I desire that you punish them, and you truly will, because you will “place them in a furnace of fire,” that is, make them like a furnace of fire. For just as a furnace contains the heat of fire within, so they contain within themselves the heat of their evil conscience.

You will place them there “at the time of your countenance,” that is, on the day of judgment, when you will show your facial expression, that is, your anger. Or “at the time of your countenance” means the time when you will show your people the perfect knowledge of your presence.

A furnace may be any oven, or more properly a vessel that becomes hot in fire so that something beneath it may be cooked, or something similar. The same “Lord” who placed them like a furnace “will trouble them in his anger” when he says: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). Once this sentence has been given, “fire will devour” them immediately—that is, material fire will torment them. By saying “fire,” he indicates the kind of torment that tortures them inwardly.

“You will place them like a furnace,” and also “you will destroy their fruit,” that is, their good works, removing them “from the land” of the living. When they ceased from doing good, their good works were destroyed, because although they may provide some remedy for punishment, they do not avail for salvation. And you will destroy “their seed,” that is, their vows, which are called seed because, just as fruit proceeds from seed, so works proceed from vows. I say “seed” separated “from the children” of true “men.” Or “seed” means their followers.

You will destroy them because “they turned the evil”—that is, the destruction they feared would be inflicted upon them by the Romans—“against you,” that is, they turned it toward you. When they handed you over to death, “they devised plans that they could not establish.” They had devised, through his death, to preserve their place and nation (John 11), but through it they instead lost both.

You will destroy them, and therefore “you will make them turn their back,” that is, bent toward earthly things and not looking upon heavenly things—asses of demons. Therefore “you will prepare your countenance,” that is, knowledge of you, which ought to be theirs, through the introduction of the Gentiles and through the intensification of glory, “among your remnants,” that is, so that those remnants may have knowledge of you. He calls those who make themselves humble and despised “remnants.”

You will make them turn their back, and in order that you may do this, “be exalted in strength,” that is, through the power of your divinity. “We shall sing with voice and heart,” and “we shall sing psalms,” by doing good, “to your powers,” praising and imitating them. In singing, we understand the contemplative life; in singing psalms, the active life.

## Psalm XXI

### Title

“To the end, for the morning reception”: a psalm of David.

[Col. 0262C] “God, my God, look upon me.” This psalm suits David, that is, Christ, and was composed “for the morning reception.” Here “morning reception” is understood as Christ’s Resurrection, which took place when the corruptible body assumed incorruption and the mortal body assumed immortality (1 Corinthians 15). Through this reception of Christ we have certainty concerning our own reception.

The fact that the Lord’s reception, that is, his Resurrection, took place in the morning is a sacrament, because it signifies that it is the beginning of our resurrection, and that this Resurrection illumined the whole world—just as the sun, rising in the morning, gradually ascends in order to illuminate the whole world.

This psalm treats of the morning reception because it proposes a new institution for us. It sets before us a just man abandoned and suffering, and also the glory of God the Father that Christ, once resurrected, displays to him. In this, too, the morning assumption is commended, because on account of that assumption the whole glorification of God takes place.

Another translation has “for the morning hind,” and then we understand the hind as Christ’s humanity, which possessed the nature of a hind, because on that morning it left behind these muddy things.

The new institution was in Christ because before Christ God usually rewarded the just, as though they were weak, with temporal goods. But to Christ, although he was more just than all others, he did not grant temporal goods; rather, he gave him the adversities of this world, so that he might obtain heavenly goods. Through this he indicated that after Christ God would no longer reward people with temporal goods, but with eternal ones.

[Col. 0263A] The subject is the Lord’s man; he treats him as follows: he shows him abandoned, and he shows him suffering. Or the subject is Christ’s Passion: afterward he shows the glory of God, and in this he also shows Christ’s glory.

His intention is to exhort us to endure adversities, so that by his example we may seek prosperity in temporal things, but, by enduring adversities, await heavenly things. Through this he directs us toward the end, that is, toward Christ.

The voice is Christ’s, directed to the Father, and it begins with abandonment as follows:

“God, my God.” By repeating “God,” he indicates that he has need of prayer. By saying “my,” he indicates that he has familiarity with him. “Look upon me”: I will not fail in this abandonment.

“Look upon me” is not found in the Hebrew; the Seventy interpreters added it, according to whom this translation was made. [Col. 0263B] “Look upon me,” I say, “because you have abandoned me,” not making me abound in temporal goods, as you did the earlier just, but rather leaving me in need. Why have you abandoned me, a just man, in this way?

He does not express amazement because he himself was amazed, but in order to show that we ought to be amazed that one so perfect did not possess temporal recompense for his righteousness, as the earlier just did. Through this he makes us understand that the reward of righteousness is not to be expected in temporal things, but in heavenly things.

And you have not merely made me needy; you are “far from my salvation,” that is, you permit me to be afflicted. This is because “the words of my sins,” namely, the sins of the faithful crying out through me, are “far from my salvation,” that is, they make you far from my salvation. They are far away because sins do not ask temporal life for me, but death, through which they may be erased.

He calls them his sins, not because he himself committed them, but because he bore punishment for them; or “my sins” means the sins of human beings.

He unfolds the abandonment. Not only have you “abandoned me,” but you also will not hear me when I cry out. This is what follows:

“My God, I shall cry out by day,” that is, for some period of time; or “by day,” that is, in prosperity, “and you will not hear” this cry “in the night,” that is, in adversity. “I shall cry out, and you will not hear.”

He cried out in the night when, at the approach of the Passion, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matthew 26). He cried out in the day when the Jews wished to make him king (John 6).

When he says that Christ cried out and was not heard, this must be understood as crying according to the natural will, not according to the spiritual will. In every just person there are two wills: the natural and the spiritual.

The natural will always concerns temporal things: that a person love the present life, fear death, and so forth. This will is not sin if it agrees with the spiritual will, as in Christ. When he asked according to his natural will that the cup be taken from him, he nevertheless, consenting to the spiritual will, added: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.” The same is true of the other just.

But if someone places the natural will above the spiritual, it is sin—for example, if someone must die for the faith but preserves his life. In all other just people that natural will exists by necessity; in Christ alone it existed not by necessity but by will. For the divinity joined to him could have expelled every such will. He nevertheless willed to fear in order to leave an example for others: if they feared during the Passion, they should not therefore despair, but should obey God’s will rather than their own.

And against what someone might say—“You cried out foolishly, since you knew you would not be heard”—he says: this “is not to be counted as foolishness for me.” For the fact that I was abandoned in this way, suffered, cried out, and was not heard was a matter of great wisdom. Through this came my glorification and the restoration of the human race.

You abandoned me; you did not hear me when I cried out; nevertheless, “you dwell” in me, “the Holy One.” You are, I say, “the praise of Israel,” that is, the one whom Israel praised because you bestowed temporal goods. Or, you are the one who makes Israel praiseworthy by granting temporal goods.

By Israel we understand any just person from the earlier people, to whom God gave temporal goods as a reward for righteousness, in a way contrary to what he gave this just man.

I rightly say “the praise of Israel,” because “in you our fathers hoped” for the possession of prosperity; they also “hoped” that dangers would be removed, and you “delivered them,” as at the Red Sea (Exodus 14). They cried out to you, as in the wilderness for water and food, and were physically saved by receiving what they requested (Exodus 15 and 16).

Why should I enumerate each instance? “They hoped in you, and were not confounded,” that is, they did not suffer shame because they were defrauded in none of the things for which they hoped.

Those fathers prospered in everything; “but I,” who was most perfect and just, “am a worm,” that is, trampled down like a worm, “and not a man,” that is, they did not consider my humanity. I am also “the reproach of men,” that is, one upon whom men cast their reproaches, “and the outcast of the people,” that is, the one of whom it was said: “The people will never be clean unless he is cast out.”

Or it may be understood in this way: “I am a worm,” possessing the nature of a worm in my birth, because just as a worm is produced from the earth without the seed of a father, so Christ came from his mother alone; “not merely a man,” but also God. Or “not a man,” that is, a sinner, because he did not possess the sin that is proper to human beings.

[Col. 0264D] I, so worthy, am the reproach of men; and since I am a reproach, “all who saw me mocked me.” They “spoke” about me “with their lips.” To speak with the lips means to speak without rational meditation. Thus they also mocked me by moving their heads (Matthew 27; Mark 15). Moving the head is a form of mockery.

Mocking, they said: “He hoped in the Lord”; now “let him deliver him” from our hands, or at least “let him save him” by raising him, “because he desires him.”

They say, “Let him deliver him,” and similar things; but you, Lord, “do not depart from me,” that is, make me rise again.

He first gives the reason why God ought not to depart, as follows: Therefore do not depart, “because you are the one who drew me from the womb,” because you alone, with no help from nature, made me be born. For whereas in other cases nature usually works together with divinity, in this one alone divinity worked without nature.

And you ought not to depart because you are “my hope from my youth,” that is, while I was still nursing at the breast, I placed all my hope in you. Here he especially indicates Christ’s perfection.

Again, you ought not to depart because “I was cast out from the womb,” that is, from the moment I was born I was regarded as worthless and needy, like any outcast. I was not cast out in Adam, that is, sin did not take hold of me, but “in you,” who preserved me free from every sin. For this reason you ought not to depart from me.

And again for this reason: because “you are my God,” that is, united to me—not merely when this was evident through miracles, but “from the womb,” that is, from the time when I was still in the womb. When he asks, “Do not depart,” he offers a prayer against abandonment.

I ask that you not depart, and there is need for this, “because tribulation is near,” that is, it is already impending for me. Or “near” because it is in my own person. Whatever happens to our possessions or friends is close; whatever happens in ourselves is nearest.

Again, there is need for this “because there is no one” else “to help.” Here he begins to speak of the Passion.

I rightly say that tribulation is near, because “many calves,” that is, the multitude of the Jewish people, who were wanton against Christ without being restrained by any yoke, “surrounded me.” They raged against him like wanton calves not yet restrained by a yoke.

These calves “surrounded me” from the time they began until the very death; “fat bulls,” that is, the rulers themselves, fierce against Christ, “besieged me.” Through delay and deliberation they sought to overcome me by death, in the manner of besiegers.

These besiegers and those surrounding me “opened their mouths,” that is, they said many things “against me,” that is, for my humiliation; “like a lion seizing and roaring,” they seized me when they dragged me before the judge.

Then “I was poured out,” that is, I was killed by the shedding of blood from my side. This is what he means by “like water.” He rightly compares Christ’s death to poured-out water, because just as poured-out water prepares a collapse and also washes, so Christ’s death is ruin for some and purification for others.

“And all my bones were scattered,” that is, the apostles, who were the stronger members of Christ’s body.

“And my heart,” that is, my teaching, in which my will is explained, “became like melting wax.” Whereas it had previously been solid and firm in the apostles, it failed in the fire of the Passion. When they saw him held by death, they lost confidence in his teaching. It did not fail in a few alone, but “in the midst,” that is, in the common body, “of my belly,” that is, of my congregation. It failed in them because, although they had previously been strong, they had now become a belly, that is, soft.

And also “my strength,” which had previously flourished in them while I performed miracles, “dried up,” being dried out, and appeared to possess no vigor, reckoned fragile “like a potsherd.” Or “it dried up like a potsherd” because, just as earthenware becomes more solid and stronger through firing, so Christ’s strength, tested by the fire of the Passion, appeared more robust.

“And my tongue clung to my jaws,” that is, whereas I had previously taught, I fell silent, so that I did not even answer Pilate when he questioned me (Matthew 27).

This can also be read allegorically, although it does not belong here: “my tongue,” that is, my preachers, through whom I speak, “clung to my jaws,” that is, to the holy Scriptures, according to which they preached. The Scriptures are called the jaws of God because through them he incorporates some people into himself, just as through jaws a beast incorporates something into itself.

“And you brought me down into the dust of death,” that is, through death you reduced me to dust—not because his body decayed, but because “dust” means any body after it has died, in accordance with the words that the Lord says to Adam: “You are ash, and into ash you shall return” (Genesis 3), giving a universal sentence concerning every human nature.

This sentence is true of those who will be found alive when the Lord comes to judge. For although they will not decay, nevertheless, at the very moment of being caught up, they will be moved into dust, according to the opinion of the Jews.

This too can be read allegorically, but it does not belong here: “you brought me down,” through the preaching of my own [followers], “into the dust of death,” that is, among the Gentiles, who were dust because they were not bound by the bond of faith or charity and were dead in sins.

All these evils came because “many dogs surrounded me,” that is, the Jews, who are called dogs because, like dogs, they bark irrationally. When they see something unusual, they bark at it even if it brings them something good; when they see something customary, they applaud it even if it is useless.

So the Jews rejected Christ’s teaching, although it was good, because it was unfamiliar. If he had preached to them according to their own law, they would have rejoiced, because they would have encountered something customary, even if it were useless.

“The assembly of the wicked,” that is, of the rulers who wished me evil, “besieged me,” that is, by deliberation it sought my death.

They also “dug out my hands.” Although they did not do this themselves, strictly speaking, they are nevertheless said to have done it because it was carried out at their command. He rightly said “dug out” rather than “pierced through,” because just as dug earth bears fruit, so this digging of Christ produced the greatest fruit. “And my feet” they also dug out; “they counted all my bones”—not because they took care to count them, but because they stretched him out in such a way that they could be counted. [Col. 0266D]

Others did the digging, but “they themselves, in their own persons, considered” what was being done to me, “and they looked upon me” as though I were a pleasing spectacle; this indicates their extreme hardness. “They divided my garments among themselves” for mockery, “and over a certain garment of mine”—that is, my seamless tunic—“they cast lots” (Matt. XXVII; John XVIII). Allegorically it is read in this way: “They divided my garments among themselves,” that is, the Scriptures, from which heretics have drawn diverse portions; “and over my garment,” that is, the Catholic faith, which always remains whole in the hands, “they cast lots,” because we understand it to be given through love alone. [Col. 0267A]

They did these things to me, but “you, Lord, do not withdraw your help from me,” that is, do not postpone my resurrection until the common resurrection of all, but rather “look to my defense,” that is, show yourself attentive to my injury by raising me up quickly.

I say “look,” namely, by doing this for me: “deliver my soul from the sword,” that is, from death, so that it may not be able to retain it, even though separated from the body. Death is therefore called a sword because, like a sword, it divides the soul from the body. “And from the hand of the dog”—that is, the Jewish people—“deliver my only one,” that is, my soul, which he calls “only one” because it alone was free from sin. He asks to be delivered so that their opinion may not prove true—the opinion by which they thought that he was being held in death. [Col. 0267B]

Likewise, “save me from the mouth of the lion,” that is, the devil, who held Christ in his mouth when he led him all the way to death. And save “my humility,” that is, me, the humble one, “from the horns” of “the unicorns,” that is, from the proud, the proud Jews. We understand the Jews by the unicorn because, just as the unicorn glories in a single horn, so the Jews glory in the Old Testament alone.

Having thus shown Christ’s abandonment and passion, lest through these we be held back from obeying him, he shows that great glorification proceeds from them for God the Father, and consequently for Christ himself. This glorification is a remedy for us against the abandonment and passion just mentioned.

And you rightly ought to save me, because “when I am saved I shall proclaim your name to my brothers,” that is, your fame, “to my brothers,” that is, to the apostles. This proclamation occurred not only through words, but chiefly through the sending of the Holy Spirit. And also “I shall praise you,” that is, I shall cause you to be praised, “in the midst,” that is, in the communion “of the Church.” He turns to them when he says:

“You who fear the Lord, praise him” in every way. He divides them into groups, exhorting both the active and the contemplative to praise. He identifies the active when he says: “All the seed of Jacob, glorify him,” that is, all his imitators. He identifies the contemplative when he says: “Let all the seed of Israel fear him,” because “he has not despised”—that is, utterly rejected—“nor disdained”—that is, regarded as worthless in any respect—“the prayer” of me, “the poor man.” [Col. 0267D]

“Nor has he turned his face away from me,” that is, I have always remained in his good pleasure. “And he heard me when I cried out,” that is, at the time when I was asking to be heard.

And because you heard me when I cried out, therefore “my praise is with you in the great church,” that is, in the Church gathered throughout the whole world. Or it may be understood in this way: Because I have been heard, therefore my praise is in the great church; that is, I am praised by you in the Church, so that, just as you are praised, I too am praised equally with you. And so that this praise may be perfect in the Church, I shall give the Church my body and blood.

And this is “my vows,” that is, my body, which I vowed to offer to God for the restoration of the human race. “I shall repay them,” that is, what I had already given on the cross I shall give again on the altar. And although some do not understand it, nevertheless it “shall be in the presence,” that is, in the knowledge, “of those who fear him.” Through this sacrament, therefore, God will receive greater praise, because this is the covenant between God and humanity; attending to this covenant, people praise God above all. [Col. 0268A]

These vows “the poor shall eat and be filled,” receiving what they desire—namely, forgiveness of sins, an increase of righteousness in this life, and a crown in the next. And because of this “they shall praise the Lord,” namely, those “who seek him”; and thus “their hearts,” that is, their souls, “shall live” in righteousness “for ever and ever,” that is, for as long as age succeeds age, namely, throughout this entire life. Or “for ever,” that is, they shall live in this life; “and for ever and ever,” that is, in the other life they shall live in glory.

I say that “the poor shall be filled,” and not merely a few, but “all the ends”—that is, some people in every end of the earth—“shall remember” and thus “shall turn to the Lord.” [Col. 0268B]

And lest we understand one order only, for example the rustic order or some similar group, as spread throughout all parts of the earth, he says: “And all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence,” that is, some from every order.

They rightly ought to worship, “because the kingdom is the Lord’s,” that is, the Lord is king of all; “and he shall rule the nations,” that is, he shall exercise dominion over his nations, because he will govern them in righteousness.

“The poor shall eat and be filled,” and also “all the rich of the earth,” that is, those made rich in earthly things, “have eaten”—that is, have tasted the Lord’s body—“and worshipped.” But although some do not see this as leading to ruin, nevertheless “they shall fall in his presence,” namely, before God, from whom nothing can be hidden. They shall fall, I say, “all who descend into the earth,” that is, all who incline toward the desire for earthly things.

“They shall praise the Lord who seek him”; “and my soul,” that is, those whom I love as my own soul, “shall live for him,” that is, for his honor. And not only shall the righteous who are presently alive do so, but “my seed,” that is, my imitators and the children of these people, “shall serve him.”

I rightly say “seed,” because “a generation” is “to come,” and it “shall be announced to the Lord” by angels, as the angel said to Tobit: “I presented your prayers to God” (Book III). Or “it shall be announced,” that is, they shall preach, “to the Lord,” that is, the generation to come shall be announced for the Lord’s honor, and through the heavens. And he says this: “And the heavens shall proclaim,” that is, the holy preachers shall proclaim, “his righteousness,” that is, God’s righteousness, “to a people who shall be born,” not by natural birth, but by water and the Holy Spirit (John III), “whom the Lord made” his own in this way. In carnal birth God and nature operate together, but in rebirth God alone operates.

## ON PSALM XXII. TITLE

“To the end: a psalm of David, or a song of David.”

“The Lord shepherds me.” A psalm of David, the voice of the prophet, whose subject here is thanksgiving for God’s gifts. He treats this subject by arranging ten gifts. He intends to persuade us that we must not despair when God grants such gifts; and before discussing the gifts, he first offers, as it were, a prologue and commendation of them.

Do not despair, but consider how “the Lord shepherds me” away from the seductions of the wicked, just as a good shepherd shepherds his sheep and carefully guards them lest wolves tear them apart. And while he shepherds me, “nothing” necessary for righteousness “shall be lacking to me.” Hence it is said: Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.

Nothing shall be lacking to me because the Lord places me “in a place of pasture” and grants the other gifts that follow. The continuation is: “Nothing shall be lacking to me.” I say this of myself, placed “in a place of pasture,” that is, in divine Scripture, which is called pasture by analogy: just as animals are refreshed in pastures, so faithful souls are nourished by the divine Scriptures. He calls this Scripture a “place” because in it alone the certainty of sufficiency is found. Although philosophers diligently sought it elsewhere, they were never able to find it in other writings. For knowledge of God is found in no writings other than the divine writings. And because he had said that he was in a place of pasture without saying who had placed him there, he adds: “There he settled me”—the Lord did so. When he says that he has been placed in a place of pasture, we recognize the first gift.

He sets forth the second gift when he says: “He settled me,” and the Lord himself “led me beside waters of refreshment,” that is, the water of baptism, which is called water of refreshment because through it we are both cleansed from sins and watered so as to bear good fruits. Previously we had been dry and barren, and had been dispersed like dust. He sets forth the third gift when he says: “He converted my soul.”

Augustine places this gift of conversion first, then the gift of baptism, and afterward the place of pasture. Yet these may also rightly be considered in this order: first someone is nourished by divine Scripture, then baptized, and afterward converted. For conversion occurs not only before baptism, when one passes from unbelief to faith, but also after baptism, namely when, having abandoned the former life, we follow the new life alone.

He sets forth the fourth gift. The same Lord who converts my soul “led me,” that is, guided me as though I were ignorant, “along the paths of righteousness,” that is, through righteous works, which are paths, because by them one proceeds rightly toward life. By saying “along” he gives us to understand that he not only knew those paths, but, as their teacher, taught others to walk along them. He did this not on account of my merit, but “for his name’s sake,” that is, so that his name might appear true—namely, the name by which he is called Savior. He sets forth the fifth gift, and joins it as follows.

I rightly say, “He led me along the paths of righteousness,” “for” he did something greater for me: if I persist among heretics, they will never be able to harm me. This is expressed by: “And if I walk,” that is, if I remain for a long time, “in the midst of the shadow of death,” that is, in the midst of heretics, who are called a shadow because their hearts are dark with respect to the knowledge of truth. They are called a shadow of death because those who enter their sect fall into death, being deprived of true life. They are like shadows of death, among which anyone who enters soon dies. Among such people “I shall fear no evil,” that is, their poisonous persuasions, “because you are with me,” defending me through the protection of your presence.

And also, “your rod,” that is, your correction, “and your staff,” that is, your help, by which a faithful person is supported when he cannot stand by himself, like a sick person supported by a staff—“they themselves have comforted me.” Although a rod does not seem to be a source of comfort, the saints are nevertheless comforted by it, because through it they understand both that they are being cleansed from sins and that in the other life they will obtain a great reward for their suffering. Hence the Apostle says: “No discipline at the present seems to be a matter of joy but of sorrow, but afterward it brings the most peaceful fruit” (Heb. XII). This is the sixth gift.

He sets forth the seventh, saying:

“You have prepared in my sight,” that is, you have made me capable of understanding, “a table,” that is, the Lord’s body. I call it a table that assists me “against all those who afflict me.” For we are not only cleansed from vices and filled with virtues by the Lord’s body; we are also sustained against every persecution.

He sets forth the eighth gift when he says:

“You have anointed my head,” that is, my mind, “with oil,” that is, with the Holy Spirit, who penetrates the soul and cherishes it as oil cherishes the flesh. Or “my head” means Christ, to whom the Holy Spirit was given without measure, from whose abundance the other members rejoice with him. By saying “in oil,” he indicates a greater abundance than if he had said simply “with oil” as an instrumental expression.

He sets forth the ninth gift, saying: “My cup,” that is, the drink of the Lord’s blood, “making drunk,” because it causes us to forget earthly things and also to despise the present life, as is evident in Lawrence and others like him. “And how splendid is that cup!” It is exceedingly splendid, namely because it bestows eternal life.

He sets forth the tenth gift, through which the other nine are preserved, so to speak, as their safeguard:

“Your mercy shall follow me.” For just as mercy goes before by granting grace, so it follows afterward for its preservation. If it merely went before, no one would be able to preserve what had been granted: “all the days of my life.” It follows for this purpose: that through the graces granted and preserved I may dwell in the house of the heavenly Jerusalem “for length of days,” that is, forever.

If the text is also taken in the other sense, it may be read as follows: May God’s mercy follow me so that I may persevere in this life, “and that I may dwell in the house of the Lord.” This is the commendation of the gifts: he shows that through them the heavenly house is given.

## ON PSALM XXIII. TITLE

“A psalm of David on the first day of the week.”

“The earth is the Lord’s.” This psalm suits the prophet David, who here speaks in contemplation of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week, that is, on the first day of the seven-day week. The Lord’s resurrection was the foundation of the Church and the beginning of our entire restoration, because in Christ’s own person our nature has already become incapable of suffering and immortal, and through him he gave us hope of immortality and freedom from suffering.

That the restoration of human nature was to be accomplished on the first day was signified by the creation of the world, according to the material creation that took place on the first day. “Sabbath” is the name of the entire week, and it derives from the dignity of the day on which the Lord rested. Accordingly, it is said in the Gospel: “I fast twice on the Sabbath.”

The subject is Christ risen. The method is as follows: he shows both that Christ possesses this order and the greatness of his kingdom; then he shows who are worthy to dwell in that kingdom. He also exhorts us to remove errors and enlarge virtues, so that we may receive the triumphant Lord. This is likewise the intention.

Just as someone might exhort the people of a kingdom to demolish its walls and enlarge its gates so that they might receive their lord with great rejoicing, so the prophet, foreseeing Christ’s possession of a kingdom throughout the whole world in his resurrection, exhorts us to receive this triumphant king.

Because “the earth is the Lord’s,” that is, the Church which he founded in his resurrection, “and its fullness,” that is, all the abundance of virtues possessed by the Church, also belong to the Lord, because the Lord gives them to the Church. And lest I understand the Church to be confined, namely to Judea alone, he shows that the Lord’s Church has been gathered from every part of the earth when he says: “the world,” that is, the Church from the entire circuit of the earth belongs to the Lord; “and all who dwell in it,” that is, all the children who are born each day in the Church.

When he says “dwell,” he indicates not everyone who approaches the Church, but those who persevere in the Church’s faith until death.

I rightly say, “The earth is the Lord’s,” “because he founded it,” that is, made it stable, “upon the seas.” By “seas” he understands the common fruits of this world. By saying “upon,” he shows that the Church cannot be overcome by the waves, but rather overcomes the waves.

“And upon the rivers.” By “rivers” he understands secular rulers, who flow into the concerns of the people as rivers flow into the sea. God established the Church above them because the Church also overcomes the persecutions of rulers. When he says “he prepared the world,” he indicates that the Church possesses these things through inward inspiration.

Having shown the extent of the kingdom, he shows how worthy the kingdom’s inhabitants themselves are. He does this through question and answer in order to show us greater certainty by this means. The continuation is: “The earth is the Lord’s, and he founded it,” as follows:

“And who” is so worthy that he “shall ascend into” this “mountain of the Lord?” That is, into the Church, which is called a mountain because of the stability and eminence of its virtues. He properly says “ascends” of one for whom it is a great ascent to pass from injustice to conformity with the Church. And because someone might ascend and quickly withdraw, he adds: “Or who [Col. 0272A] shall stand,” that is, persevere, “in his holy place?” That is, in the Church which he himself sanctified.

I ask who ascends: one who is “innocent in his hands,” that is, in his works—namely, one whose works do not harm his neighbor. Yet because this alone would not make him an inhabitant of that kingdom, he adds: “and pure in heart,” that is, one who does not harm his neighbor even by his will.

And because, although he might not sin against his neighbor, he would still not yet be worthy, he adds: “who has not received his soul,” that is, his will, “in vain,” that is, in these earthly things which are called vain, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I). By saying that vain things are not acceptable to his soul, he implies that, as far as he is concerned, he is clean from sins. And because even this would not suffice unless he showed that he had done good, he adds: “nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.” He has indeed sworn, but not deceitfully, because he has faithfully fulfilled whatever he promised his neighbor.

Having established the worthiness of the inhabitant, he shows what reward such an inhabitant will have when he says: “This” inhabitant just described “shall receive a blessing,” that is, in this life an increase of virtues, and in the next the recompense of merits, “from the Lord.” This is given not through merits, but through “mercy” granted “by God his Savior,” that is, by his Savior, who gives the blessing because salvation is bestowed through him; mercy, because sins are forgiven through him.

And lest the inhabitants he has described be thought few, he shows that they are many by naming them as a generation: “This is the generation.” He shows two parts of this generation, the active and the contemplative, when he says: “of those who seek him,” that is, of those who seek to possess God through whatever work they undertake. He places the contemplatives, as it were, behind them when he says: “who seek the face of the God of Jacob,” that is, knowledge of the deity. He says “the God of Jacob” because they labor to see God as Jacob did.

Since the kingdom is such and its inhabitants so worthy, therefore you, “princes,” that is, demons, who are called the rulers of the world, “lift up,” that is, remove, “your gates,” that is, the vices from the human beings whom you hold in error. Errors are called gates because through them one goes into eternal destruction.

And you, “eternal gates,” that is, virtues which lead to eternal life, “be lifted up,” that is, be enlarged; “and the king of glory shall enter” into those from whom errors have been removed and in whom virtues have been enlarged.

He shows the king’s dignity by asking and answering when he says: “Who is this king of glory?” It is “the Lord,” namely, “strong” in himself, even if he had never displayed it, “and powerful” in every creature. And this “Lord” is spiritually “powerful in battle,” in which he conquered the devil.

“Lift up” is repeated, by which he shows that he has great affection toward this Lord. Through this he intends to exhort us to receive this Lord with great affection.

This “king of glory” is “the Lord of the Powers,” that is, of all the angelic orders. Although “Powers” is properly the name of one order, it becomes a common designation for all of them.

It should be understood that David uses the words in his own person as the words of angels. For through the Holy Spirit he foresaw the angels who would go before Christ and say these things in hell: “O princes,” that is, demons, “lift up your gates,” that is, the closures of hell by which you hold the souls of the saints.

He also foresaw the angels who would go before Christ at his ascension and say: “Eternal gates,” that is, entrances into the heavenly places, through which no human being had yet been able to enter, “be lifted up,” that is, be enlarged, “and the king of glory shall enter.” [Col. 0273B]

The prophet also foresaw what would be answered to the angels. The demons said to the angels going before Christ into hell: “Who is this king of glory, whom you announce as coming here?” But the heavenly angels asked the same question when Christ’s ascension was announced to them by the angels who were present.

For it is certain that some angels did not know of Christ’s ascension until they saw it, and when they saw it they were greatly astonished. When both the infernal and the heavenly angels made inquiry, the angels who went before replied: “The Lord strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle.” “Lift up the gates”—they repeat their command because they seem to be announcing something wondrous and unbelievable.

## ON PSALM XXIV. TITLE

“To the end: a psalm of David.”

“To you, Lord.” In this psalm the Church speaks, signified by David, and its subject is crying out amid the hardships of this world. It treats the subject as follows: it asks that the ways of the Lord be shown to its uplifted soul; then it asks for the mercies that God was accustomed to show to the other fathers; then it describes the righteous person and sets forth the reward of his righteousness; and it promises to vow itself to be like him.

Its intention is to exhort us to endure patiently the necessities of this world. It does not urge martyrdom, but rather that we patiently bear the common troubles of this life, which all the holy confessors likewise endured unavoidably.

Before asking that the ways be shown, he first indicates that the soul has been lifted up when he says: “Lord, I have lifted up my soul,” that is, my animal nature, which belonged to this nature and could quickly be depressed by the desire for earthly things. I have raised it “to you,” that is, in such a way that, by obeying the superior power of the soul, it may serve you.

Or we may understand the superior power of the soul itself, namely the mind, as if the faithful person were saying: I have lifted my soul, that is, my mind, to contemplate you; that is, I have not allowed it to be depressed toward earthly things by its animal nature.

And because he recognizes that he is of a changeable nature, which cannot remain upright by itself, he adds: “My God, I trust in you,” that is, in the protection of your mercy; and therefore “I shall not be ashamed,” that is, I shall not withdraw from any good work once begun.

Nor will others cause me to withdraw, through which I might suffer shame. He says this: “Nor let my enemies,” whether spiritual or bodily, “mock me,” that is, make me an object of ridicule. This wish is equivalent to saying, “They will not mock me.” And truly I shall neither be ashamed nor mocked when, with my soul lifted up, I trust in you, because this is so in every case.

This is what he says: “Indeed, all who wait for you,” that is, those who confidently await your help amid the persecution of evils, “shall not be confounded,” that is, they shall not experience shame over anything.

Those who wait shall not be confounded, but all the wicked shall be confounded, both because they act wickedly and because they act uselessly. This is expressed by: “Let all who act wickedly in vain be confounded.”

Those things are said to be done “in vain,” whether good or evil, in which there is no certain expectation. And a wish has the same force as an affirmation when uttered by the good alone. By saying that those who wait are not confounded and that the wicked are confounded, he chiefly exhorts us to wait.

“I have lifted up my soul; I shall not be ashamed,” and therefore “show me your ways,” that is, your common commandments, by which one goes to you, Lord. He rightly says “show,” because little labor is required to learn the Lord’s ways. “And your paths,” that is, your stricter commandments, which are hidden from many and lead more directly to life, like paths, which are narrow roads and lead more directly to a city: “teach me” them. He rightly says “teach,” because to learn them requires not only demonstration but also the greatest instruction.

And because he might show the ways and teach the paths, yet this would be of little benefit unless God made him walk correctly along them, he adds: Lord, having placed me in your ways and in your paths, “direct me,” that is, make me walk in a straight course—“me,” namely, who have been placed “in your truth,” that is, in your Son, who is the truth; or in the law which the Son himself taught, where truth alone is found.

And when I have done good, “teach me” so that I may understand both what I have done and what I believe. A person believes and acts before understanding what he believes and does. Hence it is said: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII). And the Psalmist says: “They proclaimed the works of God and his deeds, and after they proclaimed them, they understood” (Ps. LXIII).

He gives two reasons why God should teach and direct him: because he believes that God is his Savior and because he waits for him. This is expressed by: “Because you are my God and Savior, and I have waited for you all day,” that is, at every time of my life.

Having set forth the request that the ways be shown, he moves to the request for mercies, so that God may act toward him as he was accustomed to act toward the ancient fathers. The continuation is: Because I believe that you are the Savior and I wait for you, you ought to direct me; and if this is not enough, let the custom of your mercy be enough. Thus he says: “Remember,” that is, deal with me as you have been accustomed to deal with the other fathers: “your mercies, Lord, and your compassions.”

“Miseration” is the outward bestowal of mercy; “mercy” is the inward affection of compassion. Therefore he places mercy after compassion. Although God does not grant some people the outward expression of mercy which they ask for, nevertheless compassion moves him toward them—as in the case of Paul (1 Cor. XII). Although God did not remove from Paul the “thorn” which he asked to have removed, he was nevertheless merciful toward him, even in giving him the thorn as a safeguard of his virtues. “These mercies” have existed “from the beginning of the age,” that is, from the time when the world began.

You ask for mercies; what do you want done for you? This, Lord: “Do not remember,” that is, do not punish in the other life, “the sins of my youth,” that is, of my frivolity. He does not speak of youth as a period of time, because this kind of youth can also exist in old people who possess frivolity. For this reason we understand “youth” as frivolity, because frivolity belongs to youth.

A sin is committed when what is commanded to be done is abandoned. “And my ignorances,” that is, those sins of which I am unaware, such as original sins, or those which I committed in childhood.

“Do not remember my sins,” but rather “you, Lord, remember me,” that is, remember my fragile nature—not according to your loftiness, but “according to your mercy.” Yet I do not dare to ask for mercy according to my merit; rather, “because of your goodness, remember me,” since you alone are good.

I rightly say that the Lord is good, because he is “sweet” to one who knows him, just as food is sweet to one who tastes it. This sweetness is according to mercy, “and the Lord is upright,” according to justice. “For this reason,” because he is “sweet and upright,” he “will give a law to sinners on the way,” that is, in this life: he will give them “a law,” that is, correction.

We understand “law” as correction because, just as the law both inspires fear and makes one cease from evil, so does correction. Or by “the way” we may understand the Lord’s commandments. To those who are outside this way, God gives no law.

When God punishes sinners, he acts justly. He indicates that we must understand this punishment when he says that he gives a law. That he does this “on the way,” that is, in this life, is fitting, because this life alone is the place of correction. He rightly places “sweet and upright” together, because one moderates the other. The sweetness of God’s mercy exhorts us not to despair; justice removes negligence.

“The Lord will give a law,” and through this law he “will direct the meek,” that is, those who were previously untamed and have now become tractable. When they are struck, they do not strike back; when they are cursed, they do not curse. He will direct them “in judgment,” that is, in the discernment of good and evil.

Or “in judgment” means in the correction itself which God has made for them: he will direct the meek toward the way of life. For that correction itself is his direction, because through it sins are forgiven and virtues are bestowed. “And he will teach his ways to the gentle,” that is, to those who are simple by nature and who have never been savage.

He will teach “ways” that must not be despised, because “all the ways” of the Lord “are mercy and truth.” Whatever God does for us, he does either through mercy or through truth; and whatever path we take in approaching him is either mercy or truth.

If we proceed through tribulation, it is God’s justice, by which he justly punishes us. If we proceed through some good works, it is God’s mercy, because we are unable to do any good by ourselves.

These ways are not known to everyone, but to those “who seek,” that is, those who consider them with frequent diligence: “his covenant and his testimonies.” By “his covenant” we understand the holy Gospel, because just as someone promises an inheritance in his will, commands his heirs what they should do, and confirms the will by his death, so Christ promises an inheritance in the Gospel, gives his people commandments for living, and confirms his covenant by his death.

By “his testimonies” we understand the writings of the prophets, for the prophets were witnesses to the promises that were fulfilled in Christ.

Because you are “sweet and upright,” I am confident that you “will be gracious toward my sin,” forgiving it, not because of my merit but “for the sake of your name,” because you are Jesus, that is, Savior. I rightly say “for the sake of your name,” because it is not on account of my sin—for it is indeed a great sin.

Here he begins the third part, describing the righteous person and his reward, and asserting that he will become like him. The continuation is: “You will be gracious” to me, who am a sinner. But “who” is righteous? This is expressed by: “The person who fears the Lord,” with filial fear. Who is this person? One “who has chosen a way for himself,” whether the active or the contemplative life.

By saying “has chosen,” he indicates two things: that he did so by his own will and that he separated this way from others. In this way the Lord “has established a law for him,” that is, commandments according to which he should live. The righteous person, then, is one who chooses both the life itself and to walk in it according to the Lord’s law.

He sets forth the righteous person’s reward when he says: “His soul,” that is, the soul of the righteous person, “shall dwell in good places” before the judgment; “and his seed,” that is, his good works, “shall inherit”—that is, cause him to inherit—“the land” of the living. This will take place in the general resurrection.

Against anyone who might say that no one can persevere in good because of the changeability of nature, and therefore that he will lose that good, he says:

“The Lord is a foundation,” that is, one who makes the righteous firm in goodness in this life—not the proud, but “those who fear God,” because fear of the Lord is opposed to human fear. Human fear produces distrust, whereas divine fear is a foundation of hope.

He also promised his own that he would reveal himself to them. This is “his covenant,” that is, his promise, which is of this kind: that the Lord himself “will be revealed to them.” Or “covenant” means the Gospel, which is of this kind: that it “will be revealed to them,” that is, that they will have understanding of the Gospel itself.

Since the righteous person is such and the righteous person’s reward is such, therefore, whatever others may do, I shall make myself like the righteous person. This is expressed by: “My eyes,” that is, my intentions, “are always toward the Lord,” and therefore “he will draw my feet,” that is, my affections, “out of the snare,” that is, out of the temptations of the devil, so that I may not be ensnared by them.

Others may walk with their eyes lifted up and yet fall into snares; but those who lift their eyes toward the Lord are rescued by the Lord from snares.

I look to you, and you “look upon me.” I do not ask you to regard me as your equal, but as one who is miserable. “Have mercy on me,” miserable as I am, because you are merciful, “for I am alone and poor.”

The righteous person is called “alone” because, from all the sects, he has chosen God’s one and only sect, and serves God alone. By saying “alone,” he indicates that he is to be loved as an only son is loved by his father. The righteous person calls himself poor because he has been stripped of the desire for earthly things; for this reason he is worthy to be consoled.

I say “have mercy,” and this is necessary, “because the tribulations of my heart,” namely, those which have risen even into my heart, “have multiplied.” For I am afflicted even by those who ought to be righteous members of the Church. And you, “deliver me” so that they may not prevail against me, “from my necessities,” that is, from the tribulations which are necessary for me because they are unavoidable; for no righteous person can escape tribulations. He says “my” because he had taken these upon himself through the zeal of charity.

“Deliver me,” and “see my humility,” that is, how humble I am, since I prefer myself to no one, “and my labor,” which I endure by disputing against manifestly wicked people and admonishing them. Therefore “forgive all my sins.”

Having prayed for himself, he prays for his enemies. The continuation is:

“Look upon me,” and also “look upon my enemies” with the eye of mercy, for they are the source of great harm, “because they have multiplied,” that is, they are many. Some who have even become children of the Church have become enemies, and they “hate me with unjust hatred,” because they returned evil for good.

And toward such people “guard my soul,” so that they may not make me like themselves. And if they are unwilling to convert, “deliver me” even from their bodily presence—that is, destroy them. Deliver me so that I “may not be ashamed” of this, “because I have hoped in you,” for unless you delivered me, I would then be ashamed of my hope.

Deliver me, and you, “God,” “free Israel,” that is, all who see you, “from all his tribulations.” He gives the reason why he prays that such people be delivered.

It is this: “the innocent,” that is, those who inflict no evil on others, “and the upright,” who do good, “have adhered to me,” namely, they have become conformed to me in the union of their will. Therefore “they have adhered,” because “I waited for you,” that is, they saw me patiently awaiting your reward.

## ON PSALM XXV. TITLE

“A psalm of David.”

“Judge me, O Lord.” Here David speaks, or any most perfect person who, having abandoned the company of the wicked, clings to the company of the just. This same just person is here the subject, asking in this way for two judgments according to his merits: one in this life, the other in the life to come. His purpose is to admonish us that, after abandoning the impious, we should cling to the just; for if here we have been separated from the wicked, God will separate us from those same wicked people in the judgment.

And he begins with a request for the judgment of this life, as follows: “O Lord, judge me,” that is, separate me from the impious. And he states the reason why he ought to judge him, saying: “for I have entered,” that is, I have begun to do good, “in my innocence”—I do not mean the innocence of angels, but “my own,” that is, such as human frailty can possess, since I have committed neither theft nor murder. And because he might have begun in that innocence without persevering in it, he says, “and I shall not grow weak” in that innocence. And lest he appear arrogant, he adds: “hoping in the Lord,” that is, “I shall not grow weak” not because of merits, but because I hope in the Lord.

Judge me in this way, namely, “test me,” that is, show me, “O Lord,” as having been tested and approved, both to myself and to others. God showed Job to himself as tested and approved (Job 1), because Job came to know that he could endure many things; and he showed him to others, even to the demons, who thought that he could be swallowed up by slight tribulation. “Test me,” I say, in this way: “try me,” that is, through trials show me to have been tested; and through these temptations “burn my kidneys,” that is, the pleasures of lust, “and my heart,” that is, my thoughts, so that nothing evil may be found either in my kidneys or in my thoughts. Or, “burn my kidneys” through the fire of the Holy Spirit.

“Test and try me,” and I shall bear this well, “for your mercy is before my eyes,” that is, I always keep you, merciful as you are, before the eyes of my heart; and also “I have pleased” you “in your truth,” that is, in Christ your Son, whom I have imitated, who said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14). Or, “in your truth,” that is, in the law which the Son taught, where there was pure truth. I rightly say, “I have pleased you in your truth,” because I avoided evil and followed good. And he shows that he had abandoned evil when he says:

“I have not sat,” that is, I have not lingered, either bodily or in truth, “with the council of vanity.” By “vanity” we understand earthly things, and by “council,” those who give reasons in support of the desire for earthly things.
