For some say that these things ought to be desired because they were made for human beings. “And I shall not enter,” that is, I shall not begin to be such as either to do evil with those “who practice iniquity” or to give them my assent.

“I have not sat,” but rather “I have hated the assembly,” that is, the congregation, “of the wicked,” that is, of those who wish evil upon their neighbor; “and with the impious,” that is, with heretics, who oppose divine worship and persuade others against it, “I shall not sit,” that is, I shall not remain in such a way as to consent.

He has shown that he abandoned evil and was separated from the company of the wicked. Now he shows that he both does good and has passed over to the company of the good: “I shall not sit,” but rather “I shall wash my hands,” that is, I shall show my actions to have been washed and cleansed, “among the innocent,” that is, in the company of the innocent. Through the company of the saints, anyone—even one who is lukewarm—is kindled to do good. And, with washed hands, that is, with purified works, “I shall surround,” that is, with continual devotion I shall seek, “your altar,” that is, heavenly things. For an altar is so called as though it were a high altar (*alta ara*), and heavenly things are high.

[Col. 0279A] I shall surround it for this purpose: “that I may hear,” that is, understand, “the voice,” that is, the manifestation, “of your praise,” and afterward “declare all your wonders”—not because he declares everything, but because whatever he declares is wondrous. When the just person says that he surrounds the altar and declares all the wonders, this is said by comparison. Just as the high priest in the Old Testament entered the altar in the Holy of Holies and, after hearing the divine response, reported it to the people, so Isaiah heard the voices: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory” (Isaiah 6), and reported it before the people. Until now he has dealt with the judgment which the just person asks to be carried out upon him in this life. Now he shows the judgment which he asks to be carried out upon him in the life to come. Continuation:

[Col. 0279B] “I shall wash my hands among the innocent,” and therefore you, O Lord, “do not destroy my soul with the wicked.” He divides the wicked into two classes: the impious and men of blood. By the impious we understand both heretics and all who strive against divine religion. By “men of blood” he means murderers, or men who live according to the flesh, of whom the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15). He rightly asks that his soul not perish in the judgment with those with whom he had no fellowship in action here. By saying, “do not destroy,” he means as much as if he were affirming, “You will not destroy”; and by this he especially urges us to separate ourselves from the impious. He then gives the reasons, saying. By “life” we understand the same thing as by “soul.”

[Col. 0279C] “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house.” He calls “house” all the just in whom God dwells. He understands the “beauty of that house” as the virtues with which the just are adorned. And I have loved “the place of the dwelling of your glory,” that is, of your divinity. We understand as the place in which divinity dwells the most perfect of the just, who possess a great and excellent knowledge of God.

“Do not destroy,” I said, “my soul with the wicked,” who are very unlike me, because “in their hands,” that is, in their works, “are iniquities”; “their right hand,” that is, their good works, if they perform any justice, “is full of gifts.” Here judges are especially understood, those who accept money in order to administer justice.

[Col. 0279D] “In their hands” are iniquities; “but I have entered” upon the good “in my innocence,” as above. And you, O Lord, “redeem me” through the blood of your Son. And because, once redeemed, he is not able to suffice through his own innocence, he asks for God’s mercy, saying: “and have mercy on me.”

For I am rightly suited to receive your mercy, because “my foot,” that is, my affliction, “stood,” that is, remained firmly, “in an upright place,” that is, in a high place; or “in an upright place,” that is, in Christ. Another translation has “on the straight road”; for Christ says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Or, “in an upright place,” that is, in the Catholic order. “And I shall bless you, O Lord, in the churches,” namely, dwelling in the company of the faithful.

## PSALM XXVI. TITLE

A psalm of David, toward the end, before he was anointed.

“The Lord is my illumination.” David received a first anointing in designation of the kingdom, and a second anointing in the kingdom. But before he came to the kingdom, he suffered many evils and had many enemies. So also Christ received a first anointing from the womb of the Virgin and a second in the resurrection; between the two came evils and enemies. Likewise, the faithful soul receives its first anointing in baptism, but before the second—which will be in the resurrection—it endures evil and does good.

“A psalm of David, toward the end, before he was anointed,” that is, before he was anointed for the kingdom. David composed this psalm before he received the second anointing. Before the first anointing he composed no psalm at all. Samuel anointed him first in his father’s house (2 Samuel 2; 5). Through that anointing he understood the promise of the kingdom and became certain that it could not in any way happen that he would fail to obtain both the kingdom and the second anointing, just as he had understood them to have been promised in the first anointing.

When he composed this psalm, however, he was not speaking of a bodily anointing or of the attainment of an earthly kingdom, but of spiritual anointing and a heavenly kingdom. For he considered that the children of the Church could have certainty concerning the second anointing—that is, freedom from suffering and immortality—through the first anointing which they receive in this life, namely, the remission of sins and strengthening for good works in baptism.

Just as David received his first anointing in his father’s house, so each of the faithful receives his first anointing in the house of his father, that is, of the devil. He is called “father” because through him all are born in sins. The devil’s house is called this world, into which Christ came, and in it he took some people from the devil’s power. Hence in the Gospel: “Jesus came into the house of Simon the leper” (Matthew 26; Mark 14), that is, into the house of the devil.

The subject is the first and second anointing. Of the first he treats as follows: he establishes its certainty concerning the second. Of the second he treats as follows: he sets forth frequent petitions for it and affirms that he will possess it. His purpose is to make us certain that, once we have received the first anointing, we can possess the second.

The title is explained as follows: this psalm belongs to David, the prophet, or to any just person from the earlier people. That just person, or David, speaks in this psalm. It is a psalm, I say, composed before he was anointed with the second anointing—a psalm, I say, directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. And it begins from the first anointing in this way, admonishing us in this way toward certainty concerning the second.

Be confident and certain concerning the second anointing, considering me, because “the Lord is my illumination,” that is, the one illuminating me so that I may wish to approach the faith—and this occurs before baptism—“and also my salvation,” that is, the remission of sins which takes place in baptism, and strengthening for good works, which takes place in confirmation. And what does this mean? “Whom” thereafter “shall I fear?” No one, certainly, because neither Saul, that is, the devil, nor any enemy will be able to prevent me from obtaining the kingdom for which I shall hope.

The Lord grants salvation, and the Lord himself “is the protector,” that is, the defender, so that I do not feel the devil’s arrows. He is the protector “of my life,” that is, of my salvation, or of the virtues in which the faithful soul lives. Therefore, “from whom shall I tremble?”

For while “the Lord is the protector” and I shall not fear, this is because those who wish to harm me fall. And this is what follows: “When those who do harm draw near to me,” approaching more and more by tempting me, thinking that they are acting “against me,” they draw near, I say, for this purpose: “to eat my flesh,” that is, to take pleasure in my tribulation, just as those who eat flesh take pleasure in consuming it.

“They grew weak and fell,” that is, the devil grows weak when he is unable to overcome someone by tempting him; he falls when the just person has been so strengthened that the devil does not even dare to attack him. This applies especially to “my enemies who afflict me.”

Or it may be understood in this way: “When they draw near against me” for the purpose of doing harm, as they think, in truth they draw near “to eat my flesh,” that is, to consume my carnal tendencies. And those enemies who afflict me by eating in this way “grew weak and fell.”

And because those who afflict me fall, therefore, “if camps,” that is, if the efforts of a multitude, “encamp,” that is, remain, “against me,” plotting against me, “my heart will not fear,” since I am like a fortified camp. For even if the flesh fears somewhat, nevertheless the heart, that is, the inner soul, will not fear.

And also “if battle,” that is, open assault, “rises up,” that is, increases, so that human frailty appears unable to endure it, directing itself “against me in this” battle, “I shall hope,” that is, this will be a cause of hope for me. Or, “in this,” that is, in the Lord, “I shall hope” for victory in that battle.

“The Lord” is “my salvation.” Those who afflict me will fall, and through them “I have asked one thing from the Lord.” “One” is fixed here, and “this one thing I shall seek all the days of my life”: namely, “that I may dwell,” tending toward the life to come, “in the house of the Lord.”

Or as follows: “I shall seek this, that I may dwell” in this life in the mind “in the house of the Lord,” and not for a short time, but “all the days of my life.”

I shall dwell in the house for this purpose: “that I may see the will of the Lord,” that is, what God wills me to do, “and visit his temple,” that is, frequently bring Christ’s humanity to mind, so that I may be conformed to him. Or, “I shall visit the temple,” that is, I shall reach Christ through good works.

I say that I shall visit it, and truly I am secure on this account, “because” he has already done this for me: “he hid me” so that my enemies would not attack me “in his tabernacle,” that is, in the humanity of his Son, whose member he made me, “on the day of evils,” that is, in this life, in which the wicked exercise their power. Thus “David was hidden in caves when Saul was pursuing him” (1 Samuel 24).

And he not only hid me, but also “protected me,” so that I would not feel the wounds inflicted by my attackers, “in the hidden place of his tabernacle,” that is, in the divinity which lies concealed and hidden in Christ’s humanity. “In the hidden place he protected me,” that is, in faith. Hence: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Romans 10).

And he not only protected and hid me, but also “exalted” me by giving virtues, “on a rock,” that is, in Christ, who is the foundation of all righteousness. “On a rock he exalted me,” that is, in the confession of the mouth. Hence: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (ibid.). Similarly, David placed fortifications on rocks and mountains.

The exaltation which he promised would be on a rock was still future for that just person, because Christ had not yet come; but he already possessed the exaltation which follows.

“He hid me in his tabernacle, he exalted me on a rock, and even then he exalted my head,” that is, my mind, “above my enemies,” so that I no longer fear being prevented by them from obtaining the kingdom.

After showing through the first anointing that he is secure concerning eternal life, he now sets forth a certain exultation. Continuation:

“He exalted my head above my enemies,” and therefore “I went around” everything, so that praise—therefore it is called a sacrifice offered, because just as an offered sacrifice was pleasing to God when it had its proper form, so this praise is pleasing to God—“a sacrifice,” I say, “of shouting,” that is, of great devotion. Another translation has “of jubilation.” A *jubilus* is spoken of when we conceive such great joy in the mind that the human voice is not sufficient to express it.

Hence preachers of the Church have also been accustomed, after praising God intelligibly, to burst into jubilation, that is, into a nonverbal sound, through a multiplicity of notes, thereby showing that no intelligible voice can suffice for the praise of God.

I have offered the sacrifice, and thereafter I shall praise; and this is what he says: “I shall sing,” namely, with voice and heart, which pertains to contemplatives, “and I shall sing a psalm to the Lord” by doing good, which pertains to active people.

Or, if one reads “I shall go around,” as the authors more frequently do, we shall say: “The Lord exalted my head,” and therefore “I shall go around and offer sacrifice,” namely, I shall sing “and sing a psalm.” I shall go around, I say, “in his tabernacle,” that is, in Christ.

After treating of the first anointing, he shows that he is secure concerning the future one; through the first he passes to the second and asks for it in frequent prayer. Continuation:

“I shall go around and offer sacrifice,” I shall sing and chant a psalm; therefore, “O Lord, hear the voice,” that is, my petition. And he gives the reason why that petition is worthy of being heard: it is accompanied by a cry, that is, by great affection of heart. This is what follows: “because I cried to you,” seeking to attain you alone.

And I do not merely say that you should hear my voice, but also that you should consider my very person: regard me as wretched and hear me through mercy. This is what he says: “have mercy on me,” that is, be moved by mercy toward me, and through that mercy “hear me.”

He says “hear me” twice, and gives two reasons: “because I cried” and “have mercy.” The cry is the cause of merit in a human being; mercy, which is in God, is the cause in God that the human being is heard.

I say, “hear me,” and you ought rightly to hear me, because “my heart,” that is, the intention of my heart, “said to you”—and by “the saying of the heart” he indicates great intention. “My face,” that is, my beauty, by which I am distinguished from others, “sought,” that is, sought beyond all other things. In other words, after setting aside all other earthly things, I strove to contemplate you alone and to know your presence.

The face of the just person is that virtue by which he appears distinguished from all others, as patience was in Job, humility in David, and likewise in others. “I have sought and shall seek, O Lord, your face,” that is, knowledge of you through good works.

And therefore, “do not turn your face,” that is, your knowledge, “away from me,” so that I may at some time possess that knowledge—which knowledge is possessed only in the life to come. “Do not turn aside from your servant,” that is, do not permit your servant to fall into sin. And if at some time you permit him to fall, do not do this “in your anger.”

He turns aside from his servant in anger when he permits him to reach the precipice of sin by withdrawing grace. He expresses this by comparison: just as a master turns away from a servant in anger when he does not wish to lodge with him.

Do not turn aside, but rather “be my helper” in doing good. And because he might help at the beginning and then withdraw, he therefore adds: “do not abandon me,” but continually extend your hand. And because he saw himself to be lowly and contemptible—a condition which might seem to be a reason why God would abandon him—he asks God not to regard that cause in him, saying: “nor despise me,” that is, do not regard me as worthless to you, both because “you are God” and because you are “Savior.” Whatever I may be, “you are my God,” that is, my Creator, “and my Savior,” that is, my Redeemer; for through the humanity of your Son you must save me.

And therefore you ought not to despise me, because it is not my fault that I am such: “for my father,” that is, Adam, “and my mother,” that is, Eve, abandoned me in dangers like a child exposed. “But the Lord took me up,” that is, he united my humanity to himself. By this it is especially shown that the human being is now not to be despised.

“The Lord took me up”; and you, “O Lord, establish a law for me,” that is, some correction for me—I say, while I am “in your way,” that is, in faith and in good works, by which one reaches you. “And direct me in your path,” that is, in your stricter commandments. And do this on account of my enemies, that is, the heretics who wish to pervert the meaning of the Scriptures.

I say that I ask this on account of my enemies, yet I do not ask that you refrain from handing me over into their hands, but “do not hand me over to their souls,” that is, to the wills of those who afflict me, so that they may not devour me as they wish.

Nor ought you to hand me over, because they are wicked, and they rise up and lie. This is what follows: “The wicked witnesses rose up,” that is, they raised themselves “against me,” that is, against me, “unjust witnesses,” that is, witnesses testifying to injustice. They confirmed what others had falsely said, declaring that there would be no other life besides this one, and similar things. “And iniquity lied,” that is, the wicked themselves lied “to themselves,” that is, to their own harm.

[Col. 0284A] They say: Who has seen this kingdom? Who came afterward? But whatever they may say, “I nevertheless believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord,” which “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2), “in the land of the living,” that is, in heaven, where the saints dwell and live the true life. Heaven is called “land” because of its stability, since it will then be stable.

Since you see me certain that I shall see the good things of the Lord, therefore every faithful person should “wait for the Lord” with long-suffering; and in waiting, “act manfully,” that is, persist in the virtues. And if your hands grow weary, nevertheless “let your heart be strengthened,” and thus “wait for the Lord.” That is, although you may be afflicted, nevertheless await the Lord with patience.

## PSALM XXVII. TITLE

A psalm of David himself.

“To you, O Lord, I cried.” The Word of God speaks to human beings about God, for it is itself the manifestation of God. Hence: “No one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11). And just as the whole of human nature, insofar as it possesses knowledge of God, possesses it through the Word, so does Christ’s human nature. And if the Word becomes silent for any human being, as it did for Adam, he descends into the pit. When the human nature united to the Word of God does not rely upon itself, still less do the rest.

This psalm belongs to that David. This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, who speaks here. What it says, “to this one,” may be understood either as distinction or as excellence, as though it said: “To this one”—not to a carnal king, but to the spiritual King of kings, that is, to Christ—“in excellence,” because certain words in this psalm can be applied to no one else but Christ alone, such as: “My flesh flourished again.”

The subject is Christ himself. It treats of him as asking both for himself and against his enemies, and also as giving thanks for the obtaining of his petition. This is the second part of the psalm. In the third part it shows that the things accomplished in Christ, such as the passion and resurrection and similar events, also benefited his own people for their exaltation.

Its purpose is to persuade us that we should not trust in a human being but in God alone, since it shows Christ, the most perfect just person, trusting in no one except God alone. At the end, where it shows that the people saved through Christ possess salvation only in God alone, it plainly indicates that all salvation comes from God and not from a human being. And just as in certain preceding psalms it briefly touches upon the passion and resurrection, so also here.

And thus it begins by inviting others to petition, so that they may trust and cry to the Lord, as though it said: Cry out and trust in the Lord, following my example, because I have cried and “I shall cry to you, O Lord,” Father, who alone can hear me. It uses the future tense in order thereby to indicate that he cries continually to God throughout the whole time of his obedience.

And you, “my God, do not be silent,” so that you do not fail to answer my cry, that is, to hear me. For if you were silent, then you would be far away “from me.” When he says “I shall cry” and adds “do not be silent,” he indicates the loving relationship between God and the human being, because as soon as a human being begins to cry, God hears.

The Hebrew truth does not have “do not at some time be silent from me”; the Septuagint interpreters added it. Yet they did not do so without reason, but thereby give us to understand that he cried concerning the first and second glorification.

The first glorification occurred before the resurrection, when he was free from every sin and through him God performed miracles which no one else could perform. The second glorification occurred in the resurrection, because his humanity then received freedom from suffering and immortality.

When he says “do not be silent,” we understand him to be crying concerning the second glorification. And because he could fail to be silent concerning that second glorification and nevertheless not hear him concerning the first, he adds: “and also do not be silent,” so that you do not fail to hear me concerning the first glorification—that is, so that you do not permit me to remain unheard even for a single hour.

[Col. 0285B] And if you are silent and far from me, then “I shall become like those who descend into the pit,” that is, into the misery of this world. It is called a pit because, just as a pit whose bottom is unknown is called a *lacus*, so this world is called a pit, since we do not see the depth of its miseries.

For if that man, the Lord’s man, were abandoned by the protection of the divine Word united to him, he would certainly be found like other human beings. Or, “into the pit,” that is, into corruption. For the Lord’s flesh would be corrupted in the tomb unless the divinity raised it.

He rightly says “those who descend,” because the greatest descent is to turn away from God and incline oneself toward the miseries of this world. The ascent, however, is to abandon these miseries and hasten toward eternal goods.

I say, “do not be silent,” O Lord, but rather “hear the voice of my supplication,” concerning the removal of evils. And he adds the reason why the one who prays to him ought to be heard: he lifts his hands toward him. This is what follows: “while,” that is, because, “I pray to you and lift up my hands,” and this lifting of Christ’s hands took place on the cross, “toward your holy temple,” that is, toward the Church to be established. For the establishment of the Church proceeded from Christ’s passion.

Or, “hands,” that is, “my works,” I lift up for the establishment of the Church. Or, “toward your holy temple,” that is, toward yourself, to the place where I know that you dwell. Here he refers us to the custom of those who pray, who raise their hands toward heaven, where they especially believe that God dwells.

The Jews also did this: wherever on earth they might go, they prayed facing the temple which was in Jerusalem, in which they believed that God dwelt spiritually.

[Col. 0285D] “Hear the voice of my supplication,” namely: “Do not hand me over with sinners,” that is, with Abraham and the other just predecessors of Christ. He calls them sinners because original sin had never been completely erased in them except through Christ’s blood.

I say, do not hand me over so that I am “held together” with them in darkness as they were. For Christ was with them when he freed them from the underworld. He was not with them in the same way, because he did not suffer the darkness which they endured.

“And do not destroy,” that is, do not condemn me, with the wicked. This is what he says: “with those who practice,” namely, the Jews, “iniquity.”

Or alternatively: I have heard the supplication, and I do not ask that you refrain from handing me over to death, but that you not consent to their desire. This is what follows: Hand me over indeed with sinners, but do not hand me over in such a way that you are similar to them, that is, with the same intention as theirs; do not hand me over with an evil desire as they hand me over with an evil desire.

And do not permit my soul to be held in the underworld with those who practice iniquity, that is, as one having the same intention as those who plot my destruction.

Those who practice iniquity “speak peace,” that is, peaceful words. Here the particular wickedness of the Jews is indicated: peace, I say, “with their neighbor,” namely, with me. Christ is called the Jews’ neighbor according to the flesh, because he came from their offspring, and also because he came to show them mercy.

This corresponds to what is read in the Gospel concerning the Samaritan, who is called the neighbor of the man who fell among robbers “because he showed him mercy” (Luke 10). And although they spoke peacefully when they said, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Matthew 22), and similar things, nevertheless “evil was in their hearts,” that is, in their wills.

They practice iniquity, but you, O Lord, “give them according to their works,” that is, according to their wicked life, “and according to the wickedness of their inventions,” that is, according to their devices. He calls them “inventions” because, although no evil was known about him, they nevertheless called him a sinner and said that he had a demon (John 8; 9).

And not only give them according to their shameful life, [Col. 0286C] but also “according to the works of their hands,” that is, according to that more outstanding iniquity which they committed in the Lord’s death. By adding “of their hands” after “works,” he shows that they devoted great effort and affection to that deed.

The expression “work of their hands” is taken from a craftsman, who wants those things to be called the works of his hands which he has made with care. “Give them”—and because by the preceding words he had not determined the character of the retribution, whether good should be returned for evil or evil for good, he now determines that he asks for evil to be repaid to them when he says: “their retribution,” that is, just as they repaid me evil, “repay them” in the same way.

He rightly calls it “retribution”: although Christ had done good things for them, they repaid him with evil.

[Col. 0286D] Therefore I say, repay them, “for they did not understand the hidden works of the Lord,” namely, that he was the Son of God for the restoration of the human race. And lest they wish to excuse themselves by saying that they could not recognize those hidden things, he shows them to be without excuse by saying that they had considered Christ’s manifest works, in which they could have recognized those hidden realities.

This is what follows: “and they did not understand in the works of his hands,” that is, in his power. By saying “in the works,” he indicates that they did not understand those hidden things in the manifest works. For if they had considered that he was free from every sin, they would have recognized through the miracles he performed that he was not merely a human being, but the Son of God and the Redeemer of the world.

The Hebrew has: “They did not consider the works of his hands.” This failure to understand was the reason why they devised evils against Christ, and therefore they were condemned, as follows: “and because they did not understand, you will destroy them,” spiritually and bodily, as occurred in the destruction brought about by Titus and Vespasian.

And the prophet, foreseeing that this destruction would be irreparable, says: “and you will not build them up” any longer, as God rebuilt them after the destructions of Babylon, the captivity in Egypt, and other destructions. Or, even if they had been spiritually destroyed—for example, if they had become idolaters under one leader—God freed them from idolatry through another leader.

From this final spiritual blindness, however, they will not be restored until the end, when their remnant will be saved. Bodily, they will never be restored.

They will be destroyed, but “blessed be the Lord.” And he gives the reason why he blesses the Lord, saying: “for he has heard the voice of my supplication,” namely, concerning the removal of miseries. From this verse he begins to give thanks for the obtaining of his petition.

He not only heard concerning the removal of evils, but also “the Lord is my helper” in doing good “and my protector,” so that I may not be wounded by the arrows of my persecutors. “And my heart,” that is, my intention, “hoped in him,” namely, concerning the resurrection. And because I hoped, therefore I was helped.

And he shows in what way he was helped, saying: “And my flesh flourished again.” Christ’s flesh flourished before, when it was free from every sin; it flourished again when it received freedom from suffering and immortality in the resurrection.

Or as follows: “Human flesh flourished” in Adam, who was established in complete perfection; it withered through Adam’s disobedience; it flourished again when it received freedom from suffering in Christ’s resurrection. And therefore “I shall confess to you,” that is, I shall praise him willingly, namely, in his members. Here he begins the third part, namely, that the things accomplished in Christ were useful to his own people for their exaltation.

And that “Lord” who caused me to flourish again is “the strength of his people,” that is, of those devoted to him. God’s strength consists in rescuing human beings from the yoke of the devil and making them his own. And he himself is “the protector of the salvations of his anointed,” that is, of those who have been saved through Christ. Here he clearly indicates that Christ’s mysteries benefit everyone for salvation.

And because the Lord is the strength of his people, therefore, “O Lord, do” what is yours to do, namely, “save your people,” by rescuing them from the power of their enemies and directing them toward faith. And bless them by giving an increase of virtues to that people which has been made yours: “and rule them,” so that they do not fail in virtue; “and exalt them,” leading them “unto eternity,” that is, into everlastingness.

## PSALM XXVIII. TITLE

A psalm of David at the completion of the tabernacle.

“Offer to the Lord.” After the ark of the Lord had been returned by the Philistines and brought back to Jerusalem, Nathan prohibited David from building the house of the Lord because he was a man of blood (2 Samuel 7). Nathan, speaking prophetically by the Spirit, had foretold that David would build a temple for the Lord.

David therefore made a tabernacle of tents in which to place the ark of the Lord. Once it had been completed, he invited many people to come to that temple not with empty hands, but to bring sacrifices there and offer them to the Lord.

After this completion he wrote this psalm—not because he was writing about the historical completion, but because through the Holy Spirit he was prophesying the future completion of the Church, of which the completion of that tabernacle was a figure. The prophet Ezra, knowing that David understood this, gave the psalm this title.

The title is read as follows: this psalm belongs to the prophet who speaks here; it is a psalm, I say, composed at the completion of the tabernacle, that is, in contemplation of the completion of the Church.

This psalm contains the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which the whole Church is brought to completion. These gifts are not called gifts of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit gives them rather than the Father and the Son, since the whole Trinity acts together. Rather, the name “Holy Spirit” was imposed in order to signify the love and kindness of God; because all good things are given to us from this kindness of God, they are attributed especially to the Holy Spirit.

The present Church is called a tabernacle because in it we wage war for the Lord, just as warfare is conducted in tents. The subject of this psalm is the Holy Spirit, or the Church brought to completion by the Holy Spirit. He develops this subject as follows: he invites human beings to honor the Holy Spirit, and this is his purpose.

For he foresaw that certain errors concerning the Holy Spirit would arise in the Church, namely, that the Spirit would be thought inferior to the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as in many other psalms he arms us against various errors, so also in this one, showing that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son, including by showing that he cooperates with the Father and the Son.

In the second part he gives the reasons why we ought to honor the Holy Spirit, namely, because the Spirit himself gives the gifts through which the whole Church is brought to completion. In the third part, which comes at the end, he shows that the Holy Spirit cooperates with the Father and the Son. He begins with this exhortation as follows.

[Col. 0288D] “You sons of God,” who until now were sons of the devil and have now through the Holy Spirit become sons of God; therefore you ought to honor him: “bring” here “to the Lord,” that is, to the Holy Spirit. Here we understand “Lord” specifically as the Holy Spirit because in what follows he will say, “The voice of the Lord is over the waters,” which properly applies to the Holy Spirit. He does not specify what they should bring, but we ought to understand that they should bring themselves through a pure conscience and a pure life. And I do not merely urge you to bring the sons of God; if necessary, also bring yourselves “as sons of rams to the Lord,” that is, as imitators of the apostles, offering the Church of God, if necessary, protection or leadership. The apostles are signified by rams: for just as a ram gives strong leadership to the flock and defends it with its horns, so the apostles both give leadership to the Church and defend it with horns, that is, with the Old and New Testaments.

“Bring” also, sons, “to the Lord,” that is, to the Holy Spirit, “glory,” that is, learn and understand that he is glorious—namely, omnipotent and equal to God the Father—“and also honor,” that is, serve him yourselves and invite others to serve him; “and bring glory to his name,” that is, spread his name and his honor through many nations. For his name would not be glorious if it were confined among a few nations. Thus, by bringing glory to his name, you will bring glory to the Lord himself; and also “adore,” that is, venerate “the Lord,” that is, the Spirit, “in his holy court,” that is, in your heart. It is called a court because of its breadth and because it ought not to be constricted by any tribulations. Another translation has “in his holy hall”; in that case, likewise, we understand the faithful heart as a hall, since just as a royal hall is a dwelling, so the hearts of the faithful are Christ’s hall, in which he dwells as a king in his hall.

Here he begins to describe the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. By saying “the voice of the Lord” seven times, he sets forth for us the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. He enumerates these different gifts in the same order as Isaiah does (chapter 11): first he sets forth the gift of wisdom, then understanding, afterward counsel, then fortitude, next knowledge, then piety, and finally fear of the Lord. [Col. 0289C] Continuation: You ought rightly to honor this Lord, because “the voice,” that is, the inspiration, of this “Lord,” namely, the Holy Spirit, is “over the waters,” that is, over the peoples; according to John, the many waters are the many peoples. He says “over” properly, because divine breathing rules over a person and makes that person act according to itself. We understand “voice” as inspiration because just as a voice teaches a person and reveals someone’s will, so divine inspiration reveals God’s will. Here he determines whose voice it is and what kind of voice it is when he says: “The God of majesty.” He shows him to be great and powerful when he says, “he thundered,” showing that the voice is terrifying. That voice is terrifying because it threatens the punishment of judgment. God wishes to nurture his own in terror, so that at least in this way they may serve according to his will. And that Lord not only thundered “over the waters,” that is, over the Jews, but also “over many waters,” that is, over the Gentiles, who were far more numerous than the Jews. In this verse we recognize the spirit of wisdom, because divine inspiration teaches us the knowledge of God.

“The voice of the Lord,” that is, of the Holy Spirit, is also “in power,” that is, it confers power on us—namely, understanding of the Law and of the other Scriptures, by which the objections of heretics are broken and which no one can resist. Hence we read concerning blessed Stephen: “No one could withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6). Here we recognize the spirit of understanding. “The voice” of that “Lord” [Col. 0290A] is also “in magnificence,” that is, making people magnificent; he gives us discernment concerning what ought and ought not to be done. Whoever does good and avoids evil is magnificent. Here the Spirit of counsel is signified.

“The voice” of that “Lord,” that is, of the Holy Spirit—of the “Lord,” I say, “who breaks,” that is, humbles, “the cedars,” that is, the proud. We understand the proud by the cedar because the cedar is a tall tree, raised above other trees. And that “Lord will break,” that is, humble, “the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, the great ones who are raised up in worldly pride, such as kings and princes. For “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whiteness”; therefore by Lebanon he understands those who place greater confidence in the whiteness of riches. Thus by the cedars of Lebanon we understand the more powerful who are raised up, because those cedars that grow [Col. 0290B] on Mount Lebanon are taller than all the others.

Or “the one who breaks the cedars” means the proud among the Gentiles; or “cedars,” that is, the Jews, whom we understand by the cedars of Lebanon because Lebanon is in their land. “He will break” is properly stated in the future tense, because this too is still to occur in the last times, when the remnant of the children of Israel will be saved.

“And he will also shatter them,” that is, through that breaking he will reduce them to such great humility. Here he refers to the signification; or “them,” the cedars, “like the calf of Lebanon,” that is, so that they may be pleasing to God like a calf of Lebanon offered in sacrifice. For it was the custom of the Jews to fatten the calves they were going to sacrifice to the Lord in the richest pastures of Lebanon [Col. 0290C]; and the more they fattened them, the more acceptable they believed them to be to God. Here the spirit of fortitude is signified. For God’s strength is great when a person can break his own pride and, by his own shattering, offer himself as a pleasing sacrifice.

When the preceding things appear good—namely, that the voice of the Lord is in power and in magnificence—lest this matter, namely, the breaking of the cedars, should appear evil, he also shows that the only-begotten Son of God was shattered, so that others should not grieve under such a law of shattering. He will shatter the cedars, and you ought not to be amazed, because “the beloved one,” that is, God’s only Son, “will also be shattered.” Here the prophet shows according to which nature this occurs, namely, according to the human. “He will be shattered,” I say, “like every son of unicorns,” that is, of the Jews, who are called unicorns because they take pride in one Testament alone.

“The voice” of that “Lord” is the voice of the Lord “who cuts apart,” that is, distinguishes, “the flame of fire.” By fire we understand those who burn with the love of evil desire; by flame, the fury of the evil deeds that they exercise against the holy. Divine inspiration cuts this apart when the righteous person upon whom that flame is inflicted distinguishes that it is not for his harm but judges that it turns out for his good. Here the spirit of knowledge is signified. For great knowledge of God is given to a person when he recognizes as good for himself the things that appear evil to others.

[Col. 0291A] “The voice” of that “Lord” is also the voice of the Lord “shaking the wilderness,” that is, people empty of the worship of God, and first making the barren fruitful, just as someone makes land that was previously deserted fruitful by breaking it up and cultivating it. “And” by shaking people who were previously deserted, “the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh,” that is, he will fill what was represented by the miracle performed in the wilderness of Kadesh. Kadesh is the wilderness where Mount Sinai is located. In that wilderness the Lord, through Moses, brought water out of the rock (Exod. 17), and the water followed the children of Israel through the wilderness. The fact that God made that previously dry land watered was a sign that he would make people who had previously been dry and barren watered and fruitful.

Or “the one who shakes the wilderness” means the Gentiles, who were previously deserted from the worship of God; and that Lord “will shake” in the future “the wilderness of Kadesh,” that is, the Jews, who were deserted from the holiness of the Law. For Kadesh is interpreted as “holy of the Law.” This shaking will occur when the remnant of the children of Israel is saved. The Jews have been removed from this holiness of the Law, that is, from its spiritual understanding, because they do not follow the spiritual understanding alone. Here the spirit of piety is signified.

“The voice” of that “Lord” is also the voice of the Lord “preparing stags.” That Lord, through his inspiration, prepares stags, that is, certain people to become like stags—fearful with a good fear and drinking in the poisons of this world, yet in such a way that what they drink does not harm them. For they endure persecutions and the objections of heretics, yet are not injured by them. It is the nature of stags to be fearful and to drink in poisons that nevertheless do them no harm. Here the spirit of fear is signified. This inspiration of fear “will reveal the dense thickets,” that is, the hidden things of Scripture. For just as a stag, through fear, runs through dense thorny thickets, so the grace of God opens the hidden things of Scripture to those who fear God.

And because through these gifts he perfects the Church, therefore “everyone will say glory to him,” that is, everyone will proclaim him glorious—“everyone,” I say, who dwells “in his temple,” that is, in the holy Church, which is perfected through these gifts. Here the third part is signified, namely, the cooperation of the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit.

Continuation: The Holy Spirit confers all these gifts; that same “Lord also causes the flood to dwell” there, that is, he makes his faithful dwell in baptism. The righteous live in baptism, where the crimes of the world die. This was signified in the flood, in which Noah dwelt securely because of his righteousness while the guilty perished (Gen. 7). The Holy Spirit cleanses them through the flood of baptism. “And the Lord,” namely, the Son, “will sit as king”; the Lord judges in them. He will sit in them not merely until the end of the world, but “forever.”

And to that “people of his,” thus purified by the Holy Spirit and governed by the Son, “the Lord,” the Father, will give “strength,” that is, an increase of good things, as well as all the good things mentioned above that are said to be given especially by the Holy Spirit. In this matter [Col. 0292A] the cooperation of the Father and the Holy Spirit is recognized. And that “Lord” mentioned three times, that is, the whole Trinity, will “bless his people,” established “in peace,” that is, in eternity, “giving an increase of glory.”

## ON PSALM XXIX. TITLE: A psalm of song at the dedication of the house of David.

“I will exalt you, O Lord.” This psalm is a song, that is, an expression of rejoicing, at the dedication of the house of David, that is, in consideration of the dedication—namely, the confirmation—of the house of David, that is, of the body. That body was the house of Christ according to his divinity; or it was the house of the prophet David because he was from the seed of David. The construction of this house took place in the conception, and its dedication in the resurrection. For just as a house becomes celebrated at its dedication, so Christ became more celebrated in the resurrection, having assumed impassibility and immortality.

Christ is the subject matter, which he arranges as follows. In the first part of the psalm there is thanksgiving for deliverance; in it he also urges the saints to give thanks to the Lord for that same deliverance, which is the deliverance of those who have been freed through it. In the second part the merit is shown for which it was fitting that they should be delivered. In the third part, near the end, he plainly sets forth the resurrection. His intention is to urge people to praise God for his substance, which is also theirs; this is signified where it says, “Sing to the Lord, his saints,” and so forth. He begins with thanksgiving for his deliverance as follows.

The voice of Christ: “O Lord God, I will exalt you,” that is, I will enlarge your name among many nations. Lest it seem strange that one who is humble should exalt so lofty a one, he shows that he can and ought to do this, saying: I can and ought to do so because “you received me,” by uniting your Word to my humanity. Also because you “did not delight,” that is, did not cause “my enemies” to delight, so that they might be “over me,” as though they were above me in my Passion; nevertheless, that joy was turned into sadness.

And therefore I will also “exalt you” because you “healed me,” even in those who are mine, making me impassible and immortal in them, freeing them from sins and making them righteous. He gives the preceding reason why he is worthy of salvation when he says: “O Lord my God, I cried out to you.”

[Col. 0292D] And therefore “I will exalt you,” because you, “O Lord, brought my soul out of hell,” and thus “saved me from those descending into the pit.” He was saved from the Jews when, having been made immortal and impassible, they could inflict no evil upon him.

And therefore, because the Lord delivered me in this way, you have become his saints through my deliverance. “Sing” by doing good to this “Lord,” “and confess” with mouth and heart to the “memory,” that is, to this Lord, because he remembers you. “To the memory,” I say, not proceeding from our merit, but “from his holiness,” that is, from his holiness alone. Or “to the memory of holiness,” that is, to him by whom he sanctifies others—“his” holiness, I say, which proceeds from him.

[Col. 0293A] And rightly we ought to confess, “because wrath is in his indignation,” that is, when he turns away from someone, there is punishment for the one from whom he turns; “and in his will,” that is, in his good pleasure, there is “life,” which begins in this life through righteousness and leads to eternal life. Here he intimates that we ought to confess to the Lord not only because he gives good things, but also because he removes the evils in which we were held justly.

He said that wrath is in indignation and life in the will. Now he shows through whom there is wrath, namely, through Adam, and for whom—namely, for those who imitate him; and through whom there is life, namely, through Christ, and for whom—namely, for those who imitate Christ.

Continuation: Life is in the will, but not for everyone, because for those who look “toward evening,” that is, who imitate Adam’s fall, there will be weeping. The truth of the matter is that Adam broke obedience in the evening, when the sun was declining, that is, after midday. For while Adam was at midday, that is, in the fervor of love, he kept obedience manfully. But after charity had cooled in him, and he was after midday—that is, after charity—he departed from obedience. Those who imitate him are said to be those in whom charity does not burn. For those who look toward evening, “weeping will remain,” that is, weeping will persist. But for those who look “toward morning,” that is, toward Christ’s resurrection, which took place in the morning—for his imitators—there will be “joy.”

Here he shows both the cause and the merit of his deliverance, and shows that he is opposed to Adam. For when Adam was established in perfection and abundance, [Col. 0293C] he paid no attention, indeed he withdrew. But he shows that when Christ was established in abundance, no tribulation could remove him from obedience.

Continuation: For those who look toward evening there will be weeping. “But I” am not one of them, being “in my abundance,” that is, in the perfection of knowledge and of all virtues. I “said,” that is, I resolved: “I will not be moved from that abundance” “forever.” He demonstrates this in the actual carrying out of the matter.

He said that he would preserve that abundance; now he shows that he does not possess it from himself, but from God alone. This is: “O Lord, you established strength for my beauty,” that is, for that abundance of mine—you gave me constancy; and this was not from my merit, but [Col. 0293D] from your will alone.

“You established strength,” yet at some time “you turned your face from me,” that is, you permitted me to suffer tribulation. Then “I,” as a human being, “became troubled.” Here he shows Christ’s great merit: even when tested in this way, he did not cease from obedience.

I am troubled, but in that very trouble “O Lord, I will cry out to you” for the attainment of good things, “and I will pray to you, my God,” for the removal of evils.

“I will cry out to you,” saying: “While,” that is, “if I descend into corruption,” that is, if I am reduced to dust, “what benefit will there then be in my blood?” That is, what benefit will my shed blood bring either to me or to others? [Col. 0294A] If the blood of a righteous person is shed, it ought to bring benefit; if the blood of a wicked person, no benefit should be sought.

If I am reduced to dust, no benefit will follow, because neither confession nor proclamation of the truth will then occur—things for which Christ’s resurrection was necessary. Continuation: I say that if I descend into hell, there will be no benefit, because “will dust,” that is, flesh reduced to dust, “confess to you?” That is, will it be a cause of confession, that is, of your praise? “Or will that dust proclaim your truth?” That is, will it be the cause that your cause is proclaimed concerning the restoration of the human race, which you are going to accomplish through me? Certainly not. Therefore I do not want you to permit me to be reduced to dust; raise me up quickly.

I will cry out, and the Lord will hear me, because of the merit of my cry and also because of his mercy. This is: “He had mercy on me,” and that same “Lord became my helper,” namely, he “turned my mourning” into joy. But out of familiarity he turned himself toward him when he says, “You have turned.” The pain of death was turned into joy through the glory of the resurrection. “You have turned,” I say, “for me,” that is, for my benefit and that of those who are mine; “you have cut apart my sackcloth,” that is, my flesh.

He calls Christ’s flesh “sackcloth” because just as sackcloth is penitential clothing, so Christ’s flesh is penitential clothing—not because it bore his own sins, but those of others. Hence it is said: “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. 53; 1 Pet. 2). The confession itself took place in the Passion. And afterward, in the resurrection itself, “you surrounded me with joy,” that is, with impassibility and immortality. From this verse he plainly begins to speak about the resurrection.

“You surrounded me so that my glory itself,” that is, my resurrection, “might sing to you,” that is, show that you are worthy of praise. For Christ’s resurrection brings it about that God is praised throughout the whole world. And this will not be for an hour, but henceforth “I will not be pierced,” that is, I will suffer no punishment of death. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him.” And just as that glory will be eternal, so the confession that proceeds from it will be eternal. Thus: “I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you not only in this life but also “forever,” both in me and in those who are mine.

## ON PSALM XXX. TITLE: To the end, a psalm of David.

“In you, O Lord.” This psalm applies to Christ, who speaks here not only for himself but also for his martyrs, directing them “to the end,” that is, toward Christ. Here the intention is signified, as in the other psalms. This psalm has as its subject two opposites: the help of divine mercy and the misery of human frailty. We divide the psalm into three parts. In the first, considering God’s mercy, he asks that he and his people be delivered through divine mercy, lest they fail amid miseries. In the second, he enumerates the miseries that he and his people suffer. In the third, he sets forth the joy of their deliverance and thanksgiving, and also invites others to love God. He intends to admonish people neither to despair when considering their miseries nor to foolishly grow proud by presuming upon God’s mercy. Thus he plainly directs us “to the end,” that is, toward Christ.

And admonishing others, he says: Do not presume upon yourselves, but hope in the Lord, just as I have never presumed upon myself, but “have always hoped in you, O Lord,” my God. And because I hoped, “I shall not be put to shame forever.” He does not deny that he suffers the exultation of his enemies, but that exultation will not be eternal. “I shall not be put to shame forever”; rather, O Lord, “deliver me” and those who are mine, lest I be broken by the miseries of this world—and do this “in your righteousness,” because your righteousness demands that you deliver those who hope in you.

And because my voice could not rise to you, you, O Lord, “incline your ear,” that is, your power, “toward me,” that is, toward helping me. “Incline,” that is, humble yourself, to snatch me from these miseries. This inclination is understood to have occurred in the fact that the Word of God was united to human nature, and it endures forever.

“Incline,” I say, and “hasten,” that is, quickly accomplish everything you are going to do for me—namely, give through me, according to my humanity, the perfect form of life. In my death, quickly redeem souls from hell; do not postpone the resurrection until the general resurrection. “Hasten,” I say, “so that you may rescue me,” so that the persecutors may no longer be able to harm me or prevail against those who are mine.

[Col. 0295C] And meanwhile, that is, while that hastening is taking place, “be for me a protecting God,” that is, be as strong a protector for me as you, the good God, can be, so that I may not be wounded by the weapons of my enemies. And be for me “a house of refuge,” that is, a place of security in which I may rest when my labors are finished. And because the labors might end for a time and begin again, he adds, “so that you may save me,” that is, be such a refuge for me that I may not again be roused to any labor.

Therefore I ask you to be my protector and refuge, “because” you alone are “my strength,” by which I and those who are mine may resist those who oppose us; and also “you are my refuge,” that is, the security in which both I and those who are mine may rest. God was Christ’s refuge in the resurrection; he is a refuge for Christ’s members when he makes them secure through the sacraments of the Church, namely, through Christ’s body, through prayers, and so forth. And you will be not only my protector and refuge, but also “you will lead me and nourish me.” Christ was led in his own person when his name was extended to all nations through the preaching of the apostles; those who are his are led through the spread of his fame, just as Peter was spread throughout the whole world. Christ was nourished in his own person; those who are his are nourished when they are brought from virtue to virtue. And this is “for the sake of spreading your name.”

I rightly say, “you will lead me” into knowledge, because you “will lead me out of the snare,” that is, out of death, which is called a snare. For through death they thought they would hinder [Col. 0296A] his name; it was a snare “which they secretly prepared for me,” whom no secret escapes (Heb. 4). God likewise rescues those who are his from the snares of the devil. Therefore I know that you will lead me out, “because you are my protector,” and no one who has such a protector can be ensnared.

And because you “are my protector,” therefore “I commend my spirit,” that is, my soul, “into your hands,” that is, into your power. He says “I commend” as one speaking to someone with whom he is familiar and in whom he confidently trusted to return what had been entrusted. And you, “O Lord, God of truth, have redeemed me.” The soul of Christ and the souls of others were redeemed through his perfect obedience.

And therefore, because you are the God of truth, “you hate those who observe vanities,” that is, those who desire worldly things. Truly these worldly things are vanities because they are “superfluous.” Things that bring no benefit are empty; they are superfluous because they also bring harm.

You have hated them, “but I have hoped in the Lord,” and therefore “I will exult” in body and “rejoice” in spirit “in your mercy,” not only because I hoped. By saying that he exults because he hoped, he indicates the truthfulness of God. For God would not be the God of truth unless he rewarded one who hopes in him according to God’s justice.

I rightly say that I will exult: “because you have regarded my humility,” that is, you have had mercy on my frailty, on those who are mine, and on my affliction, lest I be overcome by my persecutors. “You have also saved my soul from distresses,” that is, from sins, from which Christ’s soul was immune, and the souls of those who are his from mortal sins; or, if those who are his have had mortal sins, these did not harm them. He calls sins “distresses” because they are unavoidable for human beings and because they carry death.

And because you have saved me, therefore “you have not shut me into the hands of the enemy,” that is, into the power of the devil. He would have been shut into the enemy’s hands if he could in no way have escaped from its power. Rather, “you have set,” that is, firmly placed, “my feet,” that is, my affections, “in a spacious place,” so that I may walk without any offense, just as someone walks freely wherever he wishes in an open space. Or by the spacious place let us understand charity, in which Christ walked broadly, as did those who are his, and in which they walked with their neighbor.

[Col. 0296D] Here the second part begins, concerning the enumeration of the miseries of human frailty. After saying that through God’s mercy he was in a spacious place, yet fearing because of his frailty, he asks for mercy by enumerating his miseries, saying: “O Lord, have mercy on me,” and there is need, “because I am troubled.” He intensifies the tribulation itself: the tribulation is such that because of it “my eye,” that is, my understanding, “has been troubled in wrath,” that is, in the punishment inflicted by them; “and my soul,” that is, my animal life; “and my belly,” that is, my memory. It is called the belly because just as food is stored in the belly, so hidden and secret things are stored in the memory.

“It has been troubled,” although he was certain of the promise that had said: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12). We must not understand Christ’s life or memory as troubled in such a way that it failed in any respect. Rather, he wished to be troubled voluntarily, so that he might leave an example for others, lest, if they became troubled, they should despair.

Behold, he unfolds the aspects of the tribulation mentioned above. Truly I am troubled, “because my life,” lived up to this point, “will fail in sorrow,” in death. And because that life might have been lived in sorrow for one or two days, which would not seem great, he adds: “and my years,” that is, my life lived for many years, “in groaning,” will fail in death.

This can be said of certain members of Christ because their life was in sorrow for many years, as with Paul and others like him; of certain others, because their life failed in sorrow within a short time, as with Hippolytus and others like him.

Life failed in sorrow, and also “my strength,” that is, my soul, “has grown weak in poverty” and in consideration of my smallness, because I have nothing from myself. “And my bones,” that is, the strength of my body, are such that although anyone may think that I possess some strength, I consider that I have no strength from myself. When Christ says that he is weak both in body and in soul, he shows that all pride has been removed from him and that no one ought to presume upon himself.

He sets forth still other miseries, saying: “I have also become a reproach” greater “than my enemies,” although they themselves deserved such reproach; “and I have become greatly a terror to my neighbors,” that is, a cause of fear, because when they saw him handed over to death, they were afraid. He calls them neighbors who, although they were not the Lord’s disciples, nevertheless approached in order to hear him. “And to those who knew me,” that is, to my disciples themselves, “I became a terror.”

Or it may be read this way: “I have become a very great reproach to my neighbors over my enemies,” that is, my neighbors held me in greater reproach than my enemies did, “and I became a terror to those who knew me.” Another translation has “among my enemies,” namely, that my enemies held me in reproach.

Another misery: “Even those who saw me,” that is, those who knew me to be God, “fled from me outside,” that is, they recognized only my external features, judging me to be merely human. Hence, after his resurrection, two disciples said to him: “We had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke 24).

Or it may be read this way: “Those who saw me” treated in this manner “fled from me outside,” as above. And also “I was forgotten from their heart,” “like any dead man.” That translation confirms this interpretation which has, “I was cut off from the heart.” Or “like a dead man from the heart,” that is, like any sinner whose heart, that is, whose reason, does not live. This interpretation runs smoothly throughout.

Another misery: “I have also become like a ruined vessel,” because just as a broken vessel cannot retain liquid, so neither could I retain my apostles. For this reason they considered me worthless. “Because I heard,” that is, patiently endured, “the reproach of those dwelling round about,” that is, in my exterior, because they did not know me to be God.

Or “of those dwelling round about,” that is, in the desire for worldly things, which are always all around, because in them there is neither head nor end. Or “round about,” that is, in some error.

“In that place,” while they “came together” into an assembly “against me all at once,” that is, unanimously, “they took counsel to seize my soul,” that is, to remove it. Or, “in that place they took counsel to remove my soul.” This is another translation:

They took counsel. “But I hoped in you, O Lord,” because I knew that all these things occurred by your arrangement. And I “said” to you, with the deliberation of my heart: “My lots,” that is, my fortunes or outcomes, “are in your hands,” that is, in your power. We understand “lots” as outcomes because they occur solely through God’s arrangement, without human planning.

And therefore “deliver me from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of my enemies,” those who hate me, “and from those who persecute me,” that is, from those who inflict evils upon me.

Deliver me, and “make your face shine” upon me, “your servant,” and upon those who are mine. He says this by comparison. For just as when a lord shows his servant his bright face, others hold that servant in greater honor, so Christ was held in greater honor when the Lord showed him his face by raising him from the dead. “Make your face shine,” namely, “save me.” And do this not because of my merit, but “in your mercy, O Lord,” so that “I may not be put to shame.” And when he joins merit to mercy as the reason why he should save him, he adds: “because I called upon you.”

I shall not be put to shame, but “let the wicked be ashamed,” that is, let them appear shameful and be led, ashamed of their sins, “into hell” materially. And let “deceitful lips,” that is, those who are now talkative and deceitful, “become mute” after they have been led into hell.

Those “lips speak iniquity against me, the righteous one, in pride”; they grow proud against me, the righteous one, “and in abuse,” because they abused his teaching by neglecting it. Another translation has: “in pride and contempt.”

[Col. 0298D] The third part begins, in which the joy of deliverance, thanksgiving, and an invitation to love God are set forth.

Continuation: Have mercy on human frailty, which is so great, but your mercy, O Lord, stands against all things. Lord, “how great is the mercy of your sweetness,” that is, of your benefits, which are sweet to those who taste them; this “sweetness” you have “hidden” from those who desire worldly things, reserving it “for those who fear you,” that is, for those who fear you for the sake of your work.

And you have “perfected,” that is, will perfect, that sweetness “in those who hope in you.” This will be made manifest, namely, “in the sight of the children of men,” that is, of the carnal. For at the general resurrection the wicked will see the glory of the faithful, namely, Christ ascending with those who are his; and then the wicked man will be removed, lest he see the glory of God.

Or, “you will perfect it for those who hope in you,” so that, if necessary, they may confess you “in the sight of sons,” that is, of worldly rulers.

God begins to give this sweetness to the faithful in this life and perfects it in the other. He unfolds both aspects, placing the better one first according to its dignity.

Continuation: You will perfect that sweetness for the saints, namely, “you will hide them,” that is, you will place them in such a way that no one will be able to trouble them. You will hide them, I say, “in the hidden place of your face,” namely, among the angels, where your face—that is, your knowledge—is hidden from human beings now living in the flesh. Through this you remove them “from the disturbance of men.”

[Col. 0299B] And lest anyone should say, “Who can wait for so long?” he sets forth present consolation.

Continuation: After the resurrection you will hide them in your presence, and meanwhile “you will protect them in your tabernacle,” that is, in the present Church, in which we carry on God’s warfare, “from the disturbance of tongues,” namely, lest the tongues of heretics, contradicting the truth, be able to incorporate them into themselves.

And because the Lord does so many good things, therefore “blessed” is he, that is, exalted above all nations, “because he has made his mercy wonderful,” that is, shown his mercy to be wonderful, “by bestowing these aforesaid gifts in a fortified city,” that is, in his saints, who are called a city because they are many, and fortified because they have been strengthened by many virtues.

Or otherwise, according to Jerome: “Blessed is God, because he has made his mercy wonderful to me in a fortified city,” that is, in Jerusalem, where he performed these wonders—namely, caused Christ to be born, suffer, rise again, and all the other things that God accomplished through him in that same city. These wonders of God performed there were the cause of all the benefits that God bestowed upon the Church.

Jerome does not have “fortified,” but includes a phrase by which the city is understood to have been situated in the middle regions of the world: “in the middle of the city.” Christ chose to dwell and die there so that he might present himself as the midpoint for all.

God thus made his mercy wonderful, and yet I experienced miseries. This is: “I,” placed “in an excess of my mind,” that is, in anguish of mind, “said,” either in my heart or with my voice, “I have been cast away from your face,” that is, I have been regarded in such a way that I seem to have been cast away “from the face of your eyes,” that is, from the presence of your mercy.

An “excess” is said to occur either when a person is carried away into contemplation of divine things, as Paul says, so that we transcend ourselves in God, or when someone exceeds the limits of his senses through sadness, that is, when he no longer remains himself.

And because I thus showed myself humble, “therefore you heard the voice of my supplication,” and he supplies a certain merit for being heard when he says: “when I cried out to you,” that is, because I cried out.

And because the Lord grants these benefits to the faithful and hears those who cry out, therefore you, “all you saints, love” him, “the Lord”; for although he now permits [Col. 0300A] truth to be trampled, nevertheless he will “seek out truth among his own and repay” with punishment “those who act proudly,” and this not sparingly, but “abundantly.”

Here he gives the conclusion of the entire psalm. Continuation: Since he himself will seek out truth, therefore “act manfully; and if there is weakness or weariness in the body, let your heart be strengthened. Act manfully,” I say, “all you who hope in the Lord.”

## PSALM XXXI. TITLE: A Psalm of Understanding by David

“Blessed are those whose.” This psalm explains to us the understanding of David as a true penitent. Its subject is the penitent prophet David, or anyone who is truly penitent in understanding. It treats him in this way: although previously he had failed to recognize [Col. 0300B] his sins, he now acknowledges them. It also presents his confession, and then commends that confession. In the fourth part it presents Christ promising greater benefits of this kind to the penitent. Its purpose is to admonish us toward an understanding of such confession.

This penitent speaker already shows in the first part that he recognizes his sins when he says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities,” that is, the natural suggestions of the flesh, “have been remitted,” that is, weakened in baptism, so that although they urge one to sin, they do not bring one to the act. Or, “iniquities,” that is, sins committed before baptism, “have been remitted,” that is, utterly destroyed in baptism; and blessed are those “whose sins,” committed after baptism, [Col. 0300C] “have been covered” through penance. By saying “covered,” he indicates that the reference is to grave sins, which need to be covered lest they appear in the Lord’s sight for punishment.

That man also “is blessed to whom the Lord will not impute sin,” that is, who, although he committed a sin, did not commit one of such a kind that the Lord would regard it for punishment. This indicates a sin that can be removed by prayer alone. And although he committed only minor sins, he nevertheless imputes them to himself; this is indicated where he says: “Nor is there deceit in his spirit.” There would be deceit in his spirit, that is, in his will, if he said that he was without sin, since he knows that no one lives without sin. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth [Col. 0300D] is not in us” (1 John 1). By saying that those to whom this threefold remission is granted are blessed, he shows that he now recognizes his sins.

Now I recognize my sins in this way, but previously I concealed that I had sins; and “because I was silent, my bones grew old,” that is, my strength approached ruin in the manner of an old garment. He rightly says “grew old,” and not “were destroyed,” because they could be rebuilt. I concealed that I had sin “when I cried out” through those very works that I had sin “all day,” that is, continually. Or, “when I cried out,” namely, my own righteousness.

He shows that evils befell him because he was silent. Continuation: Previously I was silent, but now “I have turned,” that is, I am “in my misery,” [Col. 0301A] that is, I recognize myself as miserable, that is, as a sinner. And he places the cause of his conversion first when he says: “The thorn is fastened,” through suggestion, consent, and habit. “For your hand,” that is, your vengeance, “has been heavy,” that is, has become heavier, “upon me,” and “this by day and by night,” that is, continually. He says “has been made heavy” by comparison with a teacher who presses heavily upon a pupil in order to make him acknowledge his offense. “I have turned,” I say, “while the thorn is fastened,” that is, because pride is destroyed; and pride is understood through the thorn because in the thorn there is the human tendency to stand erect. I rightly say “in my misery,” “while,” that is, because, “the thorn is fastened,” that is, the piercing of sin.

Here he begins to confess. I say, “I have turned,” and then “I made known to you,” that is, I confessed, [Col. 0301B] “my offense,” that is, that I sinned by doing nothing, “and my iniquity,” that is, that I did what was forbidden, “I did not conceal,” but made it manifest to you. This does not mean that these things were ever unknown to God; rather, a person is said to make sins known to God when he recognizes himself as deserving condemnation and seeks the physician.

Here he shows what benefit comes from recognizing sin. I made my offense known to you, and from this I also “said,” that is, resolved, namely, within myself: “I will confess my iniquity to the Lord,” that is, my evil works, which is to act against myself, since previously I was accustomed to defend my sins. “You remitted” not only my sins, but also my evil works, namely, “the impiety,” that is, the “excuse for my sin.” Although God forgives sins as soon as a person repents in his will, one must nevertheless confess to the ministers of the Church, because, unless they confessed, they would be condemned through their disobedience. This was shown in Lazarus, who, after being raised, still needed to be unbound.

He commends confession when he says that the saints pray for the remission of impiety, and that this remission is obtained through confession. The remission of impiety is good, and “for this” remission “every saint will pray at an opportune time,” that is, in this life, in which prayer has power to obtain such things.

Here is another commendation of confession. The good will pray, “yet” those dwelling “in the flood of many waters,” that is, in the submersion of many sins, “will not approach” him through any confession.

[Col. 0301D] And rightly should the saints pray to you, because “you are my refuge,” that is, you make me secure “from the tribulation” of past sins “which surrounded me”; and you, Lord, “deliver me from those surrounding me,” that is, from demons and present sins. You, I say, are “my exultation,” that is, the one in whom I rejoice, secure in the knowledge that you will soon deliver me. Here he gives the fourth part, namely, the remission that Christ grants to those who confess. Continuation: I rightly say that you are my refuge, because you yourself say: “I will give you understanding,” by which you may confess your sins, “and I will instruct you in the way in which you will walk,” that is, in good works by which you proceed toward God. From now on I give you weapons with which you can fight, namely, virtues. And because, once instructed in this way, you cannot persevere without God’s protection, he says: “I will fix my eyes upon you,” that is, I will guard you through mercy.

And because I will give understanding, “do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.” They would be like a horse if they did not consider whom they were carrying, whether God or the enemy. They would be like a mule if they did not consider their burdens, whether they were carrying sins or good works. Or, by the horse let us understand the Gentile people, who, untamed and unbridled, did not care about the law; and by the mule, the Jewish people, who were hard and sluggish in fulfilling the law.

I say, do not become such; but, O Lord God, if they do become such, “break their jaws with a halter,” that is, through lesser deprivation of food and clothing, “and with a bridle,” [Col. 0302B] that is, through greater deprivation of food. A halter is a binding by which tame animals are tied; a bridle, by which untamed animals are restrained. I say “their jaws,” of those “who do not approach you” through confession.

Correct them through the halter and the bridle; and besides these there are “many scourges of the sinner,” that is, many things by which sinners ought to be corrected. “But mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord,” because mercy will fail them in nothing. These words are Christ’s to the Father, from which he said, “Break.”

Mercy will surround those who hope; therefore you, righteous people who hope in the Lord, “rejoice” in mind, “and exult” in body, “and glory,” already secure concerning glory, “all you who are upright in heart.”

## PSALM XXXII. TITLE: A Psalm of David for the End

“Rejoice, you righteous.” This psalm suits the prophet David, who speaks here as well and composes a song in praise of God, which mitigates the devil’s temptations, just as David’s song calmed Saul’s spirit. Its subject is the praise of God. It treats this as follows: it admonishes us to praise God by setting forth the reasons why we ought to praise him. In the second part it shows that those who have praised God are blessed. Its purpose is to admonish us to praise God; this is marked in the first part, from which it begins joyfully in this way.

You ungodly people ought not to rejoice in the Lord, but you, “righteous, rejoice in the Lord,” and not in worldly things. I rightly say, “Righteous, rejoice,” because “praise befits the upright,” namely, so that they may praise [Col. 0302D] God.
