Hence it is said: “God said to the sinner, Why do you recount my righteousness?” (Psalm XLIX). And again: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of the sinner” (Ecclesiasticus XV). Or, if the reading is “let them praise together,” the unanimity of those praising is understood through it.

Here he sets out the parts of the praise that he urges us to offer, saying: Since praise befits the upright, therefore you upright people “confess to the Lord on the cithara,” that is, praise him in your body and in lower possessions, namely, through almsgiving. We understand this through the cithara because the cithara is an instrument that produces sound from its lower part, and we too should resound from lower things, that is, from worldly possessions, to God’s praise by ordering them well. And not only from the lower part, [Col. 0303A] but “sing psalms to him,” that is, act well, “on the psaltery,” that is, in the spirit. The psaltery is “of ten strings,” that is, in the spirit fulfilling the ten commandments of the law. By the psaltery we understand the higher praise that exists in the spirit, because the psaltery emits its sound from its upper part. Here we note the contemplative life; where he says, “Confess on the cithara,” we note the active life.

And not only on the cithara and psaltery, but “sing to him a new song,” that is, praise him for the sending of his Son into the world. This praise concerning the Incarnation is called a new song because it had not previously been known to us. And “sing psalms to him with a shout,” that is, praise him with such intense devotion that human voices cannot express it. And because many people praise God in such compunction yet afterward fall into sins, he adds: “well,” that is, sing psalms in such a way that you do not wish to cease singing ever again.

Here he begins to give the reasons why he admonishes us to praise God in this way. Continuation: “Therefore you ought to praise God because the word,” that is, the commandment, “of the Lord is upright.” For he commanded nothing except what is right, “and all his works are in faith,” that is, right and faithful. Or, “are in faith,” that is, they can be received through faith, because no one receives remission or confession without first having faith. Or, “in faith,” because whatever God does, he does it to confirm or advance faith.

He must also be praised because “he loves mercy and judgment.” He does not say this because he himself does not love them, but because he acts especially according to them. He acts according to mercy when he forgives sins; according to judgment when he gives both good and evil people what corresponds to the quality of their merits. It is as though one asked: How do we know that he loves mercy? He gives the reason: “The mercy of the Lord fills the earth,” that is, all the people on earth.

He shows how the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, because “the heavens,” that is, the apostles, “were established by the word of God,” that is, instructed in doctrine and by the example of the Word of God, that is, the Son; “and all their power,” that is, all the miracles they performed, or their strength against adversities, was established “by the breath of his mouth,” that is, of the Son, through whom the Father speaks. I say “of his,” of the Father, and here we note the whole Trinity.

He must also be praised because he is the one “gathering the waters of the sea,” that is, worldly people who fluctuate like seawater, placing them in the Church “as in a wineskin.” For just as the waters in a wineskin are compressed so that they cannot escape, so the righteous, placed in the Church, are restrained by the instruction of the divine Scriptures, so that they cannot go out except by the permission of the one who placed them there. Through the wineskin, which is made from the hide of a dead animal, we understand the Church, which puts carnal desires to death.

He is also the one “placing the abysses,” that is, those who are profound in understanding, “in his treasuries,” that is, he gave them a share in his treasuries by granting them knowledge of his wisdom and understanding, as he did to blessed Paul, who knew him with profound understanding. Or it may be understood in this way: “Placing the abysses,” that is, those who are most deeply darkened, “in his treasuries,” that is, so that they may be part of his treasuries, in order that through them he may reward those who fight lawfully. For just as wisdom given to the saints is God’s gift, so also the wicked are God’s gift when they are given together with the saints for the sake of a greater crown. Thus Decius was given to blessed Lawrence for the sake of a greater crown.

And therefore, since “the whole earth” is such, even if it cannot praise him, let it at least “fear the Lord.” But if it does not have from itself the capacity to fear, let “all who inhabit the world” be “moved by him,” the Lord, through inspiration, so that they fear him.

And he will rightly be able to move them, because he himself created all things; and this is: “For he spoke,” that is, he willed, “and they were made,” all things, namely, formless matter, [Col. 0304B] and it was reduced to a formed state. And “he himself first commanded,” that is, willed, “and they were created,” that is, they came from nonbeing into being; namely, formless matter was made. Or thus: “He spoke and they were made,” all things; “he himself also commanded” through the angels, and all things “were created,” that is, arranged and made in due order. Thus, through the angel sent to Moses, the law was ordered and made.

The Lord made all things, and he “scatters,” that is, destroys, “the counsels of the nations,” namely, concerning the worship of idols, when he converts all things to himself. “But he rejects the thoughts of the peoples,” that is, of the Jews, who are called peoples because of the law in which they ought to have lived. These thoughts concerned retaining the law and the place, and also the belief that they could retain the Lord in the tomb. And he rejects not only the counsels of those lesser people, [Col. 0304C] but “also rejects the plans of princes,” that is, of demons, kings, leaders, and priests.

Their counsel is scattered; “but the counsel of the Lord,” concerning the restoration of the human race, which God concealed from many, “remains forever,” that is, it is unchangeable. “And his thoughts,” that is, his arrangements, which are called the thoughts “of his heart” because they were made rationally, “will endure from generation to generation,” and again into another generation. God’s arrangements are everything that exists throughout all time.

Here the second part begins. Continuation: Since the Lord himself is such, “blessed” is that “nation whose Lord is” the Lord, that is, the nation that made the one who is “its” Lord its own, whether it wished to or not. He is “its God,” that is, it voluntarily established as its Lord the one who is its Lord by power.

He begins to enumerate the blessings. I rightly say that this nation is blessed because it is the people chosen as God’s inheritance; and this is: “the people whom he chose as an inheritance for himself.” That inheritance is blessed because the Lord cultivates it through the doctrine and understanding of divine fountains. He chose it, I say, not so that he would give it to another to possess, but for himself.

That nation is blessed again because “the Lord looked upon” it, that is, he had mercy on it, “from heaven,” that is, through the humanity of his Son. For God’s mercy was great in making his Word become incarnate for our redemption. In “he looked upon” we understand that humanity had been far removed from God because of sin; and [Col. 0305A] after he made the Word become incarnate, he “saw,” that is, he now revealed himself as though out of obligation, giving strength “to the sons of men,” that is, to rational beings.

From heaven “he looked from his dwelling place,” that is, from the humanity of his Son, in which he himself dwelled. This dwelling place was “prepared,” that is, ordered through great and wise deliberation in accordance with the Lord. He looked “upon all who inhabit the earth.”

He again enumerates the blessings. Continuation: He looked upon them because he “formed their hearts,” that is, their understandings, in this way: “individually,” that is, he did not give everyone the same understanding, but gave each person an understanding of his own. “He also understands all their works,” namely, with what understanding they do whatever they do. And this is the greatest blessing. For when he understands our weaknesses, he grants us his consolations.

God does not do only the things mentioned above, but also helps kings and giants. Such aid is truly necessary from God, because without him “a king is not saved,” that is, one who governs his earthly realm well, “by his great strength,” even if God had given him many powers. And “a giant,” that is, one who is strong in fighting against God’s enemies and swift in running along the appointed way, “will not be saved by the abundance of his strength,” that is, through his strength, however great it may be, unless God helps him.

“Even a horse,” that is, human prosperity, which lifts up a person as a horse lifts its rider, “is deceptive for salvation,” which it appears to promise. And I do not say that this prosperity is merely somewhat deceptive; rather, however great it may be, it is deceptive. This is what follows: “But in the abundance of its strength,” that is, in the abundant strength of riches, in other words, in the multitude of riches, “no human being will be saved.”

The things mentioned above cannot save, but “behold,” that is, salvation is manifest: “the eyes,” that is, the mercy, “of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy.” God looks with the eye of mercy upon both those who fear him and those who hope in him.

Those who hope do so for this purpose: “that he may deliver” them “from death,” eternal death, “and feed them” in righteousness, “in famine,” namely, in this life, in which we hunger for righteousness. Or this is connected with the statement, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” namely, for this purpose: “that he may deliver their souls from death.”

And since the Lord is such, namely, since he does good to those who approach him, therefore “our soul,” namely, that of the prophet and those like him, “waits for the Lord,” because the Lord himself is “our helper” in doing good “and our protector” against the darts of our adversaries.

I rightly say that it waits, “because” it waits with joy; and this is: “in him our heart will rejoice,” that is, now rejoices and will persevere in rejoicing. And I rightly say that it will rejoice, because “we have already hoped in his holy name.”

And “just as we have hoped in you, O Lord,” [Col. 0306A] so “let your mercy be upon us.” To hope in the name of the Lord is to have hope of eternal life because one calls upon his name.

## PSALM XXXIII. TITLE: A Psalm of David, When He Changed His Countenance before Abimelech, Who Dismissed Him, and He Departed

“I will bless the Lord.” It is read in the historical account that David fled Saul’s persecution and came to King Achish. After he had served under him for some time, he was accused before the king out of envy. Fearing, therefore, that David would be condemned by them, he pretended to be insane, and for this reason Abimelech, or Achish, dismissed him. These are the names of one king, but Achish is the proper name. Thus David escaped and departed.

Abimelech, however, was the common name of the king of that land, while Achish was the proper name. [Col. 0306B] Therefore this title uses the name Abimelech because, in view of what is now being treated, it is more suitable on account of its interpretation.

After that change David composed this psalm. He did not intend the bodily change itself, but understood through it a spiritual change. The title is explained as follows: This psalm suits the prophet David and concerns the fact that he “changed his countenance,” that is, his will. For previously he had wished to remain occupied with carnal observances; afterward he understood that they were of no value and that one must trust in God alone. Although he sacrificed victims according to the law, he did not trust in them, but understood through them the sacrifice of the Church.

He changed, I say, “before Abimelech,” that is, before the Jews, who are called the kingdom of the father. The Jews were the kingdom of God the Father of all. Before the Jews he prophesied that the sacrifices of calves were of no value and that sacrifice should be offered to God alone, when he said: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Psalm XLIX). “And again: A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Psalm L). And again: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you opened ears,” and so forth (Psalm XXXIX).

And just as Abimelech regarded David as insane, so the Jews regarded him as insane when they realized that he did not trust in their rites. Then Abimelech, that is, the Jews, the kingdom of the Father, dismissed him, if not bodily, nevertheless in their will. And thus David departed, that is, he passed over to another rite, namely, the Christian one.

Christ can also speak in this psalm, and the explanation of the title will suit Christ just as it suits the historical David. The psalm suits David, that is, Christ, when he changed his countenance, that is, his will, showing the law at first and afterward showing that the law was of no value, but that only his body was to be received, when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI).

He changed, I say, before Abimelech, that is, before the Jews; and therefore the Jews dismissed him, that is, withdrew from him spiritually. The disciples too went back, and thus Christ departed from them, removed from their law.

The subject is Christ according to this new state. He treats it as follows: in the first part he praises this newness of sacrifice and admonishes his companions to praise the Lord with him. In the second part he admonishes the faithful to participate in the Lord’s body and to prepare themselves worthily for this. In the third part he admonishes the inexperienced to approach this newness. In the fourth part he gives the reasons why one should approach it in this way, namely, because God repays good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

He also urges everyone to approach this newness. Thus, whether Christ or the prophet speaks, he begins from the praise of God, saying:

Because formerly I blessed the Lord for temporal things, now I will “bless,” that is, praise, “the Lord,” not only when he prospers the Jews, as I used to do, but “at all times.” I will do this by adhering to good works; and just as I will praise him in works, so “his praise will always be in my mouth,” that is, I will praise [Col. 0307B] him with my voice. Or he speaks in this way: I who have always blessed the Lord will bless him at all times.

I rightly say that I will praise the Lord, because through this my soul will be praiseworthy. This is: “my soul will be praised,” that is, will appear praiseworthy, dwelling “in the Lord.” In this he shows that the Lord is very praiseworthy, since through the soul’s approach to him the soul is proved praiseworthy. And what I say, “let the meek hear,” that is, let the humble understand, “and let them rejoice” when they hear, namely, over this newness.

And since my soul is made praiseworthy through him, therefore you, my companions, “magnify the Lord with me,” that is, let us proclaim him glorious among many nations. And let us not only magnify the Lord himself, [Col. 0307C] but “let us exalt his name.” We exalt God when we proclaim him omnipotent; we exalt his name when we spread it through many places, striving “toward the same thing,” that is, toward unity, venerating the Lord with the same disposition and the same steadfastness.

So that the people invited to praise God might hasten to do so, he says what good things have come to him from it. “I sought the Lord,” that is, I sought him beyond all things, setting aside all temporal matters, “and he himself heard me,” that is, he made the knowledge of himself known to me, “and delivered me from all my tribulations,” that is, freed me from the tribulation of sins and demons.

After admonishing them to sing, he urges the people to approach with him for the communion of the new sacrifice itself. Continuation: Because he has done this for me, therefore you others, “approach him” by the step of the virtues, “and be enlightened” with a greater knowledge of God. For the more someone approaches God, the more abundantly God floods him with knowledge of himself. Or, “be enlightened” by sacred instruction. And after you have been enlightened, “your faces,” that is, your understandings, “will not be put to shame.” Those who do not understand are ashamed, like those who went back saying: “This saying is hard” (John VI).

I say, approach and be enlightened, and you will have the help of the angel of the Lord who guards you. This is: “The Lord sends an angel.” You can be certain of this from my example, because “this poor man,” namely, or any true poor man, “cried out, and the Lord heard him [Col. 0308A] and saved him from all his tribulations,” as was explained above.

And just as the Lord sent an angel to save me, so “he will send an angel,” a heavenly spirit; or an angel, that is, Christ, who is the angel of great counsel; or an angel, that is, any virtuous man, “around those who fear him.” That is, he protects those who fear him on every side, in every need; and he, whether the angel or the Lord who was sent, “will deliver them.”

Or, as is found in the more common reading, “he sends,” that is, he makes a sending for defense, “the angel of the Lord,” so that the sending of the angel may be a shield “around those who fear him.” This reading is confirmed by another translation, which has: “The angel of the Lord surrounds those who fear him in a circle.”

[Col. 0308B] I say, approach and be enlightened; and, having approached and been enlightened, “taste” the nourishment of the Lord’s body. For whoever, without approaching through virtues and without being enlightened, would taste it, would eat and drink judgment upon himself (1 Corinthians XI).

“Taste,” I say, “and see,” that is, understand, because the Lord himself is Christ, whom you have tasted; and the Lord himself “is sweet,” because he forgives sins, preserves people in virtue, and finally grants eternal life. And because he is such, “blessed is the man” who does not trust in the sacrifices of the law, but “who hopes in him.”

Because he had said that God is sweet, lest his sweetness produce weariness, he adds: Although he is sweet, nevertheless “fear” offending him, “the Lord,” “his saints,” that is, those sanctified by him. [Col. 0308C] I do not say this only of the lesser; however lofty your merit may be, “there is no want for those who fear him.” For how could those who possess God, who is all good, be in need? Although they endure temporal miseries, they nevertheless regard them not as deprivation but as their highest glory.

Those who fear God do not hunger, but “the rich,” that is, lovers of earthly things, “were in need” of the spiritual nourishment of the Lord’s body. Yet they did not neglect it; rather, by their nature they greatly desired it. This is what he says: “And they hungered; but those who seek,” not worldly things, but only “the Lord, will not be deprived of any good,” that is, they possess the Lord, who is every good without diminution, [Col. 0308D] because he will grant them everything necessary. Or thus: the rich were in need of virtues and hungered for the Lord’s nourishment.

Here the third part begins, in which he admonishes the inexperienced. Continuation: Since those who seek the Lord will not be deprived of any good, therefore you “children,” having abandoned impiety, “come” to the faith, receive this instruction, and “listen to me,” that is, understand my teaching, and I will “teach you the fear of the Lord,” that is, how you ought to fear the Lord.

Although they are outside the Church, he calls the inexperienced “children” with paternal affection, just as Abraham is read to have called the rich man, even while he was in hell, “son.”

I will teach the fear of the Lord, through which teaching you will have life. He states this through a question that everyone would answer affirmatively. For who is so foolish as either to say, “I do not want life,” or not to desire to see good days? This is: “What man is there who wants life,” and I do not mean a life spent in misery, but who is the one “who loves to see good days,” that is, eternal life, namely, a life spent in good days?

I say that I will teach the fear of the Lord, namely this: “Keep your tongue” from evil, that is, do not speak evil openly; and do not even speak evil with a good intention. This is: “and do not let your lips speak deceit.”

“Turn aside” also, that is, withdraw, “from evil” in action. And because these things are not sufficient, he adds: “and do good.” And because the flesh always resists the spirit and wants one not to do good, he says: “Seek peace,” restraining the flesh, that is, restrain it. And although you may never be able to find it, because it always resists, nevertheless always “pursue it,” that is, suppress it.

Here the fourth part begins. I say, do good, because “the eyes of the Lord” are “upon the righteous” through mercy; and if they ask for something, “his ears,” that is, his clemency and power, are ready to hear “their prayers.”

The Lord hears the righteous, but he condemns the wicked; and this is: “The face of the Lord,” that is, the expression of his face, namely, the Lord’s anger, is “against those who do evil, to destroy from the earth,” namely, the land of the living, not only them, but also “their memory.” [Col. 0309C] Their memory will then be destroyed when none of the saints is moved concerning them to any pious action. Hence Abraham said: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke XV).

The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous. And we can be secure about this because the Lord heard the earlier fathers; and this is: “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations.”

And just as he delivered them, so now he “is near,” that is, he is kind, to those “who are troubled in heart,” namely, through compunction for sins; and he himself “will save the humble in spirit,” that is, those who regard themselves as nothing and attribute everything to God alone.

I say that he will save them, but nevertheless “the tribulations of the righteous are many.” For it is characteristic of the righteous to be troubled, and “from all these the Lord will deliver them” when he leads them into his kingdom.

In the end the Lord will deliver them; meanwhile, he “guards all their bones,” that is, all their virtues and strengths, so that they suffer no loss of their virtues. This is: “Not one of them will be broken,” because the Lord will not allow them to fail.

These people will not be broken. “But the death of sinners is very evil,” and when it overtakes them, sinners incur eternal condemnation and a most shameful life. This is why “those who hate the righteous,” namely, the sinners themselves, “will offend,” that is, will sin. Here he gives the contrary of the righteous. Continuation: The death of sinners is very evil, “but he will redeem the souls of his servants,” that is, he will lead those redeemed through the blood of the Son into eternal life; and he will make their present life pure. This is: “All who hope in him will not offend.”

## PSALM XXXIV. TITLE: A Psalm of David for the End

“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me.” This psalm suits David, that is, Christ, directing us toward the end. Its purpose is to admonish us concerning the Passion. Its subject is the Passion and Resurrection. It treats them as follows: in the first part it presents a prayer. In the second it enumerates the Passion with the joy of the Resurrection. [Col. 0310B] In the third, it states what that Passion and Resurrection accomplish. Just as in the psalm “God, my God, look upon me” he enumerates the Passion, so he does here; but although he speaks about the same subject, he always says something different about that same subject.

In the prayer that he places first, he prays both for himself and for his enemies, both those who will be converted and those who will not be converted. By those who will not be converted we understand demons and hardened Jews, against whom he prays as follows: “Lord, judge,” that is, condemn, “those who harm me,” that is, demons or the Jews who will not be converted. And those “who fight against me,” though they do not overcome me, you “overcome,” that is, conquer.

They were overcome in Christ’s Resurrection, because they could not hold him in death, as they had supposed. And here he begins to pray for himself.

“Overcome,” I say; and so that you may overcome, “take up weapons and a shield,” that is, you who previously worked secretly, now work openly in me with weapons by which I may conquer my enemies, and with a shield by which you may defend me. These weapons and this shield are God’s will. And you who once seemed to sit, “rise up” openly “for my help,” that is, to cooperate with me.

Rise up, I say, to cooperate with me, and “draw out,” that is, make known to the world, “the sword,” that is, my soul, by which you conquered the devil, “and shut in the enemies, so that their name may not spread.” To do this will be “against those who persecute me.” They wish to confine my name and spread their own. [Col. 0310D] Let the request made in each detail be fulfilled; “say to my soul” in the very fulfillment of the matter: “I am your complete salvation.”

Here he begins to pray for the conversion of the enemies whom he had foreseen would be converted. Draw out the sword: “Let those who seek my soul be put to shame,” that is, let them be ashamed of their sins, and then “let them be reverent,” that is, let them fear and honor me.

And not only those who actively seek my soul, but also those “who think evil against me,” namely, those who consent to those who act, let them “be turned away” from their evil way, so that they are “backward,” that is, follow me; and thus, having turned away, “let them be put to shame,” that is, let them be ashamed of their past sins. The memory of those sins will be for them a safeguard of the virtues. [Col. 0311A]

And he shows by what means they can be turned backward, saying: “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind.” By the wind we understand the impulse of the Holy Spirit. He prays that, just as material wind lifts dust from the earth, so these people may be raised by the Holy Spirit from earthly things to the love of heavenly things. And if they themselves do not consent to the Spirit, let “the angel of the Lord,” whether evil or good, “constrain them,” that is, compel them toward conversion, whether through punishment, illness, or any other means. In this verse we note two kinds of correction: one voluntary, the other forced.

[Col. 0311B] “And let their way become,” that is, their evil works, which had previously seemed bright to them, let them appear as “darkness,” that is, dark, so that thereafter they may fear to walk along them as through darkness; and let the same way on which they previously thought they stood firmly become for them “slippery,” that is, a slippery path, so that they may understand that no one can stand firmly. If they do not wish to recognize this, let “the angel of the Lord” be “pursuing them” by whatever impulse. Here too two kinds of correction are noted.

And “because they hid from me the destruction of their trap,” that is, they secretly prepared traps for me, and that trap was the cause of destruction; they hid it, I say, “without cause,” that is, without any merit on my part, and because “they reproached my soul,” saying, “You have a demon,” and the like—and this “to no purpose.” It was empty, because what they said was untrue; it was also wholly to no purpose, because the Son of God was free from sin.

[Col. 0311C] And because they did this, let good things come to them in return for those evils. This is “let there come,” that is, let there be prepared, for “that” people “a trap,” that is, a teaching by which they may be ensnared, “which he does not know,” that is: just as they ignorantly prepared a trap for me, so let one be prepared for them without their knowing. And let the trap not merely be prepared; let that people also “fall” into the trap, that is, let the teaching itself be effective in them. I say that they should fall into the trap in such a way that “into the same thing,” that is, this trap, the trap may be like the one they prepared: just as they wanted to hold me completely by their trap, so may these people be held by this trap. If it is read “in the trap itself,” the meaning will be the same. I say, let the trap seize them, “and let the snare that he hid seize them,” that is, let the death which they secretly prepared for Christ seize them—that is, let it be the reason why they themselves [Col. 0311D] die in their sins.

Or it may be read with reference to evil as follows: Let these people be converted, but let the others “become like dust before the face of the wind,” that is, let them be moved at the first blow of temptations; and let “the angel of the Lord,” that is, the devil—who is called the Lord’s messenger because through him the Lord inflicts his anger on the wicked—be “constraining them” toward greater evils. “Let their way also become,” that is, let their manner of life become, “darkness,” so that, blinded by it, they may be deprived of knowledge of the truth; and let their way become “slippery,” that is, a slippery path, so that they may continually fall from one vice into another. For this reason let “the angel of the Lord pursue them,” that is, lead them from vice to vice until destruction. And “because they hid from me the destruction” [Col. 0312A] of their trap, and because “they reproached my soul without cause,” as explained above, let “a trap come upon that” people: let a hidden destruction be prepared for them, “which he does not know,” that is, which he himself does not know, just as was fulfilled in the hidden destruction brought about through Titus and Vespasian. And let it not merely be prepared; let it also become effective against them. This is what is meant by “let the people fall into that very trap,” as explained above. Or the reading may be “in the trap itself,” or “let him fall into the trap in it,” that is, by the very contrivance; and “let the snare that he hid seize him,” namely, let that force which they prepared for the Lord be the reason why they themselves are physically destroyed.

Here begins the second part. This is what will happen to them: “but my soul shall rejoice in the Lord.” [Col. 0312B] This rejoicing took place during the Passion, in hope of the Resurrection; and it “shall delight” in the Resurrection itself, “over its salvation,” that is, over its salvation, or over the divinity united to it.

And then “all my bones shall say,” in the reality itself—that is, all my powers shall say: “O Lord,” who are “delivering” by a certain violence “the helpless,” that is, the human race, “from the hand of those stronger than it,” namely, from the hand of the devils, who are stronger than the helpless human race; and also delivering “the needy and the poor,” that is, the human race, “from those who plunder it,” namely, from the ministers of the devils, who, at the devil’s command, plunder the human race by drawing it into various sins: “Who is like you?”

[Col. 0312C] The human race is called helpless because it was subject to suffering and death and was under the devil’s dominion. It is called needy because, just as someone is needy who seeks his food with labor, so the human race sought some knowledge of God; yet it was still poor, because it made only slight progress in that knowledge.

After introducing this rejoicing, he begins to recount the Passion. The continuation is: Although my soul rejoices in this way, human misery is nevertheless not removed. “Unjust witnesses rising up”—they are called unjust because one confirms another’s lie by his testimony—“were questioning me,” that is, they were bringing accusations against me through their questions, concerning things “which I did not know,” that is, deeds of which I was unaware.

They also repaid me evil for the good things “which I had done for them”—supply: in holy teaching—namely, for “the barrenness of my soul.” [Col. 0312D] My soul was barren in this respect: I could not incorporate them into myself. My food was their salvation and faith. Thus, speaking to the Samaritan woman, he said to the disciples who were asking him to eat: “I have food which you do not know” (John 4).

They repaid me evil, “but I” did not avenge myself upon them; instead, “I clothed myself,” that is, I covered my divinity, “with sackcloth,” that is, with penitential clothing. He calls his flesh penitential clothing because in it he endured punishment for the sins of the people. His divinity was covered when he did not display his own power. I was clothed, I say, with sackcloth “when they troubled me,” that is, although they troubled me, at a time when others ordinarily display their power.

[Col. 0313A] And I also “humbled my soul,” that is, afflicted my soul, “with fasting,” namely, because I could not be refreshed by their salvation—or with bodily fasting—and I also prayed for them. Because they did not receive my prayer, “my prayer shall return into my bosom,” that is, it shall be useful to me. This accords with what the Lord himself said in the Gospel to the apostles: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’; and if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him; but if not, it shall return to you” (Matthew 10), that is, if your prayer does not benefit them, it will at least benefit you.

[Col. 0313B] I humbled myself, and thus “I was pleasing to myself,” or to God the Father—namely, by having that people “as a neighbor and as a brother,” according to the flesh, because I loved him as much as if he were my own fleshly brother. And when he refused to heed me, “I humbled myself,” that is, I was afflicted on their behalf, “as” one who is “mourning and sorrowful”—mourning in body, sorrowful in soul.

Thus I humbled myself for them, “yet they rejoiced against me and gathered together,” namely, they came together in this intention, and “scourges were gathered against me,” that is, multiplied. Yet I “did not know” why they were doing this, since I had not deserved it.

[Col. 0313C] They were also “scattered” when they saw his miracles: some said that he was good, while others said, “No, but he misleads the crowds”; and during the Passion itself they were scattered when they saw the earthquakes. Yet although they were thus scattered, they were “never” “pierced with remorse.” In this their wickedness is especially aggravated. Instead, they tested me by bringing an adulterous woman before me (John 8), and also by saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 26). They “mocked me” whenever they recognized in me some weakness of human nature—not merely for an hour, but with “mockery,” that is, continually. And when they found nothing evil in me, “they gnashed” in the manner of beasts “with their teeth against me,” that is, with their bitter corrosions and slanders.

They act against me in this way, but when will you look upon them mercifully, so that you may free me from their power? Look, Lord, and “restore my soul,” returned to the body and removed “from their malignity,” that is, from the lower Jews who were acting wickedly; and restore “my only one,” that is, my very soul, which is one and undivided, because it has no part—or “my only one,” that is, my flesh, which alone is free from sin. “Restore” it: make it immortal and incapable of suffering, rescued “from lions,” that is, from the rulers of the Jews and others.

[Col. 0313D] The third part begins here. In it he shows what good comes from his Passion and Resurrection: namely, the praise of God, the conversion of the ungodly, and the rejoicing of the just. “Restore me”: if you do this, “I shall confess to you,” that is, praise you, “in a great assembly,” according to its number, because it is composed of many; yet it is not gathered from straw, but “in a weighty people,” that is, a people made steadfast by virtue, “I shall praise you.”

I shall praise you, but may those who oppose me by unjustly inflicting evils [Col. 0314A] “not rejoice over me,” that is, if they rejoice for a time, let them not rejoice to the end. Nor should those “who hate me without cause,” that is, without any fault on my part, rejoice—those who “wink with their eyes,” that is, provoke others by a gesture of the eyes to mock me.

Let them not rejoice excessively, nor ought they to do so, “because they spoke peacefully to me,” while, as they spoke peaceably, they “devised deceit” in their hearts. Their deceit was not aimed at taking away my external possessions, but was “in anger,” namely, directed toward my death. The anger is called “of the earth,” that is, on behalf of the earth and the preservation of their kingdom. For they feared losing their place and nation unless they killed Christ.

“And they widened their mouth against me” when they said, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 11), and “they said, ‘Good, good!’”—that is, “Well done, well done”—“our eyes have seen” the thing we desired.

[Col. 0314B] Thus they acted against me, but you, “Lord, have seen,” that is, you have known their wickedness and my innocence. Therefore “do not remain silent,” but pronounce judgment; and you, “Lord, do not depart from me.” Although he is certain that God does not depart from him, nevertheless, because he knows that he possesses nothing through his humanity, he prays in order to give others an example of prayer, since they ought to place no confidence at all in their own humanity.

[Col. 0314C] I say, do not depart; rather, “rise and attend to my judgment,” that is, consider what kind of judgment has been made against me—you who are “my God.” And because, if he looked only at the judgment, he would regard him as a thief, since he was condemned among thieves, he adds: “And attend to my case,” that is, consider the whole legal dispute—namely, that I always conducted myself innocently toward them—you who are “my God.”

Attend to my case and “judge me according to your justice,” that is, according to what your justice requires, “Lord my God.” And may they “not rejoice over me,” namely, may they not say in their hearts, “Good, good, our soul,” because we have kept him in death; nor let them say with their mouth, “We have devoured him,” that is, destroyed him. Here too he is not praying out of doubt concerning himself, but sets before us an example. Let them not say this; instead, let “those who rejoice in my evils all together be ashamed and stand in awe,” that is, fear and honor me.

[Col. 0314D] And not only those who consent to those inflicting evils upon me, but also “those who speak maliciously against me—let them be clothed with shame and reverence.”

Let these be ashamed, but let “those who desire justice,” namely, who desire to imitate it, “rejoice” in body and “be glad” in soul. And let those “who desire,” that is, love and seek, “the peace of his servant,” namely, the peace which I, who am his servant, established between God and humanity, “say always: ‘May the Lord be magnified’” for that peace given to humanity.

Let these magnify the Lord, “and my tongue shall meditate upon your justice,” that is, shall announce it with meditation; and not only your justice, but “all day long” it shall announce “your praise,” that is, that you are worthy of praise. Thus, concerning the creation of heaven, Christ himself announced the praise of God in his own person, and even today he is announced through those by whom he speaks. When he says that the tongue meditates—something proper to the heart—he attributes to the tongue, through the union of the members, what properly belongs to the heart.

[Col. 0315A]

## ON PSALM 35

### TITLE

“To the end. Of the servant of the Lord, David.”

“An unrighteous person spoke.” This psalm properly concerns the prophet David, the servant of the Lord. In this psalm he is rightly shown to be the servant of the Lord, because here he shows that the sinner has all his sins from himself and not from God, whereas the just person has no justice except through God’s sole mercy. I say that the psalm is directed “to the end,” that is, to Christ. Its subject is the just person, and secondarily the ungodly person.

[Col. 0315B] Its method is as follows. In the first part of the psalm, he describes the ungodly person together with his accusation. For when the ungodly person says, “I cannot restrain myself, because I was created this way; such is my nature,” he shows that the man falsely complains about his nature, and that he derives his corruption not from his creation and nature but from his will. In the second part he describes the just person, not with his own praise, but with the praise of God. For here it is shown that the just person possesses no good from himself, but all good from God alone. His purpose is to admonish us to recognize that vices come from ourselves, whereas good things come from God.

[Col. 0315C] Do not excuse yourselves for your sins, because “an unrighteous person said,” that is, someone deliberated “to commit sin within himself.” He did this not from his nature, not under compulsion, but by his own will. Nor did he attend to the fact that God would be the future judge of each person according to his merits. This is “the fear of God,” which has been set before everyone, and it “is not before his eyes,” that is, it is not present to his consideration, so that he might think of it even for that reason. His wickedness is especially evident in this: he sins by his own will and is in no way restrained by fear of the future judgment.

I rightly say that the fear of God is not before his eyes, “because” he “acted deceitfully” when he said that he sinned not by his own will but by his nature and creation, out of necessity. This was indeed deceit, because although he said this, he nevertheless knew in his conscience that the sin came from himself. He acted deceitfully only before human beings, because people thought he was speaking the truth; but before God he acted so deceitfully “that his iniquity” might be found, by that very person, to tend “toward hatred” of God and righteous people.

[Col. 0315D] He unfolds his iniquity piece by piece and shows that it exists in his thoughts, words, and actions. The continuation is: I rightly say “his iniquity,” because “the words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit” by nature: iniquity, that is, blasphemies against God; and deceit toward his neighbor, because even when he says good things, he does so with a seductive intention. And lest he excuse himself through ignorance, he shows him to be without excuse when he says that he “did not wish to understand in order to act well,” whether in words or deeds. For God had given human beings reason, by which they could understand what ought to be done; and he had restored free will, by which they could assent to divine grace.

[Col. 0316A] His words are iniquity, and iniquity also exists in his understanding. This is what is meant by “he meditated iniquity upon his bed,” that is, in his heart, which is called a bed because, just as someone rests in his bed, so the soul rests in the heart while occupied with foolish thoughts. And he not only meditates on iniquity, but also “stood” for a very long time, lingering “upon every way that was not good,” that is, upon every evil action: he stole with thieves, committed adultery with adulterers, and so forth. Although nature required him to hate evil in himself and in others, “he did not hate wickedness.” In this his wickedness is especially aggravated.

[Col. 0316B] Here begins the second part. The continuation is: The unrighteous person has his sins from himself, but, O “Lord, your mercy is in heaven,” that is, your mercy makes some people into heavens, that is, into just people, because no one has justice through himself; all possess it through you. “And your truth” extends “to the clouds,” that is, to the holy apostles. They are called clouds because they rain the dew of heavenly grace upon the faithful; from those clouds the knowledge of truth comes to us. Mercy comes from God, truth comes from God, and justice also comes from God. Hence: “Your justice”—that is, the just—“are the mountains of God,” that is, comparable to mountains. For just as the sun shines upon the mountains in the morning and descends from them into the valleys, so the knowledge of God shone in the apostles and descended through those same apostles to other human beings. And lest we understand “mountains” as the proud of this age, he adds, “of God.” And lest someone ask why he chose some and rejected others, he adds: “Your judgments are a great abyss,” that is, of such depth that no one can comprehend it.

[Col. 0316C] Truly, your judgments are a great abyss, because you will save both rational and irrational beings. This is what is meant: O “Lord,” you “will save” by spiritual salvation “human beings,” that is, rational beings, “and animals,” that is, irrational beings, making them rational, just as you made Paul rational. Or you will save them by bodily salvation, supplying them with the necessities of this life. And “you have multiplied your mercy” in many other ways by doing this, “just as,” that is, to the extent that, you have multiplied your mercy. It should be understood that although David and the Apostle knew something of God’s counsel concerning why he chose some and rejected others, they did not wish to disclose it, because they recognized that this would do more harm than good.

[Col. 0316D] You will save human beings and animals, but those irrational beings make bad use of your salvation because they do not hope in you. “But the children of human beings,” that is, rational beings, “shall hope under the shelter of your wings,” because just as young birds cannot be nourished except beneath their mother’s wings, so they understand that they cannot withstand the heat of the devil unless protected by wings, that is, by the mercy and truth of God. Or it may be understood in this way: you will save good and rational people by spiritual salvation, and they will not be ungrateful but will hope under the shelter of your wings.

They shall hope in you and will not be deprived of their hope, because “they shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house,” [Col. 0317A] that is, from the spiritual gifts with which your house, the Church, abounds. He says “they shall be made drunk” by comparison, because just as a drunken person is freed from cares, so the just person, through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, is empty of earthly desire. And “you shall give them drink” from the spirit of wisdom, which no one can resist. This is what he means by “a torrent”—I say, a torrent of your delight, that is, of grace, because you give it freely to human beings. Or “of your will,” in which you especially delight, because a torrent greatly pleases you.

[Col. 0317B] I say, “you shall give them drink,” and you will rightly be able to do so, “because with you is the fountain of life,” that is, the source of every good. “And in your light,” that is, in Christ—namely, in the knowledge of you—according to the saying, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14); and when we see that light, we shall see the Father and the Holy Spirit.

And so that we may be able to see that light, “extend” it not to those who merely wish to know you, but “to those who thirst for you,” that is, who believe in you; and extend “your justice to those who are upright in heart.”

[Col. 0317C] And so that I may reach that light, “let not the foot of pride come upon me,” that is, the inclination toward pride. By pride we understand every sin, because pride—namely, contempt for God—is present in every sin. He says “foot” in the singular rather than the plural because whoever stands in pride never stands firmly but is always inclined toward a fall, like someone standing on one foot. He has now prayed that pride, that is, the effect of sin arising from himself, may not come upon him; he now prays that another person’s suggestion may not move him to sin, saying: “And let not the hand,” that is, the persuasion, “of the sinner move me” from a good purpose.

I say, “let not the foot of pride come upon me,” because “there,” that is, in the foot of pride, “those who work iniquity have fallen.” Consequently “they have been expelled” from the kingdom of God, and afterward “they were not able to stand,” that is, to obtain the kingdom of God thereafter.

[Col. 0317D]

## ON PSALM 36

### TITLE

“To the end. A psalm of David.”

“Do not be jealous.” This psalm concerns the prophet David or any just person, and is directed “to the end,” that is, to Christ, like the other psalms. The prophet, or whatever just person is speaking here, sees the ungodly prospering and the just trampled by the ungodly. Some simple-minded just people might envy their power and wish to avenge the injuries inflicted by them; at times they might even wish to become like them. Against this he sets a most health-giving teaching, which Augustine calls a most health-giving drink.

[Col. 0318A] The subject is the just person, and conversely, though secondarily, the ungodly person. The method is as follows: he divides this subject in this way. First he deals with the just person, admonishing him not to be moved toward the ungodly by envy, imitation, or anger, while interspersing certain remarks about the ungodly. In the second part he sets out what the ungodly person does against the just person, admonishing the just person to endure it patiently. In the third part he sets out the rewards of the just, together with an admonition and condemnation of the wicked, by which he deters the just person from wishing to imitate evil. His purpose throughout is to console the simple-minded, so that they may not be moved in any way by the wickedness or injury of the ungodly.

It is as though the prophet, or the just person who is speaking, said: Simple brother, “do not be jealous.” To be jealous means to be moved toward someone, either in love or in envy. Hence the Apostle says: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” (2 Corinthians 11). Here the simple person is warned concerning both forms, so that he neither imitates the wicked by imitating their evil nor envies them. “Do not be jealous,” I say, “of those who act wickedly,” that is, in considering the wicked—namely, the malevolent—so as either to imitate or envy them; “nor be zealous,” that is, pursue “those who commit iniquity.” In “being zealous” we note a stronger affection than in “being jealous.”

[Col. 0318B] He gives the reason why the simple just person should not be moved by envy toward the wicked: “For they shall wither like grass.” Nor will this be delayed; it will happen “quickly.” We compare the powerful of this age to grass, because just as grass, adorned with flowers and green, quickly withers, so these people, adorned and flourishing in the glory of this age, quickly fail; “and they shall quickly fall, like the vegetables of the garden,” that is, like vegetables in a garden that is not well cultivated but wild. The lower classes of people are compared to these: even if they become green quickly, they nevertheless soon fail.

[Col. 0318C] And because these things quickly fail, you, good man, “hope,” not in the things of the present, but “in the Lord,” “and do good,” that is, do many good works. For goodness is not said of one thing but of many. “And” thus “inhabit the land,” that is, the Church, “and you shall be nourished by its riches,” that is, refreshed by the holy Scriptures and by many spiritual gifts.

And “delight in the Lord,” as though he were already a pleasant reality to you. For it is customary that when someone first approaches the Lord, he initially regards him as something difficult; but after becoming accustomed to him, he delights in him above all. Delight, I say, “and he himself shall give you the requests of your heart,” not carnal requests but spiritual ones.

[Col. 0318D] And because some simple people might say, “I cannot delight in or hope in the Lord, because I have many sins,” he gives this salutary counsel against that objection: “Reveal your way to the Lord” through your confession—that is, reveal the evil works by which you walk—and, once these have been revealed, “hope in him.” “And he,” the Lord, “will make your justice” for you, that is, he will give you “your judgment,” that is, discernment by which you distinguish good from evil.

And lest someone say, “Even if I possess this, I shall always be worthless,” he commends these gifts: “The Lord will make your justice,” and he will “bring it forth” from the darkness of this life, in which it is considered obscure and worthless, “like light,” that is, he will make it luminous to everyone, when the wicked say at the judgment: “We fools considered their life madness; see how they are counted among the children of God” (Wisdom 5). “And he will bring forth your judgment like midday,” that is, he will establish it in [Col. 0319A] the greatest clarity, so that it is evident to everyone. I say: reveal your way, hope in the Lord, and, having received gifts from him, always “be subject to the Lord,” that is, serve him, “and pray to him.”

[Col. 0319B] And lest the simple person, after being admonished, say: “Look, whether they act wickedly or do evil, as long as they do not harm the just, I will not be moved against them; but if they prosper and do not bring evil upon us, we cannot help being moved”—against this the prophet again offers a salutary admonition. I say: “Be subject to the Lord, and if the ungodly prosper, do not be jealous,” neither by imitating nor envying “him,” that is, in considering the one “who prospers in his way,” that is, in an evil action which proceeds toward destruction, “and in the man who commits injustices,” that is, persecutes the good.

Do not be jealous, I say; and if you have been moved in any way, let it go. This is: “Cease from anger.” And if you have been moved by prolonged hatred, cease. This is: “Abandon wrath.” And if you have at any time wished to rage, cease. This is: “Do not be jealous so as to act wickedly.”

And therefore I say, do not act wickedly, “because those who act wickedly shall be destroyed,” that is, both the malevolent and those who commit evil shall be cast outside the boundary of the heavenly Jerusalem. “But those who wait for the Lord,” that is, those who patiently endure the evils of this life while looking to the Lord as their rewarder, “shall inherit the land,” that is, they shall possess the heavenly homeland by hereditary right.

[Col. 0319C] I say that they shall inherit the homeland. And lest someone say, “Who will be able to endure for so long?” he says: “And yet a little while,” as though to say, do not grow faint in enduring; the time is short, indeed the human life is short. I say, endure for a little while, “and the sinner shall no longer be,” not that the sinner’s substance will perish, but that he will no longer exist as a sinner, since he will not be able to sin. And grant that then you “seek his place,” that is, whether in any way a sinner is necessary in the other life—“and you shall not find it.” The sinner is necessary only in this life, in which the just are tested through him.

He had said that those who wait for the Lord would inherit the land; now he determines how they wait: not unwillingly and with murmuring, but in gentleness and simplicity. To this the following is connected: you will not find the sinner’s place in the other life. “But the gentle—[the isolated reading vita, ‘life,’ is uncertain]—the gentle shall inherit the land” of the living; “there they shall delight in an abundance of peace.” There, living forever, they will be attacked in no way either by the devil or by their own flesh, nor will they be disturbed by any unrest at all.

He begins the second part. The gentle shall delight in peace, but meanwhile, in this life, “the sinner shall watch the just person,” carefully examining his life and considering whether he can harm him in any way. And when he can find no rational charge against him, like a beast he will “gnash his teeth against him,” that is, with envious biting and slander.

[Col. 0320A] Thus the sinner will gnash against the just person; but you, good man, do not care. Rather, mock him, because “the Lord will mock him.” I rightly say that he will mock him, “because he sees that his day will come,” that is, the judgment. He calls the judgment a day because there everything will be manifest, as in daylight.

The Lord rightly mocks them, because “sinners have drawn the sword,” that is, they have brought their evil works out from their thoughts, where they were hidden, into public view—just as someone draws his sword from its sheath—and they have also “bent their bow,” that is, their deceits, by which they secretly wound, as someone strikes secretly with a bow.

[Col. 0320B] They bent their bow “to deceive the poor,” that is, the simple person who has not yet advanced sufficiently in the knowledge of God, “and the helpless”—understand this as the same person, who is called helpless because he is subject to suffering and death and oppressed by the many miseries of this world. They drew their sword “to slaughter the upright in heart.”

They drew their sword, but “their sword shall enter their own hearts,” that is, while they kill the saints, they themselves shall be killed inwardly; “and their bow shall be broken,” that is, their deceit shall be rendered ineffective, so that they cannot deceive the good or make them like themselves.

[Col. 0320C] The ungodly will do all these things to you; and even when you are poor, he will prosper. But endure everything patiently, because “better is the little that belongs to the just” than “the many riches of sinners.”

I rightly say that it is better, “because the arms,” that is, the strengths and powers, “of sinners shall be broken,” that is, destroyed, and found wholly useless. “But the just,” even though they are of little means and poor, “the Lord strengthens” in their good purpose and hope of future blessedness.

I rightly say that he strengthens the just, for false is the opinion of those who think that the Lord does not know what takes place in this life, because “the Lord knows the days of the blameless,” and the Lord himself “shall be their inheritance,” that is, the inheritance of the just, “forever.” The Lord is called the inheritance of the just because, just as an inheritance feeds and supports its possessor, so the Lord is in this life the nourishment of his own, and finally, in the other life, he will be their complete refreshment.

And therefore “they shall not be confounded”; rather, their will shall be fulfilled “in the evil time,” that is, on the day of judgment, [Col. 0320D] which will be evil for the ungodly, who will then be condemned to eternal punishment. Then the just will not be confounded. In this life they are fully refreshed by God; this is what is meant by “in the days of famine,” that is, in this life, in which the saints hunger and thirst for justice, “they shall be satisfied” with spiritual food. The opposite will happen to sinners, and he states this as a proposition: thus the just will not be confounded in the evil time, because only sinners will perish.

[Col. 0321A] Then sinners will indeed perish. But in this life, “the enemies of the Lord,” that is, sinners themselves, “as soon as they have been honored,” that is, held in reverence, “and exalted,” through powers and dignities, “failing continually”—and this is what is meant by “they shall fail.” For they gradually fail, slipping every day into more serious offenses, “like smoke.” Just as smoke becomes thinner and fails the higher it rises, so the wicked, the higher the positions they occupy, fail all the more from the good. In many ways he shows that the poverty of the just is better than the riches of sinners.

Behold, he gives the reason why the sinner fails: “The sinner shall borrow” from God “and shall not repay.” We borrow from God whatever we possess. A person repays well when he uses God’s gifts for the purpose for which God appointed them—for example, if he has riches, he distributes them to the poor, and likewise with other gifts. The sinner does not repay, but the just person repays well: he “has mercy,” that is, he is moved by a pious affection toward the afflicted; and this alone is sufficient for him when he has nothing to give. [Col. 0321B] But the just person has mercy “and also repays,” if he has anything.

Therefore he has mercy and also repays, “because those who bless him,” namely, “the Lord,” that is, those who give thanks and repay what they had borrowed from the Lord, “shall inherit the land” of the living. “But those who curse him,” that is, those who do not give the Lord fitting thanks for the gifts they have received, “shall perish.”

[Col. 0321C] I rightly say that the just shall inherit the land. This will happen to them because their works are directed by the Lord. He says this: the “steps,” that is, the affections and works, “of a man” who uses reason well “are directed,” that is, are found to be upright, “before the Lord,” that is, within the Lord’s disposition. It is as though one said of a powerful person who arranged matters well concerning someone that this person’s works were well directed before him. The Lord directs the steps of the just person, and “he shall will the way,” that is, the good life of this just person whom he has directed.

Or “the way” means his commandments and instructions, which that man will wish to follow. Or “the way” means the good works which Christ performed.

Therefore, when he falls—that is, when he sins—that man “shall not be dashed down,” that is, he will neither commit a mortal sin nor remain in venial sins, “because the Lord will place his hands beneath him,” that is, he will provide his help by which he is sustained. Another translation has: “because the Lord strengthens his hand.” According to this, it should be read as follows: “When he falls,” bodily—that is, when he is killed and scourged—“he shall not be dashed down” in spirit, that is, he will not sin in his soul, “because the Lord strengthens his hand,” that is, his action.

[Col. 0321D] I rightly say that he shall not be dashed down, because I have seen the just person protected by the Lord at every time: when justice was young and small, when it was mature, and when it was old. If the whole body of the saints is speaking, it is as though he said: “I was young,” that is, youthful, as in the time of Abel and the others, when justice was practiced to some extent through the natural law alone; it became mature when the written law was received; and in the time of grace it became perfect.

[Col. 0322A] He proves that he had been young by saying: “Indeed, I grew old,” that is, I came to a venerable age, namely, to that time when the charity of many grows cold, as will happen in the time of Antichrist. If one single just person is speaking, he says, “I was young,” that is, I am like those first just people, “and I grew old,” that is, I am like those last just people, in whose time justice will be in an advanced old age—not because the just will fail, but because in many who seemed just, charity grows cold. In this way the Apostle compares himself with those last people when he says: “We who live, who remain, shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4).

[Col. 0322B] I say, “I was young and I grew old,” “and at no time did I see the just person abandoned” by the Lord, without the Lord granting him spiritual help; nor did I see “his seed,” that is, his works, “seeking bread,” that is, lacking bread—namely, spiritual vivification. For the Lord guards his faithful, gives life to their works, and makes them pleasing to himself.

Therefore God does not abandon his righteous one, because he shows himself to be such a person that the Lord ought rightly to regard him: namely, he “has mercy” with loving affection “all day long,” that is, continually, “and,” if he has anything, “lends it,” that is, gives it to one suffering need. He properly says “lends,” because the one who dispenses expects it to be repaid—not by the poor man, but by the Lord. And because the righteous man lends in this way, therefore “his seed,” that is, his good work, “will be in blessing,” that is, in increase. For this is manifestly true: if someone freely distributes some good entrusted to him by God, he abounds all the more in that same good—as when someone teaches others or distributes his possessions in alms. Hence the Apostle, exhorting people to give alms, says: “And he will increase the growth of the [Col. 0322C] fruits of righteousness” (I Cor. IX).

And because the Lord acts in this way toward the righteous, therefore you, simple brother, “turn away from evil”; and because it would not be enough to cease from evil unless one also did good, he adds: “and do good,” and thus “dwell” in heaven “for ever and ever,” that is, eternally. The righteous indeed dwell in heaven in this life by hope, and in the next life they will possess it in reality.

I say: do good—and you ought to do so—“because the Lord loves judgment,” that is, discernment, by which the righteous separate good things from evil ones. And the Lord himself “will not abandon” his “holy ones” in this life; rather, “they will be preserved,” being led “for ever.”

With the words “I was young,” the third part begins. I say: they will be preserved and will obtain that inheritance [Col. 0322D] for which they will be preserved. We have this in the intervening verse, where it says: “But the righteous will inherit the land of the living”; and this will not be for a time, but eternally. When it says, “and they will dwell upon it for ever and ever,” it has already blessed them above, because they will be the possessors and lords of that land.

He inserted a passage about the ungodly in order to deter the righteous through their punishment. The connection is this: The righteous will be preserved forever, but the ungodly will be punished forever, “and the seed,” that is, the works, “of the ungodly will perish,” because it will confer no benefit. “But the righteous will inherit the land,” and so forth. He had said that the Lord gives that inheritance to his holy ones; now, lest anyone should undervalue it, he describes it and shows it to be worthy. The connection is as follows:

[Col. 0323A] The saints will inherit the land, which is exceedingly worthy, because there “the mouth of the righteous,” that is, the heart—which he calls “the mouth” because it opens like a mouth and God fills it—“will meditate wisdom,” thinking not about something doubtful, but possessing certainty concerning the knowledge of God. And “his tongue,” that is, his affection, “will speak” in its own manner: it will praise God, namely, for his restoration.

And there too “the law,” that is, the will, “of his God”—who is called his God because he has done many good things for him—“will be in his heart,” that is, in his will. For there the righteous man will desire what he knows God desires. “And his steps will not be tripped up,” that is, his affections and works will not be hindered, so that all his desires may be fulfilled.

Nor will there be anyone there who wishes to trip up his [Col. 0323B] steps, that is, the steps of the righteous, because “the sinner,” whether the devil or a human being, “watches and seeks,” with envious affection, “to put him to death.” Envy will indeed be the torment of the souls of those who sinned through envy in this life.

The sinner seeks to put the righteous man to death, “but the Lord will not abandon him,” the righteous man, “into his hands,” that is, into the will or power of the sinner, so that he might condemn the righteous man. Nor will the Lord himself “condemn him,” the righteous man, “when he is judged,” that is, when the ungodly man is condemned “to his,” that is, to the righteous man’s, honor. For the righteous man receives vengeance when the ungodly man is condemned.

We can also read the preceding words in this way: Therefore the righteous will inherit the land, because in this life “the mouth of the righteous will meditate,” [Col. 0323C] diligently, “wisdom,” that is, the knowledge of God, “and his tongue will speak judgment,” literally. “The law also of his God,” that is, his commandments, will be “in his heart,” that is, in his will—in other words, he will wish to fulfill the law for him. “And his steps will not be tripped up,” namely, the steps of the righteous; that is, it cannot be prevented that he fulfill his desires. Nor is there anyone lacking who wishes to trip him up, because “the sinner considers the righteous man,” that is, carefully observes whether he can hinder him in anything, “and seeks to put him to death,” both in will and in deed. “But the Lord will not abandon him,” the righteous man, “into his hands,” that is, into the sinner’s power, “nor” will the Lord himself “condemn him,” the righteous man, “when he is judged to him,” as above. Or: “He will condemn him when the righteous man is judged to him,” that is, according to the sinner’s will. [Col. 0323D] For although the righteous man is sometimes scourged, killed, and judged in other ways by the ungodly, nevertheless the Lord does not condemn him, but preserves him unharmed amid destruction.

And because the Lord thus guards the righteous, therefore you should “wait” with patient endurance, while also “keeping his ways,” that is, his commandments. Then the Lord himself “will exalt you,” by giving virtues, “so that you may inherit the land” of the living. For unless a person were exalted in this way, he would be unworthy to receive your lofty possession—the land of which you now simply believe that you “will see it when sinners have perished.”

And I rightly say that sinners will perish, because I “saw the ungodly man exalted exceedingly” above some lesser men, [Col. 0324A] “and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, surpassing other powerful men in the height of this age, just as the cedar of Lebanon surpasses other trees in height.

I saw him thus exalted, “and I passed by” these present things, and foresaw the future with the affection and agility of my mind. “And behold,” there “he was not”; the sinner was no longer there. “And I sought him,” that is, I carefully considered why he was not there, “and his place was not found,” that is, I understood that he had no place.

And because the ungodly have no place there, therefore, so that you may have a place there, “keep innocence.” I rightly say “keep” it, because many wish to steal it from you through evil persuasions. “And look upon equity,” that is, recognize as equitable that you should always be punished unto your own undoing [Col. 0324B]. He therefore looks upon equity “because for the peaceful man,” that is, for one who patiently bears the adversities of this life and counts them as due to himself, “there are remains,” that is, eternal life reserved for him in the future. Or, “remains” means a good reputation after death.

The righteous have remains, “but the unjust will perish,” that is, they will be condemned; “the remains of the ungodly will perish altogether.” The ungodly, according to their presumption, leave themselves a life after death; those remains will perish for them, because they will in no way have eternal life. Or “remains” means their reputation, houses, and other things that they leave behind: these will perish, that is, they will be destroyed.

Now, lest the simple man, having been admonished, should say, “I have sufficient reasons why I ought to act well and endure the ungodly, but I am unable to do so,” the prophet [Col. 0324C] shows him that he does not lack power. Thus it may be understood: The unjust will perish, “but the salvation of the righteous,” that is, the remission of sins—in other words, the power to act well—is “from the Lord,” “and” the Lord himself is “their protector in the time of tribulation,” that is, in this life, so that they may not be wounded by the arrows of the enemy.

“And the Lord enriches them” for good works, “and he will free them” “from external punishments, so that they may no longer be afflicted in any way, even in the body; and he will rescue them from sinners” when he leads them out of this life; “and he will save them” with eternal salvation, for this reason: because they have hoped in him.

# ON PSALM XXXVII. TITLE

“Unto the end, a psalm of David, for the remembrance of the [Col. 0324D] Sabbath.”

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” This psalm suits the prophet David or another penitent. It is composed for the remembrance of the Sabbath, that is, of eternal rest. By reminding himself of this, the penitent who speaks here afflicts himself in many ways, so that he may be able to reach it. I call the psalm one directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ. Some books read: “for the remembrance of sins.”

The subject of this psalm is a penitent person, afflicted with many miseries because of his sins. Its structure is as follows. In the first part he prays that he may be so cleansed through the miseries he suffers here that after this life he may suffer nothing. In the second part he enumerates the miseries he suffers here. In the third part he shows that amid all these evils he never abandoned God, but always hoped in him, and that he is [Col. 0325A] prepared to endure still greater sufferings. At the end he sets forth, as a conclusion, a certain rejoicing over the forgiveness he has obtained. He intends to admonish us—not so that we should fear, as he did in another penitential psalm, but so that we should now patiently endure whatever evils are necessary for the cleansing of sins—as though the penitent who speaks were giving this instruction.

Do not, brother, ask God to remove the evils of this life from you; rather, through these evils, ask him to remove the eternal ones, following the example of me, who pray not concerning these things but concerning those things, as follows: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” Let this be read as it was explained in another psalm.

Nor should you rebuke me after this life because in this life I endure many evils. This is what he says: “For your [Col. 0325B] arrows,” that is, those punishments for sins which you fixed upon Adam. God threatened Adam as though with a drawn bow: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall surely die” (Gen. II). When he violated obedience, God’s arrows were fixed in him: namely, he became mortal and subject to the suffering caused by sin. These remain in the Church through the sons of Adam. Concerning them the penitent says here: They have been fixed in me, and you, Lord, have not withdrawn those arrows from me, nor lightened them; rather, you have “strengthened” “your hand” over me, as a teacher does over a corrected disciple—that is, your vengeance over me, pressing me down through those evils.

Meanwhile you have strengthened your hand over me, so that now “there is no health in my flesh,” because my flesh is possessed by [Col. 0325C] every kind of evil, such as hunger, weariness, and things of this kind. I say that there is no health in me, and this is “because of,” that is, from the presence of, “your anger,” that is, your vengeance. Since I now have before my mind the vengeance you will exact for sins, I seek no rest for my flesh. “There is no peace for my bones,” that is, the strengths of my soul are disturbed; and I do not accuse you, Lord, of this, but this entire disturbance comes to me “because of,” that is, on account of the presence of, “my sins.” For when he considers his sins and fears God’s vengeance for them, he is disturbed both in body and in soul.

I rightly say that I am troubled because of my sins, because my sins are many. This is what follows: “For my iniquities have gone over my head,” and have subjected [Col. 0325D] my mind to themselves, “and they have been made heavy upon me like a heavy burden.” For just as a heavy burden weighs down the person carrying it, so these iniquities weigh down the mind.

Here he begins to enumerate the miseries he suffers, which he gathers together in the present verse. I therefore say that they have gone over me because “my scars have become foul and have festered.” He speaks by comparison: just as scars first become foul and afterward the flesh breaks open, so sins healed in baptism become foul when we think of renewing them; they become corrupt when we bring them into action. Some books have: “They have become corrupt and have festered.” In that case the order is reversed, because they first become corrupt when they are brought into action, and afterward fester when they give others [Col. 0326A] an example of sinning, just as scars first become corrupt and then emit a stench. They have festered, I say, “because of the presence of my folly,” that is, because of my folly, which is always present to me.

And they festered to such an extent that “I became miserable,” that is, regarding myself as wretched, “and bowed down,” that is, no longer looking toward heaven as I ought, but only toward earthly things, like a brute animal. I was bowed down, I say, by my own judgment, “to the end,” that is, to such an extent that no beast is more troubled than I am by my own judgment.

Or it may be understood in this way: Because my scars festered in this manner, I became miserable, as one bearing many miseries—whether I bring them upon myself or they are inflicted upon me from elsewhere—and so miserable that I was bowed down, that is, depressed by the weight of miseries, [Col. 0326B] “to the end of my life,” or “to the end,” that is, to such an extent that no one can now be depressed further than I am by any miseries. And because I had thus become miserable and bowed down, therefore “all day long,” that is, continually, “I went about sorrowful,” passing from sorrow into sorrow. Or “I went about” means: I lived among human beings in sorrow.

I went about sorrowful, not because of any loss of temporal property, but “because my loins,” that is, the frailty of my fleshly nature, “are filled with mockeries,” that is, with the deceptions of the devil. By the loins, where the seat of lust is, that is, of carnal pleasure, we understand every pleasure of the flesh. My loins are so filled with mockeries that now [Col. 0326C] “there is no health in my flesh,” that is, there is no kind of pleasure in which I have not been deceived.

And because I have been deceived in this way, therefore “I am afflicted” in body “and humbled” in soul “exceedingly,” that is, greatly.
