I also groaned in my heart, and “from that groaning of my heart I roared,” that is, I burst into a roar—into a cry with great desire—just as a lion roars when it desires some food.

I roared, “and all my desire, O Lord, is before you,” that is, I desire nothing except what pleases you, “and my groaning is not hidden from you”; rather, it is well known and approved by you.

I rightly call it groaning, because my groaning is so great that “my heart,” that is, my soul, “is troubled.” He shows that the heart is troubled by saying [Col. 0326D] that the strength of the mind and reason have failed. This is what follows: “My strength abandons me,” that is, the strength of my mind has failed to such an extent that it can now endure nothing. “And even the light of my eyes,” that is, reason, “is not with me”; and even if it was natural to me, or “the light itself,” that is, whatever little there was, has been lost—in other words, I have lost discernment between good and evil.

“And as the culmination of all evils, my friends,” that is, those who seemed to be joined to me by a loving and faithful affection, without any kinship of the flesh, and who ought to have been a source of consolation to me, “and my neighbors,” according to the flesh, “have drawn near” by gradually approaching “against me, and have stood,” that is, have persisted toward me in evil actions.

[Col. 0327A] My friends were against me, and those who did not do me harm offered no consolation. This is what follows: “And those who were near me,” that is, joined to me by some kinship or friendship, “stood far away,” that is, withdrew from me, bringing no consolation. And when I had thus been abandoned, those “who sought my life,” that is, to take it—the demons and their ministers—“used force,” that is, inflicted manifest evils upon me.

They not only inflicted evils, but also spoke evil openly and secretly. This is what follows: “Those who sought evils for me spoke vanities,” that is, manifest lies—for example, when they said that worldly things were sufficient for blessedness, and similar things. And they did not merely speak evil openly; they also [Col. 0327B] “meditated deceits all day long,” that is, if they ever spoke good things, they did not speak them as good things, but with a deceitful intention.

“But I did not hear,” that is, I was not moved by their curses. I say that I existed in this condition “like a deaf man”: just as a deaf person has no act of hearing, so I had no act of being moved. And toward those who cursed me I was “like a mute.” Yet because a mute person, although not with an articulate voice, nevertheless expresses anger through some groan or sign in order to make his steadfastness known, he says: “and did not open his mouth,” that is, he gave no answer at all to those who reproached him.

And I not only lacked the act of hearing; I also lacked the power. This is what follows: “I became like [Col. 0327C] a man who does not hear,” that is, who is unable to hear. And since he had said above, “like a mute who does not open his mouth,” lest anyone should infer that he was mute because he had no answer to give, he adds: “and who has no reproofs in his mouth” against his persecutors—that is, although he had grounds by which he could have reproached them, he was nevertheless as though he had none.

Here the third part begins. The connection is this: I am thus afflicted, but nevertheless I hoped in you. And “because I hoped in you,” therefore “you, Lord, my God, will hear me.”

You will hear me, and you ought to hear me, “because” I “said,” that is, I resolved, “lest my enemies,” that is, the devil and his ministers—and if they now rejoice over me—“ever,” that is, at the end, “rejoice over me as one defeated.” Indeed, they would rejoice, because “when [Col. 0327D] my feet are shaken,” that is, when they have been shaken, “they spoke great things against me,” that is, against me, because they rejoiced in my weakness.

Therefore you will hear me because, although I have already endured many evils, I am prepared to endure many more. This is what follows: “For I am ready to go into” the “scourges” I must endure for love of you. And I always keep the memory of my sins, as he says: “and my pain is always before me,” that is, I always keep in my heart the memory of my former sins.

You will hear me also “because I will declare,” that is, confess, “my iniquity,” “and I will think,” that is, I will be concerned, “about my sin,” performing works through which my sin may be forgiven.

[Col. 0328A] I endure so many evils that I am even dying. This is what he says: “But my enemies live,” that is, they suppose that life consists in these worldly things, “and they have grown strong against me,” namely, for the purpose of inflicting evils upon me. “And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied,” both in number and in the severity of the harm they do.

They not only inflicted evils upon me, but also “reviled me”—those “who repay evil for good.” And they did all this for no other reason than “because I pursued goodness.”

Here he sets forth rejoicing. The connection is this: I suffer all these things, and you, “Lord, my God,” giver of my salvation—that is, you who have already heard me—“do not abandon me,” that is, do not permit me to fall into criminal sin. For God sometimes permits [Col. 0328B] his own to fall for the sake of greater correction, as he did with Peter. And if you sometimes abandon me, “do not depart from me,” that is, do not permit me to persevere in sin, but “give heed to my help,” that is, direct your attention to helping me act well.

# ON PSALM XXXVIII. TITLE

“Unto the end, a song of David, for Jeduthun.”

“I said: I will guard.” Wishing to honor Jeduthun, who was one of the four teachers when they brought back the Lord’s ark from Shiloh, Ezra places his name in the title of this psalm in his memory. Although in some writings we find that Jeduthun composed this psalm, and Heman another, and so forth, it must nevertheless be understood that all were [Col. 0328C] composed by David. They are said to have composed them because they recited them, and not only for this reason, but especially because the interpretation of the name “Jeduthun” reveals the character of the psalm itself.

For Jeduthun is interpreted as “one who leaps over,” and this psalm concerns one who leaps over all temporal things. He calls this psalm a song because it proposes a certain rejoicing—namely, our end, which is Christ. And although certain sorrowful things are proposed here, they are nevertheless regarded as joyful in hope of that end.

The title is explained as follows: This song suits David the prophet, who leaps over, or anyone who leaps over, composed for Jeduthun, that is, for the honor of Jeduthun, that is, of the one who leaps over. For when he shows such a person to be one who, having left worldly things behind, leaps toward heavenly things, [Col. 0328D] he offers him great honor. I call it a song directing us toward the end, that is, toward Christ.

The subject is the one who leaps over, that is, the perfect person who, having set aside every worldly pleasure, longs only for heavenly things, and who is so perfect that he also entirely restrains his tongue from sin. The psalm is arranged in parts as follows. In the first part it shows that this person who leaps over is silent to the world, that is, to human beings, and speaks to God. In the second part he compares worldly things with heavenly things, showing that the former are vain and the latter to be desired. In the third part he offers a prayer that he may be freed from evils and be able to obtain heavenly things. The intention is to admonish the righteous to leave worldly things behind and pass over to heavenly things.

You righteous, do not desire these worldly things. Rather, con[Col. 0329A]sider me, who “said,” that is, resolved within myself: “I will guard my ways,” by which I ought to approach God. I do not now mean that I will abstain from theft or from such things, for I have already removed all of them from me; rather, I will guard them so that from now on “I may not sin with my tongue.”

And so that I may not sin, “I placed a guard over my mouth” when “the sinner stood against me,” that is, when he wished to provoke me to curses. Thus, when the sinner stood against me, I placed a guard over my mouth. But because every action performed after deliberation is more certain, he first says: I will indeed guard myself from every evil. Reason guards as a good doorkeeper, sending out what ought to be sent out and holding back what ought not to be sent out.

“I placed a guard,” namely, “I became mute.” This was not [Col. 0329B] out of anger, but out of humility; and this is what follows: “and I was humbled,” namely, in mind. I not only became mute by refusing to speak evil, but I also kept silent about good things. This is what follows: “and I was silent from good things.” This good man rightly remains silent toward those obstinate people whom he sees prepared to trample upon the word of God. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII).

I was silent, I say, from good things, “and” as a result “my pain was renewed.” This righteous man had grieved over the sinner when the sinner provoked him to anger. Now that grief is renewed when he recognizes them to be so obstinate that he does not even dare to preach good things to them.

After showing that he is silent to the world, he shows that he [Col. 0329C] speaks to God. The connection is this: I was silent to those people, but “my heart,” that is, my affection, “grew hot within me” with the fire of love. It not only grew hot, but also burns there. This is what follows: “and in my meditation the fire blazes,” that is, I meditate with burning love. If the reading is “will blaze,” the future tense signifies perseverance.

The fire blazes in my meditation, and from that meditation “I spoke with my tongue,” that is, announcing what ardent meditation would provide. I spoke this: “Lord, make my end known to me,” that is, give me true knowledge concerning your Son Christ, so that I may understand him to be my consummator, who redeems me and restores immortality to me.

And “make known to me the number of my days” in [Col. 0329D] which I live—“what it is,” that is, what kind it is—so that I may understand that the present days are defective and thereby seek the eternal days. Or it may be read in this way: “Make known the number,” that is, the infinity, or eternity, “of my days,” namely, the days in which I shall live in the other life. Make me understand, that is, that the righteous possess eternity in the other life.

I say: make known to me, Lord, the end and the number, so that, having understood these things, “I may know what is lacking to me,” namely, Christ. For when the righteous man recognizes that Christ is the end of our labor and the rewarder at judgment according to each person’s merits, he knows that he must hasten toward him and that he must no longer place his confidence in these worldly things.

I say that something is lacking because it truly [Col. 0330A] is lacking. “And behold,” this is what is lacking: “you have made my days measurable,” the days in which I live—that is, not eternal, but subject to decline. One person has three days or years, another a hundred, another sixty; and each has a fixed measure. “And my substance,” namely, not the renewal accomplished by Christ, but the old corruptible essence that we have drawn from Adam, “is as nothing before you.” I do not say “in the sight of human beings,” who magnify human beings in comparison with animals, but “before you,” that is, in your presence. For the days are so fragile, and the substance so unworthy.

Nevertheless, although every human being, however righteous he may be, does not attend to this, “living” in this way—for there will someday be a time when he will not be subject—he “is universal vanity,” that is, he is subject to every [Col. 0330B] vanity, namely, to these worldly things. Although the righteous man does not subject himself spiritually to these worldly things, according to the body he is necessarily subject to them. For he must think about food and clothing. Hence Paul says: “The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly” (Rom. VIII).

Here the second part begins. The connection is this: Every human being is subject to vanity; for this reason he ought to cease from sin. Diapsalm. “Nevertheless a human being passes through” from sin into sin, so that he is not only subject to vanity but also passes from one sin into another, although he exists “in the image” of God, that is, is like him through reason. Another translation confirms this meaning, reading: “Although a human being walks in the image of God, nevertheless he is troubled in vain.”

I say that a human being passes through, and he not only passes through, but is also [Col. 0330C] “troubled” by many passions of the soul—joy, sorrow, hope, fear, and similar things—and this “in vain,” because all these disturbances are useless.

Here he selects a certain kind of vice in which there is both passing through and disturbance, namely, avarice. A human being passes through and is troubled because he “hoards up,” and in this there is great passing through: for he inclines toward avarice in this matter, and is disturbed by fear lest what he has amassed should be lost or diminished. He hoards up and is foolish, because he “does not know for whom he will gather” the things he has collected. Often an enemy possesses what the avaricious person gathered.

Having shown the character of the present life, he sets forth its opposite, namely, what everyone ought to desire. The connection is this: [Col. 0330D] Thus a human being is troubled. “And now,” that is, having considered this, “what is my expectation?” that is, what ought I to expect? These worldly things? Or God? “Is it not the Lord?” Certainly, the Lord is my expectation. “And my substance,” that is, the purity of my conscience renewed through Christ, “is with you,” that is, worthy for you to approve. For no substance except one renewed through Christ is worthy to be presented in your presence.

Since my substance is with you, therefore, Lord, “rescue me from all my iniquities,” so that they may not be able to rule me. And you ought to rescue me because you “have made me a reproach to the foolish,” against whom the foolish man would hurl reproaches.

And I have borne them well [Col. 0331A]. This is what follows: “I became mute and did not open my mouth,” as in another psalm. I did not open it, nor did I undertake this repentance from myself, but because “you did it” in me—that is, you produced this patience in me. And because I endured in this way, therefore, Lord, remove from me not only iniquities but also the punishments of iniquities. This is what follows: “Remove your scourges from me.” This may also be joined to what we read above, so that it means: Since you have done this, now remove those scourges from me, and so forth.

I say “remove,” and it is necessary that you remove them, because “I have failed,” that is, I have been unable to endure, “because of the strength of your hand,” that is, because of your powerful vengeance, “in rebukes.” This indicates that God inflicts his vengeance for the purpose of drawing a person back from sin.

The connection is this: I speak of your scourges and your strong hand, but I do [Col. 0331B] not accuse you; rather, I confess that I have iniquity. “Because of iniquity you chastised” me, “a human being,” with your disciplines. Here the judgment and mercy of God are indicated: judgment in that he scourges because of iniquity, and mercy in that, like a father, he scourges in order to correct, so as to lead the person back to the way of truth.

You chastised me, and to such an extent that “you made his soul waste away like a spider.” For just as a spider draws out its inward parts to make a useless work, so the sinner consumes his soul in the pursuit of worldly things. These things are so vain that the powers of the soul accomplish nothing in him. God also does this for the sake of correction, so that when a person recognizes himself to be so worthless, he may at least turn back. And although he thus fails in these useless things, “nevertheless every human being,” namely, the carnal person, “is troubled,” [Col. 0331C] that is, affected by many passions.

It can also be read in a good sense. The connection is this: You chastised the human being, and you chastised him in such a way that he entirely mortified himself to the world, just as a spider mortifies itself in its body. This is what follows: “to waste away,” that is, to fail, in anger, so that he no longer becomes angry; and in desire, so that he desires nothing and envies no one; and so that he makes himself entirely dead to the world. For a soul that is full of anger and similar passions is said to waste away, like a spider that mortifies itself. The righteous man thus wastes away in longing for heavenly things. “Nevertheless every human being,” namely, the carnal person, pursues worldly things without attending to the righteous man; and it is “in vain” that they “are troubled.”

Others are troubled, but I am not troubled because of these worldly things. Therefore you, “Lord”—Diapsalm—“hear [Col. 0331D] my prayer,” namely, that you may make known to me the end for which I ask. And hear “my supplication,” so that you may remove from me iniquity and the scourge, which I pray may be removed. This prayer and supplication are worthy of being heard because they are accompanied by tears. This is what follows: “Give heed with your ears to my tears.”

I say, hear my prayer, and meanwhile, until you fulfill it, “do not be silent,” that is, do not withdraw your grace from me, but answer me by granting grace in this life. And you ought to answer because “I am with you,” that is, I belong to your household. Especially for this reason, because I am “a sojourner”—transferred from the city of the devil, in which I was born through Adam’s sin, to your city through the grace of Christ—and I do not yet have [Col. 0332A] a fixed dwelling or seat there. Rather, I am still “a pilgrim,” journeying toward that heavenly city, “like all my fathers,” namely, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others who, in order to signify that they were pilgrims in this life and were journeying toward that true city, did not build houses for themselves in this life but lived in tents, as the Apostle testifies.

And because I am thus with you, therefore “relieve the burning,” that is, the tinder of sin, “so that I may be refreshed before I depart” from this life. For if I depart without being refreshed, without the evil suggestions having been mortified in me, “I shall no longer exist,” that is, I shall not possess true being, but will instead be afflicted by torments.

# ON PSALM XXXIX. TITLE

“Unto the end, a psalm of David.”

[Col. 0332B] “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” This psalm suits David himself, that is, Christ—not only in his own person, but also in the person of the earlier fathers, and in the person of Christ himself, and in the person of those who follow Christ, even to the last righteous person.

The subject is Christ, insofar as he establishes a limit for all legal observances and renders them useless, and proposes perfection to us in himself. He treats of this as follows. In the first part he presents testimony to this newness, namely, that the first fathers awaited and announced it. In the second part he introduces Christ himself destroying the legal ordinances and confirming his renewal. In the final part he introduces the followers of Christ, that is, those who announce him. He intends to persuade us that the legal institutions have now reached their end, and that through Christ [Col. 0332C] we must ascend to God.

The voice of the earlier righteous, as though they were saying: Do not hope in legal institutions, but wait for the Lord, just as I, never trusting in these observances, “waited for the Lord.” And I do not say that I waited only at some time, but “waiting,” with continual expectation. My expectation was not empty, because the Lord “gave heed to me,” that is, presented himself as attentive to me.

He gave heed to me not only because I waited, but also “heard me.” He explains how he heard him, saying: “and he brought me out of the pit of misery,” that is, from this world, in which many miseries are contained—namely, sins, which make people miserable and muddy. Hence he adds: “and from the mire of the mud.” [Col. 0332D] For through Christ those righteous men were freed from sin, although original sins were not entirely erased until Christ’s blood was poured out.

He not only removed evils, but also gave good things. This is what follows: “And he set my feet upon a rock,” that is, upon Christ, “my feet,” that is, my affections, so that, although we had previously been uncertain in whom we ought to trust, we might now have Christ as the certain foundation of our faith. And when my feet had been established, “he directed my steps,” that is, he made my works straight.

“And he put a new song into my mouth,” that is, he made me announce the incarnation of his Son. This “song” is a hymn—not to Jupiter or to some fictitious god, but “to our God.”

[Col. 0333A] And this which we announce “many will see and fear,” with good fear, when they see the miracles, “and they will hope in the Lord.”

And lest anyone should say that it is a small thing and contributes nothing to hope in the Lord, he shows that those who hope are blessed, saying: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord,” that is, the one who honors the Lord’s name, believing that he is the Redeemer, and believing similar things about him. I call that name his hope because, by receiving and honoring the name in this way, he hopes in him, secure that through this he will have life. And I rightly call him blessed if afterward he “did not turn,” that is, incline, the name “toward vanities,” that is, toward the enjoyment of worldly things or toward legal observances, “and false insanities,” such as believing that a stone is a god.

[Col. 0333B] People ought not to turn toward such things, because “you, my God, have done many wonders,” such as heaven and earth and the other things that they themselves can admire. They are your wonders, that is, made for your praise; and this was done not through someone else’s indication, but through your own “thoughts,” that is, through your own wisdom. Therefore it is evident that “there is no one who is like you.”

And these, your wonders, “I announced” through the earlier fathers, and afterward I myself [Col. 0333C] “spoke” your wonders in my own person. And while I was speaking, “those who believe in you were multiplied” “beyond number”—either beyond the number of the earlier believers, or beyond the number of those predestined to life, because many believed who afterward departed from the faith. Where he says, “I spoke,” he begins the second part.

[Col. 0333C] Therefore I have spoken, because you did not desire sacrifice—that is, slaughtered animals, which were not entirely burned, did not please you—“nor offering,” of candles and bread, and such things you did not desire; “but you perfected ears for me,” that is, you gave me perfect understanding. The other translation has the same sense: “you have poured over me” (*perfudisti mihi*). The Apostle, however, says: “You adapted a body for me,” that is, you made a suitable body in which divinity might lie concealed.

Nor did you desire only these things, but also “holocaust,” that is, a sacrifice in which the entire animal is burned. For *holos* means “whole,” and *caustus* means “burned”; “you did not request it.” “And” likewise you did not request sacrifice “for sin,” namely, the kind of offering that is a goat, upon which sins were laid and which was sent into the wilderness. “Then,”

[Col. 0333D] that is, having considered that such sacrifices did not please God, “I said,” that is, he deliberated: “Behold, I come,” that is, I unite humanity to myself.

I come, specifically, in order to do your will, O God; and rightly must I come, because “at the beginning of the book,” that is, in the first psalm, where it says, “He will meditate on his law day and night,” and so forth, “it is written concerning me,” namely, that I should do your will—that is, fulfill the obedience enjoined: namely, pour out my blood for the restoration of the human race. I come to do your will, “my God,” and “I desired” to do it, “and I had your law,” that is, your commandments, “in the midst of my heart,” as it is read in the first psalm: “His will is in the law of the Lord.”

Alternatively, “in the heading of the book,” that is, in Christ’s divinity, which is the head of his humanity, it is “written,” that is, foreknown and ordained, concerning me, that I should do your will. Christ is called a book because he is set before us as an example, so that we may direct our ways according to his likeness.

I have spoken in my own person, and “I proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly,” that is, I caused the great Church itself to proclaim it: namely, that righteousness does not come from legal institutions but from you. “Behold, I will not restrain my lips,” that is, even if some wish to prevent my people from speaking, they will nevertheless not be silent concerning what is said on my behalf about the martyrs. And this is: “Lord, you knew,” that is, you so ordained it, or you knew that it would happen.

[Col. 0334B] In this verse the third part begins. I will neither fear anyone nor be silent, and this is: “I did not hide your righteousness in my heart,” like the one who hid his lord’s talent in the earth. “I spoke your truth,” that is, I will proclaim that you are truthful in all your promises, “and your salvation,” that is, that salvation for all nations comes from you.

Nor will I speak your truth only before a few, but “from the great council,” that is, from the multitude of heretics, “I did not hide your mercy and your truth.”

I will proclaim, and it is necessary that you, Lord, give efficacy to my proclamation. And this is: “But you, Lord, do not remove your mercies far from me,” nor should you distance them from me, because until now you have never distanced them. And this is: “Your mercy and your truth always,” that is, at every time of all the righteous, “have received me” in order to protect me.

Therefore you should not distance your mercies from me, “because evils,” that is, sins, “whose number is without limit, have surrounded me,” that is, those whom I proclaim and who are destined to become mine. Sins surround people when they approach them through evil thoughts. “And my iniquities,” that is, those of the people who are destined to become mine, “have seized me,” that is, they have brought those who will be mine into action. “And I could not see,” that is, those iniquities so oppressed them that they could not make any use of reason.

[Col. 0334D] “They have been multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” that is, they are innumerable like hairs. And he rightly compares sins with hairs, because when hairs were shaved off under the old law, people thought that sins were being erased. They have been multiplied to such an extent that “my heart,” that is, every power of my heart, “has abandoned me,” that is, has failed.

“Iniquities have been multiplied; therefore may it please,” that is, may it please you together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, “O Lord,” this word—namely, “to deliver me,” that is, deliver those whom I proclaim and who are destined to be mine from sins, O Lord. And you, Lord, whom I ask “to help me, look upon me,” namely, by cooperating with the misery of my people, so that if they wish to fast, you may fast, and so forth.

[Col. 0335A] Here he prays for his enemies. Help me and deliver me in such a way that those “who seek my soul with all their strength,” not in order to imitate it but “to take it away,” that is, to destroy it, may be ashamed of their sin. And this is: “Let them be confounded and put to shame,” that is, let them fear and honor the Lord—likewise those who wish to destroy me.

And not only those who seek to take me away, but also “those who wish me evil”: let them turn away from the evil path, so that they may be “behind,” that is, so that they may follow you, O God, “and turn back.”

And let “those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’” that is, who speak flatteringly to me, saying, “Things are going well for you,” “bear confusion,” that is, let them be ashamed. And let them bear it “immediately,” without delay. He says this to indicate the great confusion that will crush their pride

[Col. 0335B] as a burden crushes the one carrying it.

Let the enemies be converted, but let the friends “exult and rejoice,” namely, “all who seek you” and “those who love your salvation,” that is, the salvation which you accomplish. And let them “always say: ‘May the Lord be magnified.’”

Let them say of the Lord, “May the Lord be magnified,” but of themselves let them say: “I am a beggar,” that is, one seeking knowledge of God. And however much I labor for this, I am nevertheless always “poor,” that is, possessing an insufficient knowledge of God, which no one fully possesses in this life. Although I am thus poor, nevertheless “the Lord is concerned for me,” and I do not fail, because he supplies me with everything necessary.

And “you,” Lord, who “are my helper” in cooperating with me, [Col. 0335C] “and my protector” in defending me, “do not delay” in doing for me whatever you are going to do.

Alternatively, this may be read in Christ’s person as follows: “May the Lord God be magnified”; but I am a physician according to my humanity, “and poor,” that is, in need of your deliverance, never wealthy in these temporal things. Christ says this in order to set humility before all his own: since he calls himself poor, none of his followers should dare to presume upon himself. I am poor, but “the Lord is concerned for me,” that is, he keeps me free from sin and supplies everything necessary.

And you, Lord, who are my God and my protector, do not delay in doing whatever you are going to do through me—namely, restoring the human race, and so forth.

## ON PSALM XL: TITLE

*For the end; an understanding for the sons of Korah.*

“Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy.” During the rebellion against Moses and Aaron concerning Aaron’s priesthood, when Korah was burning incense with his sons, he himself and his sons were consumed by their own fire. Hence today those who unjustly rebel against their prelates are compared with the sons of Korah.

There were also some good men among the sons of Korah who, together with the other chief singers whom David appointed in the tabernacle, were highly effective in enlarging the worship of God by reciting psalms. Therefore Ezra, judging them worthy of remembrance, assigned their name as titles to certain psalms, while observing

[Col. 0336A] especially that the interpretation of the name suited the character of the psalm. For *Korah* is interpreted as “skull,” and because the Lord was crucified in that place, by the relation of container and contained we understand the cross of Christ. The sons of the cross—namely, the sons of Korah—are Christians, and especially the martyrs, who are never ashamed to confess him crucified.

The title is explained as follows: “Understanding,” that is, this psalm, which is called *Understanding* because it explains to us a certain understanding—a very secret matter—namely, that Christ was not simply human but also God. This kind of understanding is placed before the sons of Korah to be understood, that is, before the sons of the cross, directed toward the end, that is, toward Christ, if they understand these things.

The subject is Christ, God and human: according to his humanity, insulted; through his divinity, glorified. Its method is as follows. The psalm has three parts. In the first part he exhorts, with good promises, that Christ be understood as God beyond humanity. In the second part he explains why some thought him simply human, namely, because they saw him insulted in many ways. In the third part he makes us certain that he is more than human, namely, that he was God. His purpose is to admonish us to believe that he was God above humanity.

The voice of Christ saying: Understand me as more than human, because “blessed” is the one “who understands concerning the needy and the poor,” that is, who, when he sees me needy and poor, on account of which some thought that I was merely human, understands that I am God.

[Col. 0336C] And truly such a person is blessed, because “on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” from every evil. The day of judgment is called evil because evil things will be repaid to the wicked.

He offers a prayer for such a person who understands: on the day of judgment the Lord will deliver him, but meanwhile “may the Lord preserve him” from persecutors “and give him life,” true life through faith; and “make him blessed,” that is, happy, in virtues and also in temporal matters. And this is “on earth,” that is, in this life. And although enemies then envy him most intensely, “may he not deliver him into their souls,” that is, into their wills, even if God delivers him into the hands of “his enemies,” both spiritual and carnal—that is, the enemies of the one who understands.

And because it might seem impossible for anyone to be blessed in this wretched life, Christ prays

[Col. 0336D] that he may assist this understanding person in such a way that he can be blessed. The continuation is: I say, “make him blessed”; and in order that he may be blessed, “may the Lord assist” him—that is, give strength to the one who understands—so that he may make him “upon his bed of pain.”

He calls the bed animality, namely, a certain lower power of the soul, according to which the soul itself gives life to the body and makes it perceive. It is called a bed because a certain higher power of the soul, namely reason, rests upon it. It is a bed of pain because it makes its superior power consent to carnal pleasures according to all the bodily senses and to many unlawful movements, which reason grieves over.

But this bed, which we now call a bed of pain, was formerly a bed of joy and consolation. For while the first human being remained obedient, reason ruled over animality, so that animality, according to none of the bodily senses, was moved toward any carnal pleasure. In this subjection to reason, reason rested with joy. But after he departed from obedience, it became a bed of pain.

It should be understood that God implanted the higher power of the soul, namely reason, for this purpose: so that through it the human being might contemplate God. And this same reason ought always to rule over animality, as a man rules over a woman. The function of animality is to arrange earthly matters appropriately. It ought always to be an aid to reason and subject to it as to a man. To signify these two powers of the soul—one ruling and the other subject—God created male and female: the male was to rule, signifying reason;

[Col. 0337B] the female was to be subject, signifying animality.

I rightly call it a bed of pain, because “in his weakness,” that is, in the sin which the first man committed through disobedience, “you overturned his bed,” that is, that sensuality which had formerly been laid down, or subjected, to reason. You overturned it so that it now wishes to rule and to drag reason along with it into carnal pleasures. I call the bed overturned not according to one sense but “entirely,” that is, according to all the bodily senses. For human beings are now moved toward carnal pleasures according to all the senses.

You overturned his bed, but against this I pray for him. And this is: “I said” in heart and mouth, “Lord, have mercy on me,” that is, on my people. Specifically, “my soul,” that is, my people, “because I have sinned against you,” that is, against your honor, because you alone are that physician who alone can receive praise for the healing of sinners. Out of the great affection Christ has for his own, he attributes their sins to himself when he says this.

Here the second part begins, namely, he shows Christ insulted in many ways, on account of which some regarded him as merely human. The continuation is: I pray for my people in this way, but “my enemies,” who do not care about this, “spoke evil to me,” saying, “You have a demon,” and similar things. Among other statements they said: “When will this man die and his name perish?” that is, when will his reputation be destroyed?

Not only did my overt enemies speak evil to me, but also false friends. And this is: “And if someone entered” into my company “to see,” that is, to investigate whether he could find something by which to disparage me, “he spoke vanity,” like the one who said: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman this is who touches him” (Luke 7). I say that he spoke vanity, and therefore “his heart,” that is, his wicked will, “gathered iniquity for itself.” For he approached him in order to become better through goodwill, but instead became worse because he harbored an evil will toward Christ. He gathered iniquity for himself, that is, to his own harm.

The spy came in to me and, living with me, spoke vanity. The same man “went outside,” beyond my company, and “spoke about the same thing,” pursuing the very purpose he had while he remained with me: namely, to speak evil of me with all his effort.

Why should we run through every detail? “All my enemies whispered,” that is, secretly plotted, “against me,” that is, things hostile and harmful to me. Nor was plotting enough for them; they also “thought evil against me,” that is, each one carefully considered privately what more serious and harmful thing he could devise against me. These evils were “for me,” that is, they were turned toward my dishonor and toward the benefit of my people.

They not only whispered and thought, but also “established an evil word against me,” namely, they imposed a fixed sentence of death upon me.

[Col. 0338B] This was what Caiaphas judged while unknowingly prophesying: “It is better that one man should die, lest the whole nation perish” (John 11).

They judged me in this way, “but the one who sleeps”—the one who will hand his soul over to death, namely myself, and who can release it as lightly as a sleeping person releases sleep—“will he not add,” that is, will he not add to his death “that he may rise again?” He says of himself: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again” (John 10). Through the certainty of his resurrection he rebukes their folly.

And rightly my enemies thought to judge me. “For indeed the man,” that is, Judas, “of my peace,” that is, the one with whom I had peace, although he did not have peace with me, “in whom I trusted”—I ought to have trusted him according to the merits I had conferred upon him—“who ate my bread” materially, or “my bread,” that is, the refreshments of spiritual doctrine, “magnified,” that is, made great, “deception,” that is, betrayal, by giving me the kiss of betrayal, something none even of my enemies did. He “magnified” it, I say, “against me,” that is, to my humiliation.

Here the third part begins, namely, the glorification through which Christ may be recognized beyond doubt as more than human, that is, as God. The continuation is: They judged me in this way, “but you, Lord, have mercy on me” and, by having mercy, “raise me up, and I will repay them” for what they did to me.

And truly you will raise me up, “because you desired me,” that is, I have always been pleasing to you. “And by this,” that is, because you desired me,

[Col. 0338D] “I have known that my enemy will not rejoice over me,” that is, he will not retain me in death; if he could do so, he would prevail over me.

The enemy will not rejoice, but I will rejoice, because “you received me” into immortality and impassibility, “on account of my innocence, and you established me,” that is, placed me in such a state that nothing thereafter can harm me, “in your sight,” that is, in your presence—not there for a measured time, but “forever.”

And because he has exalted me in this way, therefore “blessed,” that is, praised, let “the Lord of Israel,” that is, the one who rules Israel, namely those who see God, be recognized as he is; and “God,” that is, the creator, of “Israel.” May this blessing begin “from this age,”

[Col. 0339A] and “into the age” that follows this age, “become”: “Let it be, let it be.” Here the Hebrew has *amen, amen*—“so be it, so be it.”

## ON PSALM XLI: TITLE

*For the end; an understanding for the sons of Korah; a psalm of David.*

“As the deer longs.” This psalm is called *Understanding* because it shows us something greatly in need of understanding: namely, that in the human being there are two powers, of which the stronger strengthens the weaker. It is set before the sons of Korah for speaking or singing—that is, before the sons of the cross, namely the holy martyrs, whose voice is heard in this psalm. Through it they are directed toward the end, that is, toward Christ.

The subject is the righteous person according to both powers of the soul. Its method is this: in the first part it is shown that, according to the higher power, he desires God, seeks only heavenly things, and does not fear the adversities of this life. In the second part, through that higher power, he strengthens animality, which is quickly disturbed by the troubles of this life.

Its purpose is to strengthen the weaker, so that they may not be moved according to animality but rather, through their reason, strengthen animality. The righteous who speak also present themselves as having fallen at some time, so that the weaker may not despair if they too should sometimes fall. First they begin by showing that their reason desires God, as follows:

O God, “so my soul desires you,” that is, the higher power of my soul desires to possess you, “as,” that is, as ardently as, “the deer desires” to reach “the fountains of waters.”

The nature

[Col. 0339C] of the deer is to draw a living serpent into its body through the breath of its nostrils. After the venom burns within it, it becomes tormented by thirst and runs to a living spring. Refreshed by it, it sheds its antlers and hair and becomes young again. In the same way, the saints, imbued with the devil’s venom, namely sins, run penitently to God, through whom they lay aside all oldness.

I say that the soul desires now, and that it has desired before, and this is: “My soul thirsted to possess God.” I call God a “fountain” because he is the origin of every good. I call the fountain “living” because he lives forever, and because he makes those who taste him live forever. Or he is called a fountain because he alone can rescue us from the power of the devil.

“And when shall I come before the face of God?” that is, into his presence, so that I may know him as he is. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). Then I, who in this life appear to be of no worth, will appear as I truly am.

I say, “My soul thirsted,” and while I thirsted I had refreshments supplied by animality, afflicted by the miseries of this life. And this is: “My tears,” that is, the tears of my animality, “were bread for me,” according to reason—that is, refreshments—“day and night,” that is, continually. I call them tears because they were obtained from this: “while,” that is, because, “it is said to me, ‘Where is your God?’” For the wicked think that the righteous do not possess God when they see them subjected to such tribulations.

“These things” that were mentioned—namely, that my soul thirsted and that it received refreshment from tears—“I remembered,” although earlier I had at some time forgotten them.

[Col. 0340A] Here he indicates that he had forgotten these things through his fall, and he removes despair from the weaker; or “I remembered” means that I frequently had them in thought. “And afterward I poured out my soul,” that is, I extended it even to the love of my enemies, yet in such a way that my soul remained “within me,” that is, within my power, so subject to my authority that my enemy could not steal it.

And therefore I poured it out in this way “because I will pass over to the house of God,” that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem. “I will pass over into the place of the tabernacle,” that is, into the Church, which is called a place because outside the Church there is no certainty, whereas those who are now in the Church possess, in a certain way, a certain faith. Or it is called a place because the righteous is always advanced to a higher degree of virtue.

I will pass into the place of the tabernacle, which is “wondrous,” that is, worthy of admiration; as it was wondrous that Lawrence endured such suffering.

I will pass, I say, to the house of God “with a voice of exultation and confession,” that is, with myself exulting and praising God. I call the confession “the sound of one feasting,” that is, for me it is as great a refreshment as song is a refreshment to those who feast. “Sound” means a sweet song, and here *sound* is in the genitive case, as though it meant “the sound of one feasting.”

Alternatively, I will pass into the house of God, led by a voice of exultation and confession—that is, by the voice of angels exulting and praising God—and this voice was for me the sound of one feasting.

Here the second part begins, namely, he strengthens his animality. The continuation is: Since I will pass with a voice of exultation, therefore you, “my soul,” that is, my animality, “why are you sad?” and “why do you disturb me,” the higher power? You sometimes make me, who am grieving, grieve with you.

Do not be sad, but “hope in God,” and you must do this “because,” having confessed, “I will still confess to him.” He is the one who is “the salvation,” that is, my Savior, made a participant “of my countenance,” that is, of my humanity: he is human “and my God,” that is, my Creator.

And therefore you must hope, because “my soul is troubled” “toward myself,” that is, my soul has been troubled from no other source than myself. Another translation states this clearly, reading: “by myself.” And [Col. 0340D] because it has been troubled by me, “therefore” I will remember you, O God, who can heal me, “from the land of the Jordan,” that is, from myself insofar as I became earth made fruitful through baptism.

We understand baptism through the Jordan because Christ was baptized in it, and from him baptism came forth for us. Baptism, irrigating us and washing away sins, makes us fruitful earth. And because *Jordan* is interpreted as “descent,” we note here the humility which we have in baptism, when we reject the devil’s pomp.

And I will remember you from the land of “the Hermoniim,” that is, from myself insofar as I separate and anathematize all the sects of heretics. For *Hermon* or *Hermoniim* is interpreted as “anathema,” namely, “from the little mountain,” that is, from myself, who have become a mountain according to the eminence of virtues, but nevertheless little according to my humanity. Hermon is a certain mountain not far from the Jordan.

And for this reason also I will remember you, because deliverance is promised in both the Old and the New Testament to those who hope in the Lord. And this is: “The abyss,” that is, the New or Old Testament, “calls to the abyss,” that is, to the other Testament. The New calls upon the Old as a testimony to itself; the Old calls upon the New to complete the things promised in the Old.

We understand the Testament through “abyss” because, just as an abyss is a great depth, so in the Testaments there is a great depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God. And each abyss displays the deliverance of those who remember the Lord.

That the abyss thus calls to the abyss we recognize “in the voice of your cataracts,” that is, in the preaching of the prophets and apostles. Cataracts properly are watercourses, namely, a place from which water flows and gushes forth. In the same way, the holy apostles and prophets are those from whom true doctrine flows down to us.

Likewise, I will remember you for this reason: because “all your lofty things,” that is, more severe punishments, such as death itself, “and your waves,” that is, lighter punishments, such as hunger and similar things, “have passed over me.” That is, although they overwhelm me in this life, they will nevertheless eventually pass away.

Having stated the reasons why he should remember, he gives [Col. 0341C] the reasons by which he can remember. The continuation is: I will therefore also remember, because “the Lord commanded,” that is, promised, “his mercy in the day,” that is, in prosperity, “and in the night,” that is, in adversity. I do not mean simply mercy, but “his song,” that is, such great and evident mercy that it confers great exultation upon us. Another translation has: “And in the night he manifested that mercy.”

He gives another reason by which he can remember. God gives me mercy, and “prayer is with me,” that is, I possess within me a means by which I can remember God. I call it prayer “owed to God,” that is, directed toward God’s honor. I call God the giver “of my life.” Through this prayer I will say to God, “You are my protector,” that is, you have received me, weak as I am, in order to protect me.

[Col. 0341D] Since you have received me, “why then have you forgotten me?” And he supplies the reason why God seems to have forgotten him when he says: “And why do I walk in sorrow?” Although he is sorrowful, this righteous person says that he continually walks toward God. Therefore he says that he is sorrowful “while,” that is, because, “the enemy afflicts me.”

The enemy not only afflicts me by doing evil, but also by reproaching me. And this is: “While my bones are broken,” that is, while I am so severely afflicted that my bones—that is, my strength and my endurance, as far as my people’s opinion is concerned—are broken, “my enemies who trouble me reproached me,” saying,

[Col. 0342A] “Where is your God?” every single day.

From all the causes set out above he draws a conclusion, as though he were saying: Because I have baptism from God, mercy and prayer within me, and the other things that have been mentioned, therefore you, “my soul,” that is, my animality, should not be sorrowful. And again: “Why are you sad, my soul?” as above.

## ON PSALM XLII: TITLE

*For the end; a psalm of David.*

“Judge me, O God.” This psalm suits David, that is, any righteous person afflicted by the miseries of this life, and directs us toward the end. Its subject is a martyr afflicted by many evils. It treats of him as follows: in the first part, the righteous person, thus afflicted, finally asks to be separated from the ungodly.

[Col. 0342B] In the second part, he affirms that he will enter God’s secret place. In the third part, he exhorts his animality to hope in the Lord. His purpose is to strengthen his own animality and the weak.

The voice of the martyr saying: “Judge me, O God.” And lest it be understood that he wants to be judged without qualification, so that God might consider what good and evil things are in him—which would be arrogance in any righteous person—he specifies how he asks to be judged: namely, “distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” that is, consider my entire life, distinguished and separated from the life of an unholy nation, and finally separate me from it, which is “deliver me,” something that will occur at the judgment, “from the unjust man,” that is, one who openly does evil, “and the deceitful,” that is, one who harms secretly.

[Col. 0342C] And you must deliver me, “because you are God, my strength,” that is, my Creator and the cause of all my strength. Therefore, “why have you rejected me,” that is, why do you permit me to be so troubled that I appear to have been rejected by you? “And why do I walk in sorrow while the enemy afflicts me?” as above.

Do not reject me; rather, “send forth your light” for judgment, “and your truth,” that is, the Son, who is called light because he enlightens us, and truth because he is true in all things. “For they themselves,” that is, light and truth, “have led me” already away from the devil’s household “and brought me to your holy mountain,” that is, made me a holy mountain of God. And lest we understand this righteous person to have already been placed in security, he adds: “And into your tabernacles,” that is, into the Church in which I serve you as a soldier.

[Col. 0342D] Here the second part begins. I have already been brought into the tabernacles, and through this I will finally “enter the altar of God,” namely, “to God,” that is, to Christ, “who makes my youth rejoice,” that is, who will make my youth young again by giving immortality and impassibility. Christ is called an altar because through him we offer our prayers to God.

And because I will enter, I will now “confess to you,” that is, praise you in this life, “on the lyre,” that is, through the mortification of the flesh. I speak to you, “my God.”

Here the third part begins. The connection is this: Since I will enter the altar of God, “why,” then, “are you sad, my soul,” that is, my animality? And the rest is as in the other psalm.

## ON PSALM XLIII: TITLE

*For the end; for understanding; a psalm of David for the sons of Korah.*

“O God, with our ears.” This psalm is set before the sons of Korah, that is, Christians, for the sake of understanding—namely, so that they may understand that through the temporal goods given to the ancient people were signified the spiritual goods now given to the Christian people and to be given more fully in the future. Through this understanding the sons of Korah are directed toward the end.

Its subject is the martyrs, who also speak. Its method is as follows: in the first part it sets out the goods God gives to this people, comparing them with the things he did for the earlier people, and showing that these goods are eternal whereas those were temporal. In the second part it sets out

[Col. 0343B] the evils this people endures in the present life, although in the future they will possess many goods. The fact that the righteous suffer temporal evils in this life stands in contrast to the fact that the righteous of the earlier people were delivered from bodily evils. In the third part he prays to be delivered from the evils of this life. His purpose is to invite us to patience.

The voice of the martyrs showing what good God did for the ancient fathers when they say: “O God, we have heard,” and not without understanding, but “with our ears,” that is, with understanding, which is the inner part of the mouth. And this was not from just anyone, but “our fathers,” that is, the patriarchs and prophets, “announced it to us,” not as something fictitious but as a true reality.

“They announced this,” namely, the work which you accomplished in their days, in ancient days. We shall read it in this way: Our fathers announced to us the work which you accomplished in their days, such as the crossing of the Red Sea and similar events, as well as what you did in ancient days, such as the creation of heaven and earth and what you did for Abel, Noah, and others.

This work—namely, “your hand,” that is, your operation—“destroyed nations.” He speaks of those who formerly inhabited the promised land. And “you planted,” that is, firmly established in the land of those nations, “them,” that is, our fathers. And lest those nations be thought weak, so that their land could easily be taken from them, he adds: “You afflicted the peoples” first “and then, after they had been afflicted in many ways, you expelled them.”

And lest the Jews attribute this to their own merit, he says

[Col. 0343D] that it happened to them not through themselves but through God. The continuation is: I rightly say that you, God, planted them, “for they did not possess that land in joy,” that is, through their own weapons and strength, “and their arm,” that is, their strength and power, “did not save them.” And if they could not save themselves from those nations, then still less did they possess the land of those nations by their own sword.

By the sword we understand human virtue; by the arm, power.

The arm did not save them, “but your right hand,” that is, the favorable outcomes which you gave them, as when the walls of Jericho fell while they were circling them, “and your arm,” that is, your strength, as when one of them put ten to flight, “and the illumination,” that is, the counsel by which you enlightened them, as when you caused them to overcome some of their enemies through ambushes.

This illumination was “from your face,” that is, proceeding solely from your will—not because you wished this on account of any merit of theirs, but acting in this way “because you took pleasure in them,” or in God the Father.

And because “you yourself” did this for them, “you are” my king and my God—“you yourself,” I say, “who command salvations for Jacob,” that is, for us who struggle and are signified by Jacob. Or Jacob means the Jewish people, who were called Jacob.

You are my king and our horn, and “in you we will scatter with our horn,” that is, with our defense; that is, we will cast away and disperse,

[Col. 0344B] our enemies, both carnal and spiritual. This will take place at the judgment, where the good are separated from the evil.

We understand the horn as defense because animals defend themselves with their horns. They brandish it, that is, separate animals from themselves. And “in your name,” because here we bear your name, namely, we are Christians, “we will scorn” also at the judgment those “who rise up” against us in this life.

Behold, in this verse he has already shown that we will possess eternal goods, which are far better than the temporal goods possessed by the ancient fathers.

And I rightly say that in you we will scatter and scorn our enemies, because we will never be able to do this by ourselves. And this is: “For I will not hope in my bow,” in my lesser strength, “and my sword,” that is, my greater power, “will not save me.”

[Col. 0344C] And truly neither my sword nor my bow will save me, because you alone will rather save me; and he says this: “For you saved us from those afflicting us” in this life—not only from those afflicting us, but “you also put to shame those hating us,” that is, you will put them to shame when it is said to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” This verse can be understood of what God does for his faithful in this life, so that it may be connected in this way: We can be confident that in you we shall winnow and despise our enemies, because you have already saved us from those afflicting us, so that they could not draw us back from the good; and you have put to shame those hating us because they could not make us like themselves. And because you saved us, therefore “we shall be praised,” not only by the good but also by the wicked, as when they say: “We fools considered their life madness; behold how they have been counted among the sons of God” (Wis. V). This praise will be “in God,” that is, to God’s honor; and we “shall confess to you,” that is, we praise you; and “in your name,” that is, because here we bear your name, “forever,” that is, eternally.

Here he begins the second part. In the end you will save us, “but now,” in this life, you have “rejected us,” that is, you have permitted us to be afflicted in such a way that we seemed rejected by you; “and you have put us to shame,” not because we suffered confusion and embarrassment in our conscience, but so far as concerns the eyes of human beings, who think us worthy of shame. And thereafter “you will not go forth,” that is, you will not visibly send your angel to fight with us “in our forces,” that is, in our armies, as [Col. 0345A] you did for our fathers, for whom the angels visibly fought.

You not only rejected us, but also turned some of us “away” from a good purpose, making “us turn back after our enemies,” that is, so that we followed our enemies. Then “those who hate us plundered us for themselves,” that is, they seized us for their own portion. And this is the greatest torment of the saints: when they see their own people thus drawn away from the faith.

You turned some away, “but us” who remained steadfast “you gave like sheep for slaughter,” which are assigned not for fruitfulness but solely for killing; and among the nations you scattered us “when we were driven from city to city,” that is, you handed us over into the hands of our enemies, so that in our tribulations they might acquire some for you.

[Col. 0345B] “You sold your people,” that is, your martyrs, “without price,” because sometimes you gained no human being at all through the death of the saints; and if you did sometimes gain some, they were few. This is what he says: “And there was no multitude in their exchanges,” that is, when God gives his own in order to acquire others. You also made us a reproach, not to strangers, who rarely see us, but “to our neighbors,” who often reproached us; and he unfolds this reproach in detail, saying: “A mockery and derision to those who are around us.” Mockery is made through the nose; derision through the opening of the mouth.

You made us a likeness for the nations, namely, so that they might curse others after our likeness and say: “May a curse such as Peter’s, [Col. 0345C] or Paul’s, or Lawrence’s, be upon you.” Or, you made us a likeness of Christ, so that just as Christ endured reproaches, so might we. He immediately gives one of the reproaches Christ endured: “A shaking of the head among the peoples,” that is, they mocked those over whom the peoples shook their heads, as was said above when they said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Mark XV; Matt. XXVII), and so forth.

Why should I enumerate each item? “All day long,” that is, continually, “my shame,” namely, the shame of my reproaches, “is before me.” He says “against” because, although the martyrs confessed themselves to be just, they should never have endured such reproaches. And to intensify the shame he says: “The confusion of my face covered me.” He touches upon the natural process by which, when a person suffers some embarrassment, the inner soul sends the blood outward so that it may cover itself. This confusion, I say, was inflicted “by the voice of one reproaching and reviling” the truth, “by the face of the enemy,” namely, by evil intention, “and of one persecuting,” namely, by the actual deed.

“All these things came upon us,” namely, so that they might oppress us; “yet we did not forget you,” but always kept you in continual remembrance. “And in your covenant,” that is, in your law, “we did not act wickedly,” but always conducted ourselves according to your commandments. And in this verse the great virtue of the martyrs is indicated.

When all these evils came upon us, “our heart did not turn backward,” that is, it did not despair, “and you did not turn aside”—that is, you did not cause “our paths” by which we walk toward you “to turn aside from your way,” that is, from your commandments. For we have always acted according to your commandments. Or, omit “not”; thus it is read: “You turned aside,” that is, you caused “our paths to turn aside from your way,” as above. Or it may also be understood in this way: “our paths,” that is, the works we have from ourselves—for of ourselves we can do nothing good—those paths “you turned aside,” that is, you showed them to be turned aside and different “from your way,” that is, from your works, since you never do anything except what is good.

You showed the paths to be different, “because you humbled us,” that is, afflicted us; in this each person recognizes that he is wretched and has nothing good from himself. The passage is connected with the other interpretation in this way: I rightly say that you did not make our paths deviate, or [Col. 0346B] made them hang from your way, “because you humbled us,” that is, showed us to be humble. This humiliation is “in the place of affliction,” that is, in this life, after which there is no place for correction. Indeed, you humbled us so much that “the shadow of death,” that is, death itself, “covered us,” that is, we were killed. Or “the shadow of death” means the heretics, because if they claim someone for their own body, he is immediately deprived of true life.

Therefore we have not forgotten you, because we know that “if we have forgotten the name,” that is, the honor, “of our God,” and if we have done something still more serious—namely, “if we have spread out our hands,” both inward and outward, “to a foreign god,” that is, one who neither created us nor did us any good—namely, if we have become idolaters, “God will investigate these things.” And [Col. 0346C] because someone might say: If you spread out your hands, he will investigate this because he sees it clearly; but if you have forgotten, he will not investigate it because he does not know it, he proves that he will also investigate forgetfulness when he says: “For he himself knows the hidden things of the heart.”

Here he begins the third part. We have not spread out our hands, and therefore you, Lord, arise; and he first gives the reason why he ought to arise: “because for your sake we are put to death all day long,” and to such an extent that “we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter,” namely, as though we were considered fit for nothing whatever except slaughter. Therefore, Lord, arise to free us. “Why do you sleep?” God is said to sleep when his own are not quickly delivered, although they do not fail. He asks, “Why do you sleep?” because, although we do not know the reason, there is nevertheless some reason why God does this. “Arise, Lord”; and although you now reject some, “do not reject us forever,” but restore to your Church those who now appear to have been cast out.

“Do not reject us,” I say, “and do not turn your face away,” that is, your knowledge, from those who have now been rejected. “Why do you turn your face away?” Here again he suggests that, although we do not know the reason, there is nevertheless a reason why God turns away, and why “you forget our poverty and our tribulation.” This refers to those for whom God sleeps, although they do not fail. He is said to forget their poverty when he does not strengthen their reasoning faculties and does not give them consolations for enduring tribulation, when he neither mitigates nor removes it.

[Col. 0347A] Do not forget our poverty and tribulation, but arise; and he gives the reason why he ought to arise when he says: “For our soul has been humbled in the dust,” that is, in consideration of the defect of the human race, whose defect is signified by dust, which a penitent places upon his head. For this reason you ought rightly to arise, and it is necessary that you arise, “because our belly,” that is, our carnality, “is clinging to the earth,” that is, has adhered to earthly things, namely, it desires these earthly things.

And therefore “arise, Lord, help us, and redeem us,” that is, give the price by which you may draw us away from the devil’s power, “for the sake of your name,” so that it may be enlarged; for, once redeemed, we shall spread your name among many nations.

## ON PSALM XLIV. TITLE

“To the end, for those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding; a song for the Beloved.”

“My heart has uttered.” This psalm concerns the dignity of the bridegroom and bride, and this is indicated in the title: “for those who will be changed,” that is, for the honor of the bride, in whom a change takes place from the world to God, which is good. There is another change, from God to the world, which is evil. “For the Beloved,” that is, for the honor of the Beloved. Solomon was called Jedidiah, that is, “Beloved”; he prefigured Christ, truly beloved by the Father. Hence it says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. III and XVII). It is a song because it deals extensively with eternal exultation, and it is called an epithalamium, that is, a nuptial song.

In the first two verses he uses the image of a minstrel wishing to enter a wedding and seeking the goodwill of the doorkeeper. Anticipating the wedding of Christ and the Church, and wishing to sing about it and, as it were, to be admitted, he prepares an audience for himself by saying that he has composed a little song about the wedding and wishes to sing to the king. He praises the bridegroom in four ways and the bride in four ways.

The title is explained as follows: This psalm is called a song because the prophet, foreseeing the future union of Christ and the Church, announces it in this psalm with great exultation; from this union great exultation arises for every faithful person who understands. It is a song, I say, composed for those who will be changed from unbelief to faith. For in this psalm the Church is especially commended; it is the Church itself [Col. 0347D] that will be changed. In this life the saints are changed when they pass from the body of the devil; finally, they will be perfectly changed when they are clothed with immortality and freedom from suffering.

It is a song, I say, proposed to the sons of Korah for understanding. For it was very necessary that the mystery still unknown to many—namely, the union of Christ and the Church—be understood by the sons of Korah, that is, the sons of the cross. It is a song composed not only for those who will be changed, but also for the Beloved, that is, for the honor of the Beloved, namely Christ, who is especially called “the Beloved.” For if some just person is called beloved on account of certain virtues, much more is Christ, who possessed nothing but goodness. His honor is treated in this psalm, since he is commended in many sections; and this song directs us toward the end.

Or construct it in this way: This song is composed for the sons of Korah who will be changed, proposed to all for understanding, and also for the Beloved. Its subject is the bridegroom and bride, namely Christ and the Church. Its method is this: In the first part it presents the commendation of the bridegroom, namely Christ; in the second part it presents the commendation of the Church. Hence Augustine calls this psalm an epithalamium, that is, a praise of the bridal chamber. Its purpose is to invite us to this union, namely, so that we may understand the union of Christ and the Church.

It is the prophet’s voice. Before proceeding to praise the bridegroom, he commends the praise he is about to offer when he says: “My heart has uttered.” [Col. 0348B] Here the prophet speaks by comparison with someone who is full, because a person who has eaten his fill cannot retain his food without belching it out. Thus the prophet, full of the Holy Spirit, necessarily uttered forth something in order to reveal it. He uttered, I say, “a word,” that is, the Son of God. For if anyone attends to the psalm, he will truly be able to recognize that Christ is the Son of God.

John uses the same name when he says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). The Word is “good,” singularly so, because God alone is good, and whatever is good comes from God alone. Hence Christ, when certain people, looking only at his humanity, called him good, replied: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Matt. X). And “to this king,” namely Christ, who is God, “I speak,” that is, I dedicate my works; I devote this entire praise of mine.

And this praise of mine is not to be rejected, because I do not speak from myself; rather, the Holy Spirit speaks in me as through an instrument. This is what follows: “My tongue is a pen,” that is, comparable to a pen. For just as a pen does nothing by itself unless someone writes through it, so neither does my tongue. It is a pen, I say, “of a scribe,” that is, of the Holy Spirit, who through me and through the other prophets writes God’s law in human hearts. He is a scribe “writing swiftly,” because what teachers cannot accomplish over many years, the Holy Spirit accomplishes in a moment—as in Paul, whom he taught the knowledge of the truth in a moment, as fully and completely as Christ taught the Apostles and others over many years.

[Col. 0348D] “I speak my works to the king,” that is, this little song, these works; and I rightly ought to dedicate them to him because he is “beautiful in form.” Although this could be understood of the external arrangement of his limbs, it must nevertheless be understood of his freedom from sins. He is beautiful, I say, “beyond the sons of men,” that is, more than the sons of the ancient fathers, because no one except him was free from sin.

In making another commendation of him, he turns toward him; and because you are so beautiful, “grace has been poured upon your lips,” that is, in your words, because those who received your preaching, and also received the preaching of your disciples, received grace—that is, remission of sins and other gifts of the Holy Spirit. When he says “poured,” he indicates [Col. 0349A] that this grace was sufficiently given in diverse ways. And because you are such, “therefore God blessed,” that is, exalted, “you,” leading you to his confession; and this exaltation will remain “forever.”

Having commended the king for his beauty, he commends him for his strength. The connection is this: You, such a king, “gird yourself,” that is, use forcefully, with the “sword,” that is, the word of preaching, concerning which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). Concerning it the Truth himself also says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Luke XII). This sword separates father from son. “Gird yourself,” I say, “upon your thigh,” that is, upon your humanity. We understand humanity by “thigh” because the place of generation is in the thigh. He says “upon your thigh” by comparison with some strong man girded with a sword upon his thigh. And lest we understand by “thigh” someone fragile, he says: “O most powerful one, gird yourself” to conquer the aerial powers.

Once you have prepared yourself to preach, “direct yourself,” that is, present yourself as intent on acquiring the kingdom through preaching; and “advance,” that is, having acquired one city, pass on to acquire another through your preachers. In doing this you will have prosperous outcomes, and this is what he says: “Prosper,” and, among those acquired, “reign.” Do this “in your appearance,” because you are free from sin and beautiful in virtues, “and in your beauty,” that is, because you are God. Appearance, form, beauty, and color are found in the face.

Because of your appearance and beauty you will reign, and [Col. 0349C] also “because of truth,” since through you and through your own you will preach nothing except truth; “and meekness,” because when reproaches are brought against you, you will answer nothing in return; “and because of righteousness,” that is, because of the performance of good works, both in yourself and in your own. You may confidently direct yourself, because “your right hand,” that is, the divinity united to you, “will lead you” from the people you have acquired to seek another, “wondrously,” that is, because everyone will marvel at you, or because you will perform wonders. We understand divinity in Christ by the right hand because divinity is the better part in him.

And by this you will also be able to acquire the kingdom, “because your arrows,” that is, your judgments, by which you pierce the hearts of your hearers, are “sharp,” that is, effective. According to this interpretation, God’s words are called arrows because [Col. 0349D] they secretly entice people to fear and love God. According to another interpretation, the sword is what makes people adhere to God openly and by an almost compelling argument.

And because you are thus equipped for battle, “the peoples of the enemies of the king,” that is, many of those who have been set among your enemies, “will fall,” that is, will be humbled, “under you,” “in the heart,” that is, in true understanding. Or otherwise: “The peoples will fall,” that is, will be humbled, “under you”; and where will they fall? “In the heart of the enemies of the king,” that is, in the same heart in which they previously acted as enemies toward you, the king.

Again he commends him because, among the people he has acquired, he now sits as a judge, as it were. The connection is this: The peoples will fall under you, and, O God, “your throne,” that is, your rest, is among them; in it you sit and also judge, not for an hour, but [Col. 0350A] “forever and ever.” Again he commends him because, exercising upright justice in his kingdom, you sit, and “the rod of your kingdom,” that is, the correction you exercise over those who are your kingdom, is “a rod of uprightness,” because if they go astray, you lead them back to the right way.

I rightly say that your rod is a rod of uprightness, because “you loved righteousness,” both in yourself and in everyone else, and you loved it to such an extent that “you also hated iniquity.” And so that you might be such, “therefore, O God, your God,” specifically, the one consubstantial with you, “anointed you with the oil of gladness,” that is, with the Holy Spirit. We understand the Holy Spirit by oil because, just as oil nourishes the flesh and penetrates to the bones, so the Holy Spirit nourishes the soul in which he dwells.

This anointing took place in the incarnation itself, when the Virgin’s womb was purified by the Holy Spirit. From this anointing there was especially great reason for rejoicing both for Christ himself and for all the saints. He anointed you “beyond your companions,” because neither the Apostles nor other spiritual men possessed as much of the Holy Spirit as you. Hence it is said that the Holy Spirit was given to Christ without measure.

He gives another commendation of Christ, according to his ornaments. You are anointed with the oil of gladness beyond your companions, and also “from your garments,” that is, from your humanity, or from your Apostles, who adorn and beautify you as a garment adorns its lord. From them proceeds “myrrh, drops, and cassia,” that is, good fragrances and a good reputation.

We explain the properties of each. Myrrh is an extremely bitter ointment that drives away worms [Col. 0350C] and preserves body and soul from the rottenness of vices. The drop is an herb that drives away swellings of the lung, that is, humility, which drives away inflation and every movement of pride. Cassia is an herb that grows in a watery place to great height and gives off a strong fragrance; that is, faith, which arises in the waters of baptism, grows greatly in the just, and gives others a good reputation.

All these things have proceeded to us from Christ’s humanity or from his Apostles, who set all these things before us in themselves as an example. These same things have proceeded to us “from ivory houses,” that is, from the holy Apostles themselves, who are called houses because God dwells in them. They are of ivory because they are bright through many cuttings and abrasions, like ivory; or they are compared to ivory because they are cold, that is, chaste, [Col. 0350D] like the elephant.
