All ivory is of such a cold nature that a burning coal does not burn a cloth placed upon ivory.

“From them” come the fragrances that “the daughters of kings” have offered to you in themselves; he says “daughters” either literally or with reference to the daughters of the Apostles. “And they delighted you,” namely, by pleasing you in this way; and they did so “in your honor,” that is, not glorying in their own deeds or baptisms so as to be called Petrines or Paulines, but looking to your name, they were called Christians.

He touches upon the history in which the Law commands that, when a brother dies without offspring, another brother should take his wife; and the seed is said to be raised up not for the living brother but for the one who died (Matt. XXII; Mark XII; Deut. XXV). Thus, when Christ died, his brothers, namely the Apostles, [Col. 0351A] took his own bride, namely the Church; and they begot children of the Church not for themselves but for Christ, so that those begotten would be called Christians, not Paulines or Petrines.

Here he commends the king through his bride. The connection is this: The king is as worthy as I have said, and for you, “the queen,” that is, the Church, “stood,” namely, prepared to serve, “at your right hand,” that is, among your more excellent goods, because she does not seek temporal things but heavenly ones. She stood, I say, “in a garment,” that is, well clothed and adorned with good works, “gilded,” that is, adorned through charity. Charity is signified by gold because, just as gold is more precious than all metals, so charity is more precious than all virtues. The queen is “surrounded,” [Col. 0351B] that is, full of virtue and “variety,” namely, of nations or of different orders, because some are clerics, others married, and so forth.

“Hear, daughter.” He proceeds to the second part, namely, to the commendation of the bride. Since the bridegroom is such, O you “daughter,” that is, O Church, “hear,” that is, understand the things announced; and “see” them fulfilled. Hear, I say, and hear with humility. This is what follows: “And incline your ear, and forget your people,” that is, the sects of the Gentiles or Jews, “and your father’s house,” that is, the conduct of the devil—namely, idolatry among the Gentiles and the legal rites in Judaism. The prophet properly calls the Church his daughter and the daughter of the other prophets, because the Church is founded upon the faith of the Apostles and prophets.

I say, forget them; and if you do this, “the king,” that is, Christ, “will desire your beauty,” that is, you, who are beautiful. And lest she say, “What concern is it of his where he should look?” he adds: You ought to pay attention “because he himself is Lord,” who rules every nation; and he is “your God,” that is, your Creator. You should also pay attention because “they will worship him,” namely, all the perfect.

“And,” if he desires your beauty, “the daughters of Tyre,” that is, of narrowness—namely, the Gentiles who are constricted by the immense multitude of their sins—“will entreat your face,” that is, they will ask God to grant them the ability to attain conformity with you, “with gifts,” by giving alms and doing other similar things. And not only the lesser among the Gentiles, but also “the rich of the people.” The Gentiles are called daughters rather than sons because they are soft and inclined toward vices like girls.

Or construct it in this way: He is your God, and many others will worship him with gifts; the daughters of Tyre also will entreat your face, all the rich of the people.

After showing the dignities of the bride herself, he shows her to be praiseworthy according to her inward qualities, not according to outward ones. The connection is this: The bride herself is so glorious, and “all her glory,” that is, all her beauty in which she glories, is “from within,” that is, from the interior, namely, in the virtues of the soul. She is, I say, “the daughter of the king,” that is, of Christ. Here he commends her according to her lineage.

I say, her glory is from within, and her glory is also the glory of good works “in [Col. 0352A] golden borders,” that is, in perseverance to the end, “golden,” that is, full of charity. Her glory also consists in this: she is “clothed in varieties,” that is, in different orders—of clerics, married people, and others.

Here again he commends her through succession. The connection is this: She is clothed in varieties, and “after her virgins will be brought,” that is, those whole in soul and body, “to the king,” namely, to serve God the king. By saying “they will be brought,” he indicates that they cannot reach that dignity by themselves unless they are brought to it by preaching and with the help of grace. “And her companions,” the queen’s companions—that is, those who, although not whole, are nevertheless continent, such as good widows and others—“will be brought to you,” O king. When he says “will be brought,” he indicates their great weakness, so that they cannot even be led unless they are carried, as it were, upon shoulders in humility. This bringing about occurs through the frequency of miracles and through persistent preaching. Hence the Apostle says: “Be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Tim. IV).

And those who are brought in this way will not have sorrow, but “will be brought in gladness and exultation,” because even in the present Church the saints rejoice greatly in the purity of their conscience. And from this present Church “they will be brought into the temple of the king,” that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem.

He explains by what means they are brought and led. The connection is this: Truly they will be led and brought through every succession, because there will always be some preachers. For “in place of your fathers,” that is, in place of the Apostles, [Col. 0352C] who begot the world in faith, “sons were born,” that is, other preachers succeed them, “for you,” that is, for your work, so that they may serve you. And you “will appoint them,” that is, establish them firmly in faith and work, as “princes,” that is, teachers and doctors, “over the whole earth,” that is, over the Church spread throughout all parts of the earth.

And once appointed in this way, “they will remember your name,” that is, your fame and glory, “in every generation,” namely, throughout every land in which the Church is spread, “and in the generation” that succeeds it.

Or thus: You will appoint them princes, and I will remember through them, that is, I will make them remember your name, and so forth.

And because of such fathers, who have also been appointed, [Col. 0352D] “therefore the peoples will confess to you,” that is, praise you, “forever,” that is, throughout the whole of the present life, “and also for an age,” the age following this “age.”

Or the whole psalm can be read in the person of the Father, according to Augustine, although Jerome says that this is done more from superstition than from the truth of the text. The Father speaks and commends the Son according to his divinity when he says: “My heart,” that is, my hidden and secret things, brought forth “a good word,” that is, my Son; it “uttered” him. He is especially good because no one is “good except God alone” (Matt. XX), in which the Son is indicated to be consubstantial with the Father. We understand the Father’s divinity by “heart” and the Son by “word” because, just as a human being’s heart is hidden and is made manifest through human words, [Col. 0353A] so the divine essence was hidden from the world until it was manifested through the Son in the creation of heaven, and especially when the divinity itself was united to humanity.

The heart uttered the Word, and to this “king,” who is both God and king, “I speak my works,” that is, I arrange all things with him, without whom I do nothing. By this the Son is shown to be almighty together with God the Father. Hence it is said: “Arranging all things with him” (Prov. VIII).

I do not merely arrange all things with this king; I also do all things through him. This is what follows: “My tongue,” that is, the Son himself, who is called the tongue just as he is called the Word, and who makes the divine essence manifest, is “the pen of a scribe,” that is, of me. For just as a pen without a scribe, and a scribe without a pen, accomplishes nothing, so we cooperate with “one writing swiftly,” because he spoke and they were made.

Here he begins the commendation of the Son according to his humanity, addressing the Son himself in an apostrophe. The connection is this: Such are you according to divinity; according to humanity, however, you are “beautiful in form,” as above, and the rest remains unchanged.

And properly according to this interpretation God says to the Church: “Hear, daughter,” because the Church truly was begotten by God alone and is called his daughter on account of this. Again, God the Father rightly says: “I will remember your name,” that is, “I will make them remember your name,” O king, that is, your praise.

## ON PSALM XLV. TITLE

“To the end: a psalm of David, for the sons of Korah, concerning hidden things.”

[Col. 0353C] “Our God is a refuge.” This psalm is attributed to the prophet David or to some faithful person from Judah, so that it may be a more certain testimony. It is proposed to the sons of Korah, that is, to those marked with the sign of the cross, directing them toward the end and composed for the revelation of hidden things. For in this psalm the coming of Christ is revealed, a coming that was hidden from many; the conversion of the Apostles from the Jews to him; the salvation of the Jews in the last times; and peace between God and humanity at the time of his birth. The subject is Christ’s coming, from which the other hidden things just mentioned proceeded.

The method is this: In the first part of the psalm he admonishes his own not to fear the disturbances of the world while trusting in his coming—disturbances that will occur because of Christ’s coming. In the second part he clearly shows that coming itself and the benefits that will arise from it. In the third part he admonishes everyone to attend to the works of this Lord. The purpose is that all should place the hope of their liberation in the Lord’s coming. This purpose is indicated in the first part of the psalm: “We will not fear when the earth is disturbed.”

This is the voice of the prophet, or of the faithful soul inviting in this way: Other people reign for the sake of power, wealth, or any worldly thing; but “our God,” made such through the humanity he assumed, is “our refuge,” in that he protects us from evils so that diabolical temptations do not overcome us, “and strength,” that is, supplying endurance and steadfastness and making us unconquerable. And lest it seem that God abandons us after giving steadfastness, so that we immediately fail, he adds: “A helper in tribulations,” [Col. 0354A] that is, so that we may not only avoid being conquered but may also be able to conquer others. These tribulations “found us,” as though we had been exposed without any assistance, like orphans, “exceedingly,” that is, so grievous that they even reached the shedding of blood.

“Therefore,” because God is our refuge, strength, and helper, “we will not fear,” although there would nevertheless be reason for fear, “when,” that is, because “the earth will be disturbed,” that is, Judea, which is called earth because through the Law and the prophets it was established, made firm, and cultivated. “And then the mountains,” that is, the Apostles, “will be transferred” into the sea, that is, the Gentiles; and not merely to the Gentiles by dwelling among them, but also “into the heart of the sea,” because they will place faith in the hearts of the Gentiles.

We understand the Gentiles by “sea” [Col. 0354B] because they are always in turmoil and in pursuit of earthly things; they are tossed about and are avaricious in their vices. Or the phrase refers to those who are deeper in paganism, because even some of the more wicked were converted.

“Its waters roared,” I said; we will not fear when the mountains are transferred. And because this would not seem to be something to fear, he shows what should be feared. The connection is this: I say that the mountains will be transferred, and then “they roared,” that is, those Apostles will resound in preaching; “and their waters,” that is, the waters of the sea—for he refers to the signification when he says “their”—“were troubled” against the Apostles.

By “waters” he understands teachings or peoples. Or interpret it in this way: Once the Apostles had been transferred to the Gentiles, “their waters,” that is, the various peoples of the Gentiles, “roared,” that is, cried out against the Apostles. And for this reason “the mountains,” that is, the holy Apostles, “were troubled in its strength,” that is, in the strength of paganism, through the severe torments that the Gentiles inflicted upon them.

Or the mountains are understood as the more important people among the Gentile population, who were troubled in “his strength,” that is, God’s strength: they are indignant when they hear of God’s miracles, or they are troubled against themselves by their own disgrace, or against his Apostles by their cruelty.

Here the second part begins: “The river.” Here is a diapsalma. The connection is this: “The mountains will be troubled in its strength,” but against this disturbance there is “the force of the river,” that is, an impetuous river, namely, the Holy Spirit. He is called a river because he extinguishes the desires and burning passions of the flesh. He is impetuous because no one can resist him.

That impetuous force “makes glad the city of God,” that is, the Church, which is called a city because, just as every newcomer is received into a city, so everyone is received into the Church. Likewise, just as a city is fortified with towers, so the Church is made glad by the Apostles and by virtues, because God strengthens them through the grace of the Holy Spirit against the tribulations inflicted upon them. I say that he makes it glad, and also “the Most High,” that is, God himself, “sanctified” by giving an increase of virtues, “his tabernacle,” that is, the present Church. It is called a tabernacle because in the present life one wages war for the Lord.

“God is in the midst”: Having shown certain benefits that would come through his coming, he now announces it clearly. The connection is this: I say that God sanctifies and makes glad, [Col. 0355A] and behold by what means he does this: “God” became human and is “in the midst of it,” that is, of the tabernacle—not in the middle with regard to physical location, but “in the midst,” that is, common to all, because he is offered equally to everyone.

Or he is “in the midst” because he is the column that supports all the parts of the Church. Therefore the tabernacle itself “will not be moved” from good to evil. And he not only supports it so that it does not fall, but “God will help it,” the city, to act well and also to overcome others. He will do this “in the morning,” that is, at the beginning of conversion; and he will do it “at dawn,” that is, through dawn, namely, by administering the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Or interpret it this way: “He will help in the morning.” I do not merely say “in the morning,” that is, after the light has increased somewhat, but “at dawn,” that is, at the very beginning of conversion. Another translation has: “God will help it with his countenance,” that is, with the incarnate Son, who is therefore called the countenance of God because he is consubstantial with him and a complete representation of him.

“Disturbed”: not only is the Church firm because God is in its midst, but for this same reason the “nations are disturbed” when they hear these new things being preached; and the rulers, namely, the “kingdoms,” or whatever regions are meant, “are bowed down,” that is, humbled, because the preaching now pleases them and they now wish to receive the faith. They are bowed down because “he gave his voice”; therefore “the earth was moved,” that is, earthly people were moved to conversion. I say, “he gave his voice”—and who gave it?

“The Lord of hosts,” that is, the one who is of the angels and is with us, possessing our humanity; and through this he is “our helper,” because he led us from the lowliness of this life and its miseries to the dignity of his Church. In this it appears that he himself is the “God of Jacob,” because in us he fulfilled what he prefigured in Jacob: just as he, by giving present things, bought and supplanted his brother’s blessing, so the Church of the Gentiles supplanted what had been promised to the former people and, by giving present things, obtains heavenly ones—namely, through almsgiving and other good works.

“Come.” Here he begins the third section. Since he is with us as our helper, therefore you Gentiles, “come” to this Lord by accepting the faith, and then “see,” that is, understand, “the works of the Lord,” just as he himself says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” I speak of the works “which the Lord has set forth as wonders,” that is, as a sign. Wonders are called those things in which something other than what appears is signified: “upon the earth,” that is, in the world. These wonders are such because the Lord himself is “taking away wars to the ends of the earth”—literally, because when he was born there was the greatest peace throughout the world—not merely so that this might be said of that earthly peace, but of the peace signified by it, which Christ established between God and humanity, destroying the enemy who had risen up against human beings, namely, idolatry and the observance of the old Law, through which Jews and Gentiles were at variance. He made both one, and that peace of God was not confined to one land, but extended to the ends of the earth.

He will take away wars because he will “break the bow,” that is, deceitful attacks against the faith—namely, the deceptions of threats and flatteries—“and shatter the weapons,” that is, open attacks, “and burn the shields,” that is, the arguments by which they defend their heresies, “with fire,” that is, with the ardor of the Holy Spirit. In other words, he will kindle with the fire of charity those who previously attacked the truth deceitfully and openly and defended their sects.

He will burn them, I say, by saying: “Be still,” that is, empty yourselves of evil works, “and then see,” that is, understand through purity of life and manifest miracles, “that I,” dwelling among you and being such, “will be exalted among the Gentiles,” because, converted at the end, they will exalt me, “and I will be exalted in the earth,” that is, among the Jews. Here he prophesies the conversion of the Jews in the last times, concerning which it is said: “And the remnant of Israel will be saved” (Romans IX). He will shatter and burn, and he will rightly be able to do this, because he is “the Lord of hosts,” as above. And, being with us, he is “our helper, the God of Jacob.” Above he placed this verse for the correction of the preaching; now he repeats it to show that he is such a one as can accomplish these things. Or he repeats it because the entire psalm’s meaning is contained in this verse, and such a verse is an intercalary verse, that is, one repeated.

## ON PSALM XLVI. TITLE

A psalm of David, for the sons of Korah, unto the end.

“Clap your hands, all nations.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who here speaks in the person of the apostles. I say that the psalm is set before the sons of Korah, directed “unto the end” through this. Its subject is Christ ascending.

Its structure is as follows. In the first section he shows that God entrusted his inheritance to his apostles. In the second he sets forth Christ’s ascension. His purpose is to make us certain of the ascension: since he shows such dignity belonging to humanity that these men obtain the office Christ previously held, they may confidently believe that they too will ascend after him. Thus he begins.

One of the apostles, considering the dignity that humanity possessed, urges them to rejoice, saying: O you, “all nations, clap your hands,” that is, perform good works with rejoicing, and “sing joyfully to God,” that is, conceive in your minds such praise of God as cannot be expressed in words, so that this shout of joy may be “with a voice of exultation,” that is, do not merely praise God in your hearts, but also proclaim him with an exultant voice together with others.

“For the Lord.” You ought rightly to praise him, “for he himself is Lord,” that is, he will rule over every creature; “most high,” because he is powerful and effective in carrying out his will. And do not put your confidence in his goodness if you have done evil, because he is “terrible”: for he will be the judge who punishes the ungodly. He is “king,” because he rules his own well; “great,” because he rescues his own from the gravest dangers; “over all the earth,” because there is no part of the earth where he does not rule.

And this king is especially worthy of praise because “he subjected peoples,” that is, the Jews, “to us,” making them obedient to our preaching, “and the nations,” that is, Gentiles converted to the faith, “under our feet,” that is, he subjected them fully. Or “under our feet,” that is, under us who are feet—namely, travelers carrying God’s Gospel throughout the world.

And those whom he subjects he “chose,” that is, not on account of their merit, but by his grace alone he freed them from the mass of sinners. He chose these, I say, as “his inheritance,” whose fruits would enrich him in himself. He chose them “for us,” that is, for our work, so that we might be substituted in his place, as an inheritance—“the beauty of Jacob,” that is, like Jacob wrestling with vices. Or “the beauty of Jacob,” that is, what was signified through Jacob. This is great, because he is “the one whom he loved,” or because he chose the beauty that he loved.

Here the second section begins. He chose us—and why for us? Because “God ascended amid jubilation,” amid the exultation of the apostles who witnessed it, an exultation that could not be expressed in words. And because he ascended into heaven, he appointed us vicars of his inheritance; “and the Lord himself” ascended “with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, with the manifest voice and exultation of the angels. This is the angels’ voice: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts I).

And because he is such, “sing praise” in your minds to the honor of our God. Or, because the matter he was urging was extremely worthy, it is not enough to say it only once; and do not sing praise to him only because he is God, but also sing praise because he is ours—“God,” namely, of all the faithful. Or “king of all the earth,” that is, expelling all earthliness and ruling his own through virtue. Therefore “sing praise wisely,” that is, not for any earthly things, but for possessing him himself, discerning with great discretion what is to be done, when, why, and how.

And this same one “will reign” at last, namely, when his body has been completed, “over the nations”; but God himself also—not, I say, over the wicked, but “over the holy seat,” that is, over the angels and archangels, and over the souls of the saints in whom God already sits without any iniquity and judges.

And to him “the princes of the peoples have been gathered,” that is, they will be gathered, literally. Or these are the princes because they rule themselves well in virtues and urge other peoples toward good works. They will be gathered, I say, “with the God of Abraham,” that is, because Abraham will then appear, when God fulfills what he promised Abraham, saying: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Genesis XXII; Galatians V). There the psalm’s purpose is indicated. And they will be gathered for this reason, “because the strong gods”—that is, the apostles and preachers, who are “strong” in enduring adversities—“have been greatly exalted,” that is, judged worthy, in miracles and virtues and preaching. For this reason many will be gathered with the God of Abraham.

## ON PSALM XLVII. TITLE

A psalm, a song, for the sons of Korah, on the second day of the week.

“Great is the Lord.” This psalm is set before the sons of Korah for understanding. It is called a song because it concerns a matter over which we ought especially to rejoice: it explains to us the great dignity of the Church, namely, the Church’s expansion throughout the whole world. I say that the psalm is assigned to the second day of the week, that is, it concerns what is signified by the event that occurred on the second day of the week—namely, the foundation of the Church, which is signified by the foundation of the earth, made on the second day.

On the first day light was separated from darkness, signifying Christ’s resurrection, by which the light of immortality was separated from death. On the second day the firmament was founded, signifying the time following the resurrection, during which the holy Church was founded.

The voice is that of the prophet; or, if the words are included in the title, we shall say: This psalm belongs to the sons of Korah, that is, to the Church of the perfect, who speak in this psalm. Its subject is the Church as it is to be expanded.

Its structure is as follows. In the first section he praises the Church in many ways: through its founder, and also through the fact that certain people who wished to destroy it, recognizing its dignity, were converted to it. Then he praises it through one of its distinctive gifts, namely, that God’s mercy dwells in it. In the second section he invites those who are mute to magnify it, and those who are outside to approach it. His purpose is to urge everyone to magnify this city.

The prophet invites others in this way: Enlarge this city, because the Lord of this city is “great,” according to the power by which he does all things; “worthy of praise,” according to the fact that he does all things fittingly and skillfully; “exceedingly,” that is, more than the human mind can conceive or the tongue explain. And the fact that he is great and worthy of praise is especially perceived “in the city of our God,” that is, in the building of the Church, which is fortified by virtues, enlarged by charity, and gathered through faith for living rightly—not the city of the Babylonians and confused heretics, but “of our God.”

Here he praises the city through God as its craftsman and possessor. The city is set “on his holy mountain,” that is, on Christ, his Son, the Son of God the Father; or on the mountain of virtues; or on steadfastness.

This city is possessed by such a Lord and constructed from stones of this kind, namely, from Jews and Gentiles. It is “founded,” that is, firmly built, “in the exultation of the whole earth,” that is, from inhabitants of the entire world rejoicing over the remission of sins. He explains this by the different regions of the earth: “Mount Zion,” that is, the Jews, whose royal capital was in Zion, and “the sides of the north,” that is, the Gentiles, who formerly surrounded the coldest devil like his familiars. These are “the city of the great king,” who rules everything according to his will.

The devil is compared with the north because he remained cold toward the fervor of God’s love when he thought: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will place myself before the divine will, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV), that is, “I will reign”—in the coldness of my wickedness, just as he himself exists in truth.

“God will be known in her houses”: another commendation. This city is thus founded, and “in her houses,” that is, in each of the faithful, who are called houses because the Lord dwells in them, “God will be known,” because they possess full knowledge of God. This will happen when he “receives her” into dignity.

“For behold.” Truly the Lord will be known by her, and he will receive her, “for behold,” that is, manifestly, “the kings of the earth have gathered together,” that is, the powerful of this world, not merely in one place, “and have come together for one purpose”—the purpose of harming the city.

They gathered together to destroy it, but instead they increased it. This is what he says: “They, seeing,” that is, understanding that it is “thus” worthy, as was stated above, “were amazed,” struck by the light of such dignity; “they were disturbed” on account of their sins; “they were moved” to the faith and to good works; and “trembling,” bodily trembling because of fear of future punishment, “seized them.” Or, “they, seeing thus,” that is, immediately, “were amazed.” Another translation confirms these things, which has: “then.”

There, that is, in that very trembling, are “pains,” that is, anguish of mind, “like that of a woman in labor,” that is, extremely severe. Yet the outcome is joyful. For just as a woman, although burdened in giving birth, rejoices after a child has been born into the world and forgets that distress because of her joy (John XVI), so penitents, although previously oppressed, forget their former distress after they come to good works.

Therefore they were moved and disturbed because “in a vehement spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit, “you will crush,” O God, “the ships of Tarshish,” that is, those who explore their joy, which is confined to earthly things. For Tarshish is interpreted as “the exploration of joy,” on account of the riches they sought throughout the world. According to Jerome, Tarshish is the same as Carthage.

He says “ships” by way of comparison. For just as ships are driven here and there by storms, so lovers of the world are swept along by various anxieties. The Holy Spirit, as though violent, destroys this disposition in them, though none of their prior merits precede it. Some books have “the ships of Tharsi”; Tharsis is a city of Cilicia, from which Paul came. Herod broke its ships because the Magi passed through them and, after worshiping the Lord, fled. Yet this historical account is not found in the text, but only the allegorical sense is present.

“As.” Since all these things have been accomplished in the Church, therefore the prophecy made concerning it has been fulfilled. “As we have heard,” foretold by the prophets, “so we have seen” it fulfilled “in the city of the Lord of hosts,” that is, of the one who rules over the heavenly hosts and sends these hosts—namely, the apostles themselves—to guard his city. I speak of the city “of our God,” that is, of the one who recreates us a second time.

And what have we heard and seen? This, namely: “God founded it forever,” that is, he firmly established it through his preaching and angelic guardianship, leading it into his eternity.

“We have received your mercy, O God.” He commends the Church through that distinctive gift, the Son of God. I say that God founded the Church precisely because, O God, “we have received your mercy,” that is, your Son. He calls him mercy because, apart from him, we have no mercy. He is “in the midst of your temple,” that is, equally offered to all who wish to approach him. Some received him bodily in the temple, namely Simeon and Anna; others received him spiritually.

“According to.” Since we have received that mercy, therefore “according to your name,” that is, according to the fact that your name had spread throughout the earth—for you were called the creator of all things throughout the whole earth, although they themselves pretended that there were other gods—“so also your praise” has spread “to the ends of the earth.”

And he specifies by whom he is praised, namely, by the just, and by those many people. This is: “your right hand is full of righteousness,” that is, your propitiation is full, because it justifies many, and all praise you.

Here the second section begins. Since the right hand is full of righteousness, therefore “let Mount Zion rejoice,” that is, the faithful Jews who received the first rays of the rising sun, “and let the daughters of Judah rejoice,” that is, the Gentiles born in faith from Judah, that is, from the apostles. They are called daughters rather than sons because greater reverence and diligence are shown toward them: “because of your judgments, O Lord,” namely, because by a just judgment you blind some and admit the Gentiles, or reject certain people.

“Surround,” that is, honor, “Zion,” that is, the Church; “and embrace her” with the arms of charity, preserving the virtues and practices by which, once they have been received, you may “tell,” that is, preach, the name of the Lord, being “in her towers,” that is, imitating the apostles, so that your preaching may differ in nothing from the apostles’ teaching.

“Set your hearts”: do not merely preach, but also “set your hearts on her strength,” that is, conform yourselves to their steadfastness; “distribute her houses,” that is, establish various ranks within her—namely, the archdeaconate, the presbyterate, and all married people. Or “distribute her houses,” namely, by giving each prelate his own parish. Do this “so that you may tell it to the next generation,” that is, so that, passing down from generation to generation, you may make it endure until the end of the age.

“For.” Tell this, namely, “for this is God” who does these things for the Church that have been described. He is also “our God,” a God who will endure “forever,” that is, until the end of the world, “and throughout the age of ages,” that is, the age following this age. And he himself, being such, “will rule us,” leading us into “eternal ages.”

## ON PSALM XLVIII. TITLE

A psalm of David, for the sons of Korah, unto the end.

“Hear this, all nations.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here, and is set before the sons of Korah for understanding. Its subject is Christ, the Redeemer—not of the wicked, but of the just.

Its structure is as follows. First he gives a prologue commending the matter he is about to discuss. In the second section he presents Christ as Redeemer—not of the wicked and lovers of the world, but of the just—and in the same section, reproving their folly, he points out the vanities to which the lovers of this age are devoted. In the third section he warns the poor and just not to concern themselves with these rich people, because their riches will quickly perish. His purpose is to invite contempt for the world.

Since he was about to speak of an unusual matter, he invites everyone to listen, saying: “Hear this, all nations.” At once he captures their attention, and he rightly urges them to listen because he was about to speak of a great matter. He rightly invites everyone because, if they pay attention, what he is about to say will benefit all. He calls them all Gentiles, and he says not merely “hear” with the external ear, but “receive it with your ears,” that is, understand diligently. And you “all who inhabit the world,” that is, Jews who inhabit the promised land, hear this and receive it with your ears.

And because someone might say, “It does not benefit those who are deeply wicked to hear;” he says: You also, “earthborn,” that is, all who are earthly, as though sons of the earth, hear this, because if you wish to pay attention it will benefit you. And because the good might say, “Let the wicked hear, since they need it; we no longer need it, because we are good,” he also urges them to listen, because no one is so good that he cannot be made better, saying: “and sons of men,” that is, imitators of rational human beings, hear this.

And why should I enumerate individuals? Let “rich and poor” hear this, directing themselves “toward one thing,” that is, toward the same desire to listen. He chose these two conditions, rich and poor, especially because he will deal with them in the psalm.

“My mouth.” Here he makes them receptive to instruction by setting forth what he is about to say. The connection is: You ought to listen because “my mouth will speak wisdom and understanding.” Here he announces great things, because divinity treats of nothing other than wisdom and understanding. Wisdom is knowledge of divine things; understanding is instruction in conduct.

The prophet announces wisdom here, where he announces Christ, the Son of God, as Redeemer. He forms conduct when he teaches that worldly things are not to be attended to, that the riches of the rich are to be disregarded. And lest someone say, “You need not listen to these things because you present them without meditation,” he shows that he speaks after reflection when he says, “and the meditation of my heart,” that is, whether I speak wisdom or understanding, I do so through diligent application of the mind.

“I will incline”—namely, when I speak from meditation, it will not come from myself, but I have as my teacher the Holy Spirit. Concerning him he says: “I will incline my ear,” that is, I will incline and humble the understanding of my heart, so that with humility I may listen to a certain teacher of mine, namely, the Holy Spirit, speaking to me “in a parable.” And just as the prophet hears in a parable, so I will speak in a parable.

A parable is a saying in which one thing is said and another is understood. He speaks in this way because it was not fitting for divine Scripture to be open to everyone, lest it be trampled by enemies of the truth. “And I will open my proposition,” that is, the one whom above all I propose to follow, or the one whom I propose to make manifest in this psalm. I will do this “with the psaltery,” not only in words but also by good example, so that what I teach with my mouth I may fulfill in my works.

Here the second section and the narrative begin. The prophet speaks in the person of the wicked, saying: I will indeed fear “on the evil day,” that is, at the judgment. And “why will I fear?” Someone may say: “I have committed theft or murder; surely I shall not fear on that account, but because ‘the iniquity of my heel,’” final iniquity, “‘will surround me,’” that is, will show on every side that I deserve condemnation.

No iniquity condemns if it is abandoned and cleansed before the end. He speaks in accordance with what the Lord says to the woman deceived by the serpent: “The serpent will lie in wait for the woman’s heel, and the woman will crush the serpent’s head” (Genesis III). That is, the devil will lie in wait for the end of a human being in order to deceive him at the end; a person crushes the devil’s head—that is, his ambushes—if he avoids vices.

He has proposed iniquity and explains it in detail, showing that all iniquities are either external or internal to a person. Thus, if a person commits murder, he does so either to obtain possessions or to display his strength.

As though someone were saying: “You say that we should fear, but why should we fear, when you present a living Redeemer who ought to be feared by no one?” The prophet breaks their presumption in this way: Truly, if the iniquity of the heel surrounds them, they must fear, because “a brother,” that is, Christ, possessing our nature, “does not redeem” those “who trust in their own strength,” that is, those who do not give thanks to God for their strength and power but place their trust in those things themselves, “and” those “who glory in the multitude of their riches,” if indeed they persist in this. And if Christ does not redeem such people, will “a human being” redeem them? Certainly not.

Truly he will not redeem them, because “he will not give God his propitiation,” that is, he will not be able to make God favorable toward the wicked through any prayer or offering. Christ, however, makes God favorable toward his friends by presenting our humanity to him.

“And” no human being “will give God the price of the redemption of his soul,” that is, no price will enable him to redeem it, because only Christ’s body was found suitable for effecting redemption. And because Christ does not redeem such people, nor can a human being redeem them, they have not merely something to fear, but “that unredeemed person will also labor forever.” And just as the prophet earlier shattered the presumption of the wicked, so here he destroys their error—those who do not believe in the resurrection of the dead. I rightly say that he will labor forever, because “to the end,” that is, until temporal death, “he will still live.”

And therefore he will also labor because in this life “he will not see destruction,” that is, condemnation, since he has seen “the wise,” that is, just men, “dying” a temporal death. Or “the wise,” that is, worldly philosophers. He will not see destruction, I say, but “the foolish and the senseless will perish together.” The senseless person is one who does not believe that punishment is to come; the foolish person is one who, although he believes it, nevertheless does not take precautions.

He then points out the vanities to which these people are devoted in the world, marking their folly in them. The connection is: They will perish, “and they will leave their riches to others,” that is, to strangers, or even to their sons—yet to others, because once a person has perished, riches are of no greater value to a son than to a stranger. “And their tombs,” that is, pyramids and mausoleums, which they build like great houses, as though their tombs ought to be “their houses forever.” In this he marks their great folly: through such tombs they thought they were acquiring eternal remembrance.

“Their dwellings,” that is, their great houses, “remain from generation to generation.” Here too they appear foolish, building such enormous palaces. And they “called their names upon their lands,” namely, around their tombs.

He touches upon the custom of the Gentiles, who, when they were dying, hired certain people to invoke their names around their burial place on appointed days. And when they caused others to invoke their names in this way, they themselves are said to invoke their own names in this matter. In this the prophet marks their great folly, because although they thought by this means that they would possess eternal remembrance, it nevertheless took place only in their earthly lands.

The entire verse is to be read under one construction in this way: “Their dwellings, destined to endure from generation to generation, they called their names,” that is, their personal names, so that one might say “the palace of Tiberius” or “the tower of Crescentius.” They did this so that they might be remembered, although their memory existed only in their own lands.

They pursue all these vanities in this way, yet God is not to be blamed, for he established them with reason; they themselves were unwilling to understand. This is: “When a human being was in honor,” that is, in reason, by which he was like God, “he did not understand,” that is, he did not act intelligently. Therefore, by the wise, he was “compared with senseless beasts,” namely, in nothing except senselessness; and he is rightly compared with them because “he became like them.”

“These” evils, and the others that constitute “their way,” are “a scandal to them,” that is, an offense leading them to destruction. “And afterward,” that is, when these evils “please them,” that is, when they please themselves in them, “in their mouth,” because what they say with their mouth they confirm through their deeds.

Another translation has: “In their mouth they will bless.” This is read in the following sense: Although they do these evils, afterward they bless God, praising him with their mouths for their prosperous successes—not with the mouth of God, because God does not receive the praise of a sinner.

Such people “have been placed in hell.” The prophet rightly says that they have been placed in hell, because he knew in advance, in divine Providence, that they were to be placed there, “like sheep,” that is, like sheep. For just as sheep are often beaten, again and again, while the substance remains, so they will always be afflicted with punishments, yet their substance will not perish.

“Death will also feed upon them,” that is, the devil will feed upon them; he speaks by comparison. For just as a meadow is consumed by grazing while its roots remain, so it will be with them. “Feeding” is also used in another sense, as when a shepherd says, “I feed the flock.” Similarly, death—that is, the devil—will feed upon them, that is, lead them from one punishment to another.

“And in the morning,” that is, at the judgment, when the just will appear as light, “the just,” who in this life were oppressed by them, “will rule over them,” because they will be their judges. “And their help,” which they have in this life, “from their glory,” namely, from their power and riches, “will grow old,” becoming like an old garment that has no usefulness, “in hell.”

The just will rule; “nevertheless, God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell,” that is, from the devil’s power. He will do this “when he has received me,” that is, when he has received my humanity.

The third section begins here. The connection is: The unjust will be condemned in this way, while you, O God, will redeem the souls of the just. Therefore, human being, “do not be afraid when a man becomes rich,” and not only when a man becomes rich in himself, but also “when the glory of his house is multiplied,” that is, when each person of his household is multiplied in glory, namely, in riches.

Therefore do not fear, “because when he dies, he will not take everything,” for he takes nothing with him from his riches, nor from his glory. This is: “Nor will the glory of his house descend with him,” because when he comes to hell he will be no greater than any poor person.

The glory of his house will not descend with him because in this “life” alone “his soul will be blessed” by flatterers. This happens only during his life, so that when young men say to him, if he has committed murder or some such deed, “Ah, how well done!”—and for this reason too he will perish, because only then “will he confess to you,” that is, praise you, “when you have done good to him,” that is, when you give him prosperous outcomes.

Here he shows the completion of his wickedness. The connection is: Why should I run through everything individually? He himself will enter “as far as the generation of his fathers,” that is, he will be like all his fathers in wickedness; in wickedness he will ascend even to Cain himself. Therefore “he will not see light,” that is, in this life he will not see true knowledge, nor in the next true illumination. And this is “forever.”

He will not see because “when a human being was in honor,” as above.

## ON PSALM XLIX. TITLE

A psalm of Asaph.

Asaph was one of the precentors whom David had with him to enlarge the worship of God. David gave this psalm its title from Asaph’s name, especially because the interpretation of the name suits the character of the psalm. For Asaph is interpreted as “assembly,” and in this psalm the assembly, that is, the congregation of the faithful, speaks.

Its subject is the New Testament and, by contrast, the Old Testament.

Its structure is as follows. In the first section he sets forth Christ’s first and second coming, in order to confirm what Christ himself later says in his own person. Through the second coming he terrifies the wicked, showing that the ungodly will be condemned and the good rewarded. In the second section he introduces Christ speaking at his first coming to his friends and teaching them that legal institutions now have no value, but only the sacrifice of praise. In the third section he speaks to his enemies, rebuking them and teaching what must be done.

His purpose is to urge the Jews, after Christ’s coming, not to place their confidence in legal institutions in any way, and to prevent the Gentiles from coming to those institutions.

The title is explained as follows: This psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the congregation of the faithful, which speaks here. The Synagogue is introduced as speaking rather than the Church from the Gentiles because they rely more on the authority of the Jews than on that of others.

It is as though the faithful Synagogue were saying: Do not continue to follow legal institutions, because Christ is “God,” that is, creator, “of gods,” that is, of the just. Hence Scripture says: “You shall not revile the gods” (Exodus XX). He is the Lord of all nations, who until now spoke through the prophets; now he “has spoken” in his own person, “and has called the earth” to listen to him.

He called the whole earth, certainly, and this is “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” He also specifies the place in which he spoke when he says: “and the beauty of his adornment,” that is, the beautiful splendor of this Lord, “is from Zion.” Hence the prophet says: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word from Jerusalem” (Isaiah II).

I say that God has spoken, and that same “God,” who was once hidden because the divinity lay concealed in humanity, “will come manifestly” in judgment. And that “our God,” possessing our humanity, “will not be silent” then before Herod and Pilate, but will rebuke each person for his sins. Here the purpose is indicated.

Then “fire will blaze before him,” for material fire will precede the sight of him as he comes to judgment, and it will burn the face of the earth. “And around him a mighty storm,” that is, the holy angels, who are compared with a storm because, just as a mighty storm drives the chaff away from the grain, so they will drive the wicked away from the good.

And the Lord himself, coming, “will summon heaven,” that is, the heavenly beings from above, “to himself.” Coming from above, he will summon the heavenly beings to himself, “and” he will call “the earth,” not to himself, but “to discern his people,” that is, so that they may distinguish his people from the wicked.

The prophet rejoices over the gathering of the just and their separation from the ungodly. He urges the angels, whose office it is to do this, saying: You, O angels, “gather his saints” to the Lord. The angels’ office will truly be to gather the saints before the judge and to send the wicked away to torments. He specifies whom he calls saints: those “who arrange his testament above sacrifices,” that is, those who, having set aside legal institutions—which is the right order—follow the New Testament.

Gather the saints, “and” the gathered “heavens will announce his righteousness,” always praising God. For this reason: because he is “God, the just judge,” who separates the just, who were afflicted in this life, from the wicked.

Here the second section begins. The connection is: I say that the Lord has spoken, and now hear these words: “Hear, my people,” that is, understand carefully, “and” then “I will speak to you,” that is, I will confirm this to you through the testimony of the prophets: “I am,” that is, I possess the truth of being, “God,” indeed of all, “your familiar God.”

And “I will not rebuke you” from now on “for your sacrifices.” If you do not offer animal sacrifices, you will not offend; but holocausts “not of calves, but your own,” that is, those which are in you—namely, a contrite spirit—“are always before me.”

I say, “I will not reprove,” because “I will not accept,” that is, I do not regard as pleasing, “calves” of the heart unless you sacrifice pride to me, namely, “from your house”; nor will I accept “goats”—I do not mean goats of the heart—unless you sacrifice the foul impulses of lust, namely, “from your flocks.” I will not accept them because “all the beasts of the forests are mine,” that is, they are subject to my power; and even the untamed beasts are mine, as are these “cattle” grazing “on the mountains, and oxen,” that is, untamed animals. By untamed animals the Gentiles are signified, who did not have the Law; by tamed animals, the Jews, who were held under the yoke of the Law—but this has no place here. Not only the terrestrial animals, but also “the birds of heaven I know” to be mine, “and the beauty of the field is with me,” that is, all the produce of the earth is in my power.

And therefore, “if I were hungry”—which nevertheless is impossible—“I would not tell you: For the world is mine, and the fullness thereof.”

I say, “if I were hungry,” but I shall never be hungry; and this means: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” Here he plainly reproves the folly of those who thought that God ate or drank the blood of animals.

He determines what he had earlier said was a holocaust in his sight. Do not offer these legal sacrifices, but rather “sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise,” that is, praise your God in such a way that your praise itself is a sacrifice of praise to him. Sacrifice yourself, that is, with respect to lust, luxury, pride, avarice, and so forth, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” Offer praise, and offer it continually; and this is: [Col. 0367A] “and pay your vows to the Most High,” that is, devoutly; and if you are not now able to fulfill them, pay them when you are able.

“And” then “call upon me in the day of tribulation,” that is, in the time of this present life, and I “will deliver you” from tribulation—not in the sense that he delivers the faithful from every tribulation, but from that tribulation in which there is a true loss of good. “And” once delivered, “you will honor me” by praising God. When others see him delivered in this way, they join in praising God as the deliverer of his righteous servant.

The third part begins. Just as the Synagogue introduced Christ as speaking to its own people, so also the Synagogue introduces God as speaking to the sinner. The continuation is as though the Synagogue were saying: God said this to the righteous, “but to the sinner God said” the following: “Why do you, sinner, recount [Col. 0367B] my righteousnesses?”—those concerning the creation of heaven and earth—“and take up my covenant,” that is, the Old Law or the New, “in your mouth,” so that you may teach others from it? When he says “you take up,” he indicates that the matter itself has not been entrusted to the sinner; rather, the sinner intrudes himself by presumption.

You proclaim the covenant, but act against it; and this is: “You, however, hated discipline,” that is, my correction, because if I gave you any correction, you endured it unwillingly, “and you cast my words,” that is, my commandments, “behind your back” by failing to fulfill them.

You cast away the word, “and if you saw a thief, you ran with him.” He runs with a thief who does not rebuke the one committing theft and who consents to him. He consents to a thief either when he approves of the theft, or when, though able to rebuke him, he does not; “and with adulterers you placed your portion,” either by committing adultery or by consenting to adulterers.

“Your mouth also abounded in wickedness,” that is, it spoke openly of evil in abundance, “and your tongue contrived deceits.” He says “contrived” because those who speak deceitfully compose their words with the greatest ornamentation.

Here he adds a discussion of detraction. The continuation is: You did not commit only those evils in those ways, but also through detraction; and this is: “You spoke against your brother.” He calls any human being a brother. Nor did you do this occasionally, but “sitting,” that is, persistently; and “not only against others, but against the son [Col. 0367D] of your mother,” that is, of the Synagogue, “you placed a stumbling block,” that is, any offense whatsoever, by persuading him toward heresy or toward something of that sort which draws him back from the true way. “You did all these things, and” yet I “kept silent,” that is, I waited patiently, so that at some point you might at least be converted.

You abused this patience of mine, because you thought that, just as I was allowing you to remain unpunished for a time, so it would always be; and this is: “You wickedly thought”—whether this is a vocative or an adverbial expression—“that I would be like you,” by not punishing you. For if God were to leave the wicked unpunished, he would be found to resemble the unjust. You thought this, but I will not be like you; rather, “I will reprove you,” that is, punish you for your sins, “and set them before your face,” namely, so that you may see all your sins [Col. 0368A], which you now disregard. He speaks by comparison, because just as someone clearly sees a thing that he possesses when it is placed before his eyes, so on the day of judgment each person will recognize his sins plainly.

You also, “who forget God,” that is, who do not keep God in your memory, “understand these things,” that is, understand the punishment that will come upon the wicked. Understand, I say, “lest he seize” you for punishment, “and there be no one to deliver.”

Understand these things and offer me “a sacrifice of praise,” that is, a contrite spirit, because that sacrifice “will honor me, and there,” that is, in that sacrifice, “is the way by which” I “will show him” who offers it “the salvation of God.”

## ON PSALM L. TITLE

“To the end: a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba.”

“Have mercy on me, O God.” It is read that when David saw Uriah’s wife Bathsheba bathing on the roof of her house, he was pleased with her; and approaching her, he had intercourse with her (II Kings 11). When she became pregnant, fearing that the adultery would be exposed, he summoned Uriah from the campaign. When Uriah returned, he refused to go back to his wife’s chamber while his comrades were still on campaign. David sent him back to Joab with a letter in which he ordered Joab, the commander of his army, to place Uriah wherever the city had its strongest defenders, and, when the assault became more intense, for all Uriah’s comrades to abandon him [Col. 0368C] alone, so that he might be killed. And so it was done. David was therefore guilty of both adultery and murder.

Desiring, then, to recall his servant David, the Lord sent Nathan the prophet to him. In a certain parable Nathan sought a judgment from the king. Nathan said to King David (III Kings 12): “Tell me, king, your judgment. There was a certain man who had many sheep, and a neighbor who had only one little ewe. When guests came upon the wealthy man, he did not wish to take any of his own sheep, but seized his neighbor’s little ewe. The king judged that such a man was a son of death.” Nathan therefore said to him: “You are that man: although you had sixty wives and as many concubines as you wished, you nevertheless seized the wife of Uriah, who had only one.”

David, then, was pierced by this admonition [Col. 0368D] and began to repent, and the title was composed from Nathan’s coming. It is explained as follows: This psalm suits the penitent David, who speaks here; it was composed when Nathan the prophet came to him—not concerning just any coming of Nathan, but concerning the coming that occurred when David went in to Bathsheba, for Nathan the prophet sharply reproved him on account of that entry. The subject is David repenting and humbling himself greatly because of the serious sins he had committed.

The method is as follows. In the first part he displays his humility. In the second part, his confidence. The third follows from these: namely, that God should not regard his sins. In the fourth he asks that God establish the Church in which a holocaust pleasing to him may be offered. The intention is that, however serious the sins we may have committed, if we wish to turn back to God, we should not despair, because God’s mercy is ineffable and far greater than our sins. And just as in the other penitential psalms he does not excuse his sins but accuses himself, so in this one, confessing his sin, he entreats God on the basis of what belongs to the judge himself, saying:

“Have mercy on me, O God,” that is, regard me with the eye of mercy by reforming me. I claim no merit, but ask for your loving mercy; and this he says: “according to your great mercy.” The prophet rightly says “your great mercy,” because he had foreseen in the Holy Spirit that he would give his Son over to death for the redemption of the human race.

I say, “forgive me and have mercy on me,” but I ask you not to spare my sin; rather, “wipe out [Col. 0369B] my iniquity” from your memory by whatever punishments please you. Nor do I ask this on account of any merit, but “according to the multitude of your mercies,” because I see that you have shown many mercies to human beings, our fathers, who wished to turn back to you.

I say, “wipe out my iniquity,” and I do not seek for iniquity to be wiped out through sacrifices, but through the waters of baptism; and this is: “wash me” through the faith that I have in the waters of baptism. He asks to be washed through the faith he has concerning baptism: “wash me from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.” He calls his adultery and murder both iniquity and sin, but with different reference: he calls them iniquity with respect to his neighbor, and sin insofar as he contaminated himself in body through lust and in will through murder [Col. 0369C].

I say, “wash,” and because some things are washed while some dirt nevertheless remains, he says, “cleanse,” in both respects—so that no trace of contamination may remain in me. I say, “wash, cleanse,” and this “more,” that is, with a more abundant washing than you ordinarily perform, because just as the sin is greater, so a greater washing and cleansing is necessary.

He had spoken of God’s great mercy, but because he again saw that mercy cannot exist without justice, he wishes to point out in himself a certain reason why God ought justly to show him mercy. Just as up to this point he has entreated God as judge on the basis of what belongs to the judge, so now he begins to entreat him on the basis of what belongs to the one entreating. The continuation is: Wash me, I say, through mercy, and this is just, “because I know my iniquity”—not by knowledge alone, but by reproving and execrating it—“and my sin is always against me,” like a terrifying image that I would wish to flee in every way. We ought to understand “iniquity” and “sin” in every respect as explained above.

The sin is against me, and in committing it I sinned against no one “but you alone,” because since I am king, no one but you has the power to punish my sin. Or I sinned in such a way that I must be healed by you alone, because since no one is just except you alone, I must be healed by you alone, Lord [Col. 0370A]. And to aggravate his folly still further, he says, “and I did that evil before you,” that is, although I knew that you were present everywhere, that you saw everything, and that you would be the judge of all, I nevertheless sinned in your sight. I sinned in such a way that, if you and a human being were placed in judgment against one another, you alone would be found just, and the human being unjust—so that you may be “justified,” that is, found just, “in all your words,” because you have completely fulfilled what you promised, while I and all other human beings are found completely unjust. Hence the Apostle says: “But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Romans 3; Psalm 115).

And you are not only justified in your words, but “you also prevail when you are judged” in all things—that is, if judgment were held between you and a human being, so that you were found just. God is found just when he supplies a human being with everything necessary for him, while the human being is unjust when he does not return to God a worthy fruit. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Judge between me and my vineyard.”

You will truly prevail if you enter judgment with the human being, because—to say nothing of this new sin—“I was conceived in iniquities,” since in the very act of conception I was already guilty of Adam’s transgression and disobedience.

Therefore I confess that I am so wretched because “behold,” it is evident to all that you “loved truth.” For if I did not confess the truth about myself, I would not be worthy for you to forgive me. After accusing himself on account of his own sins, he also accuses himself on account of God’s benefits, which he used badly. Therefore, too, you will prevail, because “you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” You have made them known to me—namely, the incarnation and the restoration that you are to accomplish through your Son. These things are uncertain to some, namely, to those who, although they understand something concerning the coming of your Son, nevertheless do not understand everything fully; they are hidden from others, namely, from those who know absolutely nothing about them.

Here the second part begins. O Lord, I have sinned so gravely, but nevertheless I trust in your mercy, and, knowing this, “you will sprinkle me with hyssop.” He sends us back to the Law, in which it was commanded that a leper be sprinkled with hyssop dipped in the blood of a heifer; this was for them a kind of expiation (Exodus 12). That blood signified the blood of Christ, in which, through faith, the leprosy of sins is cleansed. Hyssop, which is a humble herb [Col. 0370D], signifies the humility by which Christ shed his blood and by which we receive that blood through faith. And just as hyssop penetrates stones and drives away swelling of the lungs, so humility penetrates stony hearts and drives away the swelling of pride.

Accordingly, he says: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop,” that is, with the blood of Christ, shed in humility and received in humility; “and” through this “I shall be cleansed” from my sins. Nor shall I be cleansed only in this sprinkling, but I shall also receive the brightness of the virtues: “you will wash me” with that blood, “and I shall be made whiter,” that is, I shall receive whiteness from you, “more than snow,” that is, more than any body could be whitened.

Thus I shall be made white, and afterward “you will give to my hearing” [Col. 0371A], that is, you will make me understand, through the Holy Spirit speaking inwardly to me, “joy” concerning the remission of sins, “and gladness” concerning the hope of eternal life. “And” then “my bones,” that is, the powers of my reason, formerly “humbled” by sin, “will exult” over their restoration.

“Turn away.” He treats of the third part, namely, that God should regard him rather than the sin. He properly places this third after the first two, because the person who humbles himself in this way and thus trusts in the Lord prays to God justly. The continuation is: He says that the bones will exult, and in order that he may be able to exult, “turn your face,” that is, your knowledge, “away from my sins,” so that you may not punish them eternally, “and wipe out” from the book of death “all my iniquities,” both these recent ones and all the others.

When the evils have been wiped away, “create in me [Col. 0371B] a clean heart, O God,” so that thereafter I may not wish to sin. He says “create” because through sin the heart had been as though destroyed. And do not merely remove evil desires from my heart, but also suggestions from the flesh; for a suggestion of the flesh could corrupt a will that had been cleansed. “And” renew “a right spirit,” that is, your Son, who rules well all those whom he inhabits, “within my inward parts,” that is, so that he may renew my inward parts, namely, the desires of my flesh. By the fact that he mentions the Holy Spirit three times, we discern the Trinity.

Cast the sins away from your face, but “do not cast me,” that is, the human nature, “away from your face”; rather, regard my merit, “and do not take your Holy Spirit away from me.” When he says “do not take away,” he indicates that he possessed him in some manner; for he could not have been so deeply moved to compunction unless the grace of the Holy Spirit had granted it [Col. 0371C].

I say, “do not take away,” but rather “restore to me the joy of your salvation,” so that, just as I rejoiced beforehand at the coming of your Son, who was to be born from my seed, so, once forgiveness has been received and known, I may rejoice thereafter. “And,” once joy has been restored, “strengthen me,” so that I may in no way thereafter be moved toward sin, “with a principal spirit,” that is, with God the Father dwelling within me. The Father is called the principal Spirit because the Son proceeds from him, and the Holy Spirit from both.

He sets forth the fourth part. I say: Restore and strengthen me; and if you do this, I shall not offer you a bull or a goat, but I shall acquire many for you. And this is: “I will teach the wicked your ways,” that is, your commandments, “and” thus “the impious,” who are opposed to divine worship [Col. 0371D], “will be converted to you.”

When he says that, after completing his repentance, he receives the ministry of teaching that he had lost because of sin, he gives it to be understood that those who are degraded in the Church on account of sins can be restored once their repentance has been completed. Against this there seems to be a certain canon which says that, after a fall and the completion of repentance, no one ought to be restored. This singular provision, however, was given with reference more to penitents who feign repentance than to the truth. Therefore the general judgment should be held: if, by divine judgment, that repentance is proved complete, the person is restored to his former dignity.

“Deliver” me, so that I may be able to teach others. O “God, deliver me from bloods,” that is, from the sins which arise through the suggestion of the blood [Col. 0372A]. We understand these sins through “blood” because such suggestions arise from the nature of the blood. He uses the plural “bloods” to show that he is entangled in many sins of this kind. “Deliver me,” I say, you who are the author of this “my salvation,” “and,” if you deliver me, “my tongue will exult,” that is, will proclaim with exultation “your righteousness,” concerning the creation of heaven and earth and also concerning the fact that you make a human being righteous.

Lord, if I am delivered, my tongue will exult in your righteousness, and you also, “Lord, will open,” that is, make very eloquent, “my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise,” that is, whenever I speak at length, everything will concern your praise.

“For” this is why I say that I shall proclaim your praise: you did not wish for any other sacrifice, because “if you had desired” another “sacrifice, I would certainly have given it”; but not even holocausts—which might rather seem to please you—“will you ever delight in.”

The sacrifice of animals does not please you, but “a contrite spirit,” that is, a soul that afflicts pride and the other vices, is “a sacrifice” pleasing “to God.” Nor will you ever despise, O God, “a broken heart” through the fruits of repentance, “and” thus “humbled.”

“Deal favorably, Lord.” He sets forth the fifth part. I say that such a sacrifice pleases you; therefore, in order that such a sacrifice may be offered to you, “deal favorably,” that is, generously—namely, build up the Church, “Zion.” I ask this not on account of merits, but from “your will,” which is especially “good” [Col. 0372C], “so that” in this way “the walls,” that is, the stronger parts, “of Jerusalem” may be “built” through virtues. The walls fell through the transgression of our first parent. Just as the walls of the earthly Jerusalem truly collapsed through the work of Nebuchadnezzar, so our cook, that is, our gluttony, destroys within us the walls of the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the virtues.

Then, I say, build up the Church; “then,” that is, once it has been built, “you will accept,” that is, receive as acceptable, “the sacrifice of justice,” that is, the offering of the Lord’s body, “and” you will accept “oblations,” that is, the virtues of the holy confessors, who, although they do not burn themselves entirely, nevertheless offer something to God, “and holocausts,” that is, the virtues of the holy martyrs, who burn themselves entirely. “Then many” from the Church “will place calves,” that is, new peoples who have not yet been under the yoke, “upon your altar,” that is, upon Christ, without whom no offerings are received by God. Or by calves are meant preachers, who bellow to God throughout the whole world.

## ON PSALM LI. TITLE

“To the end: the understanding of David, when Doeg the Idumean came to Saul and told him: David has come into the house of Abimelech.”

“Why do you glory?” When David was being pursued by Saul, he came with his men to the house of Abimelech the priest. Since Abimelech had no bread except the loaves of the Presence, he gave them to David and his men, along with the sword that David had taken from Goliath. Doeg the Idumean was there, however, a member of Saul’s household and keeper of his horses, and he reported all these things to Saul [Col. 0373A]. Saul then sent men and had Abimelech and the other priests killed (II Kings 21 and 22).

Afterward David composed this psalm—not concerning that historical event, but concerning the understanding he had that the Antichrist would come, and that through the devil’s assistance he would persecute the Church, in which the true David dwells. Doeg signifies the Antichrist. For “Doeg” means “moved,” while “Idumean” is interpreted as “earthly.” The Antichrist will always be moved toward stirring up earthly things; he will also summon others to agitation and to the pursuit of earthly things.

Doeg was his proper name; he was called Idumean from the place, from Idumea, the land that Esau inhabited. And just as that Doeg came to Saul, so the Antichrist will come through signs and miracles to Saul [Col. 0373B], that is, to the devil, and will announce to him that David—that is, Christ—has come into the house of Abimelech, that is, into the house which is the kingdom of the Father, namely, the Church, seeking how he may kill those who receive Christ, just as Saul killed Abimelech.

The title is explained as follows: “Understanding,” that is, this psalm, which explains the understanding—the mystery we have mentioned—belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here. It is “understanding,” I say, drawn from that event, when Doeg came and historically reported it to Saul. The subject is Christ and, by opposition, the Antichrist.

The method is as follows. In the first part he displays the great wickedness of the Antichrist by rebuking him. In the second he sets forth his destruction and the astonishment of the saints, who see him so exalted in the world while they will behold him so condemned [Col. 0373C]. In the third he states that those who always hope in God’s mercy will never be removed from it. The intention is to move all the faithful so that, although they see him exalted in this world, they may nevertheless understand that he will be condemned and never consent to him.

But the prophet immediately begins to rebuke the Antichrist himself for his wickedness.

O Antichrist, most wicked of all human beings, “why do you glory in wickedness,” for which you ought to blush? Others, if they do evil, are ashamed; you, by contrast, glory. Why do you glory, “you who are powerful in iniquity”? Although you commit many iniquities, you have power in them over those whom you can devour, whether through miracles or through punishments that you are able to inflict by God’s permission. The fact also that God gave him power to accomplish wickedness aggravates his wickedness.

He works through its individual parts: “all day,” that is, at all times, “your tongue devised injustice.” He attributes thought to the tongue because it belongs to fools to have the same thing in heart and mouth and to speak everything without forethought. Hence Solomon says: “The heart of fools is in their mouth” (Ecclesiasticus 21). The tongue devised injustice, and you “practiced deceit,” you, I say, “like a sharp razor,” that is, comparable to a sharp razor, because you deceive both deceitfully and keenly. Just as a sharp razor renews the skin and scrapes away what is external, so the Antichrist, by afflicting the righteous and taking away their possessions, makes the inner person more beautiful.

Or it may be understood in this way: the Antichrist promises novelty to the whole world, which he then utterly destroys. Or he is compared to a sharp razor because he cuts only by deceiving the soft and fragile, just as a razor cuts soft things such as hair and flesh, but not hard things such as bones.

“You loved wickedness more than goodness,” because if nature suggested any goodness to you, you suppressed it through your evil ways. You also loved “iniquity”—not merely to do it, but to do it “more than to speak equity.”

You loved everything. Why should I run through the particulars? You loved “all words of precipitousness,” that is, words by which you and others are precipitated eternally. You, I say, are “a deceitful tongue,” because what you cannot accomplish by violence, you attempt to accomplish by deceit, whether through perjury or through false interpretations of Scripture.

The second part begins. “And therefore,” because you are such, “God will destroy you,” not with respect to temporal goods, but “to the end,” that is, eternally, so that you cannot rise again afterward. “And he will tear you from your tabernacle and make you migrate,” that is, he will make you migrate elsewhere: from the tabernacle—that is, from this world, in which you dwell temporarily—and when he has made you migrate, you will not take root; rather, he will tear “your root from the land of the living,” on account of your greedy wickedness. For your root, that is, your wickedness, does not permit you to inhabit such a land.

Or: “He will tear you out and make you migrate from your tabernacle,” that is, from the Church, together with all your members. For the members of the Antichrist, mingled with the Church in this life, will not take root in the land of the living; rather, he will tear out your root, that is [Col. 0374C], your followers, from the land of the living.

The Lord will destroy you in this way, and “the righteous will see” it on the day of judgment, “and they will fear,” that is, they will revere the judge himself. That fear will not be one of sadness but of joy; and this is: “they will laugh at him,” that is, they will rejoice, consenting to divine justice, “and they will say: Behold,” it is evident that he is “a man,” although he called himself God, “and such a one who did not set God as his helper.”

“But he hoped in the abundance of his riches,” that is, of his gold and silver, his power and glory, “and prevailed in his vanity,” because no impious person deceived so many of the faithful.

The third part begins. He hoped in riches in this way, “but I,” being “in the house of the Lord like a fruitful olive tree” [Col. 0374D], that is, comparable to a fruitful olive tree, because just as an olive tree is always full of sap, so the prophet was full of the Holy Spirit. Although every righteous person can compare himself to a fruitful olive tree, this prophet does so more especially, since Christ was to be born from his seed.

“I hoped in the mercy of God,” specifically “for ever,” so that I might possess eternity. He does not take “for ever” as extending only to the end, but as “unto age of age.”
