And so that I may be able to compare myself to it, “I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you, “unto age,” because “you have made” this confession—that is, through your mercy—or you have made me like an olive tree. “And I will await your name,” however long it may be delayed, until in judgment you make me immortal and incapable of suffering, namely, the Son of God. “For it is good in the sight of the saints,” that is, it pleases the saints to await that good.

## ON PSALM LII. TITLE

“To the end: the understanding of David concerning Amalek.”

“The fool said.” It is read in the history (I Kings 30) that David, fleeing from Saul, placed his wives, sons, and other possessions in one of his cities, namely Ziklag, while he took with him the men whom he recognized as fit for battle and defense. Meanwhile the Amalekites, occupying David’s city, plundered everything. When this was reported to David, he pursued them; and after defeating them, he rescued his entire household. In this event he understood the future of the Church, which is signified by David, from the household of the Antichrist, which is understood through Amalek.

For Amalek is interpreted as “licking the earth,” by which the household of the Antichrist is understood, since it always licks up and desires earthly things; from these, however, God will deliver his Church. The title is explained as follows: This psalm is called the understanding of David because it explains David’s understanding—understanding, I say, acquired concerning Amalek, that is, concerning that event—and directs it “to the end,” that is, to Christ.

Amalek is also interpreted as “giving birth” or “suffering.” By this the Church is understood: she gives birth, that is, labors to bear some children for God, and grieves over the destruction of the wicked. According to this, the title is read as follows: This psalm is called the understanding of David, acquired concerning Amalek, that is, concerning the Church, in whose person the prophet speaks here [Col. 0375C].

The principal subject is the Church and, by opposition, the followers of the Antichrist. The method is as follows. In the first part he rebukes them because they belong to the household of the Antichrist. In the second he sets forth their condemnation. In the third he sets forth the salvation of the righteous. The intention is to instruct the Church concerning the members of the Antichrist.

Here he uses the same words for reproving these people that he used earlier for reproving the Jews who did not receive Christ their visitor, because he sees them as similar: just as those denied Christ, so these will deny that he was the Messiah, while they call the Antichrist the Messiah.

The voice of the Church rebukes them in this way: “Fool,” namely, the household of the Antichrist, which is without true wisdom, “said,” that is, will say: “That Christ who was called God [Col. 0375D] is not God.” And, as it was explained in another psalm (Psalm 13), he says this so as to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks, even in some way, so as to understand: “There is none who does good, there is not even one,” that is, not one among them all is found who does good.

The second part begins. All have turned aside, but “will they not know” in their condemnation—that is, will not all who now “work iniquity” recognize that they have acted wickedly?—and so forth.

“God.” They work iniquity for this reason: they “did not call upon God,” which gives great hope to those who call upon God. They will truly know that they act wickedly, “because God will scatter,” that is, destroy, “the bones,” that is, the strength, “of those who please men,” that is, themselves [Col. 0376A]. Another reading has: “the bones of men who please themselves.” “They were confounded,” that is, they suffer shame; and this is “because God despised them.”

These people will be confounded, and Israel will be saved. And “who,” coming “from Zion,” that is, from Judea, “will give salvation to Israel?” No one, of course, except Christ, whom you denied to be God. God will indeed turn away the captivity of his people, “when he has turned,” that is, completely removed, “the captivity,” that is, suffering and mortality, “of his people. Jacob will exult, and Israel will rejoice.” In this life God removes the captivity of the soul, that is, sins; in the other life he also removes that of the bodies, since they will be clothed with immortality and incorruptibility.

## ON PSALM LIII. TITLE

“To the end: the understanding in the songs of David, when the Ziphites came to Saul and said: Is not David hidden among us?”

“Save me, O God, by your name.” Ziph is a village, from which its inhabitants were called Ziphites. They were David’s kinsmen from the tribe of Judah. While David was hiding among them as he fled from Saul, they, not believing that he would become king, reported him to Saul so that he might seize him unawares. David, however, anticipating their deceit, departed from them and was delivered (I Kings 23). After this deliverance David sang this psalm—not about his own deliverance, but about the deliverance of the Church from the Ziphites, that is, from those who flourish in this world. For “Ziphites” is interpreted as “those who flourish.”

The title is explained as follows: This psalm is the understanding of David, that is, it explains David’s understanding to us—namely, the Church’s deliverance from those who flourish in the world. It is understanding, I say, acquired “in songs,” that is, in praises, which occur where he says: “I will sacrifice freely.” Even if praises were not found in the psalm, however, the subject would still be worthy of praise, since it openly declares the Church’s deliverance. It is understanding acquired from this history, when the Ziphites came, and so forth, and directs us “to the end.”

The subject is the Church. The method is as follows. In the first part he asks for his deliverance. In the second he asks for the conversion of his enemies, which begins there: “Turn away evils,” and he affirms his deliverance, for which reason he pays God sacrifices of thanksgiving. Where he says “turn away evils,” he adds: [Col. 0376D] “and behold, God helps me.” He intends to shape the conduct of the Church, so that she may pray not only for herself but also for her enemies.

It is as though he were saying: Pray for your own deliverance and that of your enemies. The voice of the Church, following my example, says to God: “O God, save me,” so that my enemies may not prevail over me. Nor do I ask to be saved through the protection of some powerful person, or through riches, but “by your name,” that is, by the name by which I am called—namely, Christian or faithful; “and by your power,” that is, when your power appears, namely, on the day of judgment, “judge,” that is, separate “me” from the mass of the lost.

After establishing the order of his prayer, he asks God to hear it, saying: “O God, hear my prayer.” This is as though he repeated the prayer, but he does so because the necessity of deliverance is great. He asks not only that his inward prayer be heard, but also his outward prayer, made with a cry; and this is: “the words of my mouth.” He does not merely say, “Hear”; rather, he asks God firmly to retain them in memory, and this is: “give ear.”

It is necessary that you hear, “because strangers,” although they are my kinsmen, are strangers to me in will, as the Ziphites were hostile to David; they “rose up” with all their strength “against me.” And the powerful, that is, the devils and their ministers, or even the princes of this world, “sought” to destroy “my soul,” just as Saul and his ministers sought David’s soul. “And” those who sought it “did not set God before their eyes,” that is, they did not consider that God was in me [Col. 0377B].

I rightly say that God is in me, because “behold,” it is evident that “God helps me” to act well, “and” the Lord himself “is the protector of my soul,” that is, he has received my soul from this lowliness and conferred virtues upon it.

He begins to pray for his enemies, and this is the second part. The continuation is: I say that God is the protector, and you, Lord God, who are the protector, “turn away evils from my enemies,” so that they may not accomplish what they wish; “and destroy them,” that is, bring them to ruin, “in your truth,” namely, by placing your truth where they now have falsehood and evil will.

And in order that you may do this, “I will sacrifice to you”—myself. And not for any temporal advantage, but “freely,” that is, from love of you alone; “and” I will also “confess to your name, O Lord,” that is, I will praise your name, “because it is good,” that is, because praising your name is sweet.

And rightly should I sacrifice and confess, “because” you, Lord, “have delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye,” that is, my inward reason, “has looked down upon my enemies.” He says “upon” because the righteous person now understands that he has been placed in a high position, while his enemies have been cast down into the refuse of this world and left to putrefy.

# ON PSALM 54

## Title

“‘For the end, in songs of understanding, of David.’

### “Hear me, O God”

This psalm is called “of the understanding of David,” namely, of Christ who was to become man, fragile according to the flesh and wavering, but possessing confidence from God alone. It is called an understanding “in songs,” that is, in praises and exultation, and because it understands God to be the firmness of our humanity. For our humanity is compared to a wavering ship: just as the ship receives its stability from an anchor, so our humanity receives its stability from God alone. The understanding which the Prophet possessed—not through history but through the Holy Spirit—he does not expound in his own person, but introduces Christ as the expositor. For Christ speaks here, and he is the subject.

The structure is as follows. In the first part, Christ, explaining his fragility, asks God for deliverance. In the second part, beginning where it says, “Cast them down, O Lord,” he curses his enemies. In the third part, beginning where it says, “But I cried to God,” he shows that his prayer has been heard, both concerning his deliverance and concerning the condemnation of his enemies. There, while speaking of the condemnation of the wicked, he inserts an admonition to the just: when they see the condemnation of the impious, they should not be afraid, but cast all their care upon the Lord. This is expressed in the words, “Cast your care upon the Lord.” Hence the Apostle says: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5).

Before he describes his fragility, he asks for deliverance, saying: “Hear, O God, my prayer,” concerning the acquisition of good things, “and do not despise my supplication,” so that you may always remove evils. For he could give good things which might be taken away by impending evils. And because my humanity is so lowly that it cannot reach your height, “attend to me,” that is, show yourself attentive by humbling yourself to me. God humbled himself when he joined himself to human weakness. “And” thus “hear me.”

It is necessary that you hear me, because “I am saddened in my exercise,” that is, I exercise myself, like a good farmer, among those near me, so that I may bear fruit; and because I make little progress in this, I am saddened. Nor am I saddened only in this, “but also I am troubled by the voice,” that is, by the reproaches, “of the enemy, and by the tribulation of the sinner.”

And rightly do I say “by tribulation,” “because they have turned iniquity,” that is, death, “against me.” For although I was saying something good to them, they nevertheless continually turned against me, plotting my death. Or they turned their iniquities away from themselves and directed them against me, calling me a sinner, and so forth. “And in anger they were troublesome to me,” that is, in their fury they inflicted troubles upon me.

Because of this, “my heart,” the carnal heart, “was troubled within me.” There was trouble when the Jews threatened him with death; “and the dread of death,” that is, the horror of approaching death, “fell upon me,” though he had no share in it, “and was destroyed.” For through this Laurentius and the other saints conquered fear by reason.

“Fear,” that is, dread, “came upon me,” and also the fear of the soul—not a necessary fear, but a voluntary one—“and trembling” of the body “came upon me” at the very hour of the Passion, when death was already imminent. “And darkness,” that is, death itself, “covered me,” because through death itself all the senses were extinguished.

### “And I said”

Having set out the evils in order, he shows how he conducted himself amid those evils. They did all these things to me, and while they were being done to me, “I said,” that is, I considered in my heart the following: “Who will give me wings like a dove,” that is, wings comparable to those of a dove, without any bitterness—wings, that is, virtues—“and I will fly away,” that is, I will remove myself bodily from those Jews, “and I will rest” from all the tumult?

The greatest wing was patience, by which he withdrew himself bodily from the Jews during the time of his persecution, so that his presence would not be for them a cause of greater madness. He remained quiet—not because he could not remain quiet amid all the tumults of this life, but in order to give us an example of withdrawing bodily from this tumult, lest we provoke others to greater fury. Exterior tumult is indeed to be fled, because it is itself the cause of interior unrest.

Behold, I sought that wings might be given, and “behold,” they were given, by which “I withdrew, fleeing,” bodily from the Jews, “and I remained in solitude,” literally.

And while existing in solitude, I “awaited him who saved me from faintheartedness of spirit,” that is, him who so guarded me that my human spirit, which in human terms was weak, would not fail; and him who saved me from “the storm” of the Jews’ tribulation, lest I in any way become conformed to them. I awaited him who did this, so that he might cause me to rise again, and so forth.

### “Cast them down”

Here begins the second part, namely, the cursing of his enemies. I withdrew, fleeing from their evils; but you, “O Lord, cast them down” from the height of their kingdom into the contempt of men, and “divide their tongues,” that is, entangle their tongues in different errors, so that they may not agree with one another in the Scriptures, as they do not even today. He expressly curses those who, building a tower against God, were cast down and divided by languages. You must cast them down and divide them, “because I saw iniquity,” that is, the actual evils which they inflicted upon me, “and contradiction” in the words with which they opposed my preaching, “in the city,” namely, the actual Jerusalem.

It may also be read in a good sense: Cast them down from pride into humility; divide their tongues, so that they may not agree with one another in evil. The rest remains unchanged.

And because they committed iniquity against me, therefore “iniquity will surround that city day and night,” that is, continually; it will exist “upon its walls,” that is, upon the city’s principal men, who are the wall and defense of the city. “And in its midst,” that is, in its common body, “there will be labor,” that is, they will labor to do evil in evil deeds, “in justice,” as in false judgments.

“And usury” in temporal money, “and deceit do not fail,” that is, they will not be absent from them. These evils they will not do secretly, but openly; and this is expressed by “from its streets.”

### “Because”

The following four verses are understood especially of Judas. They are connected with what was said above in this way: Therefore cast them down and divide them, “because” they do these evils against me through one of my intimates—something which should not be endured. But “if my enemy” openly “had cursed me,” I “would certainly have borne it,” lest I curse him in return or take revenge upon him.

Or the two preceding verses may be understood of false friends. In that case connect them thus: I say, cast them down and scatter them, because they are worse than true enemies. Thus the text reads: “Because if an enemy had cursed me…”

And not only if he had cursed me, but “if he who hated me had spoken great things against me,” namely, by degrading me and exalting himself. I do not merely say that I would have endured it, but “I would have hidden myself,” withdrawing bodily “from him”; and I say this “perhaps,” that is, truly.

### “But you, a man”

I would have endured an enemy; “but you,” who pretended to be my friend, are not to be endured. And this is what follows: “You, a man of one mind,” that is, you who pretended to be of one mind with me, “my guide,” whom I sent ahead like the other disciples to prepare lodging for me, “and my acquaintance” according to our companionship.

You, “who,” existing “with me together” with the others, “ate sweet foods,” which ought to have been the cause of sweet friendship. Or “sweet foods,” that is, spiritual doctrine, which ought to have been sweet to you and to have removed you from tradition. “And we walked in the house of God with agreement.” Even if the Pharisees sometimes contradicted me in the Temple, you agreed with me. Since you were so intimate with me, why then, O man, did you sin against me?

And because this man, who was so intimate with me, betrayed me in this way, “let death come upon them,” upon those who, agreeing with him, sinned against me. Let those who sinned against me unknowingly—that is, without understanding—be punished more lightly, so that they do not feel a severe punishment, just as those who are dead do not feel that they are burning. But let the others who sinned knowingly “go down alive into hell,” that is, let them be punished so severely as if they were being burned alive.

Here he touches upon the history in Numbers 16 and Psalm 105: Dathan and Abiram, because of the rebellion they had raised against Moses, were swallowed alive by the earth, while Korah was burned with two hundred and fifty men.

Or it may be read in a good sense: “Let death come upon them,” that is, let them die in their sins, “and let them descend alive into hell,” not dead, but with agility of mind; that is, while considering the infernal punishments prepared for the impious, let them withdraw from evil.

And death ought to come upon them, “because in their dwellings,” that is, in their hearts, “there are wickednesses,” because many evil thoughts dwell in their hearts. And this is not found in only a few, but “in their midst,” that is, in their community.

### “But I”

Here begins the third part: he shows that he has been heard, both concerning his deliverance and concerning the condemnation of the wicked. The connection is this: The wicked will be condemned in this way, “but I cried to God,” and this is what follows: I cried, “and the Lord saved me.”

And because he saved me, therefore “I will recount” what has already happened, “and I will announce” what is to come—“in the evening,” that is, when he was betrayed; “and in the morning,” when he was led before the judge; “and at midday,” when he was placed upon the cross.

The Evangelists appear to disagree. One says that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, another at the third, yet they do not disagree. What one says was done at the third hour does not concern the fastening to the wood of the cross, but the condemnation expressed in the words of the Jews; the other speaks of the actual fastening to the cross.

He recounted each matter at its proper time. In the evening, at the supper, he foretold his death, resurrection, and ascension to his disciples when he said: “Amen I say to you, one of you is about to betray me” (Matthew 26). He announced it in the morning, when he was brought before Pilate the judge, saying: “For this I was born, that I might bear witness to the truth; from this you will see the Son of Man coming with the clouds” (John 18). He was heard most fully in the Passion itself, when he appeared to have been abandoned, when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). “And,” because I will recount in this way, therefore “the Lord will hear my voice.”

Thus he will hear my voice: “He will redeem my soul from those who draw near to me,” that is, from familiar enemies, who will then be able to do no evil. I say that he will redeem my soul, which has been placed “in peace,” that is, in eternal rest, in contrast with what he said above: “My heart is troubled,” and so forth.

And it is necessary that you redeem me from them, “because they were with me,” not among the few—that is, among the number of the just, who are called few in comparison with the wicked—but “among the many,” that is, among the number of the wicked, who are many.

### “God will hear”

He will hear me concerning what I ask of him, and he will also hear me concerning what I ask against my enemies. “And he will humble,” that is, afflict, “them”—God, I say, “who is before the ages.” By this he makes known that Christ himself also humbles them, since in his divinity he existed before the ages.

### “For there is no change for them”

Therefore he will humble them, “for there is no change for them,” that is, they did not wish to be changed from evil to good. And this is why “they did not fear God,” and for this reason God “stretched out,” that is, will stretch out, “his hand,” that is, his vengeance, upon them “in requital.”

For “they polluted his testament,” that is, his law, by interpreting the Scriptures wrongly, acting perversely. This does not mean that God’s law could be polluted in itself, but that it was polluted with respect to those who defiled themselves, just as a wicked deacon is said to pollute the Gospel of God.

Therefore “they are divided” in the present from imperial rule, and in the future from the fellowship of the just; and they are divided “from the anger of his face,” that is, because they have deserved his anger. “And his heart,” that is, his will, which is now hidden, “will draw near,” that is, will be made manifest, because at last they will understand why God chose one and rejected another.

Therefore they are divided, because “they softened their speeches” with much rhetorical composition. Or, “their speeches were softened,” namely, the speeches of the Jewish people, “above oil,” because their words penetrate more deeply into the hearts of those whom they deceive than oil penetrates the flesh. Yet these same speeches, though so softened, “are arrows,” that is, they kill the hearts of men.

And when the wicked are thus divided from the anger of God, you, good man, must not fear, but “cast your thought upon the Lord.” Another reading has: “His speeches were softened.” It is then read in this way: They are divided from the anger of God, but you, good man, “cast” your thought, that is, “your care, upon the Lord”; expect everything from him and nothing from yourself.

Solomon calls care the worm of man, by which man is gnawed, like a garment by a moth, and each thing by its own particular worm. I say, cast it; and you can do so because the speeches of God, which previously could not be understood, have been softened, that is, made intelligible above oil, because they penetrate human hearts more deeply than oil penetrates flesh. And they are arrows for attacking the judgments of enemies.

I have said, “Cast your care upon the Lord,” “and the Lord himself will nourish you” in faith and by granting increase in virtues. Although you experience wavering here, nevertheless “he will not give wavering to the just forever,” that is, he will not give them disturbance, but will make them peaceful in eternal life.

But you, God, will not give wavering to the just; rather, “those whom you divide in anger, you, O God, will lead into the pit of destruction,” that is, into the depth of death, handing them over to hell.

### “Men of blood”

I say that you will lead them into the pit, and sooner than they themselves think. “Men of blood,” that is, those who kill the innocent bodily. Judges who kill spiritually those who are alive should not be called murderers or deceitful men. “They will not halve their days,” namely, the days which they suppose they will have.

“But I will hope in you, O Lord.”

Or, “they will not halve their days” means that they will not do what they ought to do: if they committed evil in the first and second stages of life, they should at least cease in the last. Or “they will not halve,” that is, they are not permitted to divide their service, serving God partly and the devil partly. Hence the Gospel says: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6).

# ON PSALM 55

## Title

“For the end, a psalm of David for the people who have been made far from the holy ones, in the inscription of the title, when the Allophyles seized him in Gath.”

### “Have mercy on me, O God, because…”

Here he touches upon the history of the New and Old Testaments. He speaks of the New Testament where he says, “in the inscription of the title,” for it is not read in the Old Testament history that David had any inscription. He speaks of the Old Testament where he says, “the Allophyles seized him in Gath.” Fleeing the fury of Saul, David came to Gath, into the land of the Allophyles, and they seized and trampled upon him (1 Samuel 21).

In this oppression David understood the oppression of the Church. “Allophyles” is interpreted as “foreigners”; similarly, “Philistines” is interpreted as “falling through drink.” “Gath” is interpreted as “winepress.”

The title is read in this way: This psalm is attributed to David, namely, so that the Church itself may be delivered from the people who have been made far from the holy ones in the inscription of the title. For when the holy ones confess Christ to be king of the Jews, as the title says, this people contradicts them—some, if not in words, nevertheless in deeds. By this they have been made far away, when, that is, because, they seized him: David, that is, Christ and the Church.

The Allophyles signify this people alienated from God; Gath signifies the winepress, namely, the oppression of this life. The subject is the Church, and it speaks about itself.

The structure is as follows. In the first part it asks to be delivered from demons and from their members, placing the confidence of its deliverance in God. In the second part, beginning where it says, “All day long my words were exercised,” it enumerates the evils committed by that people, while nevertheless saying that it does not fear those evils, since the people also yields to it. In the third part, beginning where it says, “In me are your vows, O God,” it says that it will praise God forever.

The intention is to admonish us to endure patiently the evils of this life, observing that even those who inflict evils upon us may be converted to us. And although the Church trusts in its deliverance, nevertheless, attending to its own weakness, it begins to pray in this way:

“Have mercy on me, O God.” And it is necessary that you do so, “because man,” that is, the devil, who is called man—namely, carnal and earthly—“has trampled me.” Of him the Gospel says: “An enemy man came and sowed weeds over it” (Matthew 13). This man, “all day long fighting,” by words and suggestions, “has troubled me” through open attacks.

### “They have trampled me”

He shows by what means the Church is subjected to this kind of attack. I say that he troubled me by this: “because my enemies have trampled me,” after the manner of a grape pressed in the winepress. The devil’s shadow has oppressed me. And “all day long” they were able to trample me, “because there are many fighting against me.”

They have trampled me in this way, but I “will fear” their “height,” that is, their power. Yet this power is not permanent, for it belongs to “a day,” that is, it has been granted only for a time, and it is small, so that it may be called the power of a single day. As though he were saying: I will not fear, but rather “I will hope in you.”

I say that I will hope in you, and “I will praise,” that is, I will make praiseworthy, “my words,” that is, my preaching, because they will be “in God.” I said, “I will hope in God,” and for this reason “I will not fear what flesh can do to me,” that is, whatever carnal person may do.

### “All day long my words were exercised”

Here begins the second part. I rightly say that he can do this, because they continually do evil to me. “All day long my words were exercised,” that is, they judged my preaching accursed. “And all their thoughts were for evil against me,” not because of any merit of mine, but tending toward evil for themselves, because they were thinking unjustly.

Nor did strangers alone inflict evils upon me; even those close to me did so. This is expressed by “they will dwell” bodily “with me” and “will hide” snares of death from me. If they cannot deceive immediately, then, imitating their master the devil, who always wishes to deceive a man at the end, “they themselves will watch my heel.”

Thus they will watch my heel, “as they bore my soul.” For the wicked carry the life of the just like a heavy burden. But I do not care, because you, O Lord, “will save them,” and this “for nothing,” that is, without any merit of theirs. You will save them because you will “break,” that is, humble, “the peoples in anger,” that is, through some vengeance which you will take upon them.

Or “in anger” means in consideration of the anger that is to come on the day of judgment. You will break them, and I add my own part toward their conversion: I will announce that I have committed many sins and that they have been forgiven me, so that, hearing this, they may not despair concerning their own sins. This is expressed by: “O God, I have announced my life to you,” namely, what proceeds from me—my sins—and also “my tears” poured out for these sins I have presented to you, which you “have placed in your sight.”

### “As also in your promise”

God’s promise is that he will receive the tears which are shed by the saints. Through your breaking of them and my announcement, “my enemies will be converted” from their evil way, so that they will be “behind,” that is, will follow me.

They will be converted, and “on whatever day” I, together with them, having now become one Church, “call upon you, behold, I have known” that you will hear me. And this is because “you are my God,” that is, my helper.

### “In God I will praise”

And because you will hear me, “in God I will praise the word,” that is, the Son of God in God the Father, by understanding and preaching him to be the coeternal, omnipotent Son, wholly the same with God the Father. “And in the Lord I will praise the speech,” that is, I will proclaim that Christ’s preaching was accomplished through the Holy Spirit.

Therefore “I hoped in God,” and for this reason “I will not fear what man can do to me,” that is, any carnal person.

Here begins the third part. Therefore I will not fear, because even if these temporal things are taken from me, there will nevertheless remain for me something by which I may serve you. For “in me,” that is, in my interior self, “O God, are your vows,” that is, the desires to serve you. These vows I will “render to you,” namely, praises to you; that is, I will praise you, or I will render vows of praise to you.

### “Because”

And I ought to praise you, “because you have delivered my soul,” that is, you will deliver it in the other life, “from death,” eternal death. Concerning this deliverance I am as certain as if I already possessed it. And “you will deliver my feet,” that is, my affections, “from falling,” because there my affection will in no way be moved toward evil.

You will deliver me for this purpose: that, placed “in the light of the living,” that is, possessing the knowledge of God which the truly living will have, I may “please” you and all good persons “before God,” that is, in the good pleasure of God.

# ON PSALM 56

## Title

“For the end: ‘Do not destroy David,’ in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.”

### “Have mercy on me, O God”

Here he again touches upon the old and the new history. In the old history it is read (1 Samuel 22 and 24) that David, fleeing Saul, hid himself with his men in a cave. It happened that Saul turned aside into the same cave to relieve his bowels. When David was urged by his men to kill him, he refused, but secretly cut off a part of the king’s cloak, so that Saul might recognize from this that David could have killed him if he had wished.

When the king had gone out, David came out and cried: “King of Israel, pay attention: when I cut off part of your garment, I could have killed you if I had wished.” Then the king, recognizing his own iniquity, nevertheless did not cease from persecuting him.

We should not understand the Prophet to have written here merely about this tribulation of David. Rather, he understood Christ in himself. The cave in which he hid signifies Christ’s humanity, in which his divinity was hidden; “from the face of Saul” signifies from the knowledge of the devil, or of the Jews, who attacked Christ through the devil.

Or by the cave we may understand the tomb in which Christ was hidden. Ezra, recognizing that the Prophet understood this concerning Christ, therefore gave the psalm this title, which is read in the following way:

This psalm tends “to the end,” that is, to Christ, and admonishes us: O man, whether you are Jew or Gentile, “do not destroy David,” that is, do not dishonor Christ, in the inscription of the title altered by you—that is, by withdrawing yourself from Christ’s kingdom, namely, by denying that Christ is king of the Jews.

The inscription of the title is said to have been altered by certain people at the time when David fled from the face of Saul—that is, from the knowledge of the devil and the Jews—into the cave, that is, into humanity or the tomb.

Because they knew only Christ’s humanity and saw him dead in the tomb, paying no attention at all to the fact that he was God, certain people altered the inscription of the title, denying that Christ was king of the Jews.

The subject is Christ. The structure is that in the first part, as in the other psalms in which he treats of the Passion, he first sets down a prayer. In the second part, beginning “My heart is ready, O God,” he shows that, as a result of his glorification, he offers great praise to God.

The intention is that we should not destroy David—that is, that we should always confess Christ as king. He rightly gives this admonition by showing that Christ, although he suffered at one time, was nevertheless greatly glorified, and through his glorification acquired praise for God among every people.

Christ, foreseeing his Passion, prays in this way: “Have mercy on me, O God; have mercy on me.” By repeating the prayer, he indicates to us great necessity. Therefore you must have mercy, “because my soul trusts in you.”

### “And in the shadow of your wings”

He gives the manner in which he wishes God to have mercy upon him. Have mercy, and you ought to do so, because “I will hope in the shadow,” that is, in the refreshment, “of your wings,” that is, of your mercy and power.

He speaks by comparison. Just as a hen shades her chicks with her wings and protects them from heat, so God, through his mercy and power, overshadows and protects those who hope in him. “I will hope,” he says, “until iniquity passes away,” that is, until they have fulfilled all their iniquities against me.

“I will cry; I will hope,” and not idly, but “I will cry to God Most High,” who also rules over the angels. And lest someone say, “Since he is so exalted, he will not regard you,” he says: Although he is Most High, he will nevertheless regard me, because he humbled himself to me. This is what he says: “To God who has done good to me.”

### “He sent from heaven”

This is the good he did for me: “he sent from heaven” the Word who united himself to my lowliness; “and” through this Word “he delivered me,” that is, my soul, my humanity, by removing all evils and granting glorification.

Through the same Word he “gave over to reproach those who trampled upon me,” that is, he made the Jews who trampled upon me a reproach among all nations.

In this verse the second part begins. He briefly sets forth the glorification when he says, “he delivered me,” and the Passion when he says, “those who trampled upon me.”

### “He sent”

He specifies what he sent and from whom he delivered him when he says: “God sent his mercy,” that is, his Son, through whom he had mercy upon the human race, “and his truth,” that is, the same Son, who is called truth because through him all God’s promises were fulfilled.

Through this mercy “he rescued my soul from the midst,” that is, from the common mass, because they attacked it from every side; from the midst, I say, “of the young lions,” that is, of the Jewish people, who are the children “of lions,” namely, of the evil rulers, by whom the lesser people were incited like cubs to attack Christ.

He delivered me, I say, and this was necessary because I was “troubled” by them through the evils which they inflicted upon me, and in that trouble “I slept,” that is, I died. He rightly compares his death to sleep, because just as someone is easily roused from sleep, so Christ was easily roused from death.

### “The sons of men”

I rightly say that I was troubled, and he shows by whom: namely, by the Jews. It is as though he were saying: Truly I was troubled, because “the sons of men,” that is, the Jews, who are sons of rational men—namely, generated by the prophets—and therefore ought to use reason, “prepared a snare,” that is, some deception, “for my feet,” that is, for my preaching.

“And they bent down my soul,” because according to their opinion my soul was oppressed and bent down by many sins. Or they bent down my soul because they made me grieve over their hardness. Hence he says in another psalm: “I humbled my soul with fasting.”

Someone might say: “They did not prepare the snare; rather, the Romans killed you.” To this he answers: On the contrary, they prepared it, because although they did not kill me with their hands, they killed me with their tongue. This is expressed by: “Their teeth,” that is, their corrosions, “were weapons,” that is, open attacks, “and arrows,” that is, deceits and plans by which they would strike me secretly; “and their tongue was a sharp sword,” making death, like a sword, as when they said: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

### “Be exalted”

After inserting an account of how the Jews attacked him through words, he makes another insertion concerning his deliverance. The connection is this: They attack me in this way, but you, God, who appeared humble while permitting me to be troubled, “be exalted,” that is, appear exalted; raise me up, leading me “above the material heavens.”

Or “the heavens” means above the angelic creature. “And” through this, if you exalt me, “your glory” will be poured out “over all the earth,” that is, the fame of your name.

After this insertion he supplies the clause on which the construction depended: The sons of men prepared a snare.

### “They dug”

I say that they bent down my soul, and also “they dug,” that is, they prepared a pit—namely, death—into which they might cast me, from which I could in no way escape. They did this “before my face,” that is, in my sight, when they said: “He is deserving of death” (Matthew 26).

“And” they themselves “fell into it,” because where they plotted death for me, they killed themselves.

### The third part

The connection is this: They inflicted so many evils upon me; nevertheless, “my heart” was always “ready” to sing to you, and “my heart” was always “ready” to sing psalms to you. What it was ready for, I will fulfill, because “I will sing,” that is, I will praise with heart and mouth, “and I will sing a psalm,” by acting well.

I say that I will sing a psalm and sing; and so that I may fulfill this, “rise up,” that is, appear, O “my glory,” which until now has been hidden. And you, “psaltery and harp,” that is, my flesh, “rise up,” that is, appear in the power which you possess from God.

The flesh of Christ is called a psaltery because of the works which he always performed. It is called a harp because of mortification, since in the Passion he was stretched out upon the wood like the hide of a dead animal. Hence elsewhere also: “They counted all my bones.”

I say, “Rise up,” and I do not doubt the resurrection, because “I will rise,” and, to state the time with complete certainty, I say, “at dawn,” that is, very early in the morning, on the first day of the week.

And when I have risen, “I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you through preachers, “among the peoples,” that is, among the Jews, “and among the nations I will sing a psalm to you,” that is, I will acquire good workers for you.

### “Because”

He shows through whom he will confess, namely, through the heavens and the clouds, and he shows by what means they were made heavens and clouds: through the mercy of God, which has been magnified.

The connection is this: I say, “I will confess,” and this confession will occur “because your mercy has been magnified,” that is, your Son has been magnified “as far as the heavens” to be established. For he established certain people as heavens, namely, the holy apostles in the Church.

“And your truth,” that is, the same Son, who is rightly called truth because through him the promises of God the Father were fulfilled, “has been magnified as far as the clouds” to be established, namely, the holy preachers who rain upon the Church the dew of heavenly doctrine.

Or “mercy has been magnified” means that the Son ascended above the heavens. The following words remain unchanged.

And in order that other heavens and other clouds may be established, “be exalted,” O God, “above the heavens, and your glory above all the earth.”

This verse, which is called an intercalary verse, is therefore found especially often, because in it the principal force of the whole intention depends: namely, that we should not destroy David.

# ON PSALM 57

## Title

“For the end: ‘Do not destroy David,’ in the inscription of the title.”

### “If indeed you truly…”

This psalm tends “to the end,” that is, to Christ, admonishing you—whoever you are—not to destroy David, that is, to honor Christ, with the inscription of the title altered. Always confess him as king of the Jews. This is the intention, as in the other psalm: that we should not destroy David.

The subject, by contrast, is the Jews, because Christ ought to be primary.

The structure is as follows. In the first part he rebukes the Jews by enumerating certain of their evils. In the second part, beginning “God will break the teeth of them,” he shows the condemnation of the Jews. In the third part, beginning “The just man will rejoice,” he shows that the just rejoice. By showing that the Jews who destroyed David are condemned, he especially admonishes us not to destroy David.

The Prophet’s voice begins the rebuke in this way: O you, “sons of men,” namely, of the prophets, whose reason you ought to imitate, “if indeed you speak justice,” that is, if you speak with a true and faithful heart according to God, then “judge rightly,” recognizing Christ, who has already been promised as our Redeemer and as the Son of God, and so forth.

I therefore say, “Judge rightly,” because you do not judge rightly; rather, you, placed “on earth,” that is, in the desire for earthly things, “work iniquities in your heart,” that is, you think iniquitously. And as you think evil, so you act. This is expressed by: “Your hands compose,” that is, execute in agreement, “injustices.”

They do this because “the sinners are alienated,” that is, rejected by God, “from the womb,” that is, from conception itself. Or “from the womb” means from the nourishment of the Church. They are not merely alienated, but also “have gone astray,” that is, have been assigned to errors, “from the womb,” namely, from conception, or from the womb of the Church, in which some are nourished so that they may be brought to the faith.

And they were not evil only in themselves; they also “spoke falsehoods” in order to deceive others.

### “Their fury”

“Their fury” is also “according to the likeness of a serpent,” and not merely of any serpent, but “like that of a deaf asp,” not deaf by nature, but one that stops up its own ears.

### “Which does not hear the voice of charmers”

The asp “does not hear the voice of charmers,” and not of just any charmers, but of “wise charmers,” namely, of an enchanter who is wise.

For when it is enchanted in its cave, it presses one ear against the earth and blocks the other with its tail, lest it come out into the light and its poison be drawn out. In the same way, the Jews, existing in the caves of ignorance and sins, press one ear against the earth—that is, against the delight of present goods—and block the other with the tail, that is, with the former or ancient custom of their law, so that they cannot perceive the truth of the Gospel.

Thus they cannot emerge into true knowledge, and the poison cannot be drawn out from them—that is, hatred and the other sins.

“God will crush them.” Second part, continuation: And because they are so wicked, “God will crush them,” that is, he will destroy them and expose the false “teeth of theirs,” that is, their acts of gnawing away, “in their own mouth,” that is, in their own words, because it often happens that they are convicted of falsehood by their own words. Thus Augustine, against the soldiers who said that Christ’s body had been secretly stolen while they were asleep, says: “If they slept, how did they know? And if they were not asleep, why did they not guard it?” And he will also break “the molars,” that is, their grandiloquent words—for the molars are called the larger teeth—“of lions,” that is, of the greater princes. “He will break” them, that is, destroy them, and “the Lord” will expose them as false; nor will they be able to achieve any result. And another evil: “They will come to nothing” concerning the glory of their kingdom, “like water running away.” For just as a torrent quickly swells from rains and quickly subsides, [Col. 0389A] so they will quickly fail, and thereby come to nothing, because God “bends his bow,” that is, prepares his vengeance, “until they become weak,” that is, until they are converted to God.

“They will also be taken away like wax that melts,” because they will be annihilated like wax, since they will descend into eternal fire. Therefore they will be taken away, because “fire,” that is, the ardor of their desire, “fell” upon them, “and” therefore “they did not see the sun,” that is, they did not recognize Christ. Here he turns toward them. Continuation: Fire fell upon them, and this occurred before you understood that you were to be punished for your sins. This is what is meant: before “your thorns,” that is, your sins, “understood” that they were “a thorn-bush,” that is, things that pierce. The thorn-bush is a plant that is at first soft; then, when it matures, it has very sharp spines. So sins are initially soft and pleasurable, but afterward they pierce most grievously. Another translation plainly confirms this meaning: “before your thorns produce a thorn-bush.”

Or alternatively: I say that they will be taken away, and truly you will be taken away more quickly than you think. This is the meaning: “You will be taken away before your thorns produce a thorn-bush,” that is, before they reach maturity and the completion of wickedness. I say that they will be taken away through this: he “will swallow them up,” that is, he will destroy them, as though they had been swallowed by the earth. He will swallow them, I say, “as in anger,” that is, as one who is angry. And he rightly says “as,” because God is never angry. He says that they are not living, but “as though living,” because they do not truly live; even if they appear outwardly to be alive, inwardly they are dead, [Col. 0389C] because they lack life, which is God.

“He will rejoice,” the third part. God will thus avenge himself upon them, but “the just man, when he sees this vengeance, will rejoice,” assenting to divine justice. And he “will wash,” that is, cleanse, “his hands,” that is, his works, “in the blood of the sinner,” that is, in contemplation of the blood—that is, of the vengeance that God will take upon the sinner. “And that man will say: If there is fruit for the just man,” namely, from your justice—which indeed there is—“then surely there is a God judging them,” the wicked, that is, judging them worthy of condemnation, “on the earth,” that is, while they live in this world.

## ON PSALM 58

### TITLE

“For the end: Do not destroy David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.”

“Deliver me.” Here something is touched upon from the new and the old history. For in the old history (1 Kings 19) we read that David, fleeing from Saul, went to Michal, his wife, in one of his houses. When Saul learned this, he had the house guarded so that David could not escape and so that he might kill him. But his wife, perceiving this, lowered him through a window, and thus he was freed.

Through the fact that David was thus surrounded in his house, he understood that Christ would be guarded by Saul’s servants—that is, by the devil—in his tomb, so that they might kill him, that is, extinguish his fame. The title is therefore read in this way: This psalm tends toward the end, that is, toward Christ, admonishing you, whoever you are, not to destroy David, that is, to corrupt Christ’s kingdom, namely Christ: “in the inscription of the title,” altered by certain people, at the time when Saul, that is, the devil, sent soldiers and guarded the house, that is, Christ’s tomb, in order to kill him, that is, to extinguish his fame. Certain people had this reason for altering the title: they saw him dead and placed in the tomb.

The subject is Christ, concerning whom it proceeds as follows. In the first part he asks for deliverance and exaltation. In the second part, the conversion of the nations, which proceeds from that exaltation and deliverance; it begins there: “They will return in the evening.” In the third part, the conversion of the Jews, which is found in the words “and concerning cursing and deceit.” In the fourth part, the praise that the whole Christ will offer to God for this deliverance and for the conversion of Jews and nations; it begins there: “But I will sing of strength.” The intention is: Do not destroy David. The voice of the Head, praying in this way for his deliverance:

“My God, deliver me” by your great power, so that these wicked men may not make me like themselves: “from my enemies, and free me from those rising up against me.”

“Deliver me from those practicing iniquity, and save me from men of blood.” Enemies are those who have only the will to harm their neighbor. Those rising up are people who have already been stirred by fury and anger so as to do evil, but nevertheless do not do it. Those contradicting by word and practicing iniquity are people who actually inflict evil. Men of blood are those who direct their fury toward the killing of human beings. And it is necessary that you deliver me, [Col. 0390C] “for behold,” it is manifest that “the strong have seized my soul,” that is, the demons and the princes of the Jews, “they have rushed upon me,” that is, they have attacked me without any reason.

“Neither is there iniquity.” Having shown the necessity of his deliverance, he shows the merit by which it is fitting that he be delivered. Continuation: I say, “Deliver me, free me,” because what they do to me “is neither my iniquity,” that is, I have neither sinned against them in will nor in deed. This is what follows: “nor my sin, Lord.” Or, iniquity with respect to one’s neighbor, and sin with respect to oneself: namely, I have neither sinned against them nor against myself, so that they should do these evils to me. Rather, “I ran,” that is, I completed my military service, “without iniquity,” namely, I inflicted no evil upon them; [Col. 0390D] and not only did I inflict no evil, but I did good. This is what follows: “and I directed” certain people by example and instruction, so that they might ascend to the path of true knowledge.

And because I ran in this way, O Lord—you who then seemed to be asleep, since you allowed me to be afflicted—“rise to meet me,” that is, come to me by rewarding me well. God the Father met Christ by raising him from the dead, rewarding him well for his service; Christ met the Father by deserving well of him. “Rise,” I say, “and see,” that is, make others see and recognize my exultation, so that although they may once have seen me cast down, they may now recognize me as King of the Jews. “And you, Lord, attend,” that is, present yourself as attentive, “to visiting all the nations,” which are weak and burdened [Col. 0391A] with sins; therefore it is necessary that you attend by breathing grace upon them and sending preachers to them. You are, I say, “God of hosts,” that is, of the angels, “and God of Israel,” that is, of the Israelite people. Visit them in such a way as to make the nations one body with the angels; and together with the Israelite people, visit the nations.

“And do not show mercy to all,” not meaning that you show mercy to none who wish to be converted, but not to all—namely, do not show mercy to the obstinate—“who practice” great “iniquity,” namely, my death. Or, “who practice iniquity,” that is, who persist in their wickedness. The obstinacy of the Jews served the conversion of the nations. Hence it is said: “Blindness has happened in Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter” (Romans 11).

After setting forth the prayer for conversion, he sets forth the affirmation of conversion. [Col. 0391B] Continuation: I say, “Attend,” and truly you will attend, because the nations “will be converted” from their idolatry to the worship of God, and this “in the evening,” that is, in the time of grace. “And they will suffer hunger,” incorporating others into themselves, “like dogs” barking in the preaching of God, “and they will go around the city,” that is, guarding the Church with great care, so that no heretic may find an opportunity to attack it.

I say that they will suffer hunger, and “behold,” namely, it is manifest that they “will speak” in the preaching of God “with their mouth,” that is, in a manner suited to themselves, because what they preach in word they confirm by example and deed. “And a sword,” that is, the word of God, by which the preachers kill the enemies of Christ through excommunication and defend the children of the Church from the attacks of heretics, [Col. 0391C] who are cut from both sides (Galatians 3), namely, from the New and the Old Testament, “will be on their lips.” Therefore the sword will be on their lips, “because who has heard” them—that is, someone has heard them, meaning that someone has obeyed them as they preached. Those who have heard them they defend with the sword; those who do not hear them they attack. Or: Who heard the preaching before the nations possessed the sword of God? It is as though he were saying: almost no one. Therefore it was necessary that the nations preach the word of God.

The nations will be converted, “and you will mock” those who will not be converted, that is, you will show them to be mockable. It may also be read in a good sense: The nations will be converted, “and you, Lord, will mock them,” the converted, that is, you will show them to be mockable to themselves, because they will recognize that, according to their former life, they were mockable and contemptible. “And you will bring all the nations to nothing,” both the good and the wicked. The good are brought to nothing when they abandon their former life and regard it as nothing. The wicked are brought to nothing when they are condemned on account of their former life.

“Strength.” After showing the conversion of the nations, he shows why he will not destroy his Jewish enemies, although he could do so: because, according to God’s will, he understood that their conversion and dispersion would be useful for the conversion of the nations, and also for the conversion of the Jews, which is to take place in the last times. Continuation: All the nations will be brought to nothing, but “I will keep my strength,” that is, my patience, by which I can destroy the Jews, “for you,” that is, according to your will. It is according to God’s will because “God has shown me,” as one who was “over my enemies,” since I was superior to all of them and could avenge myself upon them at my pleasure. He does not state what God showed him, but this can be understood from what follows: namely, that their preservation would be useful. I say that God showed this to me, and what he showed me I ought to do, “because” he “is my protector,” when he united my humanity to his divinity, “and also my God,” that is, my Creator. “His mercy will go before me.” For Christ was always preceded by God’s mercy, both in the very conception and ever afterward.

God showed this to me, and you, Lord, “do not kill them,” that is, do not [Col. 0392B] utterly destroy my enemies. For this reason I pray: “lest my people,” that is, the Gentiles, “forget me,” when—that is, at some time—for even if they would not forget me immediately, they would nevertheless forget me after a long time unless they had the Jews, who by their dispersion confirm the death of Christ the Redeemer; and the law they possess is a testimony to Christ. Or: lest my people forget me.

Do not kill them, but rather “scatter them” throughout various kingdoms, and this “by your power,” that is, by your might. Christ’s petition was fulfilled when Titus and Vespasian scattered them. And he begins to pray for their conversion, saying to God: “Bring them down, my protector Lord,” from their pride.

“Sin.” Bring down their pride, and also bring down “the sin of their mouth,” that is, of their heart. The heart is called the mouth because it gapes with desires like a mouth. “And” also bring down “the word of their lips,” as when they said: “You have a demon” (John 7 and 8), and similar things. “And let them be caught,” that is, convicted, “in their pride,” so that they may recognize that they have fallen into these miseries on account of their pride.

I say, let them be caught. Third part. Truly let them be caught, because “on account of cursing,” that is, because everyone regards them as accursed, “and on account of deceit.” For they were liars in wrongly interpreting the Scriptures, and they also lied about Christ when they said: “His disciples came by night and stole his body.” And they were taught concerning these things in completion, that is, in the perfection of virtues. And so others will announce—namely, it will be said that the Jews who were enemies of Christ have been converted to him—and they too will announce that they are “in the wrath of completion,” that is, perfect and completed, as they contemplate the wrath and vengeance of the Judge at the future judgment. “And” they “will not be” what they previously were, namely, blasphemers and sinners.

Or, “they will be announced,” that is, through those who announce them they will be “in completion.” Another translation has a clearer wording: “And from cursing and deceit they will be torn out in the wrath of completion.”

“And” then those Jews “will know that God will rule Jacob,” that is, the Jewish people, “and” also the ends of the earth, that is, the Gentiles, throughout all the nations [Col. 0393A] of the earth. The Jews will recognize that the same God is the God of Jews and Gentiles. Here he sets forth the manifest conversion. Continuation: They will be torn away from cursing because “they will return in the evening,” that is, around the end of the world, “and they will suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city,” as above.

And “they,” the converts who were formerly scattered unwillingly, will of their own accord “be scattered to eat,” so that they may make others their food, that is, incorporate them into themselves. “But if they are not satisfied, they will murmur,” that is, if they cannot incorporate others into themselves as they wish, they will murmur. Just as formerly in the desert they murmured for bodily food, so now they will murmur for spiritual food.

“But I.” Fourth part. Although they will thus be scattered, “I,” safe on account of all these things, “will sing,” that is, I will praise in heart and mouth, “your strength,” that is, the power by which you delivered me and converted Jews and Gentiles, “and I will exult,” that is, exulting I will proclaim “your truth” concerning the resurrection, which took place “in the morning,” both in me and especially in those who belong to me.

I rightly do this “because you have become my protector,” and the protector of those who belong to me, unto the greatest dignity, “and my refuge” when it was most necessary, namely, “on the day of my tribulation,” and of the tribulation of those who belong to me in this life. “I will sing,” and also “I will play the psaltery,” by doing good works, “to you,” who are “my helper” in good works. I will play the psaltery for this reason, “because you are my protector, God,” not a human protector, but God the protector—that is, because you deify what you have taken up—and also “my God,” that is, my Creator, [Col. 0393C] “and also my mercy,” that is, the one who through mercy does everything for me and for those who belong to me.

## ON PSALM 59

### TITLE

“For the end: for those who will be changed; an inscription of the title, by David himself, for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

“God, you have rejected us.” After Saul’s death, once David had obtained the kingdom, he burned Mesopotamia, namely, part of Syria, and Syria of Zobah, another part of Syria. Then he turned against Joab, his enemy, and struck Edom (2 Kings 8 and 10; 1 Chronicles 18), that is, the people of Idumea, because that people came from the land of Idumea, which was so called after Esau, its inhabitant. Esau was called Edom because he loved earthly things.

Through these victories David understood the victories Christ would achieve over Jews and Gentiles. The title is explained as follows: This psalm, composed for those who will be changed—that is, for the honor of those who will be changed into the end, namely, into Christ, or into perseverance—shows two changes of the just person. One takes place in this life, from sin to righteousness; the second in the other life, from mortality to immortality. This change takes place through the inscription of the title, received through faith, namely because they believe Christ to be King of the Jews. The inscription is made for David himself, that is, for Christ, and also leads to instruction, that is, to his commandments, as one conforms himself to the law of Christ so as to act according to it, because “faith without works is dead” (James 2).

They will be changed, I say, when he burns—that is, by the fact that he burns with the fire of God—Mesopotamia of Syria, that is, the Jews, whom he raised by calling them and lifted by raising them into another dignity. Previously they were exalted, that is, exceptionally proud of their knowledge of God. For Mesopotamia means “high calling.” Syria, however, is interpreted as “sublime,” that is, Christ burns Syria of Zobah, namely those same Jews, exalted and proud because of vain antiquity, that is, because of the carnal observances of the law. For Zobah is interpreted as “vain antiquity.”

And he turned Joab, that is, his enemy, namely the Gentile people, to his faith from idolatry, because they had no knowledge of God, and he struck them, that is, moved them from unbelief to faith. Edom, that is, the Gentile people devoted to earthly things or bloodstained through sins. For Edom is interpreted either as “earthly” or as “bloodstained.” He struck the earthliness of the nations, namely, so that they would no longer seek earthly things. Through this he converted Joab, that is, the Gentile people, and struck them in such a way that they would be in the Valley of Salt.

They were in the valley, that is, in humility, which is the mother of all virtues and the seasoning of all good things, like salt among foods. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind. He struck, I say, twelve thousand, that is, everyone in the four regions of the world who confesses the faith of the Holy Trinity. The number one thousand signifies perfection.

The subject is the Jews and Gentiles converted to faith through Christ’s blows. The method is as follows. In the first part, through many arguments and by the authority of God himself, he shows that they are to be changed, namely from sin to righteousness. In the second part, which begins, “Save by your right hand,” he shows that through the same change they will reach another change, namely from mortality to immortality. The intention is that no one despise these blows, because through them they receive both changes.

The voice of those converted to faith through Christ’s blows: because they were going to say that they would be changed, he first shows from what they would be changed, when he says:

“God, you have rejected us.” From that pleasant place in which you had first established our father: “and you have destroyed us,” making us mortal and subject to suffering, which was not the case before Adam sinned. This was not your fault, but ours, on account of which “you were angry” with us because of the preceding sin. “And” nevertheless “you had mercy on us” now through the Incarnation of the Son. Hence it is said elsewhere (Habakkuk 3): “When you are angry, you will remember mercy.”

He shows how he had mercy: “You shook the earth,” that is, earthly people out of error, “and you troubled it” toward repentance. And just as you began, O Lord, so complete the work: “heal its fractures,” that is, remove from it the miseries it endures, concerning which he said, “You have destroyed us.” This healing will take place in the general resurrection. Or, “heal its fractures,” that is, its sins, for which it has a contrite heart. It is just that you heal it, “because” it “has been shaken” by grace moving it through free will.

[Col. 0395A] “You have shown.” And although sins have been remitted through this shaking, you do not immediately gather them into rest; rather, you expose them to tribulations by which they may be purified. You have shaken them through this: you not only “showed” them, by mere knowledge, but through the experience of the thing itself, “hard things to your people,” that is, very severe tribulations. Or: You showed the people, who ought to imitate you, through example and preaching that they ought to suffer hard things. “And you gave us to drink,” that is, you made us take pleasure as in a good drink, “wine,” that is, tribulations, which are called wine because they cleanse the wounds of sins well, just as wine cleanses wounds of the flesh. I mean wine not of sweetness but “of compunction,” because through it we are pierced on every side.

“You have given.” I say that you gave the people wine of compunction, “and to those who fear you you gave a sign,” namely, these present tribulations, indicating and signifying to them that they should “flee from the face,” that is, from the vengeance of God, which they see before their face and consider as though present. From the face, I say, “of the bow,” that is, of divine Scripture, namely, the vengeance threatened by the Old and New Testaments. For the present tribulations that we endure for our former sin signify to us that, if we remain in sin here, we will be punished most severely at the future judgment.

Or by “sign” we can understand divine Scripture, which has been set before us so that we may follow it. Or we can take “sign” as the standard of the cross, which indicates to us that we should flee from the face of the bow. It is therefore still carried before the people, so that it may be a sign for us [Col. 0395C] not to flee from the passion of our Redeemer, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 3). Therefore you gave a sign “so that your beloved may be delivered,” having been made free from eternal punishment. Behold: through the miseries of this life he certifies the future change, which those miseries seemed to contradict.

The second part begins. I say, so that they may be delivered, and, “O Lord, deliver,” and this is the meaning: “Save the people who fear you,” “by your right hand,” that is, in your better gifts, namely, in eternal blessedness, “and” concerning this “hear me,” because I pray without interruption. Or he repeats the request because the matter is great.

“God.” I say, “Save,” and I rightly say this because I am confident concerning it, since “God has spoken in his holy place,” that is, in his Son, in whom he promised this salvation, about which he has spoken.

I, the faithful people, “will rejoice and will apportion Shechem,” that is, I will arrange shoulders, imposing burdens according to what shoulders can bear, making some presbyters, others deacons, and so forth. For Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” “and I will measure out the Valley of Tents,” that is, the Jews, who are understood through the Valley of Tents because Jacob, fleeing from his uncle Laban, rested with his sheep in the Valley of Tents (Genesis 31). He called that place the Valley of Tents because he first pitched his tents there. Through Jacob and his family the Jews are understood, since they were born from Jacob. “I will measure out,” that is, I will take some and reject others.

[Col. 0396A] “Gilead is mine,” that is, “heap of testimony,” namely, the multitude of martyrs. For Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” It was so called because it was the mound of stones that Jacob and Laban made as a sign of their covenant. Through the heap we have a multitude; through testimony, the martyrs, who by their passion bear witness to Christ’s passion. “Martyr” is Greek for “witness” in Latin. That Gilead is mine, that is, belongs to my fellowship, and will go with me to God.

“And Manasseh,” that is, “forgetfulness,” namely, the one who has forgotten his former condition, “is mine.” Hence it is said elsewhere: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 54). “And Ephraim,” that is, “those who bear fruit,” is “the strength of my head,” that is, of Christ. Through them Christ never appears weak, but strong. Or “of my head,” that is, the support of my mind.

When Joseph was in Egypt and Manasseh was born, he said: “Now I have forgotten my former sorrows.” For this reason he was called Manasseh, that is, “forgetfulness.” When Ephraim was born, he said: “Now I have borne fruit in a foreign land” (Genesis 41); for this reason he was called Ephraim, that is, “fruitfulness.”

“Judah is my king,” that is, Christ, who was to be born from the tribe of Judah, is my king. “Moab,” that is, the Gentile people, is “the pot,” that is, the refreshment, “of my hope,” that is, in which I hope for refreshment. Or, “the pot of my hope,” that is, the testing in which I hope that it will never fail, like a strong pot that, placed in the fire, is made more tested and stronger.

Moab is interpreted as “abusing the law,” or “from a father.” The people abused the law because they were born against the law. Lot, having been made drunk by his daughters, slept with both of them; by one he begot Moab, and by the other Ammon. From Moab came the Moabite peoples, and from Ammon the Ammonites.

He shows how the nations will become his, namely, through the preaching of the Gospel. This is the meaning: “I will extend my sandal,” that is, evangelical doctrine, because the Church is shod with it so that it may cross thorny and muddy places—indeed, every kind of such place. Hence the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6). This sandal, I say, I will extend “over Idumea,” that is, over the earthliness of the Gentiles, so that through the Gospel, once their earthliness has been crushed, I may make Moab mine.

“Foreigners also are mine,” that is, those who, although they adhere to me bodily, are nevertheless alien in mind, as hypocrites are. “They are subject to me.”

After the faithful who speak had said, “Save by your right hand,” and had said that they would gather many to themselves, they add that they are led by God himself into a fortified city, where they will receive the second change. Continuation: God promised this, but “who” is so powerful that he “will lead me into a fortified city,” that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem? And “who will lead me as far as Idumea,” that is, into Gentile territory, so that many from the nations may be incorporated into me and the city may be encompassed by the fellowship of its members?

“Is it not you, God,” who will lead me, “who,” nevertheless, as it appears, “have rejected” us by allowing us to be afflicted? You have rejected us, “and you will no longer go forth in our forces,” O “God,” that is, in our armies, because even today you neither order an army to be gathered nor provide visible assistance as you did to the ancient fathers.

You will not go forth so that we may live bodily, nor do we ask this. Rather, “give us help in tribulation,” namely, so that the tribulations inflicted upon us may help us and lead us to the fortified city. We do not ask for the salvation of human beings, because “the salvation of man is vain,” that is, transitory, if it comes from man.

I say that salvation is vain; therefore “in God we shall accomplish strength,” that is, we shall place the hope of our strength in God and not in human salvation or worldly things, since everything comes from him and we should attribute no good to ourselves. “And he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.”

Or, if Christ is introduced as speaking through the Church: God has spoken in his holy place, namely this: “I will rejoice” in the resurrection accomplished through me, “and I will apportion Shechem and measure out the Valley of Tents.” Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim, that is, the fruitful one, is the strength of my head, that is, of my divinity. In them my head is not weakened, but rests peacefully. Judah, that is, the confessor, is my king, whom I will establish as king. And I will extend my sandal, that is, my humanity, with which the divinity was shod, into Idumea, causing it to be proclaimed there. Who will lead me? Since Christ does these good things for me, who will lead me into the fortified city? And so forth.

## ON PSALM 60

### TITLE

“For the end: with hymns; a psalm of David.”

“Hear, O God, my supplication.” This psalm directs itself toward the end, composed with hymns, that is, with praises, by David, that is, by Christ. In this psalm the whole people, from every part of the world and through all generations, is shown crying out to the Lord Christ. It also shows that through Christ this people reaches the same inheritance that Christ himself possesses.

The subject is the faithful people, who… The method is that in the first part it shows itself crying out to Christ, as stated. In the second part, which begins, “For you, my God, have heard my prayer,” it shows that it possesses Christ’s inheritance. The intention is to oppose those who said that Christ belonged to only a few, and to show that Christ is the king of all.

It begins with prayer in this way: “Hear, O God, my supplication,” concerning the removal of evils, “and attend to my prayer,” [Col. 0397D] made concerning the obtaining of eternal life; “present yourself as attentive,” because the matter is great and requires great attention.

“Attend,” I say, because “I cried out,” that is, I carried out the act with unrelenting extension of heart, “to you,” to possess you, “from the ends of the earth,” that is, from all the ends of the earth, “while my heart was troubled,” whether by exterior or interior tribulation. And when I cried out from necessity, you “exalted me,” delivering me from evils and conferring righteousness.

I say that I was placed “upon a rock,” established in Christ through faith, in whom I am secure, as someone placed upon a very fortified rock. Or, “upon a rock,” that is, in steadfastness.

And having thus exalted me, “you led me” from virtue [Col. 0398A] to virtue, and not without merit, “because you became my hope, a tower of strength,” to which, if I flee, I will find strength, “from the face of the enemy,” that is, from every assault of the enemy.

After showing that the people from the whole earth would cry out to God, he shows that this would happen through all generations. Continuation: “You are my hope, a tower of strength,” and therefore “I will dwell in your tent,” that is, in the Church, in which one serves as your soldier, “through the ages,” that is, as long as this age lasts. And just as I am now protected, so I will always “be protected in the shelter,” that is, in the shadow “of your wings,” that is, of your clemency and power.

“For.” Here the second part begins. “Here I will be protected in the shelter,” and at last you will give “an inheritance [Col. 0398B] to those who fear your name.” I do not say that you will give it; rather, out of complete security I say, “you have given it.” And therefore I am certain of security, “because you, God, have heard my prayer,” namely, you will hear it when you give, and you have also heard it by conferring virtues upon me.

“Day upon day.” I say that you will give an inheritance, namely, “days upon the days of the king,” that is, of Christ. The days we have in this life you will add to us as eternal days, which Christ now possesses. And upon the years of the king that we have in this life, “you will add his years,” that is, the eternal years that Christ now possesses.

In this life he has the days that Christ possessed—whoever imitates his righteousness. Those who do not have years possess these days, as Hippolytus, who lived in faith for only three days, and certain others likewise. For this reason he adds [Col. 0398C] years: years, I say, you will add, which Christ himself possesses, “unto the day of generation and generation,” that is, of judgment, when the generation of body and soul will take place. Or, “of generation and generation,” that is, forever. Another translation has: “unto the age of the age.”

“He remains.” I say that you will add the king’s days, and it is no small thing to possess them, because that king with his whole household “remains forever,” that is, his days are eternal. He further commends that eternity. I say that he remains forever, and not in some insignificant place, but “in the sight of God,” because he always enjoys God’s presence. He further commends eternity because there no one will seek mercy, since no one there will be miserable. Again, another commendation: there no one will seek truth, because everyone there possesses perfect knowledge. This is what he puts in the form of a question: “Who will seek mercy and truth?”
