Here he offers praise for the things mentioned above. Continuation: “And because you will do these things for me, O God,” therefore “I will sing a psalm to your name,” that is, I will work well in order to enlarge your name, and this “for age upon age,” that is, for as long as this age lasts. And thus, “so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day,” that is, continually, so that I may let no day pass without working for your praise.

## ON PSALM 61

### TITLE

“For the end: for Idithun; a psalm of David.”

“Is not the soul subject to God?” This psalm applies to David and to the other just, composed for Idithun, that is, for those who leap across, directing itself toward the end, that is, toward Christ.

The subject is such leapers—those who can be prevented by no persuasion or tribulation from completing their leap, namely, from abandoning earthly things and pressing toward heavenly things alone.

The method is as follows. In the first part he shows that he cannot be prevented from completing his leap, rebuking the wicked who wish to hinder him either through persuasion or through tribulations. In the second part, which begins, “Nevertheless, my soul is subject to God,” he admonishes himself and others to be subject to God. In the third part, which begins, “Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain,” he rebukes the wicked for their wickedness.

The intention is to admonish us not to be prevented by any tribulation from leaping from earthly things to heavenly ones. It is as though he were saying, rebuking the wicked: You wish to prevent me from leaping, but in vain, because “will not the soul be subject to God?” That is, will it not obey him and keep his commandments?

I say, the soul is “mine,” that is, under my power, because although the body may sometimes be under your power, the soul will never be under anyone’s power except mine. It is truly subject, and it ought to be, because “from him,” namely, God the Father, “is my salvation,” that is, Christ, who is my Savior.

“For he himself.” And rightly my soul ought to be subject to him from whom that salvation comes to me, “for he,” from whom it proceeds, and he who proceeds, “is my God and my salvation,” because through the humanity he assumed he saved me, “and my protector,” because he took me from the lowliness of sin and led me to the dignity of righteousness. And therefore “I will not be moved any more,” that is, although I was once moved, nevertheless I will not be moved again.

And since I have such a Savior, by whom I shall no longer be moved, then, O fools, “how long”—that is, for how long—“do you rush upon the man,” namely, do you attack irrationally? For although you can afflict the body, you cannot touch the soul. And you rush upon us not only so as to take away our outward goods, but “you all kill yourselves”; another translation confirms this interpretation, reading: “you kill everyone.” Or in this way: You rush upon the man, and all of you kill yourselves inwardly, because, when you do evil to the good, you kill yourselves. You rush, I say, “like a leaning wall,” because, just as a leaning wall is inclined to collapse, so you think us inclined to ruin, as though we were deprived of every support, “and like a displaced wall,” because, just as a wall is fragile in itself, since it lacks cement, and, once displaced, hangs entirely over destruction, so you think us to be without every bond and utterly inclined to ruin.

For we are not a leaning wall or a wall fallen from its place. “Nevertheless,” the wicked do not cease on that account, but rather “they have thought to drive away” from me—that is, to take from me—“my price,” that is, God, whom alone I seek. Another translation has “my honor.” Nevertheless, I have always “run” through the warfare, and, “in thirst,” that is, in thirst for their salvation, I have followed this proposed path without turning aside, because I greatly thirsted for it.

[Col. 0400A] Continuation: They have thought to drive me away, and thus “with their mouths they blessed,” that is, in their mouths they wished good, “but in their hearts they cursed,” that is, if they said anything good, they said it with the intention of deception. In this verse he reveals their hidden attack. Or the continuation may be understood in this way: They all kill themselves, yet they do not cease on that account; rather, they have thought, and so forth.

“Nevertheless, to God.” The second part. They attack me through tribulations and deceits; “nevertheless, be subject, my soul, to God.” That is: Do not, because of persecutions, injuries, tribulations, and the other evils unjustly inflicted upon you, fail or depart from God’s commandments, so that you become either impatient or relapse into vices; rather, obey his word. And you ought to do so, because [Col. 0400B] “my patience comes not from myself, but from him,” since I could not endure unless he enabled me to do so.

“And again.” You ought therefore to be subject, O soul, because “he is my God and my Savior,” who received me through his humanity, redeeming me; “and” he is also “my helper” for doing good, “and therefore I shall not emigrate,” that is, depart from him by passing over to a foreign god.

I shall not emigrate, because in him I have complete sufficiency; and this is: “In God is my salvation,” that is, through God I possess salvation, “and my glory,” that is, through him I possess the glory of eternal life. He himself is also “the God of my help,” that is, he helps me to do good. And why should I enumerate each thing? Everything—“my hope is in God.”

[Col. 0400C] And since he is such, “all the congregation of the people, hope in him.” And so that you may hope securely, “pour out your hearts,” that is, empty your hearts of every defilement, so that they may be “before him,” that is, pleasing to him. For if they have not been emptied of evil and yet hope, that is not hope but presumption. I say, “hope,” because “God is our helper,” namely, the one who leads us “into eternity.”

“Nevertheless.” Here the third part begins. Continuation: God is the helper of his own; “nevertheless, the sons of men” do not attend to this, but are “vain,” that is, devoted to vanities. They are also “deceitful in the balances,” that is, in weights, since they sell false weight in silver and pepper, so that “they themselves may deceive others through their vanity,” that is, by means of their vanity, “persevering in the same thing,” namely, in vanity, tending from vanity to vanity. Or they are deceitful in the balances, in the scales of justice, because they present themselves as though they weighed everything equally—that is, as though they observed equity in all things. But since inwardly they are different from what they pretend to be outwardly, like men with beards, they do this so that they themselves may deceive others through vanity, namely, by leading them through their vanity into that same vanity, so that they may make them wicked along with themselves.

You sons of men are thus vain, but abandon your vanity. This is what follows: “Do not hope in iniquity.” And he explains this iniquity part by part. Even if you are poor, “do not desire plunder,” and do not love riches. This is also what follows: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” He does not forbid possessing riches, but forbids loving them; for one may possess them who distributes them appropriately.

For this one reason, then, do not do these evil things: God has the power to punish the wicked and reward the good. Thus: “For power belongs to God” to punish the wicked, “and to you, Lord, belongs mercy,” by which you reward the just. He demonstrates this through its effects: Truly, power and mercy belong to you, “because you will repay each one according to his works.” And as though someone were to ask: You know only now that mercy and power are in God? He says that he learned this from God’s own counsel, saying: “God spoke”—namely, creating all things. He spoke to us; I say that he spoke “once,” that is, he created all things immutably. And I, carried beyond myself and snatched up into his counsel, “heard” there—that is, understood—“these two things,” namely, that mercy and power are there, and so forth.

## On Psalm LXII

### Title

“To the end: a psalm of David, when he was in the desert of Idumaea.”

“God, my God.” Historically, David, fleeing from Saul, came into the desert of Idumaea. He understood that, in this figure, the Church is placed in the desert of this life, where there is nothing but earthly existence; and from the thing signified he sang this psalm. This psalm suits David the prophet together with all the just, while the Church itself is in the desert of Idumaea, that is, of this life.

Its structure is as follows. In the first part he shows that, instructed by the desert of this life, he hastens toward God with every desire. In the second part, beginning, “If I remembered you,” he shows the security found in this desert through God himself. Its purpose is to admonish them to choose God alone.

The voice of the whole Church speaks in this way: “I am placed in a desert land, pathless and waterless; I keep vigil,” that is, with every effort I abandon evil and do good in order to possess you. And this is “from the light,” that is, from the time when I came to know you, which is the cause of my vigilance. In this light we may especially understand illumination through the resurrection. To you I speak, O “God,” creator of all things, and “my God,” through great familiarity. By placing “God” twice, he shows that he has a great desire for God.

“He thirsted.” I keep vigil for this reason: “my soul,” afflicted here by many desires, such as anger and others of the same kind, “thirsted for you,” the living fountain, in which it will find complete refreshment. “And my flesh” thirsted for the same thing, “for you,” that is, for your praise; and this “in many ways,” that is, for far more numerous reasons than the soul, since it is subject to greater miseries, namely, hunger, thirst, cold, and other things of this kind.

“In the land.” I thirsted for you on this account, because I am “in the land,” that is, in the world—a land “deserted” in itself with respect to every good, “pathless and waterless,” not irrigated by itself in any way so as to be capable of bearing fruit. Therefore “I appeared before you,” that is, I prepared myself in such a way that you ought to look upon me, namely, because I am “in a holy” purpose, “so that I might see” in the homeland “your power and your glory,” that is, Christ your Son, who is the power and wisdom of the Father.

“For.” I ought to seek this truth “because your mercy is better,” I do not say than one life, “but than lives”: not merely better than the life of the poor, but also than the life of the rich; and not merely better than a short life, but than one however long it may be. Therefore “my lips shall praise you.”

And just as I shall praise you with my voice, “so I shall bless you in my life,” that is, in my works; and “in your name,” that is, by increasing your honor, “I shall lift up my hands,” both outward and inward. For outward hands are signs of inward ones.

[Col. 0402B] “As.” I do as much as I can, and would that I could do more. Thus “may my soul be filled as with fatness”—not bodily fat, but what fatness signifies—“and” as with “fatness,” that is, not bodily fatness, but what fatness signifies. Fat is properly inward fatness, which is around the vital organs, such as the caul and the other internal parts. Fatness is also found in the external limbs, such as the breast, and this was burned for God in the sacrifices of the old law.

By fatness we signify the knowledge of good and evil that is in the soul, with which the faithful soul desires to be filled, so that it may be able to praise God worthily. For a lean soul would not please God, just as lean flesh was said not to please him. By fatness we understand the soul’s cheerfulness, which enables the body to perform good works cheerfully. “And” then “my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation,” that is, with an exultant voice. Another translation reads: “My lips shall praise your name.”

“If I remembered you.” The second part begins. Continuation: My mouth shall praise you because you were and will be my helper; and with you as my helper, I remembered you in prosperity. This is what follows: “If I remembered you upon my bed,” that is, in prosperity, which is like a bed and a pleasant couch, because it makes people sleep in it and cling to it. And if I remembered you there, when that prosperity had blinded me, then “I shall meditate on you,” that is, I shall continually remember you, existing “in the mornings,” that is, in the illuminations you will grant me. I possess this morning because “you were my helper.” Here the Church already shows that it is secure in the desert through God’s help.

And therefore, because you were my helper, “I shall exult” in “the shelter,” that is, in the refreshment, “of your wings,” that is, in what your wings will provide for me. I shall exult because “my soul has clung” to you with every vow and affection, seeking you alone—not in such a way as to go before you, like Peter when he said to the Lord, “Be gracious to yourself, Lord; this shall never happen to you,” and the Lord said to him, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII)—but in such a way that it may be “after you,” that is, that it may continually follow you. And because it has clung in this way, therefore “your right hand,” that is, your favor, or your Son, “has received me into great dignity,” from the low condition in which I was because of my sins.

I, the Church, have been received in this way. “But they,” that is, those wicked men—“they” is added for emphasis—“sought” to destroy “my soul,” but they did this “in vain,” because they accomplished nothing and rather harmed themselves. For through this “they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth,” namely, into hell, just as Dathan and Abiron were swallowed up alive (Num. XVI). “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword,” that is, into the power of vengeance, “and they shall be the portions of foxes,” that is, of demons, who are compared to foxes because of their deceit. Or “they shall be the portions of foxes,” that is, of deceitful men; namely, they shall belong to their number.

They will thus be condemned, but “our king,” together with his own, “shall rejoice in God,” secure in eternal good. And “all who swear by him,” that is, who firmly promise him their service and fulfill it, “shall be praised,” that is, shall appear praiseworthy before everyone. This is because “the mouth of those who speak” wickedly against them in this life “has been stopped,” since they can no longer say anything.

## On Psalm LXIII

### Title

“To the end: a psalm of David.”

“God, hear my prayer.” This psalm suits David, that is, Christ, who speaks here, directing it to the end. Christ is its subject, both suffering and glorified; for it briefly touches upon his passion and glorification.

Its structure is as follows. In the first part he describes the malice of the Jews, prays to be delivered from them, and declares that he will be delivered. In the second part, beginning, “The arrows of children,” he sets forth the ridicule of their folly. Its purpose is to admonish the Jews to cease from wickedness. [Col. 0403C] As in the other psalms in which he treats of the passion, so here he begins with a prayer, saying:

“God, hear my prayer,” concerning the obtaining of good things, “and when I pray, deliver my soul.” I do not mean from fear of death, but from “fear of the enemy”: free me in such a way that I do not yield to my enemies because of fear.

“You have protected me from the assembly of the malicious,” and I am certain that you will deliver me, because “you have protected me from the assembly of the malicious,” that is, from the gathering of those who think evil against me, “and also from the multitude of those who work iniquity,” that is, those who actually inflict evils upon me.

“For.” He enumerates the wickedness of the Jews. I rightly say, “those who work iniquity,” “for” they “sharpened their tongues like a sword,” because, just as a sword is sharpened so that it cuts more deeply, so they thought with the utmost sharpness about what worse things they could say against him, as when they said, “Crucify him,” and other such explicit things. And “they bent the bow,” that is, “they prepared deceits,” specifically “a bitter thing,” when they sought how he might be betrayed by a disciple and crucified by them through the Romans, once he had been condemned by the Roman judge. For this purpose they bent the bow, “to shoot,” that is, to kill, “the blameless one,” namely, myself, who was without any stain of sin; and they did this “in secret,” with regard to their intention.

“Suddenly.” They intend to shoot, “and they will shoot him,” namely, me, whom they wish to shoot, “suddenly,” that is, secretly, with me unaware, according to their foolish opinion. “And” once I am dead, “they will not fear” punishment for that wickedness. It is certain that they will shoot, because “they established for themselves,” that is, among themselves, “an evil plan” concerning my death, as when Caiaphas, prophesying, said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XI).

“They recounted.” They established an evil plan among themselves, and afterward “they recounted,” that is, they discussed among themselves, how they might “hide snares,” when they arranged for him to be betrayed by a disciple, judged by Pilate, and so forth. “And” afterward they said among themselves: How well we have devised this! “Who will see” these snares?

“They searched out,” that is, with great effort they investigated, “iniquities,” seeking how they could keep me in death. But they, “searching,” not once but “with scrutiny,” that is, with continual investigation, “failed,” because they could not hold me in death.

“He will approach.” Those who sought evil failed, but the rational man, namely, “will approach the deep heart,” that is, so that he may raise his heart to understand lofty things, namely, God’s plan. Or let us understand this as God’s heart: the man will approach in order to understand God’s heart, that is, his hidden plan. “He will approach” is said properly, because no one will fully know God’s plan. “He will approach,” I say, “and God will be exalted” before him—not because God, considered in himself, could ever be exalted, but with respect to the man, in whom a greater knowledge of God is found.

Or otherwise: They failed, but that foolish man will approach the deep heart, namely, in order to fulfill God’s deep plan by killing me; but God will be exalted by raising me from the dead. The passage may be read in this way, even though the holy Fathers do not present it thus. They seek my death as though I would endure it unwillingly; but the man of the Lord will approach voluntarily, and the deep heart—that is, God’s disposition—will be with him, and God will be exalted.

“The arrows.” The second part begins. I rightly say that they failed, because “their wounds,” that is, the evils they inflict upon me, “have become like the arrows of children.” For just as children’s arrows do no harm, so neither do the evils they do to me. “And their tongues have grown weak,” because, whereas before the resurrection they spoke arrogantly against Christ, after the resurrection they did not speak so boldly. This happened “against them,” that is, to their disgrace. By showing clearly that they had failed, he intimates his resurrection to us.

“They were disturbed.” The wicked had thus failed, and then “they were disturbed” so as to receive the faith—“all who saw them,” namely, some from every class. “And every man feared”; being thus disturbed, he feared punishment for his sins.

And such men “proclaimed the works of God,” his incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and similar things; and at last they “understood his works,” that is, the works of God. Here it is indicated that God’s mystery is long considered before it is understood. When he says that some, considering the wickedness of the others, were converted, he shows the great glorification of Christ.

“He will rejoice.” I said that they were disturbed; and from this disturbance “every just man will rejoice,” not in himself but “in the Lord,” and “will hope in him” for eternal life. “And all upright in heart will be praised,” that is, will appear praiseworthy.

## On Psalm LXIV

### Title

“To the end: a psalm of David. A song of Haggai and Jeremiah and Ezekiel, concerning the word of pilgrimage and concerning the people of transmigration, when they were beginning to set out.”

“You are worthy.” Jeremiah prophesied to the Jews that, because of their sin, they would be taken captive and would finally return to the land from which they had departed. Haggai, however, did not prophesy the captivity; rather, he succeeded Jeremiah, who died while the Jews were in captivity. Haggai himself prophesied their return and was present at that return. After Nebuchadnezzar’s death, another king succeeded him, and, fearing God, he released the people.

Through this captivity they understood the captivity of the human race, in which they are held in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of sins. Through their return they understood our return to the land of promise, that is, to the Jerusalem above.

The title is explained as follows. This psalm suits the prophet and the others who were returning. It is the song of Jeremiah and Haggai because it explains to us that about which Jeremiah and Haggai—or Zechariah—and the others who understood it rejoiced most greatly: namely, the return of the human race to the Jerusalem above, from which they had been exiled through the disobedience of the first parent. It is a song concerning the word, that is, concerning the exultation, of pilgrimage, that is, of pilgrims; a word of exultation, I say, possessed when they began to set out, that is, to return, with Christ as their leader, to the Jerusalem above.

Or it is a song concerning the word that was the cause of pilgrimage, namely, the word by which the devil and Eve persuaded Adam. According to this interpretation, it was possessed when they began to set out, that is, to return to the Jerusalem above.

Or it is a song concerning the people of transmigration, that is, those who had migrated from the perfection in which they had been created to Babylon, that is, to the confusion of sins. It is a song possessed at the time when the people themselves began to set out, that is, to return to their former dignity.

The subject is those who are returning, who speak here. Its structure is as follows. In the first part the returning people describe, with their former exultation, the praise of their liberator. In the second part they describe the power of the one who brings them back; this begins, “The hope of all the ends of the earth.” Its purpose is to admonish us not to despair of salvation, contrary to the opinion of the philosophers, who held it certain that after death there would be eternal punishment in the underworld.

And the returning people, exulting in their return, say:

“O God,” who are our redeemer, “you are worthy” of “a hymn”—not stones, not idols. Not in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of sins, for “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccl. XV), but “in Zion,” that is, in the Church, which contemplates you. “And a vow shall be paid to you,” that is, praise shall be offered “in” the Jerusalem “above,” where there is the full vision of peace.

And because a vow shall be paid to you, therefore, O God, “hear my prayer,” so that I may be able to reach you. It is necessary that you hear me, because not souls alone but “all flesh shall come to you” in the judgment. Here the prophet openly announces the resurrection.

It is necessary that you hear me because “the words of the wicked,” that is, of the devil and Eve, who persuaded Adam, “prevailed against us,” because they plunged us into sin; “and yet you, Lord, will be merciful to our iniquities,” forgiving them.

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen.” I say that you will be merciful, and that person “will be blessed” “whom you have chosen,” that is, separated from the mass of sinners by converting him to the faith, “and have taken up” into dignity. He is blessed, therefore, because “he will dwell in your courts,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, which he calls courts because of its breadth.

He is blessed also “because he will be filled with the good things” of “your house,” that is, with spiritual goods of the present Church. But because the prophet understands everything with reference to those who are returning, he says: “We shall be filled with good things,” because “your temple,” namely, that house, “is holy,” that is, it possesses great holiness. And that temple is “wonderful in equity,” because it does nothing except what is equitable.

So that we may be filled with these good things, “hear us, God our Savior.” Here the second part begins. And you can rightly hear us, for you are “the hope of all the ends of the earth,” that is, of human beings placed upon solid land, “and in the far-off sea,” that is, in the most distant islands.

You are their hope for this reason: you are “preparing” through teaching and inspiration “the mountains,” that is, the apostles, “in your power,” that is, in the steadfastness given to them. And you can rightly prepare them, because you are “girded with power,” namely, divinity, which is not far from you but clings to you. Through those mountains you “disturb the depths of the sea,” that is, those who are sunk in the profound immutability of this world; and you disturb “the sound,” that is, the sound of those who shout in opposition, “of its waves,” that is, of those who are tossed about by persecution.

I say: You disturb the depths; namely, “the nations will be troubled” unto repentance “and will fear” punishment for their sins—those “who dwell at the ends” of the earth. And this occurs “because of your signs,” that is, through your miracles. “And you will make delightful,” that is, make pleasing to yourself, “the outlets of morning and evening,” that is, those who emerge from adversity, specifically those who care neither for prosperity nor for adversity.

Again, the nations will be troubled for this reason: “You visited the earth,” and thus “you saturated it” with the Holy Spirit; “you multiplied its riches,” that is, you greatly increased its enrichment in many ways.

And you were able to saturate it because “the river of God,” that is, his mercy, “is filled with waters,” that is, with gifts that wash like water. You not only saturated it, but also “prepared their food,” that is, your body. I rightly say that you prepared it, “because its preparation” as food “is thus,” that is, it can be prepared only through you.

And you, Lord, “make its streams,” that is, the holy apostles, who are called streams of the river because they flow from God’s mercy and can carry others, “overflow,” that is, make them abound in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. “Multiply its offspring,” that is, those generated from God’s mercy, “in number and virtues,” “sprouting,” that is, being young and undeveloped. Another translation says, “which rises.” “It will rejoice in its showers,” that is, in the drops of God’s mercy, of which the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. III).

“You will bless.” Why should I go through everything one by one? You, Lord, “will bless,” that is, you will give blessing, namely, an increase of righteousness in this life, “the crown,” that is, glory. The crown consists in the very human beings who have been acquired for glory. It is the “year of your kindness,” that is, the time in which your kindness appeared, namely, the time of grace. When he speaks of a crown, he signifies that they have been gathered from every circuit of the earth. “And your fields,” that is, those good men who remain in equality, “will be filled with abundance” of spiritual gifts.

And “the beautiful places of the desert,” that is, the Gentiles, who were formerly a desert but have now become beautiful, “will grow fat” with an abundance of grace. “And the hills,” that is, the loftier men, such as the martyrs, “will gird themselves with exultation” over the grace bestowed upon them.

And “the rams of the sheep,” that is, the priests, the leaders of the sheep or of the flock, “are clothed” with God’s blessing, that is, adorned with many virtues. “And the valleys,” that is, those who are lower, “will abound in grain,” that is, in good works; they will also “cry out” to the Lord continually and without discord, “for they will sing a hymn,” because all, by doing good, glorify God.

## On Psalm LXV

### Title

“To the end: a song of the psalm of resurrection.”

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” This psalm suits David the prophet, who also speaks here, directing it to the end. It is called a song of the psalm. It is called a psalm because it admonishes us to good works: by placing Christ’s resurrection before us, it urges us to work well so that we too may come to the same resurrection. [Col. 0407D] It is called a song because it sets before us something over which we should rejoice greatly, namely, Christ’s resurrection, since it also makes us secure concerning our own resurrection.

Foreseeing this resurrection, the prophet Ezra, in the Holy Spirit, entitled the psalm in this way: “A song of the psalm of resurrection,” that is, dealing with the resurrection. This kind of title proceeds from the figure in which, before the recitation of the psalms, a psalm was played in the melody of strings; that melody signified exultation. For it was not enough for them to sing with the voice alone; they also expressed their exultation with a living voice.

The subject is Christ’s resurrection. Its structure is as follows. In the first part he urges all nations to rejoice over that resurrection, which is placed before them as a certain indication of their own resurrection. In the second part, beginning, “Come and see the works,” he urges us to understand that the things God did for the ancient fathers have been fulfilled in us. In the third part, beginning, “Bless the nations,” he urges us to endure patiently the tribulations that God inflicts for purification and testing, since God will eventually lead us into refreshment. In the fourth part, beginning, “Come, hear,” he urges us, by his example, to be confident that our prayers will be heard. His purpose is to remove the nations spiritually from despair and make them certain of the resurrection.

Foreseeing Christ’s resurrection, the prophet admonishes the nations to rejoice over it, saying: “All the earth,” that is, the nations from every land, “shout joyfully to God,” that is, conceive in your minds such great joy that no voice is sufficient to express it. “And sing a psalm to his name” by doing good. And do not merely do good, but “also give glory,” that is, announce to others that he is glorious—not our praise, but his praise. This is what follows: “for his praise.” Hence the Apostle says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. X).

I say, “give,” and do not do this only in one way, but “say to God”—and saying means doing so with heart, voice, and deed—this specifically: “O Lord, how terrible are your works!” Although you were God, you became man, suffered, died, and rose again; all these things are terrible to the wicked. And how terrible are they? Extremely terrible, because no one can comprehend their measure. Yet although they are so terrible, “your enemies,” that is, the Jews, “will lie” about you by denying that you are the Son of God, and so forth. They will lie “to you” for your honor, because the more they lied about God, the more glorious he appeared; through the reproaches of the Jews, Christ’s name increased.

And this occurred not only when his power was not apparent, but “in the multitude of your power,” that is, when your power appeared more fully. Thus, in the resurrection, they denied that he had risen, saying that the disciples had taken him away; and likewise when they said: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke XI).

The enemies will lie about you, but in their place “all the earth,” that is, all the nations, “will adore you and sing a psalm to you,” that is, will do good in your honor. And it will “sing a psalm to you” before others, that is, it will proclaim its works, so that others may work by its example. It will do this not for itself but “for your name,” that is, for your honor.

“Come.” The second part. I say that your works are terrible. In order that you may understand these works, “come,” through faith, you nations far from the faith, “and see,” that is, understand, “the works of God,” which he performed for the ancient fathers and which have been completed in you. He is “terrible”—or, the terrible God is “in his counsels,” conceived and carried out “for the sons of men.” He says “above” because those counsels came from heaven, through which the sons of men were liberated. These counsels were those by which God blinded the Jews so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

Behold the works: “He,” the Lord, “turned the sea” into “dry land” when the Jews were approaching—that is, into solid earth. This transformation was completed in baptism. For the sea, that is, bitter and wavering human beings, tossed about in the bitterness of this world, is turned through the waters of baptism into dry land, when all the bitterness of sin is washed away.

The dry land was restored when the Church was taken up into the faith, and “they crossed the river on foot.” The Lord led them with dry feet through the river Jordan. This too has been fulfilled among the Gentiles, who cross the river of this life with unstained affection. What he says—“they will cross”—looks toward the thing signified. “There,” that is, in these works, just as it has been fulfilled in us, “we will rejoice.” And because he knew that he belonged to their number, in whom these things would be fulfilled, he says, “we will rejoice”—“in him,” not in ourselves.

[Col. 0409B] “In him,” in whom we should indeed rejoice, because he is the one “who rules” over all, and this “in his power,” that is, in his own power, “forever.” For if others rule, their rule is neither through their own power but through God’s, nor forever. He alone rules both by his own power and forever.

And although he is so high and so powerful, he does not despise his own; rather, “his eyes look down” kindly “upon the nations,” converting them to the faith, while they bear justice—those “who provoke them,” namely, the Jews—“and they are not exalted in themselves,” because they would have no exaltation in themselves but only in God.

“Bless the nations” of God. The third part. Having learned these works of God and having been converted to God through them, “you nations, bless,” that is, praise, “our God.” And do not do so only among yourselves, but “make the voice of his praise,” namely, the voice with which you praise him, “heard” by others.

And we ought to do this because “he placed my soul in” true “life,” by giving faith; and “after he converted me, he did not set my feet in motion,” so that I might look backward.

“Because you tested us.” Then, as though someone were to ask, Why should you be moved? “Because you, God, tested us,” that is, you showed us to be tested and approved both to ourselves and to others. He explains the manner of the testing: You tested us in this way—you “examined us by fire,” that is, by whatever tribulation, or by material fire, as in the case of Lawrence and others, “as silver is examined.”

“You brought us in.” He explains the kind of examination, saying: “You brought us into a snare,” that is, into bonds and prisons, and again into other affliction. “You placed tribulations on our back,” that is, we were scourged and beaten, as Paul was at Ephesus. Again, another evil: “You set men over our heads,” who ruled over us in such a way that they could pass capital sentences upon us.

And although all these evils befell us, we nevertheless always “passed through” to you “through fire,” namely, material fire, “and water,” because many martyrs were drowned in water; yet neither fire nor water could impede their course. Or we may take fire as any heat of adversity and water as prosperity, because just as water dissolves the earth, so prosperity dissolves a person.

He speaks here by comparison with a traveler. Just as a traveler, neither because of heat nor because of rain, wishes to abandon the completion of his journey, so this just man can be hindered neither by adversity nor by prosperity from completing his course. Through all these things “you led us out”—that is, you will lead us out—“into refreshment,” into which you have already led us in hope.

And finally, “I shall enter your house,” not a house made by hands, “with burnt offerings,” that is, bringing burnt offerings, namely, the destruction of vices. And there “I shall repay you,” that is, fulfill for you, “my vows,” namely, the praises that I vow to you here. These vows are not irrational, but are those that “my lips,” my inward lips—that is, reason—or my literal lips, “have distinguished,” that is, offered to you with understanding.

Cain also offered, presenting a creature to the Creator, but he did not distinguish rightly, because he withheld himself, who is more precious to God. Abel, however, offered distinctly, presenting himself first to God (Gen. IV).

And my lips distinguished those vows not only in prosperity, but also “in my tribulation,” that is, in the tribulation useful to me; “my mouth spoke” those praises. Or the continuation may be understood as follows: “I shall enter your house with burnt offerings,” and, as long as I live, I shall offer burnt offerings to you, namely, myself wholly consumed with respect to sinful works. I shall offer burnt offerings that are “rich in marrow,” that is, fat and carried forward by faith and charity. Such a burnt offering will be pleasing to God, just as in the Old Testament a burnt offering was said to please him when it was rich and full of marrow.

“And I shall offer this with incense,” that is, with prayer. Prayer is understood through incense because it smells sweet and pleases God, just as incense pleases human beings who smell it. Or I shall offer “the prayer of rams,” that is, of the apostles: I shall pray as the apostles prayed, or as those whom they will now instruct pray. I shall also “offer bulls” to you, that is, good preachers—those who will thresh and cultivate the Church well. I shall offer them by leading them to greater perfection in virtue. And I shall do this “with goats,” that is, I shall convert to you goats and those who stink with sins.

“Come.” The fourth part. Continuation: Since I conduct myself in this way, you others, stirred by my example, “all who fear God, come,” that is, prepare yourselves for understanding, “and hear,” that is, understand with the inner ear. And if you are such people, “I shall tell” you, as though reporting something not invented, “how great things God has done for my soul.”

And this, namely, I did: “I cried out to him with my mouth,” and not only with my mouth, but also “under my tongue,” that is, in my heart; “I rejoiced,” that is, I cried out exultantly.

“Unrighteousness.” I cried out not only by deed, but also without any unrighteousness, even in my heart; and this is: “If I regarded unrighteousness in my heart,” that is, if unrighteousness pleased me in my heart, namely, in my will, “the Lord will not hear me.”

And because I cried out, and without unrighteousness, “therefore [Col. 0411A] God heard me” concerning the granting of good things, and “he attended to the voice of my supplication” concerning the removal of evils.

And because he heard me, “blessed” be “God,” that is, praised by all, “who did not remove my prayer” but heard it, “and” did not delay “his mercy from me,” that is, from giving it to me; rather, he heard the prayer and at the same time bestowed mercy.

## ON PSALM LXVI. TITLE: “To the end; a psalm of a song of David, with hymns.”

“May God have mercy on us.” This psalm applies to the prophet David. It is called “a psalm of a song” because it summons us to confession, and it is called “a song” because it sets before us the greatest exultation, namely, the illumination of all the nations, which was to come through Christ. [Col. 0411B] I say that it is a psalm set “with hymns,” that is, with praises of God. For the prophets understood that God was to be praised for the illumination that he was going to give the world, on account of which everyone ought to praise him with the utmost devotion. I say that it is a psalm directing us “to the end.” Its subject is Christ, the illuminator.

Its structure is as follows. In the first part he prays for illumination. In the second part he exhorts us to both kinds of confession, namely, confession of sin and praise of God, and he gives the reason: God is a just judge. In the third part he exhorts us to the same confession, but for another reason: the earth, previously barren, has now, at the Son’s advent, given its fruit. The purpose is to exhort us to attribute everything to God’s mercy. And because he sees that all good things come from God’s mercy, before speaking of God’s illumination he implores mercy, saying: [Col. 0411C]

“May God have mercy on us,” and he explains how he asks for mercy: “and bless us,” namely, in this way: “may he make his face,” that is, his radiance, “shine upon us,” that is, make it radiate, so that he may infuse us with his knowledge, through which we may know him. For just as no one can see the sun unless the sun itself sees him, so no one can come to the knowledge of God unless God shows himself to that person. “And,” after he has illuminated us, in order to preserve this illumination, “may he again have mercy on us,” because just as illumination cannot be obtained without God’s mercy, so, once obtained, it cannot be preserved without God’s mercy.

[Col. 0411D] And may he illuminate us “so that we may know,” although we dwell “in the earth,” where knowledge is necessary, “your way,” that is, Christ the Son, through whom one goes to you; “your way,” namely, your salvation, that is, your Son, through whom salvation is accomplished for the human race—and this not among a few nations, but “among all the nations,” that is, in every place belonging to the nations, “your salvation.”

“Let them confess.” The second part. Continuation: I say, “may he illuminate,” and because he will illuminate, therefore, “O God, let the peoples confess to you” their sins, accusing themselves on account of their sins; and when those sins have been blotted out, “let the peoples confess to you,” that is, praise you—not a few peoples, but “all.”

[Col. 0412A] “Let the nations also rejoice and exult, because you judge,” that is, will judge, “the peoples with equity,” repaying each according to his merits. And because he would not be praised very much for this reason, since all would be condemned, unless God in his great mercy also visited human beings in this life, he adds: “and you direct the nations,” namely, those dwelling “in the earth,” where visitation is necessary, “to do good.”

“Let them confess.” The third part. Continuation: “Let the peoples confess,” because you judge, and “let them confess” also because “the earth has given its fruit,” that is, human beings—namely, in the earth that had previously been cursed and produced thorns and thistles, under the curse that God pronounced to Adam: “Cursed is your earth in your work” (Gen. III)—has become fruitful by giving its fruit, that is, its fitting works. “The earth has given its fruit.” [Col. 0412B] And what is required except blessing alone? Therefore, “may God bless us,” namely, the Father, multiplying virtues for us in this life; and “our God,” that is, Christ the Son of God; and “God,” that is, the Holy Spirit, “may bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” with love—that is, may the people from every end of the earth fear him. For fear is necessary for the preservation of all virtues.

## ON PSALM LXVII. TITLE: “To the end; a psalm of a song of David.”

“Let God arise.” This psalm applies to the prophet David, who speaks here. It directs us “to the end”; I say that it is a psalm of a song, which sets before us a great exultation, namely, the exultation of Christ himself and that of the Church. Its subject is Christ, exalted and exalting the Church.

[Col. 0412C] It has six parts. In the first part he presents Christ’s exaltation and what results from it for the good and for the wicked. In the second part, which begins, “O God, when you went forth,” he shows that what God did for the former people has been fulfilled in this new people. In the third part, which begins, “The mountain of God, a rich mountain,” he shows Christ’s height and what results from it for the Church. In the fourth part, which begins, “And the Lord’s, the Lord’s, are the departures of death,” he shows Christ’s humility and what it contributes to the Church. In the fifth, which begins, “Bless God in the churches,” he shows the condition of the Church: through the holy apostles, heretics are to be rebuked, and through those same apostles Egyptians and Ethiopians are to be converted. In the sixth part, which begins, “Sing to God who ascends,” he shows that the voice of the one who ascends will be powerful in judgment, and that through it the saints will be raised and glorified.

[Col. 0412D] The purpose is to admonish us concerning Christ’s exaltation, so that we may sing to Christ and exalt him. This purpose is indicated in several places in the psalm, including where it says, “Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name,” and also in the title, where it says, “a psalm of a song.”

It should be known that the prophet took these first two verses from the book of Moses. Moses sang these verses when he raised up the ark of the Lord and they went forth to battle (Num. X). At the sight of that ark the enemies were overthrown, and the Lord’s people were saved—not because Moses understood such great power to reside in the ark, but because he knew that Christ of God was signified through it. In Christ are contained all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, just as the tablets of the covenant were contained in the ark, and so forth.

[Col. 0413A] And because David understood that Moses had sung this concerning Christ, while speaking about the exaltation of that same Christ he sets down Moses’ words, saying: “May God,” who was once hidden, “arise.” This arising occurred in everything Christ did from the time of his resurrection onward. “And may his enemies be scattered” locally, as was fulfilled in the dispersal under Titus and Vespasian. “And may those who hate him,” that is, those who persisted in hatred against him, “flee,” that is, be removed “from his face,” that is, from his presence—not that they can be removed [Col. 0413B] from the presence of him who is everywhere. Hence the prophet says: “If I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Rather, they are removed from his face because they do not enjoy knowledge of him. Thus it is said: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” This retribution will occur when it is said: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

“As smoke vanishes.” Here he intensifies their punishment, because the prophet’s wish has as much force as an assertion. “Let them vanish” also “as smoke vanishes,” for such is the nature of smoke that the higher it rises, the more it disappears. So the wicked, the more they rise in the power of this age, the more they vanish from the truth; and, like smoke, they continually proceed from the fire of desire. Now he intensifies their punishment still further when he says: “As wax melts before the face of fire, so may sinners perish from the face,” that is, from the presence, “of God,” being removed from it—not that their substance is utterly destroyed, but that they perish in being separated from true being, which is God.

[Col. 0413C] After showing what comes to the wicked from Christ’s exaltation, he shows conversely what comes to the good from that same exaltation. Continuation: “Let sinners perish, and let the righteous feast,” that is, be refreshed by God himself, who will be all things in all; “and let them exult, placed in the sight of God, and in their joy,” in which they ought to delight because it is eternal, “let them take delight.”

“Sing to God.” And because the righteous will exult and take delight, therefore you others, “sing to God” with heart and voice, and “sing a psalm,” that is, act well, magnifying his name, “to his name,” namely, to Christ his Son, through whom his name became known to the world. When he says, “sing a psalm,” he not only urges us to act well, but also to make our conduct known to others, that is, to set it forth as an example. “And make a way” for him, by which way he may come into us, breaking all obstacles—namely, vices, which drive God from his dwelling in us. Make it for him, I say, “who ascends over the setting,” that is, over death, which ruled over the whole world and cast it into setting and darkness. It is fitting that you make a way for him because “his” substantial “name is Lord,” since he rules by himself and no one can rule except through him.

[Col. 0413D]

[Col. 0414A] “Exult.” I say, sing and sing a psalm, and do not do so with sadness, but rather “exult in his sight.” Let the righteous exult, but let the wicked, who harm widows and orphans, “be troubled from his face,” that is, from the face of God, when it is said: “Go, wicked, into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV). He is “the father of orphans,” because he himself is the father and protector of orphans, that is, of the simple, who possess no cunning of their own but proceed under the guidance of God alone; and he is “the judge of widows,” because he judges them with equity. Widows are those who possess and understand something in themselves that makes them cry out to God in their need, like perfect men.

“God in his place.” He offers another commendation of Christ. Continuation: He is the judge of widows, and he is “God in his holy place,” that is, in the angels and in other holy men, because he encounters no obstacle there. He is “God,” I say, “who makes” human beings “dwell with one disposition,” that is, with one will, according to faith and charity, “in a house,” that is, in his Church.

[Col. 0414B] Another commendation: He also “brings out the captives,” that is, those who were held captive by the devil in hell, or those living beings bound by the fetters of sins, “with strength,” that is, with great force; and likewise, like captives, he brings out “those who provoke,” that is, those who provoke God to anger—namely, blasphemers and those utterly foul in sins. He also brings out “those who dwell in tombs,” that is, those who consent to the pleasure of the flesh. The flesh is the soul’s tomb, because there the soul, consenting to the flesh, rots just as flesh rots in a tomb.

[Col. 0414C] “O God, when you went forth.” Here the second part begins; this is the diapsalma, that is, the division of the psalm. Continuation: I say, you, O God, will lead them forth, because what you prefigured in others you fulfill in us. This is what he says: “O God, when you went forth,” that is, when, having previously been hidden, you showed yourself openly “in the sight of your people,” illuminating them at night by the pillar of fire and cooling them by day through the pillar of cloud (Exod. XIII and XIV); and “when you passed through the desert,” leading them and showing yourself to them, always providing them guidance “by the pillar of cloud” and of fire throughout the desert, “the earth was shaken,” that is, earthly people who previously did not know the worship of God were moved toward the worship of God, including the Jews themselves, by means of the “pillar of fire,” which illuminated the people of Israel. The cloud that cooled them by day signified the same incarnation, in which all the faithful find refreshment.

[Col. 0414D] I say, “the earth was shaken,” and this because “the heavens dripped” while they rained down manna “from the face,” that is, from the presence, “of God,” because, while the manna was falling there, the presence of God was recognized. Of God, I say, “of Sinai,” because on that mountain God gave the law and commandments. Sinai is interpreted as “commandment,” and God is called the God of commandment, who dwells in all those who observe his commandment. I say, “from the face of God of Sinai,” and “from the face of the God of Israel,” that is, of the Israelite people.

Sinai may also be nominative here, as another translation shows, which has “Mount Sinai.” It may be understood as follows: “The heavens dripped, and Mount Sinai also dripped,” that is, it emitted mist and smoke from the face of the God of Israel, when God spoke to Moses in order to give the law.

[Col. 0415A] Having shown the figure, he shows the fulfillment of the figure. Continuation: Just as “the heavens dripped,” so you, “O God, will set apart rain,” that is, evangelical doctrine, signified by that manna. I call it rain “of your free will,” that is, freely given, without any merit on the part of human beings. You will “separate it,” that is, give it separately, “to your inheritance,” that is, to the people of Israel, to whom God preached separately through the presence of his body. Hence he himself said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). “And” that inheritance “was weakened,” because it did not wish to receive the word of God; it was blinded. “But you, O God, perfected it,” replenishing it with the nations.

[Col. 0415B] “Animals.” He shows from whom God perfected it, namely, from the nations, saying: “Your animals,” that is, the Gentiles, who are called animals because they are untamed and lack the law, “will dwell in it,” in that inheritance, because together with the Jews they become Christ’s inheritance. The animals will dwell there, and not through themselves or through their own worthiness, but because you “prepared” your grace “in your sweetness for the poor,” the afflicted and hungry, “O God”—not so that they would regard as sweet the things the world gives, but the things you impart, whatever they may be.

[Col. 0415C] “The Lord will give.” He shows the preparations that God makes for his poor. Continuation: “The Lord,” namely, “will give the word,” that is, evangelical doctrine, “to those who evangelize,” that is, to those who preach, “with great power,” that is, with great constancy. Or: To those who evangelize the word, the Lord gives great power, that is, confirmation through miracles. Hence the Gospel says: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed.”

“King.” “The Lord will give”—that Lord, namely, who is “king of powers,” that is, of angels. The powers are “of the beloved,” that is, of the Son; the Son, I say, “beloved,” who is loved by God. One term is substantive and the other adjectival. When he says that the powers belong to that Son, he shows that the Son is equal to the Father, and he introduces another division.

The word “will give” also means that he will “divide spoils,” that is, human beings snatched from the devil, assigning them to different orders—for example, making some bishops and so forth. Peter and the others arranged many holy men in this way. He will divide the spoils “for the beauty of the house,” that is, for the adornment of the house, namely, God’s Church, because unless God’s house were divided, it would not be beautiful, nor would it be a body. Concerning this Christ said: “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, everything that he possesses is in peace; but if one stronger than he comes upon him, namely Christ, he takes away and divides all his spoils” (John XI). This is what Christ did: he overcame the strong armed man, that is, the devil, and took away his spoils, namely, human beings.

[Col. 0415D] “If you sleep among the midst.” [Col. 0416A] He sets down still other manifestations. Continuation: He will give you this, and this is: “If you sleep,” that is, rest from the tumult of the world, “among the midst of the lots,” that is, between the two Testaments, so that you may delight in the sayings of divine Scripture, “there will be for you”—or, as another translation has it, “they will raise you up”—“feathers” (*pennae*; the source’s *poenae* is evidently an OCR error), that is, virtues by which you may be able to fly to heaven, such as “silvered doves,” that is, the Churches. The Church is called a dove because of its simplicity, and “silvered” in this life because of the brightness of its eloquence. “And its hind parts,” that is, the things the holy Church awaits after this life, “will be in the pallor of gold,” that is, like gold, because just as gold is more precious than all metals, so are the things the saints will receive in the future life.

Another translation has “in the greenness of gold,” and another, “in beauty,” but the meaning is the same. I speak of that Church which exists “for the burden of the back,” that is, as burden-bearing, because it carries burdens, namely, the afflictions of this life. We understand divine Scripture through “lots” because *cleros* is Greek and *sors* means “lot” in Latin: we did not receive divine Scripture through any human judgment, but by lot alone, that is, by God’s election alone.

[Col. 0416B] “While the heavenly one distinguishes.” He sets down other manifestations. The Lord will give you these things, and “while,” that is, because, the heavenly one, namely Christ, “distinguishes,” that is, arranges, “kings,” that is, holy prelates who rule themselves and others well, “over her,” the dove, that is, the Church, “they will be whitened,” those who inwardly constitute the Church, in the whiteness of their souls and virtues, “more white than snow.” Another translation has “upon snow.” By saying “upon snow,” it shows that this whitening is incorporeal. They will be whitened, I say, “in Selmon,” that is, in shadow—namely, in Christ, who is our shadow and refreshment against the heat of this age. For Selmon is interpreted as “shadow.”

[Col. 0416C] The third part begins. This Selmon, that is, this Christ, “is the mountain of God,” a mountain, I say, “rich,” from which flowed all spiritual doctrine by which faithful souls are enriched.

I say “mountain,” and this same Christ is a “congealed mountain,” with respect to those whom he nourishes with milk; he is also a “rich mountain,” with respect to the wise, whom he refreshes with solid food. The prophet then turns to them: Since Christ is such a mountain, why then, O Jews, “do you suppose” that you are something in comparison with this mountain—“congealed mountains,” those great men? Here he rebukes those who said that “Christ was John the Baptist or Elijah, and so forth” (Matt. IX; Mark VI).

[Col. 0416D] Another commendation of Christ: He is also “the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell,” so that “in it”—concerning which the Apostle says, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V)—I say, he dwells in it, “for the Lord will dwell to the end,” that is, to the limit of dwelling, so that he cannot dwell more fully.

After showing Christ’s height, he shows what results from it for the Church. [Col. 0417A] Continuation: This mountain is such, and the others who were thought to be congealed mountains are “God’s chariots,” carrying him, whom he himself governs as a good charioteer governs a chariot. The chariots are “many, ten thousand” peoples; by a finite number we understand an infinite one. Those thousands are “rejoicing,” because “the Lord” is “among them,” the Lord who is “in Sinai,” that is, in the commandment. By this he indicates that the Lord is with those who keep his commandments. He is also “in the holy place,” that is, in Christ; and by this he indicates that those in whom he dwells are conformed to Christ.

They have become God’s chariots for this reason: you, O God, “ascended on high,” literally, and “led captivity captive,” that is, rescued your own from the snares of the devil, which are called captivity by way of expression. And you “received” from God “gifts among human beings,” that is, human beings as gifts, just as one says, “This man received gifts in cups,” meaning that he received cups.

[Col. 0417B] And truly you received human beings as gifts, because you received even the unbelievers, so that “the Lord God might dwell in human beings,” such as the Gentiles, who did not believe that God dwelt among human beings.

And because he gave such great mercy to the world, therefore “the Lord” himself should be “blessed,” that is, praised, “day by day,” that is, continually. Someone might ask: Why do you bless him? Because I know that, by ascending, he also makes us ascend. This is “the prosperous way,” that is, without impediment, so that the obstacles of the world cannot hinder us. “God will make it for us,” and in this we can be secure. For in the present life he grants us salvations, namely, the remission of sins. This is “our salvations,” and he grants other salvations as well, namely, righteousness and so forth.

[Col. 0417C] He is also “our God,” that is, our creator, and he is also “the God of saving,” because he saves not only in this life but will also save us through eternal glorification.

Here the fourth part begins. Continuation: And lest anyone should say: You say that he is the God of saving, but this could still be so even if he himself had died and his own people also died, he answered: I rightly say that he is the God of saving, because “to this Lord, the Lord,” belongs “the departure of death,” that is, rising up, he departed from death, and he will lead all his own out of death. When “Lord” is stated twice, through one occurrence we understand what is fixed, that is, what is substantive; through the other, the exercise of lordship is signified—as if he were saying, “the Lord who rules.”

[Col. 0417D] “Nevertheless.” This is the God of saving; “nevertheless,” this “God will break,” that is, annihilate, the “heads,” that is, the minds or uprisings, “of his enemies.” He will also break “the crown of hair,” that is, the arrogance and elevation of thoughts—namely, the philosophers’ opinions and profound doctrines, and the sect of heretics, from which they were exalted and made proud. The crown of hair, I say, belongs to those “who walk,” that is, persist, “in their offenses.” We understand thoughts through hairs because, just as hairs adhere to the head, so thoughts adhere to the mind. Good thoughts adorn the mind, while evil thoughts disfigure it.

[Col. 0418A] The Lord said: He will break some, but he will convert others to himself, making some martyrs and others preachers. To confirm this, he introduces the Lord as saying: “The Lord said”: I will “convert” some to myself “from Bashan,” that is, from confusion or from dryness. For Bashan is interpreted as “confusion” or “dryness.” God converts to himself some who were previously confused in sins or in the dryness of righteousness. He will also “convert” to himself some who exist “in the depth of the sea,” that is, in the depth of vices.

[Col. 0418B] “That the foot may be dipped,” says the prophet. Continuation: You, O God, will convert them, and they will be converted so that “your foot,” that is, those converted to you who bear you within themselves—the foot that was previously dipped in love of this life—may now “be dipped in blood,” that is, may be led even to the shedding of blood. And “from your enemies” may there be made “the tongue of your dogs,” that is, may they become excellent preachers, barking well and defending the Church of God, just as dogs keep watch around the houses of their masters. This will not proceed “from” them, but from you “yourself.” Another translation has “from yourself.”

The saying may also be construed differently: The Lord will convert, and you, O people, will be converted so that your foot, that is, your affection, may be dipped in blood, that is, may be inclined toward the shedding of blood; and from God’s enemies may there be made the tongue of your dogs, that is, of your sinners—namely, those who belong to your nation and fellowship. This will be not from you, but from God himself.

[Col. 0418C] “They saw your processions.” The foot will be dipped in blood, and the tongue of your dogs will be made from enemies; and all this will happen because, O God, those who are converted “saw your processions,” that is, your works, which you worked in the world. Or he says “your processions” because God was previously alien to the world but entered the world through his mercy. To specify that these processions belong to Christ, he says: “The processions of my God, my king, who is in the holy place,” that is, who dwells in the man belonging to the Lord, namely Christ. Here he openly suggests the incarnation.

“The princes went before.” They would be converted because they saw God’s processions, and also because “the princes,” that is, the apostles, who are princes in the Church, “went before” them. Since they believed first, they gave others examples of faith and good works. They did this not alone, but “joined together,” that is, accompanied by many “who sing psalms,” that is, who act well for the honor of God.

[Col. 0418D] And lest anyone believe that this glory was given only to men—as certain heretics thought—he adds that those princes will also be “in the midst of young women.” He calls them young women because they are renewed from the oldness of sin through God’s grace. Or by young women we may understand the Churches generally, because through God’s grace they are renewed from the oldness of sin. They are young women, I say, “of those who beat the tambourine,” who make music to God through the mortification of the flesh and are like the skins of dead animals.

[Col. 0419A] “In the churches.” The fifth part begins. Continuation: The princes went before, and he gave the other good things; therefore, on account of all these things, you faithful people, “bless God in the churches,” where the place of blessing is, because those outside the Church cannot worthily praise God. Bless God, I say, “the Lord,” because he is both God and Lord. Bless him “from the fountains,” that is, on account of the fountains—namely, the holy apostles, who refresh us with spiritual doctrine. The fountains are “of Israel,” that is, proceeding from Judea; or, in the churches, you are given to drink from the fountains of Israel.

[Col. 0419B] “There.” I rightly say, on account of the fountains, because “there,” that is, in the Church, are the fountains—namely, Paul and the other apostles. This is: “There is Benjamin,” that is, Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin, that is, converted in his youth (Acts IX). Or “a young man,” namely, one who, having laid aside the oldness of the law, was renewed in Christ. This is “in an excess of mind,” that is, in fear, because he was converted through fear.

Note that there are two kinds of ecstasy. One occurs when the human mind transcends all the way to God himself, passing beyond worldly things. Hence Paul says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (II Cor. V); and this kind of ecstasy may also be understood here, since Paul was taken up “to the third heaven” (II Cor. XII). The other occurs when a person is carried outside himself through fear.

[Col. 0419C] The princes and leaders of those who are in the Church are “the princes of Judah,” that is, the holy apostles from the tribe of Judah; “the princes of Zebulun,” and “the princes” from the tribe of “Naphtali”—“they are their leaders.” He names these four tribes because the apostles were born from them.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand”; Judah, “confessing”; Zebulun, “tabernacle of strength”; Naphtali, “breadth.” These interpretations are not necessary here.

“Command.” Through such men “command,” that is, make known, “your power,” that is, your might, throughout the world; and through them “confirm what you have worked in us,” namely, faith and charity and the Holy Spirit, beginning “from your temple,” that is, from your saints, in whom you dwell, “which is Jerusalem.” For in Jerusalem the Holy Spirit was first given to the apostles, and afterward, through them and through their ministers, he was given to other human beings.

[Col. 0419D] And truly you will confirm it, because through this “kings,” that is, those who rule themselves well, “will offer gifts to you,” that is, themselves and others. Another translation puts this in the form of a wish: “May gifts be offered.” Or, as another wording has it, “to your power,” and then we may understand it as follows: Since such men are in the Church, through whom what you began can be completed, therefore command—that is, give orders to—your power, namely, your Son; and through him and through your ministers, “confirm what you have worked in us.”

“Rebuke the beasts of the reeds.” And so that gifts may be offered to you, “rebuke,” that is, convict, the “beasts,” that is, the heretics who tear the Church of God apart like beasts tear sheep. They are beasts “of the reeds,” that is, dwelling among reeds—namely, among unstable people who can quickly be moved from their purpose. For heretics attack such people, not perfect men. Or he calls them “beasts of the reeds” because, just as reeds grow in marshes, so heretics move about in marshy opinions.

[Col. 0420A] It is necessary that you rebuke them because “the assembly of bulls,” that is, of heretics, who are bull-like in their stubbornness, is “among the cows of the peoples,” that is, among peoples who quickly follow whatever they hear, like cows following bulls. The assembly was formed for this purpose: “to exclude those who have been tested by silver,” that is, by divine eloquence, from those whom he called cows—namely, to prevent inferiors from following approved men.

[Col. 0420B] Or “to exclude” means to divide from themselves those who have been tested by silver. But when heretics separate themselves from such men, they show those from whom they separate themselves to be good. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (I Cor. XI).

When they have been rebuked, “scatter” them, so that they do not come together in one will—“the nations,” that is, the heretics—“who desire wars,” that is, disputes against the faithful. And truly you will scatter them, because “envoys will come from Egypt,” that is, some who had sinned through ignorance will be converted. Egypt is interpreted as “darkness,” by which those who sin ignorantly are understood. But even those who are black with grave sins will be converted; and this is: “Ethiopia,” that is, those blackened by sins.

For Ethiopia is interpreted as “blackness,” and an Ethiopian as “a black man.” “His hand will hasten before Egypt’s hand,” that is, by its unworthiness it will surpass Egypt’s works, “to God,” that is, for the honor of God. He says “will hasten before” because the more someone is entangled in serious sins, the more, when repentant, he produces worthy fruit for God.

[Col. 0420C] Another translation has: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out its hands to God.” This is said by comparison, because just as a defeated person stretches out his hands to the victor, so Ethiopia—that is, those blackened by sins—recognizing that they have been defeated, will stretch out their hands to God, their victor. Or Ethiopia, having been convicted, will hasten before God’s hand, that is, before God’s punishments. He rightly says “will hasten before,” because they will believe before God takes vengeance on them.

Because they will thus be converted to God, therefore “kingdoms of the earth,” that is, people from every region of the earth, “sing to God” with voice and heart, and “sing a psalm” to “the Lord” through good works.

[Col. 0420D] “Sing a psalm to God.” The sixth part begins. Sing a psalm for this reason, and also because he will give “the voice of power to his voice”: “sing a psalm to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven,” literally. Or, through the highest order of angels, “toward the east,” because, literally, he ascended on the Mount of Olives, which lies in the eastern part of Jerusalem. The Lord was in Jerusalem when he ascended. That action of Christ signified to us that he was the true east, who would illuminate the whole world. Another translation has “from the east.”

“Behold, he will give.” I therefore say, sing a psalm, because “behold,” as though in manifestation, this Lord “will give to his voice,” which was humble in this world, “a voice of power,” that is, he will make his voice powerful. This will be the voice with which he will come to judgment, and by that voice all bodies will be raised.

[Col. 0421A] And because he is so great that he will give power to his voice, all of you “give glory to God,” that is, show by words and deeds that he is glorious—God, I say, reigning “over Israel,” that is, over all those who see God. For “his magnificence,” namely, that of God, by which he will make his own great, namely, incapable of suffering and immortal, will be “in the clouds,” now holy, “and his power,” because nothing will be able to resist his command, but everything he wills will come to pass—again, “in the clouds.”

[Col. 0421B] “Wonderful.” Why should I go through everything individually? “Wonderful will God be in his saints,” that is, he will make them wonderful, and not only in the other life but also in this life. This is: “The God of Israel himself will give power” against adversities “to his people, and strength,” that is, the long-suffering of perseverance. Therefore, “blessed be God” by every people.

## ON PSALM LXVIII. TITLE: “To the end; for those who will be changed; a psalm belonging to David.”

“Save me, O God.” This psalm pertains to David in its signification, that is, to Christ, who speaks here and directs us toward the end, that is, toward Christ; I mean a psalm composed for those who will be changed. In this psalm Christ speaks about his passion, on account of which he asks God for the deliverance of human beings from the evil of this life, as when he says: “Deliver me from the mire, that I may not sink in it,” [Col. 0421C] and in many other passages; elsewhere he plainly affirms their transformation when he says: “For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built up,” and in other passages. Human beings will indeed be changed in this life through Christ’s passion, from the oldness of Adam to the newness of Christ, and finally from corruption to incorruption.

The subject of this psalm is Christ, suffering according to the frailty of human nature; and he expounds his sufferings through many aspects of the passion itself. He treats the passion here differently from the way he treated it in other psalms, because here he introduces the passion all the way to its completion, when he says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

This psalm has five parts. Its method is as follows. In the first part he asks to be saved and shows the evils unjustly inflicted on him [Col. 0421D] by the Jews. In the second part, which begins, “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you,” he shows that those evils were not inflicted on him because of any merit of his own, and asks that those who, whether living and hoping in him or dead and awaiting him, should be redeemed, not be disappointed. In the third part, which begins, “But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord,” he asks that his own people be delivered from the wickedness of this life through his passion. In the fourth, which begins, “Let their table become a snare before them,” he sets out the evils which he wishes would come upon the Jews on account of his passion; and his wish has as much force as though he were affirming it. In the fifth part, which begins, “I am poor and suffering,” he sets out the blessings that come to the righteous from his passion. His purpose is [Col. 0422A] to invite us to patience, as in the other psalms where he speaks about the passion.

He begins with a request for his deliverance, as follows: “Save me, O God,” so that my enemies may not be able to hold me in death. And this is necessary, because “the waters,” that is, the Jewish people, “have entered,” that is, have drawn nearer by inflicting greater evils, “even to my soul,” in order to take it away, like waters entering a ship in sufficient quantity to drown its occupants.

I am sunk in the mire. I say that they entered in order to take away my soul, and they took it away; and this is what follows: “I am sunk,” that is, I have been so delivered into their power that they could do with my body whatever they wished. I am sunk, I say, “in the mire,” that is, in the hands of the Jews, who are mire, that is, corruption [Col. 0422B] according to human nature. I say “in the mire of the deep,” because they make themselves deep in their wickedness; and “there is no substance” in them, that is, no subsistence, because according to my humanity I could not resist them. Or there is no substance in the Jews themselves, that is, no true existence, because they do not persist as they were created by God.

I have come into the depth. I am not sunk because I was unable to foresee what would happen; rather, I offered myself willingly. And this is what follows: “I came,” that is, not under compulsion but by spontaneous will, “into the depth of the sea,” that is, among the Jews, who are called the sea because of the bitterness of their life. It is deep because of their pride, “and the storm overwhelmed me,” that is, their seditious upheaval killed me.

[Col. 0422C] They cannot be excused on this account, because I cried out to them, showing that the things they were doing to me ought not to be done. And while “crying out, I labored,” that is, I cried out or labored greatly, because by crying out so much I accomplished nothing. Someone is said to labor when he cannot succeed in what he intends. “My throat has become hoarse,” that is, it has become like that of a hoarse man; for just as a hoarse man is not understood, so neither was I understood. “My eyes have failed” in death. Or, the eyes—that is, the apostles—“have failed,” that is, they doubted, namely, they fled at the death of the Lord. All these things happened to me because “I hope,” not in the Law but in God, or “in my God,” because I still expect better things from him.

“They have multiplied.” After showing through comparisons the evils inflicted upon him, he now shows them openly. The connection is this: It is no wonder that my eyes have failed, because my enemies were many and strong. And this is what follows: “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, without reason, “have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” They have become more numerous than my friends, who are called hairs because they cling to me and adorn me as hairs adorn the head. Or “beyond the hairs of my head” may be understood literally, indicating countless enemies.
