And they are not only many, but also “they have grown strong,” that is, they have become powerful when they saw that what they wanted was going their way—those “enemies who persecuted me unjustly,” although I had done them many good things. And then, even in that tribulation, “I was paying back,” that [Col. 0423A] is, I was paying the penalty, “for what I had not stolen,” that is, for sins I had not committed.

“O God.” He begins the second part. I rightly say this, because “you, O God, know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.” That is, you know that I suffer these things not because of anything I had done through foolishness, that is, through ignorance, nor because of any offenses of mine, but because of the sins of my people.

And because I suffer not through my own fault, therefore, O “Lord,” let those “who wait for you”—that is, those who are held in hell and await being led out by me—“not be put to shame,” that is, not be disappointed “in me,” but let them have in me the deliverance they await and obtain it. You are, I say, “God of hosts,” that is, of the angels, because it is certain that you will be able to accomplish this well.

[Col. 0423B] And also let those “who seek you,” that is, who understand that you are in me—those whom I call “Israel,” that is, those who see God—for unless they were seeing God, they could not believe that God was in a man so afflicted: let such people “not be confounded,” that is, let them not be confounded because of their disappointment “over me,” that is, because of me.

I say, let them not be confounded, nor ought they to be, because my passion is worthy to redeem them. And this is what follows: “For on your account I endured reproach,” as when they said, “You have a demon” (John 7), and similar things. “And confusion,” produced by blows and spitting, “covered my face,” that is, surrounded me on every side, as when they said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who struck you?” (Matthew 26; Luke 22; Mark 14.)

[Col. 0423C] He continues the account of the passion: “I have become a stranger to my brothers,” that is, to my relatives according to the flesh, “and” also “to the sons of my mother,” that is, to the synagogue, who heard the Law with me in the synagogue, in which they could have recognized that I was the promised Redeemer. I became “an outsider,” as though unknown, as though I could not remain among them except for one night. The synagogue is called the mother of the Jews because it nourished them with the precepts of the old Law.

And therefore I became an outsider, “because zeal for your house,” from which I had driven out the sellers and buyers (Matthew 21; Luke 19), “consumed me,” that is, burned me inwardly. Here his greatest emotion is indicated, because he himself drove them out, and, angered against him, they plotted his death. “And the reproaches” of those who tested you in the wilderness [Col. 0423D] (Mark 1; John 2), and who worshiped idols—this is what follows: “the reproaches of those who reproached you,” those reproaches, I say, “fell upon me,” like a heavy burden.

At that time I did not show myself angry toward them, but “I covered my soul,” that is, my will, “in fasting,” that is, while I was fasting from them, namely, while I was unable to incorporate any of them into myself. Hence the earlier passage: “I humbled my soul in fasting” (Psalm 35). And because I endured them so patiently, so that I covered myself in this way, “it became a reproach to me,” because the humbler I was among them, the more contemptible I was to them.

He continues the account of the passion. The connection is this: I covered my soul in fasting [Col. 0424A] “and put on sackcloth as my clothing,” that is, I displayed grief, making myself like those who dress in sackcloth, namely, penitents. Yet it is never read historically that the Lord was dressed in sackcloth; rather, he always conducted himself in sadness and never laughed. “And I became a byword to them,” that is, one about whom they would make their whole story. Or “a byword” means a likeness, because they cursed others by comparing them to me. Or he spoke “in a byword,” namely, he did not speak to them lofty things according to his wisdom, but in likenesses, so that they might understand better.

Again he continues, saying that even those “who sat at the gate,” that is, at the crossroads where many gathered, “spoke against me”; and those “who drank [Col. 0424B] wine,” that is, all the banqueters, namely, all who took pleasure in worldly things, “sang about me,” that is, mocked me.

“But I direct my prayer.” The fourth part, in which Christ shows how he conducted himself amid tribulations, namely, that he prayed for the deliverance of his people. The connection is this: They sang about me, “but I directed my prayer to you, O Lord,” saying: Behold, “the time of favor, O God.” A time of favor, I say, not because of human merits, but “because of the abundance of your mercy.” And because now, O Lord, it is the time, therefore “hear me in the truth of your salvation,” that is, by granting salvation to me and to mine, and thereby showing yourself truthful.

“Hear me,” I say, namely, “deliver me,” that is, my people, “from the mire,” that is, from sin—not that my people do not touch what is unlawful, for no one can be without sin, but “so that I may not be sunk,” that is, so that my people may not cling to sins through themselves. And not only so that my people may not be sunk through themselves, but also “deliver me,” that is, my people, “from those who hate me,” that is, so that through the instigation of others they may not be led into sin; “and” also deliver them “from the depths of the waters,” that is, from those profoundly wicked people. Or, “deliver my people from the depths of the waters,” that is, from prosperity, in which falling is easy.

Deliver them in this way—not so that they may have no tribulations, but so that they may not be submerged. And this is what he says: “May the storm of water not overwhelm me,” that is, may the agitation of the people not lead me into sin. And if some storm should at times overwhelm me, O Lord, I ask that “the deep [Col. 0424D] may not swallow me,” that is, that my people may not be led into despair. Hence it is said: “When the sinner has come into the depth of vices, he despises,” and “may the pit,” that is, the depth of the wickedness of this world, “not close its mouth over me,” that is, may it not lead my people so far that they cannot at some point emerge, even from despair. This is said by comparison with someone falling into a pit: if the mouth of the pit is closed, he cannot get out.

I say, “may it not close,” but rather “hear me,” that is, my people, “O Lord.” And I am confident that you will hear me, “because your mercy is kind,” that is, abundant, because you despise no one who cries out to you. “And look upon me according to the abundance of your mercies,” which you showed to the ancient fathers, such as Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 14), and Noah in the waters of the flood (Genesis 7–8), and the others.

I say, “look,” and do this through me; and this is what follows: “Do not turn your face away from your child,” that is, from me; another translation has “your servant.” He calls himself a child because of his innocence; concerning this he himself said in the Gospel, when he had placed another in their midst: “Unless you become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18). “Do not turn away,” I say, but rather “hear me quickly.” Do not delay my resurrection until the general resurrection, “because I am in tribulation.” And therefore I say this: “Do not turn your face away,” but rather “attend to my soul,” considering how innocently I have served you, “and deliver it.” And do not deliver me only for my own sake, but [Col. 0425B] also “deliver me for the sake of my enemies,” because it is not fitting that my enemies should rejoice in my affliction.

And you ought to deliver me, because you see the evils done to me, on account of which you ought to be moved to mercy toward me. Hence he says: “You know my reproach,” that is, you recognize how shameful the words they inflict upon me are, “and” you know “my confusion,” which I had, as they supposed, when I saved others but could not save myself (Luke 23; Matthew 26), “and” you know “my reverence,” that is, those lowly things which I endure and which ought to be reverenced, such as spitting and blows. Another translation has “disgrace” or “shame.”

You see me afflicted, and also those who afflict me; therefore you ought to be moved to indignation against them. And [Col. 0425C] this is what follows: “All those who afflict me are before you.” And I endure that tribulation willingly, because “my heart,” that is, my will, “awaited reproach” in words, “and misery” in deeds.

“And I waited,” that is, I expected, “for one who would grieve together with me,” that is, who would sympathize with me. Nature requires this: when people see someone afflicted, they should sympathize with him. “And” nevertheless “there was no one” who would sympathize. “And” I waited “for one who would console me,” by coming over to my teaching, “and I found no one” who would console me.

“And they gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink,” because they gave me no other food or drink except vinegar mixed with gall. [Col. 0425D] This was symbolic: although he himself thirsted for their salvation, he received no refreshment from them; instead, they displayed bitter and harsh behavior toward him.

“Let their table become.” The fourth part. The connection is this: The Jews gave me bad food, and God gave them bad food. And this is what follows: “Let their table,” that is, their Scripture, which is set before them for nourishment, “become for them,” that is, for the Jews, “a snare,” so that through it they may be ensnared and convicted. This has indeed been fulfilled in them, for Christians very often convict them of error through the Law, and with the sword of the Law they slaughter those who observe the Law. Let it become “also” for them “retributions,” because for the Law which they do not keep, God repays them with evils. And he continues these retributions: “and [Col. 0426A] a stumbling block,” that is, let them have scandal and offense from it, either among themselves or among Christians. Let this happen “before them,” so that they themselves may recognize that they are in error, and so that the Jews may clearly know that the Gentiles possess their Law, by which the Gentiles convict the Jews themselves of sin.

As for these “retributions,” namely, “let their eyes be darkened,” that is, their reason, “so that they may not see,” that is, understand the truth. “And their back,” that is, their reason—which is called “back” because just as a person’s back is upright, so reason ought always to be raised toward heavenly things—“be continually bent” toward the desire for earthly things.

Another retribution: “Pour out,” that is, abundantly send “your wrath upon them,” for their crushing, “and let the fury of your anger seize them.” Let it be heavy [Col. 0426B] and lasting.

Another retribution follows. The connection is this: “Pour out your wrath,” namely, so that “their dwelling,” that is, their houses, fields, and vineyards, “become deserted” by them; and “in their tents,” that is, in their crowded places, such as the temple, synagogue, and Capitol, “let there not be” any of them “who dwells.” The fact that he says “who dwells,” rather than simply “who lives there,” indicates that they inhabit those places with great attachment. These wishes were fulfilled against them in the destruction brought by Titus and Vespasian.

All these evils will come upon them “because they persecuted” me, your Son, “whom you struck,” by exposing him to the miseries of this world and making him capable of suffering and mortal, “and upon the pain of my wounds [Col. 0426C] they added”: they wounded Christ when they refused to believe in him, and he grieved over this; and “upon” that “pain,” by inflicting many evils upon him, they “added” many other pains.

And because they “added” evil upon evil to me, “upon their iniquity”—the iniquity they committed against the servants sent into the vineyard, since they killed the prophets sent to cultivate them—“add” another iniquity, namely, that they should kill me, the heir of the vineyard, to complete their wickedness, “and let them not enter into your righteousness,” that is, let them not be converted to you.

Another retribution: Let them also “be blotted out of the book of the living.” The book of life is the foreknowledge of God, in which nothing can actually be written or erased. For all people are foreknown in it, either for death or for life. But according to human judgment some are said to be written in it and some to be erased. We judge that certain people, whom we previously saw as evil, are written in the book of life if they convert and act well; but if those previously regarded as good turn toward evil, we judge them to have been erased from the book of life.

Accordingly, he says: Let those Jews “be blotted out of the book of the living,” namely, let their Law—which previously made them appear righteous—be shown to be useless and harmful; “and with the righteous,” that is, with the Gentiles, “let them not be written,” because the Gentiles receive the new Law, and by this they are judged to be written in the book of life. The Jews are not written, that is, they do not receive the renewal which those who are to be saved receive.

[Col. 0427A] “I am poor.” The fifth part. The connection is this: Let those things happen to them; but I deserve something different for the work of my people, because “I am poor” for the sake of those righteous in worldly terms. Hence the Apostle says: “Although Christ was rich, he became poor for us” (2 Corinthians 8). “And I am also suffering” because of the blindness of the human race; through this he deserved that his own people should be saved. Yet, O “God, your salvation,” that is, your Son, “received me” even to the confession of God the Father, and thereby showed the power by which he can save his own.

And because “your salvation received me,” therefore “I will praise” among my people “the name of God with a song,” that is, with rejoicing, “and in that praise I will magnify him,” that is, my people will proclaim him great and almighty.

[Col. 0427B] And that praise “will please God” more than every legal sacrifice. He demonstrates this through one kind of sacrifice when he says, “more than a young bull producing horns and hooves.” The allegory of this is as follows, although it does not belong here. By that bull we understand the renewed people; by the “horns,” the defenses of the Church, by which it despises worldly things. When he says “producing,” he signifies that the saints continually advance in their defenses, that is, grow.

I say that this praise “will please God more than a bull.” “Let the poor see this,” that is, let them understand it—the poor who could not make sacrifices from those animals—“and rejoice,” knowing that they can now please God more through righteousness than the rich can through bulls. And he turns to those “poor” and says: O you “poor,” understanding this, [Col. 0427C] “seek God, and your soul will live” with true life.

The “poor” ought to rejoice, “because the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised those bound” in sins, by which they appeared to be rejected by God. I say “those bound,” namely, “his own,” that is, those who seek him; although they are bound in sins, they nevertheless aspire toward him.

He has heard the poor, and he will also save Zion. Because this was a great thing that he was saying, he first gives a kind of exhortation concerning it, so that every creature may praise God for it. And this is what follows: “Let the heavens praise him,” that is, the heavenly beings, “and the earth, the sea, and all the creatures that move in them.” Let rational human beings praise the Lord, and through humanity let every creature praise him, because [Col. 0427D] the very substance of creation is the reason why human beings praise the Lord; if humanity had not been saved, no creature would praise the Lord.

Therefore “let them praise him, because God will save Zion,” that is, those who see, namely, the Church. And those who are saved will not be few; through them “the cities of Judah,” that is, the Churches of Christ, who was from the tribe of Judah, “will be built.”

And there people “will dwell,” not for an hour, but “will acquire it as an inheritance,” so that they may possess it forever.

Nor will only one generation of the righteous dwell in it; they will do so through all successions. “And the seed,” that is, the followers and imitators, “of his servants,” that is, of the prophets, [Col. 0428A] “will possess it,” namely, Zion. And he shows whom he calls the seed, as follows: “Those who love his name,” that is, the name of God, “will dwell in it.”

## Psalm 69. Title

“For the end; a psalm of David, for remembrance, because the Lord saved him.”

“God, attend to my help.” This psalm pertains to David, that is, to every righteous person, because here any righteous person speaks. It is a psalm composed for remembrance, remembrance of the fact that the Lord saved him. Mindful of the salvation and benefits which God bestowed upon the world, as was shown in another psalm, he confidently asks to be delivered, although many evils press upon him.

The subject is any righteous person who speaks. In the first part [Col. 0428B] he asks to be delivered from pressing evils and asks for the conversion of his enemies. In the second part, which begins, “Let them exult and rejoice,” he asks for eternal benefits and declares himself secure when he says: Behold, God helps me. His intention is to make us secure concerning eternal good, although we are pressed by these evils. And he says: “God, attend,” that is, show yourself attentive by bestowing grace, “to my help,” so that you may help me overcome the evils that press upon me. When he says, “Attend to my help,” he shows that he is doing something through free choice and asks for divine assistance to cooperate with him. I say: “Attend, and hasten to help me.”

He will help me; and when they see this, “those who seek my soul” in order to take it away—this can properly be said by martyrs—“will be confounded” because of their sins, [Col. 0428C] “and will be awed,” that is, they will fear you as judge.

And not only do these “seek my soul,” but also those “who wish me evil” will “turn backward” from their purpose “and be ashamed,” that is, when they turn back, they will be ashamed of the evils they have done.

Also, those “who say to me,” that is, for my disgrace, “Good, good”—that is, “Well done, well done”—when they see some evil happening and insult him, saying, “Behold, it is evident that he is not good”: let such people “turn away in shame immediately,” that is, without delay, so that their conversion may not be postponed.

Or “those who say, ‘Good, good,’” may refer to those who applaud people doing evil—for example, if someone destroys a city and they say to him, “Ah! How well done! Very good indeed.” Or it may refer to those who do these things to me [Col. 0428D] for my harm, because their iniquity is my harm.

“Let them exult.” Let those people turn away, but “let all who seek you,” O God, “exult and rejoice,” not in temporal things but “in you” alone. The righteous exult in this life, confident that they will possess eternal life. “And” let all “who love your salvation,” that is, your Son, remembering the salvation bestowed on them by God through the Son, “say always,” in heart, voice, and deed, “The Lord is magnified.” This does not mean that he can be magnified in himself, but that, insofar as those who magnify him are concerned, the more they magnify him, the greater and higher he is always understood to be.

Let them say, “The Lord is magnified.” But concerning himself, let each person say: “I am needy” in temporal goods, and “poor” in spiritual goods; and even if he possesses some spiritual goods, they are not sufficient for him. “But I am needy and poor.” Nevertheless, this does not hinder me, because “God” helps me to act well; through this I am secure concerning eternal good. Here he clearly hints that he remembers the benefit, as he stated in the title.

And I rightly say that “God” helps me, because you, O God, “are my helper” in acting well, “and my deliverer” from evils. Only this remains for me to ask: “O Lord, do not delay,” but do what you are going to do, namely, lead me to glory.

## Psalm 70. Title

“A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the former captives.”

[Col. 0429B] “In you, O Lord.” This psalm belongs to David, or to some righteous person—not merely one speaking in his own person, but in the person of the righteous of all times. It is a psalm of the sons of Jonadab and of the former captives.

It is read in the historical account that Jeremiah, correcting the Israelite people because they did not observe God’s commands, and prophesying to them that captivity would come upon them for that disobedience, proposed the sons of Jonadab as an example. He proclaimed to them that just as those sons observed the commands of their earthly father, so they ought rather to observe the commands of God the Father (Jeremiah 35).

Jonadab, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord’s volunteer” or “voluntary one of the people,” was a priest devoted to God. He corrected his sons so that they would not drink wine, that is, so that they would not become intoxicated with the pleasures of this life, [Col. 0429C] and so that they would not build houses for themselves, but dwell in the house of the Lord; that is, they should understand that they had no enduring city here, but, serving the Lord, should strive toward what is above.

Esdras, understanding that David had proposed the sons of Jonadab—namely, the righteous, obedient to God and hoping in him—to contumacious people who did not observe the commands of their God, said that this psalm was “of the former captives,” that is, of those contumacious people who do not observe God’s commands in this life. This does not mean that the psalm concerns those people themselves, but that the sons of Jonadab, that is, those who hope in the Lord, are proposed to those contumacious people as an example, so that they may be corrected through their example.

The people of this life are called “former captives,” because they can leave this captivity, just as the Jews left the Babylonian captivity [Col. 0429D]. A second captivity is still to come, from which no one will depart.

Or, if we read “of the sons of Jonadab, the former captives” without the conjunction *and*, it can be understood that the sons of Jonadab were historically taken captive, not because of their own sin but because of the sin of others, according to the way the title is read: “This psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab,” that is, of those who hope in the Lord—of those, I say, who are “former captives,” that is, who are captive in the miseries of this life. This captivity is the former one, from which the sons of Jonadab, that is, those who hope in the Lord, will emerge. The second captivity is still to come in the other life; in it there will be no sons of Jonadab, since no one will be able to leave it.

The subject is every righteous person who hopes in the Lord, and many of God’s benefits toward those who hope in God are described.

The method is as follows. In the first part [Col. 0430A] he asks to be delivered from evils so that he may be able to praise God. In the second, which begins, “Do not cast me off in the time of old age,” he asks that just as God bestowed benefits upon him in his youth, so he may do so in old age, when there is greatest need. In the third, which begins, “What great things you have done, O God; who is like you?” he gives thanks for the benefits bestowed. His intention is to admonish everyone to place his hope in the Lord. This is indicated by the words: “O Lord, my hope from my youth.”

He presents himself as one who hopes in the Lord, thus admonishing others: Do not hope in worldly things, but hope in the Lord, following my example, since I have abandoned all worldly things. “O Lord, I have hoped,” and because “I have hoped in you,” although I may appear worthy of shame in this world, “I shall not be put to shame forever,” because at some point I shall openly obtain what I have hoped for.

I say not “I shall be put to shame,” but rather, O Lord, “deliver me,” so that this temptation may not prevail over me, “and” not only “deliver me,” but also “rescue me,” so that no further evils may come upon me. This rescue of the righteous takes place in death, when God leads the righteous person to himself. And this occurs in righteousness. Since no one can be delivered or rescued according to his own righteousness, he adds: “in your righteousness,” namely, in that righteousness of yours which always has mercy joined to it.

I say “rescue me,” and because my merits would never be worthy to reach your height, therefore, O Lord, “incline your ear to me,” that is, condescend to me through your kindness, “and save me.”

“Deliver me” in such a way that “you become a protecting God for me,” delivering me from the dangers of this life, “and” become for me “a fortified place,” in which I am safe, so that no enemy afterward dares attack me. This will take place in the other life, “so that you may save me”; this refers back to what he had said: “rescue me.”

Therefore I say, be my protector, because I seek refuge from no one but you. And this is what follows: “For you are my strength,” that is, you are the one who makes me strong. This refers to “a protecting God.” “And you are my refuge”; this refers to what he said, “be a fortified place for me.”

“My God, rescue me.” When he asks to be delivered, he indicates his need; he now specifies from whom he asks to be delivered, saying: O “my God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner,” that is, from the power of the devil; “from the hand of the one acting against the Law, and” from the hand “of the wicked,” who, although he does not have the written Law, nevertheless distinguishes through the natural law what is just and what is unjust—namely, that he ought not to do to others what he would not want done to himself.

Here every kind of sinner is indicated: those who have the Law and those who do not, as the Apostle says: “All who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law, and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Romans 2).

“For you are.” You ought to rescue me, “because you, O Lord, are my patience,” that is, that fruit and cause for whose sake I endure; and you are also “my hope,” O Lord, that is, the certainty of my future reward. Hence the Apostle says: “Patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5). [Col. 0431A] “Hope,” I say, “from my youth,” that is, from the time of my conversion. He does not speak of youth in relation to the time of life, but of the youth of righteousness; he takes strength from youth, and that strength clearly shone forth at Christ’s coming in the holy apostles and martyrs.

“In you also I was confirmed from the womb,” that is, while I was still in the womb of the Church. He calls the womb of the Church that preparation by which a person is instructed when he begins to believe, and in which he is nourished beforehand so that he may emerge into the light of true knowledge. “You” are also “my protector” from the time when I came forth “from my mother’s womb,” that is, from the Church—namely, from the time when I was reborn through baptism and received the light of true knowledge.

[Col. 0431B] And because you have done all these good things for me, “my song will always be in you,” that is, I will praise you alone. And because I praise you alone and reject the world, therefore “I have become like a portent to many,” to lovers of the world, because they think me insane and monstrous when they see me seek you alone and disregard their sects. But in opposition to all their reproaches, “you” have become for me “a strong helper.”

And therefore “let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing of your glory,” that is, proclaim you glorious, and also “your greatness,” that is, your benefits which you bestow upon me. These are the reason why I show you to be glorious. Let this happen “all day long,” that is, continually.

“Do not cast me off.” The second part. I say, “You are my hope from my youth,” and just as you do not abandon me in youth, [Col. 0431C] so “do not cast me off in the time of old age.” He explains what he understands by old age when he says: “When my strength fails, do not abandon me,” that is, although for a time you may cast me off by permitting me to remain in sins, nevertheless do not abandon me, that is, do not permit me to rot in sins.

God cast Peter off when he permitted him to sin, but did not abandon him when he caused him to repent. Behold, the one who was just now speaking in the person of the strong living righteous now speaks in the person of the old, and here he understands old age as the time when a person already appears to be failing and charity begins to grow cold, as in the time before Antichrist.

“Do not abandon me,” because if you abandon me, the weaker my enemies see me, the more heavily they will press upon me. And this is what follows: “For my enemies have said to me,” [Col. 0431D] that is, for my harm: “God has abandoned him.” And not only ignorant enemies said this, but also those “who guarded my soul,” that is, those who lay in wait for my soul with great cunning in order to seize it, namely, the devils and their ministers. “They took counsel together,” agreeing “as one” in the same desire to harm.

Saying what the other enemies said: “God has abandoned him,” that is, he does not care for him. Therefore, “pursue him,” as one who cannot flee, “and seize him,” as one who is weak and cannot resist; hold him securely, “because there is no one to rescue him.”

They think me abandoned, but you, “O God, do not be far from me,” that is, do not permit me to be afflicted by them for long. Rather, O “my God, look upon my help,” so that I may be able to overcome all these things.

Look upon me, and let those who “slander my soul be confounded,” that is, be shown to be ineffective, so that they cannot make me like themselves, “and let them fail,” that is, let them no longer dare to attack me. I say, “let them be confounded,” and let them “be covered with their great confusion,” that is, let their confusion be so great that it covers them, so that it converts them. And let them be covered not only with confusion but also “with shame” at their failure—let those who seek evils for me be covered on every side.

Let them be covered with confusion. But as for me, whatever others may do, “I will always hope” in you, “and upon all your praise,” which you possess because of the creation of the world, “I will add” another praise, namely, for the sending of the Son. And this is what follows: “My mouth will proclaim your righteousness,” and he then explains what he calls righteousness: “your salvation,” that is, the Son, who saves those hoping in him and justifies them. And this will be “all day long.”

For this reason I will proclaim your righteousness and “your salvation,” because “I have not known learning,” that is, the cunning and arts of this life. Jerome has *litteraturas* (“literary studies”); another translation has “business dealings.” And now “I will enter into the power of the Lord,” that is, the heavenly dwelling, where I will know the power of the Lord, and I myself will acquire power. Thereafter no one will dare disturb me. And there too, O Lord, “I will remember your righteousness alone,” that is, I will understand you alone to be righteous.

Therefore I will “remember,” because “God, you taught me” [Col. 0432C] not to seek literary learning and to preach your Son, “from my youth,” that is, from the time when I began to be a lover of faith. “And until now” you have taught me; therefore “I shall proclaim your wonders,” that is, the benefits you have bestowed.

You taught me, and “do not abandon me,” O “God,” to teach and preserve me “until old age and gray hairs.” “Old age” is the Church, when the Church still possesses some strength; “gray hairs” are decrepit old age, which will occur in the Church at the time of Antichrist, when the Church’s strength will be almost entirely extinguished.

“Do not abandon me,” I say, “until I proclaim your arm,” that is, your Son, “to every generation that is to come.” And until I proclaim “your power,” by which you save humanity, “and your justice” [Col. 0432D], by which you justify everyone according to each person’s merit. I say that I will proclaim this by advancing through agility of mind “to the highest places,” that is, to the heavenly creatures—to the contemplation of heavenly things, so that I may contemplate God himself and the heavenly realities. Or “to the highest places,” namely so that I may preach that certain heavenly creatures were redeemed through the Son. For it is read that certain angels, although we do not believe it, sinned by consenting to the fallen angels.

Here begins the third part. Continuation: And rightly I ought to proclaim “your power and justice,” because “the great things you have done,” O “God,” are benefits without number. Therefore above I said, “I shall sing of your greatness”; and because you have done these things, “who is like you?” No one. [Col. 0433A] I say that no one is like you, because “you have shown me how many tribulations,” in the actual experience of the matter, “many” in number and “evil” in quality—that is, grievous—“yet you have given me life,” the true life, which is God. I say that you, “having turned,” from the former condition that existed before Christ’s coming, when no one was given life, “brought me back from the depths of the earth,” that is, from the depth of sins, “again”—and again through baptism and through repentance, many times.

And to me, thus brought back, you “multiplied your magnificence,” that is, in many ways you bestowed great and manifold benefits, “and you consoled me,” making me secure in the promise of eternal good. I say that you, “having turned,” through the mediator Christ, from the wrath you held on account of the first parent’s sin against the human [Col. 0433B] race, did this.

He proves from his affection that he has been consoled in this way: Truly you have consoled me, “for I too shall confess to you,” that is, to your honor, “your truth, O God,” that is, that you are truthful in your promises—namely, that through your Son human beings obtain the security of an eternal inheritance. I say that I shall “confess” this “with the vessels of the psalm,” that is, in the psalms, which are vessels. Through the psalms we receive spiritual life; through these psalms an example of good works is offered, just as through a vessel someone receives a drink. I do not say merely that I shall confess in the psalms, that is, in the contemplative life, but, O “Holy One of Israel,” who sanctify every Israel, that is, everyone who sees God, “I shall sing to you on the lyre,” that is, in the mortification of the flesh—in the active life.

[Col. 0433C] I shall confess in the psalms, and with exultation. These are my inner lips, that is, the affections of the soul, which always gape toward God, just as “my lips shall exult when I sing to you,” that is, when I praise you. And not only my lips, but also my whole “soul, which you have redeemed,” so that the soul itself understands that it ought to exult.

And not only the “soul,” but also the whole body; and he says this through one of its parts, adding: “but my tongue also” will utter, from the affection of the heart, “your justice,” and it “will meditate on it all day,” namely when the unending day comes—that is, at the judgment. He determines what he means by “all day,” saying: when “those who seek evil for me” in this life have been “confounded,” that is, ashamed of their sins, “and have been afraid,” that is, have feared the judge’s sentence, namely: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

# ON PSALM 71

## Title: A Psalm of David concerning Solomon

“God, give judgment.” This treatise concerns Solomon, that is, Christ, who is the true Solomon, meaning “peaceful,” for he established peace between God and humanity. In this psalm Christ is the subject according to both natures, namely the divine and the human.

The structure is as follows. In the first part he asks that judgment be given to him and affirms that he will possess it. In the second part, which begins, “Justice shall rise in his days,” he speaks about the kingdom, commending that kingdom in many ways. In the third part, which begins, “May his name be blessed,” [Col. 0434A] he commends that kingdom. His purpose is to admonish us to submit to this Solomon.

The voice of the Church, foreseeing that Christ will become king, prays that the kingdom be given to him, saying: O “God” the Father, “give the king,” that is, Christ, “your judgment” over human beings. That is: just as you possess judgment, so give it to him, so that he may possess the authority to judge. And to that same “Son of the king,” that is, of you, who alone are king and who reign in your truth, give “your justice,” that is, a just judgment, because that king will always judge in justice.

This is an instance of *endiasis*, because the same thing is expressed by different terms, namely by “judgment” and “justice”; and it is *endiasis*, a saying expressed twice.

“I say, give judgment,” namely “to judge your people in justice,” that is, so that he may judge the whole people, [Col. 0434B] both good and wicked. He says “your” because even the impious can do nothing except by God’s permission. And “your poor,” give him to judge “in judgment,” that is, in just judgment.

Christ judges the good and the wicked even in this life; finally he will judge when he separates the good from the wicked. Hence Christ says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). The Father nevertheless judges—not through himself, certainly, but through the one whose substance is united with his.

I say, “give” him “judgment,” and cause him to be known throughout the whole world through the apostles. This is what follows: “May the mountains,” that is, the holy apostles, “receive peace,” that is, Christ, “for the people,” that is, for the people’s benefit—namely, so that they may make him known to the people. And “the hills,” that is, those lower than the holy apostles but higher than the peoples, [Col. 0434C] such as blessed Martin and blessed Hilary, may receive “justice,” that is, Christ himself, so that they may make him known to the people.

Christ is called “peace” because he established reconciliation between God and humanity. He is called “justice” because God justifies those who turn back to him.

“He shall judge.” He asked that judgment be given to Christ; here he affirms that he truly will possess judgment. Continuation: I say, “give” him “judgment,” and truly you will give it, because he “will judge the poor of the people,” that is, the truly poor, removing them from the wicked people. And he will also save “the sons of the poor,” that is, the imitators of the apostles. And “God will humble the calumniator,” that is, the devil, who is the unjust accuser of our brothers—he will crush him.

Here he commends that just judge. This judge [Col. 0434D] “will judge, and” this judge “will remain with the sun,” that is, always united with the Godhead. The Godhead is called “sun” because it enlightens every human being with true knowledge (John 1). And he will remain “before the moon,” that is, before the Church, because he will always be present to the Church, so that the Church may always receive light from him, as the moon receives it from the sun.

The Church is understood by “the moon,” because it wanes and waxes like the moon. I say that he “will remain in this generation and the generation” that follows, that is, the same forever, throughout generations of generations. Or “with the sun,” that is, as long as the sun exists and the firmament stands; and he was “before the moon,” that is, before the world came to be.

He had said, “he will judge”; and now he determines concerning whom he had spoken, [Col. 0435A] namely, the Son of the Virgin. Here he openly announces the incarnation of the divinity. Continuation: I say, “he will judge,” and the one who “will judge will descend,” according to his divinity, into the Virgin, “like rain upon a fleece,” so gently, without any noise or terror.

Here he refers us to the historical account. God commanded Gideon to go to battle. When Gideon was afraid, he asked for a sign of victory, and the Lord gave him this sign: after a fleece had been placed on the threshing floor, if the fleece were found soaked while the threshing floor was dry, he would know that he would be victorious. And so it happened. Still afraid, he asked for the opposite sign: that the threshing floor should be soaked and the fleece become dry. This too happened, and he was victorious (Judges 6).

The fleece, soaked first, signified the Jews, who first believed and were soaked with the doctrine of God; the threshing floor signifies the Gentiles, previously dry from faith. Conversely, the threshing floor becoming wet signifies the Gentiles later coming to faith; and the dry fleece signifies the Jews, who refused the Lord’s teaching, as the Apostle says in Acts of the Apostles: “The word of God had to be spoken to you, but since you rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

Or we may explain the comparison more explicitly: just as rain neither damages the fleece when it falls upon it nor when it departs, so neither conception nor childbirth corrupted the Virgin. And this one will water the whole world through his teaching. Hence he says, “and like drops of rain,” that is, water dripping from heaven—“drops” that are “falling upon the earth,” that is, upon the Gentiles.

“He shall arise.” The second part. Behold, “in his days,” that is, in the time of Christ, “justice shall arise,” [Col. 0435C] because through his coming every just person will be justified, “and an abundance of peace,” that is, abundant reconciliation, because it will exist throughout the whole world, since people from every region will be reconciled to God. It is a lasting peace, “until the moon is removed,” that is, until the present Church is removed—until it becomes spiritual, namely immortal and impassible. “Until it is removed,” that is, for as long as the world exists. Another translation has: “until it is lifted up.”

Here he shows the extent of the kingdom: “and” he “will rule from sea” in the east “to sea” in the west, “and from the river,” that is, the Jordan, “to the ends of the earth,” that is, around the whole world. By the river Jordan, in which Christ was baptized, we understand baptism, through which Christ is spread [Col. 0435D] throughout the whole world.

“Before him,” the king, “the Ethiopians will fall,” that is, those who are black with sins, “and his enemies will lick the earth,” and will always desire earthly things, which are the devil’s food.

“The kings of Tarshish and the islands.” “Tarshish” is interpreted as “exploration of joy,” or “contemplation.” Hence he says: some who come from the exploration of joy—that is, having set aside the joys of this world and making themselves good rulers—will offer their carnality, or others whom they will convert to him.

Or “Tarshish,” that is, the kings of contemplation, “will offer gifts,” as will “the islands,” which lie in the midst of the sea and are dry land. By the islands, which are dry land surrounded by sea, we understand [Col. 0436A] those who are dry with respect to the waves of the world and are not defiled by the storms of this life, although they are battered on every side by the tempests of this world.

“And the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba” of that other kingdom “will bring gifts.” This was fulfilled at Christ’s birth, when those kings, led by the star, offered various gifts to Christ the Lord (Matthew 2).

Or, because the Arabs are said to be extremely rich and abundant in the wealth of this life, while the Sabaeans abound in fragrances and other delights of this life, we may say: “the kings of the Arabs,” that is, those who, having abandoned the riches, delights, and fragrances of this life, make themselves kings and offer themselves to God as gifts.

Or because Arabia is interpreted as “humility,” and Sheba as “burning,” we understand humble people who set all vices ablaze within themselves. Thus made kings, they offer themselves as gifts [Col. 0436B] to God.

“And” for this reason “all kings will worship him,” the king—those who formerly used to be worshiped, that is, some from every royal kind. And “all the nations” that formerly used to serve earthly kings “will serve him,” the heavenly king.

“I say that they will serve,” and rightly so, “because he himself delivered the poor” truly “from the powerful,” that is, from the devil, whose power is shown by the one who says: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard” (Luke 11). And I do not mean “the poor” who possess some means of assistance—that is, some possibility of deliverance—but rather that “poor man who had no helper,” who could not be delivered either by free will or by any other means except through Christ himself.

Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “No other was found who could open the book, except the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5).

I say, “he will deliver the poor”; and to the one delivered he “will show mercy,” that is, he will not punish him according to each individual sin. Or he “will show mercy to the poor” because he will not permit him to be tempted beyond what he can bear (1 Corinthians 10). And he will also show mercy “to the needy,” to the one who has no help except from him. And finally, in the judgment and after death, “he will save the souls of the poor.”

And this he will do because he “will redeem” them with the price of his blood. Here he openly announces Christ’s death: “their souls from usury,” that is, from the punishment imposed for sin, “and from iniquity,” that is, from sin itself. And “their name,” namely that they are Christians, although before the powerful of this world it is despised as something worthless, will nevertheless be “honorable before him,” that is, pleasing to him.

Here are his commendations as king: “and he will live” eternally. Or “he will live,” that is, having died, he will rise again. “And gold from Arabia will be given to him,” that is, the most distinguished wise men, such as Dionysius and Paul.

By “the gold of Arabia,” which is more precious than other gold, we understand that the gold of that land is of the finest quality; by it we understand precious sages. “And they will worship because of him forever,” that is, on his account, so that he may give himself to them—just as one might say that someone worships gold who asks for gold.

Or “because of him,” that is, near him, according to what he himself instituted for prayer: they will sing, “Our Father,” and “all day,” that is, at every time, “they will bless him.”

[Col. 0437A] He himself also “will be a foundation on the summits of the mountains,” that is, of the apostles, by which he will make them firm and steadfast “on the earth,” where few can be firm and where God’s strengthening is most needed.

And “his fruit,” that is, the good work which his people perform through him, “will be exalted above Lebanon,” that is, above the whiteness of this world, because the works of the righteous are far more worthy than any power of this life. And those who have been removed “from” this “city” and led into another city, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, “will flourish,” having become immortal and impassible, “like the grass of the earth,” which is green and flowering.

“Grass” is understood in a negative sense because it quickly dries up and passes away, but not here.

“May his name be blessed.” The third part. Because he makes his people flourish, [Col. 0437B] and bestows all these good things upon them, therefore “may his name be blessed,” that is, may he himself, as one who is named, be blessed “forever.” This “name” ought to be blessed because “his name,” that is, he himself as one who is named, “remains forever” “before the sun,” that is, before the foundation of the world.

And not only will he himself be blessed, but all his people through him. This is what follows: “and all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him,” that is, some from every tribe; and through this “all the nations will magnify him.”

And because the Prophet understands that he himself has been blessed in him, he blesses God on his own behalf. Continuation: I say, “all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him,” and therefore let him be “blessed, the Lord God of Israel, who alone does great wonders,” that is, the restoration of the human race, and other things as well.

“Alone,” because no one else can do them. Or “alone,” because he does them through himself; while others, if they perform miracles, such as Peter and the others, do not do so through themselves alone but through him.

“And the name of his majesty,” that is, what his majesty—that is, he himself, the great one—bestows, namely the Christian name, “may be blessed,” remaining “forever.” I say “the name of his majesty” because “the whole earth will be filled with his majesty,” that is, his divinity. He repeats this action because he desires something exceedingly worthy when he says, “Let it be done, let it be done.”

# ON PSALM 72

## Title: The praises of David, son of Jesse, have failed. A Psalm of Asaph

[Col. 0437D] “How good is the God of Israel.” This psalm shows that God no longer gives his worshipers prosperity, as he once did, but adversity. Understanding this, Ezra understood the Prophet to have understood this in the psalm and therefore gave it the title “The praises of David.” And lest we understand “David” as Christ or the Church, he specifies David’s physical generation when he says “son of Jesse.” Through this he enables us to understand the carnal Jewish people, because David, according to his physical generation, was one member of the carnal people.

The praises of this David—that is, of the Jewish people—have failed because God no longer gives his people temporal goods, with which alone the carnal Jewish people used to praise him. And so that we may be certain that God no longer gives temporal goods, and that when these are denied the praises of the carnal [Col. 0438A] Jewish people fail, this is confirmed by the testimony of the faithful Synagogue, which ought to be believed all the more firmly because the Synagogue itself formerly praised God for earthly things alone.

This is why the psalm is called a psalm of Asaph, that is, of the faithful Synagogue. For “Asaph” is interpreted as “assembly,” and it may refer to the prophet himself or to some faithful person from the Synagogue.

The subject is the faithful Synagogue itself. The structure is as follows. In the first part it shows that it once went astray when it saw the prosperity of the wicked. In the second part, which begins, “Therefore my people will turn back here,” it shows its conversion from this error, and that of others like it. In the third part, which begins, “Nevertheless, because of their deceits,” it shows that the prosperity of this age is recognized as evil not only by means of human final destiny but also through present realities, because prosperity plunges the rich themselves into sin and causes the good to sin through envy of them. In the fourth part, which begins, “For what is there for me in heaven?” it shows that it possesses true understanding and now seeks not temporal things but God alone.

Its purpose is to restrain the simple, lest they murmur about the prosperity of the wicked and the adversity of the good.

Thus, seeing that certain simple people were still going astray and judging God to be perverse because he gave prosperity to the wicked and inflicted evil upon his own people, he restrains their error, saying: O “God of Israel,” who seem to be perverse to them, “how good” he is—that is, he is infinitely good. Or: “O God of Israel, how good he is”; but this goodness does not appear to all people, only “to those who are upright in heart,” that is, to those who judge adversity in this life to be more beneficial than prosperity.

Here he begins to explain his error. Continuation: Now I confess that God is good, but formerly “my feet,” that is, my affections, “were almost moved” away from God. And not only my wills, but also my works, almost withdrew from God toward the worship of idols. This is what follows: “my steps,” that is, my works, “were almost poured out,” that is, cast headlong.

This happened “because I was jealous of the wicked,” that is, I was indignant at the wicked, “seeing the peace,” that is, the tranquility, “of sinners.”

They had peace “because there is no regard for their death,” that is, they do not consider their death. If they considered it—and what is given to each person at death according to his merits—they would not have the peace and prosperity of this life but would mourn. And therefore they do not possess peace and prosperity because “in their affliction,” that is, in the wounds of their vices, there is no “firmness.” For even if God had moved them toward remorse through some illness, they are not thereby made firm, so that their sins might be completely healed and their souls restored.

Or, in another sense, there is no “regard” of divine mercy “for their death,” that is, God does not give them any tribulation by which they might be rescued from the death of the soul. Or he sends some adversity, though not an adversity affecting them in such a way as to heal them, but rather one affecting their wounds—that is, he does not give them an affliction that makes them firm, so that their sins are entirely erased and the soul restored to its own strength.

He speaks of God by comparison with a physician who, when he foresees that a sick person cannot escape, gives him no treatment. Thus God permits those whom he foreknows to be predestined for death to do everything, and does not withdraw them from the prosperity of this world.

Truly “there is no regard for their death,” because no medicine is applied to them. For they “are not in the labor of human beings,” that is, of rational people, so as to keep watch, live properly, or do anything of that kind. “And” for this reason “they will not be scourged with human beings” by the one who “scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

And because they neither labor on their own nor are “scourged” by God, and they obtain the prosperity of this age, “therefore pride seized them,” as though with certain hands, so that they could not be taken away. And lest they recover their senses, “they were covered,” that is, wrapped up, “with iniquity” as though directed toward their neighbor, “and with their impiety,” that is, blasphemy, as though directed toward God. He says “their own” because a human being has wickedness from himself, not from God.

And it is not enough for them to be evil within themselves; their “iniquity also came forth openly, like fat,” that is, from the superfluity of riches, by comparison with a fat animal such as a bull, so that they might give others an example of pride. And, having laid aside all fear, they “passed beyond” human custom, pressing toward “the desire of the heart,” that is, so that what their hearts desired might be fulfilled.

They did not do this as though unexpectedly, but with great attention they “thought out wickedness.” And wickedness seemed so good to them that they “also spoke,” that is, they taught wickedness to others. They “spoke iniquity” as well; and he later specifies this iniquity: “in pride.”

Behold the “iniquity” that they “spoke”: they “set their mouth in heaven,” that is, they spoke blasphemies against God, “and their tongue passed beyond” the bounds of human speech. Although they were “on earth,” living upon it, their supreme pride was evident in this: while they were on earth, they spoke proudly about the God who is on high.

Or “their tongue passed beyond” the others who are placed on earth, speaking more wickedly than the other earthly people.

“Therefore it will turn back.” The second part. Having considered that their prosperity leads them into pride and also makes them speak iniquity, “therefore my people,” that is, those like me, of whom I am one, “will turn back” from error, so that they will not be moved toward the wicked rich by the prosperity of this life. Thus they will be “here,” that is, in the judgment in which I stand.

And after they have turned back, “full days will be found in them” through their effect, because what was brought about in the time of grace will exist in them: contempt for earthly things and desire for heavenly things.

Or “full days,” that is, eternal days, will be found in them. Even if this is not now apparent, they will possess eternity.

He explains what they will turn away from. The phrase “and they said” looks ahead to what follows, where he says, “and I said.”

Continuation: I say, “they will turn back,” and they must, because before their conversion “they said: How does God know,” and how can it be true that God orders these earthly affairs? Surely he does not order them. “And” if he does order them, then this follows: “Is there knowledge in the highest place?” That is, if so, God is unjust. But he presents an incomplete statement, because an entirely explicit accusation against God would have been too blatant.

Therefore I say that either God does not order these things or he is unjust, because “behold,” it is manifest: “they themselves, sinners and abounding in the world,” who appear to prosper greatly, have “obtained riches.” For if anyone wished to take them away from them, he could not.

They said this, and I, who had once gone astray like them, “said”: since sinners abound in riches, “therefore I have justified my heart without cause,” that is, my will; “and I washed my hands,” that is, purified my works, “among the innocent,” so that I might be numbered among them.

And also without cause “I was scourged” by God’s discipline “all day,” that is, continually. And “my chastisement,” which I imposed in order to restrain lust and likewise the other vices, I practiced “in the mornings,” that is, diligently, because when we do something diligently, we begin it in the morning. It was “without cause,” that is, without benefit.

This reading may also be taken syntactically as an unfinished or suspended statement: “Thus I justified my heart without cause,” and likewise the other things mentioned.

Previously I said this, but afterward, recognizing the truth, “I said: If I tell it thus,” namely that a person “without cause” justifies his “heart,” cleanses his works, and does the other things mentioned “without cause,” a fitting consequence follows: “Behold, I would reject,” that is, judge and condemn, or separate from myself, “the nation of your sons,” Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others.

Or otherwise: They said either that God does not know these earthly things or that, if he knows them, he is unjust. To refute their opinion I said: If God is ignorant or unjust, as you say, then I and every other good person have endured God’s correction in vain, because, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 15), “We are more pitiable than all human beings” if God is believed to be unjust.

And besides this absurdity, I showed another absurdity resulting from it, because I said: “If I tell it thus,” that is, that God is unjust or ignorant, “behold, I have rejected the nation of the sons,” as above, since I would have believed that Abraham and the others were not rewarded. Or “I rejected,” that is, I found myself opposed to all the sons of God.

And I saw that this absurdity followed from that opinion; therefore I “considered,” that is, I understood—which another translation has as “so that I might understand”—why prosperity is given to the impious and adversity to the good by God. And to understand “this” “is labor before me,” that is, it is beyond me.

Or “before me,” that is, insofar as present things are concerned.

I say that it is “labor” “until I enter,” with agility of mind, “into the sanctuary of God,” that is, into God’s counsel—until I consider by what providence God does this to the wicked and this to the good: namely, that he gives the impious prosperity, by his just judgment, for their blinding, while he gives the good adversity for their purification.

Or until I enter “into the sanctuary of God,” that is, into the Holy Scriptures, which give reasons for all these things. And it is also “labor” until I “understand,” placed in mind, “their final destiny,” that is, until I consider the future punishments of those who grew proud in worldly things and the glory of those who lived amid the tribulations of this world.

“Nevertheless.” The third part. I say that understanding this is labor unless it is understood through their final destiny. “Nevertheless,” it can also be understood through present realities, because you, O God, “placed these riches before them” “for deceits,” that is, acting in a thoroughly deceptive manner, giving evil under the appearance of good for the purpose of blinding them.

And while they were “lifted up,” that is, exalted in earthly things, you “cast them down,” blinding them. The more they are exalted in temporal matters, the more they are cast down into ruin; and the very elevation becomes the cause of their fall.

I rightly say “you cast them down,” because “how they became desolation,” that is, how utterly desolate they became before you, when either as young men they lost the good things of this life that they had loved, or, when dying, “they suddenly failed,” because they died sooner than expected.

And lest someone say that the righteous also die in the same way, he adds this: “they perished because of their iniquity,” whereas the righteous live forever.

Thus they failed, “like the dream of those who awaken.” For just as sleeping people possess many riches in dreams, yet, when they awaken, find nothing and regard as empty the things they saw in dreams, so the wicked are in a dream in this life. At death they will awaken and recognize that the things they possessed in this life were empty.

And truly they will perish, because, O “Lord, in your city,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, you “will reduce their image to nothing,” that is, they will have no place in your city. This is because in this world, which is the city of the devil and his servants, they reduced your image to nothing—namely, their reason, by which they resemble you, that is, purity and innocence—and made new images for themselves: one living in uncleanness, like a pig; another living by predation, like a wolf; and others in other ways.

Therefore you “will reduce them to nothing,” because not only did their prosperity harm them, but it harmed me also, who am yours. This is what follows: “my heart,” that is, my will, “was inflamed” with envy toward them in their prosperity; and “my kidneys,” that is, the strength of my soul, by which reason ought to stand upright as a human being stands upright through the kidneys, “were changed,” so that I no longer despised earthly things as I had previously done and as reason required.

“And I was reduced to nothing,” that is, to desire for earthly things, because those who desire the world are nothing in God’s sight. “And I did not know” that I had been “reduced to nothing,” or that I was sinning.

I was also “made like a beast,” that is, completely irrational, and this “before you,” that is, in your sight, although I seemed to myself a great philosopher. And nevertheless, although at times I strayed through desire for earthly things, “I was always with you,” and this was through you.

You “held my right hand,” that is, my reason, preserving it so that it would not depart from you. God holds a person’s left hand when he leads him through prosperity in this life.

You also “guided me,” O Lord, from virtue to virtue, not through my merits but “according to your will,” and “you received me” into your house, not made by human hands, in heaven, “with glory.”

“For what.” The fourth part. I rightly say, “you received me with glory.” “For what is prepared for me in heaven?”—namely, inexpressible glory, which “no eye has seen, nor ear heard,” and so forth. “And what is there,” that is, how worthless is what I “wanted” you to give me “upon earth”? For although I had sometimes asked for temporal things, I nevertheless always wanted to possess you.

Previously I wanted earthly things, but behold, “my flesh has failed,” because my carnality, which previously desired earthly things, has now “failed,” mortifying itself. “And my heart also,” that is, my carnal will, has failed, because I no longer desire anything mortal. And “God” is “the dwelling place of my heart”; and while others make for themselves portions from the riches of this world, “God is my portion,” leading me “into eternity.”

Therefore I make you my portion, O God, because it is manifest that “those who distance themselves from you,” through a shameful and dishonorable life, “will perish.” For you, God, have already “destroyed,” by your ordering of things, those who “fornicate apart from you,” that is, live without you, with the demon, departing from the true bridegroom.

Or they “fornicate” by satisfying their own pleasure, like fornicators who seek only to fulfill their desire.

You will destroy those fornicators, but not me, because “it is good for me,” that is, it is delightful, “to cling to God,” [Col. 0442C] by observing his commandments, “and to place my hope in the Lord God.”

I cling to him “so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates.” Or “preachings,” that is, all your praises, “in the gates,” that is, in public, where everyone may hear them—“of Zion,” that is, of your “daughter,” the Church. The Church is compared to a daughter because of her adornments and because of the fecundity of her children.

# ON PSALM 73

## Title: For the end; an understanding of Asaph

“Why, O God, have you rejected us?” This psalm is called “an understanding” because it opens up to us something very obscure, namely the destruction of God’s temple, which had not yet occurred in the Prophet’s time, and the future destruction of the city by Titus and Vespasian.

This kind of “understanding” belongs to “Asaph,” that is, to the faithful Synagogue; for “Asaph” is interpreted as “assembly.” The subject is the Synagogue itself, mourning and grieving over the destruction of that people, which it foresees.

The structure is as follows. In the first part it makes a lament over the destruction of that people and begs God to have mercy on them, showing that this has happened because of the Jews’ merits. In the second part, which begins, “But God is our king,” it prays that just as God showed mercy to the world and performed many wonders, so he might also perform them for the Jews themselves. In the third part, which begins, “Do not hand them over to beasts,” it asks God that, whatever he may do with the others, he at least have mercy on the poor and those who confess him. [Col. 0443A]

Its purpose is to encourage us to sympathize with the misfortunes of others, because this is a certain degree of charity. Hence the Apostle says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12).

He sets forth the lament in this way, saying: O “God, you have rejected” your portion “to the end,” namely to the end of rejection. For although you once rejected them for a time in other captivities, this rejection is irrecoverable, because the Jews will never again rule in this place, nor will they ever again be restored, until the end of the age.

God rejected them when he did not defend them as he had been accustomed to do and allowed them to be destroyed by the Romans.

The question expresses a lament, as though he were saying: I grieve over their immense destruction. “Why has your anger raged?” That is, why have you become angry even to fury? [Col. 0443B] Namely, so as to inflict upon them extremely grievous and prolonged punishments “against the sheep of your pasture,” that is, against your people, whom you refreshed with your law as sheep are refreshed in pastures.

Here, through the benefits God bestowed upon them, he begins to gain goodwill toward them.

Do not, Lord, reject them. Rather, “remember your assembly,” which you gathered in Egypt, “which” assembly you “possessed” as serving you “from the beginning,” that is, from the time of Abraham, Noah, and Adam, and of the others.

Also, he moves God to mercy through other benefits. For this reason too you ought to “remember,” because you “redeemed”—that is, freed from the hand of the Egyptians and from other captivities—“the rod of your inheritance” [Col. 0443C], that is, your inheritance, namely the Jewish people, for whose sake you performed many miracles, as through Aaron’s rod. Or by “rod” we may understand the scepter of royal power, so that we may say: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” that is, the people whom you rule with a rod, namely with a royal scepter. And besides the other benefits, you yourself visited them bodily and dwelt among them. This is expressed by: “Mount Zion in which you dwelt,” literally, because Christ dwelt bodily in “Zion,” that is, in Judaea, whose capital is Zion. The Hebrew truth does not have “in it.” It may nevertheless be read in this way: “You dwelt in Zion,” not merely through servants sent to the vineyard, but “you dwelt in it” in your own person.

After he has sought favor through the benefits God bestowed upon the people [Col. 0443D], he seeks favor from the person of the adversaries by setting forth their pride. Continuation: Because you bestowed these benefits upon your people, therefore, O God, “lift up your hands,” that is, your works, which had been slackened when you allowed them to do with your city whatever they wished. “Lift up,” I say, “against their arrogances,” that is, against the arrogance of those who are destroying the city; and do this “to the end,” completely—that is, so that they may be converted—because “how greatly the enemy has acted wickedly,” that is, with how evil an intention that Roman people, the enemy, acted “in the holy place,” namely, in your temple.

And whereas other people who are accustomed to do evil are accustomed to be struck with remorse and sorrow, these men, “who hate you, have gloried in the midst of your solemnity” [Col. 0444A], that is, in the midst of your temple, in which your solemnity used to be celebrated.

“They also set up their signs,” that is, their eagles, the “signs” of their victory, “and they did not understand” the truth—namely, that this victory came from you—but attributed it to themselves. “They set up,” I say, “as” signs are accustomed to be set up “on the summit,” that is, above the doors of houses or temples, “at the exit,” that is, at the crossroads. He refers to the custom by which victors are accustomed to place their signs above a gate or tower.

He heightens their wickedness: they also “cut down its doors,” the doors of the temple, directing themselves “toward the same thing,” that is, toward the same intention of destruction, “as though” they were “in a forest”—not one that was guarded, but one exposed to their will for the cutting of timber—and he says this with reference to “wood.” And they “overthrew,” that is, destroyed, “it,” the city, “with axe and adze.” An adze is an iron tool especially suitable for hewing small carvings.

They also “burned your sanctuary with fire,” that is, your temple, casting down the roofs that had been built high in your honor “to the ground,” so that not one stone remained upon another. They “profaned the dwelling-place of your name,” that is, the temple in which your name had been invoked, by doing many polluted things there.

They also “said in their heart”—and not merely a few of them, but “their whole kindred together” with them—“Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth,” that is [Col. 0444C], let us destroy everything, so that feast-days may no longer be celebrated in this land.

God permitted this destruction to befall us on account of our merits, because we “did not see,” that is, did not understand, “our signs,” that is, the visitation appointed for us, which God made upon us. Here the Synagogue places itself among those who were destroyed, when it says, “we did not see” these “signs,” because “there is now no prophet” among us whom we may consult, as we formerly had. For when the prophets ceased, this was a sign of the coming of the one who was both the end and the fulfillment of the prophets: “and he will no longer know us,” God will no longer visit us through a prophet.

Or the preceding verse may be read in this way, as referring to the guilt of the Jews. Continuation: Although God had bestowed such great benefits upon the Jewish people [Col. 0444D], it will nevertheless not be in keeping with his clemency if he allows them to be destroyed, because the Jews said in their heart—that is, just as they spoke, so they held it in their heart—and not merely a few of them, but indeed their whole kindred together: “Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth,” namely, so that we celebrate no feast for him. Nor ought we to celebrate, since “we did not see our signs” which God had promised us—that is, he did not show us any signs by which we might guard ourselves against enemies, as he used to do—and furthermore, “there is now no prophet” to console us, and so forth in the same manner.

They sinned in this way; but, O “God, how long” will you allow them to remain in their sins? This is expressed by: [Col. 0445A] “How long will the enemy reproach” you—that is, the Jewish people—and how long will “the adversary,” that is, the Jewish people, “provoke” you to anger, “your name,” that is, you who can be named? Will this continue “to the end,” that is, completely? Or “to the end” of the age, when the remnant of the Jews will be saved.

And “why,” O Lord, “do you turn away your hand” from them, that is, your work by which you might convert them to yourself? Another translation has “your face.” And “why do you turn away your right hand,” that is, the Jewish people, who are therefore called the Lord’s right hand because through them God performed many miracles—as through David he slew Goliath, and so forth—“from the midst of your bosom,” that is, from the abundance of your mercy, because one who is removed from God is not in God’s mercy. Will this continue “to the end”? It will indeed continue to the end, when the Jews are converted to Christ and received into God’s bosom.

This was prefigured in Moses, who drew his hand out of his bosom and found it leprous; when he placed it back into his bosom, it was clean. This has been fulfilled in the Jewish people: when they were removed from God’s bosom, that is, from Christ, they became leprous through sins; but when they turn to Christ, they will be cleansed from the leprosy of sins.

“But God.” The second part. God now turns away his hand; yet he himself, “God our king,” existing “before the ages, worked salvation,” that is, deliverance, both before Christ’s coming and in Christ’s coming itself, “in the midst of the earth,” that is, publicly, for all human beings [Col. 0445C].

“You established.” I say that you “worked salvation,” because you, God, “established the sea,” the Red Sea, by making it dry for the passing people and making it like a wall on every side; and you did this “by your power,” that is, with all your might. Having set forth the figure, he gives its meaning when he says: “You crushed the heads of dragons,” that is, the powers and exaltations of demons, “in the waters” of baptism, because through the waters of baptism a human being emerges from the devil’s power.

And you also “crushed the heads of the dragon” above, and “to the peoples of the Ethiopians,” that is, to those who had previously been black through sins, “you gave him”—the devil—as “food,” that is, refreshment, because when his members are taken away from the devil, they are refreshed by incorporating them into himself; or they are refreshed by the tribulations which the devil inflicts upon them [Col. 0445D].

He also shows other salvations which God accomplished in the world when he says: “You also split open springs,” that is, if some spring obstructed their path, you divided it so that they might pass through easily; “and torrents,” that is, if some rushing water obstructed their passage, you “split” it into very small streams. You also “dried up the rivers of Ethan” of that land, such as the Jordan, which they crossed with dry feet.

“Ethan” is interpreted as “strong,” by which the devil is understood. We may also understand this allegorically: the springs and torrents of “Ethan,” that is, the floods of vices [Col. 0446A] which the devil sends, God breaks apart when he lightens sins; and if he does not forgive them completely, then he dries up “the rivers of Ethan,” that is, the flooding of vices, when he completely forgives sins.

Or, “you split open springs” when in the desert you brought water out of the rock, and torrents, such as that water which followed them through the desert. Or we may understand these springs and torrents as preachers, who refreshed the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel; and through these preachers “you dried up the rivers of Ethan,” the flood of sins which the devil was sending.

“Yours is the day, and so forth.” The whole passage is to be taken literally. Allegorically, however, by “day” we understand the wise person who has been illuminated by knowledge of God. By “night” the sinner is understood, who is in darkness through ignorance of the true good; yet he is God’s, because God converts him to himself.

“You fashioned the dawn,” that is, the beginning of conversion, namely, those who are newly converted; “and the sun,” that is, the most perfect wise people, who are able to illuminate others.

You also “made all the boundaries of the earth,” that is, those who make themselves boundaries and defenders of the Church against the devil and his ministers, such as holy bishops and other good shepherds; “summer,” that is, those who are most fervent, such as martyrs; and “spring” also you made, that is, the temperate, such as good confessors. And “you fashioned them,” that is, you were their beginning, because no one among them accomplished anything except you alone. Fashioning is the first creation.

[Col. 0446C] “Remember.” And you, God, who performed these wonders, “remember this,” that is, the conversion of the Jews. He says “this” without qualification; another translation has “this work.” And it is necessary that you “remember,” because “the enemy,” that is, that Jewish people, “reproached,” that is, spoke reproaches against, “the Lord,” and did this through foolishness. This is expressed by: “and the foolish people provoked” “your name,” that is, provoked you, who are nameable, to anger (sic).
