When he says that they sinned through foolishness, he excuses them and shows them worthy of compassion.

“Do not hand over.” The third part. The hostile people thus reproached the Lord; but, O Lord, whatever you do with others, “do not hand over to beasts,” that is, to the devil and his ministers, “the soul that confesses,” and “do not forget the souls of your poor” [Col. 0446D], “to the end,” that is, completely, when you reward them, because those who confess are poor, and therefore you ought to reward them.

For this reason you ought not to forget them, because you promised mercy to those who confess you. This is expressed by: “Look upon your covenant,” that is, the holy Gospel. It is necessary that you regard the promises, because you will not act on account of their merits, “because those who are darkened are filled” with iniquity, that is, they have been blinded by the use of reason, “by the houses of the earth,” that is, by bodily habitation. This excuses them for their blindness.

And, O Lord, “let not the humble person,” who supplicates you, “be turned away,” “made ashamed” if you remove him from yourself. Nor ought you to remove such people from yourself, because “the poor” and truly “needy” person, who presumes nothing of himself but attributes everything to God—that is, the humble person—such people “will praise your name.”

And for this reason you ought to rise; also because your cause is at stake. This is expressed by: O “God,” who until now seemed to have slept while allowing the unconverted Jews to persist, now “arise, judge your cause.” God’s cause is at stake when the Jews reproach God. He will judge it to his own advantage if he makes those who blaspheme into praisers.

“Judge,” I say, “your cause,” namely, “remember the reproaches” that are directed against you by the Jews. They do this, indeed, through foolishness. He adds: “their reproaches,” I say, “which are” directed toward you “all day long by the foolish” people [Col. 0447B].

And “do not forget the voices of your enemies,” that is, the voices and prayers which those who were once your enemies pour out to you. Another translation has “of those seeking you.” He ought not to forget them, both because these enemies, having become friends, cry out to you, and also because your enemies, namely the Romans, act arrogantly against them. This is expressed by: “the pride of those who hate you has continually risen,” increasing more and more.

## PSALM LXXIV

### Title

“To the end: Do not corrupt; a psalm of song of Asaph.”

[Col. 0447C] “We will give thanks.” This psalm is a song of Asaph, that is, of the faithful Synagogue, which speaks in this psalm, admonishing: “Do not corrupt,” that is, if you possess faith or any good thing, do not corrupt it; and through this directing us “to the end,” that is, to Christ.

It is called a psalm of song because it proposes to us great exultation: it introduces Christ as judge, condemning the wicked and rewarding the just. There he says, “and I will break all the horns of sinners,” and so forth. Its subject is Christ and the human being, the judge of all.

Its manner is as follows: in the first part the Synagogue speaks to him, showing him to be one to whom every form of religion ought to be offered. In the second part Christ is introduced speaking and answering the Synagogue; in his words we can understand him as God and man, the judge of all. This second part begins immediately where he says: “When I receive the time.” The intention is to admonish: “Do not corrupt.”

And the Synagogue says: O “God, we will give thanks to you” for our sins. And because it considered itself secure in remaining in confession, it repeats: “We will give thanks,” perseveringly, “and” after confession “we will invoke your name,” so that you may release us from sins and dwell in us. It proceeds in proper order, because one who does not invoke cannot worthily narrate.

And after we have invoked you, “we will recount your wonders,” namely, those concerning the creation of the world and the restoration of the human race. Here too it proceeds in proper order, because one who does not invoke cannot worthily narrate.

Hence it is said: “Praise is not comely in the mouth of a sinner.” In these words of the Synagogue, every form of religion is indicated.

“When I receive the time.” The second part. Thus Christ answered the Synagogue as it invoked him: You say, “We will give thanks,” and certainly for your benefit, namely, when I receive the time, that is, the opportunity to judge, “I will judge justices,” rendering to you according to your merit, and likewise to others.

I say “when I receive the time,” because it is necessary that I delay, since human beings are corrupt, and those who are foreknown must be prepared through mercy. He shows the corruption of human beings by saying: “The earth has melted,” that is, the element itself has melted and [Col. 0448B] become corrupt; and “all who dwell in it” have melted and become corrupt through sins, because, in accordance with the corruption of human beings, the elements themselves, which serve them, are corrupted.

The earth was more fertile and the air healthier in the time of the earlier fathers, as can be demonstrated from the length of their lives. Human beings, then, have melted, but “I,” through the mercy of God, “established its pillars,” that is, the holy apostles, who are the support of the whole Church. Through them many will be acquired who will be worthy of reward at the judgment.

“I established the pillars,” and through them “I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly”; and to those who transgress against my commands I said: “Do not exalt the horn,” that is, do not excuse yourselves for your sins. For the “horn,” that is, pride, exalts the person who considers and judges himself excusable for his sin.

And “do not lift up your horn,” that is, your excuse, “on high,” that is, against God, so that you say that you are sinners through the fault of the Creator, who did not create you as such. And what he means by “lifting up the horn on high” he explains when he says: “Do not speak iniquity against God.”

“Do not,” I say, for he himself knows whatever you do, because he is absent from no place. This is expressed by: “for” he is absent “neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the deserted mountains” [Col. 0448D], literally.

Or allegorically by the east we may understand the wise and eminent men, for whom the sun of justice rises; by the west, sinners, for whom that same sun sets; and by the deserted mountains, heretics, who present themselves as mountains yet are removed and deserted from the truth. Therefore he says that he is absent from no one, “for God is judge”: the one of whom I speak is God, and because he is God, he is everywhere.

And because he is “judge,” and just—where he expressly says “judge,” he understands a just judge—therefore he “humbles this one,” the proud person, both in this life and finally in the next; and “this one,” that is, the humble person, he “exalts,” multiplying him in virtues, and finally in the next life he will truly exalt him when he crowns him forever. He can exalt and humble, “because in the hand” of that “Lord is a cup,” namely, divine Scripture, from which many drink as from a cup.

A “cup,” I say, “of unmixed wine” [Col. 0449A], that is, of pure meaning, namely, spiritual understanding. A “cup,” I say, “full of mixture,” that is, containing a mixture, because it contains both the New and the Old Testament; and in both Testaments the understanding is sincere, pure, and spiritual.

And he “inclined this cup,” that is, by his mercy he made it intelligible, “from this” vessel “into this” other vessel. He says “this” by analogy, namely, from the Jewish people into the gentile people, for he gave his law to the Jews before giving it to the gentiles.

And although he had thus inclined it, the cup was not emptied. This is expressed by: “Nevertheless, its dregs,” that is, the remnants of that cup, “were not emptied,” because neither can it be drained down to its remnants, nor can the remnants themselves be exhausted; for however much they draw from divine Scripture, the spiritual understanding itself has no less.

By “dregs” he does not mean anything turbid, but rather the remnants alone, as some unmixed wine sometimes remains in a cup. And it has not been emptied to such a degree that “all the sinners of the earth drink from it,” that is, some people of every kind of sinners are refreshed by it: both Jews, who will drink at the end, and gentiles, who are now drinking.

Or “its dregs,” that is, of the law, namely its carnal observances, which are called “dregs” in comparison with the New Testament, have not been completely emptied, because the Jews still observe them. This is expressed by: “They have not been emptied.” And although now they “have not been” emptied, nevertheless “whoever” drinks “that law spiritually”—“all the sinners of the earth,” namely both Jews and gentiles—will drink.

Or we may understand the cup as divine judgment, so that we say: I rightly say, “He humbles this one and exalts this one,” because “in the hand,” that is, in the power, of that Lord is “the cup,” that is, divine judgment. It is called a “cup” because God pours out from it upon each person according to merit, just as drink is poured from a cup.

A “cup,” I say, “of unmixed wine,” that is, from which unmixed wine is poured: justice for the holy in this life and finally eternal glory. That cup is also “full” of “mixture,” that is, of the punishment with which the wicked will be made to drink. Just as the reward of the good is contained in that cup, so too is the condemnation of the wicked.

And he “inclined that cup from this into this,” because through that cup he pours good things upon the good and evil things upon the evil. Although he pours from it for everyone, nevertheless “its dregs,” that is, punishment, “have not been emptied,” that is, have never been exhausted; rather, “all the sinners of the earth will drink” them, that is, they will be punished forever [Col. 0449D].

They will drink from it, “but I will announce”—that is, I will rejoice, as another translation has—“forever,” that is, for as long as the age endures. And I will also “sing” in voice and deed “to the God of Jacob.”

And “after” I have done all these things, coming to judgment, “I will break all the horns of sinners,” and I will give horns to the just, who now have none; “and the horns of the just will be exalted” with ineffable glory.

When he says, “I will receive the time,” and “I established its pillars,” he shows himself to be human. When he says, “for God is judge,” he shows himself to be God and judge.

## PSALM LXXV

### Title

“To the end, with songs; a song directed to the Assyrians. A psalm of Asaph.”

“God is known in Judaea.” This is “a psalm of Asaph,” that is, of the faithful Synagogue, composed in songs, that is, in praises of God. For it proposes great praises of God to us when it says that he is known in Judaea and that he illuminates the good, where it says: “You illuminate wonderfully,” and blinds the wicked, where it says: “All the foolish in heart were troubled, and they slept their sleep.” His principal reason for praise appears there, where it says: “to save all the meek of the earth.”

This psalm is a “song” because, as has been said, it proposes to us a matter for exultation, namely the one we mentioned, “in songs.” A “song,” I say, “directed to the Assyrians,” that is, to the proud Jews. For “Assyrians” is interpreted as “directing,” and through the Assyrians the Lord chastised his people on account of their sin. These Assyrians therefore rightly signify the Jews, because these Jews too were proud of their law and persecuted the Church of Christ.

The faithful Synagogue exhorts such Jews to rejoice with it in this name, that they are called Jews, and to confess Christ, because no one can be a Jew except one in whom Christ dwells.

Or by the Assyrians, who are interpreted as “directing,” we may understand good Jews, who direct themselves toward God, according to the interpretation; and the faithful Synagogue admonishes these to persevere in love of Christ.

The subject is Christ himself. Its manner is as follows: in the first part it shows in whom Christ dwells and that from his dwelling he removes every power of the enemy, when it says: “There he broke the powers,” and so forth. In the second part, which begins, “You illuminating wonderfully,” it shows that in this life he illuminates the good and blinds the wicked, and that finally, at the judgment, he will condemn the wicked and save the good. In the third part, which begins, “For the thought of man will give thanks to you,” it shows that he is worthy to whom alone a feast should be made, and it admonishes us to make a feast for him. This is its intention.

And thus, admonishing those Jews, the Synagogue says: O you Jews, “God is known in Judaea,” that is, by all who confess Christ born from the tribe of Judah. Those to whom God is not “known” ought not to be called Jews [Col. 0450D]. All the kings of Judaea, except Saul, were from the tribe of Judah.

“And his name is great in Israel,” that is, among those who see him, because the more they investigate him, the greater he is for them. And you can know this, O you carnal Jews: if his name is not great among you—that is, if you do not honor Christ—you will not be Israel.

Or if this is said to good Jews, it may be expressed thus: Since “God is known among” the Jews, and “his name is great in Israel,” therefore you good Jews should persevere so that he may dwell in you and his name may grow in you.

“And his place was made” where he lies down “in peace,” that is, in those who cease from vices and do good. Another translation has “in Salem”; but here the translator has placed the thing signified in place of the signifier [Col. 0451A].

“And in Zion,” that is, in those who contemplate God, “is his dwelling,” in those among whom he finds no occasion of offense. Therefore, you Jews, make yourselves contemplators, so that God may dwell in you.

“There,” that is, in Zion, that is, in those who contemplate him, God “broke,” that is, destroyed, “the powers” of the devil. He enumerates them individually, saying: “the bow,” that is, hidden aggression; “the shield,” that is, the defense of iniquity; and “the sword,” that is, open aggression. And to include everything he says “war,” that is, every form of attack.

God thus broke these vices in his own people just as, historically, he broke the powers of the Amorites and Jebusites in order to lead his people into the promised land.

[Col. 0451B] “Illuminating.” The second part. Continuation: I say that you broke the “powers,” and you were indeed able to do good, because you, O God, “illuminate” your faithful with knowledge of the true good “from the everlasting mountains,” that is, through the apostles, who are called everlasting because their life remains forever.

You illuminate, I say, “wonderfully,” that is, through miracles. Or “wonderfully,” because even if knowledge of God comes without miracles, it is nevertheless wonderful: the more God is known from the beginning, the more powerful he is understood to be.

Or, if the text has “illuminating,” the construction continues until “you are terrible”; and when you illuminate, “all the foolish in heart” are troubled—not the good, but the seekers of the world.

And they “slept,” that is, rested in the joys of this world, thinking these temporal things to be good [Col. 0451C]. And because they could sleep and immediately awaken, he adds “their sleep,” that is, continuously. And just as a person awakening finds none of the riches he possessed in the dream, so “all the men of riches” found nothing in their hands.

By “riches” we understand not only the riches ordinarily so called, but every carnal desire. They “found nothing in their hands,” that is, in their power, although previously they thought those riches would always suffice and that they possessed them securely.

Here he shows them excusable from “reproof.” Continuation: I say that they “slept,” and, O “God of Jacob, at your reproof,” that is, while you reproved them through your preachers, “they dozed,” that is, they frequently slept. For when you terrified them and they saw various and unusual miracles, they were then shaken; but when these ceased, they slept again.

“They dozed,” I say, “because they mounted horses,” that is, those who roam widely through the desires of the world. Here he refers us to the historical sense: when Moses performed miracles before Pharaoh, Pharaoh said that he would quickly release the children of Israel; but when the miracles ceased and the people began to depart, he mounted horses and pursued God’s people.

And you, who do these things in this life, “are terrible” to be feared by the wicked in the judgment, “and then who will resist you?” No one, certainly. “From that time your anger” will appear, because those whom in this life you defer punishing through mercy, and invite to repentance, you will then punish severely.

[Col. 0452A] I rightly say, “your anger,” because you “made”—that is, you will make—“your judgment heard from heaven” throughout the whole world, when there is a voice in the trumpet of God and in the voice of the archangel.

The Prophet announces this in the past tense because he had already seen in God’s counsel that it was accomplished. And “the earth trembled,” that is, the earthly people will tremble, “and was still,” that is, will be still, because it will then have no power at all.

“Its trembled,” I say, “when God rises in judgment,” and he will not rise only to condemn the wicked, but also “to save all the meek of the earth.”

“For the thought of man will give thanks to you.” The third part. Continuation: Since God does all these things, therefore you must “make vows to the Lord your God, and fulfill them.” He says “make vows” because there are certain things that would not be necessary to do unless they were vowed, such as abstaining from a wife, from meat, and so forth. Therefore people must be enticed to make vows.

“Make vows,” I say, not to someone else, but let all who are “around him,” that is, existing in his service, “bring gifts” of justice and equity, and so forth. Another text has: “Those who are around him will bring gifts.” Continuation: Therefore you ought to make vows and fulfill them, because all who are around him will bring gifts.

He shows what we ought to vow and fulfill through the cause stated above. Continuation: You ought rightly to make vows and fulfill them, “because to you,” O Lord, “the thought of man will give thanks,” and “the remnants of thought,” that is, the works that remain after thought, “will keep a feast-day for you,” that is, they show you to be worthy of praise.

To celebrate a feast is to cease from evil works and offer due praises to God. Hence Augustine says: “He keeps the sabbaths badly who is idle from good works.” Or “the remnants of thought” means the recollections that a person always has concerning sins. Since this is so, therefore make vows, and so forth.

To make a vow is a counsel; to fulfill vows, however, is a command, as is proved by the authority of Moses: “What has once gone forth from your lips, you shall observe, and you shall do as you promised the Lord your God.”

“Make vows,” I say, to the Lord your God, and to the Lord, I say, “who is terrible, and who takes away the spirit of princes,” that is, their life, literally. For this reason he says “terrible among the kings of the earth,” that is, among all those who rule their earthly nature well.

## PSALM LXXVI

### Title

“To the end; for Idithun; a psalm of Asaph.”

“With my voice I cried to the Lord.” This psalm is of Asaph, that is, of the faithful Synagogue, which here speaks like David or someone from that earlier people. It is composed “for Idithun,” that is, “for the one who leaps across,” so that, just as the one who leaps across is the speaker, he may make his hearers leap across as well—that is, despising worldly things and clinging to heavenly things. This is its intention.

It is a psalm, I say, directing toward the end. We say that one of the earlier fathers speaks here because the speaker deliberates whether human salvation can come about. No faithful person doubts this concerning those who lived after Christ’s coming [Col. 0453A]. Its subject is the faithful Synagogue itself.

Its manner is as follows: in the first part it shows that it cries to God even in tribulation and that it does not wish to be consoled by temporal things, where it says: “My soul refused to be consoled.” In the second part, which begins, “My eyes anticipated the watches,” it deliberates whether human salvation is possible. In the third part, which begins, “And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High,” it shows that it has found the way of salvation and that salvation itself comes through the Son of God. In the fourth part, which begins, “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and were afraid,” it shows the wonders that God brought forth in the world through the Son.

And thus the faithful Synagogue, presenting itself as an example to others, says: “I cried to the Lord” so that I might obtain him, because he is the Lord. And this was “with my voice” [Col. 0453B], because my deeds do not contradict what I ask with my voice. “With my voice I cried to” God, and it is right to cry to him because he is God, “and he attended to me,” that is, he looked upon me kindly.

And not only at another time, but also in adversity. This is expressed by: “On the day of my tribulation I sought God,” because when the power and prosperity of this life offered themselves to me, I sought God amid everything, “with my hands,” that is, through my works.

“I sought,” I say, “at night,” that is, in this life, which is called night because perfect illumination is not possessed in it. Or “at night,” when others are sleeping; so that my seeking might be “against him,” that is, in his presence. Another translation has “before him.”

“And I was not deceived,” that is, I was not frustrated in my hope, but was taught by experience that God does not abandon his own and grants the rewards of eternal life to the just, nor denies anything to those who ask.

“I sought God,” and I did not wish to be consoled by temporal things, that is, to have consolation in them. This is expressed by: “My soul refused to be consoled,” passively, or “refused to console itself,” namely, in these temporal things.

But I was always “mindful of God, and” in that remembrance “I rejoiced,” perceiving the great goodness of God. “And I was exercised,” so that I might recognize how great his goodness was; and “in this my spirit failed,” because God’s goodness is incomprehensible.

“My eyes anticipated.” The second part. I say that “my spirit failed,” but nevertheless “my eyes,” that is, my inner reason, “anticipated the watches,” that is, were more watchful than others in seeking God’s goodness.

He says this by comparison with some diligent person who keeps vigil more than others and investigates everything more carefully than the rest. And in those vigils “I was troubled,” recognizing that the entire human race is held in sins through the disobedience of the first parent; “and” nevertheless “I did not speak,” that is, I did not murmur against God.

I was troubled for this reason: I “considered the ancient days,” that is, Adam’s sin, which occurred in ancient days. Yet I kept “the eternal years in mind,” because I always remembered what I had heard concerning the eternity promised to human beings.

“And I meditated by night,” that is, during the time of this [Col. 0454A] life, “with my heart,” that is, with my reason. For reason, attending to God’s mercy and to the fact that God made the human being for his praise, indicated that the salvation of the human race was to come; but carnality, seeing the human being decay, denied that restoration would come.

“And I exercised myself” in order to recognize what ought rather to be held; and “so that I might understand better, I swept my spirit,” that is, I cast out from myself all the dross of earthly existence. For to sweep is to cleanse.

Or “I swept” means the same as what some call “scraped out”—that is, I hollowed out—so that I might be able to understand more deeply concerning God.

“I meditated,” saying thus within myself: “Will God cast off forever” his people, “and will he not add that he may be more favorably disposed still?” He was shown above to have been gracious when he attended to me; he will be more gracious when he restores.

“Or will he cut off his mercy forever,” that is, completely, so that there may be no greater cutting off by which he removes him from good and evil? And will he do this “from generation to generation,” that is, for all time?

“Or will God forget to show mercy?”—he who formerly was accustomed to show mercies to our fathers—“or will he restrain his mercies in his anger,” that is, will his anger prevail over his mercy? I see that he is angry because of sins, yet I recognize him as merciful, and I said:

Third part. I deliberated in this way, “and” in this deliberation of mine “I said: Now I have begun” to understand what should be held concerning this. Or, “I have begun” to have true knowledge of it. [Col. 0454C] Namely, I see a certain change, as in the ram sacrificed by Abraham; I understand that Christ’s humanity was to be sacrificed for human beings. “And this is the change of the right hand of the Most High,” that is, of Christ, who is the right hand of God the Father, through whom he brings about this change, causing us to pass from sin to righteousness and leading us from mortality to immortality.

Through this I understood that change, “because I remembered the works of the Lord,” namely, that he created human beings; and just as I understood that he created them through mercy, so I understood that he would restore the same people through mercy. “I remembered,” because “I will also remember” in the future—or, as another translation has it, all “your wonders”—which you performed in the world “from the beginning,” that is, from the creation of heaven and earth. [Col. 0454D] And because I recognized that you made those things for your praise, I likewise understood that you would save human beings, for unless you saved them, you would have no praise.

And I will not merely “remember,” but “I will also meditate,” that is, diligently inquire, “into all your works,” so that from the other works that were made I may also understand that you will save humanity. “And I will exercise myself in your inventions,” that is, in your commandments, which you devised.

“God is in his holy place.” Here is what he said above: here is “now I have begun.” The continuation is: “I will exercise myself in your inventions.” This invention, indeed, O God, “your way,” by which one comes to you, “is in the holy place,” that is, in Christ. And because he sees that restoration will come through Christ, [Col. 0455A] he commends him with exultation, saying: “Who is a great God like our God?” Foolish gentiles think that their statues, or stones, are gods, but certainly this is nothing, because “you” alone “are God, who performs wonders.” He shows what wonders these are, saying:

“You have made your power known among the peoples,” that is, your Son, in whom your power will appear. And you will not merely make the Son known, but “with your arm,” that is, in the Son himself, “you redeemed your people.” He specifies which people: “the sons of Jacob,” that is, the Jewish people, “and Joseph,” that is, the gentile people. Joseph is understood as representing the gentile people because Joseph lived among the gentiles, namely, in Egypt. Or, allegorically: through “Joseph,” whose name is interpreted as “increasing,” we understand the gentile people, [Col. 0455B] who increased in the worship of God through the Jewish people.

“They saw.” Fourth part. “You redeemed the people” through this: “the waters,” that is, of the Jewish people, “saw you,” that is, they came to know you through the Son. Again, “the waters saw you,” that is, the gentiles, “and were afraid” because of their sins, understanding that you would be the future judge. “And the abysses,” that is, those deeply immersed in sins, “were troubled” and turned away from their purpose.

Then there was “the multitude of the sound of the waters,” that is, the peoples resounded, praising you in many ways for the sending of your Son, and crying out because of their sins. There was a “sound” because “the clouds,” that is, the holy apostles, “gave their voice” of preaching throughout the world.

[Col. 0455C] I rightly say, “the clouds gave their voice,” because, O God, “your arrows,” that is, your judgments piercing human hearts, “pass” from those apostles to human beings. And “the voice of your thunder,” that is, the voice of your threats concerning sins, “is in the wheel,” that is, throughout the circuit of the whole world.

And “your lightnings,” that is, the miracles performed through those same apostles, “shone upon the world.” He rightly said, “they shone upon the world,” because through these many were enlightened and converted to the faith. By the lightnings we can understand the commandments for living. And “by these lightnings the earth was moved,” that is, earthly people were moved to conversion, “and trembled,” practicing repentance for their sins.

[Col. 0455D] And through these apostles, working in this way, “your way is in the sea,” that is, among the gentile people, because through this you also came to the gentile people, and the gentile people came to you. Literally, too, this was fulfilled, because the Lord Jesus walked upon the sea, and caused Peter to walk upon the sea toward him. And “your paths,” that is, your stricter commandments, were also received “in many waters,” that is, among diverse peoples. And although the gentiles thus come to you, nevertheless “your footsteps,” that is, the signs of your righteousness, “will not be recognized” by the Jews.

Yet you performed many miracles for them, because you led “your people like sheep,” not because they themselves were good sheep, but because you were a merciful shepherd to them, “by the hand of Moses and Aaron,” literally. Through Moses [Col. 0456A] we understand every leader, and through Aaron every priest whom he appointed over his people.

## ON PSALM 77. TITLE: The Understanding of Asaph

“Attend, my people.” This psalm is suited to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which speaks here, as does the prophet David, or someone similar. It is called “understanding” because it contains not only a historical meaning, but also an allegorical meaning within the history.

Its subject is the benefits God bestowed upon the former people: freeing them from Egypt and performing the other things he later did for them up to the sending of the Son. Conversely, it concerns the Jews’ ingratitude for God’s benefits and their continual murmuring against God.

[Col. 0456B] The psalm has ten parts. In the first part he sets forth a prologue, in which he makes them attentive to what follows. In the second part, which begins, “How many things we have heard,” he rebukes the hardness of the Jews, who did not receive God’s law, although God had indicated through many benefits that they should receive his law. In the third part, which begins, “Before their fathers he performed,” he enumerates the wonders God performed for his people, leading them out of Egypt through the Red Sea and then through the desert; and in opposition to this he also presents the Jews’ murmuring. In the fourth part, which begins, “Therefore the Lord heard and delayed,” he shows that God, wishing to make known his power, about which they had unbelievingly doubted, fulfilled all their requests. In the fifth part, which begins, “While their food was still,” [Col. 0456C] he shows the vengeance God took upon them because of their hardness and unbelief. In the sixth part, which begins, “And they loved him with their mouth,” he shows that, although the Jews pretended to love God because they feared vengeance, he nevertheless displayed himself as merciful toward them. In the seventh part, which begins, “How often they provoked him in the desert,” he shows that, although they continually tested God, God nevertheless struck the Egyptians in many ways for their deliverance. In the eighth part, which begins, “And he took away his people like sheep and led them,” he shows how kindly God brought them into the promised land; and, in opposition, that the Jews, continually provoking God, continually tested him. [Col. 0456D] In the ninth part, which begins, “God heard and rejected,” he shows the vengeance God took against them in the promised land, and also against their persecutors, the Philistines. In the tenth part, which begins, “And he rejected the tabernacle,” he shows that, in addition to the other benefits, God sent them David as king, namely, the Son of God, who would rule them in innocence and righteousness, born from the tribe of Judah.

After all these things, he intends to admonish all the faithful to receive God’s law and understand it spiritually.

And so, admonishing them, he begins in this way: “My people,” that is, “faithful, like me and resembling me, attend to my law,” so that, just as I have understood the law spiritually and practice it, so you too may practice it. And so that you may be able to understand it, do not be proud, but “incline”—that is, humble—“your ear,” that is, your understanding, “to the words of my mouth.” In this way he especially makes them attentive to what follows.

[Col. 0457A] Therefore you ought to understand, because “I will open my mouth to you,” that is, I will speak many things to you; and this not only historically, but “in parables,” that is, in expressions in which something other than the literal sense is also understood. I also “speak” to you “propositions,” that is, those obscure allegories that can scarcely be understood, such as the divinations called problems—for example, what Samson proposed to the Philistines when he said: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came sweetness.” When they had explained this as referring to the honeycomb that he found in the lion’s mouth (Judg. XVI), he proposed a certain [Col. 0457B] parable in reply: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my proposition,” understanding his wife by “heifer.” I speak of propositions made “from the beginning,” that is, from the time when God began to work manifestly among that people and performed the wonders he performed in Egypt.

“How many.” Second part. Therefore you ought to attend to the propositions that I will speak, because I speak not from my own heart, but of the things that I heard and saw. This is “how many,” that is, how great, how countless, are the things “we have heard and learned” to be true through their very fulfillment, and they ought to be believed. We heard them because “our fathers recounted them to us.” When he says “they recounted,” he shows that the matter being recounted is not fabricated but true; and that narration was not conveyed only in words, but also in writing.

[Col. 0457C] And the things they recounted are known by everyone throughout the whole world. He says this: “They were not hidden from their sons,” that is, from the sons of our fathers; they are manifest to all of us in the Israelite people, “and in another generation,” that is, in the gentile people.

I say that the fathers recounted them, “recounting the praise of the Lord,” that is, every work of God in which God rightly appears worthy of praise, such as the incarnation of the human being and similar things; “and his powers,” that is, those things in which God’s power appeared, such as the division of the Red Sea; “and his wonders,” such as the manna in the desert—things which God not only spoke or promised, but “performed.”

[Col. 0457D] God performed these wonders for them, “and” afterward “he raised up a testimony in Jacob and established a law in Israel.” By the law we understand prohibitions and instructions for living. He also calls the law itself a testimony, insofar as it testifies to the eternal inheritance that God promises us. He properly says “raised up,” because the natural law in us had fallen asleep; to awaken it, God gave the written law, which was in a certain way the same as the natural law. And since God had promised that people many benefits, those who did not receive that law are greatly to be rebuked. In it he “commanded our fathers to make known to their children how many things,” that is, how marvelous things, [Col. 0458A] so that they might make them known to their descendants—not only to the Jews, but also so that “another generation,” namely the gentiles, “might know them.”

“Sons who will be born”: God gave the law so that it might be made known to our descendants. Thus what follows will be fulfilled: “Sons who will be born” from our carnal lineage, such as the holy apostles, “will arise,” that is, they will not acquiesce in temporal things, but will direct their hearts toward the Lord, “and will recount them to their spiritual sons.”

“So that they may place their hope” not in their own righteousness or in carnal observances, but “in God,” and “not forget the works of God,” that is, not be ungrateful for God’s benefits, but through created things and through the benefits done for them understand the Creator himself, “and seek out his commandments.”

[Col. 0458B] They should seek them for this reason: “so that they may not become like their fathers, a perverse and provoking generation.” That generation is called perverse because of its wicked works, such as idolatry and similar things. It is called provoking because, distrusting God’s power, it often tested God.

[Col. 0458C] I rightly call that generation perverse, because that generation was such that it “did not direct its heart,” distorted through faulty understanding, “and its spirit,” that is, its natural reason, “was not faithful with God.” That is, if at some time they were with God by understanding rightly, they withdrew from him as though God were deceiving them. Thus, if at some time they understood the things signified through figures, they drew back and did not entrust their spirit to God.

I rightly say, “that generation did not direct its heart,” because neither did the sons of Ephraim, who were the better ones among that people. He says this: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting” arrows, “turned back on the day of battle.” He speaks by way of comparison: just as someone might bend a bow, shoot arrows, and show himself ready to fight, but then immediately fail in battle, so also the leaders and superiors of that people, when they showed themselves ready for God’s service, saying after seeing the miracles, “Whatever the Lord and his servant Moses command us, we will do,” immediately withdrew from God’s service and worshiped idols. This is a parable. Through the sons of Ephraim, who were the leaders among that people, the leaders of the Church are understood: although they show themselves ready to serve God, nevertheless, because they do not resist the devil’s temptations, they turn back on the day of battle.

[Col. 0458D] They turned back in this way because “they did not keep God’s covenant,” not because the commandment was difficult, but because they did not wish to do so. He says this: “and they did not wish to walk in his law.” Wicked Christians do likewise.

Beyond this, “they forgot his benefits,” such as the refreshment in the desert, “and his wonders, which he showed them,” such as the plagues he showed the Egyptians (Num. II).

“Before.” Third part. Before these people’s fathers, namely Moses and Aaron, he “performed wonders in the land of Egypt.” And, to leave greater certainty, he specifies the place when he says: “in the field of Tanis.” Tanis is a city of Egypt, near which the ten plagues occurred; its name is interpreted as “humble command.”

[Col. 0459A] Allegorically: In Egypt, that is, in the darkness of this life, God performs wonders before our spiritual fathers when, through their ministry, he forgives us our sins and grants us the grace of the Holy Spirit. Or by the wonders let us understand invisible things; he does this for us while we are in the field, that is, on the level ground of this life. I call the field Tanis, that is, the place in which we must live by a humble command.

In Egypt he performed wonders, and, leading them out of Egypt (Exod. XIV), he “divided the sea,” the Red Sea, “and led them” as far as the opposite shore. “And he made the waters” of the sea stand “like a wineskin,” fixed and in no way flowing. Likewise, the water of baptism was divided, because it is salvation for some and death for others. God leads us from Egypt, that is, from unbelief, to the security of the heavenly homeland; [Col. 0459B] and he makes the waters, the waves of this age, stand as though in a wineskin, because he restrains them so that thereafter they cannot dominate us.

“And he led them,” after their departure from the Red Sea, “in the cloud of the day,” which was a source of refreshment for them, “and throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” By the cloud of the day he signifies Christ’s humanity, in which his divinity lay hidden and which grants us refreshment against the incitements of vices. By the column of fire we understand that same flesh of Christ, which illuminated the night—that is, the ignorance of this life—with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

“He split the rock in the desert” (Exod. XVII), “and gave them drink as though from a great abyss,” namely, in that depth of waters they could be more fully refreshed. The rock split in the desert signifies Christ, split open and wounded for us in this world, from whom spiritual and ineffable refreshment proceeded.

[Col. 0459C] I say that “he split the rock, and brought water out of the rock,” in which God’s great power and his ineffable kindness toward us are indicated. “And he led waters down like rivers,” because the stream flowing from the rock followed them through the desert and supplied refreshment. By this water we understand spiritual grace, which, proceeding from Christ, supplied refreshment to God’s people throughout the whole world. The water that flowed from the Lord’s side on the cross signified for us the washing of baptism and also the other spiritual graces by which our sins are washed away.

[Col. 0459D] God bestowed all these benefits upon them, “and” yet they “continued still to sin against him.” They “provoked the Most High to anger” so that he might take vengeance upon them, “in a waterless place,” that is, in the desert, which by nature is without water; this signifies the aridity of their hearts. Wicked Christians likewise, after receiving many benefits from God, provoke him to anger in a waterless place, that is, in the barrenness of their hearts.

They provoked him to anger, and this was not without cause, “but because they tested God in their hearts,” so that “they might ask for foods for their souls,” that is, foods by which they might preserve life. Likewise, wicked Christians, when they test God, ask him for bodily or spiritual foods, such as knowledge and similar things; yet we do not fulfill the good things that we are capable of doing.

[Col. 0460A] He shows how they tested him, saying: “And they spoke wickedly concerning God,” saying, “Can God prepare a table in the desert?” He breaks down the argument that could be brought against them, as though he were saying: Although God gave us water in the desert, he will nevertheless not be able to give us any other refreshment, because it is natural for water to come out of a rock; but to find bread and other refreshment in such a place is difficult.

And he says this: “For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed.”

“Can he,” although he had done this, “also give bread” in this desert, “or prepare a table,” that is, not merely bread but abundant refreshment? And I do not mean for a few people, but “for his people,” that is, for so great a multitude. This is certainly impossible.

[Col. 0460B] Thus some in the Church, although they confess that Christ died for us and acknowledge that the water of baptism is effective for the remission of sins, nevertheless doubt concerning the table, that is, the refreshment of the Lord’s body, not believing that God can feed them with the body and blood of his Son in the desert of this life.

“Therefore.” Fourth part. Thus they tested God; “therefore the Lord heard,” that is, understood, and fulfilled their requests, lest, if he immediately killed them, he should be thought powerless, as they had said. I say that he “heard and delayed” inflicting punishment upon them, so that he might first show his power by fulfilling their requests. “And fire,” that is, God’s anger, “was kindled against Jacob,” the carnal people, that is, the lesser ones; “and God’s anger,” that is, vengeance, “rose up” and was multiplied “against Israel,” that is, against the leaders of the Jews.

[Col. 0460C] Or in this way: God heard those Jews and delayed their punishment; and for this reason the fire of love was kindled against Jacob, that is, against the supplanting people, namely the gentile people, because blindness happened in Israel so that the fullness of the gentiles might enter.

I say that fire was kindled in the gentile people, and anger rose against Israel, that is, against the Jews, because “they did not believe in God, nor did they hope in his salvation,” that is, in his act of saving—the one who had led them through the sea, supplied them with water for refreshment, and was able to prepare a table.

[Col. 0460D] “And he commanded.” He shows how God fulfilled their requests. I say that the Lord heard them, “and” therefore “he commanded the clouds above,” that is, he commanded the upper air to rain food for them; and the Lord himself “opened the doors of heaven,” that is, the floodgates of heaven, namely, the heavenly channels through which the heavenly rain descended to them.

“And he rained manna upon them for food,” that is, for them to eat; and he determines what he calls manna by saying: “and he gave them the bread of heaven.”

Then “human beings ate the bread of angels.” When he calls that manna the bread of angels, he gives the name of the signified thing to the sign. For Christ, who is signified by the manna, is called the bread and every kind of refreshment of the angels according to his divinity.

[Col. 0461A] Allegorically, although many do not believe rightly concerning God or hope in his salvation, namely in Christ Jesus, God nevertheless commands the clouds above—that is, God opens the doors of heaven, the divine Scripture, to the supreme preachers. Through those preachers God rains manna upon them, that is, he shows and makes his Son known to them, whom he properly calls the bread of angels. And this bread, namely the Lord’s body and blood, human beings truly eat. In addition to the manna, God “sent them” other “foods,” and he did not do so sparingly, but “in abundance.”

See how he sent them: “he transferred the south wind,” that is, that wind, “from heaven,” that is, from the upper air, so that it would not blow above but near the ground; “and he brought in the southwest wind,” the other wind beside the south wind, “by his power.”

[Col. 0461B] “And through these winds he rained flesh upon them.” He shows what foods he sent them: flesh “like dust,” that is, with as great an abundance as dust possesses; and he specifies what flesh, namely “winged birds,” not dead but “feathered,” and in such infinite quantity “as the sand of the sea.”

Through the south and southwest winds, which are hot winds, we can understand holy preachers, warmed by the fervor of love. Through them God rains flesh upon us, that is, those refreshments of the soul that refresh the soul as fully as flesh refreshes the body, such as wisdom and prudence, which he compares to dust because of the subtlety of their thoughts. For this reason he calls them winged and feathered: they lift human beings from earthly things to heavenly things. He compares them to sand because they are as abundant as sand. By the sea, which is salty, we understand the seasoning of true flavor. When he says that he transferred them from heaven, we understand that God transfers his preachers from the contemplative life to the active life, so that they may care for others.

[Col. 0461C] God rained birds upon them, “and” they “fell in the midst of their camp,” that is, around their tents, “so that they could take them without any labor.”

“And” they “ate and were filled exceedingly,” that is, greatly, or with excess; “and” thus “he brought their desire to them.” “They were not deprived of their desire.”

Likewise, in our tents, that is, in our churches, and around them, that is, in neighboring places, we can find whatever teaching is necessary for us, by which we may refresh our souls, eat, and be filled exceedingly. For some grow proud of their knowledge and of other spiritual gifts, and we are not deprived of our desires.

[Col. 0461D] Fifth part. “While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them.”

“And he killed their fat ones,” that is, the proud among that people, “and” for this reason “he hindered,” that is, saddened, “the chosen of Israel,” such as Moses and his companions. Likewise, while we still have the Lord’s body as though in our mouths, God’s anger rises against us and kills the fat ones, that is, the proud and those who receive the Lord’s body unworthily; he strikes them with blindness of mind. Or, while we have been greatly refreshed by wisdom, because we grow proud on account of it, the Lord kills us inwardly; and the chosen of Israel, that is, our men and leaders, are saddened in the Church.

“In all these things,” that is, amid all these acts of vengeance, [Col. 0462A] “they sinned” again, those whose hearts were obstinate, “and they did not believe in his wonders.”

And therefore “their days,” with regard to those who did not live long, “failed,” having been spent in vanity; and “their years,” with regard to those who lived longer, “failed with haste.” Likewise, when we recognize that others are punished for their sins, we are not corrected, but, obstinate in sins, we fail and incur the deserved punishment.

And “when” he “killed them in this way, they sought him; and they returned, and at dawn,” that is, earnestly, “they came to him.”

“And they remembered that God was their helper, and that the Most High God was their redeemer.” Likewise, because of fear, we sometimes seek God.

[Col. 0462B] Sixth part. “And they loved him with their mouth,” that is, they had become well accustomed to lying, “and with their tongue they lied to him,” because they did not love him in their hearts as they professed with their mouths.

They loved him with their mouths, “but their heart was not right with him,” because they pretended to love God not for God’s sake, but out of fear of punishments. “Nor were they considered faithful to his covenant,” so as to observe his law, as they promised in fear.

“But he is merciful” by nature, “and” even contrary to their merits “he will be gracious toward their sins,” and therefore “he will not destroy,” that is, he will not utterly destroy, “them.”

[Col. 0462C] And that great mercy of God “abounded,” so that he “turned away” from them “his anger,” that is, the vengeance he had begun to take against them, “and did not kindle all his anger,” so as to exact from them the entire punishment they deserved.

“And he remembered,” as though he had forgotten while afflicting them, “that they are flesh,” namely, carnal and fragile, inclined to sin. This is the greatest reason that moves God to show himself merciful toward us. Conversely, the wicked angels remain unredeemed for this reason: no aspect of their nature—which was indeed perfect—but only their proud will impelled them to sin.

He also remembered that “the spirit is departing and not returning,” namely, that human beings are mortal. Or, “a departing spirit” means one that withdraws from God by itself and does not return to God by itself; therefore it is necessary for God to extend his hand to a human being and lead him back.

Likewise, although we love God with a deceitful heart, God patiently sustains us and continually shows himself merciful toward us.

[Col. 0462D] “How often.” Seventh part. The Lord was always so merciful toward them, but nevertheless they “provoked him,” that is, they deserved that he should be harsh and deny them every good thing, “in the desert.” By the desert place is also understood their heart, deserted of every true illumination. This happened “how often”—as though without number—and they also “incited him to anger,” that is, so that he might justly inflict punishment upon them, and they did so “in a waterless place.”

“And they turned” from the good understanding they had once had [Col. 0463A] concerning God, terrified by the signs or plagues they had seen, “and tested God,” distrusting the power of the Almighty, “and provoked the Holy One of Israel,” that is, the one who sanctifies Israel. Their great folly is condemned in this.

“They did not remember his hand,” that is, his work displayed for them “on the day when he redeemed them,” that is, liberated them, “from the hand of the one who afflicted,” namely Pharaoh.

So too we, perverse and turned away from true understanding in the desert of this life, often incite God to anger, forgetting among his other benefits that he redeemed us from the power of the one who afflicted us, namely the devil. And note that in allegory we do not attend to continuous connections, but only to the meanings of the necessary words.

[Col. 0463B] “As he set,” I say, they did not remember: “As he set his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the field of Tanis.” By signs we understand lesser miracles; by wonders, greater ones. Or the two terms may mean the same thing, but in this interpretation a sign of God is that which indicates his power, while a wonder is that which enables us to understand something else through itself. Likewise, in this Egypt of ours, while we must live in the field of Tanis, that is, under a humble command, he shows us many signs and indications of his will.

[Col. 0463C] “And he turned.” He begins to enumerate the plagues that the Lord inflicted upon the Egyptians for their sake. Although he does not list precisely the same plagues as Moses, he nevertheless lists ten, as Moses himself did. And in opposition to the ten plagues of Egypt, Augustine sets forth the ten commandments of the law that God gave to his people; by the number ten we understand all the punishments of enemies and all the instructions of the righteous.

He set signs in Egypt, and these are the signs: “He turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they would not drink.” He calls “rainwaters” the water collected from rainfall in cisterns. By the rivers we understand the deeper Scriptures, such as the Gospel; by the rainwater, the lower teachings, such as Augustine’s sermons. These are turned into blood when they are drawn into a carnal understanding, which offers death to those who drink it.

He also “sent among them the dog-fly,” that is, a canine fly, “and” that dog-fly “devoured them,” because it bit them severely, “and the frog, and it destroyed them,” because they could not remain stable anywhere on account of the frogs. By the dog-fly we understand wickedness, which continually disturbs a human being. By the frog loquacity is signified; those who attend to it are scattered away from the truth. Thus two plagues are noted in this verse.

“[Col. 0463D] “And he gave their fruits to rust.”” By the trees, and by rust—which is a harmful air or mist that secretly corrupts the crops—we understand pride, which secretly corrupts good morals when a person considers himself to be something, though he is nothing (Gal. VI). “And” he gave “their labors” as though in the fields “to locusts” that gnaw them away. By this we understand detraction, which, gnawing away at good labors, annihilates them. The locust, an unstable creature, may also signify the instability of the wicked, who believe for a time but withdraw in the time of temptation. This verse too contains two plagues.

[Col. 0464A] “And he killed their vines with hail.” By the vines we understand gatherings of people, who, in the hail—that is, in the change effected by God—are not brought to life but crushed and killed. “And their mulberry trees with frost.” Frost is a certain fragility that anticipates someone’s good intention. For example, if someone proposes to live according to a rule and chastely, he may be anticipated by the evil habit of love for nuns, through which the fruit of his good intention is brought forward prematurely and scorched. This verse also contains two plagues.

[Col. 0464B] “And he handed their cattle over to hail, and their possessions,” such as houses and similar things, he handed “over to fire.” By the cattle foolish people are understood, those upon whom God’s change falls like hail. By the fire we understand the heat of desire, by which every possession of good work is consumed. Two plagues are contained here as well.

Note that where Moses in Exodus (chap. IX) placed three plagues—namely gnats, sores from flies, and darkness—the Prophet places rust, frost, and fire, not lightning, but fire that would burn all their possessions.

[Col. 0464C] “He sent . . .” He wishes to add a more severe punishment, namely the striking of the firstborn. He first introduces a certain threat of this punishment, as though he were saying: God inflicted these evils mentioned above upon them, and in addition to these “he sent among them the anger of his indignation,” not correction, but an anger proceeding from God’s indignation—namely, the hardening of the heart, which would not release God’s people.

After this anger he sent among them “indignation,” so that they would disdain one another; “and anger,” so that they would be angry with one another; “and tribulation,” through whatever other sins by which they would be afflicted inwardly. All these things, I say, were “sendings” made “through evil angels,” namely, through the ministry of demons.

In the same way, because we provoke God to indignation, he sends anger upon us—that is, indignation, so that we are no longer pricked by remorse for the sins we have committed—and then, by his just judgment, he casts us into worse sins, so that we have indignation, anger, and tribulation among ourselves.

[Col. 0464D] “He made a way.” Through the sending by evil angels he made “a path for his anger,” that is, for his vengeance, exercised strictly and as though along a narrow path, when he struck them only inwardly; and “a way,” that is, a broad avenue, when he afflicted all the firstborn with death. Therefore he says, “he did not spare their souls from death, and he enclosed their cattle in death,” counting human beings and cattle as having the same value.

In addition to the cattle, that striking angel “struck every firstborn” of every animal “in the land of Egypt,” and also “the first fruits of all their labor,” such as barley, flax, and similar crops that ripen earlier, “in the tents of Ham.” He calls Egypt the tent of Ham because the sons of Canaan, who was the son of Ham, the son of Noah, began to inhabit Egypt.

[Col. 0465A] Likewise, God makes a way for the path of his anger in us when, by withdrawing grace from lesser sins, he permits us to descend into more serious ones. He also encloses souls in death when he allows us to be hurled down as far as contempt for God and holds us in blindness of mind. He encloses the cattle in death when he permits all chastity in us to perish. Or by cattle are understood the foolish, who are struck by God along with the crafty.

The firstborn are struck in us—faith and similar things—if we remain in Egypt, that is, in the darkness of this life. The first fruits of labor are struck when charity, which is the greatest among the virtues, or other principal virtues, perish in us. This will happen if we are found in the tents of Ham, that is, of the devil. Ham is interpreted as “cunning,” by which the devil is understood. Or “the descent of Ham” signifies the world, whose lovers continually descend into the depths of vices.

[Col. 0465B] “And he took away.” Eighth part. God inflicted these plagues upon the Egyptians and “took away his people,” namely the Jews, “from the land of Egypt like sheep”—not because they themselves made themselves sheep, but because he led them as kindly as a good shepherd leads sheep—“and led them like a flock in the desert.”

“And he led them” through the wilderness “in hope” of the promised inheritance, “and they did not fear” any of their enemies who might take away the promised homeland, “and the sea covered their enemies.” So also he leads us through the wilderness of this life like sheep, takes us from the hand of the enemy, and leads us in hope of the eternal homeland; [Col. 0465C] nor do we fear that any of our enemies can impede our journey. And he drowns our enemies—namely, sins—in the sea, that is, in the waters of baptism.

“And he brought them into the mountain of his holiness,” namely, Zion, which was sanctified by their ceremonies; “the mountain,” I say, “which their sword did not acquire,” but “his right hand,” that is, his power.

“And he cast out the nations from before them,” who had previously occupied that land, “and by lot divided the land among them,” according to the individual tribes, “by the cord of distribution,” namely, in equal measure. Thus God brings us into the sanctified mountain of his dwelling, namely, the Church, which his right hand acquired, because this could neither have been accomplished nor continued in any way except by God’s operation. And he cast out the nations from us, namely, vices, so that we should not remain in our former birth; or the nations, namely, demons, who previously possessed us, so that he removes them from before our face and we no longer behold them in ourselves. And he divides the land among us, that is, the Church, in which he makes some priests and others married; and this by lot, that is, not by human judgment but by God’s election alone; and this by the cord of distribution, because God has given each person his grace according to measure.

He cast out the nations, “and caused the tribe of Israel to dwell in their tents.” So he makes those who see God dwell already through hope in the place from which the demons fell; or, where vices previously dwelt in us, he caused virtues to dwell.

[Col. 0466A] Although God had bestowed so many benefits upon them, they, nevertheless, now dwelling in the promised land, “tempted and provoked God, the Most High, and did not keep his testimonies,” that is, they neglected to fulfill his commandments.

“And they turned away ‘from him,’ and did not keep the covenant” that they had made with the Lord, saying: “Whatever the Lord commands us, we will do”; “and they became like a crooked bow,” that is, they were made like a crooked bow, “as their fathers were.” A crooked bow is one that, when it threatens, strikes nothing; or one that, when it ought to strike the enemy, strikes its master. So we too provoke God and do not keep his law; we do not observe the covenant made in baptism, by which we renounced the devil and his pomps, [Col. 0466B] but become like a crooked bow, promising that we will do well and not fulfilling it; or because, while we prepare evils for others, we pour those evils back upon ourselves.

And “they provoked him to anger on their hills,” on which they worshiped idols, “and with their graven images they provoked him to jealousy,” when they bestowed upon their graven images the honor owed to God. Likewise, on hills—that is, in our pride—we provoke God to anger; and with graven images, when we turn to idolatry, or when we gaze upon and worship money with excessive desire, or when we serve lust or anything of that kind anxiously, as though it were God.

“God heard.” The ninth section. Continuation. Thus they provoked him, and therefore “God heard,” that is, understood, [Col. 0466C] “and despised them; and he reduced Israel to utter nothingness,” although no enemy had been able to resist him. So God despises us and makes us yield to every temptation.

“And” because of their wickedness “he rejected the tabernacle” that was “in Shiloh,” because he permitted the ark, which was in the tabernacle, to be captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel IV), “his tabernacle where he dwelt among human beings,” because God gave answers in the tabernacle. Likewise, he rejects those who serve in the Church, in whom he himself dwelt, if they are in Shiloh, that is, if they live carnally.

“And he handed over”—he shows how he rejected the tabernacle—because “he handed over their strength,” that is, the ark, which was their strength, since whenever it was present they always conquered their enemies; he handed it over “into captivity” [Col. 0466D] to the Philistines, “and their beauty,” that is, the same ark, about which they gloried above all the nations, “into the hand of the enemy,” namely, the same people. Thus, because of our wickedness, he handed over the liberty of our free choice, which is our strength and our glory, into the service of the devil.

“And he shut up his people with the sword,” because he permitted them to be killed by their enemies, “and he despised his inheritance”; likewise, he permits us to be killed by the sword of the devil.

“Their young men fire consumed,” that is, the fury of their enemies; “and their maidens were not lamented,” as custom required. Thus the young men, that is, those strong in the Church, are consumed by the fire of desire, and the maidens [Col. 0467A] in the body are not lamented by the prelates of the Church, because at times they entirely despair of them.

“Their priests,” namely, Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, “fell by the sword” of the Philistines; “and their widows were not mourned.” Likewise, our priests fall by the sword of God’s mouth when they do the opposite of what they announce well; and our actual widows are not mourned by the prelates of the Church, because at times people despair of them. Or by widows we may understand any people in the Church who vow chastity; they are rightly not mourned if, breaking their vow, they turn back to the practice of lust.

“And the Lord was awakened.” He shows how God took vengeance on the persecutors, to whom “God seemed to be sleeping,” like a drunk man, while he permitted his own people to be afflicted in this way. Continuation. Because of their sins he permitted his own people to be afflicted in this way, “and the Lord was awakened, as one sleeping, as a mighty man overcome by wine”; [Col. 0467B] for just as a mighty man, if he has drunk deeply, falls asleep, then awakens and is moved to anger and exercises the greatest fury, so the Lord seemed to exercise great fury when he took such bitter vengeance upon the Philistines.

“And he struck.” He was awakened, “and he struck his enemies,” namely, the people of Ashdod, “in their hindquarters,” because he sent mice upon them to gnaw their anuses; and “he gave them everlasting disgrace.” God strikes his enemies in their hindquarters, that is, in those who will be left behind after this life, because he takes eternal life away from them and gives them everlasting disgrace, since [Col. 0467C] they are thrust into hell.

“And he rejected.” The tenth plague. Continuation: Thus he took vengeance upon his people, “and he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph; and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,” which was the better among Joseph’s sons, to establish it as king over the people.

“But he chose the tribe of Judah” in order to make kings from it, “Mount Zion, which he loved,” in which that king, once established, would build his house.

“And he built his sanctuary,” that is, his tabernacle, “like a unicorn,” that is, powerfully, so that no one could resist it, “on the earth, which he founded for ever.” This cannot be said literally, but is better understood allegorically. Thus in this life God rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, that is, those who have increased in this world without being God’s tabernacle, and the tribe of Ephraim, that is, those who bear fruit in this world. And he chose Judah, that is, those who confess; and Mount Zion, namely, the holy Church. And he built his sanctuary, that is, the Church sanctified for himself with good prelates and other good members, like a unicorn, as above. Or “like a unicorn,” because those who are in the Church resemble unicorns: they resist their attackers courageously and are chaste. This Church he founded to endure for ever. In this way the Jews thought that their land and law had been founded for ever.

He chose the tribe of Judah, “and” from it “he chose David his servant, and took him from the flocks of sheep,” and [Col. 0468A] “received him” as king “from” going “after those that were giving birth,” that is, after the sheep.

He chose him “to pasture Jacob,” that is, so that he might pasture “Jacob his servant, and Israel,” the same people—not merely as a servant, “but as his inheritance. And” David himself “pastured them in the innocence of his heart,” providing them with an example of innocence, “and led them by the understanding of his hands,” that is, by intellectual works, performed with discernment and understanding, in which he would give others an example of working well and honorably.

By David we understand Christ, whom God took from following those that were giving birth, because he assumed him into heaven, when in this world he was making many fruitful for God; or, from the Jewish people, where, while he was making many fruitful, he took him to the Gentile people. For this purpose he chose him to pasture Jacob, that is, the Gentile people, born later and the supplanter of the Jewish people; and to pasture Israel, that is, the Jews themselves, with the same spiritual teaching with which he pastured the Gentiles.

## Psalm LXXVIII

### Title: A psalm of Asaph

“God, the nations have come.” This psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which here speaks of the devastation of Jerusalem that it sees as destined to occur under King Antiochus, in the time of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees VI); and likewise the Prophet understands it as occurring many times in the Church of Christ.

The subject is that people of God. The method is as follows. In the first part he sets forth the evils that that people endured and the pollution of God’s temple carried out by [Col. 0468C] King Antiochus. In the second part, which begins, “How long, Lord, will you be angry for ever?”, he asks vengeance upon the enemies and help for God’s people. In the third part, which begins, “Let the vengeance of the blood of your servants become known among the nations,” he asks that through vengeance God convert the enemies, and that he always possess and defend the children of those who were killed—that is, those who imitate these Jews in defending the truth, who were killed by Antiochus for the truth, such as Eleazar and the seven brothers, who chose to die rather than transgress God’s commandment (2 Maccabees V, VI, VII).

The intention is to invite us to compassion. And, lamenting the devastation of his people and of the faithful Synagogue, he begins as follows:

“O God, the nations,” that is, the Gentiles, namely Antiochus and his followers, “have come into your inheritance,” namely Jerusalem; “they have polluted your holy temple,” because in your temple they caused an idol to be worshiped, and polluted it with sexual violations and other uncleannesses; and “they have made it a guardhouse for fruit,” because they made it deserted, like the huts that are in orchards or vineyards, which are abandoned once the fruits have been gathered.

And they rage not only against the living but also against the dead; hence, “they have placed the corpses,” that is, unburied bodies, “of your servants as food for the birds of the sky,” and not only for birds, but also “for the beasts of the earth,” namely wolves and dogs. They placed “the flesh” as food—not only, I say, the flesh of servants, but also that “of your saints.”

[Col. 0469A] And they “poured out” their blood, that is, they killed them in great numbers, “like water,” that is, contemptuously, without any regard for mercy; and not only in Jerusalem, but also “around Jerusalem”; “and there was no one to bury them,” because they were either forbidden to do so or were in such great tribulation that no one had leisure for it.

And the Prophet who speaks, or any member of the faithful people, recognizing what had happened to that people and grieving over their evils as over his own loss, places himself among them, saying: “We have become a reproach to our neighbors,” who often reproached us. He shows this in two ways: we have become a reproach, namely, “a mockery,” that is, derision expressed through the nose, “and a scorn,” because they mocked us with many words, [Col. 0469B] and we were like a spectacle to them, “to those who are around us.” Through all these things the Prophet wishes to move God the judge to mercy toward his people. These same evils have likewise been found in the Church.

“How long?” The second section. These evils come upon your people, but “how long, Lord, will you be angry?” That is, how long will you, as though angry, permit your people to be afflicted? Will this continue “for ever,” that is, until the time of grace? And how long will “your zeal,” that is, the indignation displayed on account of their sins, “be kindled” against your own “like fire,” which, so long as it finds material, does not fail? As though to say: tribulation will last as long as there is some sin to be purified. Or God’s zeal is compared with fire because, just as fire consumes soft things and makes hard things stronger and tested, so tribulation consumes the soft and causes them to fail, but makes the tested strong.

Do not, I say, be angry with your people, but “pour out,” that is, send in great abundance, “your anger,” that is, your vengeance, “upon the nations,” that is, upon those Gentiles, “who have not known you,” nor believed that you are God; “and” I do not mean upon the lesser people, but pour it out “upon the kingdoms,” that is, upon the kings, “which have not called upon your name.” Whatever the Jews did, they never denied that you, O Lord, were their God.

Therefore you ought to pour it out, “because they have devoured,” that is, destroyed, “Jacob,” that is, the people of Israel, “and have desolated his place,” that is, the city of Jerusalem; they have made it desolate and devastated. Or they have devoured Jacob, that is, transferred some of them into their own body.

Pour out your anger upon them and have mercy on us. He says this: “Do not remember our former iniquities,” that is, not only those we have recently committed, but those we received from our first fathers and in which we have become accustomed to live. Do not remember them, that is, do not punish them; but may “your mercies,” that is, the forgiveness of sins and your other acts of mercy, “hasten to meet us,” that is, precede us before we are brought to judgment. Therefore I pray that your mercies hasten to meet us, “because we have become exceedingly poor,” that is, [Col. 0470A] in no way sufficient according to our merits for the reward of eternal life.

But against our inability, “God, help us” to do good works. You ought to do so because you are “our Savior,” that is, the one from whom alone we expect salvation; “and deliver us” from our sins “for the glory of your name,” that is, because by this we shall glorify your name and attribute no praise for it to ourselves.

Just as those Jews asked to be delivered from Antiochus and the other persecutors, so the Church asks not to be overcome at some time by the persecutor: deliver us, I say, “and be favorable to our sins, for your name’s sake,” so that even this persecution which we endure may be the destruction and burning away of our sins. When he says “help,” he indicates that by the liberty of free choice he can do something. “Help,” I say, “lest they perhaps say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’” For the Gentiles thought that the Jews had no God because he was invisible; and, reproaching the Jews, they said that they worshiped clouds and empty things.

The third section. Let them not say this; rather, let the following occur: “Let the vengeance of the blood of your servants that has been poured out become known among the nations,” that is, among the Gentiles, who are properly called nations because they remain as they were born, namely, living in a Gentile manner. Let them understand that God avenges himself in them, and on account of this let them be converted.

I say, let the vengeance become known—and quickly. This is “before our eyes,” so that we may see and understand our vengeance. And “let the groaning of the shackled,” that is, of those Jews who are shackled and held captive [Col. 0470C] by Antiochus and others, “enter into your sight,” so that it may please you to free them all.

“And according to”—whatever may be the case concerning the deliverance of the captive and shackled—“possess the children of those who were killed,” that is, their imitators, who are killed in defense of the truth, so that they may be able to be called defenders of the truth. This you can do well, “according to the greatness of your arm,” so that punishments may not frighten them as much as crowns may encourage them.

Do this for your own people, “and repay our neighbors sevenfold the reproach of theirs, which they reproached you with, O Lord,” when they reproached your people—“sevenfold,” that is, with multiplied vengeance. By “sevenfold” he means that, pierced by that punishment, they may be enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit. Repay it, I say, so that it may be “in their bosom,” [Col. 0470D] that is, in their innermost part, namely, in the soul.

Let that reproach be repaid to them. “But we,” who do not deserve reproach, but rather remain always “your people,” who serve you diligently, “and the sheep of your pasture,” that is, those whom you feed and refresh with spiritual nourishment, namely, teaching, “will confess to you,” that is, praise you, “for ever,” that is, for as long as any age shall exist.

It may also be connected in this way: these evils are inflicted upon us, but nevertheless we shall always confess you. Nor shall we merely confess you; we shall also “announce your praise” to others “from generation to generation,” that is, for as long as any generation shall exist.

## Psalm LXXIX

### Title: For the end; a psalm for those who will be changed; a psalm for the Assyrians; a testimony of Asaph

“You who rule Israel.” This psalm is directed toward the end and is composed for those who will be changed. For it speaks of those who are to be changed, showing that the Church will be spread throughout the whole world. Those who have been changed from Adam into Christ belong to the Church. And so that no one may doubt that this change will occur, it says, “a testimony of Asaph,” that is, the faithful Synagogue, which speaks and sets forth the Church’s expansion.
