The subject is the coming of Christ. The method is as follows. In the first part he asks for the coming of Christ, considering all God’s other benefits useless without him, and also complaining about the delay of his coming. In the second part, which begins, “You brought a vine out of Egypt,” he sets forth the expansion of the Church, which will occur through Christ’s coming, and also the Church’s great humiliation; he speaks through a certain likeness, comparing God to a farmer and the Church to a vineyard. In the third part, which begins, “God of hosts, turn again,” he asks for the completion of the Church, which will take place in the last times, when the fullness of the Gentiles and of the Jews will also be converted.

The intention is to make us certain of the change, which is also noted in the title.

The Prophet, and whoever speaks on behalf of the Synagogue, perceiving that all God’s other benefits are ineffective for our salvation without the coming of the Son, thus begins concerning the Son’s coming:

“O God, who rule Israel” in your commandments, “give ear,” namely, send the one whom you are going to send, [Col. 0471C] without whom nothing benefits us, even if we should do good; “you who also lead” from virtue to virtue “Joseph,” that is, the same Israelite people, “like a sheep, give ear.”

“You who sit above the Cherubim,” that is, above that order of angels whose name is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” God is said to sit and dwell in those in whom there is fullness of knowledge and recognition of God. As though he were saying: You who are now known only to the angels, “manifest yourself,” that is, make yourself known to us through the humanity you have assumed, “before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh,” that is, before the Jews.

He placed these names here because he saw that they were suited to signify something else for us. By Ephraim we understand all in the Church who are fruitful and grow in good works. By Benjamin, whose name is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” we understand all who pursue better things or who are to be placed at the Judge’s right hand. By Manasseh, whose name means “forgetful,” he understands those who forget the things of the world.

I say, manifest yourself in such a way as to “stir up your power,” that is, the strength by which you created all things. This power would indeed be considered dormant and useless unless that should be completed whose other works of God were signs. “And come,” that is, assume flesh, “so that” through this coming of yours “you may save us,” that is, wholly rescue us from the power of the devil.

And in order to save us, “God, turn us” toward you from unbelief, “and show your face,” that is, your Son, so that in Christ we may recognize your divinity, “and then we shall be saved.”

But to show that a little delay in Christ’s coming still remained, the Prophet, as though regarding God as angry, complains. Continuation: I say, come; and, O Lord, why do you delay so long? This is “Lord God of hosts,” that is, of the heavenly angels: “how long will you be angry over the prayer of your servant?” That is, how long will you show yourself angry with me, your servant who prays to you, by delaying to send the Son whose coming I ask for?

When he calls him “God of hosts,” he shows that God is such that he can save us well. He also indicates that God makes us, his worshipers, companions of those hosts.

And how long, Lord, “will you feed us the bread of tears?” [Col. 0472B] By tears he understands all the miseries of this life. But because he understands that these constitute for him complete refreshment and purification, he calls them food and drink; therefore he says, “and” how long “will you give us drink in tears?” That is, the tears will be like drink and good refreshment; they will be “in measure,” that is, such as we are able to endure. The Apostle says: God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.

I rightly say that we have been placed in tears, because you “have made us a contradiction to our neighbors,” since our neighbors contradict our truth. And they do not merely contradict us, but “our enemies have also mocked us,” that is, they derided us with wrinkled noses.

[Col. 0472C] But against these, “God of hosts, turn us, and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

“You brought a vine.” The second section. I rightly say that we shall be saved, because you, God, clearly demonstrated our salvation in that figure when you led your people out of Egypt and planted them in the promised land. This is what he says: “a vine,” that is, the Jewish people whom you cultivated like a good farmer cultivating a beloved vine, “you brought out of Egypt”; “you cast out the nations” from the promised land; “and you planted it,” the vine, there, that is, you established it firmly and caused it to dwell there.

“You were the guide of its journey in its sight,” because you visibly showed yourself to them in the cloud that went before them; “and you planted its roots,” that is, its leaders, by whom others were supported; “and” that people “filled the land” [Col. 0472D] of promise.

Or, if by “the land” we understand the whole world, we shall say that this ought rather to be understood of the whole Church, signified by the vine, than of the vine itself. “Its shadow,” that is, its care and concern to restore them, “covered the mountains,” that is, the greater ones, so that they would not act according to their own will but attend to the care of their subjects; and “its branches,” that is, the growths of this people, covered and obstructed “the cedars,” that is, their exceedingly lofty prelates. I do not mean the cedars of the devil, namely, the exalted ones of this world, but “the cedars of God”; for the more that people grew, the more their prelates were occupied with its care.

“It stretched out its branches,” that is, “its sons, to the sea,” by which the kingdom of Judea is bounded, “and its shoots,” [Col. 0473A] that is, its extensions, namely, it stretched out its children’s children “to the river,” the Jordan.

“Why,” since you bestowed so many benefits upon that people, “why have you destroyed its hedge?” that is, its defense; “and why do all who pass along the way,” that is, those who transgress the Lord’s commandments—or the Gentiles, who do not possess the law—“harvest it,” that is, trample it?

I rightly say that those who transgress trample it, because “the boar,” that is, Vespasian, unclean, as coming from the “forest,” that is, from uncultivated land, namely, from paganism, “destroyed it,” that is, captured it outside the boundaries of its own land; “and the solitary,” that is, Titus, “wild beast,” savage and proud, “devoured it,” that is, utterly destroyed it. For what his father [Col. 0473B] Vespasian had first crushed, he consumed completely. He is compared to a solitary beast, that is, a boar, because he is savage like a boar.

By the vine brought out of Egypt we understand the Church, brought out of the darkness of this world. Christ is the guide of its journey, set before us so that we may imitate his life. And you planted the roots of the Church, that is, the holy teachers through whom the Church is sustained, in such a way that they cannot be moved by any wind of the devil. The Church itself filled the land because it has been spread throughout the whole world. And its shadow, that is, its solicitude and care, covered the mountains, that is, it impedes the Apostles by recalling them from contemplation to the care of others; and its branches, as above.

Or “its shadow,” that is, the protection of the Church, covered the mountains, because no one in the Church is so exalted that he is not protected beneath the protection and unity of God’s Church; for if he is separated from the unity of God’s Church, he will fall from every height.

Likewise, its branches covered God’s cedars. And that vine, namely the Church, stretched its branches, that is, its preachers, to the Eastern and Western sea; and it stretched its shoots, that is, its sons through whom it is extended, to the river Jordan, making them reach through the middle of the world as far as baptism.

He mentions the river because baptism began there, through which the Church is extended throughout the whole world. God destroys the substance of that Church when he permits his own people to be afflicted or to be submerged in sins. And those who transgress the way, that is, God’s commandments—or Christ himself, through whom they ought to come to God—“harvest” [Col. 0473D] it, that is, trample and afflict it.

The boar is called *aper*, as though from *asper* (“rough”), that is, the devil, coming from the forest, namely, from savage people who are ignorant of the worship of God. He destroys the Church when he alienates its members from it. And that same devil, solitary and savage, devoured that Church, because he will almost entirely consume it in the time of Antichrist.

“God.” The third section. These evils come upon your vine; but, O “God of hosts, turn again” from your anger, since you now no longer wish to inflict evils upon it, “and look down from heaven,” that is, from the humanity of Christ, “and see,” that is, cause it to be seen that you love it by bestowing benefits; “and visit this vine,” healing it as though it were sick.

[Col. 0474A] “And perfect” this vine, that is, the Church, “which your right hand planted,” that is, your Son; “and” perfect it “upon the son,” so that he, the Son, may be the foundation of the Church, “whom you confirmed for yourself,” saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17; Mark I).

I say, perfect it, and I have no doubt, because “they will perish” in that Church “at the rebuke of your countenance,” that is, of your “Son,” who is called the countenance and image of your substance, and who rebukes sin both through himself and through his own people. They will perish, I say, “burned by fire,” that is, sins comparable to fire, such as lust and similar things, “and dug up,” that is, sins committed deceitfully. Through these two expressions he indicates the destruction of all sins.

And so that this Church may be perfected in this way, “let your hand” [Col. 0474B] that is, your operation, “be upon the man,” that is, Christ, “of your right hand,” that is, united to your Word; “and upon the son,” not of human beings, but “of man,” that is, of the Virgin, “whom you confirmed for yourself.” Here he indicates Christ as God and man, who, through God’s operation, can perfect the Church.

“And,” if this happens, “we shall not depart from you,” although previously we departed when we sought something other than you; “and you, Lord, will give us life,” the true life which is God; “and” thereafter “we shall invoke your name.”

And so that we may not depart from you, “Lord God of hosts, turn us, and show your face, and we shall be saved,” as above. This verse is repeated so many times because the whole substance of the subject depends upon it.

## Psalm LXXX

### Title: For the end; a psalm for the winepresses, to Asaph himself, on the fifth day of the week

“Rejoice in God.” This psalm belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which speaks here. It is composed “for the winepresses,” that is, for the Church, which is compared with winepresses: just as in a winepress there is wine that is kept and grape material that is cast out, so in the Church some are taken up to blessedness and some are rejected.

I say that it is for winepresses signified “on the fifth day of the week,” that is, through the works done on the fifth day of the week. On that day he brought forth fish and birds from the waters as living creatures, because he made all birds from the waters; hence they are also permitted to monks. By the birds that are lifted on high, the good within the Church are understood, because, abandoning worldly things, [Col. 0474D] they strive toward heavenly things. By the fish that remain below and are always anxious, those who cling to earthly things and are always anxiously occupied with desire for the world are understood.

I say, this is a psalm directed toward the end. Its subject is the Church, namely, all who have been reborn through the waters of baptism. The method is as follows. In the first part Asaph, that is, the Prophet, or another faithful member of the Synagogue, urges the perfect within the Church, who are signified by the birds, to rejoice in the Lord and praise him. In the second, which begins, “Hear, my people,” the faithful Synagogue introduces God speaking and rebuking the wicked within the Church, who are signified by the fish, although they do not desist. In the third part, which begins, “The enemies of the Lord have lied,” the Synagogue rebukes the wicked who do not wish to cease from their wickedness.

The intention is to urge them to take flight.

The Synagogue itself thus admonishes the perfect, saying: “Rejoice in God,” that is, for his honor, “our helper,” who helps us to work well against the deceiving world; “and shout for joy,” that is, conceive in your mind a joy that cannot be expressed in words, “to the God of Jacob.”

And so that you may be able to rejoice and shout for joy, “take up the psalm,” that is, spiritual activity, “and give” God “the timbrel,” that is, praise and the mortification of your flesh. Do this for the following reason: “the psaltery,” that is, contemplation, joined “with the lyre,” that is, with the mortification of the flesh, namely, the active life, “is pleasing” to God; for “by the psaltery we understand the same thing as by the psalm.”

“Blow the trumpet,” that is, announce God’s praise to others, “with a trumpet,” that is, in a loud voice, “at the new moon,” that is, in your invocation. In the law, as a figure of our invocation, it was commanded that that people should blow the trumpet at the new moon. *Mene* in Greek is *mensis* in Latin, “month,” while *neon* means “new.” “Blow the trumpet,” I say, “on the distinguished day of your solemnity,” that is, in the illumination of your renewal, which ought to be a great solemnity for you.

Therefore blow the trumpet, “because it is a commandment in Israel,” for them literally (Leviticus XXXII), and for us spiritually; “and,” if you neglect it, you ought to fear, because “judgment belongs to the God of Jacob,” in which he will save the obedient and condemn the negligent.

[Col. 0475C] And “he placed that” commandment, namely, his law, “in Joseph,” that is, he enlarged the people, namely, the Gentile people, which grew beyond the Jewish people, so that it might be “a testimony” to it, that is, so that it might testify what ought to be done and what ought to be omitted. “When” that people “went out from the land of Egypt” (Exodus XXII), “he heard a language that he did not know,” that is, the law.

Likewise, the Christian people, going out from Egypt, that is, from the darkness of unbelief, hears the preaching of faith and the law of life, which it had not previously heard.

God also “turned aside his back,” that is, the back of the Israelite people, “from the burdens” that they carried in Egypt, “and his hands” served “in the basket.” A basket is a vessel in which they were forced to carry dung. Likewise God turns aside the back, that is, the understanding by which the faithful are raised toward higher things, from the burdens of sins; and he turns aside the hands, that is, the works of the faithful, from the basket, that is, from the uncleanness in which they previously served the devil.

In tribulation he turned them aside, saying: “In tribulation you called upon me” with words, “and I delivered you.” Also, “in the hiding-place of the storm I heard you,” when you did not even dare to groan to me in the hearing of the Egyptians. For Pharaoh commanded, because he heard them crying out to God, that they should be burdened with work in such a way that they would have no leisure to cry out to God.

So God hears his faithful in the hiding-place of the storm when he stills within them the battle of suggestion, which has not yet broken out into open action. “And I tested you” afterward “at the water of contradiction.” God tested the Israelite people and Moses himself, who doubted the divine power (Numbers XX). Or, as others say, he tested one who presumed upon himself, and therefore could not lead the people into the promised land.

Thus God tests those in the Church at the water of contradiction, that is, at the teachings of heretics, which the good contradict and the wicked yield to.

“Hear.” The second section. The Lord has said these things to the good within the Church; now he begins to admonish the wicked. Against all these benefits I have done good to you; therefore, O “my people,” made mine in baptism, “hear me,” that is, understand; “and I will testify against you,” that is, I will confirm by the testimonies of Scripture what I shall say to you. And, O “Israel,” that is, you who see God by faith, “if you will hear me,” obeying my commandments, “there shall be no new god among you,” as you say: for although I was born in time, I am nevertheless coeternal with the Father; “nor shall you worship” in me “a foreign god.”

And truly I am not foreign: “for I am the Lord your God,” that is, your Creator, and not a recent one, “who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” that is, out of unbelief. I say, hear, and “open your mouth wide, and I will fill it,” namely, enlarge your heart to desire and to understand in those psalms, inwardly through faith and love, and outwardly through preaching and confession.

I have thus admonished my own people, “and” yet “my people,” who ought all to be mine, “did not hear my voice,” that is, my admonition; and not [Col. 0476C] only did it not hear, but “Israel did not attend to me,” that is, it did not even wish to attend to a single word. “And” therefore “I let them go according to the desires of their hearts,” so that they might satisfy their own will; and, once my grace had been withdrawn from them, “they will walk in their own inventions,” even in their own contrivances, namely, through their traditions, making God’s commandment void.

So I abandoned them; but “if my people had listened to me,” believing, and if he himself, having become the true “Israel, had walked in my ways,” fulfilling them, “I would have humbled their enemies,” so that they would be regarded “as nothing,” or I would have humbled them freely; “and upon those who afflicted them I would have laid my hand,” that is, my activity, so that my activity would prevail over their enemies and remove them.

[Col. 0476D] “The enemies of the Lord.” The third part. Continuation. The Lord had thus promised good things to his people, but his word did not take root in them. For although they ought to have been friends, they became “enemies of the Lord and lied to him,” not carrying out their promises; and therefore “their time,” that is, their alteration through punishments, “will be forever,” eternally—or, the time of their vengeance.

“And” deservedly they will be condemned, because God “fed them with the fat of wheat,” that is, with the innermost marrow of wheat, namely, with the more hidden and profound mystery of his incarnation and with other spiritual graces; “and satisfied them with honey from the rock,” that is, with stronger doctrine, because honey is a stronger food; while the rock was Christ.

## ON PSALM LXXXI

**Title: A Psalm of Asaph.**

“God stood.” This psalm is suited to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which speaks against the Jews whom, in prophetic spirit, it sees prepared to act wickedly against Christ, their visitor. Its subject is Christ’s first coming.

Its structure is as follows. In the first part, it shows that he will dwell among human beings, namely, through assumed flesh, and it warns the Jews not to judge him wickedly. In the second part, which begins, “Judge the needy,” it shows that Christ, although he was rich, became poor for us, and it admonishes them not to think less of him on this account, but to understand him as just; and it gives them a sure sign by which they may recognize him as the Son of God. [Col. 0477B] In the third part, which begins, “I said: You are gods,” it shows that, although Christ came to exalt human beings and make them children of God, because the Jews did not receive him, they did not obtain that exaltation. Its purpose is especially to admonish the Jews not to do Christ any harm, but to consent to his preaching.

It is as though he were saying: Do not despise Christ when you see him needy and poor, thinking him merely human, because he is also God. Hence he says: “God,” having become human, “stood” bodily “in the assembly of gods,” that is, among good Jews. Great men are also called gods. Hence it is said in the Law: “You shall not revile the gods” (Exodus 22)—not as though he were another human being, but he himself, God, “judges in their midst,” that is, he distinguishes [Col. 0477C] and separates the good from the wicked, but “the gods” whom he himself makes divine. In this verse he plainly demonstrates Christ’s incarnation.

“How long?” Christ is God, who also makes his own divine; therefore, you judges of the Jews, how long will you “judge unjustly,” namely, condemning Christ, the redeemer of all, as deserving death? It is as though he were saying: Since for a long time he has shown himself to be sufficiently just toward the servants sent to the vineyard, receive the heir now sent to you. “And” how long will you “take” upon yourselves “the faces of sinners” unto death? That is, how long will you consent to sinners and make yourselves like them? One takes on the faces of sinners when he adopts the manner of their wickedness by which he is distinguished from others.

“Judge the needy.” The second part. You judges, do not judge Christ unjustly, but “judge the needy and the orphan,” that is, judge Christ to his honor, judging God in addition to the human being. He calls Christ needy because he always refused to possess earthly resources, as the Apostle says: “Although he was rich, for our sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8). He calls him an orphan because he did not seek human protection for himself on earth. I say: judge him, and also “justify the humble and poor,” that is, regard him as just, and understand that no one can be just without him. You elders, judge; you younger men, “rescue this poor man” from the power of the elders, and do not allow him, once rescued, to be captured again. This is: “and free the needy from the hand of the sinful” people.

I thus admonished them, yet they “did not know” that he was their God and Redeemer. [Col. 0478A] For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. I say: They did not know, “nor did they understand”; but they did not know because they did not wish to understand, and they did not understand because “they walk in darkness,” that is, in love of earthly things. Yet they will not be excusable for their ignorance, since they had a sure sign by which they could recognize that he was God: “the foundations of the earth were shaken,” not merely in certain places, but “all of them”—through which the blessed Dionysius recognized that he was the Son of God.

“I said.” The third part. They did not understand, but nevertheless “I said: You are gods,” that is, if you wish, you can be gods—that is, made divine—and not just any gods, but “sons of the Most High,” not merely nobles and powerful people, but “all,” however powerless they may be.

[Col. 0478B] I say that you can be sons of God, “but you” did not heed my admonition; therefore “you will die,” liable to condemnation, “like human beings,” carnal people. And you elders, exercising your pride against Christ, “will fall” into the depths of hell, irretrievably, “like one of the princes” fell—that is, the devil, who was chief among the heavenly princes. Although many had fallen, he nevertheless says “one,” because all were united in evil will.

You will indeed fall in this way, but you, “O God, arise” from the tomb, and “judge the earth,” that is, the earthly Jews; condemn and blind them, “because,” once they have been blinded, “you will inherit among all the nations.” For blindness has come upon Israel in part, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter.

## ON PSALM LXXXII

**Title: A Song of the Psalm of Asaph.**

“God, who is like you?” This psalm is indeed suited to Asaph, that is, to the faithful Synagogue, which speaks. It is a song because it shows us a future event over which we ought greatly to rejoice: namely, that at Christ’s second coming our persecutors and all wicked people will be condemned. It is also called a psalm because it teaches us to act well and to endure evils patiently. Its subject is Christ’s second coming.

In the first part, it asks for Christ’s coming, by which the Church may be freed from the evils it suffers in this life; for there are many evils which the Church suffers here. In the second part, which begins, “Do to them as to Midian,” it prays that God, coming a second time, may exact a just vengeance from those wicked people, and also bring about the conversion of some to life and the greater blinding of others. Its purpose is, through fear of the second coming, to deter people—especially the Jews—from persecuting the Church.

The Prophet speaks as though saying: People think you weak and powerless when you allow your own people to be punished, but, “O God, who will be like you?” No one. Therefore, O God, who kept silent during this time of life, permitting your own people to be punished, “do not be silent”: pronounce sentence against them, saying, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” “Nor restrain yourself” from vengeance; rather, restrain them by eternal punishment.

[Col. 0479A] Therefore I say, do not be silent, because “your enemies have resounded,” that is, they have irrationally contradicted your holy ones; and therefore do not restrain yourself, because “those who hate you have raised their head,” namely, Antichrist, whom they themselves will proclaim to be the Son of God and Redeemer. Or, “their head,” that is, they have raised their pride against you.

And not only against you, but against your own people. Hence: “Against your people they have devised a wicked plan,” that is, they have deliberated with evil intent for the humiliation of your people. And they have not merely deliberated, but also “plotted” what worse sentence one of them might pronounce “against your holy ones.”

And they “said,” exhorting one another: “Come, and let us destroy them from the earth,” that is, that nation—namely, let us destroy the holy ones—to such an extent that the name “Israel,” namely, the Christian name, “will no longer be remembered.”

[Col. 0479B] And whence did they have such confidence? Because they were many and united. Hence: “For together,” that is, many of them, “they plotted unanimously,” that is, possessing the same will to inflict harm, and “they established a covenant,” that is, their agreements, “against you,” so that through their pacts they might destroy the law of God.

And who were they? “The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites.” Note that, historically, he places here the persecutors of the Israelite people; but through these names the persecutors of the Church are appropriately signified. By “the tents of the Edomites,” who are interpreted as “bloodied” or “earthly,” we understand the gatherings of those who cling to earthly things; or, by the Ishmaelites, “homicides,” we understand those who obey them.

Among the other persecutors are “Moab,” namely, one who abuses the Law; and “the Hagarenes,” that is, aliens, who, although they display a good appearance, nevertheless do harm whenever they find an opportunity; “Jebal,” that is, “a vain valley,” namely, hypocrites, who show themselves to possess humility, but do so in vanity, and nevertheless act well before human beings; and “Ammon,” which also establishes a covenant against you, that is, “a turbulent people,” like those who are distressed by the loss of earthly things; and “Amalek,” that is, “licking the earth,” namely, the avaricious of this life, who think nothing should be avoided if money can be obtained by it; and “foreigners,” namely, in meaning the same as what we had above with the Hagarenes. But the Hebrew truth has “Philistines” here, that is, “those who fall through drink,” by which we understand those who become intoxicated with the riches and prosperity of this life.

All these have established their plans against you “with the inhabitants of Tyre,” that is, “of distress.” By this we may understand merchants, who avoid no distress in acquiring money.

“For indeed” these can do this well, because “Assur,” that is, that people, “came with them.” Assur is interpreted as “one who depresses,” or “one who is exalted.” By this the devil is understood: he depresses the good and is always ready to come with others to persecute the Church of God; and he alone can rightly be called “exalted.” And Assur, together with all the others, “became an aid to the sons of Lot.”

The sons of Lot historically persecuted the people of God; through them are understood the pagans, who are sons of the apostate angel. For Lot is interpreted as “one who turns aside,” by which the devil is aptly signified.

“Do to them.” The second part. Just as through the peoples who persecuted the Israelite people he signified the persecutors of the Church, so through the peoples destroyed by the Israelite people he signified the wicked who will be condemned by Christ at the second judgment.

Continuation: These people thus devise plans against you, but you, Lord, “do to them as” you did to “Midian,” that people whom you destroyed through the Jewish people. Midian is interpreted as “turning aside from judgment”; by this are understood those who deny that a future judgment exists. And do to them as you did to “Sisera,” whose name is interpreted as “exclusion from joy”; by this are understood those who deny that any future joy awaits the good after this life. And do to them “as” you did to “Labin,” who was defeated in that place, namely, “at the torrent of Kishon.”

[Col. 0480B] Labin is interpreted as “wise in himself”; by this are understood philosophers and other wise men of this world. Kishon is interpreted as “hardness.” The wise men of this world are destroyed in the torrent of Kishon, that is, in the abundance of their own hardness.

“Others perished” “at Endor,” namely, at the place whose name is interpreted as “the fountain of generation,” “and” they “became like dung of the earth,” that is, having fallen into sins, they rotted inwardly. Hence it is said: “The animals rotted in their dung.”

Or, “like dung of the earth,” because just as dung enriches the earth and makes it fruitful, so these wicked people, by persecuting the Church, cause it to become inwardly richer and more fruitful.

“Set” also, Lord, “their princes” who persecute the Church “as” you destroyed “Oreb, and Zeb, Zebeah, and Zalmunna.” Oreb is interpreted as “dryness”; by this we understand those who are dry of spiritual dew. Zeb means “wolf”; by this we understand plunderers. Zebeah means “the wolf’s victim”; by this we understand those whom the devil incorporates into himself. Zalmunna means “shadow of disturbance”; by this we understand those who are unstable in faith, who believe for a time but withdraw in the time of tribulation.

And, to include them all universally, depose “all their princes” who said, in word and deed, this: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God,” that is, the people sanctified by God, “as an inheritance,” so that we may cultivate them with our doctrines and Christ may have no part in them.

[Col. 0480D] Those people, O “my God, make like a wheel,” so that, just as a wheel is always turning, rising at the rear and falling forward, so they may always turn in the thoughts of worldly people, rising from behind—that is, from these earthly things in which they are elevated—and falling forward, that is, toward spiritual things: namely, so that, having entirely abandoned those earthly things, they may fall away from them, forget earthly things, and desire heavenly things.

Hence the Apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind, I reach forward to what lies ahead.” And “make them like chaff before the face of the wind,” so that, just as chaff does not resist the wind, so they may not resist temptations. God brings about this downfall of the wicked in this life.

“Like fire.” In this life you will treat them in this way; but in the other life [Col. 0481A] you will burn them with punishing fire. Hence: “like fire that burns the forest, and like a flame burning the mountains.” He aptly compares them to forests, because they are wild and uncultivated with respect to the law of God; he compares them to mountains because of their arrogance.

“Thus.” Just as fire pursues the forest, “so” you “will pursue them” as they are unable to excuse themselves, “in your storm,” that is, in the judgment, which will come as suddenly as a storm and will separate the grain from the chaff. And I say that you will pursue them and, once you have caught them, “you will trouble them in your anger,” showing them that you are angry by inflicting eternal punishment.

He has asked for the condemnation of the wicked; now he asks for the conversion of those who will be saved, as though saying: You will punish those who refuse to convert in this way; but “fill their faces,” namely, the persecutors who have been foreseen for salvation, “with disgrace,” that is, so that they may be ashamed of their sins, “and” thus “they will seek your name,” namely, so that they may become Christians.

But those who are obstinate and unwilling to be ashamed here, let them in the other life “be ashamed” of their disgraceful deeds, “and be troubled” by punishments destined to last “forever and ever”; “and let them be confounded,” in soul and body. And let that confusion not be repaired, but “let them perish” in eternal torments.

“And” then at least “let them know that to you” this “name, Lord,” belongs; and those who in this life thought themselves lofty and powerful, let them then know that “you alone are the Most High in all the earth,” that is, above all earthly people, because just as you are powerful in rewarding the good, so you are powerful in condemning the wicked.

## ON PSALM LXXXIII

**Title: To the end; a Psalm for the sons of Korah, for the winepresses.**

“How beloved.” This psalm is suited to the sons of Korah, that is, to the sons of the cross, imitators of Christ, who speaks here. It is arranged “for the winepresses,” that is, for the Churches, which are compared to winepresses: just as in a winepress one learns what is wine and what is a grape, so through the pressures in the Church it becomes known who are good and who are evil.

Here he is said to act on behalf of the Church because he shows the great dignity of the Church itself, namely, that it always seeks heavenly things. Or we may say that this is not the voice of the sons of Korah, [Col. 0481D] but of the Prophet or of some perfected person. In this case, the psalm is placed before the sons of Korah to stir them up—that is, simpler Christians. Acting on behalf of the winepresses, that is, concerning the Churches, it shows the Church’s dignity and urges the sons of Korah to hasten toward the same dignity, directing them to the end.

Or in this way: This psalm acts on behalf of the winepresses, that is, in praise of pressures. It calls tribulations winepresses because, just as a winepress separates and squeezes wine from grapes, so the tribulations of this life distinguish the good from the evil—winepresses, I say, that are effective unto the end. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life.”

Its subject is the Church placed amid the pressures of this life. Its structure is as follows. In the first part, it is shown that although the Church is crushed by countless tribulations, it nevertheless desires to reach the heavenly Jerusalem. In the second part, which begins, “Blessed is the man whose help is,” it shows the aid that God gives to his own and how useful that aid is. In the third part, which begins, “For one day is better,” it shows that he would rather be rejected in the house of God than abound in the riches of sinners, so that through the aid established for him in the second part he may reach the desire set forth in the first. Its purpose is to admonish us always to desire that heavenly Jerusalem.

Showing the affection of the Church, the speaker says: O “Lord of hosts,” that is, of the heavenly angels, “your tabernacles,” that is, your heavenly dwelling, “are beloved,” that is, desired—“how beloved,” namely, infinitely so. He calls that heavenly dwelling a tabernacle because of its dwelling alone: just as people dwell in tabernacles, so they dwell in that heavenly Jerusalem.

When he says “Lord of hosts,” he suggests that he confers many virtues upon his own; therefore “my soul,” although oppressed by many tribulations, “longs” to enter “the courts of the Lord,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, which he calls courts because of their spaciousness. And “in longing it languishes,” that is, it abstains from all earthly things, so that even the body languishes. Hence in the Song of Songs: “I am sick with love” (Song of Songs 2).

Or it languishes because, however much it longs, it nevertheless cannot comprehend the joy of that city. Or by “tabernacles” [Col. 0482C] we can understand the present Church, so that we may say: Your tabernacles—that is, the present Church in which we serve you for a time—how beloved they are, that is, how glorious and joyful it is to stand and serve you in the camp. Hence the Apostle says: “We glory not only in hope but also in tribulations” (Romans 5). And Solomon says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

And because your tabernacles are so joyful, I love to serve in them, because I am confident that through this service I will reach that heavenly dwelling. Thus it longs and languishes, as stated above.

“My heart longs,” and this with exultation. This is: “my heart,” that is, my innermost part, namely, my soul afflicted by many tribulations, “and” also “my flesh,” now subject to reason and afflicted by still more evils. Hence elsewhere (Psalm 62): “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh longs for you.”

“They exulted,” that is, with exultation they endured the tribulations of this life, moving “toward the living God,” so that they might possess him who makes those who move toward him live in eternal life.

Indeed, my heart exulted—that is, my soul and my flesh. “For even the sparrow,” that is, the soul itself, “has found a house for itself, and the turtledove,” that is, the flesh itself, has found for itself “a nest where it may place its young,” that is, its works.

The soul is compared to a sparrow because, just as a sparrow leaves the forests and nests in houses, though in high places where it is safe from the hands of children and from snares, so the faithful soul, having left these earthly things, finds for itself a heavenly house in which it already dwells through hope and contemplation. Therefore it would already wish to depart and be with Christ, as Paul says (Philippians 1): “If this house of ours is dissolved, we have a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5). Through contemplation of this house the faithful soul protects itself from the snares of its enemies.

The flesh is compared to a turtledove because, just as the turtledove groans, so faithful flesh groans, pressed by many miseries. It too finds for itself a nest, that is, faith and the other sacraments of the Church, in which it may place its young, that is, make its good works secure and nourish them—those works which it generates just as a bird generates young. For just as a turtledove cannot nourish its young outside the nest or keep them safe, so the faithful person outside faith, or outside the Church, cannot perform good works pleasing to God.

Hence it is said: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). And Augustine says: “There is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.” And just as the young are not in the nest except to remain there for a time, so the faithful, even in this present service, will not remain forever.

And what nest does the turtledove find? “Your altars,” that is, the sacraments of the Church—faith and baptism and the like—upon which our works are placed and made acceptable to God, just as are the things offered upon the altar.

“O Lord of hosts,” that is, of all the angels, whose powers you send to us for aid. And in this it appears that you are “my king,” because you rule me well in the present service, “and my God,” that is, my Creator.

Or in this way: The sparrow found for itself a house, namely, your altars. He calls the altar a heavenly house because it is a lofty reality. Nothing in what was said about the turtledove is changed.

“Blessed are those.” He shows the end to which this service will lead, namely, eternal life. Continuation: You say that the sparrow has found a house and the turtledove a nest, and through this they will dwell in your heavenly house. This is no small thing, because “blessed” are those “who dwell in your house, O Lord,” that house. They are blessed in this way, namely because “through ages of ages they will praise you.” Their joy is evident from this, because if they were sorrowful, they would not praise you.

[Col. 0483D] “Blessed.” The second part. Those who dwell in your house will be blessed, and that “blessed man” is also blessed “whose help is” against the obstacles of the world “from you,” that is, from you. He is blessed because that man who has been placed “in the valley of tears,” that is, amid the miseries of this world, “has arranged in his heart”—with great reason and diligence—“ascents,” that is, certain steps of progress from virtue to virtue. These ascents lead him “to the place which he established,” namely, the heavenly house, the only place he himself set before himself to seek and love.

Or, “in the place which he established,” that is, which the human being made for himself through the sin of the first parent; for God did not create him in misery but in perfection. In this verse he shows God’s aid and how useful it is.

I rightly say that the one who has God’s aid will be able to arrange ascents, because the Lord will give him not merely the letter that kills but the life-giving Spirit. This is: “for the lawgiver,” that is, God who gives the admonishing law, “will give blessing,” that is, assisting grace, and through it “they will go from virtue to virtue,” that is, in this present Church; and finally “the God of gods will be seen in Zion,” namely, when God will be all in all.

“Lord God of hosts.” And because you do such great benefits for your own, I ask, Lord, that you do so for me also. Hence: “Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer,” and do not simply hear it, but “give ear,” that is, store it in your memory—you, I say, “God of Jacob,” who love all wrestlers who love you, and therefore ought to love me.

“Protector.” The third part. Just as he introduced a prayer in which he would ask for God’s aid, so here he asks for God’s protection, which he regards as necessary for the rejection he has described.

Continuation: Hear my prayer, and “you are our protector,” namely, in adversities. O “God, look upon” me, so that through mercy he may assist my lowliness and prevent me from succumbing. And if I am not worthy that you should look upon me because of me, “look upon the face of your Christ,” that is, the abundance of Christ’s righteousness, through which he himself was distinguished from all others, from whose fullness of righteousness something has flowed to us [Col. 0484C] and has made us conform to him according to our measure.

It is necessary that you look upon me as protector, because I “chose to be rejected in the house of God,” that is, in the present Church, “rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners,” that is, rather than to abound in riches among sinners.

This is a deliberate choice. When he says “tents,” which are temporary and inhabited for a short time, he suggests that they are not to be desired. When he says “of sinners,” he shows that they are especially to be avoided. And he gives the reason why he chose to be rejected and despised in the house: “because one day” is better—namely, that day which is “one,” that is, continuous and never followed by darkness—“in your courts,” that is, in the heavenly dwelling, “than thousands” of these passing days, which fools desire.

David showed himself rejected when he stripped himself while dancing before the ark of the Lord as he brought it back; hence his wife also mocked him.

Therefore I chose to be rejected “because God loves mercy,” that is, to show mercy by forgiving sins and giving righteousness; and he loves “truth,” that is, fulfilling promises. And because he loves mercy, he will give me, rejected as I am and walking in his house, “grace,” that is, forgiveness of sins. And because he loves truth, “the Lord will give” me “glory,” that is, the reward for my service, which he himself promised to all who serve him.

The Lord will give grace and glory not to just anyone, but to the good. Hence: “He will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence,” [Col. 0485A] that is, those who persevere in innocence. And therefore, O “Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.”

## ON PSALM LXXXIV

**Title: To the end; a Psalm for the sons of Korah.**

“You blessed, O Lord.” This psalm is suited to the sons of Korah, who speak, or to whom it is proposed; it is directed to the end, that is, to Christ. Its subject is Christ’s first coming, which confers many benefits upon the Church.

Its structure is as follows. In the first part, it shows that a blessing has been given to the earth, in opposition to the curse given to it on account of Adam’s sin, when he said: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis 3). The second part begins, “You have mitigated your anger”; there it shows the mitigation of God’s anger, which we justly endure because of the sin of the first parent. In the third part, which begins, “I will hear what the Lord will speak,” it openly announces Christ’s coming, indicates through whom this will take place, and teaches where Christ would be born. Its purpose is to admonish us to receive Christ’s coming with great exultation, through which we possess such great benefits.

It is as though he were saying: O “Lord, the earth,” which had previously been cursed in Adam’s work, now made “yours” by receiving the coming of your Son in faith, “you have blessed,” namely in this way: “you have turned away the captivity,” that is, sin, by which all people before Christ’s coming were held captive by the devil—“of Jacob,” that is, of that people which wishes to become like Jacob.

“You forgave.” By turning away this captivity, “you forgave,” that is, you will forgive, “the iniquity of your people” in baptism. And you will not merely forgive, but you have so “covered,” that is, you will cover, “all their sins” that they will no longer come before your sight for you to punish them eternally. Thus you have both removed the sin and forgiven the punishment of sin. Hence elsewhere: “From usury and iniquity you will redeem their souls” (Psalm 71).

“You have mitigated.” The second part. Suppose someone were to say: I do not believe that God has forgiven iniquity and covered sins. The Gospel answers: Truly you have forgiven and covered them, because, O Lord, the “anger” that you had because of the sins of all human beings—that is, that you had because of each individual sin—I do not say that you removed it entirely, since we are mortal and subject to suffering, but you “mitigated,” that is, made mild, because tribulations are now mild and pleasing to us, generating in us hope of eternal salvation. “And you have turned yourself away from the anger of your indignation,” namely, so that you do not inflict punishments proceeding from your indignation, namely, eternal punishments.

And so that we may not incur the anger of your indignation, “convert us” from unbelief to faith, “O God our Savior,” that is, you who through the coming of your Son confer salvation upon us; and “from us,” once converted, “turn away your eternal anger.”

I say, turn it away—and you will turn it away—because “will you be angry with us forever?” Certainly not, because you will be appeased at the coming of your Son. Or at least, “will you extend your anger from generation” to generation—from Adam, with whom it is certain that you were angry because of sin—“to the generation” of Christ? Certainly not; rather, you will be appeased toward Christ’s generation through his coming.

There are two generations: one of Adam, which belongs to carnal people, and the other of Christ, which is spiritual, namely, that of those who strive to conform themselves to Christ. Just as wicked Christians are expelled from this generation, so good people who lived before Christ’s coming are included in it.

“O God, you” will not extend your anger, but “turned” away from anger, you will “give us life” spiritually through the coming of your Son; and “your people,” once given life, “will rejoice in you,” now secure in eternal blessedness.

And so that your people may be given life and rejoice, O “Lord, show us your mercy,” namely, your Son, so that you may send him whom you are going to send. Show him, that is, so that we may recognize him—not all by the presence of his body, but at least through faith—“and” do not merely show him, but also “give us your salvation,” so that he may truly save us, and so that we may hold him in faith and imitate him in our works.

“I will hear what.” The third part. Continuation: I ask you to show him and give us your salvation, and I am confident that you will do so, because “the Lord God” speaks “in me,” and I “will hear what he will speak,” that is, I will not bark against him, but rather restrain myself from these worldly things. And I ought rightly to hear him, “because” in me “he will speak peace,” that is, he will announce to me the Son himself, who will be the author of peace and reconciliation between God and human beings—peace, I say, not to everyone, but “to his people.”

I say, to his people, “and upon his holy ones,” that is, upon those who had been sanctified before his coming, such as Abraham and others like him. Christ’s coming brought these people peace with God, freeing them from the darkness of hell. And not only upon the holy ones, but “also upon those who turn back to the heart,” that is, to reason, such as the Gentiles, who had previously abandoned the Creator and worshiped the creature but through Christ’s coming were converted to the heart, namely, so that now, with careful reason, they might worship their Creator and thus have peace with God through Christ’s coming.

Having spoken of Christ’s coming, he also determines for them the place of his birth, as though saying: Many will be converted through his coming, but Christ will not be born among them; rather, he will be born among the Jews. Hence he says: “Nevertheless, near those who fear him,” that is, the Jews, who alone were said to fear God because they had received his Law, although they served God rather for temporal than for heavenly things, “his salvation” will be—that is, his Son will accomplish salvation for the human race. His salvation will be such “that glory,” that is, the Son himself, “will dwell” bodily “in our land,” that is, in Judea.

“Mercy and truth.” He shows what Christ’s coming does for us. I say, salvation will dwell in the land, and through him “mercy and truth met one another,” that is, came together in Christ himself. He is called truth because in him all the promises made through the Prophets were fulfilled. He is also called mercy because he gave you forgiveness of sins and other benefits solely through his mercy. Thus the New and Old Testaments came together in him.

In Christ, mercy and truth came together; but in all those who await Christ’s coming, “justice and peace kissed one another,” that is, came together. For unless Christ had come, the human being would have had neither justice with God nor peace.

Therefore mercy and truth, justice and peace came together, because “truth,” Christ, “has sprung from the earth,” from the Virgin, who was fruitful earth; “and” from this “justice looked forth from heaven,” that is, from the Lordly man, or from heaven—that is, from heavenly creatures—in whom alone justice existed before Christ’s coming. “It looked forth” upon all human beings.

Or otherwise: Justice and peace truly kissed one another because truth sprang from the earth, that is, from our sinful flesh. We who previously did only empty and false things should now practice virtue: accusation of our sins, worship of God, regarding him alone as just, and other such things. And because we practice truth, therefore justice looked forth from heaven.

According to this interpretation, we shall continue in this way: I rightly say that we practice truth, “for the Lord will give goodness,” that is, the one through whom he will give goodness is to come—namely, the Holy Spirit, who will kindly inspire us inwardly. And he will give this goodness because “our earth,” that is, the Virgin Mary, “of our nature,” “will give her fruit,” that is, her Son.

According to the first interpretation, the continuation is as follows: Truly truth, that is, Christ, sprang from the earth, because the Lord will give goodness, that is, inspiring grace, which he would not give except through Christ; and our earth, that is, human flesh, inspired by that goodness of God, will give its fruit, that is, good works.

And our “justice” “will walk before him” and prepare the way by which God may descend into us. Or “before him,” that is, in his good pleasure; “and he will place” his steps, that is, his works, “in the way” by which we go to him—namely, he will multiply his grace in us.

Or the just human being himself places his steps, that is, his works, “in the way,” that is, in God’s commandments, so that he may act according to God’s commandments. Or “in the way,” that is, in Christ, so that he may act in imitation of Christ.

## ON PSALM LXXXV

**Title: A Prayer of David.**
“Incline, O Lord.” This psalm is called a prayer because it contains a prayer throughout its entire structure and urges us to pray. For the Lord Jesus wished to pray in order to leave us in himself an example of prayer; he also fled, so that in this too he might give us an example of avoiding a presumptuous and rash death. The prayer is attributed to the true David, namely Christ, who speaks in this psalm. Its subject is Christ himself in his suffering.

Its method is as follows. In the first part, before the time of his Passion, he asks that God guard him during the time of his warfare, so that his enemies may not in any way conform him to themselves. In the second part, which begins, “Lead me, O Lord,” he prays to God for his own. [Col. 0488A] In the third part, which begins, “God, the wicked,” he prays concerning what follows after the Passion, namely, his glorification. Its purpose is to invite us to pray.

Now, since Christ understood that according to his humanity he could not reach the height of God, like a sick man asking a physician, he begs God to condescend to his weakness through mercy, saying:

“Incline, O Lord, your ear to me and hear me.” It is necessary for you to incline, “because” I cannot raise myself up to you; for “I am needy,” because of myself I do not possess the riches of this world, “and I am poor,” because I do not possess these riches from another either. “Guard my soul” from conformity with the wicked; and he presents his merit, saying, “because I am holy,” [Col. 0488B] that is, free from the sin of the world. Each believer, in his own measure, can say, “I am holy,” that is, “I have been sanctified.” Hence Augustine says: A believer already does an injury to Christ if he does not say, “I am holy.” “And save,” that is, guard perseveringly, “your servant,” whom you ought to save, because I am your servant, “my God, who hopes in you,” not in worldly things.

Because I said that you ought to guard me, and also because you possess mercy in yourself, therefore: “Have mercy on me, O Lord,” that is, visit me through your mercy. And because he knows that God’s mercy is not to be given to the negligent, he shows himself worthy of receiving that mercy when he says, “because I have cried to you all day long.” [Col. 0488C] Have mercy, “and gladden the soul of your servant” with hope of eternal blessedness, “because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul,” since I have not depressed it into worldly things, but have raised it up to you alone.

Therefore I have lifted it up to you, “because you, O Lord, are gentle” toward those who taste you, “and mild” in bearing with sinners, so that they may be converted, “and of great,” that is, infinite, “mercy to all who call upon you,” because you display many good things to them.

And because you are merciful, I ask not only that you hear me, but also: “Attend with your ears,” that is, firmly store in your memory, “my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication,” concerning the removal of evils.

And you ought to attend, because “in the day of my tribulation,” [Col. 0488D] in the time of my warfare, “I cried to you, because you heard me.” For Christ, who was heard once and for all, was not uncertain about being heard. No one can say this except a holy person, who cries because he is heard, rather than crying in order to be heard. When Christ says that he cried out in tribulation, he indicates to us that in tribulation we must cry out to God above all.

“There is none like you,” and rightly I cry to you, because, O “Lord, among the gods,” whether among the powerful of this world or among heavenly creatures, there is no one “like you” in essence, “and there is none according to your works,” because no one can do what you do.

Truly there is no one according to your works, because [Col. 0489A] “all the nations that you have made,” that is, some from every nation, “will come” through faith “and will adore,” that is, will revere, and this “before you, O Lord,” that is, in your good pleasure, “and they will glorify your name,” that is, they will recognize you as worthy of being named. This does not mean that anything is added to or taken from you, since you can neither increase nor diminish; rather, together with others they will proclaim you necessarily glorious.

And rightly they ought to adore and glorify you, “because you are great,” namely, incomprehensible and omnipotent, “and you alone are God, doing wonders,” because if others perform them, they do so through you.

“Lead me.” The second part. Since you are so good, therefore, O “Lord, lead me,” that is, lead my people, “in your way,” that is, in your commandments; and, having been placed “in [Col. 0489B] your truth, I shall walk” from virtue to virtue. Another translation has “I walk”; thus I shall walk so that “my heart,” that is, the heart of my people, “may rejoice” in hope of reward, and on account of this “may fear,” that is, love, “your name.” To others joys are not given, but adversities are given, so that they may fear.

And if you should say, “I will confess to you,” that is, my people will praise you, “Lord my God, with my whole heart,” that is, with the heart of my people, because a heart emptied of all other things will be vacant solely for your praise. And my people will not confess only within themselves; they will also praise you before others. This is: “I will glorify your name forever.”

They ought to glorify you “because your mercy is great over me,” that is, over my people, “and” also because “you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.” [Col. 0489C] Abraham and the Prophets were in hell before Christ’s coming, but they were not tormented. There was a lower hell where the souls of the wicked were tormented. The contrary is likewise said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Alternatively, this world is called hell in comparison with the heavenly dwelling. The place to which the souls of the wicked descend for punishment is called the lower hell. Or “from the lower hell” means from the depth of vices. The souls of all the faithful departed who do not descend into hell have been set free.

“God, the wicked.” The third part. The continuation is: I pray that you do these things for my people, and glorify me. This is what he sets forth below. Look upon me and have mercy on me. For this purpose he first presents certain causes. It is necessary, Lord, [Col. 0489D] that you glorify me, because, O “God, the wicked have risen up against me,” and not merely inferior wicked people, but “also the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul,” to retain it in death, “and they have not set you before their eyes,” that is, they have not considered you, the God who has been united to my humbled humanity.

“And you, Lord God, are compassionate” in your manifestation, because you have shown many acts of compassion to all who hope in you, “and merciful” in your nature, “patient,” that is, not immediately punishing sins, but awaiting the sinner through patience, “and of great mercy,” because mercy is greater than guilt, “and truthful” in fulfilling all your promises.

Although you appear to be hostile in my Passion, “look upon [Col. 0490A] me,” that is, attend to my merit, “and have mercy on me” by resurrecting me through your mercy. Thus “give” to me, “your servant,” that is, one devoted in all things, “your rule,” that is, governance over the Gentiles and the Jews. “And save me,” perseveringly guarding the rule that you will confer, “the son of your handmaid,” that is, of the Virgin Mary, who said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

“Deal with me”: give me rule; and, in order that I may obtain it, make a vow. This means: make “a sign,” some notable deed, such as the Resurrection. Make it “with me,” because I labor for this by meriting it as much as I can. You ought to do this because I ask it “for good,” namely, so that good may result from it, that is, salvation may come to the Gentiles. For this purpose make the sign, “so that those who [Col. 0490B] hate me may see,” that is, understand, “and be confounded,” recognizing that they have done evil. Let them see this: “that you, O Lord, have helped me” in the struggles that I had against them, “and have consoled me” in the Passion, because when they saw him rise again, they recognized that he had been God even in his Passion.

## On Psalm LXXXVI

### Title

“A psalm of song for the sons of Korah.”

“Foundations.” This psalm is a song because it presents to us a great cause for exultation, namely, the dignity of the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Prophet proclaimed exultantly and left to us as a source of the greatest joy. The psalm is presented to the sons of Korah so that [Col. 0490C] they themselves may become citizens of this city. Its subject is the heavenly city.

Its method is as follows. In the first part, the Prophet himself commends it according to his own understanding. In the second part, which is “I will remember Rahab,” he introduces God speaking and commending the city. Again, in the third part, which begins, “As of those who rejoice,” the Prophet himself commends it through the joy of those who will inhabit it eternally. His purpose is to urge the sons of Korah toward attaining this city.

The Prophet’s voice is as though he had meditated for a long time, saying within himself: The walls of this city are indeed good, and its roofs are excellent, but “its foundations are in the holy mountains.” The mountains are the Apostles and Prophets, and the patriarchs are the foundations of this city about which he was meditating, because our faith [Col. 0490D] is founded upon them. “And the gates of Zion,” namely, of this same city, “the Lord loves.” By the gates he understands both the Apostles and those who introduce people into this Church. He loves them, I say, “above all the tabernacles of Jacob,” that is, above all the carnal sacrifices by which God was appeased in the Old Testament.

Seeing that he could not enumerate those good things by himself, the Prophet turns to the city itself, saying: O “city of God,” heavenly city, “glorious things have been spoken of you,” many things that I cannot enumerate.

### “I will remember”

The second part. The continuation is: These glorious things have been spoken to me about you: that God will make the nations inhabitants of you, because God himself said this: [Col. 0491A] “I will remember Rahab.” Rahab is interpreted as “impetus” or “breadth.” By this we understand the Gentiles who rush impetuously and without reason through the broad desires of this world. “And” I will remember “Babylon,” that is, those who are confused in sins, “who know me,” that is, I will make them know and recognize me. Or, I will remember those who know me through the Apostles.

“Behold, the foreigners.” I say that I will remember Rahab, whom I will bring into this city, and “behold,” as though you had it openly before you, “there,” that is, in this city, “foreigners have been,” that is, will be, “those who fall through drunkenness.” These are those who were once intoxicated by the prosperity and riches of this world; they will be converted and will become members of the heavenly Jerusalem. “And Tyre” [Col. 0491B]—namely, those who were previously afflicted by the difficulty of acquiring temporal goods, like merchants—will be in it. For Tyre is interpreted as “affliction.” “And the people of the Ethiopians,” that is, many of those who had previously been black through sins.

“Will it be?” The Prophet speaks as though saying: These glorious things have been spoken about that city; and, beyond all these things, more gloriously than everything already mentioned, “a man,” that is, Christ according to his humanity, “was born in it,” and “the Most High himself founded it,” according to his divinity.

Because he sees that what he is saying is wondrous and almost unbelievable, he first expresses a certain astonishment, saying: “Will” some “man,” some fleshly person, be able, O “Zion, to say,” that is, to say and understand, who and how great is the one who both founded this city [Col. 0491C] and was born in it? Christ himself was one of the Church, and these were those from whom he was born. Certainly no human being can reveal this; only the Holy Spirit can reveal it. He is the one of whom John says: “The strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to loosen” (Mark I).

“Lord.” I said that a man was born in it and that he himself founded it. You ought rightly to believe this, although it may seem wondrous, because “the Lord will narrate in the writings of the peoples,” that is, the writings set before the peoples for understanding, as though already the Apostles, through the sacred Scriptures, understood these things about Christ and proclaimed them publicly. Yet I do not say merely “the writings of the peoples,” but also “of those princes who were [Col. 0491D] in it,” namely, in the city of the holy Apostles, the Church.

### “As”

The third part. Through what has been said above, the city of Zion appears worthy of praise, and also because, O Zion, “the dwelling of us all,” which “is in you” after the Judgment, is “like those who rejoice,” that is, like those rejoicing in this life. But because he recognized that its greatness was infinite, he could not define it. Since there are such great joys there, scarcely comparable in any way with the joys of this world, he indicates that we must hasten above all toward that dwelling.

## On Psalm LXXXVII

### Title

“A song of a psalm for the sons of Korah, to the end, for Melech, for responding; the understanding of Heman the Israelite” (or, as Jerome says, “the Ezraite”).

“Lord, God of my salvation.” It is read that when David was playing this psalm on the lyre and the standing chorus responded with harmonious voice, a certain man named Heman appeared. He was an Easterner, called an Ezraite from the place named Ezra, or, as Augustine prefers, an Israelite. In this figure of David leading the singing and the chorus responding, he understood the meaning of the psalm: namely, that Christ in this psalm speaks about his Passion, and that his faithful respond well to him, that is, they endure many things in imitation of Christ. Accordingly, Ezra assigned this kind of title to the psalm, which is read as follows:

“This song of a psalm is placed before [Col. 0492B] the sons of Korah,” that is, before all Christians, “for responding,” that is, so that they may respond, “for Melech,” that is, in place of the chorus. Just as the chorus responded harmoniously to King David who led the singing, although the persons were different, so the sons of Korah, although they are different persons, respond harmoniously to Christ in faith and love. Christ first plays the lyre in the mortification of his own flesh, so that the sons of Korah also may lay down their lives for their friends, as the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps” (1 Peter II).

“Melech” is interpreted as “chorus.” I say this to the sons of Korah, directed toward the end, if they respond in this way. And rightly I say that they ought to respond in this way, because this kind of response is the understanding of Heman the Ezraite: Heman understood this kind of response [Col. 0492C] in this psalm.

Heman is interpreted as “brother”; Ezraite as “stranger” or “newcomer.” Thus Heman understood that this kind of response should be made to Christ: Heman, that is, a brother, namely, every believer, of whom the Lord says, “Say to my brothers.” I say “brother,” but also “Ezraite,” that is, a newcomer in this world, one who does not have here a lasting city but is always striving toward the heavenly one.

Alternatively, “Heman the Israelite,” that is, “the brother who sees God,” understood that the sons of Korah ought to respond to Christ in this way.

This psalm is called a song because it presents to us the Passion of Christ, which he endured with great exultation for our restoration. It is called a psalm because it urges us toward spiritual action, namely, patience. Through the example of Christ and of his faithful—whom it leads to respond to Christ by suffering [Col. 0492D]—it invites the sons of Korah to the same response.

Its subject is Christ suffering. Here it treats of his Passion differently from the preceding psalms, because here it shows more especially the insults inflicted upon him than the other evils. Its method is as follows. In the first part, he sets forth a prayer and enumerates the evils inflicted upon him. In the second part, which begins, “I have cried to you, O Lord,” he asks for the Resurrection by reason of certain necessities. In the third part, which begins, “And I cried to you, O Lord,” he shows that his own respond in Christ’s Passion, namely, by enduring many things in imitation of him. Its purpose is to invite us to patience through the example of Christ and his own, according to the Apostle: Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he himself walked.

[Col. 0493A] The voice of Christ himself praying is as follows:

“O Lord God,” author “of my salvation,” that is, of my freedom from sin, “I cried out by day and by night,” that is, I prayed at length, and not before the eyes of men, but “before you.” The one who asks for worldly things cries before the world; the one who desires to possess God alone cries before God.

And because I cried in this way, “let my prayer,” which is like my ambassador to you, “enter” and, since it could enter and afterward be expelled, he says, “into your sight,” that is, in such a way that it may be in your good pleasure. The expression is taken from the likeness of someone who places before himself something pleasing to him. And it is necessary that it enter, “because my soul is filled with evils,” that is, with anxieties. Hence he himself said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew XXIX).

Or “with evils” means with regard to their sins. “And my life has drawn near to [Col. 0493B] hell,” that is, my soul, or, at the time of the Passion, it drew near, before it descended into the underworld. Or it drew near in such a way that it was in hell, to which it descended willingly and which it despoiled.

“And I have been counted among those who descend into the pit,” that is, into hell. Or “into the pit” means into the depth of sins, because by a false opinion they regarded me as a sinner. And because they thought that, once dead, I would remain in hell, “I have become,” in their estimation, one who was merely “like a man” and not God. Although I am “among the dead” in sins, I am nevertheless “free” from every sin. Or “free among the dead” means not held in hell with the other dead, but freeing others.

I have also been regarded as being “without [Col. 0493C] help,” that is, as so contemptible that God would bring me no aid.

I have been regarded “like” the others “wounded, sleeping in tombs,” of whom, O God, “you are no longer mindful,” that is, so that they may rise again to the good. Thus they thought about me when they saw me wounded and lying in the tomb, so that I would not rise again. Or let us understand this allegorically: the wounded in sins sleep, that is, rest, in tombs, namely, in bodies in which they rot, consenting to the pleasures of the flesh. They are not those sleeping whom God recalls from wickedness, but those of whom you, O God, are no longer mindful.

“And,” although they thought that I had been rejected in this way, “they themselves,” and not I, “have been rejected from your hand,” that is, from your protection.

He intensifies his Passion and their wickedness, [Col. 0493D] saying:

“They have placed me,” in their estimation, “in the lower pit,” in the depth of vices, or as one worthy to descend into the depth of hell, namely, “in dark places and in the shadow of death,” that is, in the place where the shadow alone would kill people. Or “in the shadow” means in ignorance, which is the cause of death. Hence it is said: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians XIV).

“Your fury has been confirmed over me,” also in their estimation, that is, they think that you, O God, are continually and entirely angry with me. And besides that fury, Lord, “you have brought all your waves,” that is, the disturbances of this life, “over me.”

And I have suffered persecutions not only from strangers; my friends also failed me. This is: [Col. 0494A] “You have put my acquaintances far from me,” that is, my Apostles, “from me,” as it is read: “They left him and fled.” When the others saw this, “they made me an abomination to themselves,” that is, something to be removed from the company of human beings.

Or the Apostles themselves made me an abomination to themselves, as is read concerning blessed Peter: “He began to curse and swear, saying, ‘I do not know the man.’”

“I have been handed over” also by a disciple, “and I did not go out” to seek vengeance, because he did not display the power of his divinity, which he himself possessed. Hence he also said: “I could ask my Father, and he would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels.”

“And my eyes,” that is, my Apostles, “have languished”—they doubted concerning my Resurrection, as is read of those two who were going to the village of Emmaus and saying: “We [Col. 0494B] were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” I say that they had languished “because of lack,” that is, because they lacked the true light, since they had not yet been fully strengthened by the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Lord, reproving them for their doubt, said: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe,” and so forth.

### “I have cried”

The second part. Although I had been so abandoned by my friends, nevertheless, O “Lord, I cried to you,” asking you to grant the Resurrection, “and I spread out my hands,” that is, my works, “to you,” enlarging them through charity in order to merit it. This I did “all day,” that is, continually, or throughout the whole time of the Passion.

“Will you,” and it is necessary that you resurrect me, because, while I remain in the tomb, “will you work wonders for the dead?” “Will [Col. 0494C] physicians,” that is, the Apostles and preachers, “raise up” their preaching, “and,” once raised in soul, “will they confess to you?” No. He rightly says that they will not raise it up, because they would not even be physicians unless Christ had risen.

“Will” anyone, while I remain “in the tomb, narrate your mercy,” namely, that you grant forgiveness of sins, justify a human being, and so forth? No. Or, if I am lost “in destruction,” in corruption, will anyone narrate “your truth,” concerning the fulfillment of this promise—that all nations will be blessed in the seed of Abraham—and of the other promises? Certainly not.

Or it may be understood in this way: If I have not been resurrected, “will I,” while remaining “in the tomb,” that is, rotting in the pleasure of the flesh, “narrate your mercy?” Or will anyone existing “in destruction,” that is, in the habit of [Col. 0494D] sinning, “narrate your truth” if I have not been resurrected? No.

“And will” your wonders “be known” if I have not been resurrected—namely, the Virgin’s childbirth, the Ascension, and the restoration of the human race—by those placed “in darkness?” No, even if there were someone to preach them.

“And will your justice,” that is, the remission of sins, “be known” by those existing “in the land of forgetfulness,” that is, by those who have forgotten you because of earthly things? No.

### “And I”

The third part. I cried in this way concerning the Resurrection, “and,” having obtained it, “I cried,” through my own people; that is, my people will cry, “to you, O Lord, and my prayer,” having been made “in [Col. 0495A] the morning,” that is, continually, or “in the morning,” namely, in the light of virtues, “will precede you.” This does not mean that they possess the ability to pray without your mercy; rather, he says that their prayer precedes so that you may be made propitious before the Judgment.

I say that my people cry, but “why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer,” that is, the prayer of my people, from you? God seems to reject it when he does not immediately fulfill their desire, namely, that he should immediately strip them from the body and raise them to heavenly things.

“And you turn your face away from me,” that is, from my people, when you permit them to be troubled.

I say, “you turn your face away,” because “I am poor,” that is, my people are poor in worldly things, “and in labors,” in accordance with the persecutions of this world. This has been so “from my youth,” that is, from the time when they became my strong and steadfast people in faith; tribulation has not been absent from them.
