And if I have been exalted—and he adds “but” [Col. 0495B] in worldly things—if my people have prospered, it has profited them nothing, because afterward “I was humbled,” that is, my people were humbled to repentance, “and troubled,” that is, I was troubled in enduring labors, if my people were troubled.

And it is no wonder if I am troubled, because “your wrath,” that is, your vengeance, “has come upon me.” Yet it did not remain upon me, because my people endured it for a time in order afterward to rejoice forever. “And your terrors,” arising from fear of the future Judgment, “have troubled me,” that is, my people.

I rightly say that your wrath passed over me, because evil people, or sins, “surrounded me like waters,” that is, with great inundation, wishing to drown me as water drowns human beings. And these [Col. 0495C] “all day,” that is, continually, not one by one but “together, surrounded me,” that is, surrounded my people.

My people have suffered not only the other evils, but also: “You have put far from me,” that is, from my people, “friend and neighbor,” in kinship; “and my acquaintances,” those whom my people knew or who knew my people. This happened “because of misery,” that is, on account of their misery, for which they were despised.

## On Psalm LXXXVIII

### Title

“The understanding of Ethan the Ezraite or Israelite.”

“The mercies of the Lord.” This psalm is called “understanding” because it contains a hidden matter, namely, that God would give his mercy and truth. This was very hidden before Christ’s coming and known to very few. The psalm is not concerned only with the literal sense, but also [Col. 0495D] with the allegorical sense.

It is called “Ethan,” that is, the name of someone strong, like the Prophet David, because both the Prophet himself and whoever possesses the understanding of this psalm are greatly strengthened against the devil and stand firm in the praise of God. I say “Ethan the Israelite,” not one strong in evil, but a man who sees God; or “the Ezraite,” that is, a newcomer and pilgrim in this world.

The mercy and truth of God are its subject. Its method is as follows. In the first part, he shows that he will speak of mercy and truth, and that he has learned what he will say through God’s teaching. In the second part, which begins, “The heavens will confess,” he shows God’s great power. In the third part, which begins, “Then you spoke,” he shows God’s many promises to his Son. In the fourth [Col. 0496A] part, which begins, “But you have rejected,” he shows that God appears to have acted contrary to his promises: Christ and his own have encountered many evils, although God had promised them many good things. In the fifth part, which begins, “How long, O Lord, will you turn away?” he sets forth prayers concerning the evils that he sees will come upon the Church, and indicates that they do not harm God’s promises.

Its purpose is to admonish us to give thanks to God for the grace and truth bestowed. We may also say that Ezra placed Ethan in the title because he was one of the leaders of the singing together with the other precentors.

The voice of anyone among that former people says:

“I will sing of the mercies of the Lord,” concerning the restoration of the human race, which will endure “forever,” because they will make us eternal. “I will sing,” that is, I will proclaim with song and devotion. [Col. 0496B]

“And I will announce your truth,” that is, the completion of the promises in which you are truthful, “to one generation,” the Jewish generation, “and to another generation,” the Gentile generation. Or “to generation and generation” means through all successive generations. And this will be “with my mouth.”

He calls the same things the mercy and truth of God, namely, God’s benefits: mercy, because they are freely bestowed by God; truth, because God fulfills them according to what he promised. “I will announce,” he says, with my mouth, in which I always have the truth ready to announce to others. Or “with my mouth” means that, just as I have it in my mouth, so I fulfill it in my works.

And relying on whose authority will I announce these things? Yours, clearly. This is: “because you have said,” that is, you have revealed through an inward [Col. 0496C] inspiration to me, the following:

“Mercy will be built forever,” namely, after sins have been forgiven, many spiritual gifts will increase. It will be built, I say, not among the wicked, but “in the heavens,” that is, in the higher holy ones who contain God’s secrets, such as the Apostles. “And your truth,” that is, those same spiritual gifts, “will be prepared in them,” because through them it will descend into others.

“I have established.” You spoke in this way, saying: “I have established a covenant,” that is, I have ordered a pact, not with everyone, but “with my chosen ones,” that is, those whom I chose from the number of the predestined. “And I have also sworn to David my servant,” that is, to Christ; [Col. 0496D] I have made an immutable promise.

For where did he swear to Abraham but also to Christ, concerning whom those promises were made, as the Apostle bears witness: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed, who is Christ”? This is what I swore: “I will prepare your seed,” that is, imitators of Christ’s righteousness, leading them “unto eternity.”

“And I will build your throne,” that is, those in whom you rest and judge, “through one generation,” the Gentile generation, “and another generation,” the Jewish generation. Or: I will prepare your throne, that is, imitators who imitate you, not for a time only, but proceeding from one generation here to the generation to come.

### “The heavens will confess”

The second part. You said, “Mercy will be built,” and just as you said, so it will be fulfilled, because “the heavens,” that is, the Apostles, “will confess your wonders,” such as those concerning the creation of heaven and earth. He shows this among the wonders when he says, [Col. 0407A] “for indeed they will announce your truth.”

They will not announce it everywhere as they announce the wonders, because God’s wonders can be recounted among all nations, but God’s truth concerning the Nativity, the Passion, and so forth can and ought to be proclaimed only “in the assembly of the saints,” in which alone God’s Nativity, Passion, and the other events are both honored and loved.

And rightly the heavens ought to confess your wonders, “because who among the clouds,” that is, among the Apostles and the other higher members of the Church, “will be equal to the Lord” in power? No one.

Or who will be “like God” in substance “among the sons of God,” such as among the holy angels, who are steadfast and deified? No one, because all the others were created and deified by him.

Truly no one will be equal to the Lord, for he is “God,” and such a one [Col. 0407B] “who is glorified in the council of the saints,” that is, whom the saints glorify, and this with great deliberation, because they truly consider how they may praise him more worthily.

I say that God is “great,” because his substance fills all things, and “terrible” because of the Judgment that he himself will carry out. I say that he exists “above all who surround him,” that is, who are in his service and company, surrounding him like soldiers. This may be understood both of the angels and of holy men.

God, I say, is glorified, and God himself is also Lord of all virtues. Therefore no one can be like him. This is what he says by turning to him:

“Lord God of virtues,” whether of the heavenly virtues or the giver of our virtues, through which you make human beings like the heavenly [Col. 0407C] virtues. When you give a human being the fullness of knowledge, you make him like a seraph. Likewise, through the other virtues given to them, you make human beings like the other orders. Therefore, “who is like you?” No one, certainly.

For you are “powerful, O Lord,” from yourself alone, and no one possesses power except through you. “And your truth is around you,” in those in whom your promises have been fulfilled; it is evident that you are truthful in your promises.

Or your truth is around you because, since you have none in your service and company except those who are truthful, it is evident that you are truthful, from whom so great a household has received truth.

Truly you are powerful, because “you rule the power of the sea; you still the movement of its waves,” [Col. 0407D] literally.

Or allegorically: “You rule the power of the sea,” that is, the power of this world, in which no one can do anything unless you permit it. “You still the movement of its waves,” that is, the seditions that are stirred up in the world. “You still them,” although you do not remove them altogether. For you have left persecutions to your saints for their testing.

Literally, Christ stilled the sea when, rising from the boat in which he was sleeping, he commanded the winds and the sea.

“You humbled.” Your power, God, is shown by this also, because you humbled, casting down from heaven into this lower atmosphere, the [Col. 0498A] “proud one,” that is, the devil, who is singularly proud, “like one wounded.” The devil was wounded when he was deprived of the light and dignity with which he had previously shone.

You humbled him, I say, “by the arm of your power,” that is, by your powerful arm, your Son. Your power is also shown in this, because you “scattered your enemies,” the Jews, who were literally scattered throughout the whole world. This too you did by your arm, through which you accomplish all things.

And rightly you caused the enemies to be scattered, “because the heavens are yours, and the earth is entirely yours; the world,” also, “of the earth,” that is, the whole circle of the world, “and its fullness,” such as its fruits, cattle, and other things; “you founded” it, that is, created it. You also created the devil himself.

This is why [Col. 0498B] you created “the north wind,” which, because it is a cold wind, signifies the devil, who lacks all charity and who said of himself: “I will set my throne in the north.” And “the sea,” that is, your enemies, who grow bitter and surge against you, “you created.”

And because you are so powerful, “Tabor and Hermon,” that is, Jews and Gentiles, “will rejoice in your name,” because they will attribute their joy to you, since “your arm” is “with power,” that is, your Son is with efficacy, because nothing can resist his will.

Or, “Tabor and Hermon will rejoice,” that is, they will proclaim your arm with rejoicing, namely, your Son, understanding that he possesses power. This will be to your praise, rejoicing in your name.

Tabor is interpreted as “the coming light,” signifying the Jews, among whom the light, which is Christ, came first. [Col. 0498C] Hermon is interpreted as “anathema,” signifying the Gentiles, who, having come to know Christ, pronounced anathema against the devil.

I say that Tabor and Hermon are with power. And “let your hand,” that is, the operation of that arm, as in the conversion of the wicked to the faith, “be strengthened,” so that it may fortify them in righteousness and faith. And “let your right hand,” that is, that more powerful operation, namely, in the justification and perfection of the righteous, “be exalted,” so that it may lead them as far as heaven.

“Justice and judgment”: when people see that you judge justly, there will be “the preparation of your throne,” because then they will recognize those in whom you have prepared a throne for yourself.

There will be justice and judgment there. Meanwhile, however, there are “mercy and [Col. 0498D] truth,” that is, forgiveness of sins and the other benefits given through mercy and promise. These “will go before your face,” so that, through these benefits preceding you as the future Judge, some may be prepared to be saved with the elect in the Judgment.

And because mercy and truth will go before you, therefore “blessed” is “the people who know this jubilation,” that is, who conceive an inexpressible joy in God, so that conscience itself produces this joy, attributing praise to him and discerning rational service well.

I rightly say “blessed,” because, O “Lord,” they “will walk in the light of your countenance,” that is, in the knowledge of your Son, who is called your countenance because through him you yourself are known. “And they will rejoice all day long,” that is, continually, and “in your name,” glorifying it, “and” at last [Col. 0499A] “they will be exalted in your righteousness,” when they obtain the heavenly kingdom through the righteousness that you have given them.

Therefore they will be exalted, “because you are the glory of their strength,” that is, they attribute their strength to you, not to themselves, and regard you, not themselves, as glorious. And because the one who speaks understands himself to belong to their number, he places himself among them, saying: “And therefore our horn,” that is, our strength, “will be exalted,” that is, will grow greatly, “in your good pleasure,” that is, through your Son, in whom you were well pleased (Matt. 3).

I say that the horn will be exalted because Christ will assume our humanity, through which our humanity too will be exalted. This is what follows: “For the Lord is our assumption,” that is, the Lord will assume our flesh. And he specifies which Lord, saying: “and the Holy One of Israel,” that is, the one who sanctifies Israel, namely Christ, without whom no one has been sanctified, “our king,” that is, Christ himself, who rules us in righteousness.

“Then he spoke.” Part Three. After showing the power of the Son, he shows the promises made to the Son, through which the power of the Son mentioned above is confirmed. The continuation is as follows: You said, “Mercy will be built up for me in the heavens,” and he does not indicate a time by the word “then,” but means “similarly,” just as “you spoke to me” and to other “holy ones of yours in a vision,” that is, in some spiritual revelation. “You said,” that is, you revealed this to them through inspiration: “I have placed my help in the mighty one,” that is, in the Son, whom you established as helper for your faithful, “and” him, “chosen from my people,” because among all other faithful people he was the better, since there was absolutely no sin in him, “I have exalted,” that is, I will exalt him from strength to strength, bringing him even to my right hand.

This is what you said: “I have found David,” that is, Christ himself, “my servant,” faithful, who will offend me in nothing. “And him,” once found, “I have anointed with my holy oil,” that is, with the Holy Spirit.

I truly anointed him with oil, as is shown by this effect: “For my hand,” that is, my works, “will help him” in performing his work, “and my arm,” that is, the Word united to his humanity, “will strengthen him,” so that he will yield to no persecution but will rather grow in strength.

[Col. 0499D] Other promises of God concerning his Son: “Your arm will strengthen him.” Therefore “the enemy,” that is, the devil, “will make no progress against him,” so that when he tempts him he may cause him to consent to his persuasion. “And the son of iniquity,” that is, the devil himself, who undertook to tempt him, “will not add to harming him,” that is, to making him harmful, namely, so that his temptation might achieve an effect in Christ. Or otherwise: “the son of iniquity,” who wished to harm Christ, will at some time “not add, with the other temptations that he had inflicted upon him, to harming him,” that is, he will not even dare to tempt him, as after the resurrection, when he recognized him as truly the Son of God, he was in no way bold enough to presume to tempt him.

[Col. 0500A] And through all these things “I will cut down his enemies,” so that those who were formerly enemies may be cut down and destroyed in their enmity. And this will be “from his face,” that is, through knowledge of him. He speaks as though of some emperor from whose face enemies are scattered. “And I will turn those who hate him to flight,” that is, the vices that they previously embraced will now flee, and they themselves will follow Christ.

“And my truth and my mercy will be with him,” because in him both mercies will be bestowed and all God’s promises will be fulfilled. “And his horn,” that is, Christ’s strength and exalted status, “will be exalted,” that is, will continually increase. Or “will be exalted,” that is, will be manifested throughout the world, and this “in my name,” by extending it.

[Col. 0500B] “And I will place.” Other promises of God concerning his Son. His horn will be exalted, “and” moreover “I will place his hand,” that is, his operation, “in the sea,” that is, in the bitter waves of this age, so that through his hand these people may be turned away from their bitterness. “And in the rivers,” that is, in the waters of baptism, I will place “his right hand,” that is, his propitiation and his more powerful operation, because there all sins are forgiven. Or, “in the rivers,” that is, in rulers, whose concern flows over the people as rivers flow into the sea: Christ’s operation will convert not only the lesser people of this world but also some of the greater.

“He called upon me.” And rightly will I exalt and magnify Christ in this way, because “he called upon me,” saying: “You are my Father, my God,” that is, my creator [Col. 0500C] according to my humanity, “and my protector,” because you united the Word to my humanity, and through this you are the cause “of my salvation,” namely, of my freedom from sin, resurrection, and complete righteousness.

He called upon me in this way, “and I will make him the Firstborn,” that is, I will raise him to immortality before all others, and I will make “him the Most High,” granting him to be acknowledged, “above the kings of the earth,” literally or allegorically.

And I will do this not only for Christ according to his own person, but “I will preserve for him” in his members “my mercy,” leading them through mercy “forever.” And “my covenant,” that is, my pact, and my promises, “will be faithful to him,” fulfilling in his members what was promised concerning them [Col. 0500D].

I say, “I will preserve mercy for him,” “and” through this mercy “I will establish his seed,” that is, his imitators, enduring forever and ever. “And his throne,” that is, his kingdom—namely, those in whom he will sit as judge—I will establish “like the days of heaven,” that is, most glorious, since they are immortal and incapable of suffering.

“But if.” I say that I will preserve and establish it like the days of heaven, not only for those perfected through merit, but also that I will mercifully recall sinners. And this is what I say: “But if” those who ought to be “his sons,” that is, Christ’s, “forsake,” that is, in no way wish to receive, “my law,” “and” if those who ought to be sons [Col. 0501A] “do not walk in my judgments,” namely, in any discernment of mind—that is, if they neither judge justly nor rightly discern what should and should not be done—“I will visit their iniquities with a rod.”

And I will not merely visit those who sin lightly, but “if they profane my righteousnesses,” that is, my acts of justification, “by proclaiming them to others as profane and detestable,” so that by the example of their life the Christian law may appear something to be fled from and detested, “and if they do not keep my commandments,” that is, my rules for living.

“I will visit with a rod,” that is, with lighter correction, “their iniquities,” so that through that correction their iniquities may be erased. “And” if they do not wish to be corrected by the rod, “with blows,” that is, with more severe affliction, [Col. 0501B] I will visit “their sins.”

I will visit them with blows and with a rod, “but I will not scatter my mercy from him,” Christ, understood as both head and body, “nor will I harm” Christ as a whole, so that punishments may remain after death. I say this while existing “in my truth,” that is, as the fulfiller of promises. For God would not fulfill his promises if he harmed Christ and his members.

I say that I will not harm him, “nor will I profane,” that is, make profane and detestable, “my covenant,” that is, my pact, which I made with the ancient fathers. “And” the things “that proceed from my lips,” that is, what I promise through the holy prophets, “I will not make void,” that is, leave unfulfilled.

I will certainly not make them void because I have “sworn,” [Col. 0501C] actually swearing by the angel of Abraham, “by my holiness,” that is, by my holiness; or “by my Holy One,” that is, by my Son, through whom the entire human race is sanctified; and this “once,” that is, irrevocably. Since I have sworn, “if I lie to David” by failing to fulfill the promises, I will not be God. Any impossibility can be fulfilled, because the statement is defective. This indeed I have sworn: “His seed,” David’s seed, that is, Christ’s, “will remain forever.”

“And his throne will be like the sun in my sight,” with respect to the souls in which there will be greater brightness; “and” with respect to the body, that throne itself will be “like the moon.” I do not mean like the waxing and waning moon, as in this life, but “full.” That Christ’s throne will be such is shown by “the faithful witness in heaven,” [Col. 0501D] that is, Christ, whose ascension in our flesh the Prophet had already foreseen in the Holy Spirit.

“But you.” Part Four. You say that you will not scatter mercy and that you will do the rest, yet you nevertheless appear to act in the opposite way, because “you have rejected, despised, and delayed your Christ.” He speaks by comparison, as if some lord, angered against a faithful servant, drives him from his house; once expelled, the servant is despised by many, and that lord also delays becoming reconciled with the faithful servant. Similarly, Christ appears to have been rejected from God’s heavenly kingdom for as long as he dwelt bodily in the present age; during that dwelling Christ was contemptible in the eyes of all his enemies. You also appear to have delayed granting your grace, because you allowed him to remain longer in the misery of this age [Col. 0502A]. In the same way, Christ’s members appear to have been rejected by God, and so forth.

You appear to have rejected him because “you have turned away,” that is, you appear to have turned away, “the covenant,” that is, the pact, “of your servant,” which you made with Christ and his servants, or the things stated above: “I will not scatter my mercy,” and so forth. “And you have profaned his sanctuary,” Christ’s sanctuary, that is, his faithful, in whom he dwelt; you have made them appear profane, and this not in one place only, “but on the earth,” that is, throughout the whole world.

By this you also permit the promises of your servant to appear overturned, because “you have destroyed,” that is, permit to be destroyed, “all his hedges,” that is, all his defenses—namely, good prelates, who perform the office of hedges in defending the Church. You have also “placed,” that is, will place, “his stronghold,” that is, the Apostles, who ought to strengthen others in faith, as “fear,” because they themselves were afraid, like Peter and the others; or “fear,” because when the holy Apostles and martyrs were killed in the most shameful manner, others were afraid to approach the faith.

Once the hedges have been destroyed, “all who pass along the way,” that is, the commandments of God, or Christ himself, who is the way, “have plundered him,” that is, Christ in his members: killing some, incorporating others into themselves, or taking away their goods. Through all these things “the whole Christ has become” “a reproach to his neighbors.”

Thus you have scattered your people, and conversely you have “exalted,” that is, permitted to be exalted in temporal things, “the right hand,” that is, the power, “of those who oppress him.” In this you have “gladdened all his enemies,” that is, the malicious enemies of Christ and his members.

You have also “turned away the help of his sword,” Christ’s sword, namely, the help of the word of God, so that his own people no longer have any defense through the divine word. “And” you have also “not helped him in battle” against the heretics, so that sometimes they are overcome and incorporated into the heretics. For God permits many who, according to human judgment, appear to be transferred from the body of Christ into the body of the devil.

You have also “destroyed him,” Christ in his members, “from purification,” because the persecutions sent for their purification do not improve them [Col. 0502D] but rather destroy them and cause them to withdraw from the body of Christ. “And you have struck down his seat,” that is, those in whom Christ appeared both to sit and to rest; that is, you permit them to be destroyed. I say that they have been struck down and cast “upon the earth,” that is, into an appetite for earthly things.

You have also “shortened the days of his time,” or of his members. For when someone appears useful in the Church and destined to be preserved by God, he soon dies and is taken away. And what more can I say? You have “covered him,” Christ, “with confusion.” For the righteous will be confounded either by their past sins or by the punishments inflicted upon them.

“Where are you, Lord?” Part Five. Through all these things you appear to have turned away from those members, but “how long, Lord, will you turn away” from them? That is, how long will you permit them to appear turned away from you? Will this last “to the end,” that is, in every way? May this never happen, Lord. And how long, Lord, will “your anger,” that is, your vengeance, which “will blaze like fire,” that is, will persist or become this way until the end? Let it not be so, Lord. He compares God’s anger with fire, because just as fire consumes soft things and tests solid ones, so God’s vengeance consumes the weak and makes the strong proven.

Do not turn away, Lord, but rather “remember what my substance is,” that is, how fragile human nature is. For unless you remember this, “you have established all the children of men in vain,” because they will not be freed from the devil’s power. But did you establish all the children of men “for nothing,” without intending to receive due praise from them? Far be it, Lord.

[Col. 0503B] I say this to you so that you may remember, because there is no one else who can help. Hence he says: “What man is there who will live and not see death?” No one, certainly. And he says this: Who “will rescue his soul from the hand of hell,” that is, from the power of hell? No one.

I also say “remember” because you have been accustomed to show mercies to the ancient fathers, and you swore that you would do so. This is what he presents in the form of a question: “Where are your former mercies, Lord,” that is, the mercies that you were accustomed to show to the ancient fathers? I speak of mercies to be fulfilled, “as you swore to David,” that is, to Christ your Son, remaining “in your truth,” because you always fulfill whatever you promise. God swore, as was said above, that his seed would remain forever.

[Col. 0503C] And since you have sworn, “remember the reproach of your servants,” that is, what your servants endure. I speak of the reproach “of many nations,” that is, the reproach inflicted upon your servants by many nations. “That reproach” I “held in my bosom,” that is, in my soul, in which I retained the reproaches because I thought they would be useful to me.

“That reproach” “your enemies, Lord, have reproached,” that is, cast in my face. “That they have reproached”: I speak of a reproach not arising from any fault of Christ or his people, but from “the transformation of your Christ,” namely, that which Christ and his people did as the cause of transforming human beings from mortality to immortality. For they reproached the crucified Christ, and said that his followers were ragged and contemptible, and so forth. [Col. 0503D] By repeating “they have reproached,” he indicates the persistence of the reproach.

They reproached him, but did not prevail. And this is what follows: “Blessed be the Lord forever,” because he has freed us from all tribulations. “Let it be, let it be.” In this repetition he signifies a strong affirmation. Here he shows that the adversities mentioned above do not destroy God’s promises.

## ON PSALM 89

### TITLE

“A prayer of Moses, the man of God.”

“Lord, a refuge.” Observe that the psalm is not attributed to “Moses” because Moses composed it among his prayers, as some maintain, since this prayer is found nowhere in the books of Moses. Rather, although David composed this psalm, as he did the others, Ezra the prophet understood that in this psalm David prayed to God for the liberation of the faithful people, explaining the human defect in the manner in which Moses was accustomed to pray to God. Therefore he called this psalm the prayer of Moses, that is, one resembling the prayers Moses used to make.

This psalm is called a prayer because what it contains is either a prayer for our redemption or reasons why one ought to pray for human beings. “A prayer of Moses, I say, the man of God”: he says this to distinguish him from others who are called Moses. Or he says “man” because through the human defect that he describes in the psalm—a defect shared with every human being—he displays Moses’ nature and shows that Moses himself was human. Therefore he adds “of God,” because he shows God as the liberator from human defect, both for Moses and for the other children of God.

The subject is liberation and the overcoming of human defects. The method is as follows: in the first part, he shows God as powerful, able to free a human being from any defect whatsoever. In the second part, which begins, “Do not turn man away,” he prays for God’s liberation and describes, in opposition to it, the many defects of human beings. In the third part, which begins, “Make your right hand known in this way,” he prays for the coming of Christ, through whom he understands that all future liberation of the human race will take place. The purpose is to remove despair from us, so that although we recognize our manifold defect, we nevertheless do not despair of salvation when we attend to God our liberator.

[Col. 0504C] It is as though the Prophet who speaks were saying: “Now, brothers, let us not despair, because we have God, to whom we may flee for refuge.” And this is what he says: “Lord,” God who were previously angry with us when, through the sin of our first parent, we fled from you, now “you have become a refuge for us,” to whom we flee in every danger and in whom we find security against our enemies. God was a refuge for them through the hope of the future Savior that they possessed.

I say, “you have become a refuge,” and this not merely for a few, but “from” the first “generation” of the righteous, extending to the last “generation.” When he says that God has become a refuge for us, he implies that God wishes our liberation; when he then declares him eternal, he shows that he is one who can liberate us.

[Col. 0504D] I say, “You have become a refuge for us,” but I do not thereby say that you have come into existence in time. Rather, “before the mountains,” that is, the angelic creation, “were made,” or before “the earth” that we see, “and the world,” that is, the firmament itself, together with all that it contains, “you are,” that is, you possess true being. Hence it is said in Moses: “He who is sent me to you” (Exod. 3). And you truly are because you are “God.”

Although he had shown that God existed before all creatures, he adds “from age to age,” that is, without beginning, because God might otherwise have had a beginning and be expected to have an end. Another translation has “from eternity.” And “to age of age,” that is, without end, you are. Another translation has “forever.”

[Col. 0505A] “Do not turn away.” Part Two. It says: Because, O Lord, you are such, therefore “do not turn away” from yourself, permitting the “man” placed “in humility,” that is, in the abasement and miseries of this life, to cling to earthly things. Or he is one tending toward humility by desiring lowly and transient things. Since man is in humility, you ought not to turn him away. And for this further reason: because you have said through many prophets—and even if no other had said it, what this Prophet said to us would be sufficient—“Turn back, children of men,” because if “you turn back to me, I will turn back to you.”

“Because of mercy.” He shows the manner of human humility and abasement. The continuation is: There is need for you not to turn man away “because,” among the other evils that human beings endure, they have this: their life, however long it may be, is considered nothing. Thus “a thousand years,” that is, however long a human life may be, compared with the life that is “before your eyes,” that is, eternity, is “like yesterday.” It is comparable to yesterday only in that yesterday has passed; hence he says, “which has passed.” Just as a day that has passed is considered nothing, so too is a human life, however long. No one is recorded as having lived a thousand years, but even if someone lived that long, such a life would have to be regarded as nothing.

I say that a thousand years are like a day that has passed, “and” like “a watch in the night,” that is, actions performed in labor and blindness. A watch is always occupied with vigilance. By night we understand the blindness in which the children of the age are held. And, to say even more, “their years” “will be” among those things “that are considered nothing,” like things possessed only in a dream.

“Morning.” He enumerates other human defects. I say that the years are regarded as nothing, and so may it be, Lord. This is what follows: “In the morning” of man, that is, in infancy, “may he pass away,” that is, perish quickly, “like grass,” which easily withers. “In the morning,” that is, in youth—which is called morning because a person is still growing—“may he flower,” that is, flourish in bodily strength, knowledge, and in whatever other ways; “and may he pass away in the evening,” that is, in old age, when a person is decrepit; “may he fall,” stripped of all bodily vigor and consumed by labor and pain; “may he become hard” as a corpse, “and may he wither” when reduced to dust.

The passage may also be connected in this way: I pray that you not turn man away, but I do not thereby ask that he escape temporal defects and the punishment of sin.

I therefore allow that he should fall, pass away, and suffer similar things because I see that it cannot be otherwise, “because” “we have failed,” that is, we suffer many defects. And this is “in your anger,” that is, in the vengeance you exact for the sin of our first parent. Beyond the evils that we already endure, “we have also been troubled” inwardly “in your fury,” that is, in our consideration of the coming judgment, in which you will exercise your fury.

I say that we fail in your anger because you, God, “have placed our iniquities before your sight,” that is, you have imposed punishment for our sins. For just as God is said not to look upon sins when he forgives them, so he is said to look upon them when he punishes them. You have also placed “our age,” that is, our entire life, “in the illumination of your countenance,” that is, you have seen it most clearly, in order to punish each sin, since not even a thought will be hidden from your countenance.

“Because.” I rightly say that you have placed our iniquities before your sight, as is shown by the effect: “because all our days have failed,” that is, human life has been made short, and while we live, we live in misery and labor. This is what follows: “and in your anger we have failed.”

“Our years.” Here is how we have failed: “our years will meditate,” that is, we will meditate through our years. He says “meditate” because a person never reaches perfection in such works. He compares them to “a spider,” which makes a vain and worthless work in order to catch worthless prey, namely flies, and in this work exhausts its whole self.

Similarly, human beings perform vain deeds and expend great labors in order to obtain things that are worthless and transient. In this they consume their entrails, because they lose body and soul alike. And because in our years we might meditate sometimes well and sometimes badly, he adds: “the days of our years” will meditate like a spider, because we never cease from vain meditation for even one day. Hence Solomon says in Ecclesiasticus: “Why are you proud, dust and ashes? In your lifetime you cast out your inward parts.” And I rightly say, “our days have failed,” because “in them,” in our days, to say the most, according to the human lifespan, there are “seventy years,” that is, if someone lives a long time, he lives seventy years.

Or let them read “will meditate” passively, as follows: “Our years,” that is, our entire life, “will meditate,” that is, will be judged by the wise, like a spider.

“But if.” I say that the human lifespan is seventy years: “but if” it is “in strengths,” namely, if a person lives with bodily vigor, then “there are eighty years, and more than these.” That is, if they live longer, their life is “labor” for the body and “pain” for the mind.

Or we may understand “seventy” and “eighty” allegorically. By seventy we understand the Old Testament, which spoke of temporal things and promised only temporal things, as it says there: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land.” This entire life also turns through seven days, during which we make use of these temporal things.

By eighty we understand the New Testament, in which, after temporal things have been set aside, we are taught to desire heavenly things alone. We are taught to desire eternal rest, which follows when the seven days of this life have ended. Our nature has already received this rest in Christ, in the resurrection accomplished on the eighth day. The rest kept by the Jews on the seventh day was a sign of that rest.

According to this interpretation, the text should be read as follows: “Our years will meditate like a spider,” as above; nevertheless, there will be days, that is, illuminations, of our years, and in those days, that is, in those illuminations, there will be “seventy years” of life lived according to the Old Testament.

Another translation has “seventy years,” which may be read this way: “Our years will meditate like a spider,” but the days of our years, that is, the illuminations that we have in our years, are within seventy years. “Those” is not relative but demonstrative.

The years lived according to the Old Testament were not “in strengths,” because no one under the Old Testament, however holy—even though they are called people of the New Testament—could reach the eighth day before Christ’s death, that is, the rest signified by the rest celebrated on the seventh day and designated by the eighth day.

But if “in strengths” are our days, then they are eighty years, that is, life lived according to the New Testament. It is said to be “in strengths” because the faithful of the New Testament are led immediately into rest after death. “And more than these, their labor and pain,” that is, whatever is done outside the Old and New Testaments, is labor and pain, because if someone lives without these, he will inherit labors and pains in eternal miseries.

“Because.” God has shortened life and imposed labors and pains “because gentleness has come upon us,” that is, God’s mercy has come upon his anger and tempered it, so that God’s anger is now not for our condemnation but for our purification. “And” through that divine gentleness “we will be corrected” from our sins.

“Who?” Since God makes his anger gentle, not so that he will fail to punish us but also so that he may correct us, therefore “who knows the power,” that is, the efficacy, “of your anger,” that is, who considers that your anger has been given for correction? “And” who knows “how to count your anger,” namely, so as to consider that there are benefits in your vengeance just as there are adversities? I speak of anger inflicted “because of your fear,” that is, so that a person may fear you.

“Your right hand.” Part Three. Lord, just as you have brought anger upon us, “so,” Lord, “make your right hand,” that is, your Son, through whom you will bring liberation to the human race, “known,” namely, so that we may receive him in faith and love. “And” make us “learned in heart,” not in carnal things but “in wisdom,” namely, so that in Christ himself we may understand your dignity.

Or: you have given anger, and thus, that is, through that anger, make your right hand known, that is, your Son, so that by attending to the miseries inflicted upon us for our sins, we may recognize Christ as our liberator.

“Make your right hand known,” and through that right hand “turn” toward us, “Lord,” us who have turned, “until when,” that is, until the other aspect of conversion, namely, so that you may forgive sins. Another translation has “for a little while,” and “be approachable in entreaty toward your servants.”

I now ask you to turn, so that you may be approachable in entreaty, because now, Lord, “we have been filled in the morning with your mercy,” through hope in Christ’s resurrection, which we believe will come in the morning through the illumination of virtues. We have not only been filled with mercy, but have also “rejoiced” in hope of that mercy, [Col. 0508A] “and” have also “taken delight” amid the many evils of this life. This is what follows: “through all our days,” which are known never to pass without misery.

“And we have not only rejoiced amid evils, but the evils themselves make us rejoice.” This is what follows: “We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us.” And I do not speak only of the days but also of the “years” in “which” miseries may be more numerous than in days, years in which “we have seen” through experience itself “evils,” that is, many adversities inflicted upon us. For when we consider that these evils benefit us for eternal life, the hope of that life generates great joy in us.

I say “turn,” and “look” with the eye of mercy [Col. 0508B] “upon your servants and upon your works,” both because they are your servants and because you made them. “And direct their children” into steadfastness: “children,” that is, imitators.

I say “look,” “and” in this way “may the splendor of the Lord our God,” that is, the illumination of the Holy Spirit, be “upon us.” Or “splendor,” that is, the cross of Christ, so that we may understand Christ’s victory accomplished on the cross, where he deprived the devil of his power and restored life to us. “And” through that splendor “direct the works of our hands,” namely, every work. And may the splendor of God also be “upon us,” that is, in our soul, which is the higher part. “And” through that splendor “direct the work of our hands,” namely, charity, which is the special work.

Or we may speak under a single division: “Direct the works of our hands upon us,” that is, so that those works may lead us to a greater height than we are worthy of. Or “upon us,” that is, so that we may work for heavenly things and not for temporal things.

## ON PSALM 90

### TITLE

“A hymn of praise to David.”

“He who dwells.” This psalm is called a hymn because it sets before us a matter over which we ought especially to rejoice. It also shows us how God rescues all his faithful from every kind of temptation; in this, he himself appears as a liberator worthy of praise to all. Therefore it is appropriately called “a hymn of praise,” as if to say, “a praiseworthy hymn,” and it is attributed to the Prophet David, who speaks.

Its subject is God’s deliverance, which he grants to the entire body of the righteous from every kind of temptation; conversely, it concerns the temptations from which the righteous are delivered.

The method is as follows: in the first part, he shows what kind of person is delivered by God, namely, one who hopes entirely in the Lord. In the same part he shows what God’s protection is like, from how many dangers it delivers, and how boundless that divine protection is. In the second part, which begins, “They will fall at your side,” he shows that Christ will finally condemn the wicked, who persecute his own here through many temptations, and will reward his own. In the third part, which begins, “Because he hoped in me,” the Prophet introduces God promising Christ’s members both protection in this life [Col. 0509A] and, after this life, eternity.

The purpose is to instruct us against temptations, namely, so that we may understand that we can never resist temptations by our own strength, but must always flee to God and await deliverance from him.

It is as though the Prophet were saying: “All you righteous people, do not presume upon yourselves, but cast all your hope upon the Lord, because whoever dwells,” that is, perseveres, “in help,” that is, does not think that he has any help elsewhere, but understands that this is the place in which he ought to dwell well, because he himself is the Most High. This is what follows: “of the Most High.”

Whoever dwells in this way “will remain in the protection of God,” that is, will be continually protected by God—God, I say, “of heaven,” by which the strength and greatness of his protection are signified.

In this first verse the entire substance of this first part is indicated, although it is contained briefly. When he says, “he who dwells,” he identifies the one who is to be delivered. When he says “in the protection of God,” he identifies the protector and gives us to understand from what things that protection is granted, namely, from temptations.

“He will say.” He shows what kind of person dwells in help: he is the one who “will say to the Lord: You are my protector,” because you have taken me up from the lowliness of sin to the height of righteousness, which I could in no way attain by my own strength. Placed there, when dangers threatened, I do not trust in my own strength, but you, God, are “my refuge,” to whom I flee so that I may be delivered from every danger that presses upon me. And this is always so, because “he is my God; I will hope in him.” I will never presume upon myself in anything, but in every need I will always return to him.

I will rightly hope because “he will deliver me from the snare,” that is, from the evil deeds, “of those who hunt,” that is, of demons and wicked people, who hunt human beings as hunters hunt wild animals. This righteous person says that he has been delivered from their deeds because by no deeds can they make him conform to themselves. “And” he has also delivered me “from the harsh word.” The righteous person regards a word as harsh either when he is afflicted with insults or when he is tempted with flattering words intended to deceive him.

“With his shoulders.” Having shown what the person to be delivered is like, he shows what the deliverance is like.

The continuation is this: You say, “I will hope in him,” and God himself “will overshadow you,” that is, will protect you in such a way that you do not feel the heat, “with his shoulders,” that is, with his power and strength, which are understood by the shoulders because this is the stronger part of birds’ wings. “And under his wings,” that is, under his mercy or under his commandments, by which God’s people fly toward heaven, “you will hope.”

And if danger threatens, “he will surround you with a shield,” so that your enemies cannot harm you—“his truth,” that is, he himself, so that through this he may appear truthful. For if he did not protect his own, he would prove false to his promises. Here he sets out from how many temptations God delivers a human being.

And because he will surround you, therefore “you will not fear the fear of the night,” O Christ, together with all your members, namely, a light and hidden temptation.

And you will also not fear “the arrow flying by day” [Col. 0510A], that is, a light and manifest temptation. Nor will you fear “the affair proceeding in darkness,” that is, some grave and hidden temptation, such as the plot by which the Jews secretly prepared Christ’s death. By “affair” we understand any very serious actions undertaken to seduce someone, as when heretics labor intensely to deceive a righteous person. In saying “proceeding,” he indicates perseverance in those actions; in saying “in darkness,” he indicates a hidden temptation. Nor will you fear “the assault and the noonday demon,” that is, the assault of the noonday demon: we will not fear a very grave and manifest persecution, such as would occur if some wicked bishop were to preach and command fornication or simony [Col. 0510B], like the mad Guibertus. By saying “assault,” he indicates a violent and impetuous temptation; by saying that it was brought by a “demon,” he indicates a very grave and tireless persecutor; by saying “noonday,” he indicates that it is manifest. Jerome, in his work against Origen, calls the boldness of heresy the “noonday demon.” Here he has noted four kinds of temptation: two light ones, one hidden, through the nocturnal fear, and the other manifest, through the arrow flying by day; and again two grave ones, one hidden, through the affair proceeding in darkness, and the other manifest, through the assault of the noonday demon.

“Thousands shall fall at your side.” The second part. I say that you, O Christ, with your members, will fear neither any nocturnal fear nor any kind of temptation; rather, you will condemn [Col. 0510C] those wicked people who bring temptations upon you and yours. Hence he says: O Christ, “a thousand,” that is, innumerable people who presume that they will be at your side and judge together with you, “will fall at your side,” that is, they will not be reckoned among those who will be your counselors and judges. “And ten thousand,” that is, innumerable people who presume that they will be placed at your right hand, that is, among the saved, will fall “at your right hand,” because they will be placed on the left. He says that a thousand will fall at his side, and more at his right hand, because there are more who presume that they will be saved than who presume that they will judge together with Christ. They will fall, and “none of such people will in any way approach you”; rather, they will be hurled into hell when you say to them: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” [Col. 0510D].

I say, “he will not approach,” “nevertheless” the opposite will occur: for you, O Christ, “will look upon” everything, namely, the sins of human beings, “with your eyes,” from which not even the deepest thought can be hidden; “and” then “you will see,” that is, you will make visible and known to all “the retribution,” that is, the just condemnation, “of sinners.”

“For.” I rightly say that he will condemn sinners, because [he will save] me and the other righteous; and he says this: “For you, O Lord” Christ, “are my hope,” in whom I ought rightly to hope, because you “have made the Most High,” that is, God, “your refuge.” You have placed no security for yourself in a human being or in anything worldly, but in God alone, in whom alone security can be found, because he himself is the Most High.

And because you placed your refuge in God, therefore “evil shall not approach you,” namely, any sin: for Christ was free from every sin; “and the scourge,” that is, correction or punishment for sin, “shall not approach your tabernacle,” in which you served God for a time. When he says that Christ was saved because he made God his refuge, he intimates the salvation of the other righteous, because they place their hope in God.

Therefore “evil shall not approach you, for he has commanded his angels concerning you,” that is, he has issued an order concerning you, O Christ, “that they guard you in all your ways,” that is, in all your works, according to what is said: “And angels came and ministered to him” [Col. 0511B].

“In their hands.” I say that “he has commanded his angels,” and those angels “will carry you,” that is, they will help you, “in their hands,” that is, through their works, by ministering and serving you. Therefore they will carry you “lest you strike your foot,” that is, your affection, “against a stone,” that is, against the law, which is signified by the stone because it was written on stone tablets. Christ would have stumbled against the law if he had understood it as something to be fulfilled carnally. Or, the angels will carry you in their hands as they did at the Ascension.

The angels serve you, and you “will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.” Through these four, the devil is understood [Col. 0511C], but for different reasons. Through the asp the devil is signified, because just as the asp secretly sends forth poison, so the devil secretly sends temptations by which he may kill the souls of the faithful. Christ walked upon him because no hidden temptation of the devil could hinder him. Through the basilisk, which openly sends forth poison, the devil is understood as one who openly tempts the faithful. Christ walked upon him when, having been openly tempted by the devil in his death, he was in no way overcome by those temptations. Through the lion the devil is understood insofar as he acts violently, as when he dared to lay hands on Christ and deliver him to death. Through the dragon the devil is understood insofar as he devours and incorporates into himself all whom he can; Christ walked upon him when by his death he destroyed the devil’s power [Col. 0511D].

“For.” The third part. I say that “he has commanded his angels concerning you,” saying to them: “Because he hoped in me”—the whole Christ, although here he is speaking chiefly about his members—“I will deliver him,” that is, lest the members of Christ be struck by the weapons of the enemy. “I will protect him, because he has known my name,” namely, he did not seek his own glory but mine.

“He cried to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation,” that is, then “I will rescue him,” so that thereafter no tribulation will surround him. This rescue occurs at the end of each of the faithful’s life; “and I will glorify him,” in his members.

[Col. 0512A] Thus I will glorify him, namely because “I will fill him with length of days,” that is, with eternity. “I will show” Christ “my salvation” in his members, that is, Christ the Savior, who will be the true life and refreshment of all.

## Psalm XCI. Title

*A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day.*

“It is good to confess to the Lord.” This psalm is called a treatise because it exhorts us to act well, namely to confess and sing psalms to the Lord. It is “a psalm, I say, of a song,” that is, of great rejoicing experienced on the Sabbath day, that is, in contemplation of eternal rest, which is signified by the Sabbath. For on the Sabbath God rested from every work that he had accomplished, and that rest of the Lord was a sign of the rest that the faithful will have after the labors of this life. The Lord also commanded people in the Law to rest on the Sabbath as a sign of that same eternal rest. Since our nature fully obtained that rest in Christ’s resurrection, and since we possess, as it were, the thing signified already, we do not observe Sabbath rest as a festival.

This psalm shows that although the righteous labor in this life, they will nevertheless obtain everlasting rest, concerning which each of the faithful ought especially to rejoice. The subject is the righteous person laboring in this life and ultimately attaining the rest of eternal blessedness; conversely, the unrighteous person, resting in this life, will ultimately labor in the next. The method is as follows: in the first part, it exhorts us to act well and to labor in this life, so that at last we may rejoice [Col. 0512C] in eternal blessedness; therefore it is called “a psalm of a song,” that is, dependent upon a song. In the second part, which begins, “The foolish man,” it is shown that the unrighteous, who flourish and rest in this life, where one ought to labor, will labor under condemnation in the next life. In the third part, which begins, “The righteous shall flourish like the palm,” it shows the rest that the saints will have after this life. Its purpose is to console us amid the labors of this life, through which we are led to eternity.

The Prophet’s voice is as though he were saying: You righteous, do not despair amid the labors of this life, but rather confess and sing psalms, because “it is good to confess to the Lord,” in both senses of confession, namely, by accusing oneself of one’s sins and by praising God. After confession, it is good “to sing psalms,” that is, to act well [Col. 0512D], not for human glory but “to your name,” that is, to enlarge your name, O “Most High.” Therefore your name is rightly to be enlarged.

I say that it is good to confess and sing psalms, “to announce,” that is, so that people may announce to others “your mercy in the morning,” that is, in the prosperity of your benefits, namely, your virtues, so that if they possess any virtues, they may announce that these come not from themselves but from God’s mercy; “and” to announce “your truth,” that is, your justice, “through the night,” that is, in adversity. If they experience adversity, they should recognize that it comes from God’s justice, since he justly punishes them for what they have done.

He shows how we ought to sing psalms, namely “on the psaltery,” that is, through spiritual action, such as in the contemplative life; “with ten strings,” that is, fulfilling the ten commandments of the Law. And it is good to sing psalms to the Lord “on the lyre,” that is, in the mortification of the flesh, and this not with sadness but “with rejoicing.”

Therefore I say that it is good to confess and sing psalms, “because,” O “Lord, you have delighted me in your work,” that is, in the good “works” that you created and performed in me. Henceforth “I will rejoice” in all the good things that are “the works of your hands,” that is, of your activity, because no one acts well unless you act, rather than the person acting by himself.

And because you not only perform good things in me but also cause me to delight in those good works, I may rightly say: “How great are your works, O Lord,” and “how” greatly they have been made—beyond what can be expressed—“and your thoughts,” that is, your dispositions, which arise from thought and counsel, such as the fact that the good are afflicted and the wicked flourish, “are exceedingly deep,” that is, unsearchable. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm XXXV).

“The foolish man.” The second part. God’s thoughts are indeed so deep, yet “the foolish man,” that is, one who is wise in worldly matters and lacks true wisdom, “will not know these things” that I am about to say; and “the fool,” that is, one who is wise neither in God nor in the world, “will not understand these things.”

Namely, “when sinners have sprung up,” who are said to spring up when they attain great riches or great powers, “like grass,” that is, comparable to grass, which, although it flourishes and is beautiful for a time, quickly withers; “and have appeared,” that is, have become distinguished by their powers, “all who work iniquity” will become known to many.

They will not understand this: that when they have “sprung up” in this way, that is, however they have prospered, they will “perish forever and ever.” They will perish, but “you, O Lord,” who appeared humble in the world, will remain “the Most High forever.”

And truly they will perish, “for,” O “Lord, behold, your enemies,” that is, the gentiles, “will perish.” Or the word is repeated in order to make credible something that might appear almost incredible. “They will perish,” I say, “and all who work iniquity will be scattered.” In addition to the word “perish,” “they will be scattered” indicates that they will be separated from the good.

They will perish, “but my horn,” that is, my exaltation, which is “like that of a unicorn,” because it tends toward one thing, namely God himself. Hence it is said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord.” It “will be exalted,” by receiving immortality and freedom from suffering. “And my old age,” that is, my final state, namely what follows after this life, “will be in abundant mercy,” that is, in abundant recompense, just as, conversely, the old age of the impious will be in abundant wickedness.

I say, “my old age will be in abundant mercy,” “and” now “my eye,” the inner eye, “has looked down upon my enemies,” recognizing that their life is useless and their power short-lived; “and my ear will hear” what follows from those who rise up against me in wickedness, that is, [Col. 0514A] against me.

“Planted.” The third part. Namely, “the righteous will flourish” in the other life “like a palm tree.” He rightly compares the righteous to a palm tree, because just as the trunk of a palm is ugly below but above is lofty, beautiful, and flowering, so the righteous person, outwardly ugly in this life—which is the lower state—because of tribulations, ragged and worn down by many afflictions, will flourish in the other life “and multiply” in the ineffable glory of eternal blessedness “like the cedar of Lebanon,” which grows taller than other cedars and is imperishable. Thus the righteous will be when enriched with height and immortality.

And rightly will they multiply there, because here they are “planted in the house of the Lord,” that is, firmly rooted in the present [Col. 0514B] Church. For this reason “they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is represented by courts because of its spaciousness. Or, in the court of the house of our God, that is, at the beginning of the heavenly dwelling, namely, at the judgment itself, they will flourish.

And “still,” that is, in addition to those acts of justice that the righteous now possess, “they will multiply” “in abundant old age,” that is, in the final state, where God’s mercy will be rich and abundant. “And” meanwhile “they will be patient,” properly patient rather than falsely, as hypocrites are, “so that they may announce,” that is, so that they may be worthy to announce to others this: that the Lord our God is upright in repaying each person’s merits, and that, after repaying merits—not merely as much as those merits themselves would demand—he adds: “and there is no iniquity in him,” because he gives each person even more than he or she deserved.

Or he is “upright” when he permits his own people to be afflicted so that he may reward them in the other life; “and there is no iniquity in him” because he permits the wicked to flourish in this life, whom he will condemn to eternal punishment in the next.

## Psalm XCII. Title

*Praise of a song of David, on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded or inhabited.*

“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty.” Literally, the earth was founded on the sixth day—not because it was then formed, but because on the sixth day the human being was made. With that creation, the earth was founded, that is, made stable and possessed; it would have been empty and founded in vain if it had no human possessor.

Or, on the sixth day it was inhabited by the human being, when the human being was made. Yet we are not dealing with this literal foundation, but with what it signifies, namely, the restoration of humanity, accomplished through Christ’s blood in the sixth age, that is, in the time of grace. This sixth age is signified by the sixth day; just as the Sabbath follows the sixth day, so true rest follows the sixth age.

The title is explained as follows: this treatise is called “praise of a song,” that is, a praiseworthy song. It is called a song because it sets forth something worthy of rejoicing, namely, the foundation of the Church and Christ’s many other powers, in which Christ himself is shown to be praiseworthy. Hence it is called “praise of a song,” attributed to the Prophet David, who speaks here: “Of a song,” I say, possessed “on the day before the Sabbath,” that is, in contemplation of the first day of the sixth age. This day is so called because in it we receive true illumination. This age is before the Sabbath, that is, before eternal rest, “when,” that is, on that day, namely, in the time of grace, “the earth was founded,” that is, humanity was restored, through which the earth was founded and made stable. It would have been empty unless humanity had been restored, because although all things were made for the praise of God, no earthly creature except the human being would praise him if humanity did not live.

The subject is Christ, the founder of the Church, concerning whom he speaks through many commendations, using the demonstrative mode. Foreseeing that Christ would come in humility and therefore be despised by the Jews, the Prophet commends him in many ways so that, when he comes, we may not disparage him but render him the honor that is due [Col. 0515B]. His purpose is that we should not despise Christ because of his humility, but believe him to be God and Redeemer.

It is as though the Prophet were saying: All of you who see Christ in humility, do not despise him, because the very one who will come in humility is the same one of whom it is said, “The Lord has reigned,” that is, by his death he overcame the dominion of death and the strong armed man, namely the devil.

After establishing that he is speaking about Christ the King, he commends him, saying: He who reigned in this way “has clothed himself with beauty,” that is, he had the Godhead united to himself. This is the first part of the psalm’s commendation. That same Lord “has clothed himself with strength,” that is, with power, because he has always endured steadfastly and powerfully. This is another part. “And” because he was such, “he girded himself,” [Col. 0515C] that is, he prepared himself for the establishment of the Church. This is said by comparison with a workman, who is readier for work when girded.

He shows in effect that he girded himself. Truly he girded himself, “for he established” in faith “the inhabited world,” that is, the Church gathered from the whole circuit of the earth. This inhabited world is so firm that it “will not be moved” by any temptation. This is another portion of the psalm’s commendation.

And “from that time,” that is, from the time when you established the inhabited world, the Church itself is “your prepared seat,” in which you sit and rest. I say that the seat was prepared for you through that foundation. And lest it be understood as temporal because of this, he shows that it is eternal when he says, “you are from eternity,” that is, from everlasting—not made in the world, but the maker of the world. Or it may be understood thus: Your seat is prepared, and from that time you too have existed from eternity.

This is another commendation. Another part. Although the Church was founded in this way, nevertheless “the rivers,” that is, the powerful people of this world, “have raised up,” O Lord, “the rivers have raised up their voice,” that is, their threats and their opposition, against that holy Church of yours. By repeating “they have raised up,” he indicates the perseverance of those powerful people against the Church.

“ The rivers have raised up” their own “waves,” that is, their persecutions and disturbances, against the Church. The rivers were stirred up “by the voices,” that is, by the admonitions, “of many waters,” that is, of many peoples [Col. 0516A]. The lesser often stir up the stronger to persecute the Church.

And not only have the rivers raised their waves against the Church, but there have also been made “the exaltations of the sea,” that is, of all peoples, “wondrous,” that is, infinite and intolerable. Yet “in” all these lofty exaltations “the Lord is wondrous,” by calming such uprisings, or because he does not allow his faithful person to be overcome by any such temptation. These three verses, which contain Christ’s victory, constitute the fifth part of the psalm.

“Your testimonies,” that is, the prophecies and other Scriptures, “have become exceedingly credible,” that is, greatly so, since whatever was promised in them was fulfilled when you came. This is the sixth part of the psalm’s commendation [Col. 0516B]. And, O Lord, “holiness befits your house,” that is, the present Church in which you dwell; the holiness of that house is its fitting adornment, just as it is said: “Royal robes befit a royal house.” And this is so “for length of days,” that is, forever. This is the seventh part of the psalm’s commendation.

## Psalm XCIII. Title

*A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the Sabbath.*

“God of vengeance, the Lord.” This psalm belongs to the Prophet David, who speaks here, and concerns things signified by things made on the fourth day of the week. On the fourth day God made the heavenly lights, by which the holy men who shine in the Church are signified; these are discussed in this psalm.

There are certain kinds of darkness in this world, such as the fact that people think God does not care for earthly affairs when they see the proud torment widows, orphans, and other people of God, whom the Lord himself had commanded in the Law to be treated mercifully. Yet these darknesses neither obscure nor extinguish the lights of the holy Church, because the good are never led into the error of thinking that God does not order earthly affairs. Rather, they patiently endure these evils, confident of their reward, and continually shine among the wicked by providing examples of good action, according to what is said: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world.”

The subject is the saints, shining with the splendor of virtues amid the evils of this life; conversely, it is those proud people who, while persecuting God’s poor and flourishing in manifold prosperity, cause some to fall into the error of thinking that God does not care for earthly affairs. In the first part, he rebukes those proud people and threatens them with eternal destruction. In the second part, which begins, “Understand, you foolish among the people,” he admonishes those who mistakenly think that God does not care for worldly matters, so that they may understand and recognize that all these things are ordered by a just disposition. He also threatens them with future accusation, while showing that God never abandons the good. In the third part, which begins, “Who will rise up for me,” he demonstrates that here God helps his own and will ultimately reward them worthily, while repaying the wicked according to their iniquities [Col. 0517A]. His purpose is to remove us from that error, so that we do not think that God does not care.

It is as though the Prophet were saying: Do not think that God despises these worldly matters and does not order them, for “God of vengeance is the Lord.” Therefore, if you say that he does not order them, he will punish you, because he rules over vengeance. By this Christ is understood, to whom all judgment has been given. That same Christ, “God of vengeance, acted freely,” as when he drove the sellers from the Temple and when, throughout the whole time of his service, he kept himself free from sin.

And you, O Christ, who are the God of vengeance, who showed yourself humble, “exalt yourself” through the resurrection, “you who judge the earth,” that is, all people from the whole earth, and “repay the proud.”

[Col. 0517B] And since they act proudly, “How long, O Lord, how long will sinners glory?” That is, how long will you permit them to glory in their wickedness? It seems contrary to nature that they both do evil and glory in it, for it is natural to grieve over evils. His repetition of “how long, sinners” indicates the persistence of their wickedness.

I rightly call them sinners, because these sinners “will speak” openly, “and will utter” among their intimates “iniquity”; indeed, “all who work injustice will speak.”

He specifies what injustice they commit, saying: “They have humbled your people, O Lord,” through insults, “and have vexed your inheritance.”

“They have slain the widow and the sojourner, and they have killed the orphans” [Col. 0517C]—all of whom the Lord had commanded in the Law to be treated mercifully. Or we may understand “they have slain the widow and the sojourner, and they have killed the orphan” allegorically.

And while they were doing these things, “they said: The Lord will not see,” that is, their Lord will not pay attention. And even if he sees, “he will not understand,” that is, “the God of Jacob” will not care about these ragged people, namely, the faithful. The impious do not themselves call him God; rather, the Prophet says this on his own behalf.

“Understand.” The second part. Continuation. They say, “The Lord will not see,” and this is addressed to you, “foolish among the people,” that is, you who teach the people worldly wisdom and yet lack true wisdom. Seeing the proud flourish and God’s people suffer, you think that God does not order “these things” of the world [Col. 0517D]. “Understand,” then, and you “fools,” who are wise neither in the world nor attentive to God as the future judge, “at last,” namely, when you have seen miracles, “be wise” enough to recognize that God orders all these things.

You ought rightly to understand that God orders all these things. Say now: “He who planted the ear,” that is, he who gave the human being the capacity to hear, “will he not hear?” Surely he will hear, that is, he will understand. “Or will he who fashioned the eye,” that is, he who supplied sight, “not consider” both the inner and the outer eye? Surely he will.

And he who “chastises the nations” with his scourges, “will he not rebuke” the impious for their sins? Surely he will. And “he who teaches human beings knowledge,” that is, who gives his faithful true understanding, will he not rebuke the wicked? Or: he who chastises the nations, that is, his own people—if he does not spare his children for their correction, will he not rebuke the wicked most severely? And he who teaches human beings knowledge, will he be ignorant of our sins? You think that he is ignorant of sins, but certainly “the Lord knows” even the smallest “thoughts of human beings”; and he knows this, “that they are vain.”

Your thoughts are vain, but certainly, O “Lord, blessed is the person whom you instruct” with your rod, like a loving teacher instructing a pupil, “and whom you teach from your law.” I call such a person blessed because you give him understanding of divine Scripture.

I say that you teach him “in order to grant him relief,” that is, to make him capable of relief and patience [Col. 0518B], because knowledge of the Scriptures will otherwise be of no benefit unless he learns from them to be patient. I speak of one oppressed “by days of evil,” that is, by the tribulations inflicted in these days. “Grant him relief,” I say, “until a pit is dug for the sinner”—literally, until he dies and is buried. For as long as he lives, he does not cease to inflict evil.

Or, “until a pit is dug for the sinner” means until his wickedness is consumed. He often falls into that pit because, through the wickedness by which he inflicts evil on others, he entangles himself.

Truly blessed is the one whom you instruct, “because the Lord will not reject his people from himself,” but will rather receive them into the fellowship of the angels. “He will not abandon his inheritance” even in this life, since he always assists it according to its need amid tribulations [Col. 0518C].

I say that he “will not abandon” it “until the justice” of his people, which was trampled in this life, “is turned into judgment,” that is, until they themselves judge others. And lest we understand as few those whose justice will be turned into judgment, he says, “and those who are beside it,” that is, those who share in that justice. Another translation has, “those who hold fast to it,” namely, “all who are upright in heart.”

“Who will rise up.” The third part. Continuation. I say that the Lord will not abandon his people. Who, then, will be my defender and my helper? No one indeed except God. And this is what follows: “Who will rise up for me against the wicked,” that is, to undertake my cause and defend me from evil people? “Or who will stand with me” by helping me persevere in the struggle “against those who work iniquity?” Namely, against those who inflict evils upon me in order to make me endure their persecutions patiently [Col. 0518D].

I say, “Who will stand with me?” Yet I do not presume upon my own strength; rather, I trust in the Lord, for “unless the Lord had helped me, almost,” that is, it was very nearly the case that “my soul would have dwelt in hell,” that is, in the depth of vices—namely, that I would have thought God did not care for my soul.

I say that, unless the Lord had helped, my soul would have dwelt in hell. But why did the Lord help you? Because “if I said,” accusing myself of sins through confession, “my foot was moved,” that is, my affection was moved from the true way toward something illicit, then, O “Lord, your mercy was helping me,” drawing me back from sin and strengthening me in good action. This is therefore a great consolation for us: God not only strengthens his faithful while they persist in virtue, but also visits and comforts them when they fall.

I say that mercy helped me, because “according to the multitude of my sorrows,” that is, of my sins, for which I grieve, “your consolations,” existing “in my heart, have made my soul rejoice.”

You will make me rejoice, but not the wicked. And this is what follows: “Does the seat of iniquity cling to you?” That is, do the wicked cling to you? He calls them by an appropriate name. I address you, “who fashion labor in the commandment,” that is, who command those who ought to cling to you to labor in good works. Or, “who fashion labor in the commandment so that your commandment may be fulfilled.”

Therefore the seat of iniquity, that is, the wicked themselves, does not cling to you, because they “lie in wait for the soul of the righteous,” that is, they frequently seek to seduce the righteous soul and make it conform to themselves. And if they cannot deceive it, they “condemn innocent blood.”

They lie in wait for the soul of the righteous and pour out blood. Yet “the Lord has become my refuge” in all these things, so that I may not yield to tribulations, “and my God” himself has become “the help of my hope,” that is, he helps me to act well, so that the rest I obtain in hope through mercy I may ultimately obtain in reality.

He has become my refuge, “and to them” who pour out [Col. 0519C] the blood of the righteous, “the Lord will repay their iniquity,” that is, he will repay them according to what they have done. Someone might say: He will not repay them with evils, because their iniquity benefited the saints. He replies: He will not repay them according to the benefit their iniquity produced, but according to their evil intention.
