This is what follows: “and in their wickedness,” that is, in their evil intention, “he will destroy them; the Lord our God will destroy them.” By saying “he will destroy” twice, he assures us of their destruction.

## Psalm XCIV. Title

*Praise of a song; David himself.*

“Come, let us rejoice in the Lord.” This psalm is called a song because it sets before us great rejoicing, namely, the time of grace, in which we enter the promised land, that is, eternal rest [Col. 0519D]. It is called “praise” because he is shown to be praiseworthy through whom the entrance into rest is prepared for us. This “praise of a song,” that is, this praiseworthy song, belongs to the Prophet David, who speaks here.

The subject is Christ’s coming, through which eternal rest is acquired for us. The method is as follows: in the first part, the Prophet, speaking as though he were one of the Jews and sympathizing with them, specially admonishes the Jews to honor and worship Christ their Savior, setting forth many reasons why they ought to receive him. In the second part, which begins, “Do not harden your hearts,” the Prophet introduces God himself warning them not to harden their hearts as their fathers did, but rather to acknowledge Christ as their visitor [Col. 0520A]. His purpose is to remove the Jews from their hardness and prevent them from making God angry with them, as their fathers did.

It is as though the Prophet were admonishing them in this way: Do not be unbelieving as your fathers were; rather, “come” through Christ to faith, and “let us rejoice,” that is, let us serve with rejoicing this “Lord,” and also “let us acclaim God,” that is, let us acclaim him because he is “our salvation,” namely Christ, who saves us and redeems us from the hand of the devil. Therefore we ought rightly to acclaim him.

I say, “let us acclaim him,” and also “let us come before his face,” for he will at some time come as judge, “in confession,” namely, let us confess our sins to him before he comes to judgment [Col. 0520B]; “and let us acclaim him with psalms,” that is, let us express through good works the joy that we conceive in our minds.

Therefore we ought to acclaim and rejoice in him “because” he is “our God,” that is, the creator of all things. He is also “great,” that is, the omnipotent “Lord,” because he rules over all; and “a great king above all gods,” whether of the nations or of the angels.

There is another reason why we ought to acclaim him: “because in his hand,” that is, in his power, “are all the ends of the earth,” that is, all the people of the world; “and” his are the “heights,” that is, the exaltations, powers, and dignities, “of the mountains,” that is, of the powerful people of this life. No one can be raised up in this world except by his permission.

[Col. 0520C] There is another reason: “for the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands founded the dry land,” literally. Or, allegorically, by “the sea” we may understand those who embitter this life, who belong to God and rage by God’s permission; “and he made it,” that is, he ordered their wickedness. Hence it is said: “Making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah XLV). And by “the dry land,” that is, those who are dry from the waves of this world and thirst for the rain of justice; hence elsewhere: “My soul is like a land without water to you” (Psalm CXLII).

And because he is so powerful, therefore you Jews, who have withdrawn from God into a distant region of dissimilarity, “come” with the steps of faith; “let us worship,” that is, let us honor Christ with singular veneration, reckoning him the highest good; “and let us fall prostrate,” that is, let us humble ourselves in our desires and regard ourselves as dust and ashes; “and let us weep” for our sins, not in the sight of human beings, as hypocrites do, but “before the Lord.” We ought to do this because he is the one “who made us”; and also because he has become “our God” through the flesh that he assumed. We owe him this because he is both our creator and our restorer.

And we ought to do this because “we” are “the people of his pasture,” since he refreshes us with spiritual gifts and also with his body and blood; “and” we are also “sheep,” that is, simple and innocent. This is “the work of his hand,” that is, his activity, because we can become innocent only through God’s work.

[Col. 0521A] I say that you are a people and sheep on this condition: “if you hear his voice”—the voice of the one who formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets—“today,” that is, in this time of grace, when he speaks to us through his own Son. Hence the Apostle says: “As long as today is named among you.” I say that if you hear his voice, then “do not harden your hearts.” Or understand it this way: Since you are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand, therefore, “if you hear his voice today,” as above, “do not harden your hearts.”

## Part Two

“Do not harden,” as your fathers hardened theirs; and this means: “as at the provocation, according to the day of testing,” which took place “in the wilderness.” That is, do not follow the day of testing, so as to test God in the wilderness, “where your fathers tested me,” doubting in their hearts [Col. 0521B] my power; and then they found me to be God; and because they “tested and saw,” they heard of “my works,” that is, that I had rained manna upon them and performed many other signs for them.

And because they tested me in this way, therefore “I was offended with that generation for forty years”: for that many years they remained in the wilderness. “And I said” to them through Moses and my other chosen servants: “These men are always going astray,” not unknowingly, but “in their heart,” because they understand within their consciences that they have gone astray.

And although I had said this to them, “these men” nevertheless “did not know my ways,” that is, they did not approve my commandments. Therefore, “if they shall enter into my rest”—that is, into the eternal homeland signified by the promised land—there will be no good person there [Col. 0521C], just as “I swore in my anger” that they would not enter into my rest. This is the figure of aposiopesis, that is, a breaking off of the sentence.

## ON PSALM 95. TITLE: A Psalm of David, when the house was being built after the captivity

“Sing to the Lord.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here while looking toward that state, namely, the time of grace, when the house—that is, the Church—was built after the captivity of the devil, by whom the human race was held captive on account of sin. It touches upon the history of the rebuilding of Solomon’s temple after the Babylonian captivity; yet we understand that the Prophet dealt not only with the history but also with its meaning [Col. 0521D]. The subject of this psalm is Christ’s first and second coming.

Its method is as follows. In the first part he urges all nations, not only the Jews, as he did in the preceding psalm: “Sing to this Lord, who has come to us,” with reference to his first coming. In the second part, which begins, “Bring to the Lord, nations of the peoples,” he urges them not only to sing but also to bring offerings and to do good works for the glory of this Lord, with reference to his second coming. His intention in these exhortations is that we should sing and do good works for the glory of this Lord.

It is as though the Prophet were saying: Do not sing to the Lord an old song, praising him only for temporal benefits; rather, “sing to the Lord a new song” [Col. 0522A], that is, praise him out of love for righteousness, because through his Son he has bestowed righteousness upon us. Nor do I speak only to the Jews, but “sing, all the earth”—Gentiles as well as Jews—sing “to the Lord.”

By placing “sing to the Lord” three times, he indicates the Trinity. “And bless his name.” For we possess only the name of God, not yet the reality itself; and that name has great power, not because it is pronounced, but because it is believed. He blesses the name of the Lord who, by living well, gives others an example of living well. Conversely, he is said to curse the name of the Lord when others derive from him an example of living badly.

I say, “sing, and bless,” and “announce his salvation,” namely, the Son of God, through whom the human race is saved and the house of God is rebuilt. Do this “from day to day” [Col. 0522B], that is, continually; or, from “day”—that is, from the Old Testament, in which there was some illumination—moving toward “day,” that is, toward the New Testament. Announce his salvation: namely, prove that Christ is king and savior of all, through the authority of the Old and New Testaments.

He shows what they must announce concerning that salvation, and among whom, when he says: “Announce his glory,” namely, of the Savior; that is, proclaim Christ himself as glorious, because he was the Son of God. Do this “among the nations.” I do not say among a few nations, but “among all peoples, his wonders”: the Virgin’s childbirth, and the one who raised the dead.

And rightly you should sing to him, “because” he is “great” according to power, “and Lord” [Col. 0522C] of all, “and worthy of praise” according to mercy. And this is “exceedingly” so, because no one can search out how great his power or mercy is. He is also “terrible,” through fear of the future judgment, “above all gods” whom the nations imagine, and also above all angelic creatures who have been made divine.

Truly he is the terrible God above the gods of the nations, “because all the gods of the nations are demons.” But this “Lord” of whom he speaks “made the heavens,” whether the material heavens or whatever men are most exalted.

Again, for this reason you should sing to him, because from him you receive this benefit: confession and beauty, and finally magnificence. He says this: “In his presence,” that is, when he looks upon someone with the eye of mercy. From this proceeds “confession” [Col. 0522D], because that person confesses his sins; and afterward “beauty,” that is, adornment with many virtues; and finally, “in his sanctification,” that is, in his holy dwelling, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence another translation says, “in his sanctuary, holiness,” that is, complete purity.

Then there will be neither anger nor any such disturbance among God’s holy ones, but purity and true charity will reign. And in his sanctification there will be “magnificence,” because then they will be immortal and incapable of suffering, and companions of the angels.

“Bring offerings.” Part two. Since there is such great benefit in his presence, therefore you, “lands of the nations”—that is, you peoples from every homeland—“bring glory to the Lord,” that is, show him to be glorious [Col. 0523A] by your good works, “and honor,” that is, thanksgiving for the benefits bestowed. “Bring” also “glory to his name,” by enlarging his name and reputation; that is, let us confer glory upon the Lord himself. By saying “Bring offerings” three times, he signifies the Trinity.

Bring glory to the Lord in this way, namely, “sacrifices”: make yourselves sacrifices, giving yourselves over to suffering for God’s honor. “And” thus “enter his courts,” that is, the fellowship of the saints, who are called courts because God dwells in them. “And worship the Lord in his holy court,” that is, in the heavenly dwelling.

I say, “worship,” and would that “the whole earth be moved” to repentance “before his face,” that is [Col. 0523B], to knowledge of him. And, moved yourselves, “say among the nations,” that is, in order to move the nations. He gives them the subject of what they should say, namely this: “The Lord has reigned” from the wood. Thus another translation reads; and here we have the Prophet’s authority concerning Christ’s Passion.

He proves by the effect that the Lord has reigned, saying: “For he has corrected”—that is, by correcting them, he has directed them from sins toward works of righteousness—“the world, which shall not be moved” from the faith by any tribulation. This is what the Apostle says: “Neither death nor life will be able to separate us from the charity of Christ.”

Say also, in order to move the earth, that this Lord “will judge,” coming a second time, “the peoples in equity,” that is, giving each person what he deserves.

[Col. 0523C] Therefore, “let the heavens rejoice,” that is, the higher saints, “and let the earth exult,” that is, the humbler saints. “Let the sea be moved,” that is, those who are made bitter in this life through fear of the future judgment; “and its fullness,” that is, every life—namely, let human beings be moved, each one on account of his individual vices, toward compunction. And the more necessary it is that they be moved, I say, “let them rejoice.”

And so it will be, because “the fields”—that is, the humble and fruitful—“will rejoice” in the purity of their conscience; “and all that is in them,” that is, all their senses, because in accordance with all their senses and all their virtues they will rejoice here in hope of future salvation.

And then, that is, when he judges, “all the trees of the forests will exult,” that is, the nations that were previously wild and uncultivated, “before the face of the Lord,” that is [Col. 0523D], because of the presence which they will enjoy: “because he comes.” I do not speak of his first coming, but “because he comes to judge the earth.”

And he himself “will judge the world,” that is, the people gathered from the entire circuit of the earth, “in equity,” giving each one according to his merits; “and the peoples” in general “in his truth,” that is, according to how each one administered the truth entrusted to him.

Alternatively, we may understand “the world” literally: the Lord will judge it because, coming to judgment, he will cleanse the filth of the elements, which they have contracted from human iniquities.

## ON PSALM 96. TITLE: A Psalm belonging to David, when his land was restored to him

“The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult.” This psalm belongs to David, that is, to Christ—not because Christ speaks here, but because he is the subject. I say that the psalm was composed when his land was restored to him, that is, when the people whom he had lost through idolatry were recalled to the worship of God and thus restored to Christ.

Its subject is Christ establishing the Church for himself. Its method is as follows. In the first part it shows him to be King and commends him in many ways, as though using the demonstrative genre; and in that same part it urges people to worship him as such, rather than their carved images. In the second part, which begins, “Sion heard, and rejoiced,” it admonishes the converts to exult [Col. 0524B] and to hate the devil. Its intention is to recall people from idolatry and summon them to the worship of the one God who abides forever.

The Prophet’s voice is as though he were saying: O you nations who until now have persisted in the worship of idols, do not henceforth worship idols, but worship Christ alone, because “the Lord has reigned,” that is, he has acquired a kingdom for himself among Jews and Gentiles. Therefore “let the earth exult,” namely, Judea, which received this King.

“Let the many islands” also “rejoice,” that is, the churches established in the most remote regions, which are battered by the waves of this world and yet are not submerged, like islands in the sea.

He describes what this Lord is like to the wicked and what he is like to the good, saying: “Cloud and darkness are around him,” that is, they overshadow him—not that they remain in him, since he is the light shining in darkness—but the wicked have bleary eyes and cannot look upon the brightness of the sun. This is said solely by comparison with something that could not be seen because of a cloud.

As regards the good, “righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne,” that is, some are corrected and become his harvest through judgment, namely through the discernment of good and evil that they possess. They do righteousness because they pursue the good and avoid evil.

He shows how his own are corrected: “Fire”—that is, the charity sent forth by the Holy Spirit, concerning which Christ himself says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn”—“will go before him,” that is, it will prepare the way for the Lord. No one is worthy to have the Lord dwell within him unless he has first been prepared by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0524D]. And that fire “will set his enemies” on fire with the love of God—namely, those who were previously his enemies—“all around,” that is, on every side.

He commends him in other ways as follows: “His lightning flashes”—that is, the miracles he performed in the world—“have illumined the world,” that is, have shone throughout the whole world. “And the earth saw” this, that is, earthly people came to know it, “and was moved” to repentance.

Then “the mountains”—that is, the powerful of this age—“melted” away from their vices “like wax.” I say, the mountains melted “before the face of the Lord,” that is, because of their knowledge of God; and not only the mountains, but “all the earth” melted [Col. 0525A] “before the face of God,” that is, the people throughout the whole earth.

The miracles shone forth, and “the heavens”—that is, the holy apostles and preachers—“announced his righteousness,” how he justifies a human being. Then “all the peoples”—that is, some from every people—“saw his glory,” that is, came to know that he is glorious.

And since he is such, therefore “let all who worship carved images”—that is, painted images—“and who glory in their idols be put to shame.”

Truly you ought to abandon those idols and worship Christ himself, because the angels themselves worship him. He says this by way of an exhortation: “All heavenly angels, worship him” [Col. 0525B].

### Part two

I thus urge you to worship him, and this exhortation “Sion heard,” that is, the Church from the Jews, “and rejoiced.”

“And” also “the daughters of Judah”—that is, the Gentiles, made children of Christ, who was from the tribe of Judah—or “the daughters of Judah,” that is, daughters of confession—“exulted” over their restoration, which they understood to have been accomplished through Christ. They exulted, I say, “because of your judgments, Lord,” namely, because blindness occurred in part in Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, along with whatever other judgments of God there may be.

Therefore they exulted, “because you, Lord, are most high over all the earth,” that is, over those who dwell throughout the earth; and “you are exalted above all gods” [Col. 0525C] of the nations, or above the angelic creatures, and this “exceedingly,” in an inscrutable manner.

And because he is such, therefore you “who love the Lord, hate evil,” that is, the adversary of this Lord. Although that adversary may inflict evils upon bodies, nevertheless “the Lord guards” the souls of his saints against tribulations, lest they be incorporated into the devil; and finally “he will free them from the hand of the sinner,” that is, from the power of the devil.

And you ought to love the Lord because in the Lord himself, that is, in Christ, “light has arisen for the just,” namely, knowledge of divinity through faith; and “joy has arisen for the upright in heart,” because of the purity of their conscience.

And because light has arisen for the just, therefore you, “just ones, rejoice,” not in worldly things, but “in the Lord,” and “confess to the memory of his sanctification” [Col. 0525D], that is, praise him because he remembered to sanctify you.

## ON PSALM 97. TITLE: A Psalm of David

“Sing to the Lord.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here. Its subject is Christ’s first and second coming.

Its method is as follows. In the first part it urges people to sing to the Lord with reference to his first coming and gives the reasons. In the second part, which begins, “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth,” it urges people to shout joyfully to God and to act both through activity and contemplation, with reference to his second coming. Its intention in these exhortations is that we should sing to God. Although it deals with them alone throughout the entire context, this psalm is divided from another by the word “Sing” [Col. 0526A].

It is as though the Prophet were saying: Do not sing to the Lord only because of ancient benefits—namely, because he led you out of Egypt and showed you other wonders—but “sing to the Lord a new song,” that is, praise him for the restoration accomplished through the Son. And rightly you should, “because” he “has done” many “wonders” for us.

Among God’s other wonders he mentions one especially notable, saying: “His right hand saved for himself,” as another translation says, “His right hand and his holy arm saved him.” By his right hand and arm we understand divinity itself, namely the Word of God. It is called the right hand according to its operation, and the arm because of its strength, namely because in the humanity he assumed Christ accomplished what he did not through an alien power but through his own power [Col. 0526B]. That Word saved Christ, because it preserved him free from sin and raised him, once dead, to eternal life.

And that arm—namely, “his salvation,” that is, Jesus, through whom he saved the human race—the Father “made known,” so that through Christ’s humanity people might recognize his divinity. And he “revealed his righteousness,” that is, he demonstrated it openly, not through figures; and this “in the sight of the nations,” namely so that the nations might know him through faith.

The same one who is called salvation because he saves the human race is called righteousness because he justifies human beings.

And through making salvation known, the one who seemed to have forgotten by delaying mercy “remembered his mercy and his truth” [Col. 0526C]. This was done “to the house of Israel,” that is, for the work concerning the Jews. The same benefit of God, which he calls mercy because it was given solely from God’s goodness, he calls truth because God’s promises were fulfilled in it.

And not only to the house of Israel, but also to all the nations. Hence he says, “the ends of the earth,” that is, people situated at the remotest boundaries of the earth. And this did not happen in one place, but “all saw”—that is, came to know—“the salvation of God,” which became “ours” through the humanity he assumed.

### “Shout joyfully.” Part two

And since he remembered his mercy and did other things, therefore “all the earth, shout joyfully” to this “Lord,” that is, conceive in your mind ineffable delight in him. “Sing” to him also with mind and voice, “and exult,” that is, show the joy of the mind in the body; “and sing psalms,” that is, work well through spiritual action.

“Sing psalms,” I say, “on the lyre,” that is, descend from spiritual action to active work, as when you love your neighbor with pious and faithful love and even serve him with your own possessions. Also sing “on the lyre and with the voice of the psalm,” that is, ascend from active work to spiritual and contemplative work.

Just as we understand active work through the lyre, so through the psaltery and the voice of the psalm we understand spiritual work. Sing also “with drawn trumpets.” By trumpets, through which an exhortation to war or an announcement of solemn observances was made, we understand the exhortation of preaching. They were drawn trumpets because they were made of pure silver, which did not crack when beaten with a hammer but could be drawn out well and expanded [Col. 0527A].

It is as though he were saying briefly: Preach and exhort others to battle, and to perform solemn observances; and expand your preaching, singing also with “the voice of the horn,” that is, so that you may be comparable to a horn—hard and not ceasing from the preaching of truth because of any tribulation. A horn grows out of flesh into a kind of hardness; those who, although living in fragile flesh, nevertheless become hard and patient in labors are well compared with it. Hence the Apostle says: “Although walking in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.”

He said “shout joyfully”; now he says why this must be done: namely, because you behold, as though already present, the King himself coming to judgment. He says: “Shout joyfully in the presence of the King, the Lord.” And because he is already seen as though coming, therefore “let the sea”—that is, all who are made bitter—“be moved” to repentance, “and its fullness,” that is, let the fullness of vices be for them a reason to be moved all the more.

Let “the world of the earth” also be moved and tremble: literally, it too will be burned at the coming of that judge; “and all who dwell in it” should be moved. This is what he had said: “the sea and its fullness.”

I say, “let the sea be moved”; but let “the rivers”—that is, wise men who give others spiritual drink—“clap their hands,” that is, work well with exultation, “together,” that is, striving toward one end, namely toward God himself [Col. 0527C], holding one faith. “The mountains,” holy men eminent in virtues and firmly established, “will exult before the presence of the Lord,” that is, because they behold the Lord who rewards them.

I rightly say, “before the presence of the Lord,” because that Lord “comes to judge the earth,” that is, all people from whatever part of the earth, as though what he will judge were already present.

And he “will judge the world,” that is, all the wicked gathered from the entire circuit of the earth, “in righteousness,” giving each one according to his merits; and “the peoples” gathered for good living—namely, he will judge the good—“in equity,” likewise dealing with them according to their merits.

## ON PSALM 98. TITLE: A Psalm of David

“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here. Its subject is Christ, the powerful King.

Its method is as follows. In the first part it shows him to be King, demonstrates in many ways that he is worthy of veneration, and admonishes unbelievers—especially the Jews—to venerate him. In the second part, which begins, “You prepared uprightness,” it shows what gifts he bestows upon his own and presupposes an exhortation that we worship him. In the third part, which begins, “Moses and Aaron,” it shows that the fathers of old served this King and received many benefits from him; it then presupposes an exhortation that we worship him and not regard him as a new king. Its intention is to recall us from faithlessness and stir us to worship Christ [Col. 0528A].

It is as though he were saying: “Do not” despise Christ, because “the Lord has reigned,” that is, having conquered the devil, he obtained a kingdom for himself among Jews and Gentiles.

Now he mocks Christ’s enemies, who once used to be angry with him: “Let the peoples be angry,” as though they might consider themselves foolish, since they once grew angry with him. “The Lord,” I say, “has reigned,” the Lord “who sits above the cherubim,” that is, who rests above the orders of the angels as their Lord.

Again mocking his enemies, he says: “Let the earth be moved,” as though those who were once moved against him—together with all the orders of angels—were complete fools.

I say, “the Lord has reigned,” the Lord “who dwelt” bodily in Sion [Col. 0528B], the Lord who was “great” and of wondrous power. By this he plainly determined that he was speaking of Christ, because Christ dwelt in Sion in the presence of his body. And this Lord is “exalted above all peoples,” because no one is exalted except through him.

And since he is such, therefore “let all the nations confess” to “your name,” that is, let them praise and spread your name and reputation. To the name, I say, which is “great,” namely, which must be enlarged and praised, “because” it is great and of great value to those who believe rightly. It must be confessed because that name “is terrible” to the impious through fear of the future judgment, and “holy” to the good, because through it they have been sanctified.

And that Lord “loves judgment,” that is, he wants people to judge justly; or “judgment” means any discernment of the soul. To do this is also “the honor of the king,” namely, that the king love judgment. This too is one commendation of Christ.

### “You prepared.” Part two

The continuation is as follows: You, indeed, who are such, “prepared uprightness,” that is, by breathing your grace within them, you prepared people to be directed toward virtues. You also established uprightness—not only prepared it, but established “judgment,” that is, so that they themselves might justly discern what is good and what is evil. And you “made” this other discernment, namely “justice,” that is, so that they might do the good they recognize and abandon evil. You made it, I say, “in Jacob,” that is, in the faithful people, who received a blessing like Jacob [Col. 0528D].

And because Christ bestows these gifts upon his own, therefore you “exalt” Christ, who was made “the Lord our God” through the humanity he assumed, “and worship his footstool,” that is, his humanity, which was the footstool—his “rest and seat”—“of his feet,” that is, of the stability of his divinity. For “that footstool is holy,” namely, Christ’s humanity.

Or we may understand it intransitively: “the footstool of his feet,” taking the feet as his humanity, through which divinity, shod, came to us; that humanity was the footstool, that is, entirely subject to the Godhead.

### “Moses.” Part three

And rightly you should worship him, because he is not a recent God, as some say, but the one whom “Moses and Aaron served among his priests” [Col. 0529A]. Although Moses was not a priest, nevertheless he calls him a priest because he invoked God on behalf of the people, as the other priests did, and appointed and anointed priests.

And “Samuel” himself, although he was not from the tribe of Levi, from which the other priests came, was “among those who invoke his name,” because he was his priest.

These men served the Lord, and from this they obtained the benefit that they “invoked the Lord, and he heard them.” “He spoke to them in a pillar of cloud.” He spoke in a cloud because what he said to them was obscure, since it concerned the future, namely Christ’s coming. That cloud signified Christ, who is shade and refreshment for us against the heat of heretics. He is also signified by the pillar, for he is the pillar that supports the whole Church [Col. 0529B].

He spoke to them, and they “kept his testimonies,” that is, the common commandments of the Law, in which he testified to them both what had to be done and what had not to be done, and also the particular “commandment” concerning priestly office “which he gave them.”

Alternatively, by testimony we may understand the ceremonies they performed, which were signs and testimonies of the wonders the Lord had done for them. For example, when they ate the lamb, ate unleavened bread, and held staffs in their hands, this was a sign and testimony before the children of Israel, who had not themselves seen the exodus from Egypt.

They kept the testimonies, and you, “Lord our God” [Col. 0529C], having become so through incarnation, “heard them” in their necessities. “God, you” also “were merciful to them,” forgiving their sins, and at times “avenging all their inventions,” that is, the sins that God had not created in them but that they themselves had devised, so that through those acts of vengeance you might correct and test them.

Since Moses and Aaron served him and received these benefits from him, therefore you others “exalt”—that is, show the Lord our God to be exalted and omnipotent by serving him well—“and worship on his holy mountain,” that is, in the Church, outside which there is no place of prayer, “because the Lord our God is holy.”

## ON PSALM 99. TITLE: A Psalm of David, in confession

“Shout joyfully to God.” This psalm is called a psalm in confession because the Prophet who speaks here has both kinds of confession as its subject.

Its method is as follows. In the first part he urges us to confession of praise, namely, to praise God, and gives the reasons why we ought to do this. In the second part, which begins, “Enter his gates,” he urges us to confession of sin, namely, to accuse ourselves of our sins and to look to him alone as physician.

Its intention is to generate in us a certain moderation: we should not attend only to our frailty and sins, which would plunge us into despair, but also to God’s benefits and mercy, so that despair may be removed through them. Likewise, we should not attend only to God’s mercy and kindness, which would produce negligence and presumption in us; rather, we should look upon our own miseries and frailties, so that on account of them we may work and strive to please God.

He thus exhorts us to confession of praise: O “all the earth, shout joyfully to God,” that is, conceive ineffable delight in him in your mind; and “serve this Lord,” working well for his praise. Do this not under compulsion or with any sadness, but “in gladness, for God loves a cheerful giver.”

### “Enter.” 

He gives the reason and great benefit for which they should praise God. The continuation is this: You ought rightly to serve him in gladness, because through this you will enter [Col. 0530B] into his presence. He says: “Enter” to God himself, “into his presence,” where you will remain, “with exultation.” In his presence you will enjoy eternal joy; and because you will have joy there, you ought to serve him here with joy.

“Know,” and for this reason you ought also to be vigilant, “that he is the Lord God,” that is, the Creator of all things according to the first creation. “He” also “made us” in the creation that has greater value for us than even the first creation; “and we did not make ourselves,” because we possess no good from ourselves.

We are also “his people,” that is, instructed by his commandments and gathered for living rightly; “and sheep,” that is, simple and innocent, which he himself has worked in you [Col. 0530C]. Sheep, I say, “of his pasture,” that is, those whom he refreshes with spiritual goods, with the food of his body and blood, and with the nourishment of divine Scripture.

### “Enter.” Part two

And because you are his people and sheep, therefore “enter his gates with confession,” that is, confess your sins. Through this “enter the gates,” that is, the beginnings of reaching true life; namely, enter his mercies. And by confessing your sins, enter “his courts,” that is, the fellowship of the holy apostles and other saints, conforming yourselves to the saints in the fullness of righteousness. Then “confess” to the Lord “in hymns,” that is, in praises. For only after we have first confessed our sins can we praise the Lord acceptably [Col. 0530D].

I say, “confess,” not only among yourselves, but “praise” his name before others, saying: “For this Lord is sweet,” and is sweet to those who taste him. “His mercy” is “forever,” that is, the things this Lord bestows through his mercy lead people to eternity. And “his truth,” that is, the things that fulfill God’s promises and through which God appears truthful, are “from generation to generation,” that is, eternal. We understand the same thing through mercy and truth, but in different ways.

## ON PSALM 100. TITLE: A Psalm belonging to David

“Mercy.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here, or to any perfect righteous person. Its subject is perfect conduct, which he displays in himself.

Its method is as follows. In the first part he shows himself to live justly and to avoid the company of the wicked. In the other part, which begins, “My eyes,” he shows himself to cling to the company of the good. Its intention is to invite us through this to the practice of perfect conduct.

Before discussing this conduct, he first gives the reason why he chooses such a way of life: namely, because he regards God as not only merciful but also just. For if he regarded him as merely merciful, he would labor for nothing, thinking that God forgives everything out of kindness [Col. 0531B]. But because he recognizes him as just and understands that he will avenge sins, he considers him worthy of fear and to be pleased in every way. Hence he says: O Lord, I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, that is, I will praise you because you show mercy to others and execute judgment by punishing sins.

Having stated this reason, he now begins to show his own righteousness. It is as though he were saying: Because I understand you to be not only merciful but also judging, therefore “I will sing psalms,” that is, I will work well; and through this you will come to me, so that you may dwell in me. And “when” you “come to me”—that is, when I understand you to be my possessor and indweller—in what will I understand this? “In an immaculate way,” that is, because I walk blamelessly: I walk through good works, and I understand that you come to dwell in all who walk through “blameless” works [Col. 0531C].

I said, “I will sing psalms,” and now I have acted. He says this: “I was walking through,” that is, by my will I passed beyond these worldly things, which by their nature are always transitory. This means that I did not consider myself to possess here a lasting city, but always desired the heavenly one. And I did this “in the innocence of my heart.”

But I not only restrained my hands from harming my neighbor; I also restrained my will. I did this “in the midst of my house,” that is, in the congregation of the faithful, among whom I was one. When he says “in the midst,” he indicates that in himself he was setting before everyone an example of good works.

In addition, “I did not set before my inner eyes” any “unjust thing,” so that some injustice might please me; rather, I “hated those who act” in actual “transgressions,” that is, in offenses against the commandment of the Law [Col. 0531D].

And “a perverse heart,” that is, a person of perverse heart, some malicious person, even if he does not carry out his malice in action, “did not cling to me,” that is, he did not please me and was not intimate with me.

But one who “turns away from me,” that is, who avoids agreeing with my ways—I call that person “malignant” for this reason. Even if he displayed his righteousness before some people, “I did not recognize him” as righteous, as others think him to be, nor did I approve his life.

“I pursued the one who secretly slandered his neighbor” with diligent exhortation, so that I might draw him back from his error.

[Col. 0532A] But a man who appeared with “a proud eye” and “an insatiable heart,” that is, a greedy man, “with such a person I did not eat” bodily food, or rather spiritual food, namely the nourishment of the Lord’s body. Such wicked people must clearly be separated from the food of the good. Hence the Apostle says: “With such a person, do not even take food.”

### Part two

“My eyes.” These men will not please me, but “my eyes,” that is, my affections, were directed toward “the faithful of the land,” not of one place only, “so that they may sit with me,” that is, so that they may become like me and rest in the delight of righteousness, as I do.

But “one who walks in the blameless way, he served me.” For pure and honorable men must be chosen to serve in the house of the Lord.

[Col. 0532B] “The one who practices pride.” I do not mean in some part of the house of God, because the wicked are tolerated in the Church by prelates so that they may be corrected and desist. But “he will not dwell in the midst of my house,” that is, in the congregation of the faithful.

When he says “in the midst,” he gives us to understand that he will not make such a person his intimate companion, nor appoint him as a prelate in the house of God, lest others receive from him either a bad example or bad teaching.

Not only “the one who practices pride,” but also “the one who speaks wicked things,” namely, one who is accustomed to evil speech—even if he appears upright to such people and to those like them, “he did not walk uprightly in the sight of my eyes,” that is, in such a way as to please me.

“In the morning.” He gives the reason why he avoids the company of such people: for at some point he sees them to be eternally separated from the fellowship of the good [Col. 0532C]. It is as though he were saying: “For this reason I separated myself from such people, because I was killing”—that is, by killing I understood—“all the sinners of the earth in the morning,” that is, at the judgment, when the true light will begin to rise for the good. He was not killing those who might at some point return to mercy, but rather—“that I might destroy”—that is, that I might recognize as destined for destruction—“from the city of the Lord,” that is, from the heavenly Jerusalem, “all who practice iniquity.” He does not say “those who have practiced” but “those who persist in this.” Alternatively, we may understand “sinners” here as the demons themselves and the suggestions sent by the devil; and then the passage may be continued in this way: In others, evil things did not please me, but rather, in myself, I was killing all the sinners of the earth, that is, all the suggestions sent to me by the devil [Col. 0532D]. And this was “in the morning,” that is, at the very beginning, while those suggestions were beginning to arise: I did not carry into action what the suggestions were urging. I was killing them in order to destroy them, so that afterward all who practice iniquity would not take root “from the city of the Lord,” that is, from my soul, which is God’s fortified dwelling-place; that is, the demons, who are called sinners and workers of iniquity, since they are the cause of every sin, would no longer have a dwelling in me.

## ON PSALM 101

**Title:** A prayer of the poor man, when he is troubled and pours out his prayer before the Lord.

“Lord, hear my prayer.” This psalm is called a prayer because its first part contains a prayer, while the matters that follow give reasons why one should pray. Many books are named with reference to their opening sections. Thus, for example, one of Moses’ books is called Genesis because at the beginning it explains the generation of heaven and earth. This, then, is the prayer of the prophet David, the poor man—or of any true poor person understood in this way—when he has poured out his prayer before God. Those prayers are said to be poured out before God which are anticipated by no distracting thoughts and impeded by no obstacles of the devil, but are directed toward God himself in pure devotion.

Here the poor man speaks—David, or anyone else—not for one person only, but for each individual: the poor man himself, moreover, is troubled by his own sins and by the miseries of the whole human race, and humbly brings his prayers before God. The structure is as follows. In the first part, employing something like a supplication, he does not excuse himself but makes his prayer as one accused, and confesses himself wretched, so as by these means to move mercy in the judge. In the second part, which begins, “I have been struck down like grass,” he enumerates the miseries suffered by the human race. In the third part, which begins, “But you, Lord,” he shows the confidence he has that he will be rescued from these miseries. And through whom? Through Christ, of course. The children of God’s servants will dwell with him, and their descendants will be guided forever. His purpose is to invite us to repent in such a way that we lament both our own sins and the sins of others.

He begins the prayer in this way: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry”—that is, my inward intention, whether it is expressed with the voice or not [Col. 0533C]—“come to you,” that is, let it be impeded by no obstacle from ascending into your presence.

I say, “let my cry come to you”; and when it has come, let it not remain unheard. This is what he says: “Do not turn your face,” that is, the presence of your knowledge, “away from me”; instead, look upon my humility and weakness, and “incline toward me,” the weak one, “your ear,” that is, accommodate yourself to my weakness, “on whatever day I am troubled.” Here he indicates that he is often troubled. For tribulations and temptations of the devil scarcely ever cease for the righteous.

It is as though he were saying: “I am often troubled, and in my troubles I call upon you; and on whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly.”

[Col. 0533D] And it is necessary for you to hear me, because “the days” of my human life, “my” days spent in sin and misery, are “like smoke.” For just as smoke comes from fire, and the more intensely the fire burns, the more the smoke vanishes, so the evil acts of human life proceed from the heat of desire and blind the eyes of the heart; and the higher they rise, the more they fall away from the dignity of the true light. My days, I say, “have failed,” because they have brought no true benefit. And, likewise, your hearing is necessary because “my bones have dried up,” that is, the strengths of my soul; in other words, reason itself has dried up. By consenting to the pleasure of the flesh, it has fallen away from its strength, namely, from contemplation of the true good. “Like fuel.” This expresses the greatest dryness: the soul itself, having lost its proper richness and God’s illumination, entangled in many sins, is judged worthy and fit to be burned [Col. 0534A].

“I have been struck down.” The second part. I rightly say that my days have failed, because I, who according to nature and my first creation was “like” green and flourishing “grass,” have been “struck down” by the devil, as by an evil mower, when he drove me and my parents into sin. Through this I lost my greenness and the flowers of righteousness. Then “my heart dried up,” deprived of illumination and of the grace that nourishes the interior; it dried up because “I forgot to eat my bread,” that is, to enjoy the contemplation of God, which would have been perfect nourishment.

Behold, this penitent begins to display satisfaction [Col. 0534B] for his sins, saying, “at the sound”—as though he were saying: “I was struck down by the devil; I forgot to eat my bread; and therefore I certainly groaned. While my groaning burst forth into sound, I then so afflicted my body that I made my bones cling to my skin.” This is what he means by “at the sound of my groaning, my bone clung to my flesh,” that is, to my skin. Or we may understand it in this way: I groaned over my own sins and those of my neighbors, so that the bone—that is, the stronger part of my body, namely, the Church—clung to, or accommodated itself through sympathy and compassion to, my flesh, that is, to the weaker and more fragile members of the Church, as the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”

“And I became like a pelican of the wilderness,” because there is a species of pelican that lives in marshes; to distinguish it from that kind, he says here [Col. 0534C], “of the wilderness.” Its nature is such that, fleeing the “company” of other birds, it chooses a solitary life for itself and is always emaciated. The penitent compares himself to this bird; he speaks according to certain members of his body, namely, hermits, who choose solitude and there afflict themselves with great emaciation.

“According to other members” I became “like an owl,” which dwells “in a dwelling-place,” that is, it is not entirely remote. The *nycticorax* is a certain bird, namely, the night-raven—as some say—or an owl. This bird obtains its food at night, and it is very hateful to human beings, because when it sings, it is understood to threaten death. Yet it is neither entirely removed from human society nor does it dwell wholly with human beings. This general poor man is compared to it, speaking of himself according to those members who have neither completely abandoned human society nor dwell entirely with it: for example, good men who live in the world but do not consent to worldly conduct. They are like a nocturnal bird because they keep vigil and pray at night, or because what they do by day is as though it were done at night: they avoid the gaze of people and perform their good works in secret. They are also hostile to human beings because they threaten them with death when they refuse to find in them an example of good living.

I became like these, and therefore I also “kept watch,” that is, I was concerned and attentive to my own correction and to that of my neighbors. “And I became like a solitary sparrow,” which, avoiding snares, builds its nest [Col. 0535A] in a safe place, namely, “on the roof.” Again, according to some, this penitent poor man compares himself, in terms of his body, to a sparrow dwelling on a roof. Such are monks and good canons, who are compared to a sparrow because they are ardent in avoiding the devil’s snares. They are solitary because, having abandoned the diversities of this age, they pursue only the unity of the Church. They dwell on a roof, that is, in a safe place, namely, in the company of the good, through whose example and admonitions they are safe from the enemy’s assault.

“All day long.” He continues to enumerate the miseries suffered by the human race. It is as though he were saying: “I kept watch and made myself such a person; and then my enemies reproached me,” that is, they spoke words of abuse against me, [Col. 0535B] and this “all day long,” that is, continually. Even my friends did so; this is what he says: “Those who praised me swore against me,” like false friends. He speaks by comparison: just as some people, when they persist against someone, swear against him, so these people persist in mocking the good.

They reproached me not because they saw evil in me, but “because I was eating ashes,” that is, the tiniest sins, which are the remnants of greater sins; I was “eating” them, that is, consuming them, “like bread,” because I received as much nourishment from them as from bread. We understand ashes as the remnants of sins because ashes are the remains of coals, and by coals are understood sins that burn the heart.

“And I mixed my drink with weeping.” Literally, this righteous man did indeed weep, considering that the necessities of eating and drinking had arisen from Adam’s sin. Or we may understand the drink as the Lord’s cup, which must be received with tears and compunction [Col. 0535C].

I acted in this way because I saw as though present the anger of the future judgment. This is what he means by “from the face of your anger,” that is, because of the presence of the future anger in which you will condemn the wicked; and from the face of “your indignation,” that is, of your correction, which you exercise in this life—not to condemn the predestined, but to purify them. And I rightly say that you correct through indignation, because, “when you lifted me up” amid the prosperity of this life, “you dashed me down” with many tribulations. The poor man speaks here, not according to all his members, but according to certain ones [Col. 0535D].

I rightly say that I regard future anger as present, because “my days,” bringing me no benefit, are “like a shadow,” since here there is no true illumination. In this decline, which arises from sin, I recognize future anger: my days “have declined, and I have withered like grass.”

“But you.” The third part. I endure miseries, “but you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial,” that is, that notable deed—namely, the redemption of the human race through the Son, because of which you will be held in human memory—will endure “in this generation” and “in the generation” to come.

[Col. 0536A] And you, who are eternal and who seemed to have fallen asleep when you delayed showing mercy, will now “rise and have mercy on Zion,” that is, on the Church. I confidently say, “You will have mercy,” because “the time for having mercy on her has come,” that is, the fitting time in which mercy ought to be shown. By repeating the expression, he indicates the desire he has for that mercy.

Truly “you will have mercy on Zion,” because “your servants”—that is, the apostles and other preachers, whose task is to build up the Church of God—“have found pleasure in her stones,” that is, in living human beings who are solid and stable both in faith and in good works, and fit to be placed in the building of that Zion, namely, the Church. “And” those servants “will have mercy” by exhorting and grieving compassionately over “the land,” that is, over earthly people who are destined to be “hers,” namely, Zion’s.

[Col. 0536B] The servants will have mercy, “and” through this “the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth”—that is, whoever governs his earthly nature well—“will fear your glory,” that is, you, because they will recognize you as glorious.

They will fear for this reason: “the Lord will build up Zion,” that is, the Church, through virtues, “and he will appear” to his own people “in his glory,” that is, in eternity. Or he will appear to his own people in present glory, that is, he will be recognized by his own as glorious.

He will truly build it, because he “has regarded”—and will regard by hearing—“the prayer of the humble,” who presume nothing about themselves, just as he regarded the prayer of the publican and the Pharisee. I say that he “has regarded,” and that he also showed an accepting face; this is what follows: “He did not despise their prayer” [Col. 0536C]. By saying less, he means more. Or he did not despise the prayer made for himself, and he will not despise the prayer made for others. Or he will regard it, not merely for a time, but will never despise it.

I have said that he regarded it; now he is about to explain how he regarded it, namely, through the coming of the Son. Since he is about to speak of a great matter that must be kept in memory, he gives this warning: “Let these things be written,” that is, firmly entrusted to memory, “in another generation,” that is, among our descendants, so that they may know “these things” that I am about to proclaim; and for these things the people who will be created will praise the Lord.

These things, then, are to be written because the Lord “looked down from above,” that is, mercifully visited those who were far from the knowledge [Col. 0536D] of God, namely, the Gentiles, “from his holy height,” that is, from the humanity of his Son, which was exalted because it was free from every sin. And the Lord “looked upon the earth,” that is, upon those who cultivated the earth, such as the Jews, whom he visited as people near to him. As the Apostle says: “When he came, he preached the gospel to those who were near and to those who were far away” (Ephesians 2). And this was “from heaven,” namely, from Christ’s humanity, in which his divinity itself was concealed.

He looked down for this purpose: “that through” the Son, the mediator, he might “hear the groans of the fettered,” that is, of those who do not indulge themselves through the streets of this life but are bound by God’s commandments. He heard them in order “to release the children of those who were slain,” that is, of your fathers who died [Col. 0537A] in their sins, from the bond of the sins over which they were groaning.

He did this only so that those who had been released might “proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion,” that is, in the present Church, and “in Jerusalem,” that is, in the future Jerusalem, which is the vision of peace, “proclaim his praise,” that is, show the Lord to be worthy of praise.

I say that they should proclaim it, and not to a few, but “when peoples assemble together,” that is, when they are gathered, or, “when assembling,” that is, when addressing “peoples together,” meaning leading them into one will and one faith. “And” also by assembling “kings,” that is, the great and powerful, for this purpose: “that they may serve the Lord.”

The Lord looked upon the earth, and “it answered him” [Col. 0537B] when he called, assenting to his call, serving him, and walking “in the way,” that is, in God’s commandments through good works. It is the way “of his strength,” that is, the way in which it shows itself strong, since no tribulation can separate it from that way. Hence the Apostle says: “Neither death nor life will be able to separate us from the love of God” (Romans 8).

I say that it answered, speaking in this way: “Lord, make known to me”—that is, make me understand—“the shortness of my days,” that is, the brevity of human life, so that, having recognized it, I may hasten toward eternal life.

And while I am running toward eternal life, “do not call me back” from that course; that is, do not withdraw your grace. For then I would remain only “in the midst of my days,” that is, I would possess merely the human life spent in temporal goods [Col. 0537C]. Such a life is called half of life, that is, incomplete. Or we may understand “days” here as the life of the righteous, because true illumination is found in it, so that the passage may be understood as follows: “Do not call me back from the course of eternal life, so that I remain only in the midst of my days,” that is, so that I possess only the present life of the righteous. For that life is half, that is, incomplete and useless, unless eternal life follows it.

“My days” are half-days, but “your years,” that is, eternity—designated by the name “years,” not because of mutability, which does not exist there, but because of duration—are “in the present generation” and will endure “in the generation to come”; that is, they are eternal.

“In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth.” I rightly say that your years are eternal, because you, Lord, have neither had a beginning nor will have an end. He shows that you had no beginning when he says that you founded the earth: from this it is clear that he existed before the earth. Thus he says, “Lord, you founded the earth,” and this “in the beginning,” that is, in the first creation. “And the heavens” of the material world “are the work of your hands,” because you made them. He says so explicitly, “the work of your hands,” because the more excellent work is attributed to the person of the craftsman.

He shows that God is without end because God will exist after all things, when he says: “They,” the heavens, “will perish.” This does not mean that their substance will perish, but that their qualities will change. These lower things, which are corrupted through our habitation of them, will be purified by fire. The firmament itself will also be changed, because it will become stable. Thus he says, “The heavens will perish, but you, Lord, remain forever.”

He shows how they will perish by saying: “And they will all grow old like a garment,” because the elements themselves are corrupted in accordance with the corruption of human beings: for example, the earth, which is now less fertile than before, and the air, which is less healthy.

“And” you “will change them as a covering is changed,” when they receive another quality. Yet that change will be permanent; this is what he means by “and they will be changed,” that is, they will remain in that changed state. It will not be as certain heretics wished, namely, that the elements would at some point return to their former appearance and human beings once again to inhabit the earth.

You will change them, “but you are the same,” that is, immutable; “you yourself,” that is, almighty; [Col. 0538B] “and your years,” in which you live, “will not fail,” because they are eternal.

Alternatively, we may understand heaven and earth allegorically, so that the passage may be read in this way: I say, “Do not call me back,” and I am confident, because of the good beginnings you have already made, that you will not call me back. For, Lord, you founded the earth, that is, the Church, “in the beginning,” that is, through the Son, or from the first righteous man, Abel. And the heavens, that is, the higher men in the Church who contain heavenly secrets, are the spiritual works of your hands, in which the Lord appears especially worthy of praise.

Those heavens will perish through temporal death, but you, God, remain. All of them will grow old, age, and decay in body, like a garment that is worn out. Then you will change them, when you clothe them with incorruption and immortality [Col. 0538C], as an old covering is renewed. “And they will be changed,” that is, the new state brought about by that change will remain in them; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.

Your years are eternal, and in that eternity “the children of your servants will dwell,” that is, those who imitate the holy apostles. “And their descendants,” that is, their good works, “will be guided” by you from virtue to virtue, and will be guided “into the age” to come. For then they will never cease from praising God. Here the joyful end of the penitents is shown, as in the other penitential psalms.

## ON PSALM 102

**Title:** A psalm of David himself.

“Bless, I.” This psalm belongs to the prophet David, who speaks here. Its subject is the praises of God [Col. 0538D]. Its structure is as follows. In the first part, he exhorts himself to praise God for the benefits bestowed. In the second, which begins, “He made his ways known,” he displays God’s praises in the earlier benefits bestowed on the fathers. In the third, which begins, “Bless the Lord, all his angels,” he shows that God is praised by the angels and by all creatures. Through all of this his purpose is to invite us to praise God.

It is as though he were saying: “O my soul,” entangled in many cares and in other impediments of the world, having set all these aside, “bless the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord and magnify his praises, with all your strength. This is what he says: “And let all that is within me bless his holy name.”

[Col. 0539A] And because he sees that this must especially be done and persevered in, he repeats it, saying: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” Then he supplies the reasons, saying: “And do not forget all his recompenses,” that is, the benefits he returns in response to the evil deeds we commit against him.

He explains those recompenses when he says, “who forgives all your iniquities,” that is, pardons your sins; and another recompense when he says, “who heals all your infirmities,” that is, makes you so stable that he no longer allows you to be impeded by the devil’s temptations or by any grave sin. Or, “he heals your infirmities” because at last he will free you from corruption.

Another benefit is expressed when he says, “who redeems” through [Col. 0539B] the price of his blood “your life,” that is, the soul itself, “from destruction,” that is, so that it does not finally perish eternally. He also “crowns you” in the present “with mercy and compassions,” that is, with many benefits bestowed through mercy.

These words may be understood of the future life in this way: He redeems—that is, frees your life from destruction—so that you do not hear the sentence addressed to the wicked: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25). He crowns you because there he will adorn you with mercy and compassions, that is, with benefits granted through mercy.

There is yet another recompense when he says, “who fills” in this life “your desire with good things,” because he multiplies your acts of righteousness according to your desire. Or this may be understood of the other life, where the desire of the righteous is frustrated in nothing. “Your youth will be renewed” [Col. 0539C] even in this life, “like that of an eagle.”

The nature of the eagle is such that in old age its beak and talons grow so much that it cannot nourish itself with food. It rises up and then faces the sun until its feathers are burned by its heat; afterward it falls into living water. When it emerges, it sharpens its beak and talons against a rock, and later, obtaining food, it becomes young again.

So we, occupied by many sins and held in the old age of Adam, approach Christ, who is the true sun. Through his heat and the infusion of grace our sins are burned away. Then we are washed in the waters of baptism. There we strike and break our crooked beak—that is, our bad habit—against the rock, that is, Christ. Conforming ourselves to him, we lay aside our old age and become young again. Or we may understand this of the life in which our youth will be renewed when we are clothed with impassibility and immortality [Col. 0539D].

I rightly say that he fills your desire, because he is “the Lord who performs mercies,” and also the one who performs “judgment,” that is, vengeance, “for all who suffer injustice.” Hence the Apostle says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12; Ezekiel 9; Deuteronomy 32).

“Known.” The second part. I say that he fills your desire, and the Lord himself “made known his ways to Moses,” that is, his commandments. And through Moses he made known “to the children of Israel,” that is, to the Jewish people, “his wills,” that is, what God wished to do with that people.

[Col. 0540A] And the Lord himself is “merciful,” that is, displaying many effects of mercy—many benefits that he confers on us without any merit of ours—and the same Lord is “compassionate” in his nature; “long-suffering,” because he waits a long time for us to repent; and the same God is “very merciful,” because he forgives us our daily and innumerable sins.

And when the Lord grants us these benefits, will he “be angry with us forever”? “No.” For although in the present he may appear angry when he permits us to suffer tribulation, that anger will not be perpetual; rather, at last he will rescue us from every punishment. And he will not merely refrain from being angry; even less will he “threaten forever.” For the one who now threatens us, saying, “Unless you turn back, you will die by death,” will at some point appear gentle and mild to us [Col. 0540B].

I rightly say that the Lord is long-suffering and merciful, because “he has not dealt with us according to our sins,” namely, our original sins, as though he were to condemn us as those sins demanded; nor has he “repaid us according to our iniquities,” our actual sins, which would demand that he cast us continually into deeper depths of vice.

I rightly say, “He has not repaid us according to our iniquities,” because “instead” he did the opposite: he “strengthened,” that is, immutably bestowed, “his mercy,” the remission of sins and all other benefits, “upon those who fear him.” That mercy comes from above. Or, when he says “upon,” we may understand that the mercy is greater than the worthiness of those who receive it. He bestowed this mercy “according to the height of heaven above the earth,” because just as heaven is higher and more excellent than earth, and by watering it makes it fruitful, so God’s mercy is more excellent than those who receive it and, by raining spiritual dew upon them, makes their hearts fruitful.

I rightly say that God “strengthened his mercy,” namely, because “he has removed our iniquities far from us,” as far “as the east is distant from the west.” He rightly compares us to the west, because while we were in sins we were like the west: we were not illuminated by the knowledge and splendor of the true Sun, who is God. Once our iniquities have been removed, however, we have become like the east, because we are now illumined by the splendor of the Sun [Col. 0540D] of righteousness.

I say that he has removed our iniquities far away; and afterward, when we have sinned, “the Lord has had mercy on those who fear him, as a father has mercy on his children.” Just as a father sometimes gently consoles his children and at other times chastises them with the pious intention of correcting them, so God has mercy on those who fear him, because “he himself knew our formation,” that is, he knew that we were made from fragile material, since we cannot resist temptations by our own strength.

I rightly say that he knew our formation, because, by strengthening us, “he remembered us”—although he seemed to have forgotten us when he allowed us to remain in sins—“because” according to our condition “we are dust,” namely, bound together by the bond of faith or charity, yet not sufficient in ourselves to withstand the devil’s wind [Col. 0541A]. And because “man” is “like grass,” that is, a thing that quickly fails and dries up, “his days,” that is, the strength and splendor he possesses in youth, “will blossom,” said in a privative sense—that is, they will blossom and wither. “So,” that is, so lightly, “like the flower of the field.” Or “he will blossom” in the proper sense, but only transitorily; this is what he means by “so, like the flower of the field.”

And he remembered “that the spirit,” that is, the soul breathing within the human being, “passed through him,” that is, it does not remain in the same understanding but is always passing on to different things. Yet “even” that spirit “will not remain,” that is, it will not remain in a human being, because through death it departs from every person; and “afterward” [Col. 0541B] in this life “it will no longer know its place,” that is, it will not give life to this mortal body.

Human beings are indeed so fragile; “but the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and to eternity” and will remain “upon those who fear him.”

Mercy is upon those who fear him, “and” through that mercy “his righteousness is upon children’s children.” Through that same mercy not only the present children but also those who come afterward will be justified. “His righteousness is upon children’s children”—not upon everyone, but “upon those who keep his covenant,” that is, upon those who diligently and with good will search out God’s law.

“And” after searching it out, “they remember his commandments,” not merely in order to hear or repeat [Col. 0541C] them, but “in order to do” them, that is, to fulfill them.

I have said that the Lord is merciful and justifies. Yet the Lord himself “prepared his throne in heaven,” that is, among the highest holy beings, in which he sits as judge; “and his kingdom will rule over all,” because no one will be able to resist his authority. After encouraging us to praise him for God’s many benefits, he also admonishes us through fear of the judgment, which the wicked cannot escape, so that we may not cease praising him.

“Bless the Lord.” The third part. Since the Lord is such, therefore you, “all his angels, bless” this “Lord.” The Prophet does not use the imperative verb because the angels need to praise God at his command, or because they might cease praising God; rather, seeing them praise God continually and rejoicing in that familiar love of praise, he urges them to praise God. He identifies whom he calls his angels by saying: “mighty in strength.” It is as though he were saying: “You demons, who fell irrecoverably through pride, I do not urge to praise God; I urge those who remained obedient and therefore persevere, persisting in great charity.”

He specifies whom he calls mighty in strength by saying: “doing,” that is, fulfilling, “his word,” that is, God’s command—not that it is imposed on them in an elementary spoken form, but because they do what they understand God to will.

“Doing his word,” I say, “to hear the voice,” that is, in order to do and understand the voice that must be done by all, “of his words,” that is, of God’s commandments. Or: “Doing his word”—I mean, you who are ready and attentive “to hear the voice of his words,” that is, so that you may understand what God commands you [Col. 0542A].

Nor do I urge only one order of angels to praise God, but “all his powers,” that is, all the orders of angels, “bless the Lord.” Although the angels of one order are properly called “powers,” “powers” is nevertheless used as a common name for all the orders. You, I say, “his ministers who do his will.” For the angels complete on earth what they understand God to will; for example, the angel Gabriel, who was sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1).

“Bless the Lord, all his works,” that is, provide me with material for blessing the Lord. And you, “my soul, bless the Lord,” considering the things that are “in every place of his dominion” [Col. 0542B]. The wicked, whom the Lord awaits in his mercy, are for me a reason to bless the Lord.

Or the passage may be read under another construction as follows: “All his works that exist in every place of his dominion, bless the Lord”—as though anything outside his dominion could not be material for me to bless the Lord. And because of all these works, “bless the Lord, my soul.”

## ON PSALM 103

**Title:** A psalm of David himself.

“Bless, II.” Here the Prophet speaks, and his subject is the Creator and the whole of creation [Col. 0542C]. He shows how God arranged these created things in the world. Yet he is not dealing here only with material arrangement: through this material arrangement the Prophet understood another, spiritual arrangement, which God makes in the souls of the faithful, as he himself will indicate in certain passages. Thus the spiritual arrangement is understood here in the material subject, just as the spiritual arrangement is understood in the soul.

The structure is as follows. In the first part, he shows how God arranged the heavens through a material arrangement; what we are to understand mystically in this will be explained as we read. In the second part, which begins, “This great sea,” he shows how God arranged the remaining things. In the third part, which begins, “May the glory of the Lord be forever,” he shows that God is to be praised for this kind of arrangement and urges others to praise God [Col. 0542D]. This is his purpose.

To provide others with an example in himself, he thus exhorts his soul: “Bless the Lord, my soul,” as though he were saying: “Considering the wonders that the Lord has made, praise him and make them known to others.”

God is to be praised more for renewal than for the first creation itself. Now he turns directly to God, saying: O “Lord God,” my soul ought rightly to bless you, because you “have been magnified,” that is, have been judged great by your faithful. God cannot in his nature be either magnified or diminished; rather, he appears greater or lesser to his faithful according to how much their knowledge of him increases [Col. 0543A]. And this is “exceedingly,” that is, inscrutably. No one, however perfect, can comprehend God’s greatness.

When he says, “my God,” he indicates that he has God as someone very familiar to him, and that he is therefore fit to bless the Lord.

I rightly say that you have been magnified, because you, God, created all things. This is “confession and beauty,” that is, these creatures, which are called confession and beauty because they display their Creator, or because the things themselves, insofar as they possess their created nature, are beautiful and lovely.

Yet you “clothed yourself” with this confession. God was indeed naked, unadorned, and known by no one before he made the creatures; afterward he clothed himself with them, because through them he appeared known and adorned [Col. 0543B]. You, I say, are “clothed with light,” that is, having taken up residence in creatures, you, who are the true light, have become luminous “as with a garment,” because you are adorned by those creatures.

Allegorically, by “confession” we may understand the faithful, who confess and praise the Lord. They are beautiful according to the purity of their life, in which they especially display the beauty of the one whom they serve. God is clothed with these people, with those who are “light,” that is, luminous according to the knowledge they possess of God who dwells in them; for they are God’s ornament, like the clothing of a human being. Hence the Prophet says: “I live, says the Lord, because you have clothed yourself with all these things as with a garment.”

“Stretching out heaven.” He shows the arrangement of heaven through which God appears magnified. I say, you clothed yourself with confession; you “stretch out heaven like a skin.” For just as a skin envelops the whole animal, so heaven encloses the whole world. You, I say, “cover its upper parts” with material “waters”; hence elsewhere: “Waters above the firmament” (Genesis 1).

Allegorically, by heaven we may understand divine Scripture, which contains heavenly mysteries. It is stretched out like a skin because it protects and defends us on every side. The upper parts of this Scripture are covered by waters because Scripture itself brings before us, as though openly, the waters of baptism, so that in them we may lay aside our sins and receive the Holy Spirit.

It should be noted that we read the literal sense according to the figure, and at times draw an allegory from certain words. Alternatively, by “its upper parts” we may understand Scripture’s higher commandments, namely, love of God and of neighbor, which God covers with waters, that is, fills with spiritual graces.

He sets forth other arrangements: “stretching out the heavens”—I say, you “who make the cloud your ascent.” Literally, this was so, because the angel who was to announce God’s will to our fathers descended and ascended in a cloud; hence in another psalm he says: “He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud” (Ps. XCVIII; Num. XXII). And he further displays God as magnificent when he says: “Who walk upon the wings of the winds”—that is, you accomplish your will more swiftly than the winds accomplish any intended course; or because you, God, are everywhere. The winds are described as winged even by the divine poets, [Col. 0544A] on account of their agility. Allegorically, by the cloud we signify Christ and the other saints, through whose conformity to God we ascend; by the winged wind we understand faithful souls, who are agile and, with the agility of their minds, fly toward the contemplation of God, and who are winged with many virtues. God walks upon them because he is also in them, is better than all, and through his assistance they themselves advance.

Another arrangement in which God appears magnificent and worthy of praise is expressed by the words: “Who makes spirits”—that is, the angelic creatures themselves—“your angels”—that is, your messengers themselves. “Spirit” is the name of the substance itself, whereas “angel” is the name of an office. And he makes “a burning fire”—that is, the order of angels called the seraphim, whose name is interpreted as “burning”—“your ministers,” that is, through them you administer and fulfill your will in the world. Let us explain the allegory in this way: “Who makes spirits”—that is, spiritual men—“your angels,” because through their preaching you announce to us your will; and you make your ministers a burning fire—that is, men kindled and filled with the love of God, so that they may also burn and kindle others with the love of God.

Having shown the creation and arrangement of heaven, he shows the creation and arrangement of the earth, in which God is likewise recognized as magnificent and worthy of praise. It is as though he said: You are also magnified for this reason, because you are the one “who founded the earth upon its stability”—that is, you made it stable and firm. We understand the earth’s stability literally, recognizing its weight and the support provided by the surrounding air.
