Yet this earth “will not be moved for ever and ever,” that is, it will not be destroyed. Although its qualities may sometimes change, its substance will never perish. By the earth we understand the Church, which is founded upon its stability—that is, upon Christ—and this Church will not be moved for ever and ever, because no violence of the devil will ever destroy it.

You founded the earth, and “the abyss” of that earth, namely the Ocean, “is clothed like a garment”—that is, it surrounds “the mountains” of the earth on every side. The waters of the Flood “will stand above its mountains,” for the waters of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountain (Gen. VII). When the Prophet speaks of the waters of the Flood, which had already passed in his own time, as though announcing a future event—“Above the mountains the waters will stand”—he indicates that he is dealing here more with what is signified than with the figure itself. Therefore, we investigate the allegory throughout. According to our understanding of the earth as the Church, the passage may be explained as follows: The Church will not be moved for ever and ever, although the abyss of the deepest kind—that is, vices—is its garment, its clothing; that is, those who persecute the Church surround it on every side with persecutions, as a person is surrounded by a garment. And the waters will stand not only above the lesser members of the Church, but also above the mountains—that is, above the greater members of the Church, such as the apostles themselves. These waters are its constant attackers: persecutors wishing to overwhelm it, such as Nero, who killed Peter and Paul bodily. [Col. 0545A]

The waters will stand, but those waters “will flee at your rebuke,” just as the waters of the Flood withdrew and fled when rebuked by the winds sent by God. And those waters “will be afraid”—that is, they will show themselves afraid, withdrawing to their former place—“at the sound of your thunder,” that is, because of the great blowing of the winds. Allegorically: The persecutors of the Church will flee—that is, they will cease their persecution—“at the rebuke,” that is, because of your admonition rebuking them; and they will be afraid of what they have done, terrified by the sound of your thunder—that is, because of the threat of the future judgment.

I say that the waters fled; and when they flee, “the mountains rise and the plains descend”—that is, they appear elevated, not all at the same height or all in the same lowliness, but “to the place which you founded for them,” according to the way you arranged them. Or allegorically: When the persecutions cease, the mountains—that is, the prelates in the Church—rise, become eminent, and preach openly; while the plains—that is, the humble—descend, humbly obeying their prelates. They are not all in the same order, but in the place which you founded for them, since some in the Church are higher than others.

The waters will flee, and for them you “set their boundary,” the shores, “which they will not cross.” He shows why this is done when he says: “Nor will they return to cover the earth”—that is, the Flood will no longer occupy the whole earth. Allegorically in the same way: The Lord has set a boundary for the persecutors, which they will not cross, because no one is permitted to rage except as far as God allows; nor will they henceforth cover the earth—that is, no violence will destroy the Church.

I say, “you have set a boundary,” you “who send forth springs in the valleys,” because springs flow from the mountains into the valleys; and the flowing “waters will pass through” from place to place “among the mountains,” because no one can hold back their course. Mystically likewise, the Lord sends forth springs—that is, flowing teachings—from the mountains, namely from the holy apostles and other perfect men in the Church, into the valleys, that is, to humble and simple men who are to be taught and strengthened. Those waters, that is, those teachings, will pass from region to region, and this among the mountains—that is, among the proud—for in no way will the proud and powerful of this life be able to extinguish the course of God’s teaching. Or “among the mountains” means among the holy apostles and other perfect men, by whose authority that teaching is surrounded, supported, and guarded.

I say that the waters will pass through literally, and from there “all the beasts of the field will drink.” The wild asses, however—“onagers,” that is, forest asses—“will wait in their thirst,” that is, in the thirst they naturally possess. Although onagers are naturally thirsty, they are so foolish that, when they see water, they delay satisfying their thirst. Allegorically, therefore, from the water—that is, from the teaching of God—all the beasts of the field will drink: that is, rustic and bestial men of every human kind, such as the Gentiles. The onagers, however—that is, the Jews—are sluggish and foolish in their thirst. Although they thirst naturally and say that the promised Messiah is theirs, nevertheless, when they see him and hear his teaching, they do not quench their thirst, because they do not believe in Christ the Redeemer. Instead, they will wait to turn to him until the end of time.

I say that the waters will pass through among the mountains, literally, and “above them”—namely, above the mountains and waters—“the birds of the heavens will dwell, and they will give forth their voices from the midst of the rocks.” Allegorically likewise, the birds of the heavens—that is, spiritual men who always seek heaven—will dwell above them, because they will refresh themselves with that heavenly teaching and with the authority of the holy mountains. Thus refreshed, they will give forth their voices—that is, praises to God—“from the midst of the rocks,” that is, according to the authority [Col. 0546B] of the holy apostles and other perfect men.

From the mountains you send springs into the valleys; but the “mountains,” literally, are “watered from your higher places”—that is, by rain coming from heaven. Or, if the reading here is *suis* (“his own” or “their own”), it will belong to the preceding wording, “who sends forth.” And because you thus water the mountains and valleys, therefore “the earth will be filled with the fruit of your works”—that is, with the fruit which you produce. Literally, then: When the mountains—that is, the higher members of the Church—rain upon and water their inferiors with their teaching, God himself waters those mountains with his own gifts and inspirations. Through this, the earth—that is, the holy Church—will be filled and satisfied with fruit, namely with the virtues of your works, that is, with those which you work in them.

I rightly say “it will be filled with fruit,” because you, God, are “the one who produces grass,” literally, “for cattle”—that is, grass on which cattle may feed—“and produces plants for the service of men,” because sheep, oxen, and other livestock that serve human beings feed upon them. Or allegorically: The Church will be satisfied because you, God, produce from that Church grass—that is, bodily support—“for the service of men,” that is, of rational beings. God causes certain people in the Church, through the benefits of almsgiving, to sustain the foolish, the useless, the good, and the rational in the Church. For we are commanded (Luke VI and XI) to give alms to everyone who asks.

Literally, it is as though he said: You, God, still bring forth grass from the earth for cattle, and so forth, “in order by these things” cultivated by you “to bring forth bread from the earth,” namely grain and such things; and bread is brought forth for this purpose, “to strengthen the heart of man.” You bring forth wine from the earth, and “wine gladdens the heart of man,” just as we actually see people who drink wine become merry.

And for this reason you produce grass and make the other things mentioned: so that you may bring forth oil from the earth, for the purpose that “with oil” a person may “make his face cheerful.” The nature of oil is to warm the flesh greatly and to make it cheerful. “And bread strengthens the heart of man.” We may explain this allegorically as follows: You produce grass—that is, bodily sustenance—in order to bring forth from the earth, that is, from the faithful who share their goods with others, bread—that is, refreshment in the contemplation of God. For when they distribute their goods to others, they make themselves worthy for God to grant them knowledge of himself. Likewise, you produce grass so that they may receive wine—that is, the Lord’s blood—and that wine may gladden the inner heart of man. Those who are worthily refreshed by the Lord’s cup rejoice. Again, he brings forth grass so that those who provide the grass may be anointed with oil—that is, with the Holy Spirit—and so that the Lord may make their inner face radiant with oil, that is, because through the indwelling Spirit the Lord makes them exultant and joyful. Earlier he said, “so that you may bring forth bread,” and that bread may strengthen the heart of the inner man; for they are strengthened by good works, through which he grants them knowledge of himself.

Thus the animals are satisfied by God’s benefits, and besides this “the trees of the field” will literally “be filled” with God’s benefits. For God supplies trees with sap and other fluids, through which they live and produce fruit. “The cedars of Lebanon, which he planted,” will also be filled, since they are found to be nobler and more beautiful than all other trees; for this reason they are called a special work of God. “There,” that is, in those cedars, “the sparrows will make their nests.” Behold, not even this happens without God’s arrangement.

The heron is said to be a bird whose dwelling is in the waters, and it is thought to be the same bird as the coot; hence another translation has: “the house of the coot.” According to this, we shall explain it as follows: The sparrows will make their nests in the cedars; “their”—that is, of the sparrows—“leader” is the one who delights and refreshes them; “the house of the heron” is the water to which the sparrows come so that they may refresh and bathe themselves there. “The lofty mountains” are “a refuge for the deer,” since deer naturally delight in mountainous places and, when hunters pursue them, flee to the mountains. “For the hedgehogs”—that is, for the hairy animal—“the rock is a refuge.”

The heron is also said to be not an aquatic bird but a very rapacious one, hostile to human beings; it lives in a rock to which it retreats and where it is safe when danger threatens. According to this interpretation, “the house of the heron,” in which the heron dwells, “is their leader”—that is, the security and defense of those herons.

Allegorically we shall explain it as follows: Not only will those perfect men be satisfied with God’s bread and other benefits, but also the trees of the field. Another translation says “forests,” that is, the wild and uncultivated Gentiles converted to God; they will be “filled with the bread of God” and with other spiritual gifts. The cedar of Lebanon signifies the powerful, the exalted, and those adorned with the dignities of this age, which the Lord planted and to whom he gave those riches, not so that they might become proud or oppress the innocent, but so that with their riches they might display and defend the Church. Riches may indeed be possessed worthily; hence the Apostle says: “Command the rich not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God” (II Tim. VI). He did not say that they should reject riches altogether, but that they should not become proud.

There, that is, in the cedars, beneath the powerful of this life, the sparrows—that is, the humble, who regard themselves as small, such as monks and good canons—make nests, that is, their cells, among the benefices of the princes and powerful patrons of the Church. The sparrows, that is, the humble, those who are in the cedars—that is, beneath the powerful of this life—“will make their nests.”

The house of the herons, however—that is, the water of baptism—is the leader of those sparrows, because it leads the sparrows to eternal life. Or, according to the interpretation in which we said that the heron is a rapacious bird, we shall say: The sparrows will make their nests there in the cedars, but the house of the heron—that is, the rock, which is Christ—is the leader of those herons, namely of the rapacious creatures and beasts of this life, whom Christ leads and governs if they turn to him.

The lofty mountains—that is, the apostles and other perfect men—are a refuge for the deer, that is, for those people who avoid muddy and thorny places, namely sins. Such people flee to the authority of the apostles, because through their examples they preserve and defend their faith. For the hedgehogs—that is, for the hairy and thorny in sins—the rock, that is, Christ, is a refuge; under his leadership they are safe from the devil’s attacks.

Besides these arrangements, God also “made” other things: the material “moon,” to endure “for a time,” that is, for as long as time exists; and he made “the sun,” which “the sun knew its setting,” because through the sun and the moon God made the alternation of times.

Having set forth the alternation of night and day, he shows what God arranged to be done at night, and afterward what is done during the day. It is as though he said: The sun knew its setting; when it set, “you placed darkness,” as it were near the beginning of night; “and then night came,” that is, that greater darkness. During that night “all the beasts of the forest will pass from place to place.” For, by God’s arrangement, that is the suitable time in which those beasts may seek food for themselves.

He shows which beasts he had mentioned, namely “the young lions.” The lions themselves will pass through, and likewise the other beasts, “roaring” and crying out to God. They will pass through in order “to seize food for themselves and seek it from God.” For they do not have food for themselves except by God’s permission. When God punishes someone’s offenses, he permits his sheep or something of that kind to be consumed by a wolf.

“The sun has risen.” Having shown the arrangement of night, he shows the arrangement of day. It is as though he said: Such things occur at night; but when “the sun has risen, and the young lions have gathered,” [Col. 0548D] “they will be placed in their dens.”

When the sun has risen, and the beasts have thus been settled, “man will go forth to his work and to his labor” and continue it “until evening.”

Allegorically we may explain it as follows: Christ became a refuge for the hedgehogs, that is, for sinners, through the fact that he made the moon—that is, the Church—which, although it waxes and wanes like the moon, will nevertheless endure in time. The sun, that is, Christ, who is the true sun, “knew its setting,” that is, foresaw his own death. He died because you, God, “placed darkness”—ignorance—in the hearts of the Jews, since they did not recognize Christ their physician. Night came—that is, blindness in their hearts—when they handed Christ over to death. During that night all the beasts of the forest will pass through: that is, the demons will roam widely, thinking that, with Christ dead—the one whom they saw as the cause of all righteousness—the whole human race had been abandoned to their power.

He specifies through certain parts which beasts he means here when he says: “The young lions,” that is, lesser demons and their evil ministers, will pass through roaring—that is, gnashing their teeth in order to devour some people. They will pass through for this purpose, to seize and seek food for themselves from God, namely certain people whom they may incorporate into themselves, and this “from God”: for they cannot devour anyone except by God’s permission. God permitted Judas, by a just judgment, to be incorporated into the devil, and others likewise.

This was the situation after Christ’s death. But after “the sun had risen,” that is, after Christ had risen, and, like the rising sun, had illuminated the world, the demons gathered—not because they had come together in one place, but he speaks figuratively. Just as some people fleeing the presence of a powerful victor withdraw to their own places, so the demons, who had wished to belong to Christ, withdrew to their own. Then, persisting in wickedness, “they will be placed in their dens,” that is, they will rest in those who are truly their dens: in those who have become hardened and persevere in sins, and who in no way wish to approach the faith. They will be placed in their dens.

But the rational man will go forth to his work, that is, he will work openly—his own work, namely what is fitting for a rational man, that is, a good work—and to continue his labor until evening.

Since, O God, you have perfected all these things, both bodily and spiritually, therefore, O “Lord, your works are magnified”—that is, they are known as wondrous and magnificent—and “how” ineffably magnified they are! I say that they are magnified because “in wisdom,” that is, wisely, “you have made all things.” For all things have been arranged by God’s ineffable providence. They are also magnified because “the earth is filled with your possession,” with the multitude of its inhabitants.

Part Two. “This great sea.” It is as though he said: Lord, you have thus arranged heaven and earth, and “this sea.” He speaks as though displaying it before us. I say that the sea is “great” in its nature and “spacious,” that is, broad “for sailing with ships,” [Col. 0549D] in which many can likewise sail. “There,” that is, in this sea, are “reptiles,” that is, sea monsters, “whose number is not known” with certainty to any human being.

The reptiles cannot be counted, but I can say this one thing about them: those reptiles are both small and large. This is what he says: “small animals with great ones.” And although there are so many monsters in the sea, nevertheless “ships will pass through there” unharmed.

In that sea is “that dragon,” marvelous and of infinite size, called Leviathan, “whom you formed to mock him” (Job III), that is, so that he might be mocked. Although he is so immense and voracious (Isa. XXVII), nevertheless, with God driving him on, ships pass before him unharmed. “And all these,” namely the dragon and the animals, “wait for you to give them food in due season.”

Or we may connect the passage in this way: You, God, who made eternal things in wisdom, made this sea with your hands. Allegorically, by this sea we understand the present age, which is great and spacious for the hands of those who labor, because it is always open to those who work. There, that is, in this sea, are reptiles—that is, demons and their ministers—whose number is not known. These reptiles, namely the small and great animals, are demons, some greater than others, not in substance but in power.

There, that is, in this sea, namely in the world, ships will pass through—that is, the Churches, which are battered by the waves of this world but are not submerged. And elsewhere, that is, in this world, is this dragon [Col. 0550B]—that is, the principal devil, namely Beelzebub, signified by Leviathan—whom you created good in the first creation, but after his fall formed him to be mocked, that is, made him mockable. For even prostitutes will mock him: when he thinks that he holds them more firmly, entangled as they are in filthy vices, they slip from his hands and are transferred through repentance into the body of Christ.

And all these, namely the dragon and the others, wait for you to give them food at the appropriate time. He had an opportune time when the Lord handed Judas over into his hands. All these await food from you; and when you give them food, they “gather” both animals and human beings. But when you “open your hand,” that is, when you give assistance, “all things will be filled with goodness”—that is, with deliverance and aid—through the goodness of God bestowed upon them. For, when God provides assistance, neither can the demons conform human beings to themselves, nor can the animals themselves inflict bodily harm.

When you give, they will be filled with goodness; but if they presume upon themselves, you will turn your face away from them, and thus they will be troubled. This is what follows: “But when you turn your face away”—that is, withdraw your grace—“they will be troubled”; that is, they will realize that they are nothing. And you will take away “their spirit”—the spirit of pride—which is “theirs,” namely something they possess not from God but from themselves. Thus they will fail in their proud presumption “and return to their own dust”—that is, they will be moved.

Or allegorically, they will return to the dust when they return to humility and do nothing from themselves, but recognize that the material from which they are made is ash and dust. [Col. 0550D]

They die, and you “send forth your Spirit,” the Holy Spirit, or an angel. For the trumpet will sound, calling the dead to judgment, “and they will be created,” that is, changed, “and you will renew the face of the earth.”

Or allegorically, according to our statement that the dust is reduced to humility, we shall say: They will return to the dust—that is, to humility—and you will send your Holy Spirit into their hearts. Through this they will be recreated for good works, and thus, by conforming the face of the earth—that is, their minds, which previously yearned for earthly things—you will make a new earth.

“Let there be glory.” Part Three. The connection is as follows: Since the Lord performs all these things, therefore “let the glory of the Lord be for ever,” that is, let all of you show the Lord to be glorious, not for a time but for ever, that is, eternally. You ought to glorify him because he has made many works and has made them good. This is what follows: “The Lord will rejoice in his works.” He shows that the works in which God will rejoice are good.

“The Lord will rejoice in his works”—namely, in those by which, in his regard, the earth trembled and the mountains smoked. This is what follows: He “looks upon the earth”—that is, he mercifully visits the lesser members of the Church—“and makes it tremble” over its sins. He also “touches” the mountains, that is, the powerful, with some persecution or threat, “and they smoke”—that is, they weep over their sins in tearful contrition.

And because the Lord is so great, whatever others may do, I “will sing to the Lord” with voice and devotion. This means “in my life”—that is, not for an hour, but throughout my whole life. And I will also “sing psalms,” that is, I will do good works, “to my God”—that is, not for my own praise, but for the honor of my God—and this “as long as I exist.”

I will not sing only for myself, but will also announce it to others. And would that this “speech of mine be pleasing to him”! My speech will indeed be pleasing to him, “but I will delight in the Lord.” Here a familiar reciprocity between God and man is noted: if a person takes delight in God, God himself immediately takes delight in that person.

“I will delight in the Lord,” and would that other sinners become like me! This is what follows: “Let sinners cease from the earth”—that is, from earthliness—so that they no longer desire what is earthly; “and let the wicked” be converted, “so that they are no longer” what they previously were. And for all these benefits of God, “bless the Lord, O my soul.”

## Psalm 104. Title: Alleluia

“Give thanks.” It should be noted that *alleluia* is not a human utterance, but one that the prophet and other holy men heard from the angels singing, as blessed John, seized in ecstasy, heard them (Apoc. XIX). Nor can that utterance be interpreted by any single word. In the word *alleluia* both the name of God and praise are contained—not simply praise, but praise accompanied by exultation. What is expressed by *IA* is the name of the Lord; what is expressed by *ALLELU* signifies praise with exultation.

Whenever such a title is prefixed to a psalm, it indicates that the psalm contains praiseworthy works of God. This psalm contains God’s praiseworthy works, which are also the subject of the psalm. If we attend to them, we shall praise God, the Creator of all things, with the greatest exultation. God performed all these benefits for that people so that through them he might admonish and invite them to seek him spiritually, as he says in the final verse: “That they may keep his justifications and seek his law.”

Accordingly, in the first part he sets forth an admonition, so that all who are admonished by these bodily benefits may seek the Lord spiritually. In the second part, which begins, “Remember his wonders,” he sets forth the wonders God performed for the patriarchs. In the third part, which begins, “And he called for famine,” he shows how he delivered Jacob and his sons, preparing a place for them in Egypt through Joseph. In the fourth part, which begins, “And he established him over his enemies,” he shows the wonders he performed against the Egyptians for the liberation of his people. In the fifth part, which begins, “And he brought them out with silver and gold,” he shows with what power the Lord brought his people out of Egypt and led them into the promised land. At the end he admonishes them to seek God through all these things. He intends to admonish human beings to praise God.

The title is to be understood as follows: This psalm is called *alleluia*, that is, it contains such benefits of God that God should be praised for them with exultation.

The Prophet’s voice thus invites everyone to praise God: All of you, attending to the benefits God bestowed upon his people, “give thanks to the Lord”—that is, praise the Lord—“and invoke his name.” Do not invoke him for gold or riches, but so that he may dwell within you. Nor should this even be sufficient for you; rather, “declare his works among the nations”—that is, be concerned for the salvation of others as well as for your own, attending to this commandment of God: Whoever loves him must also love his neighbor.

I say, “give thanks to the Lord,” in this manner: “sing to him” with mind and voice, “and sing psalms to him” through good action. “Tell” also “all his wonders”—not that all of them can be told, but that all the things they will tell are wonders of God. This is what he has in view when he says: “Declare his works among the nations.” If you do this, you will truly be praised; but do not attribute that praise to yourselves. Rather, “praise yourselves in his holy name”—that is, let the Lord’s name be enlarged and shown to be glorious through your praise.

And I say, “in his holy name,” namely: “Seek the Lord,” not as one who rewards with temporal things, but so that he may give himself to you as the reward of your labor. Do this with joy. Thus he says: “Let the heart” of those who seek the Lord “rejoice.” Although the flesh may be afflicted by hardship, let the mind rejoice. I say, “seek the Lord,” and “be strengthened” by seeking him, so that neither death nor life may separate you from the love of Christ (Rom. VIII). He specifies how he ought to be sought when he says: “Seek his face always”—that is, so that here you may possess the presence of knowledge of him, and at last see him face to face.

“Remember.” Part Two. I say, “seek,” and in order that you may seek, “remember his wonders which he performed” (Gen. XI and XX), such as the fact that he caused your fathers to cross the Red Sea on dry ground; and remember “his marvels,” such as the signs he performed for the Egyptians on behalf of those fathers (Exod. IX); and remember “the judgments of his mouth”—that is, the commandments of the law. Although Moses spoke them, they must not be understood as though they came from Moses, but as though they came from the mouth of God himself. For whoever attends to God’s benefits has sought him spiritually and served him in faith.

You too must act in this way—you who are “the seed of Abraham, his servants,” and also “the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.” If you become like Jacob, you will be placed among God’s chosen.

Remember also because “he himself is the Lord our God.” And therefore, because “his judgments”—that is, his commandments—“have been made known throughout all the earth,” as was fulfilled through Christ and his apostles, just as the Psalmist himself says: “Their words have gone forth to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Remember also because, in the very fulfillment, he “remembered his covenant,” the promise he made to Abraham when he said: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. XIII). That land was a figure of the land of the living. The promise was fulfilled in figure when our humanity obtained true rest in Christ, and through him those who imitate Abraham—that is, the righteous—already enjoy that same rest at least in hope. The covenant, I say, is to remain “for ever,” that is, eternally. The faithful will possess that land without succession.

This covenant is “the word which” the Lord “commanded”—that is, entrusted to human beings—“for a thousand generations,” that is, always, with a finite expression used for an infinite duration. Or “word” means the commandment given to Abraham when he said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. XII). In its signification that commandment remains “for a thousand generations,” for spiritually all the faithful are commanded there to leave their earthliness and the allurements of their own understanding.

The covenant, I say, is the one which he “ordained for Abraham,” and he “remembered his oath”—that is, the firm and, together with the oath, immutable promise—“made to Isaac,” where the Lord said to him: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI).

“And he established that” covenant “with Jacob,” because he made the same promise to Jacob, so that it might be for him “as a commandment”—namely, so that on account of that promise he might serve God as though instructed by a divine commandment and admonished by the law. And with Israel—that is, with the one who had become Israel, “seeing God” through the multiplication of virtues—he established it “as an everlasting covenant,” because that promise will be both immutable and eternal for the faithful.

He “ordained” and established it, saying: “To you I will give the land of Canaan,” that is, the promised land, which Canaan, the son of Noah, formerly inhabited. Canaan is interpreted as “descent” or “humble.” Hence he says: “To you I will give the land of Canaan,” that is, the land acquired through humility, namely the heavenly Jerusalem. I call it a land, “the lot of your inheritance,” that is, a land divided among the individual tribes by lot. In the same way, the land of the living is distributed as if by lot, since it is assigned to each person according to God’s arrangement.

He promised this land “when” those to whom he promised it “were few in number,” so few that they were “very few, and inhabitants” of that land, living there as though they were strangers. Since it seemed impossible that so few should rule over so great a land, the promise appears to have been made rather concerning the land signified than concerning that land itself.

And although he had promised it to them, those to whom the promise had been made “passed” without attaining the promised inheritance, “from one nation” to another nation, and not merely within one kingdom but “from one kingdom to another people.” Abraham went from the land of Canaan to the land of Egypt. Since Abraham and the others to whom that promise was made did not obtain the promised land, let us understand the promise chiefly as referring to the land signified, so that we may call God truthful in his promises.

As they passed through, “he did not allow anyone to harm them,” and he “rebuked kings” who wished to harm them “for their sake.” Such were Pharaoh, who had taken Sarah from Abraham (Gen. XX), and Abimelech, who had taken Rebekah from Isaac (Gen. XXVI).

He said to those kings: “Do not touch my anointed ones.” This does not mean that they had a material anointing, but a spiritual one. “And do not act wickedly”—that is, do not act maliciously—“against my prophets.”

“And he called.” Part Three. He did these things for the patriarchs and prophets; and besides them he also “called famine,” as though calling a servant, “upon the land” of Canaan. Through that famine he “crushed every support of bread,” because bread failed that would strengthen them. This occurred in the time of Jacob (Gen. XLII).

And in order to free them from that famine, “he sent a man before them,” namely Joseph, “Joseph, who was sold as a slave” in Egypt (Gen. XXXIX).

Then the Egyptians “humbled his feet in fetters,” because the wife of his master, whose name was Potiphar, accused him of adultery, to which she wickedly wished to compel him (Ibid.). Although you say this, it is not contrary to Moses. Joseph pleased [the master of the prison,] and he placed him over the other prisoners, because both things could have happened: he could first have been placed in fetters and afterward have pleased the keeper of the prison. In that captivity “iron”—that is, harsh anxiety—“passed through his soul until his word came,” that is, until he interpreted the dreams, though he did not do so from himself.

I say that he did not interpret his word from himself, but from God. This is what follows: “The utterance of the Lord inflamed him”—that is, the spirit of prophecy enlightened him. And because he interpreted the dreams in this way, “the king,” Pharaoh, “sent and released him” from the charge (Gen. XLI), so that his master would not impose adultery upon him. And it was not just any king, but “the ruler of many peoples,” and he “dismissed him” in complete freedom.

Afterward he “appointed him lord of his house and ruler over all his possessions.”

To this end, “that he might instruct his princes as himself,” that is, Joseph—or Pharaoh—in the interpretation of dreams, “and” also “teach his elders” reverently “wisdom,” the same wisdom, so that they might know how to interpret dreams. For Pharaoh, not considering that Joseph possessed this ability through divine inspiration, thought [Col. 0555A] that he had it through human ingenuity and could teach it to others.

The Lord sent Joseph, “and” through him “Israel entered Egypt” (Gen. XLVI), that is, the Israelite people; “and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham,” which Ham, the son of Noah, had first inhabited.

“And” there “he greatly increased his people” in number. Part four. “And he strengthened him over his enemies,” because God brought his people out from the Egyptians against their will, and afflicted the Egyptians in many ways.

“And he turned their heart,” that is, the Egyptians’ heart, “so that they hated his people” (Exod. I), that is, God’s people, “and dealt deceitfully with his servants,” either by increasing their labor or by withholding their payment.

And because they acted deceitfully in this way, therefore “he sent Moses his servant” [Col. 0555B] to Pharaoh (ibid.), “and through him Aaron whom he had chosen.”

“And he placed in them,” that is, in Moses and Aaron, his messengers, “the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham.” Through these messengers he threatened the Egyptians that, unless they released his people, he would perform signs among them—such as darkness and other lesser signs—and wonders, such as the killing of the firstborn and things of that kind.

Through them he threatened signs, and he fulfilled them, because “he himself sent darkness” upon the Egyptians (Exod. X), a darkness that could even be felt, “and” thus “he made it dark.” By fulfilling them in this way, “he did not make his words harsh,” that is, he did not make them appear bitter and false; for words appear bitter and deserving of rejection if they are not fulfilled as he had [Col. 0555C] ordained.

“And he also turned their waters into blood, and killed their fish.”

“And their land brought forth frogs” in such abundance that no bedchamber could be cleared of them (Exod. VII and VIII); and this occurred “in the inner chambers of their kings.”

And he himself “spoke,” that is, willed it, “and there came dog-flies,” that is, the canine fly, “and gnats,” which entered their eyes (Exod. VIII); and this was not in a few places, but “in all their territories.”

He also “made their rains hail,” and with the hail “a consuming fire,” that is, lightning (Exod. IX), “in their land.”

And with that fire “and hail he struck their vineyards,” [Col. 0555D] “and their fig trees, and shattered the trees”—fruit trees and other trees—“of their territories.”

He also “spoke,” that is, willed it, “and there came locust and caterpillar, whose number was beyond counting” (Exod. X).

The locust and caterpillar “devoured all the grass in their land, and devoured all the fruit of their land,” which the dog-flies and gnats could not do.

“And he struck every firstborn in their land” (Exod. XII), that is, among human beings and other animals, “the firstfruits of all their labor,” namely, the first produce.

“And he brought out the people.” Part five. Here, in contrast with the plagues that he has enumerated as inflicted upon the Egyptians, he enumerates [Col. 0556A] the benefits bestowed upon the Jews. Thus he struck the Egyptians, “and he brought them out,” that is, his own people, who were held captive by the Egyptians, “from Egypt with gold and silver,” because they had carried away from the Egyptians silver and golden vessels, which they had borrowed from them at the Lord’s command. The Lord did not wish his people to lose the payment for their servitude: “And there was no weak person among their tribes.” This was exceedingly marvelous: in so great a multitude no one was sick.

Then “Egypt,” that is, those who remained in Egypt, “rejoiced at their departure,” after learning that their own people had perished in the sea. And why did it rejoice? “Because fear of them,” namely, of the Jews, “fell upon them,” that is, upon the Egyptians. For they feared that the Jews might return and kill all those remaining in Egypt.

He brought them out (Exod. XI), and “he spread a cloud for their protection,” by which he might shield them from the sun’s heat and blind their enemies; “and” he made that same cloud “a fire, so that it might give them light by night.”

They also “asked” for meat (Exod. XVI), “and quail came, and he filled them with the bread of heaven,” when manna came from the air. He names manna by the name of what it signified, namely Christ, who truly is the bread of heaven, on which the angels feed. The manna signified this bread, that is, the body of Christ, by which the faithful are refreshed.

“He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers went forth in dry places” (Exod. XVII), and these followed them through the wilderness.

[Col. 0556C] He did all these things for them, not because of their merits, but “because he remembered his holy word,” that is, his promise, which he had made to Abraham: “the word,” I say, “which he had given to Abraham his servant,” saying to him: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). For if he had destroyed all the nations, the promise made to Abraham could not have been fulfilled, because Christ was born from the Jews.

“And” therefore “he brought out his people with rejoicing,” from place to place, “and his chosen ones with gladness.”

“And he gave them the territories of the nations,” because the nations possessed the promised land; and when these had been driven out, the Jews “possessed” “the labors” of those “peoples.”

[Col. 0556D] And God bestowed all these benefits upon them “so that they might keep his statutes,” that is, live justly according to “his” commandments, “and seek his law,” that is, understand and seek what else is to be understood in the figures of the ancient law, or Testament.

## PSALM CV. TITLE: Alleluia

“Give thanks II.” Some wish “Alleluia” to be placed here twice, but blessed Jerome says that whatever psalm has “Alleluia” at its beginning also has “Alleluia” at its end. Thus we shall say that one “Alleluia” belongs to the preceding psalm and the other to the following one. In the preceding psalm he enumerated the benefits [Col. 0557A] that God bestowed upon the children of Israel, without enumerating any of their sins. In this psalm, however, he shows the mercies that God displayed toward them when they sinned. Since God is to be praised for those mercies, this psalm is entitled “Alleluia.” Its subject is the very mercies of God shown to sinners.

Considering that he is speaking of those who have turned from their sins, and of the mercies of God displayed toward sinners, as well as of God’s having sometimes punished those same sinners, he invites the wicked in this first part to confess their sins, so that they may be found worthy of God’s mercy. In the second part, which begins, “Our fathers in Egypt,” he shows that they sinned and that God’s mercy was nevertheless shown toward them. In the third part, which begins, “They acted quickly,” he shows that they sinned against God in the wilderness; [Col. 0557B] he also shows that God took vengeance on some of them and that he was finally appeased through Moses. In the fourth part, which begins, “And they treated the desirable land as nothing,” he shows that they worshiped an idol and that God’s anger toward them was appeased through Phinehas. In the fifth part, which begins, “And they provoked him,” he shows that they sinned in such a way that they also caused Moses to sin with them, that they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, and that God, because of their sins, gave them into the hands of sinners. In the sixth part, which begins, “Save us,” he prays that God may gather the Church from all nations for the praise of God. His intention, however, is to invite everyone to praise God, that is, to sing “Alleluia,” and to invite the wicked to conversion.

[Col. 0557C] And thus he begins: “Give thanks,” confessing “your sins to the Lord,” so that you may obtain forgiveness, “for he is good,” that is, merciful. And see to it that, relying complacently on his goodness, you are not led into neglect of confession, “for his mercy is in the age” only. For unless you are converted here, you will not find mercy, because then repentance is too late and is not acceptable.

Nor do I speak only of the fact that he is good and that his mercy is present in this life, for I cannot enumerate his powers and praises; and this is what he means: “Who can speak of the powers of the Lord,” and who “can make all his praises heard?” No one, certainly.

No one can enumerate his powers and praises, but [Col. 0557D] there is this one thing: those “who keep judgment,” that is, those who have discernment of what is good and what is evil, “and practice justice,” that is, those who carry out good deeds and abandon evil—these “are blessed” “at all times,” that is, continually.

Here, making himself one of them, he begins to pray for them, as though they had already been converted. Continuation: I say, “give thanks,” praying in this way: “Remember us, Lord, in your good pleasure,” that is, in the Son, whom, solely from your good pleasure and not from human merits, you sent for the redemption of humanity. “Good pleasure,” I say, “of your people,” that is, through whom your people have been reconciled to you. And he shows how he says “remember,” adding: “Visit us with your salvation,” [Col. 0558A] that is, with the Son, who may bring about the salvation that you foresaw.

“Visit,” I say, “to see us in the goodness of your chosen ones,” that is, so that we may possess that goodness which your chosen ones possess, namely, justice; and also “to make us rejoice in the gladness of your nation,” that is, so that we may rejoice in knowledge of you, as your nation also does. Let us see for this purpose, let us rejoice for this purpose, “so that you may be praised with your inheritance,” that is, so that you may be praised by us, and so that we may be praised because of you, since we are your inheritance—namely, so that others, seeing our good works, may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

Therefore I ask, “Remember; visit,” because “we have sinned with our fathers,” that is, where our fathers, such as Adam and others, sinned, we sinned [Col. 0558B] in them, since we were in their loins. Or, “we sinned with our fathers,” that is, we offended God by similar sins and a shameful life; “we acted unjustly,” with respect to the worship of God; “we committed iniquity,” toward our neighbors.

“Our fathers.” Part two. I rightly say “with our fathers,” because our fathers sinned; and he sets out those sins, saying: “Our fathers,” dwelling “in Egypt, did not understand your wonders,” that is, they did not recognize that God was inflicting these plagues upon the Egyptians for the liberation of his people, but thought that these things happened to the Egyptians through the natural forces of things. And, what is more astonishing, “they did not remember the multitude of your mercies,” that is, the plagues inflicted through your great mercy in order to free your people [Col. 0558C] from the Egyptians. If they did not attribute them to God, they ought nevertheless to have remembered them, since they were wonders.

They did not remember, “and they provoked” God “as they went up to the sea,” because, when they had come to the sea and saw the enemies pursuing them from behind, they thought that God could not free them from their enemies, although there was no reason to doubt his power, since it had been revealed in Egypt through many signs. But they said: “He brought us out in order to kill us; it would have been better for us to die in our houses.” “The sea,” I say, “the Red Sea.” He adds this because the very nature of the sea frightened them; its redness arose from the character of the earth itself. He says “as they went up” because of the position of the place, since Egypt is low-lying land. And [Col. 0558D] although they had provoked him, nevertheless “he saved them for the sake of his name” being magnified, namely, “to make his power known.”

And so that we may regard God’s mercy as even greater, he shows the manner of their salvation, saying: “And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up, and he led them through the depths,” that is, through the depth of that sea, “as through a wilderness,” because he led them across on dry ground (Exod. XIV).

“And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them,” that is, the Egyptians, “and redeemed,” that is, freed, “them from the hand of the enemy,” that is, from Pharaoh’s power. By saying “redeemed,” he speaks of the signified by means of the signifier; for this signifies the price of blood by which [Col. 0559A] we were redeemed from the hand of the enemy, that is, the devil.

“And he covered the waters over those who afflicted them,” namely, the Egyptians, so completely that “not one of them remained” who was not drowned.

“And” then, having been brought out in this way, “they believed in his word and praised his praise,” that is, they praised him because of his praiseworthy deeds.

“They acted quickly.” Part three. They believed and praised, and they did this “quickly,” that is, temporarily, because “they forgot his works,” which he had displayed among them in all his power, “and they did not endure his counsel.” For when God, according to a certain plan—that is, according to his providence—wished to delay their food in order to test them, they did not endure it, but immediately murmured.

[Col. 0559B] “And they desired” not only natural food, such as bread and water, which could have adequately sufficed in the wilderness, but “desires,” that is, delicate foods, namely birds and things of that kind, and this “in the wilderness.” And they “tested God in the waterless place,” doubting his power.

“And” although they tested God in this way, nevertheless “he gave them their request,” and this to satiety; hence it says, “and he sent fullness into their souls” (Exod. XV).

“And” yet they did not cease, but “provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord,” who had been sanctified and anointed as priest by the Lord’s command. They were unwilling to accept him as the Lord’s priest, but provoked Moses because of him, saying [Col. 0559C] that he had not acted by the Lord’s command, but because he wanted to exalt his brother (Num. XVI).

And because of that provocation, “the earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the assembly of Abiron,” that is, it swallowed Abiron and his family and closed over them.

“And in their assembly,” that is, in the congregation agreeing with these proposals that the priesthood should be taken from Aaron—namely, Korah and his sons—“fire blazed” to such an extent that “the flame consumed the sinners.” For when Korah and those with him were offering incense, the fire turned against them and consumed them. That fire was a sign of the ardor of their desire: envying Aaron, they wanted to appoint someone from among themselves as priest.

[Col. 0559D] “And” for this reason “they made a calf,” a molten image, “at Horeb,” in that place, when Moses went up the mountain to the Lord. For the Jews compelled Aaron to make a molten calf for them (Exod. XXXII), and he consented to them, partly under compulsion and partly out of desire for money; “and they worshiped” that “carved image.”

“And” thus “they changed their glory,” that is, the Lord, who was their glory, “into the likeness of a calf that eats grass.” They did not attribute the honor due to the true calf, but to the image of a calf.

By acting in this way, “they forgot God who saved them” from the Egyptians, “who did great things,” that is, great deeds, “in Egypt” in order to free them; and those deeds [Col. 0560A] were wondrous. Hence it says: “wonders in the land of Ham,” that same Egypt. Or by “wonders” may be understood the benefits that God bestowed upon them in Egypt. They forgot the “terrible things” done “in the Red Sea,” because, when their enemies were engulfed in the sea, they could have feared that the same thing might happen to them.

“And” then the Lord “said,” that is, decided, “to destroy them,” that is, judged them deserving of destruction. And he would have destroyed them “if Moses his chosen one had not stood before him,” praying for that people, “in the breach,” that is, at the time of the breach that was going to come upon them. Or, “in confession,” that is, in humility, because he humbled himself for them before the Lord, saying: “Lord, erase me from your book rather than erase this people” (ibid.). Thus, just as the Lord [Col. 0560B] was appeased toward them by Moses’ prayer, so we should understand that he is appeased each day toward our sins by the prayer of the faithful. Yet divine providence is not thereby changed, because, just as the Lord foresaw that he would be appeased, so he foresaw that this would happen through the prayer of the faithful; and if the prayers were not offered, he would not be appeased. Although Moses pleaded that the Lord should not inflict a common destruction, nevertheless, moved by zeal for God, he killed many. So also today the judges of the Church do not sin, even though, moved by zeal for God, they inflict punishment upon evildoers.

“He had stood.” For this purpose: “to turn away his anger,” that is, God’s anger, “so that he would not destroy them,” that is, so that he would not inflict a common destruction upon them (Num. XIV).

Part four. “And” although God had bestowed benefits [Col. 0560C] upon them, nevertheless they “treated the desirable land,” namely, the land of promise that God had promised, “as nothing,” because they did not believe God’s promise.

“They did not believe his word” concerning that promise. For when their scouts returned and reported that the land was very good and that there were men in it, one of whom could kill a hundred Jews, “and” therefore they murmured in their tents, saying: “Let us choose a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt; for it would be better for us still to be in slavery than to perish fighting these men” (Num. XXVI). “They did not heed the voice of the Lord,” because they doubted that land which God had promised them.

“And” then the Lord “raised his hand,” that is, prepared himself to inflict punishment, “against them, [Col. 0560D] to strike them down in the wilderness.”

“And” not only them, but also “to cast down their seed among the nations,” that is, among various nations. And he would cast them down so that they would not be alike, since their generation produced pride; rather, he would “scatter them among the regions,” that is, through distant lands.

“And” deservedly they were destroyed (Num. XV), because they “were initiated”—passively, that is, consecrated, as another translation has it—“to Beel,” that is, to that idol, “phegor,” of that place, namely Priapus, who is the god of lust. For *phegor* is interpreted as “lust,” or *Beelphegor*, that is, “the god of lust.” “Or they were initiated” can be read actively: they initiated themselves, that is, devoted themselves [Col. 0561A] to that idol. “They ate the sacrifices of the dead,” that is, idol sacrifices, namely flesh sacrificed to images of the dead.

“And” then “they provoked him by their inventions,” by the fact that they mingled with the Midianites, since they had been forbidden to associate with foreign women; at their counsel they worshiped Beelphegor. “And” therefore “ruin multiplied among them,” because many of them were killed.

“And” then, in that danger, “Phinehas stood,” pure in mind because he did not sin with the others, “and appeased” the Lord by piercing the Jew who was joined to the Midianite woman. “And” then “the shaking,” that is, the ruin, “ceased,” namely, the ruin that they were suffering.

“And it was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation [Col. 0561B] to generation forever”:  the fact that he struck that man out of zeal for God was not reckoned to him as homicide.

“And they provoked him.” Part five. And although God had thus punished them, they nevertheless did not cease; indeed, they even caused Moses himself to sin with them. This is what is meant by: “And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction,” where Moses brought water out of the rock (Num. XX), near the promised land, when the children of Israel quarreled, saying that he could not bring water out of the rock. “And Moses was troubled because of them,” that is, he was disturbed by them, “because they embittered his spirit,” that is, they made him angry on account of their unbelief and made him harsh.

“And” because he was moved by them, “he distinguished with [Col. 0561C] his lips,” that is, he spoke to them differently and with excessive confidence from his customary manner. Thus, as some say, he spoke presumptuously: “Can we bring water out of the rock for you?” and so forth.

Again he enumerates another sin, saying: “They did not destroy the nations that the Lord God had told,” that is, commanded, “them” to destroy. For the Lord had commanded them to destroy those nations from the land of Canaan, namely, the land of promise, lest they learn their customs and be moved through them to the worship of idols.

They did not destroy them, but instead “mingled among the nations” of that land, “and learned their works, and served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block for them,” because the Jews offended God. He aggravates their wickedness, saying: “And they sacrificed [Col. 0561D] their sons and daughters to demons.” For if those are idolaters who sacrifice goats, much more are those who sacrifice their children. Nor did they sacrifice their sons after finding them guilty of sins; rather, “they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.”

“And” while they were killing their children in this way, they themselves were inwardly killed. Hence it says: “The land was slain (or, *infecta*, ‘defiled’)”; that is, those earthly people were slain among themselves “with blood,” their own blood; “and by” such “works of theirs it was defiled,” that is, others acted wickedly by imitating them. “And” both groups “fornicated” against God, clinging to the adulterous demon, and this “by their inventions” [Col. 0562A] and the traditions of the elders, because, abandoning God’s commandments, they followed their own traditions.

“And then the Lord was angry,” that is, manifested the effect of anger, “against his people,” and this “with fury,” that is, with severe anger, “and he abhorred his inheritance,” no longer caring to defend them as an inheritance. “And” therefore “he delivered them into the hands of the nations,” because at that time they were defeated by the Philistines, “and those who hated them ruled over them,” namely, the Philistines and others.

“And then their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled,” that is, greatly oppressed, “under their hands.” Nevertheless, the Lord “often delivered them.”

But “they,” paying no attention to this deliverance, “provoked him by their counsel,” that is, deliberately, [Col. 0562B] “and they were humbled in their iniquities,” that is, because of their iniquities they were afflicted in many ways.

“And when” they were thus “afflicted, he saw” them, and the Lord had pity on them, “and he heard their prayer,” that is, he delivered them, both because they were afflicted and because they cried out to him. “And he remembered his covenant,” that is, the promise made to Abraham (Gen. XXII), in whose seed the promise that God had made could not be fulfilled unless he preserved them. “And he repented,” that is, he was changed in accordance “with the multitude of his mercy,” not because of their merits, but according to his mercy, which is abundant.

“And he gave them into mercies,” such as Peter, Paul, Stephen, and others, to whom he forgave sins; [Col. 0562C] and in them he multiplied the abundance of righteousness. This is what follows: “in the sight of all who had taken them captive.” For the nations that had earlier held the Jews captive, having now been converted, received them as teachers, such as Peter and the others. Or, “in the sight of all who had taken them captive” means in the sight of the demons, who had previously held them captive.

“Save us.” Part six. Continuation. Since, O Lord, you bestowed so many benefits upon our fathers, therefore do the same for us; and this is what follows: “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us,” that is, make us come together in the name of faith. “Gather us,” I say, “from the nations,” that is, from different peoples; or, by taking us away from the nations, namely, from imitation of the nations.

[Col. 0562D] Gather us for this purpose: “that we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise,” so that we may appear glorious because we praise you. This request has the same force as an enumeration.

And therefore he says that, since you will gather us in this way, God, “blessed” “is the Lord God of Israel,” with a blessing beginning “from” this “age” and continuing “into” another “age.” And all the people, namely, the Gentile people, because they are still carnal, “shall say, Let it be, let it be,” that is, May God be blessed.

## PSALM CVI. TITLE: Alleluia

“Give thanks III.” If there is another “Alleluia,” [Col. 0563A] according to Jerome it belongs to the preceding psalm. In the first “Give thanks,” he showed the benefits bestowed upon the chosen people of Israel; in the second, the mercies shown to sinners; but in this one he shows the benefits that God bestowed upon the universal Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles from the four parts of the world. Since this psalm contains benefits of God worthy of praise, it is therefore entitled “Alleluia.” Its subject is those very benefits.

Its method is as follows. In the first part he treats of ignorance and shows how God leads those wandering in the unbelief and ignorance of sin into his Church, using the likeness of someone who brought wanderers in the wilderness back to a city. In the second part, which begins, “Let them give thanks to the Lord,” he shows how God satisfies those introduced into the Church with the divine word and breaks apart the bonds of their sins, [Col. 0563B] just as someone might feed and refresh people brought into a city. In the third part, which begins with the second “Let them give thanks,” he shows how some, once satisfied by the divine word, become disgusted with it. This is deadly for them, because they cannot take food unless God refreshes them, so that they may once again delight in receiving the divine word. In the fourth part, which begins with the third “Let them give thanks,” he shows how God removes the storm and sends a breeze to the rulers of the Church, who are endangered by the many storms and tempests of this age, just as the helmsmen of ships are endangered by the waves of the sea, and finally brings them into the harbor of his will. In the fifth part, which begins with the final “Let them give thanks,” he shows that the Jews were blinded by God’s just judgment, that the fullness of the Gentiles entered in, and that they yielded the greatest fruits to the Lord. His intention is that we sing “Alleluia,” that is, that we praise God.

The prophet’s voice admonishes us in this way: Pay attention to the benefits that the Lord bestows upon the Church, and with both kinds of confession “give thanks to the Lord,” accusing yourselves of your sins and praising God for the abundance of his benefits. You ought to confess “that” he is “good,” that is, merciful, and forgives the sins of those who confess. Do this in the present, while it is the time for mercy, “for his mercy” is “into the age,” that is, in this life there is a place for mercy; after this there remains judgment.

I urge you to confess, and I say that everyone else should say the same thing I say: “Let those whom the Lord has redeemed” [Col. 0563D]—that is, let them exhort others to confess and praise God—say it. And you rightly ought to say this, because these are “those whom” the Lord “redeemed” with the precious blood of his Son “from the hand of the enemy,” that is, from the power of the devil. Nor were only a few redeemed; rather, “he gathered them” into the unity of faith “from the regions,” from different lands.

I rightly say “from the regions,” because they were gathered “from the rising of the sun,” that is, from the eastern region, “and from the setting, from the north,” that is, from the northern quarter, “and from the sea,” that is, from the southern region. By the sea, which surrounds the whole earth, any part of the world may be designated.

He shows from what he redeemed them, as though he were saying: I rightly [Col. 0564A] say that he redeemed them, because they “wandered,” obeying demons and not God, “in a wilderness,” that is, being alone without God, remaining in unbelief, “and” also “in a waterless place,” that is, in the dryness and aridity of divine teaching. They had no one to flood them, irrigate them, and make them fruitful with the dew of heavenly doctrine. And because they were in a wilderness and without teaching, therefore “they did not find the way to a city” by which they could approach the city. I do not mean just any city, but “of habitation,” that is, the city in which the faithful are to dwell, namely, the Church.

I say that they did not find that way, although they were “hungry and thirsty” for a way by which they could come to true blessedness. Such were the worldly philosophers, who earnestly inquired by various arguments what [Col. 0564B] the highest good was and by what way they could come to true blessedness. Or, “hungry and thirsty” naturally for the true good. For all people naturally tend toward the true good, but not by the true way: some through power, some through rank, some through wealth, and others through various means. And although they hungered and earnestly sought, nevertheless “their soul,” that is, their wisdom, “failed within them,” because they attributed wisdom to themselves and not to God. Therefore their wisdom produced no progress; it was found to be wholly useless and failed. Those who seek through power and other things of this kind likewise fail, because they do not walk by the right way.

“And” because they failed in this way, compelled by this necessity, “they cried out to the Lord,” having indeed been admonished by the inspiration of divine grace [Col. 0564C]; “and” he himself “delivered them” as though by a kind of force “from their necessities,” that is, from the ignorance and error of the wilderness, and, leading them into the Church, supplied them with true wisdom. “He delivered” them, I say, “when they were afflicted,” that is, when they were greatly distressed by ignorance and the other necessities of sin.

“He delivered” them, I say, “and” afterward “led them by a straight way,” that is, he inspired them with knowledge of Christ and the Catholic faith, so that “they might go” through good works “into the city,” that is, the holy Church, “of habitation,” in which they are to dwell.

“Let them give thanks.” Part two. Because of the benefits of God mentioned above, I say, “Give thanks.” And likewise, because of the benefits that follow, “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and his wonders,” that is, let the faithful praise God, having reasons to praise the mercies of the Lord wonderfully bestowed “upon the children of men.” “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies,” that is, let human beings praise God for the mercies he showed them and for the wonders accomplished for the children of men.

Therefore they ought to confess and praise, “because the Lord satisfied” “the empty soul” with the word of spiritual teaching, through which he established them in his Church. By “empty soul” he means one empty of all true knowledge, such as the foolish, the not-foolish, and the simple, but also “the hungry soul,” [Col. 0565A] such as that of the philosophers, “he satisfied with good things,” that is, he filled it with spiritual wisdom.

“He satisfied,” I say, those “sitting” “in darkness,” that is, in ignorance, from which they could in no way escape by themselves, “and” sitting “in the shadow of death,” that is, in a shameful life, which would blind them and cast a shadow leading to death. He means those “bound in poverty,” that is, in the lack of every good, “and in iron,” that is, in the hardness of sins.

They were in poverty “because they embittered,” that is, judged bitter and rejected, “the words of God,” fleeing them. For if someone admonished them concerning charity or something similar, they regarded it as something to be avoided and did not wish to be admonished in anything. Yet the natural [Col. 0565B] law indicated to them that this ought not to be done. “And they provoked the counsel of the Most High,” namely, the counsel to desire heavenly things, disregard earthly things, and cling to Christ our Redeemer. They provoked it, that is, as far as they were concerned they made it vain, since they refused to agree with Christ in anything and did not believe that he was the Redeemer. Or, despising the counsel of the Most High as stated above, they provoked it, that is, provoked God to anger.

“And” because they provoked him in this way, therefore “their heart,” that is, their soul, “was humbled in labors,” that is, in their efforts. For however much they tried and labored on their own to attain blessedness, their heart was nevertheless humbled, because they failed. Or, their heart was humbled and afflicted in [Col. 0565C] “labors,” that is, in the many miseries that God sends for the correction of the elect. “And they were weakened,” in their presumption, that is, they recognized that they could accomplish nothing by themselves, “and there was no one” among them “who could help,” that is, who could free them from the darkness and iron by which they were held. For neither could they free themselves, nor could their gods.

“And” compelled by this necessity, “they cried out,” inspired by the Lord, “to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities,” from poverty, darkness, and the other evils placed in this section. He calls them “necessities” because they could in no way escape from them by themselves. He shows how he delivered them, as though he were saying: I say that he “delivered” them, and in this way: “he brought them out of the darkness” of unbelief, [Col. 0565D] because he made them faithful, “and from the shadow of death,” because they no longer polluted their lives with shameful deeds; “and he broke their bonds,” that is, the hardness of sin by which they had previously been bound, because he placed compunction in their hearts and led them to repentance.

“Let them give thanks.” Part three. It is as though he were saying: Just as, because of the benefits of God mentioned above, it is fitting that they give thanks to the Lord, so, for the benefits that follow, “let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.”

They ought to give thanks because, when their soul had become disgusted with every food, the Lord removed not only that satiety but also all the evils that arose from it. [Col. 0566A] He first sets out the things that arose from that disgust, saying: “because he shattered,” that is, annihilated, “bronze gates,” that is, destroyed anger and desire in them, which are gates leading to eternal destruction. He calls them bronze because, although they are naturally present in human beings, scarcely anyone can master them. And “iron bars,” that is, the suggestions of the devil, by which a person is strengthened and confirmed in evil; and anger and desire, which were given to us for good purposes, namely, so that we might be angry at evils and desire good things. The Lord “broke” these bars because he made his faithful strong, so that they could overcome every temptation of the devil.

Once the gates were broken and the bars destroyed, the Lord “received them” into justice from the way of iniquity, [Col. 0566B] that is, from the shameful life they had led in sins. “Way,” I say, “of theirs,” that is, a way they had from themselves and not from God. I rightly say “their way of iniquity”: they had “injustices,” and because of them “they were humbled,” that is, afflicted by God, so that through this they might recognize their sins. Or, he received them for this reason: they were humbled, that is, had become humble, and were afflicting themselves before the Lord because of their injustices, that is, because they recognized that they had offended God in many sins.

Therefore they had the aforementioned gates, and their way was iniquity, because “their soul abhorred every kind of food,” that is, every nourishment of spiritual teaching, “and” for this reason “they drew near even to the gates of death,” that is, they nearly fell into despair, which is the direct road leading human beings to eternal death.

Compelled by this necessity, “they cried to the Lord”; yet they could not have cried out unless divine mercy had anticipated them. “When they were afflicted, he delivered them from their distress.” Here too he understands “distress” as sins, as in the earlier passage where he spoke of gates, bars, and similar things.

In this way he delivered them: “he sent his Word,” that is, he caused his Son to become incarnate, “and” through this “he healed them,” that is, he removed from them their aversion to the divine Word. Or “word” means the divine command and his authority, and he healed them—as it is said in the Gospel: “Only say the word, and my child will be healed” (Luke 7). Thus, after freeing them and healing them of their aversion, “he rescued them from their destructions,” that is, from eternal damnation, which would have arisen from that aversion, just as bodily death arises from aversion to bodily food.

“Let them confess to the Lord.” Part four. Continuation: Just as I admonished them to confess on account of the other benefits mentioned above, so also, on account of those that are now to be described, it is fitting that “they confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men,” as explained above.

I say, “let them confess,” and let them offer sacrifice to God—not a goat or anything of that kind, but praise. This is “a sacrifice of praise”: let them show by words and deeds that God is worthy of praise, in accordance with this saying: “Let your good works shine before men, so that, seeing your works, they may glorify your Father” (Matthew 5). “And let them proclaim his works,” namely, that he forgives sins and does every other good thing; and let them do this “with rejoicing,” for those who attend to these works of God ought to rejoice.

I say, “let them proclaim,” but I do not command this to everyone; rather, I speak of the rulers of the Church, of whom he says that they “go down” from the height of their contemplation into “the sea,” that is, this world, which is driven by many waves. They descend into it “in ships” in order to govern them, that is, the Churches, which are surrounded and battered by the waves and disturbances of this world, like ships by the waves of the sea. I speak of those who descend, “performing their work,” namely, preaching and confession, and dispensing the other benefits of God, “upon many waters,” that is, among many peoples.

Those rulers of the Church who descend in this way “saw the works of the Lord and his wonders,” that is, they came to know his wondrous works, “in the deep” of the heart; or, they saw works performed in the deep, that is, according to the inscrutable counsel of God.

I rightly speak of “works,” because among the other works of God they came to know that he “spoke,” that is, willed it, and that “the spirit of the storm,” that is, the devil, who stirs up every storm—the tempest of the temptations of this life—“stood,” that is, raged against the rulers of the Church and stirred up his storm within them. “And” as a result “its waves,” that is, the adversities or storms and the prosperities that most violently shake human hearts, “were raised,” that is, multiplied within them. For the devil tests these rulers of the Church both through their own prosperities and likewise through their own adversities.

“The waves were raised,” and consequently those rulers whom the waves drive “ascend to the heavens”: through many prosperities they are carried into excessive exaltation and pride. “And they descend to the abysses,” because, crushed beneath the weight of many adversities, they are driven into despair. Thus “their soul wasted away,” that is, failed, “in evils,” that is, because of the evils through which temptations were stirred up within them; it failed because they were unable to do anything good.

“They were also troubled,” that is, they did not know what they ought to do, just as the masters of ships are troubled at sea when a violent storm breaks upon them. “And they were moved” to anger against their subjects, “like a drunken man,” and thus all their wisdom was swallowed up, because they used reason well in no circumstance—neither when they enjoyed prosperity nor when they were crushed by adversity.

Since they were compelled by their distresses, “and” therefore “cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, he led them out of their distresses.” He shows how he led them out, saying: “He made its storm,” that is, the temptations and turmoil of this world, “into a gentle breeze,” which would refresh them well, namely, spiritual grace. Where previously the storm and persuasion of the devil had reigned, God now placed the Holy Spirit, who would inwardly revive them. “And” through that breeze “its waves became silent,” whether the waves of the sea or of the evil spirit, which previously had been hurling themselves upon them; for once the Holy Spirit dwelt within them, no wave and no assault of the devil could dominate them.

“And they rejoiced because they became silent, and” thus “he led them into the harbor of their desire,” that is, into as much security as they wished.

“Let them confess.” Part five. Just as in the other passages he proposed an exhortation to praise together with the benefits that followed, so here, when he says, “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men,” as above.

“And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people,” and let the whole congregation of the people praise him together, including the prelates. This is expressed in the words: “And in the seat of the elders let them praise him,” that is, let those who exercise authority over others praise him.

Let them exalt and praise him because he “made rivers into a desert,” that is, he placed the teachings of the Gospel among the Gentiles, by which their hearts are irrigated. And he placed “the outlets of waters,” that is, the teaching itself visibly issuing from Judea through the preaching of the apostles, “in a thirsty land,” that is, among the Gentiles, who thirsted for heavenly teaching through an inward longing.

But “the fruitful land,” that is, Judea, which had formerly been fruitful, he made “into saltiness,” that is, into sterility. Sterility is understood by saltiness, because if salt is mixed into the soil, it makes it completely barren. He did this “because of the wickedness,” that is, on account of the wickedness, “of those who dwelt in it.” This means that by his just judgment he blinded the Jews and brought in the Gentiles.

“I say, he made it so.” Continuation. He made Judea into saltiness. But “the desert,” that is, the Gentiles, who had previously been deserted with respect to the knowledge of God, he made “into pools of water,” that is, into the Church, which is the place where waters stand—namely, baptism. Or, he made it into pools of water in the sense that he caused the waters, that is, spiritual teachings, to stand and persevere there. “And” that same “land” which had previously been “without water,” that is, the Gentiles, he made “into outlets of waters,” so that teaching might flow from them also to others.

“And there,” that is, in the waters of that place, God “settled the hungry,” that is, those desiring to be refreshed by spiritual teachings. “And” once settled there, they “established a city,” that is, the Church, “for habitation,” that is, a place in which alone one ought to dwell.

“And” having been placed there, they “sowed fields,” that is, they converted some people by sowing the word of God without much labor. “And they planted vineyards,” that is, they built up others with great labor. Those who had been sown and planted “produced the fruit of their origin,” that is, they imitated the teaching of their teachers in their deeds. A person produces the fruit of his origin when, if chastity is preached to him, he lives chastely. He does not produce the fruit of his origin when, although chastity is planted in him through the preacher’s word, he nevertheless produces fornication—just as a field that receives wheat produces weeds, and thus does not produce the fruit of its origin.

“And God blessed them,” that is, he multiplied them in virtues; “and they were multiplied” in number “exceedingly,” that is, greatly.
