Or “exceedingly” means beyond the number of the elect, as in the saying: The fish multiplied so greatly that the net was torn, and those that were superfluous went out (Luke 5; John 21). Heretics are represented by these latter, for they depart from the Church. “And he did not diminish their beasts,” that is, the simple members of the Church: he did not make them of lesser worth than the wise, but rather multiplied virtues in them.

He blessed them, “and” nevertheless “they became few” in comparison with the wicked. “And they were afflicted by the tribulation of the wicked,” and they were also afflicted by the “pain” they felt because of the sins of others.

Because of this, “strife was poured out upon princes,” that is, upon the founders of heresies, who contend against the Church of God. Or “upon princes” means upon the powerful of this world. God “made them,” these princes, “err in a pathless place and not on the way,” that is, outside the faith—not in such a way that they might be recalled, but so that they would no longer be on the way, that is, in the Catholic faith, which is the way of life.

He blinded these people, “and,” by contrast, “he helped the poor man” truly “in his poverty,” that is, he supplied his poverty with knowledge of himself, granting him wisdom so that he could resist heretics. “And” through this poor man he “established families,” that is, many congregations in the Churches, making them “like sheep,” that is, innocent.

And when the upright see that God helps the poor man in this way and blinds the prince, “they will see and rejoice, and every iniquity will shut its mouth,” that is, it will close it. For iniquity will no longer be able to bark when it sees its accomplices remaining in a pathless place.

Since he does so many good things, therefore “who is wise?” If someone says, “I am wise,” then I know that “he will keep these things” that have been mentioned, committing to memory that God helps the poor and blinds the rich. “And” then “he will understand the mercies of the Lord,” namely, that God acts not according to human merits but according to his own mercies. Alleluia.

## On Psalm 107

### Title

A song of the psalm, for David.

“God, my heart is ready.” This psalm is appropriate to David, that is, to Christ, who speaks here. It is called a song because it sets forth great rejoicing, namely, Christ’s glorification, which the prophet announces here with exultation. It is called a psalm because it sets forth Christ’s good work, namely, his humiliation by which he liberated the human race, that is, his beloved. From this humiliation, that is, from this work, the song proceeded, because his glorification proceeded from Christ’s warfare, which he completed worthily and with such devotion.

It should be noted that in this psalm the prophet does not use new words. Rather, he borrows the first part, “so that your beloved may be delivered,” from the psalm that says: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you” (Psalm 56). What follows afterward he borrows from the psalm that says: “O God, you have rejected us” (Psalm 59). He wished to compose this psalm from different psalms because he saw that those parts of the psalms applied to Christ; and things that were pleasing in themselves as praise of God became more pleasing when joined together. For this reason also, in the Church, an antiphon or some song is joined together from different psalms or praises.

The subject of this psalm is Christ’s glorification and passion. Its method is as follows: in the first part he shows his glorification and inserts something concerning his humiliation. In the second part, which begins, “so that your beloved may be delivered,” he develops the humiliation and introduces God himself promising the deliverance of the elect, which was accomplished through Christ himself.

The purpose is to invite us, by his example, to suffer humbly and to make God our strength and security through that very patience. Hence he says at the end of the psalm: “In God we shall perform a deed of strength,” and so forth. This psalm is also one of those that demonstrate Christ to be God and man. Wherever it shows him exalted above the heavens, it shows that he is truly God; for if he had been merely human, he could never have been exalted in this way. But wherever it shows him humbled, it plainly shows that he was truly human.

Wishing, then, to show Christ worthy of glorification, he promises that he will obey God in all humility, saying: “O God, my heart is ready” to sing to you. To show that he is ready beyond the measure of other human beings, he repeats himself, saying: “My heart is ready,” that is, my heart is so ready that it is in no way hindered by sin. My heart is ready, and I will complete that for which it is ready, because “I will sing”: I will praise you with spiritual devotion and contemplation. “And I will play the psalm” for you, that is, I will work well for your honor, “in my glory,” that is, in the psaltery and the lyre, namely, in my humanity. That humanity is my glory because, through the obedience I displayed to God in it, I showed myself worthy of glory. Or “I will play the psalm” means: I will work well in my glory, that is, in contemplation of the future glory that I await.

I say, “I will play the psalm in my glory,” and, O my glory, that is, “psaltery and lyre, arise,” that is, grow in good works. Christ calls his humanity a psaltery because it resounds from above, namely, because it spiritually fulfills the divine commandments, as it did before the time of the passion. He calls the same humanity a lyre with respect to the mortification of the flesh, as it was in the passion. Therefore I say, “arise” to good works, because through this good work I am certain of my resurrection. This is expressed in the words: “I will rise at dawn,” that is, I will rise in the morning.

And after the resurrection “I will confess to you, Lord, among the peoples,” that is, I will cause many Jews from among the peoples to confess and praise you. “And among the nations,” that is, among the Gentiles, who remain such as they were born, “I will play the psalm for you,” that is, I will cause you to work well.

Therefore I will confess to you “because your mercy,” namely, your Son, through whom you mercifully restore the human race, “is great above the heavens,” that is, above the heavenly creatures, namely, above the angels themselves, who subsist through him. “And your truth,” that is, your Son, who shows you to be truthful because your promises have been fulfilled in the world through him, is great “up to the clouds,” that is, to the point of establishing holy preachers who rain heavenly water upon the Church.

And since your mercy is great above the heavens, therefore “you, God, be exalted above the heavens,” that is, lead the human being united to you above every angelic creature, as was fulfilled in the Ascension. “And” through this “your glory,” that is, your fame, will be “over all the earth,” because you will appear glorious throughout the entire world.

### Part two

And so that you may have glory, deliver your beloved from the power of the enemy. For unless they are removed from the yoke of the devil, God will have no glory in all his creatures. “And so that your beloved may be delivered, save me,” by raising me from the dead, for through my resurrection the deliverance of the beloved will come about.

He calls those “beloved” who have been forechosen by God, and he does not request the deliverance of others. He knew who the beloved were and prayed for them. The Church, however, because it does not know precisely who are to be saved, prays indiscriminately for everyone. “Save me,” I say, “by your right hand,” that is, by your power, “and hear me” as I pray for the deliverance of the beloved. Deliver the beloved both through my resurrection and through my prayer.

I ask you to save me so that the beloved may thereby be delivered. I am well assured both of my own deliverance and of their salvation, because “God has spoken in” his special “holy one,” that is, in me. He has said: “I will rejoice and divide Shechem,” that is, shoulders: I will grant my grace to different people, through which I will make them broad-shouldered and strong enough to endure labors. “And I will measure out the valley of tents,” that is, the humble who fight in my tents; “I will take them as my portion.”

“Gilead,” too, that is, the heap of testimony, such as the holy martyrs who give themselves to death as a testimony to the truth, “is mine,” that is, it has been placed among the number of those who will be saved. “And Manasseh is mine,” that is, those who have forgotten their former life, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44). “And Ephraim,” that is, those who bear fruit in good works, is “the reception of my head,” that is, of my divinity, because the divinity itself rests and delights in those who bear fruit in this way.

Or “Ephraim” means the thorny crown, which is fruitfulness because it acquires for God a crown from the circuit of the whole world. It is not my disgrace and humiliation, as some say, but “the reception of my head,” that is, it causes my head—my exaltation—to be received throughout the entire world and to be held in joy.

“Judah is my king,” that is, Christ, whom I have established over all the faithful, is from the tribe of Judah. “Moab,” that is, one who abuses the law—namely, the Gentiles, who were without the law—“is the cauldron of my hope,” that is, those who cook themselves well and make sweet foods from which I may take refreshment.

Or “Moab” means the devil, who abuses the law and is without God the Father. He is the cauldron, that is, the cooking and burning, of my hope, because through those burnings are purified those whom I hope to have.

Still concerning God’s words: Since Gilead is mine and I have others like it, therefore “I will extend my sandal,” that is, the holy Gospel with which the feet—the affections—of those who evangelize are shod, so that they are not pierced by the thorns of desire or stained by any mud. I will extend it, I say, “into Idumea,” that is, among earthly people; I will cause the Gospel to be proclaimed among the Gentiles. Through the proclamation of the Gospel, “foreigners,” namely, the Allophyles—that is, those who fall through the drink and glory of this life—“have become my friends,” that is, obedient to me.

After displaying God’s promises, Christ resumes speaking, as though saying: Since God says, “I will extend my sandal into Idumea,” who will lead me into the fortified city,” that is, so that I may make the Idumeans into a city fortified against diabolical temptations? “And who will lead me as far as Idumea,” that is, among earthly people, so that my name may be known by them and I may be able to establish a city among them?

Or “who will lead me into the fortified city?” means: among earthly people, who are now a city fortified against me, so that through the proclamation of me the defenses of that perverse city may be destroyed. “And who will lead me as far as Idumea,” that is, so that I may acquire the Idumeans for myself?

Or otherwise: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” means into hell, which is a fortified city for holding human beings in captivity, so that I may plunder it of the souls of the faithful. And who afterward will lead me as far as Idumea, so that after the triumph of my victory I may acquire those earthly people? Certainly no one except you, God. This is what follows:

“Is it not you, God”—certainly you, who nevertheless seem to do the opposite—“who rejected us,” that is, you seem to have rejected me and mine while permitting us to suffer the greatest humiliations? You seem to have rejected us in this respect because “you will not go out, God,” any longer “with our armies,” that is, you will no longer appear manifest in our forces, as you did for the ancient Fathers. Another translation reads, “with our armies.”

I say: you will not go out, nor do we ask you to do so; rather, give us tribulation. “And from” that very “tribulation give us help,” that is, make the tribulations we suffer assist us toward future glory. Therefore I ask for help from tribulation—not human help—“because the salvation of man,” that is, the support a human being can provide, “is vain,” that is, transitory.

“In God.” And because human salvation is vain, therefore “we shall perform a deed of strength in God,” that is, we shall regard God himself as our strength and steadfastness, placing no confidence in ourselves but hoping for everything from God’s mercy. “And he himself will bring our enemies to nothing,” that is, he will make our enemies accomplish nothing against us, and we will regard their persecutions as nothing.

## On Psalm 108

### Title

To the end. A psalm of David.

“God, my praise.” This psalm is appropriate to David, that is, to Christ. Its subject is his passion, about which he speaks, directing us “to the end,” that is, to Christ.

Its method is as follows: in the first part he sets forth the wickedness of the Jews—especially that of Judas and of others—which they displayed against Christ himself. In the second part, which begins, “Appoint over him,” he sets forth thirty curses, just as the Lord Jesus was sold for thirty pieces of silver. In the third part, which begins, “And you, Lord, act with me,” he asks for his glorification, inserting something about his passion and something about the curse of his persecutors.

The purpose is that, when we see those who persecuted Christ cursed in this way, we may cease persecuting the righteous.

Thus Christ speaks to the Father: “O God,” against the impious things my enemies say to me, “do not remain silent about my praise,” but cause me to be known and praised throughout the whole world. Do this because “the mouth of the sinner,” that is, of the Jewish people, which is a sinful people in its shameful life, “and the mouth of the deceitful” people, which deceitfully plots my death and speaks deceitful words such as “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” (Matthew 22), and similar things, “has been opened against me,” that is, for my humiliation. By saying, “It has been opened,” he indicates that they spoke many evils against him.

They “spoke against me with a deceitful tongue,” saying, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Mark 12); and afterward, in the passion, “they surrounded me with words of hatred,” namely, the words they uttered against me, not because of any merit but because of hatred, saying to Pilate: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23). “And they fought against me”: according to their words, they thought me convicted of guilt because I had told them the truth, saying that I was the Son of God.

Or “they fought against me” with respect to the external man, handing me over to death. And they did all these things “without cause,” that is, without any merit of mine. Or “they fought against me” means that they attacked me by despising and striking me.

Truly, “without cause,” since they did all these things to me in return for benefits. This is expressed in the words: “They slandered me for that for which they ought to have loved me,” that is, for the deed by which they ought to have loved me. “And they repaid me evil for good,” that is, in the very deed in which they sought my death, while I was seeking their salvation. “And hatred for my love; but I was praying” for them.

He indicates the final kind of malice in them. It is evil not to return good for good; worse, to return evil for evil; worst of all, to return evil for good. By contrast, he places in Christ the highest kind of goodness: Christ prayed for the salvation of those who persecuted him.

### Part two

“Appoint.” And since this people is so obstinate in persecuting me and does not wish to have me as its head and king, therefore “appoint,” O Lord, “over him”—over this “sinful people”—the devil, who is the singular sinner and the cause of every sin. Appoint him “over him,” so that he may dominate him. “And let the devil himself stand at his right hand,” that is, let him not occupy only his carnality, which is signified by the left hand, but also his reason, which is signified by the right hand, so that he may do nothing good even through reason.

Or “let him stand at his right hand” means: whatever he does at the devil’s suggestion, let him regard as right and good. Observe that this imprecation does not arise from a desire for harm; rather, Christ, assenting to divine justice, places under the form of a prayer what has the force of a declaration, because he sees that these things are destined to happen to them.

“When he is judged.” Appoint the sinner; and once he has been appointed, let him “go out,” separated from the company of the righteous, “condemned”—whether Judas or the Jewish people—“when he is judged,” that is, when he will be judged at the future judgment. At that judgment it is certain that Judas and those who agreed with him will be separated from the company of the saints.

Or, when he is judged by a hidden judgment in this life, let him go out from the company of the saints condemned, as Judas did when, after betraying the Lord, he was separated from the fellowship of the apostles. “And let his prayer become sin.” Judas’s prayer became sin when he fell into despair. When he heard that the Lord had risen, he said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” and, driven by despair, he hanged himself.

This may also be understood generally of both Judas and that wicked Jewish people. “Let his prayer become sin,” that is, lead to eternal destruction; for, as Augustine says, the prayer made with Christ leads to salvation, while prayer made without Christ leads to damnation.

Likewise, our prayer becomes sinful if, while harboring hatred or anger toward our neighbor or other injustices, we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” We ought at least to forgive our brother hatred or anger and such things as should not be demanded, so that our prayer may be acceptable to God, as it is said in the Gospel: “When you offer your gift before the altar, if you remember that your brother has a just complaint against you, leave your gift and go first to be reconciled with your brother, and so forth” (Matthew 5).

Although we are permitted to reclaim certain things justly, it would nevertheless be better to forgive everything. Hence the Apostle says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Corinthians 6 and 10).

“Let his days be few,” that is, let him remain among the apostles for only a few days; “and let another receive his bishopric,” that is, his apostolate—namely, Matthias. This is said specifically of Judas, concerning whom blessed Peter also explained this verse in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “Let us fill his place,” just as the Holy Spirit commanded when he said, “Let another receive his bishopric” (Acts 1).

“Let his children,” whether Judas’s or those of the Jewish people, “be orphans,” without a carnal father or without God as their spiritual Father. “And let his wife,” whether Judas’s or that of the whole Jewish people, be “a widow,” deprived either of carnal husbands or of God, her spiritual husband and true comforter. Although it is not recorded in the Gospel, we believe that Judas had a wife and children.

Because of these evils, “let his children,” namely Judas’s, or those of the whole people generally, “be transferred from their kingdom,” “wandering,” unstable and homeless; let them be transferred so that they possess dominion over no land. “And let them beg,” that is, deserted by God, let them lack even external necessities. I say, “let them be transferred,” and let this not happen through famine or voluntarily, but let them be expelled by force. This is what he says: “Let them be cast out of their dwellings,” as was fulfilled through Titus and Vespasian.

“Let the creditor also search out” all his substance—that is, the devil, who is called a creditor because he demands the vices committed by someone in multiplied form, since he also causes them to multiply in those people, and he pays penalties on their behalf. The substance of Judas and of the other Jews he understands as their reason, by which they ought to live and be sustained in good works. The devil searches this out when he draws them away from the good and turns their reason to perverse uses.

Or “his substance” means the devil’s substance, that is, the wickedness in which and through which he himself exists. Let him “search it out,” that is, inquire into it carefully, so that, for each of the wicked deeds they have practiced, the devil may repay them with multiplied punishments. “And let strangers plunder his labors,” as the Romans inherited their possessions. Or “strangers” means the Gentiles: let them plunder his labors, that is, the law of the Lord, in which the Jews had previously labored.

And when that people has been crushed in these ways, “let him have no helper,” that is, let there be no people who rises up to defend it. Or let God himself, who is accustomed to be moved by the miseries of others and to help them, not be a helper to that people, nor even to its children. This is what he says: “Let there be none who has mercy on its orphans.”

“Let there be none who has mercy,” but rather “let his descendants,” that is, those of the people, “come to destruction,” that is, let them die a temporal death. “In one generation let his name be blotted out,” that is, let them not have the regeneration that Christians receive through the water of baptism, but only one generation, namely, the carnal one. Whoever has only that generation will not be an inhabitant of the eternal homeland.

The same interpretation may be given if this is understood specifically of Judas. Or the phrase may have this other meaning: “In one generation let his name be blotted out,” that is, let him not have a long succession of children, but let his children die without offspring.

Because of these evils, “let the iniquity of his fathers,” that is, original sins, “return to remembrance,” that is, let punishment afflict them on account of the sins of their fathers, not only on account of their own deeds. Let it “return,” I say, “in the sight of the Lord,” that is, at the judgment in which the Lord will be seen by all. For this reason he says, “return to remembrance,” because the Lord seems to have forgotten all their sins in this life by not punishing them.

“And let the sin of his mother,” that is, of the Synagogue, in which many are carnal, “not be blotted out”; rather, let the children be blotted out because of the sins of the Synagogue. Here he understands the particular sin of persecuting the righteous. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Let all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah” (Matthew 23).

“Let the sin of his mother not be blotted out,” but rather “let them be continually against the Lord,” so that, just as in this life they are opposed to the Lord through the likeness of their life, so in the other life they will be opposed to him. While the Lord rests in glory with his own, they will be tormented by eternal punishments. “And let their memory perish from the earth” of the living, so that no righteous person may be moved toward them by any pious affection.

I ask these things for them “because that people did not remember to show mercy,” that is, to do anything by which it ought to find mercy. He says “remember” because, even if it had not previously shown mercy, it could nevertheless afterward have repented and thereby shown mercy. Or he says “remember” because, if others had done evil to Christ, they ought to have defended him, since he was descended from them and had visited them in his presence.

“It did not remember to show mercy,” but rather “it persecuted a needy man,” that is, one possessing no abundance of temporal goods, “and” me as “a beggar,” that is, one asking elsewhere for what he needed, just as he himself begged water from the Samaritan woman (John 4), “and” me as “one pierced in heart,” that is, grieving over their sins.

They did not persecute me in order to take some temporal possession from me, but “to kill me,” that is, they did so in order to put me to death. Or, if we take “pierced” in its proper sense, namely, as grieving over one’s own sins, we shall say that this is not spoken of Christ’s own person but of his members. Thus they persecuted me, a needy man, and mine. This is what follows: “those pierced in heart.”

“And he loved the curse,” as when he said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27). “And the curse will come upon him,” upon that people, because even to this day their children remain blinded on account of that sin. “And he did not desire blessing,” as when the man who had been blind and was healed said to them, “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” They cursed him and said, “You are his disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (John 9). And that blessing “will be far from him,” from that people, because, once the Jews were blinded, illumination passed to the Gentiles.

“And that people put on the curse,” that is, the sin of my death, “like a garment,” because they nevertheless thought that they appeared very adorned and respectable to their neighbors. “And that curse entered into his inner parts,” already becoming effective for their death, “like water” penetrating into the interior, “and like oil into his bones,” because, just as oil makes the face bright and cheerful, so they rejoiced over my death.

At first that sin was like a garment coming upon them, when they consented to the devil’s persuasion. Then it was like water penetrating into their inner parts, when they labored and sought by bodily means to hand me over to death. But once they had accomplished it and were rejoicing and exulting over my death, it became for them like oil.

I say that this people put on the curse, and let that curse—that sin—become blindness for them. This is expressed in the words: “Let it be for him like the garment with which he is covered.” Let them be covered and enclosed in darkness by that curse. “And” let it also become hardening for them; this is expressed in the words: “Like a belt with which he is always girded.” Let him be so surrounded by that curse that he cannot free himself from it.

Or in this way: just as my death was for them like a belt with which people commonly gird themselves so as to be more ready for work, so let my death be for them like a belt because they handed me over to death, so that they may always be ready and prepared to perform every evil deed.

I invoke these evils upon them, and “this is the work of those who slander me,” that is, this is what their deeds demand, of those who slander me, “who am with the Lord,” the consubstantial Son of God, saying: “This man is not from God; he is not the Son of God.”

Or, it is the work of those who slander me and think that this is “with the Lord,” that is, pleasing to the Lord. And this is what the work of those who “speak evil against my soul” demands—those who accuse me of crimes, saying that I am a drunkard, malicious, and the like.

Or “they speak against my soul” means against my life, as when they said: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). Therefore he says “against my soul,” and not against my body, because although they called him a poor man, the son of a poor woman, this was not evil, since the truth required it.

“**And you, O Lord.**” Part Three. Continuation: They speak this against my life, but you, O Lord, help me against them; and this is what follows: “And you, Lord, Lord.” By the repetition he displays his devotion. “Deal with me,” that is, work for me, namely for my benefit. Or, “deal with me,” that is, I work, and you work, “for the sake of your name” being magnified, and also “because your mercy is sweet”: because, through your mercy, you made me become incarnate and suffer. This was a sweet thing for me, that is, it pleased me.

This, namely, “deal with me, deliver me” from the concerted action of the wicked, and do not allow them to hold me in death, as they desire. And this is necessary “because I am needy and poor.” He was poor with respect to human wealth, of which he was deprived; needy because he sought from elsewhere. “And my heart is troubled,” by fear of death, according to the saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew XXVI; Mark XIV). And this was “within me,” that is, not from necessity but from my own will. Or, “within me,” because his soul was indeed sorrowful, yet he did not reveal this to them.

My heart was troubled by them, and I “was taken away,” that is, seized by the Jews and handed over to death, “like a shadow when it declines,” that is, as lightly as a shadow withdraws when the light arrives, displaying no force: so I was seized by them, displaying no power, but enduring humbly. And first, before the Passion, “I was shaken like a locust,” that is, I fled their hands, going from place to place in flight, unwilling to provide them with an occasion for sin, just as a locust goes from place to place by leaping.

“And my knees,” that is, the apostles, who were to carry me throughout the world and through whom I was to appear strong, “were weakened,” that is, enfeebled, “by fasting,” when I was not with them, because they did not have the nourishment of the divine word. For Christ is not read to have been weakened in his bodily knees. “And my flesh was changed,” from life to death, “because of oil,” that is, because the spiritual grace that I had previously possessed for defense against my enemies was removed from me. Or, because of oil the flesh was changed: that is, I was handed over to death because of the oil that was to be sent, namely because of the Holy Spirit who was to be sent. Or, the flesh was changed from mortal to immortal because of oil, that is, because of the divinity united to it.

“And” because of these evils “I became a reproach to them,” that is, they inflicted reproaches upon me; “they saw me and shook their heads,” as a sign of their mockery of me.

They do this, but you, “O Lord my God, help me,” lest I fail in the Passion; “save me,” by raising me from the dead. And this is “because of your mercy,” because your mercy requires that you should thus come to the aid of the righteous.

“And let them know” at last, all of them, “that this is your hand,” that is, your work gave me over to death, “and you, O Lord, have done it,” namely, this work: it is so truly yours that you have worked it entirely in me.

I say, “Save me,” and I am confident that you will do so, for “they will curse, and you will bless,” that is, you will multiply virtues and also grant resurrection. And because you will bless, therefore “let those who rise up against me be put to shame,” that is, let them have confusion; but “your servant,” namely, myself, “will rejoice” in the resurrection brought about by him.

And not only those who rise against me, but also those who slander me; and this is what follows: “Let those who slander me be clothed with shame,” experiencing embarrassment over the slander they have brought against me, “and” let them be clothed so fully “with their confusion” that they “may be covered” by it “like a double garment.” That is, just as a *diplois* is a double garment, so let their confusion be double: inwardly, in the soul, and outwardly, in the body. For although outwardly they excuse themselves in words, inwardly they are confounded by their evil conscience.

Let them indeed be covered with confusion, but I will “make confession to the Lord,” that is, cause my people to confess to the Lord, “exceedingly,” that is, greatly. And this is what follows: “With my mouth,” that is, with the mouth of my people, because what they announce with their mouth they will accomplish in their deeds. Or, “with my mouth,” that is, openly. And this not before a few, but “in the midst of many I will praise him.”

I ought indeed to praise him, “because he stood at the right hand of my poor man,” that is, he who always preserved me in good works. He stood, I say, “to save my soul from those who pursued it,” so that I would neither yield to them nor could they hold me in death.

## ON PSALM 109. TITLE: A Psalm of David.

“**The Lord said.**” This psalm suits David, the prophet who speaks here. Its subject is Christ according to both natures. In the first part it deals with both. For when it says, “The Lord said to my Lord,” it signifies him as God, according to which nature Christ was Lord of all human beings. But when it introduces God himself saying to Christ, “Sit at my right hand,” and so forth, it deals with his humanity. In the second part, which is, “With you is the beginning in the day of your power,” it deals with Christ’s divinity alone, and this through the words of God the Father himself, because there the Father shows him both coeternal with himself and begotten from himself. In the third part, which begins, “The Lord has sworn,” taking up the Prophet’s words again, it speaks of Christ’s humanity, while always saying exalted things. Or, if it says anything about the Passion, as in “From the torrent he will drink on the way,” it makes the cause one of exultation. Its purpose is to admonish us, as though using the demonstrative mode, so that we may judge Christ, thus commended, worthy of honor and offer him the honor due to him.

And to show that he did not prophesy this from his own heart, he introduces God the Father himself speaking about the Son with the Son, saying as follows: “The Lord,” the Father, “said,” that is, ordained from eternity, “to my Lord” Jesus Christ, his Son. When he says “my,” he indicates that he is especially familiar to him, because the Father is so through the assumed humanity; yet he calls him Lord according to his divinity. Hence Christ himself says to those who, thinking him only human, called him the son of David: “How then does he call him Lord, saying, The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand?” (Matthew XXII). Through this he intimates that he is not merely human but also God, according to which nature he was Lord both of David and of all others. When he calls the Father Lord and the Son Lord, he indicates equal power in both. The Father spoke, and here is what he said: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, with your warfare completed and your obedience accomplished, rest in my greater goods. Although we do not read that the Father said these words to the Son, nevertheless we know that they were ordained in this way, because we see them fulfilled in this way.

Sit at my right hand “until” I “place your enemies as a footstool for your feet,” that is, until your enemies, namely your persecutors, who now seem to possess dominion and think they can act against your will, are completely subjected to you, like a footstool beneath your feet—that is, until the day of judgment, on which they will be subjected to you. He says “until,” not because he will not sit afterward, but because at that time he will appear glorious to all, whereas some now doubt him. Or, by the feet we understand Christ’s humanity, through which the divinity came to us and became known to us; to this humanity all will be subjected at the judgment, because they will understand that this humanity deserved that every honor and glory should be conferred upon it and that every creature should and must be subjected to it.

Words of the Prophet. The Lord the Father said: “I will place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” And truly your enemies will be subjected to you, because the Lord the Father will give “the rod,” that is, royal power, with which you may break your enemies and preserve your own. The scepter signifies such power in kings. “The rod,” I say, “of your power,” that is, in which your power appears: those whom you defend, no one will be able to hinder; and, conversely, those whom you harm, no one will be able to defend. And this rod “the Lord will send forth from Zion,” so that his preaching may go forth from Zion; hence the Prophet says: “From Zion the law will go forth” (Micah IV). You will pass to the nations, so that the nations themselves may be subjected to Christ’s rule; and because he will send it forth, “rule,” O Christ. Another translation has, “You will rule: in the midst of your enemies,” that is, in the common midst of all, so that those who were previously enemies may subject themselves to you of their own will. You, I say, are like one in the midst, to whom people from every nation gather.

“**With you is the beginning.**” It is as though he said: “With you” there is for me “the beginning in the splendors of the holy,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, who adorns the holy with various splendors. In this there is for us a beginning “in the day,” that is, in the brightness “of your power,” that is, of your divinity. As if he were saying: I and the Holy Spirit have identity with you. Let no one be disturbed that the spirit is understood through “splendors” in the plural, since John says, “and spirits sent into all the earth.”

Or otherwise: “With you is the beginning.” Part Two. Words of the Father to the Son. Continuation: I say, “at my right hand,” and rightly, because of the dignity of his divinity, he must thus be exalted in the humanity he assumed, which has its beginning with me, that is, you are the beginning and creator of all things, without beginning, and I likewise. He does not say, “You have the beginning with me,” lest he seem to designate immortality in the Son. When he says, “I have it with you,” he indicates distinction of person. When he says, “we are the beginning,” he indicates coeternity. And that I am the beginning with you will appear in the day, that is, in the eternity of blessedness, because it is called “day” on account of the splendor of true knowledge. “Day,” I say, “of your power,” that is, in which your power will appear, by which you will crown your own and condemn the wicked, and so forth. “In the day of your power,” I say, namely, “in the splendors of the holy,” that is, the holy who in this life are ragged and rough-haired will then be made immortal and incapable of suffering. Then there will be true splendor, because they will understand how the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Corinthians XIII), and so forth.

I say, “I have the beginning with you,” and I “begot you from the womb,” that is, from my innermost and hidden essence, by an ineffable generation, which the angels too are believed to be ignorant of. And this was not in time, but “before the morning star,” that is, before that star was created. Through this expression we understand every creature. Or, by “the morning star” we understand the devil, who fell because he became proud on account of his excessive beauty: that is, I begot you before I created any angelic creature.

## “The Lord has sworn.” Part Three.

Continuation. The Prophet said: The Lord said, “Sit at my right hand,” and so forth. And that same “Lord,” the Father, “has sworn,” that is, firmly ordained; “and he will not repent,” that is, he will not change his decision, namely this: “You are a priest forever.” He is called a priest because he offered himself and continually intercedes with God the Father for us. And this is “according to the order of Melchizedek”: just as Melchizedek offered Abraham bread and wine (Genesis XIV), so Christ offered the cup and bread to his disciples, that is, his body in the form of bread and wine; and he instituted the same sacrifice throughout the whole Church.

Now, just as Melchizedek was without beginning and without end—not because he did not have one, but because Scripture does not record that he had one—and just as Melchizedek was without father and without mother—not because, again, he did not have them, but because Scripture does not say so—so Christ, according to his humanity, had no father, and according to his divinity, had no mother; and in many other respects also he resembles Christ. Hence the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: “Made like the Son of God” (Hebrews VII).

“**The Lord.**” The Prophet turns his words to the Father, showing the exalted character of Christ’s humanity, as though the Prophet were saying: O Lord Father, “the Lord,” that is, Christ, resting “at your right hand, has broken,” that is, will break, “kings,” that is, the proud and powerful of this life, “on the day of his wrath,” that is, on the day of judgment, when his wrath, that is, his vengeance, will appear. Therefore he says “has broken” in the past tense, because, caught up into the counsel of God, he had already seen that judgment and held it in his mind as though it were past.

I say that he will break them in the judgment; yet again he will “judge” by a hidden divine judgment, because he will enlighten some and blind others. And this not among a few, but “among the nations,” both Jewish and Gentile. Thus he will judge “ruins,” that is, those who recognize that they have fallen through their own sins and through the sins of their fathers. He will “fill” them with good things, because he will remove those things and supply what was lacking to them. But “the heads,” that is, the heights and prides, “of many” who are proud in this life, he will “shatter,” that is, crush and annihilate, and he will make them fall from judgment into a worse state. And this will be “in the earth,” that is, in this present life, where God by a just judgment blinds the wicked.

This will be given to Christ on account of his merit, both to judge in this life and finally to judge openly. For Christ himself “on the way,” that is, in the time of his warfare, in which he devotes himself wholeheartedly to God, will “drink,” that is, taste—not under compulsion but willingly and, as it were, with delight—“from the torrent,” that is, from the most fervent Passion and from the miseries of this life, which come like a torrent with a certain rush and quickly pass away. That is, he will willingly endure death and other miseries for the redemption of the human race; “and therefore he will lift up his head,” that is, he will raise and multiply his exaltation, because for this reason God will give him “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” and so forth (Philippians II).

## ON PSALM 110. TITLE: Alleluia.

“**I will confess.**” In this psalm the Prophet speaks not for himself alone but in the person of the faithful people. Its subject is the faithful people, nourished with spiritual food and redeemed at the price of Christ’s blood. In the first part he says, in the person of the whole people, that he praises God, like those who are with David, and he sets out several subjects and causes of his praise. In the second part he likewise sets out, in addition to those already mentioned, a subject for praising God. In the third part, which begins, “He sent redemption to his people,” he shows that God will free his people from the hand of the enemy. Its purpose is to invite us to sing *alleluia*, namely, to sing eternal praises to God on account of such benefits.

The Prophet, recognizing that among the other faithful he has already been nourished and redeemed by God’s benefits, says: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart,” that is, no part of it will be vacant from earthly things, but the whole heart will be occupied with the praises of God. In this I will be like those who are already “in the council of the righteous,” that is, the holy angels and the other men who already know God’s counsel and will and judge with him, and who are already “in the congregation of the righteous.” The Prophet rightly says that he is like them: what more can they do than praise God with their whole heart?

Therefore I will praise, because “the works of the Lord” are all “great” and wonderfully made. They appear great to those by whom they are “searched out,” going “into all his wills,” that is, they appear great to those who attend to what God wills in each work—what he wills when he gives adversity to someone, and what he wills when he gives prosperity.

Therefore I say that the works of the Lord are great, because “his work” is “confession,” that is, something good. Jerome has “glory and honor.” I call it good because it is so worthy that it judges and confesses its maker and makes him worthy of praise; “and” there is “magnificence,” that is, a magnificent work; “and his justice,” the justice of God, “abides forever and ever,” because he both justifies the good here and rewards them eternally, and blinds the wicked here and condemns them eternally.

## “He made a memorial.” Part Two.

In addition to the matters already mentioned, I have a subject for praising God: that the Lord, “merciful and compassionate, gave food,” that is, the nourishment of his body and blood—not food effective for life for everyone, but “for those who fear him.” By giving it, he “made a memorial of his wonders,” displayed to the ancient fathers, completing in realities what he had prefigured in figures. For when he gave us the food of the Lord’s body, he made us mindful of the manna that prefigured this food (Exodus XVI), and likewise of the other benefits of God.

And by giving this food, he “will remember,” that is, he will show himself mindful of, “his covenant,” that is, the promise made to Abraham (Genesis XXII)—a covenant, I say, enduring “forever.” Through that food the children of Abraham receive eternal blessing. In this he determines that the food is the nourishment of the Lord’s body, because no other food would give the eternal life promised to Abraham. And he “will proclaim” through preachers “the power,” that is, the efficacy and fulfillment, “of his works,” that is, of the wonders shown to the fathers in figure, “to his people,” who will proclaim Christ as the end of the Law and the fulfillment of all God’s promises.

For this purpose he will proclaim it, “so that he may give them,” namely, the proclaimers, “the inheritance of the nations,” that is, the nations as an inheritance, just as Peter and Paul had inheritance and possession among the nations.

Another subject of praise: “the works of his hands,” that is, of his divinity, “are truth and judgment.” Truth with respect to the good, to whom God’s promises are fulfilled; and judgment with respect to those for whom these works are the means by which God condemns them in his just judgment.

Another subject of praise: this too will be a reason for me to praise him, because “all his commandments” are “faithful,” that is, credible. They must be believed because they fulfill what they promise, “confirmed forever and ever,” because what they promise cannot in any way be prevented from happening, either here or in the future. Or, “confirmed forever and ever,” that is, they do not fulfill in this age what they promise, but in the future. The commandments themselves are “made in truth,” in the fulfillment of the promises, “and equity,” because nothing unjust is found in them.

## “Redemption.” Part Three.

Another subject of praise. Continuation: Therefore I will also confess to him because he “sent redemption to his people,” that is, he freed his people from the slavery of the devil. And he “commanded,” that is, caused to be proclaimed through preachers throughout the world, “his covenant,” namely, the holy Gospel, destined to endure “forever,” because it will make the righteous eternal.

Another praise: “His name” is also “holy,” that is, sweet and good to those who taste it—not because it is uttered but because it is believed; and by believing it makes people saved and holy. It is also “terrible” to the wicked with respect to the future judgment.

Another praise: “The fear” of “the Lord,” because when we fear the future judge who will exact vengeance from the wicked, it is “the beginning” of true “wisdom,” since through it we avoid evil and do good.

And “the understanding” of that fear, that is, when someone correctly understands what he must do, is “good,” that is, useful. And this is not only for those who understand, namely, without action, but “for all who do it,” that is, who complete the things that understanding requires. Or, “for those who do her,” that is, wisdom. And “his praise abides forever and ever,” because he will be praised both here and in the future.

## ON PSALM 111. TITLE: Alleluia, of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.

“**Blessed is the man.**” Long after the time of the Prophet, the Jews were taken captive to Babylon. When a certain king, moved by pity and observing that they were God’s people, had freed them, he ordered them to return to their own land and rebuild God’s temple. During this return, Haggai and Zechariah, who had already prophesied that return, saw the temple being rebuilt. Rejoicing in this and in their return, they sang praises to God. According to this history, Ezra the Prophet seems to have given this psalm its title—not because he understood it as referring to the historical event, but because Ezra himself recognized that the Prophet David, in this psalm, understood every blessed man to praise God for the fact that God had brought him back from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of sins.

The title is read as follows: This psalm is an *alleluia*, that is, praise of God—a praise, I say, of the return, that is, a praise held in contemplation of our return from the Babylon of sins to the heavenly Jerusalem—“of the return,” I say, “of Haggai and Zechariah,” that is, of all the righteous, who are signified here by a part. According to the interpretation of these names also, the righteous can fittingly be understood. For Haggai is interpreted as “mountainous,” through whom the righteous are rightly understood, since they are mountains, that is, lofty in virtues. Zechariah, however, is interpreted as “solemn,” through whom the faithful are rightly understood.

The subject is the blessed man who has returned from Babylon and praises God for his return. The arrangement is as follows: in the first part he shows what the blessed man does and what is done for him by the Lord. In the second, which begins, “Light has arisen in the darkness,” he shows that through Christ’s coming, by which human beings are enlightened, they receive whatever gifts of grace they possess. In the third, which is, “The sinner will see,” he shows that the opposite happens to the wicked from what happened to those who were enlightened through Christ’s coming. Its purpose is to persuade us to praise God, who thus brings his faithful back from the Babylon of sins.

The voice of the Prophet, or of some blessed man, speaking as follows: That “man” is “blessed” who does not seek blessedness through the byways of this world but by this short and direct path, namely, he “who fears the Lord” with true fear. And why is the one who fears blessed? Because the one who fears “will desire his commandments,” that is, will have the will to fulfill his precepts, and this “exceedingly,” that is, very greatly. Therefore he does not say “he will do,” but “he will desire,” because if the will is good and opportunity is given, he will truly carry it out. But if there is no opportunity to act, a good will is sufficient.

Having shown what the blessed man does—namely, that he “fears and desires his commandments”—he shows what happens to that blessed man, as follows: He will therefore be blessed because “his offspring,” that is, his good works, “will be powerful,” that is, will make him powerful, “in the land” of the living. Here a good work is as though powerless, because we are always in fear lest the devil hinder it, while we fear. But there no temptation and no fear will be able to hinder us. Therefore we call works “offspring” because, just as we expect abundant fruit from seed, so we sow good works in order to gather abundant fruit from them in heaven.

He is also called blessed because “the generation of the upright,” that is, the followers and imitators of the righteous, “will be blessed,” that is, will be multiplied in virtues.

He will also be blessed because “in his house,” that is, in his heart—the house in which he himself rests from worldly tumult—there is “glory” from the purity of his conscience. Hence the Apostle says: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians I). There are also “riches,” namely, of wisdom and charity. Or, riches means the observance of many of God’s commandments. And “his justice,” that is, the reward and recompense that he will receive for justice, “abides forever and ever,” because it will be eternal.

## “Light has arisen.” Part Two.

Continuation: It is as though he said: From where will it come to a blessed man that he can do this? Because the true “light,” that is, Christ, has “arisen” bodily “in the darkness,” that is, in this world, which before Christ’s coming was darkness, because darkness and ignorance of the true good reigned in it. Hence Isaiah says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah IX). And in the Gospel: “And the light shines in the darkness” (John I).

The light, I say, does not benefit everyone, but “the upright,” that is, those who wish to direct their hearts in imitation of Christ. And what is that name? It is the one who is “merciful” in nature and “compassionate” in his manifestation, as he was when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and who is also “just,” that is, punishing sins. Or, “just” (Philippians II), because he was free from sin. Through these qualifications we plainly understand Christ.

Once the light has arisen, the “man” who has become “gracious”—that is, the gracious man—“has pity” in affection on someone suffering need. This is sufficient for salvation if the one who pities does not have anything to give. “And,” when there is need, if he has anything, he “lends,” that is, distributes it to the poor. He nevertheless says “lends” because, although he does not expect repayment from the poor person to whom he gives, he does expect recompense from God, like one who lends money to someone.

Or, “has pity,” that is, supplies his money to someone in need, and “lends” to someone needy, while nevertheless requiring the same money back from him. Such a person “will order,” that is, will act in an ordered and well-arranged manner. Hence the Apostle says: “Your reasonable service” (Romans XII). He “will order,” I say, “his words,” that is, his works—works that will be effective “in the future judgment.” We understand works by “words” because, just as the well-arranged speeches of an advocate defend an accused person in court, so the works of the righteous, rationally displayed, defend the accused in the future judgment.

Therefore he will order them in this way because he knows that he “will not be moved forever,” that is, he will possess the glory of God eternally.

And this righteous man, because in this life he seems to be abandoned by the Lord and consigned to oblivion, “will be in the memory” of the Lord. This will appear when it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matthew XXV). That memory will be “eternal,” that is, conferring eternity; and such a man “will not fear from an evil report” when it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid.).

He will not fear because “his heart” was always “prepared,” that is, instructed by divine inspiration, “to hope in the Lord.” And that “heart,” hoping, “is strengthened” in hope, so that no tribulation can move him away from that hope. This is what follows: “He will not be moved until he looks down upon his enemies,” that is, until he sees fulfilled concerning his enemies what he now expects concerning them—namely, that they will be given over to punishments. Therefore he says “until,” because then there will no longer be hope, when each person sees what he does not hope for.

And because he hopes, and because he is strengthened, and so forth, therefore he “distributed” his goods. This indicates the foresight of the saints in giving alms: they do not give everything to one person so as to make him rich, but to many, so as to supply the want of many. He “distributed,” I say, and did this not for temporal reward, but “gave,” that is, freely expended and supplied to “the poor.” To do this is “his justice,” which “abides forever and ever,” that is, the recompense of justice obtains for him an eternal reward. And “his horn,” that is, his exaltation, which he possessed in virtues in this life, “will be exalted in glory,” because through those virtues he will receive immortality and freedom from suffering.

## “The sinner.” Part Three.

I say that the righteous man will be exalted, and “the sinner will see this,” because all will see Christ rewarding his own at the judgment. And then that sinner, who previously exercised anger against the good in this age, “will be angry,” angry with himself; “he will gnash with his teeth,” because “there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew XIII; Luke XIII). When it says that he will then be angry and gnash his teeth, it speaks figuratively, because they will have a punishment corresponding to the wickedness they practiced here. “And he will waste away,” that is, fail, because “the desire of sinners will perish”: the desire they had in this life will perish, since earthly things too will perish, which alone they had always desired. By contrast, the desire of the righteous will be fulfilled. Alleluia.

## ON PSALM 112. TITLE: Alleluia.

[Col. 0586D]

“**Praise the Lord, children.**” Here the Prophet speaks, having material for the praise of God. In the first part he urges praise and proposes reasons for praise, namely, that the Lord is exalted above all nations. In the second part, which begins, “Who is like the Lord?” he shows himself doing what he urged others to do, namely, praising God. Hence at the beginning he says:

“Praise the Lord, children,” that is, in your good life show the Lord to be worthy of praise. I do not urge the wicked to praise him, because “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach XV). But you, children—that is, pure and simple people—“praise” also “the name of the Lord,” proclaiming his deeds, in which he himself appears praiseworthy and through which his name, that is, his fame, will continually be multiplied.

I say, “praise the name,” and do this not for an hour, but let “the name of the Lord be” by you “blessed” and magnified, beginning “from this time forth,” that is, without any delay, “and” let this blessing continue “forever,” “until,” that is, continually. In other words, let it begin immediately and remain eternally.

I say, bless him always, and extend that blessing of yours throughout the whole earth. This is what he says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting.” By this we understand the whole earth. Through your proclamation, “the praiseworthy name of the Lord” is to appear.

He gives reasons and subjects for which they ought to praise him, as though he were saying: You ought therefore to praise the Lord because this “Lord,” that is, Christ, is “exalted above all nations,” because he made all nations. And he is not only above all nations but also “above the heavens,” that is, above the heavenly and angelic creatures; and “his glory,” that is, he himself is glorious, because he is also the life and nourishment of the angels.

## “Who is like the Lord?” Part Two.

And truly he is to be praised, because no one can be found like him in any dignity. He says this by way of a question: “Who is like the Lord our God?” No one, certainly. He is the Lord “who dwells on high,” that is, in the holy through the excellence of virtues. They are “on high” because they become exalted through his dwelling in them. Yet he does not despise them if we are willing to humble ourselves before him. From that height of his seat he “looks,” that is, by showing mercy he visits “the humble,” that is, those who wish to humble themselves, “in heaven,” that is, among the heavenly creatures. Just as he does not look upon the proud angels, so he looked upon the angels who remained and who were humble, and he confirmed them in true obedience, so that thereafter they could not become proud. And he looks with the eye of mercy upon those humble ones who are “on earth,” that is, upon humble men, because he both forgives their sins and bestows righteousness upon them.

He looks upon the humble who are on earth, conferring this benefit upon them, namely “raising up the needy,” that is, the one who does not consider himself to possess any good from himself, “from the earth,” that is, from the desire for earthly things. He rightly says “raising up,” because human beings were asleep and resting in the love of earthly things when God awakened them from it through Christ. He also “raises the poor in spirit,” namely the humble man, “from the dung heap,” that is, from the filth of this life. Hence it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

He raises him for this purpose: “to place him” once raised “with princes,” that is, with the holy angels, “and with the princes of his people,” that is, with the holy apostles, whom the Lord placed over his people.

He shows through what means God raises the poor: he will make his preachers, who before his coming were barren, now fruitful and producing good fruit. Continuation: He is indeed the one who raises up, “who makes the barren woman dwell in a house,” that is, in the Church. The “barren woman” means his preachers, who before Christ’s coming, although inwardly good in the secret of their minds, were nevertheless barren because they did not beget children for God. He makes her dwell in a house so that she becomes “the mother of children,” because she gives birth to many for God in faith, and therefore “rejoicing.” When he says that they dwell in a house, he indicates the care of administration and consolation that the holy preachers exercise in the Church. Alleluia.

## ON PSALM 113. TITLE: Alleluia.

“**When Israel went out.**” In this psalm the Prophet speaks, and its subject is the benefits that God bestowed upon the Church, signified through the benefits he conferred upon the ancient people. For certain things are said here that remove us from the historical account, such as: “The mountains exulted and the hills.” In the first part he sets before us the benefits that God bestows upon the Church, signifying them through figures. In the second, which begins, “What is wrong with you, sea, that you fled?” he poses a question, as though wondering: Who can bestow such great benefits upon his people? And he answers it, showing that it was done by the Lord. This is not because the Prophet himself is amazed, but because he leaves us to marvel at God’s goodness. In the third part, which begins, “The idols of the nations,” he makes a comparison between the worship of the false gods of the nations and that of Christians, showing that the worship of the nations is folly, while that of Christians is supremely useful. He intends to admonish us to sing *alleluia* to the Lord for those benefits completed in us and to draw allegory from the historical account.

[Col. 0588C]

First let us read the history in this way: “When Israel went out of Egypt,” that is, when the Israelite people went out of Egypt, namely, the departure of the “house,” that is, the whole family, “of Jacob.” From Egypt, from which it rightly went out because it was “from a barbarous people,” that is, because the people was barbarous.

At that departure “Judea,” that land, “became his sanctuary,” that is, the sanctuary of that people, because there they were able to perform those ceremonies and sacrifices to God through which that people was sanctified. And “Israel” became “his power,” that is, powerful in that land. Then Judea appeared as mistress of all lands.

And how did it go out? Through this: “the sea,” the Red Sea, “saw,” that is, recognized, the face of God and his will, “and fled,” that is, divided itself. And when they came to the Jordan, then “the Jordan was turned back,” because it made a way for them.

And when they came into Judaea, “the mountains,” that is, the greater ones among the people, such as Joshua and Caleb, “exulted like rams; and the hills,” that is, the lesser ones among the people, “like lambs of sheep.”

Allegorically: By Israel we understand the Christian people, who are rightly called Israel, that is, “seeing God” through faith, when they came out of Egypt, that is, from the darkness of unbelief. By the house of Jacob we understand the people who wrestle against vices; they are rightly called Jacob, that is, “wrestler,” when they came out of the barbarous people, that is, from the dominion of vices or from fellowship with demons, who are called a barbarous people because they are alienated from God.

And after this Israel came out of Egypt, Judaea—that is, Christ, who is understood through Judaea because he was born from the tribe of Judah, from whom Judaea received its name; he is also properly called Judaea because he is our confession, since we understand him to be our Savior—and Christ himself is our land, through whom we subsist, just as the Israelite people did through that Judaea. That Judaea, namely Christ, became the sanctification of its Israel, that is, of the Christian people, because through Christ the Christian people possesses all sanctification. And Israel, that is, that Christian people, became the power of its Judaea, that is, of Christ: it showed Christ to be powerful, from whom it received the strength by which it can stand so firmly and fight against vices.

And through this that people became Israel and came out of the Egypt of unbelief, because “the sea saw and fled”: that is, all those embittered by sins saw the face of God. And “the Jordan,” that is, certain people flowing with various desires into the sea, that is, rushing through the world, “turned backward,” so that they ceased from sins and returned to Christ, that is, to their fountain, from whom they were created in perfection.

And then those “mountains,” that is, the greater ones in the Church, sanctified by Christ, “exulted” in their virtues “like rams,” because they are leaders of the flock, like rams. And “the hills,” that is, those lesser ones who had been cultivated by those greater men, became through their preaching “like lambs of sheep,” that is, innocent, and exulted.

“What is the matter with you, sea?” The second part. Continuation: The sea fled its former life. And, O “sea,” that is, O you who are embittered by sins, “what is the matter with you that you fled,” that is, abandoned your former way of life? And you, “Jordan,” what is the matter with you “that you turned backward,” toward God, your fountain?

And you, O “mountains,” that is, holy apostles, what reason caused you to “exult like rams”? And you, O “hills,” why did you exult “like lambs of sheep”? He supplies the answer.

I ask why you fled, and so forth. Behold the reason. The sea fled, and the other things happened (Exod. XVII), because “the earth,” that is, earthly people, “was moved” from the old life to the new. And this occurred “from the face of the Lord,” that is, on account of the face of God, which they saw present—namely, because they possessed knowledge of God. And lest we understand “new” in this way, he says, “from the face of the God of Jacob”: that is, the God whom we saw present in the body was that same God whom Jacob worshiped.

That God, showing us his face through the presence of his body, “turned the rock,” that is, the stony Jews, of whom it is said, “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III)—that is, from these Jews. He turned them, I say, “into pools of water,” that is, so that they might be a pool containing waters, namely, that they might become the Church, in which the waters of baptism are contained. And he turned not only the Jews, but also “the rock,” that is, the Gentiles, dry and parched from the true dew and from the knowledge of God, “into fountains of waters,” that is, so that the Gentiles themselves might become fountains and sources from which waters—that is, teachings—flow forth to others.

“Not to us.” And since, O Lord, you thus turn the rock and perform the other benefits for us, I ask you, “Lord, grant us mercy and truth.” And upon that mercy of yours, “grant glory to your name, not to us”: that is, make us understand that your mercy is given to us without any merit of ours, but for the enlargement of your name, so that we may attribute no praise or glory to ourselves from it, but ascribe everything to your name. In one instance of “not to us,” we understand the Jews; in the other, “not to us,” the Gentiles—namely, let neither Jews nor Gentiles presume that mercy is given to them according to their merits.

“Grant glory,” I say, “upon your mercy,” that is, for the remission of sins and for the other things mercifully bestowed; “and upon your truth,” that is, for the fulfillment of your promises. Thus grant glory to your name, “lest at any time the Gentiles say, ‘Where is their God?’” For they either think that we do not have a God, or, if they think we do have one, they suppose him powerless when they see us poor and in rags.

“But our God.” The Gentiles think that we do not have a God, or, if we have one, they suppose him powerless. But “our God” is “in heaven,” as is shown by the fact that “he has done everything whatsoever he desired.”

“Idols.” The third part. Our God is in heaven, powerful over all things. But the gods “of the Gentiles,” who are “idols,” are “silver” and “gold” according to their material. He names these two, which are the more precious metals, because if it is foolish to worship images of gold and silver, it is much more foolish to worship images of iron or of any cheap metal. According to their material they are silver and gold; according to their construction they are “the works of human hands.” And in this their greatest folly is noted: they venerate as their Creator the things that they themselves make.

And in order to mock the folly of idolaters as fully as possible, he describes the powerlessness of idols, saying: “They have mouths,” which their craftsmen make for them, “and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see.”

“They have ears, and they will not hear; they have nostrils, and they will not smell. They have hands, and they will not touch; they have feet, and they will not walk.” I do not say merely that they will not speak like human beings, but “they will not cry out” like certain irrational animals. In this he especially mocks the folly of those who worship such things, which cannot even cry out like asses or any irrational animals. I say that they will not cry out, yet in such a way that they cry out “in their throat.” He says this because sometimes demons speak through idols of this kind.

“Let those who make them become like them,” that is, the craftsmen of idols. Just as those idols do not see and possess no other bodily sense, so may the makers of idols be deprived of every power of the soul. “And” not only those “who make them,” but also “all who trust in them,” that is, those who ask them for help as though they were asking God.

The Gentiles, hoping in idols of this sort, gained nothing useful. But “the house,” that is, the assembly, “of Israel,” that is, of the Christian people, “hoped in the Lord,” and he is “their helper” for doing good, “and he is their protector” against evils.

“The house of Aaron,” that is, the assembly of priests, “hoped in the Lord,” and not without fruit, but “he is their helper and their protector.”

What does this mean in each case? All, of whatever condition, “who fear the Lord, have hoped in the Lord”; and they found help in him, because “he is their helper and their protector.”

And the fact that he was our helper did not arise from our merits, but from his mercy: “the Lord remembered us.” This appears especially from the fact that he caused his Son to become incarnate for our redemption, “and he blessed us,” that is, increased us in number and virtues.

And whom did he bless among us? “He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron”; and he also “blessed all who fear the Lord.” Nor did he bless only the powerful of this world, but also “the little ones,” according to human status, “with the great,” or the little and the great according to their merits.

The Lord bestowed these benefits upon us, and may the Lord still “add” blessing, or the succession of children, “upon you,” converts from the Jews; or upon us, converts from the Gentiles; or may he add it upon the greater; or upon you, the little ones. “And upon your children” may he add blessing, or the succession of children.

I say “may he add,” and truly he will add, because “you” will be “blessed,” that is, multiplied in virtues. And this will be “from the Lord,” that is, for the honor of the Lord, not for your glory. He can rightly bless his faithful, because he is the one “who made heaven and earth,” literally.

“[The] heaven of heaven,” that is, the highest heaven, he gave “to the Lord,” that is, to Jesus, so that he might reign there; “but he gave the earth to the sons of men,” so that they might serve God in it and merit the dwelling of heaven. By “the heaven of heaven” we may understand the firmament, which contains the other heavens, namely, the regions of the planets, from which the devil was cast down. Or by “the heaven of heaven” we may understand another heaven above the firmament, toward which, as Jerome says, the devil aspired, and for this reason was cast down. The Lord gave that heaven to Christ.

Allegorically: By “the heaven of heaven” we may understand the greater ones in the Church, who contain and govern others. They have been given to the Lord because the Lord dwells especially in them. By the earth we understand the lesser ones in the Church, who are not only subject to the Lord but also to the sons of men.

For this I pray you to add your blessing, so that we, once justified, may worthily praise you, because those who are “dead in sins will not praise you, Lord,” with an acceptable praise, as it is said: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). Hence the Psalmist says elsewhere: “God said to the sinner, ‘Why do you recount my justices?’” (Ps. XLIX). “Nor all,” that is, not all those “who descend into hell.” Yet some praised in hell, such as the prophets and other righteous people before Christ’s coming.

The dead will not praise you, “but we who live,” namely, with the true life that consists in virtues, “bless the Lord,” that is, beginning “from this moment,” namely, from the present time, and persevering in praise of God alone “unto the age,” that is, forever.

## ON PSALM CXIV. TITLE. Alleluia.

“Because I have loved.” The prophet speaks, and has as his subject himself and others who have been converted and heard after their sins, and who pray for what remains, that is, for eternal life. In the first part he shows that, when he was in sins, God sent him many tribulations, which compelled him to cry out on account of his sins; and, when he cried out, he was heard. In the second part, which begins, “O Lord, deliver my soul,” having already been heard concerning his sins, he asks for what he sees still remaining for him, namely, eternal life. His intention is that, for such deliverance, we sing alleluia to the Lord with exultation.

While, admonished by many tribulations, I cried out to the Lord on account of my sins, the Lord heard me. And because he heard me, I loved the Lord. Love of God is spoken of in two ways: liberally and servilely. It is servile when we love God for temporal goods; this is scarcely pleasing to God, since even the worst people love him in this way. Liberal love is the love by which we love God for his own sake and cannot be separated from him by any tribulation. Hence the Apostle says: “Neither death, nor life, nor any other creature can separate us from the love of God” (Rom. VIII). This love is pleasing to God; and it is with this kind of love that the righteous man who has been afflicted says he loves God. Therefore, “I loved, because he himself, God, will hear”—that is, just as he heard, so he persevered in hearing—“the voice of my prayer.”

I know, therefore, that he will hear me, “because he has inclined his ear to me,” that is, by condescending and humbling his clemency and power, he delivered me. And because he inclined his ear in this way and heard me in this way, therefore “I will call upon” him, so that he may make me persevere in guarding myself from sins. And this will be “in my days,” that is, in this fragile life, where we are always in fear and inclined to fall.

I say “he will hear” and “I will call upon him” because I experienced many tribulations in which I cried out. I needed him to hear me, and this is what follows: “The pains of death surrounded me,” that is, the most grievous anxieties of the soul; “and the dangers of hell,” that is, the most grievous dangers and bodily tribulations such as the wicked endure in hell, “found me,” that is, came upon me. But they found me for this reason: because I lay exposed, as though without a helper, cast down in sins and making no provision for my salvation.

These things found me and seized me, and I “found tribulation” of the body “and pain” of the soul, that is, I came to understand that these things had been sent to me by the Lord for correction. To find tribulation means to recognize that it has been imposed upon one by God for the correction of sins. And when I found this, admonished by those tribulations, “I called upon the name of the Lord.”

“O Lord.” The second part. Continuation: Since you admonished me through tribulation and heard me when I called upon you concerning my sins, accomplish what remains, namely, “deliver my soul” from every impediment of the world; that is, bring me into eternal rest, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII). I say “deliver,” and I know that he will deliver. And he turns in direct address to his hearers, because “the Lord” is “merciful” by nature “and just,” correcting sins. “And our God himself has mercy,” because he saves those who have been corrected, making them immortal. Another translation reads, “he will have mercy.”

And he is truly just and merciful, because he is the Lord “who guards the little ones” from sins, that is, the humble who make themselves little. I then show an argument from my own case, because “I was humbled,” becoming little; “and he delivered me” from the burden of sins.

And because he delivered me in this way, O “my soul, return” from every delight in earthly things “to your rest,” that is, to God, who is truly your rest, from whom you proceeded, created in perfection, and to whom you ought to return, “because the Lord has dealt favorably with you,” that is, he forgave your sins, made you worthy of his glory, and in the end will make you immortal and incapable of suffering.

He turns to his hearers: Truly the Lord will deal favorably with me, “because he has rescued”—that is, he will rescue by force—“my soul from death,” that is, from every fear of death. And thereby he will rescue “my eyes,” that is, my affections, “from tears,” because I will do nothing there that would cause me to weep.
