Hence it is said: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. XXI). And he will rescue “my feet,” that is, my affections, “from falling,” because there we shall be so secure that we shall be moved by no sin. In this life the opposite is true: here we are always in fear of death, we shed tears for our sins, and we are always inclined to fall.

[Col. 0593D] And then “I will please the Lord,” because he will find no offense in me there, when I have been taken from the region of the dead and placed “in the region of the living,” that is, of the saints. He says that he will please God in an exceptional sense, because while no righteous person here can be without sin, no one can please God in every respect.

## ON PSALM CXV. TITLE. Alleluia.

“Because I believed.” This is the voice of the martyrs of the Lord. He speaks as though in the person of one, assuming the person of all the martyrs, and the martyrs themselves are his subject, since by their martyrdom they imitate the Lord’s death. In the first part the martyr who speaks shows that, since in himself he is nothing but vanity and falsehood, he has received from the Lord so great a gift that he does not fear repaying the Lord, since Christ himself chose to die for our salvation. In the second part, which begins, “O Lord, because I am your servant,” he shows himself to be Christ’s servant and to remain in the Catholic faith, and therefore to obtain the benefit of his martyrdom. His intention is that we praise God for these benefits and that he give us such constancy that we may wish to repay the Lord’s death with our own.

The martyr who speaks says, inspired by God’s grace: “I believed” in my heart. Hence the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. X). He rightly begins with “I believed,” because we can do no good unless we believe. Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV). “For which reason,” that is, because I believed, “I spoke,” because, when necessary, I did not keep silent about the truth. This confession is effective, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). I spoke, “but I”—not my preaching—“was humbled,” not in mind, but through bodily tribulation, and this “exceedingly,” that is, unbearably or to a great degree. Although I was afflicted by many miseries, I nevertheless did not cease preaching God. Hence the Apostle says: “I am held in chains, but the word of God cannot be bound” (II Tim. II).

“I believed, I spoke, I was humbled.” Thus I appear to call myself strong. Yet whenever I examined my nature more wisely, I understood that I was nothing but vanity. And this is what follows: “I said,” that is, I considered inwardly within myself. Nor did I do this foolishly, but “in my ecstasy,” that is, by reason rising above human emotions. I said this, namely, “Every man is a liar,” that is, every man who is merely human.

I said, “I believed, I spoke, I was humbled.” And since the Lord conferred these good things upon me, “what shall I repay the Lord for all the benefits that he has repaid to me?” He did not give good things for good merits, but gave good things for evils.

I say, “What shall I repay?” I will “take the cup of salvation,” that is, by my death I will imitate the Lord’s death. And I will not do this in such a way that I appear unwilling to do it, but I will “take it,” that is, I will seek it with great desire. I call it the cup of salvation, that is, of the Savior, which he himself endured for our redemption. When he says “of salvation,” he indicates that through this cup he too will attain salvation. I say, “I will take it,” “and” so that I may be able to fulfill it, “I will call upon the name of the Lord.” We understand the cup as death because the saints receive it with a certain delight, and for them it is perfect refreshment.

I will call upon the name of the Lord; “I will fulfill my vows,” that is, I will complete in action what I had desired: I will bring myself to completion through suffering, just as I had desired. And I will do this “in the presence of all his people,” so that others may take an example from me. I will fulfill my vows in this way because “in the sight of the Lord the death of his saints,” which is contemptible in the sight of human beings, is “precious,” that is, pleasing. Or: the death of the saints, which is “in the sight of the Lord,” that is, pleasing to him, is precious, that is, purchased by Christ’s blood. For this reason he died, so that we too, if necessary, might die for him. And what has been bought at a great price is precious.

“O Lord.” The second part. I endured these things because you granted them; this suffering of mine, O Lord, will be useful to me because I persist in your faith and service. Before showing its usefulness, he shows that he remains in God’s service when he says, “because I am your servant,” that is, because I regard you as the Most High and as my Lord. And to show greater humility he repeats: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid,” namely, the Church, an imitator of the ancient fathers.

Because I am thus a servant, “you have broken my bonds,” that is, through martyrdom you have released me from every bond of sins. We are certain that all those who endure martyrdom for Christ in the Catholic faith, even if they are burdened by serious crimes, nevertheless have everything washed away in the blood of martyrdom. When he says that his bonds are broken because he was Christ’s servant, he makes us understand that if anyone suffers martyrdom without being a true Catholic, his martyrdom does not break the bonds of his sins. Many have died for their heresies, and it benefited them nothing.

And because I know that you will break my bonds, “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice,” not of beasts, but “of praise,” that is, myself as an acceptable sacrifice, putting all vices to death in myself; “and,” so that I may be able to do this, “I will call upon the name of the Lord.” This is not found in the Hebrew truth, but the translators added it. Therefore Jerome, here and elsewhere, where something is not in the Hebrew truth, places an asterisk, that is, a sign of prohibition; he places an obelus where the opposite has occurred, namely, where he finds something removed that the Hebrew truth retains.

I vow praises to God, and I will “render those praises to the Lord,” namely, “my vows.” And I will do this “in the presence of all his people,” so that I may offer others an example of praise. I will do this “in the courts of the house of the Lord,” that is, in the present Church, which is called a court because of the spaciousness of the house, since God dwells in it. Or by the house we understand the heavenly house, and by the court the present Church, which is a court—that is, an entrance—to the heavenly homeland. And I will render those vows of mine, already in hope, “in the midst of you, Jerusalem,” the heavenly city.

## ON PSALM CXVI. TITLE. Alleluia.

“Praise the Lord, all nations.” The prophet has as his subject the Lord’s mercy and truth, and he urges the singing of alleluia. Therefore he says, “all nations,” that is, all peoples, “praise the Lord”; and you, “all peoples,” that is, the peoples of all nations—Romans, Latins, or Greeks—“praise him.” Or let us understand “peoples” as all who live under one law, and “nations” as the inhabitants of a single city. Or by “nations” let us understand converts, and by “peoples” Gentiles.

He sets forth the reasons for praise, saying: “For his mercy,” that is, the remission of sins and the other graces that justify, “has been confirmed upon us,” that is, has been given to us so firmly that the devil, though he lies in wait, can no longer tear it away from us. “And the truth of the Lord,” that is, the fulfillment of his promises, “remains forever,” because it begins here and will remain forever and beyond.

## ON PSALM CXVII. TITLE. Alleluia.

“Give praise to the Lord, for.” In this psalm the prophet has as his subject the goodness of God, and treats it in this way. In the first part he shows that God helps his own in such a way that they do not fear what a human being may do, and even despise their enemies. In the second part, which begins, “It is good to trust,” he shows that God acts for those who trust and hope in the Lord in such a way that no tribulations can harm them; rather, they even take vengeance on their enemies, and also convert them. And if they sometimes fall, God raises them up. In the third part, which begins, “Open to me the gates,” seeing certain gates through which one is led to Christ, who is the gate leading to eternal glory (John X), he asks to be brought into those gates. In the fourth part, which begins, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” seeing that someone blessed has come into the world, from whom others will be blessed, he urges the other faithful, once blessed through this Lord, to establish a solemn day for him.

His intention is to admonish us to return due praises to the Lord for such benefits. It is the voice of the prophet, or of some righteous person speaking not for himself alone but in the person of all the righteous: “Give praise to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord. And you ought to do so, “because” he alone is “good” in himself; and whatever are good are good from him. Hence Christ said to a certain young man who called him good without understanding that he was God: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII). Do not be negligent in giving praise, “because his mercy” endures “forever,” that is, as long as this age endures, because after this life confession comes too late.

And let what I urge, namely, confession, be said “now,” that is, in the present age, by “Israel,” that is, by all subject Christians who set this reason for praise before themselves: “For the Lord is good, and his mercy endures forever.”

And let not only subjects exhort one another to praise God, but also “the house of Aaron,” that is, the entire body of priests and other prelates, “let it say now,” exhorting people to praise God, “for his mercy endures forever.”

And what does this mean in each case? Let “all” also “say now,” from whatever people, condition, or nation, “who fear the Lord”: let them say this, “for his mercy endures forever.” I rightly say that he is good, because this is evident in me, since “I called upon the Lord from tribulation,” that is, through many tribulations I was admonished to call upon the Lord, “and the Lord heard me,” when I called upon him, “in a broad place,” that is, in the breadth of charity, so that I might even pray for my enemies. Or, “he heard me,” already placed in hope in the breadth of the heavenly homeland.

He heard me; and since “the Lord” is “my helper,” “I will not fear what man can do to me,” no matter how fiercely he rages.

And I will not merely fear no human being; since the Lord is my helper, “I will despise my enemies,” my spiritual enemies, that is, demons, when I see them condemned in God’s judgment. Or, in this life I will despise my enemies, so that we may say: “I will despise my enemies,” that is, the demons themselves. Although they are invisible, I will show them to be despicable, because I will yield in no way to their temptations.

“It is good.” The second part. Continuation: Since the Lord helps me in such a way that I do not fear human beings, “it is good to trust in” this “Lord rather than to trust in man,” because one must in no way trust in a human being, neither in oneself nor in another, but in God alone. He trusts in the Lord who considers him powerful and sufficient to forgive sins and grant righteousness. But he trusts in a human being who thinks that he can act well by free choice alone, without the help of grace.

“It is good to hope in the Lord,” that is, to await from the Lord the reward of one’s righteousness, which the Lord himself has given, “rather than to hope in princes,” whether secular princes or “holy angels and other holy men,” because neither angels nor other saints can confer anything by themselves. “Rather than” is a comparative conjunction, and the thing to which it is joined it plainly indicates ought to be removed.

Therefore I say, “It is good to hope in the Lord,” and “it is good to trust in him,” because I have proved this in myself, and I demonstrate its certainty: “All nations surrounded me” with flatteries and threats, and even by taking away my external possessions. “And” this, namely, “that I took vengeance on them,” happened “in the name of the Lord,” not through me but through the Lord’s help. In this way the righteous man takes vengeance on those sinners: he converts them in such a way that the evils which they previously inflicted upon the righteous they now inflict upon themselves, and punish themselves for those sins. Here a lighter form of tribulation is indicated.

“Surrounding me, they also surrounded me,” namely, persevering in inflicting evils upon me in my own person; “and I took vengeance on them,” such grave persecutors, as above: “in the name of the Lord.”

“They surrounded me” also “like bees,” namely, as fiercely and bitterly as bees sting someone. He rightly compares them to bees, because just as bees sting someone and, in stinging, break off their stinger and then die or remain useless, so persecutors of the righteous either destroy themselves inwardly or become temporarily blind. Or, “they surrounded me like bees” surround a honeycomb. Another translation has “honeycomb”: they surround it in order to pour in and increase the honey. So they, surrounding me in order to afflict me, increased virtues in me, “and they burned like fire among thorns.” Just as thorns provide fuel for fire so that it burns more fiercely, so their thorns, that is, their sins, provide greater fuel for their fury.

Or in another sense: Just as fire consumes thorns and does not prevail against a trunk that is firm and solid, so tribulation destroys the thorns, that is, the sins, of the righteous, without harming the firmness of the soul. “And in the name of the Lord, because I took vengeance on them.” Here he shows the manner of the most grievous tribulation, and he says that he endured these persecutions in the person of other righteous people of the primitive Church.

After showing that he thus avenges himself upon his enemies, he shows that, even if he is driven toward a fall, God raises him up. Continuation: For this reason it is also good to hope, because “I was pushed” by the devil and his ministers “so that I might fall” into sin. The righteous person is said to be pushed when he doubts whether he should act. Thus we read about Marcellus and Marcus, who were almost seduced by the flatteries of women, but the Lord, through blessed Sebastian, took hold of them so that they would not fall. And I was also “overthrown.” He says this in the person of others: I was thrown headlong into the act of sin, “so that I might fall,” that is, so that I might perish completely. “And” from there “the Lord took hold of me.” From this it is evident that he is “my strength,” making me strong after my fall; “and the Lord is my praise,” making me praiseworthy in this respect, that he makes me resist my enemies. Or he is my strength against enemies, and my praise insofar as he raises me from sins. And by doing this, “he became my salvation,” that is, the salvation of my soul. When he says “became,” he signifies the incarnation of the divine Word, through which all these things were accomplished for us.

And because the Lord is my strength, therefore “in the tents of the righteous,” that is, in their consciences, in which God dwells and in which they serve God, there is “a voice of exultation,” that is, great exultation, by which we show our will to God, as one friend does to another through his voice; “and a voice of salvation,” that is, the exultation itself is held in the heart because of the salvation which the righteous understand they will possess.

Therefore let the righteous exult in the tents, because “the right hand of the Lord has done virtue,” that is, his Son and his power have made me steadfast against persecutors. That same “right hand of the Lord has exalted me” in virtues, multiplying me in those virtues and guarding me by protecting me. This is what he says: “The right hand of the Lord has done virtue.”

And because “the right hand of the Lord has done virtue,” therefore “I will not die,” that is, I will not fall away from the virtues granted to me, “but I will live” with the life of the soul; “and I will recount the works of the Lord,” that is, I will proclaim them to others.

Therefore “I will not die, but I will live,” because those evils which you think were inflicted upon me for my destruction, the Lord inflicted for my correction. And this is what follows: “The Lord chastising chastised me,” that is, he persevered in chastising me through very frequent tribulations, “but he did not hand me over to the death” of the soul. Hence the Apostle says: “Chastised, but not put to death.”

[Col. 0599A] The third part. And since I live with the life of the soul and have been chastised by many tribulations, yet have not been put to death, therefore you, holy apostles and other ministers of the holy Church, “open to me the gates,” that is, release me through the sacraments of the Church, and by opening the holy Scriptures, which are all gates “of righteousness,” that is, through which a person obtains complete justifications. After saying that he lived, he rightly asks to be released, because it is necessary for every faithful person to be absolved by the ministers of the holy Church in order to reach eternity. We recognize this now because, after the Lord Jesus had given Lazarus life, he commanded that he be unbound (John XI).

“Open,” I say, and I, “having entered through them,” that is, already absolved and justified, “will confess to the Lord,” that is, I will praise the Lord. And once introduced through these gates, I will reach Christ the Lord, who is the true gate, introducing those conformed to him into eternal life. And as though already seeing Christ himself present, he says of him: “This is the gate of the Lord,” that is, the gate through which one goes to the Lord. Yet not just anyone will enter through it, but “the righteous will enter through it,” that is, through that gate they will enter into eternal rest.

Or in another sense: Since your tribulations are not death for me but chastisement, therefore, you persecutors, open to me the gates of righteousness, that is, prepare tribulations for me which will lead me into the perfection of righteousness. And when I have entered through those gates, I will not murmur but will confess to the Lord, that is, praise the Lord. And why will I praise him in tribulation? Because this was the gate of our Lord Jesus Christ: through many tribulations the Lord Jesus entered into the glory of the Father. And because it is “the gate of the Lord,” therefore “the righteous will enter through it,” that is, if anyone wishes to become righteous, let him not flee suffering for the name of Jesus Christ when necessity requires it.

“Having entered, I will confess to the Lord.” And therefore, O Lord, “I will confess to you because you have heard me,” bringing me to the gate which is Christ; “and you became for me,” through the humanity you assumed, “salvation,” that is, the enlivening of the soul.

“The stone.” He determines who it is that was made salvation, namely Christ, called a rejected stone because of its solidity. And for whom? For the Jews and the Gentiles, who through Christ, the cornerstone, are joined into one faith [Col. 0599D] and one order.

Continuation: He was made salvation for Jews and Gentiles, and this is that stone, “which stone,” that is, Christ, who is called a stone because of his solidity, “the builders,” that is, the Jews, “rejected.” They are called builders because they were built up through carnal observances, namely, abstaining from evil and serving God. Although they did not complete the work so as to be found perfect—except for those who awaited Christ the Redeemer—they were like children who are educated through flatteries until they can bear heavier things and fulfill God’s law. Thus the Jews were built up through these temporal benefits until at some point they recognized the truth and therefore judged that one ought to serve for the sake of heavenly things alone.

This stone, which the builders rejected, “has become the head of the corner.” Just as a cornerstone joins two walls, so Christ joins two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, in the same faith. When he says “the head of the corner,” he indicates that Christ is the entire completion of our building and religion, like the stone placed at the completion of the corner.

I say that the rejected stone was made the head of the corner, and “this”—that is, this stone, or this such union of peoples effected through that stone—“was made by the Lord,” as though no one else could make such a man, born of a virgin, who keeps himself free from every evil and performs many other wondrous deeds; and therefore it is called a special work. And the union of the peoples [Col. 0600B] was a special work of God, “and” this work of God “is wondrous in our inward eyes”: for if we consider that God caused the Son to become incarnate for our liberation and even gave him over to death, we truly understand the wondrous operation and goodness of God.

I say, “made by the Lord,” and “this day”—on which Christ was born and made man, or on which the aforesaid union of the peoples was made, namely, the time of grace—is the day “which the Lord has made.” Although the Lord made all days, this one is said to have been made specially because in this time he specially enlightened us and poured the light of his knowledge into our hearts. Therefore, “let us rejoice” according to the body, “and let us be glad in it” according to the soul, rejoicing in it [Col. 0600C] through the purity of our conscience that we have been redeemed on this day.

I say, “Let us rejoice,” saying this: “O Lord, save me”—that is, make me a participant in the salvation that you have brought to the world—“O Lord, prosper well,” namely, against the miseries that you endured here; make me, at some time, be clothed with immortality and impassibility.

Next comes the fourth section. It is as though he were saying: Since Christ was made the head of the corner, therefore you others “establish a solemn day”; and the reasons for this have been set forth above. He is, as it were, saying: You ought therefore to establish a solemn day for him because he who “came into the world,” shod in our humanity, is “blessed,” that is, full of every perfection of virtues. I say that he “came,” not [Col. 0600D] to acquire his own glory, as Antichrist will do, but “in the name of the Lord,” to enlarge it.

From this blessed one we were blessed, and we “blessed you from the house of the Lord.” For those who are outside the house—that is, the Church—do not have the power to bless. I say that we blessed, and while we were blessing, “God the Lord” blessed us, “and,” through his blessing, “he shone upon us” together with us: that is, he drove darkness from us and poured the true illumination into our hearts. We must believe that Christ gave this power to his ministers, so that those whom they bless are also blessed by his blessing.

And because you are blessed, therefore “establish a solemn day [Col. 0601A] amid dense throngs,” going “as far as the horn of the altar”—that is, so that you may partake of the food of the altar. Or, allegorically: “Establish a solemn day,” that is, keep sabbath for the Lord in your hearts by ceasing from vices; and do this “amid dense throngs,” that is, amid a great abundance of virtues, going as far as the horn of the altar, that is, to the imitation of Christ’s height, so that you may make him your altar, upon which your offered prayers are received.

I admonish others to establish a solemnity for God, but whatever others may do, I shall always praise the Lord. This is what he says, turning himself toward God: “You are my God, and I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you. He repeats the same thing out of excessive affection, [Col. 0601B] saying: “You are my God, and I will exalt you,” that is, I will announce your loftiness and your power to others, so that you may be exalted among them.

I say, “I will confess and exalt” you; therefore I will “confess” and exalt you “because you have heard me,” praying for my sins, “and” because “you have become my salvation.” He repeats this verse because the greatest reason why we praise God depends upon and revolves around it.

And since God has granted us the aforesaid benefits through his goodness, therefore “confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” ending at the same point from which he began, namely, that we should continually occupy ourselves in the praises of God. Alleluia.

## ON PSALM 118. TITLE. Alleluia.

### Aleph

“Blessed are the undefiled.” Aleph is not the title; rather, Alleluia is the title. The prophet divided this psalm into twenty-two sections, after the manner of the Hebrew alphabet, which has twenty-two letters; and each section has its own letter, according to the order of the alphabet, from which the individual verses of that section begin. Thus, among the Hebrews, the verses of this first section begin with the letter Aleph, those of the second with Beth, and so on with the others. But the same identity could not be preserved in this translation or in the translations of the other translators, so that among us or among the Greeks the eight verses of each section might begin with the same letter. Nevertheless, nothing prevented the same meaning that the prophet had—writing according to the order of the alphabet—from being arranged as the foundation of perfect doctrine, just as the alphabet is the foundation of all learning.

These sections are divided according to the number eight, because each contains eight verses. By this we are shown that, even if someone cannot fulfill everything contained in all the sections, nevertheless, if he fulfills what is treated in any one section, through this he will be led to the eighth, that is, to eternal rest, which will follow these seven days through which this world revolves.

In this psalm the prophet has as his subject the law of God. Under the name “law” we understand both the natural law, the law written through figures—namely, the law of Moses—and the New Testament. He treats this subject by commending it and showing that, through this law, God bestows blessedness. This first section is the prologue to all the others, because it shows in general that a person is made blessed through the law. And because it comprehends the subject of the whole psalm in a general way, it receives the name of the whole psalm: it is called “law” and “teaching,” and for this reason Aleph is prefixed. Aleph is interpreted as “teaching”; the remaining sections then unfold in various ways the blessedness that this first section sets forth generally.

Thus the section beginning, “In what way does he correct,” shows that through his law God frees people from the confusion of sin and brings them back to conversion; and [Col. 0602B] the section beginning, “Repay your servant,” shows how God supplies the needs of the faithful through the fulfillment of that same law; and the third section, beginning, “My soul has clung to the pavement,” shows that through observance of that same law God removes the necessities that the body necessarily bears, namely, fear of falling, weariness, and whatever similar things there may be. And because God brings about such blessednesses through his mercy, the title “Alleluia” is prefixed to this psalm. Its purpose is to invite us to sing Alleluia to the Lord.

The universal voice of the just person, from the first just person to the last, is as though saying: Brothers, keep the law of the Lord, because those who keep it will become “undefiled” and through this “blessed.” Hence he says “undefiled,” that is, those whose sins have been forgiven, and who are therefore undefiled because they are “in the way,” that is, in Christ or in the law of the Lord. They are blessed: keeping the law and imitating Christ are the way to blessedness—not the way that some people desire. For some seek to arrive at blessedness through riches or through power. But since these are rather distortions and deviations, they cannot reach blessedness through them.

People are not called undefiled because they can be entirely without every stain, since Christ alone is without stain, but because their sins are forgiven through confession. For if we were to say that people are without sin, we would contradict the Apostle, who says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, because we all offend in many things [Col. 0602D] (1 John 1).” Therefore he says “undefiled” in the plural, so that we understand many people to be undefiled and thus understand that we ourselves are made undefiled. For if he had said “undefiled” in the singular, it could be understood of Christ alone. And the undefiled are blessed, “who walk in the law of the Lord,” that is, who continually increase through the multiplication of virtues.

Also blessed are “those who search,” that is, those who seek with every diligence “his testimonies,” that is, his commandments, which are called testimonies because they testify to what must be done and what must not be done. If someone asks whether murder ought to be committed, through the law he can know the testimony, which says: “You shall not kill (Deuteronomy 6).” The law also commanded that good be done when it says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22).” Or they are called “testimonies” because they make us certain of eternal good. Thus I say that those who search become blessed if they search these things not for some temporal advantage, like those who study the law of God in order to receive money from others by teaching them, but if, by searching the commandments, they “seek him,” God, “with their whole heart.” The summary is briefly this: Those are blessed who in all God’s commandments seek God’s will with all their strength.

Those who walk in the law of the Lord are blessed, because those “who practice iniquity,” that is, the defiled, “have not walked in his ways,” that is, in his commandments. Or we may understand the ways as the saints, through whose imitation we can reach the Lord.

I say that the law makes one blessed, and that this law must be kept, because “you,” Lord, “commanded it to be kept.” This is what he says: “Your commandments exceedingly,” that is, to such a degree that nothing should be left unkept through fear. God commanded his law to be kept through the prophets, the apostles, and other holy men.

And since your law makes one blessed, and you, Lord, command it to be kept, therefore, Lord, “would that my ways might be directed,” that is, my actions, “to keep your justifications,” that is, those ceremonies which, understood spiritually, justify a person.

He shows how the ways can be directed: namely, if we always have God’s commandments before our eyes. Continuation: I say, “May my ways be directed.” The ways are directed when I “look upon all your commandments”; that is, the ways can be directed if I always have your commandments before my eyes. And “then,” when I have done this, “I shall not be put to shame” because of my sins, by doing something shameful, lest it be said of me: “This man began to build, and was unable to finish.”

I say, “I shall not be put to shame,” but rather “I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you, “in the uprightness of my heart,” that is, with my heart made upright and justified by you. I do not arrogantly discover something new in my heart, but rather I confess “in what I have learned” from the Holy Spirit speaking inwardly to me, or from the holy Fathers: “the judgments of your justice,” namely, the judgments by which he himself condemns some and justifies others. He does all these things from his own justice, although this is unknown to everyone.

I say, “I will confess,” and I will persevere in your obedience. This is what he says: “I will keep your justifications,” that is, I will remain in the keeping of your commandments, which justify a person. And so that I may be able to remain and keep them, O Lord, “do not utterly forsake me,” that is, in any respect. He says “utterly” because he sees the devil always ready to enter wherever God withdraws his grace.

### Beth

“In what way does he correct.” Beth is prefixed to this section and is interpreted as “confusion.” This letter is appropriately prefixed to this section, because here we are taught how people are led out of confusion—that is, from their former life—and converted to the true life.

The text is as follows. Continuation: I say, “I will keep your justifications,” specifically because through those justifications my ways will be corrected. He shows this more clearly by posing a question and giving the answer, when he says: “In what way does a younger man correct his way,” that is, a foolish person, more prone to sin, correct his way—that is, his action and the habit of his wickedness, in which he has been accustomed to live? He sets the answer before his blinded hearers by means of a question when he says: “By keeping your words,” because he fulfills your commandments by acting well.

Or “a younger man” means a renewed people, made young again. In what way does he correct [Col. 0604B] his way—that is, through what is he thus renewed? “By keeping your words.”

And because the correction of wicked action lies in keeping the words, therefore “I have sought you,” that is, I have fulfilled your law—but for another purpose, namely, so that knowledge of you might increase in me. And I have sought you “with my whole heart,” that is, no part of my heart will be empty of seeking you. Therefore, Lord, “do not cast me away from your commandments,” but rather reveal your will to me in them.

I say that I have sought, and that once found I have hidden, proclaimed, delighted in, practiced, considered, meditated upon, and not forgotten. Through all these things he is shown to come out of confusion and to be very perfect, as perfection ought to be found in each group of eight. The letter is read as follows: “In my heart,” that is, in my memory, “I have hidden your utterances,” that is, I have carefully entrusted your commandments to memory. But when he says “I have hidden,” he indicates something more: that he would not make them known to his enemies, as it is said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw pearls before swine (Matthew 7).” Therefore I hid them “so that I may not sin against you,” who forbade your commandments to be given to dogs.

I have hidden them, and, O “Lord, teach me” in the very act “your justifications,” that is, make me act as your commandments require, for they justify a person. Or, teach me to whom I ought to reveal your commandments and to whom I ought not. I have dared to ask you to teach me because you “are blessed,” that is, praised by your own and kind toward your own, namely, providing your own with whatever is necessary.

I hid them from my enemies, but to my friends I “have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth,” that is, the things you spoke through your mouth, namely, through your Son. This does not mean that anyone could proclaim all the judgments of God, but that whatever judgments I proclaim are the judgments of God. Here he calls “judgments” whatever God does by hidden judgment, such as condemning some, choosing and justifying others. And this is “on my lips,” that is, corresponding to my action, because what I teach with my mouth I fulfill in my deeds.

I say, “I have hidden” and “I have proclaimed,” and because of these things “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies,” that is, in proceeding toward the fulfillment of your testimonies, “as” a carnal person would delight “in all riches.” [Col. 0605A] That is, I have delighted in your commandments because they are all riches to me.

I have not merely delighted, but thereafter “I will practice your commandments,” fulfilling them, “and I will consider your ways,” that is, the true meaning in your commandments. He rightly places “I will consider” after saying “I will practice,” because true understanding cannot be possessed unless good action comes first.

I say, “I will consider,” and “I will not forget” your “words,” once known, because I will always “meditate on your justifications,” that is, I will always keep in continual meditation your commandments, in whose observance justice is found.

### Gimel

“Repay your servant.” This letter is appropriately prefixed to this section. Gimel is interpreted as “retribution,” and in this section a great retribution from God is shown: namely, how God, once the person has been stripped of confusion, as was said, supplies the needs of those who seek God himself and leads them to great perfection.

We call this supplying of needs “retribution” because God first grants his faithful the desire to pray. For this grace God repays them with another grace, namely, the supplying of their needs. Continuation: I say, “I will meditate on the commandments and will not forget,” and therefore, O Lord, for me, “your servant,” that is, one who recognizes you alone as my true God and myself as your servant, “repay”—that is, you who granted me the gift of knowing you, grant me another repayment, namely this: “Give me life,” that is, restore to me the ability to act well, which I lost in my first parent. “And,” thus made alive, “I will keep your words,” that is, I will act according to your commandments.

And once I have been justified and am already acting well, “reveal my eyes,” that is, remove the veil from my inward eyes, so that I may have full understanding of your law. “And” then “I will consider the wonders of your law,” that is, the things signified by the figures placed in the Old Testament. I will consider Christ signified by the slaughtered lamb, and the nourishment of the Lord’s body signified by the manna, and other things of this kind, which no one can understand unless God has revealed his eyes.

You ought therefore to reveal and give life because I have prepared myself as far as I could, namely because “on earth,” that is, in this world, “I am a sojourner,” that is, I regard myself as an immigrant, and I have no permanent city here, but always strive toward the true homeland. Therefore, “do not hide your commandments from me.”

And therefore reveal them and do not hide them, because “my soul has desired” with the greatest affection “to desire your justifications,” that is, so that my soul itself may be refreshed by the fulfillment of your words. And this is not for an hour, but “at every time,” that is, continually.

“I have desired in this way so that what happened to the devil and to the other proud might not happen to me. You rebuked the proud by threatening eternal punishment and sometimes scourging them [Col. 0606A] in this life as a sign of the future judgment or punishment; and these proud are ‘accursed,’ that is, rejected, because they are the ones ‘who turn aside from your commandments.’ Those are not said to sin proudly or to turn aside from God’s commandments who, although they do not set before themselves a will to sin, nevertheless sometimes sin because the weakness of the flesh compels them. But those are said to sin proudly and to turn aside from God’s commandments who sin by their own will and the delight of their mind, and who do not care to hear God’s commandments or trample them underfoot once they have heard them.”

My soul has desired, and so that they may not be able to take away from me the fruit of my desire, “take away from me reproach,” so that those who afflict me may not lead me into the act of sin, by which I would justly become reproached and [Col. 0606B] mocked. “And” also take away “contempt,” so that they may not turn me back from the good undertaking and make me sluggish in acting well. I rightly ask that these things be taken away from me “because I have sought,” that is, from all the other teachings I have chosen “your testimonies” for my instruction.

I say, “Take it away,” and it is necessary, “for princes,” that is, the powerful of this world, “have sat,” that is, have occupied themselves attentively, “and spoke against me,” attacking the truth that I set forth. “But your servant” did not fail; rather, he “was exercised in your law,” that is, speaking and acting according to your commandments.

Therefore I was exercised, “for your testimonies are also my meditation,” that is, through frequent meditation I keep your commandments, “and your justifications are my counsel,” that is, I have always deliberated within myself to fulfill the commandments. A person who does not first propose to follow God’s justifications is quickly shaken when tribulation comes upon him.

### Daleth

“My soul has clung to the pavement.” Daleth is prefixed to this group of eight because it is interpreted as “fear.” The faithful person who speaks is one who has already been recalled from confusion, and whose many needs have already been driven away, so that he is filled with God’s benefits.

Yet, observing that the human body is always prone to sin and brings with it certain necessities that lead to sin, he fears falling back and prays to the Lord against these necessities. Continuation: I say, “My soul has desired,” and your justifications are my counsel, but nevertheless “my soul has clung to the pavement,” that is, it once consented to the body in certain illicit matters. “Pavement” is derived from *pavire*, “to strike,” because stones are called pavement when they have been crushed and well leveled, so that they do not injure the feet; and pavement lies beneath the feet of those who walk.

By this the human body is understood, crushed and leveled by many fasts and other afflictions so that it does not injure the feet of the soul; it is also subject to the soul. But because the nature of the body, however much it may be afflicted, is always prone to sin, even if the soul consents to the body, it is immediately precipitated into a fall. And because the soul, clinging to the body, has already [Col. 0607A] been led into a fall, therefore, O Lord, “give me life,” that is, restore to me the ability not to let the soul consent to the body. Do this “according to your word,” that is, according to your promise, because you ordained that “the one who is righteous must be made righteous still (Revelation 22).”

Although it has clung to the pavement, you nevertheless ought not to reject me, because I have revealed my sins to you. This is what he says: I have “declared” to you “my ways,” that is, my sins, in which I had walked, by confessing them, “and” you “have heard me,” that is, you have forgiven my sins. And because you have already heard me by granting forgiveness of sins, therefore, O Lord, “teach me your justifications,” that is, make me act according to your commandments.

And after you have taught me to act well, “instruct [Col. 0607B] me in the way of your justifications,” that is, give me true understanding in your commandments. “And” thus instructed, I will “practice” through manifold action “your wonders,” that is, spiritual works and graces understood through the figures of the old law.

There is another bodily necessity for which the faithful speaker thinks he must fear. Continuation: I say, “I will practice,” but at some time “my soul became drowsy,” that is, it was somewhat sluggish, and this was “because of weariness,” since it had already grown disgusted with the divine word. But you, Lord, “strengthen me,” so that I may not afterward fall into weariness. Strengthen me, I say, “in your words,” that is, in the fulfillment of your commandments. When he says “became drowsy,” he indicates that he sinned more lightly than if he had said “fell asleep.”

I say, “Strengthen me,” and so that I may be able to remain strengthened, “remove from me the way of iniquity,” that is, the devil, who is the way of every iniquity, so that he cannot prevail against me, thrust me back into weariness, or plunge me into some vice. “And have mercy on me according to your law,” that is, through your mercy grant me to fulfill what is commanded in your law.

And you ought to remove the way of iniquity from me because I “have chosen the way of truth,” that is, to imitate Christ and follow his law. And I “have not forgotten your judgments,” but have always considered them within myself.

“I have not forgotten your judgments,” but rather I “clung” to them, because I was firm and stable, “to your testimonies,” that is, to your commandments by which you testify to your will. Therefore, “O Lord, do not put me to shame,” that is, do not make me shameful, but make me complete [Col. 0607D] what I have begun, lest it be said of me: “This man began to build, and could not finish.”

I did not merely cling to your testimonies, but also “ran,” that is, I acted readily, “in the way of your commandments,” that is, in your commandments, which are the way to life. And this was because “you enlarged my heart,” that is, expanded it through charity, patience, long-suffering, and similar virtues.

### He

“Establish the law.” In this group of eight the faithful speaker asks that Christ come through his new law—not only through commandments, but also through assisting grace and through the understanding that demonstrates the commandments—and establish it in them. Therefore He, which is interpreted as “to be,” is appropriately prefixed to this section, because in Christ’s law true being is found and the life of the soul is renewed. It seems to be the voice of those who were awaiting Christ’s present coming and earnestly desired it. The order is also good: after showing himself converted and filled with God’s benefits once his needs have been removed, he shows himself strengthened against the necessities imposed by the body and asks that the law be given to him—that is, Christ himself, whom he sees as sufficient for every justification.

Continuation: I said, “Do not put me to shame,” but rather “establish your law for me, O Lord,” namely, this “way of your justifications,” that is, Christ himself, who is the way by which the faithful are justified. Establish the law for me [Col. 0608B] so that I may direct my life according to his imitation. Establish the law, I say, “and” I will “seek it,” namely, the law, so that in it I may find God’s will. And this not for an hour, but “always.”

I say, “I will seek the law”; and so that I may be able to seek it, “give me understanding, and” through this “I will search your law, and” once sought, “I will keep it,” fulfilling it in deed. I will keep it “with my whole heart,” because I will devote all my strength to fulfilling the commandments.

I say, “I will keep it”; and so that I may be able to keep it, being placed “in the path of your commandments,” that is, in the imitation of Christ, who is the straight path, namely, the narrow way, “lead me,” that is, make me continually advance toward a greater imitation of Christ, “because I desired that path,” that is, I loved Christ himself for his intrinsic worth. Or we may understand the path as the stricter commandments, because “in keeping them there is great reward.”

And so that I may be able to desire this, “incline”—that is, humble—“my heart toward your testimonies,” so that they may be fulfilled, “and not toward greed,” that is, so that I may not observe your commandments for the sake of some earthly advantage.

I say, do not incline me toward greed, but rather “turn my inward eyes away” so that they may not “see vanity,” that is, so that they may not delight in earthly things, which are vain and fleeting. Instead, “give me life in your way,” that is, strengthen free will and make me despise earthly things and love heavenly ones.

Turn away my eyes, incline my heart, and so forth, “and establish,” that is, make stable, “your utterance,” that is, make me fulfill steadily what you command. Do this for me, I say, “your servant,” and therefore I am worthy that you should do these things for me; and do so “in your fear,” that is, through the fact that I fear you as judge and love you. For those who fear the Lord in this way fulfill his commandments.

Establish the utterance, and “cut off,” that is, remove, “my reproach, which I have suspected,” that is, the reproach of suspicion. For I have often been deceived in my suspicion, suspecting someone good who is evil, and conversely. Therefore I say, “Cut it off,” because, even if I cannot know the truth, I nevertheless delight in the truth. This is what he says: “For your judgments,” that is, whatever you determine through your hidden judgment, [Col. 0609A] “are pleasing,” that is, the scourges that you send me for my correction are agreeable to me.

I said, “Cut off my reproach,” lead me, and do whatever I have asked. And behold, whatever I asked, I have. This is what he says: “Behold, I have desired to fulfill your commandments.” Whoever desires in this way can be secure, because he will obtain what he asks. I say, “I have desired,” and thereafter, Lord, “give me life,” that is, make me persevere in your commandments. I say that I am placed “in your equity,” that is, acting according to your commandments, which command equity alone.

### Vau

“And let it come.” In this section the faithful speaker, who has now received Christ’s law at Christ’s coming, asks that Christ himself be his protection against heretics and persecutors, who immediately rise up against those who receive Christ’s law. Therefore Vau, interpreted as “he himself,” is appropriately prefixed to this group of eight; through it we understand Christ as the outstanding helper whom the speaker asks to assist him in this group of eight.

Continuation: I say, “Give me life,” “and let your mercy come upon me,” that is, in such a way that it may be my head. Or “upon me,” that is, coming from the heavenly realms: “your mercy, O Lord.” And he specifies what mercy he seeks, namely, “your salvation,” that is, your Son, who brings salvation to all, so that he may be my protection against those who attack me. Or, “according to your utterance,” let it come, that is, let him instruct me concerning your law.

“And” if he comes in this way, then “I will answer with a word,” namely, your Son, “those who reproach me,” reproaching me on account of that Son. If anyone reproaches me by saying that Christ is not the Son of God but merely a crucified man, and so forth, I will show him through arguments that he was the Son of God and coeternal with him. And I will answer in this way, not because I trust in my own strength, but “because I have hoped in your words,” which are good weapons for me. For you said: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not prepare beforehand what you should answer; for what you should say will be given to you in that hour (Matthew 10),” and again: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom (Luke 21).”

I will answer the heretics. And, O Lord, take care that your word not be taken away from me through tribulations. This is what he says: “And do not take the word of truth from my mouth,” that is, do not permit it to be taken away through tribulations or flatteries, “the word of truth,” that is, the word of preaching, so that I may never be silent among anyone concerning the preaching of the divine word. Do not permit it to be taken away even for a time because of tribulation, as you did with Peter, who denied the truth at the voice of a maidservant (Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18). Nor permit it to be taken away “utterly,” that is, in every way and at every time. You ought not to take it away, “because” I have “hoped beyond measure in your judgments,” that is, in the tribulations that you impose upon me through your judgments; I have hoped for a greater fruit than any temporal tribulation could merit. Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory (Romans 8).”

I say, “Do not take it away,” and, having received Christ himself as my protection, “I will always keep your law,” that is, “for ever and ever.” In this life the one who loves his neighbor, prays for his enemies, and does similar things keeps God’s law. In the other age we shall keep the law that the angels now possess, because then, like the angels, we shall commonly praise God and also love our brothers, as it is said: “Charity never fails (1 Corinthians 8).”

I say, “I will keep it,” and I have already kept it. Here he indicates that he has received what he was asking for above, namely, the coming of Christ, and that he will keep the law. This is what he says: “I walked” from virtue to virtue, having received Christ as a guest, existing “in spaciousness,” that is, in the abundance of charity and knowledge. I was given this spaciousness [Col. 0610B] because “I sought your commandments.”

“I will answer those who reproach me with a word,” and I have also answered them. This is what he says: “And I spoke,” that is, I have spoken, being established “in your testimonies,” that is, in your commandments. Not only in the presence of the people, but “in the presence of kings,” that is, of the rulers of the world, I preached the word of God; “and I was not put to shame,” that is, I was not ashamed because of the scandal of the cross. Or, “I was not put to shame” means that I did not yield to them or remain silent because of them.

I spoke and “meditated on your commandments,” that is, I frequently considered how I might fulfill them; this indicates contemplation. I did not do this under compulsion, but because “I loved” those commandments, and therefore fulfilled them.

And I did not merely meditate, but also fulfilled them in deed. This is what he says: “And I lifted up my hands,” that is, I raised my actions “toward your commandments” in order to fulfill them, “which I loved.” As though to say: What I taught in words, I fulfilled in deed. Here active life is indicated. I say, “I lifted them up,” and I fulfilled this action perseveringly. This is what he says: “I will practice your justifications,” that is, I will strive to fulfill them without any delay.

### Zain

“Remember.” The just person who has received Christ’s law, and Christ himself as helper against heretics and persecutors, now has hope of eternal good. In this group of eight he prays for the completion of that hope. Therefore Zain, interpreted as “led” or “here,” is appropriately prefixed to this section, because through both meanings we understand that we do not have a permanent city here.

Continuation: I practiced because you gave me hope in your word, that is, in your promise, when you said: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8).” And “remember your word to your servant,” that is, for the honor of your servant, by fulfilling what you promised. You seem to have forgotten it because you have delayed for so long the word “in which” you gave me hope of eternal good.

This “hope comforted me in my humiliation,” that is, in the degradation of our first parent. The hope of which he speaks here works patience in us [Col. 0611A] against adversity, and proven character amid adversities. Or, “it comforted me in my humiliation” means in tribulations, because for the sake of that hope I endured the tribulations inflicted upon me. I say, “It comforted me,” because “your utterance,” that is, your commandment, “gave me life,” that is, gave life to my soul. For whoever is given life by fulfilling God’s commandments is thereby secure concerning eternal good and joyfully endures the miseries of this age.

I rightly say that “your utterance gave me life,” because when my enemies pressed me, I did not fail. This is what he says: “The proud acted wickedly,” that is, they inflicted evils upon me without cause, “utterly,” that is, in every way they could; “but I did not turn aside from your law,” that is, I did not cease because of them in any way.

And why did I not turn aside? Because, O “Lord, I remembered your judgments,” made “from the beginning.” That is, I considered that from the first just person onward God rewards those who obey and condemns those who neglect him. Or, “judgments from the beginning” means that, from the beginning—that is, from the first just person—because judgment begins from the house of God, you justly judge those to labor whom you wish to reward in the other age. Hence it is said: “God scourges every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12).” And Solomon says: “Whoever is not among those who are scourged will be excluded from the house of sons.” And because I recognized such things to be your judgments, therefore “I was comforted” in my tribulations.

“‘I was comforted’ with regard to myself, but I grieved over sinners; and this is what he means: ‘affliction,’ that is, distress, ‘seized me’—I mean affliction and grief—‘because of sinners’: [Col. 0611C] not because of those who inflicted evils upon me, but because of those ‘who forsake your law.’

I was faint on their behalf, but in order to remove all weariness from myself, I sang psalms and hymns to the Lord in my heart; and this is what he means: while existing ‘in the place of my pilgrimage,’ in this life in which I recognize myself as a pilgrim, ‘your justifications were songs for me,’ that is, psalms and hymns, which justify the person who sings them purely, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: ‘With hymns and psalms and spiritual songs, singing in grace in your hearts to God’ (Col. III).

Therefore the justifications were songs because, O ‘Lord, in the night,’ that is, in the time of persecution, ‘I remembered your name,’ that is, I recognized that you are Lord, that I am a servant, and that it is right for the Lord [Col. 0611D] to correct; ‘and’ therefore ‘I kept your law,’ that is, the patience of Jesus, which is commanded in the law.”

And “this” night, that is, tribulation, “came to be for me,” not because of my offense, but “because I sought your justifications,” desiring to fulfill them. Note that “this” cannot refer to “law” in this passage, because, as Augustine testifies, in the Greek translation *law* is masculine in gender, whereas the pronoun “this” there is feminine. Therefore it necessarily refers to “night,” according to the sense in which that word signifies pilgrimage.

## Heth

“‘My portion, O Lord.’” This letter is interpreted as “terror,” and it is appropriately prefixed to this octave, because [Col. 0612A] here the faithful speaker displays his great terror and anxiety—namely, that he searches and labors with much concern to discover how he may reach the hoped-for object. Note that terror is a trembling of the heart, not something arising from courage.

Continuation: I therefore sought your justifications because, O “Lord, you are my portion”—that is, I did not choose gold or anything worldly as my portion, but you alone, who are the true way to blessedness. And because I chose you as my portion, therefore I “said,” that is, I resolved within myself, “to keep your law,” that is, that I would keep your law by fulfilling it.

Nor did I merely say this; I also “entreated your face” to be granted to me, so that I might see you present face to face (I Cor. XIII), and know as I have been known [Col. 0612B]. Nor did I entreat this only a little, but “with my whole heart,” that is, to such an extent that my heart would be empty of everything else and would seek to obtain your face. And so that I might reach that face, “have mercy on me,” that is, by your mercy forgive my sins and bestow spiritual graces upon me, “according to your word,” that is, your promises.

And to show himself worthy that mercy should rightly be granted to him, he shows that he has turned away from the perverse path, not through fickleness but after mature reflection. Continuation: I therefore pray you to have mercy, because I “considered my ways”—that is, the works I perform according to myself, which are always sinful—“I considered” them, that is, I examined them with careful reasoning, recognized them as evil, and therefore “turned my feet,” that is, my affections, [Col. 0612C] “toward your testimonies,” in order to fulfill them.

I say “I turned them,” so that, even if evils should come, “I am prepared to keep your commandments.” But because I am prepared, therefore, when evils come, “I am not troubled.”

Prepared against what? Against sins or tribulations, which, surrounding me on every side, seek to entrap me. And this is what he says: “The cords of sinners”—that is, sins, namely the suggestions of the flesh, which are cords by which the sinner is bound so that he cannot stretch himself toward good acts—“have encircled me,” because they surround me on every side; “and” nevertheless “I have not forgotten your law,” but have always kept it in mind. Hence the Apostle says: “I see another law in my mind, warring against the law of my flesh” [Col. 0612D] (Rom. VII). Or we may understand the cords as tribulations by which human beings are ensnared: “of sinners,” that is, cords which sinners cast out.

I say “I have not forgotten,” but rather “I rose at midnight to confess to you.” Literally: Religious men rise at night to praise God, taking this passage as an example for themselves, and because at midnight the Lord liberated his people after striking the Egyptians (Exod. XIII). Likewise, because at midnight those virgins went out to meet the bridegroom (Matt. XXV). Likewise, because the Lord is said to have risen at midnight (Matt. XXVIII). Likewise, because he will come at midnight to judge—although this is unknown; nevertheless, some infer it from the words of the Gospel, where it says: “At midnight a cry was made” (Matt. XXIX). [Col. 0613A]

Or, allegorically, it may be understood in this way: “at midnight,” that is, in the greatest tribulation, I did not grow sluggish, but rose—that is, I lifted myself up to perform good works—and, intent upon good action, rose to confess, that is, to praise you, “because of the judgments of your justification”: that is, because through the scourges which you judge and permit to be inflicted upon your faithful, you justify them; or, “of your justification,” that is, which you inflict through justice.

What does each detail mean? “I am a participant in all”: I do not say “in Christ,” since that might appear presumptuous, but in all “who fear you.” I speak of those “who fear” in the sense that they keep your commandments; that is, “and of those who keep your commandments.” When he says that he is a participant, he suggests that we should understand the unity of the Church, by which all are bound together by the bond of faith and charity. [Col. 0613B]

And through all these things, O Lord, I show my anxiety; and you, “Lord, teach me your justifications,” that is, make me accustomed to your commandments and enable me to persevere. I therefore ask this confidently because “the earth,” that is, the whole world, “is full of your mercy,” since throughout the world the faithful are now justified through mercy.

## Teth

“‘Goodness.’” In this octave the faithful speaker shows that he not only patiently endures the adversities that come upon him, but that they are even pleasant to him. Therefore the letter Teth, which is interpreted as “good,” that is, “pleasant,” is appropriately prefixed to it, because the tribulations inflicted upon this faithful person are pleasant. Alternatively, it is interpreted as “exclusion”: the faithful speaker here excludes every sadness through his patience, and proceeds in an appropriate order. For after someone has been established in hope and is anxious to attain the hoped-for object, what remains is that he should patiently endure whatever evils may occur.

I therefore say confidently, “teach me justifications,” because you have already begun to do so. And this is what he means: “You have made” tribulations “good”—that is, caused them to appear good—“with your servant,” O “Lord.” Therefore I say “with me,” because he himself does what he can on his own part; and this is “according to your word,” that is, according to your law, because the law itself instructs me so that tribulations may be pleasant to me.

[Col. 0613D] You have already taught goodness, and still, O Lord—that is, from now on—“teach me goodness”: make me such that, through the breadth of charity, tribulations may be pleasant to me. “And,” so that I may possess that goodness, teach me “discipline,” that is, send tribulation for my correction. “And,” so that I may receive that discipline—that is, understand it as given for my correction—teach me “knowledge,” that is, understanding of useful things, so that I may understand that through sins I am corruptible and miserable and cannot be freed from these evils except through your discipline. These are placed in reverse order: knowledge comes first, then discipline, from which goodness proceeds. Therefore I say, “teach me,” because I have believed in your commandments, [Col. 0614A] in which goodness, knowledge, and other such things are promised.

Therefore I pray you to teach me discipline because “I have sinned,” and I could not be freed from that sin except through discipline. I say “I have sinned” “before I was humbled,” that is, before you corrected me with scourges. And “therefore,” because you humbled me, “I kept your words,” that is, I fulfilled your commandments.

And because through tribulation you caused me to keep your word, therefore “you are good, and in” this “your” great “goodness teach me your justifications,” that is, make me accustomed to your commandments, so that if tribulations come upon me I may no longer be shaken.

And it is necessary that you teach me, because “the iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me,” that is, they inflict more tribulations than human endurance can bear. “But I,” through all these things, have not grown weary; rather, “I will search out your commandments,” and not merely a little, but “with my whole heart.” [Col. 0614B]

They have multiplied, and they have done so with an obstinate spirit. And this is what he means: “Their heart,” which ought to be tender and to be moved by mercy toward those like themselves, “has been congealed,” that is, hardened, “like milk”; “but I,” amid all these things, “have meditated on your law,” that is, I have kept your commandments in frequent meditation, through which I resisted the obstinate.

And because I meditated on your law, what you humbled me pleased me. And this is what he means: “It is good for me that you humbled me,” that is, it is pleasant to me that by sending tribulations you afflicted me. And this is also what he means: The tribulation sent upon me is good for me, “so that I may learn your justifications,” by fulfilling and knowing them.

Therefore I say that the humiliation itself, which teaches the law, is good, because the law itself, which is acquired through that humiliation, is pleasing and pleasant. And this is what he means: “The law of your mouth is good for me,” that is, the Gospel, which you spoke with your mouth—that is, through your Son—I say is good “above thousands of gold and silver,” that is, above however great the riches of this world may be.

## Iod

“‘Your hands.’” Iod is prefixed to this octave; it is interpreted as “beginning” or “knowledge,” because the faithful person speaking here asks God to lead him back to his beginning, in which he was created—namely, to grant him the blessedness of the knowledge in which he was created, together with immortality and freedom from suffering. He recognizes that he was cast down from this by the disobedience of his first parent. [Col. 0614D]

Continuation: It is therefore good that you humbled me, so that through this I may return to the beginning in which you created me. And this is what he means: O “Lord, your hands”—that is, your activity—“made me,” with respect to my soul, “and fashioned me,” with respect to my body. Although God made all things, the creation of human beings is nevertheless attributed to God’s hands because of its dignity. And because you made me, and I cannot immediately return to the perfection in which you created me, “give me understanding,” that is, enlighten my reason, “so that” through this “I may learn [Col. 0615A] your commandments,” that is, understand and fulfill them. Through these precepts I shall finally be able to return to the perfection of my beginning.

Therefore you ought to enlighten my understanding because “those who fear you,” that is, holy men, your faithful, “will see me” thus enlightened, “and” consequently “will rejoice.” Again, you ought to give understanding because I “have hoped beyond hope in your word,” that is, in your Son: I have hoped for a greater good from your Son than my merit could deserve. Or, “in your words,” that is, I have placed an extraordinary hope in the fulfillment of your words. Or, if I ask for understanding in order to obtain this fruit, then those who fear you with merely servile fear will see me—that is, they will observe me enlightened and justified from sin—and, having become imitators, will rejoice.

[Col. 0615B] Therefore I ask you to give understanding, by which we may return to our beginning, because I recognize that our fathers, and we their children, have been cast down from that dignity through disobedience. And this is what he means: O “Lord, I have recognized that your judgments”—namely, that you made our first parents subject to suffering yet immortal, and subjected them to misery—“are equity,” that is, were justly made. “And” you also “humbled me,” that is, afflicted me in these miseries, and did so “in your truth,” that is, by your just judgment.

Through this judgment we are in miseries; but against those miseries, “let your mercy be done” to me, “your servant, so that it may comfort me” in my miseries. And I ask this “according to your word,” that is, your promises, for you said: “Turn back to me, and I will return to you.” And elsewhere: “Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. CXXXI). By the widow he understands the Church.

Let mercy come to comfort me amid evils, and let the mercy that makes us live with eternal life also come. This is what he means: “Let your mercies come to me,” that is, the effects of your loving disposition and mercy, “and” through it “I shall live” with eternal life, restored to the dignity of my beginning, “because your law is my meditation,” that is, I always meditate on the fulfillment of your law.

Let your mercies come to me, “but let the proud be put to shame,” that is, let them feel shame over their sins, “because they have acted wickedly against me,” and have done so “unjustly,” without any offense on my part. “But I was exercised,” that is, I will be exercised, “in your commandments,” fulfilling them.

[Col. 0615D] Let the proud be put to shame, and through this let them become “those who fear you” and seek your testimonies; and thus “let them turn toward me”—that is, let them turn in such a way that they become like me. “And let those who know your testimonies,” by knowledge, even if not yet by reflection, turn toward me.

I say, let your mercies come so that I may live; and so that I may be able to live, “let my heart,” O Lord, “be blameless” through the remission of sins “in your justifications,” that is, “so that,” through fulfillment of the commandments, “I may not be put to shame” with the impious when it is said to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones,” and so forth (Matt. XXV).

## Caph

[Col. 0616A]

“‘It has failed for salvation.’” In this octave the faithful speaker is shown already weary from a long campaign, desiring to be released and to rest with Christ, yet still not refusing labor. Therefore Caph, which is interpreted as “bent down,” is appropriately prefixed to him. The order seems fitting: after someone has regarded sufferings as pleasant and has obtained the law of God through continual meditation, he desires already to rest and to regain his natural beginning.

Continuation: I therefore desire that your mercies come to me and that I live with eternal life, because “my soul,” out of desire for my beginning, “has failed” with respect to every present delight, going “toward your salvation,” that is, toward your Son. I therefore despise earthly things so that I may reach the eternity which our nature already possesses in our Lord Jesus. “And in your word,” the very Son whom he previously called salvation, “I have hoped beyond hope,” that is, I have believed that I shall obtain a reward greater than a human being could deserve through his campaign. Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

The soul has failed with respect to every desire for earthly things; and also “my eyes,” the interior eyes—that is, reason rightly enlightened—“have failed” with respect to every consideration and enjoyment of earthly things, tending “toward your word,” that is, toward contemplation of your utterance, namely your Son, through whom you show and declare your will. Or, “your word,” that is, your commandment: [Col. 0616C] “my eyes,” I say, “saying,” that is, considering within themselves, “When will you comfort me?”—that is, when will you lead me to the desired beginning, so that I may now rest with Christ?

Therefore I need consolation, because the wicked here seek to draw me back from the good through many scourges. And he says this: “Because I have become like a wineskin in frost.” By comparing himself to a wineskin, which is the hide of a dead animal, he indicates his own mortification—namely, that through fasting, vigils, and other such practices he mortifies his flesh. And just as a wineskin holds the liquid poured into it well, so he will carefully preserve the preaching entrusted to him and committed to him by God. And just as a wineskin placed in frost contracts and dries out, so that it can no longer preserve the liquid entrusted to it, so this faithful person, placed among the wicked—people constrained by the cold of unbelief and the stains of a shameful life—is compelled by many persecutions to abandon and pour out the liquid of the divine word entrusted to him. And although I have thus become “like a wineskin in frost,” nevertheless I “have not forgotten your justifications,” that is, your commandments, by which human beings are justified, but have always kept and fulfilled them.

And since, O Lord, I have become like a wineskin, then “how many are the days of your servant?”—that is, how long will I endure these miseries? In other words, “When will you execute judgment,” that is, separation, so that those “who persecute me,” who in this life are mingled and living together with us, can no longer harm me?

[Col. 0617A] And it is necessary for you to execute judgment because “the wicked have told me tales”: in this he includes all the arguments by which heretics and other evil people seek to make the just person a participant in their perversity. “But” those tales “did not” please me “as your law” does.

Therefore, because “all your commandments” are “truth,” that is, because I have proved them to be true while I regard their tales as fables, and because they cannot gain anything against me through their tales, the wicked “persecuted me,” inflicting many evils in order that at least through this they might subject me to their will. But you, Lord, “help me.”

And it is necessary that you help me because “they nearly consumed me in the earth,” that is, they made me perfectly devoted to earthly things, as they wished. Yet “a little was lacking,” that is, only a little was lacking for them to entangle me in love of earthly things. Or, “in the earth,” that is, in this life, “they nearly consumed me,” that is, they almost killed me; “but I did not forsake your commandments.”

I did not forsake your commandments, and therefore, concerning the future, O Lord, “give me life,” that is, make me persevere in your commandments. Nor do I ask this trusting in my merits, but “according to your mercy.” And thus, having been given life, “I will keep the testimonies of your mouth,” namely the evangelical precepts.

## Lamed

“‘Forever, O Lord.’” In this octave it is shown [Col. 0617C] that the just person who has just displayed himself as afflicted, when he understands that God does not yet wish to lead him to the desired rest, does not refuse but shows himself ready to endure labors here. Therefore Lamed, which is interpreted as “the heart of servitude,” is prefixed to this octave.

Continuation: I ought therefore rightly to keep your testimonies, Lord, because “your Word,” that is, your Son, “remains in heaven,” that is, among the heavenly creatures, “and this forever.” Or he ought to keep them because the angels also keep them. And this is what he means: Your Word, that is, the fulfillment of your commandments, remains in heaven, that is, in the angels, because they always fulfill God’s commandments, and this forever.

And not only in heaven, but also “your truth,” [Col. 0617D] that is, your Son, remains “in the generation” of the earlier just, “and in the generation” of the just of the New Testament. Or, truth—that is, your law itself—remains from generation to generation, that is, from the beginning to the end of the world. Just as in Abel and in the other holy men you “established,” that is, set firmly, “the earth,” that is, the Church, “and it remains,” because it can never be completely destroyed by any tribulation.

And not only is the earth—that is, your universal Church—founded by your arrangement, but also “the day,” that is, wiser and more eminent men in the Church who are able to enlighten others, “endure by your ordinance” against the waves of the world. I rightly say that the day endures by your arrangement and the earth is founded, and so forth, [Col. 0618A] “because all things serve you,” in which it is evident that you are most omnipotent.

You are such a one as arranged the day in this way, established the earth, and whose law is such “that if your law itself were not my meditation,” I would have perished in the persecution of my enemies. “Then,” that is, when enemies persecute, “I would have perished in my humiliation,” perhaps; he says this as though, by his own free choice, it lay with him whether to yield to them or not.

“‘Forever.’” After presenting certain reasons why he ought to serve God, he shows that he possesses the heart of servitude. Continuation: Because through meditation on your law you freed me from destruction and did the other things mentioned above, therefore “I will not forget your justifications forever,” that is, throughout my entire life, “because in those justifications [Col. 0618B] you gave me life,” freeing me from conformity with the wicked and bestowing virtues.

And what does each detail mean? “I am yours,” that is, serving you in all things; therefore “save me,” leading me to eternity, “because I sought your justifications,” in order to understand and fulfill them.

And it is necessary that you save me because “sinners waited for me,” seeking an opportune time and suitable deceptions “in order to destroy me.” Nevertheless, “I understood your testimonies,” and through this fortified myself against heretics.
