And in those testimonies, once understood, namely “I saw the end of every perfection” of virtues: I recognized that eternity is the end reached through the perfection of virtues. Therefore “your commandment,” specifically the commandment concerning charity, “was exceedingly broad for me,” that is, very great, because, so that I might reach eternity, it enlarged me even to the love of enemies. Or, alternatively: in the commandments that I loved, I saw “the end of every perfection,” that is, I understood that every worldly consummation and perfection has an end, but your commandment—that is, the precept of charity—is exceedingly broad, extending into eternity. Hence the Apostle says: “Charity will never fail.”

## Mem

“‘How I have loved.’” In this octave the faithful speaker is shown to love God’s law with intimate affection, and therefore to possess understanding in the Lord’s law above all his enemies, however clever they may be. Accordingly, Mem, that is, “the inward parts,” is prefixed to this section, through which we understand intimate love. The order is also good. For after someone has obtained the heart of servitude, if he applies intimate love to the law, he will reach a great accumulation of perfection.

Continuation: Your commandment is exceedingly broad, and I “loved your law.” And, “Lord, how I have loved it!” As though I could not show how much I love it. Nevertheless, he displays certain indications of his love when he says: “It is my meditation all day long.”

And because I loved it in this way and kept it in meditation, therefore “you have made me prudent through your commandment above my enemies,” that is, I understood more about your law than my enemies. [Col. 0619A] Therefore I say “above my enemies,” “because” your commandment “is with me forever,” that is, it leads me to eternity, which it does not do for my enemies.

You have not merely made me prudent above any particular enemies, but “I understood above all who teach me,” that is, above the scribes and Pharisees and any others who wished to teach me their sect of error. I understood in this way because I think constantly about your commandments. And this is what he means: “because your testimonies are my meditation.”

And among the other teachers “I understood above the elders,” that is, above the older and more eminent wise men. And this was because “I sought your commandments.”

“I understood above the elders,” and “I restrained my feet,” that is, my affections, “from every evil way” of theirs. [Col. 0619B] I restrained them for this purpose: “so that” in practice “I might keep your words.”

“I will keep them,” and “I did not turn aside from your judgments,” because I guarded them in such a way that I deviated in nothing from your precepts. Therefore I did not turn aside “because you established a law for me” which held me fast in persevering in your commandments.

I say that I understood, fulfilled, and proclaimed to others; in this, “your words” were sweet “to my throat,” and “how sweet” they were—that is, they were infinitely sweet. I say they were sweet “above honey to my mouth,” that is, they were sweeter to me in tasting than honey is.

Your words were sweet to me, and “therefore I hated every way of iniquity.” And so that this good may be confirmed, the author shows the authority of God’s precepts when he says: “From your commandments,” O Lord, “I understood” that I ought to hate the way of iniquity, and therefore I hated it.

## Nun

“‘A lamp for my feet.’” In this octave the subject is humility, because the just person speaking shows that he possesses nothing from himself, but everything from God, even the beginning of good will. Therefore Nun, which is interpreted as “the unique one” or “pasture,” is prefixed to this section, because God is one and alone, from whom he receives whatever good he possesses; and that same God is his pasture and complete nourishment. The order is also good. After showing that he possesses the heart of servitude, that through intimate love he has attained understanding of the law, that he does not turn aside from God’s judgments, and that he has hated the way of iniquity, he attributes all these things [Col. 0619D] not to himself but to God’s grace.

Continuation: I understood above the elders; I did not turn aside from the judgments; I hated the way of iniquity. And I did all these things not by my own strength, but because “your Word,” that is, the divine commandment, became “a lamp,” that is, an illumination by which I can guard myself against the snares of the devil that they set for me in the darkness of this life. I say it is a lamp “for my feet,” that is, for my affections and wills, through which our soul now proceeds toward good action, because we cannot even will what is good unless we are enlightened by God’s grace. Your Word is a lamp for our will, and “for my paths,” that is, for my narrower works; your Word, namely the divine precept, is “a light” for me, that is, something greatly illuminating. [Col. 0620A] For the more earnestly someone acts, the more he is enlightened by knowledge of God.

Or, “your Word,” that is, your Son, became a lamp through the flesh he assumed. For just as a lamp contains light and a clay vessel, so in Christ divinity is the light, while humanity is like the vessel containing the light. This lamp illuminates my feet, that is, advances me so that I may now be able to will what is good. And the same Word became a light for my paths, that is, for strict and arduous works. He does not say “lamp” but “light,” because the more narrowly someone serves God, the greater light he possesses and the more knowledge he receives concerning that divinity itself.

And because the will is enlightened through you, and you provide light on the paths—namely, because we have all illumination from you—therefore “I swore and resolved,” that is, firmly determined, “to keep the judgments,” which are your acts of justice, that is, which you perform through your justice. He keeps the judgments because, if he has adversities, he is not broken but understands that they have been given to him by God’s judgment. If, however, he has prosperity, he is not lifted up but dispenses it according to God’s will. I say that he keeps them; I also say that he swore to keep them, that is, just as he resolved, so he steadfastly fulfilled them.

Because I resolved to keep them, therefore “I have been humbled,” that is, afflicted, “exceedingly,” that is, in every way and by every kind of affliction, because I was steadfastly observing your judgments and testimonies. I have been humbled, but you, “Lord, give me life,” so that I may not yield to those afflicting me, “according to your word,” that is, according to [Col. 0620C] your promise.

I say that I have been humbled, and in that very humiliation I offered you sacrifices “of my mouth,” that is, praises that proceeded from my mouth, because what I said with my mouth I fulfilled in action. And I did this “voluntarily,” that is, with good intention and pure will. And because I sacrificed to you in humility and voluntarily, therefore, O Lord, “make my vows pleasing” to you, “and teach me your judgments,” that is, make me accustomed to them and cause me to fulfill them in practice.

And therefore it is necessary that you teach me, “because my soul,” that is, the life of my soul, “is always in my hands,” that is, in my works: for if I cease to act well, my soul will die. This is said by comparison with a good soldier who defends his life with his own hands in battle. “And,” so that I may be able to guard my soul, [Col. 0620D] “I have not forgotten your law,” but rather to ponder it in meditation and fulfillment.

I say, “I have not forgotten,” and yet “sinners placed a snare for me” by which they thought to drive me to consign God’s law to oblivion. He calls it a snare, such as threats, blandishments, every kind of evil persuasion, and persecution. “And,” although they thus spread a snare for me, nevertheless “I did not err from your commandments,” whether by understanding them wrongly or by acting against them.

“I did not err,” but rather “I acquired” your testimonies “forever,” by diligently exercising myself to understand and fulfill them. “I acquired” them “by inheritance,” that is, in the manner of an inherited possession, namely so that I might possess them firmly [Col. 0621A] and receive them from my fathers and others like them. Therefore I sought them, “because they are the rejoicing of my heart”: however much I may be afflicted, I shall nevertheless fulfill God’s commandments with rejoicing, confident of the reward.

I say “I sought them” in this way, namely by humbling myself in every respect before God. Hence he says: “I inclined my heart,” that is, I humbled my will in every respect, “to perform your justifications for the sake of an eternal reward.” As blessed Jerome says, this is the order in the Hebrew. Nevertheless, we may also say: I will keep your justifications forever, that is, throughout the whole period of my life.

## Samech

[Col. 0621B]

“‘The wicked.’” In this octave the just person, who shortly before displayed his humility, now shows himself so firmly established that he wishes to flee the company of the wicked. Therefore Samech, which is interpreted as “strength” or “help,” is appropriately prefixed to this section. It is as though he were saying: Here, where you say that you hate the wicked, this must be heard and considered with great care, because great caution must be exercised in dealing with the wicked. For the Gospel commands us also to love our enemies (Matt. V). They must therefore be loved in such a way that, whatever evil they do to us, we do not retaliate but pray for them; and as long as we think we are making progress with them, we must persist with them according to divine admonition. But if we can make no progress with them and cannot live with them without compromising religion, we must separate ourselves from their familiarity [Col. 0621C] and dwelling. For this reason we must even leave father and wife if we cannot preserve the Christian religion with them—namely, if through them we are driven toward the worship of idols or something similar. We owe nothing to any neighbor against God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X).

Continuation: I kept the justifications for the sake of the reward; and so that I may reach it, “I hated the wicked and loved your law.”

And while I avoid the wicked and keep the law, “you are my helper” for acting well, “and my supporter,” because through the humanity assumed by Christ you have greatly exalted me. “And in your Word,” that is, the Son, or the divine commandment which I fulfilled, “I have hoped beyond hope,” that is, for something greater than the present things. Or, “I have hoped beyond hope” because I have added a greater hope to my former hope.

I hated the wicked, saying: O you evil ones, depart from me. Or the passage may be connected in this way: Because God is my helper and I have hoped beyond hope in your Word, therefore, “you wicked, depart from me,” that is, separate yourselves from my company, in whose presence I cannot maintain divine religion. “And,” once you have departed, “I will search out the commandments of my God” freely. The Apostle says concerning avoidance of the wicked: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Titus III).

[Col. 0622A] You wicked, “depart”; but you, Lord, “receive me” into your protection, so that I may not yield to my enemies, “according to your word,” that is, according to your promise. Or, “according to your word,” that is, so that I may follow your precepts by fulfilling them. “And” then, would that I “may live” in soul; and when I have awaited eternal life, “do not put me to shame” in “my expectation” of it, but grant me what I hope for.

I say “do not put me to shame,” but rather “help me” to act well, “and” through this “I shall be saved” with eternal salvation. And through your help, so that I may reach that salvation, “I will meditate on your justifications always,” that is, continually. For whoever lives according to God’s law is said to meditate on God’s law while he lives, sleeps, or eats.

Therefore “I will meditate,” because I consider that you “have despised all who depart from your judgments, because their thought is unjust.” For if they say that they sin through weakness, or that God pardons them through mercy, or that they do not care about earthly things, their thought is unjust.

And not only have you despised them, but I too have despised them. And he says this: “I have regarded all the sinners of the earth”—namely the pagans, who do not have the written law—“as transgressors,” at least of the natural law. In this he increases the accumulation of their evils: because of the act of sin they are transgressors of the natural law, or of Scripture, or of both. And because I saw that sinners were transgressors, “therefore,” so that I might not be a transgressor, “I loved [Col. 0622C] your testimonies.”

“‘Nail me with your fear.’” Because this just person saw the same enemy lying in wait for him who made others transgressors through suggestions of the flesh, he asks God to restrain that enemy. Continuation: I regarded sinners as transgressors; and so that I too might not be a transgressor, “nail my flesh,” that is, my carnal desires, “with your fear,” that is, with the nail of your fear. I therefore pray you, nail me, “for I feared your judgments,” that is, I feared when I considered your future judgments. He says “nail me” because he knew that the old person would be nailed to the cross and destroyed in Christ’s passion.

## Ain

“‘I have done judgment and justice.’” Ain, which is interpreted as “eye,” is prefixed to this octave because here the just person is shown to possess an inner eye that is well enlightened—namely, a certain shrewdness for repelling the slanders of the wicked and defending God’s law against them. Such shrewdness was necessary even for the just. For the wicked, whom they hated, brought many slanders and accusations against them.

Continuation: Because he loved your testimonies and regarded others as transgressors, therefore: “Do not hand me over to those who slander me”—that is, do not allow me to succumb to their slanders, which they bring against me in great number. Because I regarded them as transgressors, I also separated myself from them; nor ought you to hand me over, because “I practiced judgment”—that is, discernment between good and evil—“and righteousness,” because, abandoning evil, I followed good.

“Do not hand me over to those who slander me”; and if they drive me into some danger, then “receive” me, “your servant, for good,” and at some point make all their slanders cease. This is expressed by: “Let not the proud slander me.”

And you ought to receive me because “my eyes”—my inner eyes—have withdrawn from every desire for earthly things, reaching toward “your salvation,” that is, toward your saving power; and so that I may reach that salvation, they reach toward “the word of your righteousness,” that is, toward the commandments of yours that are to be fulfilled.

Because my eyes fail, “deal with your servant according to your mercy”; do this in particular: “teach me your ordinances.”

I rightly say “with your servant,” because “I am your servant,” obeying you in all things. Therefore “give me” an enlightened “understanding, so that I may know your testimonies”—by knowing and fulfilling them.

And you ought to do this because “it is time” to do so, Lord: namely, to give me understanding of your law, by which I may defend it against heretics, because they have “destroyed” your law by understanding it wrongly, introducing heresies, and corrupting it in various other ways. Or, it is necessary for you, Lord, to act by giving me understanding for the defense of your law; and because others have destroyed your law, “therefore,” kindled by zeal for God, “I loved your commandments” in order to defend them, “more than gold”—that is, more than every desire for worldly possession—“and” more than “topaz.” Topaz is a precious stone whose nature is always to attract the gaze of those who look at it, while the eyes of those who behold it cannot be satisfied with looking at it. By this we understand every beautiful object in the world that is pleasing to the sight.

And because “I loved your commandments, therefore” I was not idle in my work, but was “directed” always toward fulfilling all your commandments; and conversely, “I hated every way of iniquity,” in accordance with the Gospel: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6).

## Phe

“Your testimonies are wonderful.” The letter Phe, which is interpreted as “error,” is rightly prefixed to this octonary, because in this section the faithful speaker shows that he grieves over the error of those whom he earlier said were destroying God’s law; and he appropriately shows them that the Lord’s law must not be destroyed but loved.

It is as though he said: You must not destroy it; rather, you must embrace and preserve it, because, O “Lord, your testimonies” are “wonderful”—that is, worthy of admiration—because they make their observers such that they enlighten the blind, raise the dead, and accomplish other things of this kind; and “therefore my soul has searched them out.”

The soul searches them out, and can rightly advance in understanding, because “the disclosure”—that is, the fulfillment—“of your words,” such as the coming of Christ and the evangelical teaching that disclose and fulfill all the prophets, “enlightens” the whole Church in general and brings it to faith; and “gives understanding” of an excellent kind, such as the wiser members of the Church possess, “to the little ones”—that is, to the humble, who consider themselves little and presume nothing about themselves, but are little in malice, as the Apostle instructed: “Be little ones in malice” (1 Corinthians 14).

And because it gives understanding only to the little ones, I made myself little; namely, “I opened my mouth”—that is, I enlarged the desires of my heart. By “mouth” we understand the heart, because it now desires to be refreshed by spiritual benefit. “And I drew in the Spirit”—the Holy Spirit, namely, the health-giving breeze. The person who desires to acquire the Spirit strives and makes himself worthy for the Holy Spirit to dwell in him, since he desires to keep God’s commandments. Therefore I opened my mouth; therefore I drew in the Spirit, “because I desired your commandments,” in order to understand and fulfill them.

And because I desired them and opened my mouth, therefore “look upon me” with the eye of compassion, so that you may confer some good upon me; and “have mercy on me,” wiping away any stains you find in me. I ask this “according to the judgment of those who love your name”: that is, judge me as you judge that mercy ought to be shown to other lovers of your name. Although God visits his faithful and has mercy on them through mercy, he nevertheless says “judgment,” because he understands that in this life mercy is always joined with God’s judgment: there is some merit of faith for which God spares a person.

I say, “Look and have mercy,” and “direct my steps”—that is, my works—so that they may be “according to your word”; and through this “let no iniquity rule over me”—that is, let no iniquity, meaning the sin that dwells in our mortal body, rule in us so as to be able to drive us toward unlawful impulses. Instead, let the tinder of sin be restrained by enlightened reason. Therefore he says “let none rule,” because he understands that one ruling iniquity is as effective for condemnation as all iniquities ruling.

I say, “Direct my steps,” so that iniquity may not rule; and also “redeem me” by the price of the blood of your Son. Redeem me “from the slanders of men”—that is, from the false accusations and inventions of men—so that they cannot conform me to their wickedness, “so that” then I may freely “keep your commandments,” whereas now I am hindered by their many slanders.

And so that I may keep your commandments, “make your face shine”—that is, show me your manifest presence, not with a veiled face, as Moses taught the Jews (Exodus 3), signifying the veil of their minds, since they could not understand spiritual teaching. Christ, however, our teacher, openly taught the truth and made the knowledge of God known to the faithful. Illuminate this face—that is, this knowledge—“upon” me, “your servant,” and through this “teach me,” by understanding and fulfillment, “your ordinances.”

And I am worthy for you to teach me, because I grieve greatly over the error of others. He says this: “Streams of waters”—that is, abundant outward weeping and many inward sorrows—“have flowed,” not merely for one hour but for many days, from “my eyes,” inward and outward, “because they did not keep your law.”

## Sade

“You are righteous, Lord.” Sade, which is interpreted as “consolation,” is rightly prefixed to this section, because the righteous man who shortly before showed that he grieved over the error of the wicked now shows that he has a twofold consolation arising from God’s just judgment. When he recognizes that he has been enlightened by God’s judgment, he has great consolation for enduring evils and hoping for heavenly things. Likewise, when he understands that the wicked have been blinded and rejected by God’s just judgment, he is consoled in them, understanding that he must be tested and reproached through them. What the furnace does to gold and the file to iron, the wicked person does to the godly.

[Col. 0625B] Continuation: Until now I grieved, and my eyes poured out tears; but now I do not grieve, but rather am consoled by attending to this: that, O “Lord, you are righteous” in your nature, “and your judgment is right,” because you do rightly in choosing and enlightening some while rejecting and blinding others.

The fact that the judgment is right appears in this: you cause the commandments that you set before us to be accepted by some and rejected by others. He says this: “You have commanded your testimonies as righteousness,” and this “exceedingly”—that is, very greatly—namely, through innumerable messengers. I say that the testimonies are righteousness, that is, commanding only equity; “and your truth,” that is, they judge and fulfill whatever they promise, and therefore ought rightly to be accepted by all.

And although your testimonies were just and fulfilled every promise, nevertheless “my enemies,” who wish me evil because I am not like them, “have forgotten your words” according to their fulfillment—the words that rational reason persuaded them of and the preaching of certain people made known to them. Because they have forgotten these things, therefore “my zeal,” which I had for them because they despised the testimonies, “made me waste away”—that is, fail and grow emaciated in body.

“Your testimonies are truth and righteousness,” and your very “word” is “burning exceedingly,” because it burns away vices and kindles a person to the love of God; “and your servant loved it”—namely, I and those like me.

[Col. 0625D] And because I loved it, therefore “I am a young man”—that is, renewed, stripped of the old man and made a member of the new man. “And” because I have thus been renewed, I am “despised” by the wicked, considered worthless and subjected to torments; nevertheless, “I have not forgotten your ordinances,” so as not always to meditate upon and fulfill them.

And I rightly say that I fulfill and observe them, because “your righteousness,” which the execution of your commandments confers, is “righteousness” leading a person “into eternity”; and “your law is truth,” that is, it fulfills the promises.

I am despised, I say, but I have not withdrawn. Rather, “tribulation” inflicted upon the body “and distress”—that is, anxiety of mind—“have found me” ready to endure all things; and all these things have not made me ready to withdraw from your commandments, but always “your commandments are my meditation.” And because he understands that all these things are given to the righteous by God’s just judgment, he receives consolation from them all.

Therefore your testimonies are my meditation, because your “testimonies” themselves are “equity”—that is, commanding nothing wicked or dishonorable—and leading “into eternity.” Therefore “give me understanding” of them, so that I may receive consolation in them, “and” through understanding them “I shall live”—that is, reach eternal life.

## Coph

“I cried out.” Coph means “conclusion.” Here the blessed man is gravely hemmed in on every side by enemies; hoping for help from nowhere else, he directs his cry to God. The order is also appropriate: after receiving consolation following the experience of error, when he is surrounded by the wicked, nothing remains except to direct his cry to the Lord.

Continuation: Because tribulation and distress have found me, therefore “I cried with my whole heart: Hear me, Lord”; and he adds what he cried for, namely, that “I may seek your ordinances”—that is, grant me the ability to seek in order to understand your ordinances.

And I did not cry out only so that I might seek; I also cried out so that you might grant me to keep the commandments. This is expressed by: “I cried out to you, and” you “save me,” with this kind of salvation: “so that I may keep your commandments.”

[Col. 0626C] And I did not merely cry out, but also “anticipated” others “in maturity,” because while others ordinarily come to you at a mature and fully developed age, I hurried to you as a child and immature. Or, “I anticipated in maturity”—that is, before your coming, before the time of fullness and grace—to gain your favor; “and I cried out.” Therefore I anticipated and cried out, “because in your word”—that is, your commandment, or your Son—“I hoped exceedingly.”

I anticipated at dawn, and I also anticipated others in greater illumination, because I was more enlightened than others. This is expressed by: “At dawn”—that is, from the beginning of my conversion, when I received the true light—“my eyes,” my inner eyes and perceptions, “anticipated” others, reaching “toward you”; and they anticipated for this purpose, “that I might meditate upon your words.” Or, if one reads “dawn” as the time of the resurrection, my eyes anticipated.

And because I cried out and anticipated, “hear my voice,” so that I may not be broken by the tribulation of those hemming me in. I dare to ask this not according to my merits, but “according to your mercy”: “Lord, give me life,” so that I may not succumb to evils, and also multiply me in virtues; do this “according to your judgment.” For you judge so that “the one who is righteous may become righteous still” (Revelation 22).

And it is necessary for you to give me life, because those “pursuing” and killing “me have drawn near to iniquity,” since they have almost conformed me to their wickedness and persuaded me of it; “but they have gone far from your law” by acting in this way. For the more someone approaches iniquity and binds himself to the devil, the farther he becomes from God and God’s law.

He approaches iniquity, but “you, Lord, are” near “to me” in order to defend me against them. They are far from your law, but your law pleases me. This is expressed by: “All your ways are truth to me”—that is, I understand as true the commandments by which one comes to the Lord, and as deceiving in nothing.

“All your ways are truth to me,” and “I have known this from your testimonies,” namely, “because you founded them” so that they might endure “forever”—that is, so that they might lead people to eternity. I learned this “from the beginning,” from Abel and the other righteous, in whom I saw Christ who was to come and to establish his Church immutably.

## Res

“See my humility.” Res, meaning “head,” is prefixed here, because this section concerns humility, which is the head and guardian of the virtues. The righteous man, hemmed in by enemies, preserves humility as a serpent preserves its head while exposing its body to blows. For just as a serpent, if it preserves its head, does not perish even if its other limbs are cut off, so a person who preserves humility is not deprived of true life even if his body is beaten.

Continuation: Those pursuing me have drawn near, and I have displayed humility toward them. O Lord, “see my humility”—that is, let it please you—“and deliver me,” so that their persecution may not overcome me, “because I have not forgotten your law,” which you commanded concerning humility: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14 and 15).

“See and deliver me,” and “judge my judgment”—namely, what I decide ought to be done, such as holding fast to the faith and other matters of this kind, which, because of human weakness, I cannot properly discern. For I judge a person who is good to be evil, and conversely, and so forth. You “judge” it—that is, examine it; make me judge rightly in all things. “And redeem me”—that is, free me by the price of the blood of your Son from the power of the enemy—and “give me life” with eternal life, “because of your word” given concerning the humility that I have preserved, just as that word itself commanded. Or, “because of your word”—that is, because of your promise, which is to be fulfilled. For in the Gospel you promised that those who are in the tombs and have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life.

If I keep your law and commandments, you will give me life, but “salvation will be far from sinners”; and you will not be blamed for this, but they will, “because they did not seek your ordinances.”

Salvation will be far from them, but “give me life according to your judgment”—that is, according to what you judge concerning giving life to your faithful. I ask this confidently because “your mercies,” O Lord, “are many”—that is, from the first righteous person onward you have been accustomed to show many mercies to your faithful.

And it is necessary for you to give me life because there are “many who pursue me,” driving me from place to place, “and afflict me,” beating me; “yet I have not turned aside from your testimonies.”

I “saw transgressors, and wasted away” with grief, “because they did not keep your words.”

I did not turn aside, but rather grieved over those who turned aside. This is expressed by: I saw them as transgressors, and just as I saw them, so you, “Lord, see” me deserving of favor in this respect, “because I loved your commandments.” In contrast to the fact that I was wasting away with grief, “give me life” with true life; and my merits are not sufficient for this, but do this for me “in your mercy.”

I rightly loved your commandments, because “the beginning of your words” is “truth,” just as you first commanded the human being, saying: “You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; on whatever day you eat from it, you will die by death” (Genesis 1). This word was true, because he was condemned when he ate the forbidden food. And “all the judgments of your righteousness,” which you will carry out according to your righteousness on the last day, separating the good from the evil, remain “forever”—that is, unalterable, because they will not return to earthly life and the cultivation of the earth after a hundred thousand years, as Origen and other heretics supposed.

## Sin

“Princes.” Sin, which is interpreted as “upon a wound,” is rightly prefixed here, because the faithful man who shortly before displayed his humility now shows that he gratefully accepts tribulations that heal the wounds of the soul and are for him like a plaster placed upon a wound.

[Col. 0628C] Continuation: Many pursue me, and not just any people, but “princes”—that is, the powerful of this age—“have persecuted me especially,” and have done so “gratuitously,” that is, without cause. Although my flesh then feared their words, nevertheless “my heart”—that is, my will and reason—did not fear their words, but feared your words, because you said: “If anyone denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father” (Matthew 10). And likewise: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10 and 24).

And in doing this, “I,” founded “upon your words”—that is, fearing the one who can destroy both body and soul—although I might perhaps appear to be saddened by the persecution of the wicked, “will rejoice like” one “who has found much spoil.” Just as an enemy, after defeating an enemy, joyfully seizes the spoils, so too the devil, when he incorporates some people among those subject to himself, carries off the reward of eternal life.

I say, “I will rejoice,” and by this I can rejoice because I loved your law. To show his perfect love, he first says: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it”—that is, I regarded it as accursed—“but I loved your law,” rather than hating it.

That I loved the law is evident from this: “In my illumination I praised you,” and this “seven times”—that is, always, throughout the whole period of my life, which revolves through seven days. Or literally: “Seven times a day”—that is, at the appointed hours commemorating the sevenfold Spirit—I praise you, attending “to the judgments of your righteousness,” that is, recognizing that all those persecutions are inflicted upon me by your just judgment, namely, for correction.

And while I was amid tribulations, I was able to praise you because great tranquility and peace were in my mind, since “there is great peace for those who love your law”—that is, tranquility of mind, though not perfection. For although they are beaten outwardly, they are nevertheless not shaken in mind. Hence it is written: Even in this life rest is given to many of the saints, whose souls the world does not hold slain; “and” also “there is no stumbling block for them”—that is, no offense ever harms them or separates them from the Church, because they cause no offense.

Therefore I was also able to praise you and hate iniquity because I, O “Lord, awaited your salvation.” We await Christ, who will come at the final judgment; the ancient fathers awaited his first coming. For unless we awaited him as coming a second time, we would neither love the law nor hate iniquity. I awaited him; “and I loved your commandments”—that is, the moral precepts, such as “You shall not kill, you shall not steal,” and similar commandments.

And I did not merely love your commandments, but also “my soul”—that is, my reason and will—“kept your testimonies”—that is, the commandments of your old law, namely, the figures themselves. This does not mean that a person of the New Testament fulfills them by carrying them out literally, but he nevertheless preserves them, knowing that they are the proof and testimony of his law, just as the Lord himself, through the testimony of those prophets, confirmed the resurrection when speaking to the disciples on the way (Mark 16; Luke 24); “and it loved them exceedingly.”

I say, “I loved the commandments,” and not only this, but also “I kept your commandments and” likewise “your testimonies together with the commandments,” to show that I observe both Testaments, the Old and the New, equally. Therefore I kept them “because all my ways”—that is, all my works—“are before you”—that is, you direct my ways and works. No works are said to be before God except those of the righteous alone.

## Tau

“Let it draw near.” Tau, meaning “completion,” is prefixed to this octonary, because this righteous man, who earlier showed that he had kept God’s law, prays for completion, so that his prayer may reach God’s presence, and so that God himself, having become his shepherd through the flesh he assumed, may lead him, the sheep wandering in the wilderness because of the offense of the first parent, back to the true and everlasting fold. The order is also appropriate: after the blessed man has been brought to the point where tribulations become medicine for him, nothing remains except to strive to reach the promised reward.

Continuation: Because I loved and kept the commandments, therefore, O “Lord, let my supplication draw near” to you, so that it may be “in your presence.” That is, may my prayer itself cause me to draw near to you—not locally, but by resemblance in righteousness, from which I have become unlike you through the multiplicity of my unrighteousness. And so that I may draw near, “give me understanding,” not in worldly sciences, but “according to your word”—that is, concerning heavenly things, an understanding taught by your words.

Let it not merely draw near, but also “enter”—and remain—“my petition,” that is, my prayer, “into your presence.” Let this petition enter: “deliver me” from the prison of the flesh and from this body of death; do this “according to your word”—that is, according to your promise, by which you said in the Gospel: “Whoever does what I command, I will reveal myself to him” (John 14).

I say, “Give me understanding,” and “when you teach me your ordinances”—that is, when you give understanding—“my lips will pour forth a hymn”; that is, from the great abundance of fullness I will offer you praise.

And I will not praise you only within myself; “my tongue” will also “proclaim your word” to others. That word ought rightly to be proclaimed, “because all your commandments” are “equity”—that is, they command nothing unjust.

And so that I may enter your presence and these other things may come to pass, “may your hand”—that is, your Son—“be ready,” so that he may “save me”—that is, become my Savior, also for us at this time. For Christ becomes Savior daily by forgiving sins and conferring spiritual graces. May this rightly be done for me, “because I have chosen your commandments.”

Therefore let your hand also save me, because I “desired your salvation, Lord”—that is, to be saved through that very Son whom I recognized as the Savior of all. And I ought also to be saved for this reason: I did not merely love the law, but “your law itself is my meditation,” and I meditate diligently on its fulfillment.

I desired salvation, and not in vain, because through you, the Savior, “my soul will live” with eternal life; “and” in that life “it will praise you,” according to the words: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83). And so that my soul may reach that life, “your judgments”—that is, corrections, namely, the scourges that you inflict upon me for correction and judge ought to be accepted—“will help me,” because through them sins will be punished and I will be proved.

And so that my soul may live that true life, which I cannot reach by myself, you, Lord, “seek” me, “your servant,” by inspiring, calling, and multiplying virtues, because I “went astray like a sheep that has perished”—that is, I went astray in the sins of the first parent, withdrawing into the land of unlikeness. And I am worthy for you to seek me, “because I have not forgotten your commandments.” For just as God neglects those who neglect him, so he seeks those who seek him.

## IN PSALM 119. TITLE: A Song of Ascents

“To the Lord, when I was in distress.” This title is prefixed to each of the fifteen psalms. Each of them teaches certain virtues that are most certain steps by which we may ascend to the heavenly Jerusalem. Solomon likewise made fifteen steps in the temple of the Lord, by which one ascended from the first tabernacle into the Holy of Holies, prefiguring in them the way to the heavenly city that the prophet displays in these fifteen psalms.

Through this number fifteen, which is composed of seven and eight, both the prophet who speaks here and Solomon in his steps wished to signify the completion of the Old Testament, which is represented by the number seven as able to ascend to the heavenly Jerusalem. By seven, we understand the Old Testament. For that law did not give the eighth day—that is, eternal rest—nor did it speak about it, but about the sign of that rest. This was its whole end, because the law commanded a Sabbath rest (Leviticus 23), which was a sign of the rest to come.

By eight, we understand the New Testament, because in it we now obtain true rest. For in Christ’s rising again our humility received eternal blessedness; and we, who are his members, already possess it in hope, and at last will reign perfectly with him after the seven days through which this world revolves.

Note that in these fifteen steps the New and Old Testaments are signified. In the preceding seven, the Old Testament is represented, and the title is simply “A Song of Ascents”; in the following eight, the New Testament is shown, and they are entitled “A Song of Ascents of Solomon.”

The title is to be read as follows: This psalm is a song because it sets forth great exultation—namely, how we may ascend to the heavenly dwelling and recover what we lost in the first parent. It is a song of ascents, that is, one of those songs that set steps before us. Each psalm sets forth one step; and the step itself—that is, the particular virtue displayed in each one—is the proper subject of that psalm.

In this psalm he sets forth the first step, namely, avoiding vices and renouncing the world in mind. For even if someone uses the world, he should nevertheless not be a lover of it. Hence the Apostle says: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice” (1 Corinthians 7).

This is the voice of the prophet showing that he has ascended these steps, and he does not speak only of himself but also of those like him. He intends to invite others to climb these steps by his example.

He makes two parts in this psalm. In the first part he shows that, when he cried out, he was heard, and he prays not to be driven into sin thereafter. In the second, which begins, “Alas for me,” he groans and laments that he has remained for so long a stranger and sojourner among the wicked.

It is as though he said: Brothers, when you are troubled amid the multiplicity of the sins of this age, cry out to the Lord, and he will hear you, following the example of me, who, “when I was in distress” because of the attraction of the many vices of this age, recognizing this to be harmful, “cried out to the Lord, and he heard me.”

[Col. 0632A] After the Lord heard him, both forgiving his sins and removing him from the love of earthly things, he saw that many dangers threatened him which might again drive him toward what lay behind him, such as the deceitful tongue that cast the first parent down from his perfection. He therefore prays God to free him, so that he may not again be drawn into sin. It is as though he said: “Lord,” who have already heard me concerning the past, henceforth “free my soul from lying lips”—that is, from lips openly persuading me to evil—“and from a deceitful tongue,” that is, one that introduces some authority or reasoning by which it deceives.

The devil spoke to Eve with a deceitful tongue when he tried to persuade her to eat the forbidden food. He added a deception by which he persuaded her, saying: “You will be like God himself” (Genesis 3).

[Col. 0632B] He turns to himself, counseling himself; this indicates his great diligence and how much caution must be used against a deceitful tongue. It is as though he said: O my soul, which is tempted by the gravest temptation, namely, the deceitful tongue, “what can be given to you?”—that is, what can be given to you?—“or what can be added to you?”—that is, what example can be set before you that would be effective for you “against a deceitful tongue,” so that you may not be seduced by it?

Here is what is given to you: “sharp arrows”—that is, divine commandments, which swiftly pierce human hearts—are given to you as weapons against the deceitful tongue. Arrows, I say, “of the Mighty One,” that is, of God himself. By this he indicates that these arrows make people strong against the deceitful tongue. Arrows, he says, are given “with desolating coals.”

He calls the saints “coals,” because they were at one time extinguished, but afterward through Christ became burning and kindle others to the love of God. They are called desolating because they burn up and consume buildings—that is, vices—if we wish to shape ourselves according to their example. This is what is given to us against the deceitful tongue.

“Alas for me!” The second part. It is as though he said: Although I have been heard in my distress, possessing arrows and coals against the deceitful tongue, nevertheless there is still “alas for me”—that is, a great groaning—“because my sojourning has been prolonged,” that is, my pilgrimage and exile from the true homeland have been extended too long. This does not mean that human life is long, but that he would already wish “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 2). Therefore there is “alas for me,” because “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar”—that is, with those who remain in darkness. For Kedar is interpreted as “darkness.” And therefore I say, “Alas for me!” because “my soul has been a long-time sojourner”—that is, it has endured great hardship in this exile.

I say that this pilgrimage is grievous to my soul because those with whom I lived hated the peace that I sought and attacked me. This is expressed by: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful.” Although they were seditious, I did not curse them but prayed for them; nevertheless, I did not remain silent instead of preaching the word of God. “When I spoke to them” the word of truth, “they attacked me” with many tribulations, and did so “gratuitously”—that is, without any merit of mine. Or “gratuitously,” because they achieved nothing.

## IN PSALM 120. TITLE: A Song of Ascents

“I lifted up my eyes.” This psalm contains the material of the second step. Here the righteous man who earlier escaped from vices and renounced the world shows that he directs his thoughts toward the saints, so that through their intercession he may obtain divine help by which, having been made righteous, he may resist every temptation. Through his example the prophet intends to invite others to ascend by the same steps.

In the first part, lifting his eyes to the saints, he asks that the Lord’s help be given to him through their intercession. In the second part, which begins, “The Lord guards you,” he affirms that he possesses this help and shows what it can accomplish for him.

It is as though the prophet invited others in this way, saying: O brothers, who have already stripped off your sins, lift your inner eyes toward the saints of God, so that through their intercession you may receive the Lord’s help, following the example of me, who “lifted”—that is, raised up—“my eyes,” that is, my thoughts, “toward the mountains”—that is, toward the holy angels and other saints who stand in God’s presence—“from where,” that is, from whom, “my help will come.”

I say that help will come to me from them, but not because they themselves give it; rather, “my help” will be “from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” From this it is evident that his help is powerful and strong for protection.

I say that help will be mine from the Lord; and, O my soul, may he “who guards you”—that is, God, whose help you have received while the saints pray—“not let your foot”—that is, your affection—“be moved,” so that you may not be moved toward anything unlawful. Nor should he “slumber”—that is, he should not allow you to act negligently.

The Lord our guardian is said to slumber when he permits us to act negligently. Thus the Lord slept in the boat (Matthew 8) while they were negligent and secure because of the calmness of the sea. But when they were stirred up and cried out during the storm at sea, the Lord awoke and guarded them diligently.

[Col. 0633D] Truly, the one who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep for you, because he does this for all who are Israel. This is expressed by: “Behold, he will not slumber”—that is, he will not permit Israel to act negligently—“nor will he sleep”—that is, he will not permit the foot to be moved so that it is driven toward some vice.

### Second part

“The Lord guards you.” Continuation: I pray that the Lord may not let your foot be moved, and so it will be, because “the Lord guards you” in the good things we possess; and “the Lord” is “your protection” against evils, “over your right hand”—that is, over your spiritual action, which he himself guards so that it does not turn from good toward evil.

A person’s left hand is called human action because of temporal advantage; the right hand, however, is spiritual action, performed only for a heavenly reward.

And because the Lord is protection over your hand, therefore “by day”—that is, in a time of prosperity—“the sun,” that is, prosperity no matter how exalted, “will not burn you”—that is, it will not take away any good from you or lead you into pride. Nor will “the moon”—that is, the gravest adversity, which often burns some people, just as the moon scorches people at night—“burn you by night,” that is, in a time of adversity, when adversity presses most heavily. In other words, you will neither be exalted in prosperity nor broken in adversity.

Or interpret it according to Augustine, who takes the sun as Christ according to his divinity and the moon as that same Christ according to his humanity.

Continuation: Because the Lord guards you, therefore by day—that is, in the knowledge of the illumination you will have concerning his divinity—the sun, that is, the divinity of Christ, will not burn you; that is, it will not permit you to err in your knowledge of his divinity. Nor will the moon, that is, Christ himself according to his humanity, burn you by night—that is, in your knowledge of his humanity, so as to permit you to think wrongly about that humanity.

What does each phrase mean? “The Lord guards you from every evil,” that is, from every sin; and because he sees evils impending by which a person is usually driven into sin, he says to himself: “May the Lord,” who guards you, henceforth “guard your soul.”

In this sense, namely: “May the Lord guard your entrance [Col. 0634C],” or, when you are led before kings and governors, may you not be silent about the truth, nor yield to their threats; “and your departure,” that is, when you are led to death, may you not deny the truth through fear of death. And may he do this beginning “from this time forth,” that is, from the present moment, “and forever,” that is, for as long as this age endures.

## ON PSALM 121

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“I rejoiced.” Here we have the joy of this faithful speaker at the third degree: he recognizes that he is going to the house of the Lord, above in the heavenly Jerusalem; he already dwells there in hope, and intends to invite others to this kind of degree. In [Col. 0634D] the first part, he says that he rejoices over that heavenly house in which he himself is going to dwell, and he displays the great dignity of that city, so as to stir hearts most strongly toward desiring it. In the second, which begins, “Pray for the things that make for peace,” he tells its citizens that he speaks many good things about them. He proceeds in a fitting order. For one who has acquired divine help for himself through the intercession of the saints ought to exult and rejoice in the hope of an eternal dwelling.

It is as though he were saying: You who have been stripped of vices and have already received divine help through the intercession of the saints, rejoice in the security of an eternal dwelling, following my example, for I “rejoiced in the things that were said to me” by the Holy Spirit, or by any of the prophets—from [Col. 0635A] Moses, for example, or David, he might have received them. These things were indeed said to me: “We shall go into the house of the Lord,” that is, we shall reach the heavenly dwelling, I and others like me who, having now abandoned their vices, have received divine help through the intercession of the saints, just as I have. Although I say, as though of the future, “we shall go into the house of the Lord,” nevertheless I already dwell in that house in my mind. This is what is meant by: “Our feet,” that is, our affections, “were standing,” that is, were firmly established and rightly raised, O heavenly “Jerusalem,” “in your courts,” that is, in your spaciousness. By specifying Jerusalem, he shows that he is speaking not of the earthly but of the heavenly Jerusalem.

It is as though he were saying: O Jerusalem, we shall stand in your courts; and this “Jerusalem” is the one “that is built as a city” every day from living stones. It is “as a city” because the heavenly citizens [Col. 0635B] come together to preserve unity, so that they may live rightly and offer a single praise to God. “The participation” of that city, that is, the thing in which its citizens participate, tends toward “that same thing,” that is, toward the unchangeability of the divine essence itself, which is the refreshment of all who dwell in that city. Or, I may say that the participation of that city—namely, something belonging commonly to all—is directed toward that same thing, that is, toward something wholly unchangeable, namely, “that same thing,” God; and God himself is the participation of that city. Those citizens share in this good, though not equally.

And rightly do I say that “we shall go into the house of the Lord,” because “tribes have ascended there,” that is, to that heavenly dwelling—not just any tribes [Col. 0635C], but “the tribes of the Lord,” namely, those tribes that served God with great solicitude. He specifies which are the tribes of the Lord: “the testimony of Israel,” that is, those who by their good conduct testify that they are Israel. They ascended there so that the name of the Lord might be praised. This is what he says: “to confess the name of the Lord,” in accordance with: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83).

He does not say “they ascended” because, in the time of the prophet David, some people had already ascended; rather, he announces it in the past tense because he was certain that, through the merits of the patriarchs and other righteous people, they would ascend to that heavenly Jerusalem at the advent of the Mediator.

And truly they ascended, because judges have also been [Col. 0635D] appointed there. This is what is meant by: “For there,” that is, in that dwelling, “thrones sat,” as judges—that is, those in whom God sits and rests in this life. They will sit, I say, “in judgment” in the future, so that they themselves may judge, namely, by consenting to the divine sentence. For the saints will judge the nations. They will judge, I say, as “thrones set over the house of David,” that is, over the household of faithful Christians, whom they will judge for salvation.

“Pray.” The second part. It is as though he were saying: You tribes who already sit there, “pray,” that is, ask and obtain for us by your prayers and merits those things “that are” useful “for” attaining “the peace of Jerusalem.” Pray in this way, that is, seek it, “and” through [Col. 0636A] this there will be “abundance” for all “who love you.”

And so that by our abundance we may be able to reach your dwelling, “let there be” for us “peace,” that is, rest and tranquility of mind; and let this be “in your strength,” that is, in charity, which reigns especially in you. “And in your towers,” that is, in the holy apostles and others who exposed themselves to death in defense of the Church, “let there be abundance” of virtues, or of those acquired through their preaching, so that they may present themselves to God at the judgment with many children.

I ask not only that there be peace and abundance in your towers, but I will also speak well of you to others. This is what is meant by: “I spoke peace” to others “concerning you,” that is, that peace abounds in you, and that those who are restless and live here without true peace cannot attain your tranquility. I spoke [Col. 0636B] this “for the sake of my brothers and my neighbors,” namely, so that I might establish in them such peace as would enable them to reach the peace and dwelling of the heavenly city. By “brothers” he means those more closely joined to him and like him in good works; by “neighbors,” all Christians indiscriminately.

And I did not speak of you only in words, but also in work and labor: “I sought good things for you,” that is, I attracted many citizens. And this because you are the house of God. This is what he says: “for the sake of the house of the Lord our God.”

## ON PSALM 122

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“To you I lifted up my eyes.” As has been said in other places, and as he also shows in the preceding psalm, the faithful speaker [Col. 0636C] rejoices in the heavenly dwelling. Now, having already become familiar with God himself, he directs his eyes toward him while placed amid the troubles of this life. In the first part, he shows that he directs his eyes toward God. In the second, which begins, “Have mercy on us, O Lord,” he begs for mercy. His purpose is to exhort us to this degree; and especially in these first seven psalms he speaks about the Old Testament.

It is as though he were saying: You who are placed in tribulation, lift your eyes to God, as I “lifted up my eyes” inwardly “to you,” O God, who are powerful enough to hear. He indicates this by saying: “who dwells in the heavens.” He is said to direct his eyes toward God who, not trusting in earthly things, places his confidence in the Lord alone.

[Col. 0636D] He shows how he directs his eyes toward that same God: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters,” so that they may receive some benefit from him—or, if they are punished by their master, so that they may be set free.

And “as the eyes of the maidservant” are likewise “on the hands of her mistress,” so our eyes are on the Lord our God until he has mercy on us, either by freeing us from tribulations or by granting us whatever benefits he chooses. After speaking of male servants, he then speaks of women, so that future salvation may be understood in that sex. By women, whose bodies are naturally fragile, we understand not only females but also certain physically weak men; and among men we again understand certain strong women. And just as a mistress is said to be more ready to show mercy [Col. 0637A] than a master, so God is compared to a mistress because he is quickly moved toward the fragile. He is also compared to a master when he permits the stronger to be severely tormented, assigning to each according to his capacity. Hence the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Corinthians 10).

“Have mercy on us, O Lord.” The second part. Since we direct our eyes in this way toward the Lord, therefore: “O Lord, have mercy on us; have mercy on us.” He asks twice for mercy because he sets forth a twofold misery, namely, according to body and according to soul. “Have mercy,” I say, “because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt” according to the body.

For this reason also “have mercy,” because not only the body but also “our soul has been filled [Col. 0637B] exceedingly” with contempt. And I will not merely say that it has been filled; rather, it has become “a reproach to those who abound” in riches. For the rich judge the good to be contemptible and foolish because they do not seek riches as the rich themselves do. “And” it has become “a contempt to the proud,” those lifted up in mind; for they despise them when, on account of the heavenly things—which they regard as eternal—they reject earthly wealth.

## ON PSALM 123

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Unless the Lord.” Here we have the righteous man who, in another psalm, raised his eyes to the Lord and, amid distress, cried out for deliverance. The deliverance he received—or whatever other good he possesses—he attributes not to himself but entirely to God’s mercy. He also [Col. 0637C] intends to invite others to this same degree, so that they may attribute everything to God’s mercy. In the first part, he shows that from the Lord alone he has the ability to withstand tribulations. In the second, which begins, “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give,” he gives thanks to the Lord for his deliverance.

It is as though he were saying: You who have received deliverance amid distress, ascribe your deliverance to the Lord, following our example, for we give good thanks to the Lord: “unless” this had been the case, that “the Lord was with us,” strengthening us, “when people rose up against us, they would have swallowed us,” that is, incorporated us into themselves, “alive,” that is, knowingly. For although we recognized that it was evil, nevertheless, because of the magnitude of the tribulations, we would have had to consent to them. And this [Col. 0637D] “perhaps,” that is, it could happen—or not happen. And just as we speak, so “let Israel speak,” that is, the man who sees God, “now,” that is, without delay, saying: “Unless the Lord had been with us when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

At the beginning we would have failed, and even more so “when their fury,” that is, their onslaught, “was enraged,” that is, burned fiercely, “against us.” The “water,” that is, the flood of tribulations, “would have swallowed [Col. 0638A] us,” that is, drawn us irrecoverably to itself. And this would “perhaps,” that is, truly, have happened, unless the Lord had been with us.

“Unless the Lord had been with us,” the water would have swallowed us; but because he was with us, “our soul,” however the body might have been treated, “passed through” unharmed “the torrent,” that is, the violent tribulation. I say that, with the Lord’s help, our soul passed through it. Perhaps someone might say that, without the Lord’s help, “our soul would have passed through the water,” that is, the flood of evils, “which was intolerable” insofar as human strength is concerned. This appears impossible from the fact that the water was intolerable.

“Blessed be the Lord.” The second part. And because we passed through by his help, therefore “blessed be the Lord, who did not give us over as prey,” so that they might capture us and incorporate us “with their teeth,” that is, with their gnawing and their savagery, “for” they wanted to tear us apart like wild beasts.

[Col. 0638B] “He did not give us over,” I say, but rather “our soul, like a sparrow, has been snatched from the snare,” that is, from the deception “of the hunters,” that is, of those seeking an opportunity to deceive me.

And not only has our soul been snatched away, but “the snare,” that is, those who ensnared us, “has been broken,” because they themselves will finally be crushed by a twofold crushing, “and we have been set free,” that is, established by God in great dignity.

And this “help of ours,” by which we have been so delivered, is not from us, but because we are “in the name of the Lord,” who is fully able to guard us, for he is the one “who made heaven and earth,” either literally or allegorically.

## [Col. 0638D] ON PSALM 124

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Those who trust in the Lord.” Here the subject of this degree is confidence; he also intends to invite others to it. In the first part, he shows what confidence itself accomplishes: namely, that those who trust in the Lord cannot be separated from the charity of Christ. In the other part, which is, “Do good, O Lord,” he asks good things for those who trust in the Lord. The order is appropriate. After receiving deliverance from God and attributing everything to God’s mercy, it is right that he should trust in him most firmly.

It is as though he were saying: You who attribute your benefits to God’s mercy, henceforth trust in the Lord, because none of those “who trust in the Lord,” not presumptuously but as one “who dwells in Jerusalem,” that is, who is righteous—who dwells in heaven by hope, or devoutly in the Church—“will be moved forever” from Christ or from a good purpose by any tribulations, “like Mount Zion,” that is, Christ himself, who dwelt bodily on Mount Zion.

Therefore the one who trusts will not be moved, because “the mountains,” that is, angels, or apostles and other holy men, by their merits, prayers, and examples, are “around him,” fortifying such people who trust against their enemies. “And” the “Lord” himself is “around his people,” to fortify and protect them “from this time forth and forever.”

[Col. 0639A] Although for the present he permits them to suffer tribulation, nevertheless he is truly around them, because he will not leave his faithful in the power of their enemies, lest they too be compelled to sin. This is what is meant by: “The Lord will not leave the rod,” that is, the power, “of sinners over the lot of the righteous,” that is, over the religion which the righteous make their lot. Therefore he will not leave it there, “lest the righteous extend their hands to iniquity.” For if the wicked had power over the righteous, they would compel the righteous to sin by necessity.

“Do good.” The second part. Continuation: I said that the Lord will not abandon them; and you, O “Lord,” as you began, “do good,” that is, persevere in guarding them and in doing other good things, “to those who are good,” that is, to those who follow your commandments, “and to those who are upright in heart [Col. 0639B],” those whom no distress compels to sin.

The Lord will do good to these. “But those who turn aside,” that is, who fall away from God’s commandments because of certain tribulations, “the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity,” that is, he will permit them to be bound by many sins, just as he does with the other workers of iniquity. “But upon Israel,” that is, upon the man who sees God, there will be “peace,” partly in this life and supremely in the other. When he announces evil to the wicked, he rightly exhorts us to confidence, lest we suffer evil together with those who lack trust.

## [Col. 0639C] ON PSALM 125

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“When the Lord turned.” Here the prophet’s subject is the expectation of future deliverance through Christ’s coming. Through him the faithful and the earlier righteous—who had still been held by the devil, both living and dead, because of the guilt of original sin—were set free. This expectation was the end of all the righteous under the Old Testament. From this it is clear that the preceding six degrees are directed especially to the people of the Old Testament. The prophet intends to invite the people of the Old Testament to place their hope of deliverance in Christ’s coming. In the first part, he shows that those righteous people had such consolation at Christ’s coming that even their enemies praised their consolation. In the second, which begins, “Turn again, O Lord,” he asks God that he too may share in deliverance at Christ’s coming [Col. 0639D], because he sees the joyful end of those who have been liberated.

It is as though he were saying: You ought to await consolation, brothers, at Christ’s coming, because “when the Lord turned,” that is, when the Lord turns, “the captivity of Zion,” that is, of those who are contemplation and who look ahead for themselves, “we became like those who are consoled,” that is, like those who receive consolation when good things arrive.

“Then,” that is, in that turning of the captivity, “our mouth,” namely, the heart itself, “was filled with joy.” And not only the heart, but also “our tongue,” the outward tongue, was in “exultation,” that is, it joyfully proclaimed to others the deliverance which it saw being brought about through Christ’s coming. By using the present and past tense [Col. 0640A], he announces a future event because of its certainty.

“Then,” that is, when the Lord turns our captivity, certain people “among the nations” will say: “The Lord has done great things with them,” that is, has magnificently arranged to act with them. For when they understand that people are liberated from sins through Christ, they will recognize them as children of God and as destined finally to be carried in angelic hands into everlasting rest.

They themselves will say: “The Lord has magnified what he did with them.” Nor are they foolish or ignorant in saying this, because it is true. But they will also say: “The Lord has done great things with us,” that is, he determined that he would make us great; and, hoping for this, “we became rejoicing.”

“Turn again, O Lord.” The second part. Continuation: And because “you have magnified what you did with us,” therefore, O [Col. 0640B] “Lord, turn our captivity,” by which we are bound through the cold of sin. Turn it in such a way that we may reach the course of good works. Turn it “like a torrent” that is bound by the cold of winter and is changed “in the south wind,” in that warm wind, so that through the south wind—that is, through the warmth of the Holy Spirit—the cold, namely the sluggishness of sin, may be changed in us.

I say “turn,” because then, when the turning has taken place, “those who sow in tears will reap in exultation,” that is, they will joyfully receive the reward of eternal life—those who sow their good works, from which they await abundant fruit, “in tears,” that is, in the grief and sadness of this life.

Who are those who will reap in exultation? Those, clearly, who were going toward the eternal city through their good works [Col. 0640C], and who did not cease even for an hour but were continually “going.” They were going, I say, “and weeping” over the death and misery of this life. These, I say, were “carrying their seeds,” that is, their good works, or especially their almsgiving.

“Going, they went.” But when they come—that is, when they approach death—they “will come” to the judgment with exultation, bringing, that is, presenting to the Lord “their sheaves,” namely, their good works, from which they will receive their reward.

## [Col. 0640D] ON PSALM 126

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees of Solomon

“Unless the Lord builds.” Just as we directed the seven preceding degrees especially to the people of the Old Testament, so we refer these eight that follow properly to the people of the New Testament. These degrees are said to belong especially to Solomon, that is, to the peaceful one—namely Christ—who was truly peaceful because he reconciled God to humanity and made peace between Jews and Gentiles. Hence the Apostle says: “He made both one” (Ephesians 2). These degrees properly belong to this peaceful one because, through the presence of his body, he brought manifest help to the human race, displayed in himself an example of complete righteousness, and taught others to ascend by the degrees of the virtues to the heavenly Jerusalem.

In this psalm he speaks to people who, at Christ’s coming—which in another psalm he says is awaited with great exultation—received an abundance of benefits [Col. 0641A], as the holy apostles did. He intends to remove all presumption from them: they must not presume to be able by themselves either to build or to preserve what has been built. Nor should they consider themselves secure before Christ’s second coming, because no one in this life can be secure, since anyone can immediately fall into sin.

It is as though he were saying: You who received many benefits at Christ’s coming and were also appointed builders of others, do not presume upon yourselves, because you can do nothing by yourselves unless the Lord acts. This is what he says: “Unless the Lord builds the house,” that is, unless the Lord prepares someone for his dwelling through inward inspiration, “those who build it have labored in vain,” that is, those who labor to build it. [Col. 0641B] “For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God, who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

I say that no one can build by himself, nor preserve by himself what has been built. This is what is meant by: “Unless the Lord guards the city,” that is, the Church itself, which is called a city because it is gathered from many people and well fortified by virtues, “the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.” When he says “keeps watch,” he indicates the care and concern which the pastors of the Church have as they watch over their flocks. Hence in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me” (Song of Songs 3).

Since God alone builds and guards, therefore “it is vain for you to rise,” that is, to presume upon the security of eternal blessedness, because whoever [Col. 0641C] is in this life is inclined to fall. Hence it is said: “Let the one who stands beware lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10). “It is vain,” I say, “to rise before the light,” that is, before Christ’s second coming, in which true light and manifest knowledge will exist for everyone. Or, “before the light,” that is, before the knowledge which each faithful soul receives after the dissolution of the body alone. It is vain to rise before the light—namely, “after you have sat down,” that is, once you have passed through the sitting and abasement of this life, then “rise,” that is, be secure. I tell you to rise, you “who eat the bread of sorrow,” that is, you for whom the miseries of this world are nourishment, as bread is for someone.

I say, “Rise after you have sat down.” And as though someone were to ask: When will that sitting be complete? [Col. 0641D] It will be “when” the Lord “gives sleep to his beloved,” that is, death. And when he gives it, “behold,” there will appear “the inheritance of the Lord,” namely, of the Son, that is, of the righteous man: these are sons. These sons are “the reward,” that is, the recompense which the Lord gave to Christ for the fulfillment of his obedience. It is a reward, I say, “the fruit” of Christ himself, who was the fruit of the virginal “womb.” When he says, “Behold the inheritance,” he begins the second part, in which he shows the great dignity of those who are the Lord’s inheritance. In the first part he dissuades from presumption.

I say that the sons will be a reward, and those sons will be “the sons of those who have shaken out,” that is, of the prophets, who are called those who shake out because they shook out and revealed what was hidden, namely, the rejection of the human [Col. 0642A] race. They will be “like arrows in the hand of the Mighty One.” For just as an archer directs an arrow wherever he wishes, and the arrow itself does not stray but strikes whom he wills, so God the Mighty is called an archer because he sends his arrows, that is, the holy apostles and other messengers, to distant regions which he himself chooses, and through them pierces human hearts with divine love.

And not only are the apostles blessed, along with those others who welcomed Christ’s coming, but so are all who imitate them. This is what is meant by: Every such “man is blessed who has fulfilled his desire from them,” that is, who ordered his life according to their example. And he is truly blessed because “he will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies at the gate,” that is, in public.

Or by “the gate” [Col. 0642B] we can understand Christ, who is the gate through which one goes to life, as he himself says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). Thus we may understand it as follows: “When he speaks with his enemies,” that is, heretics, “at the gate,” that is, in Christ—speaking about Christ himself—he will not be put to shame, whether by saying something erroneous about him or by being refuted in some way by the heretics.

## ON PSALM 127

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Blessed are all.” In this psalm the subject of this degree is the fear of the Lord, and he intends to admonish those whom he previously warned against presumption to undertake this same degree. In the first part, he shows [Col. 0642C] what the fear of the Lord produces. In the second, which begins, “May the Lord bless you from Zion,” he offers a prayer wishing good things for those who fear God.

It is as though he were saying: You who have received Christ’s good gifts and yet do not presume, fear the Lord, because “all who fear the Lord” with a chaste fear “are blessed,” namely those “who” fear him and “walk in his ways,” either in his commandments or in imitation of him.

You will truly be blessed, “because you will eat,” that is, take nourishment from yourself, “the labors of your hands,” that is, the works of your hands, performed with great labor. And because you will eat this, “you are blessed” in this life, “and it will be well with you” in the future. When he first speaks of the Church in the plural, he refers to the multitude of persons [Col. 0642D]; when he later speaks of the same Church in the singular, he refers to the Church’s unity.

You will also be blessed in this: “your wife,” that is, your animal nature, which ought to be subject to the man, namely, to reason by which it is governed, will be “abundant” in good fruits and works, “like a vine.” I say, a wife placed “at the sides of your house,” that is, near your “good conscience,” because she will be a good neighbor to her husband, namely, to reason. Through this the wife herself will not be deceived, as Eve was deceived. We call the conscience a house because in it we prepare a lodging for the Lord.

Or by “wife” we can understand wisdom, so that we may say: Your wife, that is, wisdom, which, like a wife, cherishes and nourishes the man, is [Col. 0643A] “abundant” in good fruits, because she makes you work like a vine. I say, a wife placed at the sides of your house, that is, in the two Testaments; for through the wisdom contained in those Testaments she makes both herself and the man work well, and teaches others to work well. These two Testaments are the sides, that is, the supports, of a good conscience; and this is your house.

You will also be blessed in this: “your sons,” whom you beget for God through preaching and example, will be “like young olive trees,” that is, like young olive trees. For just as young olive trees are always green, that is, bear more fruit than others, so your sons will be green with virtues and fruitful in good works. I say, sons placed “around [Col. 0643B] your table,” that is, the divine Scripture, so that they may be refreshed by your teaching.

Or, “around your table,” that is, the altar, where they are nourished by the refreshment of the Lord’s body. He rightly chooses these two trees rather than other fruit-bearing trees, because by the vine we understand the austerity of justice, and by the olive the gentleness of mercy. Every faithful person ought to have both within himself. These are the two things which the Samaritan is read to have poured into the wounds of the man “who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 10).

It is clearly evident that the one who fears the Lord will be blessed, because “behold, thus,” as has been said, “the man who fears the Lord will be blessed.”

“May he bless you.” The second part. In this wish he shows the affection he has for those who fear the Lord. Continuation: I say, “thus he will be blessed”; and you, O man who fears the Lord, “may the Lord bless you from [Col. 0643C] Zion,” coming from there, because he was born bodily in Zion.
