Or, “from Zion,” that is, from the fact that you have been made from Zion, that is, one who contemplates eternal things. “And may you see the good things of Jerusalem,” namely, of the heavenly Jerusalem; may the Lord lead you to those good things. May you see them, I say, “all the days of your life,” that is, in eternity.

“And” may you not alone see this, but also “see” in that Jerusalem “the sons of your sons,” that is, the imitators of those who were begotten through your preaching. And what does each phrase mean? May you see “peace upon Israel,” that is, eternal tranquility, which is “upon,” that is, greater even than any man who sees God can merit.

## ON PSALM 128

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees of Solomon

“Often they have attacked me.” After warning against presumption and teaching the fear of God, he gives instruction concerning endurance, and makes this same degree his subject. In the first part, he exhorts the people of the New Testament to endurance through the example of all the righteous, beginning with the first righteous man. In the second, which begins, “Let them be confounded and turned backward,” he prays for evil against the obstinate. Through this he exhorts us to endurance, lest we be condemned together with the impious at the Judge’s coming.

It is as though he were saying: You who no longer presume upon yourselves, while fearing God with filial fear, when the wicked persecute you, practice endurance following my example [Col. 0644A], because “they often attacked me,” that is, afflicted me with tribulations so severely that they sometimes even killed me. Here he speaks in the person of all the righteous of the New Testament. This was “from my youth,” that is, from the time of the first righteous man, when the Church began. And as I speak, so “let all Israel speak,” that is, the man who sees God, “now,” that is, immediately in the present. He says “now” because there will be a future time when Israel will no longer cry out about its persecution, namely, when it is in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Let him say this: “Often they attacked me from my youth.” And truly often, “yet they could not prevail against me,” because if they had killed me once, there would no longer have been any need to fight them.

I say “they attacked me,” and not merely face-to-face [Col. 0644B], so that they might oppose me openly; rather, “sinners constructed,” that is, inflicted many evils “upon my back,” that is, upon those in the Church who do not possess the true light by themselves but follow others, and they did this for a long time. This is what is meant by: “They prolonged their iniquity.”

Those people persecuted the Church arrogantly. “The Lord,” alone, “will cut down,” that is, bring to humility, “the necks,” that is, the heights and pride, “of sinners,” namely, of all those who persecute the Church.

The second part. I say, “he will cut down the necks of sinners.” But those who are obstinate—namely, “all who hate Zion,” that is, the Church, obstinately [Col. 0644C]—“will be confounded” when it is said: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25), “and they will be turned backward,” that is, deprived of the power which they exercise over the righteous in this life.

They will also “become like the grass of the rooftops, which has withered before it is pulled up.” The proud, who raise themselves on high, are rightly compared to the grass of rooftops, because just as rooftop grass raises itself high and yet has no root, so they raise themselves up. Before they are pulled up, that is, before they die, they wither away with respect to the goods of the soul because they neither seek nor love the reasoning of heavenly doctrine.

“From that grass,” that is, from those wicked people, “the angel who reaps,” that is, separates the good from the wicked, “will not fill his hand,” nor will “the angel who gathers sheaves” fill “his bosom” from it, that is, gather [Col. 0644D] the good (Matthew 13). By the hand is understood work; by the bosom, rest. Therefore angels are said to carry in their hands those who were good workers, and in their bosom those who were contemplatives.

They will not be gathered by the angels because in this life they did not receive a blessing from the apostles or from other holy men. This is what is meant by: Those “who passed by,” that is, the apostles and other holy men who, rejecting earthly things, pass onward to heavenly things, “did not say” to them: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” that is, the multiplication of virtues. Nor did they say: “We have blessed you” on our own behalf, in such a way that “in the name of the Lord” we bless you, that is, so that the name of the Lord may be honored through your blessing.

## ON PSALM 129

### TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Out of the depths.” In this psalm the degree and subject are repentance. He places it after many degrees of virtue to show us that, however far anyone may have advanced in virtues, repentance is nevertheless necessary for obtaining God’s mercy, because no one is so righteous that he has no stains, which must always be removed by the remedy of repentance.

In the first part, this penitent asks God to hear him crying out over his sins and not to judge him according to his iniquities. After he has thus pleaded on the basis of his own miseries, he seeks to win the judge’s favor through the judge’s goodness and shows the joyful end of his repentance [Col. 0645B]: namely, that he waits for the Lord and hopes in him, by which he can especially persuade through repentance. In the second part, which begins, “From the morning watch,” he urges other righteous people to place their hope in the Lord as well. His purpose is to invite them to repentance.

It is as though he were admonishing them: You, brothers, who possess endurance and have climbed the other degrees mentioned above, repent of your sins and cry out to God following my example, for I “cried to you, O Lord, from the depths,” that is, from the depth of iniquity. I cried because I recognized myself to be in this depth.

The righteous man understands by this depth even the lightest sins, and also the whole conduct of this present life, in which no one can refrain from [Col. 0645C] sin. And because I cried out in this way, listen; and because I recognized such things to be deep, therefore: “O Lord, hear my voice.” It is as though he were saying: It is right for you to hear me when I cry out in this way.

Nor do I merely say, Hear me; also attend to me, so that you may not only forgive the sins over which I cry out, but may also multiply and preserve me in every good thing. This is what he says: “Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication.”

Therefore I ask you to hear me and forgive my sins, because “if you observe iniquities, O Lord, O Lord,” wishing to judge according to them, “who will endure” your judgment, so as to be saved by merits? No one, certainly.

[Col. 0645D] If you take note of iniquities, no one will be able to bear the judgment; but because you are merciful, therefore we endure. This is what he says: “For with you there is forgiveness,” that is, because out of mercy you pardon sins; “and” likewise “because of your law,” namely, the evangelical teaching that instructs us concerning your forgiveness, “I endured you,” O “Lord.” That is, no matter what tribulations were inflicted, I never departed from you, but always held fast to the faith and fulfilled your law. In this verse he makes the judge whom he had previously entreated favorably disposed toward him, recognizing his own iniquities.

Not only because of forgiveness and the law, but also “in his word my soul endured,” that is, in his Son, whom I recognized as destined to be incarnate for our redemption [Col. 0646A] and recognized as the reason for enduring; and because I endured in this way and cried out in this way, therefore “my soul hoped in the Lord.”

“From the watch.” The second part. And just as my soul hoped, so let “Israel,” that is, the man who, repenting of his sins, cried out and endured adversity, “hope in the Lord,” and this “from the morning watch,” that is, from Christ’s first coming, which is called morning because through him the light of true knowledge became known to us. In this light a watch must be kept, so that there we may receive faith and understand Christ our Savior. Or, “from the morning watch,” that is, from the time of the Resurrection, when Christ, having been guarded by the soldiers, rose in the morning, “until night,” that is, until death.

[Col. 0646B] You ought therefore rightly to hope, because “with the Lord” there is “mercy,” because he freely pardons sins; and “with him” there is “redemption,” because he himself gave the blood of his Son as the price of our redemption. I say that the redemption is “abundant”: he does not release only slight and original sins, but sins however great.

And that this redemption is with him is evident in its effect, because “he himself will redeem all Israel”—that is, all who see God—“from all his iniquities.” In this it is evident that the redemption is abundant.

## ON PSALM CXXX. TITLE: A Song of Degrees of Solomon

“Lord, my heart is not.” This degree has humility as its subject. The Prophet intends to invite others to ascend this same degree, so that, however just they may be, they may always remain in humility and retain the memory of sins, without which they cannot exist; this memory is the safeguard of the other virtues.

It is as though he said: You, brothers, who have already obtained the remission of sins through repentance and now firmly hope in the Lord, do not presume upon yourselves, but always be humble, following my example, for I have exalted myself in nothing. This is what he says: “Lord, my heart is not exalted,” that is, I was not inwardly proud; “nor have my eyes been lifted up,” that is, I have not displayed any outward sign of pride.

And although I possessed great things, namely virtues and other gifts, [Col. 0646D] nevertheless “I did not walk in those great things,” that is, I did not present myself as one who possessed great things, namely, as a proud man. And although I possessed marvelous powers, namely, the ability to perform wonders, I did not walk “in marvelous things,” even though they existed “above me,” that is, were much greater and more worthy than I was.

Not only did I not walk in great things, but I also thought humbly of myself. And “if I did not think” this while existing “like a weaned child,” that is, separated from milk, which lies and rests “upon its mother,” because it cannot subsist by itself unless its mother provides assistance—if I did not consider myself like a weaned child, and God as the mother who nurtured me; if I did not do this [Col. 0647A] but instead “exalted my soul,” being foolish like the weaned child who places himself upon his mother, that is, who thinks he can subsist without his mother’s help, “so” may “the recompense be upon my soul.”

Let the one who is proud receive the recompense of pride. But “let Israel,” that is, the humble man who does not presume upon himself, “hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever.”

## ON PSALM CXXXI. TITLE: A Song of Degrees of Solomon

“Remember.” This psalm has the incarnation of Christ as its subject. In the first part it sets forth the promises that Christ makes to God the Father, namely, that he will prepare a dwelling for himself; the Prophet’s entreaty is placed first, so that God may regard Christ’s dignity and merits. In the second part, which begins, “Behold, we have heard,” it shows that Christ’s promises have been fulfilled and expresses his wishes that they may be completed. In the third, which begins, “The Lord swore to David,” it shows the Father’s promises to Christ: namely, that because of Christ’s merit he will make those conformed to Christ into sons and imitators of Christ, so that they may teach here what Christ taught, judge in judgment, and share in his blessedness. Through all this he intends to invite us to understand that nothing comes through our own merits, but through Christ’s sole merit; to pray that righteousness be given to us; and to be brought into conformity with Christ. We are urged by this psalm to ascend to this degree. He composed this psalm against heretics and Jews who thought that Christ’s coming was not necessary for salvation.

It is as though he said: Although we possess fear of God, cry out concerning our sins, and think humbly, as was shown in the preceding degrees, nevertheless we are not sufficient by our merits to attain conformity with Christ. Therefore, O “Lord, remember David,” that is, Christ, through whose unique merit we can be saved. He names David, the prophet, after the name of the bodily David from whose seed Christ proceeded, in order to signify Christ’s true humanity. “And remember all,” that is, his complete “meekness,” through which he fulfilled that unconquerable service, because he was obedient for our sake even unto death [Col. 0647D] (Philippians 2), and was led like a sheep to the slaughter.

I speak of meekness displayed “as” Christ himself “swore to the Lord,” that is, firmly resolved. And this was not under compulsion, but willingly. Thus he says: “He made a vow,” willingly and with affection, to you, “God of Jacob,” that is, the helper of those who wrestle. I say that he “swore,” speaking as follows: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house,” if I ascend into heaven, which is the tabernacle and dwelling in which my habitation is; and also, “if I ascend upon the bed of my couch,” that is, into complete rest, as upon a bed spread with fine coverings.

And also, “if I give sleep,” that is, death, “to my eyes”—that is, to me, who previously kept watch because of the guardianship of the flock entrusted to me. He rightly compares his death with sleep, because he rose so lightly, as someone rises from sleep. He describes how sleep comes upon a person: first the eyelids grow drowsy, then rest is given to the temples, and thus sleep takes possession of the whole body. So Christ began to sleep as he approached death, when he was handed over to the Jews, because then he neither performed miracles nor, before Pilate, spoke the truth. He gave rest to his temples when he ascended the cross. Therefore he says: “and” if I give “slumber to my eyelids,” that is, if I first come with my power shut up in the hands of the Jews.

“And” if I first give “rest to my temples,” that is, if I first ascend the cross, near to death, “until I find a place for the Lord,” that is, until human beings possess such a portion in which God may dwell; and until I find a “tabernacle for the God of Jacob,” to whom I made my vow, namely, people in whom God may dwell. This is an aposiopesis, that is, an omission in the sentence, and any impossible expression may be supplied, such as “I will not be God,” or something of that kind. It should be understood that before Christ ascended, he prepared everything that he recognized as necessary for establishing the Church: namely, he instructed the apostles in the evangelical teaching, so that they might sow it throughout the whole earth for those willing to hear and be converted.

“Behold, we have heard.” The second part. The continuation is this: Christ thus promised the building of the Church, and “behold,” just as he promised, we have recognized that it has been completed. This is what he says: “We heard these things” that Christ promised “in Ephrata,” that is, in Bethlehem; that is, we understand, through the Holy Spirit revealing it to us, that Christ would be born in Bethlehem of a Virgin, and through this we became certain that the remaining promises would be fulfilled. Or, allegorically, by Ephrata, which is interpreted as “mirror,” we understand the prophecies, in which, although the truth is announced, it is not openly declared. Or let us say this: “in Ephrata,” that is, in the sayings of the prophets, we heard and read these things, namely the promises; and just as we heard them there, so “we found them” fulfilled “in the fields,” that is, in the paths, which, although previously “forests” and thorny with sins, have now become arable and fruitful for God.

We found Christ’s Church, foretold in the prophets, in the fields—that is, fulfilled—and we ourselves “will enter into his tabernacle,” that is, into the service of Christ, because, having become members of the Church, we serve him. And “we worshiped in the place where his feet stood,” literally, because people still worship where the Lord ascended; the green turf remains as a witness to his ascension, and its greenness cannot be removed by any pavement. Or, “we worshiped in the place,” that is, with complete faith, “where his feet stood,” that is, where the traces of his righteousness appear. For whoever possesses perfect faith does not possess it idly, but acts in imitation of Christ. Through this the Church came into being, and Christ’s other promises were fulfilled, because he rose and ascended into his glory, and from there sent the Spirit, through whom the strengthened apostles built the Church for him. And where he ascended, he causes his ark, that is, the Church, to ascend. The Prophet announces this not declaratively but desideratively, thereby displaying the affection of his mind.

Continuation: Since the promises have been fulfilled and the tabernacle has been perfected, therefore, O “Lord, arise into your rest,” that is, ascend, “and” after you let the “ark,” that is, the Church, ascend—the ark in which wisdom and knowledge are contained. I call it the ark “of your sanctification,” that is, the ark which you sanctify.

And so that the ark may be able to ascend after you, meanwhile let “your priests,” devotedly serving you, “be clothed with righteousness.” Let them possess virtues as their priestly bands, virtues that are ornaments of the soul, “and” let “your saints rejoice” in their righteousness. Or, let your lesser saints rejoice in their progress and in the imitation of good people.

[Col. 0649B] And because he sees the Jews being blinded as the nations are enlightened, he beseeches God at least to visit them near the end. Continuation: Let the priests be clothed with righteousness, and O “Lord, do not turn away” the face of your Christ—that is, the present and clear knowledge of your Son, which is now turned away from the Jews—from ever showing it to the Jews, at least around the final times. I do not ask this because of their merits, but rather “because of David your servant,” that is, because of Christ’s merit. Here it is plainly understood that no one ought to presume upon his own merits, but should expect all salvation from Christ’s merits.

“The Lord swore.” The third part. I say “because of David,” and I do not despair, “because the Lord,” the Father, “swore,” firmly decreed, to “David,” that is, to Christ, [Col. 0649C] “the truth,” because just as he promised, so he fulfilled it; “and he will not disappoint him,” saying: “From the fruit of your womb,” that is, from those generated through your teaching—which is called a womb because it contains within itself God’s mysteries and nourishes human beings, just as the womb nourishes a child—from those generated in this way “I will place upon your throne,” that is, I will make them teachers, as you were in this life, and also judges of the whole world.

I say that I will “place” them on this condition: “if your sons will keep my covenant,” that is, the precepts of the old law and of the prophets, which bear witness to our faith, “and these testimonies of mine which I will teach them,” not those that they invent for themselves.

Your sons will sit upon your throne, “and” also “their sons,” that is, their imitators, “forever,” that is, as long as this age lasts. Even the sons of the final times “will sit upon your throne,” as stated above.

He promised Christ that his sons would sit in this way, and not according to their merits, “but because the Lord chose Zion,” that is, the Church. He chose “it as his dwelling,” so that he might inhabit it not for an hour but continually. I say that he chose it, saying: “This,” namely Zion, “is my rest, in which I rest,” not only in this life, but “for the age that follows this age.” “Here,” that is, in this Church, “will I dwell, because I have chosen her.”

“I will bless her widow,” that is, those of the Church who are desolate amid earthly things, yet preserve their chastity for God and do not fornicate with the demon. “I will bless abundantly,” that is, continually increasing them in virtues; “I will satisfy her poor,” the poor of Zion, “with bread,” that is, with spiritual nourishment.

“I will clothe her priests with salvation,” that is, with the conformity of Christ, the Savior, namely my Son. “And her lesser saints,” who imitate the priests, “will rejoice with rejoicing,” that is, they will possess such great joy that it can in no way be taken away from them.

“There,” that is, in that Zion, “I will bring forth,” that is, I will extend at the future judgment, “the horn of David,” that is, the heights of Christ himself, revealing his power to all. And meanwhile “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” namely John and the other heralds who would prepare the way for the Lord.

I will clothe his priests with salvation, “but I will clothe his enemies with shame,” that is, with disgrace, when they descend into eternal fire. “But upon him,” Christ, “my sanctification will blossom,” because his sanctification and glory will never wither.

## ON PSALM CXXXII. TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Behold, how good.” This psalm has both a subject and a degree: the Prophet’s subject is love of neighbor, which he commends in several ways. He intends to invite us to ascend this degree, without which we cannot reach the heavenly Jerusalem.

It is as though he said: You, brothers, who have been gathered through Christ’s merit and have become Zion, “behold” what remains for us: “to dwell together” as “brothers,” that is, to show one another fraternal charity. He chose to commend fraternal love rather than the love between a father and sons, or some similar relationship, because the love between brothers is greatest in equality. By saying “to dwell together,” he does not merely urge us to live in one physical place, although it is also good to dwell together locally. Rather, he understands as dwelling together any people who are diverse and distant, including persons who serve one another through their different offices and tend toward unity, bound together by the bond of the same faith and love. Thus the greater should not say to the lesser, “I do not need your help,” but they should pray for one another, and the others should fulfill their duties with love. Let the peasant feed the cleric, and likewise the others. You ought to dwell together, because it is “good,” that is, useful: by the example of those who dwell well, many gain for themselves the benefit of good dwelling. And how good is it? Certainly infinitely so. And how “pleasant,” that is, how sweet and delightful? Likewise, infinitely so.

I rightly say that it is pleasant for brothers to dwell together, “like ointment on the head, which descends into the beard, the beard of Aaron.”

“It” also “descends to the edge of his garment.” He introduces the likeness of ointment because the flesh is especially delighted and comforted by ointment. He mentions Aaron because he was the first anointed priest, and his anointing was so abundant that it flowed down into his beard and onto his outer garments. This likeness is mystical: by the ointment on the head is signified the Holy Spirit, who was in Christ, our head, in whom the Holy Spirit dwelt without measure. From that head he descends into the beard, that is, into strong men, and, by adhering closely to the head, especially into the apostles, who are the beard—not of just anyone, but of Aaron, that is, of Christ, who is signified by Aaron because of the priestly office, and also according to the interpretation of the name: Aaron is interpreted as “mountainous,” whereas Christ always dwelt on a mountain and at the greatest height of virtues.

Or, “into the beard” means into virile and wise men, who are signified by the beard. And that ointment does not descend from our head only into the beard, but also onto the edge of his garment, that is, onto the last saint who will ever exist in the Church. The Holy Spirit will descend from the same head of ours, whose garment is called his faithful people because they honor him as garments honor their master. Through this likeness he wishes it to be understood that such concord and such common dwelling bestow the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in our body.

And truly it is so pleasant to dwell together “like the dew of Hermon, which”—the dew is not entirely the same as that which is on Hermon, but similar to it—“descends upon Mount Zion.” It is as though he said: Just as dew, that sweetest moisture, makes that mountain, Hermon, grow green and produce fruit, so Zion, dwelling together in this way, makes the faithful fruitful.

Yet something is also understood in this likeness. By dew spiritual grace is understood. By Hermon, which is interpreted as “anathema,” we understand the Gentiles, who were once accursed and separated from God; spiritual grace nourishes them, pierces their hearts, and leads them to the faith. And it makes them Zion: once made Zion, it nourishes them and makes them produce good fruits. Through this likeness he wishes it to be understood that those who were once Hermon and separated from God become Zion, that is, the Church beholding God, through dwelling together in unanimity.

Having given these likenesses, he sets forth the reason why people should dwell together. It is as though he said: It is therefore good to dwell together, “because there,” that is, in harmonious dwelling, “the Lord commanded” that there should be “blessing,” an increase of virtues, “and life forever,” that is, eternally.

## ON PSALM CXXXIII. TITLE: A Song of Degrees

“Behold, now.” This psalm likewise has both a subject and a degree, to which we rightly ascend through love of neighbor. “For if we do not love the brother whom we see, how will we love God whom we do not see? (1 John 4).” In the first part he shows that God must be loved both in praise and in action. In the second, which begins, “May the Lord bless you from Zion,” he expresses his wish for blessing upon those who love the Lord. He intends to invite us to ascend this degree, in which the completion of all the others will be found.

[Col. 0652A] It is as though he admonished us in this way: Brothers, since you already abide in love, “behold,” complete what remains for you, namely, “bless the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord for having made you what you are in this age. The words of this praise are set forth in the following psalm, “Alleluia.” Do this “now,” that is, without delay. Nor do I admonish just anyone, because “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15), “but all you servants of the Lord,” that is, you who serve the Lord in love, bless the Lord.

You servants, bless him—not those who serve for an hour, but those who stand, that is, serve as soldiers perseveringly, “in the house of the Lord.” And you also who are “in the courts,” that is, in the entrance of “the house of our God”—even the imperfect and the newly converted—praise the Lord.

[Col. 0652B] After urging them to praise, he also urges them to act well. It is as though he said: I urge you not only to bless, but also to “lift up your hands,” that is, raise your works, “in the holy places” of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, to God himself. Do not perform works for human praise like hypocrites, or give alms from what you have seized; direct your works to the Lord with a pure intention. “Lift them up,” I say, “in the nights,” that is, throughout this whole life, in which we are always in the darkness of ignorance, so that through your good works you may be worthy to be led from these darknesses into the true light. And always “bless the Lord,” that is, praise him also because he has allowed you to act well.

“May he bless.” The second part. Having spoken up to this point to the servants of God in the plural, he now turns to a singular person to show that unity must be preserved in the Church. Continuation: “You, man, bless the Lord, and may the Lord bless,” that is, multiply “you” with his gifts. The Lord, I say, who comes “from Zion,” who was born from Judah, whose blessing is great, because although he was great, he is nevertheless the same one “who made heaven and earth.”

## ON PSALM CXXXIV. TITLE: Alleluia

“Praise the name.” The Prophet’s subject here is praise of the Lord. In the first part he urges us to praise the Lord, presupposing many of his great works through which he appears worthy of praise. In the second, which begins, “House of Israel, bless the Lord,” he urges all the orders of the faithful together to praise God. His intention is to exhort us to sing “Alleluia” to the Lord and to encourage continual praise of the one who granted us the degrees mentioned above.

It is as though he said: You who have received the preceding degrees, “praise the name of the Lord,” that is, make the Lord worthy to be named. Nor do I admonish just anyone, but you: “servants, praise the Lord.”

You who are such, “who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God,” you who are such, “praise the Lord, because the Lord is good”—said antonomastically, he is good in himself and makes others good—“sing praises to his name, because it is sweet,” pleasant, and delightful to sing praise to him.

[Col. 0653A] You ought also to sing praise to him because “the Lord chose Jacob,” that is, the wrestler against vices, “as his possession,” so that all things might be possessed by God with joy. Or, “for himself,” that is, for his service. But he chose “Israel,” that is, the man who sees God face to face in the life to come, not so that he might now wrestle against vices, but as his possession, that is, so that he might possess him with himself, placed in joy.

Praise him also “because” the “Lord is great,” that is, almighty. And believe that he is great, because “I have known” it through the Holy Spirit. And this same “God of ours” is “above all gods” whom he himself established—not only above the false gods of the nations, but even above the angels and other gods.

[Col. 0653B] And truly he is above all those gods, because “whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea,” navigable and passable, “and in all the abysses,” as in the Ocean.

He presents certain wonders that he performed on earth. These include: “Bringing clouds from the end of the earth.” All this can be read literally, but it can also be read allegorically. Thus he brought forth clouds, that is, holy preachers, from the end of the earth, that is, from the most insignificant class of this age. The prophet Amos, for example, was taken from guarding sheep, as were Peter and many others. Likewise, he made “lightnings,” that is, the threatening declarations of their preaching, “into rain,” that is, fruitful teaching, insofar as concerns those who received their teaching well.

[Col. 0653C] He did these things, “who brings forth winds,” that is, the holy apostles, rushing most swiftly throughout the whole world, “from his treasuries,” that is, from the fullness of wisdom and knowledge with which he had filled them. He “struck down the firstborn,” that is, original sins, “of Egypt,” that is, of the world itself, because this world always remains in the darkness of ignorance. He struck them “from man,” that is, from the rational and wise person, “to beast,” that is, to brutish people, because in the wise as well as in others he killed original sins through the waters of baptism.

“And he sent signs,” that is, lesser miracles, “and wonders,” that is, greater ones, “in your midst, Egypt,” that is, in the midst of the world. “In the midst,” because they were manifest to everyone. He sent them, I say, “against Pharaoh,” that is, against the destroyer, namely the devil, “and all his servants,” that is, his ministers, namely the lesser devils, because through those signs some people were taken away from the devil’s power.

He sent them, “who struck down many nations,” that is, the multitude of vices, “and killed powerful kings,” that is, demons, depriving them of their power. They were powerful because they were able to drive people into great crimes.

These kings are “Sihon, king of the Amorites.” Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes.” For the devil transforms himself into an angel of light and deceives people through hypocrisy. The Amorites are interpreted as “those who make bitter.” By Sihon the demon is understood who tries to deceive the eyes of human beings and is king of all who make life bitter through sins.

“And” he also struck “Og, king of Bashan.” Og is interpreted as “confinement,” and Bashan as “confusion.” By this we understand the demon who confines those confused in sin, preventing them from finding the way of salvation. And he struck “all the kingdoms of Canaan.” Canaan is interpreted as “descent,” and by this we understand those who decline from good to evil.

“And he gave their land as an inheritance,” that is, the heavenly homeland, which the demons lost through their pride. He gave it “as an inheritance to Israel,” not to just any Israel, but “to his people.”

And because you have done all these things, O “Lord, your name,” that is, your fame and praise, will be “forever.” And “your memorial,” that is, your words, O Lord, which continually bring you to our remembrance, will be “from generation to generation,” that is, until the eternal day, because heaven and earth will pass away, but your words will not pass away.

It will not pass away, and this memorial will be eternal, “because the Lord will judge,” by blinding “his people” through his just judgment; and among “his servants,” who are faithful to him, he “will be entreated,” that is, he will be worthy to be entreated.

## “Images.” The Second Part

Continuation: So great is our God, who performs such great wonders. But “the images of the nations” cannot do this, because they are “gold and silver, the work of human hands.” In this those who worship them appear foolish: they venerate as creator what they themselves produced.

“They have mouths, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see.”

“They have ears, and they will not hear,” as we explained above. “At the departure of Israel.” These instruments do not perform their functions because “there is no Spirit,” the Holy Spirit, “in their mouth.”

“Let those who make them become like them, and” also “all who trust in them.”

“House of Israel, bless.” Let what was stated above come upon those who worship idols. But “house of Israel,” you “bless the Lord,” namely, the universal Church. He divides the universal Church into parts, adding: and also “house of Aaron,” that is, the assembly of priests, “bless the Lord.”

“And also house of Levi,” that is, the assembly of ministers, “bless the Lord.” What is meant by each group? All of you “who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”

I urge you others to bless, and I for my part will bless, saying: “Blessed is the Lord,” the same one who was born “from Zion” and “who dwells in Jerusalem,” that is, in the Vision of Peace. Alleluia.

## ON PSALM CXXXV. TITLE: Alleluia

“Give thanks to the Lord.” The Prophet’s subject here is the Lord’s mercy. In the first part he shows his power, namely, that through his mercy he created the whole world, prefacing an exhortation to praise. In the second part, which begins, [Col. 0655A] “He who struck Egypt,” he shows how many mercies the Lord bestowed upon the Israelite people. In the third, which begins, “And he gave their land as an inheritance,” he shows what benefits the Lord bestows upon the Christian people. Through all this he intends to persuade us that “Alleluia” must be sung to the Lord.

It is as though he said: All you nations, “give thanks to the Lord” with both kinds of confession, because he is “good” in himself and makes others good. Likewise, for this reason give thanks, because “his mercy” is “forever”: in this life he pardons sins through mercy and grants many spiritual goods; in the other life he rewards the faithful far beyond their merits.

Likewise, “give thanks to the God of gods,” that is, to the one who is creator of angels and of the other saints whom he himself justifies and builds up, “because his mercy is forever.” He adds this same phrase to each verse, indicating that everything has been accomplished solely through God’s mercy.

“Give thanks to the Lord of lords,” that is, because he rules over all the lords and princes of this life. At the beginning and the end he places “Give thanks,” and throughout the middle we may also repeat it, saying as follows:

Give thanks also to him “who alone does great wonders,” that is, without anyone’s assistance; he also made the ministers themselves.

Give thanks, I say, to him “who made the heavens.” This too is part of his wonders. He says “heavens” in the plural because he understands there to be several heavens, although their number has not been defined for us. He did not make those heavens according to any model, but by “understanding,” in accordance with what he arranged in his mind; rather, he made them through his wisdom. From this we understand that those heavens were made beautifully and perfectly.

Give thanks also to him “who established the earth,” literally, “upon,” that is, beside “the waters,” because the Ocean flows all around it. Or by earth we understand the Church, which God established upon the waters, that is, the floods of this age; or upon the waters of baptism, so that the Church might overcome these floods and never be submerged by them, just as the actual earth rises above the waters and is never submerged by them.

Give thanks to him “who made the great lights.” By this we can signify the holy angels, whom the Lord created in the greatest brightness.

[Col. 0655D] He explains those lights, saying: “He made the sun to rule the day.” The sun’s rule over the day is evident because it illuminates the air and provides us with light. Allegorically, by the sun we can understand wisdom, which illuminates the hearts of the faithful and makes a kind of day shine within them, namely knowledge of the Divinity itself.

He also made “the moon,” the material moon, “and the stars to rule the night.” By the moon we can understand the universal Church; by the stars, the Church’s various offices. The Church illuminates the night, that is, this world filled with errors and ignorance, just as the moon prepares light for the night.

## “He who struck.” The Second Part

For this reason also give thanks to him “who struck Egypt,” that is, this world, “with its firstborn,” that is, with its original vices and its other greater vices.

“He who led Israel out from its midst,” that is, once a man has become Israel, Egypt—namely, the darkness of this world—will no longer rule him, nor will original sins rule him.

He “led him out,” I say, “with a powerful hand,” that is, through a powerful and unconquerable action, “and with an outstretched arm,” that is, through the omnipotence from which the powerful action proceeded and through which it achieved its effect.

Give thanks also to him “who divided the Red Sea into divisions.” Literally, he speaks in the plural because there were twelve paths. By the Red Sea we understand baptism, which is red because it has been consecrated by Christ’s blood. The Lord divided it because for some it is unto life and for others unto condemnation, namely, for those who despise it, because in this way transgressors are found in greater number. He divided it “into divisions” because there the faithful begin the paths by which they hasten toward the Lord.

Or by the Red Sea we understand the world, which is called a sea because it is always in flux and full of every bitterness. It is called red because of the blood of the holy martyrs. He “divided it into divisions” because he gave different people different ways by which they might hurry through this world toward the Lord: one through fasting, another through almsgiving, others through other virtues.

“And he led Israel through its midst,” that is, through the midst of the sea, or through the midst of this world, because the man who had become Israel could not be hindered by any allurements of this world. Or, through the midst of baptism, because Israel was led out through the Catholic faith that he received in baptism.

“And he cast Pharaoh,” that is, the devil, “and his power,” that is, his ministers, “into the Red Sea,” that is, into baptism, in which each person is expelled from the devil’s power.

Praise him also, “who led his people” from virtue to virtue, “through the desert,” that is, through this world, through which the saints pass like pilgrims, hastening toward the true land of promise.

“He who struck down great kings,” that is, the great vices that lay in wait for them and wanted to obstruct their journey toward the heavenly kingdom.

“And killed powerful kings,” that is, those vices which, although they were not great in everyone, were nevertheless powerful in some for expulsion because of habit.

These powerful kings are “Sihon, king of the Amorites,”

“and Og, king of Bashan,” as explained above.

## The Third Part

“And he gave their land as an inheritance.”

The land previously given over to the vices of this age—to whom did he give it for cultivation? To those very same people. This is what follows: “as an inheritance to Israel his servant,” so that, having become Israel, they might now cast out the thorns from themselves and nourish good seed. Or, he gave Israel the heavenly land that the demons had possessed—not to just any Jew, but to his servant.

Understanding that the Prophet was one of those who possessed that inheritance, he says: He did all these things for us “because he remembered us,” as when he caused his Son to become incarnate, for example, “in our humiliation,” because we showed ourselves humble, recognizing that neither the natural law nor the written law was sufficient for us unto salvation.

And because he remembered us, therefore “he redeemed us,” giving the price of his Son’s blood, “from our enemies,” the demons, in whose power we were held captive.

Also confess to him, “who gives food,” that is, spiritual nourishment, “to all flesh,” that is, to the faithful of every nation. Or by “all flesh” let us understand every animal, for which God provides bodily food.

[Col. 0657B] And because he does all these things, therefore “confess to the God of heaven,” that is, to the one whom he previously called “God of gods.”

And likewise for this reason confess, since he himself rules over all the powerful. This is what he says: “Confess to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is everlasting.” By placing “Confess” at the beginning and at the end, he indicates to us that the whole psalm is occupied with the praise of that God himself. Alleluia.

## ON PSALM 136. TITLE: A Psalm of David concerning Jeremiah.

“By the rivers of Babylon.” This psalm belongs to David, and concerns one of the captivities of the inhabitants of Jerusalem; this captivity was brought about by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians. Another captivity, which he describes in the words, “O God, the nations have come” (Psalm 78), was brought about by Antiochus, king of those same Babylonians. The third—“Why, O God?” (Psalm 73)—was brought about by the Roman emperors Titus and Vespasian. Thus this is David’s psalm concerning Jeremiah and the Babylonian captivity; the other psalms belong to David alone.

Ezra, understanding that the prophet David lamented in this psalm the captivity of the citizens of Jerusalem, not so much bodily as spiritual, and that Jeremiah lamented the spiritual captivity together with the bodily one—which he saw and had prophesied to them as future—attached the following title, which is read in this way: This psalm of David, in which David laments the captivity of the citizens of Jerusalem, belongs to Jeremiah and concerns the Babylonian captivity, which Jeremiah lamented not only as bodily, since he saw it present, but also as spiritual, which he signified through the bodily captivity.

[Col. 0657D] The subject of this psalm is the citizens of Jerusalem held captive in Babylonia. For there are two opposing cities: one called Jerusalem, namely, the city of the faithful; the city called Babylonia is the city of all evil people. The city of the faithful is captive in this world to the Babylonians, that is, to evil people, who continually attack the faithful, and to demons, who never cease tempting the faithful. Righteous men also have another enemy, namely, their own flesh, which always fights against the inner man. Hence the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5).

In the first part he shows the citizens of Jerusalem placed in the captivity of Babylonia, yet never forgetting their homeland, namely, the Jerusalem above. In the second, which begins, “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom,” he prays for vengeance upon the enemies and says that he will avenge himself in part, namely, upon the daughter of Babylon, that is, upon his own flesh. His purpose is to admonish us to compassion, so that we may grieve over the evils of our neighbors, especially their spiritual evils, namely, the loss of the soul.

The prophet’s voice, not only in his own person but also in that of others, as though he were saying: Brothers, lament with us our captivity and that of our fellow citizens, because we, having been taken captive through the sin of our first parent by the devil in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of sins—are there. We are not merely now in the rivers of Babylon, that is, in the depths of vices, which submerge a person like any extremely swift river, but “by the rivers of Babylon,” that is, beside the great depth of vices, because we have so many enemies among the citizens of Babylon who wish to make us conform to their will that we are submerged in the depth of the Babylonians’ wickedness, yet we remain above it, because we do not consent to them.

And we, dwelling “there,” that is, among the Babylonians, “sat,” that is, we remained somewhat upright. For although we have endured miseries in this life, that is, in Babylon, and through the suggestions of the flesh have extended our hand there toward certain unlawful things, nevertheless, because we abstained from more serious offenses, we are said to have remained upright and to have sat. Therefore, when tempted, he used one word, “to sit”: if he had said “we stood,” it would have seemed presumptuous; but if he had said “we lay,” we would appear to have suffered ruin.

I say, “we sat and wept,” over the prolongation of our dwelling and the miseries that we endure. I say “we wept,” while we remembered you, O heavenly “Zion,” who are the true land of our promise.

Because we are weeping and dwell among pigs, therefore “we hung our instruments,” that is, we cease from the word of preaching. I say that we are “in the willows,” that is, among those who are fruitless and barren like willows. For the word of God ought not to be sown among pigs. And this is “in the midst of it,” namely, of Babylonia, that is, in the fullness of confusion, because we are surrounded on every side by the citizens of Babylon.

Therefore we hung them up, “because there,” that is, in this Babylon in which we are held captive, “they asked us for words of songs,” that is, of divine preaching, which was sweet to us, as a song is pleasant and entertaining to one who hears it, almost like a story. Those, I say, asked us—those “who led us captive,” that is, who cast us into sins, at times bringing us back into conformity with themselves.

Not only those who cast us into evil asked for the words of songs, but “those who carried us away,” that is, who caused us to be removed from the good, commanded us, saying: “Sing us a hymn,” as though they were saying to you who call this the praise of our God, “from the songs of Zion,” that is, from those praises which you sing in Zion, namely, in the Church.

[Col. 0659A] They urged us to sing, but because they were like strangers, dogs, and pigs, we did not sing to them in any way. This is expressed in the words: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord,” sowing the divine word, “in a foreign land?” He calls it a foreign land because, if the word of God is sown there, it does not bear fruit but is choked by the thorns of wickedness.

We shall not sing to those who are strangers; but, O heavenly Jerusalem, we have never forgotten you. Thus: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand,” that is, my good work, “be given over to forgetfulness” by God, that is, may I receive no reward from all my good deeds.

I do not merely say, “If I forget you, may these evils befall me,” but also, “If I do not remember you,” that is, if I do not always keep you in present memory, “may my tongue cling to my jaws,” that is, may I become mute.

And also, “If I do not set you,” Jerusalem, “at the beginning of my joy,” that is, if you are not the beginning and cause of all my joy, may my tongue likewise cling to my jaws.

“Remember.” The second part. Because I make Jerusalem the beginning of my joy, therefore, O Lord, remember those who persecute us, in order to judge them. This is expressed as follows: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom,” that is, the earthly or blood-related people who shed our blood and wish to lead us toward the desire for earthly things. Then I say, “Remember the sons on the day of Jerusalem,” that is, when the glory of the faithful will appear, namely, on the day of judgment.

Those who are the sons of Edom “say,” not in words but by their deeds: “Empty, empty,” that is, completely empty out whatever justice is in them. I say, “empty” all of it “down to the foundation,” which is “in her,” namely, empty out what appears in them. The foundation of this Jerusalem is Christ, or faith; so long as it remains, this city cannot be destroyed. In this they show themselves foolish, because, when the foundation remains, everything else will immediately be rebuilt.

“Daughter.” We pray that you may avenge us upon the sons of Edom, and we ourselves avenge ourselves in part. Thus: O “daughter of Babylon,” that is, our flesh, born in confusion and always urging confusion—and therefore “wretched”—blessed is the one “who repays you with the repayment that you repaid us,” that is, who, in return for the affliction in sins to which you continually urge the inner man, will inflict affliction upon you by fasting, keeping watch, and by other forms of mortifying you, the flesh, daughter of Babylon.

And also blessed is the one “who will seize your little ones,” that is, the suggestions of sins which you generate in a person. They are called “little ones” while they arise but are not carried through into action. Blessed is the one who “will seize” them so that they do not proceed as far as action, “and will dash them,” that is, suppress and crush them, “against the rock,” that is, against Christ, namely, through remembrance and conformity to Christ.

[Col. 0660A] For when evil suggestions and those unlawful impulses creep in, we ought to bring back to memory how courageously Christ acted in his life and conform ourselves to him, so that we may be wholly able to extinguish those impulses within us.

## ON PSALM 137. TITLE: A Psalm belonging to David himself.

“I will confess.” The prophet who speaks here has as his subject the liberation accomplished through Christ’s coming. Note that this psalm is read as having possessed extraordinary holiness in the Old Testament. For it is read in Chronicles that, when those singing this psalm were in the tabernacle, God’s mercy surrounded them like smoke of marvelous fragrance. Now, however, it is believed to possess no lesser holiness, since, if it is sung purely, God’s mercy is immediately present to those who sing it.

In the first part he promises to praise God and to act well, placed amid the troubles of this life. In the second, which begins, “Let all kings confess to you, O Lord,” he urges others to praise God for another reason, the same reason for which he himself praises him, namely, in consideration of liberation. Here his purpose is evident. For he intends to urge us to rejoice and praise God for the liberation accomplished through Christ, just as elsewhere he urged us to grieve over the Babylonian captivity.

As though he were saying: You, brothers, confess to the Lord after my example, because I am not ungrateful to you, O “Lord,” for your benefits. I will always “confess to you” with a confession of praise, “with my whole heart,” because “you have heard the words of my mouth,” since you sent your Son to become incarnate in order to free us from the power of the devil, from which we continually cry out to you.

And I will not merely confess, but also “sing praise to you,” that is, I will act well for your praise. And this will be “in the sight of the angels,” that is, according to their good pleasure. For now the angels, knowing that we are their fellow citizens, rejoice in our good works and assist us.

“And I will worship toward your holy temple,” that is, toward Christ’s humanity itself. I will venerate that humanity with the veneration that is due and complete, and I will adore the divinity dwelling specially in him. “And” also “I will confess to your name,” that is, I will praise you.

“For your mercy and your truth,” because you accomplish redemption through mercy, and through Christ fulfill the promises that you had made through the prophets; or, this refers to the mercy that you show to the human race in the present life, “and” to “your truth” that will be fulfilled when you reward your faithful according to what you promised. Mercy and truth, I say, are exhibited because you “magnified,” that is, made great, “your holy one,” the unique one, namely Christ, “above every name,” that is, above everything that can be named. Hence Paul says: “He gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 1).

Although this righteous man had received liberation at Christ’s coming, nevertheless, because he sees evils threatening, he prays for assistance against them. The continuation is as follows: Because you are so great, therefore, O Lord, “hear me on whatever day,” that is, at whatever time, “I call upon you.” When he says “all day,” he names the whole time of the righteous person, because the righteous always walk in true knowledge and illumination.

I say, hear me, and I am secure, because you “will multiply,” that is, will give multiplied, “strength in my soul,” by which I may be able to resist the evils that press upon me.

“Let them confess.” The second part. Here he reveals his purpose. And because I will confess to you, therefore, after my example, O “Lord, let all the kings of the earth confess to you,” that is, let all those praise you who rule their earthly nature well. And unless they have confessed, they will be without excuse, “because” they “heard all the words of your mouth,” which you commanded through your Son to be observed, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and so forth” (Psalm 18).

And let these kings, placed “in the ways of the Lord,” that is, in his commandments, “sing,” that is, announce the Lord’s praises to others. Therefore let them sing, “how great is the glory of the Lord,” which has been set before Jews and Gentiles alike.

And truly his glory is great, “because the Lord is exalted” above every creature. “And,” although he is so exalted, he will not despise his faithful, but rather “regards the humble,” that is, he looks upon the humble with the eye of mercy, granting them assistance and increases of virtue, and so forth.

And when the proud person might say: Since he regards only the humble, I can therefore sin safely, because he will not see me, he removes this objection as follows: He regards the humble “and also knows the proud,” that is, those who are high, but he knows them “from afar,” because even here he withdraws his grace from them, and at the judgment will separate them from his own, saying: “Depart from me, you accursed,” and so forth.

That he regards the humble is apparent in me, because “if I walk in the midst of tribulation,” you, God, “will revive me,” that is, you will make me receive those tribulations with a joyful spirit. “And” also “against the anger of my enemies,” that is, against the enemies who do evil to me out of anger, not because I deserve it, “you stretched out your hand,” that is, your operation, because you have taken vengeance on some and converted others. “And your right hand,” that is, your reconciliation, “saved me,” that is, it preserved me unharmed from conformity to them.

“The Lord” has already stretched out his hand against the enemies, and still “will repay on my behalf” vengeance upon the enemies. But this righteous man, moved by compassion for his neighbors, turns toward God himself, praying for God’s mercy upon them, and says:

O “Lord, your mercy is forever,” because you have shown mercy to the whole world. Therefore, O Lord, “do not despise the works of your hands,” that is, human beings themselves, who are called your special work. Do not despise them, that is, do not withdraw your grace from them here, on account of which they would be condemned in the other life.

## ON PSALM 138. TITLE: To the end, a Psalm of David.

“Lord, you have tested me.” This psalm properly concerns the true David, who speaks here. I say that the psalm directs us “to the end,” that is, toward conformity to Christ himself.

In this psalm Christ is the subject according to both natures. It touches briefly upon his divinity, but treats at greater length of his humanity. For it shows him enduring lowly things in the manner of other human beings, so that by his humility he might prove his true humanity. It also shows him undergoing the highest things, such as the resurrection, and illuminating the darkness of this world through himself, along with other great deeds, so that by these he might prove himself not merely human.

The same point is expressed elsewhere: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40). The prophet wished to proclaim this concerning Christ against the sects of certain heretics who denied that he was truly human; he presents his exaltation against the Jews, who considered him merely human and not God.

In the first part a summary is given, which he later demonstrates through the exposition of the psalm: namely, God’s knowledge concerning Christ, made wondrous through Christ himself. In the second, which begins, “Where shall I go from your spirit?” he shows such great power of God that no one can escape it, and on account of which the darkness of the world could not remain hidden; rather, through that power Christ illuminated the darkness of the world.

In the third, which begins, “I will confess to you, for you have been terribly magnified,” he shows himself praising God for the benefits that God confers upon him. In the fourth, which begins, “But to me your friends have been exceedingly honored,” he shows that the good are to be exalted and the wicked cast down and condemned. At the end he adds a kind of conclusion when he says, “Test me, O God.”

By describing such exaltation in Christ, he intends to persuade us that Christ is worthy of honor, so that we may render him the honor due to him.

The Son’s voice to the Father: “Lord” Father, you “have tested me.” This does not mean that anything concerning Christ or anything else had been uncertain to God the Father. Rather, when he says “you have tested me,” he means: you have shown me to others as tested through many trials, as when he was tempted by the devil (Matthew 4) and in no way consented to him, and confirmed himself to be truthful through his own death.

“You have tested me,” I say, “and known me,” that is, you have held me as one known and pleasing to you. “You,” Lord, “have known,” that is, approved, “my sitting,” that is, my rest, namely, my death, in which I rested from the tumult of this world. “And” you have known “my resurrection,” because you both accomplished it and held it pleasing to yourself.

In this verse, when he says that he was tested as other human beings are tested, and says that he has a sitting, that is, a death, he speaks of lowly things concerning himself and signifies to us his true humanity. But when he names his resurrection, he speaks of exalted things concerning himself. Thus, in this verse the summary of the whole psalm is touched upon briefly.

Note that here he uses an artificial order: he begins first with glorification, then with resurrection and passion, and finally with the womb, that is, the incarnation.

You have tested me, I say, and “known” me; you have also “understood my thoughts from afar,” that is, long before I thought them, since from eternity you also “searched out,” that is, fully knew, “my paths,” namely, my hidden works and the hidden things of my will, “and my cord,” that is, my judgment, namely, the discernment that I possessed between good and evil.

You searched me out, that is, you knew me perfectly, just as things fully searched out are known completely. Another translation has “my direction.” By “cord” we can understand direction and right judgment, because by a carpenter’s cord and other workers’ cords they direct their work.

And you not only knew, but also “foresaw all my ways,” that is, all my manifest works, long before they came to be. Therefore I say “you understood, you foresaw,” and similar expressions, “because there is no speech” without a reality corresponding to it.

Hence another translation says, “There is no deceit on my tongue.” When he says that he did not sin with his tongue, where it is more serious to stand firm, he implies that he did not fall in other matters either, and thereby that he pleased God well in every respect.

It is as though he had said: When you searched out the thoughts of Adam, our first parent, his paths, judgment, and ways, and those of his sons, and found them deceitful, they displeased you. But when you knew me completely, you found nothing in me at which your eye could take offense.

“Behold,” why should I enumerate everything individually? “You, Lord, have known all things last,” namely, those concerning my humility, “and” all my “ancient things,” such as those concerning my divinity, which from eternity you possess consubstantial with yourself. “You formed me” according to my humanity, and “upon me,” the formed human being, “you placed your hand,” that is, your Word, namely, your Son, through whom you act; you clothed my humanity with him.

I say, you formed me, and I made your knowledge wondrous. This is what follows: “Your knowledge,” that is, your law, namely, evangelical teaching, in which your will is manifested, “has been made” wondrous “from me” for human beings, that is, through my preaching and action. It is wondrous because through it they know that forgiveness of sins is accomplished through Jesus, that eternal life is given to the righteous, and everlasting punishments to the ungodly. Therefore they marvel at that knowledge.

It has not only been made wondrous through me, but through me it has also “been strengthened”; it does not waver, but has been so firmly established in human hearts that they cannot be moved away from it even by the danger of death.

I made it wondrous in this way and strengthened it; “and” nevertheless, according to my humanity, “I cannot” be made equal “to that knowledge,” that is, to God himself, in whom knowledge is nothing other than divinity itself.

## “Where shall I go?” The second part.

I rightly say that I cannot be made equal to that knowledge, because such power is present in it that no one can escape it. This is what he says: “Where shall I go,” removed “from your Spirit,” that is, from the Holy Spirit? “And where shall I flee,” removed “from your face,” that is, from your present and manifest knowledge?

By “face” he understands here the person of the Father. He calls it “face” because everything is present to him as though placed before his face.

Nowhere can we escape his face, because “if I ascend into heaven,” as he truly ascended, “you are there; if I descend into hell,” where his human soul truly descended together with his divinity, “you are present.”

“If I take my wings,” that is, the works of divine power which I set aside from the time when I myself was in the power of the Jews, because I neither performed miracles nor preached, “at dawn,” that is, in the resurrection which took place at dawn, “and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea,” that is, at the extremity of the age, no longer living a mortal life—for “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Romans 6).

That he would live outside the life of the world he signified when he stood on the shore while the disciples were sailing on the sea (Matthew 14). This signified in them that they were still living the life of the world. Before Christ rose, while the disciples were sailing, he himself walked above the sea on foot, signifying in himself that he was still living in the storm-tossed world.

If I take my wings in this way, you are present, and truly you are present there, namely, so that I may dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, that is, so that I may be outside mortal life. “Your hand,” that is, your operation, “will lead me,” and will also make me persevere in immortality. And this is expressed as follows: “And your right hand,” that is, your Son, namely, your Word united to me, “will hold me.”

I say that the right hand will hold me, “and” I also “said,” that is, deliberated, “perhaps darkness.” This is ironic, as though he were saying: Since his power is so great and his right hand holds me in this way, it is foolish for anyone to think that the darkness, that is, the darkness of this life, can trample me.

The darkness will not “trample him”; rather, “night,” that is, people full of ignorance and sins in this life, or even the dead held in the death of hell, will become “my illumination,” that is, illuminated by me, and will be “in my delights,” that is, in paradise. For paradise is interpreted as “delights.” He led those whom he found in the underworld into paradise. Those who are living are already in paradise by hope, although not yet in reality.

Therefore the illumination of night will come to be, because you, God, will illuminate the darkness and the night. This is what follows: “For the darkness,” that is, those who are dark because of ignorance, “will not be darkened by you,” that is, you will not allow them to remain dark, but rather they will be illuminated. “And” also “night,” that is, those who are obscure and ruined in sins, “will be illuminated” by you, and thereafter will be “like day,” that is, like a wise person who has never remained in such a depth of sins.

I say, “night will be illuminated,” and “as its darkness is, so also is its light,” because to the extent that some recognize their sins, to that extent they will receive illumination. Hence Augustine says: “To the extent that a person recognizes, to that extent God forgives.”

All these things will result from this: “because you possessed my reins,” that is, my strength and direction; namely, you made me strong and free from sin, and directed, not inclined toward unlawful things.

I do not merely say “you possessed” me, but also “you received me from my mother’s womb.” You willed that I be conceived without the pleasure of the flesh, and afterward preserved me without sin.

## “I will confess to you.” The third part.

And because you so possessed my reins, illuminated the darkness through me, and accomplished the other things, therefore “I will confess to you,” that is, I will praise you. And rightly so, “because you have been magnified,” that is, you appear great, and this “terribly,” with respect to the wicked, who in judgment await their future condemnation.

You have been magnified because “your works,” concerning the restoration of the human race and the other things that you accomplish, “are wondrous,” and “my soul will know” those works “exceedingly,” that is, very greatly. Here he attacks those who think that Christ possessed only a human body and did not receive a human soul.

Your works are known not only to me, but also to those below. This is what follows: “My bone,” that is, the Church, “which” bone “you made” at some time “in secret,” that is, in the time of the prophets, who through mere figures judged the body of Christ to be the Church—this bone of mine “was not hidden from you,” because you did not conceal it; rather, you made manifest what belonged to my bones.

Or “in secret,” that is, in baptism, the consecration of the Lord’s body, and the other sacraments of the Church. “And my substance” was not hidden “in the lower parts of the earth,” that is, among the Gentiles, who are lower than the Jews because previously they were without the law and without the worship of God.

For the Gentiles know Christ’s substance and believe him to be true God and true man. That the Church is called Christ’s bone is figured in the creation of the woman from the first man (Genesis 2). Just as a bone was taken from the man to create the woman, and the place of the bone was filled with flesh, so Christ bestowed his bone upon his Church, that is, his strength and divinity, because he made all his faithful sharers in the Holy Spirit, having himself become a participant in their humanity.

Hence the Apostle, when discussing man and woman, says: “This is indeed a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

My substance was not hidden in the lower parts, but “my imperfect thing,” that is, the completion of my body, which will exist in the other life and is not yet perfect, “your eyes saw,” that is, you alone knew it. And all those who, although currently absent, will complete your body in eternal life “will be written in your book,” that is, they will remain indelibly in your eternal memory, and they will be made equal: “days will be formed,” shining and possessing divine knowledge.

Or, as another translation has it, “gods will be formed,” or “the gods,” namely, from the divinity that will form them from darkness into light. Or they will be formed, “and no one” will be formed “among them,” because no one will be able to confer justice upon them. Hence the Apostle says: “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3).

Alternatively, by “imperfect thing” we can understand what is still lacking from Christ’s body, unless that person belongs to the Church. Or, if “my imperfect thing” means those who in this life will complete my body, then “your eyes saw” them, that is, you foresaw them. And just as you foresaw, so you will fulfill it, because all those whom you foresaw for that perfection will be written in your book, that is, in your memory.

Or they will be written in me, who am the book, according to whose conformity others are written, and no one is among them; for no one says, “I am Paulinus,” or “I am Petrinus,” but “I am a Christian.”

## “But to me.” The fourth part.

Those whom you foresaw will be written. But those who are already “your friends,” O “God,” such as the apostles, “have already been honored,” and this “exceedingly,” that is, very greatly. And this is “to me,” that is, to my honor, because through me comes their honor, and “their dominion,” that is, the power which they possess over the kings of the earth, “has been exceedingly strengthened,” because it still appears in the successors of Peter and the other apostles.

[Col. 0666B] I say, “their dominion has been strengthened,” and they are not few; rather, “I will number them, and” they “will be multiplied” in number and virtues “beyond the sand,” so that they may be far more worthy than the sand, that is, than fruitless human beings.

This multiplication will result from the fact that I “rose,” and yet “am still with you,” hidden as I was before, because my power is not yet manifest to all; ultimately it will be known to all at the judgment.

Note the promise made to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven,” and so forth (Genesis 22 and 26). By the fruitful stars we understand those who, although fewer in number, are greater in virtue and in God’s benefits. By the sand we understand the sterile.

[Col. 0666C] Your friends have been honored, and so forth. But, O “God, if you kill,” that is, condemn, “sinners,” saying to them, “Men of blood, depart from me,” because of their dissimilarity—for one can approach you only through similarity.

Or in this way: Truly I am with you, because I also give life to those whom you give life to, and I kill those whom you kill. This is expressed in the words, “if you kill.” By this he marks Christ as equal to the Father.

Therefore depart, “because you say in thought” the following: “Let those Christians take away from us their cities,” that is, their assemblies, those who dwell “in vanity,” that is, uselessly, because they worship clouds and empty things.

If you kill in this way, I too will kill. This is what follows: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?” that is, do I not withdraw grace from them? Certainly I hate them, “and” also “I wasted away over your enemies,” that is, I failed through grief on account of the enemies who attacked you and your name.

“With perfect hatred I hated them.” He hates perfectly who hates what is evil and loves what is from God, namely, the creature. And because I hated them in this way, just as they are your enemies, so also “they became enemies to me,” holding me in hatred.

Or, if the reading is, “Let them take their cities in vanity,” let us explain it as follows: If you, God, kill sinners in their sins and convert them to justice, saying to those obstinate in evil, “Men of blood, depart from me,” because they say in thought—that is, murmur against me—if you kill them in this way, then let those who have been killed receive their cities, that is, their former sects, in vanity, because they will consider vain the things they previously loved. You say to those obstinate in evil, “Depart,” and do I not hate those same people? And so forth.

This is the conclusion from what has been said, as though he were saying: Since you have tested me in this way, and these good things will result from it, therefore, O “God, test me,” that is, show me as tested through certain temptations; “and know my heart,” that is, make my will known; “and question me,” that is, make my will be examined through the greatest torments, namely, through interrogations; “and know my paths,” that is, make my narrow and hidden ways known and approved.

“And” in this way “see whether there is a way of iniquity in me,” that is, whether the traces of the devil appear in me. He says this by comparison: just as the tracks of a serpent do not appear on stone but in dust, so the traces of the devil did not appear in a strong man, namely, Christ, however much he was tempted by the devil.

“And,” when you see that there is no iniquity in me, “lead me in the eternal way,” that is, into eternity, which has been made passable through me.

## ON PSALM 139. TITLE: To the end, a Psalm of David.

“Deliver me.” The prophet’s voice, or that of some righteous person, not only in his own person but also in that of the Church, and it directs us toward the end.

The subject is the Church itself, placed amid dangers both external and internal. In the first part he prays to be delivered from external dangers, which demons cause by tempting or which their agents inflict by doing evil, as well as from the tongues of heretics.

In the second, which begins, “I said to the Lord: You are my God,” he prays to be delivered from internal dangers, namely, from inward desire, so that the tinder of sin, stirred by the devil’s prompting, may not be able to dominate him.

In the third, which begins, “The head of their circuit,” he announces the condemnation of those who persecute the Church and the reward of those who patiently endure their evils. Through this he intends to admonish us to courage, so that with a manly spirit we may resist temptations both outwardly and inwardly, secure in the knowledge that we shall dwell in the Lord’s presence.

Before setting forth the dangers, he asks for deliverance, saying: “Deliver me, O Lord,” that is, make the evils cease, “from an evil man,” that is, from the devil, whom he calls a man because, although he was created a spirit, he made himself muddy earth through perverse desires.

Also, deliver me “from an unjust man,” that is, from a human agent of the devil, who is called unjust because he sins against his neighbor without cause. He calls him a “man” because such people are powerful and strong in this world. From such a man, “deliver me,” that is, make the evils which they inflict upon me cease.

He shows the external dangers from which he asked to be delivered, as though he were saying: It is necessary that you deliver me because the evil man and the unjust man have plotted against me. They “carry out what they have devised in their heart,” that is, they have investigated iniquities with great care. And they not only devised them, but also “prepared battles” against me, and this “all day,” that is, continually, because the Church is never without the attack of the devil and his agents.

He shows what kind of battles these are: heretics persecute the Church with their wicked doctrines. Therefore he says: “They sharpened their tongues like serpents.” They prepared sharp and carefully devised doctrines by which they could quickly pierce the hearts of their hearers, just as serpents send forth venom through their tongues, because their words were poisonous and harmful like the bite of a serpent.

Nor is it surprising that their words were poisonous, because “under their lips,” that is, beneath their tongues, namely, in their hearts, there was “the venom of asps,” that is, hatred and envy against the Church. These things are said to be beneath their tongues because what lies hidden in the heart is made manifest through the tongue. The venom was “of asps,” that is, incurable, because it could not be removed from them by God’s preachers, just as snake-charmers cannot draw venom from an asp.

I say “deliver me,” so that the evils may cease. Meanwhile, while the evils are being inflicted, “guard me from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of the sinner,” that is, of the devil, who is the cause of every sin.

“And from unjust men deliver me, O Lord,” so that the evils which they inflict upon me may cease.

“Those” wicked men “thought to trip up my steps,” that is, my good works, as though they were making a pit in the road into which they might hurl me. A heretic trips up a step when he imposes his perverse interpretation upon someone who possesses a right understanding of Scripture, and thereby leads that faithful person astray. Likewise, “the proud,” such as heretics who presume upon themselves and understand themselves to be justified by their own power, “hid”—that is, secretly prepared—“a snare for me,” namely, a concealed deception.

I say that “they hid a snare,” and they made it manifold and strong.
