He says this: “and they stretched out ropes,” that is, twisted opinions, interconnected with one another, by which they might bind people firmly, as with ropes. They “stretched them out,” that is, prepared them extensively and in many forms, so that if I escaped one of their opinions, I might fall into others. “They stretched them out,” I say, “into a snare,” so that through those ropes they might ensnare me, and this “beside the way,” not on the way—that is, if they can turn the faithful person aside from the straight path, then they can ensnare him; but while he is on the way, he is not caught by their snares. And when they could not ensnare me by hidden persuasions, “they placed a stumbling-block before me,” that is, an open attack by which they might make me conform to themselves. This too was beside the way, because no attack can harm the righteous person while he walks on the straight path.

“I said to the Lord.” The second part. Here there is a diapsalm. And because you preserved me amid so many dangers, therefore “I said to the Lord,” that is, I prayed to the Lord in this way, because “you are my God,” that is, the one whom I make familiar to myself. Therefore, “hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication,” against the inward dangers about which he is going to speak.

I say, “hear,” and, O “Lord, Lord”—by repeating the name he declares the greatness of his affection—because you are “the strength,” that is, the one who gave me strength against external dangers. You are the “strength,” I say, “of my salvation,” that is, the strength that made me safe from the dangers mentioned above, because you “overshadowed”—that is, you placed your shadow so that he would feel no heat—“over my head,” namely, over Christ; and this “on the day of battle,” that is, on the day of the Passion, when he himself fought with the devil. Having defeated him, he set the human race free.

And because you have already bestowed benefits upon me, therefore, O “Lord, do not hand me over to the sinner,” that is, to the devil, “from my desire,” namely, so that the tinder of sin, which still remains in our flesh, may not be so inflamed by the devil’s suggestion that we thereby be handed over to the devil’s dominion. Therefore it is necessary to pray, “Do not hand me over,” because “they have plotted against me”—the devil and his ministers. But you, Lord, “do not abandon me,” by withdrawing your grace, “lest they be exalted” and boast if they are able to make me conform to themselves.

“His head.” The third part. A diapsalm. Nor is it right that they should be exalted, because “their head,” that is, the devil, “is a circuit,” since he never proceeds rightly but always goes around. And “the labor of their lips,” that is, falsehood, requires labor to compose; for whoever speaks the truth does not labor—the truth shows itself credible by itself. That very labor will cover them, that is, envelop and ensnare them. Or: “Do not hand me over to the sinner,” separated from my good desire, by which desire I wish to reach you.

And because they are such, therefore “coals will fall upon them,” that is, the burning passions of evil desires will crush them, and at last “you will cast them down into the fire,” the eternal fire. These people, placed “in miseries” as though in a fire preceding the face of the Judge, “will not endure,” because they will be enveloped by that fire and brought into eternal darkness. The righteous, however, rebuked by that fire, will pass through it.

He also sets forth, together and in combination, the cause of their condemnation and their condemnation itself, as though he were saying: They will not endure for this reason: they are talkative, and “a talkative man,” that is, one who speaks without reflection and does not consider what he says, “will not be directed” toward good works. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. X). “In the land,” that is, in this life, at least, “evils will seize the unjust man in destruction,” that is, at the end.

I rightly say that evils will seize them, since through the Holy Spirit I “have known” that the Lord will execute judgment, that is, recompense according to his just judgment, “for the true poor man,” “and” will exact “vengeance for the poor,” because he will condemn those who persecute his poor.

The wicked persecute the poor in this life; “nevertheless,” amid their tribulations, “the righteous will confess your name,” that is, praise you, “and” therefore they “will dwell upright” eternally “with your face,” that is, in your presence, seeing you face to face and knowing as they are known.

## ON PSALM 140

**Title: A Psalm of David.**

“Lord, I have cried out.” In this psalm too the prophet, or another righteous person, speaks about himself and other righteous people, who are its subject as they cry out to the Lord amid dangers. In the first part he cries out to the Lord not to think evil; or, if he does think evil, not to let his thoughts break forth into words; or, if he even speaks evil, not to defend his wickedness. He sees himself inclined to this not only by the nature of the flesh but also through association with wicked people, who do all these things: they think evil, speak evil, and defend their wickedness. In the second part, which begins, “The righteous man will correct me,” he shows that he would rather choose the corrections of the righteous than oil, that is, the flattery of the sinner. He also shows that, when the wicked cannot advance through deceit, they carry out open persecutions as well; and against this he sets forth his supplication. The intention is that in tribulation we should choose divine help alone as our refuge.

It is as though he were saying: You who are placed in tribulation, take divine help alone for yourselves, following my example, because I, in tribulation, have always “cried out to you, O Lord.” Therefore “hear me.” I have cried out and will cry out, and when I cry out to you, “attend to my voice.” By saying “I have cried out” and “I will cry out,” he indicates the constancy of prayer.

I say, “attend,” and through that attention “let my prayer be directed in your sight like incense.” Just as incense placed upon fire gives off a good odor, so may my prayer, kindled by the fire of repentance, please you; and let it be “an evening sacrifice,” that is, at the end of my life. Nor should it be just any sacrifice, but “the lifting up of hands,” that is, the direction of “my” good works.

I say, “I have cried out,” and you, “O Lord,” made favorable by this lifting of hands, “place a guard over my mouth,” that is, over my heart, so that I may not think evil. The heart is called the mouth because, just as the mouth gapes for nourishment, so the heart yearns and desires to be refreshed by divine grace. “And place a surrounding door”—one that stands around and closes the lips so that they may not speak evil—“around my lips.”

And even if forbidden words occasionally break forth, “do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness.” He specifies what wickedness he means, namely, “toward making excuses” “in sins,” so that I may excuse my sins. And because he often sees many excuses being offered, he adds, “toward excusing” excuses.

Under the old law there were morning and evening sacrifices, but the evening sacrifices were said, mystically, to please God more. For by the morning sacrifice our sacrifice, made at Christ’s coming, is signified; by the sacrifice of the lamb at evening, Christ’s sacrifice at the end of time is signified. In the same way, these are called morning sacrifices—that is, good works performed in youth—and evening sacrifices—good works performed at the end.

If I do this, I will be “with people who practice iniquity,” that is, one of those who excuse their sins. Jerome reads: “But I will be joined”; but I will not share with people who practice iniquity. And not only will I refuse to share with the lesser among them, “but I will not share with their chosen ones,” that is, with those more powerful and prominent in wickedness, so that through their companionship I might excuse my sins, as they themselves do.

“He will correct me.” The second part. I will not share with them, but rather “the righteous man will correct me and rebuke me.” To correct refers to the fact that he will cause me to desist gently; to rebuke refers to the fact that many threats are necessary. Hence the Apostle says: “Reprove in season and out of season” (1 Tim. IV). And again: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort.” I say, “rebuke in mercy,” with pious affection, so that he may remove me from an evil purpose. The righteous man will correct me, but “the oil of the sinner,” that is, flattery or blandishments, which soothe and anoint like oil, “will not fatten my head,” that is, will not produce any elation in my mind.

Therefore it is necessary that the righteous man correct me and that the oil not fatten me, because I still have something of sin within me. This is what follows: “For my prayer is still in their pleasures,” namely, the pleasures of sinners, because the things that please them still please me as well, such as earthly things. Therefore I say, “Let not the oil of sinners fatten me,” because “their judges,” that is, their wise men, “joined to the rock,” namely, to Christ, and founded upon him—not so that they may possess the right faith, but because in a certain way they speak well of him, not because they love him but so that they may deceive others, as heretics do. Another translation has: “Beside the rock, and such people have been swallowed up,” that is, placed in the deepest vices.

Their oil will not fatten my head, but they themselves will rather “hear my words,” that is, my preaching. These words deserve to be heard, “for they have been able,” that is, they are true. But although they heard them, it did them no good, because “as the thickness of the earth, when dug up, is thrown upon the earth,” that is, as earth brought up from the ground corrupts the air and sends destruction upon people, so “our bones have been scattered” by them, that is, the stronger members of the Church, namely, the martyrs. “Scattered,” I say, “beside hell,” that is, in the manner of those considered worthy of hell. But “because my eyes, O Lord, Lord, are toward you,” and because “I have hoped in you,” therefore “do not take away” from me “my soul,” that is, whatever may happen to the body, do not permit them to take my soul away.

Rather, “guard me from the snare,” that is, from flattery and other hidden plots, “which” snare they “set for me” in order to ensnare me, “and from the stumbling-blocks,” that is, from the open persecutions, “of those who practice iniquity.”

You will indeed guard me, but “sinners will fall into its net,” the net of iniquity, by which they are ensnared through their own wickedness; and they will be caught in the net. But “I am alone,” that is, unjoined and not associated with them, until I pass from this life.

## ON PSALM 141

**Title: The Understanding of David When He Was in the Cave; a Prayer.**

“With my voice.” From the historical account he leads us to allegory. Just as David, fleeing Saul and hiding in a cave, prayed (1 Sam. XXIV), so by the cave we understand mortal flesh, since it was, as it were, an unworthy dwelling for the Divinity. To detach us from the historical account, he adds “understanding,” as though he were saying: This psalm is called “understanding,” that is, it contains a certain secret—not dealing with the history but with what the history signifies. This psalm is David’s prayer, that is, Christ’s prayer; a prayer offered when Christ himself was in the cave, namely, in mortal flesh. This psalm is called a “prayer” because whatever it contains is either a prayer or introduces a reason for prayer, and through this psalm we are instructed to pray. Its subject is Christ praying in the time of his weakness. In the first part he sets forth the prayer and that against which it was directed, namely, the deceitfulness of the Jews. In the second, which begins, “I cried out to you, O Lord,” he again sets forth his prayer to the Father and asks that his soul be snatched from hell, upon which the entire expectation of the faithful depends. The intention is to instruct us to pray by his example.

It is as though Christ, who speaks here, were saying: Brothers, placed amid the evils of this life, do not cease from prayer. Follow the example of me, who, placed in the cave of fragile flesh, “cried out to” the Father, “the Lord,” and did so “with my voice,” because my works do not disagree with my prayer: what I ask with my voice, I confirm by my works to be worthy of being granted to me. I say, “I cried out,” and not merely for an hour, but I “prayed” to the Lord, that is, I pray continually, and I do so “with my voice.”

I say, “I cried out,” and still I “pour out,” that is, I express with great abundance, “my prayer,” which remains “in his sight,” that is, in his good pleasure, “and” I also “declare my tribulation,” so that it may be “before him,” namely God, and in his good pleasure.

I say, “I pour out my prayer,” and I do so with complete humility. This is what he says: “in the failing,” that is, in abandoning “my spirit.” I do not mean the spirit given by God, but rather the spirit that is “from me,” that is, from the nature of humanity, which is never good but always stirs up some elation. But because I abandoned that spirit in this way, therefore “you,” Lord, “knew,” that is, approved, “my paths,” that is, my works.

After setting forth the prayer, he sets forth that against which he prayed, as though he were saying: I prayed in this way and with such humility, and “on this way in which I walked, the proud,” namely, the Jews, “hid a snare for me,” that is, a hidden death and every kind of concealed evil.

They sought to bring death upon me. Then I “looked toward the right hand,” that is, toward the better part, namely, the disciples, “and I saw them, and there was not” among them “one who knew me” to be God, although Peter had previously said to him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). Likewise: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI). Here he signifies the time of his Passion, when the apostles went away backward, abandoning him (ibid.).

They did not know me, but fled “from me.” “Flight perished,” that is, I did not flee, but rather promised to be given over to death for the liberation of others. “And there was not” then found anyone “who sought my soul,” that is, anyone who wished to imitate my Passion.

“I cried out to you, O Lord.” The second part. I had no help from others, but, recognizing you as my only refuge, “I cried out to you, O Lord” and Father, with complete devotion. I said, “You are my hope,” as when on the cross he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). Christ commends his great humility to us: he always cried out to God the Father and entrusted his spirit to him, although he possessed within himself the same united divinity to which he could cry out and to which he could commend his spirit. In this humility he wished to conform us to himself, so that we should place no confidence in ourselves but await everything from God. I said, “You are my hope,” and I said, “You are my portion in the land of the living,” as though I were seeking to be one of those who will live in the heavenly land.

I said, “You are my hope,” and you, Lord, in whom I hope, “attend to my supplication,” made for the removal of evils, “because I have been humbled exceedingly,” because I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).

Thus indeed attend to me; “deliver me from those who persecute me.” And it is necessary that you do so, “because they have been strengthened against me,” with respect to the body, which God permitted them to deliver over to death.

Thus, I say, “deliver me,” namely, “lead my soul out of custody,” that is, out of hell, where the souls of those faithful people are held and guarded by the devil. “Lead it out,” I say, “to confess your name,” that is, let your name be praised for my deliverance, both by me and by others liberated through me. And it is necessary that you lead it out, because “the righteous await me,” their liberator, “until you repay me,” granting resurrection for my obedience. Another translation has: “Lead me out of prison.”

## ON PSALM 142

**Title: A Psalm of David, When His Son Absalom Persecuted Him.**

“Lord, hear my prayer.” This psalm applies to David, that is, to every true penitent. It was composed when his son—that is, a carnal impulse—and every other evil act, which a person has begotten for himself through his own fault, persecuted him, that is, afflicted him with many troubles and cast him out of the kingdom, namely, from the dignity in which the human being was created, just as Absalom persecuted his father and cast him out of the kingdom. The subject here is the true penitent; and, as in the other penitential psalms, it shows the penitent’s good end. In the first part he sets forth a prayer of concession, without excusing his fault, and recounts his wretchedness so as to move the judge to mercy. He also shows himself rightly turned toward that judge, so that he may appear worthy of receiving the judge’s movement of pious affection. In the second part, which begins, “Hear me quickly,” he asks to be heard quickly and to be led onto the right path, and affirms that this will happen to him. This psalm is one of the seven penitential psalms; their number signifies something to us. Since there are seven days through which the whole of time proceeds, so the seven penitential psalms show us that repentance is necessary on each day. The intention is to invite us to repentance by his example.

It is as though he were saying: When I was proud and took pleasure in sinning, it was not right that you should hear me. But because I now grieve over my sins and afterward strive to cease from them, therefore, “O Lord, hear my prayer and my supplication,” that is, my supplication through the cross, the Nativity, and similar things. Such supplication is indeed to be made when great necessity presses. I will not merely say, “Hear” that mercy and supplication, but “give ear,” that is, attend carefully. And do so “in your truth,” that is, so that you may prove true in your promises, because you promised to hear the one who humbles himself, saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. I). This is also what follows: “Hear me in your righteousness,” that is, your righteousness requires you to fulfill your promises. He rightly says “in your righteousness,” because he understands God’s righteousness always to consist in mercy.

I say, “Hear,” and “do not enter into judgment with your servant,” that is, do not judge me according to my merits, “because no living person will be justified in your sight,” since, in comparison with you, no one is found righteous—not prophet, apostle, or even angel.

Therefore I pray that you not enter into judgment, “because the enemy,” namely, my son, that is, the carnal impulse, “has persecuted” my soul by making a wicked suggestion, that is, my reason; and he “has humbled,” that is, brought low, “my life upon the earth,” so that my soul might cling to earthly things. He also “placed me in dark places,” that is, in the depths of vices, “like those who have been dead for ages,” that is, any unbelievers whom the world entirely possesses after they have been entangled in sins. “And” therefore “my spirit was distressed within me,” that is, because of me: I felt repentance and grief over my sins. “And my heart,” that is, my reason, “was troubled within me,” because, left to myself, I did not know how I could escape from this captivity.

And in this disturbance “I remembered the days of old,” that is, the days in which you showed mercy to other penitents. “I meditated on all your works,” that is, I brought all your works back into meditation, so that from them I might prepare some consolation for myself, “and on the works” that are called “of your hands,” namely, the works that you mercifully performed for the ancients, for Abraham, the Israelite people, and other righteous people—and for me as well, when I humbled myself before you. On such works “I meditated.”

And I not only “meditated,” but also “stretched out,” that is, lifted up, “my hands,” that is, my works, not for the sight of human beings, not for popular favor, but “toward you,” in order to obtain you. What more can be said? “My soul is like land without water before you.” Just as land without water gapes and desires the infusion of water, so the soul desires the infusion of spiritual grace. By this he shows himself worthy of receiving the judge’s pardon.

“Quickly.” The second part. Because my soul thirsted in this way, and because I stretched out my hands in this way, therefore, O “Lord, hear me quickly.” And you ought to do so, because “my spirit has failed,” namely, that spirit which is from human beings, the spirit of pride.

And because the spirit of presumption has failed, since I humble myself before you, therefore “do not turn your face from me,” that is, your knowledge and presence. And if you turn your face away, there will be no difference between me, the humble one, “and” the other proud people. Rather, “I will become like” those proud people “who descend into the pit,” that is, into the depths of hell.

Do not turn away, I say, but rather “make me hear your mercy,” that is, let me hear your merciful sentence concerning the remission of sins; and do so “in the morning,” that is, at the beginning of my illumination and repentance. Some hear mercy, as David did through the prophet Nathan concerning the forgiveness of his adultery (2 Sam. XII); others understand through an angel; others, through the purity of their conscience, understand that they have obtained remission of their sins. Therefore make me hear mercy, “because I have hoped in you.”

And through the mercy I have heard, “make known to me the way in which I should walk,” because I have lifted up my soul to you.

And when I have walked on the way, if some enemies come who wish to hinder me, you, “O Lord, deliver me from my enemies,” because I “have fled for refuge” not to any human refuge, but “to you.” Therefore “teach me to do your will,” which you ought to do, “because you are my God,” whom I make familiar to myself.

I say, “Deliver me; make the way known to me,” and you will do so, because “your good Spirit will lead me” along the paths of righteousness “into a level land,” that is, into the land of the living, which only the upright will possess. Meanwhile, “you will give me life” so that I may fulfill your commandments, “for your name’s sake, O Lord,” because you are called Jesus, that is, Savior, and this is not on account of my merits but on account of your mercy. And do so “in your equity,” because your equity requires you to give life and lead the one who humbles himself before you.

You will give me life, and “you will lead my soul out of tribulation,” that is, out of the suggestion of sins; and “in your mercy you will destroy” all “my enemies,” that is, the unlawful impulses that rise up within me.

“You will destroy them,” so that they may no longer rise up against me, “and you will destroy all those who trouble my soul,” both wicked people and demons, “because I am your servant.”

## ON PSALM 143

**Title: A Psalm of David Against Goliath.**

“Blessed.” This psalm applies to the prophet David, who speaks here, and was composed against Goliath, that is, the devil. The psalm speaks of the victory that Christ won over the devil; through this victory the holy Church is rescued from the enemy’s power. David understands this victory of Christ to be signified by his own victory, which he himself had over Goliath. Its subject is Christ’s victory itself, through which our liberation was accomplished. In the first part he gives thanks for his victory, which he nevertheless attributes to the grace of Christ’s signified victory, and asks that the one who will defeat Goliath and free us from Goliath’s power may become incarnate and come. In the second part, which begins, “O God, I will sing a new song to you,” the Prophet says, both in his own person and in the person of all those who have been liberated, that he will sing to the Lord in both the New and the Old Testament for the liberation that the Lord accomplished for him and for those like him from the devil and wicked people. He describes their wickedness at length. He intends to invite us to give thanks to the Lord for the victory of our liberation, just as the prophet himself gives thanks both for his own victory over Goliath and, above all, for Christ’s victory, through which the prophet understands that he himself, together with the other righteous, has been liberated. He places this psalm last among all those in which something was signified through historical events, or in which he exhorted us to patience and other similar virtues. The following seven are called the praises of David, because here he sets forth the victory of our liberation. By this he intimates that if someone carefully observes what was previously taught in the other psalms, he will find liberation from Goliath in Christ’s victory.

It is as though he were inviting others, saying: Brothers, if you have been freed from the devil, do not ascribe it to yourselves, but give thanks to the Lord. Follow my example: I accomplished nothing by myself against Goliath, but everything through the Lord. Therefore “blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands,” that is, my works, “for battle.” By myself I would not have known how to fight against Goliath. “And he trains my fingers,” that is, my counsels, “for war.” The fingers are understood as counsels because, just as fingers proceed from the hand, so counsels proceed from the heart, as though emerging through a certain reasoning. God taught him a good plan, for example, when he was to fight Goliath from a distance; likewise, when he taught him to carry a sling with him and to carry selected stones in the shepherd’s bag.

He then sets forth other benefits of God, to increase his thanksgiving, as though he were saying: Therefore let God be blessed and exalted, because “he trains my hands”; likewise, because he is my mercy. Since it would take too long to enumerate everything he did for him, he comprehends many divine benefits in a few words, as follows: “My mercy,” that is, the one who showed me mercy. He wishes this mercy to be understood as follows: God chose him from among all his brothers, who seemed far more worthy, and had him anointed king (1 Sam. XVI). The first anointing took place in the house of his father Jesse by Samuel, as a sign of the future kingdom. “And” God himself is “my refuge,” to whom I fled, laying down all the weapons with which I had been clothed, lest I be suffocated in combat by Goliath. Thus, pressed by the great weight of armor, I found with God a different plan for fighting; through him I was secure against Goliath. He is “my protector,” because God received me into such great dignity that, although I was a mere shepherd, a man of humble lineage, he made me Saul’s son-in-law, “and” almost the equal of the king himself. He is “my deliverer,” because he freed me from all Saul’s persecution.

He is “my protector,” who brought all Saul’s attacks to an end, as at Saul’s death. And he did this because “I hoped in him,” that is, I placed all my hope in him, “who subjects my people,” namely, the people of whom I was one, the Israelite people, “under me,” because he made me their king.

He shows that he was unworthy of the benefits mentioned above, and likewise that every human being is unworthy of the liberation which he sets forth as accomplished through Christ’s victory. The connection is as follows: You bestowed all these benefits upon me, but I was unworthy of them all. And, O “Lord, what is” a human being—that is, how insignificant a thing is “man,” to whom you did something so marvelous—“because you made yourself known to him”? God made himself known to human beings through his own presence at Christ’s coming. Previously, God had made known to David through inward foresight what a human being is, that is, how dear and precious a thing he is. And this is because you made yourself known to him through the humanity you assumed, although he was in himself most insignificant. I say, what is man, “or the son of man,” that is, of what dignity, when in himself he is nothing at all? And this is for the following reason: “because you reckon him” that is, esteem him as being of great worth, because you make him a participant in eternal blessedness.

When he says “man,” he understands the first parent, the human being who was not created through carnal desire, because God formed him from the clay of the earth (Gen. I). But when he says “son of man,” he shows the lowliness of every generation, as though he were saying: Whatever kind of man he might be, whether born through carnal desire or not, in himself he was nothing.

Therefore I ask what “man” is, because “he was made like vanity,” that is, like something light, empty, and quickly passing away. He says “was made” because he was created in perfection and stability; but by violating obedience he made himself empty, mortal, and transient, and he does not blame the Creator for his evils. I rightly say “like vanity,” because he was made like a shadow. This is what follows: “His days pass away like a shadow.”

Now he shows how God, who possessed such great dignity, made himself known: he descended and assumed our flesh. The connection is as follows: Man was made like vanity, but you, O “Lord,” the Word, “incline your heavens,” that is, humble the heavenly beings, such as the holy angels, whom God humbled when he placed our humanity above them. Those who had previously been accustomed to being worshiped by human beings he made servants of human beings. “Incline,” I say, “and descend,” that is, join our flesh to yourself. Concerning this descent the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II). Descend, I say, and thus “touch the mountains,” that is, the powerful and proud of this life; breathe inwardly upon them, “and they will smoke,” that is, they will send forth great sighs and tears from the fire of devout repentance.

I say, “Descend,” and also cause “your lightning,” that is, the sayings of the prophets and the other divine Scripture, which shines and flashes in itself, to “flash forth”—both forms, *fulgura* and *fulgora*, are used—that is, make them manifest. And through this “you will scatter them,” namely, the mountains mentioned above, that is, separate them from the mass of the lost, because some of them will be saved. “Send forth your arrows,” that is, your apostles, who pierce human hearts with the love of God, “and you will trouble them,” the mountains, toward the good, because they will be moved to repentance.

He turns to the Father. You, Lord Son, I say, “descend,” and you, Lord Father, “send forth your hand,” that is, your Son, through whom you accomplish all things, “from on high,” that is, from the sublimity in which you are; “snatch me” from the devil’s power, “and deliver me from many waters,” that is, from the flood of evils, “and from the hand,” that is, from the power, “of foreign sons.” They are called foreign sons because they are sons of the devil and foreign to us. Therefore it is necessary that you rescue me from them, because they are those “whose mouth has spoken vanity,” namely, anything contrary to the divine judgment; “and their right hand,” that is, their activity, which seems better to them, “is a right hand of iniquity.”

“O God, I will sing a new song.” The second part. I say, “Deliver me,” and if you do this, “I will sing a new song to you,” that is, through baptism I will proclaim that sins are forgiven, that the body and blood of Christ are true nourishment, and the other matters belonging to the New Testament. I will also “sing praise to you,” that is, I will act well, “on the psaltery,” that is, through a spiritual activity resonating from above. The psaltery is “ten-stringed,” that is, it resonates with ten strings, fulfilling the ten commandments of the law.

To you I say this, “who give salvation to kings,” that is, remission of sins to the faithful who govern themselves well. You are the one who “redeemed” me, “David your servant, from the evil sword,” that is, from the power of the devil or from heretical persuasion. Or we may understand David himself as Christ: he was redeemed from mortality and suffering by the price of his blood. And you, who gave the price for us, “rescue me” from that same evil sword, that is, from the power of the devil, who is called a sword because he separates the wicked from the fellowship of the good.

“And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

“Whose sons.” Here he describes their wickedness. Their “right hand” is “a right hand of iniquity” because they judge only the person who abounds in temporal goods to be blessed. We can nevertheless read the passage allegorically in this way: “The sons of whom,” that is, their disciples, are “like plantings,” because they cling firmly to their teachers’ opinions; they are “young shoots,” because they do not receive the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, but follow novel sects in their heresies. Such people always remain “in their youth,” because they never return to the antiquity of the truth of the fathers, but always follow new sects and discover still other new ones.

“Their daughters,” that is, their thoughts and teachings, which they generate from themselves. He calls them daughters because they are unstable and have no root in truth. Such daughters are “adorned,” that is, devised and fashioned with artifice; they are also “ornamented all around,” because they are furnished on every side with rhetorical colors and other devices, “like the likeness of a temple,” so that they may resemble a temple, that is, the dwelling of God. He rightly says “resemble,” because they themselves are not the dwelling of God.

“Their storehouses,” that is, their hearts, from which they bring forth evil opinions, are “full,” that is, overflowing with many evil arts, “and belching forth,” because from their excessive fullness they utter opinions. But those opinions are unstable, because if someone attacks them, they flee “from this to that,” that is, from one argument to another and then to another, and thus, without stability, they make many detours through their arguments.

And it is necessary that you free me from them for this reason: “Their sheep,” that is, their inferior and less learned followers, are “prolific,” because they immediately have many disciples; for no one among them is so weak that he does not immediately acquire many followers. But such sheep are “abundant in their going forth,” because the more they multiply in their heresies, the more they are removed from fellowship with the holy Church. “Their oxen,” that is, those stronger members and teachers of others, are “fat,” that is, made fat by temporal desires.

“Their walls,” namely, those of their art or fortification, “have no breach,” as far as their own opinion is concerned, because they do not consider it possible for the solidity of their arguments to be attacked in any way; “nor is there a passage,” again with respect to them; “nor is there a cry” of the word of God “in their streets,” that is, amid their broad desires.

Because they flow away through the broad desire for this world, the divine word does not resound among them; rather, “they called that people blessed to whom these things belong,” namely, to whom all the aforesaid things belong, such as having sons of this kind [Col. 0679D], and so forth. They call such a people blessed; but I, who hold the true interpretation, say for my part that “that people is blessed whose” “Lord” is “his God”—that is, the one who has chosen his Creator as his Lord, whom he may serve.

When, in the literal sense, he says that their sheep are fruitful, in order to point out their foolishness, he adds: “abounding in their goings-out,” that is, such sheep are not stable but quickly go out of life; in other words, all riches of this kind are unstable.

## ON PSALM 144. TITLE: A Praise to David.

“You will I exalt.” Here David himself, that is, Christ, is praised by the speaking Prophet, and the praise of Christ is the subject [Col. 0680A]. The structure is as follows: in the first part he says that he will praise God. In the second he sets out nine ways in which he praises him; this part begins, “Generation shall praise your works.” In the third, beginning, “The Lord is compassionate and merciful,” he explains those ways, answering each of the individual forms of praise. He intends to invite others to praise God by his own example.

He places the following seven psalms continuously concerning the praise of God, signifying through this number—which is equal to the number of days by which all time revolves—that we should praise the Lord on each day.

It is as though he were inviting others in this way: Praise the Lord by my example, because I will “exalt you, my God and King”; according to your essence, I will announce to others the dignity of your essence, insofar as I am able to make it known, “and I will bless [Col. 0680B] your name,” that is, I will magnify your name, both “for ever” in the present age and “for ever” in the age following this “age,” in which the saints especially praise God. And just as he urged us to pray, so he urges us to praise.

And this not once during life, but “each day I will bless you” according to your essence, “and I will praise your name for ever and ever,” which must be done because “the Lord” is “great” in power and “worthy of praise” because of the works and benefits that he performs for his faithful. And this to an extreme degree, since no one can praise God with sufficient dignity; “and” just as his praise has no end, so “there is no end to his greatness,” because no one can adequately proclaim his power.

[Col. 0680C] “Generation.” The second part. I will praise him, and I will not do so alone, but “the generation” of the Jews “and the generation” of the Gentiles “will praise your works,” that is, they will attend to his works; and likewise because of his power. He says this: “and they will proclaim your power.” This is another way of praising God.

Likewise, “they will speak of the magnificence of your glory,” that is, of your magnificent glory; and I speak of the glory “of your holiness,” that is, the glory possessed because of your holiness. This is another way of praising him, which Jerome sets out more clearly, saying: “They will speak of the glory of your majesty and of your holiness, and they will recount your wonders,” that is, the miracles you performed, such as in the dividing of the Red Sea. This is another manner and another reason [Col. 0680D] for praising.

“And they will declare the power of your terrors,” namely, that power of yours in which you appear terrible, such as what was done in Egypt to Pharaoh and his people. This is another manner. “And they will recount your greatness” in essence.

This too is another manner. “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” that is, remembering your most sweet and abundant goodness, as in the restoration of the human race through grace, they will pour it forth and proclaim it to others. This is another manner. “And they will exult in your justice,” that is, they will announce it with exultation.

This too is another manner. “Compassionate.” The third part. He responds to what he had previously said, “Your works shall be praised,” and explains how God should be praised because of his works. The connection is as follows: They should exult and pour forth because the Lord, who is “merciful” in his nature, has also become “compassionate,” that is, he has shown us many acts of compassion, as in the first creation and especially in the re-creation.

In response to what he said, “They will proclaim your power,” although he could have displayed many other powers of God, such as the fact that he holds the earth suspended in the void, and similar things, he nevertheless chose one in particular: that God waits for sinners and forgives their sins. Hence he says “patient,” because he does not punish immediately but awaits conversion; and “abounding in mercy,” because however great and innumerable sins may be, he nevertheless forgives the one who [Col. 0681B] humbles himself and turns back to him.

In response to what he had said, “They will speak of the magnificence of glory,” he replies by saying that this magnificent glory is sweet to those who examine it. The connection is as follows: The Lord is patient, and so forth as has been said, and the Lord himself “is sweet,” that is, gentle and delightful, “to all” who taste him, as it is also said elsewhere: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33). “And” he is so sweet that “his mercies” are “over all his works,” because, beyond all his benefits and powers, he performs another act of mercy for us, namely, he grants the rewards of eternal life.

The works possessed by us, however, are punished by God. The devil also, according to his substance—for he is a creature and work of God—will have this mercy: his substance will not perish eternally, but because of his wickedness he will be afflicted with eternal fires. And because he is sweet, and thus makes mercies for all his works, it is evident that his magnificence is glory.

“Let all your works confess to you, O Lord.” He shows God’s holiness, since to some the Lord may appear unjust when he permits the wicked to prosper in this life and the just to be troubled by many adversities. It is as though he were saying: Because you do such things, “let all your works confess to you, O Lord,” that is, let them be the reason why rational creatures praise you, “and let your saints bless you,” attending to the holy and praiseworthy ordering of your works. For example, if clear weather comes when we are expecting rain, or the reverse, they recognize that this has been sanctified by God and brought about according to a definite ordering.

In response to what he had said above, “They will recount your wonders,” he explains those wonders. The connection is as follows: I say, “the saints will bless you,” and “they will speak of the glory of your kingdom,” that is, they will show this world and the firmament in which you reign to be glorious and adorned together with itself, “and they will speak of your power,” because they will show that by your own power you govern all these things.

He responds to this with, “and the power of your terrors.” The connection is as follows: They will speak of your power and declare the glory of your kingdom, “to make your power known to the sons of men,” as Peter and John did when they had healed the lame man and everyone marveled; they said that it was not their work but that of the Lord Jesus [Col. 0682A] Christ (Acts 3). “And” they will also make known “the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom,” that is, how glorious and how magnificent your kingdom is.

In response to this he says, “and they will recount your greatness.” The connection is as follows: I rightly speak of “the magnificence of your kingdom,” because “your kingdom” is “a kingdom of all ages,” since it is eternal, and in that kingdom you possess eternal dominion. And he adds: “Your dominion is in every generation and generation.”

In response to this he speaks of “the abundance of your sweetness.” The connection is as follows: Your dominion is in every generation, and the Lord himself is “faithful in all his words,” that is, truthful, because he faithfully fulfills whatever he has promised; “and holy in all his works,” [Col. 0682B] that is, irreproachable, although to fools he may seem to arrange certain things unjustly.

Through this also the abundance of his sweetness becomes evident, “because the Lord lifts up all who fall,” that is, those who are inclined to sin. If they are willing to consent to him, they do not carry their will through into action. “And he raises up all who have been cast down,” that is, those who have already fallen into the act of sin, forgiving them, if they are willing to repent and give thanks.

In response to this he says, “They will exalt your justice,” and he shows God’s justice. The connection is as follows: Because you lift up and raise, now “the eyes” of all, that is, their intentions, “hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food,” whether spiritual or bodily, as, for example, to Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6). And this “at the proper time,” because even if someone worthy is not given something immediately when it is requested, he gives it when he judges the time appropriate.

In this also your justice will appear, because “you open your hand,” that is, dispensing your benefits generously, “and you fill every animal” that serves you with reason and devotion “with blessing,” that is, with an increase of virtues.

The Lord is “just in all his ways,” that is, in all his dispensations, “and holy in all his works,” that is, in all the effects of those dispensations.

He shows how God is just—just toward the good. The connection is as follows: The Lord is just in the good things mentioned above, and it is evident that he is just because [Col. 0682D] “the Lord is near to all who call upon him. To all who call upon him,” I say, “in truth.”

To call upon him in truth is to cry out to the Lord with a pure and undefiled intention, for the salvation of one’s soul, and not frivolously, but to ask for what can contribute to the soul’s salvation. But because Paul prayed for something frivolous (2 Corinthians 12)—since the removal of the thorn of the flesh was not conducive to the soul’s salvation—he was not heard by the Lord. Thus the Lord is near to those who call upon him: in mercy he fulfills what they ask. Hypocrites, however, who seek the favor of the people, do not call upon God in truth.

And truly he is near, because he himself “will do the will [Col. 0683A] of those who fear him,” that is, he will fulfill it, and even if they remain silent, “he will hear their prayer,” uttered in a continuous voice, “and” at last “he will save them” in eternal salvation.

Until now he has not shown that God is just toward the good; from this point onward he explains generally how he is just toward both the good and the wicked, saying: “The Lord preserves all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners.”

This is the conclusion of the praises mentioned above. Since the Lord will do all these things, whatever others may do, “my mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and,” by my example, “let all flesh bless his holy name.” Here his intention is clear. “All flesh,” I say—that is, servants and free persons, children and old men—and this not for an hour, but “for ever” in the present age, [Col. 0683B] “and” also “for ever” in the age following this “age.”

## ON PSALM 145. TITLE: Alleluia.

“Praise the Lord, my soul.” In this psalm the subject is the praise of God, and he intends to invite us to praise God by his own example. The structure is as follows: in the first part, after exhorting his own soul to praise God, he warns others not to trust in princes, that is, either in the devil or in human beings, who can provide salvation neither for themselves nor for others. In the second part, beginning, “Blessed is he whose God is Jacob,” he shows that one ought to hope in the Lord, describing him as one who worthily rewards those who hope in him.

[Col. 0683C] It is as though he were saying: The higher reason, governing and restraining his carnality, says: “O my soul,” that is, my animal nature, which ought to serve me, “praise the Lord.” The soul, now well strengthened, says: “I will praise the Lord in my life,” that is, in the other life, which will be my own and blessed life; “I will sing psalms,” that is, I will act well, “to my God as long as I exist,” that is, throughout the whole period of this life.

And in the same way, you others, sing psalms by my example. You ought to follow the counsel I give myself, namely: “Do not put your trust in princes,” that is, in demons, who are the princes of this world; hence in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12); “nor in the sons of men,” that is, in human beings, “in whom,” whether princes or other people, “there is no salvation,” because they cannot save themselves, much less save others.

Or, without the second “nor,” it may be understood in this way: Do not put your trust in princes, that is, in the powerful people of this life, because they are the sons of men; and this is what follows, “in the sons of men,” and so forth.

I rightly say that there is no salvation in them, because “his spirit,” that is, the spirit of a human being, “will go out” from the body, “and” that person, in bodily form, “will return to the earth” to become ashes. I say “his own” earth, from which he had been made and from which he had received his beginning. “And on that day,” when the spirit goes out in this way, “their thoughts” will perish—thoughts by which they had supposed that they should acquire riches and lay great kingdoms beneath themselves as though they were king of the angels.

[Col. 0684A] The second part. One must not hope in the sons of men, since they can help neither themselves nor others; rather, one must hope in him who gives blessedness and does the other things that follow. This is the meaning: “Blessed is he whose” God is “the God of Jacob,” that is, the one who makes him his God whom Jacob had as God. And this God is “his helper” in doing good. He is therefore also blessed because “his hope” is “in the Lord his God,” in whom one ought rightly to hope, because he is the one “who made heaven and earth, the sea,” literally.

And to remove the error of certain people who said that some beasts had been made by the devil, he adds, “and all that is in them”: God himself made them. For peasants say that the devil made the goat, and others say that he made the toad. And since all the praises of God are drawn from the preceding psalm in nine ways, this passage refers to his works.

One should also hope in him because he is the one “who keeps truth,” that is, fulfills his promise, “for ever,” that is, throughout all the ages of this world. This pertains to what he said above: “the abundance of sweetness.” And he is the one who “executes judgment for those who suffer injury,” because at some time he has judged them. “He gives food to the hungry,” both spiritual and bodily. For he gives spiritual nourishment only to the hungry, that is, to those who desire it, namely, those who thirst for righteousness. These two matters pertain to justice.

This Lord also “sets free those in fetters,” whether by the bond of sins or by demonic possession, that is, the demoniacs; or literally those in fetters, as Peter in prison (Acts 12). The Lord also “gives light to the blind,” that is, he gives knowledge of himself to the ignorant; or literally, as to Tobit (Tobit 11) and many others.

“The Lord raises up those who have been cast down,” by forgiving sins. “The Lord loves the just,” because he strengthens them in virtues.

“The Lord protects the sojourners,” that is, those who do not seek a lasting city in this world but seek an eternal one (Hebrews 13). He protects them from committing sins and from conformity with the wicked. He will receive “the orphan,” that is, the one whose father is the dead devil and whose mother is worldly will, “and the widow,” that is, those who have been deprived of the support of this world, into the eternal tabernacles; “and,” conversely, “he will destroy [Col. 0684D] the ways of sinners,” that is, he will render them useless.

These things just mentioned show the abundance of his sweetness. The connection is as follows: The Lord will destroy the ways of sinners, and this “Lord will reign for ever.” He specifies which Lord he means, saying: O “Zion,” that is, O Church, this is “your God,” who will reign “in this generation” and “in the generation” to come.

## ON PSALM 146. TITLE: Alleluia.

“Praise the Lord, for.” Here too the Prophet makes the subject the praise of God, specifically that God gathers his Church into unity of faith from every part of the world. Note that in the title of this psalm they add “of Haggai and Zechariah.” These men, detained in the Babylonian captivity, prophesied the future return after seventy years, understanding more fully the spiritual return to the heavenly Jerusalem than the bodily return to their own homeland [Note: [Col. 0685] These words seem to belong to the exposition of the preceding psalm.].

The structure is as follows: in the first part he urges the religious and more perfect members of the Church to praise the Lord, showing that God builds his Church from those scattered throughout the whole world and bestows many benefits upon them. In the second part, beginning, “Sing in advance to the Lord with confession,” he urges others who are still negligent to praise God, and shows them that the Lord is pleased with the humble but not with the proud. Through these things he intends to invite them to praise the Lord.

[Col. 0685B] Hence he says: “Praise the Lord,” with voice and deed, “for a psalm,” that is, praise of this kind accompanied by good action, “is good” and beneficial to anyone who praises in this way, “to our God,” who is not like the gods of the Gentiles. “Let there be praise”: not just any kind, but “joyful,” that is, performed with a pure intention, not for temporal advantage but solely to gain God’s favor. “And let it be comely,” that is, proceeding from a pure conscience, so that it may not be cheapened by the sins of the one who performs it. For you have heard that “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15).

Another division may be made in this psalm, but it is not derived from authoritative tradition, as follows: “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let it be to God, but let the praise be joyful.”

Therefore I say, “praise,” because “the Lord is building [Col. 0685C] Jerusalem,” that is, his Church, which already pursues peace here and will finally see God in complete peace; “and he will gather” into that Church—not locally but spiritually and into unity, or unanimity—“the dispersed of Israel,” that is, those whom he makes Israel, scattered through every part of the world.

He will gather them, “who heals the brokenhearted,” that is, those who have a contrite and humbled heart. He rightly specifies “the brokenhearted,” because however much the body may be afflicted, if the heart is exalted, God does not regard its afflictions. The Lord heals the brokenhearted by forgiving sins, “and he binds up all their wounds,” that is, the brokenhearted themselves, deprived of true dignity, and he strengthens them in order [Col. 0685D] to restore them to their former dignity.

He speaks by comparison with a physician who binds broken bones so that they may be restored and brought back to their former health. God binds us with the bandage of mercy and bestows his graces, by which he reforms us according to the former appearance that we lost through the sin of our first parent.

“He numbers the multitude of the stars, and he calls all of them by name.” If this is taken literally, it nevertheless signifies great power. We may also interpret it allegorically as follows: The Lord heals and binds up the wounds of the brokenhearted, and thus makes them shining stars in the Church. He numbers the multitude of those stars, that is, he comprehends all of them in his numbering, because he rejects none [Col. 0686A] but provides all with what they need.

“And he calls all of them by name,” or, “calling them,” he knows each one according to his own particular quality: he knows this one as simple, like David; that one as gentle, like Moses; and likewise others through their own qualities, which he himself has produced in them. He signifies such qualities by names, because just as someone recognizes a distinct person by a name, so the Lord recognizes persons as distinct through these qualities.

And because he does such things, “the Lord” is “great.” I do not mean the Lord whom the Gentiles make their own, but “our” Lord. Here the person of the Father is understood. “And great is his power”: here the person of the Son is understood, whom he calls the power of God, because through him God [Col. 0686B] rules all things powerfully and exercises dominion over all. “And of his wisdom”: here too the Son is understood. “There is no number,” because that wisdom of God is infinite and incomprehensible.

Or, “there is no number” because it is unique and singular. Or, “of his wisdom,” that is, of the Son, “there is no number,” meaning that he cannot be numbered as different from the Father, because he is the same with the Father, according to Augustine, who says in this exposition: We read in holy Moses that there is no number of his wisdom, for no other wisdom can be compared with it; but many other things can be compared with the wisdom of Plato and of other philosophers. He calls the Son himself the wisdom of God because through him the Lord made and ordered all things wisely.

I say that the Lord does these things just mentioned, and not for just anyone, [Col. 0686C] but for the meek. He says this: “The Lord receives the meek” into glory, “but he humbles sinners even to the ground,” that is, to the desire for earthly things.

“Sing in advance.” Another translation has “Begin,” by which we understand that this was spoken not to the perfect but to the negligent. The connection is as follows: Since the Lord receives the meek and rejects the others, therefore “sing in advance,” that is, do not be negligent and wait for judgment, but sing in advance at once, “to the Lord with confession,” that is, by confessing sins. “Sing psalms” also to our God “with the lyre,” that is, through bodily works, namely, in the active life.

“He covers the heavens,” that is, divine Scripture, which contains God’s secrets, “with clouds,” that is, with certain enigmas or obscure prophetic figures, so that heavenly secrets may not be open to everyone; “and” nevertheless in those clouds “he prepares rain for the earth,” that is, for the Church—“rain” meaning spiritual doctrine. He rightly says “prepares,” because God sometimes opens the Scriptures in such a way that his faithful are refreshed by them.

He himself opens them, “who brings forth hay on the mountains,” that is, among the higher men, such as the holy apostles—“hay” meaning solid food, for the support of the greater and stronger. “And grass,” that is, more tender food, namely, gentle and humble doctrine, as the Apostle says: “I speak wisdom among the wise” (1 Corinthians 2). And elsewhere: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

Or by the mountains, which are open places in this world, we may understand those places in which God prepares for the work of preachers and of all who serve him “hay,” that is, harsher food, “and grass,” that is, gentler food. For sometimes he gives his preachers only bread and water, and at other times good fish. All these things are “for the service of men,” that is, for the servants of men, namely, preachers and the other ministers of the Church, who truly serve human beings while day and night they intercede with God for them in prayer.

“He also gives” to “the beasts of burden,” that is, to the meek, who no longer refuse to bear the burden of the day, “their food,” food suitable for them, both spiritual and bodily; “and to the young of ravens,” that is, [Col. 0687B] to the sons of the Gentiles, who are ravens, blackened by sins—not like their wicked fathers, but “calling upon him,” that is, becoming unlike the blackness of their fathers.

Likewise, in the literal sense, God is said to feed the young of ravens, whose fathers abandon them, with the dew of the air, as long as they are white and until they become like their parents.

And this Lord “will not have pleasure,” that is, approval, “in the strength of a horse,” that is, in the proud, “nor in the legs of a stubborn man,” that is, in legs slender and fit for kicking well, namely, in bodily cultivation, which he signifies by one part, the legs. “In these he will have no pleasure.” Another translation has, “in the tents of a man”; by this we understand the gatherings of the proud.

In such people the Lord has no pleasure, but “the Lord has pleasure in those who fear him”; and because they fear him, they cease from evil, “and in those who hope,” not in their merits, but “in his mercy,” and therefore they act well.

## ON PSALM 147. TITLE: Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah.

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” The Church which above he showed to be gathered by the Lord from the dispersion of this world, now gathered and placed in the heavenly realms, is urged in the first part to praise God for such great peace and such great security. In the second part, beginning, “Who sends forth his word,” he shows the many benefits that God has done for us in this life, so that through them he may make us secure concerning eternal security. He also intends to urge us, as he does others, to praise God.

Hence he says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” which has now been placed in eternal security; and “O Zion,” which now beholds, “praise your God.” He calls the same reality Zion and Jerusalem, but Zion insofar as it contemplates the divine presence, and Jerusalem insofar as it reigns with God and is established in perpetual peace and tranquility.

Therefore “praise him, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates,” that is, he has placed you in security. Jerusalem is said to have eternal gates because of its entrance; it is said to have strengthened bars because no one will be able to enter it after the day of judgment. He strengthened the bars, I say, “and he blessed your sons who are” present “within you” with every kind of blessing.

He blessed you—he who “made your borders peace,” because even among those who will be in the final dwelling there will be peace and exultation. “And he satisfies you with the fatness of wheat,” that is, with the very divinity of Christ.

“Who sends forth his word.” The second part. “Who sends forth his word,” that is, his Son, “to the earth,” that is, into the world; and “his speech,” whether the speech of his word or of God himself—namely, preaching—“runs swiftly,” that is, spreads throughout the whole world.

He also “gives snow,” namely, those who are cold and hardened in sins, “like wool,” so that they may warm others through his teaching; and he “scatters the cloud,” that is, those blinded by much ignorance—he scatters them, meaning that he enlightens them and separates them [Col. 0688B] from the mass of the lost, “like ashes.” For just as ash spread over the earth enriches it and makes it fruitful, so those who were previously a cloud enlighten others and make them fruitful.

He also “sends his ice like morsels,” that is, those who for many years had been cold and hardened in sins, like a morsel of bread, so that they may become nourishment for other people. But “before the face of his cold,” that is, before those whom God hardens in sins by his just judgment, “who will endure?” That is, who will be able to persist without immediately consenting to them? Thus Moses could scarcely persist before Pharaoh (Exodus 7), because Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.

No one, I say, will be able to endure before the face of the cold. But God “will send forth his word,” the word of preaching, [Col. 0688C] “and” through it “he will melt them”—the snow and the ice, and the other things mentioned above. “His Spirit,” namely, the Holy Spirit, “will blow” upon them, “and” also “the waters will flow,” that is, many teachings will go forth from that people.

Or here he shows the authority of the matter, because God will send the Word into Judea, since it was foretold in this way.

He will send the Spirit, who, “through the presence of the body,” announces his word, that is, his preaching and teaching, to “Jacob,” that people; and he announces to them “his righteousnesses,” that is, how people become righteous, “and his judgments,” that is, how he disposes all things in time—by what judgment he chooses some and rejects others—to “Israel,” that people, through the presence of the body.

Or he announces his word through the apostles and other preachers, and his righteousnesses and judgments to Jacob and Israel, that is, to those who make themselves like Jacob, meaning wrestlers, and like Israel, meaning those who see God.

These things he did for Jacob. “He did not” do “so for every nation,” namely, “he did not manifest his judgments to them.”

## ON PSALM 148. TITLE: Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens.” Here again the Prophet makes the praise of God his subject. The structure is as follows: in the first part he urges the heavenly creatures to praise God. In the second, beginning, “Praise the Lord from the earth,” [Col. 0689A] he exhorts earthly creatures to praise that same God; this praise will be performed more fully and perfectly in the other life. His intention is to invite everyone to praise, saying:

You creatures “from the heavens,” that is, heavenly creatures, “praise the Lord.” And not only you who are lower, but you who are “in the heights,” that is, cherubim and seraphim, “praise him.” He does not invite the angels to praise God because they might ever cease or because, when admonished by him, they might praise more; rather, by admonishing them in this way he shows his own affection, namely, that their praise is pleasing to him.

“Praise him, all his angels,” that is, you whom he sends into the world on his embassy; and you also, “all his powers,” namely, you who are not messengers, “praise him.”

[Col. 0689B] “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars;” and what does he mean individually? Let the entire “light” praise him. If the sun, moon, and other stars are said to have a spirit, they can praise God by themselves; if not, they praise you well because they are the material by which we praise you. This is not because the powers of one are meant, although they are sometimes used for all, as here; rather, it is because it would be lengthy to enumerate them all individually.

“Praise him, heavens of heavens.” He says this because he understands there to be many heavens. “And let the waters that,” in reality, “are above the heavens”—from which rain descends to us through the cataracts of heaven—“praise the name of the Lord,” that is, let them provide us with material for praising God. Among other things, we may marvel greatly that those waters, which are of dense substance, are held by the exceedingly subtle substance of heaven; and we ought not to cease from praising God.

Therefore praise him, “for he spoke,” that is, he willed it, “and they were made,” all things, that is, ordered through the composition of the four elements. He also made the matter itself; and this is what follows: “He commanded,” that is, firmly decreed, “and they were created,” namely, the elements themselves, from which he later ordered the remaining things. In this verse he rightly speaks against those who say that the world is coeternal with God.

Among other things he ordered the elements, and afterward he “established them” to remain “for ever,” that is, throughout the whole period of the present life, “and for ever,” in the age following this “age.” Although it is said in the Gospel, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew [Col. 0689D] 24), and here they are said to remain, the statements are not contradictory, because they are not said to pass away according to their substance but only according to their qualities. And once he had established them in this way, “he imposed a command, and it will not pass away,” that command, because just as he ordered them, so they still remain.

“Praise the Lord.” The second part. You heavenly creatures should praise him in this way, and you also “from the earth,” that is, earthly creatures, “praise the Lord.” He selects certain seemingly harmful creatures, in which he sees many people accusing God and considering him unjust, and he proposes to us that if anyone understands God’s ordering, he recognizes that God is to be praised in these creatures just as in the others. Hence he says: “Dragons, praise the Lord,” through which, as we see, God punishes his enemies according to their merits.

Or, according to Augustine, “dragons” means those subterranean regions through which dragons move, especially those in which there is water, because they are of a fiery nature and cool their heat there. “And all abysses,” that is, the depths of the sea, in which God punishes his enemies, praise the Lord; that is, provide us with material for praise, and so forth.

Whatever the case may be in this life, although things may appear to have been made unjustly, in the other life, when we understand according to what purpose of God they were made, they will be for us material for praise.

“Fire” also, that is, the sun’s great burning heat, and “hail,” which crushes crops and causes harm in many ways; “snow” also, and “ice”; “the spirit of storms,” that is, the great force of winds which sinks ships at sea and avenges God upon the iniquity of sailors—all these should provide us with material for praising God. Although all these things seem to fools to have been made unjustly by God, they ought nevertheless to provide us with material for praising him, since they “do his word,” that is, serve the will of God in every respect.

“Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars,” should provide us with material for praise.

“Beasts,” that is, lions, bears, and the other untamed animals, namely, savage beasts, “and all cattle,” such as oxen and other animals, domesticated animals in particular, should offer praise to God through the rational creature; “serpents and winged birds.”

All the things mentioned above, understood literally, praise God in the manner stated, namely, by providing us with material for praising God. They may also be examined allegorically in this way.

By dragons, abysses, and the other things mentioned above are signified the wicked according to the various kinds of evil found in them: dragons, that is, exceedingly cruel people; abysses, that is, those sunk most deeply in vices; fire, that is, those who are in the heat of their desires; hail, that is, those who crush the saints through their tribulations; snow, that is, those who are cold in sins; ice, that is, those frozen by the cold of unbelief; the spirit of storms, that is, people who create storms—meaning persecutions—against the saints, driving them from place to place.

All these do God’s word when they return to the faith and law of God.

Mountains signify the proud; hills, those who are less proud; fruit-bearing trees, those who produce the fruit of good works; cedars, those who possess within themselves the fragrance of spiritual virtues; beasts, wild creatures, namely, the uncultivated and unlearned; cattle, the meek; serpents, poisonous people, such as heretics; and winged birds, philosophers who possess wings, that is, the wisdom of various books, by which they are said to fly, meaning that they are superior to others.

All these wicked people, once converted, praise the Lord. That is, from all these groups the Lord has chosen certain people who, placed in rest in the future life, will praise the Lord.

“Kings of the earth and all peoples,” such as consuls, “princes and all judges of the earth.”

“Young men and virgins,” that is, the different sexes; “old men with the young,” that is, the different ages—let them “praise [Col. 0691A] the name of the Lord, because his name alone is exalted,” as the Apostle says: “He bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2).

What does each phrase mean? “His confession,” that is, the praise owed to God himself, is “above heaven and earth,” because neither the heavenly nor the earthly creatures can praise him sufficiently. “And” that God “has exalted the horn of his people,” that is, its height. For although it possesses some height in this life, that very height is brought low by many adversities; but in the other life it will be so exalted that no adversity will be able to bring it low. And for “all his saints,” thus exalted, there is “a hymn,” that is, praise accompanied by song; they praise the Lord without interruption. I mean the saints, namely, “the sons of Israel”—and I do not mean carnal sons, [Col. 0691B] but “a people drawing near to him,” namely to God, making itself like God.

## ON PSALM 149

### TITLE: Alleluia

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” Here again the subject is the praise of God. In the first part he urges the saints, already dwelling in eternal rest, to praise God. In the second, which begins, “The saints shall exult,” he describes the joy and powers that those saints will possess in the other life; and he invites us to praise, saying:

You Israelites, now seeing God in that eternal Jerusalem, “sing” to the “Lord” about the creation of heaven and earth, and so forth, “a new song,” namely about the restoration [Col. 0691C] that God effected through the incarnation of his Son. Nor do I urge everyone to praise him, because “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner (Eccli. XV),” but “his praise” is made “in the assembly of the saints.” I urge you not only to sing, but also: “Let Israel,” that is, the more perfect, “rejoice in him who made him,” because it already enjoys his presence; “and let the sons of Zion,” that is, the more fragile and lesser ones, “exult in their king,” whom they possess as present and by whom they are refreshed. Or he says “daughters” so as to include both sexes, against those who say that the female sex was not redeemed.

Let them also “praise his name in the choir,” that is, in harmony, and “sing psalms to him with timbrel and psalter,” not because they will use these instruments in the heavenly homeland, but because they will rejoice over the reward they will receive for having been a timbrel and a psalter here. [Col. 0691D] By the psalter are understood those who serve God through spiritual activity, such as contemplatives. By the timbrel, which is made from the hide of a dead animal, are understood those who hand themselves over to death for the testimony of truth, such as the holy martyrs.

Note that a choir is a pleasing harmony of diverse voices, signifying the harmony of charity in which God is to be praised, as the Apostle says: “Let all your deeds be done in charity (I Cor. XVI).” Or a choir is a musical instrument whose strings produce equal voices and do not render them discordant. Here we may also note the principal virtues: faith, when he says, “Praise in the assembly of the saints”; hope, when he says, “Let Israel rejoice”; charity, when he says, “Let them praise his name in the choir.” [Col. 0692A]

Continuation: Therefore sing psalms, and so forth, “because the Lord is well pleased” in that dwelling “with his people,” because he finds nothing in them by which he may be offended; and also for this reason let them sing, because “he will exalt the meek unto salvation,” eternal salvation.

“They shall exult.” The second part. Those “saints,” thus exalted, will likewise “exult in glory” and “rejoice,” not with an outward song, but “in their chambers,” that is, in their consciences.

And they will exult not only inwardly but also outwardly, as he says: “The exultations of God,” that is, praises of God made with exultation, will be “in [Col. 0692B] their throat,” that is, in their body and mouth; and in “their hands,” that is, in their powers, there will be “two-edged swords,” that is, the word of God, by which they themselves will cut and separate the good from the evil (Matt. XIII and XXV). These swords are two-edged because they cut on both sides, namely through the Old and New Testaments; or because in this life they separate vices both from the body and from the soul. He says “swords” in the plural because each person will use that sword.

For what purpose will the swords be in their hands? “To execute vengeance upon the nations,” that is, upon those who did not have the law; and to make “reproofs among the peoples,” who used the law wrongly.

And “to bind their kings,” that is, the kings of those peoples, “with fetters,” namely with eternal punishments, from which they will in no way be able to free themselves; “and their nobles,” that is, the nobler ones among them, “with iron chains,” because they will be punished in the very hands with which they inflicted evil and injuries in the present life. [Col. 0692C]

Why should I enumerate every detail? They will have the sword in their hands “to execute upon them,” kings and peoples, “the judgment written,” that is, to judge them according to what has been written in the prophets and other books; for example, when they say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire (Matt. XXV).” And this “glory” will belong not only to the holy apostles or to the highest saints, but “to all his saints” as well: they will possess this authority, for they consent to the divine sentence, as happens daily in the holy Church. The bishop indeed excommunicates as the mouth of the Church, and the whole Church consents, saying: Amen. [Col. 0692D]

## ON PSALM 150

### TITLE: Alleluia

“Praise the Lord among his saints.” Here again the Prophet invites us to sing alleluia—not those still striving toward the homeland, but those already placed in the king’s chamber, already rejoicing in the wedding feast, already conformed to the image of God, to which he had admonished us from the beginning of the book. The subject is the praise of God, now indeed a nuptial praise.

He shows from what things and in what manner they ought to praise the Lord, saying: “Praise the Lord among his saints,” that is, in contemplation of the saints whom he mercifully justified and wondrously rewarded; [Col. 0693A] “praise him” also “in his firmament,” that is, in contemplation of the firmament—namely, that he has made us so firm and placed us in such great rest that now no one, neither human being nor devil, can in any way harm the “firmament of his strength,” namely of God, which God himself made with great power. For in order to place us in that rest and conform us to his image, he caused his Son to become incarnate and also to be afflicted with the torment of death.

“Praise” also “him in his powers,” that is, for the fact that he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father. Another translation has, “in his mighty deeds.” “Praise” him also “according to the multitude of his greatness.” As God’s greatness is without end, so praise him without end. In this life, which is brief and has an end, God cannot be praised according to his greatness. [Col. 0693B] Having shown from what things God is to be praised, he shows how he is to be praised, saying: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet.” By the trumpet, which urges people to war or to a festival, are understood the holy preachers, who urge us to battle against vices and to celebrate a festival for God. It is as though he said:
