You holy heralds, praise God for the reward of your trumpet and your exhortation: “praise him” likewise “with psalter and harp,” that is, for the reward of the psalter, meaning the contemplative life, and for the reward of the active life, which is signified by the harp, as was shown earlier.

“Praise him with timbrel and choir,” that is, for the [Col. 0693C] reward of your mortification, as the holy martyrs are represented by the timbrel; and for the reward of the harmony and unanimity that you possessed in this life, which harmony is understood through the choir, in which a concordant sound is produced. “Praise him with strings and organ.” By the strings, which are greatly thinned and stretched and produce a sweet sound, are understood those who thin themselves by afflicting themselves with fasts, vigils, and other means, and who continually stretch themselves toward God, doing nothing for human favor but everything out of love for God, and producing for God through their works a sweet and pleasing song. By the organ, in which many pipes produce one harmony, are understood those in whom many kinds of virtues tend toward one goal and are joined together by the harmony of charity. It is as though he said: Praise [Col. 0693D] him for the reward of your self-discipline and for the reward of the harmony that you maintained amid many things.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” By the cymbals, in which two objects are struck together, are understood those who exhort one another so that they may sound forth well for God in the active life; or so that they may jubilate, that is, conceive such great joy in their minds that they cannot adequately express it with their voices. It is as though he said: Praise God for the reward of your good exhortation.

Why say more? “Let every spirit praise the Lord,” that is, all of you who have become spiritual, possessing a spiritual and subtle body. Blessed be God. Amen. Praise him.

[Col. 0694A]

“Glory to the Father.” This verse is sung after each psalm, specifically because every psalm—whether it is exhortatory, treats of the praise of God, concerns history, or is composed in any other manner—is always accomplished through the cooperation of the Trinity. Thus it should be explained:

“Glory,” that is, fame, frequently sung and proclaimed by us with praise, be “to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” so that in all our works God may always be honored and praised, as the Apostle urges: “Whether you eat, whether you drink, or whatever else you do, do all things for the glory of God (I Cor. X).” God is then glorified in all our works when, turning away from evil actions and thoughts, we will and do what is good—not out of desire for earthly things, but out of longing for heavenly things—and whatever good we do, we attribute entirely to divine mercy. [Col. 0694B] Nor do I say this as though the Father’s glory had only now acquired new grounds on which I should urge him to be glorified. Rather, “so,” that is, for these reasons, glory is to be offered “as,” that is, for the reasons for which glory “was” to be offered and rendered “in the beginning,” namely before the foundation of the world, “and now,” that is, in the present, “and always,” and it “will be” in the future “ages,” through the constancy of many “ages.” “Amen,” that is, let it be so, and let it be so again.

For God was always merciful, although at some times there were none toward whom he might show mercy; yet he was always almighty and benevolent. What he was, he is and will be, because he is immortal and eternal. For all these reasons it is both fitting and just that he should always be honored and magnified by his creatures. Blessed be God. Amen.

[Col. 0694C]

It must be known that there are three kinds of wicked thoughts. One kind consists of those that contaminate the mind through deliberation and a purpose to sin. Another consists of those that disturb the mind through the pleasure of sinning, yet do not draw it into consent to sin. The third consists of those that pass through the mind by a natural movement but do not entice it to commit sins; nevertheless, they hinder it from the good things it ought to think about. This happens, for example, when we recall to memory mental images of things that we once know to have been done or said needlessly. Their frequent reconsideration, like the troublesome insolence of flies, is accustomed to circle around the eyes of the heart and disturb its spiritual vision rather than blind it.

Solomon admonished us to be chastened from all these kinds of wicked thoughts when he says: “Guard your heart with every vigilance, for from it life proceeds (Prov. XIV).” [Col. 0694D] Following his admonition, let us act diligently: if we have sinned in our mind by consenting to commit some crime, let us quickly wipe it away through confession and worthy fruits of penance. If we perceive that we are being tempted by the pleasure of sinning, let us drive away that harmful pleasure through frequent prayers and tears and through frequent remembrance of perpetual bitterness. If we see that we are not sufficient by ourselves to repel it, let us seek the assistance of our brothers, so that what we cannot obtain by our own strength, we may obtain through their counsel and intercession. “For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power (James V)”; and as the same Apostle promised: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him [Col. 0695A] (ibid.),” because we cannot entirely avoid superfluous thoughts.

Let us drive them away as far as we can through the intercession of good thoughts, [Col. 0696A] and especially through frequent meditation on the Scriptures.

[Col. 0695]

# COMMENTARIES OF HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT, ON CERTAIN CANTICLES, WHICH THE CHURCH USES JUST AS IT USES THE PSALMS OF DAVID

(G)*

## CANTICLE OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH

[Col. 0695A]

“I will confess.” Here the title “Canticle of the Prophet Isaiah” is assigned because Isaiah, in the preceding words of his prophecy, prophesies the fall of humanity, the appeasement of God’s anger, and humanity’s restoration to its former dignity through the incarnate Son. The subject is Christ’s coming. The manner is that he shows what benefits come to human beings from that coming. The purpose is to urge praise for the incarnation of the Son.

The voice of the prophesying Son: “I will confess to you, Lord,” that is, I will praise you, “because you were angry with me,” that is, with the whole human race, through the fault of its ancestor, “and your wrath has been turned away,” that is, your anger has been removed through the forgiveness of sins, “and you have comforted me” [Col. 0695B] with the hope of eternal blessedness. He does not confess because he understands that God was angry, but because God has turned from anger to mercy.

Behold, you have comforted me in such a way that you, God, who were formerly angry, have now become my Savior, cleansing me from original sin. Therefore henceforth “I shall act,” that is, I shall advance in the virtues, “confidently,” that is, secure in the hope of reward if I do anything good. I will not fear the devil or the sin that dwells in mortal flesh, because this Savior will restrain both.

Therefore I will not fear, because the Lord is my strength against them, and he is my praise, that is, he will make me praiseworthy in eternal life. All these things are mine because the Creator has become powerful for me, his creature, unto eternal salvation.

[Col. 0695C]

“You shall draw water.” He turns to those who were present at the time of the incarnation, as though saying:

I see in the prophetic mystery, through the Spirit, the one who is to save me; but you will openly draw the waters of teaching and baptism in spiritual joy from the springs, that is, from the Savior’s manifold abundance. On that day of the incarnation you will say to one another and admonish others: “Confess to the Lord and invoke his name,” that is, prepare yourselves as worthy to invoke him.

“Make known.” You will also say this: “Make known among the peoples,” by preaching, “his discoveries,” that is, salvation and every path of wisdom and knowledge that he found and showed to his faithful. Do not wish to claim God’s name for yourselves, as Adam did; rather, [Col. 0696A] always remember that his name is exalted and that he punishes the proud.

You will also say this: “Sing to this Lord,” because he has done great things in these matters and is worthy of praise. You will also say: “Announce this,” that is, this salvation, “throughout the whole earth,” everywhere among the nations; this Savior gathers all people.

“Exult.” It is as though salvation must now be announced to everyone. But you, O habitation of Zion, that is, you Jews in particular, exult and praise for this reason: because the Holy One of Israel, that is, the one who sanctifies Israel, is great in your midst, born from you and having lived among you.

## CANTICLE OF HEZEKIAH, KING OF JUDAH

[Col. 0696B]

“I said.” This canticle was written by Isaiah, yet it is not titled with his name but with the name of Hezekiah, who is introduced as speaking through Isaiah. Although Hezekiah served God in many ways, he sinned in this respect: he did not remove the high places. Therefore he was struck by God with a serious illness and deserved to hear from Isaiah: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.” He then turned toward the wall in deep contrition, wept over his sins, and again deserved to hear from the same Isaiah that God, appeased by his repentance, had added fifteen years to his life.

After Hezekiah recovered from his illness, he sang this canticle to God his deliverer. In it he recalls both his sin and his illness, so that, by contrast with the tribulation, the manner of his deliverance may appear more gracious. The subject is Hezekiah himself, placed in illness and delivered from illness. The manner [Col. 0696C] is that he shows why he fell into that illness—because of his sins—how he behaved in his illness, namely, how deeply he repented, and how, once his sin had been cleansed through repentance, he recovered. The purpose is to urge repentance.

It must be noted that Isaiah, speaking in the Lord’s name and announcing an impending death, did not lie to Hezekiah, even though Hezekiah recovered. For the Lord is accustomed to speak conditionally, as when he says: “You will die, unless you repent.”

The words of Hezekiah, recalling how he conducted himself in his illness:

“When I became ill, I said,” that is, I resolved: “I shall go to the gates of hell in the midst of my days,” because I had not completed my days in the pursuit of good works.

[Col. 0697A]

“I sought,” and for this reason: because I saw that, on account of my sins, I was to be placed in hell before completing my life. I sought from the Lord, through prayers and contrition of heart, the remainder of my years, so that, by an extension of my life, I might complete what was unfinished in me.

Therefore I sought good things in order to complete them. For if I did not complete them, I said, that is, I resolved: “I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living.” I used to rejoice in the company of the one who was to restore the rest that Adam had lost, but I shall no longer see him among those who are the land of the living.

“I shall not see.” An exposition of the preceding verse. Truly I shall not see, because, if I die now, I shall no longer look toward salvation: I shall not see the man whom I understand to be destined to come in humanity, nor shall I behold that same inhabitant [Col. 0697B] who will be the habitation of rest. It is as though he said: He will indeed come to places of unrest, but he will be an inhabitant of rest, no longer dying.

“My generation has been taken away.” It is as though he said: If I die incomplete, so that I do not finish the good works, then that distinguished one who is to be born from my seed will be taken away from my salvation. Or, the generation of the devout and elect has been removed far from me—my generation, that is, those among whom I understood I would be. And it has been rolled up from me like a shepherd’s tent.

He speaks by comparison, as though to say: The fellowship of the saints has been removed from me with such speed, if I die incomplete, as quickly as shepherds’ tents—that is, pastoral shelters—are rolled up when they change pasture.

“It has been cut off.” Therefore I shall not look upon it, because my life has been cut off, that is, I have not completed the good works I ought to have completed, like a piece cut off by a weaver. He speaks by comparison of a weaver who, before the whole fabric has been completed, cuts off the part he has woven. And my weaver, namely God, has cut me short—not, I say, after I had woven something, but while I was still beginning, that is, while I was preparing myself to do good, he cut me short. [Col. 0697C] He says that his life was cut off, not because he was dead, but because, owing to the excessive severity of his illness, he came very near death.

“From morning to evening you will finish me.” It is as though he had cut me short for this reason, and as though I had been dead, because each day, owing to the excessive severity of my illness, I said: “O Lord, from this morning until evening you will finish me.” And in the evening I hoped and said: “Until morning you will finish me.”

[Col. 0697D]

Therefore I hoped in this way because the illness sent by God crushed all my bones, just as a lion breaks all that it has seized.

“From morning.” Because of the contrasting comparison with the lion, he repeats the phrase. And because the illness resembled a lion, I therefore said: “From morning until evening you will finish me.”

Up to this point he has spoken about the severity of the illness. Since it occurred on account of sins, he now begins to speak of the repentance he practiced in the illness itself, as though saying:

I see that this illness has come upon me because of my sins, but I shall cry out to the Lord with the full intensity of my mind, like a young swallow, which opens its mouth widest when crying out; and I shall meditate like a dove, lamenting my sins as I cry out.

[Col. 0698A]

“They have grown thin.” Because I was preparing to cry out and groan, my eyes, that is, my affections, have grown thin, that is, having shed their earthly thickness, they have become clearer and more refined, and through this they look upward, being directed toward the heights, namely toward God.

“Lord.” I say that my eyes speak thus: “Lord, I suffer the force of illness,” like one who is oppressed in a lawsuit and seeks an advocate. Therefore he says: “But you answer for me,” that is, be my advocate.

“What shall I say?” As though amazed at his own sins and at the justice of the one whom he invokes, he says:

I invoke you to deliver me, but what shall I say as I invoke you? Or what will God himself answer me? How will God himself become my advocate, when he himself has inflicted this illness upon me because of my sins? It is as though he said: [Col. 0698B] Although I understand that he is angry and is inflicting punishment on me because of my sins, nevertheless through contrition of heart I know that he has been appeased and will heal me from my illness.

“I will reflect.” It is as though he said:

If you answer for me and raise me up from my illness, I will reflect to you all my years, repaying good for each of the good things I did in my former years, in the bitterness of my soul, that is, in deep contrition of heart.

“Lord.” He presents the weakness of the flesh not as an excuse, but as a means of obtaining more easily:

Lord, if this is how one lives, and if life exists amid such weakness of the flesh, which cannot resist sins—and if the life of my spirit, that is, of my sensuality, is such that my flesh teaches and suggests nothing except sins, which is indeed the case—so long as a human being remains in the flesh, then you will rightly “correct” me, that is, you will correct and amend me [Col. 0698C] through this illness, grant me time for amendment, and afterward give me life, making me just and holy.

And truly I ought to be corrected and amended if my time is prolonged, because now I recognize this: while all the people are at peace and secure from enemies, this bitterness of mine is the bitterest illness. When the whole people was in danger with me amid wars, I could not attend so carefully to my fault. But because I alone am punished while the people remains unharmed, I therefore discover that this has happened on account of my sins.

“But you.” He now begins to show how he recovered, as though saying:

The illness is bitter for me, but you have delivered my soul, forgiving me and extending my life so that it would not perish. You delivered me in this way because you cast [Col. 0698D] all my sins behind your back, consigning them to oblivion by forgiving them.

For you delivered me so that, once delivered, I might confess; otherwise I could not confess, because hell will not confess to you. No one, once placed in hell, can praise you. Nor could I, if I were placed there because of my sins. Nor will death—that is, someone dead in sins—even in this life praise you as is fitting; nor could I, if I were to persist in sins. And those who descend into the pit, that is, into hell or the depth of vices, will not await your truth; that is, they do not understand as beneficial for themselves the truth promised in the flesh of your Son. Nor would I, if I died in sins or persisted in sins, understand that the future incarnation of your Son [Col. 0699A] would benefit me.

“Living.” They will not confess, but the living person—that is, the one who lives in the virtues in the present and in blessedness after death—he alone will confess to you. Therefore you have given me life so that I might confess to you.

He will confess to you, I say, and one of those who have been given life, having become a father and teacher to others, will make your truth known to the children whom he teaches, that is, your promises: that you do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezech. XVIII). Thus I too make it known today through my illness and healing.

And so that I may confess, Lord, as you have begun, henceforth save me and the others, and together we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord, not in the high places, as you have promised up to this point.

## CANTICLE OF HANNAH

[Col. 0699B]

“She exulted.” Hannah, having long endured the reproach of barrenness from her rival Peninnah and her sons, was at last made fertile. When her son Samuel had been brought to the temple, as was customary, she sang this canticle to the Lord, as if in thanksgiving. In it she also prophesies the salvation that the Lord would accomplish for the Israelite people in Samuel’s time and through Samuel himself.

Through Hannah, formerly barren and afterward made fertile, the Gentiles are signified: formerly despised by the Jews, they were later converted and placed before the Jews. Through Peninnah is signified the Jewish people, formerly accepted by God and afterward rejected. Through Samuel is signified Christ, who was to be the salvation of the Jewish people, that is, of every believer. [Col. 0699C]

The subject is Hannah’s son, given by God. The manner is that she shows how Hannah behaved concerning the son given to her: namely, that she gave thanks to God the giver, and what occurred through Samuel, namely the salvation of the people and the destruction of enemies. The purpose is to urge praise of God for the obtaining of some benefit.

The voice of Hannah rejoicing over the son she had received:

“My heart exulted in the Lord,” because he gave me a son; “and my horn,” that is, my defense against the reproach of barrenness, “was exalted in my God.” I did not become proud in myself, but showed myself grateful to God in all things.

And my mouth, which previously did not dare answer those who reproached me, is now opened wide against my enemies, because I have something with which to answer my rival and her sons. Therefore I have been exalted because I have rejoiced in your salvation, that is, in the son whom I foresee will be the salvation of your people, given through you.

“There is none holy.” Since he gave a savior, it is evident from this that there is no one holy like the Lord, who possesses equal power. Truly there is no one equally holy, for there is no other besides you. No one is holy except through you, and there is no one powerful in granting benefits, mighty like our God.

Therefore, my rival and you sons of the Philistines, whom I understand to be destined to be overcome through the priesthood of my son, do not continue to speak exalted things as you have done until now in your boasting. Do not merely cease to multiply new boasts, but let even the old things you used to utter [Col. 0700A] depart from your mouth. Let them depart because God, who foresees all things, will prepare punishment for your boasting, although you do not understand the outcome of events. This is what he says: “For God is the Lord of knowledge,” and thoughts are prepared, that is, they are known before they come to be.

And because he knows your proud consciences and my humility, he has brought you down and exalted us. This is what he says: “The bow,” that is, the power, “of the strong,” namely of my rival, her sons, and the Philistines, “has been overcome” by my fertility and by the strength of the Jews; and “the weak,” that is, I and my people, or even the Hebrews, have now been girded with strength through this son.

Those who were formerly filled with power and riches have now hired themselves out for bread with which to be satisfied [Col. 0700B] and will serve as laborers; while those who were formerly hungry, like myself or the Jews, have been filled.

“Until.” I gradually grew so much, and my adversaries declined, until they reached the greatest humiliation. This is what he says: “Until the barren woman,” that is, I, or rather Judea, powerless to resist the foreigners, “has borne many,” while that rival who had many sons, or the foreigners who had many warlike men, has become weak.

And the fact that I have been filled while they have become weak is the work of the Lord, who kills those whom he wishes and gives life to those whom he wishes. He brings the dead down to hell, so that they may remain there forever, and he brings some back because he foresaw that the just would be brought back in Christ’s resurrection.

The Lord also makes poor and enriches with riches; he humbles and raises up to positions of power.

[Col. 0700C]

He himself, I say, raises the needy from the dust, that is, from a lower rank, as he has raised me or my people; and from the dung heap, that is, from great reproach and rejection, he raises the poor to great dignity.

He raises him for this purpose: that he may sit with princes and hold a throne of glory like an emperor.

And he himself can do this, for the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord—that is, the farthest limits of the earth—and he has set the world, that is, the firmament, upon those hinges.

After the Lord himself has exalted the saints, he will also keep the feet of his saints from sinning, that is, their ends, because he will lead them to a good end. And conversely the wicked will fall silent, not daring to murmur and having nothing good to utter, placed in the darkness of hell. And because only the man [Col. 0700D] will be strengthened in the future, this strength will not be his own but God’s.

A strong man will indeed appear, but his adversaries, deprived of divine strength, will tremble and appear fearful before the Lord. And he, existing in heaven, will thunder terribly over them through the archangel’s trumpet, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire (Matt. XXV).” Or, before he comes to that judgment, he will thunder from heaven in the present age, that is, through the apostles, who will announce the future misery to them by preaching.

Nor is it surprising that they will be afraid, because at that judgment the Lord will judge all the ends of the earth, that is, human beings of every kind, and he will do this through the Son. This is what he says: [Col. 0701A] “And he will give authority to his king, Christ”; and at that judgment he will exalt the horn, that is, the height, which appears depressed in some people, so that everything may be subjected to the humanity of his Christ, that is, of the Son signified through Samuel.

Allegorically the whole psalm may be read in this way.

The voice of the Church from the Gentiles:

“My heart exulted in the Lord,” because I have been taken up into the faith; “and my heart was exalted in my God,” because I possess a defense against the Jews who reproach me.

“My mouth was opened wide against my enemies,” because I have something with which to answer them, since they have now been blinded by my illumination; “because I have rejoiced in your salvation,” because I have received the faith of your Son, the Savior.

O Jews, do not continue to speak exalted things against me in your boasting. [Col. 0701B] Let the old things that you used to use as reproaches depart. Let them depart because “the bow,” that is, the power of the strong Jews, has been overcome by us, who now understand more than they do; and “the weak,” that is, we, have been girded with the strength of knowledge.

The other Jews, formerly filled with wisdom, have now hired themselves out for bread; they have become a light for the Gentiles, so that they might receive the bread of understanding, which is life. And the hungry Gentiles, formerly ignorant of God, have been filled with knowledge.

The Gentiles, formerly barren, grew until they bore many into the faith; and that Judea, which formerly had many sons instructed in the worship of God, became weak and blind. Nor is it surprising that the Gentiles grew in this way, because the Lord did this: he kills by blinding and gives life by illuminating [Col. 0701C]; he leads the slain down to hell and brings the living back.

The same Lord makes the Jews poor and enriches the Gentiles; he humbles the proud Jews and exalts the humble Gentiles.

He raises the needy Gentile from the dust, that is, from ignorance, and raises that poor one from the dung heap of idolatry.

He does this so that the Gentile may sit with princes, that is, with the apostles, and hold a throne of glory in eternal blessedness.

“For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord,” as has been explained up to the end.

## CANTICLE OF MOSES TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL

[Col. 0701D]

“Let us sing to the Lord.” After the children of Israel had been led out through the Red Sea, Moses sang this canticle of praise to the Lord, as if in thanksgiving, because he had drowned their enemies (Exod. XV), and he taught the children of Israel to sing it, with his sister Miriam going before and playing the harp. In it he prefigured the joy of the saints, who, after their vices have been drowned through baptism, have escaped and give thanks to God.

The subject is the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea and the drowning of their enemies. The manner is that he shows himself giving thanks to God for his deliverance and the drowning of the enemies, and by what means this passage occurred, namely through God’s right hand and strength. He also prophesies what would happen during the journey after the passage, namely how God would deliver them from everything that opposed them on the way, until he brought them into the promised land. [Col. 0702A] The purpose is to urge praise of God on account of this passage.

The voice of Moses applauding the deliverance:

“Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified.” When he performed many deeds in Egypt, he appeared more glorious in this drowning of the enemies, because he cast “the horse,” that is, all the pomp and pride, and “the rider,” that is, Pharaoh himself and his soldiers, into the sea.

“My strength.” He determines who it is that has been so gloriously magnified, namely the Lord. It is as though he said: The one who has been so magnified is my strength and my praise; he makes me strong and praiseworthy, and he himself has become my salvation when the enemies were drowned.

This same one is my creator and therefore I will glorify him. [Col. 0702B] He is not a new god, but the God of my father Abraham and of the others. I will exalt him, and therefore he is worthy of praise.

“The Lord.” He was able to cast them down and to become my salvation, and the Lord himself is like a warrior, fighting powerfully against his enemies. And if you do not know who he is, I tell you: “the Almighty” is his name.

“Chariot.” He now determines which horse and which rider he understood above, as though saying: Since he is a warrior and almighty, he therefore cast Pharaoh’s chariot and Pharaoh himself, together with his pride and pomp, into the sea. And not Pharaoh alone, but his army also, that is, his entire retinue, he cast into the sea.

And not merely any men, but his chosen leaders were drowned in the Red Sea. [Col. 0702C] And because they might have been drowned and then emerged again, he adds: “The depths,” that is, the depths of the waters, “covered them.” They descended into the deep like a stone, that is, in the manner of a stone descending downward, forever.

Your right hand, O Lord. He begins to determine by what means He brought about that drowning, namely, by the strength of His right hand, that is, by His operation. He says this: O Lord, so they were drowned, and in this your right hand—that is, your operation—was magnified in strength, that is, in this mighty deed. Or, “was magnified in strength” means that it was recognized to be strong. And truly your right hand is strong, because your right hand—that is, your operation and power—not chance or a change in the element, struck the enemy Pharaoh; and in the multitude of your glory, that is, in manifold glory, you cast down my adversaries, the whole household of Pharaoh.

You sent forth your anger. He still shows how He acted: you sent your anger upon them, and it devoured them in the water as quickly as fire devours stubble; and in the spirit of your fury, in the whirlwind of wind which you sent in anger, the waters were gathered over them.

But before they entered, the wave stood still, that is, the water was divided—which is marvelous, since by its nature it is flowing. And the water was not divided only beside the bank; in the middle of the sea also the depths were gathered like a wall on the right and on the left: the depths, that is, the deep waters. And therefore, because he saw the water standing still, the enemy said: “I will pursue and overtake them; I will divide the spoils among my soldiers, which they seized from the Egyptians; my soul shall be filled with those spoils; I shall satisfy my desire.”

And against them I will unsheathe my sword; I will not draw it back from the slaughter, and my hand shall kill them.

He was planning thus, but your spirit, or the whirlwind, blew when sent forth, and the sea covered them; they were drowned like lead in mighty waters.

And because you acted so powerfully, O Lord, who is like you among the strong, that is, among the mighty? And beyond strength, who is magnificent like you in holiness? Who is so fearful and praiseworthy, and does wonders like you?

And in that drowning you stretched out, that is, magnified, your hand, that is, your operation, and the earth devoured them, that is, the hope of the earth, since they saw the bare ground.

You were their guide. Here he begins to show prophetically, in part, how He led them through the desert as far as the Promised Land. Once the people had been led across, you were their guide in your mercy, to the people whom you redeemed.

And you carried them in your strength to your holy dwelling, that is, to Jerusalem, where you are sanctified.

Meanwhile, while they were crossing the desert, peoples came up to meet them and to harm them, angered that they were crossing their borders. He determines which peoples: namely, anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia.

[Col. 0703C] Then the princes of Edom were troubled, that is, of the Idumeans, who descended from Esau. Trembling seized the mighty men of Moab as they passed by; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew rigid with fear.

Let dread fall upon them. Speaking prophetically, he says, as though he were saying: They will fear, and I grant this: let terror of mind and bodily panic fall upon them in the greatness of your arm, in great strength.

And I pray that they become immovable against Israel, like a stone, until your people, O Lord, pass through—that is, pass through their regions—and not merely through certain places, but until this people of yours, whom you have acquired, pass through entirely into the Promised Land.

And as I pray, so it will happen, because you will bring them into the Promised Land and firmly plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, namely, the highlands of Judaea, in your most firmly established dwelling, which you, O Lord, have made and prepared for them.

And that dwelling which you gave them is your sanctuary, O Lord, because there you will sanctify what your hands established, so that, as long as they obeyed you, they might hold it firmly. And this Lord who accomplished all these things will reign forever, that is, for as long as anyone can imagine and beyond what anyone can imagine.

And we can be certain that He will accomplish all the things that still remain; this can be seen from the beginning of His works, so that the presentation of past events may be certainty regarding future ones. He says this: For Pharaoh entered into the sea with his chariots and horsemen, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them.

But the children of Israel walked on dry ground in its midst.

It may be read allegorically. It is the voice of the faithful, purified in baptism, glorifying God for the destruction of the devil and of vices. Let us, purified in baptism, sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously magnified in this our restoration, more than in the first creation. Therefore let us sing, because He cast the horse—that is, all the devil’s pride—and the rider of this horse, the devil himself, into the sea, since in the baptized he lost the power which he exercised over the whole human race.

The Lord is my strength and my praise, as has been explained; and although He is the Creator of all, He became a creature, bringing me eternal salvation.

This is my God, and I will glorify Him, the God of my father Abraham and of the others; or, the head of Christ, who is the father of the baptized. Hence the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). The Lord, as a warrior, has the omnipotent name. The reference to the chariot determines who the rider of the chariot is: namely, those wicked beings who gather in the same army to carry Pharaoh—that is, Beelzebub, the prince of demons—and his entire army, that is, the lesser devils. He cast them into the sea, because they no longer have such power to harm the baptized.

His chosen princes were drowned in the Red Sea, [Col. 0704C] in the blood of Christ.

The right hand. As though he were saying: You accomplished all these things through your Son. Your right hand struck the enemy, that is, the devil; and in the multitude of your glory, that is, in the manifold glory of His birth, passion, and resurrection, you cast down my adversaries, the evil spirits.

You sent forth. He still shows how He cast them down and drowned them: you sent your anger, which devoured them like stubble; and in the Holy Spirit, minister of your fury, just as He is minister of grace, the waters were gathered and multiplied over those evil spirits—that is, tribulations, which will occur in the future, when they are tormented in hell.

[Col. 0704D] But meanwhile, before the day of judgment, the wave stood still and the flowing wave was prolonged—that is, the punishment was held back, since they are not yet being tormented. He further increases the reserved punishment by saying: “the depths,” that is, those deepest punishments, were gathered—that is, reserved and multiplied—in the middle of the sea.

And therefore, because the devil saw that punishment had been delayed in the present time, he said: “I will pursue these whom I see taken away from me, and I will overtake them through sins. I will divide the spoils,” that is, I will take away their virtues. “My soul,” that is, my desire, “will be filled,” because I do not want substitutes to be placed in the position from which I fell.

And if I cannot succeed through deceptions, I will draw my sword through my ministers, so that they may be moved by terror, [Col. 0705A] and my hand shall kill them bodily.

He blew. He was planning to pursue and kill them in this way, but your Holy Spirit blew and troubled them, diminishing his power. And the sea covered them—the water of baptism. It covered them so that they might not rise again into their former power. He says this: They were drowned like lead in mighty waters, which possess great power.

Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? As has been explained.

You stretched out your hand in baptism; thus you deprived him of power. And with regard to the day of judgment, you stretched out—that is, prolonged and enlarged—your hand, that is, your vengeance, which you will inflict upon them.

[Col. 0705B] And once they had been thus overthrown and destined for greater punishment, you were their guide through the desert of this life after baptism, to the people whom you redeemed by the price of blood, in your mercy—that is, in the manifold bestowal of graces.

And you carried them in your strength to your holy dwelling, as far as eternal blessedness.

As they journeyed toward that blessedness, peoples rose up to detain them—that is, a multitude of vices or wicked people—and they were angered against them, afflicting them. He explains the wicked in parts, as though he were saying: And because they could not overcome them, therefore anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia. “Philistia” is interpreted as “falling by drinking,” and signifies those made drunk by earthly things, who wish to corrupt the saints. Because they cannot do so, they grieve.

Then the princes of Edom, that is, “blood-colored,” who persecute the saints, were troubled. Trembling seized the mighty men of Moab. “Moab” is interpreted as “one who abuses the law,” and signifies those guilty of incest and subject to other vices. All these grieve over the perseverance of the good and fear the punishments announced through them: all the inhabitants of Canaan. Canaan means “descent,” and signifies those thrust down into the lowest depths of vices, who grieve because they cannot hold the saints back.

Let it fall upon them. As though he were saying: These wicked people wish to corrupt the saints in this way, but let terror and panic fall upon them in the greatness of your arm, that is, of your Son.

Let them become immovable like a stone until the people pass through this life [Col. 0705D] into heavenly life—the people of yours whom you have acquired.

And so it will happen: you will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, that is, in heavenly blessedness, namely, in your most firmly established dwelling, which you, O Lord, have made for those who fear you.

That work, I say, is your sanctuary, O Lord, because nothing defiled will enter it. The rest is self-evident.

## THE PRAYER OF THE PROPHET HABAKKUK

### For Ignorances

O Lord, I have heard. Among the other words of his prophecy, Habakkuk also prophesies the birth of Christ. Because he understood that great benefit would arise from it, he sang this song of rejoicing to God, in which he treats Christ’s incarnation and passion. Its method is to enumerate and define the benefits bestowed upon humankind through that birth. Its purpose is to exhort people to praise God for the incarnation of the Son.

O Lord, I have heard through inward speech your utterance—that is, what you cause others to hear concerning you, namely, the incarnation of the Son—and I was afraid, because I understood something contrary to nature.

O Lord. As though he were saying: The event is indeed marvelous, but I shall marvel at it still further, because I understand that you are powerful enough to act contrary to nature. He says this: This is your work, O Lord, that is, something fitting to your omnipotence; and this work of yours, O Lord, vivify—that is, show it to be living, powerful, effective, and known to many. This will not occur during the time of my barrenness, but in the middle of the years, in the fullness of time, when it will be as the heart of the years.

In the middle of the years. As though he were saying: And just as I pray, so you will make that work—that is, that incarnation—known. In accomplishing the work, you will remember the mercy placed before the first human being, but withdrawn because of sin and, as it were, consigned to oblivion, since you had previously been angry with that human being.

God. Because he had spoken obscurely in an enigma, he now openly determines what work and what utterance he had understood. God will come from the south, that is, from Egypt, from where the south wind blows, to the land of Israel after Herod’s death. Hence it is said: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Matt. 2; Hos. 11). And that same holy one will come from Mount Pharan. Pharan is a place in Egypt called Pharos, a tower on the shore of the sea; hence the kings of that land are called Pharaohs. “God,” by nature from the Father; “holy,” by humanity.

He covered the heavens. And although He is both God and holy, His glory covered the heavens, that is, it darkens those who are greater by its brilliance; and it also illuminates their lesser light, flooding it with the greater radiance. And the whole earth is full of His praise, that is, earthly people praise Him, or become praiseworthy through Him.

His splendor. Behold, this concerns the passion. And after His splendor has become like light throughout the whole world, then the horns of the cross will be in His hands.

[Col. 0706D] And although He is so great, He will nevertheless be able to be crucified, because there, that is, at the time of the passion, His strength was hidden, when He handed Himself over entirely to the power of those crucifying Him. And from this crucifixion great benefit will arise, because when He rises again, death will go before His face—that is, His presence—and will be destroyed, because through Him the power of rising again is granted to all.

And through His resurrection the strong, armed devil will come out from the house which he had previously possessed, before His feet, wherever He Himself proceeds through inspiration. And the devil, losing his right, stood and, raised up into immortality and incorruptibility, measured the earth—that is, by measure, He received from the earth those whom He wished and rejected those whom He did not wish.

[Col. 0707A] And He looked upon them—that is, weighed the merits of each—and dissolved the nations from the coldness of unbelief. And the mountains of the world, that is, the more powerful and prouder people in this world, were crushed, that is, humbled and deeply pierced by recognizing their sins.

And the hills of the world also, that is, the powerful among worldly people, were bent toward repentance by His eternal paths, through the paths which eternity makes in the world by preaching through Christ’s humanity and through His apostles.

I also saw—that is, I understood by the prophetic spirit—that the tents of Ethiopia, that is, those who are black with vices and continually dwell in tents, serving in them, would be troubled through repentance for their former iniquity. And the skins would also be troubled through repentance, [Col. 0707B] that is, those serving in tents which were made of skins. “Skins,” I say, of the earth, that is, possessed by earthly people, who are Midian—that is, those declining judgment, meaning those who do not believe that they will be punished for their sins. Midian is the people who opposed Israel when it was entering the Promised Land, and they signify those who prepare obstacles for the saints as they strive toward blessedness.

Will you perhaps...? He determines by what means this conversion takes place, namely, through teaching and baptism. He says it thus: O Lord, who previously exercised your vengeance in the waters of the Flood (Gen. 7), and turned the waters of Egypt into blood, and overturned the waters of the sea upon the Egyptians (Exod. 14), are you still angry with the rivers of Scripture, so as to turn them into blood, [Col. 0707C] that is, into a false literal meaning, so that they kill those who drink? As though he were saying: He is no longer angry; rather, there is now a true and salutary understanding. Or is your fury still present—that is, the continuation of your anger—in the rivers? As you previously exercised your anger, so may you now exercise it continually in the rivers? As though he were saying: No; just as you previously exercised your anger continually through the waters, so now you continually show mercy through the teachings of Scripture. Or is your indignation still in the sea? It is not; rather, just as in the sea you killed Pharaoh and his people, so conversely you now save people in baptism.

You who ascend. Behold how you make the Scriptures salutary. I speak thus because you ascend upon your horses—that is, upon your apostles, who carry you through the world—[Col. 0707D] and your chariots are salvation, namely, the four Gospels, the salvation of your people. The Gospels are called chariots because of the four things preached concerning Christ: His birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension.

And through these horses, continually raising up, you will raise your bow—that is, the old law, which was previously useless when understood literally. Now you have directed it through the new law, as though you had placed the string on a bow, and you have aimed it toward the knowledge of many. You will also raise up the oaths—that is, the firm promises—which you spoke not to one tribe only but to many, such as Isaac and Jacob and others, saying: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), or “all the nations.”

[Col. 0708A] You will cleave the rivers. Through that revived teaching of the law you will cleave—that is, refute—the rivers of the earth, that is, the abundant teachings of earthly people who wish to deny the Virgin’s childbirth and other such things. And when you cleave them in this way, the waters saw you—that is, those overflowing with many-voiced wisdom. Those mountains mentioned above, because of their pride, grieved over the falsified and destroyed wisdom. And when they had been weakened, the torrent of waters passed through—that is, the abundance and force of your teaching passed unharmed through all their sophistries, as far as the ends of the world.

And in that passage the abyss, the most profound depth of secular knowledge, gave its voice to restrain it—that is, a false argument. And when the height—that is, the proud and powerful—could not prevail through deceptive arguments, it lifted its hands by striking.

Nevertheless the sun—that is, Christ Himself—and the moon—that is, the Church—stood firmly against those assailants in their dwelling, in the steadfastness of their minds. And because they stood in this way, the nations will go to the faith in the light of your arrows, that is, the apostles; and especially they will go in the brightness of your flashing spear, that is, through the preaching of Christ, who was like a flashing spear in comparison with the arrows.

And those people would not be converted by these gentle and peaceful words; but you will trample the earth—that is, those earthly people—and convert them by convincing them, in a roar, that is, in a roaring and forceful preaching. And you will stupefy—that is, render those nations devoted to paganism stupid and immovable with regard to their former works—in fury, that is, in a furious and threatening preaching, when you threaten infernal punishments.

And then you will be able to act well, because while you were previously hidden and known to few, now through the incarnation of the Son you have gone forth for the salvation of many, being powerful for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ—as though he were saying: Through Christ you will give that salvation.

You are salvation for your people, but you struck the head—that is, the devil—out of the house of the wicked, that is, out of the hearts of the wicked. And you stripped his very foundation—that is, those in whom he was firmly established—of that devil, as far as the devil’s neck, to be bound and punished eternally. He speaks by comparison, as of a captive who is led to punishment with his neck bound [Col. 0708D].

Meanwhile, while you do not abandon them thus for ever, you have cursed his scepters, that is, you have diminished the power which they previously exercised over everyone. And you have cursed the head of his warriors, that is, those princes who are the heads and superiors among the warriors and persecutors. “The head,” I say, and “the scepters,” coming to scatter me as a whirlwind stirs the sea.

They come to scatter me, but they will gain nothing, because if they kill the body, they cannot kill the soul (Matt. 10). He says this: The exultation of those persecuting me is like the exultation of one who devours a poor man in a hidden place. When he had previously believed that the man was rich and that through his death he would possess wealth, after killing him he realizes that the man was poor, and therefore that he has gained nothing.

The way. Truly their exultation is empty, because through the midst of those persecutors you made a way and a passage for your horses—that is, for the saints who carry you—in the sea, that is, in the world, namely, in the mire of many waters, in the place where there are many waters: carnal desires, which generate mire, into which the feet of the affections become fixed. But the saints, with the good soles of their affections, emerge from such mire.

I heard. As though he were saying: The saints pass through, but nevertheless they are grievously troubled on this road. He says this: I heard what they were plotting on this road against those who passed through; and my belly—that is, the weakness of my flesh—was troubled by the frailty of my flesh; and my lips trembled, [Col. 0709B] that is, in the fear of the flesh they proclaimed the word of God at the sound of their voice—that is, when I understood what they were preparing.

Let it enter. The flesh was afraid, but nevertheless I will not cease because of that. Rather, let decay enter beneath me, and corruption into my bones, even to the bones; and let that decay itself also bubble up beneath me. This means that I would sooner permit myself to be so afflicted that worms would pour from my body.

I suffer for this reason: so that on the day of tribulation, when those persecutors are tormented in hell, I may rest and ascend into heaven to our people, to the company of those who were our people—that is, like us in faith and works—who in this life were well-girded and prepared.

The fig tree. And truly they are troubled, for they will lose there all the good things which they loved in this world. He sets this out in detail concerning earthly goods: For the fig tree will not blossom, and there will be no shoot on the vines.

The work of the olive will disappoint, and the fields will yield no food.

The sheep will be cut off from the fold, and there will be no herd in the stalls.

But I. They are saddened by the loss of their goods, but I, having obtained blessedness, will rejoice in the Lord and exult in my God Jesus.

And that same God the Lord is my strength in the present time. He will make my feet in this life like those of deer; He will make me ascend as quickly as a deer ascends, and in the future He will lead me, victorious, over the heights of heaven, singing in psalms.

## THE SONG OF MOSES

[Col. 0709D]

Hear, O heavens. The Lord had foretold (Deut. 32) that Moses would die, and that after his death Israel would be led into the Promised Land and would sin there, even worshiping foreign gods; and that for this reason God would afflict them marvelously. Therefore, lest it seem that this happened through the weakness of God, who had previously protected them, the Lord commanded that it be written down that this occurred because of their sins, not because of God’s weakness. He afflicts those who sin and permits them to be trampled by their enemies. He therefore wanted it written down so that the same might be believed concerning what followed: when they are punished and abandoned by God, it is because of their sins. Nor should this be charged to God, who, if they did not sin, would protect them.

Here Moses enumerates the good things God did for them and, conversely, the evil things they returned to Him, even after He had rescued them from so many dangers and led them into the Promised Land. For this they deserved to be severely punished and trampled by their enemies. In the first part he shows that what he teaches here is exceedingly useful, and therefore he calls both greater and lesser beings as witnesses. This is what he says:

Hear, O heavens, what I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth. As though he were saying: Let everyone hear, acknowledge, approve that it is true, and announce it to posterity.

Let my teaching condense into rain. Behold its usefulness: it causes the barren hearts of hearers to condense and become fertile, like water makes the earth fertile. Let my discourse flow like dew [Col. 0710B] for the benefit, once again, of earthly people who think wrongly about the judgments of God.

Like rain upon grass and like drops upon the plants, because I will call upon the name of the Lord. As though he were saying: You must all listen, because I will invoke the name of the Lord as witness to what I say.

Give. Here he begins to recount the good things He did for them, and therefore first invites them to act well. This is what he says: Give magnificence to our God, that is, exalt, insofar as you can, Him who is great in Himself. You ought to do so because all the works of God are perfect; there is perfection in everything He has done, and all His ways by which He comes to human beings are judgments rightly ordered, even if some are hidden.

God is faithful and without any iniquity. He commends Him: God is also just and upright; this is what His ways are.

Or, if He is just and upright, they sinned against Him, because even those who appear just are sinners by comparison. And “not”—that is, are even His sons in filth? They certainly are, even those who appear to be sons. Or thus: The Lord is just and upright, and the sons did not sin against Him; and those who are not His sons are in filth.

A crooked and perverse generation. This is a rebuke, as though he were saying: They are not sons but a crooked generation. Is this what you return to the Lord, foolish and senseless people? Evil and perverse things, namely.

Is He not your Father? As though he were saying: You ought not to return such things, because your Father did many things for you. And this is what he says: He who acquired you by ruling you, and made and created you. The order is inverted.

Remember the days of old, in which He showed benefits; consider the successive generations, to each of which He did good.

Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, after Abraham, Isaac, then Jacob, and so on individually, will tell you the good things He did for the ancients.

When He was dividing. He adds what He did, namely, when the Most High was dividing the nations. The division of the nations is not said to have occurred before the construction of the tower; it began then. And as many heads and princes as there were among those giants, so many divisions of languages were made among them. In Hebrew, the Hebrew language remained with its own people because it did not join the others. Later the number of those who worshiped the one God was so greatly diminished that in Abraham’s time scarcely twelve could be found. He too was told: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12). And this is what he says: When the Most High was dividing the nations—that is, when He separated the sons of Adam through the diversity of languages—that separation took place; and when He established the boundaries of the peoples. The thought is suspended until that point: “But the Lord’s portion...” The peoples are delimited according to languages, through which the principal division occurred, although afterward the peoples were divided within the same language.

Under the division according to the number of the angels of God, some place it, because angels were assigned to individual peoples for their protection, and according to the number of those angels is the number of the greater peoples. Angels are also assigned to unbelieving peoples to preserve in them their first nature, which is God’s good creation. Whether every human being has an angel is not certain to us. This is the meaning: “according to the number of the sons of Israel,” so that the angels may be called the sons of Israel. Or “according to the number of the sons of Israel” because Israel—that is, Jacob—brought that many souls, namely seventy, into the land of Egypt; that is, there are that many varieties of languages, according to the languages of the peoples.

But the Lord’s portion. As though he were saying: He placed the others under angels, but the Lord’s people are His portion, because He guarded them spiritually as though in His own hand. Nevertheless, He assigned His familiar servant Michael to them, and Jacob. This is that people, the cord of His inheritance, which He chose for Himself as His dwelling.

He found. He continues to recount the good things He did for that people. He found him in a desert land: Abraham in Ur of the Chaldeans, and His people in Egypt. In a place of horror, namely the desert and vast wilderness, He led him around, taught him, and guarded him like the pupil of His eye. As an eagle, rousing its young to fly and hovering over them so that neither heat nor wind might harm them, so God acts toward His own: He spread His wings—His protections—far and wide, took him up, and carried him on His shoulders.

The Lord alone was his God. As though he were saying: He did everything, and no foreign god was with that people. After it went over to foreign gods, it was destroyed.

He established him on the high land of Jerusalem, which is on a summit, or on the Church, so that there he might eat the fruits of the fields, both bodily and spiritual.

[Col. 0711D] And that he might suck honey from the rock. Even if that land is literally stony, nevertheless honey abounds there and is found in the reeds. The symbolic meaning is clear. And oil from the flinty rock, because olive trees grow among the rocks.

Curd, corruptly rendered, as though “cheese of cattle”: curd from the herd signifies the teaching of the elders, and milk from the sheep signifies teaching among the lesser ones, together with inner devotion as rich fat, from the lambs and rams, the greater and lesser sons of Bashan. The land of Bashan is pastureland and lies beyond the Jordan; two tribes dwelt there.

And goats, through which penitents are signified, together with the marrow of wheat; and they would drink the blood of the grape, which literally is red. The mystical meaning is evident.

[Col. 0712A] When he grew fat, as he abounded in these things, he became proud in foreign gods, that is, in idols different from God.

You abandoned the God who begot you and forgot the Lord, your creator. This is an inserted rebuke.

The Lord saw and was provoked to anger, because sons and daughters provoked Him.

He repeats the narrative. He saw the evils they were committing and said: “I will hide my face from them.” Previously He illuminated them while His face was turned toward them; but He hid His face when He withdrew His help. “And I will consider their end,” because they are rushing into the gravest evils.

And deservedly so, because they are a perverse generation and unfaithful children.

With one who is not God, that is, by worshiping an idol instead of God, which is not God; with one who is not a people, that is, by receiving nations which are not My people.

Here he prophesies the conversion of the nations: “In a foolish nation”—that is, among the Gentiles, who were previously foolish while living without the worship of God—I will provoke them, so that they may envy those who have been received into the faith. And it will burn down to the lowest depths of hell. For in the present the punishment of the wicked begins, lasting into eternity; God does not punish twice.

For this reason it will devour the earth—that is, earthly people—altogether.

I will gather: I will multiply.

With famine. In the literal event, birds devoured those who had fallen in the bodily desert; through those people the spiritual meaning is signified. Demons are the birds which devour spiritually.

Of those that drag themselves upon the earth and of serpents: that is, those who are serpents among earthly and pleasure-loving people. Outside, the sword will lay them waste, and inside, terror. Thus it happened to them literally; spiritually the same occurs, because they are afflicted outwardly and tormented inwardly. It spared neither the young man nor any sex or age.

And I said. When these evils were occurring, I said to them—that is, I caused them to say this when they saw it: “Where are they?” Those who had previously been powerful through God. “I will put an end to the words of God.”

This will happen in the future; but meanwhile I delayed it because of the anger of the enemies, that is, the Gentiles, who would attribute this to themselves.

A nation without the words of Moses: all this concerns them.

How one pursued a thousand. They had done this previously, [Col. 0712D] but the opposite now happens to them.

And this is because God, who had formerly been theirs, sold them—that is, alienated them from Himself—and the Lord shut them up among enemies, so that they could not be freed.

And our enemies are also judges and witnesses to this, because they never dared to attack them unless they knew that God was angry with them because of their sins.

From the vineyard of Sodom. Their vineyard is from the vineyard of Sodom, because they were begotten from its evil root and are like them. And “cluster” is feminine: it belongs among those words which end in -os in Greek but are feminine in our language, such as synod, and so forth.

Are these things not stored up? The words of God, as though he were saying: These things which they did are not hidden from Me in My treasures, that is, in the secret arrangements of My providence.

At a time suitably appointed by Me, so that their foot may slip—that is, so that they may sin in the present.

The day is near, that is, it is close; and the times when they will be punished hasten to arrive, that is, they are approaching.

He will see—that is, He will make it be seen—that the hand, that is, the operation, has been weakened, either for defending them against enemies or for those shut up within walls so that they might defend themselves, namely, the stronger survivors, the lesser and weaker ones. And seeing these things, they will say:

I will raise my hand to heaven. This concerns Christ ascending, or His own whom He causes to ascend.

[Col. 0714A] I live forever. Behold the oath of God, and He adds what He swears in this way:

If I sharpen—this will indeed happen.

I will intoxicate my arrows with the blood of the slain, and with the captivity of the head, that is, of him who is the head of the enemies—the head, I say, then stripped of all his power. The words are drawn from the practice by which captives were shorn and sold.

Praise, O nations, His people, because He will avenge the blood of His servants. And He will repay vengeance upon their enemies, and He will be merciful to the land of His people. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, and unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0713]

## THREE BOOKS OF THE COMMENTARIES OF HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT, ON ISAIAH

By the same author, while he was alive, enriched throughout with many additions that are lacking in most other copies, and everywhere meticulously revised in a final recension.

(Cologne, by the honorable citizen Peter Quentell, in the year 1531 [Note: [Col. 0713B] The title of the very rare edition which we follow. At the foot of the page, the following is additionally written about our author: “Moreover, reader, there is no reason for you to doubt about the author, since the Reverend Father in Christ and most learned man Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, testifies in his book on ecclesiastical writers that Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, wrote three books on Isaiah, beginning as follows: ‘Isaiah the prophet, of noble lineage, etc.’”].) (G)*

## TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST AND LORD, THE LORD CUTBERT

Bishop at Dorren among the English, most distinguished bishop, or prelate of Durham, a man of the highest authority, Peter Quentell, printer of Cologne, sends respectful greetings.

[Col. 0713B] Franciscus Birckman, our common friend while he lived, a bookseller, before departing from human affairs and yielding to nature and God, brought with him from England, in your name and also at the commission of your reverend fatherhood, Haymo on the prophet Isaiah, long desired by all students of sacred Scripture, so that I might have it printed in a more polished form. I therefore humbly and reverently dedicate to your eminence and your most devout fatherhood this orthodox teacher—one whom all men of letters and languages should extol—recently printed by me, for the praise and glory of your most illustrious name. In the time to come, I shall gladly print all the works of that same holy Haymo, including these expositions on Isaiah, not in the small format, as they say, but rather in a larger and more distinguished one, suitably divided into volumes, for the greater honor of your eminence.

May Your Reverence prosper happily in Christ, and may you regard favorably this little work, humbly dedicated by me; forgive me if I have not entirely satisfied the title or honor of the same—honors that, alas, are now unknown to me. From our literary workshop at Cologne, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the year 1531 after the birth of Christ.

## F. Nicolaus Herborn, Minister of the Order of Friars Minor of Regular Observance in the Province of Cologne, Sends Greetings and Best Wishes to the Candid Reader

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715A] Although, Christian reader, this public office of ministry, as they call it, to which I was unwillingly appointed, has so enslaved me that I scarcely have the opportunity to devote anything to good authors, study, or work—even though I openly lament my misfortune—I nevertheless do not want it to bind and plunge me so deeply into the abyss that I should at some time have nothing further in common with the Muses.

For I am engaged in that embassy for the glory of Christ which I neither ought nor can properly carry out without good letters, and therefore without reading, frequent meditation, use, and practice of the divine Scriptures. And, in my judgment, I have rightly persuaded myself of this. I know how much Paul was indebted to all the churches; I know with what concern he looked after the interests of everyone; how many sleepless nights, how inexhaustible labors, and how many dangers he undertook for this purpose—namely, that he might win everyone for Christ. Yet at the same time he devoted himself so completely to the sacred writings that he even ordered Timothy to bring the parchment sheets.

This matter frequently comes to my mind here, and it has persuaded me never to let books by illustrious men fall from my hands except when I am asleep, or perhaps when, with the strength of my body exhausted, I am satisfying my hunger at a standing meal. It may have happened by chance that this splendid exposition of the most distinguished man, Haymo, was offered to me by friends. As I examine it, I often find myself admiring that man’s talent, judgment, sincerity, and zealous devotion to the divine writings. He did not handle the sacred Scriptures carelessly or sluggishly, although in the meantime he seems to have touched upon many matters briefly and in the Laconic manner rather than treating them at length; nor did he handle them in such a way that he failed to accomplish splendidly what he had promised.

He completed, weighed, treated, and explained everything in such a way that he does not depart from the genuine meaning, while nevertheless explaining each point that contributes to the continuity of the text. He also avoided a fault that is almost characteristic of many in these times in which we write—learned and unlearned alike—namely, that we ambitiously seek to thrust our own work upon others rather than benefit them: despising the labors of others, mocking their efforts, and criticizing their errors.

For this author is approachable and courteous, and, at least among all those whom I have seen, exceedingly modest. He injures no one except those whom their own evil deeds injure. He torments no one except those whom their own conscience torments. [The text is corrupt here.] I have read many little commentaries by him on Paul and on the Apocalypse, as well as homilies and expositions of the Gospels, yet nowhere did I find jests, nowhere that factional language: “He is a heretic,” “He is Antichrist,” “He is Papistic.” Yet I often read passages that are directed squarely against heretics, Antichrists, and pseudo-Papists.

Whoever does not wish to believe this should read these little commentaries on Isaiah; then he will perceive that I am speaking truths more truthful than truth itself. In them he unfolds the prophet’s oracles in such a way that he both draws out their authentic meaning and, more than once, sprinkles in many allegories as embellishments, like fresh little flowers. As far as allegories are concerned, however, I should have wished him to treat them more fully, since he seems to have handled those he touched upon quite successfully.

Therefore, whoever you are who will read this man, whoever you are who will make him familiar to yourself, believe one who has experience: you will neither be ashamed of nor regret your reading. For he is so composed that he breathes Paul, if you desire severity; Christ above all, if you desire modesty; and Peter, if you desire authority—yet he is always like himself, that is, a bishop, genuine, and perpetually answering to his office. May God grant that the common multitude of bishops follow this one bishop, even from behind!

He acted as a bishop, he acted as a teacher, and he acted as a writer—something granted to few. Let our bishops do what belongs to them; let them do what Paul commanded. Let them devote themselves to teaching, reading, and exhortation; let them learn, write, and teach. Then we shall dedicate to them as well that praise which we have dedicated to our Haymo. I hope that one day, through this single Haymo, we may all learn universally what fruit, what power, and how great a benefit lie hidden in the divine utterances.

May God Almighty grant that, even in so turbulent an age, we may at last become wise. Christ will be present with us, provided that we do not abandon ourselves. Farewell, Christian reader, and pray to God that he may one day restore me completely to good letters.

Cologne, on the Nones of February, in the year 1531.

# Haymo’s Preface

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715C] The prophet Isaiah, born of noble lineage, was the son of Amos—not, however, of that Amos who is regarded as third in the series of the twelve prophets. Thus, among the Hebrews, one is written with different letters from the other. But if anyone wishes to agree with the tradition of the Jews, who say that the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers of the prophets were themselves prophets, and that their names are placed at the beginning of their prophecies, he may observe that Amos was the father of Isaiah the prophet.

The same prophet Isaiah prophesied at the same time as Hosea, Joel, and Amos, namely under the kings whom he mentions at the beginning of his book. He also prophesied under Manasseh, who had taken his daughter as his wife. Under that king, when the Jews accused him, Isaiah was cut in two with a wooden saw because he had said of them: “Hear, princes of Sodom, and people of Gomorrah” (Isa. I), taking occasion from the fact that he had said that he saw the Lord, whereas the Lord himself had said to Moses: “No one shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII).

Whatever he prophesied under each king, he carefully distinguished in his book. He was not only a prophet because he foretold future events, but also an apostle, which in Latin means “one who is sent,” because he deserved to be sent by the Lord, who said to him: “Whom shall I send?” When he answered, “Send me,” the Lord said to him: “Go to this people” (Isa. VI).

He spoke not only about the ten tribes—which, under Uzziah king of Judah and Jerusalem, had already begun to be devastated while Pekah son of Remaliah and Zedekiah were reigning among them—but also about many different nations and kingdoms. Yet he prophesied especially about Judah and Jerusalem, by which the tribe of Benjamin is understood, since Jerusalem was situated within its allotment.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0717]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0717A] “The vision of Isaiah, son of Amos, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

It is the custom and established practice of writers who provide us with the sacred Scriptures that, whenever something is narrated by one of them, when he comes to himself he speaks about himself as though about another person. Moses did this when he said: “Now Moses was a very meek man.” He did not say: “I was very meek.” Job likewise says: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.” So too blessed Matthew, John, and the apostle Paul. Finally, the prophet Isaiah did the same: he did not wish to say, “The vision that I, Isaiah, saw,” but inserted himself into the order of his narrative as a writer of events, not as a praiser of himself.

Yet the one who speaks silently about himself in this way at the beginning later, strengthened in what follows, speaks confidently and says that he saw the Lord. Finally, it must be noted—and it is worthy of inquiry—why the prophet says: “The vision of Isaiah, son of Amos, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem,” when at the beginning he does not recount visions of the sort that he saw, as Daniel does (Dan. X), nor say what he saw, but immediately adds, saying: “Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth,” and, “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom,” along with other similar expressions.

The answer is that there are three kinds of vision. The first kind is bodily, by which we see heaven, earth, and all bodily things. The second is spiritual, by which in dreams we see mountains, trees, and people walking about and fighting with one another, yet when we awaken we have no idea what that thing was which we saw. The third kind of vision is intellectual; in it the rational faculty of the soul consists, and through it, recognizing our Creator, we understand what we ought to say according to his will, when the Holy Spirit reveals this to our minds.

“Seeing” is often used to mean “understanding.” Thus we commonly ask someone whether he sees this or that—that is, whether he understands. The prophets, too, who understood the things that were to come, could say: “Our eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. XXIV), and, “To you I have lifted up my eyes” (Ps. LXXXIV), that is, the eyes of my heart. And when the Psalmist says, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (ibid.), those prophets were first called “seers,” that is, understanding men.

Isaiah therefore saw a vision of this kind: inspired by the Holy Spirit, he understood; and he saw what was to happen to his people and said: “The vision of Isaiah,” that is, the understanding which he understood, concerning Judah and Jerusalem.

[Col. 0717D] “Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.”

Just as Moses (Deut. XXX) summoned heaven and earth as witnesses when, through him, the Lord gave a blessing and a curse, so Isaiah once again calls them to witness after the people’s transgression, so that all the elements may know that God was justly moved to anger in order to avenge the violation of his commandments.

In a metonymic sense—that is, taking the containers for what they contain—we may suitably understand by the name “heavens” the heavenly and angelic powers, and by “earth,” human beings, the inhabitants of the earth. They are commanded to hear and listen because the Lord has spoken what the prophet adds next.

But let us hear what the Lord has spoken: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me.”

The almighty God has deigned to call the Jewish people, whom he regards as servants under the common law, “children”—not only here, but also in Exodus, where he says to Pharaoh: “Let my firstborn son go” (Exod. IV). In his most compassionate mercy, the almighty God nourished and exalted these children, bringing them out of the harsh slavery of the Egyptians, where they served in mud and bricks.

But, ungrateful for his benefits, they despised him by trampling upon his commandments, scorning his servants the prophets, and worshiping the gods of the nations, deaf and mute as they were. If anyone asks how he nourished and exalted them, let him consider how, through many signs and wonders, he brought them out of Egypt and made them cross the sea on dry feet (Exod. XIV), overwhelming their enemies in those same waters; how for forty years he supplied them with manna while most patiently tolerating their evil ways, murmurings, and rebellions (Deut. VIII); and how he destroyed seven nations before them, bringing them into a land better than all others, flowing, as it were, with milk and honey (Deut. VI). Let him recall many similar things, which it would now take too long to recount.

But let the prudent reader foresee with an alert mind that, according to the Hebrew truth, it is better to read “I have nourished children” than “I have begotten children,” as blessed Jerome witnesses, lest the former seem contrary to what the apostle John says in his epistle: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John III).

[Col. 0718C] “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger. But Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood me.”
