To the shame of the Jews, who were created rational by God and ought to have used reason, brute, senseless, and extremely foolish animals are brought forward as witnesses that they did what these people did not do—namely, recognize their shepherd and nourisher, as the ox and donkey do.

At a higher level of understanding, the ox, which is accustomed to bear the yoke and is a clean animal, signifies the people of Israel, who bore the yoke of the Law and preserved purity of mind and body. The donkey, however, lustful and unclean, which likewise carries a burden, signifies the gentile people weighed down by the burden of sins.

Thus “the ox knew its owner”: that is, the Jews who were unwilling to believe in the Son of God recognized him, the one by whom they had been possessed in their fathers. These are those of whom it is said that on one day three thousand believed at the apostles’ preaching, on another day five thousand, and thereafter many thousands.

The donkey also knew its master’s manger when the gentiles believed the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, who, as we read in the Gospel, when he was born, was laid by his mother in a manger. While these people recognized God the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit, Israel did not recognize him—namely, the Pharisees, scribes, and other Jews, who preferred to die in unbelief rather than believe in Christ.

They are called Israel—not because they were true Israelites, since they did not behold God with the mind.

[Col. 0719B] “Woe to the sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children.”

No other nation or people is meant here. Israel itself is called a nation, a people, and wicked children. “Woe” signifies eternal punishment and eternal condemnation. The Jews, therefore, who were once called children of God as they walked in the commandments of their Father, almighty God, are now called an evil seed and wicked children because they have departed from the will of God. He threatens them with eternal condemnation and eternal destruction because they did not wish to recognize the Son of God, who came into the world for their redemption.

The Savior himself likewise calls them children of the devil and offspring of vipers, saying in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII), and, “Offspring of vipers, flee from the coming wrath” (Matt. V; Luke III).

“They have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned backward.”

They forsook the Lord God almighty when they worshiped idols and when they did not receive his Son. They blasphemed the Holy One of Israel—that is, Christ, the Son of the living God—when they said to him: “You have a demon” (John VIII), and, “You are a Samaritan” (ibid.). Moreover, they blasphemed him when, with envious lips, they cried out: “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid. XIX), and, “Crucify, crucify this man!” (Matt. XXVII; Luke XXIII), and, “Release Barabbas for us” (ibid.).

To blaspheme means to inflict some insult or reproach. Because they forsook God and blasphemed Christ, they turned backward—that is, although they ought to have directed the steps of their works forward and followed the commandments of God, according to what had been said to them, “Walk after the Lord your God” (Hos. XI), having been alienated from God they turned back to their iniquities, acting contrary to what the Savior commanded: that no one who has put his hand to the plow should look back.

[Col. 0719D] “Upon what shall I strike you further, as you continue to transgress?”

This is the voice of almighty God speaking through the prophet to the foolish Jews: “Upon what,” or “in what place, shall I strike you further, since you are always adding transgression?” It is as though he said in other words: “I cannot find what remedy I can apply to your wounds, because all your members are full of injuries. I have often applied treatment, and now I find no part that has not already been struck and filled with wounds.”

Or it may certainly be understood in this way: “I find no wounds and no blows by which I can break the hardness of your hearts, because the greater the torments, the more impiety, murmuring, and rebellious pride increase.”

In these words, as blessed Jerome says, we can perceive that God strikes sinners in order to correct them, so that affliction may be for them not so much punishment as amendment.

That there was no suitable place in which he could apply a healing remedy to them is shown when he adds: “Every head is sick, and every heart is faint.”

Since among all the bodily senses and among all the members the head holds, in a certain way, the chief place, and since doctrine and wisdom reside in the heart, it is not inappropriate to understand metaphorically by “head” the rulers by whom the people are governed, just as the members are governed by the head, and by “heart” the wise and teachers.

“Every head,” he says, “is sick, and every heart is faint”—that is, from the rulers to the beggar and the lowest common people, and from the teachers to the ignorant and unlearned crowd, there is no soundness of mind. All have been weakened in their impieties, and all waste away in their iniquities.

Just as cheerfulness of spirit sometimes eases bodily pains, while if weakness of mind is added to bodily sickness the infirmity is doubled, and if the head suffers, all the members are weak, so too, while the people were weakened in their impieties, if the rulers and teachers had maintained a state of uprightness, that people might in some measure have deserved the remedy of salvation.

But because all were weakened together, salvation and the medicine of souls were therefore prolonged for them. Hence it also follows:

[Col. 0720C] “From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it.”

He preserves the metaphor and says, “from the sole of the foot to the crown”—that is, from the lowliest to the highest, and from the last to the first, there is no one flourishing in soundness of mind.

“A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore: it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.”

Properly speaking, a wound is what is made with a staff. A bruise results from blows with rods. A swollen or inflated sore is usually made by a sword and often by a staff.

It should be noted that these words refer especially to the Lord’s coming and to the final devastation of the Jews. The wound of their impiety, because of which they were led away to Babylon, was later healed when under Zerubbabel and other leaders they returned from captivity and afterward rebuilt the Temple (1 Esd. V). Therefore this must be referred to the final captivity, after which they deserved no remedy.

But what the prophet says here is fulfilled in them: the wound of malice, the bruise of iniquity, and the swollen sore of the Jews—that is, their sin, inflated and distended—has not been bound with the cloths and bandages of prayers, nor treated with any medicine of good works, nor softened, that is, warmed or healed, with the oil of repentance. It is no wonder that their wound was not healed, since they themselves killed the most compassionate physician sent to them.

[Col. 0720D] “Your land shall be desolate; your cities shall be burned with fire. Strangers devour your region before your eyes”—for “they shall devour”—“and it shall be desolated as in an enemy’s devastation.”

These things were partly fulfilled under the Babylonians, when the cities were burned, Jerusalem overthrown, and the Samaritans inhabited their region, while the whole land was desolated, so much so that it was ravaged by lions.

But they were fulfilled more fully and perfectly at the coming of the Romans. This devastation will remain until the end of the world, and strangers will consume the region of the Jews before their eyes.

[Col. 0721B] “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field, and like a city that is laid waste.”

The likeness of the devastation of the Temple and Jerusalem is taken from farmers. As long as a vineyard is full of grapes, they place guards in shelters. In a cucumber field as well—where the Septuagint rendered the phrase as “a guardhouse for fruits”—huts are made, that is, small cottages, to ward off the heat and rays of the sun; from there they drive away people or small animals that commonly harm the newly growing crops.

But when such fruits have been gathered and the guard has departed, because he has nothing further to guard there, the dry shelters among the shrubs and the ruined huts remain.

Similarly, almighty God made Jerusalem and the Temple desolate and abandoned the people, because it no longer produced the fruit of good works, whose guardian he himself had once been, when it produced the fruits of good works.

That the same people were called a vineyard is shown by the same prophet Isaiah, who says a little farther on: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (below, V). And the Psalmist says: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX).

As long as this vineyard bore the richest fruits, it had a guardian, of whom the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). After it lost its good fruits, he abandoned it, as the Lord himself says to the Jews: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

He calls the same people the daughter of Zion to show that he possesses the affection of a most compassionate father. Nor is it surprising that Zion is called a daughter, since Babylon too is very often called a daughter. By nature we are all children of God, but through our own fault we become alienated.

In the moral sense, through Zion—which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “speculation”—and which is designated by the name of a vineyard, we may understand any soul that ought to dwell in contemplation of God and bear acceptable fruits. As long as that soul lives rationally, producing good fruits, it has God as guardian of its mind. But if vices and sins, like certain small animals, ravage the fruits of virtue, it is abandoned by God its guardian, and everything belonging to it is reduced to nothing.

[Col. 0721D] “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom, and we would have become like Gomorrah.”

This is to be understood of the remnant of the apostles and of the other faithful who, after the Lord’s coming, believed among the Jews. In the Acts of the Apostles it is said of them (Acts II) that three thousand believed on one day, five thousand on another, and thereafter many thousands.

The outstanding preacher also speaks of this remnant in his Epistle to the Romans: “The remnant according to the election of grace has been saved” (Rom. XI).

The prophet therefore speaks in his own person and in the person of the other faithful from that same people: Unless the Lord of hosts, whom the hosts of angels serve, had left us a seed in the apostles and their followers, then, just as the Sodomites and Gomorrhites perished because of their sins, so our entire lineage, lost through the sin of unbelief, would have been utterly consumed.

[Col. 0722B] “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; listen with your ears to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.”

It is a tradition of the Jews, as blessed Jerome says, that the prophet Isaiah was killed for two reasons: either because he called the rulers princes of Sodom and the people people of Gomorrah, or because, when the Lord said to Moses, “No one shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII), Isaiah dared to say: “I saw the Lord of hosts sitting upon a lofty throne.”

These words may be referred to the Jews of that time, but they apply especially to the scribes and Pharisees and to the people who cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (John XIX) against such a man.

They are therefore called princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah because, just as the Sodomites and Gomorrhites sinned openly, plotting a wicked scheme against the righteous man Lot and saying without any blush of shame, “Bring out the men who have entered your house, so that we may abuse them” (Gen. XIX), so these people plotted a wicked scheme against the Lord Christ, saying without any shame: “Come, let us devise plots against the righteous,” and, “He is guilty of death,” along with many similar things.

Hence the same prophet says later: “They proclaimed their sin as Sodom did, and did not conceal it.”

[Col. 0722D] “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord.”

It is as though he said: “Why do you offer me a multitude of sacrifices? Do you think that I need them?” Then he immediately adds: “I am full”—that is, I lack nothing. “For the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII).

Or the statement “I am full” may also be understood in this sense: “I am full,” that is, your sacrifices are a disgust to me, because you do not offer them with a simple and pure mind.

“I did not desire the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats.”

The content of this chapter up to the place where he says, “Judge the fatherless, defend the widow,” rejects the sacrifices of the Jews and teaches obedience to the Gospel. By saying “I did not desire,” using the past tense, he shows that he was never pleased by the sacrifice of the Jews. Especially when the new sacrifice arrived, the old sacrifice was counted as nothing. For only a good will together with the purest faith brings liberation.

This may also be understood of those who, although they do not perform God’s commandments, wish to placate him with various gifts and offerings acquired through plunder.

[Col. 0723A] “When you came to appear before me, who asked this from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?”

The almighty God did not ask for the offerings and sacrifices of the Jews because he himself needed them, but so that they would not sacrifice to idols and so that, through carnal and figurative remedies, they might more easily arrive at the spiritual and true sacrifice.

“Do not offer sacrifice any longer in vain. Incense is an abomination to me”—that is, I detest it and count it as nothing, because it is not performed with a pure intention.

“I will not endure the new moon, the Sabbath, and your other festivals”—that is, I will not tolerate them in such a way that they please me.

The term “new moon” is formed from *neo*, “new,” and *menne*, “moon.” Hence *neomenia* means the festival of the new moon, which the Jews celebrate at the beginnings of the months.

[Col. 0723B] “Your assemblies are wicked; my soul has hated your calends and your solemnities. They have become burdensome to me.”

“All these things that he has mentioned” is understood. “Your festivals,” he says—not mine—“my soul has hated,” because you misuse them. He does not mean that God possesses a soul, but speaks according to our manner of feeling and speaking. It is as though he said: “Your assemblies and your solemnities have not pleased me, nor have the things I mentioned; rather, they have become burdensome to me, because you have carried them out with an evil mind.”

“I have labored in bearing with you”—that is, you have made me labor by waiting for your conversion and repentance.

[Col. 0723C] “And when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you.”

The eyes of the Lord signify the regard of his mercy. With these eyes he looked upon the people of Israel in Egypt and therefore took pity on them. Hence he also said: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people, and I have heard its groaning, and I have come down to deliver it” (Exod. III). “Seeing, I have seen” means: I saw and took pity.

When, therefore, you stretch out your hands to me in a time of tribulation, so that I may hear and deliver you, I will turn my eyes away from you—that is, I will remove from you the regard of my mercy.

“And when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear.” The same is said to Jeremiah concerning this people: “Therefore do not pray for them, because I will not hear you.”

He gives the reason why he turns away his eyes: “For your hands are full of blood”—that of the prophets and the righteous is understood.

The Jews have always been murderers, ready to pour out the blood of the righteous, and even the blood of the Lord who was sent to them. Hence the Savior reproaches them, saying: “Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers” (Matt. XXIII). This means: What they did less, you complete. They killed the servants; you kill the Lord.

In the moral sense, “hands” signify action, while “blood” signifies sin. Hence the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from bloods”—that is, from sins. I will therefore not hear you because the work of your hands is full of sins and impiety, namely murder, adultery, fornication, and other vices.

[Col. 0724A] “Wash yourselves; be clean.”

It is as though he said in other words: In place of all the things mentioned above, which I said I hated, the religion of the Gospel is pleasing, so that you may be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity. Therefore wash yourselves in my blood and in the water of baptism. Be clean by remaining innocent in life after the grace of baptism.

Or wash yourselves through repentance and through the tears of compunction. Be clean, lest you again defile yourselves by falling into the snare and mire of sins. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

This agrees with what the Lord says in the Gospel to someone who had been healed: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin any more.”

“Take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes.”

He had commanded them to wash and be clean; now he teaches them how they must act, saying: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from before me”—that is, from my presence. If you think anything evil, do not carry it out; uproot that wicked thought completely from your hearts and destroy it.

[Col. 0724B] “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good.”

This is what the Psalmist commands in the same sense, though not in the same words: “Turn away from evil,” he says, “and do good” (Ps. XXXI).

It is appropriately said, “learn to do good,” because virtue must be learned and imitated. Mere natural goodness is not sufficient for justice unless one is trained by suitable disciplines.

“Seek judgment.” From whom should judgment be sought? Certainly from the wise, because it is not given to everyone to judge or to offer sound counsel. In truth, it belongs only to the wise.

“Assist the oppressed”—that is, rescue him from the hand of the powerful person who inflicts violence upon the poor.

“Judge for the fatherless”—that is, assist him in judgment—“and defend the widow” from the hand of one stronger than she.

[Col. 0724C] “And come and argue with me, says the Lord.”

“When you have done all these things,” he says, “argue with me”—that is, rebuke me and contend with me in judgment—if I do not give you the rewards that I promised.

“If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow. And if they are red like crimson, they shall be white like wool.”

Scarlet and crimson are the same thing. Therefore what is signified by scarlet is also signified by crimson: namely, grave sin, such as murder, adultery, theft, and other such offenses.

What is signified by snow is also signified by wool: namely, the cleansing of sins and the washing away of crimes.

“If,” he says, “you do what I command you—turn away from evil, do good, assist the fatherless, and defend the widow—then your enormous sins and most wicked deeds, which were formerly blood-red like scarlet and red like crimson, shall be made white through repentance and the tears of compunction, and shall become white like snow and wool.”

[Col. 0724D] “If you are willing” to walk in my commandments, and “if you obey my words, you shall eat the good things of [this] land.”

Or, what is greater, you shall eat the good things of the land of which the Psalm says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XX; Matt. V), and of which the Truth says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land.”

Since all the elements are in motion, only the earth remains immovable and solid. Therefore it is not improperly understood as signifying the solidity of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0725A] “But if you are unwilling”—to walk in my commandments is understood—“and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

This means the word of God the Father, or even, “I the prophet have spoken,” because I am the mouth of the Lord, since through me he deigns to speak his mysteries. The prophets were called the mouth of the Lord because the Lord spoke through them.

When he says, “the sword shall devour you,” this signifies both the physical sword of the Babylonians and that of the Romans. But we may also understand that sword to signify mortality, pestilence, famine, or the vengeance of almighty God, which the wicked will endure after death, when they are placed in the punishments of hell.

For in this passage, by the name “sword” is understood whatever tortures, whatever punishes, and whatever burns.

Free choice is also preserved in part when he says, “If you are willing” and “if you are unwilling,” so that in either direction punishment or reward may arise not from God’s judgment, but from the merit of each individual.

“How has the faithful city become a prostitute, full of judgment? Righteousness once dwelt in her, but now murderers.” Fornication is not only bodily but also spiritual. Hence the psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Psalm 72), that is, those who depart from you. To fornicate is to worship idols instead of God, as it is written: “Israel fornicated at Baal-peor” (Numbers 25). Therefore the Israelite people are called a prostitute—not so much because of bodily fornication as because they departed from God. These words, however, concern not the prophet’s own times but especially the time of the Lord’s incarnation, when they completely departed from God by choosing Barabbas and killing the Son of God.

The Prophet therefore wonders and says: How has the faithful city become a prostitute by departing from God, the city once full of judgment? Righteousness once dwelt in her, but now there are murderers. The city, I say, of the faithful, which formerly was full of judgment and in which righteousness once rested, has now become a prostitute, full of murderers who killed the prophets and the very head of the prophets, namely the Savior of the world.

This may also be applied morally to every soul. It is a faithful city full of judgment so long as it obeys God’s will and has God himself dwelling within it, God who is substantial righteousness because he justifies all his faithful. But when it departs from God through evil works, it becomes a prostitute—not in place but in merit. What was previously full of judgment and had God as its inhabitant then begins to be inhabited by demons and wicked spirits, whose will it obeys.

These are the murderers, namely the slayers of souls. “Your silver has become dross.” The refuse and filth of metals are called *scoria*, “dross”; it may also be called rust. “Your silver,” that is, the utterances of the divine Scriptures, of which the psalmist says: “The utterances of the Lord are silver tested by fire” (Psalm 17), has become dross or filth—namely, the perverse teaching of the scribes and Pharisees.

Alternatively, by silver are understood religious men, bright and approved in every aspect of life; by dross, sinners, stained with the rust of sins. The meaning is: holy men who formerly lived brightly and clearly in your midst have afterward been changed into the rust and filth of sins. Or: whereas formerly you had bright men, approved in complete purity, now you have others in their place, defiled by the rust of sins.

“Your wine has been mixed with water.” Wine has austerity. Therefore the legal commandments are understood by wine, because they possess austerity—that is, they are strong, pure, sincere, and established in truth. They have been mixed with water, that is, violated by the traditions of the Jews and Pharisees. The Lord makes this clear in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who corrupt the law of God, wishing to establish your traditions” (Matthew 15; 25).

“Your wine,” he says, “has been mixed with water,” because the legal commandments, pure and most sincere, possessing austerity within themselves, have been corrupted and softened by the false traditions of the scribes and Pharisees. Every teacher who turns the austerity of the sacred Scriptures—by which he can correct his hearers—toward their favor, and speaks in such a way that he does not correct but pleases his listeners, violates and corrupts the wine of the sacred Scriptures by his own interpretation. This is what heretics and utterly wicked tavern-keepers do: they corrupt evangelical truth through their perverse teaching.

“Your princes are faithless and companions of thieves.” In this passage the princes of the Jews also mean the priests, who appeared to judge and teach the people. They are called faithless and companions of thieves because they walked unfaithfully in God’s commandments, accepting gifts from the scribes and Pharisees—gifts which those men extorted from the poor by violence and robbery. Thus the priests were companions of the thieves, namely the scribes and Pharisees.

They were also faithless during the Lord’s Passion, unwilling to believe in him; and they were companions of thieves, namely the scribes and Pharisees, as well as of the traitor Judas. We too must take the greatest care not to accept gifts from those who amass wealth through robbery and the tears of the wretched, lest we be called not only thieves but also companions of thieves, and it be said of us: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him.”

“All retributions pursue those who love gifts,” and therefore such people are counted among the ranks of vices. For there are many, as Jerome rightly says, who consider no one a friend unless they have received gifts from him. They do not consider the faces of their friends but their hands, and they judge those holy whose purses they empty. Retributions pursue such men because they repay those from whom they hope to receive similar things. To such people God says: “You have received your reward” (Matthew 6).

Or retributions pursue them because they raise up and praise only those whom they favor, from whom they receive something. “They do not judge for the orphan,” that is, they do not assist him in judgment, “and the widow’s case does not come before them,” because they regard it as worthless.

“Because of these things the Lord of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, says: Ah! I will be comforted over my enemies, and I will avenge myself upon my foes.” Almighty God grieves over the miseries of his people, yet he calls them his enemies and foes. These are understood especially as the scribes and Pharisees, to whom he also says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matthew 23; Luke 11).

Here he is said to be comforted over his enemies when he exacts vengeance from them. God’s consolation consists in this: his enemies and foes, who were unwilling to possess his benefits in prosperity, are corrected by punishments and afflictions.

[Col. 0727B] “And I will turn my hand toward you, and I will smelt away your dross for punishment, and I will remove all your tin.” This is the voice of God, turning in direct address to the people themselves. By dross are understood vices and the filth of vices. By tin, which is accustomed to resemble silver, is understood the false doctrine of the scribes and Pharisees, which appeared true and resembled the divine utterances.

The extension of the hand signifies divine vengeance. Thus he says: I will turn and extend my hand toward you to punish you; I will smelt away—or cleanse by the fire of tribulation—all the filth of sins; I will remove the false doctrine of the scribes and Pharisees, and I will give you the most sincere and perfect knowledge of the Law and the Gospel.

[Col. 0727C] “And I will restore all your judges as at the beginning, and your counselors as in ancient times.” The former judges and ancient counselors were Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Gideon, Samuel, David, and the others who judged God’s people according to God’s will, and with whom almighty God took counsel, revealing to them the secrets of his mysteries.

Judges and counselors like the former were restored not only after the captivity, in the persons of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and other leaders who ruled the people up to Hyrcanus, but also after the Lord’s coming, in the persons of the apostles and the leaders and rulers of the churches.

“After this you will be called the city of the Just One, the faithful city.” The city of the Just One—that is, of the Lord Savior. The faithful city is understood as the one of which the Truth says in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden,” namely, the Church founded upon Christ.

After I restore your judges as they were formerly, and your counselors as in ancient times, then you will be called the city of the Just One, that is, of Christ, and the faithful city, because you will preserve the faith of the Lord Savior with complete integrity.

[Col. 0727D] “Zion will be redeemed in judgment, and they will bring her back in righteousness.” In other words, it is as though he said: Not all Israelites will be redeemed, but those remnants of whom it was said above (Romans 19). This is what he means by saying that she will be redeemed in judgment, that is, in discernment, so that those who wish to believe may be saved and redeemed. Those who brought them to faith in Christ in righteousness are understood to be the apostles and the other preachers.

[Col. 0728A] “And he will crush the wicked and sinners together, and those who abandoned the Lord will be consumed.” The wicked and sinners are understood to be those who consented to Christ’s death and afterward refused to accept his faith. They were rightly crushed and consumed, both by the Romans and by the punishments of hell, because they abandoned the Lord and remained in their wickedness.

“For they will be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed, and you will be ashamed because of the gardens that you chose.” “Confusion” is very often used in the sense of shame. By the gardens he mentioned we should understand sacred groves and forests in which they sacrificed and offered victims to demons, shamelessly committing their lust before the altars of idols.

At what time they should be ashamed because of the idols and the gardens they had chosen, he clearly reveals when he says: “When you become like an oak with falling leaves, and like a garden without water.”

The meaning is this: just as leaves fall from an oak shaken by dryness, and just as a garden cannot produce the fruit of herbs if it lacks the water by which it is irrigated, so, when you lack water—that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures and the spiritual grace which the Lord promised would flow from the belly of those who come to him—you will not be able to retain and preserve your works; your fruits will be empty and of no use, because you will be dried up by aridity. That is, you will fail in your sins.

It should be noted that, in prophetic fashion, he suddenly changes persons. While speaking in the third-person plural he had said, “They will be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed,” but suddenly he turns the eye of his mind toward the second person of the people, saying: “And you will be ashamed because of the gardens that you chose,” and so forth.

[Col. 0728C] “And your strength will be like the ash of tow, and your work like a spark.” When the time of their persecution and captivity came, all the strength and pride of the Jews who had abandoned the Lord, in which they trusted, were reduced to nothing, just as a spark of tow is easily consumed. All their work, by which they hoped to protect themselves, suddenly passed away, just as a spark of fire quickly flies off.

“And both will burn together, and there will be no one to extinguish them.” That is, both the strength of their pride and their false work will perish together. There will be no one to save them, because the Lord will destroy them.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0728D]

“The word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.” It is exceedingly remarkable and must be weighed carefully that the prophet says he saw the Word. For how can a human being see the Word? And what is this Word? Surely it is the one of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). This Word—the wisdom of the Father, namely his Son—the prophet saw. That is, he understood mentally that he would come, and therefore he added:

[Col. 0729A] “And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills.” These are the last days of which the patriarch Jacob said: “Come, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father, and I will announce to you what will happen in the last days,” that is, in the final age of the world. Immediately he added: “The ruler will not fail from Judah until the one who is to be sent comes” (Daniel 2).

It should be noted that this is the mountain which he earlier called the Word. This is also the stone which Daniel saw growing into a great mountain and filling the whole earth. This mountain is indeed the mountain of the house of the Lord, that is, of the Church, which is the house of the Lord founded upon Christ. Concerning it the psalmist sang: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 26). The outstanding preacher likewise says to Timothy: “Know how you ought to walk in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God” (1 Timothy 3).

Christ himself is also the mountain and house of God, of which it is said: “The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Psalm 67). But who has ever seen a mountain above the summit of mountains? Christ is the mountain, as we have said. The mountains, however, are the angels and the heavenly heights: the apostles, patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, and confessors, who shone mightily through their teaching, faith, works, and signs of miracles.

The hills are the ordinary faithful: hermits, those practicing continence, widows and widowers, and good married people. Although they did not shine through teaching and miraculous signs, they were perfect in faith and conduct.

Concerning these mountains and hills the psalmist sings: “The mountains are round about him.” And the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills” (Song of Songs 2).

The mountain of the house of the Lord, therefore, has been prepared at the summit of the mountains and exalted above the hills: namely, Christ, upon whom the Church has been founded, prepared and exalted by God the Father above every principality, power, and dominion.

[Col. 0729C] “And all nations will flow toward him, and many peoples will go and say:” When the Lord came into the world and, redemption accomplished, passed through the heavens, all nations and peoples flowed together to his faith. Concerning them the Father had also said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2).

But these peoples and nations, by no means content with their own salvation, encouraged one another, saying: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths.”

Who the mountain of the house of the Lord is, and what the house of God is, we explained a little above: namely, Christ and the Church. It should be observed that, after saying, “Let us go up to the house,” he immediately took care to add whose house it was, adding “of God.” He then added: Whose God? The God of Jacob. This is to say: Come, let us go up to the house of that God who is the God of believers, just as Jacob believed.

After we have come in faith to the mountain of the Lord and gone up to the Church of God, he will teach us his ways, that is, the commandments of life through evangelical teaching; and thus we will walk in his paths, that is, in his works, imitating him. But first the ways of the Lord must be learned—that is, his commandments—as blessed Jerome says; afterward we must walk in his paths.

[Col. 0730A] “For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” It is as though he said: For this reason all nations and many peoples will encourage one another to come to the mountain of the Lord and go up to the house of the God of Jacob: because the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

By Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” the primitive Church is understood—the Church that existed among the apostles and the other believers from the Jews. From it the law of the Old Testament, understood spiritually, and the word of the Lord, the teaching of the Gospel, proceeded to all nations.

This may also be understood of the universal Church, from which the law and the teaching of the Gospel flow daily.

[Col. 0730B] “And he will judge the nations and rebuke many peoples.” Some take this in a single sense, as though judging the nations and rebuking many peoples were one thing. But it is better to understand distinctly by “nations” the Gentiles, both believers and unbelievers, and by “many peoples,” or “the numerous people” as the Septuagint translated it, the unbelieving Jews.

The Lord therefore judges the nations daily, and will judge them universally on the day of judgment—that is, he will make a distinction between believers and unbelievers. Believers will be judged in one way and unbelievers in another, because the one who does not believe has already been judged. But he will rebuke many peoples, that is, condemn the unbelieving and faithless Jews.

[Col. 0730C] “And they will beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into sickles.” This means that all zeal for waging war will be changed into peace, and that in the whole world there will be harmony instead of discord. Swords will indeed be changed into plowshares, and spears into sickles, so that, once the fury and pride of warfare have been abandoned, they may serve agriculture.

Spiritually, swords are changed into plowshares and spears into sickles when the seditions of discord are driven far from us, and the hardness of the heart is broken by Christ’s plow, that is, by the admonition of God’s word. The thorns of vices are then uprooted, so that the seed of God’s word may grow into crops, and afterward we may eat the labor of our hands when the time of harvest arrives, that is, death.

[Col. 0730D] “Nation will not lift up sword against nation, nor will they train for war any longer.” What was said above about the transformation of swords, and what is now being said, was fulfilled at the time of the incarnation. For, as both sacred history and especially the histories of the Gentiles relate, there was such great discord throughout the whole world before the Lord’s birth—up to the twentieth year of Octavian Augustus, under whom the Lord was born—that no one was permitted to pass from one kingdom to another, that is, from one province to another, since all were inflamed with eagerness for battle, not only against foreign nations but also against neighboring peoples and cities.

But after the Lord and Savior arose, he who came to give peace to the world and reconcile us to God the Father, and at whose birth the angelic citizens sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2), all wars ceased. They no longer began to exercise themselves in the zeal for war but devoted themselves to cultivating the fields.

When it says, “nor will they train for war any longer,” we should understand: as they had done previously. For we read that many battles were later fought, but they were not as severe as those that had occurred before.

[Col. 0731A] “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.” After the calling of the Gentiles and the manifestation of God’s mountain, the prophet turns to his own people, who were called the house of Jacob because they descended from Jacob’s family. He urges them to come forth from the darkness of unbelief and error and to receive the light of truth, that is, Christ, who said: “I am the light of the world.” Thus they are to walk in the light of the Lord, that is, in the faith and commandments of the Lord Savior.

“You,” he says, “house of Jacob, house of my people, come with me, and together let us walk in the light of the Lord,” concerning which the psalmist says: “Come to him and be enlightened” (Psalm 33).

[Col. 0731B] “For you have cast away your people, the house of Jacob.” The prophet addresses and exhorts his people to walk in faith in the Lord Savior. After seeing through the Holy Spirit the hardness of the Jews’ hearts and their impenitent heart, he suddenly turns the eye of his mind toward God, saying: I therefore urge them to come to you and enjoy your light with me, because on account of the multitude of their sins you have abandoned and cast away them—your former people, namely the house of Jacob.

He gives the reason why he cast them away: “Because they have been filled as in former times, and they have had diviners as the Philistines had.” Since different people attempt to explain this passage in different ways, it must be discussed according to the tradition of the teachers, and whatever appeared more sound to them must be stated.

“They have been filled,” he says, “with idols, unbelief, and the crime of sins as in former times”—that is, as once in Egypt and afterward in the promised land, in the times of the judges and in the times of Jeroboam and Ahab. And they had their augurs and diviners as did the Philistines, or their neighboring Palestinians, from whom the law forbids them.

Augury is divination, so called because it is taken from the chattering of birds. Hence *augurs* are those who derive divination from the chattering of birds. The Palestinians were especially devoted to this superstition among the other nations.

It should be noted that in the time of Uzziah, Jotham, and Ahaz, under whom Isaiah prophesied, the Jews had idols just as they had once had them.

It follows: “And they clung to foreign boys,” that is, they fornicated with boys alienated from God. This can be understood in two ways: either they satisfied their lust with boys of their own nation, who through this crime were alienated from God, since every sinner is far from God; or with boys from the Gentiles. The Jews were so devoted to this detestable and horrifying vice that they even bought handsome boys from the Gentiles in order to satisfy their lust through them.

[Col. 0732A] “The land has been filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to its treasures.” Among the other vices to which the Jews were devoted, excessive avarice and greed are also signified by the words: “There is no end to its treasures,” that is, to their avarice and greed. This does not mean that treasures have no end, but that the mind of those who possess them is never satisfied, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “The avaricious person will not be filled with riches” (Ecclesiastes 9). The treasures of the Jews indeed had an end, but their greed was without end.

[Col. 0732B] “And its land has been filled with horses, and its chariots are innumerable.” This too was contrary to the Lord’s command, for in the Law he forbids the multiplication of chariots and horses. Those animals were indeed given for human assistance, not for pride; but humanity abused them in pride. Hence an animal is called *iumentum*, from assisting or raising up.

Concerning those who proudly abused such things, the psalmist says: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Psalm 20).

“And its land has been filled with idols; they worshiped the work of their hands, what their fingers had made. And the human being bowed down, and the man was humbled.” This means that both the weak and the powerful—indicated by the human being, who is so called from earth—and those who ought to have been strong and virtuous, understood by the word *man*, which derives from virtue, all alike bowed down and were humbled in order to worship idols. This also happened in Isaiah’s time.

“Therefore do not forgive them.” The Septuagint interpreted this differently, under the persona of God saying: “Therefore I will not forgive them.” Consequently the passage admits a twofold interpretation.

If it refers to God’s person, so that God himself spoke these words, it is to be understood as follows: Because they have committed such great evils, I will not spare them, nor forgive their countless crimes.

If the prophet is speaking, the meaning is: Therefore do not forgive their sins, since they have perpetrated such great evils.

It must be observed, however, that the prophet is not invoking evils against his own people. Rather, the things that were truly going to happen are understood; these had to be announced to them in prophetic fashion, from the earlier passage where it says, “They have been filled as in former times, and they have had diviners as the Philistines,” up to this point.

This refers both to the Jews in the way we have explained and to the Chaldeans and Romans, who were the plunderers of that people and inhabited their land. It means that, with the Jewish people protected [the wording is contextually problematic], foreigners who were filled with idols inhabited Judaea, had diviners, and clung to foreign boys.

“And its land has been filled with horses, and its chariots are innumerable.” This signifies the avarice of the Jews and Romans, than whom, as blessed Jerome testifies, no one is more avaricious. The land of the Israelite people was also filled with the horses of the Chaldeans and Romans, and its chariots were innumerable—that is, its vices.

[Col. 0732D] “Enter into the rock; hide in a pit in the earth, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty.” This is the voice of the prophet urging his people to enter into a rock and hide in a pit, covered over with earth from above.

In other words, it is as though he said: I urged you to walk in the light of the Lord, but because you were unwilling to listen, behold, I announce and urge you to enter into a rock and hide in a pit—or in caves—from the face of the fear of the Lord, or from the face of the Babylonian army, which is signified by the fear of the Lord; and from the glory of his majesty, because through them he sent his fear upon the Jews and glorified himself over his Jewish enemies by exacting vengeance.

Concerning this tribulation, out of fear of which they hid themselves in caves and wells, as the histories relate, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then they will say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the rocks, ‘Hide us’” (Luke 23).

In a higher sense, however, all of us are commanded to enter into the rock from the face of the fear of the Lord, that is, to flee for refuge to Christ, concerning whom it is said: “The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Psalm 103). Christ is like a rock, as the apostle Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

Whoever truly believes and takes refuge in him enters into the rock, so that, when he comes to destroy the reprobate, that person may not be condemned. He is hidden in a pit in the earth who enters his room and prays to his Father. Or he is hidden in a pit in the earth who, established in an earthly body—signified by earth—hides and conceals his bodily weaknesses, so that he does not display outwardly through his actions all the enticements that the flesh desires to accomplish.

[Col. 0733B] “The lofty eyes of the human being will be humbled, and the height of men will be bowed down; but the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.” By the lofty eyes of the human being that are humbled, and by the height of men, are understood the arrogance of power and nobility of lineage.

When, he says, the enemies arrive, neither wealth, nobility of lineage, nor the power of offices will be able to defend anyone, since there will be one captivity for all. The eyes of the powerful and wealthy person will be humbled—of the person who looked harshly and arrogantly upon others. The height of men will also be bowed down, that is, the nobility of lineage will be despised and regarded as worthless.

The Lord alone will be exalted on that day, that is, at the time of the arrival of the Chaldeans and Romans, whose anger and vengeance no one will be able to escape.

These same words may also appropriately be referred to the day of the final judgment, on which every creature will be humbled before the divine majesty and power and, in comparison with it, will recognize that it is nothing.

He then gives the reason why it must be humbled and bowed down.

[Col. 0733D] “Because the day of the Lord of hosts is against every proud and lofty person and against every arrogant person, and he will be humbled.” Whenever prophetic speech speaks of the Lord’s vengeance and victory, it is accustomed to call him the Lord of hosts—that is, of armies, which in Hebrew is called *Sabaoth*. He is the Lord of his armies, whether of angels or of human beings.

The day of the Lord, that is, the day of his vengeance, is understood in two ways: namely, as the time of the Jews’ captivity, which came upon every proud and lofty person and every arrogant person. These three expressions convey one meaning, signifying the princes of the Jews, the priests, the Pharisees, and the scribes.

It also means the time of the final judgment, in which the proud devil will be condemned with all his followers and will be humbled, together with all the arrogant and proud.

[Col. 0734A] “And against all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, and against all the oaks of Bashan.” “The day of the Lord will come” is understood. Lebanon is a mountain in the region of Phoenicia containing exceedingly lofty cedars which, as Cassiodorus says in his exposition of the Psalms, surpass the height of every other tree by their stature.

Bashan, however, is a region of Arabia ruled by King Og, containing oaks that produce acorns, whose fruit is food for pigs, not for human beings.

In a metaphorical sense, the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon signify all the proud; the oaks of Bashan—which is interpreted as “shame”—signify those who perform shameful deeds and wallow in the mire of lust, whose fruit belongs to pigs, that is, to demons. Against all such people the vengeance and day of the Lord’s wrath will rise.

Concerning such cedars it is said in the psalm (Psalm 28): “The voice of the Lord shattering the cedars.” And again: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure, like the cedars of Lebanon.”

[Col. 0734B] “And against all the lofty mountains, and against all the hills and elevated places.” “The day of the Lord will come” is understood. Mountains and hills are often taken in a good sense, as referring to the saints adorned with a variety of virtues. But often the wicked themselves, especially the proud, are called mountains and hills because of the diversity of their vices, as in the present passage.

Concerning these mountains and hills the prophet Ezekiel says: “Thus says the Lord to the mountains and hills: Behold, I will bring a sword against you” (Ezekiel 36).

[Col. 0734C] “And against every lofty tower and every fortified wall.” “The day of the Lord will come” is understood. As far as the literal sense is concerned, when the Roman army arrived, the Lord’s day of vengeance came against the tower and every wall of the Jews, because all of them were utterly overthrown.

In a metaphorical sense, the tower and wall signify those who trusted more in the height of towers and the strength of walls than in God. Against them the Lord’s day of vengeance came, because they were consumed by famine, pestilence, and the sword, and were sold for a price.

The tower may also be understood particularly as those who stood out among the people, like a tower in a city. By the fortified wall are understood the rich and powerful, who fortified themselves with their wealth; against them the Lord’s day will come.

[Col. 0734D] “And against all the ships of Tarshish, and against everything beautiful to the sight.” “The day of the Lord will come” is understood. The Hebrews call all seas “Tarshish,” and they call a gathering of waters by the name “sea,” in accordance with the passage in Genesis: “He called the gatherings of waters seas” (Genesis 1).

Therefore in this passage “that sea” should not be understood simply as the sea adjoining the promised land, but also as all the neighboring rivers on which the Jews were accustomed to sail and conduct commerce. In a figurative sense, the ships signify those who, sitting in ships, sailed the open sea and rivers for the sake of trade.

Against them the Lord’s day of vengeance came. For, as Josephus relates, when the Romans arrived, those who lived in the ports were seized and their ships were burned.

What follows—“and against everything beautiful to the sight”—is to be understood as referring to the temple and sanctuary, where there was the greatest beauty, and to all virgins and young men: against everything that was delightful to behold, the day of vengeance came, when all the goods of that people were simultaneously destroyed and emptied out.

[Col. 0735A] “And the loftiness of human beings will be bowed down, and the height of men will be humbled.” By the loftiness of human beings and the height of men are understood the arrogance of power and nobility of lineage, as was said a little above, because they were bowed down and humbled when some were killed and others were sold into slavery.

“And the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and the idols will be utterly crushed.” This means plainly: On that day, that is, at the time of the devastation of the Jews, the Lord will be exalted—that is, he will appear lofty, glorious, and strong—when he delivers his Jewish enemies into the mouth of the sword of the Chaldeans and Romans. Then the idols of the Jews will be utterly crushed together with their worshipers.

Although the Jews are not recorded as having worshiped idols at the Lord’s coming, they did worship idols when they were taken captive by the Chaldeans, as was shown to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 8). Therefore, because the prophetic speech speaks in a mixed manner of both captivities and devastations, the statement that the idols will be utterly crushed should be referred especially to the earlier one. The idols of the Jews were indeed crushed by the Chaldeans, and their metals were carried off to Babylon.

[Col. 0735C] “And they will enter into the caves of the rocks and into the hollows of the earth, from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth.” The present words and those that follow concern both devastations of the Jews, when, attempting to flee God’s vengeance, they hid themselves in caves and hollows of the earth.

It is rightly said: “From the glory of the Lord’s power, when he rises to strike the earth.” In a certain sense almighty God rises to strike earthly people—those who think about and seek only earthly things—when he severely inflicts punishment upon them through his ministers, just as he inflicted it upon the Jews through the Chaldeans and Romans.

[Col. 0735D] “On that day”—that is, at the coming of the Chaldeans or also the Romans—“the man” (the Jew) “will cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he made for himself in order to worship moles and bats; and he will enter into the clefts of the rocks and into the caves of the stones, from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth.”

“Of the Jews,” or “those Jews who pursue earthly things,” is understood. This happened when, as the hostile army came upon them, the Jews cast away their idols and hid themselves in caves so that they might escape the Lord’s anger.

When it says “in order to worship moles and bats,” this should not be understood to mean that they had images in the likeness of a mole—which is an animal lacking the light of sight—or of a bat, which is a bird that flees the light. Rather, he spoke contemptuously and mockingly, comparing their idols to moles and bats, which, although they appear to have eyes, do not see at all, as the psalmist says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have eyes and do not see” (Psalm 113).

“Therefore cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted.” The prophet Isaiah, considering that his fellow Jews were to be destroyed because of the evils which they inflicted upon Christ with treacherous intent, exhorts them, saying: Behold, I have foretold to you in the prophetic spirit what may come to pass. I therefore warn and command you to cease from the man Christ, who according to the flesh is truly human, possessing a soul, breathing, and drawing breath through his nostrils, just as we ordinary human beings breathe and live; but according to his divine majesty he is accounted exalted and believed to be equal to God the Father. Beware lest you offend him in anything, for although he breathes as a human being, he is nevertheless true God. And if you do so, all the evils described above will swiftly come upon you. That our Redeemer is exalted the Psalmist indicates, saying: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.” And what he says, “whose breath is in his nostrils,” is as though he had said: In whose nostrils there is breath, which is generally called spirit.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0736C] “For behold, the Lord, the ruler of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the strong and mighty man.” The prophet’s voice is directed to the Jews who persecuted the Lord. Because, he says, you were unwilling to cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, who must be believed to be exalted, but instead shed the blood of the innocent, behold, the Lord, the ruler, will take away from Jerusalem the strong and mighty man, and every warrior, so that no one will remain who possesses any strength, but all will be weak and feeble. “All the strength of bread and all the strength of water.” Understand: he will take away from Judah and Jerusalem. The strength or supply of bread and water is understood as every kind of food and drink—things which the Lord took away from the Jews, to such an extent that, driven by hunger, they ate their own children. [Col. 0736D] Allegorically, however, bread and water signify divine Scripture, which in some passages is food and in others drink. The Lord took it away from the Jews and gave it to the nations, so that they might produce its fruits, as he himself says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21). Wherever it is difficult to understand and is taken in with difficulty, it is food, because it is swallowed, in a manner of speaking, by chewing. Where it is easily understood, it is drink. Another prophet testifies concerning this kind of bread and water: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I shall send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8).

“Strong man and warrior, judge, prophet, diviner, and elder.” Understand: the Lord will take them away from Judah and Jerusalem. There is no doubt that the Lord took all these from the Jews. They have no strong warrior at all; rather, all are weak and full of fear. It is also evident from this that they have no judges, since they themselves are judged by Roman governors. The true prophet and the wise elder have already ceased to exist among them. The Lord took away from them not only the others but also the diviners themselves—whom the Septuagint translated as “soothsayers.” Diviners are enchanters who accomplish things by means of certain spells. Through them future events are also often foretold, as we read of the diviner Balaam (Numbers 24), and of the diviners of the five cities of the Philistines (1 Samuel 6). The meaning is that both truth and falsehood alike are taken away from the Jews.

“A commander over fifty, and one honorable in appearance, and a wise counselor among the craftsmen, and one skilled in mystical speech.” Here, taking the part for the whole, by “a commander over fifty”—who is called a *quinquagenarius*, “a leader of fifty”—we understand that all the princes of the Jews are taken away. Among the other gifts, the Lord will also take this from the Jews: that they will have no one honorable in appearance, worthy of respect on account of his dignity; no counselor, but will do everything without counsel. He will also take away the chief of craftsmen, such as Bezalel, and the one skilled in mystical speech—that is, the wise teacher who teaches mystical or divine utterances—or, as some wish to say, the wise listener who is able to discern the teaching of the preacher. The saying of a certain Greek poet is admirable: he says that the first blessed person is the one who is wise by himself, and the second the one who listens to a wise man.

“And I will give children as their princes, and the effeminate will rule over them.” While the prophet was speaking in his own person the things stated above, suddenly, according to prophetic usage, God speaks through the prophet in his own person, saying: I will give children as their princes—that is, after removing those whom I had previously given as princes, namely the leader of fifty, the elder, and the wise counselor, I will give them instead wanton and dissolute princes, behaving like children. We must not understand “children” as referring only to age, but also to character and conduct. We read of such child-princes in Ecclesiastes: “Woe to you, land whose king is a boy” (Ecclesiastes 10)—that is, one who acts boyishly. Such was Rehoboam, who, scorning the advice of the elders, followed the counsel of the young (1 Kings 12). This does not mean that he was a child or young in age when he received the kingdom—for he was forty-six years old—but that he behaved childishly and irresponsibly. What follows, “and the effeminate will rule over them,” has the same meaning. The effeminate are those who have reduced manly strength and firmness to feminine softness. Such are the Jewish leaders today: they do everything childishly and possess no strength at all.

[Col. 0738A] “And the people will rush, man against man, and each against his neighbor. The child will rebel against the elder, and the ignoble against the noble.” When their princes are children and the effeminate rule over them, then no order of age or dignity will be preserved. The people will rush or rise up against themselves, the bond of peace and civic concord having been dissolved: man against man and each person against his neighbor. A child in age will also murmur against an elder, or a fool against a wise man, and the ignoble against the noble. This often happens in the holy Church because of the sins of the people. Strong princes, fit to wage the Lord’s battles, and religious rulers who know how to govern God’s people according to his will are removed, as are counselors and wise teachers. Thus every order is thrown into confusion, and a man rises against his brother: a child takes the liberty of murmuring against an elder, and one ignoble in birth and conduct against a noble.

“Then a man will seize his brother, a member of his father’s household”—that is, a servant whom his father raised. When Jerusalem was surrounded by the Roman army in a siege, the Jews, shut inside the walls of their city, were divided into three factions. Some held the Temple and the citadel of Zion; others held the upper part of the city; and others the lower part. Each man appointed as his prince whomever he wished, not only a servant of his father’s household but also another person, saying: “You have clothing; be our prince. This ruin is under your hand.” The sense is: You have food and clothing; be our prince—only free us from the famine that is pressing upon us, and let our misery be sustained by your assistance.

“And he will answer on that day, saying: I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me prince of the people.” The man who has been chosen as prince, considering his poverty and weakness, will answer: I am not a physician—that is, I cannot meet your need—for I have neither bread nor clothing. Therefore do not appoint me prince.

“For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty.” This is not spoken by the man whom they wished to appoint as prince, but rather by the prophet, who says that no one wishes to rule over a sinful people because the city of Jerusalem and the province of Judea alike have fallen into the hands of their enemies. He gives the causes of their impiety and destruction: they blasphemed against the Lord, saying, “You have a demon,” and, “You are a Samaritan,” and, “He is guilty of death,” and, “Crucify him,” as well as many similar things (John 8; Matthew 26; Luke 23). They also brought forward their devices against the Lord when they produced false witnesses against him, saying: “This man said, ‘I can destroy this temple made with hands and in three days rebuild another not made with hands.’” Therefore they provoked the eyes of the Lord’s majesty—that is, his merciful regard and clemency—to bitterness. Although the Romans came for their own reasons, inasmuch as the Jews refused to pay tribute, the cause of their destruction was nevertheless the death of the Son of God. And because they provoked him to bitterness:

“The recognition of their face will answer them”—that is, the knowledge that, although they saw Christ in the flesh, they refused to believe in him. The Lord will answer them when, placed in misery and tribulation, they remember that these things befell them because of the death of the Son of God. Or alternatively: “The recognition of their face will answer them,” because they received what their sins deserved, or because they continually had their own offenses before the eyes of their mind. “And they proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not conceal it.” Just as the Sodomites, polluted by unspeakable crimes, shamelessly said to Lot, “Bring the men out to us, so that we may have intercourse with them,” so these people, ensnared in the same sins, proclaimed their sin impudently and without any sense of shame, shouting against the Lord: “Crucify him, crucify him!” and, “He is guilty of death.” Hence, by the same prophet, they are called the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah.

Morally, each person publicizes his sin like the Sodomites when he shamelessly reveals to others the vices by which he himself is polluted and enslaved, in order to make them like himself and turn them into his imitators. It is not enough for him to show his impurity to one person unless he also entices many others. Therefore, just as the Sodomites perished in body and soul, so he too will be condemned on the day of judgment in body and soul alike, hearing from the Lord that terrifying voice: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). “Woe to their soul, for evils have been repaid to them”—that is, they receive the condemnation due to their crimes.

“Tell the righteous man that it is well, for they shall eat the fruit of their devices.” The prophet addresses those who will read this prophecy: You who have read the book of this prophecy, or who have heard of the destruction of the Jews, praise the Lord’s justice and say to the righteous man—that is, to Christ—that he has done well in repaying the Jews the punishment which their devices deserved.

“Woe to the impious man for evil; the recompense of his hands will be done to him.” This means: Eternal destruction will come upon the Jewish people, because they will receive such things as they have done. They handed over their prince to Roman authority, and they themselves were subjected to Roman slavery. This also applies to every impious person: whatever he has done, such things will come upon him.

“My people—those who exact from them have plundered them, and women have ruled over them.” The prophetic word speaks against the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23; Luke 11), calling them the people’s exactors, because, in order to be able to demand tribute, tithes, and firstfruits from their subjects and turn them to their own uses, they denied the Son of God for the sake of shameful profit. They are called exactors not only because they plundered the people, but also “women,” contemptuously, because they lived in a womanish manner, serving lust and every pleasure. They were so devoted to greed that if their subjects did not hand over everything that ought to be paid, they publicly scourged them and afterward demanded it from them in many ways, saying: “It is written: You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Exodus 23).

It may also be understood in this way: women ruled over them—that is, the wives of the scribes and Pharisees. Therefore teachers and instructors of the Church must beware lest they become exactors who oppress the people subject to them so that they may enrich themselves with their wealth, and, serving greed, live in a womanish manner.

“My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps.” The scribes and Pharisees, who were called exactors above, used to call those from whom they received gifts blessed, flattering them and saying: You are holy and chosen by almighty God; you honor his ministers and are pillars of the house of God. By such and similar flattering words they deceived them, and by excessively exalting their conduct with their praises they destroyed the path of their actions, acting against the saying: “Do not praise a person during his lifetime” (Ecclesiastes 11).

“The Lord stands to judge; he stands to judge the peoples.” He does not sit to judge in order to destroy them in the present age, as is written in the book of Daniel (Daniel 13); rather, he stands—that is, he considers and discerns everyone’s works, wishing to establish in faith and good works those whose path has been destroyed. Or he considers how he will reward his benefactors in the future, but destroy his evildoers in the future.

“The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people”—that is, with the patriarchs and prophets, and with his princes, namely the apostles, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “You will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44). “But you have devoured my vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses.” The divine word speaks against the scribes and Pharisees, the exactors of the Jews: they have devoured the Lord’s vineyard—that is, the Israelite people, plundering the people of whom the Psalm says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” Isaiah also says elsewhere: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (below, chapter 5). In their houses there was the plunder of the poor—that is, of the innocent: orphans and widows who had no means of defending themselves.

“Why do you crush,” or afflict, “my people, and grind down”—that is, impoverish, weaken, or wear away—“the faces of the poor,” that is, the needy and orphans? To grind down means to weaken, consume, or crush. Hence in the Gospel (Matthew 6) the scribes and Pharisees are said to fast because they disfigure their faces—that is, make them thin. They themselves also seized the substance of the poor and needy, and thus, through the deprivation caused by hunger, weakened their faces.

This may also be referred to wicked leaders of the Church, who plunder the needy and publicly condemn the innocent. In their houses there is the plunder of the poor, and they weaken their faces.

“And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion have exalted themselves, walked with outstretched necks, went about with glances of their eyes, clapped their hands, walked about, and stepped along with measured tread.” Above, both the Lord and the prophet rebuked the people and their leaders. Now the prophetic word is again directed to the wives of the scribes and Pharisees, of whom he had said above, “and women have ruled over them,” so that they may not consider themselves free from guilt. On account of their luxuries and wantonness, their husbands plundered the Lord’s people. They were adorned and decked out in pleasures, walking with outstretched necks and speaking with glances of their eyes. They went about clapping their hands and playing with their feet because of excessive wantonness and irresponsibility, and they walked with a measured step because of their pride. This testimony should correct the women and wives of the holy Church who imitate these women. “Because,” he says, “they have done this.”

[Col. 0741B] “The Lord will make the crown of the daughters of Zion bald”—that is, he will cause their heads to be shaved.

“And the Lord will uncover their hair,” so that disgrace may take the place of adornment.

“On that day”—that is, at the time of the captivity of the Jews, which will come upon them through the Romans—

“The Lord will take away the ornament of their footwear and their crescent ornaments,” together with their other feminine adornments. Women have pendants or clasps made in the shape of the moon. A necklace is made of gold and encircles the neck. Hence, when Belshazzar saw the fingers of the hand writing on the wall, he said (Daniel 5): “Whoever reads this writing and declares its interpretation will be clothed in purple, and a golden necklace will be placed around his neck.” Necklaces are, in general, all women’s ornaments. Bracelets are right-hand ornaments worn on the arms. A *mitra* is a covering for the head; among men it is called a cap or tiara, while among women it may be called a *cusia*. Hair-partings are the implements with which the hair is parted; they are also called *squinones*. With these women divide and arrange the hair of their heads. *Perischelides* are golden necklaces resembling bracelets, worn around the neck. *Murenulae* are golden rods, twisted with gold and silver, containing pearls inserted into them and hanging from the neck. *Olfactoriola* are so called from smelling; women carry musk and other feminine perfumes in them. Earrings are ornaments hanging from the ears. *Sindones* are linen coverings made with delicate workmanship. A *teristrum* is a kind of woman’s cloak made from the finest linen, so delicate and thin that if someone wore a tunic made from it, it could not conceal the body’s blemishes. Women of Arabia, Mesopotamia, and Spain especially use this garment in *tou thereos*, that is, in summer; hence it received its name, for *theros* means “summer.”

“And there will be stench instead of sweet fragrance, and instead of a belt”—that is, instead of a golden girdle—“a cord, and instead of curled hair,” which women customarily arrange by curling their locks, “there will be baldness. And there will be sackcloth instead of a breast-band.” A breast-band covers the chest and occupies in women the place that the breastplate occupies among priests. It is placed upon the chest to restrain the breasts so that they do not grow too large, which is unattractive.

Jeremiah also spoke mystically concerning this breast-band: “If a bride can forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band, then I will also forget you, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 2). In some regions, certain coverings are made of raw leather, as large as one wishes, to serve as breasts. They are applied to young girls’ breasts and then tightened from above with a breast-band. Thus the breasts neither grow excessively nor, through the hands and touch of lustful young men, become broken and swell.

“Your most handsome men will also fall by the sword, and your strong men in battle.” Both the most handsome young men of the Jews and their strong warriors fell to death by the sword of the Romans, and perished while fighting against them. Although they did not fight the Romans at close quarters in the open field, they nevertheless fought against them while shut within the walls of their cities, as Josephus and Hegesippus relate most clearly.

“And her gates will mourn and lament, and she will sit desolate upon the ground.” By a metonymy, the gates of Jerusalem, which are said to mourn and lament, signify those living outside the gates or in the gates themselves according to ancient custom, since the seats of kings and princes were above the gates. Thus we read of David (2 Samuel 19) that he sat at the gate. The princes of Jerusalem may also be understood by the gates of Jerusalem, since afterward they remain in mourning and grief. The city itself, made desolate of its inhabitants, sits upon the ground, utterly overthrown. Or the desolate and abandoned people themselves, deprived of their inhabitant, almighty God, sit upon the ground—that is, in humiliation and rejection—while they are daily despised and scorned by all the nations.

## CHAPTER IV

“And seven women will seize one man on that day, saying: We shall eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us—take away our reproach.” When Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took captive Zedekiah, king of Judah, together with all the princes of the Jews and all the people of the land, namely of the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin (for the ten tribes had already been led away beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians, from where they afterward did not return), it could have happened that many more women remained in the land, so that, because of the scarcity of men, seven of them seized one man, saying: We have bread and clothing, but we are deprived of husbands. Therefore, lest we remain without offspring and the curse of the Law come upon us—“Cursed is the barren woman who has not left seed upon the earth”—come and take away from us the reproach of barrenness. Let your name be called over us; that is, be our husband, so that we may not appear to be without a husband and be called your wives.

Allegorically, however, the seven women are understood as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the same prophet mentions later, saying (below, chapter 11): “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding,” and so forth, “of the fear of the Lord.” The one man is understood as the Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom Zechariah says: “Behold, a man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah 6). “On that day,” he says, “seven women will seize one man.” That is, at the time of the Lord’s incarnation, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit will seize one man. This signifies the Lord Jesus, whom they had long desired because they could find no other in whom they might rest eternally. Hence John says: “I saw the Spirit descending and remaining upon him” (Mark 1).
