These are the seven women, that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Zechariah designates under the name of eyes, saying: “Upon one stone there are seven eyes, and upon one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven channels” (Zechariah 4). The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, signified by the seven women, did not first seize the Lord Jesus so that they might dwell eternally in him when, at the time of his baptism, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and the Father’s voice thundered (Matthew 3; Luke 3; John 3): “This is my beloved Son.” Rather, the Spirit dwelt fully in him from the time of his conception, as the blessed Augustine and Boethius testify in their book *On the Holy Trinity*.

What is said—“We shall eat our own bread and wear our own clothing”—must be understood to mean that the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things together with the Father and the Son. And because the Spirit continually suffered reproach among human beings, being excluded from their hearts through sin, since no one lived in such a way as the gifts of the Spirit required, they therefore desire that the name of Jesus be invoked over them, so that through him who is Savior and is called Jesus or Christ, human beings may be saved and called Christians, and so that he may thereafter dwell in them.

It may also be understood in another way. The seven women, he says, signify the seven churches to which John writes in his Apocalypse. These seven churches represent all the churches spread throughout the whole world. For the number seven is frequently taken in sacred language to signify universality. When he speaks to one of them, he speaks to all, just as at the end of each sentence addressed to them he says: “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2).

At what time, then, did these women seize the Lord Jesus? Certainly after his ascension, when, through the preaching of the apostles, they received faith in him and began firmly to believe in him. But what did they say to him? “We shall eat our own bread”—that is, we shall receive your body in the Church, because you are the true bread that descended from heaven. “And we shall wear our own clothing”—that is, we shall be adorned with the ornaments of virtues, which are woven together from the two pieces of wood, namely love of God and love of neighbor (John 6). “Only let your name be called over us”—so that from you, Christ, we may receive the name of Christianity. “Take away our reproach”—that is, be our husband, protecting us amid adversity and prosperity, so that we may grow throughout the whole world and leave behind us the seed of good works, or spiritual children who are children of God. Before the Lord’s coming, the Gentiles were held in reproach by the Jews because they did not have as their husband the almighty God. But after the Lord’s ascension this reproach was removed from them, when through faith in him they received as their husband their almighty God.

“On that day there will be a branch of the Lord in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth will be exalted, and rejoicing for those of Israel who have been saved.” He calls the Son of God the branch of the Father, concerning whom the prophet says: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root.” And: “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples.” And elsewhere: “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior.”

The fruit of the earth is the Son of the blessed Virgin Mary. It must be noted that when we say that he is the Son of God and the son of the Virgin, we do not divide the person, which is one; rather, we distinguish the natures, divine and human. He is the fruit concerning which the Father says to David: “From the fruit of your loins I will place upon my throne” (Psalm 131). And the Psalmist says: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will give its fruit” (Psalm 84).

On that day, therefore—that is, at the time when the seven women seized one man—there was a branch of the Lord, the Son of God, in magnificence and glory, because through the power of his miracles and heavenly teaching he appeared great and glorious. The fruit of the earth, that same Son of the Virgin, was also exalted when he was raised above all the orders of angels. Then there was great rejoicing for those of Israel who had been saved, namely the apostles and the other Jewish believers, concerning whom Luke says: “They believed on one day three thousand, on another day five thousand, and afterward many thousands” (Acts 2, 4). On the other hand, for the scribes and Pharisees and the others who remained in unbelief and did not deserve to be saved, there was no rejoicing but the greatest sorrow, when they saw the apostles preaching the name of the Lord Jesus and spreading his faith far and wide.

“And it will be: Everyone who has been left in Zion, who remains in Jerusalem, will be called holy, everyone who has been written in life in Jerusalem.” Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and Jerusalem, which is called “vision of peace,” signify the holy Church, which by contemplation of the mind gazes upon heavenly things, striving with all its strength toward the vision of peace. Therefore everyone who has been left and remains in the Church through faith and good works will be called holy, because he will be called a Christian by Christ. That is, everyone who has been written in life in Jerusalem—in the memory and predestination of almighty God. At this point the apostles and the other faithful from the same people are understood, concerning whom the same prophet says: “Unless the Lord had left us seed, we would have been like Sodom.” The Lord also spoke to these people: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Not in a material book, but in the memory of almighty God. For in the heavenly Jerusalem there is no other book than the memory and presence of God.

“If the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanses the blood of Jerusalem from its midst, by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.” This particle “if” sometimes has a negative meaning, as in: “If I have repaid those who repaid me evil” (Psalm 7)—that is, “I have not repaid them.” At other times it is used affirmatively, as in the present passage and many others. It is as though he said: All who believe in him will be called holy. The Lord will wash away the filth of their sins from them through the grace of baptism, and he will cleanse from its midst the blood of the prophets which they and their fathers shed, as well as the blood which the erring people invoked upon themselves, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

He will bring about this purification by the spirit of judgment—that is, in baptism—and by the spirit of burning, that is, through the shedding of his blood. Or the spirit of burning or consuming may be understood as the Holy Spirit, who consumes the sins of the elect. Hence it is also said: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4). The spirit of burning may also be understood in a third way: as the tribulation and torment of the Passion by which the elect are purified. This, however, must be understood as having been spoken concerning the apostles and the other believers from the same people.

“And the Lord will create over every place of Mount Zion, and wherever he is invoked, a cloud by day, and smoke, and the brightness of flaming fire by night.” Zion here signifies the holy Church. The cloud signifies divine protection. Smoke signifies his glory, as the same prophet says: “The house was filled with smoke,” that is, with the glory of the Lord. Or smoke may signify the compunction of repentance. The brightness of fire signifies the remission of sins.

“Over every place,” he says, “of Mount Zion”—that is, over the holy Church—and wherever he is invoked by his faithful, the Lord will create a cloud by day, that is, protection amid prosperity, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night, that is, assistance and deliverance, or glory and compunction, together with the remission of sins, through the grace of the Holy Spirit who protects amid adversity. It is as though he said: He will protect those who hope in him amid prosperity and adversity, so that they neither become proud and fall into sin amid prosperity nor fail through despair amid adversity. Just as he protected the children of Israel in the daytime with a pillar of cloud to ward off the heat, and at night with a pillar of fire to inspire fear, so also he will protect and govern his elect in prosperity and adversity.

## CHAPTER V

“I will now sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard.” The prophet sings a mournful song for the people of Israel, composed by the one of whom it was said in the Gospel: “When he saw it”—there is no doubt that this means Jerusalem—“he wept over it and said: If you too had known the things that are for your peace, for enemies will come upon you and surround you with fortifications, and hem you in, and overthrow you and your children” (Luke 19).

That Christ is called “the beloved” is taught by the superscription of Psalm 44, “A song for the beloved,” and by the voice of God the Father in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). This beloved, then, composed a mournful song for his vineyard, which I will sing for my beloved and pitiable people. Or certainly it should be understood in this way: I will sing to almighty God the Father the song of Christ, who is my kinsman—that is, born from the same people as I.

That the people of Israel is called the Lord’s vineyard is said in Psalm 79: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.” In the Gospel also, the Lord constructed a parable in almost the same words with which the prophet now speaks: “There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard.” Thus, as we have said, Jerusalem is mourned, and its ruin is sung in prophetic speech.

“A vineyard was made for my beloved, on a horn, the son of oil.” We often read that a horn signifies a kingdom and power, as in the Gospel: “He raised up the horn of our salvation in the house of David his servant.” And: “In you we shall toss our enemies with the horn.” And in Zechariah, four exceedingly powerful horns signify kingdoms.

“And he fenced it, and chose stones from it, and planted it with the vine Soreth; and he built a tower in its midst and constructed a winepress in it.” By metaphor, as we said earlier, he described the Jewish people as a vineyard, which he fenced with the assistance of angels. “And he chose stones from it”—that is, idols, or everything that could obstruct the worship of God. “And he planted it with the vine Soreth.” The Hebrews say that *Soreth* is a kind of very fine vine that produces abundant and lasting fruit. Finally, some interpret *Soreth* as *callicarpos*, “beautiful-fruited,” which we may render as “producing very beautiful fruits.” “He also built a tower in its midst,” namely the Temple in the middle of the city. “And he constructed a winepress in it,” which some think signifies the altar.

Everything said about the vineyard can therefore also be referred to the condition of the soul: planted by God for good, it produced not grapes but wild grapes; afterward it was handed over to beasts to be trampled, and it did not receive the divine rain of teachings because it had despised the gifts previously bestowed.

[Col. 0746D] “And I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes. Now then, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done for it? Or was it that I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes?”

“I did,” he says, “everything that I ought to have done. I planted the vineyard in a fertile place; I surrounded it with a hedge, chose out stones, and supported its branches with stakes and reeds. The vine itself was not one among many, but chosen. Therefore, since I did what I ought to have done, let the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judah answer me—or rather, let them judge between me and my vineyard: what was there that I ought to have done and did not do?” Here this people is questioned as though concerning a vineyard, so that it may answer against itself [Col. 0747A]. The Savior expounds this passage more fully in the Gospel (Matthew 21). What is omitted here, he asks the scribes and Pharisees. In Isaiah nothing is said about the cultivators, nor is it indicated what they will suffer; there the subject is simply the vineyard. But there, as though the vineyard were one thing and the cultivator another, he speaks about the people and its teachers, so that “he may destroy the evil men miserably” and “lease the vineyard to other cultivators,” signifying the apostles and those who will succeed the apostles. Above, he speaks silently to himself; here, he questions others about what he had intended.

“And now I will show you what I shall do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be exposed to plunder. I will tear down its wall, and it shall be for trampling. I will make it desolate; it shall not be pruned and shall not be dug, [Col. 0747B] and briars and thorns shall grow up over it.” Because I did everything that I ought to have done for my vineyard, and it produced wild grapes instead of grapes, I shall remove everything that I had given it. I shall take away the assistance of the angels, concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them”; and he will deliver them from their adversaries. I shall destroy its walls, and it shall be subjected to hostile nations. It shall be desolate and shall never be pruned, nor shall it be dug, so that it may be reduced to briars. God’s help, however, is taken away from those who are unworthy, so that, because they did not recognize God through benefits, they may recognize him through punishments. Or he threatened them with certain savage and harsh things for this reason: so that, turning to repentance, they might avoid the torments that threatened them. “And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” We can understand this not only of the prophets, [Col. 0747C] but also of the apostles. Let them not bring forth thorns instead of grapes, but, because of their barrenness and dryness, let them entreat him who is able to provide rains of virtues.

“The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his delightful plant,” that is, God’s. Beautifully, Israel—that is, the whole people of Israel—is called the house of God; but Judah is called the delightful plant, because afterward it sprouted forth when the tribes had been separated. For a young shoot is called delightful. This too must be noted: according to prophetic custom, what was first said metaphorically or by way of parable is afterward explained more plainly—that the vineyard and the young planting are Israel and Judah. “I expected him to execute judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, a cry.” [Col. 0747D] God expected the Jewish people to execute judgment—that is, to produce grapes—but it produced iniquity, that is, wild grapes. He expected righteousness, so that it might receive the one sent by the Father, the giver of such great gifts; but it produced a cry, by which it shouted against the Lord and cried out, saying: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John 19). Hence the apostle Paul also writes: “Let all anger and shouting and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4). Or certainly, because they had shed the blood of the righteous, and the blood of the Lord’s Passion cried out to God, they returned a cry instead of righteousness.

“Woe to you who join house to house and attach field to field, up to the boundary of the place. [Col. 0748A] Will you alone dwell upon the earth?” I think this was said both generally against all those for whom nothing is sufficient, and specifically against the vineyard of the Lord, which produced wild grapes instead of grapes—that is, iniquity instead of judgment, and a cry instead of righteousness. What madness is it, when roofs in the fields seem to be kept for warding off the rain and sowing crops, to desire to possess things whose combination makes it impossible for you to dwell there, and which you are unable to cultivate—and to make another person’s necessity your will? According to the tropological interpretation, some consider this to have been said against heretics. When they have moved their feet from the east, they come to the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking off of teeth,” and build a city of confusion and a tower of pride. These people join houses to houses—that is, [Col. 0748B] doctrines to doctrines. Heretics continue trying to join new things to old and to alter the same things with more recent ones until both human understanding and speech fail.

“In my ears are these things, says the Lord of hosts: Unless many houses become desolate, great and beautiful, without inhabitant.” That is, the words spoken by the Lord still resound in my ears. The Lord said that after the captivity great and very beautiful houses would become desolate, having no inhabitant.

“For ten yokes of vineyards shall produce one small jar, and thirty measures of seed shall produce three measures.” That is, a chorus shall produce one ephah, which the Septuagint translated as three measures, that is, three modii [bushels]. A bath is the term for this measure in the case of liquids, while an ephah or oiphi is the same measure for dry goods. That building and agriculture refer to spiritual understanding, the apostle Paul also teaches elsewhere (Ephesians 3), testifying that believers are “founded and rooted in love.” Hence Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 2) not only built houses for himself, but also planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, established every kind of fruit-bearing tree, and constructed pools in order to water the woodland. Heretics, however, possessing only the image and shadow of virtues, and not the truth itself, promise leaves of words without the fruit of deeds. Concerning such trees the Lord says (Matthew 15): “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” Concerning the vineyard of Sodom: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot is from Gomorrah.”

[Col. 0748D] “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that you burn with wine. Harp, lyre, tambourine, flute, and wine are in your banquets, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.” In accordance with the sequence of the explanation already begun, he rebukes the cultivators of the vineyard, who, while barrenness is imminent and a nearby fire is at hand by which the briars and thorns are to be burned, have given themselves over to luxury and pleasures—not only in eating and drinking, but also in the delight of the ears and in various kinds of musical art. When they do these things, they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor [Col. 0749A] consider what is going to happen to them. According to a higher understanding, every disturbance of the soul can be called drunkenness. It is conceived from the wine of the dragons’ fury and from the incurable poison of asps. Some drink this from youth into old age—that is, from morning until evening; others rise from the banquet at the third, sixth, or ninth hour, or at the tenth. To them it is said: “Awake, you who are drunk with wine” (Joel 1). Most wretched are those who, occupied from morning until evening with drunkenness, gluttony, and various pleasures, do not understand God’s works within themselves, nor consider why they were created.

[Col. 0749B] “Therefore my people have gone into captivity, because they had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished from hunger, and its multitude has dried up from thirst.” That these things literally happened to the Jewish people under the Roman rulers Vespasian and Titus is related by both Greek and Latin history. This is also understood spiritually today: they suffer who endure not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but hunger for hearing the word of God (Deuteronomy 8). That every word of teaching is called bread and water is shown by the Gospel (Matthew 4; Luke 4; John 4): “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” And: “Whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst.” And in the Psalm it is said: “He led me beside the waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22). Some wish to interpret the statement, “My people have gone into captivity because they had no knowledge, and its nobles have perished from hunger, and its multitude has dried up from thirst,” [Col. 0749C] generally of hell and Gehenna, in which everyone who has not had knowledge of God will suffer.

[Col. 0749D] “Therefore Sheol enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit, and its mighty ones and its people shall descend to it, and its exalted and glorious ones; and man shall be bowed down, and the man shall be humbled, and the eyes of the exalted shall be brought low.” Because they rose early to pursue strong drink, remained in drunkenness until evening, and, occupied with pleasures and delights, refused to regard the work of the Lord or contemplate the works of his hands, therefore they were led into captivity, because they did not have knowledge of the Son of God, who said to them: “You know neither me nor the one who sent me” (John 8). Sheol is said to have a soul—not because it is an animal, according to the error of some, but because in the language of human custom we express the disposition of inanimate things, namely, that it is insatiable and is never filled by the multitude of the dead. Whatever we have said about the Jewish people can be referred tropologically to those who, occupied with the pleasures of the world and not regarding the works of the Lord, are led captive into sin, do not possess knowledge of God, and therefore perish from hunger and thirst—that is, from a lack of good works and virtues. They will be dragged down into Gehenna, and there, consigned to eternal fires, they will see their power and pride changed into misery and humiliation.

“And the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, [Col. 0750A] and the holy God shall be sanctified in righteousness”—that is, when man has been bowed down and the man humbled, and all have received according to their merits, then the Lord shall be exalted in judgment. At first his judgment will seem uncertain, and the holy God will be sanctified in righteousness, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 16). And: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17).

“And lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the desolate places that have been turned into abundance.” When the Lord has been exalted in judgment, and holy David has been sanctified in his righteousness, so that the evil cultivators perish miserably and the cedar raised up is cut down by the Lord’s axe, then those who belong to the number of the lambs, not of the goats, shall feed in the meadows of the Church and shall say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 20). And what has been made desolate by the Jews, having been turned into abundance, the people of the nations shall consume. This is the tropological interpretation. But, to complete the historical sequence, the same thing is said in other words as what we discussed above: “Strangers devour your land in your presence, and it is desolate and overturned by foreign peoples.”

“Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart rope, who say: Let his work be hastened; let it come quickly, so that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel approach and come, and we shall know it.” We frequently read that sins are called bonds. Among these is the following: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” [Col. 0750C] (Proverbs 5). He does not lament those who have begun to sin and then immediately ceased. For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins; rather, the reference is to those who have drawn out the long cords of sin. That they are called cords of vanity signifies that sin is easily woven for those who commit it, and is so empty and useless that it is woven like spiders’ threads; but when we wish to escape from it, we are entangled in the strongest bonds. Those understand the cart, full and loaded with sins, who remember what is written in Zechariah (Zechariah 5): that wickedness sits upon a talent of lead. These words are addressed to the leaders of the Jews, who above were convicted of greed and luxury, because, challenged to repentance by the Lord [Col. 0750D] and afterward by his apostles, they have persisted in blasphemies, and even to the present day in every synagogue they anathematize the Christian name under the designation “Nazarenes.” The meaning is: Woe to you who think that the day of judgment will not come, or that the captivity foretold by the prophetic word will not come. For you are the ones who say to the prophet: How long will you threaten us with God’s anger? We wish to know whether it is already near and about to come. They speak ironically, since they do not think it will come, but pretend that this word has been fabricated by the prophet.

[Col. 0751A] “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter.” That is, it is the same offense to call good, light, and sweet by contrary names as it is to call evil darkness and bitter by the name of virtues. This is said against those who do not think it a sin if they disparage what is good, and do not consider it a transgression if they praise what is evil. The Jews make good evil, light darkness, and sweet bitter when they accept Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucify Jesus (Matthew 27), who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, in order to save what had perished (Matthew 15). We can also say that all doctrines opposed to the truth are bitter, while the truth alone is sweet. Therefore we must beware lest we follow falsehood instead of truth, or darkness instead of light. [Col. 0751B] For there are many ways that seem right to human beings (Proverbs 14), but their end leads into the depth of hell. And, to say what I think, who can easily avoid this curse, when we often flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty? To this meaning corresponds what Solomon says in Proverbs: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the just are both an abomination before God” (Proverbs 17). The scribes and Pharisees also, refusing to receive the Savior’s words but accepting human traditions and empty fables, made good evil and evil good.

“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight.” That is, who, [Col. 0751C] he says, seem wise to yourselves, who follow not the prudence of God but that of human beings, who do not receive the power of God and the wisdom of God, and who think yourselves wise (1 Corinthians 1).

[Col. 0751D] “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing strong drink.” That is, to those of whom he had said above: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that you burn with wine.” He now speaks this woe also to those who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing strong drink, who, drunk with the wine of the dragon and the incurable poison of asps, slandered the Lord’s virtues and, themselves drunk, intoxicated the peoples, so that, raging with the same madness, they shouted against the Lord. Between wine and strong drink, according to the anagogical interpretation, I think there is this distinction: wine is one disturbance among many—for example, lust, greed, gluttony, and envy. Strong drink, that is, drunkenness, contains within itself all the passions of the vices. We may more correctly call these in Latin perturbations, because they overturn the mind’s condition, make people drunk, and cause them not to know what they are doing. Therefore, whoever has great power ought to be free from vices, and especially from anger, which is the sister of madness, lest, the more powerfully they can act, the more harm they do to their subjects.

“Who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him.” This too is a vice of the vineyard, which produced wild grapes instead of grapes, and, while the Lord expected it to produce judgment, produced iniquity, [Col. 0752A] justifying the wicked for gifts and considering not cases but presents, which blind even the eyes of the wise. Therefore we must beware lest we become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery (Ephesians 5), and the woman of our shame be exposed, lest we flatter the wicked for gifts and despise the righteousness of the righteous because of poverty. This too is commanded in the Epistle of James: that, honoring wicked rich people and despising holy poor people, we should not become judges of iniquity.

“Therefore, just as a tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of the flame consumes, so their root shall become like embers, and their shoot shall rise like dust. For they rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel.” That is, because of the preceding causes—pride, drunkenness, and greed—[Col. 0752B]because instead of grapes they produced thorns, hay, wood, stubble, and burning briars, therefore the root of their wickedness shall be reduced to embers, and every flower of pride and beauty of riches and body shall be compared to dust. They did not merely do these things, but by these steps arrived at blasphemy, so that they did not receive the law of the Lord as the law of the Lord, and blasphemed the words of the Holy One of Israel. Concerning these words we read above: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The root may also be understood as evil thoughts, and the fruit or shoot as evil deeds and words, so that what lies hidden in the root may be shown in the shoot.

“Therefore the fury of the Lord’s anger was kindled against his people, [Col. 0752C] and he stretched out his hand over them and struck them; and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the midst of the streets. In all these things his anger was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out.” Because they rejected the law of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord promises through Jeremiah that he will give, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31). And they blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel, saying (John 8; Matthew 13; Mark 6): “He has a demon,” and “He is a Samaritan.” And: “Is this not the son of the carpenter?” [Col. 0752D] Therefore the fury of the Lord’s anger was kindled against his people, who had previously provoked his anger against the leaders and the powerful, who were wise in their own eyes. God is said to be angry not because he is subject to human disturbance, but because we who sin, unless we hear the Lord as angry, do not fear him. Hence the Apostle also writes that “the goodness and patience of God lead us to repentance” (Romans 2). But, according to our hardness and impenitent heart, we store up anger for ourselves on the day of anger and the revelation of God’s just judgment. What hand it is that is stretched out or raised over the sinful people, Job explains more clearly in chapter 9: “The hand of the Lord has touched me.” Hence the devil, knowing that power is in [Col. 0753A] the Lord’s hand and in his arm, which has been revealed to all the nations, says to the Lord: “Stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, unless he bless you to your face” (Job 2). As for what follows, “and he struck him”—that is, his people—“and the mountains were shaken,” we think this is hyperbolical: because of the magnitude of the evils, even the mountains are shaken, and all the streets of the cities are filled with the corpses of the dead. No one doubts that this happened to the Jews after the Lord’s Passion, under Vespasian and Hadrian. When these things had happened, his anger was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out, thereby showing the posture of one who is angry and striking. It should also be noted throughout all these passages that he does not reproach them for idolatry, nor for the other sins by which they offended the Lord, but because they rejected the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the word of God.

[Col. 0753B] “And he will raise a sign among the nations from afar and whistle for him from the ends of the earth. And behold, he will come quickly and swiftly, and there will be no one failing or growing weary among them. He will not slumber or sleep; his belt around his loins will not be loosened, nor will the strap of his sandal be broken. His arrows are sharp, and all his bows are bent. The hooves of his horses are like flint, and his wheels [Col. 0754A] like the force of a storm. His roar is like a lion’s; he will roar like young lions, growl, seize the prey, and embrace it, and there will be no one to rescue it. On that day he will roar over it like the roaring of the sea. We shall look upon the earth, and behold, darkness of tribulation; the light has been darkened in its gloom.”

He therefore signifies nations situated far away and dwelling at the ends of the earth—without doubt the Romans, and all the peoples of Italy and Gaul, and those who are in Spain, who were subject to Roman power under Vespasian and Hadrian. The divine word thus describes the speed of the army that comes—not by its own will, but by the Lord’s, indeed drawn by him and summoned by his whistle; an army that neither fails nor grows weary on so long a journey, and that, in its eagerness for plunder, does not allow sleep to enter its eyes. Its sandals are not worn out. The passage describes the movement of the archers, the multitude of the cavalry, the squadrons of horsemen, and the violent rush of the wagons and four-horse chariots: it has come like a lion, not so much to fight as to plunder and devour, and the howling of the victorious army is compared with the waves of the sea. From this it should be noted that wherever the roaring of the sea is mentioned in Scripture, this passage demonstrates what it signifies.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0753]

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0753B]

“In the year in which Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting [Col. 0753C] upon a throne, high and raised up.” The Lord appeared to Isaiah upon a high and raised throne, in order to display the posture of a king. For sacred history relates that Uzziah, because he had claimed for himself an unlawful priesthood, was struck with leprosy. After his death, the Lord is seen in the temple that he had polluted. From this we perceive that, while a leprous king reigns, we cannot see God in his majesty, nor know the mysteries of the Holy Trinity. Hence in Exodus, after Pharaoh who oppressed Israel had died, the people—under clay, straw, and bricks—cried out to the Lord, something they could not do while he was alive. Who this Lord is who is seen, we learn more fully in the evangelist John and in the Acts of the Apostles. Among these, John says: “Isaiah said this when he saw his glory, [Col. 0753D] and spoke of him”—with no doubt that he signified Christ. Again, Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, when he speaks to the Jews at Rome, says: “The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive.” The Son was seen in the posture of one who reigns, and the Holy Spirit spoke through the sharing of majesty and the unity of substance. Someone may ask how the prophet now says that he saw the Lord—not simply “the Lord,” but “the Lord Sabaoth”—when the evangelist John said: “No one has ever seen God” [Col. 0754B] (John 1). To this we shall reply: it is not possible to behold with the eyes of the flesh not only the divinity of the Father, but even that of the Son and the Holy Spirit—for there is one nature in the Trinity—[Col. 0754C] but only with the eyes of the mind. Concerning these the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). God’s nature is not perceived, but he is seen by human beings insofar as he himself wills.

“Seraphim stood above it; six wings for one and six wings for the other. With two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried out one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.” Seraphim is interpreted as “burning ones” or “those who consume,” in accordance with what we read elsewhere: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 103), and his ministers a burning fire. The Lord [Col. 0754D] is shown in the seraphim partly and concealed partly. They cover his face and feet because we cannot know either what came before the world or what will come after the world, but contemplate only the middle things, which were made in six days (Genesis 1). Nor is it surprising to believe this about the seraphim, since the apostles also disclose the Savior to believers and conceal him from unbelievers, and there was also a veil before the ark of the Testimony (Exodus 11). They are said to have wings because of their speed in all their movements, or because they always dwell in higher places. For when Scripture says of the winds, “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 103), it does not truly testify, according to the fables of poets and painters, that the winds have wings; rather, it signifies that they are swift in all their movement. [Col. 0755A] Each has six wings because we know only about the making of the world and of the present age. That one cries out to another—or, according to the Hebrews, “this one to that one” (that is, one to one)—means that they exhort one another to the praises of the Lord and say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts,” displaying the mystery of the Trinity in one divinity. They testify that no longer, as before, is the temple of the Jews full of his glory, but the whole earth is full of it—of him who for our salvation deigned to assume a human body (Galatians 4) and descend to the earth. Some Latin writers understand the two seraphim as the Old and New Testaments, since they speak only about the present age. Hence they are said to have six wings, to cover God’s face and feet, to offer their testimony to the truth in rivalry with one another, and to reveal in everything they cry out the mysteries of the Trinity. They marvel at one another that the Lord Sabaoth, though he was in the form of God the Father, [Col. 0755B] took the form of a servant and humbled himself even to death, and the death of the cross (Philippians 2); and that they now know him not only as heavenly, as before, but also as earthly.

“And the lintels of the doorposts were shaken by the voice of the one crying out, and the house was filled with smoke.” When the seraphim were crying out and proclaiming the mystery of the Trinity throughout the whole earth, when the entire earth came to know the Passion of the Lord and Savior, immediately the lintel of the temple was shaken—or removed—and all the doorposts fell into the streets, in fulfillment of the Savior’s threat: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” [Col. 0755C] (Matthew 23). And how beautiful is the order of these words! For after the earth had been filled with the glory of the Lord Sabaoth, the temple of the Jews was filled with the darkness of ignorance, gloom, and smoke, which is harmful to the eyes. Or certainly, the fire of the temple is indicated by the smoke. First the Savior’s Gospel was preached throughout the whole world, and afterward, forty-two years after the Lord’s Passion, Jerusalem was captured and the temple burned.

“And I said: Woe is me, for I was silent, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.” [Col. 0755D] Abraham too (Genesis 13), after he saw the Lord and heard his voice, says that he is earth and ashes. The prophet laments that he was not worthy to praise the Lord Sabaoth together with the seraphim, whom we understand to be angelic powers. He did not dare to praise God because he had unclean lips. His lips were unclean because he lived among a sinful people. Or certainly the passage should be understood in this way: Because I was silent and did not boldly rebuke Uzziah, the impious king, my lips are unclean, and I do not dare to sing the Lord’s praises with the angels, lest it be said to me: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Psalm 49). For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. We say this not to teach that Isaiah was such a person, [Col. 0756A] but because, out of humility, he confesses himself unworthy of God’s praise on account of his unclean lips alone.

“And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said to me: Behold, I have touched this [these]—your lips— and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed.” One of the seraphim—which is interpreted as “the burning one”—flew to cleanse the prophet’s unclean lips and to purify them with the coal or live ember that he had taken from the altar. Many think that there were two seraphim because one cried out to the other, although individual beings, whether among two or among many, can each cry out to another; and the Septuagint version more clearly indicates a multitude, since it translates: “Seraphim stood around him.” If the reference were to two, they would have said not “around him,” but [Col. 0756B] “on either side.” This also agrees well with the multitude of angels prepared for God’s service. Seraphim is used both in the plural and the singular—that is, Seraph—just as Cherubim and Cherub. We understand the altar beneath which the souls of the martyrs are in heaven, as John speaks in the Apocalypse (Revelation 9), to be the Lord’s altar, full of carbuncles—that is, fiery stones or embers that cleanse sins. Hence we read concerning God: “Coals were kindled by him” (Psalm 17). And it is said of God himself that “he is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4). In the Gospel the Savior says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” so that I may baptize “with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Luke 2; Matthew 3). For the fire will test what sort of work each person’s work is. And the one who is to be saved is saved as though he had [Col. 0756C] passed through fire. It should also be noted that to Jeremiah it was said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1), because his lips were not unclean; he had merely said: “I do not know how to speak, because I am young.” The Lord himself stretched out his hand, touched his mouth, and said: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.” But to Isaiah, who had said: “I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips,” the hand of God is not extended; rather, a seraph is sent. The hand is sent both by the Lord and by the Seraph, so that, seeing the member of his own body touched, the prophet would not be frightened by an external agent. Some of our writers think that the tongs by which the coal is grasped signify the two Testaments, which are joined to one another by the union of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0756D] “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here am I; send me.” When “for us” is spoken from God’s person, it must be understood in the sense in which we also read in Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1), so that it may indicate the mystery of the Trinity. For just as in the Gospel we read the Lord saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), we refer “one” to nature and “are” to the diversity of persons; so, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives the command. Therefore the Lord does not say whom he should order to go, but presents the hearers with a choice, so that the will may receive its reward. And the prophet does not promise to go through rashness or the arrogance of his own presumption, [Col. 0757A] but through the confidence of good hope, because his lips have been cleansed, his iniquity removed, and his sin purified.

“And he said: Go and say to this people: Hear with hearing and do not understand; see with sight and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and healed.” At what time this prophecy was fulfilled, the apostle Paul also explains in what follows: “Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the nations; they will listen.” Hence in the same Acts of the Apostles we read that Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews who were unwilling to believe: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first, but since you reject [Col. 0757B] it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13). For thus the Lord commanded us, saying: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49). This is not God’s cruelty, but mercy: that one nation might perish so that all might be saved; that part of the Jews might not see, so that the whole world might see. Hence the Lord himself, in the Gospel, turns the mystery of the man blind from birth who received his sight toward the tropological meaning and says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). And elsewhere Simeon says: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke 2). While they are as though unable to see, we see; while they fall, we [Col. 0757C] rise. Understanding this, the prophet says in a manner through other words: “O Lord, you command me to speak to the Jewish people, so that they may hear and not understand the Savior, and see him and not recognize him. If anyone wishes to fulfill your command and save the whole world—which I too desire to happen—you blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, so that they may not understand, hear, or see. For if they see, are converted, and are healed, the whole world will not receive healing.” From this we perceive that, however grave the sin may be, if someone turns, he can be healed. At the same time, we must understand that because of the magnitude of their crimes they were judged unworthy even of repentance, as the Lord himself says to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children”—understand, [Col. 0757D] as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings—“and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23).

“And I said: ‘How long, O Lord?’ And he said: ‘Until the cities are laid waste without inhabitants, and the houses without human beings, and the land is left desolate; and the Lord removes the people far away, and what had been abandoned is multiplied in the midst of the land, and even then there will be a tenth in it. And again it will be given over to plundering, like a terebinth and like an oak that has cast off its fruit. The holy seed will be what remains in it.’”

When the Lord says, “Go and tell this people that they hear and do not hear, see and do not see,” this is why they neither hear—for they will not understand the Lord’s words—nor recognize his works: because they have grown fat and [Col. 0758A] swollen, and have forgotten their Creator. But the prophet answers and anxiously asks concerning his people: “How long will this sentence remain, so that those who hear do not hear, and those who see do not see?” The Lord answers him: They will neither hear nor see for so long, and will have a blinded heart, until the cities of the Jews are utterly overthrown while Vespasian and Titus are waging war, so completely that not even their former name remains; and the houses, if any survive, are without inhabitants; and the land is reduced to solitude; and the Jewish people are scattered throughout the whole world, whether by flight or captivity; and the Jewish people multiply no longer in Judea as before, but among all the nations. When he says that it is multiplied, the misery of the remnant people will be so great that, in comparison with the former multitude, [Col. 0758B] scarcely a tenth part will remain, while even in that land there will be desolation.

For this passage can be understood in two ways: either that a tenth part remains throughout the whole world, or that in Judea itself scarcely a small portion of the people is preserved. These very remnants will again be given over to plunder when, after approximately fifty years, Hadrian comes and utterly ravages the land of Judea—so completely that it is compared with a terebinth and an oak that have lost their acorns. Finally, after the final devastation, even public laws were posted, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been expelled.

But if someone believes in Christ, and what we read above is fulfilled—“Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah”—then, when, according to the Apostle, the remnant is saved, this will be the holy seed, and from the stock of the apostles all the churches will spring up.

## CHAPTER VII

“And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but they could not defeat it. And they announced to the house of David, saying: ‘Syria has allied itself with Ephraim’; and his heart and the heart of his people were shaken, as the trees of the forests are shaken by the face of the wind.”

We read in the book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles XXVIII; 4 Kings XVI) that Rezin, king of Damascus, after defeating Ahaz, transferred many people from Judea to Damascus; and that Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes—which were called Israel and reigned in Samaria—struck down, in a single day, one hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judah, and led away captive to Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys, and girls, together with immeasurable plunder.

The prophet now says nothing about that battle, but reports a second one: when, having tested their own strength and victory, and enticed by the magnitude of the spoils, they come again against Judah and desire to defeat Jerusalem, but cannot, because the Lord helped it. In this way, under the pretext of mercy by which he was delivering the besieged people, he announced that his Son would be born from a virgin. When the house of David—that is, the royal house—heard that Syria and Ephraim, Rezin and Pekah, were coming with a united army, it was terrified and trembled; king and people alike trembled so greatly that one might think the leaves of trees were being tossed by blasts of wind.

According to the anagoge, the interpretation is straightforward: while the impious king Ahaz reigns, the king of Aram—which is interpreted as “lofty” and “exalted,” indicating the arrogance of worldly wisdom—and Pekah son of Remaliah, who likewise, according to the prophet Hosea, represents the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam son of Nebat had established golden calves at Bethel and Dan and had separated God’s people from the house of David, are referred to heretics, who agree among themselves in order to attack the Church.

When the house of David hears this—the house of David whom we read in Ezekiel (Ezekiel XXXIV) will be raised up as the good shepherd—and his people, believing simply in God, will tremble. They will tremble for this reason: they are compared not with fruit-bearing trees, but with a fruitless forest.

“And the Lord said to Isaiah: ‘Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Jasub, who has been left behind, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field; and you shall say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and do not let your heart be afraid because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, at the fury of the anger of Rezin king of Syria and the son of Remaliah, who say: “Let us go up against Judah, let us rouse it, let us take it for ourselves, and let us set the son of Tabeel as king in its midst.” Thus says the Lord God: “This shall not stand, and it shall not happen; for the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And after another sixty-five years Ephraim will cease to be a people; and the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you will not remain.”’”

Jasub, son of Isaiah, whose name is interpreted as “left behind” and “turning back,” represents the people of Judah, who were to be delivered from the hands of the two kings. He is commanded to go out with his father and meet Ahaz, king of Judah, at the place of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field, where we will later read that, under Hezekiah king of Judah, the Rabshakeh stood.

The two tails of firebrands—that is, of smoking torches—are Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Samaria, that is, of the ten tribes, which were also called Ephraim. Although these two most wicked kings took counsel together to go up against Judah, whose territory is situated in the mountains; to rouse it from its rest, as though it were negligent and sleeping; to subjugate it to their rule; and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, whose name is interpreted as “good God,” whether it signifies a man of that name or an idol, nevertheless the Lord God says: “This plan shall not stand.” For the present, the head city of Syria will be Damascus, and in Damascus itself, the capital, Rezin will rule.

In Ephraim, moreover, because of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who first reigned, the head of Ephraim will be Samaria—that is, the royal house in the city of Samaria—and the head of Samaria will be the son of Remaliah, that is, Pekah. But the kingdom of the ten tribes, that is, of the people of Ephraim, will cease to exist after sixty-five years. This cannot stand unless we examine the matter carefully.

In the fourteenth year of Ahaz son of Jotham, in the tribe of Judah, Uzziah reigned over Samaria, and in the ninth year of his reign he was captured. Ahaz reigned over Judah for sixteen years. After his death, Uzziah was captured in the seventh year of his reign, Samaria was destroyed, and the whole people was transported to the Medes. Thus, if we count the sixteen years of Ahaz and the seven of Uzziah, there are twenty-three years, or at most twenty-four. Where, then, are the sixty-five years in which the kingdom of Israel is said to be brought to an end?

Accordingly, the Hebrews explain this passage as follows: Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, at the same time that Isaiah began his prophetic ministry, first prophesied against Israel, saying: “Israel will surely be led captive from its land.” The title of his prophecy was also directed against Samaria, and he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, two years before the earthquake—which they believe occurred at the time when Uzziah entered the temple of God and claimed the priesthood for himself. The earth was struck, the ashes of the altar were scattered, and the king himself was struck with leprosy.

They hold that this was the twenty-fifth year of King Uzziah, when these things occurred, leaving twenty-seven years of his reign. For Uzziah reigned fifty-two years. After him his son Jotham reigned sixteen years, and Jotham’s son Ahaz reigned another sixteen years. After him Hezekiah reigned, and in the sixth year of his reign Samaria was captured. Thus the total becomes sixty-five years. Although the Lord proclaimed these things through the prophet, King Ahaz and his people did not believe what was to come.

We have spoken of this according to the historical sense. According to the tropological interpretation begun above, however, we must consider that Isaiah is commanded to meet the impious king, and, leaving his own place, to go not to the beginning of the conduit but to the furthest boundaries of the upper pool, which was in the fuller’s field, where dirt and stains were cleansed.

The two tails of smoking torches, as we said earlier, signify worldly wisdom and heretical discourse, whose end is burning. They took counsel in vain to go up against Judah, to seize it as though it were negligent and sleeping, to join it to their errors, and to set over it the son of Tabeel, that is, “good God.” Each adversary believes that truth and sound doctrine are on his own side.

While they say these things, the Lord threatens them that their plan will not stand. Yet, for the time being, so long as this present world remains and the things of the world endure, they will dominate within their own boundaries and cities. But when the time of consummation arrives—that is, the sixty-five years—and both the affairs of the world, which were made in six days (Genesis I), and everything pertaining to the five senses have reached their end, then all things will be dissolved.

“And the Lord continued to speak to Ahaz, saying: ‘Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depth of the underworld or in the height above.’”

“Because,” he says, “you think it difficult that the most powerful kingdoms should come to an end in a short time and that you, together with your people, should be delivered from great danger, ask for yourself a sign—not from the idols by whose error you are held, but from the Lord your God, who promises you assistance. And the sign you choose is yours to request, whether from the depth or from the height. Do you wish,” he says, “that the earth be split and that the underworld—which is said to be in the heart of the earth—be opened by a great chasm? Or that the heavens be opened?” Both alternatives refer typologically to the Lord’s death and ascension: “For he who descended is also the one who ascended” (Ephesians IV).

“And Ahaz said: ‘I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord.’”

Is this response one of humility or of pride, that he does not wish to ask the Lord for any sign? Although it is written in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy VI), “You shall not test the Lord your God,” and although the Savior used this testimony against the devil, nevertheless, when he was commanded to ask, he ought to have fulfilled the command in obedience—especially since Gideon and Manoah (Judges VI) had asked for and received a sign.

Yet, because of the ambiguity of the Hebrew expression, in which it is written “Yloenassem Adonai,” which everyone has translated alike, “I will not test the Lord,” it can also be read as: “I will not exalt the Lord.” For the impious king knew that if he asked for a sign, he would receive it and the Lord would be glorified.

“And he said: ‘Hear, then, O house of David. Is it not enough for you to trouble human beings, that you also trouble my God?’”

Who is the one who said, “Hear, then, O house of David”? It was certainly not God, who had earlier said to Ahaz, “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God,” but the prophet, as is proved by what follows, when he says, “because you also trouble my God.” The meaning is: Since you not only persecute the prophets and despise their deeds, but also resist the judgment of the God who is present and gives commands, so that you impose labor upon him who says elsewhere, “I have labored,” he says, “enduring” (Isaiah I), therefore the Lord will do what follows.

It should also be noted that, because the most impious King Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, the prophetic word turns to the house of David—that is, to the royal tribe—from which we read above: “And they announced this to the house of David, saying…”

“Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and will bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel.”

When it says, “The Lord himself will give you a sign,” the sign must be new and marvelous. But if a young woman or girl, as the Jews maintain, and not a virgin, will give birth, what kind of sign can it be, since this term refers to age and not to virginity?

Indeed, to contend with the Jews on their own ground and not give them cause to laugh at our ignorance through a contentious dispute, a virgin is called in Hebrew *betulah*. But that word is not written in the present passage; instead, *almah* is used. Among them *almah* is an ambiguous word. It means both “young woman” and “hidden” or “concealed”—*apocryphos*. Hence, in the title of the ninth psalm, where the Hebrew has *halinanoi*, the other interpreters translated it as “for youth,” while the Septuagint translated it as “for hidden things.”

In Genesis (Genesis XXIV), we read of Rebecca, where she is called an *almah*; and Aquila translated the word not as “young woman” or “girl,” but as “hidden.” Therefore *almah* means not merely “girl” or “virgin,” but, with emphatic force, “a hidden and secluded virgin,” one who has never been exposed to men’s gaze but has been guarded with great care by her parents.

The Punic language also, which is said to flow from Hebrew sources, properly calls a virgin *almah*. And, as far as my memory serves—for I do not think I have ever read *almah* of a married woman—it refers to one who is a virgin, not merely a virgin but a virgin of younger age, in the years of adolescence. For it is possible for a virgin to be an old woman. This virgin, however, was in the years of girlhood.

Therefore, O house of David, let this child who is born from a virgin now be called by you Emmanuel, that is, “God with us,” because by the facts themselves you will prove, after being delivered from the two hostile kings, that you have God present with you. Later he will be called Jesus, that is, “Savior,” because he will save the whole world; but now, by you, he is called Emmanuel (Matthew I).

“‘He will eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good.’”

Do not suppose that he will be born as a phantom: he will use the foods of infancy, and will eat butter and honey. Although, many ages later, the Evangelist testifies concerning him, saying, “The child grew and advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and with human beings” (Luke II), and although this is said to establish the reality of his human body, nevertheless, while still wrapped in swaddling clothes and nourished with butter and honey, he will possess judgment of good and evil, so that, rejecting evil, he may choose good.

This does not mean that he actually did this, rejecting or choosing, but that he would know how to reject and choose, so that through these words we may understand that the infancy of his human body did not prejudice his divine wisdom. Finally, angels announce him lying in the manger to the shepherds, and magi coming from the East worship him (Luke II; Matthew II)—men who must certainly be believed to have been chosen. Conversely, Herod, the scribes, and the Pharisees are rejected; they slaughtered many thousands of infants because of one child.

“‘For before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land that you detest will be abandoned from before its two kings’”—that is, in the mystery and renewal of the name Emmanuel, the land of Syria and Samaria will be devastated by the Assyrian, and the house of David will be delivered from the two kings whom it fears, namely Rezin and Pekah.

“‘The Lord will bring upon you, upon your people, and upon your father’s house days such as have not come since the days of the separation of Ephraim from Judah, with the king of the Assyrians.’”

For the present, the two kings, Rezin and Pekah, who are besieging and hastening to devastate you, will soon be overthrown. But the time of your devastation will come when the Assyrian arrives—something you had never hoped for, indeed something you had never feared. Through this he teaches the house of David that it is not Syria and Samaria but the Assyrians whom it must fear. Thus he delivers it from its present dread and threatens it concerning the future.

“And it shall come to pass on that day that the Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the farthest reaches of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. And they will come and rest in the ravines of the valleys, in the clefts of the rocks, in all the thickets, and in every opening.”

When the land of the two kings—namely, Damascus and Samaria, which you now detest and fear—has become desolate, then the Lord will bring upon you, O house of Judah, and upon your people days such as you have never before seen: that is, the king of the Assyrians.

Therefore you fear present things in vain—half-burned torches that are merely smoking and possess no real fire. You must know that by his whistle the Lord will summon the flies of Egypt and its rivers, clearly meaning the seven channels of the Nile, and the bee that is in the land of Assyria.

He calls the Egyptians “flies” because of the filth of idolatry and the weakness of the people. He calls the Assyrians “bees” because at that time their kingdom was most powerful and most ready for war, or perhaps because nearly the whole region of Assyria and Persia used arrows.

All these, then, will come and occupy the whole land—in the ravines of the valleys, in the clefts of the rocks, in every thicket, and in the openings and wooded places. These things are said metaphorically, so that, because he had once named flies and bees, he might preserve the metaphor in what follows.

“On that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor—with those who are beyond the river, with the king of the Assyrians—the head, the hair of the feet, and the whole beard.”

They understand the hired razor to be the Syrian himself, whom in Jeremiah (Jeremiah XXV), in vengeance for the sinful people, he even calls his dove. Therefore, with this exceedingly sharp razor, and with those who dwell beyond the river Euphrates—namely, with the king of the Assyrians—the Lord will shave all the hair and bodily growth from head to feet, as well as the beauty of the beard, which is a mark of manhood, from Judea. Nothing strong, nothing beautiful, will remain there; rather, the people will be compared with effeminate men, or even with dishonorable women.

“And it shall come to pass on that day that a man will nourish a cow and two sheep, and from the abundance of milk he will eat butter. For everyone who is left in the midst of the land will eat butter and honey. And it shall come to pass on that day that every place where there were a thousand vines worth a thousand silver pieces will become thorns and briars. With arrows and a bow they will enter there. For briars and thorns will be throughout the whole land, and all the mountains that are tilled with the hoe will not be approached because of the terror of thorns and briars; and it will become pasture for cattle and a place trampled by sheep.”

On that day, then—that is, at that time—when all the wealth of the Jews has been transferred to Chaldea, the desolation of the land of Judah and its devastation will be so great and so unbelievable that they will no longer have herds of cattle or flocks of sheep as they formerly did. Scarcely will a rare inhabitant be able to nourish one cow and two sheep, not for plowing but for food and for clothing from milk and wool.

Because of the scarcity of grain and of everything that the earth produces for food, they will live on milk, butter, and wild honey. When he says that they will eat butter from the abundance of milk, this signifies that the land, because of the scarcity of cultivators, will be more fertile and better suited to pasture.

At that time, because of the small number of people, there will be such a scarcity of wine from the deserted vineyards—which, because of fear of the enemy, will not be pruned—that individual vines will scarcely be bought for individual silver pieces. The whole land will be turned into briars and thorns, and fear will be so great, with swords raging everywhere, that no one will dare visit his field without a bow and arrows.

They will abandon the level country and flee to the mountains; fortified there by the difficulty of the terrain, they will scarcely dig the harsh mountains by hand, since they will have no oxen, plows, or plowshares. Thus, wherever a rare cultivator is found in the mountains, they will sustain their miserable life from that place. The rest of the land will lie open to pasture and, without any inhabitant, will be trampled by wild animals.

## CHAPTER VIII

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Take for yourself a large book and write in it with a man’s stylus: “Hasten quickly: plunder, strip, hurry to despoil.”’ And I took as my faithful witnesses Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Barachiah. And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: ‘Call his name “Hasten, plunder, strip, hurry to despoil,” because before the child knows how to call his mother and his father, the strength of Damascus will be taken away, and the spoils of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians.’”

Again, the virgin birth is described under another figure. The Lord told the prophet not to proclaim openly among the people the mystery of the new birth, but to write it in this great volume that we now read. He is to write it in this great volume which we now read and, what is more marvelous than can be expressed in human words, to comprehend the mysteries of God with the stylus men customarily use.

What is it, then, that is written with a human stylus? Clearly this: that the child who is born will swiftly strip away the spoils and quickly plunder—that is, that he will no longer endure the kingdom of the devil’s domination. He will not send angels or prophets; rather, he himself will descend to save his creatures.

The prophet therefore does what he has been commanded and takes as his faithful witnesses Uriah the priest, who is a teacher of the law, as Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Malachi II), because “he is the angel of the Lord of hosts”; and Zechariah son of Barachiah, who was certainly a prophet.

We read (4 Kings XVI) that, while Ahaz was reigning, a priest presided over the temple of the Lord, and Ahaz commanded him to make an altar like the altar of Damascus. The Book of Chronicles (4 Kings XVIII) also relates that Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, having been instructed in the fear of God.

Isaiah showed himself worthy of the prophetic Holy Spirit and presented himself to the prophetess—that is, to the Holy Spirit, which in Hebrew is called by the feminine gender, *ruha*—according to what is written: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII).

Thus the Lord Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Although human speech cannot explain the mysteries of his birth, Gabriel speaks to the virgin who conceived: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Before God assumed a human body and, according to infancy, called God his Father and Mary his mother, the strength of Damascus was taken away and the spoils of Samaria were carried off by the king of the Assyrians. Thus, while the Lord was not yet born, he saved his people, the house of David, by invocation alone.

Uriah is interpreted as “light of the Lord”; Zechariah as “memory of the Lord”; and Barachiah as “blessing of the Lord.” By these witnesses Christ’s birth is confirmed. For the Lord himself, in the Gospel (Luke XXIV), explained to the two who were going to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and the prophets, that all the Scriptures had prophesied about him.

According to the tropological interpretation, in a virginal soul, unstained by any defilement, the Word of God conceived from the Holy Spirit swiftly strips spoils from the hostile powers and makes all things serve him. Although now he sees in part and prophesies in part, before he can be perfect, and before he can rightly call God his Father and heavenly Jerusalem his mother, while still in infancy he will defeat the strength of Damascus—that is, the teaching of worldly wisdom—and will carry off the spoils of Samaria, with which the heretics have despoiled the Church, saying: “We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse,” while the king of the Assyrians, the devil himself, was present but unable to help them.

Such children were begotten not only by Mary the prophetess, the perpetual virgin, but also by the holy women who gave birth to the patriarchs: Sarah, whose name is interpreted as *arcusa*, that is, “a princess,” and Rebecca, whose name in our language signifies “patience.”

“And the Lord continued to speak to me, saying: ‘Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah, which flow quietly, and has chosen Rezin and the son of Remaliah, therefore, behold, the Lord will bring upon them the strong and abundant waters of the river: the king of the Assyrians and all his glory. He will rise over all its channels and flow over all its banks; he will pass through Judah, overflowing, and, passing through, will reach up to the neck. And the spreading of his wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel.’”

Above, the prophet had said that the strength of Damascus would be taken away and the spoils of Samaria carried off in the presence of the king of the Assyrians, and that the two kings would be captured when the Assyrian fought against them. Now God speaks to the prophet in the customary figurative language of Scripture, comparing the fountain of Shiloah in Jerusalem with the exceedingly violent river of the Assyrians, which will cleanse the entire land of Israel with its waters, enter the banks of its channel, and rush with such force that, after occupying the land of the ten tribes, it will reach Judah and, passing through it, rise as far as the neck. By this he signifies the captivity that was near at hand.

Judah was not captured at that time. Rather, after all the cities of the two tribes had been subjugated, only Jerusalem remained; and it was delivered by the Lord’s incredible mercy. Thus the power of the Assyrian and his innumerable army, which he had described under the image of a flood of waters, he now displays through another metaphor: with his wings—that is, with his commanders and his boundless multitude—he covered the land of Emmanuel, that is, God defended it, so that the Assyrian did not possess it.

We cannot doubt that Shiloah is a fountain at the foot of Mount Zion, whose waters do not bubble continuously but at uncertain hours and days, and which flows through hollow ground and caves of exceedingly hard rock with a great sound—especially since we live in this province. The meaning is this: the people of the ten tribes preferred to be subject to Rezin and the son of Remaliah—that is, to the kings of Damascus and Samaria—rather than to the stock of David, which had begun to reign over it. “I will make him,” says the Lord, “not subject to the kings whom he chose, but serve the Assyrian king.” Since his power occupied the land of Samaria, it is compared with the flooding of a river.

There is also an apostrophe to Emmanuel, that is, to the God who is present: the Assyrian has raised himself so high that he even attempted to possess the land of Emmanuel himself, that is, Judah.

According to the anagoge, every heretic who joins worldly wisdom to his own assistance and wishes to attack Jerusalem—that is, the Church—abandoning the waters of the fountain of Shiloah, whose name means “sent,” and which springs up into eternal life (John IV), will be handed over to the prince of the Assyrians. We will read this meaning more fully later, namely, to whose power he must be handed over, because “the sinner will come into the depths” (Proverbs XVIII).

For his arrogance is so great that he dared to display all the kingdoms of the earth to the Savior and say: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew IV). He will also attempt to enter Judah—that is, the house of confession—and, often through those who are negligent in the Church, he will come up to the neck, desiring to choke those who believe in Christ and to extend his wings, filling the whole region of Emmanuel. But he will not be able to possess it, because Judah has God present with him.

“Gather yourselves together, peoples, and you will be conquered; hear, all you distant lands. Strengthen yourselves, and you will be conquered; gird yourselves, and you will be conquered. Form your plan, and it will be destroyed; speak your word, and it will not come to pass, because God is with us.”

Therefore, O two peoples of Samaria and Syria, recognize that you are weak and powerless and that, with Emmanuel present, you can do nothing against Jerusalem, the city of the Lord. Let not only you who are near know this; let the distant land know it as well.

Although you gather an army, gird yourselves for battle, and the number of those besieging is greater than that of those being besieged, nevertheless I shall say, not once but again: you will be conquered. Whatever plan you form against Jerusalem will be destroyed.

We can also use this testimony against the nations in a time of persecution: although they may appear strong in those who have fallen away, they are defeated in those who shed their blood for Christ. For peace is restored to the churches after the battles, and all their plans against Emmanuel are destroyed, because God is with us.

Those who contradict the truth will also hear this to their advantage, so that they may finally be overcome by reason and may not wish to triumph in falsehood. Whatever they say, no perversity can ever overcome what is right.

[Col. 0767A] “For thus the Lord said to me: ‘As he instructed me with a strong hand, so that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying: “Do not call it conspiracy.” For everything that this people says is conspiracy. And you shall not fear its fear, nor be terrified. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; let him be your fear, and let him be your terror. And he will be for you as a sanctuary, but as a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal to the two houses of Israel, as a snare and a ruin to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
