And many among them will stumble, and they will fall and be crushed, and they will be caught in the snare and taken captive.’”

The Lord spoke these things to me; because of the good works and the grace that I obtained through good works, he instructed me with a strong hand. He taught me not to walk in the way of this people and not to be held by the same error. Or certainly, he caused me to withdraw from the exceedingly wicked way of this people and said to me: Do not fear the conspiracy of the two kings; rather, consider that everything this people says against me is conspiracy.

But you, prophet, and those who are with you, say: Do not fear the people’s ambushes; fear the Lord, and let him himself be your fear. “For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs I).

For believers he will be a sanctuary, but for unbelievers a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal (Luke II)—namely, to the two houses of Judah and Jerusalem, and especially a snare and a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will strike against it and fall and be crushed; entangled in the bonds of their sins, they will be led into captivity.

The Apostle also takes his testimony from this passage: Christ became a stumbling block to the Jews but foolishness to the nations (1 Corinthians I). And again: “Israel, pursuing righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works of the law” (Romans IX). They stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone, a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal. And everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah XXVIII). Therefore those who did not receive Emmanuel, but for whom he became a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, will be crushed and led away captive.

“‘Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples; and I will wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob, and I will await him.’”

This is the voice of the Lord speaking to the prophet. “Because,” he says, “the Lord has become a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal to the two houses of Israel, and they were unwilling to receive Emmanuel sent to them, bind up the testimony of the Old Testament and deliver it to my disciples who have received the Gospel—that is, to the apostles or apostolic men.”

Or certainly, the law and the prophecy continued until John. It is read among them, and among them it has been closed and sealed, so that they do not understand what they read. Because of the ambiguity of the Hebrew expression, we may also interpret “disciples” as “teachings.” Therefore the prophet replies that, when the Gospel succeeded it, the law was closed and sealed among the Jews, and commands that it be assigned not to the Jews but to the nations.

For this reason I will await the Lord Emmanuel, whom you promise is to come, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob—that is, from the Jews, because they were unwilling to receive him.

“Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me as signs and portents for Israel, from the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.” The Lord, he says, commanded me to bind the testimony among the Jews and to deliver and seal his law to his disciples, he who hides his face from the house of Jacob; therefore I shall await him and look for my Lord. And not I alone, but also my children whom the Lord has given me—namely, the other prophets, the sons of the prophets: “who were born not of the will of flesh and blood, but of God.” Concerning them the Apostle also spoke: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (John I; Gal. IV).

These children, that is, the prophets, were given as signs and portents to Israel, according to what we read in Ezekiel: “And Ezekiel shall be a sign” (Ezek. XXIV). In Zechariah also holy men and disciples of the prophets are called men of portents and signs, because the prophets have always gone before as signs of things to come. This is so according to the literal sense for the present. Moreover, the blessed Apostle, in the Epistle written to the Hebrews, teaches—although Latin usage does not receive this testimony among the canonical Scriptures—that it must be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord and Savior: “Behold, I and my children whom the Lord God has given me.” Since, therefore, the children shared in blood and flesh (Heb. II), he himself likewise became a participant in the same sufferings.

But how these children were a sign and portent to the wisdom of the world and the pride of the Jews, the same Apostle teaches: he says that the Lord chose the foolish things of the world and the weak things, in order to confound the wise and the strong (I Cor. I). Hence the Savior also said to the Apostles: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” The preacher of the new Gospel becomes a child when he lays aside the old man, who is corrupted by the desires of deception, and puts on the new man, who is renewed from day to day according to the knowledge of the image of the Creator (Eph. IV). That the Lord of hosts dwells on Mount Zion, the same Apostle writes: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. XII).

[Col. 0768B]

“And when they say to you: ‘Seek answers from the ventriloquists and diviners who hiss in their incantations: Surely a people does not seek from its God on behalf of the living and the dead? To the law rather and to the testimony.’ And if they speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them, and it will pass through it; and he will fall and hunger. And when he has hungered, he will grow angry and curse his king and his God. And he will look upward, and he will gaze upon the earth, and behold: tribulation and darkness, dissolution, distress, and pursuing gloom; and he will not be able to fly away from his distress.”

This must be said in the person of Christ: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me.” He himself also speaks these words to the Apostles and to believers from the Gentiles who received his Gospel. “If,” he says, “your fathers whom you have left behind tell you: ‘Seek ventriloquists’”—by whom we understand the *python* spirits, for in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 0769A] [Acts XVI] we read also of a servant girl who brought her masters great profit—“and those who speak from the earth,” who promise through magical invocation to perform the evocation of souls, as well as the other kinds of the arts of sorceresses, you must know that every nation consults its own gods and asks the dead about the safety of the living. But to you the Lord has given the law as an aid, so that you may say: “There is no such divination among the Gentiles, whose worshippers they deceive with hope, as there is in our case, which is proclaimed without any payment from the law.”

A very severe famine will come upon the unbelieving: not a famine of bread or thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God (Amos VIII). And when you hunger, you will grieve and curse your ruler and the traditions of your fathers—that is, the devil and ancient errors. He speaks this [Col. 0769B] to those who have suffered hunger for the truth and will look up toward heaven and down upon the earth. They will be in distress, in darkness, and in tribulation, so that they will not see for a time, until they too turn to God.

## CHAPTER IX

“At the earlier time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was relieved, but at the last time the way of the sea was burdened, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. For those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has risen.”

At the beginning it is said to have been praised because it was relieved of the burden of sins, since the Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of the two tribes. Hence it is also said in the sixty-first Psalm [Col. 0769C]: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel.” There is Benjamin, the younger—that is, Paul, in an ecstasy of mind—who elsewhere also said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (II Cor. V). The prince of Zebulun and the prince of Naphtali are their leaders. There were villages in these tribes from which our Apostles came as leaders; according to Symmachus, they believed by hearing swiftly from the Lord: “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. IV). They immediately left both their father and their little boat.

But at the end the faith of the Jews was burdened, while many remained in error. Here he calls the sea the lake of Gennesaret, which is formed by the Jordan flowing through it; on its shore lie Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin. The Lord dwelt especially in this region, so that the people who sat or walked in darkness might see the light—not a small light like that of the other prophets, but a great one, like that of the one who is read in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII). And for those who dwelt in the region and shadow of death, light arose.

I think this is the distinction between death and the shadow of death: death belongs to those who went down to the underworld with the works of death. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). The shadow of death, however, belongs to those who sin but have not yet departed from this life; for, if they wish, they can do penance. Although the holy Apostles rejoiced at the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, they were nevertheless deeply concerned for the Israelite people [Col. 0770A], who had held the Lord’s preaching in contempt, since they themselves had sprung from that people’s lineage, as the outstanding teacher says: “For I myself could wish to be accursed for my brethren, who are Israelites” (Rom. IX).

“They will rejoice before you.” The prophet addresses the Apostles of Christ directly, saying: O Lord Jesus, your Apostles will rejoice before you, “as harvesters rejoice in the crop.” He calls the Gentiles the harvest and the peoples the harvesters, just as the Lord himself says in one place: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX; Luke XVI), and so forth.

“As victors rejoice, dividing the spoils.” *Spolia* is plural; in the singular one says either *this spoil* or *that spoil*. He calls the Apostles victors because they conquered the temptations of the flesh and the devil himself. [Col. 0770B] The spoils are the human beings who had been held captive by him. He therefore calls the Apostles victors because they took their spoils away from the devil—that is, the human race which he had taken captive—and restored it to God.

“The yoke and the rod,” of the devil—that is, domination and power. “And the scepter,” that is, the rule which he held throughout the whole world: “You have overcome it,” O Lord Emmanuel. This is an address to Christ concerning the exactor, that is, the one who exacts. Properly speaking, an exactor is one who demands or compels peoples to pay royal taxes. The devil was an exactor, compelling the whole world to do his will.

“As on the day of Midian.” We read in the Book of Judges that at the time of harvest and vintage the Midianites came into the land of promise, gathered the fruits of the earth, and returned. But when they had done this frequently, an angel of the Lord was sent to Gideon, saying (Judg. VI): “Hail, most valiant of men.” And he replied: “Where are,” he said, “the signs and wonders which the Lord showed to our fathers when they came out of Egypt with a strong hand?” And the angel said: “Go in this strength, and with three hundred men you will deliver Israel.” And he did so.

Choosing three hundred men from Israel, he commanded each one, as the history relates, to hold in one hand a jar with a light inside and in the other a trumpet. When they sounded the trumpets and held up the lights after breaking the jars, the army of the Midianites was thrown into confusion, and they killed one another. On that day the Jews gained the victory without the shedding of their own blood. Thus the prophet says: Just as that victory occurred without blood being shed from the people of Israel [Col. 0770D], so Almighty God gave victory to his chosen ones, conquering the devil and thrusting him into hell—or, alternatively, conquering the multitude of peoples engaged in battle.

“For every violent plunder with tumult.” He speaks about the devil himself. The sense is: The spoils—that is, the human race which the devil had plundered—when Jesus, its Savior, comes, he will take away from him by force and violence. He will cast him, or shut him up, amid tumult—that is, with a great crash—in hell, as the Psalmist says (Ps. IX) both of the reprobate and of the devil: “Their memory has perished with a crash.”

“And the garment mixed with blood.” What is meant by the garment except the devil, who was full of the blood of human beings, committing many murders throughout the world? We may also understand by the garment all murderers, with whom the devil was surrounded as though by a garment, and whose hands were full of blood. When he says, “It shall be for burning, and fuel for fire,” this means that the devil, together with his imitators and followers, has been handed over to eternal fire as fuel, just as wood is given to the hearth.

“For a child is born to us.” This is the child Emmanuel, who was born of a virgin and dwelt among us. According to his humanity he appeared small, but according to his divinity he is above all. “And his rule has come to be,” that is, the rule of the child, “upon his shoulder.” He carried his rule upon his shoulder because he himself carried the cross of his passion when he was led away to be crucified. For this reason, as he himself said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (John XIX). And, “For this reason God exalted him” (Matt. XXVIII)—that is, because of that punishment—“and gave him the name which is above every name,” and so forth.

“And he shall be called Wonderful,” and so on. These words must be divided as follows. He is “Wonderful” because he is God and man. He is “Counselor” because without him there is no good counsel, as the angel says of him: “He will be the angel of great counsel” (Luke I). He is “God” because he made all things. He is “Mighty” because no one can be strong without his help. He is “Father of the age to come” because he himself will remain without end. He is “Prince of peace” because he has reconciled us with the angels and restored us to God the Father.

“His dominion shall be multiplied.” How will it be multiplied? Because throughout the whole world his name has been made known through the preaching of the Apostles, and every day the name of Christianity increases. “He shall sit upon the throne of David,” that is, among the Jewish people, or also in the hearts of those who are gentle, meek, and humble like David. “From now on,” that is, for ages of ages.

“The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this.” Zeal is hatred and envy. But zeal also means love and affection, and this is the sense here. The zeal—that is, the love—with which the Lord has loved his people, namely the whole human race, will do this: it will send his Son and free the human race from the jaws of the devil.

“The Lord sent a word into Jacob.” The prophet speaks. Here he calls the tribe of Judah Jacob, and the remaining tribes Israel. What was this word? According to the literal sense, the Lord sent a word into Jacob because it pleased him and he decreed that kings should always be chosen from the tribe of Judah over all Israel, from the time when David, the most gentle king, began to reign.

“But it fell upon Israel,” that is, upon the ten tribes, because they destroyed that ordinance when they cast off the house of David and chose Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim as their king. From him they were afterward generally called Ephraim (III Kings XII).

Or otherwise: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob,” that is, evangelical teaching into the Apostles and holy preachers, “and it fell,” that is, the preaching of the holy Gospel was violated by heretics.

Or otherwise: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob,” that is, into the Jewish people, “but it fell upon Israel,” that is, upon the Gentile people. This is the word of which the outstanding Evangelist John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I). When was this Word sent into the people of Jacob? When he assumed flesh from a virgin. Then it came to the Gentiles, when the Jews refused to receive the preaching of the Lord and of the Apostles and the Lord said to the Apostles: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI), and so forth.

“And all the people of Ephraim shall know.” He calls the ten tribes Ephraim. They were exceedingly proud because they were much more numerous than Judah and Benjamin. Indeed, this was so, since in comparison with ten, two is a small number. Or they also boasted because Rezin and the Syrians had joined themselves to them. And what will Ephraim know? He will know that Rezin and the Syrians, who had been joined to him, will eventually withdraw from him and fight against him, as he makes clear in what follows. What were those ten tribes saying against Judah and Benjamin?

“The bricks have fallen,” and so forth. What is signified by the bricks is signified by the sycamores: namely, fragile and weak men. What is signified by squared stones is signified by cedars: exceedingly strong and warlike men. The sycamore is a fruitless and foolish tree, which they call the wild fig. The cedar is imperishable wood.

We said above that Rezin and the ten tribes said: “Let us go up against Judah, tear it away to ourselves, and set the son of Tabeel in its midst” (Isa. [Col. 0772C] VII). And, rising up in pride, they spoke contemptuously of Judah and Benjamin: “The bricks have fallen,” that is, the weak and feeble have fallen from Judah into the hands of the enemies. But when we have brought those two tribes under our power, “we shall build” for you from “squared stones” a house—that is, we shall establish for you a rule and dominion consisting of the strongest and most warlike princes and fighters.

And they added: “The sycamores have been cut down,” that is, the enemies who fought against them have killed the fragile and powerless men from those two tribes. But when we have subjected those who remain, in place of those weak men we shall replace them from among ourselves with cedars—that is, with the strongest princes. Just as the cedar, whose wood is imperishable, never gives way, and just as a squared stone always stands on whatever side it is inclined, so they too will remain firmly stable amid every adversity.

That he does not mention the enemies who cut down those two tribes—that is, killed them—and into whose hands they fell, refers to the time when the Philistines, or Rezin and the Syrians, fought against them and killed many thousands of them.

“And the Lord will raise up the enemies of Rezin against him.” The prophet speaks against Rezin and the Syrians. “He will raise up,” that is, bring, the enemies of Rezin—namely Sennacherib—against him, that is, against Rezin, “and he will turn his Assyrian enemies into tumult,” that is, into battle against him. And why? Because he had made war against Judah.

“The Syrians from the east.” The prophet speaks to the ten tribes. This is what he said above: “All Ephraim shall know.” What will it know? That the Lord will bring Syria from the east, although previously it had been allied with Ephraim, “and the Philistines from the west,” because the Israelites were from the eastern region, while the Syrians and Philistines were from the west. When did this happen? When Sennacherib captured the Syrians and Philistines and came with them together against the ten tribes.

“To the one striking him,” that is, God. “Bending.” To bend is to turn something straight toward another side. “And perverting.” Some manuscripts read “restraining,” but this is written falsely. He says “perverting” because that people perverted and corrupted the law of God and the path of their steps.

[Col. 0773B]

“And those who bless this people will be thrown down, and the people who are blessed will be thrown down.” The thorns—that is, all their evils—will be consumed upon them.

“A man will not spare his brother.” This was fulfilled at the time when they were besieged by the Romans, for then brother killed brother.

“And he will turn to the right,” that is, away from justice, “and he will hunger”—for evil. “And he will eat on the left,” that is, wickedness will grow fat, “and it will not be enough for him.” Manasseh and Ephraim will fight together against Judah. Manasseh and Ephraim were hostile to one another, yet they were united in making war against Judah.

## CHAPTER X

“Woe to those who enact unjust laws.” The prophet speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, who placed their traditions above the law of God (Matt. XV; Mark VII).

“What will you do on the day of your visitation?” The prophet grieves over the wickedness of his people. Here “visitation” is used in a negative sense; he calls visitation the punishment and vengeance which God exacted from them, either under Sennacherib or also under the Romans.

“Woe to Assyria.” God speaks to Sennacherib and his people: “Woe,” that is, the ruin of destruction threatens you. Why does God threaten Sennacherib? Although he permitted him to wage war against the ten tribes, he did not command him to crush them utterly, but only to scourge and trample them like the mud of the streets. But he, lifted up in pride, thought that he did this by his own strength and power. He not only led those ten tribes into captivity but also destroyed a very great multitude of them. He calls him the rod and the staff because through him he struck and scourged the twelve tribes.

“Are not my princes kings?” Sennacherib says this because when he came against the ten tribes, he brought with him many kings whom he had already subjected.

“Are not Chalamno, Arphad, and Emath under my power just as Carchemish is?” The prophet speaks in the person of Sennacherib, for he gloried in this way. Carchemish and the other cities he enumerated were cities of the nations [Col. 0774A], which he had already captured.

“Is not Samaria under my dominion just as Damascus is?” Damascus is a metropolitan and royal city, founded by Abraham’s servant Eliezer, over which Rezin reigned.

“How has my hand found” —that is, my power—“the kingdoms of idols?” Sennacherib speaks, marveling at his own power. This should not be read affirmatively but as an exclamation and question. What follows requires an understood continuation. The sense is: Just as the idols and kingdoms I mentioned above have been reduced under my dominion, so the idols of Samaria and Jerusalem are mine as well.

He nearly fulfilled his boast. For he plundered all the cities of the ten tribes, Benjamin, and Judah, except Jerusalem. From Jerusalem also he captured the lower part, which Shebna the scribe handed over to him (IV Kings XVIII). [Col. 0774B]

“Will I not do to Jerusalem as I did to Samaria?” The Lord did not permit him to do this to Jerusalem because of Hezekiah.

“And it shall be, when the Lord has completed all his works.” The prophet speaks. “I shall visit,” that is, I shall avenge and vindicate myself against him, “upon the fruit,” that is, upon his works.

“He removed the boundaries of the peoples.” Sennacherib captured many kingdoms and enclosed them under one boundary, that is, under one power.

“My hand found it as a nest.” Just as a nest is destroyed when the fledglings withdraw from it by the one who finds it, so he destroyed all the kingdoms. He speaks metaphorically and says:

“And as eggs left behind by birds are gathered.” He maintains the metaphor. Just as he means kingdoms by the nest, so by the eggs we may understand the inhabitants of the kingdoms. Some manuscripts read “grapes,” but this is written falsely. Since he first spoke of a nest, he then speaks of eggs. These are Sennacherib’s words.

“And there was none who moved a wing,” that is, who dared to raise a hand against me, “or chirped.” Chirping properly belongs to birds, but he uses it for muttering.

“Will the axe boast?” The prophet speaks about Sennacherib. The sense is this: Sennacherib did not attribute the vengeance he inflicted upon the ten tribes to God’s will, but to his own strength. The prophet says to him [Col. 0774D]: If an axe, a saw, a rod, or even a staff of wood were to rise up in pride and say, “What we do, we accomplish by our own strength and skill,” this is what Sennacherib was saying.

Just as the things mentioned above cannot work or accomplish anything by themselves unless someone works through them, so Sennacherib would not have accomplished what he did unless the Lord had permitted it because of the sins of the people.

“Therefore the Lord will send leanness upon his fat ones.” By the fat ones we must understand the commanders, princes, and powerful warriors whom the Lord weakened when he sent his angel—as we shall see below—who killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them (IV Kings XIX).

[Col. 0775A]

“And beneath his glory, kindled, it shall burn like the burning of fire.” Blessed Jerome says somewhere that when his army was killed, all the bodies were consumed by heavenly fire, while the garments remained unharmed. The Jews came and took the edges of the clothing and shook off the dust of the bodies, which had been reduced to dust. Therefore he says: “His glory, kindled, shall burn like the burning of fire”; and, kindled, it shall burn beneath—that is, beneath the garments. He calls the multitude of the army its glory, because the multitude of a people is the glory of a king (Prov. XIV).

“And the light of Israel shall be in the fire.” He calls the angel who set them alight the light. “And his Holy One in the flame.” The light and the Holy One are one: he was in the fire and flame for the Assyrians, all of whom he burned with fire. He calls the angel “Israel’s light” because an angel is appointed by God as an emissary to each nation. The Hebrews say that it was the archangel Michael who had been entrusted with that Israelite nation, as we read in Daniel.

“His thorn shall be devoured,” that is, his glory and riches, “and the brambles also shall be consumed,” that is, iniquities and sins shall seize him.

“On one day: the glory of his forest and of his Carmel.” He calls the multitude of peoples glory. Carmel is a great mountain containing a multitude of trees. The sense is: Your army, which is so great, like the trees in the forests and on Mount Carmel, will perish in body and soul.

“And he shall flee in terror.” When Sennacherib rose in the morning and saw his entire army burned with fire [Col. 0775C], terrified by fear, he fled to his own land. When he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons killed him (IV Kings XIX).

“And a child shall write them down,” that is, those whom previously he had brought in such a multitude as the sand on the seashore and the trees in a very great forest will be countable by a little child. And this happened. For of that entire multitude only ten men remained, who escaped in flight together with him.

“And it shall be on that day.” Understand “day” as “time.” “The remnant of Israel shall not continue.” He calls the remnant of Israel those who remained from the two tribes and were not captured by Sennacherib. He had captured all the fortified cities of Judah and Benjamin and also the lower part of Jerusalem, which Shebna the scribe handed over through fear.

When he says, “who have fled from Jacob,” he refers to the fact that when all the cities of Judah were being devastated, everyone who could find refuge in flight fled to Hezekiah in Jerusalem. And when he says, “he shall not continue to rely,” that is, to place confidence, “upon the one who strikes them,” it must be understood as follows (IV Kings XVI, XVIII):

At the time when Pekah and Rezin wished to come—that is, to wage war against the two tribes—the king of the two tribes, Ahaz, sent to the king of Egypt to rescue him from the hands of the two kings, saying: “I am your servant; only come and remove from my neck the yoke of Pekah and Rezin.” But he did not rescue them; the Lord did so because of his servant David.

When Ahaz died and his son Hezekiah took up the reins of the kingdom, he broke all the idols that were in Jerusalem and recalled the people of God, whom his father had turned to the worship of the nations, to the worship of God. For that faithless Ahaz had set up idols of various kinds in every corner of the streets, upon the houses, in the groves and sacred places; his son Hezekiah broke them all into pieces and reduced them to dust.

When Sennacherib heard this, inflamed by the spirit of wickedness, after he had plundered the Syrians, the Philistines, and the ten tribes and had led them captive under the burden of plunder, he came from Egypt with an innumerable multitude, directing his route straight toward Jerusalem. He had already ravaged the cities of Judah a second time, except Jerusalem. [Col. 0776B]

Therefore the prophetic word is directed to the two tribes, who had previously placed their hope in the Egyptians and Assyrians, who often struck them, so that they should no longer rely upon them but place their hope in the Lord God of Israel. “In truth,” not falsely or with a divided heart, “the remnant” that remained and that the Lord of hosts delivered.

“They shall turn to him. For if your people Israel should be.” This pertains to the coming of Christ. The prophet speaks: O house of Israel, although such a great multitude is in your midst, like the sand of the sea, nevertheless, in comparison with them, whatever remains in hardness of heart will, when Christ comes in the flesh, turn from among them to him like a remnant (Rom. IX, XI). [Col. 0776C]

What was this remnant? The Apostles and the others among the Jews who believed before the Lord’s ascension. And those of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When Peter preached, three thousand believed in one day, and five thousand on the next” (Acts II, IV).

“Consummation,” that is, perfection or completion, “will overflow,” that is, will cause “righteousness” to overflow. These words concern the coming of the Lord. How was the completion abbreviated? Because all the things that had been foretold about the Lord in the law and the prophets over long preceding ages, he himself fulfilled in a short time, namely in three and a half years.

And how did he make righteousness overflow, that is, abound? Because the preaching of the Apostles went out into all the earth, and their words reached to the ends of the earth (Ps. XVIII). What was this righteousness? The human race, which the devil possessed through deception, he himself freed from the bond of death through the triumph of his passion.

“Consummation,” that is, perfection or completion, “and abbreviation the Lord will make in the midst of the earth,” as we have already said.

Or, to put it more briefly, the Lord made an abbreviation when in three days he completed everything that had been foretold about his passion, resurrection, and the liberation of the human race (Luke XXIV). He says “in the midst of the earth” because Jerusalem, where this saving mystery was accomplished, is said to be the navel of the earth (Ezek. XVI).

Or he made an abbreviation when he slew the entire innumerable multitude of the Assyrians in one night [Col. 0777A], except for ten men. These are God’s words through the prophet.

“Therefore the Lord says,” so that Hezekiah and his people may not fear Assyria, that is, Sennacherib and his people: he himself will strike them in a short time and in an instant. And although he strikes them with the rod—that is, through the plundering of their cities—nevertheless he will in no way prevail in destroying them utterly, because I shall deliver the city of Jerusalem from his hand for the sake of David my servant and Hezekiah my servant (IV Kings XIX).

But when he says, “He will raise his staff against you on the road to Egypt,” this is to be understood as follows: After Sennacherib had plundered the ten tribes, he returned through the cities of Judah and Benjamin that were on the road to Egypt, and he overturned them all. Or “his staff,” that is, his sword, he will raise against them on the road to Egypt, because after he had once captured all the cities of the two tribes, and even part of the city of Jerusalem had been handed over into the hands of the commander of his army, the Rabshakeh, by Shebna the scribe—as we have already said above—and he had returned toward Egypt, when he came back again to capture Jerusalem, he overturned all their remaining cities that lay along the road from Egypt to Jerusalem.

“A little while longer.” After a long period, once these things had been foretold, they were fulfilled. But all ages, compared with God’s eternity, will be considered brief. For everything that is yet to happen already appears to have happened in God’s presence.

[Col. 0777C]

God’s words to Sennacherib and his people: “And my anger shall be completed against their crime,” that is, against the Egyptians, the Assyrians, and Sennacherib.

“And he will raise up against him”—that is, against Sennacherib—“a scourge,” that is, vengeance, “according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb.” The prophet speaks against Sennacherib. We have already explained above how the Midianites were killed without the shedding of the blood of the children of Israel (Judg. VI, VII). Therefore he compares the killing of the Midianites with the slaughter of the Assyrians. Just as the former were killed without the shedding of the blood of the Jewish people, so were the latter.

“And his rod over the sea”—understand: he will raise it. By the rod understand strength. The sense is: Before he comes against you, he will go against Tharaca, king of Ethiopia, cross the Red Sea, and raise that same rod over Egypt. Then he will return with a large army, coming against Jerusalem.

“And it shall be on that day.” Understand “day” as “time.” God speaks to the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. On what day or at what time was the dominion of Sennacherib removed from the necks of the two tribes? When his army was killed by the angel.

“And it shall rot,” that is, fail, “the yoke”—that is, dominion and servitude—“from your shoulder,” O people of the two tribes, “before the face of oil,” that is, before the presence of God’s mercy. For mercy is signified by oil.

“He shall come to Aiath.” The prophet speaks. This is a description of the roads and places by which Sennacherib came from Egypt as far as Nob, where his people also perished, as we shall see below. O my people, Sennacherib will come from Egypt to Aiath and will not pitch his tents there, “but will pass through Magron and entrust his vessels in the great city,” together with his provisions, that is, his baggage.

“They passed through swiftly.” The prophet speaks of the future as though of the past: the peoples who came with Sennacherib passed swiftly, and they passed through the Jewish cities we have enumerated. Or, after quickly passing through the great city where they had entrusted their baggage, they came to Gabaah. When they arrived there, they said: “Gabaah shall be our lodging.” For he had a lodging there, as blessed Jerome says. And the neighboring city of Rama was terrified.

Some wish to distinguish the passage so that it reads: “They passed through the lodging of Gabaah quickly,” taking “lodging” as plural, and then joining it to “our Rama was astonished.” But this is not so. Blessed Jerome says that when they had swiftly passed through the great cities, entrusted their provisions there, and reached Gabaah, they had a lodging there, as we have already said.

When Gabaath of Saul heard this, it fled. One is Gabaa and another Gabaath. Gabaa is a Hebrew name, and therefore whether we say *Gabaae* or *Gabaa* makes no difference, since it retains the property of another language. Gabaath, however, is called Saul’s because it was once the royal seat of Saul, the Lord’s chosen one.

[Col. 0778C]

“Raise it with your voice, O Hinni [reading uncertain].” The prophet speaks. Gallim, Laish, and Anathoth were Israelite cities through which they passed.

“Medemena has moved.” From its place to another. Medemena and Jabin are cities of Judah.

“There is still a day for one to stand in Nob”—that is, for Sennacherib to dwell there. Nob is a city of the land of promise, from which came Gesbi, one of David’s thirty commanders, as we read in the Book of Chronicles (I Chron. XXVII). It is not far from Jerusalem. Why does he say, “There is still a day for him to stand in Nob”? Because when Sennacherib reached that place, only a small part of the day remained.

“Therefore he will shake his hand,” that is, move it, [Col. 0778D] threatening Jerusalem with many evils. He does this “against Mount Zion and the hill of Jerusalem,” because Zion is a mountain and Jerusalem is situated around the hill—that is, around the valley of that mountain. When Sennacherib departed from Egypt, he hastened his steps as quickly as he could, directing his route toward Jerusalem, as has been said above.

When he came to Nob, he pitched his tent there, intending to seize Jerusalem at dawn. After he arrived, he did not cease until midnight from threatening the desolation of Jerusalem, saying: “Will this one city alone be able to be rescued from my hand? It will not be so; but as I did to Samaria and its king, so I shall do to Jerusalem and its king Hezekiah.”

But after they went to sleep, they were all struck down by the angel of the Lord.

“Behold, the Lord Ruler will shatter the little flask in terror.” The prophet’s voice concerns the Lord’s Passion. *Laguncula* (“little flask”) is a diminutive formed from *lagena* (“flask”). The little flask, being made of clay, signifies the Lord’s body, which was broken at the time of the Passion. He says “in terror” because the tombs were opened, a great earthquake occurred, and the other events that were manifested in his Passion took place. “The lofty ones were cut down,” that is, the Jews were humbled, cut off from their native soil, and cast out.

“And the thickets will be overturned,” that is, the dense growth of the “forests” by the sword. He calls Jerusalem a forest because of the multitude of peoples who were cut down by the sword of the Romans. [Col. 0779B] “And Lebanon will fall with its lofty trees,” that is, Jerusalem with its priests and rulers. By Lebanon we should understand either the Temple or the city, as it is said through the prophet: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars.”

## CHAPTER XI

“A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse.” The prophet’s voice concerns the Lord’s birth. The prophets do not preserve the order of the history. Above, he spoke of the Lord’s Passion; now he speaks of his birth. The shoot went forth from the root of Jesse because the Virgin Mary arose from David’s lineage. “A flower will rise from his root,” that is, Christ was born from the seed of Jesse, the father of David: the flower of virtues, the crown of angels, [Col. 0779C] and also the garland of the elect among humanity.

“And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him,” that is, upon Christ. This was fulfilled when he was baptized by John in the Jordan. The Holy Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father was heard (Luke 3). Nevertheless, this should not be understood to mean that the Holy Spirit began to dwell in the Lord Jesus Christ only from that time. According to his divinity, he possessed the same Holy Spirit equally with the Father before all ages. Rather, just as from the time of his conception, according to his humanity, such grace was bestowed upon him—the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ—that he was true God and true man, so also, insofar as he was man, the Holy Spirit rested upon him when, through the operation of that same Holy Spirit, he assumed in the Virgin’s womb the flesh of our frailty (Luke 1). [Col. 0779D]

These seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are enumerated here, rest in Christ, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians 1 and 2).

“He will not judge according to the sight of his eyes.” That is, he will not show partiality toward a person, because it is written of him: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

“He will rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth.” The Lord rebuked those who reproved the humble when his disciples, walking through the grainfields, plucked the ears of grain, rubbed them in their hands, [Col. 0780A] and ate them (Matthew 12; Mark 8; Luke 6). For when certain people saw this, they reproved the apostles. But what did the Lord do? He refuted the apostles’ opponents and said to them: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matthew 4; Hosea 6).

“And he will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth.” He puts “earth” for the inhabitants of the earth, and “rod” for evangelical doctrine. When did he strike them with the rod, that is, with evangelical doctrine? When, through the preaching of the chief of the apostles, Peter, after the Lord’s ascension, three thousand believed in one day, five thousand on the next day, and thereafter many thousands. Those who had believed after hearing his preaching said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” And Peter said to them: “Repent and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out.” [Col. 0780B] Likewise, through the preaching of the apostles, he struck the hearts of the peoples when, abandoning their own wills, they were baptized in the name of Jesus.

The rod may also be understood as the sentence of divine judgment. When the Lord came in the flesh, he first began to preach repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4). Afterwards he added: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7). By this sentence of the coming Judge, the hearts of earthly people, abandoning their former vices, began to stream toward his baptism. The disciples of John, envying Christ, said to their teacher: “Rabbi, look, more people are coming to Jesus, whom you baptized, than to you” (John 3). [Col. 0780C]

“And with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.” That is, the Antichrist, as the distinguished preacher says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2). And although he will be struck down by Michael, as some say, nevertheless this will be accomplished at the Lord’s command.

“And righteousness will be the belt of his loins.” Who has ever seen a belt made of righteousness, or a girdle made of faith? By righteousness and faith we should understand the saints, who, by working good through faith and righteousness, cling to the Lord like garments. Hence Isaiah, speaking elsewhere of the Son in the person of the Father, says: “As I live, you will clothe yourself with all these as with a garment.”

“The wolf will dwell with the lamb.” According to the historical sense, this lacks meaning. Allegorically, however, by the wolf we can understand a fierce and faithless person, while the lamb is compared to one who is humble, gentle, and faithful. Thus the wolf dwelt with the lamb after the Lord’s coming: Paul, the cruel persecutor, with the gentle Ananias, or with Peter. The same interpretation should be applied to many who came from the hardness of unbelief to faith in the Lord. [Col. 0780D]

The leopard signifies a person stained by many crimes and errors, yet enjoying the honors of this age.

The kid is compared to a humble sinner. “Thus the leopard dwelt with the kid,” that is, the proud sinner will remain with the humble sinner within the holy Church, not despising him, even though he abounds in earthly riches, because he will be ashamed of his own evils. The kid [Col. 0781A] is not compared with the gentle because it is among those on the left, but because it mortifies itself for the Lord (Colossians 3). By the calf and the sheep, likewise, we should understand the humble and innocent, who mortify themselves with their vices and desires. By the lion we can understand some ruler of this age who dwells in the Church together with the innocent. The same should be understood of the calf and the bear.

“The lion will eat straw like an ox.” By the lion, a king or, as was said, some ruler is understood; by the ox, any simple person. Thus the lion eats straw like an ox, that is, a simple understanding, because the rulers of this age are content with the literal surface and historical sense, as are ordinary people.

“And the infant will take delight.” Here we can understand the Lord Jesus Christ as an infant, on account of his innocence; or Peter, or the other apostles and the most illustrious saints, who were children in malice but mature in understanding (1 Corinthians 14). To them the Lord gave power to cast demons out of possessed bodies (Matthew 10; Mark 6; Luke 9 and 10). [Col. 0781B]

The asp signifies the devil, who “dwells” in caves and openings—that is, in the hearts of perverse people. “Separated from the breast,” he says, that is, withdrawn from carnal desires. “And the weaned child will put his hand into the den of the basilisk.” The basilisk is a serpent, the king of all serpents, which by its breath or gaze kills not only beasts but also birds flying through the air, and it signifies the devil. One is called “weaned” because one has been separated from milk.

Therefore, the saints who have been withdrawn from the breast—that is, from carnal desires—and who have been weaned, separated from milk because they now receive solid food (Hebrews 5), that is, because they are already perfected in faith and action, take delight in putting their hand—that is, the work of their preaching—into the hole of the asp and the den of the basilisk, that is, into the hearts of the faithless, and drawing out from there the serpent called the devil.

“The serpents themselves will not harm” “on my holy mountain,” that is, in my Church. This is the Lord’s voice. And why will they not harm? The prophet explains: “because the earth is filled with evangelical doctrine.” For the sound of preaching has gone out to the ends of the earth (Psalm 18). And how is it filled? “As the waters cover” the floor of the sea. Some manuscripts have *aperientes* (“opening”), [Col. 0781D] but this is written incorrectly. It differs from the sense. But it is written incorrectly. For it differs from the sense. Thus, just as the waters cover the depths of the sea, so the whole earth is full of the knowledge of God.

“And it will happen on that day: the Lord will add a second time.” The prophet’s voice concerns the Jews who believed in the Lord. “Day” should be understood as a period of time. In what period will this happen? When “the Lord’s tomb has become glorious,” that is, after his resurrection and ascension. Why does he say “a second time”? Because before his Passion he first preached, saying: “Repent” (Matthew 4). After his resurrection and ascension, he added his “hand” a second time, that is, preaching through the apostles, teaching them to produce fruits worthy of repentance (Luke 3). [Col. 0782A]

By “the remnant” he means the survivors of the two tribes whom those peoples, who are enumerated, had left alive rather than killing; instead, they had driven them into exile throughout all the regions of the world. Alternatively, he will add his hand a second time on the day of judgment, when, with Elijah and Enoch preaching, all Israel who are found will be saved.

“And he will raise a standard”—the standard of victory, that is, the sign of the cross—“over the nations” through the preaching of the apostles, so that all peoples may know by what means they were redeemed after the devil had been conquered. “And he will gather the fugitives of Israel,” that is, those who were scattered from the tribes throughout various kingdoms. “And he will collect the dispersed of Judah,” that is, those from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

This pertains to the time when, on the day of Pentecost, the apostles, inflamed by tongues of fire, began to speak in various languages (Acts 2). [Col. 0782B] For histories report that, from all the places where the Jews had previously been scattered, some of them returned to their native land for that festival, just as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven.” Of these, on the one day mentioned above, when Peter preached, three thousand believed, and on the next day five thousand (Acts 2:4), and thereafter many thousands.

“And the jealousy of Ephraim will be removed, and the enemies of Judah will perish.” When Isaiah was preaching this, the ten tribes were hostile to Judah and Benjamin. In the time of the apostles, however, those who believed, both from Judah and from Benjamin, no longer fought among themselves as before, since they had been joined together in the unity [Col. 0782C] of faith and love.

“And they will fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines by sea.” Who will these be who fly? The apostles, of whom it is written elsewhere: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” They are said to fly because of the speed of their journey, since the apostles crossed the great sea by ship to the islands of the Philistines. Thus the blessed apostle Paul taught the word of life on the island of Rhodes and in Pamphylia (Acts 27). They are said to fly over the shoulders of the Philistines because, just as a bird suddenly flies over a branch, so the apostles, inspired by the Lord, approached them and likewise plundered the children of the East through their preaching.

“Idumea and Moab will be under the command of their hand”—understand, they will follow it. For the Idumeans and Moabites submitted themselves to the evangelical command, believing in Christ the Son of God. “And the children of Ammon” likewise “were obedient” to their teaching.

“And the Lord will lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt.” Just as the Idumeans, Moabites, and Ammonites became obedient to the evangelical commands through the apostles’ preaching, so the Lord himself will lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt. It is called the sea of Egypt because of the multitude of its peoples. It should be noted that the sea has no tongue; the prophet is speaking metaphorically.

Thus the Lord laid waste the tongue of the sea—that is, the people of Egypt—when he changed those who had formerly been accustomed with their lips to praise and worship idols made by human hands through the apostles’ preaching, [Col. 0783A] so that they could and would know how to praise their Creator and Redeemer. For the Egyptian nation was more devoted than all other peoples to idolatry and the most vain superstition concerning demons, to such an extent that they worshiped the hawk, the dog, and the ass as gods. The Lord then changed its tongue when he destroyed the images that it had previously worshiped and praised, and it began to confess its wickedness to its Creator, having turned to repentance.

“And the Lord will raise his hand over the river,” that is, over the kingdom of Egypt, “in the strength of his spirit,” that is, in the strength of the Romans. “And he will strike it in its seven channels, so that they may pass through it shod.” When Isaiah was preaching this, the Nile had not yet been divided into a great river. Later Alexander of Macedon divided it [Col. 0783B] into seven channels.

In the reign of Caesar Augustus, when the flower had arisen from the root of Jesse and the first census was made in the Roman world (Luke 2), the exceedingly powerful kingdom of Egypt, which had remained united for many years, was destroyed at the death of Cleopatra. All Egypt was divided into seven channels, that is, into seven rulers, whereas previously it had been under the government of one man. The Nile too, a river of many waters that before Alexander divided it had been impossible to cross, was so dried up as it flowed through the lowest valleys, after the Romans had enlarged the channels, that it could be crossed on dry feet.

The kingdom is said especially to have been struck in seven channels because, having seven rulers instead of one, its glory and power were diminished. [Col. 0783C] Libya had one ruler, Pentapolis another, Alexandria another, and Thebaïs another. The river Nile is therefore divided metaphorically into parts and cut into channels so that the apostles, wearing sandals—that is, without impediment—could travel freely while preaching the word of the Gospel and reach the most distant peoples of Egypt.

“And there will be a road through Egypt for the remnant of my people who will be left by the Assyrians, as there was for Israel on the day when he came up from the land of Egypt.” Before the Lord’s birth, it was not permitted for any people to pass from one nation to another; after his Passion, however, anyone who wished was free to go from one region to another.

The Lord speaks of the apostles, the primitive Church, and the Jews who believed in him, through whom the Gospel was disseminated throughout the four regions of the world: just as Israel crossed the Red Sea without resistance, so they would cross not only through Egypt but also through the ends of the earth (Psalm 18), without any obstacle. [Col. 0783D]

## CHAPTER XII

“And you will say on that day.” The prophet speaks to the assembly of believers, so that on that day—that is, at that time—it may confess the Lord, when Egypt has been divided among seven rulers and its tongue has been changed to praise God.

Just as Israel sang a song to the Lord when it came out of the Egyptian prison after crossing the sea, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified,” so let it sing again when their imperial power has been dissolved and the Lord has begun to reign over them, praising with joy and exultation and saying:

“I confess to you, Lord,” that is, “I will glorify and magnify you,” “because I deserved wrath, but your fury has been turned into mercy, and you have comforted me,” that is, “you have received me and redeemed me from the hand of death and calamity.”

“Behold, God is my savior.” *Jesus* is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as *Salvator*, “Savior.” And why “Savior”? Because “he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1).

“Behold, my God, my Jesus, has now come; he has now redeemed me with his precious blood; he has now removed the revolving sword that stood before paradise (Genesis 3), shattering the bronze gates of the abyss; [Col. 0784B] he has now opened for me the gate of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore I will act confidently” in his commandments, “and I will not fear,” since they are not to be feared. I will no longer place my hope in idols, but in the Lord my God, who is my “strength” and my protection against all adversity, “and who has become my salvation,” my refuge and deliverance from the enemy.

“You will draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior.” The prophet addresses believers from among the Jews and foretells saving things for them. Earlier he called him Emmanuel and said, “He will strip the spoils,” so that he would not seem to be someone other than the one whom the archangel Gabriel announced to the Virgin, saying: “And you will call his name Jesus” (Luke 1). Now he calls him Savior and speaks of water to be drawn from his spring, that is, from evangelical doctrine.

Not from the waters of the river of Egypt, which were struck, but from the spring of Jesus. For in the language of the Hebrews this name expresses “Savior.” These are the waters that he himself promises to give to believers in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; and from his belly will flow living waters.” The Evangelist himself explains what he meant: “Now this he said concerning the Spirit whom those who believed were to receive” (John 7).

The springs of Jesus are evangelical doctrine and the mysteries of both the Old and the New Testament. If we understand them rightly and fulfill them in action, we will draw from them waters—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“And you will say on that day,” that is, at that time, when you have received the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit from the springs of the Savior:

[Col. 0784D] “Give thanks to the Lord,” all you who believe in him, “and call upon his name,” so that, because he is called Jesus, he may save and protect you. “Make his inventions known among the peoples,” that is, the evangelical doctrine and the commandments that he taught; and “remember that he alone is exalted,” the one to whom song should be offered.

“The Lord has acted magnificently,” because by his single death he destroyed our double death, rising from the dead and ascending to the heights; and because he carried into heaven the flesh of our frailty that he had assumed in the Virgin’s womb (Matthew 28).

“Announce this throughout the whole earth”: that the one who created us has himself restored us; and, after conquering the author of death, has opened the way into the heavenly kingdom for believers. [Col. 0785A] The prophet addresses the apostles and the remaining believers, both from the Jews and from the nations, so that they alone may confess the Lord, abandon idols, call upon his name, and proclaim all his works to the unbelieving and faithless, so that they too may turn to faith in Christ, proclaim his wonders and mighty deeds throughout the whole world, and announce how by his mercy he redeemed us when we had been lost.

“Exult and praise, habitation of Zion, because great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” The prophet exhorts the primitive Church and says: “O Zion, dwelling place of God, exult and praise your God, because the one who previously seemed to be your God alone, confined within the narrow boundaries of the land of Judea, is now proclaimed throughout the whole world. He reigns among the nations, and the peoples of the nations worship him.”

Nevertheless, a second time—that is, before the day of judgment—he will add his hand, gather the fugitives of Israel, and collect the elect of Judah: “For when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11), and it will draw water from the spring of the Savior.

This may also be referred to the Church from the nations. For Zion, which is interpreted as “mirror” or “watchtower,” signifies the holy Church. And rightly so. The holy and faithful preachers who dwell within the Church seek nothing earthly but, with the whole desire of their minds, long for heavenly things, watching over their actions and works lest they suddenly be deceived by the devil. Without doubt, at the judgment they will not be excluded from the contemplation of God, but will see him as he is (1 John 3).

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0785C]

“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw.” In the prophetic books, wherever we read “burden,” what follows is full of punishments, miseries, and the weight of tribulation. When he says “the burden of Babylon,” it is as though he were saying: “This proclamation is the weight of Babylon’s miseries.”

Babylon was the metropolis and most powerful city of the Chaldeans. It was of such size—as Herodotus and many other Greek historians relate—that it extended in a square from one corner to another for sixteen thousand paces, that is, sixty-four thousand paces in all, making forty-two leagues and two-thirds of a league. It was also built by the queen called Semiramis.

In its midst stood a citadel, or capitol—that is, a tower—which the sons of Adam built after the Flood, before they were scattered throughout the whole world. It is said to have been three thousand paces high, that is, two leagues, gradually narrowing from a broad base to a narrow summit so that the impending weight might more easily be supported from the sides.

Because the language of the whole earth was confused there, it is called *Babel* in Hebrew and *Babylon* in Greek (Genesis 11). Its exceedingly powerful king Nebuchadnezzar devastated, among other nations, even Judea. Therefore the Holy Spirit, for the consolation of the Israelite people, foretells through Isaiah, long beforehand, its destruction by the Medes and Persians under the leaders Darius and Cyrus.

Isaiah saw these things not with the eyes [Col. 0786A] of the body, but with the eyes of the mind, as the Holy Spirit revealed them.

“Raise a standard on the dark mountain; lift up your voice.” He calls Babylon a mountain, not because it is situated on a mountain, but because of the swelling of its pride. He calls it dark because of the sorrow and weeping of the captives and the affliction of those whom the Babylonians had reduced to slavery there. Alternatively, he calls it dark because of the great conflagration that he foretold, when it was burned by the Medes and Persians.

The prophet addresses the angelic powers or his fellow prophets so that they may proclaim Babylon’s desolation, saying: “Raise a standard of angelic victory upon the dark mountain, O angelic powers, or my fellow prophets; lift up your voice,” that is, proclaim Babylon’s destruction by the Medes and Persians. “Raise your hand,” as though for victory, [Col. 0786B] and the leaders of the Medes and Persians, Darius and Cyrus, will enter Babylon’s gates.

“I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have summoned my mighty ones in my anger, rejoicing in my glory.” He calls the Medes and Persians his sanctified and mighty ones—not because they were holy, but because, obeying God’s command, they fulfilled his will. In comparison with those who did not obey God’s orders, they were holy.

“I,” he says, “commanded my sanctified ones, the Medes and Persians, to come against Babylon; and I summoned my mighty ones, mentioned above, in my anger, or in my vengeance.” He summoned and commanded them to come when he inspired their hearts. By adding “rejoicing in my glory,” he shows that they did not accomplish this by their own power, but that, relying on God’s help and [Col. 0786C] strength, they were able to overthrow so exalted a kingdom.

“The voice of a multitude, like that of peoples gathering in the mountains.” He describes the assault of the Medes and Persians, who came with many peoples’ assistance to overthrow Babylon. “The voice of a multitude of peoples in the mountains of Babylon, like that of peoples gathering,” that is, of many peoples. “The voice of the sound of kings”—understand, Darius and Cyrus, and the others who were with them—“of nations gathered together,” who were assembled by Darius and Cyrus against Babylon.

“The Lord, and the vessels of his wrath, to destroy the whole land.” Understand: “The Lord will come, and the vessels of his wrath”—namely, Darius and Cyrus, his ministers of vengeance—“to destroy the whole land of Babylon.”

[Col. 0786D] “Wail, because the day of the Lord is near.” He turns to the Chaldeans so that they may lament the evils that are to come: “Wail,” he says, “because the day of the Lord is near,” that is, the day of his vengeance and of Babylon’s destruction. “Desolation will come from the Lord,” that is, it will be reduced to solitude.

“Because of this”—understand, because the Lord will come with the Medes and Persians—“all the hands of the mighty men” of the Chaldeans “will be loosened” by fear, “and every human heart will melt,” or fail.

“And it will be broken. Pangs”—understand, of the belly—“and pains” of the limbs “will seize” the Chaldeans; “they will writhe like a woman in labor.” “Each one will be astonished at his neighbor,” that is, they will marvel because of their misery [Col. 0787A] and calamity and will be driven mad, so that no one will wish to console another over his misery. “Their faces will be scorched,” or “their countenances will wither,” from excessive pain; alternatively, because many were burned in the fire.

“Behold, the day of the Lord will come, cruel and full of indignation,” or vengeance, “and wrath and fury, to make the land”—understand, of Babylon—“a desolation, and to destroy its sinners from it.” Here we should understand “the cruel day of the Lord” as the day of captivity, or also the day of the universal judgment—not because the one who torments the cruel, or in which the cruel are tormented, is cruel in his own merit, but because it appears cruel to those who suffer affliction.

“For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread their light; the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light.” To those who are afflicted and placed in tribulation, everything seems darkened. Alternatively, by the sun we may understand King Belshazzar, by the moon the queen, and by the stars the rulers, all of whom were darkened in death when the Medes and Persians arrived.

We may also refer this to the day of the final judgment, when all the heavenly lights will seem darkened in comparison with the greater light of Christ.

“And I will visit evil upon the world.” Because of the magnitude of its kingdom and the immense multitude of its people, Babylon is called “the world.” But he threatens that it will be visited not for its good but for its harm, so that where there had previously been an innumerable multitude of peoples, there will be desolation and a wasteland of human beings.

[Col. 0787C] “A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure refined gold.” Whatever is rarely found is precious. Hence this means that after Babylon’s destruction and the slaughter of its people, a Babylonian man will be more precious than gold, that is, a man will be found more rarely than gold. Likewise, a Babylonian human being will be found rarer than refined gold, that is, red gold. Something similar is read in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 3): “The word of the Lord was precious,” that is, it was rarely found.

This can likewise be referred to the day of judgment, when the Lord will visit the evils of the whole world and cause the pride of demons and faithless human beings to cease; and few will be found among the elect because of the persecution of the Antichrist.

“Because of this I will shake heaven,” that is, over the throne [Col. 0787D] of Babylon, “and the earth will be moved from its place because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts and because of the day of his wrath and fury.” As we said above concerning the darkening of the stars, that to the afflicted everything appears darkened, so this too can be understood as meaning that such terror seized them when the Medes and Persians arrived that not only human beings but even the elements seemed to rise up against them. It may also be understood that, as Babylon’s overthrow approached, the heavens were shaken by thunder and the earth was shaken to its foundations. It can appropriately be referred also to the day of judgment.

“And it will be like a fleeing doe, and like a sheep; and there will be no one to gather it.” When the Medes and Persians arrive, all Babylon’s warriors will flee from their presence [Col. 0788A] as a doe flees from a lion’s roar, unable to resist or free itself. They will flee like a sheep from the howling of wolves, having neither a defender nor one to gather them. “Each one will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land.”

All Babylon’s allies who had come from various regions by which it had previously been defended, after being captured, will return to their own lands if they are able to escape the enemy’s sword. Alternatively, all the peoples who were held captive and enslaved in Babylon, after their masters—those who had previously ruled them—have been killed, will return to their own lands.

“Everyone who is found” in it “will be killed; and everyone who comes upon it”—understand, to bring aid to the Chaldeans—“will fall by the sword of the enemies.” Whoever does not flee but wishes to resist will be punished by the sword; and whoever comes for the purpose of resisting will likewise be punished by the sword.

“Their infants,” that is, the infants of the Babylonians, “will be dashed” or struck “before their eyes.” Of this the Psalmist foretold long beforehand: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136). “Their houses,” that is, their households and wealth, “will be plundered, and their wives will be violated” by the enemies before their eyes.

This is the most savage cruelty of conquerors: they spare neither the innocent in age, allow all the wealth of the houses to be plundered, nor preserve the chastity of wives in the sight of their husbands.

“Behold, I will raise up the Medes against them, who do not seek silver” [Col. 0788C] and so forth “and whose eyes will not spare their children.” Here he shows which nations he had mentioned above, and that they overthrew the power of so exalted a kingdom not by their own strength but by God’s aid, since he raised them up against the Chaldeans. For they had been subject to the Chaldeans and therefore would in no way have done such things unless God had willed it.

At the same time he describes the cruelty of the Medes and Persians as so great that, in their eagerness to shed blood, they regarded gold and silver as worthless and pierced nursing infants with their arrows.

“And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms,” that is, which was once glorious among kingdoms, “renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans,” that is, in which the Chaldeans gloried and took pride, “will be destroyed and overturned into desolation,” [Col. 0788D] “as God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.”

“It will not be inhabited forever, and it will not be founded from generation to generation,” that is, it will never again be established for eternity. It must indeed be held as true that it was not rebuilt afterward. But, as some say, there is a lake there, in its midst, full of serpents, and groves and thickets in which beasts and birds dwell; and there is a royal hunting ground there. But because, as is said below, there are monsters of demons there, it has been made uninhabitable.

Two exceedingly powerful cities were built among the Medes in place of Babylon: Seleucia and Ctesiphon, which are said still to remain. “Nor will the Arab”—that is, the Saracen—“pitch his tents there, nor will weary shepherds rest there after the tracks of their flocks.”

“But beasts will rest there; and their houses”—that is, the houses of the Babylonians—“will be filled with dragons; and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy beings will dance there. And owls will answer one another there in its houses, and sirens in its pleasure shrines.”

Because of the multitude of beasts, serpents, and demons, no shepherd—that is, no seeker of the desert—dares to dwell there. The ostrich is a bird of remarkable size that seeks solitude. It has this nature, as natural philosophers say: it forgets its eggs in the desert. Through it we should understand all kinds of birds that love solitude and dwell there.

The hairy beings are wild, shaggy men, or apes, [Col. 0789B] whom some also call incubi or satyrs, or else they are kinds of demons. The owls are horned owls, as large as ravens but covered with various spots; they are accustomed to thrust their beaks into the marsh and cry out loudly.

The sirens are dragons, crested and winged, as the poets’ tales relate; they are sea creatures resembling women. “Sirens” may also be understood as monsters of demons.

“Houses” means large dwellings. Shrines were temples of the gods, called *delubra* either from *deludendo* (“deceiving”), or because people hoped there to “wash themselves clean,” that is, to cleanse themselves from sins through the multitude of sacrifices; for beside those temples there were springs in which the victims were washed.

He says “in the pleasure shrines” because before the altars of their gods they indulged in debauchery and satisfied every carnal pleasure. But where they had most aroused against themselves the anger of almighty God, there the prophet now threatens that various kinds of serpents and demonic monsters will dwell.

## CHAPTER XIV

“Her time is near to come, and her days will not be prolonged.” Every period of time, however long it may be, is very short in comparison with God’s eternity. The prophet therefore threatens Babylon’s destruction and says: “The day of Babylon’s overthrow and captivity is near to come, and the day of its tribulation will not be prolonged.”

“For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will again choose Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil.” This pertains to the time of Cyrus, in whose first year the captivity was dissolved, when the Lord had mercy on them [Col. 0789D] by bringing them out of captivity and chose from Israel those who returned with Zerubbabel and the other leaders.

Allegorically, however, we can refer this to the time of the incarnation of the Son of God, which was near when he had mercy on Jacob—that is, on those who had become supplanters of vices—by forgiving them their sins, and when he chose from Israel the apostles and other believers, whom he makes rest upon his own soil, that is, in his Church.

“The sojourner will be joined to them”—understand, the sojourner who will return from captivity—“and will cling to the house of Jacob.”

“And peoples will take them”—understand, not into servitude, but in affection and the highest honor—“and they will bring them,” that is, the foreigners, “to their place” [Col. 0790A] in Jerusalem. It is understood that many Gentiles followed the Jews returning from captivity and adopted their religious practice. “And the house of Israel will possess them” until “they subject their taskmasters.”

If they came of their own will, as was said above, how did they possess them as male and female slaves? This can be resolved in two ways: either because they themselves voluntarily submitted to their power and dominion, or because, after returning from captivity, they were of such great dignity that they bought many male and female slaves from various nations. The statement that follows—“They will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subject” to themselves “their taskmasters,” or tributaries—is to be referred to the time of Ahasuerus and Holofernes.

“And it shall be on that day: when the Lord gives you rest” [Col. 0790B] “from your labor and from your trembling,” that is, from the violence by which he was led into captivity, “and from the harsh servitude in which you formerly served”—understand, the Chaldaeans—“that is, when the captivity has been completely ended—“you will take up a parable,” or proverb, “against the king of Babylon,” expressing astonishment that the Lord and conqueror of the lands, who despoiled everything through tribute, has been crushed and reduced to nothing.

It should be understood that what follows is spoken both of Nebuchadnezzar and of the devil, from the person of the elect on the day of judgment. “How has the taskmaster ceased”—whether Nebuchadnezzar or the devil, who exacts tribute or punishments—“how has the tribute rested?” Understand: the tribute that was formerly paid. A taskmaster is one who exacts tribute from peoples. The devil too is a taskmaster, because he forces us to serve him and demands the servitude of sin. [Col. 0790C] Since, therefore, the tribute has rested not through human power but through the Lord’s power, once the taskmaster has been killed, the prophet makes this clear in the words that follow, speaking from the person of the Israelite people, or of the elect.

“The Lord has broken the staff of the impious, the rod of rulers, striking peoples with an incurable blow,” that is, with irreversible death, “pursuing them cruelly”—understand, all peoples. He calls either Nebuchadnezzar or the devil the staff of the impious, because just as the impious were scourged by God through him, so those who are in the punishments of hell are scourged through the devil. Or, while he forces them to sin in this world, he scourges them with his suggestions and depraved pleasures.

“Every land has rested”—understand, from labor—“and has fallen silent from weeping,” that is, from cries. After he was crushed, “it rejoiced” at his death, “and afterward exulted.” At his ruin the whole land indeed fell silent and gave forth a voice of joy.

“The fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon.” By the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon are understood the princes of various nations who were afflicted by Nebuchadnezzar—or, better, the sons of princes whose fathers were killed by Nebuchadnezzar, since they rejoiced greatly at his death, saying: “Since you have lain down,” that is, since you have died, “no one has come up to cut us down,” that is, to kill us, as you killed our fathers.

“Hell beneath has been stirred up to meet your arrival [Col. 0791A] and has raised up giants for you.” From this we learn that hell is beneath the earth. Its inhabitants are designated here by the name “hell,” or this may mean the angel appointed over the punishments of hell. The giants are to be understood as earthly and powerful princes. These things are said not as though they actually happened, but as things that could have happened. “All the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones.” The souls of the princes whom he himself had killed came to meet him, taunting him, so that they might afterward marvel at him in punishment, although previously they had honored him for his power. It is a consolation for the wicked when they see their enemies suffering the same things.

“And you have been wounded as we have, and you have become like us.” As though they were saying in other words: We thought that you alone could resist the power of God; but, as events show, you too have been wounded as we have, and you have become like us—that is, mortal and cast into hell. Therefore we grieve less that we were cut down, since you too have fallen beneath the same axe.

“Your pride has been brought down to hell; your corpse has fallen”—understand, into death—“beneath you”—understand, beneath you who formerly reclined upon the breasts of other kings—“the moth will be spread,” and you who were formerly covered with cloaks and clothed in gold and jewels: “worms will be your covering.” Through these two images the magnitude of the punishments of hell is expressed, or the material of the punishments that arises from bodies themselves: just as worms arise from a corpse while some moisture remains in it, and moths from clothing.

“How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who were rising at dawn!” [Col. 0791C] In the literal sense, he calls Nebuchadnezzar “Lucifer” in this passage (Dan. IV), because through pride he fell from the throne of power. For just as Lucifer, scattering darkness, proceeds bright and radiant at his rising, so your public progress seemed to resemble the highest star.

“You who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven” until “I will be like the Most High.” Thus Nebuchadnezzar spoke in his heart, lifted up in pride, thinking that he had acquired such power by his own strength: Since the whole earth is subject to me, what remains for me except to ascend into heaven and be like the Most High?
