Alternatively, he calls the Jews “heaven and stars,” since they shine with knowledge of the God of heaven. He calls Mount Zion the “mountain of the Testament,” because on its northern side it had the Temple, in which was the Testament of God given through Moses. By the “height of the clouds” he means the patriarchs and prophets. Concerning these clouds the same prophet Isaiah says elsewhere, speaking from the person of God: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon them.” Thus Nebuchadnezzar spoke in his heart, and indeed also in words, before he captured the Jews.

What remains for me except to ascend over the Jews, who possess knowledge of the God of heaven, where the prophets proclaim future events and where the magnificent Temple is? We can also refer these things allegorically to the devil, who, at dawn—that is, at the beginning of the world—rose or was elevated among the other angels, but fell from heaven. In accordance with what the Lord says in Luke chapter ten: “I saw Satan [Col. 0792A] falling from heaven like lightning.” He may have said such things by thought before he fell, or after he had fallen. Before he fell, while he was in the firmament, he desired to ascend into heaven, where the Lord’s throne is. But after he was rebuked through words of arrogance, just as that one was, he boasts of ascending into heaven above the angels and above the clouds—or above the hearts of the elect—and of sitting “on the mountain of the Testament,” that is, in the Church, “and on the sides of the north,” that is, in the cold minds where he dwells.

“Nevertheless, you will be brought down to hell, to the depths of the pit.” Nebuchadnezzar or the devil, who through pride had said, “I will ascend into heaven; I will be like the Most High,” fell from the throne of glory not merely into hell, but into its furthest regions; [Col. 0792B] for the higher the position, the deeper the fall.

“Those who see you”—understand, placed in the furthest regions of hell—“will bow toward you and will look upon you”—understand, saying: “Is this the man who troubled the earth,” namely Nebuchadnezzar, “who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities?” This is the voice of kings and princes taunting him and marveling that the devastator of all has himself been devastated. For what he did, he received—and even more.

The statement that follows, “He did not open the prison to his prisoners,” that is, to the captives of the world, expresses the magnitude of his cruelty and impiety. He not only burdened captives with chains but also shut them up in darkness, to such an extent that he would not open the prison even for his son Evil-merodach, whom he held captive with the others (IV Kings XXV; Jer. LII).

“All the kings of the nations, all of them, have slept in glory, each man in his own house,” that is, in his own tomb.

“But you have been cast out from your tomb like a useless, polluted shoot, and you have been wrapped together with those who were killed by the sword”—understand, by your sword—“and they have gone down to the foundations of the pit.”

The sense is this: once all those whom you killed by the material sword or through captivity have been buried, you alone will lie unburied. Alternatively: even if all the souls who are in hell have at some time received some rest, you alone will be confined in the furthest reaches. You will be covered by the blood of all, and the gore of everyone will press upon you, as though you were wrapped in the putrefaction of the dead.

In the verse where he says, “You have been cast out from your tomb [Col. 0792D] like a useless shoot,” the true story of the Jews appears to be indicated. They say that after Nebuchadnezzar had returned to his former condition, he placed his son Evil-merodach—who had ruled for those seven years during which Nebuchadnezzar dwelt among the beasts—in prison. Evil-merodach remained there throughout his father’s life with Jehoiachin, king of Judah, who was also captive. When Nebuchadnezzar died, Evil-merodach did not dare to assume the kingdom, fearing that his father might rise again; for he said: “My father dies when he wishes and rises again when he wishes.” He therefore consulted Jehoiachin, who advised him to take three hundred birds from different parts of the world and, after digging up his father’s body, tear it limb from limb and bind a part of it to each bird, saying: “When these birds eventually come together, then your father will be resurrected.”

As for what is added, “like a useless shoot”: properly speaking, a shoot is what grows from the roots of trees. It is called useless because it takes strength away from a tree that bears fruit.

“For you have destroyed the land; you have killed the people.” That is, those whom God had given to you for correction, you destroyed by killing them. Alternatively: because of your pride the kingdom of the Chaldaeans was destroyed; it would still have remained if you had acted humbly. Or in this sense: You were so cruel that you afflicted and oppressed not only foreign peoples but also those subject to you and similar to you in wickedness.

“The seed of the wicked will not be called forever,” that is, the seed of Nebuchadnezzar and his sons. Here all the histories seem to agree that, after Belshazzar was killed, no one afterward from the seed of Nebuchadnezzar ruled; rather, because of their father’s pride and impiety, the entire offspring was destroyed.

“Prepare his sons for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers,” that is, on account of the iniquity of their fathers. “They will not rise”—understand, his sons will not rise to the kingdom—“nor will they inherit the land,” that is, their father’s kingdom.

“And I will rise against them,” that is, against the sons of Nebuchadnezzar, through Darius and Cyrus.

“And I will destroy Babylon’s name”—understand, so that it will no longer be called mistress of kingdoms—“and its remnants and its shoot,” that is, its sons, “and its offspring”—understand, I will destroy them—“says the Lord.”

“And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and into pools of water.” By the hedgehog are understood all the beasts, birds, [Col. 0793C] and serpents that are there. Finally, it can be seen today that this was fulfilled just as the prophet foretold: there is nothing in it except royal hunting grounds, apart from the baked-brick walls, which, in order to enclose the beasts there, are restored after many years.

“And I will sweep it with the broom of destruction, says the Lord of hosts,” or of armies. Just as nothing dirty remains when a broom is dragged across a surface, so no names will be left in it.

“The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: If it is not as I have thought,” or planned, “so shall it be; and as I have considered in my mind, so shall it happen: that I may crush the Assyrian in my land and trample him on my mountains.” Thus far he has spoken about Babylon, its kings, and its peoples; now he returns to Sennacherib and to what at that time [Col. 0793D] threatened the Assyrians, who had devastated Samaria and Judah, except Jerusalem (IV Kings XIX). Because they had been lifted up in pride against the Lord, one hundred and eighty-five thousand of their army were killed by the angel of the Lord in one night in the land of Judah and on its mountains, just as the Lord had foretold.

When he says, “The Lord of hosts has sworn,” he speaks in human fashion. The speech of almighty God should be taken as an oath because of its immovable firmness: the one who is truth cannot lie. Nor does he have anyone greater by whom to swear (Hebr. VI). What he adds—“If it is not as I have considered in my mind”—means the same as if he had said: Since I have planned to crush the Assyrian, it cannot happen otherwise.

“And the yoke”—or power—“of the Assyrians will be removed from them,” that is, from the inhabitants of Jerusalem, because they were under siege, “and his burden,” that is, the weight of affliction, “will be lifted from their shoulder.”

“This is the plan that I have planned over the whole earth, and this is the hand”—or power—“stretched out over all the nations.” This is the voice of the almighty Lord, specifically against the land of the Assyrians or generally against the whole world: against those who are subject to the power of Sennacherib or of the devil and obey his will. Here the plan of almighty God is called that of which it was said a little earlier: “If it is not as I have thought, so shall it be, that I may crush the Assyrian in my land.”

“For the Lord of hosts has decreed,” that is, established it. “And who will be able to weaken”—understand, his decree, so that he will not crush the Assyrian? “His hand is stretched out,” that is, his power is extended to strike, “and who will turn it away?”—understand, no one, so that he does not strike. The extension of the hand shows the posture of one who is striking.

“In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came to pass.” From the beginning of the book to this point, during the reigns of three kings—Uzziah, Jotham, and Ahaz—the prophet foretold the matters contained in between. From here to the end of the book, they belong to the reign of Hezekiah, and some of them were fulfilled.

“Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of your smiter has been shattered.” It is natural, as blessed Jerome says, that when a king dies, the enemies of other nations rejoice, expecting civil wars and rebellions from the new circumstances. When the exceedingly wicked and already aged King Ahaz died—he had harshly afflicted the Philistines, or Palestinians—they rejoiced at his death and mocked the Israelites, because, after losing a mature king, they were subject to his young son Hezekiah, under whose authority they thought they could invade the borders of Israel.

“From the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth, and its seed”—that is, the basilisk’s offspring—“will devour the bird.” The basilisk is called the king of serpents; the Greeks call it a basilisk. It is said to possess the power of killing birds flying above it not only by its breath but even by its gaze.

He calls Ahaz the rod or staff of the smiter, and the serpent, because Ahaz struck and wounded the Philistines severely, but did not completely devour them. He calls Hezekiah the basilisk. The prophet therefore addresses the Philistines, telling them not to mock Israel because of Ahaz’s death, saying: “Do not rejoice.”

“All Philistia, over the death of Ahaz,” who had reached mature age, “because the rod of your smiter,” Ahaz, who used to strike you, “has been broken; for from the root of the serpent,” that is, from the seed of Ahaz, “a basilisk will come forth,” namely Hezekiah, “and its seed will devour the bird.” How, he says, no bird can pass the basilisk’s gaze unharmed, but, however far away it may be, it is sucked in by its mouth, so you too will perish entirely at the sight of Hezekiah. For Hezekiah afflicted the Philistines more than all the kings of Israel.

[Col. 0795A] “And the firstborn of the poor will feed,” that is, the Israelites, “and the poor will rest securely.” These are the firstborn concerning whom the Lord says through another prophet: “Israel is my firstborn son.” And: “Let my firstborn son go” (Exod. IV). They are called poor because they placed their confidence not in riches or power but in God. Of such people the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V).

Therefore, O Philistia, when the basilisk has devoured you—that is, when Hezekiah has completely destroyed you—you will no longer lie in wait for my poor one. Rather, overcome by troubles, you will mourn your own calamity. “And I will kill your root in famine,” that is, your strength or offspring, “and I will kill your remnants”—understand, those whom Hezekiah leaves behind—“through” [Col. 0795B] the Assyrians and Chaldaeans.

“Howl, O gate; cry out, O city: all Philistia has been overthrown.” As far as literal reality is concerned, neither a gate can howl nor a city cry out. He therefore uses “gate” for those who are in the gate, and “city” for the inhabitants of the city. The prophet accordingly directs his speech to the cities of the Philistines, so that they may mourn and lament their misery, which has come upon Sennacherib, because all Philistia has already been overthrown by the sword of the Assyrians.

“For smoke will come from the north, and there is no one who will escape his formation.” Here “smoke” is used for the multitude of Sennacherib’s armies. Or by the smoke of his name is understood that he was going to devastate all the nations, since he came from the northern region to Jerusalem. The prophet might have said in other words: I therefore command you, O Philistines, to howl, because I already foresee Sennacherib’s army coming from the north, together with the report that he will capture you, so that no one among the many nations will be able by his own strength to escape his multitude.

“And what will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people will hope.” Since, in saying above that no one would escape his formation, Judah too seemed to have been included in the general sentence, he therefore added: If, he says, the angels appointed over the Assyrians should ask why Jerusalem alone is saved from Sennacherib’s hand, they must be answered that the Lord founded Zion and by his own power delivered his humble people who hoped in him.

It can also be understood simply in relation to that passage in Jeremiah where the prophet himself placed wooden yokes upon the necks of those who had been sent to him. The prophet therefore says to the Lord: What will be answered to the messengers of the various nations when they come to inquire about Sennacherib’s arrival? The Lord replies: They must be answered that the nations are to be captured, while Jerusalem alone, which placed its hope not in man but in God, is to be delivered.

## CHAPTER XV

“The burden of Moab.” Because the Moabites rejoiced at the captivity of the Israelites, as the Philistines had, the Holy Spirit through the prophet Isaiah foretells to them [Col. 0796A] the weight of the miseries they were going to suffer.

Moab was the son of Lot, conceived through incest. All those descended from him were called Moabites, and their province Moab. This one name is used for the entire people of that nation. It should also be known that they were first devastated by the Assyrians and then by the Chaldaeans.

“Because Ar was devastated in the night, Moab fell silent,” or was quiet. It dared nothing against the Assyrians or Chaldaeans. “Because the wall was devastated in the night”—understand, the wall of the city of Ar—“Moab fell silent.”

Ar was the metropolis and royal city of the Moabites. Today, formed from the Hebrew and Greek languages, it is called Areopolis—not because it is the city of Ares, that is, of Mars, as some have claimed. Ar was rightly devastated in the night, because Moab was conceived from the incest of Lot’s daughter during the night. Or “night” signifies the magnitude of grief.

Therefore, when the royal city Ar had been devastated and its walls destroyed, the province of Moab, in Arabia, fell silent; this is the province in which the city itself was built.

“The house”—understand, the royal house—“and Dibon,” which is a renowned city, “ascended to the high places”—understand, of their idols—“for mourning,” that is, to lament; they had these high places on their mountains or roofs.

Some incorrectly read: “The house of Edibon ascended,” as though it were the proper name of a man and his house were said to ascend. But this is not so. It should be read and understood as follows: “The house,” or royal family, “ascended to the high places of its idols, Edibon”—that is, its inhabitants ascended to the high places—not to sacrifice but to weep over their misfortunes.

“Over Nebo and over Medeba [Col. 0796C] Moab will howl.” These are the names of renowned cities, over whose destruction the entire province of Moab will howl.

“On all its heads there will be baldness; every beard will be shaved.” He touches upon the custom of the ancients, who in a time of affliction and mourning shaved their heads and beards. Thus we read of blessed Job that, after having his head shaved, he fell to the ground.

“In its streets they gird themselves with sackcloth upon its roofs, and in its squares there is universal howling. It will descend into weeping.” Teachers explain and punctuate this verse in two ways.

Some read it as follows: “In the streets,” that is, in public places, “they gird themselves with sackcloth,” which is a garment of repentance. “Upon its roofs and in its squares,” understand, all Moab, howls. From the roof or high places, or from joy, it will descend to the earth into weeping, that is, to lament.

The sense is: It will indeed ascend to the high places to weep before its idols, and when it finds no help there, it will descend to its house, or to the earth, in weeping.

Others punctuate it in this way: All Moab’s howling will descend, or reach, weeping. Thus some Moabites will not weep while others rejoice; rather, the entire multitude will weep, proceeding through the squares and through the crossroads, which is so called because of its three roads.

“Esebon and Eleale will cry out”—these are the most powerful cities of the province of Moab—“as far as Jasa”—understand, the city—“their voice has been heard,” that is, the voice of the Moabites.

This indicates that from the beginning of the kingdom, where the city of Esebon is situated, to its furthest borders, where another city, Jasa, stands, all the inhabitants will resound with cries of grief and captivity.

“Because of this”—understand, because of the evil of captivity—“the unencumbered men of Moab will howl. Its soul will howl for itself,” that is, each Moabite will howl for himself.

The prophet calls the armed men the strongest warriors, who are still free from wives. Of such men we read in Genesis (Gen. XIV), where Abraham chose the unencumbered household servants born in his household—that is, those who had no wives. The sense is: Not only will those weep and howl who are advanced in age and married and have children, but also those who ought to have defended others and have no one to mourn except themselves.

“My heart will cry out to Moab.” The prophet says that he has compassion for Moab’s miseries. Although they were his enemies, they were nevertheless God’s creatures. They were oppressed by such great calamities that they became pitiable even to their enemies. Similarly, the prophet Jeremiah says that he sympathizes with Moab’s miseries: “Therefore,” he says, “my heart for Moab will resound like a flute.”

“His bars as far as Zoar, the three-year-old heifer (*conternantem*).” Zoar is one of the five Sodomite cities, which was spared for Lot at the time of the destruction (Gen. XIX). It is called a heifer because of the impurity of its lust. As for the word “trembles,” some manuscripts have *consternantem*, “terrifying” or “disturbing,” but this is incorrectly written.

The Hebrews report that, after enduring two earthquakes, it fell at the third. This is one way of taking “as far as Zoar, the three-year-old heifer (*conternantem*)”: namely, as falling in a third earthquake. Or by *conternantem* he means “robust,” as animals are usually strongest in their third year, just as a human being is strongest at thirty. It can therefore be understood that Zoar would have remained exceedingly strong if it had not afterward sinned, after being spared for Lot’s sake.

By the bars, too, boundaries and strength are to be understood. The sense is: The bars or boundaries of Moab will be deserted as far as the city of Zoar, situated at its borders, once all its strength has been lost and destroyed.

“For by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping”—understand, Moab will go up into captivity—“and on the road to Horonaim they will raise a cry of devastation,” or captivity. Luhith is a slope on the route used by the nations of the Assyrians; Horonaim is a city of Moab facing the Assyrians. When the Moabites were being led captive to Assyria, they proceeded weeping along the slope of Luhith and through their city Horonaim, [Col. 0797D] raising a cry of mourning.

“For the waters of Menri will be desolate, because the grass has withered and the shoot has failed; all greenery has perished.” Menri is a settlement above the sea, with many springs and waters, but they are salty and bitter and therefore barren. It should nevertheless be noted that the grass in Moab did not wither and fail because Menri’s waters were barren; he has spoken metaphorically.

The sense is: Throughout Moab there will be salty and bitter waters, like the waters of Menri, which has bitter springs and is therefore barren. Every grass will dry up, and all the greenery of the grasses and vineyards will perish.

“According to the greatness of the deed is their visitation.” Here “visitation” is taken in a negative sense, as in the Psalm: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Visitation is also used in a positive sense, as when Zechariah says through John: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke I).

The sense is this: Just as a physician visits a sick person according to the magnitude of the disease, so Moab will receive vengeance according to the measure of its sin.

“They will lead them to the torrent of the willows,” that is, the Moabites.

“For a cry surrounds the boundary of Moab.” Thus far he has spoken about the captivity that came upon the Moabites through the Assyrians; now he speaks of that which occurred through the Chaldaeans. By “the torrent of the willows” we should understand the rivers of Babylon, concerning which the Psalm also says: “Upon the willows in its midst” (Ps. CXXXVI), and so forth.

“As far as the settlement of Gallim is its howling, and as far as the well of Elim is its cry,” that is, the cry of Moab from the beginning to the end of its kingdom.

“For the waters of the city of Edibon are filled with the blood” of the Moabites who have been killed. He might have said in other words: Moab will howl for this reason: where previously there was luxury and every delight because of irrigated fields and springs flowing continually, streams of blood will flow because of the multitude of the slain.

“For I will place an addition upon Edibon.” This means an increase of affliction, namely, tribulation upon tribulation: “a lion upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnants of the land.”

He now explains what addition he will place, namely the lion, and upon whom he will place it: upon those who have fled from the Moabites and upon the remnants of the land that remain.

I will place, he says, upon Edibon—that is, upon its inhabitants—affliction, so that those who have not been killed by famine and pestilence and who wished to flee will be overtaken by a lion: that is, by enemy persecutors, or by fierce beasts that will devour them. And not only upon those who have fled, but also upon the land that remains, I will send Chaldaean persecutors, or truly lions and savage beasts.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Send forth the lamb, Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.” The prophets are difficult to understand because they suddenly change persons and times; while speaking about one subject, they suddenly pass to another.

While the prophet Isaiah was speaking about the captivity and miseries of Moab, he suddenly turned the eye of his mind in the middle of his discourse toward Christ’s birth and began to address Moab and promise good things, saying: O Moab, do not despair of salvation, but do penance; for although you are to be taken captive by the Assyrians or Chaldaeans, nevertheless from your offspring will be born a lamb who will take away the sins of the world and rule over the whole earth (John I).

For Christ is the ruler of the whole world, in accordance with what God the Father said to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). And after his resurrection he himself said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

From where, then, was this lamb sent? “From the rock of the desert”—that is, from Ruth the Moabite woman. After being widowed by the death of her husband, she married Boaz, by whom she bore Obed; Obed begot Jesse, [Col. 0799A] the father of King David. From his lineage came the undefiled virgin Mary, who bore Christ, made pregnant by the work of the Holy Spirit and not carrying a child conceived from a man’s seed.

Ruth the Moabite is called the rock of the desert because the Gentiles from whom she came worshiped stones instead of God and were hard of heart, and therefore were desert and abandoned by the Creator.

To where, then, was that lamb sent? “To the mountain of the daughter of Zion,” that is, to the place where he preached and performed miracles and where he redeemed the human race. Or, better, he was sent to the Church, which consists in the mirror of the mind and the height of virtues.

Therefore, whoever seeks the reason why Boaz took Ruth the Moabite as his wife should read the Book of Ruth; there he will find the matter explained most fully. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was arranged by divine providence, so that just as Christ came to redeem Jews and Gentiles, in whom every kind of human being is included, so he would also derive his bodily origin from both peoples.

“And it will be like a bird fleeing, and like chicks flying away from the nest; so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon.” You see how he passes from one subject to another. He returns again to the captivity of Moab.

As a bird, he says, flees before a hawk, and as chicks fly away with the greatest speed, so the daughters of Moab will quickly migrate from their land at the crossing of the Arnon. By them we should understand cities and towns, or literally men and women. Arnon is a city and the boundary of the Moabites and Amorites. He speaks of a crossing because of the captivity. “So will they be at the crossing of the Arnon,” [Col. 0799C] that is, they will pass into captivity by way of Arnon.

“Take counsel” against the Moabite woman. Alternatively, “enter into counsel,” that is, enter into deliberation. “Take counsel”—that is, gather your counsel and consider how you may escape captivity.

“Make your shadow like night at midday; hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives will dwell with you. Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator.”

It should be noted that Jerusalem was devastated first by the Assyrians and afterward by the Chaldaeans, before Moab was devastated. Therefore Moab is commanded to receive and conceal the fugitives from the people of God who come to it.

“Make your shadow like night,” that is, offer protection to my people fleeing from the Assyrians or Chaldaeans, so that you may conceal them from the face of their pursuers. Fulfill this at midday, that is, hide the fleeing Israelites in the midst of open persecution and captivity. Do not destroy the wanderers who flee from place to place, or hand them over to their enemies.

For Jerusalem, which is near you, has been devastated; therefore my fugitives will dwell with you. For this reason I command you, Moab, to be their hiding place from the face of the Assyrians or Chaldaeans.

“The dust has come to an end.” The prophet suddenly passes to the killing of Sennacherib, who is called dust and wretched because all his glory and dominion quickly pass away like dust carried off by the wind. Wretchedly he passed from this life, having been killed by his sons in the presence of his god (IV Kings XIX).

“The dust has come to an end, Sennacherib;” [Col. 0800A] “he is finished,” or has been killed, “the wretched one; the one who trampled the earth” by devastating it and killing its inhabitants “has failed.”

“And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment and swiftly rendering what is just.”

Although the Jews refer these words to Hezekiah, who ruled in peace after the death of Sennacherib, they are better understood of Christ. Some of them pertain to his first coming, while others pertain to his second.

The statement, “A throne will be prepared in the mercy of God the Father,” that is, the kingdom of Christ, “and he will sit upon it in the tabernacle of David,” that is, in the Church, is to be referred to his first coming and to the sixth age, in which we now live. For great indeed was the mercy of God the Father, who sent his only-begotten Son to redeem us for our salvation. He now sits upon the throne, or in the tabernacle of David—that is, in the Church—resting and reigning in the hearts of the faithful through faith and love.

But what follows—“judging,” that is, discerning, “and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just”—properly belongs to the day of judgment, when he will distinguish between the elect and the reprobate and render to each what is just: good things to the good and evil things to the evil. He will do this swiftly, saying to the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and to the reprobate: “Depart from me, accursed ones” (Matt. XXV).

“We have heard of Moab’s pride; he is very proud. His pride and his arrogance and his indignation [Col. 0800C] are greater than his strength,” that is, his pride is greater than his strength.

“Therefore”—understand, because his pride and indignation against the Lord are greater than his strength—“Moab will howl against Moab,” citizens against citizens, brother against brother; “all”—understand, all Moab—“will howl.” The prophet returns once more to Moab.

“Speak of their wounds to those who rejoice over walls of baked brick, because the outskirts of Heshbon have been laid waste, and the vineyard of Sibmah”—understand, has been deserted. By saying this—“Speak of their wounds,” that is, their death and captivity, to those Moabites who trust in the joining of brick walls—he both indicates the power of their former prosperity and the wound of their sudden [Col. 0800D] overthrow. Outskirts are the villages and hamlets adjoining cities. Heshbon was a famous city of the Moabites, as was also Sibmah, which is called a vineyard because of the multitude of its people. “The outskirts,” he says, “of Heshbon have been deserted by their inhabitants”—and not only the outskirts, but the city itself. “The lords of the nations,” that is, the princes of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, who ruled over many nations, “have cut off its branches,” that is, they have killed the inhabitants of Sibmah; “they have reached Jazer,” the city; “the lords of the nations have wandered in the desert,” surveying the whole land of the Moabites. Since he had earlier said that Sibmah was a vineyard, he preserves the metaphor by adding “branches.” [Col. 0801A] He likewise preserves the metaphor when he says: “Its shoots have been left behind; they have crossed the sea.” Who has ever heard of anything like this—that vine-shoots should cross the sea? Understand “shoots” as its fugitive sons, who crossed the sea while they were being led to Babylon, abandoned by God.

“Because of this I will weep in the weeping of Jazer over the vineyard of Sibmah.” This is the voice of the prophet lamenting the magnitude of the devastation of the once-famous cities of the Moabites. “Because of this,” he says—that is, because of the devastation of the cities of Moab—“I will weep”; and “in the weeping of Jazer I will also weep over the vineyard of Sibmah.” “I will drench you with my tears”—or, “O Heshbon and Eleale”—that is, I will weep bitterly over you, or I will make you weep as I mourn over you—“because a cry of tramplers has burst upon your vintage and upon your harvest.” [Col. 0801B] The tramplers in this passage are understood as the Chaldean and Assyrian plunderers, who seized for themselves their vintage, harvest, and all their goods.

“And joy and rejoicing will be taken away from Carmel, and in the vineyards he will not rejoice or exult”—understand, Moab will not do so, as the former vintager did. Carmel is an exceedingly fertile mountain between Phoenicia and Palestine, overlooking Ptolemais, on which Elijah prayed (3 Kings 18). It is often used in Holy Scripture for every kind of fertility. “All joy,” he says, “will be taken away from Carmel,” that is, all the fertility over which the Moabites rejoiced will be taken from them. “He will not tread wine in the winepress”—understand, the Moabite will not do so; “I have taken away the sound of the tramplers,” that is, the song which they were accustomed to sing at vintage time.

[Col. 0801C] “Because of this my belly.” This is the voice of the prophet grieving over the ruin of Moab. “Because of this,” he says—that is, because of the destruction of Moab—“my mind will sound like a lyre” as I lament Moab, “and my inward parts,” or the innermost places of my heart, will sound “toward the wall” of the city of Arnon, “of baked brick,” that is, because of the destroyed wall which had been built of baked bricks.

“And it will be, when it appears that Moab has labored on his high places”—that is, on the mountains and roofs—“that he will enter his sanctuaries,” that is, the idols which he thought were holy, “to pray, and he will not prevail”—understand, he will not be able to find help in them. For it is the greatest misery not to have support even in those whom one has always worshiped. [Col. 0801D] When the Assyrians and Chaldeans arrived, Moab went up to his idols, which he had previously worshiped and whose protection he hoped would defend him from his enemies; but this did him no good, because they were senseless. Then it became evident that he had worshiped vanity.

“This is the word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab,” that is, against Moab, “from that time”—understand, from the time when Moab was created. The Lord also said: “The Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter my Church.” Or “from that time” means from ancient times, from the time when he determined these things in his presence, and now the Lord has spoken, saying: “Within three years, like the years of a hired laborer,” and so forth. The meaning is this: just as very few grapes remain after the vintagers, so only a few of the multitude of [Col. 0802A] Moab will remain when the enemies come. But what he says—“Within three years the glory of Moab will be taken away”—can be understood in two ways.

We said above that this prophecy against the Philistines and Moabites began to be directed, after the death of Ahaz, from the time when the prophet uttered it. It may be understood that in the third year after the death of Ahaz the Moabites were devastated by the Assyrians. The meaning is: just as a hired laborer awaits sunset and looks forward through days and nights to the end of his work so that he may receive his appointed wage, so after three years Moab will be destroyed by the Assyrians. It may also be understood of the Babylonian captivity: that after the capture of Jerusalem it was to be devastated by the Chaldeans in the third year; or that within three years no secure respite would be available to it.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0802B] “The burden of Damascus.” Damascus was once the metropolis of the province of Syria, founded by Eliezer, Abraham’s servant. Its king Rezin, because he always offered assistance to the ten tribes in waging war against Judah, is therefore threatened by the Holy Spirit through the prophet Isaiah with captivity and his own destruction. By Damascus, therefore, the royal city, we should understand the whole province of Syria, which was likewise devastated.

Damascus is interpreted as “shedding blood,” or “the blood of sackcloth.” In its literal sense, it can rightly be called “shedding blood,” because there the blood of Abel was shed by Cain (Genesis 4). With reference to these people, however, “shedding blood” or “the blood of sackcloth” is interpreted because they were murderers and shed much blood; they ought to have done penance, which is signified by sackcloth. But because they did not do this, they went into captivity and plunder.

[Col. 0802C] “Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city”—understand, a most powerful city—“and it will be like a heap of stones in a ruin,” after it has been overthrown by the Assyrians.

“Abandoned”—understand, by human beings—“the cities of Aroer will belong to flocks”—understand, as pasture—“and they will lie there,” namely, flocks of sheep in those pastures; “and there will be no one to frighten them.” The meaning is: such desolation will be there that there will be no ambusher to fear, but they will graze there without fear. Aroer is a region of the province of Syria containing many cities. Aroer is interpreted as “tamarisk,” an unfruitful tree that grows in desert and salty places. [Col. 0802D] It is as though he said: just as the tamarisk, an unfruitful tree, grows in solitude, so all the Syrians will be in solitude and without fruit.

“And assistance will cease”—understand, from Damascus—“from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus”—understand, will cease—because it will no longer reign as before. “And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord.” Here “glory” is used ironically for disgrace: what glory will Israel have when it is led into captivity, because it placed its hope in human beings rather than in God? Such glory will also be possessed by the Syrians who promised them assistance in order to turn them away from the fear of God—which they did. Both peoples were led into captivity, they and the others.

[Col. 0803A] “And it will be on that day”—understand, when Syria has been devastated by the Assyrians and Damascus has ceased to be a city—“the glory of Jacob will be weakened,” namely Syria and Damascus, in which he gloried and placed his confidence. “And its fatness will waste away,” that is, the strength of the confidence which he had in the Syrians will fail. Some manuscripts read “its fatty flesh”; but it is better, as the teachers hand down, to read “fatness,” by which the refuge and strength that the ten tribes had in the Syrians are understood.

“And it will be like one gathering in the harvest what remains, and his arm will gather ears of grain,” and the rest that follows up to “on the tops of its fruit.” He gives three comparisons, but they have one meaning. Just as, he says, very sparse ears remain after [Col. 0803B] the backs of the reapers, and just as very few grapes remain—called *racemi* because they remain—after the vintagers, and just as a few olives remain after the olive tree has been shaken, so very few will remain in Damascus and throughout Syria when the Assyrians first, and afterward the Chaldeans, arrive. For under the Assyrian captivity a few remained merely to cultivate the land, while the greater part was transferred to Cyrene, a region beyond Egypt.

“On that day”—understand, when Damascus’s assistance to the ten tribes has failed—“a man will turn toward his Maker,” and so forth. This is said about the remnant of the ten tribes. After the greater part of the people had been taken captive among the Assyrians because of the idols they worshiped—one in Dan and another in Bethel—they were admonished by letters from King Hezekiah, turned to the worship of God, and came to the temple of the Lord which was in Jerusalem, as the book of Chronicles recounts (2 Chronicles 30–31), abandoning the idols which their hands had made and which their fingers had fashioned.

This is what he means: when Damascus has been destroyed by the Assyrians, and the Syrians in whom the ten tribes had placed their confidence have been destroyed, then the man who has been left from those ten tribes will turn and convert to his Maker, Almighty God, and will no longer worship the works of his hands.

“He will not look to the groves and shrines”—understand, the man who has been left from the ten tribes. Groves are wooded and shady places in which, because of their pleasantness, they placed their idols and practiced every delight and pleasure before the altars of the idols. Why they are called shrines has been explained above.

“On that day”—understand, when the Assyrians come and devastate not only Damascus but also the land of the ten tribes—“the cities of his strength,” that is, the cities of the ten tribes, “will be abandoned” by their inhabitants, “like ploughs and fields which were abandoned before the children of Israel.” This is not spoken against Damascus, but against the ten tribes called Israelites. He says that just as, when the children of Israel once came, the Amorites abandoned their ploughs and fled, so the ten tribes themselves will flee when the Assyrians come—fleeing from those before whose presence foreign peoples had once fled.

“And you will be desolate,” O people of the ten tribes, [Col. 0804A] “because you have forgotten the God who saves you.” “You will suffer these things,” he says, O Israel, because you abandoned the God your Savior, who delivered you from Egypt and who by his strength subjected to you the fiercest nations.

“Therefore you will plant an unfaithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot.” As blessed Jerome says, this should be read more explicitly and with irony. The meaning is: because you have forgotten the God who saves you and have not remembered your strong helper, O people of the ten tribes of Israel, should you therefore plant a faithful planting rather than sowing a foreign seed which the Assyrian enemy will eat? You will not therefore plant a faithful planting. A faithful planting is when someone plants and cultivates a vineyard and gathers its fruit himself. An unfaithful planting and a [Col. 0804B] foreign shoot occur when what is sown is not gathered by the one who sowed it, but enemies seize it.

“On the day of your planting, there will be a wild grape, and in the morning your seed will blossom.” It is as though he said: because you have forgotten the God who saves you, you will reap these fruits. When you plant your best vineyard, the Soreth, it will degenerate; and on the day of ripening, when you seek the fruit of your planting—that is, grapes of the finest kind—there will be a wild grape.

“And in the morning,” he says, that is, at the beginning of the harvest, “your seed will blossom.” This can be understood in two ways. In its blossom, you will seem to see the appearance of salvation in it; but before it reaches maturity, it will be consumed by blight. Or “in the morning” means before the proper time your seed will blossom, and therefore it will not reach maturity, as we see with seeds that sprout quickly. [Col. 0804C] Hence what follows: “The harvest has been taken away on the day of inheritance,” that is, when it ought to have been stored in the granary, it was taken away either by enemies or in the manner described above. “And he will grieve bitterly,” that is, over the harvests that have been taken away.

“Because of the multitude of many peoples”—understand, those coming with Sennacherib against my people—“like the multitude of a roaring sea, and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters.” The prophetic word threatens Sennacherib and his army, which he had gathered from various nations in order to destroy the people of the Lord, with a “woe,” that is, eternal damnation and eternal punishment. He came with such a great multitude that the sound of the armies could be compared with the sound of the sea roaring from afar, [Col. 0804D] or even with the sound of many waters.

“The peoples will roar”—understand, those coming with Sennacherib—“like the roar of overflowing waters. And he will rebuke him,” that is, Sennacherib, the lord of such great armies, “and he will flee far away,” from Jerusalem to Nineveh, “and he will be carried away,” from Jerusalem or from this world, “like the dust of the mountains before the wind.”

Did the Lord not rebuke him when he killed his whole army except for ten men? Was he not carried away like dust from Jerusalem when he fled to Nineveh with only a few men? Was he not carried away from this world when he was unexpectedly killed by his sons? The text continues:

“At evening time”—understand, at night, that is, in the final part of the night—“behold, trouble” came upon that multitude, with the angel of the Lord waging war. “In the morning,” likewise, there was trouble, “and his army will not remain.” “This is the portion of those who devastated us, and the portion of those who plundered us.” The prophet speaks in the person of the people of Israel and joins himself to them. What, then, was the portion of the Assyrians who devastated all Israel and seized their goods for themselves? That they should be reduced to dust and ashes, consumed by spiritual fire.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the river of Ethiopia.” The true prophetic word now turns to Egypt and calls it “the cymbal of wings” for the following reasons. [Col. 0805A] The great river Nile is the Gihon, [Col. 0805B] coming through Ethiopia and flowing through Egypt. Before it was divided into seven channels by Alexander the Great, and afterward as well, it flowed with a great sound, descending as it did through mountainous regions—like the sound that is customarily made by the chattering of many birds. Therefore the multitude of this people is compared to the sound of wings: for the swift and rapid flight of birds produces the sound of a cymbal.

It can also be understood simply in this way: since the river itself flows with great speed, it has the sound of wings in the manner of a cymbal. It is called “the cymbal of wings” because of the speed of the crops growing there: just as a bird flies quickly, so that river, by comparison with other lands, quickly produces crops, God so ordering it.

Let us give a fourth interpretation as well, understanding by “the cymbal of wings” [Col. 0805C] the help and protection which they promised to the two tribes. That wings should signify help and protection is shown by the Psalmist, who says to God: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16). Therefore the Lord threatens Egypt with evils because, just as Syria did for the ten tribes, these people, trusting in their own strength and promising protection to the two tribes, removed from them the fear of the Lord.

“Woe,” he says, “to the land of Egypt, because it promises help to the two tribes in the shadow of its wings, just as Damascus did to the ten tribes”—for the land of Egypt is beyond the river of Ethiopia, that is, beyond the channels of the Nile River which flows from Ethiopia. [Col. 0805D] As for what follows:

“He who sends ambassadors by sea”: since among grammarians Egypt is always expressed in the feminine gender, the passage may be construed as follows: the Egyptian people, or Mesraim, who is also Egypt, sends ambassadors—that is, messengers—to the two tribes “in vessels of papyrus upon the waters”; understand, it sends letters promising them assistance.

When it says “in vessels of papyrus,” we should understand either boats made from papyrus, which is of such great size among them that, as is said in the history of Alexander, ships are made from it; or we may understand by “vessels” sheets made from papyrus, on which writing was done in ancient times. For just as something is contained in a vessel, so writing is contained on sheets. A third possibility is that small boxes for messages, made from papyrus, are meant.

With those letters, then, the Egyptians sent their messengers to the two tribes, saying: “Go, swift messengers”—that is, our [Col. 0806A] messengers—“to a nation torn apart,” that is, separated from God and already, for the greater part, from its land, and torn apart by the assaults of the Assyrians; “to a people once terrifying,” while it had God as its protector. “After which”—understand, after that people—“there is no other” so terrifying, that is, no people whose power can be compared with it; “to a nation awaiting”—understand, the help of God or of us—“and trampled down” by various nations, “whose land the rivers,” that is, various kings and princes, “have plundered,” or laid waste.

[Col. 0806B] As for what follows—“to the mountain of the name of the Lord of hosts”—the mountain of Zion can be understood in two ways. First, it may be spoken from the prophet’s perspective, as though someone had asked to what nation or land they should send those messengers, and he had answered: “To the place of the name of the Lord, Mount Zion, to Jerusalem.” It may also be spoken from the perspective of the Egyptian rulers, as though the messengers had asked them, “Go, swift messengers—where,” they say, “do you order us to go?” They replied ironically, sending them to the place where the name of God had once been—that is, to Mount Zion.

“All inhabitants of the world who dwell on the earth, when the standard is raised on the mountains, you will see it, and you will hear the sound of the trumpet.” Almighty God now addresses all the nations dwelling throughout the world, saying: “Pay attention, all nations. When the standard of victory of the Assyrians has been raised on the mountains of Egypt, then you will see”—that is, you will understand—“what I have thought and commanded concerning Egypt, because then you will hear the sound of the trumpet, when the Assyrians begin to fight.”

[Col. 0806C] “For thus the Lord says to me: I will rest in my place,” that is, I will sit in the heavens, “and I will consider”—understand, what the outcome will be. This is what the Lord spoke to the prophet. What follows is this: “As,” he says, “a clear midday is bright, and as a cloud of dew on the day of harvest.” The meaning is: just as nothing in the whole day is brighter than midday, and just as dew is most welcome to weary reapers because it both gives them refreshment and makes the dry stalks easier to tread, so every word which I consider in my place against Egypt will be most welcome to all who believe in me. Or, just as what is said about dew pleases the reapers, [Col. 0806D] so the victory granted by me will please the Assyrians.

“For before the harvest it has blossomed completely”—understand, the Egyptian people—“and ripeness, having germinated.” He speaks metaphorically about the Jewish people under the symbolism of the harvest, but the wording cannot be explained word for word in every respect. The sense, however, is as follows: just as crops that spring up quickly before maturity perish, and those that germinate before the fullness of time are useless, so Egypt will perish, and like useless little branches will be cut down by the Assyrians with sickles or swords.

Hence what follows: “Its little branches will be cut off with sickles,” that is, its inhabitants will be killed by the sword of the Assyrians. “And whatever is left behind” by the Assyrians “will be cut off by the Chaldeans.” “They will be shaken out”—understand, from their land—[Col. 0807A] “and will be left together for the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth”—understand, to devour and tear apart—the very people who have been killed; “and throughout perpetual summer birds will be upon it,” that is, upon the slain people, “and all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it,” that is, upon the slain people.

He speaks hyperbolically. Not all the beasts will come to devour their bodies; rather, by this he wishes to show that a very great multitude of Egyptians were killed there—so great that the beasts which gathered would have enough for themselves in summer and winter and would not need to seek other prey.

“At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts by a people”—understand, Israel—“scattered,” that is, separated for a time from God, from its land, and from its people, [Col. 0807B] “torn apart” by enemies, formerly the most terrifying of all—understand, no other people was so terrifying—“acting, awaiting,” awaiting the help of God for a long time, “whose land the rivers have plundered,” namely, kings and princes of various nations, “to the place of the name of the Lord, Mount Zion.”

The prophetic word turns again to Israel and promises it good things, saying: at that time, after Egypt has been devastated, Judah will no longer hope in the shadow of Egypt, but will bring the gift of faith and good works, as well as other gifts, to the place of the name of the Lord, that is, to his temple. This was fulfilled under Zerubbabel and the other leaders, when, by Cyrus’s permission, they returned from captivity after seventy years. We read about these gifts in Zechariah, where crowns were made in the house of the Lord at his command.

[Col. 0807C]

## CHAPTER XIX

“The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt before him.”

What is said here about Egypt can refer both to its destruction, which came through the Assyrians, and to the Lord’s advent. Let us explain how it applies to Egypt. He calls the swift Assyrian army a “light cloud.” The prophet therefore says that the Lord will not strike Egypt through an angel; rather, he himself will ascend upon the exceedingly swift Assyrian army and enter Egypt. [Col. 0807D] For the Lord ascended upon the cloud of the Assyrians because he inspired them in their hearts to strike Egypt, and he gave them the power to wage war so that he might avenge himself upon his enemies, who had deceived his people through their promises.

When he entered Egypt with the Assyrians, the idols of the Egyptians were shaken. The Egyptians worshiped idols above all nations, and these idols were broken by the Assyrians. Or it happened through the Lord’s action that, when the Assyrians came, the demons worshiped in the idols could no longer give responses. Then the heart of Egypt melted, or its counsel failed, since it found no way to escape its enemies.

The Lord also ascended upon a light cloud when he assumed a human body, not weighed down by any seed of human intercourse, [Col. 0808A] and, with Mary and Joseph, at the angel’s word, fled into Egypt through fear of Herod (Matthew 2). At his entrance it may be that the idols of the Egyptians fell, or even that they were struck dumb, and that the hearts of the wise men of Egypt melted with fear.

Alternatively: Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” signifies this world, which before the Lord’s advent was covered by the darkness of unbelief. The Lord therefore entered Egypt—that is, this world—with a light cloud, that is, with a body not weighed down by the burden of sin. The idols were shaken when people abandoned the idols, hastened in faith to God, and shattered the idols.

“And I will cause Egyptians to rise against Egyptians,” that is, citizens against citizens; “and a man will fight” [Col. 0808B] “against his brother.” This was fulfilled when the Assyrians or Chaldeans came: some wished to surrender themselves, while others strove to resist. Hence a considerable sedition arose among them. This is the gravest evil and great misery: when an enemy arrives, citizens should stir up sedition among themselves.

At the Lord’s advent also, and through the preaching of the apostles, the same discord was fulfilled among believers and unbelievers throughout the world, with some wishing to believe and others unwilling. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father” (Matthew 10), and the rest that follows.

“And the spirit of Egypt will be torn apart in its midst, and its counsel”—understand, the counsel by which it would strive to rebel—“I will cast down,” that is, I will bring it to nothing; [Col. 0808C] “and they will consult their idols and their lords, and the mediums and the diviners.”

When sedition arose in Egypt and the enemy threatened, its spirit would be torn apart—that is, the will of Egypt—because all would think differently and desire different things. Then they would go and consult the demons residing in their idols, and the diviners or prophets, as well as the mediums and soothsayers, asking why this had happened; but it would not help them.

Likewise, at the Lord’s advent the spirit—that is, the will—of this world was divided: some wished to believe, while others resisted. Then the persecutors of the saints and of believers consulted their idols and diviners, asking why such things had arisen in the world, so that human beings, abandoning their ancient custom, might adapt themselves to the new faith.

Mediums are those also called ventriloquists, because they have within them an evil spirit, by whose inspiration they sometimes speak falsely and sometimes, with God’s permission, even speak truthfully. Soothsayers are enchanters who accomplish matters through certain incantations and songs.

[Col. 0808D] “And I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel lords, and a strong king will rule over them, says the Lord.” We read that Egypt was delivered into the hands of many lords. First it was conquered by the Assyrians, then by Nebuchadnezzar, third by Alexander, and finally by the Romans, when Augustus, after defeating Antony and Cleopatra, subjected it to Roman rule. Of all these, the Chaldeans were evidently the most cruel, and the Romans the most powerful.

[Col. 0809A] “And the water will dry up from the sea, and the river”—understand, the Nile—“will be desolate and dry.” This is not said of the great sea, but of the lake called Mareotis. For according to the particular usage of the Hebrew language, as was said above, all collections of waters are called seas. “And the rivers will fail,” that is, the seven channels of the Nile will be diminished in their waters. “The reed and the rush will wither.”

“The riverbed will be stripped from its spring,” that is, both the river and the spring will dry up together. It is natural, as blessed Jerome says, that when captivity comes through God’s anger, pestilence should follow his indignation, and that all the elements should rage against sinners. It could therefore have happened that, when the captivity of the Egyptians came through the Chaldeans or even through the Romans, the waters of the [Col. 0809B] Nile and of the springs failed. It may also be understood hyperbolically, so that because of the excessive tribulation the rivers too are said to have dried up, and the things that were in the rivers to have perished.

Metaphorically, however, in the dried-up river we understand a kingdom laid waste; in its channels, its leaders; and in the reed and rush, all the abundance of Egypt, which is exceedingly fertile in these things.

“And the fishermen will mourn,” or lament, because of the drying of the rivers; “and those who spread nets upon the surface of the water will wither,” that is, will fail. “Those who worked with flax will be ashamed,” that is, those who made seines and nets from flax, “plaiting and weaving fine things”—understand, garments, or even various kinds of vessels which they wove from rushes—“its irrigated places will be,” that is, those of Egypt, “drooping,” that is, dry. [Col. 0809C] “All who made pools for catching fish”—understand, will fail when the enemies arrive.

All these things, as we have said, should be understood hyperbolically; the prophet expressed them in such terms because of the magnitude of the devastation.

“Foolish are the princes of Taphnes; the wise counselors have given Pharaoh foolish counsel.” “Of Taphnes” is a Greek genitive. Taphnis is a metropolitan city of Egypt, in which Moses performed many signs, as is recorded in Exodus. He said this because, when the Babylonian or Roman captivity came, all the counsels of the magicians were nullified. The princes of Pharaoh, who were thought to be wise, gave foolish—that is, useless—counsel, telling him to prepare himself to resist Nebuchadnezzar or the Romans.

[Col. 0809D] “How do you say to Pharaoh: ‘I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings’?” Thus each of his counselors spoke to Pharaoh, wishing to show that his own counsel was good and therefore that it should be adopted: “You are the son of the wise men of Egypt and of ancient kings, and therefore you must fight bravely against the Assyrians or Romans.” For the Egyptians boast that heroes and great gods were the founders of their nation—namely, Isis, Osiris, and Typhon.

“Where are your wise men now?”—understand, when devastation arrives—“Let them announce to you and declare what the Lord of hosts has planned concerning Egypt.” The prophet speaks to Egypt, asking where its wise men are and why they do not announce to it what the Lord has planned concerning it. [Col. 0810A] He then answers himself concerning why they were unable to announce it.

“The princes of Taphnes”—or Taphnis—“have become fools,” understand, those who were thought to be wise; “the princes of Memphis have withered,” or failed, “and they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples.” Memphis is a city of Egypt once filled with magical arts. But where they were thought to be wise, not only did the others fail, but they themselves did as well. When he calls Egypt “the corner of its peoples,” he speaks according to the idiom of the divine Scriptures, which use “corner” for a kingdom because it contains peoples, just as a corner contains two walls, and because it is the strongest part of the whole house.

“The Lord has mixed within it”—that is, within Egypt—[Col. 0810B] “a spirit of dizziness, and they have caused Egypt to err in all its work, as a drunkard errs and vomits.” “The Lord has mixed,” he says, within it—that is, he permitted the wise men of the Egyptians to have a spirit of dizziness, meaning a spirit of error, so that they would not know what they were saying. “And they have caused Egypt to err,” like a drunkard who has departed from his senses and is alienated from every rational understanding, to such an extent that he does not know where he is or what he is doing.

“And Egypt will have no work which the head and the tail, the one who bends and the one who restrains, can do.” Blessed Jerome says that instead of translating “the one who bends and the one who is wanton,” that is, “the old man and the boy,” he was deceived by the ambiguity of the word and translated “the one who bends and the one who restrains.”

[Col. 0810C] The meaning, therefore, is this: when the Assyrians or Chaldeans come, Egypt will have no work—that is, no counsel—which has either a head or an end, or which suits old men or boys. Some, because of excessive age, lose their understanding and become foolish or delirious; others, because of wantonness and childishness, do not know what they are doing.

“On that day Egypt will be like women,” and what follows. On that day, when the devastation of Egypt comes through the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and Romans, Egypt will be like women—weak, unarmed, and without any strength. “And the Egyptians will be astonished,” or will be thrown into extreme amazement, “and they will fear before the face of the movement of the Lord’s vengeance,” which is understood by his hand. “This vengeance he will move through him”: through Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar.

[Col. 0810D] “And the land of Judah will be a terror to Egypt.” Some manuscripts read “a festival.” But blessed Jerome rebukes himself for having translated it in this way, because it is more correct to say “a terror” or “a cause of fear.” The meaning is this: when all the hands of the strong men of Egypt, like the hands of women, have been loosened by excessive fear of the enemies, then the name of Judah will be terror and dread to Egypt, because, while Egypt wished to offer it assistance, it suffered such great evils.

For Egypt will remember that, because of the fear of Almighty God and the love which it took away from the Jews by promising them assistance and protection, such great evils came upon it from the Lord. Hence what follows: “Every”—understand, Egyptian—[Col. 0811A] “who remembers him,” that is, the land of Judah, “will fear before the face of the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he himself has planned concerning him,” that is, concerning Egypt.

What, then, did the Lord plan concerning Egypt? To crush it and devastate it through the Chaldeans and Romans, and to reduce it to nothing.

“In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts. One will be called the City of the Sun.”

Here “day” must be understood as “time.” The priest Onias, not understanding this passage, came to Egypt with a multitude of Jews—as Josephus’s history relates—and built a temple of the Lord and an altar in the city of Heliopolis, in order to fulfill the prophecy of this passage, acting, in fact, against the Lord’s command [Col. 0811B], which says: “You shall not build an altar for me throughout all your cities, but in the place that I shall choose.”

It should be noted that the prophecy speaks not only of that city where the temple was built, which was called Heliopolis, that is, “the City of the Sun,” but also of four others nearby, situated beside the river Corura, which plainly speak the language of Canaan, that is, Syriac. Some think that Syrians and Arabs were settled by Nebuchadnezzar in the cities of Egypt and that, down to our own time, as we have said, they speak the language of Canaan, or Syriac. Others understand the five cities as the five books of the Law, which were first translated in Alexandria.

But it is better to refer all these things spiritually to the Lord’s coming. “In that day,” he says—that is, after the Lord’s Passion—“there will be five cities in the land” [Col. 0811C] “of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan.” Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” signifies this world. Canaan, however, is interpreted as “changed.”

The five cities, therefore, are the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. One of these cities is the City of the Sun, that is, the eyes, through which we draw in light. Whoever serves vices and does not restrain these five bodily senses from evil thoughts and pleasures speaks the Egyptian language, because he remains in the darkness of sins. But those who devote themselves to virtues speak the language of Canaan, that is, the language of the changed, because they have been changed from vices to virtues.

“In that day,” that is, in that time after the Lord’s Passion, “there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt,” that is, in this [Col. 0811D] world, “and a monument beside its boundary belonging to the Lord.”

“And it will be”—understand, that altar or monument—“for a sign” of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, “and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt,” that is, throughout the whole world. By the one altar we should understand all the altars throughout the world. For just as there is one faith of believers, one baptism, and one Church, so there is one altar.

The monument beside that altar is understood as the Gospel and the teaching of the Apostles, which has reached to the ends of the earth. This altar may also be understood as the faith that is one for all believers. For just as sacrifices are offered to God upon the altar, so whatever good we do is offered upon faith. The monument beside the faith is understood as good works [Col. 0812A] and imitation of Christ’s Passion.

“For they will cry to the Lord because of the persecutor, and he will send them a savior and defender who will deliver them.” When, he says, the Lord’s altar has been established in this world, and the Gospel teaching has begun to be proclaimed everywhere, and the time of persecution has come upon them, then those who have believed—namely, the Apostles, their martyrs and followers, and the other faithful—will cry to God the Father because of their persecutors, imploring his mercy. Immediately he will send them a savior, that is, the help of his Son Jesus, whose name is interpreted as “Savior,” and he will be their champion, or defender, delivering them.

Whenever the elect are afflicted, either by persecutors or by the attacks of demons, and they have God’s help by which they are protected, it is as though the Son [Col. 0812B] of God himself is sent by God the Father, since they are saved through his aid.

“And the Lord will be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day.” When God’s mercy has looked upon believers placed in the struggle, the Lord will be known by Egypt, that is, by this world, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day—namely, the inhabitants of this world, whether the persecutors who have been overcome or the believers who have been delivered by God’s help.

“And they will worship”—understand, those who have believed—“God with sacrifices,” namely, of his body and blood, which is offered daily in the Church, “and with offerings,” that is, spiritual ones; “and they will make vows,” that is, good works, “to the Lord, and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike Egypt with a plague, and heal it; and they will return to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them, and he will heal them.”

Let what has been said about the holy martyrs and the other believers suffice. The Lord will strike Egypt—that is, he will permit the elect to be struck by persecutors—and he will heal that same wound, because he will crown the holy martyrs who suffered for him. Persecution does not lead believers to denial, but to testing and reward. “For whom the Lord loves, he reproves” (Prov. III). He scourges every son whom he receives. And even if, he says, they have withdrawn from him for a time, they will return to him, and he will heal them from their sins and from every tribulation.

“In that day,” that is, in the time of the Lord’s coming, “there will be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian will enter Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will serve Assur.”

Before the Lord’s coming, each nation had its own kings, and no one was permitted to pass from one region into another, because travelers were taken for spies. But in the Roman Empire all became one, especially after they believed in Christ. For the entire region between the Euphrates and the Tigris belonged to the Assyrians, and those whom the ancients called Assyrians we now call Syrians, naming the whole by one part.

After the Lord’s Passion, therefore, there was a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, because whoever now wishes to pass from Egypt to Assyria or from Assyria into Egypt has free permission to do so, especially their merchants, who travel from kingdom to kingdom.

As for what he says, “The Egyptians will serve Assur,” he does not mean that afterward they were subjected to him [Col. 0813A], but this refers to the Roman legions, which, being equipped with Assyrian soldiers, guarded Egypt; or because each nation transfers to the other, for purposes of commerce, whatever goods it possesses in abundance.

“In that day Israel will be third with the Egyptian, and the Assyrian will be a blessing in the midst of the land, which the Lord of hosts has blessed.”

We read in the book of Maccabees that the kingdom of Israel was at times claimed by the kings of the Assyrians and at times by those of the Egyptians. But at the Lord’s coming it was subject neither to the Assyrians nor to the Egyptians; rather, the city was established under Roman rule, and it was in the same condition as they were. For just as the Egyptians and Assyrians served the Romans, so did Israel.

It is as though he said in other words: Israel will no longer be harassed as the intermediary between the Assyrians and the Egyptians; it will be third, because those two peoples will serve the Romans just as Israel does, and Israel will be a blessing to them in the midst of the land.

Why a blessing? Because “the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”; that is, Israel will be blessed throughout the world, in the Apostles and in the other believers.

To whom, then, will Israel be a blessing? To that people whom the Lord blessed—that is, Israel will be blessed by the one by whom it was formerly cursed, the one whom the Lord blessed.

“Blessed be Egypt, my people, and Assyria, the work of my hands.” These regions abound above all other regions in a multitude of monks, and therefore they deserve to be blessed by the Lord.

“But Israel is my inheritance.” Why an inheritance? Because he was born there, was raised there, suffered there, and there redeemed the human race; there also he rose again.

## CHAPTER XX

“In the year in which Tartan entered Egypt, when Sargon, king of the Assyrians, had sent him and he had fought against Azotus and captured it, at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amos.”

Azotus is one of the five most powerful cities of the Philistines. Sargon, king of the Assyrians—who is also called Sennacherib and who, as blessed Jerome says, was known by seven names—sent the commander of his army, named Tartan, and through him captured and held it.

At the time when this city was captured, the Lord spoke “by the hand of Isaiah,” that is, through his activity. For the prophet performed such deeds that he was worthy to hear the word of God.

“Go and remove the sackcloth from your loins.” Sackcloth is a garment made of haircloth. This was the prophetic clothing of one mourning the people’s sins.

“And he did so,” going naked and barefoot. What remarkable obedience on the prophet’s part: a man of the highest nobility was not ashamed to walk naked, but obeyed God’s commands, judging nothing more honorable than to remove the sackcloth and, once it had been cast aside, to remain naked. For he had only one tunic, as blessed Jerome says, and that too was made of haircloth.

We have said that he was of the highest nobility because, as the Hebrews relate, he was of such distinguished birth that Manasseh, the king of the two tribes and son of King Hezekiah, took his daughter as his wife.

“And the Lord said: Just as my servant Isaiah [Col. 0814A] walked naked and barefoot, so it will be for three years as a sign and portent against Egypt and against Ethiopia.”

The prophets were men who foreshadowed things, because not only what they said but also, for the most part, their actions prefigured something else, as we can recognize in this passage.

It should be noted that when he says, “It will be a sign for three years,” we must not suppose that the prophet walked naked for three years. Rather, by the number of years we may understand days, as is shown in the book of Ezekiel, where the Lord says to him: “A day for a year”—that is, “I have assigned you a day for a year.”

“So the king of the Assyrians will lead away the captivity of Egypt and the deportation of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks uncovered.”

Understand: for three years, just as my servant Isaiah walked for three days. Then “all will see the disgrace of Egypt,” when he thus threatens it with captivity.

“And they will fear”—understand, the Jews—“and will be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and because of Egypt, their glory.”

The Jews gloried in the Egyptians, who promised them protection, and placed their confidence in the Ethiopians, who were allied with the Egyptians. When, therefore, they heard and saw that both the Egyptians and the Ethiopians were being shamefully threatened with captivity by the Assyrians, they were greatly afraid and ashamed that they had placed their hope in them.

“And the inhabitant of this island will say in that day” [Col. 0814C]. An island is so called because it is situated in the open sea, that is, in the sea. Jerusalem too is called an island because it was battered by the various persecutions of its adversaries.

“Was this our hope, to whom we fled for help, so that they might deliver us from the presence of the king of the Assyrians? And how will we be able to escape?”

“Is this our hope that we had in Egypt and Ethiopia? We fled to them so that they might provide us assistance, yet they were unable to rescue themselves from the evil of captivity. And if they have been captured, how will we be able to escape?”

God’s providence should be considered here: how he destroyed all the kingdoms that had raised themselves against one another in pride and reduced their power to nothing.

Against God’s will, Israel placed its hope in Damascus and the Syrians. Therefore both those who promised assistance to God’s adversaries and those who hoped in them were devastated and taken captive by the Assyrians. Judah—that is, the two tribes—trusted in Egypt, and the Egyptians in the Ethiopians; yet they too were defeated by the Assyrians and Chaldeans.

The Assyrians were proud, thinking that they were victorious by their own strength, but their kingdom perished through the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans and Babylonians raised their heads against the Lord, but were subjected by the Medes and Persians. The Persians and Medes were overcome by Alexander the Great. Alexander the Great, thinking himself to be like God, perished by poison, and his kingdom, divided into parts, was conquered by the Romans and brought under their power.

The Roman Empire, which tore the flesh of the saints as though with iron teeth and claws, now appears to have been destroyed [Col. 0815A], and it will be destroyed on the day of judgment, when the kingdom of Christ arrives.

## CHAPTER XXI

“The burden of the desert of the sea.”

Babylon is called “the sea” in this passage because of the multitude of peoples that was in it. Hence it is also said through Jeremiah to Nebuchadnezzar: “The Lord will make its sea a desert” (Jer. LI). It is called a desert because it has been abandoned by God and emptied of its inhabitants.

“As storms come from the south, it comes from the desert; a harsh vision has been announced to me from a dreadful land.”

This is Babylon’s voice. Just as a violent storm customarily comes from the south, that is, from the southern region, so devastation came to me from the desert of the Medes and Persians, and from a dreadful—that is, terrifying—land, whose very name I cannot hear without fear. A harsh vision has been announced to me: namely, the coming of the Medes and Persians. What is harsher than the evil of captivity? And what is harsher than having not only one’s temporal goods but also one’s present life taken away by those who had themselves been subject?

“He who is unbelieving,” that is, he who is unfaithful to God or to his lord—Darius or Cyrus—“acts faithlessly,” understand, against his lord Belshazzar by killing him; “and he who ravages” or devastates “ravages,” understand, me.

This is Babylon’s voice. Although this happened by God’s permission, Darius and Cyrus nevertheless acted faithlessly against their lord Belshazzar.

“Go up, Elam; besiege Media.” This is the voice of the Lord addressing the multitude of the Persians and Medes. Elam is a province and city of Persia, and by it the people of Elam and Persia are understood.

“Go up,” he says, army of Elam—that is, you who come from the province of Elam—and army of Media, you who are from Media; besiege Babylon.

The meaning is: Do not be afraid, Medes and Persians, to devastate Babylon. Mount your horses and besiege the city.
