“I have caused all her groaning to cease.” This sentence can be understood in three ways: “I have caused all her groaning to cease,” by which she made you and other nations groan; or, that no one now groans under Babylon’s power; or, that she has been afflicted with such great evils that she dares not groan before you.

“Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor.”

This is the prophet’s voice, mourning Babylon in the prophetic spirit. “Therefore,” he says, because Babylon has been filled with such miseries, “my loins are filled with pain,” like the loins of women in labor. Anguish has seized me as I foresee the blood of such a multitude being shed, just as there is anguish in childbirth.

“I collapsed”—understand, into sadness or onto the ground—when I heard, understand, of Babylon’s misery; I was troubled when I saw its destruction in the spirit.

“And my heart,” or my strength, “dried up,” that is, failed; “darkness,” that is, distress and pain, “stunned me,” that is, transformed me into great astonishment.

Or darkness itself stunned him because his eyes grew dim from the multitude of his tears.

“Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me” [Col. 0816A]. This is the prophet’s voice. He calls Babylon beloved because he was a human being and was speaking about human beings; for that reason he could not fail to grieve over their great miseries. It had been made a wonder to him because it had been overthrown so quickly by its subjects.

“Set the table; look out from the watchtower; eat and drink. Rise, princes; seize the shield.”

This can be understood in two ways.

The Persians and Medes are told: Take food, preparing yourselves for the coming battle, so that you may be strong enough to fight and kill the Babylonians. When you have eaten and drunk, rise, take up your weapons, and conquer Babylon. When you have conquered it, look out from the watchtower—that is, complete what has been written on the wall, because God has numbered the kingdom of this man.

Alternatively: O Babylon, prepare a table for your king Belshazzar, and watch what will happen to him after the meal. But you, Darius and Cyrus, who eat with the king, rise and kill the lord, the man.

Or, “look out,” O Belshazzar, and see what has been written on the wall: “Mene, Tekel, Parsin” (Dan. V).

“For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and whatever he sees, let him announce.”

By the watchman in this passage we understand the prophet Isaiah, who watched for what the Lord was about to command concerning Babylon. The prophets were called watchmen, as is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III).

It is as though he said: Appoint yourself as a watchman, and whatever you hear from me or see in the prophetic spirit, announce.

“And he saw”—that watchman, that is, I saw—“a chariot of two horses,” that is, a two-horse chariot, “a rider of a donkey and a rider of a camel”—understand, I saw them; that is, the rider seated there used different animals instead of horses, namely a donkey and a camel.

This rider of two animals is understood as Cyrus, who became ruler of two kingdoms, Persia and Media, after the death of his maternal uncle Darius. The donkey is the kingdom of the Persians, which before Cyrus was insignificant and had no dignity among the other kingdoms. The camel is the kingdom of the Medes, which had always been extremely powerful.

The prophet therefore saw the rider of the two-horse chariot coming because Cyrus himself came with the Medes and Persians against Babylon, together with his uncle [Col. 0816D] Darius.

“And the watchman looked,” that is, I looked, “carefully, with a long gaze.”

“And he cried out like a lion.” The prophet himself, who is called a watchman, is now called a lion because of the strength of his spirit. And because there was doubt about the identity of the watchman, he explains it more clearly, saying:

“Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights.” “Upon my guard,” he says, “I am,” so that I may guard myself from every sin and be worthy to hear God’s words. And upon the Lord’s watchtower I am continually—that is, I am always placed in contemplation of God, and by day and night I am prepared to hear and speak whatever he commands.

“And he answered”—understand, the lion who had cried out above—“and said: Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all the carved images of her gods have been crushed to the ground” [Col. 0817A].

When he says, “Babylon has fallen,” it must be understood that it had already fallen in God’s prophecy. When Cyrus, with Darius, devastated Babylon, not only was the city destroyed, but its idols also were reduced to nothing, when the temple of Bel was destroyed and burned with fire.

“My threshing floor and daughter of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.”

He turns his address toward Jerusalem, which he calls his threshing floor because it was threshed or trampled by various nations. To thresh is to trample.

She is also called “daughter of my threshing floor,” that is, daughter of the temple that was built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, who was also called Araunah (II Reg. XXIV).

The meaning is: O my threshing floor, Jerusalem, which has been crushed by many nations, and O daughter of my threshing floor—that is, of the temple situated on Araunah’s threshing floor—do not consider what I have said about Babylon unbelievable. For these are not my words, but those of the Lord of hosts, and what I heard from him I have announced to you.

“The burden of Dumah.”

Instead of Dumah, the Septuagint translated Idumea, which is a province of the Saracens. Dumah, however, is a region of the province of Idumea, and its inhabitants are descended from Esau, who was also called Edom or Seir.

It is certain that the Idumeans were conquered by the Assyrians or Chaldeans, just as the two tribes were. But when they saw that, after seventy years, the two tribes had returned from Chaldean captivity while they themselves remained in servitude, they implored divine assistance, asking why they too had not been liberated, since they were descended from Abraham and Isaac.

Hence the Lord says: “To me he cries from Seir”—that is, any Idumean who is from Seir and has been carried captive to Babylon and Media, where he is still detained.

“Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Understand: Liberate your people.

The meaning is: O almighty Watchman of Israel, who guard your people with everlasting vigilance and, as though they were sleeping at night, keep watch lest the enemy break in upon them, delivering them from the night of captivity—why do you not protect us too, who are of the same lineage, with similar mercy?

“The watchman said”—there is no doubt that this means almighty God—“Morning has come,” that is, freedom for my people, “and night,” that is, the time of tribulation, has come upon the nation of the Idumeans.

I will give my people the light of joy in returning from captivity, but I will abandon you in the darkness of captivity and servitude, because you rejoiced over the devastation of my people. Since the Idumeans rejoiced at the captivity of the Israelite people, they too were later led into captivity.

“If you seek, seek; turn back and come.” The meaning is: If you seek me, return from captivity with your whole heart.

Alternatively: If you seek my help in a time of need, seek me likewise in prosperity. Turn back to me with your whole mind, and come, drawing near to me through good works, and I will receive you as penitents.

“The burden of Arabia.”

The Arabs are the Saracens and Ishmaelites, tracing their origin to Ishmael and his son Kedar, whose region is called Arabia. Although they ought properly to be called Hagarenes, after their mother Hagar, they prefer, having changed the name, to call themselves Saracens rather than Hagarenes, as though they had sprung not from the slave woman Hagar but from the free woman Sarah (Gen. XXV).

Because, when the Jews were fleeing from the presence of the Chaldeans, the Arabs ought to have given them water and bread, but gave bread while withholding water, so that the Jews might burn more fiercely with thirst and die, the Arabs too were led into captivity.

Although the Arabs did this, almighty God addresses the fleeing Jews, saying:

“In the forest you will sleep in the evening, on the paths of Dodanim.” You, O Jews, who were able to escape the Babylonian siege, will sleep—or rest—in the forest, that is, in the woods of the Saracens, while fleeing from the Chaldeans [Col. 0818B]. You will also rest on the paths of Dodanim. Dodanim is interpreted as “near ones” or “kinsmen.” You will sleep on the paths of Dodanim, that is, on the road leading to your Saracen kinsmen.

“Meet the thirsty one”—understand, my people—“bring water.” The address turns to the Ishmaelites, so that they may bring water to their Jewish brothers fleeing to them.

“Run,” he says, “and bring water to your fallen brothers and to those endangered by the burning heat of thirst, so that they may not perish in the wilderness from the excessive heat of the sun.”

“You who inhabit the land of the South,” that is, the southern land, “meet the fugitive with bread,” my people.

Bring not only water, he says, but bread to the fugitives, so that those whom siege and the persecution of their enemies have afflicted may be relieved by your mercy.

“For they fled from the face of swords, from the face of the sword”—understand, of the Babylonians—“that was threatening, from the face of the drawn bow,” that is, from the face of the Elamites, who are highly skilled archers and came with the Chaldeans, “from the face of grievous battle.”

It is as though he said: Do not despise the wretched, because your captivity will soon come.

“For thus the Lord said to me: Still one year, as one year for a hired man, and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away,” that is, the people and wealth of the Saracens, “and the remnant of the number of archers among the sons of Kedar will be diminished.”

After one year of the Jews’ captivity and the destruction of Jerusalem, the Saracens too were devastated. Therefore he says: Just as a hired man considers the year short and swift, thinking little of his labor as long as he reaches the wages he desires, so very little time remains before you are taken captive, O Saracens!

He therefore gives the reasons why he commanded them to meet the fugitives. They fled, he says, the Babylonian sword; they fled the bows of the Elamites; they fled the threatening sword; and because you did not show them mercy, when their one year of captivity is complete all your glory will be taken away.

As for what he says—“the remnant of the number of the strong archers among the sons of Kedar will be diminished”—this is understood as follows: The remnant of the Saracens left by the Assyrians will be diminished by the Babylonians. The Saracens are archers, as was their father Ishmael, because they dwell in the wilderness.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0819A]

“The burden of the valley of vision,” that is, the weight of miseries and punishments.

He calls Jerusalem a valley. That city, mistress of the nations, which had formerly been called the city of the great king, is now contemptuously called a valley by the Holy Spirit—not because it is situated in a valley, for it lies on a mountain, but because of its transgression of God’s commandments and its idolatry.

So too, when the Lord came in the flesh, he contemptuously calls it a fortress. He says to the Apostles: “Go into the fortress that is opposite you” (Matt. XXI).

And he rightly says, “valley of vision.” For there were the righteous prophets who were worthy to see the Lord’s visions, such as Samuel, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the other saints (IV Reg. XVIII; IV Reg. XXIV; II [Col. 0819B] Par. XXXVI).

It should be noted in this passage that what the prophet says does not refer to the siege carried out by Sennacherib in the time of Hezekiah, but rather to the siege carried out by Nebuchadnezzar in the time of Zedekiah.

“What is the matter with you?” This is the prophet’s voice in the person of the Holy Spirit. “What is the matter with you too, O Jerusalem, that you have gone up, you and everyone else, onto the roofs?”

He rightly says “you too.” For Moab first went up onto the roofs to worship idols, as did the Philistines and the other nations, before Jerusalem did.

It is as though he said in other words: Even if all the nations have gone up onto the roofs to worship idols, why have you gone up, abandoning me, your Redeemer? Therefore he says:

“Full of shouting”—understand, the city—because before the siege it was full of shouts of exultation and [Col. 0819C] joy while they worshiped their idols. When Nebuchadnezzar arrived, it was likewise filled with the cries of sadness and fear.

Those most wretched people went up onto their roofs to worship their idols and ask them for help, but it did them no good.

It is called “a populous city” because of the multitude of peoples who were there; its king continually lived there, as did his army.

It was once “a rejoicing city,” as in the times of David and Solomon.

“Your slain are not slain by the sword.” As we have said, this refers to Nebuchadnezzar and Zedekiah. How, then, was its people killed during the siege? By hunger and thirst. And why was it not in battle? He himself explains.

“All your princes fled.” For, as we read in the book of Jeremiah (Jer. XXXIX), when the city was being besieged by the Chaldeans, King Zedekiah went out at night through a certain opening in the wall, with the princes fleeing with him across the plains of Jericho.

But they were not thereby delivered, because they had not trusted in the Lord. The Chaldeans pursued them, captured them on those same plains, and brought them to Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah. He himself had not gone up to Jerusalem, but had sent his people to capture the city.

Then Nebuchadnezzar ordered Zedekiah’s sons to be killed before his eyes. Afterward he gouged out Zedekiah’s eyes and took him, blinded, in a cage to Babylon. All the princes and everyone whom the Chaldeans were able to capture were either killed or tightly bound, shackled, and taken to Babylon.

“Therefore I said” [Col. 0820A]. This is the prophet’s voice. Because I knew the desolation that would come upon my people, I said to my fellow prophets and fellow disciples: “Withdraw from me, for I will weep bitterly”—that is, grievously—over the desolation of my people.

We said above that when the prophet heard of the evils that were to come upon Babylon, he wept; how much more, then, over the devastation of his own people.

“Do not lean upon me.” This is the prophet’s voice to his fellow disciples, who wished to console him. He was so weighed down with grief as though he were sick in bed; therefore he says: Do not lean toward me, that is, bend over me, to console me.

“For the day of slaughter comes from the Lord God”—understand, it arises—“in the valley of vision,” that is, upon Jerusalem.

“Searching out the wall.” The Lord himself searched out the wall of Jerusalem, because, as will be seen below, each of the Chaldean princes who besieged the city destroyed the section of wall opposite him.

The magnificent one was also over the mountain—that is, over the temple—because the Lord permitted it to be destroyed.

“Elam took up the quiver.” Elam is a city and province in the province of Persia, and the Elamites are excellent archers.

Elam, therefore—that is, the Elamites—will take up the quiver to shoot at the Jewish people. They will also take up “the chariot of a mounted man,” so that they may move quickly through the streets of Jerusalem. Although a chariot has two horses, the one riding above it may nevertheless appropriately be called a horseman.

“And the shield will strip the walls of the house of the Lord” [Col. 0820C]—that is, the strength of the Chaldeans. The shield stripped the walls of the house, which had been covered with plates of gold and marble; that is, the strength and power of the Chaldeans stripped them. For in this passage “shield” stands for strength.

“And your chosen valleys will be full of chariots.” This is the prophet’s voice addressed to Jerusalem. Jerusalem was situated on a mountain and had pleasant valleys around it. When Nebuchadnezzar’s army came against it, a multitude of chariots spread throughout the breadth of the valleys.

The horsemen who entered the city—for that city could not contain the entire multitude—established their positions at the gates, so that none of the Jews could escape by flight.

This is what is said in Jeremiah: “Behold, I will gather all the families of the kingdoms of the north, and they will attack Jerusalem” [Col. 0820D] “and place their princes’ seats above its gates. O Jerusalem, your formerly chosen valleys will be full of chariots, and horsemen will place their seats above your gates” (Jer. XXV).

“And the covering of Judah will be uncovered,” that is, destroyed. He calls the temple of the Lord a covering because it had formerly been covered, that is, hidden, from lepers and unclean people, and also from Gentiles, since they were not permitted to enter within.

Then it was uncovered because the Chaldeans and the nations violated it by entering.

“And you will see”—understand, destroyed—“the armory on that day,” on the day when the Chaldeans capture the city and destroy the temple. Then you will see, O Jews, my fellow citizens, the armory of the [Col. 0821A] “house of the forest” destroyed.

An armory is a place where weapons and missiles are stored. There was a building near the temple of the Lord that David had built for storing weapons, and trees had been planted around it; therefore it is called the house of the forest. The building itself did not have walls of cement and stone, but of wood. For they say that rust forms on iron from the moisture of cement and stones.

“And you will see the breaches of the city of David.” By the city of David he means Jerusalem. As we said above, the city wall was pierced in many places by the enemy, and the breaches multiplied.

“And you gathered the waters of the lower pool,” O daughters of Judah and Benjamin. This is the prophet’s voice. A pool is a lake or cistern where water is collected.

The Promised Land, as blessed Jerome says, although it was extremely fertile, suffered from a great scarcity of water, especially around Jerusalem; therefore they made cisterns to collect water.

The river Jordan flows between Galilee and Judea. The spring of Siloam rises at the foot of Mount Zion. In Jerusalem there were two pools, one upper and the other lower. The upper one could not be seized by the enemy; the lower one could be taken.

When they heard of the Chaldeans’ arrival, they led the water that was in the lower pool—the water that could be seized—through certain pipes and channels into the city, gathering it in one place. They counted the houses of Jerusalem and determined how much water each house would receive. They demolished some houses, fortified the city against the enemy, and caused the pool itself, of which we spoke above, to flow between two walls.

“And you made a pool between two walls.” He speaks of two walls because Jerusalem was surrounded by a double wall, as we read in Ezra: “These dwell in the first Jerusalem, and these in the second.”

“And the water of the old pool,” which once had no water—understand, you will restore it—placing more trust in the water than in the Lord who created it.

“And they did not see its maker,” that is, the Lord, “from afar” until tribulation came upon them.

“And the Lord will call on that day to weeping.” This means that at the time when Nebuchadnezzar comes, he will summon the Jews.

We read in Jeremiah (Jer. XXXVIII) that when Nebuchadnezzar was coming against Jerusalem, before his people began to besiege the city, the Lord sent Jeremiah to Zedekiah and the Jews so that they might repent and he might have mercy on them. But they treated Jeremiah’s word as worthless.

They feasted and said, in their despair: “Let us eat and drink; tomorrow”—in the future—“we shall die.”

He also summoned them to baldness, because in ancient times it was customary, at a time of repentance, to shave the head and cut off the beard.

“‘In my ears this voice of the Lord sounded.’ What was that voice? ‘Will this iniquity of this people be forgiven?’—that is, it will not be forgiven. “If” is used in place of “not.” The Lord says this to Isaiah: “Go to Shebna [Col. 0822A], the master of the temple, who dwells in the tabernacle”—understand, of the Lord. This Shebna was high priest, proud and arrogant, a transgressor of God’s law, oppressing the entire people and turning them away from the Lord’s commandments and worship. Out of fear, he himself handed over the lower part of the city to Sennacherib’s army; therefore the Lord promises him evils that are to come. The things said here, however, do not concern the captivity mentioned above, which occurred in the time of Zedekiah. And what does the Lord say to him?

“‘What are you doing here’”—understand, what are you doing? You who are proud and a ravenous wolf, why do you remain in my house, “or as though anyone were here?” As though he were saying in other words: Why do you sit in my house, not fearing to go into captivity, as though anyone could remain here forever? [Col. 0822B] “For you have cut out a tomb for yourself here.” He did not cut out his tomb within the temple itself; rather, in the city he built a little house in the rock, in a lofty place, hoping that he would not go into captivity, so that the pride and power he had obtained while alive might also be displayed in his death. But he was not buried there, because he was led captive to Babylon. “As a cock is carried away.” A cock is a castrated rooster, which we call a capon. The meaning is: Just as that bird is carried without any impediment, and just as a sack is lifted onto the shoulder without difficulty, so he was carried away from his land. “He will crown you with a crown.” He calls the golden plate a crown, on which the name of the Lord was written and which the priest wore once a year on his [Col. 0822C] forehead. Because of that crown he was afflicted with tribulation. “Like a ball he will throw you into the land.” Just as, if a ball is placed on some mound or mountain, it quickly rolls down into the valley, so he quickly fell from glory and pride into ruin. “And there shall be the chariot of your glory”; he used “chariot” for all glory, power, and dignity, all of which were carried away together with him, and disgrace—that is, the defilement of the Lord’s house—was returned to him.

“And it shall be on that day”—that is, when you have been removed from your position, from your place—“I will call my servant Eliakim, son of Hilkiah.” Eliakim was one of the twenty-four priests, who received the dignity of the high priesthood in place of Shebna, because he was found to be righteous. Shebna was like a ravenous wolf toward the entire people. But he, like a father to both people and priests, [Col. 0822D] calls the house of David the house of the Lord, where there was a golden key. He calls Eliakim himself a peg metaphorically. He calls him a faithful place, where the faithful gather. “And he will be there as a throne of glory”—whose?—“for the house of his father.” His relatives and kin indeed had great honor when they saw him so glorified. “And I will hang upon him”—that is, upon the peg. He still preserves the metaphor. Just as various utensils are hung upon a peg, that is, upon a stake, so the entire adornment of the Lord’s temple rested upon his governance. “On that day, says the Lord, the peg will be removed.” It should be noted here that the things being said do not concern Shebna’s captivity, but rather the final captivity, which occurred in the time of Zedekiah and which we mentioned above [Col. 0823A]. It should also be considered that although above he wished the peg to be understood as the priest Eliakim, he now turns to something else: by the peg he signifies the priesthood itself, which was destroyed after Eliakim’s death. For as long as he lived, everything was conducted honorably in the Lord’s temple. But when he died, that too declined, to such an extent that when the captivity came in the time of Zedekiah, they were without a priesthood.

We can also understand allegorically what is written about Eliakim and Shebna. By Shebna, who was proud and arrogant, the priests of the Jews, the scribes and Pharisees, are signified. By Eliakim, however, humble and righteous, whose name means “rising again,” the Lord Jesus is signified, who rose on the third day and who was made a priest [Col. 0823B] according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX). By the fact that Shebna was expelled from the ministry and Eliakim was appointed in his place, it is signified that the Jewish priesthood was destroyed and that the holy Church was established by the Lord among the nations in its place. He is now the father of those dwelling in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church.

The key of the house of David is understood as knowledge of the Scriptures, which the Lord opened when he granted his disciples understanding of everything that had been written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. He also closed it, because whatever he himself has not opened remains closed. By the key that he carried upon his shoulder we can also understand the authority of the kingdom and the sign of victory—that is, the cross, which he himself carried upon his own shoulder (John XIX)—as we have already said in the passage where it is stated: “Whose authority is upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX). He fixed him in a faithful place—that is, in the Church of the faithful. Hence it rightly follows: “And he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father.” The house of God the Father is the angels, or the hearts of the saints, in which he himself dwells. The throne of glory of that house is the Lord Jesus Christ, because he rises above the whole Church, and he is the head of all the elect and their glory, presiding over them and bringing them into contemplation of himself and of the Father.

“And he hung upon him.” He directed his elect toward his teaching. “He hung various kinds of vessels”—that is, the hearts of the elect. By the vessel of mixing-bowls, that is, by the wine vessel, we should understand the apostles and teachers of the holy Church, who intoxicate us with wine—that is, with the mystery of the divine Scriptures—and who, themselves intoxicated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, also intoxicate us. By the musical vessel, however, we should understand the singers of the holy Church, who by their melodies summon the hearts of their hearers to the love of God.

What is said—“On that day the peg that had been fixed in a faithful place will be removed”—is to be referred to the day of judgment. For when Antichrist comes, after the fullness of the nations has entered, and when Elijah and Enoch preach, all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI). At that time what was said will be fulfilled: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). For many, out of fear of Antichrist and because of affliction, will deny Christ. Then the peg will be broken—that is, the Gospel that had been in the Church—and it will partly cease and pass over to the Jews [Col. 0824A].

## CHAPTER XXIII

“‘The burden of Tyre.’” A burden—that is, a weight of miseries and punishments. Tyre was a very famous city of the Canaanites, full of riches and abounding in wealth. But when Isaiah was prophesying this against it, it had been built on an island in the Great Sea. Later, after a long interval, when Nebuchadnezzar came with his entire army, he wished to make it contiguous with the mainland. As we read in Ezekiel (Ezek. XXIX), every shoulder was stripped bare and every head made bald in his service; but this did not benefit him, because he could not bring it level with the ground.

When those who were in the city saw that they could not resist Nebuchadnezzar, all of them who were able to board ships—I mean those who possessed ships—fled to Egypt, and beyond the sea to Moab and to other neighboring regions. When Nebuchadnezzar saw this, he was inflamed with immense fury, boarded ships, overthrew the entire city, and led away captive all whom he found there, as we shall see below. He returned to Chaldea, and the kingdom of Egypt was given to him by the Lord in place of Tyre.

Later, after it had been rebuilt following seventy years, Alexander the Great came while proceeding to seize Egypt. He divided part of his army there against Tyre, so that they might bring it level with the ground, but they could not. After subduing Egypt, however, he came with a people of Ethiopians [Col. 0824C] and of various nations, went into the forest, cut down trees, brought them to the sea, and filled it with stones, trees, and earth, so that he could reach the city on dry feet—which he did. He captured everyone who was in the city and overthrew it.

The prophet, however, is not speaking of this destruction, but of the one Nebuchadnezzar accomplished. Why did this happen to it? This is the reason. When Jerusalem had been captured by the Chaldeans in the time of Zedekiah, its people had been led into captivity and the temple had been destroyed, Tyre mocked its devastation. Therefore, because it rejoiced over Jerusalem’s tribulation, the Lord did the same to it, sending Nebuchadnezzar against it. Through the prophet he foretold the evils that would come upon it.

“‘Howl, ships of the sea.’” The prophet speaks metaphorically, because ships cannot howl, but rather the people who are in them. In Greek it is stated more clearly: “Howl, ships of Carthage, you who used to come to Tyre for the sake of trade.” Carthage was a colony of the Tyrians, because it was built by them and they inhabited it. And why does the prophet say, “Howl”? “Because the house”—that is, the city of Tyre—“has been laid waste,” from which gold used to come to you, or your commerce.

“‘From the land of Cethim it has been revealed to them.’” He uses Cethim for Greece, as we read in the Book of Maccabees (1 Macc. I) concerning Alexander the Great, that he came forth from the land of Cethim—that is, from Greece. And what was revealed to the Carthaginians by the Greeks? That Tyre had been laid waste. For merchants came to Tyre from Greece, as they did from various nations and cities. When they returned to their homeland, they announced Tyre’s destruction to the Carthaginians.

“‘Be silent’”—that is, do penance—“you who dwell on the island” of the sea: O Tyrians, you are the commerce of Sidon, because their city was built by the Sidonians, and the Sidonians themselves often came to Tyre for the sake of trade. The prophet speaks to the inhabitants of Tyre, as he does also in what follows: “You who cross the sea.”

Who were these people crossing the sea and filling Tyre, set amid many waters, with their wealth? Sidonians, Carthaginians, Greeks, and others who came together there from various nations—especially Egyptians, as is stated below.

“‘The seed of the Nile, the harvest, its produce from the river.’” This verse requires rearrangement, and its connection is as follows: Its produce—that is, Tyre’s produce—is the seed of the Nile River, and its harvest is the seed of the Nile River. The land of the Canaanites, in whose midst the city of the Tyrians is situated, is infertile. But the land of the Egyptians, which the River Nile irrigates, is extremely fertile and very abundant in crops. Therefore the merchants of Tyre crossed the sea and bought from the Egyptians grain, beans, barley, flax, and the other things that land produces, giving in exchange gold, silver, garments, and such valuables. This is what he means: the Egyptians sowed for Tyre; Tyre took the produce, and the harvest and fruit of Egypt were its food. “And it became the commerce of the nations”: all the nations around it flocked to it, because it was wealthier than all the others.

[Col. 0825C] “‘Be ashamed, Sidon,’ says the sea—the strength of the sea—saying:” This verse can be understood in two ways. It may be understood as the prophet speaking in the person of the sea, as though the strait itself possessed a soul and grieved for the city of Tyre. Or it may be understood as the inhabitants of the various cities situated on the sea, to whom Tyre supplied merchandise, saying to the Sidonians who built Tyre, out of compassion for their miseries: O city of Sidon, be ashamed—that is, be confounded—and have mourning and shame over the desolation of your daughter Tyre, because through its pride and fornication it has been reduced to nothing.

“‘I have not labored in childbirth, and I have not borne children.’” This is the voice of the people dwelling on the sea, or even of the sea itself, if one may speak in this way. It does not say that it did not bear children for this reason, but in grief it says that its children were not such as could defend Tyre; or else that they did not reach maturity—that is, completion: its virgins and sons were killed by their enemies before they had fully grown.

“‘When it is heard in Egypt.’” The voice of the prophet. Egypt was close to the city of Tyre, and they were joined to one another by bonds of friendship. For the Tyrians brought to Egypt what the Egyptians lacked, receiving grain and the other things more fully mentioned in Ezekiel in return. Therefore he says: When the Egyptians hear that Tyre has been overthrown, they will grieve over it.

[Col. 0826A] “‘Cross the seas.’” The prophet’s voice, giving counsel to the Tyrians. As we said above, when they had considered that they could not resist Nebuchadnezzar, most of them boarded ships and fled across the sea; another part, lacking ships, remained in the city. The prophet therefore speaks to those who escaped by flight, saying: Cross the seas. To those who remained behind in the city he says:

“‘Howl, you who dwell in Tyre,’” for you will be captured by the Chaldeans. “Is this not your”—understand, your city—“which gloried because of its antiquity?” The prophet speaks to the merchants of Carthage and of the other cities. Tyre was lifted up in pride, saying: I was built in ancient times, I have been filled with riches, and I am mistress of all merchants. And because it gloried, puffed up by pride, “its own feet will carry it to Chaldea.” He now speaks of those whom Nebuchadnezzar led to Babylon.

“‘Who planned this against Tyre,’” so that it might be destroyed, though “formerly” it was “crowned”? The prophet asks who planned this, and he himself shows who planned it when he says: The Lord of hosts planned this. In what way was it crowned? Just as a king, wearing a diadem on his head and a scepter in his hand, stands higher and more distinguished than all his people, so Tyre, sitting in the midst of the sea and full of riches and commerce, was wealthier and loftier than all the cities. It is also called crowned because all the cities and merchants situated around it flocked to it from every side, surrounding it as though with a crown. Traders are called *institores* because they are occupied with business and commerce. The prophet therefore says that it had such distinguished and noble merchants and traders that they could have been princes and renowned men in kingdoms.

“‘The Lord planned’” that it should be brought down “from pride to ruin, and that he should put all the renowned men of the earth”—understand, of the Canaanites—“to shame. Cross over your land,” O daughter of the sea, “like” someone who quickly crosses “a stream.” Why this? “Because you have no belt,” that is, you no longer have the strength to resist the Chaldeans. By “belt” understand strength or power, because human strength resides in the loins that are girded with a belt (Job XXXVIII).

The prophet gives the Tyrians counsel: “He will stretch out his hand over the sea.” This is the voice of the prophet. Who will stretch out his hand? The Lord. For what purpose? So that the kingdoms may be disturbed. Which kingdoms? Those of the Egyptians, Moabites, and the others around Tyre. When all the kingdoms around Tyre heard that Tyre was suffering the ruin of plunder, they were struck with immense fear and said: What shall we do now, when our queen has been given over to plunder? Certainly we shall be captured by the Chaldeans.

So it happened with the kingdom of Egypt. We read in Ezekiel (Ezek. XXIX) that the Lord gave the kingdom of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar for the overthrow of Tyre, saying: “Son of man, [Col. 0827A] Nebuchadnezzar has not been given payment for the service with which he served me against Tyre; give him Egypt in place of Tyre.”

“‘The Lord commanded against Canaan.’” What he said above—“He will stretch out his hand”—he now says as “he commanded.” The stretching out of God’s hands is his commanding. His command is his will; his will is action. By that power he commanded Nebuchadnezzar. What did he command? That he should come against Canaan “and crush its strong men”—that is, the strong men of the Canaanites. As we have already said, Tyre was a city of the Canaanites; their strongest men lived in Tyre, and in the crushing of Tyre their strong men were killed.

“And he said”—understand, the Lord—“You shall no longer add,” and so forth. Calumny is accusation. Tyre is called the daughter of Sidon because the Sidonians built it. Tyre gloried in its riches, but was accused by all around it of being proud. Therefore he said: O rod, daughter of Sidon, after you have been destroyed you will no longer glory, and the peoples will no longer accuse you of being puffed up with arrogant pride. “Rise up, cross over to Cethim.” The prophet speaks to Tyre. If you go to Cethim—that is, to Greece—you will have no rest. He speaks of those who crossed the sea and fled to Egypt and Greece. And why did they have no rest there? Because they were seized by Nebuchadnezzar.

“‘Behold, the land of the Chaldeans—such a people did not exist.’” It should be noted that he did not say, “will not exist,” but “did not exist.” For it is true that until the death of Nebuchadnezzar the Chaldeans and Assyrians were the strongest of all nations [Col. 0827C]. Afterwards, however, the people of the Greeks and Romans became stronger.

“‘Asshur founded it’”—understand, that land. Asshur was a very powerful and strong man, from whom it was founded—that is, from whom it took its origin. This is the voice of the prophet. Asshur himself came against you, O Tyre; “they led its strong men”—or its captives—“into captivity.” Whose captives? Tyre’s. “They undermined its houses.” When Nebuchadnezzar came to Tyre by ship, he overthrew not only the walls but also all the houses; and what had previously been the commerce of cities became a drying-place for salted provisions for seventy years.

“And it shall be on that day: You will be forgotten, O Tyre, for seventy years, as the days of one king.” The prophet’s voice: Just as Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed and the people remained in captivity for seventy years, so too Tyre, which mocked their misfortunes. But it is not without significance that he says, “as the days of one king.” Do we read in any history of a king who reigned for seventy years? David reigned for forty years, and his son Solomon for the same length of time. Uzziah, however, who is also called Azariah, was struck with leprosy and held the government of the kingdom for fifty-two years. The prophet therefore says: O Tyre, just as the days of some king who reigned for seventy years are consigned to oblivion after he has breathed out his spirit—perhaps if it happened to him to reign for so many years—so you and all your glory will be forgotten by all peoples for seventy years.

“‘After seventy years, Tyre will be like the song of a prostitute.’” [Col. 0828A] This verse concerns its restoration, which occurred after seventy years. Prostitutes who have had many lovers, after being abandoned by them either because of deformity or old age, commonly sit in their house, compose songs for themselves, and sing in order to receive consolation. Or, recalling what they previously did, they commemorate it in song. So too Tyre acted after it returned.

“‘Take up the lyre,’” O prostitute. The prophet gives it advice about how to do penance so that it may escape the Lord’s judgment, saying: “Take up the lyre and go through your city,” singing your miseries, so that the Lord may have mercy on you. “Sing well; repeat the song.” What follows from this burden concerns its return. Therefore the prophet urges it to sing and to repeat the song of its miseries, so that it may recall its former evils, because of which it departed from its own soil and was destroyed, lest similar things happen to it again. For the teachers say that the power of musical art is such that if it finds a joyful person, it makes him more joyful; but if it finds someone sad, it increases his sadness.

“‘The Lord will visit Tyre after seventy years.’” This visitation is to be understood positively, because after its return it was filled with merchandise, as it had been before. “And again she will fornicate.” “Fornication” is used here for commerce, because after its restoration it conducted business with all the nations.

“And its commerce will be consecrated to the Lord.” In what way was its merchandise consecrated to the Lord? Blessed Jerome says that after the children of Israel returned from captivity under the leaders Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, and the Tyrians followed them, they were joined in friendship not long afterward. Their riches were neither concealed nor stored in treasuries out of greed; rather, they came to Jerusalem and offered gifts and sacrifices to the Lord—gold, silver, garments, gems, sheep, oxen, and linen cloth. Part of these remained for the adornment of the Lord’s temple, while another part went toward the needs of the priests. Therefore its commerce was consecrated to the Lord.

We can also understand this in another way. After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, when the outstanding preacher Paul preached to the Tyrians and Sidonians, they were converted with the full desire of their minds to faith in the Savior. Then its commerce was consecrated to the Lord, because they did not hide it in the secret places of their treasuries out of greed and avarice, but built churches from it, provided expenses, and supplied what was necessary for the disciples preaching the Gospel—namely, the disciples of blessed Paul, whom he left among them—as well as for the poor and needy for the name of Christ.

What he adds, “so that they may eat,” understand, those who dwell before the Lord, “until they are satisfied, and be clothed until old age,” can be referred to both groups, Jews and believers, who dwelled before the Lord—that is, fulfilled his will. They ate from their goods until they were satisfied, as we have already said, and were clothed in their garments until old age—that is, until sufficiency [Col. 0829A].

## CHAPTER XXIV

“‘Behold, the Lord will lay waste the earth.’” Up to this point the prophet has described the burdens of various nations and cities—namely, those of the Babylonians, Assyrians, Egyptians, and many others. But the things said here concern the day of judgment, generally concerning all the inhabitants of the world. For he passes from the particular to the general.

What does the prophet mean by saying that the Lord will lay waste the earth? Will it be so destroyed that it will cease to be what it is? The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Luke XXI). How? Through change and improvement, as John clearly shows in his Apocalypse: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. XXI). For if it passed away in such a way, it would cease entirely to exist. Solomon would certainly not speak in this way: “A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. I). Therefore the Lord will lay waste the earth at the final judgment—that is, he will make it pass through fire, changing it from the form it now has into a better one.

“And he will strip it bare of its inhabitants”—of human beings, beasts, serpents, trees, and every filth or impurity—“and he will afflict its face,” because it will pass through fire. For when a physician treats a sick person with fire, although he restores him to health, he nevertheless afflicts him. “And he will scatter its inhabitants”—that is, he will divide them. When will this happen? When the sheep are separated from the goats, “the righteous from the unrighteous” (Matt. XXV). In the present age the good and evil are mixed together. Then it will be otherwise, because the wicked will go into the punishment of eternal condemnation, and the righteous into the joy of eternal rest.

“And it will be: as with the people, so with the priest.” A good layperson will be rewarded with a good priest, and an evil layperson will be condemned with an evil priest. There will be no distinction between master and servant, between maidservant and mistress, if both are good, or both women are good or evil. The same must be said of the rest.

A moneylender (*foenerator*) is one who lends or provides something to someone. Some say that *mutare* means to return changed money, as a horse in exchange for silver. Others say that because a loan is called a *mutuum*, it means, “what is mine is yours.” The expression is derived from legal usage.

“‘The earth will be utterly laid waste,’” because everything in it will be laid waste and burn. Why? “Because it will be plundered by the Lord.” And how will it be plundered? Because its inhabitants will no longer be in it.

“‘It mourned and flowed away,’” for “it will mourn and flow away,” that is, it will fail. And how can the earth mourn? By “earth” we should understand its inhabitants. “It flowed away”—that is, the world and the height of the peoples will fail: all the proud and powerful will become weak on that day.

[Col. 0830A] “And the earth has been killed.” Who can kill the earth? Does it have a soul? By “earth” earthly people and those living according to the flesh are understood. Therefore the earth has been killed by its inhabitants: that is, earthly people have been killed by other earthly people who dwelt on the earth. “Because they transgressed the laws and changed the right.” These words pertain to what follows. What is law is also right, covenant, and friendship. Whoever observes the law well and properly undoubtedly deserves to be joined to God through good works, and after being joined to him will have a covenant with him—that is, friendship. As he himself says to the apostles: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV).

The Jews boasted of the nobility of their lineage, saying: We are a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and children of Abraham; the law was given to us alone. But in this they were lying, that they alone had received the law. For almighty God commanded all human beings to observe the natural law. What is the natural law? “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.”

The Jews therefore despised both the natural law and the written law, and, in addition, the Gospel, regarding them as nothing. The nations, however, transgressed both the natural law and the Gospel; and it should be understood that this was said concerning those who did not imitate Christ.

“‘Therefore a curse will devour the earth.’” Why? Because they transgressed the laws. By “earth” earthly people are to be understood. And what will that curse be which will consume and destroy the whole earth? A terrifying sentence against all, when the judge of all says: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

“‘Therefore its inhabitants will go mad.’” To go mad is to be turned into madness and extreme stupor. The inhabitants of the earth are its lovers, who devote themselves to earthly desires and worldly cares. They will be turned into madness by their love of it, because they will see the one whose commandments they despised and will hear their own perpetual condemnation.

“And few human beings will be left.” This pertains to the elect. When all the reprobate have been plunged into the abyss of eternal torment, a few elect will remain. As the Truth himself said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX and XXII). But if we pay close attention, they will not be few. They will possess perfection in their own number, but in comparison with the reprobate they appear few in number.

“‘The vintage mourned.’” The prophet speaks of the future as though it were past. “It mourned and became weak,” for “the vine will mourn and become weak.” How can a vintage or vine mourn? It must be understood metaphorically. By the vintage or vine we should understand wine-drinkers and drunkards. As the prophet said above: “Woe to those who are powerful for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness.” When will these people mourn? On the day of judgment, because, as the Apostle says: “Drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI).

“‘The sound of those rejoicing ceased’”—for “it will cease on the day of judgment.” The remembrance of the joy of this age will be the greatest sorrow.

[Col. 0831A] “Bitter will be the drink” for those who now, in this age, delight in various meals and various drinks. On the day of judgment it will be bitter for those who drank it in this age.

“‘The city has been crushed,’” for “it will come to an end.” By one city all cities are to be understood; or by this city of vanity, Babylon, which was the city of cities, it may be understood. Or otherwise: by one city this world may be signified, which will then come to an end. And why does he call it vanity? Because whatever passes away and is changeable is vanity, according to what Wisdom says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Wis. I).

“‘There will be a cry over wine in the streets.’” *Platos* is a Greek word, and it derives from breadth. What, then, should “street” signify in this passage except those who wander through the breadth of this age? Hence the Truth himself says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII). “Wine” here signifies error, because those who are drunk err and go mad. Therefore, when the day of the final judgment comes, there will be a cry among those who serve earthly cares and desires over their own error, because when they ought to have produced grapes, they produced sour wild grapes.

“‘Solitude has been left in the city.’” What we have already said above about one city must also be said about one town, “because these things will be in the midst of the earth.” What will be in the midst of the earth?

“‘Therefore there will be solitude in the city’”—that is, in this world—“because these things will be fulfilled in the midst of the earth,” namely, what has been said up to this point: the Lord will change the earth. By “the midst of the earth” he means Jerusalem, which is the navel of the earth.

Many who hold this opinion say that the Lord will sit upon the Mount of Olives, from which he ascended into heaven. The Lord will not descend to the earth for judgment, but will sit in the air, in a cloud opposite the Mount of Olives. He will not therefore descend to the earth, but will sit in a cloud in the expanse of this air opposite the Mount of Olives, surrounded by the ranks and powers of heaven. He ascended in a cloud, and in a cloud he will come again, as the angels said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). And the Lord himself says: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds” (Luke XXI). He who came before in humility will then come with great power [Col. 0831D] to avenge himself upon his enemies.

“‘As when a few olives remain, and clusters after the gathering.’” This pertains to what follows. The prophet speaks of the elect, saying that just as a few clusters remain when the vintage has ended, so a few elect will remain on the day of judgment—not few in their own number, but few in comparison with the reprobate.

Those who remain “will praise the Lord when he has been glorified, and will neigh from the sea”—that is, from this world, understand, having been delivered. They will not neigh like horses; rather, just as those who rejoice utter a neighing sound, so those who remain will emit a voice of joy.

“‘Therefore glorify the Lord in teachings.’” The prophet urges the apostles and teachers of the holy Church to praise the Lord, and says: O apostles and teachers who have been taught, because the Lord has been glorified and you have seen your reward and the punishment of the reprobate, glorify the Lord in your teaching. “And in the islands of the sea”—understand, preach—the name of the Lord.

“From the ends of the earth we have heard praises.” The voice of the elect on the day of judgment. Who are the ends of the earth? The patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and teachers of the holy Church. And why are they called the ends? Because just as the earth stands by its boundaries and limits, and cannot stand without them, so this world stands by their teaching and merits. For in Hebrew, as blessed Jerome says, it is written, “From the wings of the earth we have heard praises.” The wings of the earth are to be understood as the saints, who fly from earthly things to heavenly ones, from transitory things [Col. 0832B] to those that endure and are everlasting.

For the elect will say on the day of judgment: “From the ends of the earth,” or “from the wings,” “we have heard” these things which we now see, O Lord our God—your praises and your greatness—you who always foretold these things to us, inviting us to them and admonishing us to fulfill your will with all our strength. We have also heard the glory of the righteous—either specifically the glory of the Lord, who is the way and the truth, or generally the glory of all the righteous.

And I said: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me; woe is me.” The voice of the prophet. It is as though he were saying in other words: “I know, indeed I know—but I cannot say it. And because I cannot say it, woe is me.” When the prophet had seen and understood in the spirit the incomprehensible torments of the reprobate and the ineffable glory of the righteous, and because of their magnitude could neither express nor write them with his mouth—things which, as the Apostle says, will be such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man”—he said in his anguish: “Woe is me, because I am not worthy to utter what I have seen.”

“Transgressors have transgressed,” that is understood to mean, the impious have transgressed the law of God. To transgress is to cross over; to cross over is to go beyond. The voice of the prophet concerning the reprobate. “Terror” means fear. A “pit” means a ditch, a snare, or destruction.

The prophet therefore says: O you who dwell on the earth—that is, you who live according to the flesh and devote all your efforts to earthly things—terror will come upon you. These words can suitably be referred both to the times of the apostles or martyrs and to the times of Antichrist. For when persecution arose from without against Christians, there were many Christians who were still imperfect in faith and who, fearing torture, said within themselves: “Since this persecution is pressing us so hard, I will deny Christ in words only and afterward do penance. Otherwise I cannot escape.” But while saying this, through fear he fell into the pit of denial. And while he wished to do penance, he was killed by his persecutors at the instigation of the devil. Then from the pit he fell into the snare of eternal damnation. So it will also be in the times of Antichrist.

“For the floodgates from on high have been opened,” that is, from the heavens. In Greek, *cataractae*; in Latin, they are called “windows.” And why have those windows been opened? So that almighty God may take vengeance on his enemies. Blessed Jerome says: “For wherever they turn, they will not escape the judgment of God.” And how are those windows opened? Because he sees everywhere and is present everywhere; in our mouth he speaks. For when almighty God does not punish sinners, he appears to be absent. When he strikes them, he then appears to draw near to them.

“And the foundations of the earth will be shaken.” According to the historical sense, all these things will be fulfilled, because there will be a great earthquake. Allegorically, however, by the foundations of the earth are understood the rulers of this age who live according to earthly things. Likewise, by the earth are understood people who cling to earthly things.

“The earth will be violently shaken”—that is, it will be moved by disturbance, whether the earth itself or its inhabitants. For in an instant everything will pass away from it. “And its iniquity will weigh it down” [Col. 0833B]—the earth cannot commit iniquity. Therefore the earth will be weighed down by the iniquity of earthly people, “so that it will not rise again,” that is, so that it will no longer be the habitation of human beings.

“And it will come to pass on that day”—that is, on the day of judgment—“that the Lord will visit,” for evil, namely, and not for good, “the host of heaven on high.” The prophet calls Antichrist and his companions, the demons, the host of heaven; they move through heaven, that is, through this air. “And the kings of the earth.” The kings of the earth are those who pursue earthly things and never raise their minds to heavenly things. Upon such people almighty God will visit on the day of judgment, for he will repay them according to what they deserve (Matt. XVI; 1 Cor. III). The princes of the demons may also be called kings. Thus the angel says to Daniel (Dan. X): “But the prince of the Persians resisted me.” And shortly afterward: “And behold, the prince of the Greeks was coming.” And the distinguished preacher says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI).

“And they will be gathered into one gathering, like a bundle, into the pit; and they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited.” Many have discussed this verse of the prophet Isaiah in various ways, but they have not all held the same opinion. Origen says that after they have received from the Lord that terrible sentence, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), they will be visited after many days—that is, after a thousand years, when the judgment has been completed by the Lord.

None of the holy Fathers, however, confirms this opinion; rather, they all reject it, keeping before their eyes that sentence of the Lord: “The impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Whatever is eternal is without end. Therefore, just as the Lord appointed eternal joy for the righteous, so he appointed eternal punishment for the impious. This sentence appears obscure for the reason that after the prophet said, “and they will be shut up there in prison,” he immediately added, “after many days they will be visited.”

When the presbyter Acca asked Bede by letter about this sentence, Bede replied in these words:

“I confess, dearest brother, that I would by no means dare to say that I understand what the prophet Isaiah thought and intended to be understood in this sentence. Nevertheless, what the prophet himself understood purely and catholicly in these prophetic words must be stated.

“‘And they will be gathered,’ he says, ‘into one gathering, like a bundle, into the pit.’ This can be understood of the souls of those whose bodies, when the Lord visits them, will be given over to death. Although they do not all depart from their bodies at the same time, nevertheless each and every one, in its own order, will be gathered into the same bundle, and they will be enclosed in the same prison of everlasting punishments, according to the disposition of the strict Judge. Thus those who attacked the Church with a like mind, because they entered into battle against God together, may together suffer punishment. For those who are equal in guilt are to be condemned together in punishment: the greedy with the greedy, the lustful with the lustful, the perjurers with the perjurers.

“This is what the Lord makes clear when he says concerning the weeds: ‘Bind them into bundles and burn them.’ Therefore, when Antichrist has perished, the ministers of his deceptions will be gathered into the prison of infernal punishments. ‘And after many days they will be visited’—namely, at the time of the resurrection of all, when their souls will be summoned briefly from the underworld for this one purpose: that, having received their bodies, they may immediately, after the judgment has been completed, return with the other sinners to their punishments.

“For that the universal judgment will not come immediately after Antichrist has been destroyed, the prophet Daniel testifies. In the final vision of his prophecy, while describing the events of that kingdom and encompassing the duration of the same kingdom in one thousand two hundred and ninety days, that is, three and a half years, he suddenly added: ‘Blessed is he who waits and reaches the one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days’ (Dan. XII).

“Blessed Jerome explains this verse as follows: ‘Blessed,’ he says, ‘is the one who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits forty-five days beyond the appointed number of days, during which the Lord will come in his majesty.”’ Why there should be a silence of forty-five days after the killing of Antichrist belongs to divine knowledge—unless perhaps we say that the delay of the kingdom is a testing of the saints’ patience.

“It must also be noted that he says, ‘and after many days they will be visited.’ For the expression ‘many days’ is more suitably assigned to the times of this age, which are multiplied by the alternating succession of days and nights, than to the future age, when the passage of hours will cease: the Lord will be eternal light for the saints, and the impious will be sent into outer darkness [Col. 0834D] (Matt. XI). Therefore it must rightly be understood that those who are now held in the prison of infernal darkness will be visited after many days of this fleeting age—at that hour, certainly, when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. ‘And those who have done good will come forth into the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment’ (John VI).”

Thus far the sense and words of the distinguished teacher Bede.

It is also possible, as some say, that the order is inverted. After the prophet had said somewhat earlier, “it will not rise again,” speaking of those who, in the times of Antichrist, denied faith in the holy Trinity and died before he was killed by the Lord, he should have added: “And after many days [Col. 0835A] after the killing of Antichrist they will be visited,” and then have added:

“And it will come to pass on that day”—that is, on the day of judgment—“that the Lord will visit him, and the kings, and the host of heaven,” that is, the multitude of those who imitated him, “and he will shut them up in the prison” of eternal punishment.

As for what was said above, “The Lord will visit the host of heaven on high,” it is to be understood in this way: The Lord will visit the host of heaven on high by sending an angel from heaven, who by divine power will destroy the man of sin, the son of perdition, who is lifted up and exalted above everything that is called God or that is worshiped (2 Thess. II). Blessed Gregory judges or understands that this will be done through the archangel Michael.

Therefore the host of heaven will be visited when Antichrist is destroyed, because, once he has been killed, the power of the evil spirits that had aided him by displaying lying signs will be weakened and brought to nothing. He himself can also, not without reason, be counted among the host of heaven, because he will presume to exalt himself not only above all angels but also above every height of the divine majesty.

The kings of the earth will also be visited—those who are upon the earth, namely the ministers of Antichrist and the supporters and accomplices of his factions, frauds, and schemes, who exercise impious dominion over weak and earthly minds. There is no doubt that they will perish, as is recognized to have happened among those who rose up against the Church. It should be noted that he does not say explicitly, “over all the kings of the earth,” just as he does not say “over the whole host of heaven,” but simply: “The Lord will visit the host of heaven and the kings of the earth.” This is understood to have been said not concerning the downfall of all in general, but concerning the particular downfall of certain evil human beings and angels.

“And the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded.” This too will be fulfilled at the time of the visitation, that is, on the day of judgment. “The moon will blush,” that is, it will waste away. Will the moon blush and the sun be confounded in such a way that they fall from heaven? No. But how this will happen the Lord makes clear when he says: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Matt. XXIV; Luke XXI).

Blessed Augustine says that neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars will lose their light, since elsewhere the same prophet says: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days.” Rather, in comparison with the true light, which is Christ—as he himself said, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII), and John said of him, “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I)—all the stars and lights will appear to be darkened. What brightness does the light of a candle provide if it is placed in the midst of the sun’s rays, or what increase of light does it give to those who see it? None.

Or otherwise: When the reprobate are placed in indescribable fear and terror, everything will appear to be darkened. As for what the prophet adds, as though in the same passage at its conclusion, saying: “When the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the sight of his elders” [Col. 0836A], this will rather be fulfilled after the judgment has been fully carried out. When the impious have been removed so that they may not see the glory of God, all the saints will enter the dwelling of the heavenly city to contemplate forever the appearance of their Creator.

He calls Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints “elders.” In their sight the Lord will be glorified when the impious go into eternal punishment, but they themselves into eternal life (Matt. XXV). The glorification of the Lord, however, is not to be understood as that by which he will appear to all, both the impious and the righteous, in the judgment, but as that by which he will be revealed only in the sight of his elders, that is, the elect.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0836B]

“Lord my God, I will exalt you.” The voice of the prophet speaking about the day of judgment: “I will exalt you,” that is, I will proclaim you to be great. “I will confess your name,” that is, I give you thanks. The prophet gives thanks to the Lord God “because he has done marvelous things and faithful ancient purposes. Amen.”

He did marvelous things when he repaid the righteous and the impious according to what they deserved. His purposes were ancient because he predestined his elect before the foundation of the world. As the Apostle says: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I).

“Because you have made the city into a mound.” Some copies read “into a tumult.” It was made into a mound when it was destroyed. For when a city is destroyed, it is reduced to a mound. “The house of foreigners”—that is understood to mean, you have humbled it—“so that it is no longer a city and will not be rebuilt forever.”

The Jews are called foreigners because they are alienated from God, as it is written in the Psalm: “Foreign sons have lied to me” (Ps. VII). And in the Gospel, the Lord says: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII). As for the statement that they will not be rebuilt forever, this is understood as above. For it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings XXV), but afterward rebuilt by Nehemiah and Jesus the high priest (1 Esd. I). It was destroyed again by the Romans, but later restored by Aelius Hadrian—not, however, in the same place where it had previously stood. And although it was rebuilt, afterward it did not return to its former condition, as it had been in the times of David and Solomon.

[Col. 0836D] “Because of this”—that is, because you repaid the impious Jews what they deserved—“the strong people of the nations will praise you, and the city,” that is, the Church of the nations, “of the strong will fear you.” For the nations were strong and powerful in enduring torments for the name of Christ.

“Because you have become strength for the poor.” The prophet praises God the Father. He calls the Lord Jesus “poor”: “Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor” (2 Cor. VIII). For he himself says: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII).

He also calls him needy: “You were hope from the whirlwind”—that is understood to mean, you were consolation amid the storm of his Passion—because, with you working through it, he endured the Passion patiently. For he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again.”

“You were a shelter from the heat,” that is, you were protection from the heat of death, so that he might rise on the third day. “For the spirit of the powerful is like a whirlwind driving against a wall.” He calls the Jews “the powerful,” and the Lord “the wall”; the whirlwind is their power. For just as a wall struck by a whirlwind remains unmoved, so the Lord was indeed struck by the Jews at the time of his Passion, but they could not prevail over him. Although they killed his humanity, he quickly rose again through his divinity, giving it life.

For they said: “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” that is, the wood of the cross into his flesh, “and let us destroy his memory from the earth” (Jer. XI). But by the very means through which they attempted to remove his memory, they spread his name throughout the whole world.

“Just as the tumult of foreigners is in heat and thirst”—that is, you will humble the Jews—“and as, in the heat beneath a scorching cloud, you will cause the shoot of the powerful to wither.” He gives two comparisons concerning the Passion of the Lord. Some manuscripts read: “Just as heat in thirst,” which can be understood in two ways. Just as the tumult of people is brought to nothing by distress amid thirst and heat, and just as vine shoots wither beneath a cloud when the sun’s heat scorches intensely, like a flower that falls, so the power of the Jews against the Lord came to nothing.

But if you read, “as heat in thirst,” you will explain it thus: Just as heat humbles a person afflicted by thirst, so they failed.

“And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a banquet.” The prophet returns to the day of judgment, and says that he will make it specifically on the day of judgment. When he says “for all,” he speaks by synecdoche, using the whole for a part. By “all peoples” he means all the elect; “on this mountain” means in the Church of the heavenly kingdom.

Or “on this mountain” means upon the Mount of Olives, upon which the Lord will come in a cloud. He will not, however, descend to the earth, but will sit in the expanse of this air. And what banquet will he prepare for them? “A banquet of rich foods and purified wine.” Dregs are the sediment of wine. Purified wine is pure wine without dregs.

It must be observed, however, that in that blessed state the saints will neither eat nor drink. He therefore says that a banquet will be prepared for them because they will be filled with every delight and sweetness and will never lack anything.

“And the Lord will cast down on this mountain the face of the bound-up covering.” What he calls a “covering” is death; it is also a “web.” The covering of death, which was woven like a web from our first parent over the entire human race, the Lord will cast down—that is, destroy—on the day of judgment, making all immortal, both the elect and the reprobate. The righteous will be immortal in glory, and the impious in punishment; afterward there will be neither bodily nor spiritual death, as the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in the victory of Christ” (1 Cor. XV).

He also calls the devil himself the covering and web of death, for the devil had bound all nations with his bond and woven the web itself, drawing everything toward bodily death and many toward the death of the soul. When he is dragged forth on the day of judgment, his power will be swallowed up.

“And the Lord will remove the tear from every face,” that is understood to mean, from the faces of his elect. In the present age the saints afflict themselves with tears; therefore, in eternal rest they will all lose their weeping and tears. Hence John also says in his Apocalypse: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. XXI), and so forth.

“And he will remove the reproach of his people”—that is, the servitude and dominion of the devil. After our first parent sinned by eating the wood of the forbidden tree in paradise, the human race was subjected to the devil’s servitude (Gen. III). The Lord will destroy this reproach, both of death and of servitude, on the day of judgment, shutting him away from the confines of hell, he who had ruled over the whole world.

“And the righteous will say on that day”—that is, on the day of judgment—“Behold, this is our God,” up to “the hand of the Lord will rest”: that is, the power of his divinity “on this mountain,” namely, in the Church and in the kingdom of heaven. He calls the Church of the elect a mountain, for they will reign with the Lord.

“And Moab will be trampled beneath him, as straw is trampled on a threshing cart.” The voice of the prophet concerning the devil and his princes. To thresh is to crush. There are certain regions where hay is lacking; their inhabitants gather the straw of their crops in the field and drive a cart back and forth over the straw with serrated wheels, crushing it so that animals may ruminate it more easily. Thus Moab will be crushed beneath him, that is, beneath Christ, on the day of judgment.

Moab was the son of Lot (Gen. XIX), from whom the Moabites took their origin; they were always hostile to the children of Israel. For when the Israelites were leaving Egyptian slavery under the Lord’s protection and were approaching the region of the Moabites, Balak, king of the Moabites, using the counsel of Balaam the diviner, caused them to sin against the Lord (Num. XXV). Therefore in this passage we must understand Moab as the devil, who is always hostile to Israel—that is, to the elect, who are signified by Israel. On the day of the final judgment the devil and his princes will be crushed beneath Christ, just as straw is crushed beneath carts.

“And as a swimmer stretches out to swim.” Thus the devil will stretch out his hands beneath him, that is, beneath Christ. When someone falls from higher to lower places, he falls with his hands extended, like one who swims.

“And the Lord will humble the glory” of the devil on that day “with a striking,” that is, with the crushing, “of his hands”—that is, of his activity.

“And the fortifications of your lofty walls will fall.” The prophet addresses the prince of the demons himself. The devil’s fortifications are his satellites. His wall is the people who follow him and imitate him, by whom he is surrounded as by a wall. On the day of judgment he himself, his ministers, and all whom he deceived will fall into the abyss of eternal damnation.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0839A]

“On that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah.” This can be referred both to the present Church and to the heavenly Church, which will be completed on the day of judgment. The holy Church now sings a new song when it praises and proclaims the Lord’s birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and when it sings of the elect penetrating the heavens. For it is an ancient thing for human beings to descend into the confines of hell, but a new thing to penetrate the heavens.

“Our city of strength is Zion: the Savior will be established in it as a wall and bulwark.” The voice of the righteous, whether in the present Church or in the future one. The city—that is, the protection of the saints—is Christ, who grants them strength amid adversity; he himself is their wall and bulwark, for he fortifies and defends them.

Or again, the prophets were the bulwark and Christ the wall. Or otherwise: the bulwark is faith, while the wall is action. For from him we have both the will and the ability.

“Open the gates.” The voice of God to the angels: O my angels, open the gates—that is understood to mean, the gates of righteousness and the gates of glory—so that the righteous nation may enter, that is, all my elect who have kept the truth of the Gospel. For just as there are gates of righteousness, so there are gates of death and iniquity. The gates of righteousness are faith, charity, humility, and the other virtues. The gates of death and iniquity are hatred, greed, and the other vices.

“Ancient error has gone away; you will preserve peace.” The voice of the elect. Ancient error is the worship of handmade idols and the placing of creation before the Creator. Therefore the saints will say on the day of judgment: O Lord our Redeemer, since ancient error has now departed far from us and we have hoped in you, you will preserve for us eternal peace, both of body and of soul.

“You have hoped in the Lord,” O saints and elect of the Lord; “through the ages and forever”—that is understood to mean, continue to hope. The voice of the prophet.

“Because he will bend down those who dwell on high.” The prophet now speaks of the Jews, and this belongs with what he said above concerning the saints: “Hope in the Lord.” Why? Because he will bend down—that is, humble—the Jews, who opposed our preaching.

“He will trample it down”—that is understood to mean, the city—“the foot of the poor.” The prophet is now speaking about the captivity and destruction of Jerusalem in the time of Vespasian, addressing the apostles and teachers of the primitive Church.

In certain manuscripts it reads: “The foot of the foot of the poor will trample it down.” This very clearly appears to have been written incorrectly. For it seems to say as though a foot had another foot. He calls Christ poor, because he became poor for our sake (2 Cor. VIII), and he calls the apostles needy because they imitated the Lord’s humility.

The meaning is: Jerusalem will be trampled by a foot—that is, by a passing over. Whose foot or passing over? The foot of the poor one—that is understood to mean, of Christ—and also the step of the needy apostles.
