Therefore, because they condemned their Lord and God to death and despised his preaching and that of his apostles, they were trampled down and laid waste by the Romans.

[Col. 0840A] “The path of the righteous is straight.” The voice of the prophet. “Path” and “road” are to be understood as one thing, namely, the evangelical teaching. Therefore the path—that is, the Gospel of Christ—is straight, proceeding from the truth, which is Christ (John XIV).

“On the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have waited for you.” The voice of the elect on the day of judgment. Here he calls the Gospel a path, because it contains all the judgments and commandments of both the Old Testament and the New.

“My soul will desire you in the night”—that is, in tribulation—up to “I will keep watch for you.” The voice of the prophet. For he says: Certainly, both in the night—that is, in tribulation—and in the morning—that is, in prosperity—I will always keep watch, desiring to see you.

Or otherwise: “From morning I will keep watch for you”; that is, day and night I labor in the work of your commandments [Col. 0840B], hoping to receive a reward from you.

“When you execute your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness.” The voice of the prophet concerning the Jews: O God and immeasurable mercy, as long as you do not execute your judgments upon the inhabitants of the world, are you not known by the impious? “Strike the impious,” says the prophet, “and they will learn your laws.”

“Let us have mercy on the impious.” The voice of the prophet concerning the impious; it must be divided by question and answer. The Lord says: O prophet, “let us have mercy on the impious,” so that he may do penance. And the prophet replies: “And will they not learn to practice righteousness?” The meaning is: Will you not display your power to them? Surely they will not believe otherwise unless you scourge them.

The prophet added, speaking: “He has acted wickedly in the land of the saints.” By synecdoche, all the reprobate are understood through the singular. He calls the apostles, martyrs, and all the saints “the land of the saints,” because they suffered many things from the impious. It is as though he were saying: Therefore you ought not to spare him, because he killed the saints. The prophet grieved over the death of the saints that was to come and, as it were, argued with him so that he would destroy the wicked.

“And he will not see the glory of the Lord.” The voice of the Son of God to the prophet. The glory of God the Father is the Son, to whom the Father gave all judgment (John V). It is to be read as a question. The meaning is: Is it better that he should see the glory of God the Father—that is, me—on the day of judgment and be ashamed of his evils? But what did the prophet answer him?

“Lord, let your hand be exalted,” that is, your power [Col. 0840D] on the day of judgment over the impious, “and let them not see”—that is understood to mean, the glory of God the Father. He said this both as an entreaty and as an affirmation. The prophet does not wish the impious to behold the glory of the Lord on the day of judgment.

“Let them see and be confounded, those who are jealous”—that is, envious—“of the people,” and may fire devour your enemies or those of my saints. The voice of God to the prophet. The meaning is: I want all the peoples who envy my elect to see me exalted and the greatness of my elect on the day of judgment; and afterward let fire—whether the fire of repentance, of Gehenna, or of burning anguish—devour your enemies and those of my saints.

And, his spirit rejoicing, the prophet said:

“Lord, you will give us peace.” It is as though he were saying: When you have done this, handing the impious over to death, then you will give [Col. 0841A] us peace. For all the good things we perform you grant us through your mercy.

“Lord our God, other lords besides you have possessed us; only in you let us remember your name.” The voice of the prophet in the person of the Jewish people, who came to faith after the Passion of the Lord.

“Lord, other lords have possessed us”—namely, the demons whom we worshiped in idols, abandoning you, our Creator and Lord. “Only in you let us remember your name.” It is as though he were saying in other words: Although we sinned before you by worshiping idols, make us believe in you and deem us worthy to remember your name, so that we may be called Christians by you, who are Christ.

“May the dying not live; may the giants not rise again.” [Col. 0841B] The prophet is not speaking by wishing evil upon them, but foreseeing what was to come upon them, he spoke in this way. “The dying”—that is understood to mean, those dead in sins and iniquity—“may they not live in glory as long as they remain in sins.” “Giants”—that is, the proud and those who are strong for committing evil—“may they not rise to glory on the day of judgment.”

There are two deaths, of the body and of the soul. Bodily death is the breathing out and departure of the soul. The death of the soul is sin and the commission of crime, as it is said in the Law: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII). For just as the life of the righteous is faith, good action, and love toward God and neighbor, so the death of the impious is pride, hatred, greed, and the other vices.

“Therefore you will visit them.” The prophet speaks of the future as though it were past. “Therefore”—that is understood to mean, because they are dead through sin and strong in doing evil—you will visit them on the day of judgment for evil and not for good; you will crush them and destroy their memory from the kingdom and blessedness of the righteous.

“You have spared the nation,” as though he were saying: You have often spared them and had mercy on them, Lord, but for that reason they were not converted to you. “Have you been glorified”—that is understood to mean, by them? As though he were saying: Although you had mercy on them, did they glorify you? You were not glorified by them.

“You have extended all the boundaries of the earth”—that is, you permitted all nations to be separated from you, so that they might remain in their error.

“Lord, in distress they sought you,” in place of “they will seek you.” The meaning is: Lord, strike them so that, even when placed in distress, they may seek you; so that those who did not wish to seek you in a time of prosperity may seek you in a time of distress and persecution.

“In the tribulation of murmuring, your instruction to them”—that is understood to mean, may it be. It is as though he were saying: Those who did not wish to learn your teaching in a time of peace, instruct them through tribulation, and let your teaching remain in their memory. Strike them in such a way that, because of fear, they do not dare to cry out to you openly, but do so as if in a murmur.

“We conceived and gave birth to a holy one.” The voice of the prophets in the person of the holy martyrs. Those who were placed in the struggle did not give birth to children of the flesh, but to the Spirit of salvation, so that, illuminated and inflamed by the Holy Spirit, they might be tortured more intensely, burn more ardently with the love of God, and believe in him with the whole fervor of their minds.

“We have not produced salvations”—that is, good works—“therefore the inhabitants did not fall,” that is, the lovers of the earth who oppress and persecute us. Who are the lovers of the earth? Those who place all their hope in earthly things, serving the world more than God.

“Your dead will live,” that is, your martyrs. “My slain”—that is, my companions—“will rise again.” The prophet speaks to the Lord. The martyrs of Christ are those who were killed by the impious for his name. The prophet Isaiah calls them his companions because he himself was cut apart with a wooden saw for the name of God.

“Awake and praise the Lord, you who dwell in the dust.” The prophet also exhorts the saints: O holy martyrs, awake—that is, rise from your tombs [Col. 0842B]—and praise the Lord, “for the dew of light is your dew.” The prophet addresses the Lord directly. He uses dew to signify mercy. “The dew of light is your dew”—that is, your illuminating mercy, which enlightens the hearts of those over whom it rests.

He offers a great comparison drawn from the crops of the earth. Seed is cast into the earth, and through the moisture of dew it grows into a plant; then it makes it grow into fruit. So the mercy of God produces faith, and turns faith itself toward action.

“And you will drag down the land of the giants into ruin.” By the land of the giants he means the bodies of earthly and proud people. Therefore the bodies of the saints, together with their souls, will be transferred on the day of judgment to everlasting rest, and the bodies of the reprobate, together with their souls, to everlasting damnation.

[Col. 0842C] “Go, my people, enter your chambers” up to “until my indignation has passed.” The voice of almighty God to the martyrs: O my most glorious martyrs, enter your chambers—that is, rest in your tombs—and close the mouths of the tombs until the day of judgment comes and my vengeance passes over the impious, when I will repay each person according to what he has done.

“For behold, the Lord will go out from his place to visit”—that is, to avenge—“the iniquity of the inhabitants of the earth against him.” The prophet speaks about the day of judgment. What is the Lord’s place? Does he not himself say through the prophet Jeremiah: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXXIII)? The Lord’s place is mercy and compassion. When he is therefore said to take vengeance on his enemies—that is, when their evils have deserved this—then he is said [Col. 0842D] to go out from his place. Not because he moves from one place, since he is everywhere.

He calls the proud and those who are wise according to earthly things the inhabitants of the earth. On the day of judgment the Lord will go out from his place—that is, he will not extend mercy to the reprobate—in order to avenge their iniquity against them.

“And the earth will reveal its blood, and will no longer cover its slain.” This can be understood in two ways. On the day of judgment the earth will reveal its blood—that is, the blood of the holy martyrs that it received—and will no longer retain the bodies of those whom it has slain, that is, the bodies of the holy martyrs. The earth received blood, as the Lord says to Cain: “Cursed is the earth in your work, which has received the blood of your brother from your hand” (Gen. IV).

Or otherwise: The earth—that is, the souls of the impious—will reveal on the day of judgment the blood of the holy martyrs that they shed, and their crime will no longer remain hidden. For on that day it will be apparent and known to all people whom each person
will have killed.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“On that day”—that is, on the day of judgment—“the Lord will visit,” God the Father, “with his harsh sword upon Leviathan” down to “and he will kill the blind one that is in the sea.” What is this sword with which God the Father will judge the whole world on the day of judgment? The Word of God, that is, the wisdom of God the Father, through which the Father himself made all things. Concerning this sword the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Ephesians 6). This sword is harmless to the just and holy, but to the impious and sinners, and to their father the devil, it will be harsh on the day of judgment, when he says: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). And plainly this sword will cut—that is, divide—the just from the unjust on that day.

Leviathan is interpreted as “their addition” or “adversary”; it signifies the devil, who always strives to oppose the human race. Why is he called Leviathan, the bar-serpent and the winding serpent? Because, while he always stands in uprightness, he is crooked, deceiving many by his cunning. He is called the serpent, the Leviathan, and the blind one—that is, the devil. For they say that the dragon swims in the waters like a fish, crawls on the earth, and flies in the air.

“On that day”—that is, on the day of judgment—“the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him.” To whom will it sing? To the Lord. Yet it will not be a song of joy, but of pain and sorrow. There is a song of joy, and there is a song of sorrow. Moses, Deborah, David, and Solomon sang to the Lord a song of joy; Jeremiah, however, sang a song of sorrow. In the same way, on the day of judgment the vineyard of pure wine will sing—that is, the people of Israel, who killed the Lord and his Holy One. The Greeks call *merum* “pure.” And why is this vineyard called “pure”? Because the Lord often drank pure wine from it, and it often produced pleasing clusters and shoots, namely, in the prophets and righteous kings. But when Isaiah said this, it was no longer pure; instead of grapes it was producing wild grapes.

The vineyard of pure wine—that is, the vineyard of the people of Israel—will sing to the Lord on the day of judgment a song of sorrow, because it will be condemned for having hung our Maker and Redeemer upon the gibbet of the cross. I speak of those who afterward were not converted to the faith.

“I, the Lord who guard it, will suddenly give it drink.” This is the voice of the Lord. It is as though he said in other words: I, who now guard it from hostile people, will suddenly—that is, on the day of judgment—give it the drink of eternal condemnation, lest some calamity visit it. “By night and by day I guard it,” that is, in prosperity and adversity; but it is always inclined in the opposite direction, toward falling.

“Is there no indignation in me?” This is the voice of almighty God, and it must be read as a question. It is as though he said in other words: Do I not know how to become angry, if I am provoked by you? You always act wickedly against me, while I constantly confer good things upon you; shall I not therefore become indignant against you?

“Who will give me thorns and briers in battle?” The Lord’s voice addressed to the Jews. “Who will give me”—that is, who will make me harsh, cruel, and rough? Or who will teach me to be a tyrant, so that I may rise up in battle against you? Although I am gentle and most merciful, your wickedness arouses me and makes me harsh toward you.

“I will advance against it; I will burn it up altogether.” The voice of God speaking to the vineyard: I will advance against this wicked vineyard, burn it up, and destroy it.

“Or rather, shall I hold fast to my strength?” This is the voice of God the Father. In some manuscripts one finds *tenebit fortitudinem meam*, “he will hold fast to my strength,” but that is erroneous. Here God the Father appears to speak hesitantly. But how can he hesitate, in whose presence all things have already been done and who knows all things? He speaks according to our manner.

The strength of God the Father is the Son, because through him he made all things (John 1), through him also redeemed the human race, and through him decreed to judge all nations. He therefore says: Shall I permit my strength—that is, my Son—to become incarnate for the redemption of the entire human race? Or rather shall I hold him with me? I will send him to assume flesh from a virgin, so that by his incarnation he may make peace for me.

He will make peace for me—that is, the human being whom I created through him, who withdrew from my peace by transgressing my law, he will reconcile to me through his incarnation and passion. For he himself, as the Apostle says, will reconcile us to God the Father (2 Corinthians 5).

“Those who enter violently against Jacob: Israel will blossom and sprout, and they will fill the face of the world with seed.” This is the prophet’s voice, concerning the apostles of Christ. Who are those who enter? “The apostles,” he says. We cannot in every respect adapt the words that the prophets speak when illumined by the Holy Spirit to the sequence of their discourse; nevertheless, their meaning will become very clear to those who investigate carefully.

The meaning of this verse is as follows: When the apostles of Christ enter—that is, when they return with force toward Jacob, meaning eagerly or swiftly—then Israel will blossom in faith and sprout in works. I speak of those who were converted to the Lord through the apostles’ preaching. The apostles themselves also filled the face of the world with the seed of their preaching, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm 18). When did the apostles fill the whole world with their preaching? When, having heard the Lord say, “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel” (Mark 16), they set out preaching everywhere, with the Lord working with them.

“Did he strike him according to the stroke of the one striking him”—that is, the Jewish people? “Or was he killed as he killed those whom he slew?” The words “by him” are understood. This is the prophet’s voice speaking about the Son of God. The sense is: Did the Son of God strike the Jewish people in the way that he himself was struck by them? Or did they kill him in the way that they killed his martyrs? Certainly not. They were merciless toward him, mocking, scourging, and crucifying him. He, however, did not strike them at that same moment as they deserved; rather, over the course of forty-two years he granted them a delay for repentance, so that they might repent of the evils they had committed in killing him and his disciples.

But what does the Lord’s prophet say about those who were unwilling to turn to repentance?

“Measure against measure. When it has been cast away from you, you will judge it as a people.” This means: What they did, they will receive from the Romans. They are already suffering eternal punishment in hell, and on the day of judgment the punishment of Gehenna will be increased for them.

It should be noted that he says, “when it has been cast away from you,” referring to the time when they refused to repent of their iniquities and drove his apostles away from them, unwilling to receive their preaching.

“He meditated in his harsh spirit during the day of heat.” This is the prophet’s voice. Who meditated? Almighty God himself meditated—that is, he thought and spoke—during the day of heat, meaning during the time of tribulation, whether his own or that of the apostles, when he suffered at their hands. What was he going to repay them? Evidently, whether he would send against them the Roman devastator.

“Therefore, on account of this the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven; and this is all the fruit: that its sin be removed, when he has made all the stones of the altar like stones beaten into ashes.” This is the prophet’s voice. Someone might say: What did this people deserve, or what happened long after the Lord’s resurrection, so that one of them should be someone to whom God would forgive his sin, giving him a heart to believe in him?

The Prophet responds to this: “Therefore, because of this”—that is, on account of this—“the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven, and all its fruit,” its evil fruit, because the apostles derived their origin from their lineage. They earned this from the Lord: that some of them should be saved, because they destroyed all their altars by their preaching throughout almost the entire world and reduced the stones of those altars to ashes.

Therefore the Prophet says: “When you have set the choirs of apostles against all the stones of the altar dedicated to the devil, making them like ashes, the sin of the house of Jacob will be removed.” I speak of those who were baptized and received the faith of the Holy Trinity. Concerning them Luke says: “They believed: three thousand on one day, five thousand on the next, and afterward many thousands” (Acts 2 and 4).

“There will not stand”—that is, they will not remain—“groves and shrines,” wherever the apostles preached. Shrines are temples of idols; groves are wooded places where the altars of demons had been built.

“The fortified city will be desolate.” The Prophet turns to the overthrow of Jerusalem, which was accomplished by the Romans. He calls Jerusalem a fortified city, since once it had been protected by angelic guardianship and by walls. The “beautiful” city, which in the times of David and Solomon was filled with every dignity, “will be left like a wilderness and will be abandoned” by God.

“There the calf will graze, and there it will lie down and consume its summit.” He calls Titus and the Roman army a calf; in the Psalm David called him a boar, saying: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it” (Psalm 79). Just as a vineyard dries up if its shoots and branches are cut off, so that city was dried up of its inhabitants. And because the Prophet said above, “There the calf will graze,” that is, in the vineyard, he preserved the metaphor when he said, “And it will devour its summit.”

“In the dryness of its harvest the women will be crushed, coming and teaching it.” The Prophet speaks metaphorically, using harvest or vineyard to signify the people of Israel. Here he calls women the synagogues of various nations—the Egyptians, Philistines, and others. When Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans and all its people became prey to the nations, the synagogues of the various peoples that surrounded it gathered to her. They were crushed with pain and mourning—not because of the Lord’s passion, but because of the overthrow of so great a city.

Alternatively, he may mean the wise Jewish women who had been scattered through different regions. They had formerly been accustomed to come before that captivity and teach the people how to prepare themselves against their enemies. When they heard that the city had been destroyed and came to see the disgrace of their relatives, they were crushed and worn down by immense grief.

For just as it was shameful that Deborah went to war, and just as it was shameful that the woman Huldah prophesied while the men remained silent when the Chaldean captivity was imminent, so it was exceedingly disgraceful that women came to teach the people when Roman captivity was imminent. Thus, in the dryness of Jerusalem’s devastation, the women who had been accustomed to come and teach them were crushed when they saw the disgrace of their own people.

“For it is not a wise people; therefore the God who made it will not have mercy on it.” Here the Prophet shows why the women gathered to them: namely, to teach them, because they were ignorant, and for that reason fell into their own condemnation.

“And it will be on that day”—that is, at the time of Jerusalem’s captivity—“the Lord will strike the whole land of the Jews, from the riverbed of the river”—that is, from the Euphrates River—“to the torrent of Egypt,” that is, to the Nile. It is better rendered in the Septuagint translators, who say, “from the Euphrates to Rhinocorura.” This is a river, not especially large, which divides the land of promise from Egypt; the city of Rhinocorura is situated upon it.

The verse is to be understood in this way: From the place where the region begins to the place where it ends, the whole territory of the Jews was plundered by the Romans.

“And you will be gathered, one by one, and all the children of Israel.” This is the prophet’s voice addressed to those who, after the Lord’s ascension, were converted to the Lord through the preaching of the apostles. It is said of them in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2 and 4) that three thousand believed on one day, and so forth. Because of their small number he says, “one by one.” Compared with those who remained in treachery and unbelief, they were few in number.

“And it will be on that day”—that is, after the Lord’s ascension, or after the city’s overthrow—“a great trumpet will be sounded” by the apostles, that is, in evangelical teaching, “and the Gentiles will come together,” those who had been lost through idolatry, “from the land of Assyria and those who had been expelled by the Lord into the land of Egypt, and they will worship the Lord on the holy mountain at Jerusalem,” that is, in the Church.

And this is the present time. For from the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is praised (Malachi 1). Here it should be noted that through these two peoples all the nations are to be understood that will come to faith in Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the fading flower, and to the glory of its exultation.” Above, the Prophet spoke about the day of judgment, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the faith of the Gentiles. Now the divine discourse speaks against the ten tribes that were called Ephraim.

They were called Ephraim either after Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin and was the first king established over those ten tribes, or after Joshua son of Nun, who succeeded Moses in governing the people. These ten tribes were proud, trusting in their multitude. They were greater and stronger than the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, in number and power.

Therefore they are called the “crown of pride,” because just as a king’s head is adorned with a diadem or crown made from gold and a variety of gems, so they adorned their king by surrounding him on every side. The multitude of a people is the king’s glory.

They are called drunkards not because of bodily drunkenness, but because of idolatry, error, and the worship of demons. They are called a fading flower because the beauty and glory of their exultation quickly fell away. For that reason they heard from the Holy Spirit: “Woe to the crown of pride of Ephraim, to the fading flower, and woe also to the glory of its exultation, because it will be desolated and reduced to nothing.”

They were at the summit—that is, at the temple—which was built above the very fertile valley of Gethsemane. Gethsemane is a most fertile valley where the Lord was seized by night; above that valley stands Mount Zion, or Jerusalem. Gethsemane is interpreted as “valley of the fat ones” or “valley of fatness,” because of the abundance of crops, since it was extremely fertile.

They are not said to have been at the summit of the valley of Gethsemane because they lived there, nor because it had fallen to them by lot. Rather, in the times of David and Solomon, whenever they came to Jerusalem either for festivals or at the king’s command, they stayed there for a short time. Their ascent passed through that valley, and while they stayed with the king, erring through wine, some of them were accustomed to pitch their tents there for amusement.

Jeroboam their king mixed and offered them a bitter drink when he cast the two calves, and they worshiped them, saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the slavery of Egypt.” From that time they wandered away from wine—that is, from idolatry and the error of demons.

“Behold, the Lord is powerful and strong” down to “and those sent upon the broad earth,” that is, the level earth. This is the prophet’s voice. He compares hail and overflowing waters with the army of Sennacherib, and a windstorm with the broad land filled with the ten tribes. He gives two comparisons.

Just as a whirlwind is confined by hail—that is, by a storm—and just as, through the force of overflowing waters running across a level land, all lightweight straw is carried away, so, through the force and multitude of the Assyrians, the ten tribes were devastated, trampled down, and led into captivity.

“With their feet” the Assyrians “will trample the crown,” that is, the multitude, “of Ephraim.” Those ten tribes were of such beauty and dignity in the times of David and Solomon that they were called by the Lord a crown and a most beautiful flower. But at the time when Isaiah foretold this to them, they had already abandoned the glory of their dignity by worshiping idols.

“And it will be a fading flower”—that is, its beauty and adornment—“of its glory” down to “will devour it.” This is the prophet’s voice. He calls the summit of the fertile valley the house of the Lord, which was situated above the summit of the valley of Gethsemane, for the reason mentioned above.

The Prophet gives a comparison for how those ten tribes were scattered. “Just as,” he says, “if a cluster is found before the ripeness of autumn, or fruit on any tree before summer, as soon as someone sees it, driven by desire, he immediately devours it, so Sennacherib and his army desired the glory of the ten tribes and carried away all their goods.”

“On that day the Lord of hosts will be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation for the remnant of his people.” Here “day” must be understood as a period of time. What is the crown, and what is the garland? Some say that a crown is made of gold and gems, while a garland is made of flowers, such as boys customarily wear on their heads.

By “the remnant of his people” he means the two tribes that were not led into captivity by the Assyrians in the time of Hezekiah. “On that day,” he says—that is, at that time—“when the ten tribes have been led captive by the Assyrians, the Lord will be a crown of victory and a stronghold of protection for Judah and Benjamin, so that he may deliver them from the hand of Sennacherib.”

“And a spirit of judgment for the one sitting in judgment, and strength for those returning from battle to the gate.” The Lord himself will be the spirit of judgment. For whom will the Lord be the spirit of judgment? For King Hezekiah, sitting in judgment.

Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz, was beloved by the Lord because he taught the Lord’s people justly and judged justly. Therefore the Prophet says that the Lord himself will be for him a spirit of judgment—that is, he will inspire him concerning how and in what manner he should judge—because Hezekiah sits in judgment, that is, desires equitable and just judgment.

And the Lord himself will be strength for those returning from battle to the gate. We do not read anywhere that Hezekiah waged war against any nation. Why, then, is it said, “The Lord will be strength for those returning from battle”?

This should be understood as referring to that battle which was carried out from heaven, when the Lord sent his angel and killed 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians (2 Kings 19). When the Jews saw such a slaughter of their enemies without danger to themselves, they went and gathered the spoils and returned with joy and exultation to the gates of Jerusalem.

“But these too were ignorant because of wine, and they wandered because of drunkenness.” Because Judah and Benjamin quickly transgressed the law of the Lord, just like the other ten tribes that had been led far away into captivity, and did not remember the Lord’s benefits, by which he had delivered them from the hands of their enemies, the Prophet speaks against them and says:

“But these too”—that is, Judah and Benjamin—“were ignorant because of wine,” that is, because of the error by which they had been deceived, they did not know their Creator and Deliverer; “and because of drunkenness”—that is, because of idolatry—they wandered, withdrawing from God.

“The priest,” the wicked one, “and the prophet,” the false one, “did not know” their Creator “because of drunkenness,” that is, because of the worship of demons whom they served. “They were swallowed up by wine,” that is, by false error. The priest and prophet “wandered in drunkenness,” that is, in idolatry.

“They did not know the seer,” that is, they did not consider that God, who penetrates all hidden things by his gaze, saw their thoughts and deeds. “They were ignorant of judgment,” not knowing how to distinguish between the just and the impious, the holy and the profane.

“All their tables” “are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no longer any place” in them. He uses “vomit” and “filth” for every kind of uncleanness, impurity, and foulness.

He says this because after they had been delivered by the Lord from the hands of their enemies, they immediately returned to their former error, worshiping idols in groves and woods, and even upon rooftops. They consecrated all the food they ate to demons, setting tables before their altars.

Thus no place was found in them for the Lord, because their hearts were filled with hatred and every kind of iniquity. As he himself says in the Gospel to the teacher of the law: “Foxes have holes in their hearts, and the birds of heaven have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head” (Matthew 8).

“Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand what is heard? One weaned from milk, torn away from the breasts.” This is the prophet’s voice.

One is called “weaned” as though drawn away from milk: someone who feeds on solid food. “Torn away from the breasts” means rejected or separated.

The Prophet therefore speaks to the Jews: Whom among you will the Lord teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand what is heard—that is, so that he may understand that what he has heard is true, and, retaining it in his mind, fulfill it in his conduct?

It is as though he said: He will not teach those who suck milk, that is, who live childishly and without understanding, imitating the works of infants. Rather, he will teach those who already possess the solidity of faith and who are nourished not by milk but by solid food (Hebrews 5).

There are people in the holy Church who still suck milk—that is, who fulfill easy commandments, unable to take solid food, meaning to carry out demanding commandments. Concerning them the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Like newborn infants, desire the milk” (1 Peter 2). And the excellent preacher says: “As to infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food,” and so forth, down to: “For you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3).

There are also some who take solid food, that is, who fulfill the greater commandments of the Law and the Gospel, despising earthly things and desiring heavenly things. In accordance with what the Lord commanded: “Go, sell everything that you possess, and follow me” (Matthew 10).

Such people go from virtue to virtue until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Psalm 8). Even while remaining in the flesh they can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

One of us sucks milk when he says: “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 6). The one who knows how to say what must be said feeds on solid food: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and what follows.

“For command, recommand; wait, rewait; a little here, a little there.” Almighty God, by whose mercy all things subsist, “who does not desire the death of the sinner, but wills that he turn through repentance and live” (Ezekiel 18), used to foretell through his prophets the captivities and the evils that the people would suffer from Nebuchadnezzar or Sennacherib, so that they might abandon their error and turn back to him.

But that people, always stiff-necked, provoked God by their deeds. Because the captivity did not come upon them immediately when it was announced, they mocked the prophet, saying: “Command, recommand”—that is, prescribe what we should do and threaten us with evils. The evil will not come upon us at that time.

But the Prophet replied: “Wait, and wait again, and a little there”—understand, remain in that waiting—“because the calamity will certainly come upon you.” And what if it has not come now? It will undoubtedly come eventually.

Yet they did not correct themselves from their crimes and wickedness. Instead, they took the Prophet’s own words and said to him: “Command, recommand; wait, rewait; a little here, a little there.” It was as though they said in other words: Command us again what we should do, and order us repeatedly to wait for and expect the captivity, remaining for a little while in that waiting. Before it comes, we will all die and pass from this life to another.

“For in the speech of the lip and in another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said.” This is the prophet’s voice. What is that “other speech” in which he will speak? It is this: As soon as he has threatened captivity, he will bring it upon them, leaving no further opportunity for repentance.

The sense is: Because you despised the words of the prophets, treating as nothing all that they said, and because you said, “What these men prophesy will happen in the future, and evil will not overtake us,” behold, I speak to you in another speech. As soon as I speak, tribulation and captivity will come upon you.

I will no longer announce through my prophets what evil is going to come upon you, until it rushes upon you and you are captured. For I told you:

“This is my rest; refresh the weary.” This is the prophet’s voice. He says that he himself has been wearied by their iniquities.

When we devote ourselves to prayers, fasts, vigils, almsgiving, and other good works, then we refresh the Lord and make him rest within ourselves. But when we labor at greed and other evil works, we make him labor. As he himself says through the same prophet: “You have made me labor in your iniquities” (Isaiah 45). And also: “I have labored while enduring.”

“And this is my desire”—the words “that you refresh me by your good works” are understood. For my rest is to sit and dwell in the hearts of the elect. “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7).

“And the word of the Lord will be to them, ‘Command, recommand,’” down to the words “a little there.” The Prophet speaks against those who took the word of the Lord as a mockery and says:

Because you held the words of the Lord and of his prophets in contempt, treating as a lie what they announced to you, and even turning it into a jest, the word of the Lord will be for you ruin and calamity.

Alternatively, for those to whom it comes, the Word of the Lord will be given “so that they may go into their own destruction and fall backward,” killed by their enemies.

“Therefore hear the word of the Lord, mocking men, who rule over my people.” This is the prophet’s voice in the person of the Lord, directed against the high priests, scribes, Pharisees, and rulers of the Jews. They are called “mockers” because they treated the Prophet’s words as a joke when they said, “Command, recommand,” and so forth.

“For you said: We have struck a covenant with death”—that is, with the devil—“and with hell we have made an agreement.” “Covenant” means the same thing as “agreement.” An agreement is so called as though it were an augmentation of peace.

The most impious Jews, not remembering the judgments and benefits of the Lord by which he had once preferred and exalted them above all nations, giving them a land more fertile than every other land, said:

We labor in vain under the Law, observing the commandments contained in it, since we are going down to the gates of hell just as all the nations do. It will be easier and more tolerable for them than for us, because they appease the rulers of hell daily with sacrifices and gifts. It is therefore better for us to turn to the rite of the nations and establish an agreement with the devil and the punishments of hell, offering them incense and sacrifices.

“When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us,” meaning the scourge of captivity and tribulation, “because we have made a lie our hope”—that is, we have our hope in the devil—“and we have been protected by falsehood,” that is, by the devil. In place of “we have been protected,” the sense is “we will be protected” or “we will be shielded.”

He calls the devil “falsehood,” in accordance with what the Lord says (John 8): “He is a liar, and its father”—that is, the father of falsehood—“always fleeing from the truth.”

Therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, I will lay a stone in the foundations of Zion.” This is the prophet’s voice, speaking in the person of God the Father about the Son of God.

Because you have done all these things that have already been mentioned, placing your hope in falsehood, the Lord speaks, saying: “Behold, I will lay a stone in the foundations of Zion,” that is, in the foundations of the Church.

Zion, which is interpreted as “mirror” or “contemplation,” signifies the holy Church, which always raises the mirror of the heart and the contemplation of the mind toward God.

The stone is called the Lord Jesus because of his firmness and solidity. For everyone who is founded upon him is not moved by any flood or storm. As the Apostle Peter says: “Approaching him, a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen by God” (1 Peter 2).

This is the stone that Daniel saw “cut from the mountain without hands,” that is, “born from the seed of the Jews without sexual intercourse with a man,” which filled the whole earth (Daniel 2).

This is the stone rejected by the builders (Psalm 117), but called approved by God the Father. It is called “cornerstone,” because just as a cornerstone holds together two walls, so he joined two peoples in himself and established one Church from the two. He “made both one,” as the Apostle says (Ephesians 2).

He is precious because he did not commit sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (Ephesians 2). Therefore he is founded in the foundations of the Church.

“Whoever believes”—understand, in that stone—“will not hasten,” that is, when he sees the Son incarnate, he should not think that his second judgment will immediately follow, but should await it. As the Prophet says: “If he delays, wait for him, because he will certainly come and will not be late” (Habakkuk 2).

“And I will place judgment in the balance,” that is, in consideration, “and righteousness in the measure,” so that he may repay each person according to his works. This is God the Father’s voice concerning the Son.

The sense is: When I send my Son, who is the approved stone, to redeem my elect for me, then I will set everything in measure, judging all nations through him with a just examination.

Concerning the judgment given to him, the Son says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). For through him he made and redeemed all things; through him also he will fulfill his judgment.

“And hail will overthrow”—that is, the multitude of torments—“the hope of falsehood,” where they placed their hope; “and waters will flood the protection,” that is, the multitude of punishments and tribulations will overwhelm the devil, from whom they thought they were protected, and will overwhelm those who said, “We will be protected by falsehood,” that is, by the devil.

“And your covenant with death will be erased”—that is, with the devil—“and your agreement,” which you established, “with the punishments of hell will not stand,” although you said that it would be easier for you in hell if you worshiped demons according to the rite of the nations.

The scourge, whether of captivity or of death, when it comes from Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar, will trample and destroy you.

“For morning after morning it will pass through, by day and by night.” Dawn is so called as though it were uncertain light. By “morning” and “dawn” we should understand continuous time; by “day” and “night,” continuous punishment is signified.

“And only the distress of tribulation will give understanding to your hearing,” that is, punishment. The suffering and penalty to which you will be subjected will make you understand that the things the prophets spoke in my name were true.

“For the bed has been made too narrow, so that one falls out; and the short blanket cannot cover both.” This is the Lord’s voice addressed to Jerusalem. It is drawn metaphorically from a husband and wife, referring to God and Jerusalem.

For example, if someone said to his wife: O adulterous wife, this bed is narrow; it cannot hold me and the one with whom you violate it. And this blanket is short and narrow; it cannot cover me and the adulterer.

The sense is: O Jerusalem, if you wish to have me as your spouse and protector, you must abandon foreign gods, which are always bringing you ruin and calamity. For you cannot do both things: worship foreign gods and have me as protector; commit adultery with lovers and please me. “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6).

“For just as on the mountain of divisions the Lord will stand, so in the valley that is in Sabaa he will be angry.” This is the prophet’s voice against Jerusalem. Ellipses are necessary in this passage.

“Just as the Lord stood on the mountain of divisions,” dividing the Philistines while David fought (1 Chronicles 14), so the Lord will stand against you, O Judah and Benjamin.

The history of the Kings relates that when the Philistines had gathered in one mass, David came upon them; with the Lord assisting him, he divided them from one another. Those who remained dead were separated from those who were scattered far and wide through different deserts, as David pursued them. Hence that place was called Baal-perazim (Joshua 10).

“And just as he was angry in the valley that is in Sabaa” against the Canaanites when Joshua fought against them, when, at his command, all the stars stood at the summit of the middle heaven for the space of one day, so “will the Lord be angry over Jerusalem, to do his work?”

This should preferably be read as a question rather than as an affirmation. The Prophet says: “Will the Lord therefore become angry in order to do his work?” No. “His work is foreign to him.”

Why is it foreign? Because God’s work is to show mercy and spare, and to provide everyone with the aid of his mercy. But when, provoked by human evils, he strikes them and takes vengeance upon them, the work he performs resembles that of a cruel man and tyrant. Therefore it is foreign to him that he should perform his own work.

Thus, if it is to be pronounced interrogatively: “Will he therefore become angry against the impious, so as to perform his work?” Certainly not. “For the work that he performs is foreign to him.” Indeed, as we have said, when he takes vengeance on those who despise him, he performs the office of a savage and bloodthirsty man.

Blessed Gregory gives another interpretation: The Lord came into the world in order to do his work, that is, to redeem the human race from the power of the devil and to have mercy upon it. But his work was foreign to him because it was not fitting to the divine nature that he should be spat upon, scourged, and crucified.

“Now therefore do not mock, lest perhaps they be bound.” The Prophet exhorts those who took his words in derision, saying, “Command again, command again,” and the other things stated there, to cease and desist from mocking, lest, bound by the chains of their sins, they should also be bound by the chains of captivity [Col. 0854A] and be led more swiftly into plunder. “I have heard from the Lord a consummation and an abbreviation over the whole earth.” For this reason I announce these things to you: I have heard from the Lord of the shortening of your captivity and calamity. He will not delay, as you suppose when you mockingly say, “Wait, wait again; rebellion,” but it will come suddenly, if you do not turn to repentance. What he says, “over the whole earth,” may be understood specifically of the land of the Jews, or also generally of the day of judgment, when the whole world will be visited by the Lord.

“Give heed with your ears and hear my voice.” The Prophet’s voice is addressed to the scribes and Pharisees.

“Does the plowman plow all day,” that is, at all times, “in order to sow his seed?” No. The one who works the soil will then break it up—that is, before the season of sowing arrives, he will plow that land once or twice so that, when the time for sowing comes, it will be prepared; “and he will make,” that is, he will hoe his ground with a rake. What cannot be broken up with a plow and a share because of the narrowness of the place, where the plow cannot turn, he also hoes with a digging tool at the proper time. “Is it not when he has leveled its surface,” that is, when he has made it even and softened it, “that he will sow,” that is, sow “black cumin and scatter cumin?” Gith is a kind of legume, having grains as large as cumin but black, and it is customarily put in bread because of its sweetening flavor.

[Col. 0854C] “And he will place wheat in rows,” with the locations of those rows understood. For not all areas of the earth are equally suited to the seeds. “And he will scatter vetch within its boundaries,” because vetch is sown along the edges of fields, around the crops.

“And he will instruct the farmer in judgment,” that is, in discernment. In other words, his God will teach him when he ought to plow and break up the soil, where and when to sow wheat and where millet. A major pause should be placed at the point where it says, “And he will instruct him in judgment,” and what follows should be attached: “His God will teach him.” Who will instruct him? His God. The word “God” must be understood there, so that the sense is: “And his God will instruct him.”

When the time of harvest comes, “neither will gith be threshed with saws,” that is, it will be beaten out, [Col. 0854D] “nor will a cartwheel roll over the cumin, but with a rod,” that is, with a whip and staff, “they will be beaten out.” There are some regions where, because of the scarcity of hay, people gather wheat into one place, bring carts with iron wheels over it, and thresh the wheat; the straw is also reduced to chaff so that the animals may consume it more easily.

“But bread will be crushed,” with iron wheels and a cart being understood. He calls wheat, barley, and everything from which bread is made “bread.” “Yet the threshing cart will not thresh it,” that is, this bread or wheat, “forever, nor will its cartwheel wear it down,” that is, the bread, “nor will it crush it with its hoofs.” What will not crush the bread itself? [Col. 0855A] The cart or the wheel; it has already been beaten out. He used “hoofs” for the upper parts of the wheel-saws.

“And this” plan “comes from the Lord God of hosts”; the meaning is that the farmer should know at what time he ought to furrow the earth and at what time he ought to sow. We have explained these things according to the literal sense: how God instructs the farmer not to devote himself perpetually to the work of one kind of cultivation at one and the same time, but to foresee what he should do at one season and what at another.

The sentence must again be taken up from the beginning, and we must consider what he wishes to disclose spiritually. “Give heed with your ears.” The Prophet speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, whom he earlier called mockers. Does the plowman plow all day, that is, at all times, in order to sow? Almighty God, [Col. 0855B] merciful and compassionate, has arranged every kind of human being and their dispositions in various ways. Therefore, in this passage he is compared to a farmer, who is occupied in different ways at different seasons and desires to receive fruit from the earth he cultivates.

Sometimes almighty God breaks up the earth—that is, the inhabitants—by striking it with pestilence; sometimes he has mercy and spares; sometimes he causes his despisers to migrate into captivity; sometimes he recalls them from captivity. He does this so that they may turn to repentance and so that he may receive from them the fruit of good works. For he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII).

He continues: by the cumin that is beaten with a rod we can understand all the nations that did not receive the knowledge of God, who will be beaten with a rod—that is, with the punishments of hell. By the wheat and barley from which bread is made, the Jews may be understood, who received the knowledge of God in the Law but did not wish to fulfill it; and therefore they will suffer greater torments than those who have not yet known God.

Or otherwise: by the wheat and barley may be understood the leaders of the holy Church and the rulers of this world, who ought to guard themselves and also recall others to the joys of the heavenly homeland. While these entangle themselves with all their strength in earthly profits and, by their evil example, cause their subjects to stray from the way of truth, without doubt, unless they have practiced perfect repentance before the final day of judgment, they must be handed over to the punishments of hell, because the powerful will suffer powerful torments (Wis. VI).

By cumin and gith, moreover, the common people and all the simple are understood. By living badly they corrupt the faith of the holy Trinity and the baptism of regeneration; unless they are cleansed by tears and repentance, they must be handed over to the punishments of Gehenna. Yet the bread will not be threshed forever, nor will the cumin be beaten with a rod. In this passage he gives consolation to sinners. For the merciful Lord will have mercy on his creature on the day of judgment, if in this age the creature has practiced repentance before death overtakes it.

There are indeed many in purgatorial fire who began repentance here but, when the moment of death snatched them away, did not bring it to completion; through the Lord’s generosity, they will be saved on the day of judgment. It must be noted, however, that we are not speaking of the ungodly who departed from this life in their very ungodliness, but of those who, after committing wicked deeds, turned to repentance. [Col. 0856A] And this arrangement of human actions proceeded from the Lord God, who thus ordered them and magnified his justice.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“Woe, Ariel, Ariel, the city that David captured.” Almighty God speaks to Jerusalem with the emotion of one mourning. He did something similar in the Gospel, when he saw the city and wept over it, saying: “If only you had known” (Luke XIX).

Jerusalem is not called Ariel by the Lord because it once bore this name, but because of the interpretation of the name. Ariel is interpreted as “lion of God.” Jerusalem is therefore called the lion of God because it has always been exceedingly strong and powerful. Before it was captured by David, it possessed such strength that the Jebusites who lived there mockingly said to David: “The city is so strong, they say, that you are repelled by the weak, and you will not be allowed to enter within unless you first drive out the blind and the lame” (III Kings V). Hence the proverb arose: “The blind and the lame will not enter the temple.”

After it had been captured by him, it was increased and multiplied still more over many cycles of years by the strength of its warriors, the circuit of its walls, and, above all, the abundance of its wealth. This was especially so in the time of Solomon, when that most glorious temple was built and there was in it such an abundance of silver and gold that it was like stones. Therefore he foretells that woe is impending over it—that is, everlasting condemnation—because all that glory and exaltation would be taken away on account of their sins by the Chaldeans and the Romans, as we shall see in what follows. [Col. 0856C]

“Year has been added to year; the festivals have come to an end.” For this reason he said, “Woe to you, Ariel,” because this was destined to happen to it. He speaks of the future as though it were past. A year was added to a year because, when they were led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, they did not offer sacrifices, since the temple was absent; and the festivals of Tabernacles and Passover came to an end, that is, perished. Just as the first year of captivity continued through all these things, so did the following year; therefore it is said that year was added to year.

Blessed Jerome says that this is remarkable: at one and the same time the city was destroyed, the temple burned, and the people led into captivity, at the time when Zedekiah was captured. The same thing also happened at the arrival of the Romans. [Col. 0856D]

“And I will besiege Ariel,” that is, Jerusalem, “and it will be sad and mournful.” It will be surrounded by the hostile army of the Chaldeans, just as the Lord also foretold through Jeremiah: “Behold, I will gather the ancient kindreds of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord, and they will set up their seats over the gates of Jerusalem.” And so it happened. For when Zedekiah and the princes with him fled through a certain opening in the wall and were captured by Nebuchadnezzar’s cavalry in the fields of Jericho, the Chaldean princes, already holding the gates, had placed their seats above them.

“And it will be to me like Ariel, and I will surround you as a sphere around you.” This refers to the time of the Romans. “And it will be to me like Ariel, and I will surround it as a wild beast.” It is as though he were saying in other words: When Vespasian and Titus come, crowded with Roman soldiers, you will be to me like Ariel—that is, you will retain only your former name, but you will be deprived of all the dignity and glory in which you flourished in former times. You will indeed have a temple and priests as in the time of Solomon, but neither a temple of such splendor nor priests of such dignity. You will retain only the name by which you are called Jerusalem, but you will lack your former possessions in every other respect.

What he adds, “and I will surround you as a sphere around you,” agrees with what he says in the Gospel: “Your enemies will surround you with a rampart,” that is, with fortification or siege, “so that you will be unable to escape from their hands” (Luke XIX).

[Col. 0857B] “You will be humbled”; when these things come upon you, “you will speak from the earth,” not about heavenly matters. It is as though he were saying in other words: Formerly you used to bring forth prophets who spoke with the Lord and discussed heavenly things; after the Romans come, you will cease to speak of anything except earthly matters.

“And your speech will be heard from the ground.” By this, blessed Jerome says, the Lord wished to show that magicians would arise from that people, as we later heard that many did, such as Simon Magus. There were magicians who, by necromancy—which is called the raising of the dead—summoned souls from the underworld and uttered very subtle voices, predicting what those who consulted the magicians were asking about.

The same are also called pythonic spirits, and their practitioners are called ventriloquists, because they have a demon in their belly. For this is what the pythoness at Endor did: urged by Saul’s request, she summoned Samuel from the underworld (I Kings XXVIII). “And your speech will mutter from the ground”: this is the same as what was said above.

“And it will be,” O Ariel, “the multitude of those who fan you, like fine dust and like passing ash.” He compares the multitude of the Romans who came against Jerusalem to the finest dust and to ash—not on account of their smallness or insignificance, but because it was innumerable, like the dust of the earth. It was also like a mass of ash which, when carried past by the wind, cannot be counted.

“And it will happen suddenly,” that is, immediately, “from the Lord of hosts”—that captivity. “And Jerusalem will be visited,” either by the Lord from heaven, or with his permission, “with thunder and a great shaking.” The Romans had peace with the Jews, but the treaty was quickly and suddenly broken because the Jews refused to pay tribute. Then the Roman emperor sent his two commanders, Vespasian and Titus, to destroy the city.

The statement that it “will be visited with thunder and devouring flame” can be understood in two ways. Before the Romans came to the city, there were thunderclaps from heaven and earthquakes, and voices were also heard in the air, along with storms; in addition there was devouring fire—that is, lightning striking people—so that it might be shown that not only human beings but also all the elements had been stirred against them.

It may also refer to the Romans, who came upon them with thunder—that is, with a great assault—and like a storm, so that by their multitude the earth seemed to move. They themselves saw flames of fire that set the temple and the city ablaze and consumed everything like the heat of fire.

“And the multitude of all the nations that fought against Ariel will be like a dream of a nighttime vision.” The Prophet turns his speech to the Romans who destroyed Jerusalem. When, with the Lord’s permission, they had captured the city and the temple, together with all the wealth both of the Lord’s treasures and of the people, and had enriched themselves with it, they did not give thanks to the Lord who had granted this to them. Instead, they glorified their own gods, as though they had been protected by their power and enriched by the resources of the Jews.

Therefore the Prophet speaks against them [Col. 0858B] because they would soon pass away and die, giving three comparisons. “Just as,” he says, “a dream”—that is, a vision seen when someone sees trees and mountains passing by, but as soon as he awakens his mind is empty—“so quickly will the nations of the Romans who fought against Jerusalem pass away,” because they did not give thanks to God, who gave them all the goods of the Jews, but thought they had accomplished this by the power of their deities.

“Be stupefied,” O scribes and Pharisees, “and be amazed” at your misery; “waver,” that is, stagger, “and totter,” that is, turn yourselves this way and that. Again the divine word speaks against the scribes and Pharisees.

“Be drunk, but not with wine,” rather, with the grief of your heart and the contrition of your body, because evils will come upon you. “Stagger, but not from drunkenness,” that is, do penance so that you may escape the danger of calamity, “because the Lord has mixed for you a spirit of stupor,” that is, alienation of mind, on account of your countless crimes.

“He will close your eyes,” so that, although you see the words of the Law and the Prophets, you will not understand them. “He will cover your prophets who see visions,” that is, he will hide them from you, “and he will cover your rulers,” in whom you trust—that is, he will remove and take them away from you.

“And the vision of all things will be for you like a sealed book,” that is, as though the prophecy of all the books had been sealed. “And when he gives the book to one who knows letters,” that is, to a scribe, Pharisee, or teacher of the Law, “he will say: ‘The book is sealed,’” that is, “its meaning is obscure, and its interpretation is difficult for me.” “And when it is again given to one who does not know letters,” that is, to the common people who have never learned letters, or to some Gentile, “he will answer: ‘I do not know letters.’”

This should not be understood only of one book of the Psalms, as some have thought, but of the whole Old Testament. It was fulfilled then, when they lost the priesthood and their dignity, and the city was destroyed and the temple overthrown by the Roman rulers.

“And the Lord said: ‘Because this people draws near,’” with “to me” understood, “with its mouth, and glorifies me with its lips, but its heart is far from me.” The people of Israel seemed to draw near to their God when they did not worship idols and glorified him alone [Col. 0859A] with their lips; but in their hearts they were far from him, because they worshiped God the Father in such a way that they did not believe in his Son. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe in the Son does not believe him who sent him” (John III).

How, then, can one become distant from God, who is everywhere and fills all things, as he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXXIII)? But when we do good, fulfilling love of God and neighbor, then we draw near to God and he draws near to us, because we prepare a temple for him within ourselves, and he makes his dwelling in us. But when we do evil, serving fornication, adultery, or other vices, God withdraws from us, because he does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis. I; Matt. XV; Mark VII).

“And they feared me,” that is, they worshiped me, “because of the commandment of men,” that is, on account of the commandment or tradition of the scribes and Pharisees. The scribes and Pharisees, setting aside the commandments of the Law, placed their own traditions above God’s commands. Therefore the Lord also says to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who set aside the commandments of God for the sake of your traditions,” saying: “Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you.”

And the wretched Jews followed their commands rather than God’s. Therefore, “because they established their own righteousness” (Rom. X) and were not subject to my righteousness, “behold, I will add” something “so that I may cause astonishment.” What was that astonishment? He himself explains it.

“For the wisdom of the wise will perish,” that is, of the scribes and Pharisees. He did not say that wisdom would perish from all human beings, but from the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed wise to themselves although they were foolish (I Cor. III). The Jews lost this wisdom when, in the time of the Romans, they lost the land given to them, the city and temple, and all their dignity.

“Woe to you who are deep of heart, so as to hide counsel from the Lord.” The Lord speaks against the scribes, Pharisees, and rulers of the Jews. Outwardly, through hypocrisy, they pretended to be holy and innocent, while in darkness—that is, at night or in a private room—they carried out many evil deeds. For they said: “Who can know our will and our actions?”

So our father Adam spoke when, after his eyes were opened by tasting the forbidden tree, he made loincloths from fig leaves and hid beneath the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thinking that he would not be seen by God. So Cain spoke when he said: “I will be a wanderer and a fugitive, and I will be hidden from your face” (Gen. III and IV). The same should be understood of the wise men and philosophers of this age, and of the heretics.

“Your thought is perverse, as if clay were to say to its maker: ‘You did not make me.’” For just as clay, if it could speak and said against its maker, “You do not know how to mold well,” so their words sound. Every creature is known to its Creator, and it cannot think or do anything without him seeing all things. With him there is no night and no darkness; everything is naked and open to his eyes.

“Will not Lebanon, in a short and very brief time, be turned into Carmel, and Carmel be reckoned as a forest?” He calls the time short from when Isaiah proclaimed these things until the Lord’s ascension. For all times and ages, compared with the eternity of almighty God, appear brief and small because they have an end. God’s eternity, however, is neither begun by a beginning nor enclosed by an end.

Lebanon is a mountain in the province of Phoenicia, and its name is interpreted as “whitening.” Carmel likewise is a mountain on the boundary of Palestine and Phoenicia, adjoining the city of Ptolemais, and its name is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision.” There is also another mountain of the same name in the Promised Land, from which Nabal the Carmelite came. But what we call Carmel, the Hebrews call Chermel.

Blessed Jerome says in this passage: Let those who refuse to accept the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, being content merely with the literal surface and seeking everything historically, answer us now: When did Mount Lebanon pass into Carmel, and again Carmel into Lebanon? Their sense and reasoning will fail them in this passage.

By Lebanon, whose name is interpreted as “whitening,” the Gentiles are signified: they were whitened and cleansed through the preaching of the apostles and were turned into Carmel—that is, into the true knowledge of circumcision, which is the truest circumcision of regeneration and renewal.

By Carmel, which, as stated, is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” the Jews are represented. They circumcised themselves bodily but not in mind, and therefore were reckoned as a forest—that is, as an unfruitful woodland. Before the preaching of the apostles, the Gentiles were indeed unfruitful, because although they produced fruits, those fruits were nevertheless bitter and sour.

After the Lord’s ascension, when the Jews rejected the preaching of the apostles and the apostles came to the Gentiles, Lebanon was turned into Carmel and Carmel into a forest: the Gentiles, who had previously been the tail, were turned into the head, while the Jews, who had once been the head, were reckoned as the tail.

“And it will happen on that day,” that is, at that time, when the preaching of the Gospel has passed to the Gentiles, “the deaf will hear the words of the book,” the sealed book, “and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see.” The Gentiles had not previously received the knowledge of God and were oppressed by the darkness of ignorance and the gloom of sins, with the eyes of their hearts blinded. On that day—that is, when Lebanon is turned into Carmel and Carmel is reckoned as a forest—they will understand the words of the sealed book, that is, the Old and New Testaments, which had been sealed to the scribes and Pharisees, and they will see the mysteries and hidden meanings of the divine utterances.

“And the meek will increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men will exult in the Holy One of Israel.” The apostles are called meek, of whom the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth” (Matt. V). When the apostles therefore saw the multitude of the Gentiles hastening to the faith of Christ, great joy was added to them.

The apostles are also called poor, because they were poor in spirit. We too may call the Gentiles poor. For our fathers were poor because they did not possess spiritual riches and remained without the abundance of hope and love. But when they have been made drunk with spiritual waters from the Savior’s fountain, they will exult in the Holy One of Israel.

“For the one who prevailed has failed; the mocker has been brought to an end.” Before the coming of our Redeemer, the devil prevailed over all the nations, because he held them subjected to his dominion, until the Lord Jesus, stronger than he, came and took away everything that belonged to him, as it is written in the Gospel: “But when one stronger than he comes upon him, he will take away all his weapons in which he trusted” (Luke XI).

He prevailed because he was the prince of this world. As the Lord said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” [Col. 0861B] (John XIV). And: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” He is also called the mocker, because he mocked every kind of human being and led them astray into his error.

“All those who watched over iniquity, who caused people to sin by their words, have been cut down.” Those who have been cut down are understood as the disciples of the prince of this world, namely the demons, who were always watching for evil. Those who caused people to sin by their words were cut down when, having blinded the hearts of the Jews with the poison of their iniquity, they said to the Lord: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, you cast out demons” (Luke XI); and: “Crucify him, crucify him”; and other things of this kind.

“And they used to trip up the one who reproved at the gate.” Who is the one who was tripped up at the gate? The Lord Jesus, or also one of the prophets who announced at the gate to the people that, by doing penance, they should turn to the work of faith. Yet he was not tripped up, because the righteous person, living by faith, remained immovable (Rom. I).

“And they turned the righteous aside in vain.” In some copies it is found as “from the righteous,” but blessed Jerome explains “the righteous” in this way: As far as those demons themselves were concerned, they tried to turn the righteous one away from righteousness, but in vain, because he was firmly founded.

We may also refer this to the scribes and Pharisees, who were always watching for iniquity and caused simple people to sin by their words when they said of the Lord Jesus Christ that he was not the one promised in the Law and the Prophets. They attempted to trip him up when they plotted how they might catch him in his speech (Matt. XXII).

Both readings agree with this interpretation: “And they turned the righteous aside in vain,” or “from the righteous.” The scribes and Pharisees tried in vain to turn the righteous one aside, because they did not prevail. Or this may refer to when they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John X). In vain they turned away from the righteous one—that is, they acted foolishly by departing from life and choosing death.

After this had happened—because the devil had prevailed, and both his ministering demons and the scribes and Pharisees had been cut down—the meek increased their joy, and the poor in spirit, the Gentiles, exulted in the Lord.

“Therefore the Lord says this to the house of Jacob, who redeemed Abraham.” How did the Lord redeem Abraham? We read in the histories that the Chaldeans threw Abraham and Haran into the fire, which in their language is called Ur, because they refused to worship him. Haran died there before his father Terah, while Abraham came out unharmed (Gen. XI). Hence the Lord also says to him: “I am God who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.”

“Jacob will not now be ashamed, and his face will not now blush; but when he sees his children, the work of my hands, sanctifying my name in his midst.” Almighty God speaks through the prophet Isaiah and says: Jacob will not now—that is, at this time—blush, that is, be ashamed and grieve over his iniquities, but when he sees his children, namely my apostles, the work of my hands, whom I created, restored, and instructed in spiritual knowledge, sanctifying my name in his midst.

After the Lord and Redeemer of the human race “had conquered the dominion of death, risen again, and ascended to the right hand of God the Father,” on the tenth day after his ascension “he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in fiery tongues, and they began to speak of the mighty works of God” (Acts II).

When the Jews who had handed the Lord over to death heard this, they blushed because of their sins, since they had condemned their Lord and God. Moved to repentance, they said to the apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” And Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.”

What is said here was fulfilled: “When you see your children, my apostles, made into those who sanctify my name, you will blush over your crimes and be ashamed of your errors.”

“And they will sanctify” the holy name of Jacob, “and they will proclaim the God of Israel.” This is the voice of the Prophet. The Holy One of Jacob in this passage is Christ, who blossomed from his seed and lineage. The God of Israel is understood as the Lord Jesus together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

“And on that day those who err in spirit will learn understanding, and the murmurers will learn the law.” Those who err are called Jews, led astray by false error, who worshiped idols after departing from the true God. They are also called murmurers, because they were always grumblers and mutterers, both in the wilderness and after they had been introduced into the land better than all others.

## CHAPTER XXX

“Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord.” Woe, as we have already said above, signifies the destruction of ruin and death. The Jews are called rebellious because they abandoned the Law of the Lord and transgressed his covenant.

Now Isaiah, intoxicated by the Holy Spirit, foretells the history that was fulfilled in the time of Jeremiah, when Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, came to Jerusalem, led away Zedekiah after putting out his eyes and killing his sons, and took captive nearly the entire population of the land. He placed over those who remained Gedaliah, who was of royal descent.

Then Ishmael and other wicked men came with him and killed Gedaliah, driven by envy against him. At that point, all who remained, terrified by overwhelming fear, came to Jeremiah and said to him: “Pray for us to the Lord [Col. 0863A] God, and tell us what we ought to do.” For they knew that, because of the killing of Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had placed over them, they would suffer evil.

On the tenth day after they had consulted Jeremiah, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Say to those who remain: Remain in this place, and I will protect you, and it will be well with you.” When Jeremiah had reported these words to them, they said to him: “We will not remain here, but we will flee to Egypt, lest perhaps we die here, killed by the Chaldeans.”

“You made a plan, but not from me, and you wove a web, but not by my spirit.” They wove a plan and a web without the Lord’s will when they said: It is better for us to flee to Egypt and be saved there than to be killed here by the Chaldeans.

[Col. 0863B] “You who walk in order to descend into Egypt and have not consulted my mouth.” When he says “you who walk,” he speaks of the future as though it were present. For from Isaiah, who foretold this, to Jeremiah, in whose time it was fulfilled, there were one hundred and fifty years.

“My mouth,” he says—that is, Jeremiah. For the prophets are called the mouth of the Lord, because through their mouths almighty God foretells the hidden mysteries. Hence the prophets customarily say: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

“And the strength of Pharaoh will be for you a shame.” Pharaoh is a title of rank among the Egyptians, just as among the Romans people were called Augusti and Caesars. The Pharaoh in whose time these people fled to Egypt was otherwise called Vafres, as was also Pharaoh Necho.

“For your princes had gone to Taphnis, and your messengers reached as far as Anes [Thanes].” This verse should be read ironically. It is as though he were saying: You departed from me in order to go to Taphnis—what benefit did that bring you? Taphnis is a royal city of Egypt, where the magicians performed signs against Moses. Anes is also a city on the borders of Egypt.

“All were ashamed because of the people who could not benefit them.” Blessed Jerome says that, when they went to Egypt, to the city of Taphnis, hoping to be protected by Pharaoh’s power, Jeremiah went there with them. He took large stones, carried them to the entrance of the city, and said: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring Nebuchadnezzar, my servant, and he will set up his seat upon these stones. He will capture you together with all the Egyptians in whom you have trusted, and you will perish by famine, harsh captivity, and the sword, because you refused to hear my voice and remain in your own land.”

“An oracle concerning the beasts of the South.” After ten oracles concerning various nations, in the eleventh place an oracle concerning the remaining two tribes is given, namely the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. They remained after Zedekiah and the leaders of the people had been led away to Babylon. They are called beasts because of their insensibility: they did not avert the scourge of God impending over them by repentance. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “When a man was in honor, he was compared to senseless beasts” (Ps. XLVIII).
