[Col. 0864A] The oracle concerning the beasts of the South is so called because those tribes lived in the southern region. “In a land of tribulation and distress.” The land of tribulation and distress is the expanse of that wilderness through which Johanan son of Kareah and the other leaders of the remnant led those survivors into Egypt, contrary to the Lord’s command. Or it is the very land into which they were led, afflicted by many miseries.

As for what he says, “a lioness and a lion,” Jerusalem and its people are to be understood by the lioness, and Johanan and the other leaders by the lion. He continues within the metaphor when he says, “from them”—with “from the beasts” understood, that is, from the lioness and the lion—“was born a viper and a flying serpent,” that is, one passing away swiftly.

Who has ever heard of such a thing, that a viper and a flying serpent should arise from a lioness and a lion? According to the historical sense, these things should not be held to by a firm literal argument. We have said that the lioness and the lion signify Jerusalem and its leaders, while the metaphor is maintained. By the viper and the flying serpent their children are understood: born, as it were, from poisonous parents, they remained venomous and passed away swiftly, just as their fathers had.

Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. XII), and “evil generation.” Moses says: “A crooked and perverse generation” (Deut. XXXII).

“Carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts.” Those fathers, together with their children, carried their riches and treasures on beasts and camels, fleeing to the Egyptian people, who did not benefit them. For when Nebuchadnezzar came, as has already been said, they perished together with the Egyptians in whom they trusted, by famine, captivity, and the sword.

Egypt had promised them aid vainly and emptily, because the Egyptians themselves were likewise captured by the Chaldeans. “Therefore”—with “because Egypt vainly helped it” understood—“I have cried: there is only pride,” with “in Egypt and in the power of the kingdom” understood, and not strength in war.

“Be still,” that is, remain here in your own land. This is the voice of almighty God to the remnant. What was fulfilled in the time of Jeremiah is foretold in the time of Isaiah.

“Now, having entered, write for them on boxwood.” The Lord speaks to Jeremiah: “O Jeremiah, when you have entered Egypt with them, write carefully on boxwood and in this book what I foretold to them, so that they should not go to Egypt but remain in this place. And why do I command you to write this? So that all [Col. 0864D] who read it may know that I had permitted good things for them, and that they had done evil against me. “And it will be” for them “a written testimony on the last day,” that is, at the time of this consummation, when Nebuchadnezzar comes upon Egypt and captures both the Egyptians and those who had fled to their aid; “and it will be a memorial forever” for all who read or hear.

“For the people is provoking to anger, and deceitful are the children.” The Jewish people, not only in the wilderness but also in the land given to them by the Lord, were always ready to provoke the Lord to anger. They were deceitful when they said, [Col. 0865A] “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we will do” (Exod. XXIV). Immediately afterward, turning to idolatry, they made themselves a golden calf and worshiped it, and it became their downfall. These people likewise provoked the Lord to anger and proved deceitful when they came and said to Jeremiah, “Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God, that he may tell us what we ought to do” (Jerem. XLII). For when the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah on the tenth day, saying, “Tell the remnant who remain: stay here, and it will go well with you,” they provoked the Lord to anger by saying, “We will not stay here, but we will flee to Egypt.”

“Who say to the seers”—that is, to the prophets Jeremiah, Baruch, and Huldah [Col. 0865B]—“Do not see” for us favorable things. Prophets are called seers because they foresee what is to come. For they said to the prophets, “Do not announce the word of the Lord to us, because we will not listen to it.” When he says, “And to those who look, do not look upon for us the things that are right,” that is, the things that the Lord commands—that we remain here—the meaning is the same. “Speak to us,” O Jeremiah, Baruch, and Huldah, “pleasing things,” namely, that we should go to Egypt, “and we will carry them out.” “See for us errors,” that is, allow us to go astray.

“Take away from me the way,” that is, allow righteousness to withdraw from us, “and turn aside from me the path,” that is, remove truth from me. “Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before”—that is, from the presence of—“us”: the one whose admonitions you often proclaim, saying, “Thus says the Lord.” “Therefore,” because you rejected God, saying, “Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before us,” “thus says the Lord: [Col. 0865C] Because you rejected this word, so that you might dwell in your own land, and trusted in oppression”—that is, in deception—“and relied upon it,” that is, placed your hope “in tumult,” namely, in the pride of Egypt.

“Therefore this iniquity of yours”—that is, this sinful transgression—“will be like a breach,” that is, a collapse, “falling.” The meaning is this: Just as a lofty wall, collapsing in a fall after a long period of neglect, is repaired only with difficulty, and just as, when a clay vessel has been utterly shattered, no part of it remains from which either fire or water can be taken, so you will quickly be crushed by the Chaldeans, and none of you will remain fit for any work.

“For thus says the Holy One of Israel: If you return” [Col. 0865D] from iniquity in order to repent, “and rest” in this place, “you will be saved” from evil. The divine word, long before calamity comes upon the remnant people, urges them to repentance, so that they may turn back from all their crimes and rest in their own land, in order that they may be saved, the Lord’s anger having been changed into mercy. I told you: “In silence,” remain here, “and in hope” of my protection, “your strength will consist”—that is, your defense. It is as though he said in other words: “Have confidence and firm hope in me, and I will deliver you—not through the pride of the Egyptians, but through the strength of my mercy. And you were unwilling” to hear me, that is, to obey my words, placing your confidence in the shadow of Egypt.

“And you said, ‘By no means’”—will we remain here—“but [Col. 0866A] ‘to the horses’”—of the Egyptians—“we will flee. Therefore,” because you said these things, “you will certainly flee, but those who pursue you”—the Chaldeans—“will be swifter,” and you will not be able to escape their hands. “A thousand men” of the Egyptians in whom you trust will flee “from the face of one” Chaldean, and five thousand of you will flee “from the face of five” Chaldeans, “until you are left like a mast on the top of a mountain.” The meaning is this: Just as, after a shipwreck, the mast of a ship, when set upon the summit of a mountain or on a hill, serves as a sign of the ship’s destruction, so whoever remains of you will be a sign of the most terrible devastation of the temple and the city.

“Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you.” It is as though he said: “Because the things mentioned above will come upon you”—unless you repent. The Lord still waits for this reason, so that he may have mercy on you, “and therefore he will be exalted,” that is, he will be recognized as great in his mercy, because God—that is, Christ, the Lord of judgment—“the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). “Blessed are all who wait for him,” namely, in hope of future glory.

“For the people of Zion will dwell in Jerusalem.” The prophet’s voice. The Jews refer this to the time when, after seventy years of captivity, they were brought back to Jerusalem by Jesus the priest and Zerubbabel, and mourned the good things they had formerly possessed. But it is better to refer it to the Church of the elect. Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” signifies the holy Church, which, placed bodily on earth, contemplates the Lord in mind, saying with the Apostle, “Our commonwealth is in heaven” [Col. 0866C] (Phil. III). Jerusalem, however, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies heavenly blessedness, in which those who are now in Zion—that is, joined to the body of the Church—will rejoice forever with God after the labors of this life have ended, following the Lamb wherever he goes.

“While weeping, you will no longer weep.” Although the children of the Church grieve while they dwell in the exile of this pilgrimage and sorrowful life, on account of their own sins and those of others, or because they are delayed from entering the kingdom, as the Lord says, “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful” (John XVI), nevertheless they rejoice in their hearts because of the reward that exists in hope. But when they have completed the course of this affliction, their sorrow will be turned into joy, because the Lord will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Apoc. II).

“Having mercy, [Col. 0866D] he will have mercy on you.” These words display the abundance of Christ’s mercy, and the Prophet says this to confirm his statement. For every day almighty God has mercy on his elect when he frees them from the afflictions of this life and causes them to reach the joys of the heavenly homeland. But this mercy will be accomplished more fully after the day of judgment, when, having received their bodies, they will be rewarded in body and soul forever and ever.

“At the voice of your cry,” that is, of your prayers, “as soon as he hears,” that is, as soon as he receives your vows, “he will answer you,” having granted you forgiveness. The Prophet speaks to the people who remain in the faith of Christ. O Christian people, when you cry out to God, he will hear you immediately and say, “Here I am.” We read of many [Col. 0867A] believers who cried out to the Lord and yet were not immediately heard. Blessed Paul prayed that the spirit of Satan might be taken away from him (II Cor. XII), but he did not obtain this. And why? So that he would not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations. For this reason our petition is also customarily delayed, so that we may receive a greater reward for perseverance.

“And the Lord will give you scarce bread and scant water.” The Hebrews say that when they came out of captivity, they had scarce bread and scant water—that is, a shortage of food and drink—and they wish to apply this to themselves. But blessed Jerome says that it should rather be referred to the people gathered into the unity of faith. Therefore, in this passage [Col. 0867B] bread and water signify evangelical teaching, which is narrow in comparison with the Law. For what is narrower than that the Law and the Prophets should consist in two commandments? The Lord says in the Gospel, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII). And he added, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (ibid.).

Moreover, it must be understood that Holy Scripture is sometimes bread for us and sometimes water. It is bread in those passages where the mysteries are deep and hidden, so that they are not easily understood by us but are swallowed, as it were, by chewing, as in the statement, “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). It is water, however, when it is easily grasped, as in the literal surface or in clear mysteries, such as, “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

“And he will no longer cause your teacher to fly away from you.” [Col. 0867C] Our teacher is Christ, who teaches us inwardly (Gregory). Unless the Lord illumines the heart of the hearer, the tongue of the teacher labors in vain. Therefore God the Father will not cause your teacher to fly away—that is, to depart—from you, O Christian people. On account of the Church’s sin, he does not remove the Son from it through the common consent of the two persons of the Godhead, but teaches through inward inspiration. This will be fulfilled more fully when God will be all in all (I Cor. XV), and they will reign with him without end.

“And your eyes”—that is, the eyes of your mind—“will see your instructor,” Jesus Christ himself. Now the Church sees God in hope through contemplation of the mind; then it will see him directly.

“And your ears will hear the voice of one admonishing behind you.” [Col. 0867D] When almighty God first created the first man, from whom we all derive our origin, holy and just in body and soul, he spoke to his face, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, III). But when he had sinned by tasting the food forbidden to him, he turned his back, as it were, upon Christ, because, recognizing that on account of his sin he had fallen from his original state of dignity, he no longer heard the Lord before him but behind him, saying, “Cursed is the earth in your work.” In his fall we all went backward, because, being a sinner and transgressor of God’s commandments, he begot sinful and transgressing children.

But Christ says to us, “Repent” (Matt. IV), and again, “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. I), and “Return to me [Col. 0868A] with all your heart,” so that, bent by these admonitions, we may seek what lies before us. “This is the way,” that is, the rectitude of faith, which is Christ; “walk in it.” Christ’s voice to believers, urging them to advance from virtue to virtue. This is the way, that is, Christ, who said in the Gospel, “I am the way and the truth and the life.” What is it to walk in the way except to imitate Christ? For he himself said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and follow me” (Matt. XIX). And, “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me,” that is, let him imitate me.

“Do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” How can someone turn aside to the right? If he walks on the right, does he not proceed rightly? For Solomon said, “The Lord knows the ways that are on the [Col. 0868B] right” (Prov. IV). But elsewhere he himself shows what it is to turn aside to the right when he says, “Do not be excessively wise, and do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. VI). Everything is good when kept in measure. Therefore, he turns aside to the right who displays holiness beyond the holy conduct of religious people.

Thus each righteous person ought to appear in such a way that what was said of Zechariah and Elizabeth may truthfully be said of him (Luke I): “They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments of the Lord without blame,” that is, without reproach. To turn aside to the left, however, is to depart from good toward evil. Nothing, therefore, is better than to walk along the royal road.

“And you will defile the plates of your silver idols.” The divine word speaks [Col. 0868C] to the nations coming to the faith, which had been devoted to idolatry and were lying in the mire of vices. O Christian people, when my apostles come preaching the word of the kingdom, you will defile—that is, cast away as defiled—all idolatry, both the carved and the cast image made of gold or silver, together with the garments, that is, with all its adornments, into an unclean place, and you will scatter it into fragments like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman.

“Go out and say to it.” The voice of almighty God. O Isaiah or Jeremiah, go out and speak to the Christian people.

“And rain will be given to your seed wherever you sow in the land.” The prophet speaks concerning the nations. He calls the grace of the Holy Spirit “rain,” and the word of teaching “seed.” It is as though he said in other words: O Church [Col. 0868D] gathered from the nations, heavenly grace will be given to your teaching, so that wherever—that is, among whatever nation—you pour out your preaching, it will produce the fruit of good works.

“And the bread of the grain of the land will be most abundant and rich.” Our bread is Christ, who says, “I am the living bread” (John VI). Christ, therefore, who bears fruit in the hearts of the elect through faith and love, is most abundant, because his teaching shines throughout the fourfold world, and churches have been founded in his name that produce the richest fruits of good works. That bread also—that is, Christ—is rich, because he refreshes the hearts of his elect with the grace and richness of the Holy Spirit.

“He will feed in your possession,” O Christian people, [Col. 0869A] “the lamb in that day, in a spacious place.” The possession of Christians is the Church, where the lamb is fed—that is, every gentle person upon the teaching of the divine utterances. When he says “in that day,” this refers to what he said above, when the gentile people shattered idols and images.

“Your bulls and the colts of your asses will eat a mixed fodder as on the threshing floor, when it has been winnowed.” We know that bulls lead herds, and therefore they appropriately signify the apostles and prelates of the holy Church, who provide it with leadership, showing how and by what paths it ought to walk. We read in the Gospel (Matt. XXI) that when the Lord was traveling toward Jerusalem, he had with him an ass and a colt. By the ass we understand the Jewish people, and by the colt the gentile people, who were dissolute and wanton in following idols. Therefore, in this passage the colts appropriately signify their children, joined together in the unity of faith.

[Col. 0869B] *Migma* is barley together with chaff. By the chaff the outward literal sense is understood; barley signifies inward understanding. The bulls and colts, therefore—that is, prelates and subjects united in the holy Church—eat the mixed fodder, because they spiritually understand the things that are to be understood spiritually, and grasp historically in the historical sense the things that are to be taken historically. Whatever applies to both senses, they grasp in both ways with the mind, just as it is contained on the threshing floor—that is, in Scripture.

“And there will be, upon every high mountain and upon every hill, streams of running waters, on the day of the slaughter of many, when the towers have fallen.” These [Col. 0869C] words appear to concern the day of judgment. Mountains and hills signify the saints because of the height of their virtues, or the expositors of the divine utterances, such as Augustine, Jerome, and the others. Streams of running waters are the spiritual teaching of the Gospel. The day of slaughter signifies the day of judgment. The towers signify the devil and all the proud and powerful of this age.

On the day of judgment, therefore, when all the ungodly perish, and all the rejected are slain by the sword of God’s word, and the demons themselves fall—those who now fortify their own as towers—streams will run through the hills and mountains, because the good works of the saints will also appear, which they fulfilled through observance of God’s commandments, and throughout nearly all nations the teaching of the Gospel, which now does not shine among them, will become clear as the day of judgment approaches and Elijah and Enoch preach.

[Col. 0869D] “And the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds”—that is, heals—“the wound of his people, and heals the blows of its affliction.” This will take place after the day of judgment, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth, whose fulfillment the Prophet foretells. For everything that almighty God accomplished over the span of six days was made for the sake of man, and at man’s fall all the elements suffered harm. Previously the earth did not produce thorns and thistles. This air was not so dense but pure. Thus the sun, moon, and stars suffered a diminution of their light.

On that appointed day of judgment, [Col. 0870A] when all the rejected have been shut up in hell together with the devil after the examination, the Lord Jesus will rise into heaven together with his body—which consists of all the elect. Then the moon will borrow the sun’s radiance, and the sun will shine seven times more brightly than now, like the light of seven days—that is, manifoldly—and it will recover the light and splendor that it lost when the first man sinned.

For blessed Isidore says in the *Book of Creatures* that thereafter neither the sun nor the moon will set, but will remain forever in the place in which they were created. This accords with Habakkuk III: “The sun and moon stood in their habitation,” meaning, “they will stand.” And why is this? So that those who will be in the lower regions may not enjoy the brightness of the sun or moon. Concerning this state a certain prophet also says, “Your sun will no longer set for you” (below, LX).

[Col. 0870B] When he says, “on the day when the Lord binds the wound of his people,” he calls his people all the elect, from the first man to the last righteous person who will be born on the day of judgment. By “wound” and “affliction” he means the mortality and ruin that we contracted when our first parent sinned, at which time we lost the image and likeness of God. Man was made in the image of God because he was created holy and just (Gen. I); the Lord commands us to retain this image when he says, “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. XI). He had the likeness because he was created immortal. On the day of judgment the Lord will heal this wound and affliction in his elect, when he makes them immortal and incorruptible in body [Col. 0870C] and unchangeable in soul.

“Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar,” that is, the Son of the Father, the true God Jesus Christ, comes in the Father’s name, because he is true God just as the Father is. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one name, according to what the Apostle himself says: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII). He does not say “in names,” but “in one name,” which is God. Although there is a Trinity in persons, there is nevertheless unity in the Godhead.

“Behold,” he says, “the true Son of God comes from afar,” that is, after a long time he will come to condemn the rejected and reward the elect. Hence it is also added: “His wrath is burning and grievous to bear” for the rejected. Can God become angry? Is he therefore changeable? Let this be far from the hearts of the elect. Almighty God [Col. 0870D] is said to rage then, in the manner in which Scripture speaks according to our way of understanding, when he takes vengeance and retribution upon his enemies. For on the day of judgment he will appear severe and unbearable to the rejected, but gentle and merciful to the just.

“His lips,” that is, the lips of the Son of God, “will be filled with indignation” when he says to the rejected, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. XXV). “His tongue will be like consuming fire” when he says, “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire.” For that sentence will be a sharp sword, because it will slay all the wicked together with their author, the devil, as the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

“His spirit is like an overflowing torrent.” Just as the force of overflowing waters, when it reaches “to the middle [Col. 0871A] of the neck” of a human being or animal, suffocates it, so the spirit of the Son of God—that is, his judgment—will destroy all the ungodly and suffocate them on the day of judgment “into nothingness,” that is, so that they will be nothing.

“And the bridle of error,” that is, of idolatry, “which was in the jaws,” that is, in the praise or activity, “of the peoples,” he will destroy and break. Here he calls the devil a bridle, because he held all the nations as though under a bridle—that is, under his dominion. When Christ accepted the flesh of our frailty for the redemption of the human race, through his single death he destroyed our double [death?]. The devil is called the bridle of the peoples in this passage, not because he guided them toward the salvation of their souls, but because, just as a mounted rider turns and leads a bridled horse wherever he wishes, so the devil, having brought the whole human race [Col. 0871B] under his power, led it to carry out his will and to its destruction. On the day of judgment this bridle will perish, because he will be shut up in eternal fire to be tormented.

“There will be a song for you like the voice of a sanctified solemnity, and joy of heart.” Until now he has spoken about the punishment of the rejected; now he speaks about the glory of the elect. Just as the children of Israel, destined to be liberated by the Lord’s power from Egyptian slavery, ate the lamb toward evening while celebrating the solemnity of Passover (Exod. I), and, after crossing the Red Sea, saw Pharaoh and the Egyptians submerged in the morning and sang a song to the Lord, saying with immense joy of heart, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. XV), so the saints on the day of judgment, after crossing the sea—which signifies [Col. 0871C] this world—when they see Pharaoh, that is, the devil, handed over to eternal damnation together with all his followers, who are signified by the Egyptians, will sing praises to the Lord with great exultation and joy of heart.

“Like one who goes with a flute to the mountain of the Lord.” The Prophet continues his comparison concerning their praise. The Lord commanded the children of Israel, when they entered the promised land, to bring to the house of the Lord tithes from all the crops and good things given to them by God (Lev. XXVII; Num. XVIII; Deut. XII). And just as at that time they carried their tithes to Jerusalem, to worship in the Lord’s temple, bringing them with a flute—that is, with joy and gladness—and praising God, who gave them the good things of the land, so the saints, when they enter the heavenly homeland on the day [Col. 0871D] of judgment—which signifies the promised land—will rejoice and exult, carrying tithes in their hands, that is, good works, and praising their Creator, by whose help they fulfilled the works through which they reached the eternal homeland.

Thus far, according to Saint Jerome. Blessed Gregory, however, speaks differently, referring this to the time of the apostles and to the present, when through their preaching the nations abandoned idols and idolatry ceased from their mouths. He calls idolatry and the worship of demons a bridle. For our fathers, who formerly said to Jupiter or Mercury, “You are my god, and you begot me,” after abandoning and destroying that bridle—that is, idolatry—sang to the Lord, and we too now sing: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens; and the idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. XCV); [Col. 0872A] “there is no spirit in their mouths.” The bridle of error—that is, idolatry—will, he says, become a song to the Lord, and you will praise him as the children of Israel praised him after crossing the sea, or as they praised him when they brought their offerings and tithes to the temple with joy of heart.

“And the Lord will make the glory of his voice heard, and will show the terror of his arm.” Again the Prophet returns to the ungodly, speaking about the day of judgment. On the day of judgment the Lord God the Father will make the glory of his voice heard. The voice of God the Father is his Son, his arm, through whom he accomplished all things, through whom he redeemed the world, and through whom he will judge the whole world in equity.

[Col. 0872B] For on the day of judgment the person of God the Father will not appear to the rejected, but the person of the Son, so that he who appeared humble at his first coming may appear terrible, to destroy all the ungodly together with their father, the devil, and judge those justly by whom he was judged unjustly. The glory of the Son of God, therefore, will be the vengeance and retribution by which he condemns the wicked. God the Father will make that glory heard by all the heavenly powers and by all his elect, and he will show its terror when he says, “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

Alternatively, he will make the glory of his voice—that is, of his Son—heard because all will rise at the voice of the Son. As he himself said, “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John V). “With the threat of wrath and of devouring fiery flame.” When God the Father shows [Col. 0872C] the rejected the terror of his Son, he will threaten them. “The voice of the Son of God” will be “with the threat of wrath and the threat of devouring fiery flame.” For the judge’s sentence will devour them, “and will strike them down in a whirlwind,” that is, in a storm, “and in a stone of hail,” that is, in tribulation.

“For at the voice of the Lord Assyria will tremble, struck by the rod.” If only the Assyrian will tremble on the day of judgment, what will all the rejected do? By Assyria we should understand the devil and all his satellites, together with those whom he has led astray by false error and who have imitated him. He calls the terrible sentence of the judge a rod.

When he adds:

[Col. 0872D] “And the passage of the rod will be established,” that is, the persecution of the Lord’s sentence, he clearly shows that this harsh and severe sentence will always remain upon them. The Lord will not relieve it after he has imposed it, as Origen says; rather, he will cause it to rest upon them forever.

“With tambourines and lyres and with outstanding battles he will fight against them.” It is as though he said in other words: In the joy of all his saints and in surpassing glory he will conquer all the rejected together with their prince, handing them over to be tormented in eternal fire—the very ones who persecuted him and his saints.

“For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday,” that is, from former time, from the beginning of the world, in the presence of God, by the almighty King, “and it has been made broad.” [Col. 0873A] “Its fuel”—that is, the fuel of Gehenna—“is fire and much wood,” that is, all sinners. “The breath of the Lord,” that is, the spirit of the Lord, “like a stream of sulfur, sets it ablaze,” namely, Gehenna. Sulfur emits a stench from the earth and generates heat. All these things will be for the ungodly in hell. There will be unquenchable fire and intolerable foulness and stench, and they will be tormented with incomprehensible torment.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting in the horses of Egypt.” Until now he has spoken about the glory of the elect and the punishment of the rejected. Now he returns again to the remnant that remained in the land of Judah after Zedekiah and all the princes had been led away to Babylon, concerning whom he has already said much above.

But there is this difference [Col. 0873B] between what he said above and what he now says: there he warned them not to go to Egypt but to remain in the land of Judah, and promised that it would go well with them. Here, however, he threatens evil to those who went against the Lord’s commands, placing greater trust in Egypt than in the Lord, and says: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt, hoping in the horses and chariots of Egypt, and who did not seek the Lord,” when they said to Jeremiah, “Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord, that we may know what we ought to do” (Jerem. XLII). They sought him in words, but not in their hearts. For when, on the tenth day, as we have already said above, the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah—“Go,” he said, “and tell the children of the remnant: Remain in this place, and I will protect you”—they answered him, “We will not [Col. 0873C] do so, but we will flee to Egypt.” Therefore he says that they did not seek him: although they sought him in speech, they did not seek him with a pure heart.

“But he himself, being wise,” that is, almighty God, whom they despised, “brought” evil “upon them, and did not remove his words,” which he had spoken through the mouths of Isaiah and Jeremiah, but brought Nebuchadnezzar upon them, as what follows will teach. “And he will rise up” in the anger of his fury “against the house of the wicked.” That is, against those who fled to Egypt, “and against the help of those who work iniquity,” that is, against the Egyptians, who tried to provide them assistance.

“The Egyptian”—the king, namely Pharaoh Vaphres, or his people—“is a man and not God, and their horses,” [Col. 0873D] in which they trusted, “are flesh and not spirit. And the Lord has inclined his hand.” He speaks according to the metaphor of a charioteer. Just as a charioteer who controls a cart or chariot loosens the reins when he wants the horses to run faster, so almighty God quickly brought his anger and vengeance upon the Egyptians and upon those who had fled to them. For we said above how Jeremiah foretold to them that Nebuchadnezzar would come against the Egyptians and against those who had fled to their aid, and how he would destroy them all, either by the sword, famine, or captivity.

“And the helper,” he says, the Egyptian, “will fall” from the strength of Nebuchadnezzar, “and the one receiving help”—the remnant people who fled to him—“will fall, and all will be consumed together,” both the Egyptians and the Jews who had placed their trust in them.

[Col. 0874A] “For thus says the Lord to me.” Above he spoke about the remnant who went to Egypt, trusting in Pharaoh’s strength. Now he speaks about those who were led away to Babylon with Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes, but who, after seventy years, by the Lord’s mercy, returned to Jerusalem under Jesus the high priest, Zerubbabel, Ezra, and other princes. He promises them good things, giving two comparisons to show how they were protected there by the Lord, and says:

“As when a lion and a lion’s cub roar over their prey,” and so forth. Just as a hungry lion, when it sees a flock of sheep, runs and seizes a ram, and when a multitude of shepherds confronts it, [Col. 0874B] is not frightened by their shouting, trusting in the strength of its own power; and just as birds, to defend their young, fly about over their nests, and whether they see a human being or a serpent, or other birds approaching their chicks, fight with beak and claws, forgetting their own weakness, and, if they can do nothing else, redouble the distress of their breasts with chattering cries:

“So the Lord of hosts will descend to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill, and will protect it, protecting and delivering it, passing over and saving it.” It should be noted that he does not say “against Mount Zion,” but that, standing upon Mount Zion, he will fight against its enemies. Thus he acted at that time when the Samaritans wanted to prevent the temple from being rebuilt, [Col. 0874C] and in the time of the Maccabees, when many victories were granted by the Lord to a few faithful people.

The Lord is compared to a lion, because he is the strongest lion, who rose on the third day. Concerning him the Evangelist John says in his Apocalypse (chap. V), “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered.” Or he is also likened to a hen, as he himself said in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets who are sent to you: How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, but you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII). And in Deuteronomy (chap. XXXII): “As an eagle stirring up its young, and spreading its wings, and carrying them,” and many other things of this kind.

[Col. 0874D] “Return,” children of Israel, “as you had withdrawn into the depths” of evils. A little above he spoke about those who returned from captivity under Jesus the high priest. Now he returns again to the time of Hezekiah. Prophecy does not preserve the order of time or of history. Before Sennacherib, returning with the Assyrians from Egypt, came to Jerusalem, the prophet warned the tribe of Judah and Benjamin to return to their God, so that, just as they had withdrawn into the depths of evils, they might turn to the Lord in the depths of good things with their whole heart’s devotion, lest they be handed over into the hands of the Assyrians.

“For on that day a man will cast away his silver idols and his golden idols, which your hands made for you as a sin.” These words of the Holy Spirit are to be understood not according to history but spiritually. If you return, O children of Judah and Benjamin, to the Lord [Col. 0875A] your God, and cast away your golden and silver idols, which you made for yourselves for your sin.

“Assyria will fall by a sword not belonging to a man,” that is, the Assyrian people, “and a sword not belonging to a human being will devour him.” When Sennacherib came with his Assyrian people against Hezekiah and his people, he was struck down during the night, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them were killed (IV Kings XIX), “and he himself will flee,” Sennacherib, “not from the face of a sword,” but from fear of the Lord, “and his young men” who remained “will become tributaries,” that is, tributary subjects of the Medes and Persians. For that most powerful Assyrian kingdom was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and afterward by the Medes and Persians, both the Assyrians and the Chaldeans, under Darius and Cyrus, who killed Belshazzar.

“And its strength”—that is, the multitude of Sennacherib—“will pass away from the torrent” of the angel, “and its princes, fleeing, will be afraid.” For, as the Hebrews report, as mentioned above, only ten remained from that entire multitude, and they returned with Sennacherib. “The Lord said”: Since Sennacherib and his people will perish, if you turn to him “whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.”

As far as the literal sense is concerned, the Lord’s fire and furnace were in Jerusalem, because the temple was there, containing altars: on one of them a perpetual fire was maintained, and on the other holocausts were burned daily. In the higher sense, however, by Zion, which is interpreted as “mirror” or “watchtower,” the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles into the faith of Christ is understood; Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies the heavenly homeland. By the fire and furnace is understood the ardor of love and devotion with which all the elect burn and glow toward God and neighbor, both those established in the present age and those in the Jerusalem above.

That fire signifies love of God and neighbor is made clear by the Lord when he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). But it must be considered that, in comparison with a furnace, a fire may be small; and as great as the difference is between a small fire and a very large furnace, so great—and much greater—is the difference between the love and fervor of devotion toward God possessed now by the elect in the present age and that possessed by the saints already joined to the Lord in heaven.

The Lord therefore, whose fire is—that is, the fervor of devotion in the Church still established on earth—and whose furnace is—that is, the fullness of devotion in the heavenly Jerusalem—said, he for whom to speak is to act: “For if you cast away your idols and appease him by your good works, he himself will fight for you, and Assyria will fall, not by the sword of a man, but will be devoured by heavenly fire.”

Some teachers also explain in another way what is said: “On that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver”—that is, when Assyria has fallen by the sword of no human being and its terrified princes have fled, a man will cast away the idols of his silver and turn to the Lord. This was fulfilled in the time of Hezekiah. For since he was righteous and the Lord had delivered him from the hands of the Assyrians, he turned the people of Judah away from the evils by which his father had caused Judah and Benjamin to deviate from the way of the Lord (2 Chronicles XXIX). And he converted not only those who lived under his rule, namely Judah and Benjamin, to the worship of God; through his churches he also recalled those who remained in the ten tribes.

## CHAPTER XXXII

“Behold, he will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in judgment.” The prophetic discourse now speaks of the Lord and his apostles. The Lord himself reigns in righteousness, because he teaches us how to live justly and rightly. For he is the king who governs the minds of his elect. He is the king who will give his elect the kingdom of the Father on the day of judgment, saying: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). Christ will also reign in righteousness because, at his second coming, he will not show partiality toward any person in judgment, just as he did not at his first coming. His princes are called the apostles, who, taught by truth and righteousness, proclaimed judgment. Through their preaching, the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord by the judgment of the Spirit (Psalm XVIII); and they themselves, when judging, will not show partiality toward anyone.

“And a man will be like one who hides from the wind.” He now speaks of the people of believers, who are protected and defended by the Lord from the assaults of demons. He gives three comparisons: “Like one,” he says, “who hides himself in a house because of a violent wind and a tremendous storm, and rests; and like one who is thirsty and, when he finds streams of water, drinks and his soul is refreshed; and like one who walks through the desert under a burning sun and, when he finds a rock of extraordinary size, is sheltered from the excessive heat beneath its shade: so will be the one who believes, protected by the king, the Lord God, and the one who flees beneath the shadow of the holy Church.”

“The eyes of those who see will not be dim, and the ears of those who hear”—will “listen attentively” to Christ and his admonitions. In this passage the apostles are called those who see and hear. For they heard from the Lord: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear” (Matthew XIII), and so forth. For what the prophets foretold and saw in an enigma and a mirror, these men saw both with the eyes of the body and with the eyes of the mind. The apostles and believers may also be called ears, because they gladly received the words of the Lord. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII). John likewise speaks in this way in the Apocalypse (Chapters II and III) to the seven churches.

“The heart of the foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers will speak swiftly and clearly.” Those who had neither knowledge nor faith before the Lord’s coming were called foolish; the apostles were among them. A stammerer is one who cannot speak readily, or one who does not possess perfect faith. But what did the Lord do when he came into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation? He called the foolish, ignorant, and uneducated, those who did not possess the light of true faith; he filled them with his wisdom, and through them reduced the wise of this age to nothing. “For God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians I).

The heart of the foolish may also signify the Gentile people, who were foolish—that is, estranged from Christ—before the apostles’ preaching. After the Son of God’s ascension into heaven, therefore, through the apostles’ teaching and miracles they were converted from the foolishness of idols to true knowledge; and the tongues of unbelievers, who had not known how to say, “I believe in God,” now possessing right faith, began to praise God clearly, that is, with a tranquil mind.

“He who is foolish will no longer be called a prince, nor will the deceitful be called great.” He calls philosophers of human wisdom foolish, men who appeared to hold authority among the peoples, such as Plato, Aristotle, and very many others. After Christ’s teachings, they were considered foolish, because Christ’s teaching surpasses all their wisdom. Therefore their empty teaching was judged foolish, just as the eminent preacher says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians III). And again: “God made the wisdom of this world foolish.” The wisdom of Christ, however, flourishes, refreshing the hearts of the faithful.

The scribe and Pharisee is called deceitful because they defrauded the simple of Christ’s law on account of their traditions, and were also deceitful against the Lord himself. After the Lord’s coming, therefore, they were neither called princes in the holy Church nor great men; the holy Church did not receive them into its unity, but received conquerors—those founded upon the truth, which is Christ.

“For the foolish man speaks foolishly, and his heart will practice iniquity.” Again, the scribe and Pharisee is called foolish. They spoke foolishly when they said: “You have a demon, and you cast out demons by Beelzebub” (John VIII; Luke XI). Their heart practiced iniquity when they said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX).

“To utter hypocrisy and speak deceitfully against the Lord.” They were hypocrites because they presented themselves as righteous, although they were full of iniquity. To them the Lord also said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees and hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs.” They spoke deceitfully when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth,” continuing: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew XXII). But what did they hear from the Lord? “Why,” he said, “are you testing me, hypocrites?”

“And he will make the soul”—that is, the mind—“of the hungry empty,” that is, alienated from the bread of God’s word, that scribe and Pharisee; “and he will take away drink,” that is, knowledge. For the Jewish people wished to receive from the Lord spiritual bread and water, that is, saving instruction, but were prevented by the scribes and Pharisees. Those teachers—or rather, seducers—said to them: Why do you accept this man’s preaching, and why do you believe in him? He is not the one promised to us in the Law and the Prophets. “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from” (John IX). They spoke lies, because they had been taught by the devil, who is a liar and did not stand in the truth (John VIII).

“The vessels of the deceitful are utterly bad.” He calls the scribes and Pharisees deceitful, as above. Their vessels are their hearts, or even the hearts of their subjects, which they had made such through their evil and deceitful teaching. For bad children are born from bad parents, and the worst disciples from the worst teachers. Just as a viper gives birth to a viper, so the scribes and Pharisees taught the worst disciples. Of them it is also said: “Brood of vipers,” and: “Evil and adulterous generation” (Matthew III, XII, XVI, and XXIII).

“For he himself”—understand, the order of the scribes and Pharisees—“contrived what was unjust and false,” that is, prepared and devised it, “to destroy the meek through a word of deceit.” They devised perverse thoughts to destroy the meek, that is, all the simple, when they said to Nicodemus: “Search the Scriptures carefully, and you will see that Christ will not arise from Galilee” (John VII). Likewise, when they said to the blind man whom the Lord had given sight: “Give glory to God”—that is, deny what you have received, and do not say that Jesus enlightened you, but God the Father (John IX). For they filled them with their false teachings in order to withdraw them from the true preaching of Christ.

“When the poor man spoke”—that is, Christ—“judgment,” that is, discernment, “they reproved him.” He calls him poor because, although he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty he might enrich us (2 Corinthians VIII). He spoke judgment when he said: “If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me” (John X).

“But the prince”—that is, Christ—“will think on the things worthy of a prince, and he himself will stand above the leaders.” The Lord Jesus spoke and thought upon things worthy of him when he said: “I proceeded from God and came”; “I and the Father are one”; and: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” The apostles are called leaders because they provided leadership to all believers. Of one of them the Psalmist speaks: “But you are a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance” (Psalm LIV).

“Women of wealth, rise and hear.” The prophet speaks to the women of the Jews, who were led away as plunder by the Romans in the final captivity, and commands them to listen attentively to his words. Through these women we should understand the synagogues of the Jews, or the cities; or even noble and wealthy matrons, who are called wealthy because they abounded in works.

And what does he say to them? “O women who were once wealthy but are now held captive, rise.” One lying down or sitting is told, “Rise.” They were lying in the mire of vices, sluggish in good works. And what does “Rise” mean except “Do penance” (Matthew IV)? “And hear my voice”—that is, understand with your heart, and ascend from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things. “Daughters who were once confident in your riches, receive my words with your ears.” These are the same as the women, for repetition of the discourse confirms the matter under discussion.

“For after days and a year, you too will be disturbed, you who are confident” in your possessions. He calls the period of the Lord’s preaching “days” and “years.” For example, he includes two and a half years when he says “days”; and a third when he says “after days” and adds “a year.” The entire period of the Lord’s preaching may also be intended, as Isaiah himself says elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” continuing to: “and to proclaim the year of the Lord” (below, LXI, LXIII); and: “For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of recompense for the judgment of Zion” (Jeremiah XLVI).

After the Lord’s ascension into heaven they began to be disturbed, although not immediately. Nevertheless, in the forty-second year after his ascension they were scattered and plundered by the Romans. Therefore, because they refused to receive the Lord’s preaching and condemned him to death, the prophet addresses them so that they may return to repentance: “Recall,” he says, “that you were unwilling to hear the words of salvation, and even while placed in captivity return to him, so that he may have mercy on you and deem you worthy to gather within the holy and undefiled Church.”

“For the vintage is finished; the gathering will come no more”—understand, upon you. He calls the final captivity a gathering and a vintage. “The vintage is finished,” he says, that is, your captivity has been completed and fulfilled. It will no longer be necessary for you to go into captivity, because you have been scattered throughout all the nations.

“Be astonished”—that is, marvel at your misery. O most wretched women of the Jews, who were once “wealthy” and abounded in riches, “be disturbed,” you most miserable women who trusted in your riches—that is, do penance. “Strip yourselves”—that is, bare your breasts, as another edition reads—“and be ashamed,” that is, blush over your wickedness. “Gird your loins” with the sackcloth of repentance, and weep so that you may be able to appease the Lord’s anger.

“Mourn over the breasts”—that is, over the children of your breasts, who were killed by hunger, the sword, and captivity, and scattered among all the nations. For the Lord said to them: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children” (Luke XXIII), and the rest that follows. For the curse that they uttered—“His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII)—was extended over their subsequent generations.

“Over the desirable land”—that is, on account of your desirable land, flowing with milk and honey—weeping because you have been expelled from it and made exiles, scattered far and wide. “Over the fertile vineyard”—that is, the rich vineyard—understand, weep. This is the vineyard of which he says elsewhere: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah V); and: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Psalm LXXIX).

“Upon the soil of my people briars and thorns will rise; how much more upon all the houses of joy of the exultant city?” He calls the soil of his people the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, because the temple and altars were there, where sacrifice was offered morning and evening. He calls the houses the cities of the other tribes and says: If calamity came upon that land, how much more upon their other cities and regions. For when the city and temple had been destroyed (Luke XIX), just as the Lord had foretold, thorns and brambles rose up in those places where formerly there had been the greatest glory and dignity.

“For the house has been abandoned”—that is, the temple has been deserted by God. “The multitude of the city”—that is, the multitude of its houses—“has been left” by its inhabitants, just as the Lord foretold to them: “Behold, your house will be left desolate” (Matthew XXIII). “Darkness and groping” means that the darkness is tangible. We read something similar in Exodus: “And tangible darkness came upon the land of Egypt” (Exodus X).

The treasury buildings, porticoes, and courtyards adjoining the temple are now contemptuously called caves. For when thorns and briars had grown up, darkness came to those places. “The joy of wild asses, the pasture of flocks”—understand, will be there. The wild ass is a solitary ass; through it we should understand all beasts that love solitude, and also the birds that dwelt there for long periods.

Allegorically, however, the wild ass signifies the pagans who later inhabited that land and were senseless like beasts, worshiping various apparitions of demons. But when the prophet adds:

“Until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high,” the passage seems to sound as though someone were saying to him: How long will the joy of wild asses remain there—that is, how long will pagan and bestial people inhabit that place? The prophet answers: It will remain so long as this: until the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts II), returns to us, with Elijah and Enoch preaching, and softens our hearts of stone. Blessed Isaiah joined himself to those who will be found righteous at Christ’s coming; therefore he says, “upon us.”

“And Carmel will become a desert, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest.” Carmel is a mountain in the province of Phoenicia. We have already said above that by the desert, or Lebanon—which is interpreted as “whitening” or “making white”—the Gentiles are signified, for they were a desert, that is, abandoned by God. But they were made white in baptism through the apostles’ preaching, and were changed into Carmel, which is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision.” What the Jews practiced carnally, the Gentiles now truly and spiritually fulfill through baptism, having been changed into true circumcision. The Jews, however, were changed into a desert or forest, that is, into the unbelief of the Gentiles. This was fulfilled after the Lord’s ascension, when the apostles, expelled by the Jews, went throughout all the nations and preached everywhere.

“And he will dwell in the wilderness”—that is, among the Gentiles. “Judgment and righteousness”—that is, Christ—“will sit in Carmel.” By judgment understand the judge of judgment, the Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). Christ therefore dwells in the wilderness, that is, in the hearts of the Gentiles through faith and love; and he who is righteousness and truth sits in Carmel, that is, in the congregation of the faithful who possess true circumcision.

Thus the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians III, 6); and: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians III); and the Lord himself: “He who remains in me, and I in him” (John XV); and through the prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (Leviticus XXVI).

“And the work of righteousness will be peace”—that is, of Christ, who said: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV), in place of “I will give.” For he came for this purpose: to reconcile the world to God the Father through his blood.

“And the service of righteousness will be silence.” Service—that is, the religion of Christ—is faith and sincere action. When he says that the service of righteousness will be silence, he shows that the Gentiles, who perceive that God is present everywhere, do not believe that they will be heard through much speaking, as the scribes and Pharisees do, who love to pray in the corners of the streets and in the marketplaces, so that they may be seen by human beings (Matthew VI).

“And security forever.” And where is this security? In the Church, that is, in the congregation of the faithful. For although the saints often endure the adversities of this age, they nevertheless dwell in security, certain of the hope of eternal recompense. While they still remain in the flesh, they already possess heavenly things in their minds, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians V).

“And my people will sit in the beauty of peace, in tents of confidence, and in abundant rest.” Here he calls the people not Jewish but Gentile, who now sit in the Church, where there is the greatest beauty in the splendor of faith, dignity, peace, and concord. For the Church sits in beauty, possessing bishops, presbyters, Levites, and the other ranks by which it is adorned; moreover, it possesses the three orders: prelates, virgins, and married people. This is its most splendid beauty.

“And in tents of confidence.” Although the holy Church is one in faith and in baptism, it is spread throughout the four regions of this world, dwelling in tents of confidence. And how does it dwell in tents of confidence? Because it is founded upon Christ, who is the cornerstone (Ephesians II), joining one Church to himself from the two peoples. Or it dwells in tents of confidence in mind, not in body; of these the Lord said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV). Since the saints desire nothing earthly but contemplate heavenly things with the full ardor of their minds, they dwell, as it were, in heavenly tents in hope.

“And in abundant rest”—that is, rest full of riches. The holy Church sits in abundant rest because it is nourished by the mysteries of the Old and New Testament. Or it will sit in abundant rest when it sees the Lord Jesus Christ in the glory of the Father’s majesty, how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father (John XIV), and the Holy Spirit in both. And when it sees how Christ is in his body, which is the Church, and the Church remains in him, when God will be all in all (1 Corinthians XV).

“But hail” will be “in the descent of the forest, and the city will be humbled with utter humiliation.” He calls the Jewish people a forest, because it was changed into the unbelief of the Gentiles. This was fulfilled, is fulfilled daily, and will finally be fulfilled on the day of judgment. Hail—that is, a storm of tribulation and calamity—came upon the Jews when they were killed by the Romans, their city and temple were burned, and they themselves remained and were scattered throughout the whole world. Even now there is a hailstorm of misery upon them, because they have been reduced to servitude under the nations. And what is more grievous, since they are alienated from God, their most wretched souls are daily taken captive by the devil.

On the day of judgment, however, the wrath and sentence of almighty God will come upon all who have despised the Lord’s preaching and that of his apostles and have remained in the error of unbelief; they will be handed over to perpetual fire, to be tormented in body and soul.

“Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the ass.” The divine discourse has thus far spoken of the overthrow and misery of the Jews; it turns again to the apostles and holy preachers, who called people to the faith, saying: Blessed are you who sow the word of the Gospel beside all waters, that is, in the hearts of all nations, sending forth the foot—that is, the action—of the ox and the ass into the bonds of God’s commandments.

By the ox, which is a clean animal and bears the yoke, the Jewish people are signified, because, keeping God’s commandments over a long period, they were clean and bore the heavy yoke of the Law. The ass, however, which is unclean, signifies the Gentiles, who through the worship of idols were unclean and wicked, far removed from knowledge and service of God.

The divine discourse therefore says: Blessed are you, holy preachers, who sow the doctrine of the Gospel and the word of faith in the hearts of Jews and Gentiles, introducing—that is, bringing—their action and practice into the bonds of heavenly commandments, so that from the two peoples you may build one holy and undefiled Church for the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

“Woe to you who plunder; will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise, will you not yourself be despised?” He now speaks against Sennacherib. For he had plundered all the provinces and regions around him, and moreover the ten tribes, and finally all the cities of Judah and Benjamin except Jerusalem. Because of this he was lifted up in pride and boasted that he had done all these things by his own strength and power, not remembering that, on account of their sins, the Lord had handed them over to be trampled upon. Therefore the divine discourse is directed against him: O most proud Sennacherib, you who plunder others will certainly be plundered by others. And you who despise—that is, look down upon—all nations will yourself be despised and scorned.

“When you have finished plundering” Egypt or Judaea, including the part of Jerusalem that Shebna surrendered, “you will be plundered; when, wearied, you cease to despise, you will be despised.” This was fulfilled, as it is foretold here (2 Kings XIX). For when he came back weary from Egypt, because of the many troubles, against Jerusalem and King Hezekiah, the angel of the Lord went out—as the following events show—and killed 185,000 men in his camp.

This may also be referred to all who act impiously and plunder the houses of the poor and orphans, and even to the devil himself. For those who continually practice robbery and pursue pride, and who are entangled in other evils, if they do not produce fruits worthy of repentance (Luke III), although they are not punished temporally in the present, nevertheless, after the course of this life has ended, they will be humbled by sentence and will pay the penalties of judgment.

“Lord, have mercy on us; we have awaited you. Be our arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation.” The prophet Isaiah now speaks in the person of the people of Jerusalem, who were besieged by the army of Sennacherib, and entreats the Lord, saying: Lord, have mercy on us, free us from the hands of the Assyrians, and protect this city, because we have awaited you in faith, trusting that you would free us. We have not sought idols and images, because they cannot help us, but you, who alone are powerful.

“Be their arm in the morning.” Some manuscripts read, “Be our arm.” If we say, according to blessed Jerome, “Be their arm,” the meaning will be: Be their arm—that is, their conquest and repulsion of the enemy. If, however, we say “our,” the meaning will be: Be our arm—that is, our strength and defense—and defend us by your power and might.

It must not be overlooked why he says “in the morning.” When the army of the Assyrians was killed in the manner described above, those who remained of Sennacherib did not know what had happened in their camp until they rose in the morning and saw all the bodies burned. Then, struck by immense fear, they fled to their own land. Therefore, because in the morning they learned what had happened and in the morning they took flight, the prophet says: “Be their arm in the morning”—that is, their conquest and repulsion—and “our salvation in the time of tribulation.”

“At the voice of the angel the peoples fled; at your exaltation the nations were scattered.” Some maintain that it was the angel Michael, who was appointed prince of the Jewish people, as it is written in the book of Daniel: “No one is my helper in all these matters except Michael your prince” (Daniel X). Others say that it was Gabriel, whose name is interpreted as “strength of God,” because he presides over the peoples. The teachers of the Jews also affirm the same thing: that he struck those many thousands of Assyrians and filled the hearts of those who remained with overwhelming terror (3 Kings XIX).

This is what he means by “at the voice of the angel”: the peoples fled at Gabriel’s terror—that is, the ten leaders who remained, who had also come with Sennacherib. Therefore he says: “At your exaltation, Lord, the nations were scattered,” because almighty God was then exalted and proclaimed great by all who heard that by his power he had struck down, through one of his angels, so many thousands of men who had risen up in pride against him. Almighty God is said to be exalted whenever he takes vengeance upon his enemies, because those who refused to know him in a time of peace will know him in a time of tribulation.

“And your spoils will be gathered as the locust is gathered, as when ditches are filled with it.” Some manuscripts read, “our spoils.” If we say “your spoils,” the meaning will be: O wretched and most proud Assyrians, when you come against Jerusalem, your spoils will be gathered by the Jews, and their houses will be filled with your spoils, just as a ditch is filled by a multitude of locusts. If, however, we read “our spoils,” the meaning will be: O Jews who dwell in Jerusalem, do not fear the face of the Assyrians, because all their spoils and all their riches are already ours, and they will be gathered by us as the locust is gathered.

The bruchus is born from the locust and is called by that name until it has wings. But when its wings begin to grow and it attempts to fly, it is called an athelech. When it is finally able to fly fully, it again becomes a locust. The bruchus is much more destructive than the locust and the athelech, because it lacks wings and cannot move quickly; therefore, wherever it comes, it completely devours the crops.

The people of those regions to which locusts come customarily gather them into ditches and cover them with earth, so that, if the wind should happen to cast them into the sea, and the waves should cast them back onto the land, bruchi may arise from their offspring. For it often happens that they are born from eggs that were still in the mother’s body.

“The Lord has been magnified, because he has dwelt on high.” He has been magnified—that is, proclaimed great and praised—by Hezekiah and by those who saw the Lord’s victory over his enemies (2 Kings XVIII). He will dwell on high, either in the temple of his glory in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles XXIX), or in the height of the heavens, or in the hearts of the elect who long for heavenly things.

“He has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness,” because King Hezekiah judged justly the people dwelling in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem, recalling them from idolatry to the worship of God. This was accomplished through inward inspiration, so that he himself might live justly and judge the Lord’s people justly.

But what the prophet adds—

“And there will be faith in your times”—may be understood in two ways. Some manuscripts read, “in their times.” If we say “in your times,” the meaning will be that the prophet is addressing Hezekiah: O Hezekiah, when God has struck your enemies, faith—that is, its truth—will be proven in your times. If, however, we read “in their times,” the meaning will be: When almighty God has delivered his people from fear of their enemies, the faith of the besieged people will be proven in their times. It was proven in this way: abandoning their idols, they served the Lord with devotion of mind.

“The riches of salvation”—the judgments of the people—“were wisdom and knowledge.” Blessed Augustine makes this distinction between wisdom and knowledge: wisdom is understanding of divine things, while knowledge concerns human things. That people possessed wisdom because they were converted from iniquity to righteousness, from idolatry to the worship and service of God. They possessed knowledge because they did not surrender themselves to the Assyrian, although he had threatened them with many evils.

“The fear of the Lord itself is his treasure,” that is, the treasure of salvation. Without the fear of the Lord, neither wisdom nor knowledge will be of any benefit, nor can salvation be attained. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX). And Tobias says to his son: “You will have many good things if you fear God” (Tobit IV).

“Behold, those who see will cry out outside; the angels of peace will weep bitterly.” The divine discourse returns to the final captivity. These are the seers of whom he said above: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Mach. XIII). They are also those of whom the Lord said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke X). And to the Jews: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes” (Matthew XXIII).

They were the angels of peace—that is, messengers who announced the words of Christ, who is true peace and who said to them: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John XIV), and who reconciled us to God the Father and to the holy angels (Col. XIII).

After the Lord’s ascension, therefore, as the time of captivity approached, the apostles no longer cried out in Jerusalem announcing the word of the Gospel, but outside, that is, to the Gentiles. When the Jews themselves had rejected them, the apostles said (Acts XIII): “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.”

The angels of peace—that is, the apostles, messengers of peace and of the Gospel—wept bitterly because of the unbelief of the Jews, grieving over the destruction and wickedness of those from whose stock they had descended. One of their number says (Romans IX): “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, who are Israelites. I myself wished to be accursed for them”—that is, to be killed for their salvation.

«The roads of Jerusalem have been scattered; the one passing through it has ceased.» This happened after the Romans’ devastation. The roads were scattered because no one remained to come to the temple at the time of the solemn festival, as Jeremiah says: [Col. 0885D] “The roads of Zion mourn, because there is no one who comes to the solemnity” (Lam. I). “The covenant was annulled,” which God had made with Abraham and their fathers, saying: “I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven” (Gen. XVI and XVII). And through a certain prophet: “You shall dwell in this place from now and forever” (Eccl. XXXVII). And to Solomon: “My name shall be there forever.” He “cast away their cities” and “did not regard” them as “human beings.” Therefore they were regarded by the Lord as beasts, because, not recognizing that they were human beings, they lived after the manner of beasts, living in lust and sprouting with every kind of uncleanness. “The land mourned and languished.” It mourned, that is, it failed. It was not the [Col. 0886A] land that wasted away, but those dwelling in it. “Lebanon was confounded and became deaf”: there is no doubt that Lebanon signifies the temple. Of it we read in Zechariah: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. II); and in Ezekiel: “A great-winged eagle came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar” (Ezek. XVII). That temple, in which the prayers of those making petitions had previously been heard, was therefore reduced to deafness at the time of the final captivity because of the people’s sins; for although they prayed to the Lord to have mercy on them, they did not deserve to be heard because of the killing of the Son of God and his apostles. “And Sharon became like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel were shaken.” Sharon is the name of the entire province between Joppa and Lydda, where broad and fertile plains extend. [Col. 0886B] Bashan is likewise a region beyond the Jordan that belonged to King Og; Moses gave it to two and a half tribes for possession, and its name is interpreted as “very fruitful” or “fat.” Carmel, however, is the most fertile mountain of the Promised Land. By Bashan, Sharon, and Carmel we must understand all the fertility of the land of the Jews, which they lost because they rejected the Lord together with his disciples.

“Now I will arise, says the Lord,” from my excessive peace, to strike and kill the Jewish people. “Now I will be exalted,” that is, I will be glorified by the nations when they see that I have done this, “and I will be lifted up,” that is, I will be proclaimed great. This may also be referred to the Lord’s resurrection and ascension. “Now I will arise,” says the Lord, from the dead, having conquered the dominion [Col. 0886C] of death. And I will be exalted and lifted up by ascending to the Father.

“You will conceive heat”—O wretched Jews, when I have ascended to heaven, you will conceive heat, that is, you will be filled with the fervor of envy when you hear my name proclaimed by my apostles (Acts V and XIII). For thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealous envy” (Acts XIII). “You will give birth to stubble,” that is, words of blasphemy, which will be regarded as nothing, like stubble. For we read that they contradicted what Paul was saying, blaspheming. Let us also explain it another way: “You will conceive heat,” that is, anguish and ill will, and you will give birth to empty words or an evil deed. Nevertheless, both the conception and the birth—that is, the thought and the deed—[Col. 0886D] will be devoured, either by the fire of the Romans’ arrival or by the fire of the torment of Gehenna on the day of judgment. “Your spirit,” that is, your evil desire, “will devour you like fire, and the peoples will be like ashes from a fire.” Just as, after a fire consuming a great quantity of wood, only a few ashes remain as evidence, so after the captivity had ended only a few Jews remained from the multitude of Jews (James I). “Thorns gathered together”—that is, the Jews’ sins gathered together—will be burned by everlasting fire. For when sins have reached completion, they give birth to death. That thorns signify the pricks of sins is demonstrated where it is said: “Your land”—that is, your flesh—“will bring forth thorns for you” (Gen. III).

[Col. 0887A] “Hear,” O Gentiles, “who are far away,” whether from this land or from God, “what I have done, and know, you who are near,” Moabites and other nations, what I have done—how I avenged myself upon my enemies, the Jews. Once the devastation of the Jews had been accomplished, the divine word turned itself toward the Gentiles.

“They have been crushed,” that is, destroyed, “in Zion,” that is, in Jerusalem, “the sinners”—those who killed their own Lord. “Fear seized the hypocrites,” namely, the scribes and Pharisees, because of the Romans’ arrival.

To them he also said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Luke II). “Who will be able to dwell,” that is, to remain, “among you” who are faithful “with devouring fire?” The prophetic word addresses either the righteous among the Gentiles after recounting God’s mighty deeds. It calls God almighty [Col. 0887B] “fire,” of whom Moses says: “God is a consuming fire.” The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). He is fire, because by the fire of tribulation he crushed the Jews, and on the day of judgment he will condemn all the reprobate by the fire of his sentence. “Or who among you will dwell with everlasting burning?” God almighty is the burning, because he himself makes the hearts of the elect burn with love for him, and he himself will consume the sins of penitents with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

“Who walks in righteousness”—that is, who advances in virtues—“and speaks truth”; understand, he will be able to dwell with God. Righteousness is faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues that consist in righteousness. To speak truth is to speak not with deceit and fraud, but with upright faith. “Who rejects avarice arising from slander [Col. 0887C] and shakes his hands free from every gift.” He calls avarice an evil desire. Slander is sometimes a false accusation; but in this passage it means harm. Therefore, whoever has no evil desire arising from another’s injury and shakes his hands free from every gift—understand, he will be able to dwell with God. He says “from every gift” because there is a gift from the hand and a gift from the mouth. A gift from the hand comes from giving and receiving; a gift from the mouth is human praise and favor, which accomplishes nothing. “Who stops his ears so as not to hear bloodshed,” that is, so as not to consent to sin or commit it, “and closes his eyes so as not to see evil”—that is, who turns his eyes away from lust—such a person will be able to dwell with God.

“And he will dwell in the heights,” that is, in eternal happiness [Col. 0887D] with Christ. For blessed is the conscience that neither consents nor acts. “His exalted place is the stronghold of rocks.” The saints are called rocks because of the solidity of their faith founded upon Christ. By their examples and words we are instructed to seek heavenly and exalted things. “Bread will be given to him; his waters are faithful.” Because of his merits, bread and water are given to him—that is, the teaching of the divine Scriptures, which is bread in obscure passages and water in clearer ones. His waters are faithful because divine teaching is true.

“His eyes will see the King,” namely, the almighty Lord, “in his beauty,” that is, in the splendor of his divinity—that is, the eyes of all the saints after the day of judgment. “His eyes will behold the land,” [Col. 0888A] that is, the solidity of eternal rest, now in hope but then in reality. Of this land the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI).

“Your heart”—that is, your mind, O righteous one—“will meditate on fear.” Holiness is difficult to preserve without fear; hence it is said: “Wisdom is to fear God” (Eccl. I). And Simeon the righteous is read to have been devout and God-fearing. “Where is the learned man? Where is he who weighs the words of the law?
