Where is the teacher of little ones?” The divine word asks the righteous one where the learned man is—that is, the grammarian among the Jews, or the philosophers of the Gentiles with their human wisdom—and where the one who weighs the words of the law is, the scribe and Pharisee who burdened and weighed down the law by their false interpretation, and where now the teacher of little ones is, that is, the scribe of the foolish Jews.

[Col. 0888B] “You will not see an insolent people,” O righteous one, in the heavenly Jerusalem; nor will you see there a people of lofty and profound speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of their language. “In whom”—understand, the philosopher or Gentile—“there is no true wisdom.” He calls Plato, Aristotle, and the other philosophers of the nations an insolent people, because they shamelessly mixed falsehoods with truths. Likewise, he calls philosophers of human wisdom a people possessing height and eloquence of language: they speak elegantly and polishedly, some according to Cicero, some according to Aristotle; they possess only a display of words, not knowledge of divine mysteries.

“Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity.” The prophet Isaiah addresses the righteous man of whom he spoke above, and joins himself to the number of the elect, speaking of the heavenly Jerusalem: O righteous one, to whom it was said above, “Your heart will meditate on fear,” and “You will not see an insolent people”—look upon heavenly Zion, the city of solemnity and everlasting joy. “Your eyes will see,” O righteous one, “the wealthy Jerusalem.” It is as though he said in other words: You who now contemplate her in your mind will then see her truly wealthy, that is, filled with the riches of the vision of almighty God. “The tabernacle that can never be moved, whose nails will never be removed.” Now he is speaking of the present Church, which the ancient tabernacle [Col. 0888C] prefigured. It cannot be moved or shaken so that it falls, because it has been established upon the firm rock, of which the Apostle says: “The rock [Col. 0888D] was Christ” (I Cor. X). The Jews had a tabernacle, but it was carried from place to place: from [Cremo?] to Shiloh, from Shiloh to Nob, from Nob to Jerusalem, and from Jerusalem—as is read in the Book of Maccabees—Jeremiah carried it to the tomb of Moses. But this tabernacle, that is, the present Church, will not be transferred from place to place; that is, it will not change from good to evil, because it has Christ as its dwelling and is fixed upon him. When he says that its nails will not be removed, he speaks metaphorically. Just as a tabernacle, tent, or pavilion is secured by nails and stretched by ropes, so the holy Church is strengthened by nails—that is, by holy teachers, through whose miracles it is instructed—and stretched [Col. 0889A] by ropes, that is, by the foundations of the divine utterances.

“For there,” that is, in the hearts of his elect, “the Lord our God is magnificent”—not in the gatherings of heretics or in the synagogues of the Jews—“a place of rivers”; understand, there are also “streams, very high and broad.” He calls the prophets and apostles rivers, because they drew from the true fountain what they brought forth for us. He calls broad streams the interpreters of the Holy Scriptures, who clearly explained for us what the prophets and apostles had uttered obscurely, such as Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory. “No rowing ship will pass through it,” understand, through the tabernacle, which is the congregation of the elect—“nor will a great trireme [Col. 0889B] cross it,” understand, the holy people of God. A trireme is a ship having three rows of oars. Here it signifies the devil because of his pride: before the Lord’s coming, he had subjected the three parts of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa—under his power.

“For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us,” understand, from the devil. This is the voice of the elect who still dwell in the penitent Church. Our judge is almighty God, because he is the discerner of judgment, and he will judge the whole world in equity. He is also our lawgiver, because he gave us the natural law, which is: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” He also gave the law through Moses, and finally the law of evangelical [Col. 0889C] truth.

“Your ropes have been loosened, but they will not prevail.” Thus far he has spoken of the heavenly Jerusalem and of the Church of the present age. Now he returns to the earthly Jerusalem, speaking of it under the figure of a ship. “Your ropes have been loosened” means that all the strength of your people will be loosened and extended as it strives to fight against the Romans; but it will not prevail, because the Lord will bring them to your destruction. “So will your mast be,” that is, your celebrated temple, in which the most precious sails once hung, “that you cannot spread the standard,” that is, so that it will not be apparent where it was first built, because not one stone will be left upon another. “Then,” that is, when Jerusalem and the [Col. 0889D] temple have been burned, “the spoils of many plunderings will be divided” by the Romans—that is, all the wealth and every possession of the Jews. “The lame will plunder the spoil, and the neighbor will not say, ‘I am weak,’” that is, the Roman will not say to the Roman, “I am weak,” because Christ will furnish them with strength so that they can destroy the nation in their hostility. The Romans are called “lame,” not because they were lame, but because what they did against the Jews was not accomplished by their own strength, but by God’s power. “The people”—understand, the Roman people—“who dwell in it,” that is, who hold that land reduced under their authority. “Iniquity will be taken away from him.” The meaning is: If the Roman people were worthy and had any sin arising from the fact that they killed the Jews and inhabited their land, their iniquity would be taken away from them on account of this [Col. 0890A] deed, because they exercised the Lord’s vengeance.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“Come near, nations, and hear; and pay attention, peoples.” He speaks of the general sentence of the day of judgment and calls all nations to hear the just retribution rendered to the Jews. He also calls the earth and its fullness—that is, all human beings—and says:

“For there is indignation”—that is, vengeance—“of the Lord against all nations.” This does not mean that the Lord’s anger will rage on the day of judgment against only certain nations, but against all the reprobate. When he adds, “and fury against their entire army,” that is, against the army of the reprobate, this must be understood of the evil angels [Col. 0890B] who range through the regions of this air, with whom the Apostle says that we wrestle (Eph. VI). Christ killed them by his sentence when he said: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). “And he gave them slaughter,” that is, he permitted them to go into eternal condemnation.

“Their slain will be cast” into hell, “and a stench will rise from their corpses.” Those whom the devil killed by persuasion, and wicked men killed by living wickedly and teaching through evil examples—not in body but in soul—will on the day of judgment be cast together with those by whom they were deceived into eternal condemnation, there to be tormented; and they will give off a foul odor, because they will be tormented both in body and in soul.

“The mountains will waste away from their blood, and the whole army [Col. 0890C] of heaven will waste away.” Here he calls the kings, princes, and tyrants of this age mountains, such as Nebuchadnezzar, who shed the blood of many nations upon the people subjected to him, and such as the killers of the holy martyrs. By the army of heaven he means the angels of this air who preside over the individual kingdoms, as we can learn from the Book of Daniel (ch. X), where the prince of Persia and the prince of Greece are mentioned. And the outstanding preacher says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world” (Eph. VI). Kings will fail because of the evils of their subjects, since they themselves were the authors of their wickedness; and the ruling demons of the various nations will fail, by whose evil counsel and deception both kings sinned and their subjects perished. “And they will be folded up [Col. 0890D] like a book, and their entire army”—understand, the army of heaven—“will flow away, as a leaf flows from the vine and from the fig tree” when winter approaches, “because my sword has been drunk in heaven.”

He used the plural “heavens” instead of the singular when he said “heavens,” because this is to be understood of this air. Air is commonly called heaven; hence we also say “the birds of heaven.” The army of heaven will flow away—that is, the sun, moon, and stars, or also the evil spirits. The stars will not flow away in such a way that they fall, but when Christ, the true light, arrives, they will be darkened. Hence the Savior also says: “The stars will fall from heaven” (Matt. XXIV), that is, [Col. 0891A] they will appear to fall. The evil spirits, however, will flow away because they will lose all power and will be shut up in hell. This air will be folded up because it will be enveloped in fire and will appear to be folded like a book. Let us also consider another interpretation of the folding of the heavens. He does not say that the heavens will perish, but that they will be folded like a book: after all sins have been disclosed, they will be folded up, though previously open, so that the sins of the wicked may no longer be written in them. Daniel speaks of books of this kind (ch. VII): “The court sat, and the books were opened, in which the deeds of each person had been recorded.” All these things will happen because my sword has been drunk—that is, filled—in heaven, that is, in this air, to destroy the demons and all the reprobate. “My sword,” he says, “has been drunk with the wickedness of human beings”—that is, the sentence, revenge, or vengeance for destroying the reprobate has been completed. “Behold, [Col. 0891B] my sword will descend upon Idumea, and upon the people destined for my slaughter for judgment”; understand, it will come for condemnation. Idumea, which is interpreted as “earthly,” signifies this world. Once the demons have been condemned in the air, vengeance will come upon the reprobate on earth.

“The sword”—that is, the vengeance—“of the Lord is filled with blood,” that is, with the sins of human beings. “Made fat,” that is, filled, “with fat,” that is, with the iniquity “of the wicked,” that is, “filled with the blood of lambs and goats,” understand, it is filled with this. Here “lambs” does not mean the meek and righteous, but powerless and ordinary people. “Goats” are the powerful and princes of this age. This is what [Col. 0891C] follows: “with the blood of the fat ones.” Yet by goats we may also understand the lustful. The day of judgment will come upon every condition and every kind of person: upon free and slave, upon kings and princes and their subjects, upon the powerful and the powerless, and upon all who died in their iniquity. “For the sacrifice of the Lord”—that is, vengeance—“is in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.” Bozrah, which is interpreted as “fortified,” “surrounded,” or “strengthened,” and Edom, which is interpreted as “earthly” or “bloody,” signify this world, which is fortified and surrounded by waters—understand, filled with the blood and wickedness of human beings.

“And unicorns will descend” [Col. 0891D] into hell “with them,” those of whom we spoke above, “and bulls with the powerful.” Unicorns are called kings and emperors who possessed the monarchy of the whole world, such as Octavian, Nero, and the other Roman emperors. Bulls are called petty kings, counts, and princes. The powerful are the friends and advisers of kings and all the nobles. Earthly kings, living with their princes and friends like themselves, will descend into hell, so that, just as they were united in evil, they may be joined in punishment. “The earth is drunk,” that is, hell, “with their blood,” that is, with the wickedness of the reprobate, “and the soil”—that is, the abyss of eternal condemnation—“will be filled with the fat,” that is, the pride, “of the fat ones,” that is, of the prosperous and powerful.

“For the day of the Lord’s vengeance is the year of retribution [Col. 0892A] for the judgment of Zion”—understand, it will come. What is said here does not pertain to what precedes. After the consummation of the whole world, the prophetic word returns to Jerusalem, to which it was speaking at that time, and describes its devastation in full: the devastation carried out by the Romans. The day of the Lord’s vengeance is the avenging of Christ’s blood. He calls the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion the entire period of Christ’s preaching, namely, three and a half years. During that time the inhabitants of Zion scorned receiving their Savior and lawgiver, and during that same period they handed him over to death. This is the year of which Isaiah later speaks (ch. LXI), in the person of the Son of God: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor and to proclaim [Col. 0892B] the acceptable year of the Lord.”

“And its torrents will be turned into pitch, and its soil into sulfur.” Because of the Romans’ excessive savagery and the frequent fires by which the entire Promised Land was surrounded—and because both the city and the temple were consumed by fire—its torrents and soil are said to have been turned into pitch and sulfur. “And its land will become burning pitch; night and day it will not be extinguished.” Night and day are to be understood as the continuation of time. It should be noted, however, that he does not say this because that land will burn forever, but because of the Jews’ immense tribulation and the desolation of that land. “Its smoke will rise forever,” that is, the sign of their extermination and calamity; “from generation” [Col. 0892C] to generation—understand, the vengeance of almighty God will remain upon them until the final generation. “It will be desolated for ages of ages,” that is, it will be reduced to solitude forever. “There will be no Jewish man passing through it.” Many Jews did pass through it after that final captivity, but not freely as they had formerly been accustomed to do, nor did they live there afterward. For the Romans established a law forbidding any Jew to return to the land of his birth.

“And they will possess it,” understand, the land of the Jews. “The onocrotalus and the hedgehog, the ibex, and the raven will dwell there.” The onocrotalus is a water bird hostile to serpents, possessing a very sharp and long beak. Josephus says that Moses brought these birds during the war against the Ethiopians because of the multitude of serpents with which the land through which he had to advance against the Ethiopians [Col. 0892D] was filled. It climbs upon the serpent’s head and kills it with a blow of its beak. These birds or animals seek solitude, and after the desolation of the human inhabitants they dwelt where previously the temple and royal residence had stood. “And over it”—understand, over the land—“a measuring line will be stretched,” that is, God’s sentence, so that the Jews will have no habitation there, but demons will; “it will be reduced to nothing, and the plumb line to desolation,” understand, it will be reduced to this. A plumb line is the instrument by which masons bring a wall into alignment, and that land, by the decision of God’s sentence, has been assigned to solitude.

[Col. 0893A] “Its nobles,” that is, the apostles and believers, “will not be there” when captivity and calamity come. They will call upon “the king,” Christ, while “all its princes,” that is, the priests and Pharisees, “will be reduced to nothing.” When the Romans came against Israel, the apostles had already been dispersed throughout the four quarters of the world. The believers and saints who remained there, having been warned by the Holy Spirit, crossed the Jordan to the kingdom of King Agrippa, who was at peace with the Romans.

“Thorns and nettles will arise in its houses,” once most beautiful and full of riches, “and the paliurus”—a kind of thistle with extremely sharp spines—“will be born in its fortifications,” understand, it will grow there. “And there will be a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches.” [Col. 0893B] The ostrich is a bird that seeks solitude.

“And demons will meet the onocentaurs, and the hairy creature will call to another.” Some manuscripts read “demons will meet,” dividing the words so that “to one another” is understood: “The onocentaur and the hairy creature will call to one another.” But it is better to punctuate it as follows: “Demons will meet the onocentaurs.” Onocentaur is a compound name from Greek and Latin, formed from *onos* and *taurus*. For in Greek *onos* means “donkey.” An onocentaur is a monster that begins as a donkey and ends as a bull. By the donkey, an animal ready to satisfy lust, are signified lustful people who always lie in the stench of debauchery. By the bull are signified the proud. Demons are said to meet them because they favor them by persuading their hearts through [Col. 0893C] evil suggestion, so that they act even worse while imagining that they are acting well. Some say that the hairy creatures are apes; others, wild men. Still others say they are incubus demons who have intercourse with women. “There the lamia will lie, and the hedgehog will find rest for itself.” A lamia is a monster with an entirely beautiful female face and body, but with the feet of a horse.

“Yet seek diligently in the Lord’s book and read.” By “the Lord’s book” the prophet means this book, which he received from the Lord and wrote down. He summons those who were to come in the future to read these things. “Not one of them”—understand, of the monsters mentioned above—“was missing. One did not seek another,” that is, neither the male the female nor the female the male, because the Lord brought them all to that place. “For that which proceeds from [Col. 0893D] my mouth.” The prophet’s voice. “He,” that is, Christ, “commanded,” that is, ordered, “and his spirit,” that is, the Holy Spirit, “gathered them,” those living creatures; the Spirit himself gathered them.

“And he cast lots for them,” understand, for their dwelling, where all might remain in their proper places. “And his hand,” that is, his power, “divided it,” understand, the land, “by measure,” that is, into a desert habitation where dragons would dwell, where the lamia would dwell, where the ostrich would dwell, and where various beasts would dwell; they will inhabit it from generation to generation. As far as the literal sense is concerned, these birds or animals are not there to this day, although they may have been there for a time. As far as the spiritual meaning is concerned, by the birds and beasts we must understand all [Col. 0894A] those who have inhabited that land from that time onward, living like beasts and worshiping various monstrous things.

## CHAPTER XXXV

“The desert and the impassable place will rejoice, and the solitude will exult, and it will flower like a lily.” Thus far he has spoken about the devastation of the Jews; now he speaks about the conversion of the Gentiles. The Gentile world is called “desert” because it had been abandoned by God on account of the corruption of the natural law and idolatry. It was “impassable” because Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), was not in it. It was also impassable because no prophet, apostle, or teacher had passed through it to show it the way of truth. Once Judea had been abandoned, therefore, the Gentile world would rejoice, be glad, and flower [Col. 0894B] like a lily. Just as a lily gives off a pleasant fragrance when it sends forth flowers, so the Gentile world, coming to faith, produced from itself the fragrance of virtues. Thus the outstanding preacher says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II).

“Budding”—understand, faith and hope—“it will bud forth” in action, “and it will exult, rejoicing and praising” its Creator. Previously it remained in the sorrow of sins; converted to faith, it began to exult and rejoice in the Lord. Thus the Apostle says: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear children; break forth into joy and cry aloud” (Gal. IV). “The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon.” Here he calls the temple Lebanon, as was said above, while Carmel and Sharon signify the fertility of the Promised Land. The glory and worship that once existed in that temple are now found in [Col. 0894C] the holy Church, and in a much greater form. “They,” the faithful, “will see the glory of the Lord,” that is, the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, “and the beauty of our God,” that is, how the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. Now they see this in hope; then they will see it in reality.

“Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees.” He addresses the apostles and their followers, of whom he said above, “They will see the glory of the Lord,” so that they may strengthen the hands of the Gentiles, which are empty of good works, and he says: O my apostles, strengthen the hands of the Gentiles, wearied by wickedness, and make firm their feeble knees—that is, their steps, which limp in the worship of God—establishing them in faith.

“Say,” O my teachers, to the fainthearted Gentiles in faith: “Be strengthened,” that is, place your hope [Col. 0894D] in Christ, “and do not fear” the devil. “Behold your God,” O faithful ones; “he will bring vengeance, the reward of retribution.” The prophet addresses the Gentiles strengthened in faith: Behold, he says, your God will render to the wicked on the day of judgment a vengeance worthy of their deserts, “and he will come to save you” in his great mercy—you who have received the preaching of his apostles and fulfilled it in your deeds.

“Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.” These things are to be referred to the Lord’s first coming. The Lord fulfilled them bodily, as he said to John’s disciples: “Go and report to John that the blind see, the deaf hear, and the lepers are cleansed” (Matt. II), together with the other things [Col. 0895A] contained there. Spiritually, this is fulfilled every day in the holy Church, when an unbeliever whose eyes of the mind have been blinded and whose ears have been closed to hearing the word of God is converted to Christ and, after being baptized in the water of saving baptism, is enlightened. The eyes of the Gentiles, which had been blinded to knowing their Creator, were enlightened by the apostles’ preaching. Likewise, their ears, which had not at all been open to hearing the word of God, deserved to receive hearing when the apostles preached.

“Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute will be opened.” Every Gentile who, not yet possessing the steps of faith in his works, limped in God’s service, will come to faith and leap like a stag, when he passes from unbelief to faith, from vices to virtues, and from earthly things to heavenly things [Col. 0895B], striving to grow in virtue. Let us take Paul, once a persecutor of the Church and now an apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, as one example among all, and let us see how great a leap he made. For he who was an unbeliever and persecutor of Christians crossed over from treachery to faith and from iniquity to the worship of true righteousness. Passing from virtue to virtue, he said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I). The tongue of the wicked, which had no confession of true faith but was mute in confessing its sins and praising its Creator, was opened by the apostles’ preaching to confess the right faith. “For waters have burst forth”—that is, have been opened—“in the desert.” The tongue of the mute was opened because the waters of saving baptism were opened in the desert that had once been the Gentile world [Col. 0895C], “and streams arose in the solitude” of the Gentiles—that is, various spiritual graces, or the teachings of the Old and New Testaments.

“And what was dry,” that is, the Gentile world with respect to faith in God, “became a pool”—understand, it was turned into knowledge of the Old and New Testaments. “And what was thirsty became fountains of water,” that is, it was turned into the teaching of the divine utterances. “In the dens”—that is, in the hearts of the Gentiles—“where dragons,” that is, demons, “formerly dwelt, the greenness of reed and rush will arise.” By the reed, with which Scripture was formerly written, the preaching of teachers is signified. By the rush, the attentive hearing of those subject to instruction is signified. Reed and rush grow upon waters and retain their greenness. So too the hearts of the Gentiles, attentive to hearing the word of God, possess greenness when they strive to fulfill in their deeds what they receive through the ear.

“And there will be,” understand, in the solitude of the Gentiles, “a path and a [Col. 0895D] way”—that is, Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). “And that way will be called holy. The unclean will not pass through it,” understand, through the Church—the devil, who has been defiled by the blood of many and by every impurity. “And this will be a distinct way for you,” that is, the clear faith of Christ, “so that fools”—formerly the Gentiles, who worshiped the creature in place of the Creator—“will not go astray upon it” after being converted to the faith of Christ.

“There will be no lion there,” namely, the prince of demons, of whom the Apostle says: “Our adversary the devil [Col. 0896A] prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V). “And the evil beast,” that is, the devil’s satellites, “will not ascend through it,” that is, through the congregation of the faithful. “Nor will it be found there,” in the hearts of the elect, because it has been expelled by the confession of faith. “And those who have been set free will walk,” from virtue to virtue, “and those redeemed by the Lord” with the blood of the true Lamb “will return” to repentance, and afterward “will come to Zion,” that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, “with praise” of their Creator. “And everlasting joy” because of the hope of eternal reward “will be upon their heads,” that is, in their minds. Some manuscripts read: “And those who have been set free and redeemed by the Lord will return,” dividing the words in this way. But [Col. 0896B] this is written incorrectly. Blessed Jerome explains it as stated above: “They will obtain joy and gladness” when they come to the heavenly Jerusalem, “and sorrow and groaning will flee” from them. For although they groan and mourn amid the troubles of this age over their own errors or those of others, they rejoice in hope because of the reward they are destined to receive. Then they will rejoice in reality, already possessing the joys of eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXXVI
“And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.”

After the ten tribes had already been led into captivity and all the cities of Judah had been devastated, Jerusalem is reached. But at this point there is a considerable question: Who was this Sennacherib? For, as the history of the Kings and the book of Chronicles makes clear (ch. XXXII), in the seventh year of Hezekiah’s reign Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, came and transferred the greater part of the people of the ten tribes beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians. Among them the just man Tobias was also led into captivity, as is recorded in his book. For it says there: “When Tobias had been taken captive in the days of Shalmaneser” (Tobit I). After Shalmaneser, however, Pul came again, and he too carried off part of the people into captivity. Then Teglath, Phalassar, and Sargon succeeded to the Assyrian kingdom, down to Sennacherib. If, therefore, in the seventh year of Hezekiah’s reign the ten tribes were first led into captivity by Shalmaneser—and this is entirely true—how can it be that within a period of eight years so many kings succeeded one another in a single year? For eight joined with six make fourteen.

Blessed Jerome says: Because Jewish tradition reports that one man, Sennacherib, was called by all these names. For he was called Shalmaneser, and Pul, and Tiglath-pileser, and Sargon, and Sennacherib. This does not appear to differ from the truth.

“And the king of the Assyrians sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish.” Lachish was a city of Judah, which Sennacherib was then attacking. Therefore he sent the Rabshakeh “to Hezekiah with a great force,” that is, with a multitude of troops. “And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field,” that is, where the fuller lived. It is called the upper pool because there was another, lower one there.

“And Eliakim, who was over the house of the Lord, went out to him,” that is, the high priest. This is the Eliakim who succeeded the exceedingly proud Shebna in the priestly office, concerning whom the Lord said above: “Behold, I shall call Eliakim my servant, and he shall be my priest” (above, XXII). “And Shebna the scribe” also went out, that is, the grammarian. We must not think that this is the Shebna to whom the prophet earlier said: “What are you here, or who are you here?” “And Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder,” went out. A recorder was called one who wrote down the deeds of events, that is, a chancellor. This Joah too, coming from the chancellors or recorders over whom he presided, went with the men mentioned above. [Col. 0897B]

“And the Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king of the Assyrians.” He attributed to his own king, because of his rank and power, the words of God that he had often heard from his father: “Thus says the Lord,” so that his speech might be strengthened by greater authority. “What is this confidence in which you trust, or with what counsel or strength do you intend to rebel?” The Rabshakeh was speaking these words in the person of the king. At first Hezekiah had become tributary, but afterward he rebelled, unwilling to pay tribute. Therefore he says: “With what strength do you intend to rebel?” And because Hezekiah had withdrawn from him, he was coming against him for this reason.

“Behold, you trust in this broken reed-staff, in Egypt.” He means the Nile, because of the abundance of its waters, where there are many reeds. Through this mocking image he indicates the powerlessness of Egypt: “Thus Pharaoh, king of Egypt,” is powerless.

“But if you answer me: We trust in the Lord our God—surely he is the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem: You shall worship before this altar, which is in the temple of the Lord?” Thus this man recounted the words of his king as though the two kings were both present and were contending with one another. In his own time King Hezekiah destroyed the altars and idols that his father Ahaz had made. But what Hezekiah had done for the sake of religion, the Rabshakeh twisted into an accusation.

“And now surrender yourself,” O Hezekiah, “to my lord, and I shall give you two thousand horses, and you will not be able from your own resources” [Col. 0897D]—that is, from among your soldiers—“to provide riders for them.” He spoke this in the person of the king. The Jewish people did not lack the skill of riding through weakness, but because they observed the commandments of God, who commanded through Moses concerning the king of Israel: “He shall not multiply horses and chariots for himself, nor many wives” (Deut. XVII). Because Solomon did this, he fell under the anger of the Lord. Hezekiah could have possessed chariots and horses, but for this reason he abstained, fearing to fall into sin.

“And now,” that is, “have I come up without the Lord”—that is, without the Lord’s command and will?

“Speak to your servants in the Syrian language,” that is, Chaldaic. [Col. 0898A] “For we understand it” in Hebrew. He was speaking Persian, because he had learned it in the school of his father Isaiah. They said this so that he would not frighten the people standing on the wall with his words.

“Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you, and not rather to the men who sit on the walls, so that they may eat their own excrement and drink the urine of their feet with you?” Inflated with pride because of their humiliation, he addresses one of the messengers mentioned above in this fashion. He says “urine of their feet” because it reaches the feet. The sense is this: This city will remain under siege until, compelled by hunger, they consume their excrement and the urine of their feet for their own sustenance; and whoever is not killed by the enemy will perish from famine.

[Col. 0898B] “And he cried out in a loud voice”—in Hebrew, so that he might terrify the people with his threats—“Hear the word of the great king of the Assyrians.” He uttered this arrogantly and with excessive pride.

“Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to rescue you.” The Rabshakeh’s blasphemy bears witness that Hezekiah trusted in the Lord after all the cities of Judah had been captured. For that wicked man had heard that Hezekiah had strengthened the people of the Lord, so that they would not fear the Assyrians, saying: “Do not fear or be afraid, for those who are with us are far more numerous than those who are with them. With them is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, who will be our helper and will fight for us.” The people were strengthened by these and similar words.

“Make a blessing for us,” that is, praise me, bless me. Or, as another edition has it: “Do what is useful for you, so that, if you receive me, peace may remain with you.” “And let each one of you eat the good things of your land in security, until I come,” namely, from Egypt, where I have decided to go.

“And I shall take you to a land like your own land.” He does not name the region that he promises them, because he could not find one equal to the Promised Land; rather, he promises a likeness. Blessed Jerome nevertheless says that the land of the Medes has a certain resemblance to the Promised Land in its cultivation and situation, and there is no doubt that he promised them that land.

“Where is the god of Hamath and of Arpad? Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim?” Understand: They have been crushed. These cities, worshiping different gods, perished. It is as though he had said in other words: If many gods could not resist me, will one God be able? From his statement, “Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” it is shown that the ten tribes, among whom the royal city stood, worshiped many gods before they were led into captivity, and therefore they perished.

“And they were silent and did not answer him a word.” Why they did not answer is made clear by what follows: “For the king had commanded them: Do not answer him.” Or they also did not answer because they remembered Solomon’s saying: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. XXVI). And also: “Do not stir up the coals.” [Col. 0899A] For this reason too they did not answer him, lest they provoke him to greater blasphemy against the Lord or cause him to instill terror in the people hearing these things.

“And they entered before the king with their garments torn.” It was the custom of that people that, whenever they heard blasphemy against the Lord, they tore their garments. We read that the high priest did the same when the Lord said: “From now on you shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds” (Matt. XXVI). Paul and Barnabas also did this in Lycaonia when the people offered them garlands and wanted to worship them as gods (Acts XIV).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“And it came to pass, when King Hezekiah heard these words,” [Col. 0899B] “he tore his garments and was wrapped in sackcloth,” that is, instead of purple, in poor clothing, “and entered into the house of the Lord.” They tore their garments because of the blasphemy they had heard; he did so because, hindered by his sins, he considered the siege and devastation to have come upon them.

“Thus says Hezekiah.” He does not say, “Thus says King Hezekiah,” but speaks with complete humility: “Thus says Hezekiah.” “This is a day of tribulation”—understand, for us—“and of God’s correction, and a day of blasphemy” by the enemies. “For the children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to give birth; perhaps”—that is, perhaps—“the Lord your God will hear.” The sense is this: Just as a woman, at the time of childbirth, is distressed when she cannot deliver the child and has no idea what she can do, so we, now besieged on every side, do not know what we ought to do. Or, in another way: Our children are our plans; and when we conceive a plan but are unable to fulfill it in action, we are gravely distressed. Thus they gave birth to a plan but were entirely unable to accomplish it. “Therefore lift up a prayer to the Lord your God for the remnant that has been found, only in Jerusalem.” For the ten tribes had already been led into captivity, and all the cities of Judah and Benjamin had been devastated. Even the lower part of the city had been delivered into the hands of the enemy through the agency of the most wicked high priest Shebna, who had already completed his priestly office. Therefore he says, “for the remnant that has been found.”

“And the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.” [Col. 0899D] The men mentioned above are called servants. Indeed, all leaders are called servants, except advisers, who are called the king’s friends. Hence the expression: “Why are these men not with your friend?”

“And Isaiah said to them.” The prophet anticipated those messengers, because through the spirit by which he foretold the future he knew what had happened, what the Rabshakeh had said, and what the king had commanded him. “This is what you shall say to your lord”—understand, not to mine: “Thus says my Lord.” The leaders of kings who serve their kings are called boys.

“Behold, I shall put a spirit in him,” and he will return to his own land, that is, to Chaldaea. I shall put in him not a holy spirit but an evil one, “and I shall cause him to hear a report.” In what follows we shall see that he spoke of Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians.

“But the Rabshakeh returned.” With the Lord permitting, he came; and at the Lord’s command he withdrew. “And he found his king fighting against Libnah, Lachish already having been conquered.” Libnah was a city of Judah. He had been believed to be at Lachish, from where he had been sent to Jerusalem; but he had already departed from there and, following him, the Rabshakeh went to Libnah.

“And Sennacherib heard concerning Tirhakah the king.” This is the report mentioned above.

“Behold, you have heard all that the kings of Assyria,” my fathers, “have done,” who, with God permitting, devastated many regions; “Bozan and Aran and the kings of Assyria” were exceedingly powerful, “and the sons of Eden”—understand, they overthrew them. Eden is a region of the East. Ana and Ava were very renowned peoples or cities.

“And Hezekiah took the books,” that is, the gifts that Sennacherib had sent him.

“And he went up into the house of the Lord, and prayed, saying.” He is said to have gone up into the house of the Lord because it was situated above. The first time, when he went up into the house of the Lord with torn garments while the city was besieged, we do not read that he prayed to the Lord, because he considered this to have happened on account of his sins. Now, however, more confident of deliverance, he prays, saying:

“Lord of hosts, who are Lord of all,” both angels and human beings, “incline your ear and hear; open your eyes and see, and take vengeance.” God almighty is said to incline his ear when he hears those who pray. He is said to open his eyes when he has mercy.

“And they cast their gods into the fire,” that is, the idols on account of which they perished, “for they were not gods.” He explains why they perished. Sennacherib despised them.

“He has mocked you,” that is, he has ridiculed you, “virgin daughter of Zion. After you he has shaken his head, daughter of Jerusalem.” The people of Jerusalem are called virgin and daughter because, while all the nations worshiped images of dead human beings, this people alone preserved the chastity of devotion to God and the worship of the one God. Virginity belongs not only to the body but also to the mind. That people then despised and mocked Sennacherib and the Assyrians, when Eliakim and the other men sent by Hezekiah did not answer his messengers. But afterward, when the Assyrians had been killed and Sennacherib returned in disgrace, the daughter of Zion, or Jerusalem, made him captive, mocking and trampling upon him.

“Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed?”—through your servants? Hezekiah speaks mockingly to Sennacherib. “Against whom have you raised the height of your eyes?” Against the Holy One of Israel, that is, against almighty God, not against me. It is characteristic of the proud to raise their eyebrows.

“You said,” O Sennacherib, “I shall climb to the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon, and I shall cut down its lofty things, its throne, and its choice firs.” By cedars and firs, metaphorically, pride, kingdoms, and the kings of various nations who stood under his dominion are indicated. By Lebanon and its summit or height, Jerusalem and the temple are meant, to which he wished to ascend. By the forest of Carmel, the people of Jerusalem are meant.

“I dug and drank water, and with the sole of my foot I dried up all the streams of the embankments.” Such was the multitude of his army that he dried up all the streams of the land of Judah; and therefore they were compelled to dig wells for themselves. Metaphorically, however, by the streams of the channels and by the water we should understand the kingdoms and regions that he dried up by killing their inhabitants.

“Have you not heard”—that is, have you not understood, O Isaiah—“what I did to him long ago,” that is, what I predestined for him? These are God’s words to the prophet concerning Sennacherib. “From ancient days,” that is, from the beginning [Col. 0901B] of creation, “I formed it”—understand, the evil that Sennacherib inflicted upon all the nations. “And now,” what was in my predestination, “I have brought upon him,” so that he may receive what he did. “That evil came to pass” for the destruction of hostile hills and fortified cities.” By the hills we should understand the kings and rulers who fight among themselves and against one another; these are the ones whom Sennacherib, coming with the Lord’s permission—not because of his own merits but because of their sins—destroyed. It also came to pass for the destruction of fortified cities.

“Their inhabitants” of those lands or cities “trembled with weakened hands,” that is, because I did not provide them with my customary assistance and withdrew my help from them; “they were confounded” and consumed in their evils. Therefore they are not compared with fruitful olive trees, vineyards, and trees, but with hay, pasture grass, and roof-grass, which hinder crops and wither before reaching maturity. “Their inhabitants”—namely, those of the cities—“became like the hay of the field and the grass of the pasture, and like the grass of the roofs.” The grass in this passage is a plant that among us is called *trinua* [a plant-name of uncertain identification]. By the hay and the other things mentioned here we should understand the peoples who, because their sins hindered them, perished quickly before the time of their death had arrived, having been delivered into Sennacherib’s hands.

“Your dwelling-place”—namely, Babylon—“I have known, O Sennacherib, and your departure” from there, “and your entrance” into the Promised Land, “and your madness” against me—that is, your insanity. [Col. 0901D] He went mad when he said: “What god will be able to deliver you from my hand?”

“Therefore I shall put a ring in your nostrils.” By the bridle and the ring we should understand the power of divinity. It is as though he had said in other words: “By the power of my strength I shall bridle your blasphemous mouth and lead you back from Jerusalem to your own land in disgrace.”

“But to you,” O Hezekiah, “this shall be a sign” of your salvation. The prophet addresses King Hezekiah concerning what he must do. “Eat this year, you and your people, what grows of itself,” that is, what you sowed before the Assyrian came, “and in the second year eat fruit.” At that time, when the harvest season was already approaching, the Assyrians came and trampled their crops, vineyards, and olive groves. Because the fields had been devastated by the excessive siege, what was later restored from the grain served them as food in the first year, and likewise in the second year; for in the year of the siege they were unable to sow, and they consumed what they found among the grain and fruit. “But in the third year,” when the Assyrian had already been driven away and they were secure, “sow and reap, and plant vineyards” again, which the Assyrians had devastated and uprooted.

“And it shall send out”—understand, the human race—“what was saved” by the Lord “from the house of Judah, and what remains shall send down roots and produce fruit above.” Just as a tree sends its roots downward in its season and is filled with fruit above, so the entire land of the two tribes was filled from a small people. [Col. 0902B] Therefore he adds:

“From Zion and from Jerusalem the remnant shall go forth,” because the ten tribes and all the cities of Judah had been devastated. “The zeal of the Lord”—that is, the fervor of love and mercy—“shall do this,” what was said above, not their merit.

“He shall not enter this city.” He did indeed besiege it, but he shall not enter it. “He shall not shoot an arrow there,” so as to kill anyone there.

“And I shall protect this city in order to save it, for my sake,” not because of your merit, “but for the sake of David my servant.” When he says “for the sake of David,” he shows that some were there who possessed something of David’s merit and faith. From this it is understood that almighty God has mercy on wicked children for the sake of good fathers.

“And the angel of the Lord went out,” understand, from his place, “and struck down eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians.” He did not kill them with a material sword, but by the power of God. They were killed without a wound and reduced to ashes. “And they rose in the morning”—namely, Sennacherib with only a few, just ten men, as the Jews relate—“and behold, all” those slain were “corpses of the dead.”

“And Sennacherib departed from the borders of Judah and went to his own land, to the city of Nineveh. And it came to pass, while he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down.” It is asked why he did not perish with the people over whom he ruled, since the wickedness for which they perished had been carried out at his command. The answer is that he was shown to be even more wicked in this respect: he was not worthy to die in the land of the Lord, but in his own land, and to be killed by his sons before his own god. Pharaoh too was preserved through the ten plagues so that the Lord might be glorified more fully.

It may also be asked what caused him to be killed by his sons. Hebrew tradition says that he had many wives, by whom he had three sons: Adrammelech, Sarasan, and Esarhaddon. But because he loved Esarhaddon’s mother more than the others, he decided that Esarhaddon should succeed him in the kingdom. When the other two saw that they had been disinherited, they killed their father. And because their brother Esarhaddon already held the reins of the kingdom, they fled to the land of Ararat, which is a region of Armenia.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0903A]

“In those days,” when the Assyrian had been killed, “Hezekiah became ill with a very serious sickness.” Here it is not made clear why he became ill or why he was stricken. But in the book of Kings and in Chronicles it is shown more plainly that he became ill because he did not sing praises to the Lord or give him thanks for the victory granted to him, but became proud (IV Kings XX; II Chronicles XXXII). “Set your house in order,” that is, arrange who should succeed you in the kingdom.

“And he turned his face toward the wall,” of his house or of the temple, so that those standing around would not hear his groaning or see his tears.

“I have walked before you in truth,” that is, in [Col. 0903B] the worship of religion, “with a perfect heart,” not limping after idols. “I did what was good in the eyes of the Lord,” because he destroyed the idols that his father had made. He himself opened the doors of the house of the Lord, which his wicked father had closed, and he broke into pieces and scattered to the wind the bronze serpent that was in Gibeon, which the Jews worshiped. “And Hezekiah wept with a great weeping.” He wept because he was without children. He saw that, because of his sins, the promise that the Lord had made to David was perishing in him: “When you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your offspring who shall come forth from your loins, and I shall place him upon the throne of Israel forever. And he shall be a son to me, and I shall be a father to him” (I Chronicles XXII; II Samuel VII; Hebrews I).

“Behold, I shall add fifteen years to your days.” In God’s predestination they had first been given to him, but because of his pride and sins they were taken away from him; on account of his humility, however, they were restored. Some say that a person can anticipate the end of his life in two ways: either by living badly, so that because of his sins he is not deemed worthy to reach that end; or by living well and justly and afflicting himself, so that, before the natural end of his life, he may deserve to be called by the Lord to the joys of eternal life as a reward for his merits.

“This shall be a sign for you.” The Jews are always seeking signs. “And the sun returned ten lines.” From the eleventh or tenth hour it suddenly returned to the first, and the day was almost doubled.

“The writing of Hezekiah, when he had been ill and had recovered [Col. 0903D] from his illness.” In the Septuagint interpreters there is a prayer, but this is rather the truth of the matter, because it recounts what truly happened: When almighty God, in his goodness and mercy, had given Hezekiah victory over his enemies without any labor on his part, and he had not given him thanks for the gift bestowed, he fell ill, so that the man who had been unwilling to sing praises for his prosperity might afterward utter them concerning his affliction. And after he recovered, he said what he had considered within himself while placed in distress.

“I said”—understand, at the time of my distress—“in the middle of my days: I shall go to the gates of hell.” I shall not complete the number of my days so as to reach old age in goodness like my fathers; rather, I shall die and go to the underworld. For he knew that before the Lord’s coming all descended there, though the righteous went one way and the wicked another.

“I sought the remainder of my years,” that is, in prayer I sought from God the years taken away from me because of the sin of pride. “I said” within myself, while lying in sickness: “I shall not see God, God, in the land of the living.”

“I shall not look upon a human being any longer, nor upon an inhabitant of rest.” Some manuscripts have “the Lord God,” but this is written falsely. “God” must be repeated twice, as blessed Jerome says. Some also divide it this way: “I shall not look upon a human being any longer, nor upon an inhabitant,” ending the verse there; and they join the following words to it: “My generation has ceased.” Blessed Jerome, because of the ambiguity of the word, first translated it in this way, but later corrected it to “an inhabitant of rest.”

The sense of this verse is as follows: If I descend to the gates of hell and am condemned there because of my crimes, I shall not see the Lord, that is, almighty God, in the land of the living, that is, in the rest of the righteous and in heavenly blessedness. I shall not look upon a human being any longer if I am eternally condemned to the punishments of hell; afterward I shall not see how the Son of God, who was promised to us, exists as true God and true man. Or else, I shall not see any of the saints in the glory of eternity. I shall not see an inhabitant of rest either. True rest and true rejoicing in eternal life consist in the contemplation and vision of the Trinity. Who is the inhabitant of eternal life except almighty God himself and his elect? “I shall not see,” he says, “any saint, an inhabitant of rest,” who, dwelling there, rests from all evils.

“My generation has been taken away from me,” that is, the children who ought to have succeeded me are not present, “and it has been rolled up from me like a shepherd’s tent.” Just as a tent is folded up and its size is no longer visible, so the greatness of my lineage has perished because there are no children to administer it.

“My life has been cut off as by a weaver.” He gives another comparison. The sense is: Just as a woman cuts off an unfinished cloth that she ought to have completed, so my incomplete life is cut off and taken away from me while I am still in the age of youth. “From morning until evening you will finish me.” He spoke in the manner of one suffering from fever or some other illness, as blessed Jerome says: In the morning the sick person, afflicted, says in his heart, “When evening comes, either I shall die or my illness will change.” When evening comes, he says, “In the morning either I shall die or I shall feel somewhat better.” Thus he spoke while lying ill, saying:

“I hoped until morning; like a lion he has crushed all my bones.” He compares almighty God to a lion. Just as a lion, he says, crushes everything by eating, not only flesh but also bones, so I have lost not only the strength of my body but even the strength of my bones because of the severity of my illness.

“From morning until evening you will finish me.” He spoke in suspense. It is as though he had said: “Either in the morning or in the evening you will bring me to an end. [Col. 0905A] Like a swallow’s fledgling, so shall I cry out,” as a swallow’s fledgling cries out to its father and mother so that it may be heard and receive food; and as a dove moans, so I persisted in crying and groaning before God, so that he might restore my health.

“My eyes have become weak,” that is, they have become thin and feeble, as I looked toward heaven to my God, who had worn me down with his scourges.

“Lord, I am oppressed.” This is the voice of one pleading. I am afflicted more than I deserve and beyond what my strength can bear. “Stand surety for me.” Some manuscripts have “answer for me,” but this is written falsely. “Stand surety” is better, because blessed Jerome explains it in this way. It is as though he had said: “If I have gone astray, I shall turn toward what is better; stand surety for me; that is, be my guarantor and receive me into your faith and protection.” “For it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans IX).

“What shall I say”—understand, to my maker—“when I justly endure these things? Or what will he answer me,” he who made me and gave me what he willed? Therefore I must endure everything that he has decreed.

“I shall recall to you all my years,” that is, I shall bring all the days of my happiness back to memory and shall consider that they were all bitter, because my present tribulation finds nothing good in any of them. Truly, as blessed Jerome says, human happiness possesses no security.

“Lord, this is how one lives.” Some manuscripts have “if this is how one lives,” but that is not correct. The king is philosophizing about the condition of this life, as blessed Jerome says. “Lord, this is how one lives,” that is, human happiness is so fragile and fleeting; “you chastise me” with your scourge, “and you will give me life,” restoring life and health to me.

“Behold, in peace”—understand, in the peace of Jerusalem and of my people, who are now not being attacked by enemies—“my tribulation is unbearable to me.” He says “in peace” because, once the Assyrian had been struck down, there was great peace among the people.

“But you have rescued my soul” so that it would not now go to the underworld because of my pride and my many sins; “you have cast all my sins behind your back,” that is, you have removed evil from your presence and placed it behind you, so that you would not condemn me now.

“For the underworld shall not confess to you, nor shall death praise you.” By the underworld in this passage we should understand the reprobate; by death, the devil. Those who descend to the gates of hell are condemned without end. They do not repent there, nor do they offer praise to almighty God, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” “Those who descend into the pit” shall not await “your truth,” that is, the Son of God, who said: “I am the truth” (John XIV). The saints who descended into the underworld before the Lord’s coming withdrew to its more secluded places to await his arrival, so that they might deserve to be freed from the torments of Gehenna. But the wicked, who have been handed over to eternal torments, have no hope of being recalled to the world above, having been placed in despair.

“The living, the living person shall confess to you,” that is, he shall praise you. The sense is: Whoever lives in your protection in perpetual rest, as I, now quieted from my enemies, shall praise you, “as I do today,” praising and glorifying you in the present. “The good father shall make your truth known to his children,” that is, he shall teach the true worship of religion. By the good father, good kings such as David and Hezekiah are understood, for they taught their children to keep the law of the Lord; or else holy and religious men, who make the Lord’s justice known to their subjects.

“Lord, save me” from Sennacherib and from eternal death, “and we shall sing our psalms to you.” [Col. 0906B] Lord, if you save me and my people, we shall sing praises to you. The Jews do this to the present day, although it does not benefit them. Nevertheless, conversely, the faithful in the holy Church continue to do so to this day.

“And Isaiah commanded” the king’s servants “to take a lump of figs and apply it as a poultice to the wound, and he was healed.” To apply a poultice means to warm or foment. Blessed Jerome says that he suffered from jaundice, for which everything sweet is said to be harmful, whether in food or in touch. But so that the power of God might become better known, he was cured with opposites, as Isaiah instructed. Here it must be noted that they did not foment the whole body with it, but only the wound that he had received from the Lord, apart from the jaundice, which we call *aerugo*.

[Col. 0906C] “And Hezekiah said: What will be the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?” The order is reversed. These words were spoken before the matters concerning his health and prayer that were explained above.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“At that time,” after the Assyrian had been killed and Hezekiah had recovered his health, “Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books,” that is, letters, “and gifts to Hezekiah.” It was said above that Esarhaddon, the son of Sennacherib, who ruled over the Assyrians and Babylonians, succeeded his father in the kingdom. Here it is said that Merodach-baladan sent messengers to Jerusalem to Hezekiah while Esarhaddon, who was king of the Babylonians, was still alive. [Col. 0906D] But it should be known that at this time the kingdom of the Assyrians and that of the Babylonians had been divided, and each ruler governed his own realm. Histories relate that this Merodach-baladan was the father of Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful king, who later subjected all those kingdoms to himself and united them, as they had previously been.

And why did those messengers come to Hezekiah? Because of the portent they had seen in the sun. For they were astrologers. Since they could not discover through their art why it had happened that the sun moved backward from the tenth hour to the first, they came to Jerusalem to learn from the prophets or wise men what the cause had been.

“And he showed them the chamber of spices.” Epiphanius of Cyprus says that the chamber of spices was a large and splendid house [Col. 0907A] in which the bodies of kings were buried, and that many spices were kept in their tombs, above, and around them. “He also showed them the silver and gold”—understand, the treasures—“and the spices,” of which there were many among them at that time, “and the storehouses,” that is, the storerooms of his possessions. “There was not a word that he did not show them.” Sacred Scripture often uses “word” for “thing,” as here. It says that he showed them everything in his house, in his treasures, and in his power; but among these were the treasures of the house of the Lord, which he offended by revealing to foreigners.

“What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?” The prophet asks two questions, but the answer he receives concerns human pride, not the praise of God for the portent on account of which they had come. “They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon,” which is a very powerful city. The remoteness of the lands increased his pride [Col. 0907B] and arrogance. Blessed Jerome says that this should be read with an expression of pride, since the king spoke arrogantly, saying: “They came to me from a distant land.” He ought to have said: “They came to praise God on account of the greatness of the sign.”

“They saw everything that is in my house,” understand, everything precious. “There was no thing”—however dear and honorable—“that I did not show them in my treasures.” He was silent about the treasures of the house of the Lord, which he had revealed to foreigners, and in this he offended, fearing that the prophet might rebuke him.

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “and everything that is in your house shall be carried away to Babylon,” things that you did not gather by your own labor but that belonged to your fathers. The retribution for the crime is foretold: the man who had exposed the Lord’s secrets to foreigners, together with his house, was to be carried away by that same people into destruction, along with all the possessions of his ancient fathers that he held and his own possessions as well. Indeed, the house of the Lord too was to be destroyed because of the sin of that people. “Nothing shall be left of them, says the Lord.” Behold, the sentence is fixed.

“And from your sons who will go out from you,” that is, who will spring from your stock, “they will take away, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” The Hebrews report that this prophecy was fulfilled in the three youths and Daniel, who is mentioned in that book, when Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, was captured and the people were led away to Babylon, together with Daniel and his companions, who afterward became eunuchs in the king’s palace. For one must not suppose [Col. 0907D] that they had been physically mutilated, but that they were placed in service and lived chastely. Of such men the Lord says in the Gospel: “There are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God” (Matt. XVI).

“Let there be only peace,” that is, so long as I live, may I not be attacked by Sennacherib, “and truth,” that is, the true worship of God, “in my days.” This was not right. He ought rather to have confessed his sin, like David, and removed the Lord’s anger from his descendants; or he ought to have shown compassion, as Moses did toward the people when, because of the crime of the people condemned to death, he asked that he himself be erased from the book of life, saying: “Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. XXXII). Therefore the Prophet did not answer him, but, turning to the people, said:

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0908A]

“Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.” The meaning is: O people of God, you who are believers from among the Jews, take comfort in Christ, for your king shows compassion neither for himself nor for you. This may also be referred to the Gentiles, concerning whom the Lord says through Zechariah: “Behold, I will gather the people of the East, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Zech. VIII).

“Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call to her.” The prophet addresses Eliakim and the other faithful who existed at that time. Or alternatively, he addresses the apostles and teachers of the Gentiles, saying: O Eliakim and other faithful ones, or apostles, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. One speaks to the heart when he gently addresses and [Col. 0908B] consoles someone who is sorrowful or sad. Thus we read of Shechem, son of Hamor, when he violated Dinah: “Shechem spoke to her heart and consoled her” (Gen. XXXIV). It should be noted, however, that when he says, “Call to her,” Jerusalem—or, by implication, the Gentile world—is to be called from tribulation or sadness to joy, from evil to good, and from idolatry to the mourning of repentance. “For her wickedness is completed.” Wickedness is not always used for sin, but also for affliction, as in what the Lord said through the Prophet: “If there is evil in the city,” that is, affliction, “which the Lord has not caused” (Amos III). Her wickedness, then, is completed—that is, the affliction of persecution that occurred in the death of the martyrs and that, by God’s gift, is now absent. “Her iniquity has been pardoned” [Col. 0908C]—that is, if she ever sinned, it has been forgiven her. This applies especially to the Gentiles or the Jews who, coming to faith in the Lord, have been cleansed through the regeneration of baptism. Or it may refer to martyrdom, where their sins were forgiven them as they are in baptism. “She has received from the hand of the Lord double,” implicitly, torments. If we refer this to Jerusalem, she received a double punishment from the Chaldeans and the Romans, and perished in body and soul. If we refer it to the Church, she received a double punishment from her persecutors, because she was tortured in body and suffered anguish in spirit during the time of persecution; therefore her iniquity was pardoned.

“A voice of one crying,” implicitly, Christ through John, “in the wilderness” of Judea. John is called a voice because he preceded the Word. Or it may be the voice of Christ crying to the apostles [Col. 0908D] in the wilderness of the Jews or of the Gentiles. Just as John cried out in the deserted and abandoned land of Judea, “Repent,” so the apostles preached the word of salvation in the wilderness of the Gentiles, hearing from the Lord: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI). “Prepare the way of the Lord,” that is, perform such works as will please God, believing rightly and acting well, so that he may come to you. “Make straight in the wilderness,” that is, in the wilderness of the Gentiles, “the paths of our God.” The paths may appropriately be understood as thoughts, just as the way may signify actions; and the meaning is that those who desire Christ to come to them should be pure not only in body but also in heart. This is commanded to those who believed in Christ in the wilderness of Judea, and to those who lived in the wilderness of the Gentiles.

“Every valley shall be exalted,” that is, the simple Jews who believed, or the Gentiles, were magnified in right faith and holy conduct, “and every mountain and hill shall be humbled.” This means that the scribes and Pharisees, and wicked kings such as Nero, together with those who existed before and after him, were humbled like hills, falling into the depth of the pit. This is what the Lord said: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XIV, XVIII). “And crooked places shall become straight.” The crooked places are the twisted hearts of tax collectors and Pharisees, who came through the preaching of the Lord and his apostles to faith; they were made straight so as to perform good works. “And the rough places,” that is, the unmanageable and hardened hearts of the scribes and Pharisees [Col. 0909B] and of the Gentiles, “shall become level ways”; that is, they were changed into gentleness and mildness when they came to the faith, as Matthew relates.

“And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed,” that is, it shall be made manifest. The Son is the glory of God the Father: the Lord, namely Jesus Christ. Of him God the Father says in the psalm: “Rise up, my glory” (Ps. XLIII). For when the apostles preached, the Son of God was revealed among the Gentiles. “And all flesh shall see,” that is, every human being shall see, “the salvation of God.” This pertains to the day of judgment. For while the Prophet, speaking of Christ’s first coming, stretched the eye of his mind toward the second, not everyone saw him at the first coming, but at the second all will behold him—both those who saw him and those who did not. “The mouth of the Lord has spoken,” that is, through the prophets [Col. 0909C], by whom he foretold what was to come. What he said, “and all flesh shall see,” may also be understood in this way: all flesh shall see—that is, then everyone will understand that what the Lord foretold through his prophets was true.

“A voice of one saying,” implicitly, Christ to Isaiah: “Cry out,” implicitly, to the Israelite people—or to the whole human race. “And I said: What shall I cry?” He did not ask without reason, “What shall I cry?” For he had seen the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne and had heard the Lord say, “Whom shall I send?” He answered: “Here am I; send me.” And because at that time he had announced harsh things to his people, he was afraid to announce similar things now. Therefore he did not offer himself willingly, as above, but asked about the substance of his task. The Lord said to him: “All flesh,” that is, every human being, “is grass, and all its glory,” which it possesses in the present [Col. 0909D], “is like the flower of the field”—both health and youth, and also temporal riches. The meaning is this: just as grass, when it is born, has greenness, and when it sprouts, beauty, but when cut it dries and is reduced to dust, so a human being, through the successive stages of life, loses the greenness of vigor and beauty and ceases to exist.

“Grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the breath of God blew upon it.” Grass grows suddenly from the earth and suddenly falls, because a scorching wind and burning heat dry it up. Likewise, a human being is suddenly born and suddenly falls into death, because the breath of God—that is, the sentence of almighty God—takes away his present life. “Truly, the people are grass.” He now explains what he said above. Blessed Jerome says that when a young man’s fortunes seem prosperous and he serves his vices, especially lust, he is as though in flower. But when God’s sentence suddenly overtakes him, he is reduced to nothing.

“But the word of the Lord remains forever,” that is, Christ, the Son of God, together with his body, which is the Church that clings to him through faith and action; he will reign forever. John speaks of this Word: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I).

“Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion.” Some manuscripts have *qui evangelizas*, “you who evangelize,” in the masculine gender, but this is written incorrectly. Blessed Jerome explains it in the feminine gender, saying that this is how it stands in the Hebrew truth and in the Septuagint translators. The construction of this verse [Col. 0910B] is as follows: O Zion, you who evangelize and teach good things, go up upon a high mountain—that is, upon Christ, who is the mountain of mountains and the sublimity of virtues—and preach what Christ taught. He speaks similarly to Jerusalem: O “Jerusalem, you who evangelize,” that is, you who announce good things, “raise your voice with strength,” so that you may be heard by many; raise up your preaching. “Do not fear” the savagery of persecutors or the cunning of the devil. By Zion and Jerusalem he wishes the company of the apostles and teachers to be understood; divine speech addresses them so that they may preach and announce what they have heard from the Lord and received from the Holy Spirit. The expositor of this passage says: Every preacher ought to climb to the heights of virtue, so that by his example [Col. 0910C] the hearts of his hearers may be lifted toward the pursuit of heavenly things. “Say to the cities of Judah,” O company of teachers—that is, to the synagogues, or to the people of the Jews, or to the universal Church: “Behold your God.” O Jews, the one promised to you in the Law and the Prophets, whom you were awaiting, has now come. He has now redeemed us from the snare of death; only believe in him. And you also, O Gentiles, believe in him who has now come—that is, in Jesus, whom the patriarch Jacob promised to you, saying: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

“Behold, the Lord God shall come in strength, and his arm shall rule,” that is, his strength shall rule. This is the voice of the apostles concerning the Lord’s second coming: Behold, they say, the Lord God whom you, Jews and Gentiles, despised when he came in humility and in the form of a servant [Col. 0910D], will come in the power of judgment. As he himself says: “When the Son of Man comes in great power and majesty” (Luke XXI). “Behold, his reward is with him,” that is, the recompense of the good and the condemnation of the reprobate. “And his work is before him,” that is, the power of judgment, as he himself said: “For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father, and he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. XVI). And again: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

“As a shepherd he shall feed his flock.” This is the Prophet’s voice concerning the Lord’s first coming. It is as though he said in other words: He who will later come in majesty to judge the whole world in righteousness will first come in the form of a shepherd, as he himself says: “I am the good shepherd” (John X). For he is the good shepherd who now feeds his elect through contemplation of the mind; then he will satisfy them with perfect vision, first teaching them and afterward leading them into eternal joys. “With his arm,” that is, with his strength, “he shall gather the lambs”—that is, he will gather the simple, gentle, and innocent, and those newly coming to his faith—not the proud and swollen. “In his bosom,” that is, in his protection, “he shall lift” implicitly, his elect, to heavenly things, those who imitate the innocence of the lamb. “He himself shall carry the ewes with young.” By the ewes with young we may understand the apostles and apostolic men, who daily give birth to spiritual children in the Church through their preaching, examples, and miracles; they still travail for the salvation of many and say with the Apostle: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” [Col. 0911B] (Gal. IV). And again: “Through the Gospel,” he says, “I begot you” (I Cor. IV).

“Who has measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with a span?” We call a fist a handful made with contracted fingers. A span is an extended hand measured crosswise from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger. The calling of the Gentiles and their recompense have therefore been foretold above. Now, lest anyone should doubt their calling, the greatness of the one who calls is expressed in these words. When a fist and a span are attributed to the almighty Lord, this is not to be understood as meaning that he who is spirit possesses human bodily members; rather, it is a likeness used to express the greatness of his power [Col. 0911C]. Who could measure all the waters, or reduce heaven and earth to a weight, except the one who made everything from nothing? “Who has hung the mass of the earth on three fingers,” that is, who has suspended the earth over nothing, except the power of the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? “And who has weighed,” that is, suspended, “the mountains in a balance, and the hills on scales,” that is, reduced them to a weight?

“Who has assisted the spirit of the Lord,” namely, in the creation of every creature, which was made by the majesty of the Trinity? No one. For he who gives strength to the weary requires no one’s help. “Or who was his counselor” (Wis. IX; Rom. XI), that is, the counselor of the Holy Spirit, “and showed him,” implicitly, what he should do? [Col. 0911D] No one except the Father and the Son, whose power is one and whose divinity is inseparable; and who are three in persons but one in divinity. He is a counselor of the Holy Spirit who gives him sound counsel, in whom that same Holy Spirit dwells.

“With whom did he take counsel” concerning how that Holy Spirit ought to work, “and instruct and teach him the path of justice,” that is, the uprightness of action, “and educate him in knowledge, and show him the way of prudence?” No one. Prudence consists in seeking good things and avoiding evil ones.

“Behold, the nations,” namely those who worship idols, or the whole human race in comparison with God, “are counted as a drop from a bucket,” and as a moment of the scales. [Col. 0912A] Just as a small drop falling from a bucket is counted as nothing by the person carrying it, “and as a moment of the scales,” which is tipped to the other side by a light weight, so all nations, compared with God’s eternity, “are counted as nothing.” A *moment* derives its name from movement. It is the slightest and swiftest inclination of a balance toward one side, caused by a small weight. “Behold, the islands”—all the lands that are in the rivers, or all nations, so that by islands we may understand nations—are “like fine dust” in comparison with God, which is seen in a sunbeam and is felt in the eyes more than it is seen.

“And Lebanon would not suffice for burning, nor its animals for a burnt offering.” He speaks in this way to call the nations back from idolatry. Lebanon is a mountain [Col. 0912B] of extraordinary size, abounding in very rich pastures; all its trees and the animals grazing there could not suffice for the Lord’s sacrifices. This is a kind of likeness. It is as though he said in other words: Even if you were to sacrifice all the animals and burn the wood to consume the burnt offerings, they would not suffice to appease the power of such majesty.
