“All the nations,” implicitly, those under heaven, “are as though they did not exist before him”—that is, in comparison with the one who fills all things.

“To whom, then, have you likened God,” the living God, O Gentiles, from among all your man-made images, “or what image will you set up for him” from among all your gods, since he is spirit?

“Has the craftsman cast a carved image? Or has the goldsmith [Col. 0912C] fashioned it,” that image, from gold, so that it could be like God, who is everywhere? It is as though he said: Has anyone made him by carving, rather than the one who made all things, who himself was made by no one? This voice of almighty God rebukes the folly of the nations, so that they may withdraw from the worship of images.

“Perhaps the craftsman chose wood,” that is, durable wood, “to make his god from it.” In ancient times they made images from incorruptible woods, gold, silver, and other metals, so that they might endure for long periods. These words show that idols possess no strength in comparison with God.

“Do you not know,” O nations, through the natural law and knowledge of created things, that I am eternal and that an idol is nothing? “Have you not heard” the Law given through Moses? [Col. 0912D] “Has it not been announced to you” from the beginning, in the book of Genesis, chapter seventeen, that I alone am the living God? “Have you not understood the foundations of the earth,” implicitly, that they are founded upon a thin element?

“He who sits,” that is, who dwells, “above the circle,” that is, above the circuit, “and its inhabitants,” that is, the inhabitants of the earth, are in comparison with him or with the angels “like locusts.” Let us consider all the kinds of human beings living between these climates, from east to west and from south to north, and we shall see that, in comparison with God, who fills all things and is everywhere, they are small and insignificant. “He who stretches out the heavens like nothing,” [Col. 0913A] implicitly, the most subtle and delicate things, like smoke, “and spreads them out like a tent for dwelling.” Such are the heavens prepared by God, so that above them the multitude of angels and elect human beings may dwell, while beneath them lies the multitude of human beings, as though beneath a tent.

“He who brings investigators of secrets to nothing and makes the judges of the earth like emptiness.” He calls investigators of secrets the philosophers who investigated the condition of the present life, the natures of animals and trees, and of land and sea. By the judges of the earth are meant the kings and rulers of this age; he reduces all of them to nothing. Where is that multitude of Hebrews that was in the wilderness? Where are all the kings who existed with their armies from the beginning of the world until now? They are as though they had never existed.

[Col. 0913B] “Indeed, neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted,” that is, established, “and their trunk in the earth”—that is, the statues of them in the present life—“he suddenly blew upon them, and they withered”; that is, Christ’s sentence came upon them, and they died; “and a whirlwind will carry them away like stubble,” namely, the kings, rulers, and powerful men, from the condition of the present life, since they did not possess perpetual existence or power—for they were flesh. Some manuscripts read: “Neither planted nor rooted is their trunk”; but it is better to use the ablative construction: “neither sown nor rooted.” As a storm carries away stubble, so almighty God by his power removes the reprobate from this life.

“To whom have you likened me and equated me, says the Holy One”—that is, God? This is a rebuking address to both the Jews and the Gentiles who worship idols. “To whom have you likened me,” he says, O Jews or Gentiles, from among all your gods?

“Lift up your eyes on high,” that is, to heaven, “and see,” that is, understand, “who created these things” that exist there. If you are unwilling to do so in any other way, understand the Creator through the creature. “He who brings out their host in number,” that is, the host of the heavens—he who has angels and stars according to their number—“and calls them all by name”; implicitly, he created these things. We understand the host of heaven in two ways: either as angels or as stars. For the Psalmist says of this: “He numbers the multitude of the stars” (Ps. CXLVI). And Daniel says: “A thousand thousands served him” (Dan. VII). “Because of the abundance of his strength [Col. 0913D] and power,” that is, of almighty God, “not one” of those things we have mentioned “was lacking,” that is, outside his reckoning. Here it is shown that almighty God knows all visible and invisible things and made everything according to number, weight, and measure.

“Why do you say, Jacob,” that is, the two tribes, “and speak, Israel,” that is, the ten tribes, “My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed away from my God?” When the Prophet spoke these words, the ten tribes had already been led into captivity, while the two still remained in the promised land. What the ten tribes were saying after being led away to the Assyrians, and what the two were going to say when they were to be led away to Babylon, [Col. 0914A] the Prophet foretold. For they said: “My way is hidden from the Lord,” that is, he does not see my justice and good works. “And my judgment has passed away from my God,” that is, he has not judged me justly, because he allowed me to be led into captivity although I had done good. The meaning is: Earthly matters do not concern God, and, sitting in heaven, he does not consider what each of us does; therefore we are unjustly oppressed by our enemies. Just as fish swim here and there in the waters, and beasts and animals run this way and that, having neither shepherd nor ruler, so we, placed upon the earth, have no one to govern and defend us, because the Lord does not care for us; indeed, he does not even see us.

“Do you not know,” that is, do you not believe, “or [Col. 0914B] have you not heard” in the Scriptures that the “everlasting God,” the one “Lord who created the ends of the earth” from nothing, “does not grow faint,” as a human being does, because he is spirit, “nor grow weary,” because he is Lord of all creatures, holds all things, and administers everything by his majesty? “There is no searching out” of his wisdom by any mortal, because he knows everything. How, then, can you say that he does not understand judgment and that your ways are hidden from him? “He gives strength to the weary,” that is, to the human being, implicitly, the strength of faith or bodily strength. “And to those who are not” in wickedness, as once they were, he gives “strength” for good action. For almighty God possesses such great strength that he not only himself needs no one’s help, but also grants strength to all who hope in him. “Boys shall faint and grow weary, and young men shall fall in weakness.” A human being rejoices in childhood, youth, and health, but grows weary in sickness and old age and soon falls. But God, who is eternal, always is and always will be; he suffers none of these things, because he is one and the same forever and immutable. Allegorically, those who are not established in faith and live like children will faint and grow weary—that is, in the present they will have the burden of earthly cares, and afterward they will fall, utterly condemned.

“But those who hope in the Lord shall change their strength.” It should be noted that he does not say that they will lose their strength, but that they will change it: that is, they will change the strength of sin into the strength of good action. Those who do not place their confidence in their own powers, but have hope—implicitly, in God—and await his mercy, undoubtedly change their strength [Col. 0914D]. For just as they were strong in committing evil, so then they will be strong in doing good and enduring adversities for the name of Christ. We read that many saints acted in this way. Let us take, by way of example, one among many: Paul, formerly a most vigorous persecutor, afterward a most vigorous preacher. The stronger he had previously been in persecuting the elect, the more fervent he afterward became in preaching to the Gentiles and calling them to the faith. Alternatively: those who hope in the Lord—that is, in the hope of eternal blessedness—will change their strength after the death of the flesh, having become incorruptible.

“They shall take wings like eagles,” that is, the renewal of the future life, or the ability by which they may go to meet the Lord in the air. The teachers say that it is the nature of the eagle, when worn out by old age and no longer able to seize prey, with its beak bent and its talons contracted, to be inflamed by anger and rub its beak against a hard and lofty stone for so long that only a trace of it remains. In this way its feathers and its entire body are renewed. So the saints, who have worn themselves down here by mortifying themselves, will be renewed through incorruption, contemplating Christ, the sun of justice, just as the eagle looks upon the sun with unblinking eyes. And when they have reached the end of life, they then begin to live, when they seem to be ending life. “They shall run,” migrating to Christ, “and shall not grow weary,” because the vision of the Holy Trinity will be everything to them. “They shall walk,” from virtue to virtue, “and shall not faint,” living with the Lord forever.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Col. 0915B]

“Let the islands be silent before me, and let the nations change their strength.” This is the voice of God. We read something similar in Exodus: “Hear, O Israel, and be silent.” They are called islands because they are situated in the salt sea. By islands we should understand the Gentiles, who are battered by the salty and bitter waves of this age. “Let the islands be silent,” he says, so that they may first hear me—that is, so that the Gentiles may hear me through the apostles. “And let them change their strength.” How should the Gentiles change their strength? In the way we explained above: those who were strong in evil should become stronger in carrying out good works. Blessed Gregory says that the elect have one kind of strength and the reprobate another. The strength of the elect is to conquer the desire of the flesh—that is, lust—the appetite for earthly things, and other vices; and, if necessity arises, to endure willingly the torments of death for Christ’s name. The strength of the reprobate is to commit murders, to seize the goods of others through robbery, and, for the sake of temporal profits, to expose themselves to the danger of death. “Let them draw near,” implicitly, let the Gentiles draw near to me by believing, “and then let them speak,” that is, let them preach to others what they have believed. “Let us likewise approach judgment,” so that they may distinguish between me, their Maker, and the idols fashioned by them, and discuss whether the God of all acts justly in all things.

“Who has raised up the just one from the East,” that is, Christ? This is the voice of God the Father, teaching the Gentiles by his question what they do not know. God the Father raised up our Lord Jesus Christ from the East, because Judea lies in the regions of the East, and it was there that he first ordained that Christ should become incarnate. “He called him to follow,” that is, to obey his will. The Son followed the Father because he obeyed his will in all things. Whatever he did, he referred entirely to the Father’s glory; he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. He also raised him up from the East (Isa. XV) when, in that place in the land of Judea, he made him rise from the dead and brought his name through the apostles to all the nations and to the ends of the earth. He also called him from the tomb on the third day, according to what the Psalmist himself says to the Son in the forty-fourth psalm: “Rise up, my glory” (Ps. XVIII), and so forth. For the Son followed, obeying his voice, and rose from the dead on the third day, according to what he answered the Father: “I shall rise at dawn.” “He will give”—implicitly, God the Father will give—“nations in his presence,” that is, before the Son, and peoples who will believe in him, “and he will gain possession of kings” through the preaching of his apostles. For many kings and rulers came to faith in the Lord when the apostles preached. “He will give,” almighty God the Father will give, “to his sword,” that is, to the Gospel teaching of his Son, the hostile powers “like dust; like stubble carried away by the wind he will give them to his bow,” that is, all his adversaries to his power. Gospel teaching is a sword, and the word of preaching cuts and separates those who observe it from the company of the reprobate. The Apostle speaks of this sword: “And the sword, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0916B] “He shall pursue them,” namely, the kings and rulers of the nations who were unwilling to believe in him; “he shall pass in peace” from the world to the Father, calling everyone to peace so that they may be reconciled to God; “the path shall not appear in his footsteps,” that is, he will feel neither the labor of the journey nor any weariness arising from human weakness.

“Who has worked and done these things?” That is, the things we mentioned above. Who, namely, handed over kings and rulers to the bow and sword of the Son of God? “And who called” the just one from the East, “calling generations,” implicitly, to the faith, “from the beginning of the world?” Surely it was the one who, while all remained silent, answered himself, saying (below, XLIV and XXVIII):

“I, the Lord, am first,” that is, before whom there was no one, [Col. 0916C] “and last,” after whom there is no one. “I am he” who foretold all these future things and fulfilled them in deed. He is the one who speaks in John’s Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega,” that is, the beginning and the end (Rev. I and XXII).

“The islands saw” God through faith, that is, the Gentiles of the Church who endure the storms of this world, “and they feared” him, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Without fear, virtues are difficult or entirely impossible to preserve. “The ends of the earth were astonished,” implicitly, when they heard the apostles’ preaching. For their sound went out into all the earth. “They drew near,” implicitly, to God through faith, “and approached”; the Gentiles approached not in place but in merit, because they had been far from him.

[Col. 0916D] “Each one,” implicitly, of the believers, “shall help his neighbor,” that is, his believing brother, “and shall say to his brother: Be strong” in the faith of Christ. Some Gentile converted to the faith of Christ has already been strengthened in him. The ironwork, not yet fully hardened, will be strengthened in God.

“The coppersmith strengthened him, striking the form of the images with a hammer, who was forging at that time,” when idols were worshiped, “saying: I join,” that is, “with fastening; it is good,” this fastening, “and he strengthened it,” implicitly, his god, “with nails so that it would not move,” implicitly, if the wind came. The meaning of this verse is as follows: The one who had become perfect in faith will help his brother, saying: You see these idols, brother; surely they are not gods, but the works of human hands, deaf and mute. Be strong in the faith of the living and true God.

“And you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham, my friend, in whom,” that is, in Abraham, “I took hold of you.” The Jews understand this as referring to themselves, because they descended from the seed of Abraham; but it is better to refer it to the spiritual Israel, that is, to the apostles, who sprang from the seed of Abraham. With affectionate gentleness he addresses that company of apostles, saying: “And you, Israel, my servant.” Prophecy does not preserve the order of the historical narrative. After the calling of the Gentiles, certain islands saw and feared. The apostles too are called and strengthened by him (Matt. X). The Gospel speaks of these men as well, because he chose twelve disciples whom he named apostles (Luke VI). It should be noted that they are first called servants and afterward introduced into friendship. Earlier we received the spirit of servitude for fear; afterward, having been chosen, we are joined to the friendship of God. They are called the seed of Abraham not only because they descended from his lineage according to the flesh, but because they possessed Abraham’s faith and were obedient to God. In him—that is, in Abraham—he took hold of them from the ends of the earth and called them from its distant regions, because he gathered from all nations the Jews among whom they had been scattered, and many of them believed through the preaching of the apostles. To you, however, O company of apostles, who are my servant and my chosen one, who are going to preach to the Gentiles and suffer many persecutions for my name, I say:

[Col. 0917C] “Do not fear” the face of persecutors, “for I am with you,” as I said to you in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). “Do not turn away from me, for I am your God,” implicitly, I am truth and life. Do not go astray, lest a false persuasion deceive you into thinking that by your own strength you can penetrate the forest of the Gentiles and call the fiercest nations to the gentleness of the Gospel (John XIV). “I have strengthened you, and I have helped you,” O company of apostles; “and the right hand of my righteous one has received you,” that is, I have strengthened you by the power of my Son.

“All,” implicitly, Jews or Gentiles, “who fight against you shall be as though they did not exist, because they shall perish” from before you.

“I, the Lord, have taken hold of your hand,” that is, of your action; and I have helped you, in place of “I will help you.”

“Do not fear, worm of Jacob, you who are dead from Israel,” implicitly, dead through sin. The company of the apostles is called a worm because of its humility, imitating the one who says in the psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI). Just as a worm penetrates the earth, so the apostolic word penetrated the hearts of the Gentiles. Those among them who say with the Apostle, “Every day I die for your glory, brothers” (I Cor. XV), are dead to sin. And again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). “I have made you like a new threshing cart, having sharp teeth.” It has already been said several times above what the threshing cart is and why it has sharp teeth [Col. 0918A]. In a deeper sense, however, this signifies that the preaching of the apostles crushes hostile powers and the spiritual wickedness that raises itself against the knowledge of God. “You shall thresh mountains and crush hills.” By mountains are signified the kings and powers of this age, just as by hills are signified rulers of lesser power and dignity, who are lifted up in pride for the sake of temporal profits. We may also say that an ecclesiastical man possesses the sharp teeth of evangelical preaching in order to crush the hardest hearts of unbelievers.

“And you shall winnow them,” separating the wheat from the chaff—that is, all the elect from association with heretics. “And the wind shall carry them away,” that is, their own pride will destroy them. “And you shall exult in the Lord” when you see demons going out and the humble in heart being exalted to the heights of virtue. For the apostles rejoiced greatly when through their preaching they saw the Gentiles converted from error to faith.

“The needy and poor seek waters, and there are none; their tongue has dried up from thirst.” The Gentiles are called needy and poor because they had neither the Law nor prophets nor apostles, nor any teacher who might invite them to the joys of their heavenly homeland and offer them spiritual bread. The needy and poor Gentiles seek waters—that is, spiritual teaching—from their philosophers, but there is no spiritual teaching in them. Therefore their tongue dried up with thirst, without the Law and the utterances of the prophets. For this reason the Lord God of Israel did not utterly abandon them, nor did he allow them to thirst forever [Col. 0918C], but opened rivers on the high hills and springs in the midst of the plains. In this passage the hills are understood in a favorable sense.

“In high places” — that is, among the defiled or lowly nations — “I will open rivers,” that is, the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. Almighty God opened among humble human beings a knowledge of the divine utterances, as in Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and the other teachers who disclosed the divine mysteries to us, drawing waters from him who said through Jeremiah: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II), that is, the gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this river the Psalmist also says: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God,” and “The river of God is filled with waters” (Ps. XLV and LXIV). What he says, “and in the midst of the plains, springs,” means the same thing, as we said above.

“I will make the wilderness” — that is, the Gentile world — “into pools of water,” that is, through the outpouring of the Scriptures, “and the impassable land into streams of water.” The impassable land is called the Gentile world because, before the coming of the Son of God, no prophet and no apostle had been sent to it; and there was no one among it who said: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV).

“I will give in the wilderness a myrtle, a thorn, and an olive tree.” After waters had been given in the wilderness, or solitude, of the Gentiles, trees began to grow there. Let us see what the names of these trees signify for us.

The cedar is a tree of remarkable fragrance and imperishability. By it are signified holy men who perform miracles, who will live forever and give forth a good fragrance; they say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II).

But where he adds “thorn,” the Septuagint has *seta* (“bristle”). This is a tree resembling the white thorn, possessing extraordinary lightness, extraordinary strength, and extraordinary beauty, and being imperishable; from its wood the Ark was made. Hence the region, or land, where it grows is called Sethim. The thorn was given to our first parent as a punishment, as the Lord says: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). But afterward it was given to the Gentile world as a glory.

What, then, is meant by the thorn that pricks, except the holy preachers in this passage? For they do not flatter people’s sins but openly rebuke them. Whenever a holy preacher discusses vices and virtues, the punishment of the reprobate and the glory of the elect, he stimulates the hearts of his listeners with certain pricks, urging them toward the compunction of repentance.

“Myrtle.” The myrtle is an aromatic and imperishable tree. Its sap strengthens and restores weary limbs. Through it are represented holy preachers who, by their preaching and consolation, strengthen and fortify the hearts of the weak for the performance of good works, saying with the Apostle: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every affliction” (II Cor. I).

“An olive tree.” In Greek, *eleos* means “mercy”; and by the olive tree are understood those who practice almsgiving, who shine through mercy like oil. Our mercy consists in feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, helping a brother in every tribulation and distress, teaching the ignorant (Matt. XXV), and other things of this kind. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall see God and shall obtain mercy. I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. V).

“I will place in the wilderness of the nations a fir, an elm, and a box tree together.” The fir is a tree of remarkable height, from which pitch is made. What, then, is signified by the fir, whose crown rises almost to the clouds, except the holy preachers who, though still placed bodily on earth, possess heavenly things in mind? They say with the Apostle: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. III).

The elm is a fruitless tree. Yet it sometimes bears a vine with a cluster of grapes. By the elm, therefore, are signified the rich of this age, who do not possess the office of preaching and perform no miracles, but, having only simple faith, support by their works and wealth the one who administers the word of preaching both to himself and to others; moreover, if necessary, they protect him from the attacks of enemies.

The box tree is a low-growing tree that rejoices in its greenness; some say that it is imperishable. By the box tree, therefore, are signified the saints who follow the Lord’s humility, excel in the greenness of faith, and adorn that greenness of faith with the flowers of good works.

If we carefully consider all these things that we have said, we shall find them in the holy Church. And why did the Lord give this in the wilderness of the Gentiles?

[Col. 0920A] “That they may see” — those who are still imperfect — “the cedar,” that is, those who shine with the most illustrious miracles of the saints and with the fragrance of virtues, “and know that the Lord made it,” that is, gave the cedar to the wilderness, “and reflect,” that is, recall to mind, his miracles and good works, “and understand together,” that is, by understanding, imitate him.

For example, when they see the cedar — that is, any saint shining with miracles and giving forth a good fragrance — let them strive, as far as they can with God’s help, to imitate him. Likewise, when they see the fir — that is, any saint dwelling bodily on earth while yearning for heavenly things through contemplation of the mind — let them imitate him, scorning earthly things and desiring those above.

[Col. 0920B] “Bring your judgment near,” says the Lord; “bring forward whatever you may perhaps have,” says the King of Jacob. Just as we said that Jacob and Israel are twofold — namely, those who do not believe and those who believe in the Lord the Savior — so the Gentile world must also be understood as twofold: consisting of believers and unbelievers.

Here the divine word speaks to those from the Gentiles who refused, through the preaching of the apostles, to believe in the Lord. They are summoned to judgment because they refused to see, know, recall, and understand that the hand of the Lord — that is, his power and strength — caused the cedar to grow in the wilderness, so that they might imitate it and the other trees, through which the orders of the elect are signified.

“Bring your judgment near,” says the Lord; that is, draw near to judgment, and let us be judged together. What ought I to have done for you that I did not do? I gave a cedar in the wilderness — that is, an illustrious man who performed miracles and gave forth a good fragrance — and you refused to imitate him. “Bring forward whatever you may perhaps have” — understand, an idol — said the King of Jacob.

“Let your strongest idols,” he says, “in which you trust, come forward; or bring forward one that is stronger than all the rest, and let us judge which should be worshiped. I am the one who made you and redeemed you, or the one who was made by you?”

“Let them come forward,” your idols, “and announce to us the things that are to come,” whether concerning the coming of my Son, or the redemption of the Gentiles and their own expulsion. “Announce the former things that were, and we shall set our heart upon them, and we shall know their latter things.”

He addresses these words to the idols, which possess neither the ability to hear nor to answer but are insensible. O idols, if you can announce the former things — that is, how or in what manner I and my Son, together with the Holy Spirit, made all things from nothing — “and the future things,” namely, the coming of my Son, the calling of the Gentiles, and your expulsion from human hearts, announce them; “and we shall set our heart upon them,” that is, our will, so that we may regard you as true gods, “and we shall know their latter things.” That is, when you have announced the former things to us, then we shall know their latter things — namely, to what faith they will attain.

“Declare to us the things that are to come,” O idols — that is, the coming of my Son and the other matters stated above.

“Do something good or evil, if you can,” O idols, “and let us speak and see together” which God ought to be worshiped by human beings. These words show that after the coming of the Son of God all the idols fell silent and were unable to prophesy anything about Christ, or anything about the destruction and overthrow of their temples. For if they were unable to predict their own destruction, how could they announce good or evil things to others?

There is also another sign that idols are not gods: they can do neither good nor evil. This does not mean that idols, or the demons dwelling beside idols, often did not perform evil deeds, but that they could not do so unless power had been granted to them by the Lord. Demons entered into images and, with the Lord permitting it, often foretold future events. Above all, however, they gave such responses that they could be understood in two ways. For example:

“I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans.”

“Let us speak together,” that is, just as I speak of future things, so let them also speak.

“Behold, you are from nothing,” O idols — understand, because you were made by human beings, who are nothing. The Apostle Paul says: “An idol is nothing, and the makers of idols are nothing” (I Cor. VIII). As it is found in the Psalm: “Let those who make them become like them” (Ps. CXXXIV). That is, the idols are nothing, and, insofar as worship is concerned, those who make them are nothing.

“And your work,” that is, the idols, is “from what does not exist”; that is, what you have fashioned into gods is nothing, because they are not gods. We can also refer this statement to the idols: “Behold, you are from nothing,” as we have said; and the statement “your work is from what does not exist” can refer to the worshipers of idols. As far as the material from which the idols were made is concerned — gold or something of that kind — it was something; but the worship itself was nothing. Moreover, in comparison with the gold, bronze, or other material from which they were made, it was nothing.

“He is an abomination who chose you”: that is, the man who cast you, O idols, is a rejection and an object of abhorrence.

“I raised him up from the north; he will come from the rising of the sun.” This is the voice of God the Father. The north wind is cold and contrary, and it signifies the devil. Therefore God the Father raised up the Gentiles dwelling in the north — that is, those who suffered the cold of error, whose hearts did not burn with love of God and neighbor.

“And he will come” — understand, Christ — “from the rising of the sun,” in whom they will believe. He is said to come from the rising of the sun because Judea lies in the eastern regions. He will come from the rising of the sun, of whom it was said above: “He who raised up the righteous man from the East” (above, IX); and elsewhere: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising” (Zech. VI). Therefore he will raise the Gentiles from unbelief to faith, so that they may believe in him who came from the rising of the sun.

And why does he say that the Lord comes from the rising of the sun to the Gentiles, when he himself did not preach to the Gentiles? He came indeed through his apostles, because everything the apostles accomplished, they did through him, in his name, and to his praise. And unless he himself had come and illumined the hearts of the Gentiles, they would have spent their preaching in vain.

“He called my name” — understand, the one who will come from the rising of the sun — “and he will bring down,” that is, reduce, “rulers like clay,” that is, the princes of this world or the demons who held authority over the human race, “and like a potter trampling the earth.” A potter is a *plastes*, a maker of vessels [literally as printed: “a maker of bows”]. Just as a potter tramples clay and earth in order to form pots, so the Lord Jesus, at his coming, trampled down and reduced to nothing all the power of this age, so that from it he might make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

“Who announced it from the beginning, so that we might know, and from the outset,” he foretold future things among creatures, “so that we might say, ‘He is righteous’”? The meaning is: What god among the Gentiles announced the coming of the Son of God? If there is any god who did these things, we shall say that he is righteous.

“For there is none among all your gods who announces,” past times, “or foretells,” future things, “or hears your words,” because they are mute and deaf. This is what we already said above: after the Lord’s coming, and after his faith began to spread throughout the world, the demons fell silent concerning the responses they had previously been accustomed to give.

“The first one will say to Zion, ‘Behold, I am here,’ and I will give an evangelist to Jerusalem.” Zion, which is interpreted as “mirror” or “watchtower,” and Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signify the choir of preachers and the universal Church.

“The first one” — that is, my firstborn Son — says to Zion, that is, to the holy apostles and preachers: “Behold, I am here, O my apostles; and I will give an evangelist to Jerusalem,” that is, I will give holy people who will be in the Church, so that they may be preachers and proclaimers of the truth. An evangelist is called a good interpreter, and one has been placed for the many.

“And I looked,” I, almighty God, “and there was none among these” — understand, the images or demons — “who entered into counsel,” that is, who entered into deliberation, “and, when questioned” by their worshipers, “answered a word.” For although they were questioned, they could not answer.

“Behold, all of them,” understand, the worshipers of idols, are “unjust.” “And their works are worthless,” that is, their worship is like “wind,” and their images are “empty,” that is, useless.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Col. 0922D] “Behold, my servant; I will receive him.” The voice of God the Father concerning the Son. The Lord Jesus Christ is God and man. With respect to divinity, he is God, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father. With respect to humanity, however, he is called a servant, because he was made a little lower than the angels. He was also called a servant because “although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II).

Almighty God the Father received his servant, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, on the fortieth day after the resurrection, raising him above all the stars and above all the heavens and placing him at the right hand of his majesty.

“My chosen one; my soul has been pleased with him.” The Lord Jesus was chosen by God the Father, just as, at the time of his baptism and also on the mountain, a voice sent from the Father declared: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III), that is, in whom I have placed my pleasure. He was chosen because in him is all the fullness of virtues (Col. I and II); indeed, he himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Almighty God the Father does not possess a soul, but here he uses the word according to the will. This is what is meant by “my soul has been pleased with him”: it has pleased my will that he should dwell in him.

“I have given my spirit upon him,” either from the day of his conception, as the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke I), or also at the time of his baptism, when the Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove.

“He will bring forth judgment to the Gentiles,” which they previously did not know. Why does he not say “and to the Jews,” since he himself rather announced judgment and righteousness to them? Because the Jews regarded his preaching as nothing, and few of them believed in him. But after the Gentiles heard their error from the apostles, although they had not seen the Lord present, they did not delay in believing in him and turning from their evil way.

“He will not cry out,” that is, he will not raise his voice aloud, because he will be gentle and meek. As it is written elsewhere (below, LIII): “He will be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent.”

“Nor will he show partiality,” understand, in judgment; rather, he will judge with righteous judgment.

“Nor will his voice be heard outside,” understand, outside Judea or Galilee. Although we read that he preached and approached the borders of Tyre, Sidon, and Caesarea Philippi, cities belonging to the Gentiles, nowhere do we find it written that he entered those cities or regions; rather, he remained in Judea and Galilee, especially around Jerusalem.

“A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering flax he will not extinguish.” By the reed, which is bright on the outside and hollow within, we can understand the kingdom of the Jews: outwardly bright through pretense in the scribes and Pharisees, but inwardly empty of good works. Or it was bright because at that time it did not worship idols, but empty because it did not possess faith.

By the smoldering flax, from which priestly garments were made, is signified the Jewish priesthood, which was already failing and was, as it were, smoldering. Therefore, when the Lord came and found the Jewish kingdom shaken — for they no longer had a king from their own people but a foreigner — and their priesthood already close to extinction, he did not crush or extinguish it, but called everyone to repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matt. XII).

“He will bring forth judgment in truth,” understand, on the day of judgment, when he will repay each person according to his works. On the day of judgment only the person of the Son will appear. He who was unjustly condemned will render to each person, by a just judgment, according to what that person has done, whether good or evil.

[Col. 0924A] “He will not be sorrowful or troubled.” At all times he was cheerful and always joyful.

“Until he establishes judgment on the earth,” that is, on the day of judgment, over earthly human beings.

“And the islands will await his law.” This is expressed more clearly in the Septuagint translators: “And in his name the nations will hope for the law.” We must not understand the law of Moses, but the evangelical law. Why the Gentiles are called islands was stated above.

“Thus says the Lord God, creating the heavens,” when they did not exist, “and stretching out” the dwelling of the angels, “establishing the earth” upon the most tenuous element, “and creating what grows from it,” understand, “giving breath,” that is, the soul, “to the people who are upon it.”

Concerning this breath it is said in Genesis that “God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life” (Gen. II), that is, he gave him a soul, “and spirit to those who tread upon it,” understand, the earth. This is to be understood of the Holy Spirit. For those deserve to receive the Holy Spirit who trample upon earthly desires and subject the wisdom of their flesh to his power.

It was ambiguous who had spoken the preceding words about the coming of the Son of God — namely, “Behold, my servant; I will receive him,” and the other statements made there. Therefore he shows more clearly that the creator and Lord of the universe spoke them when he added: “Thus says the Lord God, creator of all things.”

This too must be known and stated at the place where he says, “giving breath to the people”: just as at the beginning of creation he created the soul from nothing and gave it to the first man (Gen. I), so each day he creates new souls, which he grants to human beings at birth.

“I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness, and I have taken your hand.” He who did all the things we have discussed above addresses his Son, saying: “I, God the Father, have called you from the East to the West,” that is, from Judea to all the Gentiles, “in righteousness,” that is, with righteousness through the preaching of the apostles, “and I have taken your hand,” that is, I have received your work.

Everything the Son accomplished, the Father accomplished through him, as he himself says: “The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works” (John XIV).

“And I have preserved you,” that is, I recalled you from death to life, because you preserved everything that you heard from me.

“And I have given you as a covenant of the people of Israel,” that is, into a fellowship of friendship with the Jewish people — namely, with those among them who wished to believe in you, to whom I had previously promised that you would come — “as a light to the Gentiles,” understand, those who sat in the darkness of unbelief and in the shadow of death.

“So that you may open the eyes of the blind,” who previously did not see the Lord, “and bring out from confinement,” understand, of sins, “the bound” Gentile people. For each person is bound by the cords of his sins, as Solomon says (Wis. XVII). And in the Gospel the Lord freed the woman whom Satan had bound (Matt. XV).

“From the prison house,” understand, “you may bring out those sitting in darkness,” who were placed in the night of error and unbelief and in the gloom of sins.

“I am the Lord. This is my name,” understand, so that I may be called Lord by all, because I rule over every creature.

“I will not give my glory to another.” He does not exclude the Son from his glory, because the Son himself says in the Gospel: “Glorify me, Father” — that is, honor me, Father — “with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John XII, XVII).

For he did not say, “I will give my glory to no one”; if he had said that, he would certainly have excluded the Son. Rather, he says: “I will not give my glory to another,” understand, apart from you, to whom I have given it and to whom I will give it. For he thus replied to the Son concerning what the Son had said: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again.”

So that we may understand more fully through this statement that the Son is not excluded from the glory of God the Father, the following words bear witness: “And my praise,” he says, “I will not give to graven images.”

“The former things — behold, they have come; and I announce new things also.” What were those former things that he spoke? Through the patriarchs, through Moses, and through the other prophets, he spoke of his coming. But he calls the preaching of the Gospel, the calling of the Gentiles, and the newness of faith “new.”

The meaning is: Everything I spoke through the prophets about my birth, my preaching, my miracles, my passion, and my resurrection has been fulfilled. But now I announce new things to you: the calling of the Gentiles, the rejection of the Jews, and the overthrow of Jerusalem.

“Before they arise, I will make you hear them.” Therefore I announce new things to you, so that, just as you see the former things fulfilled in events, you may also believe that the things I now proclaim will come to pass.

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” Who are those commanded to sing a new song to the Lord? The apostles and apostolic men. The new song is the evangelical preaching.

The holy apostles and holy preachers are commanded to sing a new song — that is, to preach the teaching of the Gospel — not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit, and not only in the old instrument but also in the new.

“And let them resound with his praise to the ends of the earth,” that is, let them announce throughout the whole world the praise of his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

“You who go down to the sea, and its fullness, the islands and their inhabitants” — understand, sing a new song and proclaim his praises. Who those are who must sing is made clear by what follows in the Gospel.

“You who go down,” he says, “to the sea and sail upon it” (Matt. IV). The apostles were repairing their nets on the shore beside the Sea of Gennesaret when they were called by the Lord. After the Lord’s ascension they crossed dangerous seas to the Gentiles (Rom. XV). Some preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and as far as Spain, capturing by their preaching, in a short time, many kinds of people, even the power of the city of Rome, so that what the Lord said to them might be fulfilled: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.”

Alternatively, by the sea we can understand this world, into which they descended when they heard the Lord say: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel” (Mark XVI). Going forth, they descended into the sea — that is, into the world of the Gentiles — where they endured the storms of persecutions and the tempests of tribulation.

He calls the fullness of this sea human beings, but the islands the various peoples and churches. O peoples who descend into the sea of this age, and its fullness — that is, the human beings dwelling in it — and islands, that is, the diverse peoples and diverse churches, and their inhabitants: praise the Lord and sing the new song of evangelical preaching.

“Let the wilderness raise its voice,” that is, the people of the Gentiles, “and its cities,” who were deserted and abandoned by God because of idolatry. Some manuscripts have “Let the wilderness rejoice,” some “Let the wilderness praise,” and some also “Let it be lifted up.” But only one of these can be appropriate.

If we say “Let it rejoice,” the meaning will be: Let the wilderness rejoice because the Lord redeemed it from death to life. If we say “Let it praise,” the meaning will be: Let the wilderness praise its Creator, who redeemed it from the bonds of sins and adopted it as a son. But of all these it is better to say “Let it be lifted up.”

Therefore, let the wilderness — that is, the Gentile world — raise its voice, and let its islands raise theirs in praise of the Lord, rejoicing that it has been snatched from unbelief to faith, from darkness to the true light, and from death to life.

“Cedar will dwell in houses.” Cedar was a son of Ishmael, and the province where the Saracens live took its name from him (Gen. XXV). They ought not properly to be called Saracens but Agareni, from Hagar, because Ishmael, from whom they derived their origin, was the son of Hagar, Sarah’s slave woman. But because they know for certain that they are sons of a slave woman and not of a free woman, they improperly appropriated a name of freedom for themselves. This applies not only to those who derived their origin from Cedar, the son of Ishmael, but to all their descendants who came from all the sons of Ishmael, because he fathered twelve princes.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, Cedar — that is, the Saracens — do not dwell in houses but in tents and tabernacles. In the higher meaning, Cedar will dwell in houses — that is, in churches — coming to faith through the preaching of the apostles and acting contrary to his former custom: he who was unaccustomed to dwelling in houses will dwell in churches, now existing as a believer.

It can also be understood in another way. Through Cedar, which is interpreted as “darkness,” the Gentiles are signified, who were placed in the darkness of error and unbelief. But after they came to faith, hearing the apostles sing the new song of evangelical preaching, they began to dwell in houses — that is, in churches.

“Praise the Lord, inhabitants of Petra.” In this passage Petra is the name of a city situated in the province of Palestine. It signifies that the people of the Gentiles, previously deserted by knowledge of God and bound by the errors of idolatry, are converted to the praises of the Lord.

“From the summit of the mountains they will cry out” — understand, the apostles and holy preachers, proclaiming the Gospel with a loud voice. Every preacher cries out from the summit of the mountains when, placed at the height of virtues, he sets earthly things aside and contemplates heavenly things with the full attention of his mind; and he adorns by his works what he preaches in words.

To such men it is said above (XL): “Ascend upon a high mountain,” that is, ascend to the summit of virtues, “you who evangelize Zion.”

“They will give glory to the Lord,” understand, the apostles and preachers of the word, in the hearts of their subjects, “and they will announce his praise in the islands,” that is, among the nations. For the sound of their preaching went out into the whole earth.

“The Lord will go forth like a strong man; like a warrior he will stir up zeal,” that is, vengeance and retribution, against the Jews, his enemies, and through the strength and power of the Romans. The events read here were fulfilled by the Romans, with the Lord permitting it.

When it is said, “The Lord will go forth like a strong man,” it is to be understood as referring to his coming forth from his great clemency and gentleness when he takes vengeance on his enemies. It does not mean that he literally goes forth, but that this is how it appears to those against whom vengeance is taken.

He is compared to a very powerful warrior because he fights against his adversaries and stirs up in his mind zeal and the fervor of vengeance against his enemies.

“He will cry out and shout,” openly rebuking their madness: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII).

“And he will prevail over his enemies,” namely, the Jews.

“I was silent; I was always quiet; I was patient. Like a woman in labor I will speak.” Some manuscripts have *parturiens*, “being in labor,” but *pariens*, “giving birth,” is better.

He speaks against the Jews, and the meaning is: For a long time I carried and endured you in your wrongdoing, waiting to see whether you would remember me. But because you do not wish to repent and return to me, I will no longer remain silent. Rather, just as a woman giving birth brings an infant into the light and reveals what was previously enclosed within her womb, so I will now bring forth what I have long kept silent while enduring your sufferings, and I will display the pain and the pretense that I have always maintained concerning your crimes.

“I will scatter” your counsels “and swallow them up together,” that is, I will destroy my enemies, the Jews.

“I will make the mountains and hills desolate, and I will dry up all their grass.” By the mountains let us understand the princes, scribes, Pharisees, and priests. By the hills, the lesser judges, namely, tribunes and centurions. By the grass, the people subject to them.

At one time the princes, young men, old men, and the whole of their people were swallowed up and dried up — that is, killed by the Romans through famine, the sword, and captivity.

“I will place rivers in the islands,” that is, an abundance of knowledge among the Gentiles.

“And I will dry up the pools,” that is, I will make you who appear to possess knowledge of the Law devoid of the knowledge of God. The meaning is: When I have destroyed you from the greatest to the least, then I will cause the rivers of my teaching to flow toward the islands of the Gentiles; and the pools — that is, you who once possessed a depth of knowledge — I will reduce to dryness, so that, although you read the words of the Law and the prophets, you will be unable to understand them.

[Col. 0928A] “I will lead the blind by a way they do not know.” The Gentiles were blind, not in body but in mind, because they lay in the darkness of sins. The way by which the Gentiles now walk is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

“I will make them walk in paths they have not known.” These paths are understood as the prophets. Just as one reaches the road by a path, so through the words of the prophets and their examples we reach Christ, because they contain his birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, as well as our calling.

“I will place darkness before them as light, and crooked things as straight,” that is, before the Gentiles I will place true light and the knowledge of almighty God. And the crooked things — understand, their hearts — I will make straight. The crooked and twisted hearts of the Gentiles were turned straight, so that, when they read the words of the prophets, they might understand what is contained there and clearly behold the light of Christ with the eyes of their hearts.

“I have done these things for them” — for what is meant is “I will do,” understand, the devastation by the Romans that I mentioned above. “And I have not abandoned them” — for what is meant is “I will not abandon them,” if they repent. But what did they do, refusing to repent?

“They turned backward,” that is, toward unbelief. After the Lord ascended into heaven, he left the apostles in Judea to preach to the Jews and baptize in the name of the Holy Trinity, and he gave them a period of forty years in which to repent. But they not only refused to believe in him; they also drove the apostles themselves from their territories.

For this reason — namely, because they unjustly crucified the Lord, persecuted his apostles, and refused to repent — they were handed over into the hands of the Romans.

“Let those who trust in a graven image be confounded with confusion, who say to a cast image, ‘You are our gods.’” He speaks of the Gentiles who refused to believe the apostles when they preached, remaining in their errors.

“Deaf ones, hear; and blind ones, look up in order to see.” To whom this prophetic word refers, he shows in what follows, saying: “Who is blind except the one to whom I sent my servants and messengers, the prophets?”

“Deaf ones, hear.” There is no doubt that this is said about the Jews, who were deaf not in the ears of the body but in those which the Lord requires in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII), that is, whoever has understanding, let him understand what I say.

For the Prophet had said to them above (chap. VI): “You will hear with the ears of the body, but you will not understand with the ears of the mind.”

“Blind ones, look up in order to see,” that is, you who are in the darkness of unbelief, open the eyes of your mind to see your Savior.

“Who is blind except my servant Israel, and who is deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers, the prophets? Who is blind except Israel, who was sold” into sins? For whoever serves someone is that person’s servant.

“Who is blind” except the one who was previously “the servant of the Lord”? To him it is said:

“You who see many things,” O Israel — that is, you who understand the Law [Col. 0929A] and the prophets — “will you not keep them,” the things spoken there? “You who have open ears” of the body, “will you not hear,” that is, will you not obey?

“And the Lord desired to sanctify him,” understand, the people, “and to magnify the Law,” that is, to make it great by observing it, “and to exalt,” that is, to raise them from vices to virtues. But because he did not wish to fulfill his will, [sentence continues beyond the supplied text].

“‘He was plundered and laid waste,’ either by evil spirits or by enemies—namely, the Chaldaeans and the Romans. ‘The snare of the young men, all together, and they have been hidden in prison houses.’ Now he returns to the time of the Lord’s preaching, speaking of the scribes and Pharisees. The scribes and Pharisees are compared to a snare because by their perverse teaching they ensnared the minds [Col. 0929B] of the simple. Their subjects are called young men on account of their simplicity. For they were easily deceived, so that they would not believe in Christ. But because they deceived those subject to them and set snares for the Lord, what Solomon says happened to them: ‘Whoever prepares a pit for his neighbor will fall into it first’ (Prov. XXVI). They prepared a snare for the Lord, but they themselves were ensnared in their sins. Thus it is rightly said: ‘The snare of the young men, all together’—the scribes and Pharisees preparing ambushes for the Lord—‘and they have been hidden in prison houses.’ The breasts of the scribes and Pharisees are not inappropriately compared to a prison. Were they not hidden in a prison when, testing the Lord, they said to him: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth’ (Matt. XXII), and other things like these? ‘They have become plunder,’ that is understood, of enemies, ‘and there is no one to rescue them.’ There was no prophet or priest to intercede for them, as Moses did in the wilderness, turning the Lord’s anger toward mercy (Exod. XXXII). ‘Into plunder’ by enemies—that is, into captivity and spoil—‘and there is no one who says, “Restore,”’ that is understood, their liberty to them, O Lord.

“‘Who among you will hear this? Let him attend and listen to what is to come,’ that is understood, what I announce, whether good or evil. The Prophet urges them that, if they cannot all hear what he is about to announce, at least a few should learn what is to come, understand from whom they have suffered these things, and consider the causes of their devastation.

“‘Who gave Jacob over to plunder, and Israel to those who laid him waste? [Col. 0929D] Was it not God himself, against whom we sinned?’ God the almighty Father, against whom they sinned by unjustly condemning his only-begotten Son, himself handed them over to plunder—that is, to the trampling-down of the Romans—because they refused to repent of their crimes. ‘They were unwilling to walk in his ways,’ that is, in his commandments. ‘And they did not listen to his law,’ which he was giving them through his Son.

“‘And he poured out upon them the indignation of his anger’ through the Romans, ‘and mighty war.’ By “mighty war” he means an exceedingly severe defeat, in which all perished through famine, the sword, and captivity. ‘And he burned him all around,’ that is, consumed him with the fire of tribulation. ‘And he did not know’—that is understood, that they suffered these things because of the killing of the Son of God [Col. 0930A]. ‘And he set him on fire,’ either the people themselves with the fire of tribulation, or the temple. ‘And he did not understand’ for what reason he was suffering. Histories relate that neither did the Romans know that they were being delivered into their hands in vengeance for the Son of God, nor did the Jews themselves understand this, blinded by their wickedness.

## CHAPTER XLIII

“‘And now thus says the Lord, who created you, Jacob, and formed you, Israel.’ As we have already said above, the people of Israel are divided into two groups: believers and unbelievers. The Gentiles likewise. In the preceding passage he spoke of the Jews’ final captivity and of the unbelief of those who persisted in wickedness. Now, however, he addresses the primitive Church, which [Col. 0930B] consisted of the apostles and of those among the Jews who believed through them. ‘And now,’ he says, ‘thus says the Lord.’ It is as though he said in other words: Because they remained in their faithlessness, refusing to receive my preaching or yours, O chorus of apostles, thus says the Lord who created you in the body and formed you in the soul (Gen. XXVII). Jacob—which is interpreted as “supplanter”—and Israel—which is interpreted as “the man who sees God”—signify the apostles and apostolic men, who supplanted vices and merited to see God. ‘Do not fear,’ O chorus of apostles, ‘because I redeemed you’ with the blood of my Son, ‘and I called you by your name,’ that is understood, so that you might be called Israel, meaning “the man who sees God.”

“‘You are mine,’ that is understood, my servant. ‘When you pass through the waters,’ O chorus of apostles, ‘I will be with you, and the rivers will not cover you.’ By these words the divine discourse shows that the apostles would suffer many torments and dangers for Christ’s name. Through waters, rivers, fire, and flames it wishes to signify the assault, savagery, and fury of persecutors, who begrudged salvation to the Gentiles and did not wish the evangelical message to be preached by the apostles. The Hebrews, however, wish to understand by the waters the Egyptians, because of the great river Nile; by the rivers, the Chaldaeans, who have many rivers; by the fire, the Macedonians, because of their harshness; and by the flame, the Romans, who attempted to destroy the preachers just as flame consumes everything. Through all these kingdoms the holy apostles and preachers passed, announcing the word of the Gospel. The divine discourse also exhorts them not to fear or [Col. 0930D] dread their hardness and fierceness, because the Lord, the God of Israel, is their savior and protector. Although they were killed bodily, delivered over to diverse and extraordinary torments, they nevertheless reached the joys of the heavenly homeland unharmed in soul, their course completed.

“‘I gave Egypt, Ethiopia, and Seba as your ransom,’ O chorus of apostles. Ethiopia is a region situated at the ends of the earth. Seba is a great city at the borders of that same region, from which came the queen of Seba, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. What, then, are we to understand by Ethiopia and Seba except the ends of the whole world, to which the apostles’ preaching reached? ‘Their sound has gone out into all the earth,’ says the Psalmist, ‘and their words to the ends of the world’ (Ps. XVIII). Thus the apostles’ ransom and righteousness became the salvation of these and other regions.

“‘From the time when you became honorable in my eyes,’ O chorus of apostles, ‘and glorious, I loved you.’ The chorus of apostles became honorable and glorious in the Lord’s eyes when, hearing from the Lord, ‘Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel’ (Mark XVI), they set out and preached everywhere, with the Lord working with them. ‘And I will give men in exchange for you, and peoples in exchange for your life.’ The meaning is: For all those whom you are able to convert to faith in me through your preaching from among all the nations, you will receive a reward.

“‘Do not fear,’ O chorus of apostles, the kings and princes of this age and the savagery of persecutors, ‘for I am with you,’ I who redeemed you and said in the Gospel both to you and to all the faithful: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. XXVIII). ‘From the East I will bring your seed,’ O chorus of apostles, to my Church, ‘and from the West I will gather you.’ By these two parts of the world we should understand the four quarters, from which people are collected into faith and gathered into the unity of the Church—even if not bodily, at least in mind. Hence he says in the Gospel: ‘Many will come from the East and the West, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. VIII). If we ask what the apostles’ seed is of which he speaks here, it is clear that spiritual seed is intended [Col. 0931C]. For all who believed through their preaching are their seed, as the outstanding preacher says: ‘My little children, with whom I am again in labor’ (Gal. IV); and: ‘Through the Gospel I fathered you.’

“‘I will say to the north,’ that is, to the devil, ‘Give,’ that is understood, my sons whom you hold captive, to my apostles. ‘And I will say to the south, “Do not hinder”’ my sons who are coming to the faith of the Church. ‘Bring my sons from afar,’ O chorus of apostles—that is, the people of the Gentiles, who are far from knowledge of God—‘and my daughters,’ that is, souls destined for the kingdom, ‘from the ends of the earth,’ namely from India and Ethiopia. Or by daughters we may understand women who came to the Lord through faith. Men believed, and women believed as well. To this statement, ‘Bring my Gentile sons from afar,’ belongs what the blessed Apostle says: ‘You who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ’ (Eph. II).

“‘And every person who invokes my name for my glory’—that is understood, I will bring into the fellowship of my elect. ‘I created him’ in the body, he who was destined to believe in me. ‘I formed him’ in the soul, ‘and I made him’—that is understood, a Christian, or any apostle, or a Gentile.

“‘Bring the people out,’ from unbelief to faith, from death to life, from the darkness of error to the true light. This is the voice of God the Father to the Son concerning the Jews, who had eyes in the body but were blind in mind. Likewise they had bodily ears, but they were deaf because they had the ears of their minds stopped up, so that they could not hear the law of God. For the Holy Spirit had also foretold this very thing through the prophet Isaiah, saying: ‘You will hear with the ear and will not understand, and you will have eyes and will not see’ (above, VI). It should be noted that the calling of the Jews took place first, and then that of the Gentiles, as the Lord said: ‘I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (Matt. XV). The blessed Apostle Paul is also read to have said something similar in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles’ (Acts XIII).

“‘All the nations have been gathered together, and the tribes have been collected.’ After those who had been predestined from the Jews believed in Christ, the Gentiles too were gathered. Thus the Gentiles were gathered, and the tribes—that is, the Jews—were collected. Both from the Gentiles and from the Jews there came to be one fold of the Lord (John X), in which they are gathered daily in the unity of faith, in baptism, and in the one reception of the body and blood of Christ. ‘Who among you,’ O Gentiles, ‘will announce this’—that is understood, what God spoke concerning the coming of his Son—‘and will make us hear the first things?’ If your gods are true, let them announce to you past or future things, as does our Lord. The Prophet addresses the Gentiles, wishing to remove them from idolatry and the worship of demons. ‘Let their witnesses come forward,’ that is, let the gods themselves bring forward their witnesses, ‘so that they may be justified,’ that is, so that they may be called just and true, ‘and let them hear,’ those who do not know them to be true gods, ‘and let them say’ that they are true gods. At this point the verse should be punctuated and joined to what follows.

“‘You are truly my witnesses, says the Lord.’ Truly you are my witnesses, prophets and apostles, says the Lord Father, because I have spoken through you. ‘And my servant,’ that is understood, Christ, ‘whom I chose,’ in whom I was well pleased (Matt. III; Luke III), that is understood, he himself also being a witness to my words, ‘so that you may know that I am God.’ Concerning this servant he said above: ‘Behold my servant; I will receive him’ (above, XLI, XLII); and: ‘It is a great thing for you to be called my child’ (below, XLIX). ‘Before me there is no God who is a former, and after me there will not be.’ This is the voice of God the Father. Some manuscripts have: ‘Before me no God was formed.’ But it is better and more correct to say “former.” The pagans said of their gods [Col. 0932D]: ‘This is our god; he made all things.’ For example, they might say to Jupiter: ‘Jupiter, you are my true god, because you created and rule Olympus,’ that is, heaven. Against this the almighty God says: Before me there was no God who formed anything. I am the first former, because when nothing existed I made all things from nothing. For how could any of the false gods have been the former of anything, when there was nothing from which he could form it? Idols are deaf, mute, and insensible, formed by human hands. But if this is referred to the devil, who often gave responses through idols, how could he have been the former of all things, since he himself was made by God in time? If we say, ‘Before me no God was formed,’ the meaning will be: Before me no idol was fashioned, because I formed the righteous human being, from whom idols were afterward unjustly fashioned. But this meaning does not fully fit. As for what he says, ‘and after me there will not be,’ it is the same as what is said in the Apocalypse: ‘I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end’ (Rev. I, XXII).

“‘I am, I am the Lord, and there is no savior apart from me.’ The repetition of the words confirms the matter. When God the Father says, ‘There is no savior apart from me,’ he does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit from himself, because neither is the Son apart from the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit, through whom they are one. As the Lord says: ‘I and the Father are one. I am in the Father, and the Father is in me’ (John X). But when he says, ‘There is no savior apart from me,’ it is as though he said: In me is the savior, namely my Son, through whom I have determined to save the human race. And just as the one Christ the Lord does not prevent the Father from being Lord, so the one God the Father, the savior, does not prevent the Son from also being savior. For the Son says in the Gospel: ‘As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whomever he wishes’ (John V). Because just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself—that is, he begot the Son having life.

“‘I announced’ the birth of my Son, the calling of the Gentiles, and the expulsion of demons. ‘I saved’ the human race through my Son, with “I will save” used in its place. ‘I made it heard,’ past and future, ‘and there was no’ prophet or apostle or ‘alien’ god among you, as the Gentiles said. ‘You,’ prophets and apostles, [Col. 0933C] ‘are my witnesses, says the Lord,’ that is understood, because what I foretold would come to pass in the future will come.

“‘There is no one who can rescue anything from my hand,’ that is, from the power of my Son or from mine. ‘I will act,’ for the salvation of the Gentiles, ‘and who will turn it aside,’ who will destroy ‘what I have done’? Who has brought about the salvation of the Gentiles except the one who is truly God? No one.

“‘Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.’ This is the voice of God the Father to the apostles. The following words are spoken by the Lord, your redeemer, ‘for your sake,’ O apostles, my sons: ‘I sent into Babylon, and I brought down all the bars, and the Chaldaeans boasting in their ships.’ In the literal sense, Babylon is interpreted as ‘confusion,’ because there the language of the whole earth was confused. In the higher sense [Col. 0933D], it signifies this world, which, when the Lord came in the flesh, lay in the confusion of sins. By the bars we should understand the kings, princes, and powerful men of this age, because just as something is carried by bars, so the pomp of this world was borne along by their protection. In the historical sense, he says that the Chaldaeans boasted in their ships because, possessing many great rivers, they were highly skilled sailors. In the higher understanding, he says this because the demons—who are signified by them—made the souls of wretched human beings wander through the waves of this world. ‘For your sake,’ he says, O my apostles, ‘I sent into Babylon,’ that is, into the world that dwelt in the confusion of sins, ‘and I brought down all the powerful of this age from their pride; I also brought the demons down from the hearts of human beings,’ demons who gloried in the souls they had deceived, ‘so that through perfect faith and steadfast love my Son might reign in the hearts of human beings,’ instructed by your preaching.

“‘I am the Lord, your Holy One,’ O apostles, ‘creating Israel,’ your king, O chorus of apostles.

“‘Thus says the Lord who gave’ the sons of Israel ‘a way in the sea,’ the Red Sea, ‘and a path in the waters of torrents,’ that is, of very powerful waters, ‘in the Jordan,’ or also in the Arnon, as Moses said: ‘Just as he acted in the Red Sea, providing you a path through the dry sea, so he will act in the torrents of Arnon’ (Num. XXI). The one who gave a way in the sea and a path in the waters of the Jordan—so that the exodus from Egypt and the entry into the promised land might be accompanied by a miracle—himself, I say, cast down the rulers of this world from their pride, converted them to the humility of the Gospel, and expelled the demons from the hearts of the human beings over whom they ruled, providing a way for his apostles and preachers in the sea (Exod. XIV), that is, in this world, so that they might preach freely.

“‘I led out the chariot from Egypt, and the horse, the host, and the mighty one.’ He said “chariot” and “horse” for many chariots and horsemen, just as “host” and “mighty one” stand for many hosts and a multitude of mighty men. ‘They slept together,’ that is, they died together. ‘Nor will they rise again,’ because they are wrapped in perpetual sleep. ‘They were crushed’ by many waters in a moment. ‘They were extinguished like flax.’ Just as flax is set alight in a moment and quickly extinguished, so they died in a moment and were extinguished from the earth.

“‘Do not remember’—O apostles—‘the former things’ that I said (2 Cor. V), namely, the way made by me in the sea and the path in the Jordan, ‘and do not consider the ancient things,’ because I will do greater things, and you will do them through me; in comparison with these, the past will be judged insignificant (Rev. XXV).

“‘I will place in the wilderness’ of the Gentiles ‘a way,’ that is, Christ, because he is ‘the way, the truth, and the life’ (John XIV). ‘And in the trackless place, rivers,’ that is, in the wilderness of the Gentiles, where there was no spiritual teaching, I will give rivers: namely, knowledge of the Old and New Testaments. These are the new things that he previously promised to do.

[Col. 0934D] “‘The wild beast of the field, dragons, and ostriches will glorify me, because I gave waters in the wilderness and rivers in the trackless place, to give drink to my people.’ He calls the Gentiles wild beasts, because they lived like beasts, ignorant of the Creator and worshiping the creature (Rom. I). By dragons, which have venom and kill, we may understand murderous and wicked people, full of the blood of their neighbors. The ostrich is a large bird with short wings, incapable of flight. By it are signified hypocrites, who appear indeed to have the wings of virtues but cannot rise to higher things. ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘the Gentiles will glorify me—those who were previously murderous and wicked, living like beasts—because I gave them knowledge of the Old and New Testaments in their wilderness, so that I might give my people who believe in me a drink for the mind,’ namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit, as I said in the Gospel: ‘Let anyone who thirsts come to me and drink. And from his belly will flow living waters’ (John VII).

“‘This people,’ that is understood, the Gentile people who believe in me, ‘I formed for myself,’ so that it might be Christian. ‘It will proclaim my praise,’ that is, my birth, my Passion, the triumph of my resurrection, and the glory of my ascension.

“‘You did not call upon me, Jacob, nor did you labor for me, Israel.’ As we have already said above, there are two Jacobs, the carnal and the spiritual, and two Israels. Wherever Israel or Jacob is mentioned without an interpretation of the name—for example, ‘Jacob my elect’ and ‘the upright one whom I chose’—it should be understood of the spiritual. ‘You did not call upon me, Jacob,’ he says. We may refer this to those who worshiped idols before the Lord’s coming, or to those who refused to believe after the Lord’s ascension, remaining in their unbelief. Let us speak first of those who transgressed through idols before the Lord’s coming. Israel often called upon the Lord, and he heard him. But at the time when Isaiah spoke these words in the Lord’s person, although Israel called with his mouth, he did not call with his actions. ‘You did not call upon me, Jacob,’ he says, as I ought to have been called upon, because you called upon me with your mouth but called upon idols in mind and deed. ‘Nor did you labor for me, Israel,’ that is, you did not make yourself labor to obtain precious things to offer me; or, you did not labor for me alone.

[Col. 0935C] “‘You did not offer me the ram of your burnt offering, and you did not glorify me with your sacrifices.’ Often he seemed to offer burnt offerings to the Lord, but the Lord himself did not accept them, because they were shared with the idols. He took them away from the Lord with his hand and sacrificed to the idols in his heart. It is as though he said in other words: You think that you offered victims to me and sacrificed rams, but know that they were not accepted by me, because they were shared between me and the idols. He repeats the sense of what he said above: ‘Why do you offer me the multitude of your sacrifices, says the Lord?’ (above, I). ‘I am full,’ that is, I lack nothing. This is like what he says through the prophet Amos: ‘Did you offer sacrifices to me, house of Israel, for forty years, and not rather to your god Moloch?’ (Amos V). For God does not want a part, but the whole. Nor does he delight in a carnal sacrifice, but in a spiritual one, of which the Psalmist says: ‘A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise’ (Ps. XXXIX). ‘You did not make me serve through an offering, nor did you burden me with incense.’ The Lord commanded offerings to be made to him and incense to be offered on each Sabbath. Why, then, does he now say these things? It is as though he said in other words: I did not make you serve for that reason, because I did not demand anything costly from you, so that I would make you labor in preparing such things. Or he did not make you serve for that reason because he accepted your sacrifices.

“‘You did not buy me aromatic reed (*calamus*) with silver, nor did you intoxicate me with the fat of your victims’ [Col. 0936A], that is, I was not delighted. *Calamus* is an aromatic twig. He uses incense and *calamus* for all spices. ‘You did not buy,’ he says, ‘aromatic reed with silver,’ that is, I did not command you to give your gold and silver in order to buy various kinds of precious fragrances and spices from them to offer me, because they did not please the eyes of my majesty, since they were shared with the idols. ‘Yet you made me serve in your sins.’ We make almighty God serve in our sins when we refuse to turn from our iniquities, while he, compassionate and merciful, waits for us to repent. ‘You gave me labor in your iniquities.’ The meaning is the same. This may also be referred to the Jews who refused to convert after the Lord’s ascension, and to those who have persisted in unbelief until now and still hold in figure the true sacrifice that has already been fulfilled, making worthless everything they seem to offer to the Lord, although they do not sacrifice these things to idols.
