Thus the Lord says to Jacob and Israel acting carnally: ‘You did not call upon me, Jacob, nor did you labor for me, Israel.’ The meaning is: While the wild beasts of the field, dragons, and ostriches—that is, the Gentiles—praise me, you were entirely unwilling to call upon me or to labor so that you might erase the sin of denial through repentance. And although it may seem to you that the burnt offerings, victims, and incense you offer please me, I am not delighted in them, because, remaining in the oldness of sin, you do not wish to pass over to the newness of the Gospel.

“‘I am, I myself, he who blots out your iniquities [Col. 0936C] for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.’ He now addresses the Jews and urges them to repentance, promising them forgiveness of their offenses. ‘I am,’ he says, ‘compassionate and merciful; I will blot out your iniquities if you repent—for my own sake, not for yours. And I will no longer remember your sins after you have produced fruits worthy of repentance.’

“‘Recall me to memory, and let us be judged together.’ That is: Remember all the good things I did for you when I led you out of the house of slavery and brought you into a land superior to all others in signs, miracles, and great power, and how I removed many strong nations from before you. ‘And let us be judged together,’ that is, let us determine what I ought to have done for you that I did not do, and bring an accusation against me. This meaning is expressed more fully in Micah: ‘My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I wearied you? Answer me’ (Mic. III). ‘Tell me if you have anything, so that you may be justified’: you, sinner, speak if you have done anything good, lest, if I begin to speak, you should say that because of my many words you cannot answer.

“‘Your first father sinned, and your interpreters transgressed against me.’ Their father may be understood as Abraham, who sinned by doubting the promise and asking for a sign; or the entire people who died in the wilderness by sinning against the Lord (Gen. XV). Interpreters are so called as though they stood between parties, moving between two sides and bringing peace. In this passage we may understand Moses and Aaron, who transgressed at the waters of contradiction [Col. 0937A] (Num. XX), that is, departed from the will of God.

“‘And I permitted the holy princes to be defiled,’ that is, I permitted Moses and Aaron to be defiled. He says that he defiled them for this reason: they did not enter the promised land. ‘I gave Jacob over to destruction,’ that is, to slaughter, ‘and Israel to reproach,’ so that no one except two of those who came out of Egypt would enter the promised land, but their corpses would lie in the wilderness, apart from Joshua and Caleb.

## CHAPTER XLIV

“‘And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I chose.’ Above he spoke of carnal Israel and Jacob; now he addresses the chorus of apostles [Col. 0937B] and the believers from the Jews, together with the privilege of the name and the dignity of honor. ‘And now,’ O chorus of apostles, because carnal Israel remains in unbelief and does not wish to hear me, you who are my servant, my chosen one, hear my commandments and fulfill them in deed.

“‘Thus says the Lord, who makes you’ in the body ‘and forms you’ in the soul, ‘your helper from the womb,’ because I made you when you did not yet exist. ‘Do not fear, my servant Jacob and Uprightest One, whom I chose.’ Blessed Jerome says that Israel, according to the proper meaning of the Hebrew language, is properly interpreted as ‘upright’ or ‘most upright.’ But the interpretation ‘the man who sees God’ does not lie in the written letters; it consists in the sound of the word. Thus what is said here—‘Do not fear, my servant Jacob and Uprightest One, whom I chose’—is as though it said: ‘and Israel whom I chose.’

“‘For I will pour out water,’ that is, the teaching of the Old and New Testaments, ‘upon the thirsty one,’ the Gentile world, ‘and streams’ of divine utterances ‘upon the dry land.’ The Gentile world that was thirsty was also dry, because it did not possess the moisture of love for God and neighbor. ‘For I will pour out my spirit upon your seed,’ O chorus of apostles, ‘and my blessing upon your offspring.’ The apostles’ spiritual seed and offspring are all believers who, enlightened by their preaching, examples, miracles, or writings, came to the faith or will come to it until the day of the final judgment. Upon this seed the Lord poured out his Holy Spirit when, in baptism and through the laying on of bishops’ hands, he granted it the grace of his Spirit [Col. 0937D]. He also poured out blessing upon their offspring, because unless he himself had enlightened the hearts of the Gentiles, they would expend their preaching in vain. For unless the Lord enlightens the hearer’s heart, the teacher’s tongue labors in vain.

“‘And they will sprout among the grasses, like willows beside flowing waters.’ Grass rejoices in its greenness. Therefore those who are renewed in baptism and deemed worthy to receive the Lord’s blessing are compared with green grasses, because, possessing the greenness of faith and good works, they will produce fruits of good action among believers who, already strengthened by roots, themselves possess full greenness. By the willow—which is fruitless and grows quickly, especially if it is situated beside flowing waters, that is, if it is surrounded on every side by water, and which, even if taken in food or drink, as physicians say, makes the person who takes it sterile—the Gentile world is signified. Before the Lord’s coming it was sterile of the fruits of good works; but afterward, having beside it the waters of evangelical teaching, it produced, contrary to nature, the fruit of virtues, though previously fruitless. We may also understand by the grasses and willows the twofold calling of the nations, namely of the Gentiles and the Jews: by the grasses, the multitude of the Gentiles coming to the faith; and by the willows, the primitive Church from the Jews, which quickly grew when the apostles preached.

“‘This one’—that is understood, one believer and faithful person—‘will say, “I belong to the Lord,”’ a servant through faith and action, not belonging to idols, because he has been redeemed by him. ‘And that one,’ another faithful person, ‘will call’ sinners to repentance ‘in the name of Jacob,’ that is, so that he may supplant vices, just as Jacob did. ‘And this one,’ that is, another, ‘will write with his hand: “I belong to the Lord; I am a servant,”’ or, according to what the Septuagint says, ‘I am God’s soldier,’ so that he may glory in being a soldier of Christ from his new enlistment. Some manuscripts have: ‘He will write on his hand, “To the Lord.”’ But blessed Jerome, according to the Hebrew truth, says, ‘I belong to the Lord,’ and, according to what the Septuagint says, ‘I am God’s soldier.’ It is also clearer to say ‘he will write, “I belong to the Lord; I am a soldier,”’ than ‘he will write with his hand, “To the Lord.”’ Nevertheless, if we say ‘to the Lord,’ the meaning will be that he writes to the Lord that he is a Christian, that he possesses his faith, just as the outstanding preacher says at the beginning and end of his letters: ‘Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle.’ And: ‘I, Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, wrote this with my own hand.’ ‘And he will be likened in the name of Israel’—each one of them—so that what he does not possess by flesh, he may possess through faith. Thus the Gentiles, who according to the flesh are not descended from Abraham’s line, are likened in name to Israel, which is interpreted as ‘the man who sees God,’ because through faith and action, while placed in the present age, they merit to contemplate God, and in the future they will contemplate him face to face. Not all Gentiles, however, are likened to Israel, but only believers, who now possess the law and the prophets and all the graces of the Holy Spirit that were promised to the people of Israel.

“‘Thus says the Lord, the king of Israel: “I am the first,”’ before whom there is no one, ‘“and I am the last,”’ after whom there is no one, ‘“and apart from me there is no God,”’ true and savior. After the calling of the Gentiles and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which he promised he would give to all believers, when, according to the diversity of their merits, one will say, ‘I belong to the Lord,’ another will call sinners to repentance in the name of Jacob, another will write with his hand that he belongs to the Lord, and another will be likened in the name of Israel, so that, having abandoned idols, there may be the worship of one God: he speaks against the worshipers of idols who refused to convert.

“‘Who is like me’ among the idols? Let him ‘call’ things that do not exist as though they existed, ‘and let him explain to me the order’ of my creatures. I created [Col. 0939A] everything when it did not exist; let him ‘explain’ how they were ordered. ‘From the time when I established the ancient people, let them announce to them the things to come and what will be in the future.’ He calls either the entire human race from Adam or the Israelite people, whom he chose in Abraham, the ancient people. The meaning is: From the time when I established the ancient people from the first human being, so that they might serve me, or the Israelite people so that they might be my special people, I announced future things to them. And just as I announced future things to them, if they are true gods, let them likewise announce what is to come.

“‘Do not fear,’ O believers, the savagery of the persecutors who worship idols, ‘nor be troubled’ because of their threats. ‘From that time,’ that is, from the time when I established the ancient people, ‘I made them hear, and I announced’ that [Col. 0939B] an idol is nothing but the work of human hands. ‘You are my witnesses,’ O my peoples, because I am God of the whole earth. ‘Is there a God apart from me, and a former whom I do not know?’ If there is another God and former besides me, another world must necessarily be shown to exist. But since neither another former nor another world will be found, there is in no way another God besides me, who formed this one.

“‘The image-maker of an idol’—that is, the makers of idols—‘are nothing,’ as the Psalmist says: ‘Let those who make them become like them’ (Ps. CXXXIV). ‘And their most senseless things,’ that is understood, their idols, ‘will not profit them,’ namely their worshipers, on the day of each person’s examination. *Plastes* is Greek and means ‘former’ or ‘composer.’ ‘They themselves,’ the image-makers, ‘are witnesses of them,’ that is, of the idols, [Col. 0939C] ‘because they do not see or understand, so that they may be confounded’ over their error—that is understood, and for this reason they are witnesses. For the Psalmist says: ‘They have ears and do not hear; they have eyes and do not see, because there is no spirit in them.’

“‘Who formed a god, and cast a sculpture for something useless?’

“‘Behold, all who share in it will be confounded,’ namely both the one who formed it and the one who worshiped it. ‘For they are craftsmen from among human beings’ for fashioning idols. ‘All will assemble,’ that is understood, the makers and worshipers of idols on the day of judgment; ‘they will stand’ for judgment, ‘and they will tremble,’ remembering their sins, ‘and they will be confounded together’ because of their error.

“‘The ironworker worked with a file’ on the idol. ‘He will hunger,’ its maker, because his god will not give him food, ‘and he will grow faint’ from his labor; ‘he will not drink water, and he will grow weary,’ that is, if he does not drink water from elsewhere he will become exhausted, because his god will not provide him drink.

“‘The woodworker stretches out the measuring line,’ that is, he prepares a rule so that he can bring the idol to straightness. ‘He fashioned it into’ an idol, that is, with a plane (*runcina*). A plane is a certain tool of the woodworker, slender and curved, by which boards of a house are hollowed out so that one may be joined to another. ‘He made it’—the idol—‘with corners,’ that is, square; ‘and he shaped it with a compass,’ that is, on a lathe and into roundness; ‘and he made’ there, whether in the square or in the round, ‘the image of a man, like a handsome human being dwelling in a house.’ For who could believe that God is formed with an axe, a file, a chisel, and a hammer, and that images are first cast and turned on a lathe and suddenly rise up as gods—especially when the craftsman’s poverty is demonstrated by his hunger and thirst?”

“The woodcutter cuts down cedars” to make idols, “takes holm oak and oak, which had stood” for many years “among the other trees of the forest,” and fashions an image from them. “He plants a pine” to make a god from it, “which the rains” nourish “for many days.”

“And it becomes” that pine, in part, “for human beings as fuel. He takes some of them”—namely, from the cedar, holm oak, oak, and pine—“and is warmed by them.”

“But he makes the remainder of it into a god,” that is, he fashions what remains into an idol for himself.

“They do not reflect in their mind” that I made them, “nor do they understand” that they themselves are not gods, but works of human hands; “nor do they perceive”—and they do not understand—“so as to say”: “I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread over its coals; I roasted meat with it and ate it, and shall I make an idol from what remains? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?” I shall not do so—why?

“Because part of it is ashes: an unwise heart worshiped it, and it did not save its soul; nor will it say: ‘Perhaps’—that is, perhaps—‘there is a lie in my hand.’” When he was worshiping or fashioning the idol, he ought to have considered and said to himself: Certainly there is a lie in my hand—that is, in my handiwork—because this thing, which I worship and hold as a god, is the work of my hands. The worshipers of idols ought to have weighed these matters with a vigilant mind, but they did not. They will be seized in their iniquity and will not be delivered by the help of their gods.

“Remember these things, Jacob, and Israel, because you are my servant.” Now he addresses the Israelite people and the faithful who believed at the Lord’s coming. Since everything is as I have said, and you know that idols are fabrications and constructions of human beings, “do not forget,” O Israel, “your Creator,” so as to worship the idols that are to be destroyed at the coming of my Son, and so as to wrong yourself by worshiping the works of your hands.

“I blotted out”—for “I will blot out”—“your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist.” If, O Israel, you listen to me and attend to what I command you, then at the coming of my Son I will blot out your iniquities and your sins just as a dark cloud dissolves, or a mist is thinned by the sun’s heat or by a driving wind. “Return to me,” O Israel, and repent, “for I have redeemed you”—for “I will redeem you”—with the precious blood of my Son.

“Praise, O heavens, for the Lord has shown mercy to Jacob; shout for joy, ends of the earth.” By “heavens” we should understand the highest angelic powers dwelling in heaven, and by “ends of the earth,” likewise, the angelic powers who preside over human beings living on earth. Alternatively, by “ends of the earth” the apostles and prophets are to be understood, by whose teaching, miracles, and intercessions the human beings living on earth are sustained, because they are founded upon them. As the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians III). “Resound, mountains, with praise”—that is, you saints who stand upon the summit of virtues—“forest and every tree in it,” that is, all the elect and the righteous. And why is this? “Because the Lord has redeemed” Jacob with the precious blood of his Son; “and Israel will be glorified,” that is, will become great. O Israel, if you return to me with your whole heart and repent, the angels in heaven, those who preside over human beings on earth, the apostles and prophets, and all the elect will rejoice over your salvation, knowing that you have been redeemed by his Son’s blood.

“Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer” [Col. 0941B], O Israel, who is to redeem you, “and your fashioner from the womb,” that is, when you did not yet exist: “I am the Lord, who make all things.” Above, he spoke about the overthrow of idols and the redemption of Israel, if it should repent. Now he speaks about the greatness of his power: that he himself made all things alone, so that no one might doubt Israel’s salvation, provided only that Israel should turn to him. When he says, “stretching out the heavens alone, and establishing the earth, and there was no one with me,” he does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, because they are one and cannot work separately, as the Son himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). But, as we said above, by this statement he wishes to exclude idols from the formation of creation.

“Bringing to nothing”—that is, making empty—“the signs of diviners, and turning soothsayers into madness,” that is, into insanity. Soothsayers are enchanters who always accomplish everything by means of certain incantations. Diviners are the same as Pythons (*pythones*), that is, ventriloquists, who have an evil spirit in their belly and utter many signs and portents. Many people practiced these things before the Lord’s coming; but as the faith of Christians increased, they were partly eradicated. “Turning the wise men” of this age “backward,” that is, into folly, “and making their knowledge foolish,” because he chose what was foolish and made the wisdom of the philosophers foolish.

“Raising up the word of his servant and fulfilling the counsel of his messengers.” Who is this servant of God the Father, if not the one of whom we spoke above: “Behold my servant; I will receive him”? And also: “Is it too little for you to be my servant?” This is the servant who is also the child. This word is the evangelical teaching, which God the Father raised up throughout the whole world through the messengers of his Son, that is, through the apostles. The apostles’ counsel was that, dispersed throughout the four regions of the world, they should preach one Gospel, teach one faith, and proclaim that the almighty God possesses a Trinity in persons and a unity in substance. God the Father fulfilled in deeds this counsel, which they had expressed in words. “I who say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be inhabited,’ and to the cities of Judah, ‘You shall be rebuilt,’ and I will raise up its deserts.” He is speaking about the restoration accomplished through Zerubbabel and the other leaders with Cyrus’s permission; that captivity still awaited its fulfillment. I am God, who did this—or who will complete it. I say to Jerusalem that it will be founded again, and I also say to the cities of Judah, “You shall be rebuilt,” and I will raise up its desolate places.

“I who say to the deep”—that is, to Babylon, which sat in the depths of sins—“‘Be desolate’” of your inhabitants; “and I will dry up your rivers,” the Tigris and the Euphrates. This was accomplished by Darius and his grandson Cyrus. For on the night when Belshazzar was killed by them, their army divided the Euphrates, which flowed through the middle of the city, into many channels far from the city and dried it up, to such an extent that they entered the city through the riverbed along which it had previously flowed and devastated it (Daniel V). The preceding statements may also be referred to the present Church, and these to the present world. “I who say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be inhabited’” by believers from both the Gentile and Jewish peoples; “and to the cities of Judah”—that is, to the churches of those who confess, established throughout the whole world—“‘You shall be rebuilt,’ and I will raise up what was formerly desolate.” “I who say to the deep”—that is, to this world—“‘Be desolate’” of your worshipers and lovers. “And I will dry up your rivers,” that is, I will annihilate the wisdom of this world. The Lord’s wisdom made the wisdom of this world foolish.

“I who say to Cyrus, ‘You are my shepherd’” among my faithful; “and you shall fulfill all my will” by releasing the captivity of my people. “I who say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be built’” by Jesus the great priest, Ezra, and the other leaders returning from captivity, “and” I who say “to the temple, ‘You shall be founded.’” The meaning is the same as in the preceding verse.

## CHAPTER XLV

“Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subject nations before his face”—the Babylonians, Chaldaeans, Egyptians, Medes, and the others surrounding them—“and I will turn the backs of kings” to flee before him. Many kings turned their backs before him, because the Lord granted him assistance.

“Thus,” he says, “says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus.” *Christus* means “anointed.” In ancient times among the Jewish people, just as among the Romans they fashioned a diadem and made someone king, so those anointed with chrism were made kings and priests, as Aaron was by Moses and David by Samuel. Why, then, is Cyrus called “anointed,” although he was not anointed with the oil of blessing? Because imperial dignity served him in place of chrism. “Thus says the Lord to my anointed,” in place of “to his anointed,” or “to his anointed one,” that is, to his king: “and I will open doors before him, and the gates of the city shall not be closed. I will go before you,” O Cyrus, “and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth,” that is, the Babylonians and Chaldaeans, who were considered glorious throughout the world. “I will shatter bronze doors” before you, O Cyrus, “and I will break iron bars.”

“What city,” says blessed Jerome, “did not lie open to him? What king did not submit his back to him? Which walls, previously impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege?” Whoever wishes to know these things more fully should read Xenophon’s history of Cyrus the Great, and will find that what Isaiah foretold long beforehand was fulfilled, the Lord making it known.

“And I will give you,” Cyrus, “the hidden treasures” of kings “and secret hoards” of various cities, “and the concealed stores of secrets,” that is, the things that kings and queens always kept in their private chambers; I will give them to you. And why will I do this? “So that you may know that I am the Lord, who call you by your name, the God of Israel,” long before you were born. Just as long ago I called Isaac and Jacob, and foretold many things about you, as about Isaac and Josiah.

And I did not do this on your account, nor because of your merit, but:

“Because of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel,” so that you might release him from captivity and recognize what I foretold to you before you were born, so that you might strive to bestow benefits upon my servants. “And I called you by your name,” that is, so that you would be called Cyrus; “I likened you” in the name of my Son, “and you did not know me.”

Many wish to refer to the Lord Jesus Christ the things spoken in this passage, but they do not say what is true. Cyrus, whose name means “heir”—for he himself also inherited the kingdom of his maternal uncle Darius, namely, the kingdoms of the Babylonians, Chaldaeans, Medes, and Persians, as well as the Egyptians—and who is also called *Christus* because of the dignity of his empire, is said to be likened to the Lord Jesus Christ only in name, because he received an inheritance from his father, as it is written in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II). He too was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. “I likened you,” he says, “in the name of my Son, and you did not know that I am the true God, who made you victorious over many nations; but you worshiped idols that profited you nothing.”

“I am the Lord, and there is no more”—that is, no other true—“God; besides me there is no God.” He does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit when he says, “Besides me there is no God,” because the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is one God, as the Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” And, “I and the Father are one” (John XIV, X). “I girded you” with power so that you might acquire kingdoms for yourself, “and you did not know me” as you ought to have known me. Therefore I girded you with power and gave you the glory of kingdoms.

“So that those who are from the rising of the sun and those from the west may know through you that besides me there is no God. I am the Lord, and there is no other.” It is read in the book of Ezra that Cyrus wrote to all nations that there was no other God besides the Lord, the God of Israel. Alternatively, it may be understood in this way: through the release of the captives, the mercy of almighty God became more widely known among all peoples. Josephus says in his *History of Antiquities* that the people were released from the bonds of captivity for this reason: he had read in the book of Isaiah what the Lord had foretold about him through Isaiah the prophet.

“Forming light,” that is, the day, “creating darkness,” that is, the night; “making peace and creating evil,” that is, war or affliction: “I am the Lord, making all these things.” Alternatively, we may understand light as the release from captivity, darkness as captivity, and evil as labor, as in the Gospel: “Sufficient,” he says, “is its evil” (Matthew VI), that is, its labor. It is as though he said: I am the Lord who sends you, acting evilly and departing from me, into captivity, and who, when you return to me with a pure heart, brings you back to the homeland of your own land.

“Drip dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the righteous one; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up at the same time.” Earlier the divine word spoke about Cyrus, king of the Persians, who released the captivity, and how this had long beforehand been foretold by the Lord. Now it speaks about the coming of the Lord the Savior and his conception.

O heavens, “drip dew from above,” that is, send forth dew. By “heaven” we should understand the angels who inhabit the heavens, and the plural number is used in place of the singular. By “dew,” angelic words. Blessed Augustine says: Let the archangel Gabriel come and send forth dew for us, that is, let him announce the birth of the Lord the Savior.

“And let the clouds rain down the righteous one.” What should we understand by “clouds” except the prophets, who gave us saving rain by which our hearts are watered, announcing the Lord’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, as well as the blessedness of the elect and the punishment of the reprobate? Concerning them it is also said above, in the fifth and seventh chapters: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon them.” Let us take Isaiah the prophet as one cloud among many and consider what he brought forth for us: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” And also: “Send forth the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.” Behold the saving rain by which our hearts are watered so that we may understand the birth of our Redeemer.

It follows: “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior.” He calls the most blessed virgin Mary “earth,” because she brought forth the Lord the Savior. “Let the earth open,” that is, let the Virgin’s heart open to belief. For when she heard from the angel (Luke I), “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son,” she said, “How shall this happen to me, since I do not know a man?” And the angel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” When she heard this, her heart was opened to belief, and she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

“And let it bring forth the Savior.” Jesus means “Savior.” And why “Savior”? Because he himself will save his people from their sins. It is as though he said, “Let it bring forth the Savior,” meaning Jesus. For the angel said: “His name shall be called Jesus” (Matthew I).

“And let righteousness spring up at the same time.” He himself is righteous, because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. He himself is righteousness, because he justifies those who believe in him. Of him it is also said: “But my righteous one shall live by faith” (Romans I).

“I am the Lord”—understand, the Father—“I created him.” In respect of divinity, God the Father did not create him, because he is consubstantial and coeternal with him. In respect of humanity, however, he created him, because through the operation of the Holy Spirit he assumed a body in the Virgin’s womb, as the angel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

It should be noted that when we say that he was formed in the Virgin’s womb through the operation of the Holy Spirit, we do not separate the power of the Father and the Son from him, as though he formed that body without the Father and the Son. For the Holy Trinity is inseparable and indivisible; therefore the whole Trinity brought this about. Whatever the Father does, the Son does the same, and the Holy Spirit does the same. Yet how this was accomplished is not granted to human weakness to investigate. Hence Isaiah also says: “Who will declare his generation?” (below, LIII). And his forerunner says: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John I), that is, I am unable to unravel the mysteries of both his births.

“Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth.” Samus is a city in which the art of fashioning vessels was first discovered. Thus, “a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth” is as though he said, “a potsherd among the vessels of the earth.” Almighty God is compared with a maker and potter, because by his power he formed the whole universe. Woe to him who contradicts almighty God, his maker, about anything, since he himself was formed by him. It is as though he said: Woe to him who does not believe that Christ would come in the flesh, contradicting the word of almighty God.

“Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and, ‘Your work is without hands’?” Just as that potsherd or clay cannot contradict its maker by saying, “What you are making is without hands,” so the human creature cannot resist its creator.

“Woe to him who says” to God the Father, “What are you begetting?”—understand, a Son equal to you—“and to the woman,” namely, the blessed Mary, “What are you giving birth to,” something that you did not receive from the seed of a man? Concerning this woman the Apostle says: “Christ was made from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians IV).

“Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, its fashioner,” that is, its creator or former. *Plastes* is Greek, and means “former” or “fashioner.” Its fashioner is God the Father, because he fashioned him in the Virgin’s womb.

“Ask me about the things to come,” O Jews, “concerning my sons”—understand, adopted sons—who are going to believe through my Son: how I ought to govern them; “and command me concerning the work of my hands,” that is, instruct me how I should govern the things I have created. These words are to be understood ironically.

“I made the earth, and created the human being upon it. My hands stretched out the heavens,” so that they might be the dwelling place of angels, “and I commanded all their host”—namely, the angels and stars of the heavens—that is, I ordered what they should do. I commanded the angels to praise me, their creator, and to fulfill their ministries. I commanded the sun to illuminate the earth, completing its course in three hundred sixty-five days and four hours and moving toward the west.

If, then, I made the earth so that human beings might inhabit it, and stretched out the heavens above and adorned them with the variety of the stars, so that the worshipers of God might dwell on earth, what wonder is it if I sent my righteous Son and king into the world to acquire many adopted sons for me? And what wonder is it if I raised him from the dead, so that by his death he might free everyone from the bond of death, which is present to all who live so that they may have life?

“I raised him up for righteousness”—understand, so that he might be Savior not only of the Jews but also of the nations—“and I will direct all his ways,” that is, his actions and works, so that he might not commit sin and no deceit be found in his mouth.

“He,” my Son, “will build my city,” that is, my Church, from both the Gentiles and the Jews. “And he will release my captivity”—understand, he will set it free. Some wish to refer this to Cyrus, in whose time the captivity was released and permission was given for the temple to be built. But the preceding statements do not fit, since not all his ways were directed, and to him it was said: “I likened you, and you did not know me.” Nor did he himself build it, although he permitted it to be built, because the building was not completed in his time but in the time of Ahasuerus.

Let us return to the preceding statements, referring them to the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom they must be attributed in their fullest sense. He built the city of the Father, namely the holy Church, against which the gates of hell will not prevail, because it was founded upon the firm rock (Matthew XVI), that is, upon him himself; and because it is set upon a mountain—that is, upon him who is the mountain of mountains—it can never be hidden.

Concerning the foundation of this city the excellent preacher says: “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians III). We must consider what captivity he refers to when he adds, “and he will release my captivity.” When our first parent sinned in paradise (Genesis III), he was taken captive by the devil and, made an exile from his own soil, was placed in the exile of this pilgrimage. All his sons were bound by the chain of captivity until the Son of the Most High came through the mystery of the Incarnation and by his single death destroyed our double death, restoring us to the joys of paradise, from which we had been expelled.

Hence it is also added: “Not for a price,” he says, “nor for gifts”—understand, he did not free and redeem us in order to receive a price from us—but freely and out of abundant mercy.

“Thus says the Lord: ‘The labor of Egypt’”—that is, the worship of idols, which it fulfills more than all the nations—“and ‘the commerce of Ethiopia’”—understand, earthly commerce—“will cease at your coming, most beloved Son; and ‘the Sabaeans, men of stature, will pass over to you,’” believing in you, “and they will be yours” through faith and works.

He calls the worship of idols that the Egyptians offered their gods “labor,” because they labored greatly in offering sacrifices to various monsters, namely birds, sheep, goats, and many other creatures. But when Christ came into the world, and after his ascension the apostles went to Egypt and to the other kingdoms preaching the grace of the Gospel, where previously a multitude of images had been worshiped, the worship of one God began to be revered. Indeed, more than in all the other kingdoms, companies of monks have continued to dwell there, fighting without material weapons against the prince of this world. What the Apostle says was fulfilled there: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V).

Likewise, the Ethiopians, who had previously pursued earthly profits, after being converted to the faith of Christ began to set earthly things aside and to desire heavenly gain with the full affection of their minds.

Sabaim is the same as Saba, a region or city situated at the borders of Ethiopia, from which the queen of Saba also came. They are called “men of stature” because they have always been exceedingly powerful and learned; they too passed over to the faith of the Lord. Concerning them the prophet says: “All those from Saba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (below, LX).

Through these three that we have mentioned, all the kingdoms and regions are understood, from which people are gathered daily into the faith of the Lord. “They will walk after you,” believing rightly and living well. “Bound in their hands they will proceed,” that is, bound by the Lord’s commandments, they will go from virtue to virtue, “and they will worship you,” having now abandoned idolatry, “and they will pray to you” with pure devotion of mind.

“Only in you is God, and there is no true God besides you.” This is the voice of the Father concerning the Son. Thus they will say: “Only in you is God,” that is, in the Son. For he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV). “And there is no God besides you,” as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (ibid., X).

“Truly you are a hidden God.” These words are spoken because of his humanity, since in his humanity the divinity was hidden. “He himself is God, the Savior of Israel,” because he himself saves his people from their sins.

“They were all confounded and ashamed; they went together into confusion”—that is, into destruction—“the makers of them.” He speaks against the scribes and Pharisees, who became makers of errors when they sowed falsehood throughout the world, saying that the Lord had been secretly removed by the apostles (Matthew XXVIII). The scribes and Pharisees were therefore confounded, handed over in their wickedness into the hands of the Romans, and were ashamed—not so that they might repent, but, placed in tribulation, they went together into the destruction of body and soul. They indeed perished.

“But Israel,” that is, the chorus of the apostles and those who believed through the apostles, “was saved with eternal salvation. You shall not be confounded,” O apostles and other believers, “and you shall not be ashamed” when placed in punishment for my name, “unto ages of ages,” that is, neither in this age will you be ashamed to endure torments, secure in your hope of glory, nor in the future, when established in eternal blessedness.

“For thus says the Lord, who created the heavens—he himself is God”—so that they might be the dwelling place of angels—“and formed the earth and made it,” so that worshipers of God might inhabit it, “he himself is its fashioner,” that is, the one who formed the earth. “He did not create it in vain, but so that it might be inhabited,” by human beings who worship and understand their Creator and despise idols; for this reason he formed it.

“I am the Lord, and there is no other God” who does such things. These words are spoken against the worshipers of idols.

“I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth.” Once he spoke in secret on Mount Sinai, when he said to the children of Israel, “You shall have no strange gods,” because he spoke only to one people and remained hidden from the others. But what he says—“I have not spoken in secret”—is to be understood of the evangelical teaching, which resounded to all the ends of the earth through the preaching of the apostles.

“I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, ‘Seek me in vain,’” because he first came to them saying: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew XV), and promised to give them the kingdom of heaven if, abandoning the images of the Law and its ceremonies, they followed the truth of the Gospel.

“I am the Lord, speaking righteousness,” by which everyone who wishes to fulfill it will be justified, “announcing upright things,” so that every creature might worship its Creator. The Lord spoke righteousness when, after the Jews rejected his preaching, he said to the disciples: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel” (Mark XVI).

“Gather yourselves,” O faithful, to my faith, “and come” to me—not in place but in merit, because I am everywhere—“and draw near together” into one fold, “you who have been saved” by my blood “from the nations,” from error and sins. Because the Jews refused to repent and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, he addresses the Gentiles so that they may be gathered into one fold. Therefore, when he says “gather yourselves,” he shows that not all nations would believe immediately, but gradually and in parts.

“They did not know”—understand, the Gentiles—my words, remaining in their own error, weighed down by the burden of their images, “and those who lift up the sign of their sculpture,” that is, those who carve seals for their images, “and pray to a god who cannot save.” Hence the apostles and believers are commanded to proclaim the truth “in season and out of season” and to enter into the council of the nations (2 Timothy IV).

“Announce,” he says, O apostles and believers, to the nations still remaining in error the faith that you have received, “and deliberate together” concerning their salvation. This was fulfilled when, before they were dispersed throughout the whole world, they chose a common council so that they might proclaim unity, without disagreeing among themselves. At that time they also composed the creed concerning the Trinity and unity, the communion of the Church, and the general resurrection.

“Who made this known from the beginning” concerning the salvation of the nations, except me, who spoke to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXIII), and many things like these, which I foretold through the mouths of the prophets?

Or it may be understood in another way: Who made known from the beginning that an idol, which is nothing, should not be worshiped, except me, who said: “You shall have no strange gods, nor shall you make for yourself a carved image” (Exodus XX; Leviticus XIX; Deuteronomy V)? “From that time”—that is, from the time when I brought my people out of Egypt—“I foretold it,” namely, that an idol is nothing.

“Is it not I, the Lord, and is there no God beyond me? There is no just God and Savior besides me.” The Son is in the Father, and in the Son—understand—the Father.

“Turn to me, and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth.” Turn from idolatry to my faith, all nations, and I will save you from destruction in Gehenna. I fulfill what the Father promised the Son, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm II).

He added concerning himself:

“I have sworn”—I, God the Father, understand—that the decision of my mouth and the word that I once uttered concerning the salvation of the nations will by no means be rendered void, but will be fulfilled in deed. We must not think that almighty God swears by some oath; rather, he is said to swear because his speech is utterly firm and immutable.

“A word of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth,” that is, my Son will become incarnate, for he is my Word; or else, the sentence of justification by which the nations are to be justified. “And it shall not return to me”—my Son with the flesh he has assumed—until he redeems the human race. Alternatively, the word and sentence of preaching will not return to me without fruit.

Why?

“Because every knee shall bow to me”—understand, every race of human beings, which previously bowed before idols—and not only the knees of the body, but also the will of the mind.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “At the name of the Lord every knee shall bow” (Philippians II), and so forth. “And every tongue,” he says, “shall swear”—understand, to me. In this passage the faith of the nations is especially demonstrated. The divine word does not say these things because it commands us to swear, but because every word of Christians ought to be firm, as though under oath, so that those who confess themselves to be sons of truth may utter truth from heart and mouth.

“Therefore in the Lord,” said the Christian people, “are my righteousnesses”—the righteousnesses of the Law and the Gospel, as well as baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, not belonging to the Jewish people—“and dominion”—understand, I possess dominion throughout the whole world. “To him,” that is, to Christ, “all nations will come,” believing rightly and living well, “and all who oppose him” by rejecting his words “will be confounded” in their error.

They will indeed be confounded—that is, they will be ashamed of their evils—not so that they may perish, but so that they may repent, as the Apostle says: “What fruit did you have then in the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans VI). Or certainly those who remain in their error will be confounded on the day of judgment when they hear from the Lord: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew XXV).

“In the Lord he will be justified,” in the present age through baptism and repentance, “and every offspring of Israel will be praised,” that is, the whole chorus of the apostles, or those who sprang from their stock and believed in Christ, possessing everlasting righteousness and glory. Concerning this praise and glory the Lord says: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew V). And the Psalmist says: “The righteous will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart will be praised” (Psalm LXIII).

## CHAPTER XLVI

“Bel has been melted down [broken]”—that is, reduced to monetary value. “Naboth has been crushed.” After the calling of the nations, the overthrow of idols is immediately added.

Bel, or Saturn, was originally an idol of the Babylonians. Later other nations also adopted it from them. It was called Bel after Belus, the father of wine. It was held in such great honor and religious reverence among the ancients that they sacrificed to it not only human victims—captives and people of low status—but even their own sons.

Naboth is also an idol, but in this passage it is not placed for an idol, but for the interpretation of its name. For it means “prophecy” or “divination.” It should be noted that when he said, “Bel has been melted down,” he immediately added, “Naboth has been crushed.” He passed from the species to the genus, signifying that after the Lord’s ascension and the preaching of the apostles almost all idols were melted down and reduced to nothing, and that their worship and religious observance, as well as every prophecy of demons and divination of magicians, ceased.

“Their images were made for beasts and cattle”—that is, their gods’ images were made to be worshiped by people living in the manner of beasts and cattle. “For human beings,” as the Psalmist says, “when they were in honor did not understand; they were compared to senseless cattle” (Psalms XLVIII and CXXXIV), and so forth.

“And let those who make them become like them. Your burdens have wasted away under a heavy weight, even to weariness.” “Your burdens,” that is, your images, are of heavy weight; they contain within themselves great masses of metal. Or it may be understood another way: your images are nothing other than burdens for the priests and bearers, weighing them down even to weariness. The images themselves have wasted away—that is, they have failed and been annihilated—after the ascension.

“They could not save the one carrying them” from tribulation, “and their soul”—that is, the soul of those who fashioned, carried, and worshiped them—“will go into captivity” to demons. It must not be thought that mute and senseless images possess a soul; the statement plainly refers to the souls of their worshipers.

“Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel.” He did not say, “Listen to me, my servants and my chosen ones,” with an added expression of honor, but “Listen to me, house of Jacob”—that is, the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, together with Levi, living according to the flesh and having gone far from me—and “all the remnant of the house of Israel,” that is, the remainder of the ten tribes, who likewise have gone away from me through the worship of idols. When the Prophet was saying these things, three tribes were still dwelling in Judea, while ten had already been led away into Assyria; therefore he said, “the remnant of the house of Israel.” But when he adds [Col. 0951A], “who have been carried by me from the womb, who have been borne by me from the uterus,” we must not suppose that almighty God, who is spirit, has a vulva or a womb. Rather, by “vulva” and “womb” we must understand his clemency and mercy, by which we are protected. As far as the literal sense is concerned, that people, like infants and nursing children, was carried from Egypt into the promised land as though by a mother pregnant in her womb and vulva. As far as the higher meaning is concerned, it was carried by God’s mercy through the wilderness, because he endured it in its sinfulness, unwilling immediately to destroy so great a multitude. Likewise, after he had brought it into a land better than all others, and it had often withdrawn from him, provoking him to anger by worshiping idols, he endured it for a long time and bore its iniquity [Col. 0951B], awaiting its repentance—as he also did for forty-two years after his Passion.

“Until your old age”—understand, your old age, not mine—“I am the same,” understand, I am the one who once said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. III). Or else: “Until your old age I myself will protect you, and until your gray hairs”—yours, not mine, that is, until the day of judgment—“I will carry you,” I will sustain you, so that, when the fullness of the nations has entered, you may be saved by believing in me. “I made you, and I will carry you,” that is, I will await you for repentance, “and I will save you” if you are willing to believe in me.

“To whom”—understand, to a manufactured god—“have you likened me?” Now he speaks especially against those who, in the time [Col. 0951C] of Ahaz and Hezekiah, worshiped idols, setting them up in all the corners of the streets, in gardens and groves, and upon houses.

“You who bring gold from the purse,” as in the time of Aaron in the wilderness, “and weigh silver on the scales,” wishing to know how much each person contributes (Exod. XXXII), “hiring”—that is, summoning—“a goldsmith,” that is, a maker of statues, “to make you a god. And they fall down” before it, all who have looked upon it, “and worship it; and they carry it,” the image, priests from place to place, because it cannot move itself, “and it will stand in the place” where it has been set, “and it will not move from its place” by its own power. “But even when they cry out to it,” its priests and worshipers, “it will not hear them. Remember [Col. 0951D] this,” you makers and worshipers of idols, who have committed such great evils, “and be ashamed,” acting in faith and doing penance. The Lord now addresses them and calls them to repentance, not desiring their death but rather wishing them to be saved (Ezek. XVIII). “Return, transgressors, to your heart,” that is, to your mind and to an understanding of justice.

“Remember the former age,” that is, bring back to mind all the good things that I supplied to you through my servants, the prophets and judges, from the day when I brought you out of the squalor of the Egyptians’ prison, “for I am God,” the true God who provided these things for you, “and there is none like me.”

“Announcing from the beginning” of the world “the end” [Col. 0952A], and “from the origin” of creation “the things that have not yet been made”—understand, I announced them. It is as though he were saying in other words: There are manufactured gods, but they cannot announce the future. But I announce the end from the beginning, that is, the coming of my Son, the choice of the apostles, and the calling of the nations. From the beginning he announced the coming of the Son of God and the calling of the nations when he spoke to Abraham: “In your seed”—that is, in Christ—“all the nations shall be blessed.” And through Jacob: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XXIII and XLIX). Likewise through Moses, David, and the other prophets. Why, then, did he say “the end”? “Because when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. II). [Col. 0952B] And John says concerning this final age: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II). And the outstanding preacher says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X). “My counsel”—understand, the counsel that I established—“shall stand,” namely, that through my Son I should redeem the human race, “and all my will shall be done.” The will of God the Father and of the whole Trinity was that the Son of God should assume flesh and, by his death, redeem the human race that was being held captive.

“Calling from the east a bird, and from a distant land a man of my will.” The Hebrews refer this to Cyrus, king of the Persians, or Darius, king of the Medes, comparing them to a bird because they came swiftly from the east and fulfilled the Lord’s will against Babylon. [Col. 0952C] We, however, asserting what is truer, should say that our Lord Jesus Christ was likened by God the Father to a bird, because, just as a bird passes swiftly from place to place, so the Lord’s preaching, beginning from Jerusalem through the apostles, quickly spread far and wide throughout the whole world. Indeed, the earth failed before their tongue did, as the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII), and so forth.

From the east, therefore, God the Father called the bird—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ through the mystery of the Incarnation—because the promised land in which the Lord was born lies in the eastern regions; and he himself is called “the rising man,” as the Prophet says: “Behold, the man whose name is Rising” (Zech. VI). From a distant land he also called the man of his will [Col. 0952D] when, through the mystery of the Assumption, he raised Christ from this land of pilgrimage, which is far from eternal blessedness, to the right hand of his majesty. “I have spoken,” through the prophets, concerning the coming of my Son and the redemption of the human race, “and I will bring it”—understand, my counsel—through the mystery of the Incarnation, namely, my Son, who is the angel of great counsel. “And I created,” that is, I arranged with him and with the Holy Spirit how it should be fulfilled, “and I will do it,” this counsel, according to my will.

“Listen to me, hard of heart, who are far from justice.” To those whom he had earlier addressed without the privilege of an honorific title—“Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel” [Col. 0953A]—and to whom he had said, “Return, transgressors, to your heart,” the divine word now speaks again: “Listen to me,” he says, “hard of heart,” that is, unbelieving, you who have always resisted the prophets and finally my Son, “and who are far from justice,” that is, from Christ, who justifies all who believe in him. Concerning such people the protomartyr Stephen, standing in the arena, said: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did” (Acts VII).

“I have brought my justice near; my salvation shall not be far away.” “I have brought near” stands for “I will bring near.” The Son is the justice of God the Father. Therefore I will bring my justice near—that is, it is near at hand, so that I may send my Son through the mystery of the Incarnation. [Col. 0953B] “It shall not be far away”—understand, because he will be born among you and come for your work; “and my salvation,” that is, my Son, who will save those who hope in him, “shall not delay.” This is the salvation of which the angel says to Mary: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I).

“I will give salvation in Zion,” or, as the Septuagint said, “the Savior.” “And my glory in Israel.” Zion and Israel signify one thing. “I will give,” he says, “salvation in Zion,” or “the Savior,” my Son, concerning whom we have already said that the angel spoke to Mary. And concerning him Simeon says: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II). But when he adds, “and my glory in Israel,” it means the same thing, because the Son is the glory of God the Father [Col. 0953C]: everything he did, he did for the praise and glory of God the Father, saying: “The Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (John XIV). These words may be referred specifically to Jerusalem and the Jews, among whom and from whom he was born. More generally, they may be referred to the universal Church, which is founded on faith in Christ and contemplates heavenly things in the mirror of the mind.

## CHAPTER XLVII

“Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon.” Until now he has spoken concerning the Jews and the coming of the Lord; now he speaks against Babylon and the Chaldeans, under the figure of a captive woman who was once a queen, who killed almost all his people and oppressed the survivors with severe captivity. “Come down,” O Babylon [Col. 0953D], from your pride and from the throne of your power; sit in the dust like a captive.

She is called “daughter of Babylon” because that populace and people were born in Babylon, or also because they were made by God. She is called “virgin” not because of integrity of mind, but because of the barrenness of good works. Therefore it is said to her: “Sit on the ground,” like a servant, or humble yourself. “There is no throne of a kingdom,” that is, there is no longer the dignity and power of reigning. “Daughter of the Chaldeans, for you shall no longer be called soft and delicate,” that is, luxurious and overflowing with pleasures; or else, so that you may be supported from every side by the assistance of various nations, as though by the hands of maidservants.

Queens and noblewomen commonly support themselves on every side by the hands of maidservants, and even servants, so that they scarcely set the soles [Col. 0954A] of their feet upon the ground and their garments do not touch the dust of the earth. Therefore, under the appearance of a queen or noblewoman, the divine word speaks these things to Babylon.

“Take the millstone and grind flour” for your masters, the Medes and Persians. It is a great misery that a woman who was once a queen should grind flour; this is an indication of harsh captivity and extreme servitude. Blessed Jerome says that the task of grinding in this passage may refer to sexual intercourse, so that the sense is: “Take the millstone and grind flour,” that is, offer sexual intercourse to your conquerors, the Medes and Persians, who are exceedingly ardent in intercourse. According to this interpretation, the Hebrews explain what is said about Samson in the Book of Judges (Judg. X): the Philistines made him grind, that is, they compelled him to lie with [Col. 0954B] women of their nation, so that from him they might obtain men of great stature.

“Uncover your shame,” that is, your vulva, so that it may be exposed to the lust of your conqueror. “Uncover your shoulder,” so that you may appear to be a woman. “Bare your legs,” so that you may be prostituted by your plunderers. Or uncover them for this purpose: “that you may cross the rivers,” namely the Tigris, Euphrates, and Chebar, and go into captivity. Women customarily bare their legs when crossing rivers, so that their garments will not be touched by the water.

“Your disgrace shall be uncovered,” understand, before your enemies, “and your shame shall be seen” [Col. 0954C], that is, your misery and the evil of captivity. “I will take vengeance”—understand, on you; that is, I will avenge my people—“and no human being shall resist me,” understand, neither the angel who presides over you nor a prophet, should he ask me for your liberation, as Moses once did in the wilderness when I wished to destroy his people (Exod. XXXVII). And why will this happen to you? Because, although I commanded you to strike and afflict my people, I did not command you to destroy them utterly and kill them to the last person.

“The Lord our Redeemer of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel.” This is the voice of the people returning from captivity after seventy years. “Our Redeemer,” they say, “is the Lord of hosts,” that is, the God of angels and human beings, who redeemed us from the [Col. 0954D] most severe captivity. “The Holy One of Israel is his name.” He alone is properly holy who says: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. XI, XX). He himself also sanctifies those who hope in him.

“Sit, be silent, and enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans.” He returns again to Babylon and transfers the figure from a city to women, and from a queen who once existed to one who has become a servant. The sense is: Sit—that is, humble yourself. Be silent; consider your calamity, as sorrowful people commonly behave. Enter into darkness, lest anyone see your shame. She is called “daughter of the Chaldeans” because the Chaldeans built that same city. And why this? “Because you shall no longer be called mistress of kingdoms”—understand [Col. 0955A], of the Egyptians, Assyrians, and many others over whom you formerly ruled.

“I was angry with my people, I defiled my inheritance, and I gave them into your hand.” He now gives the reason why he was angry against the Chaldeans, lest someone should say that he struck them without cause, or lest the Chaldeans fail to recognize that they had conquered them with the Lord’s permission. “I was once angry,” he says, “with my people; therefore I handed it over to your power. I defiled my inheritance,” that is, I permitted it to be defiled by you, so that for a time the dignity of the priesthood and the rites of the ceremonies might be taken away from it. “And I gave them into your hand,” that is, into your power, not so that you might kill them utterly, but so that you might chastise them.

“You showed them no mercies,” that is [Col. 0955B], you pitied no one, neither old man nor child, whose age is venerable even among enemies. “Against the holy seed you made your hand heavy.” This is the same as what we have said: she spared no one.

“You said, ‘I shall be mistress forever,’” that is, “I shall reign always.” “You did not set these things upon your heart,” that is, you did not foresee or consider the calamity of your present misery, “nor did you remember your end”—understand, your danger or misfortune; that is, you did not think that you could ever be humbled. Many who are placed in temporal prosperity and honor never believe that they will fall, but are lifted daily into pride.

“And now hear these things [Col. 0955C], luxurious woman,” that is, enriched and overflowing with pleasures, “who dwell confidently”—understand, fearing no enemy. “I am,” understand, mistress of the whole world and queen, “and there is no one besides me”—understand, no one who reigns. “I shall not sit as a widow,” that is, I shall always have a king, “and I shall not know barrenness,” understand, because there will always be someone reigning from me. So she spoke. The husband of this woman was Nebuchadnezzar, together with his sons.

“These two things shall come upon you suddenly,” O Babylon, “in one day,” that is, at one time, when Cyrus and Darius come: “barrenness and widowhood.” Barrenness, so that you may lose the peoples subject to you; widowhood, so that you may lose your king. These things came upon her suddenly and unexpectedly, because she could in no way imagine that the Persians and Medes, who [Col. 0955D] were subject to her and were of no strength in comparison with her, could overcome her.

“All these things,” understand, the evils foretold by me and by the prophets, “shall come upon you,” O Babylon, “because of the multitude of your sorceries,” that is, the enchantments of your magicians, whose counsel you used. By the phrase “your sorceries” we may understand that she had sorcerers and magicians who seemed to predict the future for her. Magicians are those who strip the bodies of the dead and dwell in tombs, and who also make use of human blood. But when he adds, “and because of the hardness of your enchanters,” understand, in whom you placed your trust, it should be understood that those magicians and enchanters attributed [Col. 0956A] hardness to her, so that she spared no one, saying that she would reign forever.

“And you trusted,” understand, in reigning, “in your wickedness,” that is, in the enchantments of your magicians, “and you said, ‘There is no one who sees me,’” that is, no one who can restrain me from my evil. “Your wisdom,” that is, your diviners, magicians, and haruspices, “and your knowledge,” that is, divination and observation of the stars, “have deceived you. And you said, ‘I am,’” understand, mistress throughout the whole world, “and besides me there is no other,” understand, no other queen.

“Evil shall come upon you,” understand, the captivity and misery that you have prepared for all the nations until now, “and you shall not know its rising,” that is, its beginning. Suddenly Cyrus and Darius, with the Medes and Persians, besieged the city; and, unexpectedly killing the king [Col. 0956B], they devastated everything that was in it. Their magicians and sorcerers could not foresee that she would be humbled by a people whom she despised and held subject to herself.

“Calamity of devastation and captivity shall rush upon you; you will not be able to expiate it,” that is, to prevent it from coming upon you. “Misery shall suddenly come upon you,” the misery of slaughter, “which you shall not know”—understand, beforehand.

“Stand now with your enchanters,” against Darius and Cyrus and their peoples, if perhaps you can resist them, “and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have labored from your youth,” that is, from the beginning of your empire. He speaks ironically. From the beginning when Babylon began to hold imperial power, it always [Col. 0956C] had magicians and diviners in whom it labored, because it did everything with their counsel, as the Book of Daniel demonstrates, which reveals that the king of Babylon did everything according to their advice.

“You have failed amid the multitude of your counsels,” understand, by which you overcame many nations. “Let them stand and save you now, the observers of the heavens,” that is, astrologers, who in common speech are called *mathematici*. “Those who contemplated the stars” and supposed that human affairs were governed and ruled according to the course and decline of the stars, “and reckoned the months,” saying, “This will happen in this month or that month, or in this year,” “so that from them they might announce future things to you.”

“Behold, those magicians have become like stubble; the fire” of the city or of tribulation “has burned them with you. Your sorcerers shall not deliver their own souls [Col. 0956D],” that is, their lives, “from the hand of the flame,” whether of the city or of devastation. “They are not coals” for them “by which they may warm themselves,” that is, they do not possess the true and divine wisdom that they imagine themselves to have, by which they could escape the danger of calamity through their counsels. “Nor is there a hearth for them at which they may sit,” that is, by which they might dispel the darkness; rather, they are to be burned.

“Thus have they become for you, in all the things in which you have labored.” It is as though he were saying: Just as you lack the illumination of true wisdom, so all good things will pass away from you. “Your merchants,” that is, your magicians and sorcerers, who acquired much by their art, “and those who from your youth,” that is, from the beginning of your empire, “led you astray—each of them has wandered in his own way. [Col. 0957A] There is no one among them who can save you” when tribulation comes.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“Listen to this, house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel and have come forth from the waters of Judah.” We have often said above that whenever Jacob or Israel is mentioned without a designation of dignity—for example, when one does not say “Jacob, my servant,” or “Israel, my chosen one”—it should be understood of carnal Israel and Jacob. In this passage the Prophet speaks to those who were falsely called Israelites and Jacobites: they were not supplanters of vices, nor men who saw God, but carnal people embracing earthly things.

“Listen,” he says, “house of Jacob,” that is, the two tribes together with Levi, to what I am about to say, “who are called by the name of Israel,” that is, who are falsely called Israel, “and have come forth from the waters of Judah,” that is, have proceeded from his seed. When he says, “you have come forth from the waters of Judah,” he does not say this to confer honor upon them, but to show that they are in no way children by the virtue of the patriarchs, but only according to the flesh. Therefore he mentions Judah, because the ten tribes had already been led into captivity, and only the tribe of Judah, remaining in the promised land together with Benjamin and Levi, preserved the royal seed of David.

“Who swear by the name of the Lord”—understand, not to honor that name, but to establish and strengthen a true lie. The Lord commanded them not to swear by the name of foreign gods, but by his name, wishing to separate them from idolatry. Yet, while worshiping false idols, they swore by his name, saying, “The Lord lives”—not for the sake of honor, but so that the error of their lie might be made more secure. But when he adds, “and remember the God of Israel, not in truth nor in justice,” he says this because they said with their lips that they worshiped the God of their fathers, while in heart and deed they were far from him, just as he says elsewhere: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV; Mark VII).

“For they were called from the holy city,” understand, so that they might be called Jerusalemites from Jerusalem, “and they were established”—that is, founded—“upon the God of Israel.” Here the Prophet speaks ironically. For they boasted and gloried in the nobility of their ancestry and the greatness of their city, saying: We are the sons of the prophets and patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, the friends of God, and inhabitants of the city of God. We are called Jerusalemites from the holy city, and we are founded upon the God of Israel (John VIII). “The Lord of hosts is his name,” understand, the name of him whose servants we are.

“I announced the former things,” that is, ancient things, “to you from that time,” understand, from the time when I began to speak against Babylon, saying, “The burden of Babylon.” “And they went out from my mouth, and I made them heard by you.” From my mouth, says the divine word, went forth the things that I foretold—that is, from the mouth of the prophets, who are called the mouth of the Lord, just as they themselves say: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I).

What were the former things that he announced beforehand? The miracles that he performed in their midst from the day when they came out of [Col. 0958A] Egypt, and the captivity by Nebuchadnezzar that was impending. Now, before they are led away, he foretells their liberation and return, and the devastation of the Chaldeans, and adds: “Suddenly,” understand, the things that I now foretell, “I acted,” standing for “I will act,” “and they came,” standing for “they will come”—namely, the overthrow of the Chaldeans and your return.

“For I know that you are hard,” that is, unbelieving, “and your neck is an iron sinew,” that is, your pride is inflexible, “and your forehead is bronze,” understand, because you were unwilling to feel shame.

The divine word speaks these things to those who had come forth from the waters of Judah and were still dwelling in Judea, namely, Judah and Benjamin. That they were always [Col. 0958B] stiff-necked is attested by the protomartyr Stephen: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you always resisted the Holy Spirit.” And concerning their shamelessness the Lord speaks to them through Jeremiah: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you were unwilling to feel shame” (Jer. III; Ezek. III).

“I foretold to you” the things that are destined to happen to you and to Babylon, “from that time”—understand, from the time when I began to speak through my prophets concerning Babylon—“lest perhaps you should say, ‘My idols have done these things,’” understand, so that Cyrus and Darius might come and avenge me upon the Babylonians.

“What you heard” at that time through the prophets—O people of the two tribes—“see all things,” understand, as already fulfilled, standing for “you will see.” “But you did not announce,” understand, to your children, the things that were to come upon Babylon. “I made new things heard by you,” [Col. 0958C] namely, the things already mentioned concerning Babylon’s devastation, “from that time,” from the time when I began to speak against it, “and things that you do not now know have been preserved.”

This verse should be divided at this point. It is as though he were saying: I have done many things for you that I could recount, but because you do not remember them, I too shall omit them for now, announcing to you the things that are to come.

“The things that are to happen to you were created with me, and not from that time”—understand, you heard or knew them—when they were established with me. “And before the day”—understand, of your devastation—I have determined them, “and you did not hear them” from your gods.

And why did you not hear them? “Lest perhaps you should say, ‘Behold, I knew them,’” understand, from my gods. “Nor from that time”—understand again, from the time when they were predestined [Col. 0958D] with me—“was your ear opened,” so that you might hear or understand them. “For I know that, transgressing, you will transgress,” understand, at the coming of my Son: you will transgress the law given through Moses and the law of the Gospel that you are to hear from my Son, by not believing in him. “And from the womb”—or, “from the uterus”—“I called you a transgressor,” that is, from the day when I gave you the law, when you worshiped the idol, forgetting what you had previously promised when you said: “Everything that the Lord has spoken to us, we shall hear and do” (Exod. XXIV). Or else, from before you entered the promised land.

Just as a woman who carries a child in her womb, after giving birth, nourishes and cherishes it, so almighty God, carrying them through the wilderness of desolation by his mercy [Col. 0959A], after they entered a land better than all others, nourished them through judges, priests, prophets, and kings, until they transgressed by withdrawing from him.

“For the sake of my name,” that is, so that my glory might not be annulled, “I will put my wrath far away,” understand, by bringing you back from captivity; “for the sake of my praise,” that is, on account of my praise, so that I may be praised, “I will restrain you” with my law, “so that you may not perish.”

We may also refer this to the time of their departure from Egypt, so that he speaks of the past as though it were future. “For the sake of my name,” he says, “so that it might not be violated, I will put my wrath far away,” standing for “I did so,” when you worshiped the calf, so that I might not destroy you; and “for the sake of my praise,” that is, on account of my praise, “I will restrain you,” standing for “I restrained you,” by giving you the law so that you might not perish.

[Col. 0959B] “Behold, I have refined you,” that is, I have tested you with various scourges, “but not as silver”—understand, I have tested you, because you have not been purified—“and I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty,” that is, in the tribulation of poverty and want, handing your riches over to your enemies. Or else, in Egypt, where you were as though in a very poor furnace.

From this it is understood that almighty God tests human beings sometimes through riches and sometimes through poverty. For example, those who abound in riches, if they use them badly, he makes descend into poverty; but those who use them properly, he makes abound still more. Likewise, those who patiently endure poverty, he gives riches; whereas those who murmur, he brings into greater want. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not give me riches or poverty” (Prov. XXX).

“For my own sake I will act,” that is, for the sake of my mercy I will free you from captivity, [Col. 0959C] “so that I may not be blasphemed,” that is, lest those who keep you in captivity forever say that their gods have kept you and that I was unable to free you (Isa. XLI and XLIV). “And my glory,” that is, my praise, “I will not give to another,” to another of the gods, so that he may be God, even if he is called so by human beings, except for my Son and the Holy Spirit, who are consubstantial and coequal with me.

“Listen [Another copy adds: to me], Jacob,” to what I am about to say, “and [Col. 0959D] Israel, whom I call” to repentance and salvation. God the Father does not say, “Listen to me, Jacob, my servant, and Israel, my chosen one,” so that it might be understood as spoken of spiritual Jacob or Israel; rather, he says, “Listen, Jacob and Israel,” who are carnal. “I am the same, the first,” before whom there was no one, “and I am the last,” after whom there is no one. The same is found in the Apocalypse of John: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.”

“My hand also”—that is, my Word, my Son, and my Wisdom—“founded the earth” upon the subtle element, “and my right hand measured out”—that is, extended—“the heavens.” The hand of God the Father and his right hand are the Son, because through him he made all things (John I), just as the Psalmist says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Pss. CIII and XXXII). And: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” And: “God founded the earth in wisdom, and his right hand measured out the heavens.”

“I will call them”—understand, the heavens—“and they shall stand together” in my sight. “Gather together [Col. 0960A], all of you”—whether the heavens, or all creatures, or the whole multitude of the children of Israel—“and hear” what I am about to say. “Who among them”—understand, among the heavens or creatures—“announced these things,” concerning Cyrus, that he would destroy Babylon, or concerning my Son, that he would be born of a virgin?

The following words properly concern Christ, though they may also be referred to Cyrus and Darius, as blessed Jerome says, up to the place where it says, “His way has been made straight.”

“The Lord loved him”—understand, Cyrus, or Darius, his uncle—“so that he might release the captivity of his people, and he will do his will in Babylon,” because he will capture it, “and his arm among the Chaldeans,” because he will kill them (Isa. XLV).

“I, I have spoken” concerning Cyrus through my prophets [Col. 0960B], “and I have called him” by his proper name before he was born, speaking through Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus.” He brought him from the east against Babylon, so that he might devastate it and repay it according to what it deserved.
