But when the divine word adds, “and his way has been made straight,” it is in no way clear how this can refer to Cyrus, a worshiper of idols, as having had his way made straight.

Let us also refer it to the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father loved his Son as one who is unique and consubstantial with him, because he himself said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III; Luke III). “He will do his will in Babylon,” that is, in the confusion of this world, because he will redeem the human race, which was dwelling in the confusion of sins. In everything that the Lord Jesus did [Col. 0960C], he fulfilled the will of God the Father, as he himself said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

“And his arm,” that is, he extended his strength and power, “among the Chaldeans,” that is, among the demons, because he took power away from them. For he himself said: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII). “I, I have spoken” concerning my Son through Moses and the other prophets, “and I have called him” by his proper name before he was born of a virgin, speaking through the archangel Gabriel to Mary: “Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.” “I brought him,” that is, I determined that he should become incarnate; “and his way has been made straight,” because “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Luke I).

“Draw near to me,” nations, “and hear this.” This is the voice [Col. 0960D] of the Son of God. “I have not spoken from the beginning in secret”—understand, to Moses, speaking with him on Mount Sinai through an angel, because many heard my words. “From the time before these things came to be, I was there.” Understand, in the Father. The Son of God spoke with Moses together with the Father; with the Father he made and arranged all things, just as he speaks through Wisdom: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything in the beginning,” and so forth, up to the words about arranging all things with him. And again: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him, and it is before the age” (Prov. VIII).

“And now the Lord the Father has sent me,” that is, he has determined that I should become incarnate, “and his Spirit.” In this brief verse the mystery of the Trinity [Col. 0961A] is shown to us. The man assumed by the power of the Word says that God the Father and his Spirit sent him, that is, determined that he should become incarnate.

“Thus says the Lord God, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.” At this point he addresses the chorus of the apostles. He is called its Redeemer because he redeemed it at a price, namely, by his blood. “I am the Lord your God, teaching you what is useful,” that is, what pertains to salvation, through the Gospel, “guiding you on the way in which you shall walk,” that is, in the present age, or in the ministry of preaching. Thus he promised you, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII), and when he said: “Go, teach all nations.”

“If only you had attended to my commandments! Your peace would have become [Col. 0961B] like a river,” that is, you would have had profound security. We may refer this in part to Israel: O Israel, if you had attended to my commandments and fulfilled them in deed, your security and peace would have become profound. Through all the things that follow, the abundance and fullness of every good thing that this people would have possessed, had it not become transgressive, are shown.

But if we refer it to the chorus of the apostles, the sense will be: O chorus of the apostles, if only you would attend to my commandments! If you do what I have commanded, your peace will be like a river that always flows and is never diminished; that is, your security and peace will always remain in eternal blessedness. “And your justice shall be like the waves of the sea,” rising and falling, and advancing from virtue to virtue.

“And your seed shall be,” that is, [Col. 0961C] all believers through your preaching, whether Gentiles or Jews, “like the sand”—understand, which cannot be counted because of its multitude. “And the offspring of your womb,” that is, the children of your teaching, “shall be like the pebbles of the sand.” The seed and offspring of the apostles are all believers, as the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor,” and: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (Gal. IV; 1 Cor. IV).

“Your seed would not have perished,” understand, O Israel, if you had attended to my commandments, “and its name would not have been worn away”—understand, the name Israel—“from my face,” so that they might always be called men who see God in their minds. But now, because you have transgressed, your name has been worn away, except among the apostles, in whom you preserved the seed and name of the patriarchs. As Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord had left [Col. 0961D] us a seed, we would have become like Sodom” (Isa. I).

Although they are called Israelites, their name has nevertheless been worn away from my face, because they do not deserve to see God. And if this is referred to the apostles, the sense will be: O chorus of the apostles, if you attend to my commands, your seed will not perish, and the name of your sonship will not be worn away from my face, so that, from Christ, you may be called Christians.

“Go out from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans; proclaim it with a voice of rejoicing.” This address may be understood in two ways: either of the Jews who were in Babylon, from the two tribes, or also of those who believe through the apostles. For Babylon signifies this world. The divine word therefore addresses the Jews—or the apostles, or believers—and says: “Go out,” O Jews, from Babylon, with Cyrus granting permission; or, you believers, go out from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of this world. If you cannot do so bodily, then at least do so in mind and contemplation. “Flee,” you, from the Chaldeans into the promised land. Or you, apostles, withdraw far from the company of demons and wicked men. “With a voice of rejoicing and gladness proclaim”—understand: you Jews, your freedom to the other nations; and you apostles, the redemption of your souls. “Make this heard,” O Jews, because you are fleeing from Babylon, and O apostles, because the Lord has redeemed you. “Carry it as far as the ends of the earth,” that is, preach throughout the whole world, so that succeeding generations may themselves proclaim it. “Say,” O Jews or apostles, to those who are ignorant: “The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob” from Babylon—or all the nations that overthrow vices, from the confusion of sins.

“They did not thirst in the desert”—understand: when they went out from Babylon under Zerubbabel and the other leaders. For when they went out from Egypt, they not only thirsted but also murmured. But what follows—“when he led them out, he brought water forth for them from the rock”—we read as having been fulfilled by no means after they had received the promised land, unless one asserts that it was fulfilled hyperbolically, in imitation of their former happiness, when they passed through the desert of the covenant into Judaea and were freed from captivity; or unless it is referred to their departure from Egypt and understood as saying that they did not thirst in the desert so as to perish. If, however, we refer it to the apostles, they did not thirst in the desert of this life, because when he led them out of Babylon, that is, from the confusion of sin, he brought forth water for them from the rock through their faith—that is, he filled them with the grace of the Holy Spirit, which proceeded from Christ. “And he split the rock, and waters flowed forth”: that is, he promised that Christ’s side would be opened, from which the waters of our cleansing and redemption came forth. We read in the Lord’s Passion that, after he had given up his spirit, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately there came out the blood of our redemption and the water of baptism (John 19).

“There is no peace for the wicked,” that is, for the Jews, “says the Lord.” Although I have granted them so many benefits, they have no peace with me—that is, they do not believe in me. Or alternatively: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord,” namely, for unbelievers who know that the Son of God endured so much for their salvation, yet do not wish to believe in him or to possess him who is our peace and who made both one. Whoever therefore believes rightly lives well: he has peace within himself, that is, Christ.

## CHAPTER XLIX

“Hear, islands, and pay attention, peoples from afar.” After the calling of the remnant of Israel and the rejection of the people who remain in unbelief—of whom he had said, “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord”—the divine word turns to the Churches gathered from the nations and addresses them under the name of islands, speaking in the person of the Son of God. An island is so called because it is situated in the salt water, that is, in the sea. The Church is compared to an island because, just as an island is struck by waves and is not moved, so the Church, founded upon Christ, is struck on every side by the disturbances and raging waves of this age, yet is not moved. For it has been founded upon a rock.

“Hear,” he says, “islands”—that is, understand, Churches of various nations, what I am about to say—“and pay attention, peoples from afar,” that is, from the remotest ends of the earth. “The Lord called me from the womb”—understand: through the archangel Gabriel, when he said to Joseph, “Do not be afraid, Joseph, son of David, to take Mary your wife. For she will bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus” (Matthew 1). “From my mother’s womb,” that is, before I was born, “he remembered my name,” by which I would bear the name of Savior.

“He made my mouth”—that is, the words of my mouth—“like a sharp sword.” The Lord’s mouth is called in this passage the teaching of the Gospel and his word. The Lord himself speaks of this sword: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10). And to the apostles: “With the breath of his mouth,” he says, “he will kill the wicked” (2 Thessalonians 2). And also: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). “In the shadow of his hand he protected me,” that is, in the protection of his divinity, so that I might remain without sin and perform miracles, lest the flesh assumed by the Word be brought low. Therefore he says “in the shadow,” because the divinity itself is invisible.

“And he made me like a chosen arrow.” When he says “chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not all of them are chosen. The arrows of almighty God are the prophets, the apostles, and apostolic men who run throughout the whole world, concerning whom it is said: “Your arrows are sharp; the most powerful peoples will fall beneath you” (Psalm 44).

“He hid me in his quiver,” that is, in a human body. He is now speaking in the person of the divinity. A quiver is so called because it bears death. Elsewhere the Lord is compared to a hook: just as a fish is caught by a hook hidden in bait, so the devil was caught by the divinity hidden in humanity. Hence the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will you catch Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40).

“And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel, because I will be glorified in you.” He himself, the Son of God, is called a servant because in all things he obeyed the will of God the Father. He is called Israel because he took the origin of his flesh from Israel. And he is blessed in the words, “I will be glorified in you,” because everything that the Son himself accomplished, he did for the praise of the Father, saying: “The Father who dwells in me performs the works” (John 14).

“And I said”—understand: to the Father—“I have labored in vain; for nothing and in futility I have consumed my strength.” As though he were saying in other words: When the Father said to me the things I have related, I answered him: “How have I glorified you, Father? I have labored in vain, and I have been unable to bring the greater part of the Jews back to you.” These words are spoken to demonstrate the freedom of the human will. It is God’s part to call, and ours to believe. Thus, insofar as those Jews who remained unbelieving are concerned, he labored in vain by enduring the Passion, and consumed his strength uselessly—that is, he was wearied and suffered for them in vain, because it benefited nothing in those who refused to believe.

“Therefore my judgment”—that is, my discernment—“is with the Lord,” the Father, because he will judge whether I have done for them everything I ought to have done, saying in the Gospel: “I have performed many good works for you” (John 10). “And my work is with my God,” that is, his presence.

“And now the Lord says, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, that I might bring back to him”—understand: “Jacob”—therefore I am a servant. “And Israel will not be gathered,” that is, will not be converted to faith, although I came for this reason. From this it is understood that, when he says “forming me from the womb as a servant for himself,” he called the one who was formed a servant both above and in this passage. The Son of God came in order to bring wandering Jacob back to his Creator, as he says to the apostles: “Go to the house of Israel. I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 15).

“And I was glorified in the eyes of the Lord”—understand: because he gave the whole world to me, as I said when rising from the dead: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28). As though he were saying: “I have lost one nation, and behold, the whole world will believe in me.”

“My God became my strength,” because I rose on the third day. Although, hanging on the cross, he said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 28), speaking in the feeling of his humanity, nevertheless he did not forsake him.

“And he said to me”—God the Father—“It is too little”—understand: for you—“that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the dregs of Israel.” They are called “dregs” on account of their misery and contempt. The meaning is: It is too little for you to endure death for Israel alone; rather, do so for all the nations. The Son himself also prayed something of this kind: “Father,” he said, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26)—namely, if it is possible for the salvation of the nations to occur without the destruction of the Jews, let this cup of suffering pass from me.

“I have given you as a light to the nations,” that is, so that you may enlighten all the nations that come to my faith. “And that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth,” that is, so that through the apostles you may announce the salvation by which the peoples are to be saved. The Son is called the salvation of God the Father because through him he decreed to save the human race.

“Thus says the Lord, the redeemer of Israel,” that is, of the faithful and of those who believe in him. “His Holy One,” that is, of the people of Israel, “to the contemptible soul, to the abominated nation, to the servant of rulers.” The prophet’s voice addresses the Son in the person of the Father. The Son of God is called the redeemer of Israel—that is, of those who see God—because he himself redeemed us by the shedding of his blood.

“To the contemptible soul” means to Christ, who was despised and rejected by the Jews when they cried, “Crucify him” (John 19), and many other things of this sort. He calls Christ and his Nazarenes an “abominated nation,” because among the Jews they are so abominable, detestable, and rejected that every day in their synagogues they are cursed three times, with the claim that on their account they have lost their kingdom, their place, and their nation.

He calls the Lord Jesus Christ “the servant of rulers,” because, like a servant, he did not disdain to stand before Pilate, Annas, and Caiaphas and to be judged by them as a robber and criminal, although he was the only-begotten Son of God the Father.

“Kings will see” him coming to judgment in great glory and majesty; “and princes will rise”—understand: the rulers of the Churches will rise from their thrones to honor you—“and they will worship” you “because of the Lord” the Father, “because he is faithful,” namely, because he fulfilled in deed what he promised you concerning your glorification and the salvation of the nations. “And because of the Holy One of Israel who chose you.” This is the prophet’s voice addressing the Son of God.

By “kings” and “princes” he means the apostles and apostolic men, and all the rulers and teachers of the holy Church, who on the day of judgment will judge the world with the Lord in righteousness, as he himself said: “Amen, I say to you, you also will sit judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22).

“Thus says the Lord”—understand: God the Father to the Son—“In an acceptable time,” that is, on the day of the Passion and Resurrection, “I heard you,” by raising you from the dead; “on the day of salvation,” that is, when you endured the Passion for the salvation of the human race, “I helped you.” He calls the time of his Passion and Resurrection the acceptable time because it pleased him to redeem the human race through him. God the Father heard him when he prayed, saying, “Glorify me, God the Father, with yourself.” And he answered him: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John 12).

The acceptable time means the time of his Passion and Resurrection. Or the acceptable time may also be understood as extending from the beginning of his preaching to the final day of judgment. The Apostle speaks of this time: “Behold,” he says, “now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6).

“And I preserved you” from death to life, “and gave you as a covenant of the people,” namely, to those among them who wished to believe, in friendship with the apostles, to whom he himself said: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15). Why, then, did I raise you up? “That you might raise up the earth,” that is, the inhabitants of the earth from unbelief to faith and from the error of idolatry to the true worship of God; “and possess as an inheritance lands laid waste,” which had no inhabitant of God—that is, the multitude of nations predestined to life. Concerning this inheritance the Father says in the psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2).

“That you might say to those who are bound, ‘Come out’”—from the bonds of sins, concerning which Solomon says: “Each person is bound by the bonds of his sins.” “And to those who dwell in darkness”—understand that you should say—“Be revealed,” that is, be enlightened. To those who were in darkness—that is, in unbelief—and who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death and could not see the light (Luke 1), that is, Christ, who is the true light that enlightens all that enlightens (John 1), the Son of God himself said that they should be enlightened when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4).

“Upon the roads,” that is, in the teaching of the apostles and prophets, “they will pasture,” those who have come out of the darkness of unbelief, saying: “The Lord shepherds me, and I will lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Psalm 22). “And on all the level places”—understand: the paths of the Scriptures, explained and clarified by the holy teachers—“will be their pasture.”

“They will not hunger” for the words of God, “nor will they thirst,” being established in those teachings. Concerning this hunger and thirst the Lord speaks through the prophets: “I will send a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8). “Holy Scripture is food in some passages and drink in others. For wherever it is taken with difficulty, it is food; but wherever it is easily understood, it is drink.” “They will not hunger,” he says, “nor thirst,” the faithful established in the holy Church; that is, obscure and clear things will be opened to them.

“The heat and the sun will not strike them,” that is, the adversities of this age will not harm them, “because their merciful one,” Christ, “will guide them,” those whom he redeemed with his most precious blood, “and will give them drink at springs of water,” the teaching of the Old and New Testaments, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “You will draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior” (Isaiah 12), or the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“And I will make all my mountains into a road,” that is, before the face of my apostles and preachers I will turn all the impediments of this age into tranquility. “And my paths will be raised up,” that is, those who imitate my humility, according to the saying: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14; 18).

The mountains are called the apostles and apostolic men, either because they are founded in Christ, who is the mountain of mountains, or because they are set before the world as an example. The paths are called all believers who humble themselves for Christ’s name. Who these are for whom the way is prepared, he shows more clearly when he says:

“Behold, these believers will come from afar,” that is, from the east to faith and the unity of the holy Church—not by location but by faith. “And behold, other faithful will come” “from the north and the sea,” that is, from the west, “and these from the southern land.” Here is shown the multitude of believers joined together in the unity of faith from the four regions of the world, concerning whom the Lord also says: “Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8).

This should not be understood as their being gathered into one place, but into one faith. Although they are separated bodily, those whom Christ’s inviolable charity binds cannot be separated in mind.

“Praise, heavens,” that is, angels who dwell in heaven, “and exult, earth,” whether the angelic powers set over the earth or the righteous human beings who inhabit it: rejoice over the salvation of the human race. “Shout for joy, mountains, praise”—namely, angels and righteous men established on the heights of virtue—“because the Lord has consoled his people,” those who believe in him, through the coming of his Son: namely, the apostles and the other believers from the Jews, and all those coming to his faith from the four regions of the world. Concerning them he had already said above: “And he will have mercy on his poor”; and of them it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for they will be consoled.”

In this passage the poor may be understood as the gentile people, who did not possess the riches of the Law and the prophets but, abandoned and forsaken by God their creator, were subject to demons through the worship of idols and the slavery of lust.

“And Zion said: ‘The Lord has abandoned me,’” that is, annihilated or annulled me, “and has forgotten me.” Jerusalem and Zion are understood in four ways in the holy Scriptures.

First, the earthly Jerusalem among the Jews is intended—the city that we read the Lord lamented and to which he speaks in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets” (Matthew 23), and so forth.

Second, the congregation of the saints, which consists in the Lord’s peace and the contemplation of virtues, while still situated on earth, will be called Jerusalem and Zion. Of it it is said: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Psalm 86).

Third, Jerusalem or Zion is called the multitude of the holy angels and dominions and the other powers, together with the elect human beings already reigning with Christ. Of this the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4).

Fourth, Jerusalem is the city which the Jews and those among us who Judaize say will descend from heaven adorned, according to John’s Apocalypse (chapter 21).

It must therefore be asked which of all these is meant by the words, “The Lord has abandoned me.” This should be understood: Jerusalem—that is, the congregation of the saints—which had formerly been among the Jews is being recalled here; placed in the captivity of Babylon, it says that it has been abandoned by God. But what does the Lord say to her in the affectionate manner of one who comforts? Let us listen.

“Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the child of her womb?” Certainly not. The meaning is: Just as she cannot forget her infant and fail to have mercy on it, so I will not forget you, but will have mercy.

He says something more: “And even if she”—understand: if she should prove so cruel and hard that she “forgot” to have mercy on the child of her womb—“yet I will not forget you,” says the Lord Almighty.

“Behold, in my hands,” that is, in my presence, “I have inscribed you,” or “painted you,” so that I may always remember you. “Your walls are continually before my eyes.” Who are these walls of which he speaks? The patriarchs, prophets, and righteous men born from that people, who continually intercede for it, and by whose prayers it has long been surrounded, just as a city is surrounded by a material wall. Your walls—that is, the prophets and patriarchs—are in my presence, praying continually for you; therefore I will have mercy on you.

“Your builders have come”—understand: the apostles and preachers, the builders of the primitive Church. He speaks of the future as though it were past, as though they had already come. The apostles rebuilt Jerusalem—that is, the congregation of the faithful—which had been destroyed by unbelief, at least among those of them who wished to believe.

“Those who destroy”—understand: the scribes and Pharisees, who always placed their traditions before the law of God—“and those who devastate you by their examples—will go out from you,” led into captivity by the Romans.

“Lift up your eyes all around and see: all these gathered together have come to you.” He addresses the apostles and the primitive Church. We read in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 2) that on the day of Pentecost, while the apostles were preaching, a multitude of Jews gathered who had assembled from various parts of the world to which they had been scattered because of the excessive persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes, in the time of the Maccabees. Of these, as Luke says, three thousand believed in one day, five thousand on the next, and thereafter many thousands.

He is now speaking of them to the primitive Church: “Lift up,” he says, “your eyes, O primitive Church, and see” (Acts 2; 4)—that is, consider—“all these Jews gathered from various regions have come to you,” that is, through you they may believe and be joined to you in the unity of faith. This may also be referred to the multitude of the nations, which daily flows together from all the regions of the world to the faith of the Church.

“I live,” says the Lord, “because you will clothe yourself with all these”—understand: believers, both from the Jews and from the nations—“as with an ornament,” that is, you will be adorned, “and you will surround yourself with them like a bride.” If it is permissible to speak in this way of the expression “I live,” it is God’s oath, just as he often spoke in the Old Testament and as in the New Testament he says, “Amen, amen.” He is said to swear according to our custom so that all his speech may be held as firm as an oath.

These words, which the prophet speaks in the person of God the Father, may be understood in two ways, as referring both to the person of Christ and to the Church. For all the saints are Christ’s adornment and clothing, and he himself is the adornment of all the saints.

Let us also explain it another way, referring the same words to the Church: just as a bride is adorned with gold and jewels and various ornaments of clothing, so the holy Church is adorned by the multitude of believers and by the various orders that exist within her—bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and also the multitude of married people, the continent, and virgins. Concerning these it is said in the psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded by variety.”

“Your deserted places”—understand: your abandoned localities—“and your solitudes and your ruined lands”—understand: all the places destroyed by those who refused to believe—“will now be too narrow because of the inhabitants,” that is, because of the multitude of believers coming to the faith. “And those who devoured her will be driven far away,” namely, the scribes and Pharisees, by the Romans—those who separated you from your God by evil example or perverse teaching.

“Even now they will say in your ears”—O son, or O primitive Church—“the children of your barrenness.” This is the father’s voice addressing the son and the primitive Church. As far as the literal sense is concerned, the “children of barrenness” are those who were indeed born in unbelief but afterward believed when the apostles preached.

“The place is too narrow for me”—understand: in the synagogues. “Make room for me that I may dwell”—understand: among the nations and throughout the whole world. After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the faith of believers grew so greatly that they could no longer dwell only in Judaea unless they were spread throughout the whole world.

“And you will say in your heart,” O primitive Church: “Who has begotten these for me”—understand: these spiritual children? “I am barren”—understand: barren in that I did not nourish spiritual children for God—“and not giving birth, transported” into Babylon “and led into captivity. And who nourished these?”

She says that she is barren and not giving birth because, after Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—who is called Ezra—they had no prophets to nourish their children in the law of God. “I was abandoned” by God “and desolate” of my own husband, God Almighty. “These”—understand: the Jews or the gentiles who believe in the Son of God—“where were they?” This kind of generation is spiritual: it gives birth to many at once in faith, and therefore the Church marvels at how they were gathered together so quickly.

“Thus says the Lord God”—understand: the Father—“Behold, I raise my hand to the nations, and I will lift up my sign to the peoples.” The Church had said that she wondered where so many children had come to her faith; therefore God the Father answers and says: You wonder how these things have happened; I will show you.

“Behold,” he says, “I raise”—that is, I reveal or demonstrate—“my hand to the nations,” namely, my Son through the mystery of the Incarnation; or I raise him from earth to heaven through the Ascension. “And I will lift up my sign to the peoples,” that is, the sign of the cross. For the sign of the cross has now been so greatly exalted that all nations believe that, with God’s help, they are protected by it from all the snares of the devil.

“And” when I have raised my Son, either over the hearts of the nations or by lifting him up to heaven, “they will bring,” O primitive Church, “your sons” to the faith, “in their arms,” that is, by their examples and preaching. Or the angelic powers will bring them to eternal blessedness after the course of this labor has ended, just as we read concerning Lazarus (Luke 16).

“And your daughters,” that is, bringing the female sex to the faith, or leading the souls of the saints to paradise, “upon their shoulders”—that is, the apostles by their merits, or the angels by their prayers—“they will carry them.” He says “your sons and your daughters” because the holy Church consists of both sexes (Acts 21). For we read that Philip had four daughters who were prophetesses.

“And kings will be your foster-fathers, and queens your nurses.” These words must not be understood carnally, as the Jews understand them. They say that at the advent of their Christ—whom they still await—they will have kings as foster-fathers and queens as nurses, and will be carried in their arms and upon their shoulders by them.

Rather, by “kings” and “foster-fathers” we should understand the apostles and preachers, who diligently sought to rule themselves and others well and to nourish them in the way of truth. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “You will appoint them princes over the whole earth” (Psalm 44).

They were the queens who were also kings and foster-fathers. Were Peter and Paul not kings and queens, when by their preaching they subjected the hearts of proud men to Christ (Galatians 4)? Was Paul not a foster-father or nurse when he said: “Through the Gospel I begot you, and as to little children in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3)? Was Peter not a foster-father when he said: “Like newborn infants, desire the milk” (2 Peter 2)? The same should be understood of the other apostles.

It follows, therefore, and is said to the primitive Church: “With face bowed to the earth,” that is, humbled, “they will worship you,” that is, they will honor you, O primitive Church, in your head, which is Christ—namely, earthly power and worldly dignity. Whoever worships or honors Christ, who is the head of all the elect, honors all the elect, who are Christ’s body (Colossians 1 and 2).

And what he adds—“and they will lick the dust of your feet”—signifies that kings and queens, by whom the apostles and preachers are represented, will cleanse and wipe away by their word and example whatever earthly work or sin has clung to the feet, that is, to the actions, of the Church. “They will lick the dust of your feet,” he says: they will remove earthly conduct and forgive sins, in accordance with the power they received from the Lord, who said to them: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18).

“And you will know,” O Church, “that I am the Lord”—understand: together with my Son and the Holy Spirit—“in whom,” that is, in me, “all the elect who await him,” by believing rightly, living well, and persevering perfectly, “will not be confounded in judgment.”

“Can spoil be taken from the strong, or can what has been captured by the powerful be saved?” The Lord proposes a question, which he himself explains in what follows. He who spoke these things through Isaiah also brought forth similar words in the Gospel through himself, saying: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, what he possesses is in peace” (Luke 11).

By “the strong” and “the powerful” he wishes the devil to be understood. The devil held the human race captive with such strength that none of the saints could take it from him—not Solomon through his wisdom, nor Job through his holiness—unless the Son of God did so through the mystery of his Incarnation. Can the prey of the human race therefore be taken from the strong devil by any saint? Or can what is held captive by the powerful devil be saved?

“For thus says the Lord: Indeed, the captivity”—understand: the captivity that took the human race captive—“will be taken from the strong,” at my coming through my Passion; “and what had been taken away” from God “by the powerful one,” through persuasion, “he will save” from death to life.

“But I will judge,” he says, “those”—understand: demons, or Jews, or even gentiles—“who judged,” that is, unjustly condemned you, O Church. I will judge them justly on the day of judgment, handing them over to the punishments of hell. “And I will save your sons,” that is, all believers, giving them the kingdom of eternal rest.

“And I will feed”—that is, I will satisfy or reject—“your enemies with your flesh,” which means: consumed by your corruption and misery, they will perish—not cease to exist, but be perpetually tormented. “And they will be intoxicated with their own blood as with new wine.”

These things must not be understood carnally, as though the wicked and the persecutors of the saints would eat their own flesh and drink their own blood. Rather, their flesh will be devoured by worms and infernal beasts; that is, they will perish in their misery and corruption. And just as a person is made drunk by new wine, so they will be filled with miseries because they shed the blood of many saints.

We can also refer this to the present time, when the flesh of persecutors of the saints is eaten by worms and their blood is drunk. This happened, for example, to Herod, who killed the children and, consumed by worms, breathed his last. Such men experienced what the prophet says: “Crush them, Lord, with a double crushing,” namely, in the present and in the future (Jeremiah 17).

“And,” he says, “when I have done these things on the day of judgment—or when I punish the reprobate in the present—‘all flesh will know,’” that is, every elect person who will see the Salvation of God, “that I am the Lord who saves you,” O Church, “and your Redeemer,” who redeemed you with my blood: “the Strong One of Jacob,” that is, the one who gave Jacob strength in his struggle with the angel.

Or by Jacob we may understand the Lord, who proved strong at the time of his Passion, so much so that he prayed for those crucifying him, saying: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23).

Some think that Jacob wrestled with the angel in the manner in which two men appear to fight, holding one another and struggling with their arms and their whole bodies. But how a bodily being could wrestle by bodily touch with an angel, who by nature is incorporeal and invisible, is not at all apparent. The question must be resolved in this way.

When Jacob was fleeing to Mesopotamia, to Laban, from the face of his brother Esau, and had come to Bethel, he saw in a dream at night a ladder reaching to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it. He also heard the Lord leaning upon the ladder saying: “Jacob, I will give you the land on which you sleep, and to your offspring” (Genesis 28). Then the guardianship of angels was given to him, to protect him in Mesopotamia.

When he was returning and came again to the same place, as morning approached, he saw the camp of God. Hence he called that place Mahanaim, that is, “camps.” An angel also appeared to him—the one who had protected him for as long as he had stayed in Mesopotamia—and said to him: “Let me go” (Genesis 32), understanding: so that I may go to the one who sent me.

Immediately falling to the ground, Jacob began to pray and say: “I will not let you go,” that is, “I will not cease from prayer until you bless me.” And he blessed him, saying: “If you are strong with God in prayer, how much more will you prevail against human beings?” That is: If you persevere in prayer, how can you be defeated by Esau? Then he released him by ceasing from prayer. For he did not hold him in any other way, nor did he wrestle with him except through prayer.

## CHAPTER L

“Thus says the Lord: Where is the bill of divorce of your mother”—understand: the Synagogue—“with which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor to whom I sold you?” That is, who is the one to whom I owe so much that I have nothing with which to repay him unless I hand you over to him?

He addresses the Jewish people, who had withdrawn from him, speaking according to the custom of those who gave their wives bills of divorce—that is, a document of rejection—so that they could take other wives. He therefore says: O Jews, perhaps you say that I rejected your mother, who was once called my bride; but now tell me how I dismissed her. I did not dismiss her, nor did I give her in exchange for property. Rather, she herself withdrew from me, handing herself over to the devil, and by abandoning her own husband she became an adulteress.

“Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities,” to the devil, “and in your crimes I dismissed your mother.” One must not think that he himself first dismissed her; rather, when she committed adultery and withdrew from him, he permitted her to depart. A person is sold in iniquity when, for the sake of luxury and lust, he submits himself to the devil.

“For I came”—understand: through the mystery of the Incarnation—“and there was no man,” that is, no one bearing the likeness of God who would fight manfully against vice and the devil. Rather, all lived like beasts, in accordance with John’s reproach to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3).

Therefore he adds: “I called,” through repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 23). “And there was no one who listened,” that is, no one who obeyed or understood, because there was no man.

“Has my hand become shortened and small,” that is, my power, “so that I cannot redeem” my people from Babylon or from the captivity of the devil—those who are going to believe in me—just as formerly I redeemed the children of Israel from Egypt? “Or is there no strength in me” to free my people, or to free myself from death?

“Behold, at my rebuke”—that is, in my indignation or vision—“I will make the sea desolate,” that is, I will empty it of its waters if I wish, as once at the crossing of the children of Israel. “I will put the rivers”—understand: other rivers—“into dryness,” if I wish, as formerly the torrent of Arnon and the Jordan.

“‘The fish will rot without water and die of thirst,’ just as in that river of Egypt.” And the meaning is: I who did those things and can now do similar things have lost nothing of my power. Allegorically, however, [Col. 0972D] the sea signifies this world, which is always in motion. “Behold,” he says, “in my indignation I will make this world a desert on the day of judgment, empty of all bitterness and of all its inhabitants. And I will make the rivers dry,” that is, I will dry up the teaching of heretics and the wisdom of philosophers. “And the fish will rot,” that is, the curious and sinners will fail without water, namely, without the grace of the Holy Spirit; “and they will die of thirst,” having none of that water of which the Lord said: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly will flow living waters” (John VII).

“‘I will clothe the heavens,’” namely, the atmospheric heavens, “‘in darkness, and I will make sackcloth their covering.’” Philosophers say that the heavens extend no more than ten stadia above the earth; [Col. 0973A] the thickness of the air sometimes deprives us of the sun’s brightness across that distance. Therefore the heavens are not wrapped in sackcloth; rather, when the sun is positioned in the middle of the heavens, the air is sometimes darkened for us. Allegorically, however, the meaning here is: “I will clothe the heavens in darkness,” that is, I will cause the saints to recognize that they are sinners, in accordance with: “The righteous person is an accuser of himself at the beginning” (Proverbs XVIII). And: “If we say that we have no sin, we shall be liars” (1 John I). “And I will make sackcloth,” that is, haircloth, “their covering,” so that, doing penance, they may say with the Psalmist: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth” (Psalm XXXIV).

“‘The Lord gave me a learned tongue,’” that is, an instructed one, “‘so that I might know how to sustain the one who has fallen by a word.’” The Hebrews do not wish to refer this to Christ, [Col. 0973B] but rather to Isaiah, to whom the Lord gave a learned tongue so that he might sustain the Jewish people, and who endured many insults from them, even to the point of being sawn apart with a wooden saw. But it is better to refer this to the Lord Jesus Christ, who had a learned tongue for consoling the sorrowful and calling sinners back to repentance, and who willingly suffered these things for the salvation of the human race. “The Lord,” he says—that is, God the Father—“gave me a learned tongue in the law and in every kind of wisdom, so that I might know how to sustain by a word the one who has fallen,” namely, into sin and death: the human race. By what word does he say that he sustains the human race? By the word of preaching and repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew IV). And: [Col. 0973C] “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI). When he says, “The Lord gave me a learned tongue,” this is the voice of his humanity; in accordance with this, after his passion and resurrection he also said: “All authority has been given to me” (Matthew XXVIII). For as regards his divinity, he eternally possesses everything with the Father. “He raises,” that is, lifts up, “in the morning,” namely, from the beginning of my birth or preaching.

“‘Morning by morning he raises my ear,’” that is, the understanding of my mind, “‘so that I may hear him as a teacher,’” and speak nothing other than what I have heard from him. Concerning this he himself says in the Gospel of John: “I do not speak from myself” (John XIV). [Col. 0973D] The Lord speaks in the manner of a disciple who is taught by his teacher in the morning.

“‘The Lord God opened my ear,’” that is, my understanding. “‘But I did not contradict,’” that is, I did not act against his will. “‘I did not turn back,’” that is, I did not withdraw from his will, because I always do what pleases him.

“‘I gave my body to those who struck it,’” namely, to the Jews and the Roman soldiers, for the salvation of the human race (John VIII), “‘and my cheeks to those who plucked them.’” The cheeks are the places where the beard first grows. He then gave his cheeks, or beard, to be plucked when they covered his face and struck him with blows, and he did not resist. “‘I did not turn away,’” that is, I did not withdraw, “‘my face,’” namely, my patience, or the face of my body, “‘from those who reproached [Col. 0974A] and spat upon me.’” We read that all these things were fulfilled in his passion.

“‘The Lord God,’” namely, the Father, “‘was my helper,’” namely, in the passion; “‘therefore I was not confused,’” therefore I was not ashamed, nor did I endure disgrace. He would then have suffered shame if he had not risen on the third day. Therefore, because he himself is my helper, “‘I set my face like the hardest rock,’” so that I would not turn away from the passion. “‘And I know that I shall not be confounded,’” that is, I shall not perish.

“‘Near,’” that is, close at hand, “‘is God,’” the Father, “‘who justifies me.’” He justified him when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And he justified him when he raised him on the third day. “Who will contradict me?” That is, who can say that I am not just? [Col. 0974B] “‘Let us stand together,’” namely, for judgment. “‘Who is my adversary?’” Let him “‘approach me.’” The same idea appears in what he says in the Gospel: “‘Who,’” he says, “‘among you will convict me of sin?’” (Luke III.) And the meaning of the preceding verse is: “If anyone among you Jews thinks that I was justly crucified and that I committed some sin, let him approach me so that we may judge together.”

“‘Behold, the Lord God is my helper; who among you will condemn me?’” No one can condemn me. “Behold, all the Jews who contradict me will be worn away like a garment; the moth will eat them,” that is, their own conscience. Just as a garment is consumed in two ways, by the passage of time and by the moth, so they, because they refused to turn to repentance during the forty years [Col. 0974C] granted to them, were crushed when the Romans arrived, and in that tribulation their own conscience tormented them because they had not believed in Christ. Or even now, placed in the punishments of hell, they are tormented by the recollection of their own conscience.

“‘Who among you,’” namely, unbelieving Jews, “‘fears God, hearing,’” that is, understanding, “‘the voice of his servant,’” namely, of his Son, who says: “‘Repent’” (Matthew IV), “‘and obeys it in action?’” No one. There are two kinds of fear, and two kinds of servitude. There is servile fear, by which a servant fears his master, afraid of being scourged by him; and there is the fear of love, by which a son fears his father while hoping to receive an inheritance from him. It is of this fear that he speaks here to the Jews, who ought to have served and feared God, so that they might deserve to receive from him [Col. 0974D] the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. Concerning this fear it is also said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs I). And: “The fear of the Lord surpasses everything” (Ecclesiasticus XXV), and other similar passages.

There follows, therefore, a statement about the Son of God himself: “‘Who,’” namely, the Son of God, “‘walked in darkness, and there was no light for him,’” that is, no glory in that people, as he himself said: “No prophet is without honor except in his own homeland” (Matthew XIII; Mark VI; Luke IV). What light or what glory did the Son of God have when he was spat upon and beaten with blows? Let us give another interpretation, referring this to the gentiles. Which gentile people walked in the darkness of unbelief, and had no light in its heart—that is, Christ, who said: “I am the light [Col. 0975A] of the world” (John VIII). But what follows? Therefore, because there is no light for it—whether this is understood of Christ or of the gentile people—“let it hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon its God,” namely, and then it will come to the light of my joy and gladness.

“‘Behold, all of you,’” namely, Jews, “‘who kindle a fire,’” the fire of envy, or the fire of devastation against yourselves because of your sins, “‘and gird yourselves with flames,’” that is, surround yourselves with sins. They themselves kindled the fire by which the city was burned by the Romans when they handed the Son of God over to death, inflamed against him by the fire of zeal and envy. Therefore he says “girded with flames,” because just as every righteous person is surrounded by virtues, so the sinner is surrounded by iniquities. “‘Walk in the light of your fire,’” that is, in the tribulation of captivity that you prepared for yourselves, “‘and [Col. 0975B] in the flames’” of devastation and misery “‘that you kindled. From my hand,’” that is, from my power, namely, this evil will come upon you, O most impious Jews. The same idea is expressed elsewhere: “Is there evil in the city that the Lord has not done?” (Amos III.) “‘You shall sleep in pains,’” namely, in the pains of devastation and captivity; or, lying in the pains of hell, you shall endure these things, namely, the flame and fire of tribulation.

## CHAPTER LI

“‘Hear, you who follow what is just and seek the Lord.’” Above he spoke against the unbelieving Jews who remained in unbelief; now he addresses the apostles and the entire company of believers: “Hear me,” he says, O apostles [Col. 0975C]—that is, by hearing me, understand what I say—“you who follow and imitate by faith what is just,” namely, Christ, “and seek the Lord” by faith and devotion, and not earthly profits. “‘Pay attention,’” O peoples, “‘to the rock from which you were hewn,’” that is, to Abraham, who was a rock because of the firmness of his faith, and from whom you proceeded, “‘and to the hollow of the pit,’” that is, to Sarah, from whom you were hewn.

Or alternatively: Pay attention to the rock, that is, to Christ, from whom you were hewn, from whom you received faith, and from whom you are called Christians. Concerning this rock the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X). We can understand “the hollow of the pit” as the side of Christ, which was pierced by a spear, just as he himself said in the psalm: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm XXI). We were hewn from it when the blood of our redemption and the water of baptism came forth. [Col. 0975D] We can also understand “the hollow of the pit” as the Lord’s tomb, from which, rising again, he brought forth innumerable sons for himself. In a third way, we can call the Church “the hollow of the pit”; she was barren for a long time, and from her we are daily hewn, that is, born through the washing of baptism.

“‘Pay attention to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you.’” The meaning is the same as above, because “I called him,” that is, him alone, saying: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Genesis XII), and the other things that follow there: “And I blessed him in all his works, and I multiplied him in gold and in sons.” Therefore “the Lord will console Zion,” that is, the Church, in the apostles.

[Col. 0976A] “He will console all her ruins,” coming from the gentiles to the faith and filling them. The meaning is: I, almighty God, who once multiplied Abraham, can also console the Church and increase her children. “And he will make her desert,” that is, the primitive Church, “like delights, and her solitude like the garden of the Lord,” that is, she who previously was deserted by God—abandoned and reduced to solitude—will have God dwelling within her and will produce the flowers of virtues and the fruits of good works. “Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise,” for the benefits conferred upon her by God. And because he redeemed her by the blood of his passion, she will render him thanks and praises of faith and confession.

“‘Pay attention to me, my people,’” that is, my apostles, [Col. 0976B] “‘and my tribe,’” namely, you who have believed from the Jews or from the gentiles, “‘hear me.’” This is the people, and these are the tribes, of whom Gabriel speaks to Joseph: “For he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I). And what does he command them to hear? “‘For the law,’” he says—namely, the law of the Gospel—“‘will go forth from me, and my judgment,’” that is, my decree, “‘will rest in the light,’” namely, in the faith of the peoples, “‘who were in darkness,’” the darkness of unbelief, “‘as it is written: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light’” (Isaiah IX). It was a judgment of discernment that, when the Jews refused to believe, the gentiles should be called to the faith.

These words that we have stated were spoken in the person of the Son of God; what follows, however, is the voice of the Father concerning the Son.

[Col. 0976C] “My righteous one is near,” that is, my Son is near, who will be born from a virgin; “he will not delay any longer. My Savior has gone forth,” that is, he has now been begotten by me; in time he will go forth from his mother. The Lord calls his Son righteous and Savior because through him he justifies and saves all his elect. But when he adds, “‘and my arms will judge the peoples,’” he wishes the apostles and apostolic men to be understood, who will judge all the nations on the day of judgment, just as the Lord himself promised, saying: “‘When the Son of Man sits,’” he says, “‘on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel’” (Matthew XVIII). “‘The islands will hope in me,’” that is, the gentiles or the Churches, “‘as Jacob said: The ruler will not fail from Judah, until [Col. 0976D] the one who is to be sent comes; and he will be the expectation of the nations’” (Genesis XLIX); “‘and they will sustain my arm,’” that is, my Son, “‘through whom I made all things.’”

“‘Raise your eyes to heaven,’” O gentiles or Churches, “‘and see,’” that is, consider or understand, “‘that the heavens,’” namely, the atmospheric heavens, “‘will dissolve like smoke,’” that is, vanish, “‘and the earth will be worn away like a garment,’” that is, it will fail, “‘and its inhabitants,’” namely, all the beasts, birds, and all the creatures that will then be found upon it, “‘will perish in the same way,’” that is, everything will die. The Lord says the same thing in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew XXIV), through change [Col. 0977A]—namely, into something better—and not in essence. In accordance with this Solomon says: “A generation passes away and a generation comes; but the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes I). But although everything passes away, “my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will not fail.” The salvation and righteousness of God the Father is the Son, because through him he saves and justifies those predestined to life. This is the salvation of which Simeon said: “My eyes have seen your Salvation” (Luke II). And Jacob: “I will await your Salvation, Lord” (Genesis XLIX).

“‘Hear me,’” O peoples and believers, “‘who know the righteous one,’” namely, Christ: the faithful people. “‘My law,’” that is, the law of the Gospel, “‘is in their hearts,’” namely, in the hearts of the faithful—not in the mouth alone, [Col. 0977B] but in the heart and in their actions. This is the voice of God the Father to believers. Hearing in sacred Scripture must be sought in a spiritual sense. “Hear me,” that is, understand the Gospel teaching and strive to fulfill it in action. “‘Do not fear,’” O apostles, “‘the reproach of men,’” that is, their insults and oppression, “‘and do not be afraid of their blasphemies.’” The same idea is contained in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew X).

“‘For just as a garment,’” namely, is consumed by the worm or by time, “‘so the worm will eat them,’” that is, their own conscience. “‘And as the moth devours wool, so the moth will devour them,’” because this likewise signifies their own conscience. Alternatively: just as a garment is consumed by age and by the moth, so their reproach [Col. 0977C] will pass away together with their persecutors. “But my salvation,” namely, Christ, “will be forever, and my righteousness from generation to generation,” that is, throughout all future times. Or, in the generation of the Jews and the generation of the gentiles.

“‘Arise, arise, clothe yourself with strength, O arm of the Lord.’” This is the voice of the prophet and of the faithful people, entreating the advent of the Son of God. O arm of the Lord, that is, O most exalted Son of God, rise from the glory of the Father’s majesty to fulfill the mystery of your incarnation; arise to redeem the human race. Clothe yourself with the strength of your divinity against the demons. “‘Arise as in ancient days, in the generations of past ages.’” The meaning is: just as in ancient times you helped your people by bringing them out of Egypt, and just as in the generations of our fathers you displayed your strength, [Col. 0977D] so now come in the flesh to free the human race from the hand of the devil. “‘Have you not,’” O Lord God, who are equal to the Father in all things, “‘struck down the proud one,’” namely, the devil, casting him from heaven, “‘and wounded the dragon,’” namely, Pharaoh, in the sea—or the devil?

“‘Were you not the one who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty abyss,’” so as to provide a passage for your people? “‘Who made the depths of the sea a road, so that the redeemed might pass over?’” your elect. The meaning is: just as you did all these things, so also come to save your chosen people.

[Col. 0978A] “And now those who have been redeemed by the Lord,” namely, by the blood of his Son, “will return,” from iniquity to righteousness, “and will come to Zion,” that is, to the present Church—or, better, to heavenly blessedness—praising him. “And everlasting joy will be upon their heads,” that is, in their minds. In accordance with what the Psalmist says in the eighty-third psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.” The saints cannot possess these things while situated in the present age; hence it follows: “They will obtain joy and gladness,” namely, in the heavenly Jerusalem. “Pain and groaning will flee,” as it is said in the Apocalypse, chapter twenty-one: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying.”

[Col. 0978B] “‘I, I myself,’” namely, the Son of God, “‘will console you,’” by redeeming you and giving the Holy Spirit, who is the true Comforter. Because the faithful people had earlier said in prayer to the Lord, “Arise to save us,” he himself responds through the prophet: “I,” he says, “will console you, and no other”—not the powerful of this age, nor the wise of this world. “‘Who are you,’” O company of the faithful, “‘that you should fear,’” that is, that you ought to fear, “‘a mortal man and the son of man, who will quickly wither like grass? And you have forgotten the Lord, your maker?’” He addresses the company of the apostles, so that they would not fear the savagery and tortures of men, because they themselves will perish and pass away like grass that quickly withers, since all flesh is grass. [Col. 0978C] And he also addresses those who, terrified by fear of the passion, had denied him, so that they might be ashamed of their wickedness and be strengthened in faith by doing penance. “When,” he says, “you feared a mortal man at the time of affliction, you lost fear of your Creator”—“who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth.” “And you were continually afraid all day long,” that is, throughout the entire time of the passion, “before the face of the fury of the one who oppressed you,” namely, the persecutor who tormented you in body “and had prepared to destroy” in soul, without remembering: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X). “Where now is the fury of the one who oppresses?” He addresses the faithful people, so that they may consider how all persecutors and all human beings pass away from the present world, and by this he may strengthen them in faith.

[Col. 0978D] “‘He will come quickly,’” namely, my Son, through the mystery of his incarnation, “‘walking,’” according to his humanity, “‘to open’” the hearts of proud men—or also to open hell. “And he will not kill to destruction,” that is, he will not immediately condemn sinners when he comes, but will wait for repentance, just as he himself preached, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew IV). And: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn from his iniquity and live” (Ezekiel XVIII). What he adds—“his bread will not fail”—may be understood of the Son himself, who said: “I am the living bread” (John VI); or of his body and blood, concerning which the same Son said: [Col. 0979A] “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” Or, in a third way, it may be understood of the teaching of the Gospel, because it will never fail, but will always nourish those who observe it with the food of life.

“‘I am the Lord your God, who stirs up the sea,’” that is, the inhabitants of this world, “‘and its waves swell,’” that is, the persecutions of wicked men are stirred up against the elect. “‘The Lord of hosts is my name,’” that is, the Lord of the armies of angels and men. He turns his address directly to the Son himself. When did God the Father stir up this sea? When he permitted the Jews to rage, first against his Son, and then against the apostles and those who believed in him. And if he himself stirred it up, why are those who persecuted them held guilty? [Col. 0979B] He is said to have stirred them up when he permitted them to be stirred up.

“‘I placed my word in your mouth,’” that is, I gave you the fullness of wisdom and knowledge. “‘And in the shadow of my hand I protected you,’” that is, I guarded you in the protection of divinity, so that you would not sin and so that the flesh assumed by the Word would not be dishonored, “‘to plant the heavens,’” namely, the new heavens, “‘and to lay the foundations of the earth,’” namely, the new earth, “‘and to say to Zion,’” that is, to the Church, “‘You are my people.’” God the Father speaks these words to the human being assumed by the Word, in whom, from that time onward, all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. For as regards his divinity, he received nothing from the Father in time, but possesses everything in common with the Father, since he is the power of God and the wisdom of God, through whom all things were made from nothing. By the new heaven and [Col. 0979C] the new earth that God the Father commanded the Son to plant and establish, we ought to understand the apostles, apostolic men, and all the faithful, who have been planted by the Lord and founded in him through faith and love of God and neighbor, and who have been renewed from the oldness of sin into the newness of faith and holy conduct.

“‘Rise up, rise up, arise, [Col. 0979D] Jerusalem, which drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath.’” The divine word addresses those who, during the Lord’s passion, fell into the sin of denial and unbelief, saying: “Crucify such a man, and give us Barabbas; for we have no king except Caesar” (Matthew XXVI). And just as one lying in bed is told, “Rise,” so they too are commanded to rise from vices to virtues, from unbelief to faith. When he says, “‘Rise up, rise up, Jerusalem,’” we must not suppose that he commands the walls of the city, which were destroyed by the Romans, to rise again into their former state; rather, this is to be understood metonymically, through the container for the contained. “Rise,” he says, O people of the Jews, from vices to virtues, from unbelief to faith. “Arise, Jerusalem,” that is, do penance, you who drank from the hand of the Lord—that is, from the power of the Lord—the cup of his wrath.

By the cup of his wrath we should understand the devastation by the Romans, the magnitude of the punishments, and the affliction. That the cup signifies affliction and tribulation, the Psalmist makes clear when he says: “The cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine. And he will pour it out,” and so forth, up to what follows: “[Col. 0980A] All the sinners of the earth will drink it” (Psalm LXXIV). And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Take,” he says, “the cup from my hand, and you shall give it to all the nations to which I send you” (Jeremiah XXIV). “‘You drank the cup of stupor,’” that is, of death, “‘to the bottom, and you drank it to the dregs,’” that is, you will endure this captivity to the end of the age. Therefore he says, “You drank to the bottom” and “to the dregs,” because after that captivity no other will come upon them, since they will always remain in it.

“There is no one to sustain her among all the sons whom she bore, and there is no one to grasp her hand and raise her who lies fallen,” that is, no one to strengthen her action, “among all the sons whom she nourished.” When they came out of Egypt, they had Moses, who sustained [Col. 0980B] them and prayed for them, saying to the Lord: “Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from your book” (Exodus XXXII). Again, when they were led into Babylon, they had Daniel and his companions, and other prophets, who grasped their hand—that is, their action—and sustained them by their prayers. In this final captivity, however, they have neither priest, nor prophet, nor apostle to intercede for them, because they did not wish to have them. For the apostles wished to extend their hand—that is, to offer consolation as to how they might be raised up—but, rejected by them, they left them and went over to the gentiles.

“‘Two things have befallen you,’” O Jerusalem. “Who will grieve over you?” Namely, as Jeremiah and Daniel once [Col. 0980C] grieved; or as Christ grieved over you when he wept over you, as is contained in the Gospel (Luke X). He says “two,” but mentions four, and these four are again reduced to two: “Devastation,” he says, “and destruction,” which signify one thing, “and famine and sword,” which likewise are one thing; namely, these will come upon you. “And who will console you?” Either no one, or one will be found only rarely.

“‘Your sons have been cast out,’” namely, from their dwellings, led captive among all the nations. “‘They have slept at the head of every road,’” that is, they have died along the streets of various nations, their naked bodies lying upon the bare earth. “‘Like a snared wild beast,’” namely, they slept in this manner. “‘O people full of the indignation of [Col. 0980D] the Lord,’” that is, the vengeance of the Lord, “‘with the rebuke of your God.’” Where the Hebrew says, “They slept like a snared wild beast,” the Septuagint translated, “like a half-cooked beet,” a plant that quickly becomes limp in the heat of the sun. Other interpreters said, “like a snared oryx,” a wild beast unsuitable for sacrifice. The meaning is: just as the animal called an oryx is caught in hunters’ nets, with no way to escape, and, exhausted from struggling there for a long time, finally lies down to rest, so your sons have been caught in the bonds and ropes of their sins; everywhere they lie dead and slain, having no help by which to escape the Lord’s wrath.

“‘Therefore,’” namely, because you have no comforter to sustain you, “‘hear this, poor little woman, drunk [Col. 0981A] not with wine.’” She is called a poor little woman because she was effeminate and possessed no spiritual riches.

“‘Thus says your Lord, the Lord and your God, who fought for his people.’” The almighty Lord often fought for the Jews and bestowed many good things upon them, which it would take too long to recount in full. “‘Behold, I have taken,’” for “I will take,” “‘from your hand the cup of stupor,’” that is, the captivity of death, “‘the bottom of the cup of my indignation.’” Namely, I will take it away if you do penance. Above he foretold the captivity and misery that would come upon them; now he urges them to repentance, saying: “If,” he says, “you produce fruits worthy of repentance, I will take from you the evil of captivity and the wrath of my indignation.” “‘You shall not add any more,’” namely, after you have done penance, “‘to drink it,’” [Col. 0981B] namely, the cup—that is, to endure tribulation.

“‘And I will place it,’” the cup, “‘in the hand of those who humbled you,’” namely, kings and peoples, or demons, who will receive punishment for all whom they deceive. And in the hand of those demons “who said to your soul: Bend down, so that we may pass over you,” that is, submit yourself to vices, so that afterward we may rest in you and trample upon you. “And you laid your body down like the earth,” that is, so that it adhered to the ground; or, just as the earth is trodden upon, so that you might offer yourself to be trampled. “And like a road,” namely, you gave your body to passing demons and evil spirits, so that just as a road lies open to everyone, you might likewise lie open to lust.

As regards the literal sense, what he said above has been fulfilled: “I will humble those who humbled you.” Let us see how [Col. 0981C] it was fulfilled. The Chaldeans humbled them, and they themselves were humbled by the Medes and Persians. The Romans humbled them, and afterward the Romans perished and suffered many evils. Likewise, the evil spirits who humbled them by persuading them to crucify Christ were humbled, because through the Lord’s passion they lost the power they had held throughout the world; and on the day of judgment they will be humbled still further when they are handed over to the punishments of hell. Each soul dies when it sins by serving vices; it falls into death and is taken captive by the devil. When, therefore, it does penance, it is raised up and rises into the state of good action; and the evil spirits who had humbled it by dragging it into guilt are humbled in hell.

## CHAPTER LII

[Col. 0981D]

“‘Arise, arise, clothe yourself with your strength, Zion; clothe yourself in the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, city of the Holy One.’” The prophet Isaiah, long before the Lord’s coming, foreseeing that the Jews would fall and collapse into denial of Christ and unbelief, and that afterward many of them would come to the faith, addresses those who, after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, believed through the preaching of the apostles—three thousand on one day, five thousand on the following day, and many thousands thereafter (Acts II)—so that they might rise from unbelief to perfect faith and from earthly things to heavenly things. He says: “Arise, O Zion; clothe yourself with your strength,” you who fell through denial; “clothe yourself in the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, [Col. 0982A] city of the Holy One,” namely, of God’s temple.

What are these garments with which she is commanded to clothe herself? Faith, hope, love of God and neighbor, chastity, humility, and the other virtues with which the saints are clothed and adorned. It is as though he said in other words: Abandon the error of unbelief, and accept faith and the honor of every virtue, together with all the adornments of teaching, and be a city of the Holy One.

Some manuscripts read “city of the Holy One,” others “holy city”; both readings can stand. If we say “city of the Holy One,” we must supply “of God,” because the holy city of God existed among the patriarchs, that is, of almighty God. Or “city of the Holy One,” namely, of the temple, which had within it a temple sanctified to the Lord. Their city can also be called holy because, while all the nations worshiped idols, it alone throughout the world possessed knowledge of God [Col. 0982B] and awaited the coming of the Son of God. Hence, even after the Lord’s resurrection, while retaining its former name, it is called the holy city, as the Evangelist says: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and appeared to many in the holy city,” which at that time could not truly have been holy, since it had laid hands upon the Son of God (Matthew XXVII).

The difference between Jerusalem and Zion is that Zion was called the citadel and city of David, whereas Jerusalem was the remaining part of the city. What follows—“For the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you”—belongs specifically to the heavenly Jerusalem, through which no uncircumcised person passes, that is, no one who has not been cleansed from sins, and no unclean person. [Col. 0982C] It can also be referred to the present Jerusalem, that is, the Church, with an implied condition: “The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you if you rightly observe what I say.” This circumcision must be understood spiritually, not in one bodily member alone, but in every sense, will, and evil desire, so that in every respect we may be purified and clean.

“‘Shake yourself free from the dust’” of sins, that is, cleanse yourself from sin; “arise” to repentance. “Sit” in the state of your mind, O “captive daughter of Zion,” that is, you who are now held captive; “loose the bonds of your neck,” that is, the bonds of sins and blasphemies, so that you may say with the Psalmist: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice an offering of praise.” [Col. 0982D] At that time she was not a daughter, but was held captive—that is, captivity was already threatening her—because by denying the Son of God she had become effeminate and lost her virginity. Then Zion loosed the bonds of her neck, speaking of those who believed, when they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus through the preaching of the apostles.

“‘For thus says the Lord: You were sold without payment, and you shall be redeemed without silver.’” You were sold without payment—that is, willingly and voluntarily—to the devil, because they received no good from Pilate when they handed the Son of God over to death. Nor did they gain any advantage from it, nor did they escape any disadvantage. He says, “You shall be redeemed without silver,” because without any profit or reward, and without any merits preceding on our part, the Son of God redeemed us by his grace and mercy. [Col. 0983A] Hence the Apostle Peter says: “You were not redeemed from your empty way of life with perishable gold and silver, or with a precious stone, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter I).

Because the Lord says this: “‘My people went down into Egypt at the beginning,’” that is, in the person of Jacob, “‘to dwell there as a settler,’” namely, to inhabit the land of Goshen. “‘And Assyria,’” that is, the Assyrian people coming with Nebuchadnezzar, “‘oppressed him without any cause,’” after they had entered his land. The meaning is: the Egyptians indeed wished to keep my people in servitude, for this reason, namely, because they had rescued him from the scarcity of famine. And in truth they appeared to act justly in part; but I delivered him by leading him through the wilderness into the land previously [Col. 0983B] promised to him. And if he sinned against the Assyrian, so that the Assyrian expelled him from his own soil and oppressed him—that is, so that he might crush him and seek an opportunity to do him harm—

Morally, however, Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” signifies this world. Therefore the human race, at the beginning—that is, in our first parent—descended into this world to dwell there as a settler. In accordance with what the Psalmist says: “I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim” (Psalm XXXVIII). But the devil oppressed him without any cause, that is, sought to deceive him without cause, because he had committed nothing to him. Therefore I say that the human race is a settler here for this reason: if it had not sinned at the devil’s persuasion, once the number of the elect had been completed, it would immediately have passed from the earthly paradise to the joys of eternal rest.

[Col. 0983C] “‘And is this mine?’ says the Lord.” It is as though he said: Why should I remain any longer here in Judea, when few there will believe in me? I will go to the gentiles, “because my people have been taken away without payment from their land,” or have been taken away from God by living wickedly.

“Those who rule over him”—understand, the peoples of the ten and the two tribes—“act wickedly, says the Lord, and continually, all day long, my name is blasphemed”—understand, in their synagogues, as blessed Jerome says: three times daily in their synagogues they curse the Lord and all his Nazarenes; or else it is blasphemed among the nations, according to the saying: “Through you the name of God is blasphemed among the nations.” For when they displayed their evil deeds before the nations, the name of God and the worship of God were mocked. And when, on account of their sins, they were led into captivity and handed over to the power of their enemies, the Egyptians, Moabites, Idumeans, and their other neighboring peoples said (Rom. II): “Where is their God now? Now it is evident that our gods are greater in power and strength than theirs, since their god cannot protect them from their enemies or govern them.” By “those who rule over him,” acting wickedly, we should understand kings and princes, as well as priests, scribes, and Pharisees, on account of whose sins the people were handed over to plunder.

“Therefore”—understand, because I am blasphemed by the Jews—“my people”—all the faithful and believers—“shall know my name on that day,” that is, at the time of my incarnation, “because I myself who was speaking” [Col. 0984A] through the patriarchs and prophets—“Behold, here I am,” through the mystery of the incarnation. He calls that one his people of whom the angel said to Joseph: “For he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I). This is the day of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day” (John VIII).
