Therefore all believers know his name, because Christians are called after him.

“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one announcing, preaching peace, announcing good things, preaching salvation, saying: ‘Zion, your God will reign.’” Some manuscripts have “those announcing and preaching peace,” but this is written incorrectly. The order of the words is therefore this: How beautiful are the feet—understand, of Christ—of the one announcing [Col. 0984B] and preaching peace above all! We may understand “mountains” in two ways: either literally, as the mountains of the Jews, upon which the Lord often preached while present in the flesh, and on which he also refreshed the crowds; or, what is better, as the apostles, who were mountains because of the height of their virtues. The Lord preached upon them because he sat within their hearts, saying: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you.” Of them it is said in the Psalm: “You who wondrously illuminate from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LVII). He therefore preached and announced himself to them, because he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II), and who reconciled us to God the Father. The feet of Christ, who announces peace, are therefore beautiful because they have not contracted the dust of sins. [Col. 0984C] “For he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II).

And he says: How beautiful are the feet of Christ, who announces what is good—whether himself or his Gospel—and preaches salvation, that is, redemption and the reward of life! And how beautiful are the feet of Christ, who says: “O Zion”—that is, the universal Church—“your God will reign!” This is the prophet’s voice, preaching of and announcing the Son, proclaiming peace upon the apostles, and saying to the Church: “Your God will reign.”

The passage may also be understood of the apostles, who were the Lord’s feet when, running through the whole world by means of them, he announced the Gospel. The sense is therefore: How beautiful, he says, are the feet—that is, the apostles—of Christ, who announces peace upon the mountains, that is, upon the other elect, through their adornment. It is like what the same [Col. 0984D] Isaiah says elsewhere: “The voice of Christ crying in the wilderness through the mouth of John.” The apostles, therefore, were the Lord’s feet, and whatever they announced, Christ announced through their mouths; therefore he says, “of Christ who announces.”

“The voice of your watchmen”—understand, it has been heard throughout the whole world—“they have raised their voice”—understand, the voice of preaching that announces the Gospel. Just as in the Old Testament the prophets and priests were called watchmen, so in the New Testament the apostles and preachers are called watchmen, because they ought to be in the mirror of the mind, always contemplating heavenly things; and they ought to watch over the life of their subjects and announce the snares and the coming of the hostile evil ones. The voice of these [Col. 0985A] watchmen has indeed been heard throughout all the earth, and their words have resounded to the ends of the world.

And he rightly says, “They have raised their voice,” because they have spoken of things above. Hence what follows: “Together they shall praise”—understand, all the apostles and all the preachers—“because they shall see eye to eye,” that is, face to face, “when the Lord converts Zion,” that is, when he brings the Church to his faith. He speaks of those eyes of which the Psalmist says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. XXIV).

“Rejoice and praise together, desolate Jerusalem, because the Lord has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem.” He now addresses the primitive Church, which believed from the Jews, and comforts it concerning the multitude of the nations, which succeeded the Jews who remained in unbelief. After the people had been led into captivity by the Romans and the cities had been burned, scarcely any Jewish inhabitant, or none at all, remained there. But the Church that had once existed among them was restored from the number of the nations coming to faith, and it was even multiplied.

Hence it is said to those among them who believed—namely, the apostles and apostolic men who were saved from the hands of the Romans and by whom the Gospel was preached among the nations: “Rejoice and praise,” he says, “desolate Jerusalem,” that is, the primitive Church from the Jews, and believers who were left behind after the captivity of your brothers, “because the Lord has comforted his people,” who believe in him, through the coming of the Holy Spirit and through the multitude of the nations assembling for the faith; [Col. 0985C] “and he has redeemed Jerusalem,” that is, the universal Church, by his blood. Although the apostles and the believers from the Jews grieved over the destruction of their brothers who persisted in error, they nevertheless received great joy from the fact that what had perished among the Jews was restored from the nations.

“The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations,” that is, he revealed his Son in the minds and hearts of all the nations through the preaching of the apostles, when they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them (Mark XVI). And how did he reveal his Son through the apostles’ preaching? Because he comforted his people who believed in him, both from the Jews and from the nations, and redeemed Jerusalem by the blood [Col. 0985D] of his Son—that is, the Church.

Hence what follows: “And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,” that is, the Lord Jesus Christ. The arm of God the Father and his salvation is the Son, as we have said, because through him he created all things, as John says: “All things were made through him” (John I). And through him he determined to save the human race.

All the nations, or all the ends of the earth, did not see this arm or salvation of God the Father in bodily presence; but all human beings, good and evil, will see him in mind and contemplation of heart on the day of judgment, because the Father gave him all judgment (John V).

“Depart, depart, go out from there; do not touch what is polluted.” The Jews refer these words to the time when, with Cyrus’ permission, they returned gloriously to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Ezra, carrying with them the vessels of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon, and from which Belshazzar was drinking when he was killed by Cyrus himself and his uncle Darius. They are commanded to cleanse themselves through repentance, since they are to bring the vessels of the Lord to Jerusalem. And it is promised that they will not go out in flight or tumult from the Chaldeans, as they once did from the Egyptians.

The Jews indeed hold this view, but it is better to refer the passage to the apostles and the primitive Church. They are commanded to leave Jerusalem and go over to the nations, as the Lord says to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 0986B] XXVIII).

Before the Romans came against Jerusalem, divine providence arranged that the apostles should be distributed among all the nations, and that the believers dwelling there should move into the territories of King Agrippa, who was at peace with the Romans. When the Holy Spirit revealed this to them, the divine word addressed them and said: “Depart, apostles, from Jerusalem; go out from there, lest you become entangled in sins; do not touch what is polluted”—that is, do not have fellowship with the Jews, polluted by the death and blood of the Son of God—“for whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Eccl. XIII).

Hence the apostles themselves say: “Since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts III). It follows, therefore, and is said to these same people: “Go out from her midst,” that is, from the midst of Jerusalem, lest you be enveloped in their sins. “Be cleansed”—understand, from vices—“you who carry the vessels of the Lord,” apostles. They themselves were the vessels of the Lord, because he dwelt in them through faith and love. Concerning one of their number he says: “He is a vessel chosen for me, to carry my name before the nations and kings” (Acts IX).

We may also say that the vessels of the Lord are the spiritual armor that each believer ought to carry in his mind. Concerning it the apostle spoke: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day” (Eph. VI). He explains in what this armor consists in what follows: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and finally the sword, which is the word of God.

“For you shall not go out in tumult”—that is, in fear [Col. 0986D] or terror—“from the Jews,” “nor shall you hasten in flight,” as the children of Israel did from Egypt. Although the apostles were scourged and beaten by the Jews in the synagogues, they did not withdraw from them as fugitives, but as though they were victorious and at peace. “For the Lord will go before you”—understand, to the nations—as he promised you, saying: “Behold, he will go before you into Galilee.” “And the God of Israel will gather you” into one sheepfold (Matt. XXVIII), establishing one Church from Jews and nations alike, just as he himself says: “So that there may be one sheepfold and one shepherd” (John X).

“Behold, my servant shall understand”—that is, my Son shall understand—my will, “and he shall be exalted” after his resurrection in the hearts of the nations through the preaching of his apostles [Col. 0987A]; or he shall be exalted from the grave to the heavens, from death to life; “and he shall be lifted up” above all the heavens; “and he shall be very high,” sitting in the glory of his former majesty.

The Son of God is called a servant according to his humanity, because, although he was “in the form of God, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II). And because he did this, God the Father exalted him at his right hand, giving him the name that is above every name, so that he might be called the Son of God.

“As they were astonished [obstupuerunt]”—that is, as many “were amazed at you”—understand, before your passion, seeing signs and miracles performed by you—“so without glory shall his appearance be among men” at the time of his passion, when they saw him spat upon and scourged, [Col. 0987B] and finally crucified; “and his form”—that is, his appearance—understand, shall be without honor “among the sons of men.”

This is the voice of God the Father to the Son. In this passage the historical order is not preserved. Earlier the Prophet spoke in the person of God the Father about the ascension of the Son of God; now he returns to his passion.

Here a question arises: why does the Psalmist say, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XXXXIV), while here God the Father says through the prophet that his appearance will be without honor among the sons of men? The question is resolved in this way: this dishonor is not to be referred to his face and countenance, but to the disgrace of his passion. When they saw the Lord spat upon, crucified, and reckoned among the wicked, those who had seen his miracles before his passion and had said, “Who is this?” [Col. 0987C] supposed that he was not the Son of God, but despised and the least of men.

“This one shall sprinkle”—that is, wash with his blood—“many nations.” In the Old Testament the people were sprinkled with the blood of a lamb, but they were not cleansed from sins. When the Son of God came and poured out his blood for us, however, he cleansed all believers who had been predestined to life. It is therefore fittingly said, “He shall sprinkle many nations,” and not all, because his passion benefited no others except those who received his faith and were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity.

“Kings shall shut their mouths because of him,” that is, the wise men of this age—Plato, Aristotle, and the others who were wise according to the flesh and seemed to rule themselves and others. When the apostles preached the teaching of the Gospel, all human wisdom and all worldly eloquence fell silent, and the faith of Christ was spread far and wide through the grace of the Gospel.

Why this happened is explained in what follows: “For those to whom nothing was told about him”—understand, by the patriarchs and prophets—“shall see,” that is, shall understand that he came for the redemption of the human race, “and those who have not heard” the prophets before his coming “shall contemplate him” through faith and desire.

By those to whom the prophets did not announce the Lord’s coming, and who had not previously heard, we should understand the gentiles, of whom he himself says: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XXVI). While the Lord was preaching in the flesh, very few gentiles saw his presence; nevertheless, afterward they contemplated him with faith and love.

## CHAPTER LIII

“Who has believed what we have heard, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Isaiah now speaks to the Lord in the person of all the prophets, saying that there were few among the Jews who would truly believe that what they had heard from them concerning the coming of the Son of God was true. Therefore he says: “Who has believed what we have heard?” “Who” is used here because of the rarity. The sense is: Although we had foretold all the things stated above, which of the Jews believed what we heard—that is, who considers true what we learned from you concerning the coming of your Son?

The arm—that is, the Son of God the Father—to whom has he been revealed? That is, to whom has he been manifested so that he might believe in him? [Col. 0988B]

“And he shall ascend like a young shoot before him”—that is, before God the Father—“and like a root from thirsty ground.” He rightly says that the arm of God the Father will ascend like a young shoot before him, that is, by the will of God the Father, as he himself said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI). This demonstrates the ascent of his birth: how, having become human, he was exalted by rising from the dead and ascending to heaven, and how, through the preaching of the apostles, his name was exalted above all the nations.

This is the young shoot and the root of which Isaiah says elsewhere: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. II), that is, Christ from the Virgin Mary, who arose from David’s line. When he says, “and like a root from thirsty ground,” we should understand the virgin herself, whose womb was thirsty because it was not moistened by human and male seed.

What follows—“there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no beauty”—understand, in him—is the voice of the prophet in his own person and in that of all the prophets, who through the Holy Spirit knew all that was to be accomplished in the Lord Jesus Christ, or who believed when the Lord came in the flesh.

A considerable question arises here: Why does the prophet Isaiah say, “There is no beauty in him, nor comeliness,” when the Psalmist sings of him that he is “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV)? The question is resolved in this way: he had no beauty or comeliness because the fullness of divinity, which lay hidden in him, did not appear outwardly; or, insofar as those who inflicted insults upon him were concerned, he appeared to have lost all beauty.

Let us therefore examine each point, although these words were spoken in the person of the prophet and his companions: “There is no beauty in him, nor comeliness.” While God was scourged, spat upon, and enduring the other insults, he appeared to the Jews not to have beauty or comeliness, because the power of his divinity lay hidden within.

“And we saw him through the Holy Spirit”—I and my companions, who lived before him, saw him in the mind, as did the apostles who were present. “And there was no appearance”—understand, at the time of his passion—“and we desired him”—understand, I and my companions, the prophets who preceded him, desired to see him.

[Col. 0989A] “Despised” by the Jews, “and the least of men,” that is, counted as nothing; “a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness”—understand, patiently enduring it—“and as one whose face was hidden and despised,” that is, whose divine splendor was concealed.

When he says, “we desired to see him” as he was despised by the Jews and counted as nothing, he joins himself to the Fathers who preceded the Lord’s coming and desired with immense love to see him. Concerning them the Lord said to the apostles: “Truly I say to you, many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. XIII). And: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day” (John III).

Therefore David, inflamed with great love to see him in the flesh, said: “Stir up your power, O Lord, and come” (Ps. LXXIX), through the mystery of the incarnation. And Isaiah said: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend” (Isa. LXIV).

What follows—“we desired to see him, a man of sorrows,” that is, placed in suffering and patiently enduring weakness—must not be understood doubtfully, as though he did not truly endure the pain of his passion, as certain heretics claimed. Rather, just as he truly possessed a body, so he truly felt the greatest pain of his passion according to his humanity; but his divinity remained without pain. Hence on the night when he was seized he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI).

“Therefore”—understand, because the appearance of his divinity was hidden—“we did not regard him” as the Son of God. He speaks in the person of the Jews who later came to faith, and in his own person and that of all the prophets.

“Truly he himself bore our weaknesses”—that is, our sins—understand, away from us, as a physician bears an illness away from a sick person, not by taking it into himself but by curing it—“and he himself carried our sorrows,” that is, our sins, in his body upon the wood. “And we thought him like a leper,” that is, a sinner, “struck by God” on account of his own sins, “and humbled.”

This is the voice of those who, after the Lord’s ascension, believed the apostles who preached and, pierced with compunction, said in repentance: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts II). The prophet continues and says:

“But he himself was wounded for our iniquities”—understand, not for his own, as he says in the Psalm: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. XXI). “He was crushed,” that is, weakened or delivered over to death, “for our crimes.” For our sake he endured the curse, so that he might free us from the curse. “The discipline of our peace was upon him,” that is, the scourging that we ought to have received he himself received, so that he might reconcile us to God the Father and to the holy angels. “And by his bruise,” that is, by the wound caused by his rods and blows, “we were healed” from sins. For he suffered for us to reconcile us to God, because “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

“All of us, like sheep, have gone astray,” handing him over to death and needing his mercy, according to the apostle’s saying: “There is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Rom. III). Hence what follows: “Each one has turned aside to his own way,” that is, to his own conduct; or else, away from the way of uprightness, which is Christ. For he is the way, the truth, and the life.

They turned away from the way when they said to Christ: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon”; and when they decreed that he should be crucified and Barabbas released (John VIII). “And the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all,” that is, he handed him over for our sins, so that what we could not bear because of the weakness of our frailty, God himself might bear for us—not so that he would carry our sins in such a way as to possess sin, since he remained without sin, but as a physician takes the sick person’s illness away from him, not receiving it into himself.

Hence the apostle says: “God the Father made him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (John X), that is, a sacrifice for sin.

“He was offered”—understand, by himself, not upon the altar of holocausts but upon the altar of the cross—“because he himself willed it.” Yet he says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again”; and: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down myself.”

He was therefore offered not for his own sins but for ours, because he himself willed it. “And he did not open his mouth”—understand, during his passion, when questioned by Pilate or Herod, lest he appear to resist. When questioned by Pilate, he answered briefly, when Pilate said: “Will you not speak to me?” (Matt. XXVII). And when he was sent to Herod and questioned by him, he said very little.

For he could, if he had wished, have shown himself free from guilt, but he did not wish to do so, lest the salvation accomplished through his passion be delayed. For unless he had endured the cross, the human race would have remained subject to eternal death.

“As a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth.” He who was offered to Pilate because he willed it and did not answer when questioned repeatedly, lest the benefit of his passion be delayed by excusing himself from guilt, was also led of his own will to be sacrificed, as the apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V).

Therefore, just as a lamb is silent before its shearer and does not bleat, so he remained silent while being unjustly condemned. For he is the true Lamb in whose figure the Israelite people ate the lamb when leaving Egypt. He is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, as John the Baptist said (John I), and whom John the Evangelist says in his Apocalypse that he saw slain (Apoc. XII).

Christ is called a lamb because of his innocence and gentleness. He refreshes us spiritually with his flesh and blood, and clothes us with his fleece, that is, protects us with his protection.

Some manuscripts have: “And as a lamb before the one who shears”—that is, the one who strikes him—“he shall be silent,” which does not differ from the faith. Although “before the one who shears” is the more fitting reading, since while he was being beaten—that is, scourged by the soldiers of the governor—[Col. 0991A] he is not recorded to have answered anything, but to have remained silent like a lamb while being beaten and scourged by the shepherd.

And because he was unjustly condemned and patiently endured everything, the things that follow happened to him for his glory.

“From distress,” he says, that is, from the passion, “and from judgment,” the unjust judgment of the Jews, “he was taken away,” that is, removed; on the third day he was raised from the dead, when according to his humanity all heavenly and earthly power was given to him.

It follows: “Who shall declare his generation?” No one. This may be understood in two ways: either of his divine generation, concerning which he himself says through Wisdom: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. VIII); or of his human generation, concerning which Mary says to the angel: “How shall this happen, since I do not know man?” And the angel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I).

Who among human beings can comprehend how the supreme and life-giving Spirit, God, assumed the flesh of our mortality in the womb? No one. The judgments of almighty God are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable.

What he adds—“because he was cut off from the land of the living”—belongs to what was said above: “From distress and judgment he was taken away.” In this passage “the land of the living” means human society, from which he was removed by the persecuting Jews, who said: “Come, let us put wood in his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living” (Jer. XI).

“For the crime of my people I struck him,” that is, on account of the sins of my people, whom I have always held as my own possession, “I struck him”—that is, I permitted him to be struck—so that he might redeem and free them for me. God the Father struck him when he permitted him to be struck. The same is meant by: “I will strike the shepherd”—that is, I will permit him to be struck—“and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. XIII).

What follows—“And he shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death”—may be understood in two ways.

“He shall give the wicked Jews to the Romans for his burial” (Matt. XXVII), that is, because they persecuted him even to the burial, crying, “Crucify such a one!” and because, after he had died, they placed guards at the tomb and sealed the stone. “And the rich for his death”—namely, the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed rich because of their knowledge of the Law and the prophets—he will hand over to the Romans, because through envy they handed him over to death.

Or otherwise: he will give the wicked gentiles to God the Father for his burial. They were far from the piety that is God and from love, because Christ’s death was their price; and unless he had died, been given to burial, and risen on the third day, the nations would in no way have been saved.

Likewise, he gave the rich Jews who believed through his preaching or through the preaching of his apostles to God the Father for his death, through faith and works; previously they had been possessed by the devil.

And he will do this “because he committed no iniquity,” that is, no sin or transgression against the Law, “nor was deceit found in his mouth.” Whatever is done against the Law is iniquity. Hence among the Greeks it is called νόμος, *nomos*, “law.” Ἀνομία, *anomia*, means whatever is without law or against the law.

The Lord committed no iniquity in thought, speech, or deed—something that cannot truthfully be said of any other human being. “For there is no person upon earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII), even if his life upon earth were only one day.

“And” this happened—that is, he died for us—“because the Lord”—the Father—“willed to crush him in the weakness” of the flesh that he assumed. He says that the Lord the Father willed to crush him because the Father himself first ordained that he be killed.

“If he”—the Son of God—“sets down his soul,” that is, his life, “for sin” on behalf of the human race, “he shall see a long-lived seed” in the hearts of believers, that is, the word of the Gospel, which is eternal, since no other Law will succeed it. Concerning this seed he himself says in the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow his seed” (Luke VIII).

Or he will see his seed, who are all believers, because they will reign with him eternally. “And the will of the Lord”—the Father—“shall prosper in his hand,” that is, in his work and virtues; it shall be directed, that is, completed.

The will of God the Father was that he redeem the human race through the blood of his Son, as he himself said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke III), that is, “in whom I have placed my good pleasure.”

“Because his soul labored”—understand, in preaching among the Jewish people, performing miracles, and even enduring death for them, though they refused to turn to him through repentance—“he shall see,” understand, churches established throughout the whole world in place of the Jews, [Col. 0992C] “and he shall be satisfied,” that is, he shall delight in the faith and good works of believers.

For the faith of the elect is food and drink for almighty God. As he himself said to the disciples when he was speaking with the Samaritan woman while seated beside the well: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John IV). He said this concerning the faith of the Samaritans who believed in him.

“By his knowledge,” that is, by his teaching, “my righteous servant shall justify many”—understand, Jews—“and not all, because many are called but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). “And he himself shall bear their iniquities” through his grace, which they could not bear and under whose weight they were oppressed.

The Son of God is righteous because he committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth (Matt. XVII). Hence Judas the betrayer said: “I have sinned by betraying righteous blood.” And Pilate’s wife said: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.”

He did not receive this righteousness in time, but according to his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father and of one divinity and power with him—not according to the humanity of our frailty. Likewise, he is the servant of God the Father according to his humanity, by which he is less than the Father, because, although he was “in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II).

He bore—that is, took away—our iniquities, that is, he endured in his body upon the wood the punishment of our sins and took sins away from us, as a physician takes away the illnesses of the sick. The text continues.

[Col. 0993A] “Therefore”—understand, because he suffered for the salvation of the human race and did everything that the preceding discourse recounts—“I shall distribute,” or divide, “to him many”—understand, peoples—so that, in place of the one people that does not wish to believe in him, he may possess all the nations. As the Father says to him through the Psalmist: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

Hence what follows: “And he shall divide the spoils of the strong”—understand, among his disciples. He therefore handed over the plunder of the strong to his apostles when he took from the devil the peoples who had been under his power and divided them among the apostles, so that one would preside over one people and another over another. Thus Peter presided over the believing Jews, Paul over the nations, John and Andrew over the Achaeans, Thomas over the Indians, and the others over the others.

[Col. 0993B] Let us see what was said about blessed Paul the apostle long beforehand: “Benjamin,” he says, “is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. XLIX). And concerning all the apostles: “They shall rejoice before you, as victors rejoice over captured prey when they divide the spoils,” dividing churches throughout the whole world among themselves.

And why will this happen? “Because he himself delivered” the Son of God “his soul to death,” that is, his life, “and was reckoned among criminals”—not by God the Father or the saints, but by the Jewish persecutors—according to what is said elsewhere: “He was reckoned among the wicked.”

“And he himself bore the sins of many” by his blood, by the regeneration of baptism, and by their faith; “and he prayed for the transgressors”—the Jews, or the persecutors—saying, while hanging on the cross: “Father, forgive them” (Luke XXIII).

As it is found in the Gospel of the Nazarenes, at this saying of the Lord many thousands of the Jews standing around the cross believed.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0993]

## CHAPTER LIV

[Col. 0993B]

“Praise, O barren woman who do not give birth; sing praise and neigh, you who did not give birth.” Up to this point the Prophet has spoken about the Lord’s birth, passion, and the glory of his resurrection; now he returns to the calling of the nations and to those who believed in him, both from the Jews and from the nations.

“Barren” in this passage specifically means the gentile world, which was not begetting spiritual children for God because it had neither the Law, nor prophets, nor patriarchs. Now it begets more children of God than the Synagogue, which thinks that it has God as its husband. The Church that was desolate among the Jews may also be called barren, because, when the Lord came, it was not giving birth to his children. We may therefore refer this to both Churches, from the Jews as well as from the nations, according to what the outstanding preacher demonstrates in his words.

Taking the testimony from Isaiah that we now have before us, he referred it to the children of the promise, to the Church from the nations, or to the Church gathered from both peoples. It had been desolate and abandoned by God and remained barren, not having God Almighty as its husband.

“Praise,” he says, “your Creator and our Redeemer, O barren Church, from both Jews and nations, because now you will begin to give birth to children for God. Sing to your Savior, and shout for joy”—that is, rejoice greatly—“you who did not give birth to children for God.”

Because of the greatness of the joy, he alluded to the neighing of a horse advancing toward victory, predicting why he commanded her to exult and praise the Lord.

“For the children of the desolate”—understand, the Church of the nations, once abandoned by God—“are many more than those of her”—that is, the Synagogue—“who has a husband, says the Lord”; that is, who thinks that she has God Almighty as her husband.

This should be noted: when it is said, “The children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband,” the Synagogue is not entirely excluded from giving birth. For through the apostles and in the apostles she herself bore many children for God; but the immense multitude of the nations is placed before her.

“Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins [Col. 0994B] of your dwelling-places; do not spare. Lengthen your cords, and strengthen your pegs.” To her who was earlier told, “Sing praise, barren woman who do not bear,” and the rest of what is said there, it is now said again that she should enlarge her tent in the likeness of Moses’ tabernacle, and, possessing everything that that tabernacle possessed, make all of it greater and stronger.

Moses’ tabernacle, which was one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, and which had coverings, red-dyed and hyacinth-colored skins, cords, and pegs, signified the holy Church. Those who dwell in tents [Col. 0994C] in tents pass from place to place, journeying toward a house and toward the promised land, as the Jews did. The saints also dwell in tents in the present age—that is, in churches—because they are pilgrims and strangers in this world. As the Psalmist says: “I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim” (Psalm 118), journeying toward the house of which the same Psalmist says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26). And they journey toward the promised land, of which he likewise says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” The Lord also speaks of it in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5).

The holy Church therefore has the place of its tent enlarged, because churches bearing the name of Christ have spread toward the east [Col. 0994D] and the north, toward the west and the south. The skins of the holy Church are the preachers and pastors who protect her from the heat of vices and demons and from every adversity. The tabernacle had, as we have said, goat-hair coverings, by which penitents are signified, since sackcloth is the garment of penitence. It had red-dyed skins, by which martyrs are signified; it also had hyacinth-colored skins, by which all who bear the pallor of abstinence are signified. It had cords, by which the divine commandments are signified, and pegs by which the cords were stretched and the entire tabernacle was secured. By these we may understand [Col. 0995A] understanding and reason, by which the divine commandments are made firm—namely, when we fulfill in rational action the things we rationally understand.

He therefore says to the holy Church: O Church, enlarge the place of your tent through the four regions of the world, and do not confine yourself to one corner of Judea alone. Stretch out and spread your skins—that is, your preachers—throughout the world. Do not spare or cease multiplying them, so that by their protection you may be guarded from the heat of demons. Lengthen your cords—that is, extend your preaching far and wide, and lengthen the divine commandments. Strengthen your pegs—that is, confirm and fortify your understanding and reason. It continues:

“For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left,” [Col. 0995B] that is, you shall possess all nations; or, alternatively, you shall endure prosperity and prevail both here and in the future, because you will neither be lifted up by prosperity nor crushed by adversity. We may also understand “right” and “left” as the two lives, namely the present and the future: by the left, the present life; by the right, eternal life. In accordance with what Wisdom says: “In her right hand are length of days, but in her left hand riches and glory” (Proverbs 5).

The holy Church has riches and glory in the left hand, that is, in the present life, because she possesses knowledge and understanding of the divine words, which are spiritual riches; and she possesses the virtue of good works, by which she is glorified among the nations. In the right hand she has length of days and life, because, setting aside present things, she hastens toward those that are future, [Col. 0995C] in which she will remain eternally with the Lord and enjoy eternal joys.

And what follows—“and your seed shall inherit the nations”—may be understood in two ways: either of the seed of the Gospel, concerning which it is said in the Gospel, “The sower went out to sow his seed”; or of the apostles, who were sown by God, and concerning whom Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom.” The nations now inherit the seed of the Church—whether this is understood as evangelical doctrine or as the apostles—because everything possessed by Christ, who is the head of the Church, is also possessed and inherited by the Church, which is his body. “And it shall inhabit deserted cities,” that is, it shall inhabit nations, or churches, or souls abandoned by God.

“Do not fear,” O Church of the nations, “for you shall not be confounded [Col. 0995D] nor shall you blush; for you shall not be ashamed”—understand, that you were once abandoned by your husband—“because you shall forget the shame of your youth,” when you come to the faith and your husband receives you, “and you shall remember the reproach of your widowhood no more.”

Almighty God now addresses the Church from the nations as she comes to his faith. She is understood to have been abandoned by him when the tower of Babel was built. But a question arises here. Why does he say here, “You shall remember the reproach of your widowhood no more,” when above he said that she had been barren and had no husband, and that she would have more children than the Synagogue, which thought that she had a husband? This question can be resolved from the words of the Lord speaking through the prophet Zechariah. For there [Col. 0996A] it is said: “And I took for myself two staffs,” he says, “one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord” (Zechariah 11).

By the two staffs he wishes the two peoples to be understood: the nations and the Jews. By the one he called Beauty, the Gentiles are understood, whom he chose in Noah and his sons. By the other, which he called Cord, the Jewish people are shown, whom Almighty God chose at the building of the tower, in the family of Eber, and in Abraham. Hence it is said in what follows: “And I cut off from my service and grace the staff called Beauty, and I joined myself to the staff called Cord.”

In the confusion of languages, the Gentiles were cast away from their husband until the time of his incarnation, while the Jewish people were chosen. Therefore the former is said to be a widow and without a husband, while the latter is said to have a husband. [Col. 0996B] Hence Moses also says in the song of Deuteronomy (chapter 32): “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam at the tower of Babel, he set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God”—or, according to the number of the sons of Israel. “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.”

He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God because he appointed an angel over each nation. He therefore says, “You shall forget the shame of your youth, and you shall remember the reproach of your widowhood no more,” because, when she was abandoned by God at the building of the tower, she was still like an adolescent and a young girl. But although she endured the reproach of her widowhood for a long time, after she came to the faith she cast off all shame, having now been joined to her proper husband through the bond of faith and love. Why was this so? It is made clear [Col. 0996C] in what follows:

“For he who made you shall rule over you,” he says; “the Lord of hosts is his name”—that is, of armies or of angels—“and your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel,” who redeemed you with his blood. He shall be called the God of the whole earth, not merely of one region or one corner of Judea, but of all creatures, both heavenly and infernal.

“For as a woman abandoned”—understand, by her husband—“and sorrowful in spirit, he has called you” to his faith, so that you might cling to him; “and your God has said that you are a wife rejected from her youth.” The Gentiles were a woman abandoned by her husband when, because of idolatry, they lost their husband, Almighty God [Col. 0996D], and this happened during their youth. The Gentiles had their youth in the sons of Noah and in the building of the tower.

“For a brief moment I abandoned you, and with great mercies I will gather you.” Why does he say that the Gentiles were abandoned only briefly, when they served the devil for many thousands of years and did not cling to their Creator? Because all periods of time, when compared with God’s eternity, are exceedingly brief and small. Concerning these great mercies of the Lord the Psalmist says: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32), and: “His mercy is over all his works” (Psalm 144). His mercy was therefore indescribable, since, without any preceding [Col. 0997A] merits of ours, he recalled us to his life and grace. What follows is:

“In a moment of my indignation I hid my face”—that is, my presence for a little while—“from you,” understand, because of your idolatry; “but with everlasting mercy I have taken pity on you,” redeeming you with my blood, “says the Lord, your Redeemer.” This contains the same meaning as the preceding verse.

Almighty God is said to hide his face from us, although he is everywhere, when on account of our sins he withdraws from us his customary grace and his customary help. He rightly says, “With everlasting mercy I have taken pity on you,” because the Gentiles will possess the everlasting mercy of Almighty God, clinging to him through faith and love.

[Col. 0997B] “As in the days of Noah”—understand, when the flood came on account of the sins of the human race—“this is to me,” understand, the oath that I swore not to bring the waters upon the earth again; “so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you,” O Church, “and will not rebuke you.” The meaning is: Just as I have not violated the oath that I swore to Noah, namely, that I would no longer bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, so I will no longer be angry with you, O Church, to the point of casting you away as I have done until now.

“For the mountains shall be moved and the hills shall tremble, but my mercy shall not depart”—understand, from you—“and the covenant of my peace that I made with you shall not be moved,” that is, it shall not be dissolved by you. “Says the Lord, who has had compassion on you.” The meaning is: The mountains and hills will be moved sooner, and heaven and earth [Col. 0997C] will pass away, as it is said in the Gospel, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24), than my mercy and the covenant that I made with you will depart from you. It continues:

“O poor little one, shaken by the storm, without any consolation,” that is, without any consoler. He still addresses the Church from the nations and calls her poor because she had been weakened through idolatry. Or she was poor because she did not possess the spiritual riches of the Law, the prophets, and the Psalms. She was shaken by the storm—that is, trampled and torn apart—because she had endured many whirlwinds of the world, the terrors of demons, and had been tossed amid various errors concerning idols. Without consolation—that is, without any consoler—she remained for a long time, because she had no patriarchs, no prophets, no apostles, [Col. 0997D] and did not even possess the true Consoler, the Holy Spirit, who is called the Paraclete, that is, the Consoler.

“Behold, I will lay your stones in order,” O Church, “and will establish you upon sapphires; I will place your battlements in jasper, and your gates in carved stones.” What are the stones of the holy Church? They are the holy preachers and the other faithful. Concerning them Peter says: “And you, as living stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2).

Let us take one stone as representing all: the Lord Jesus Christ, upon whom the other stones were built and ordered. Daniel saw him (chapter 2) cut from the mountain without hands, and concerning him the prophet Isaiah earlier spoke in the person of God the Father [Col. 0998A]: “Behold,” he says, “I lay in Zion a cornerstone, precious and chosen” (Isaiah 28). This, then, is the stone rejected by the builders (Psalm 117), namely the scribes and Pharisees. But it grew into a great mountain and now contains two walls, namely the two peoples, those of circumcision and of uncircumcision.

Although the holy Church is adorned with various orders of stones, that is, of the faithful, she nevertheless contains three more excellent orders: preachers, virgins, and the continent. These too are represented by the names of three righteous men mentioned by Ezekiel: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

Noah, who guided the ark amid the waters of the flood, represented the holy preachers, who amid the waves and storms of this age guide and govern the holy [Col. 0998B] Church by their protection, so that she may reach the harbor and shore of eternal stability unharmed between Scylla and Charybdis—that is, between heretics and pagans. Daniel, who preserved virginity both of body and of mind while placed in the court of the king of Babylon, signifies the saints placed in the Church who, with all their strength, sincerely preserve virginity of mind and body. Job, however, a just and upright man who had a wife and children, represents the order of married people. Although they are bound by marital ties, they render the debt owed to their wife in such a way that they do not displease their Creator.

Since the two names of stones placed here are sapphire and jasper, let us also see what they signify. “I will lay your stones in order,” he says, “and will establish you upon sapphires; I will place your battlements in jasper, and I will place your gates in carved stones.”

Sapphire, a stone [Col. 0998C] that preserves the likeness of a clear sky, signifies the saints who shine with serenity of mind, enduring the adversities and prosperities of this age with equanimity for Christ’s name, and who can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Jasper, which has a green color, signifies the holy preachers who shine with the freshness of faith and charity. The holy Church therefore has battlements made of jasper, because she has preachers radiant with the freshness of faith and charity, who fight on her behalf against demons, heretics, and all persecutors, to such an extent that they even lay down their lives for her at the risk of death.

What follows—“And I will place your gates in carved stones”—must be referred to those same [Col. 0998D] preachers and pastors of the Church, who bring the multitude of believers into the holy Church through the regeneration of baptism. They are rightly said to be carved, because they ought to impress the words and examples of the preceding Fathers upon their hearts, so that at the appropriate time they may make them clear to their hearers.

“And all your boundaries”—understand, I will make them—“desirable.” These are the boundaries of the Church, which are also her gates: namely, the preachers and teachers. They are rightly called boundaries because hearers ought not to transgress the faith and doctrine of the preachers. And just as the earth is held together by its boundaries and limits, so the holy Church is established by the faith, preaching, and miracles of the preceding Fathers and preachers. [Col. 0999A] She is not confined to one corner of Judea alone, but extends far and wide through all the boundaries of the earth.

“All your sons shall be taught by the Lord”—understand, I will give them or make them so—“and I will give your sons an abundance of peace.”

“And you shall be founded in righteousness,” that is, you shall be made firm. He now explains whom he earlier called stones: namely, the sons of the Church. All the sons of the Church are taught by the Lord, because through his teaching they become sons of God. As he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6). And in the prophets: “They shall all be taught by the Lord,” he says.

“I will give your sons an abundance of peace,” that is, I will reconcile your sons to you. When he says, [Col. 0999B] “You shall be founded in righteousness,” by righteousness he wishes all the virtues to be understood, so that the meaning is: You shall be founded in righteousness—that is, you shall be made firm by the faith of Christ, by eternal justification, and by the fullness of virtues.

“Depart far from oppression,” that is, from violence, robbery, or iniquity, “because you shall not fear”—understand, the devil, nor the attack of heretics or persecutors—“and from terror”—understand, do not fear it—“because it shall not approach you.”

Earlier he consoled the Church from the nations by promising her spiritual graces; now he teaches what she must do if she does not wish to fear the assault of her adversaries. The meaning is: Do you not wish to fear your enemies? Do what I say: depart from oppression and iniquity, and do not fear the terror of men.

[Col. 0999C] “Behold, the sojourner shall come who was not with me; your former stranger shall be joined to you.” This is the voice of Christ speaking to the primitive Church about the multitude of the nations coming to the faith. Before the Lord’s coming, they were strangers and far from God. “Behold,” he says, “the sojourner”—namely, the Gentile people—“shall come to me through faith,” believing rightly and living well, “who previously was not with me,” serving idols and various errors. “The stranger,” that is, your former proselyte, O primitive Church—namely, the people of the nations, who were formerly far from you and from your faith—“shall now be joined to you” by the name of Christian and by the unity of faith.

The holy Church, which previously existed among the Jews alone, now consists of both peoples, those of circumcision and of uncircumcision, gathered into one fold. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “And [Col. 0999D] I have other sheep,” he says, “which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10). The Jews foolishly think that this is said of Jerusalem, because many from the nations would become proselytes at the time of their Christ.

“Behold, I created the smith who blows the coals in the fire and brings forth a vessel for his work.” In this passage he calls the devil a smith, the inventor of every evil and the craftsman of all wickedness and iniquity. This does not mean that Almighty God created him evil with respect to his nature; rather, having become evil through his own fault, he fashions weapons of iniquity every day.

By the fire and coals we must understand the incitement of lust toward vices and other sins, as well as persecution, [Col. 1000A] all of which the devil blows upon—that is, excites. He also brings forth vessels for his work, namely every heretic and pagan who does his will. Thus he brought forth Simon Magus and Elymas: one resisted blessed Peter and inflicted many evils, while the other opposed the distinguished preacher Paul.

Let it therefore be said: “I created the smith,” that is, the devil, “who blows the coals in the fire,” that is, who excites persecution and wickedness, “and brings forth a vessel for his work,” that is, any heretic or perverse person to do his will.

“And every vessel that has been fashioned” by the devil against you, O Church, “shall not prosper,” because it will suffer present and future punishments; “and every tongue” of heretics, scribes, Pharisees, and even philosophers, [Col. 1000B] “that resists you in judgment you shall judge,” or even condemn, or certainly distinguish and discern through disputation with them.

As it is written elsewhere: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject” (1 Corinthians 1). Simon and Elymas indeed attempted to resist the holy apostles, as we have said, with their doctrine and wisdom, but they were condemned by them and judged not to be speaking the truth. So Hilary, so Augustine, so Jerome, and Athanasius fought against the vessels of the devil through their disputations.

“This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord.” So that the elect would not think that they were enduring the labor of the present life for Christ’s name in vain, he adds the rewards of their merits. “This,” he says, “is the inheritance of the servants [Col. 1000C] of the Lord,” namely eternal life, the kingdoms of heaven, and the recompense of their labors—those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 1). And this is the righteousness of those who belong to the Lord: that they receive eternal rewards for the labor of the present life, and that present tribulation be encompassed by future joy.

## CHAPTER LV

“All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy, and eat.” The divine word addresses everyone generally, both Jews and Gentiles, so that they may come to the waters of salvation, of which Isaiah says elsewhere: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isaiah 12).

Thirst is to be understood spiritually here, as is the spiritual [Col. 1000D] water concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). The Evangelist consequently explained what this meant, saying that he spoke of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.

“All you who thirst,” that is, who desire or seek knowledge of the Old and New Testament, “come to the waters” of baptism, or to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. “And you who have no silver,” that is, the divine words, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested” (Psalm 11), “hasten,” quickly coming to my faith. “Buy” the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the water of baptism—not at the price of gold or silver or anything of that kind, but by believing and [Col. 1001A] living well. “And eat” that water itself, namely spiritual doctrine or the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by hearing, reading, meditating, and retaining it in the heart.

How, then, can we eat water? Holy Scripture is food in some places and drink in others. Wherever it is grasped with difficulty, it is food; where it has an easy meaning, it is drink.

“Come,” O peoples of the Gentiles, and all who need the words of the Old and New Testament, “and buy without silver, and without any exchange, wine and milk.” Human wisdom was bought at a price by philosophers, but the apostles were told: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10).

Scripture gives us wine when it says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Exodus 20), and in the words of John: “In the beginning was the Word.” [Col. 1001B] It gives us milk when it says: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and other things of this kind. By wine, therefore, the mysteries of the divine words are to be understood; by milk, simple doctrine suited to the faith of beginners, as the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able.”

“Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread,” that is, not for spiritual doctrines, “and your labor for what does not satisfy?” He now rebukes the scribes and Pharisees, the heretics and philosophers of the nations, and all who follow their perverse doctrines and fabricated traditions. Why do they spend or consume the brilliance of eloquence on the surface of the letter and on human wisdom, in which spiritual bread is not found [Col. 1001C]—the bread by which the soul is satisfied, namely spiritual understanding, in which there is knowledge of the true bread, which said: “I am the living bread” (John 7)?

Silver, as we have said in other places, signifies the brilliance of eloquence. There are many, says blessed Gregory, who read the sayings of the prophets and other divine Scriptures but do not find in them bread by which they may reach satisfaction, because they seek only the letter that kills and refuse to pursue the spiritual understanding that gives life, where the spiritual bread is found by which the soul is nourished (1 Corinthians 3). Gentiles also read human books and labor greatly over them, consuming the brilliance of eloquence; but they do not deserve to be satisfied, because spiritual understanding is not contained in them.

“Listen, listening to me, and eat what is good, [Col. 1001D] and your soul shall delight in richness.” Hearing is to be sought spiritually in the sacred word, as in the saying: “Let the one who has ears hear” (Revelation 2)—that is, let the one who has understanding of mind understand what I am about to say.

This eating is likewise to be sought spiritually, as in the passage said elsewhere: “If you listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Deuteronomy 28). Just as the body is made fat by bodily foods, so the soul is refreshed and nourished by spiritual doctrines and virtues. Concerning this richness the Psalmist says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Psalm 62), and: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Psalm 22).

“Listen,” he says, “listening to me”—that is, understand what I, who am speaking, will say, you who possess understanding [Col. 1002A]—“and eat what is good,” that is, understand Christ by believing rightly and living well, him who said: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Or understand and receive what is good, the word of the Gospel, concerning which it is also said: “Lord, did you not sow good seed?” (Matthew 13). “And your soul shall delight in richness,” that is, in virtues and spiritual doctrine.

“Bend your ear,” that is, listen to me humbly, “and come”—understand, to me—not spatially, but in merit, by believing rightly and living well. “Listen,” that is, obey my words, “and your soul shall live,” understand, possessing God within it in eternal life, him who grants life to those who believe in him.

“And I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.” He addresses the Jews here. To make a covenant means to strike it. [Col. 1002B] Hence it is said: “Abraham struck a covenant” (Genesis 15)—that is, he struck a victim for the covenant and agreement. As we read in the Old Testament, the Lord confirmed the covenant he struck with the sons of Israel by the blood of goats, calves, and lambs, giving them statutes.

The covenant that he made with us in the New Testament he confirmed by the blood of his Son, when he gave us the Gospel. Why, then, does he say, “I will make with you an everlasting covenant,” since it did not remain with them eternally? We must understand that he is speaking of the grace of the New Testament. For “the Law and the prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of God”—that is, the Gospel—is proclaimed (Matthew 11). It is called everlasting because another law will not succeed it. Hence John also says in his Apocalypse that he saw “the everlasting [Col. 1002C] Gospel” (Revelation 14).

When he says “the faithful mercies of David,” that is, the faithful promises, understand: “I will confirm them with you.” This is not to be understood of David the king, the son of Jesse, but of Christ, in whose figure David acted. For all the promises made to David concerned Christ.

“Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and instructor of the nations.” This is the voice of God the Father concerning the Son, whom he gave as a witness to the peoples—that is, as a testimony for the peoples—so that he might announce to them his precepts and commands. He speaks of himself and the Father: “For this I was born, that I might bear witness to the truth” (John 18). And again: “This Gospel must be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations” (Matthew 24).

He is the witness of all, whom the Father promised [Col. 1002D] and granted to the world. He is the leader, because he provided his faithful with guidance in righteousness, and he himself brings us from earthly things to the contemplation of God the Father and of himself, as he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). He is also our instructor and teacher, teaching us the way of truth; he said: “One is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23).

“Behold, you shall call nations whom you did not know, and nations that did not know you shall run to you.” God the Father addresses his Son concerning the calling of the nations to faith, and concerning the nations’ hastening to him, although previously they did not know him through faith and love. “Behold,” he says, “you shall call nations whom you did not know,” because of their idolatry, from empty worship to your faith through the preaching of your [Col. 1003A] apostles. “And nations that previously did not know you through faith shall run to you,” saying: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Psalm 45). “This is our God, whom we awaited.”

The faith of these people was spoken of above: “Those to whom nothing was preached about him shall see.” And the Lord speaks of them in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

It follows: And this will happen “because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, for he will glorify you.” Sometimes Holy Scripture speaks of the divinity of the Son of God, and sometimes of his humanity. When it speaks of him as God, who “in the beginning was God the Word with God the Father” (John 1), the Father is called the Father of glory. When it speaks of him who says in the Gospel, “You are persecuting me, a man who tells you the truth [Col. 1003B]” (John 8), he is called the Father of our divine Jesus Christ.

So here, when it says, “because of the Lord, your Father and God, and the Holy One of Israel, for he will glorify you,” it refers to the fact that he will glorify him in time with that glory which his divinity itself possessed eternally with the Father before all ages. God the Father glorified the Son at his baptism, when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He also glorified him in his death and passion by raising him from the dead.

“Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.” The prophet addresses the Jews who refused to receive the mercies and promises made to David, telling them to seek the Lord while there is time and opportunity—that is, while they live in this age. It is as though he said: Since you refused to receive the mercies made to David, while the nations received them, “do penance and turn back to the Lord while you have time.”

The Apostle speaks of this time: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6). He can indeed be found in the present—not spatially, but through the merit of faith. In the future, however, there will be neither opportunity nor time to seek God, but only to live. Therefore, “seek him while he may be found, while you are in the body, while an opportunity for repentance is granted.”

Let us also seek him—not spatially, but through faith. Let us seek him by believing rightly, living well, and persevering well, with simplicity of heart, as it is written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom 1).

It continues: “Call upon him while he is near,” that is, while there is opportunity, while [Col. 1003D] there is time. For the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth (Psalm 144), but he is far from those who depart from his will by sinning. Just as we draw near to him by serving him through good works—not spatially—so we draw away from him by laboring at vices. Hence he says through Jeremiah: “I am God who draws near to those who draw near to me in faith, and who withdraws far from those who withdraw far from me in unbelief” (Jeremiah 23). And the Apostle says to believers: “Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you” (James 4).

“Let the wicked man,” namely the Gentile people, “abandon his way,” the evil way of his former life, “and the unrighteous man,” namely the Jewish people, “his thoughts,” evil [Col. 1004A] and ancient, by which he was turning away from the Lord, when he said to them: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9). “And let him return to the Lord,” in accordance with the saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36). “And he will have mercy on him” who returns to him, “for he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18).

“And let him return to our God”—understand, let both peoples return by doing penance—“for he is abundant in forgiving,” that is, he is always ready to show mercy. Thus the Psalmist says: “His mercy is over all his works” (Psalm 144).

What we have said pertains specifically to the Gentile and Jewish peoples—“Let the wicked man abandon his way,” that is, his depraved conduct, “and the unrighteous man his perverse [Col. 1004B] thoughts”—can also appropriately be referred to every sinner who sins in thought and deed, so that by doing penance he may obtain God’s mercy. We then return to the Lord, and he has mercy on us because he is abundantly merciful, when, abandoning our former thoughts and ways, we devote ourselves to the virtues.

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord.” So that no one would doubt the salvation of both peoples, or think that he could not forgive everyone’s sins in deed and thought, he said these things. The meaning is: Do not think it difficult or impossible for me to save the Jewish people and all the Gentiles who do not know God. Consider that there is a great difference [Col. 1004C] between my counsels and yours, between my thoughts and yours, and between my nature and yours.

For just as my thoughts are unchangeable, so your thoughts are not, because human thoughts are vain. Nor are your ways—that is, your actions—like mine, for your ways are crooked and evil, whereas my ways are unchangeable and straight (Proverbs 19). “There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel and thought of the Lord will remain firm forever.” Hence it is added:

“For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted”—firm—“above your ways,” which are fragile, “and my thoughts,” fixed, “above your thoughts,” which are vain. As far as heaven is from earth—since one is the dwelling-place of angels and the other of human beings—so far do God’s thoughts and ways differ from human thoughts [Col. 1004D] and ways, and much farther still, because human thoughts and ways are crooked and unstable, whereas God’s are unchangeable and most direct.

Concerning God’s thoughts and ways it is said: “His judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable.” Concerning human counsel, however, it is said: “They devised a plan that they were unable to establish.”

“And just as rain and snow descend from heaven”—that is, from the clouds—“and do not return there again, but saturate the earth” with their dew, “and soak it, and make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater: so shall my word be”—that is, my decree—which shall go forth from my mouth. “It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it.” [Col. 1005A] Here he gives another comparison, showing that his counsel and will are unchangeable. The meaning is: Just as this thing I say is unchangeable, so that when rain has descended upon the earth it does not return upward, but saturates the earth with its dew so that it may produce various fruits, so what I have said concerning the salvation of the Jewish people and the calling of the nations will be firm.

Allegorically, however, by “rain” we may understand evangelical teaching, which comes from the clouds—that is, from the apostles—upon the dry hearts of earthly people and fertilizes them with its dew, so that they may produce the fruits of righteousness and virtues. By “the word,” which he says goes forth from his mouth and accomplishes his will, we may understand the Word of God the Father, of whom John says (Chapter I): “In the beginning was the Word.” [Col. 1005B] Nevertheless, when he says that it will go forth from his mouth, we must not think that almighty God possesses members such as human nature does; rather, he speaks according to our manner of expression, so that through our nature we may learn about God’s words.

God the Father therefore sent this Word so that through him he might fulfill his will and purpose—that is, so that through him he might redeem the human race—as the Son himself says: “I always do the things that please him” (John VIII). He therefore did what the Father willed by redeeming the human race, and he prospered according to his humanity when, through his preaching and the faith proclaimed throughout the whole world, the nations believed in him; and thus he returned to the right hand of the Father’s majesty.

“For you shall go forth in joy, and shall be led forth in peace.” [Col. 1005C] God the Father addresses both the Jews and those who come to him through faith. “In joy,” he says, “you shall go forth, O Gentiles,” from the error of unbelief and the worship of idols to the light of faith and knowledge of me. Or, “O Jews,” from the shadow of the Law to the grace and truth of the Gospel. And “in peace”—that is, in Christ—you shall be led to the heavenly homeland, away from the darkness of sins. Concerning this peace the Apostle says: “Grace to you and peace” (Romans I). And again: “He himself is our peace, who made peace between us and God the Father” (Ephesians II).

“The mountains and hills shall sing praise before you, and all the trees of the region shall clap their hands.” By the mountains and hills are understood the angelic powers and the souls of the saints—patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and the other saints—which, on account of the variety of their virtues, are called mountains and hills, and which rejoice in the salvation of both peoples. [Col. 1005D] Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is joy in heaven among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV). What follows, “and all the trees of the region shall clap their hands,” is to be understood of the multitude of the nations and the faithful, who preceded the Gentiles. One of these trees says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm LI).

“In place of the thornbush the fir shall grow, and in place of the nettle the myrtle shall grow.” The thornbush, or thorn plant, is an herb full of spines and pricks. The fir, however, is a tall and lofty tree, suitable both for constructing a house [Col. 1006A] and for producing pitch. It is as though he were saying in other words: In place of vices, virtues shall rise; and in place of unbelievers, the faithful. For example, when any unbeliever comes to the grace of baptism—one who previously was a thornbush, that is, an unfruitful tree—he rises to the heights of virtues and becomes a fir.

By the nettle, which is of a fiery nature, are signified the lustful and greedy, and those who are alienated from the faith of Christ and pricked by the thorns of sins. They are changed into myrtles—which are aromatic and fragrant trees—when they pass from vices to virtues and give forth from themselves the good fragrance of virtues. Were the apostle Paul and Zacchaeus not like a thornbush, that is, unfruitful trees, and like a nettle, when one pricked Christians with the thorns of persecution and the other burned with the thorns of greed and the fever of avarice? [Col. 1006B] But when they were quickly converted to the faith, they grew into firs and myrtles, so much so that one of them said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians II).

“And the Lord shall be named as an everlasting sign, which shall not be taken away.” When, he says, the faithful have risen in place of unbelievers, and the chaste and those who despise riches have grown in place of the lustful and greedy, the Lord shall be named throughout the whole world as an everlasting sign, because Christians are called from Christ; and this sign of salvation shall not be taken away from the hearts of the faithful. By this sign—that is, by the name of Christ—all the faithful shall be marked until the day of judgment.

## CHAPTER LVI

[Col. 1006C] “Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment”—that is, judge all alike, not showing partiality toward the person of the poor in judgment. When he adds, “practice righteousness,” by righteousness we must understand all the virtues that justify God’s elect. And why do I command these things? “Because my salvation is near, so that it may come”—that is, my Son Jesus, whose coming is near; he is interpreted as “Savior,” because “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I)—“and my righteousness is near,” so that it may be revealed in its proper time, according to the Apostle’s statement: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians IV). The salvation of God the Father and his righteousness is the Son, because through him he saves and justifies all the elect.

“Blessed is the man who does this,” namely, judgment and righteousness, and does everything with discernment. [Col. 1006D] “And the son of man who grasps this,” namely, judgment—that is, who holds Christ firmly by believing in him, to whom “the Father has given all judgment” (John V). Similar to this verse is what the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times” (Psalm CV).

He speaks of two persons: a blessed man and a blessed son of man. The one who labors manfully in the commandments of the Lord, forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead until he comes to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, “to mature manhood and the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians IV), will without doubt deserve to attain adoption as a son of God.

It follows: “Keeping the sabbath, so as not to profane it, keeping his hands from doing any evil.” [Col. 1007A] He keeps the sabbath who fulfills God’s commandments and turns away from vices. “Keeping,” he says, “the sabbath by ceasing from vices, so as not to profane it,” he is blessed; and keeping his hands from robbery and every iniquity, so as not to do any evil—that is, any sin—because “whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James II).

“And let not the son of the foreigner who clings to the Lord say: ‘The Lord will surely separate me from his people.’” They called Gentiles “foreigners” who, abandoning the practice of paganism, passed through circumcision to Judaism, clinging to the Lord through faith and conduct. [Col. 1007B] These words are directed against the Jews who, boasting of the nobility of their lineage, said that Christ’s coming concerned no one but themselves, since he took his bodily origin from their stock.

Hearing their words, the Gentiles who were joined to them despaired of salvation, thinking that they could not equal them in eternal glory, and saying: “The Lord will separate me from his people when he comes.” But in that spiritual regeneration there is no distinction of sex or status, whether a male or female, free person or slave, comes to faith and is cleansed by the baptism of sanctification. For “in every nation, whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X). In accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free; but all are one” (Galatians III).

Therefore the Prophet consoles the Gentiles and says: Let not the son of the foreigner, or the stranger, who clings to the Lord through circumcision and faith say: [Col. 1007C] “The Lord will separate me from his people when he comes to save his Jewish people,” because more are to be saved through faith from the Gentiles than from the Jews.

“And let not the eunuch say: ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’” There are three kinds of eunuchs. There are eunuchs made so by other human beings, and there are others who are born from their mother’s womb in such a way that they have no capacity to beget children. Finally, there are eunuchs of both sexes who keep themselves from every impurity and preserve virginity for the love of God. Concerning them the Lord says: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX)—not by cutting off their genitals, but by restraining lust. [Col. 1007D]

The Prophet here consoles all of them in the person of the Lord, so that they may not despair of eternal salvation or be saddened because they do not have bodily children, on account of which the person who did not leave offspring upon the earth was cursed in the Law. There, however, the reference is not to the seed of procreation but to the seed of good conduct. They thought that whoever had no children would have no rest in the kingdom of heaven with the holy fathers.

Allegorically, by these eunuchs we should understand all persons of both sexes who preserve virginity for the name of Christ. The divine word now addresses them, so that they do not lose hope of the heavenly homeland, although they lack bodily children, because they will not be separated from the glory of the elect if they have produced spiritual seed here—that is, if they have done good work. [Col. 1008A] Rather, they will receive from the Lord the crown and prize of virginity.

It follows:
