“Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs”—that is, to virgins—“who keep my sabbaths”—that is, who cease from every vice, through which a person becomes a son of the devil—“and choose the things I have willed”—that is, who preserve virginity—“and hold fast to my covenant”—that is, the pact or commandment that I made with them and that they fulfill in their conduct, devoting themselves continually to prayer, in accordance with the statement: “One ought always to pray” (Luke XVIII), and also considering what is said: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians V). [Col. 1008B]

It should be noted that he does not say, “and choose the things I have commanded,” but “the things I have willed,” because the Lord shows that he loves virginity, yet does not command it when he says: “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew XIX). The Apostle likewise says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Corinthians VII).

Let us see what reward the Lord promises them.

“I will give them,” he says, “in my house”—supply: a place—that is, in the present Church I will give them the highest honor, so that they may exercise the priestly office in it and have many spiritual children in place of bodily children. Or, I will give them a place in my house, namely in the heavenly Jerusalem, where there are many dwelling places (John XIV).

“And in my walls I will give them a place”—that is, I will establish them among the number of preachers, so that they may become the strongest towers of my city, fortifying and protecting those subject to them by the word or example of their preaching.

“And a name better than that of sons and daughters”—that is, a name more excellent than that of others who beget bodily sons and daughters. [Col. 1008C] “I will give them an everlasting name”—that is, the name of Christianity, so that they may be called Christians from my Christ—“a name that shall never fail.”

“And the sons of the foreigner”—that is, of the Gentiles—“who cling to the Lord,” believing in him, I will give [them], supply: to his holy name, “so that they may worship him,” confessing him, “and love his name”—that is, the name of the Son—“so that they may be his servants,” as the Apostle speaks of himself: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ” (Galatians I).

“Every one,” supply: whether eunuch or foreigner, “who keeps my sabbath, so as not to profane it”—that is, who ceases from evil conduct—“and holds fast to my covenant,” so that he may always devote himself to prayer.

“I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer”—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, where the elect will do nothing other than offer praises to God and devote themselves to prayer. [Col. 1008D] The holy mountain to which he promises to bring them may be the doctrines of truth and the confession of the Trinity; or the present Church; or even the Lord himself, who is the mountain of mountains. Concerning him the same Prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah II). To contemplation of him he himself will bring his elect.

“Their burnt offerings and sacrifices”—that is, those of the eunuchs and foreigners—“will be pleasing to me upon my altar, because my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations.”

Burnt offerings are those that are entirely consumed by fire, for “holocaust” means something wholly burned and consumed. [Col. 1009A] Sacrifices are so called from being bound, because they were brought bound and tied to the door of the Lord’s house and handed over to the priests. Part of them was offered upon the altar, while another part was given to the priests.

By these words he does not command the eunuchs or foreigners to offer sacrifice according to the Jews; rather, he commands them to offer a spiritual sacrifice, concerning which the Apostle says: “I urge you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans XII). And elsewhere: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.” To preserve virginity of mind and body is to offer spiritual sacrifices to God.

To make some distinction, however: whoever devotes himself to prayer for a time and then, for the sake of children and not because of lust, renders the due to his wife for a time offers sacrifices. But whoever abandons everything for the name of Christ offers a burnt offering, in accordance with what the Lord says: “If you would be perfect, go, sell everything, and give to the poor” (Matthew XIX). [Col. 1009B]

Or, whoever, living in the world, keeps part of his substance for himself, for his own needs and to meet the needs of his family, and distributes another part to the needy and poor for the name of Christ, offers sacrifices. God therefore commands eunuchs and foreigners—that is, virgins and believers from the nations—to offer such burnt offerings and sacrifices: they are to despise the world entirely, preserve virginity, devote themselves to prayer, and offer these things upon the altar—that is, in the true faith.

For just as sacrifices and burnt offerings were placed upon the altar and consumed there, so all virtues and all good works are established in faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God. Hence it is said: “But my righteous one lives by faith.” [Col. 1009C]

It follows: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Habakkuk I). He is not speaking only of the one temple of the city of Jerusalem, where prayer and the gathering of only the Jewish nation took place, but of the Church, which has been spread throughout the whole world and to which many peoples daily flock.

“Thus says the Lord, who gathers the dispersed of Israel” into one fold and one Church. He calls the twelve tribes “the dispersed of Israel,” to whom Peter was writing; or all believers, concerning whom the Lord says to the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matthew XIX), and so forth.

The Evangelist speaks of this gathering, or of the dispersed: “Jesus,” he says, “was about to die for the nation” (John XI), [Col. 1009D] “and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were dispersed.” “I will still gather others to him”—that is, to Christ—“in addition to those already gathered to him”—that is, all those predestined to life—“and I will bring them” to his faith and to the Church, or to the heavenly Jerusalem. These are the words of the Father to the Son.

It follows:

“All the beasts of the field, come to devour; all the beasts of the forest”—supply: come and prepare to devour the Jewish people, who refused to believe in Christ. “Gather,” says the Prophet, “all the nations, so that they may come and destroy the wretched Jews who remained in unbelief.”

He calls them beasts because they lived irrationally like beasts, worshiping the creature instead of the Creator, venerating various apparitions of demons, and dwelling in the forest of vices. [Col. 1010A] When the Romans came against the Jews in the forty-second year after the Lord’s ascension, soldiers from nearly every nation came, for they held the whole world under their dominion. Therefore it is now said: “all the beasts of the field”—that is, soldiers from all the nations. The field is the world, as the Lord explains in one place in the Gospel (Matthew XIII).

By the beasts of the field we may also understand the demons, to whom the wretched Jews were handed over for punishment, in accordance with Jeremiah’s statement: “Israel is a wandering sheep; lions drove it away” (Jeremiah L). And the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion.”

“All his watchmen are blind; they have not known”—supply: they have not known God or the true light. [Col. 1010B] “Mute dogs, unable to bark.” It is the custom of the Scriptures to call kings, princes, and teachers “watchmen,” as here it calls the scribes, Pharisees, and priests of the Jews, who were blind and did not know how to behold “the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). Or they were blind because they did not possess the light of faith or the splendor of virtues.

Hence the Lord says to them: “Woe to you blind men who say: ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the altar is bound by his oath’” (Matthew XXIII). The word “watchman” is used in both a good and a bad sense. In the good sense, as when the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel III); and Isaiah says: “Upon the watchtower [Col. 1010C] of the Lord I stand by day and by night” (Isaiah XXI). It is used in the bad sense here and in very many other places.

Not only are they called blind watchmen, but also “mute dogs unable to bark,” because of their laziness. Just as dogs guard the flock from wolves by barking, so they ought to have uttered the barking of preaching and driven demons from the hearts of those subject to them.

“Seeing vain things”—that is, being wise in evil—“and understanding useless things, sleeping”—that is, lying in sins, serving lust, and being sluggish in good works—“and loving dreams,” by which they were deceived by demons. Hence they said: “I dreamed, I dreamed” (Jeremiah XXIII). Those watchmen were indeed asleep, paying no attention to the words: “Do not give sleep to your eyes” (Proverbs VI), or to the Gospel’s command: “Watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matthew XXV). [Col. 1010D]

To heighten their wickedness, he adds:

“Dogs utterly shameless”—that is, without restraint—“they have not known satiety,” supply: of error and wickedness. Just as shameless dogs return to their vomit, so they, after satisfying the wickedness they had conceived in their hearts, immediately returned to their former vices, in accordance with the proverb: “A dog returns to its vomit” (Proverbs XXIV).

Or, alternatively: Just as dogs shamelessly bark while pursuing a wolf or even a robber, so they shamelessly cried out against the Lord: “Crucify him, crucify him; he is guilty of death” (Matthew XXVII).

“The shepherds themselves have not known understanding”—supply: of the Law and the prophets. [Col. 1011A] Those whom above he had called watchmen and dogs he now calls shepherds, namely the scribes, Pharisees, and teachers of the Jews—not because they were truly shepherds, but because they were hirelings who did not know the divine Law, as the Lord says to them: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew XXII).

“All have turned aside to their own way”—that is, to their own wicked conduct. These were the scribes and watchmen of the Jews, who, departing from God’s will and following the devil, fulfilled the words: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalm XIII, 52).

“Each one has turned aside to his own greed,” seeking what is his own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians II). And they did this “from the highest to the lowest”—that is, from the greater to the lesser, from the prelates to the lowest subordinate—as the same Prophet says: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, there is no soundness in it” (Isaiah I). [Col. 1011B]

“Come, let us take wine; let us fill ourselves with drunkenness,” or *sikera*, as it is found in the Hebrew. The term is used for anything capable of causing intoxication. “And it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more.”

Thus those wretched men spoke to their companions and associates, who ought diligently to have observed and governed the conduct and actions of their subjects. And because they refused to repent after the Lord’s Passion, but persisted in wickedness, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah XXII), they were handed over to the Romans and miserably killed by them. [Col. 1011C]

## CHAPTER LVII

“The righteous man perishes, and no one considers it,” and so forth. The Hebrews report that Isaiah said this about himself: that he was cut in two with a wooden saw by Manasseh, and that he called the other prophets, whom that most impious king killed, “men of mercy.” But it is more truly understood of him who justifies every ungodly person. Concerning him Pilate’s wife said: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” And Pilate said: “What shall I do with Jesus who is called righteous?” (Matthew XXVII). [Col. 1011D]

The righteous Christ perishes in his Passion, and no one among the Jews—that is, among the reprobate—considers or reflects in his heart that he suffered such things not for his own sins but for the salvation of the human race. The expression “perishes” is spoken according to their estimation; or else because “perdition” does not always mean abolition or destruction, but may refer to the magnitude of suffering. For the Lord did not perish, since he rose on the third day.

By “men of mercy” we should understand the apostles, who came to us not because of our merits, in order to snatch us from the power of the devil. “These men of mercy are gathered” to the heavenly homeland, “and there is no one who understands”—that is, none of the reprobate considers that they are slaughtered for their righteousness and endure such things.

“From the presence of wickedness”—that is, from the presence of sin—“the righteous man has been gathered” by God the Father: Christ, rising from the dead; or, because of the wickedness of the people whose sins he bore in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness, he ascended victoriously to the Father (1 Peter II). [Col. 1012A]

“Let peace come; let him who walked in his right way rest in his bed”—that is, in uprightness. Blessed Jerome says that in Hebrew the reading is *let them rest*, although the singular number is found in some books. This can be understood in two ways.

The Prophet, desiring the coming of Christ, may be saying: Let true peace come—Christ, through the mystery of the Incarnation, to reconcile the human race to God the Father; then, rising from the dead, let him rest in his bed—that is, in the glory of the Father’s majesty, or in the Church in which Christ himself walked in his uprightness.

If we read it in the plural, “let them rest in their bed,” it is to be understood of the apostles in this way: Let the peace of Christ come through the apostles to the Gentiles, the peace that he left to the apostles when he said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV). [Col. 1012B] When that peace comes, which “surpasses all understanding” (Philippians IV), let the apostles rest in their bed—that is, in eternal blessedness. He himself, however, who is peace and grants peace to the faithful, walked in uprightness, because by a straight path he returned to the Father.

“Draw near here, sons of a diviner, offspring of an adulteress.” Jerusalem worshiped many idols, especially in the time of Isaiah, and among its other impurities also practiced divination. Hence the Jews are now called sons of a diviner and offspring of an adulterous woman; in some copies it reads “offspring of an adulterous people,” or “offspring of a fornication-practicing people or woman,” so that, thus confounded, they might repent.

A woman is called adulterous when she abandons her own husband and clings to another. Jerusalem is likewise called adulterous because she abandoned her own husband, God, and clung to another, the devil. Therefore he now says to her: “Draw near to me, sons of a diviner, and hear my words, you who are the offspring of an adulterous and fornicating woman. Over whom did you mock, and at whom did you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue?” [Col. 1012C]

These are the words of the Son of God recalling the Jews’ cruelty toward him, which he endured at the time of his Passion, as the Evangelists indicate: they mocked him, opened their mouths, and thrust out their tongues to blaspheme him when they covered his face, struck his head with a reed, and said, “Hail, King of the Jews”; when they placed a crown of thorns upon his head; and in the other things that the Gospel narrative records (Luke XXIII; Matthew XXVII; Mark XV; John XIX). [Col. 1012D]

Did they not open their mouths and thrust out their tongues to blaspheme God when they said: “You have a demon; you are a Samaritan; he casts out demons by the prince of demons” (John VII, VIII)? And at the time of his Passion, when they said: “Crucify him; he is guilty of death,” and, “Woe, you who destroy the temple.” “Against whom,” says the Son of God, “did you do all these things, if not against me?”

“Were you not wicked sons, a lying offspring, who take comfort in foreign gods beneath every leafy tree”—that is, every wooded tree—“sacrificing little children in the torrents beneath overhanging (or projecting) rocks?” [Col. 1013A]

They were sons of the devil and of sin, as the Lord says to them: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII)—not by nature, but by imitation. A wicked person is called cruel. They acted cruelly and wickedly when, abandoning the true God, they served idols and sacrificed their children to foreign gods. They were a lying offspring because they imitated the devil, who is a liar—as the Lord says—and its father, that is, the father and author of lying.

What he says here about those who take comfort in foreign gods beneath every leafy tree, sacrificing little children in the torrents beneath overhanging rocks, is made clearer in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, where it is said that they made their sons and daughters pass through fire and offered sacrifices to idols beneath wooded trees, in torrents, and beneath overhanging rocks. Concerning this sacrifice the Psalmist says: “They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons” (Psalm CV). [Col. 1013B]

“Among the parts of the torrent”—that is, on the banks of the torrent—“is your portion, O Jerusalem,” you who abandoned the altar of the Lord’s house and sacrifice in the torrents. “This is your portion,” supply: in the worship of idols, “and to them you poured out a libation; you offered a sacrifice.”

Libations are made from liquids, from oil and wine. Sacrifices are made from dry things, from bread and victims. “Over these things”—your most wicked deeds—“shall I not be indignant,” supply: so that I do not repay you according to your evil works?

“Upon a high and lofty mountain you set your bed,” and so forth. Blessed Jerome says that these things happened especially in the time of Isaiah, when under King Ahaz all the mountains were filled with the worship of demons. [Col. 1013C] For they placed their beds on high mountains so that there they might satisfy their lust and fornication. Nor was this evil sufficient for them: they also placed images behind the door and behind the doorpost, so that, entering or leaving, they might always worship them, as the following words make clear.

“Behind the door,” he says, “and behind the doorpost you placed your memorial”—that is, you worshiped images not only on mountains and in valleys, but also behind the door and behind the doorpost, which are one and the same place. You placed your memorial—that is, idols—there so that they might always be in your memory, and so that, leaving or entering the house, you might worship them.

“For beside me you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer”—that is, the devil—“you enlarged your bed and made a covenant with him,” supply: so that you would not return to me. [Col. 1013D] The Lord speaks to Jerusalem and reproves her as a prostitute and adulteress, because she abandoned her own husband, God, and clung to another, the devil, committing fornication with stone and wood through the worship of idols.

For example, it is as when someone reproves his wife, saying: “While I sleep beside you, you secretly uncover my bed and receive an adulterer beside me, and you have made a pact with him not to return to me.” Or it can be understood in this way: she revealed her entire will to her lovers without shame; and she did not commit fornication only in Jerusalem, but also established brothels throughout all the villages and small towns.

“You loved their bed with an open hand, and you adorned yourself with royal ointment.” [Col. 1014A] By “bed” here we must understand adultery, which is practiced in bed; and by “hand,” shameless activity, so that the meaning is: You loved adultery with an open hand—that is, without shame and with irreverent action—and you adorned and prepared yourself with royal ointment, that is, demonic ointment, since the devil is king over all the sons of pride.

Or, “you prepared yourself with royal ointment,” that is, for the idol of the Moabites, which some call Moloch or Melchon and which is interpreted as “king.” Jerusalem prepared herself for it and multiplied perfumes, so that by her adornment and fragrance she might please her lovers.

“You sent your messengers far away,” supply: to bring idols and hire lovers, “and you humbled yourself as far as the underworld”—that is, because of your evil works you were plunged into death. [Col. 1014B]

The meaning is: It was not enough for you merely to worship the gods that the nations around you worshiped; in addition, you sent far away to Babylon and Egypt, so that, worshiping their gods as well, you might complete your fornication with their worshipers.

The statement “you humbled yourself as far as the underworld” is not to be understood as humility in the good sense. There is a humility that belongs to glory, as in: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV and XVIII), and so forth. There is another that belongs to destruction and downfall, as in the passage read in the Book of Kings: “Because Amnon humbled Tamar his sister” (2 Samuel XIII). And the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.”

“You have labored in the multitude of your way”—that is, in your many wicked actions. [Col. 1014C] “And you did not say, ‘I will rest,’” supply: from the worship of idols or from wicked conduct.

“Whoever walks by the royal way, not turning to the right or to the left, does not labor” (John XIV), and so forth. The straight way is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

For example, prudence is a straight and royal way: it shows us how to consider good things with foresight and avoid evil things carefully. Whoever is wiser than one ought to be wise undoubtedly turns to the right. Whoever is foolish and acts without caution undoubtedly turns to the left. And the person who is always devoted to wicked actions labors on the way.

“You found the life of your hand; therefore you did not ask”—supply: me. And if you asked in words, you did not ask through deeds, as in: “This people honors me with its lips” (Isaiah XXIX). [Col. 1014D]

Here he uses “life” for riches and the abundance of earthly possessions, in which they had placed the hope of their life. It is as though he were saying: You found the riches you desired and were filled with abundance in every way; therefore you did not ask me as you ought to have asked.

“For what were you anxious and afraid, because you lied,” and so forth. This verse requires punctuation and supplied words. “For what were you anxious?” For riches. A middle division should be placed there. The meaning is: You were anxious about the riches I had given you, wondering how you might preserve them.

“And you were afraid,” supply: of enemies or of the gods from whom you hoped that all these things had been given to you. “Because you lied,” supply: when you were leaving Egypt, saying: “All that the Lord has spoken to us” (Exodus XXIV), and so forth. [Col. 1015A]

“And you did not remember me,” supply: in the time of your prosperity. What follows—“nor did you consider in your heart that I, being silent and as though not seeing, you had forgotten me”—has this meaning: When you abounded in riches and enjoyed profound peace, serving lust, avarice, and other vices, because I did not immediately repay you what you deserved, you thought that I would always remain silent, not recalling what I had said elsewhere: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?”

“I will announce your righteousness and your works”—that is, your images—“will not profit you.” He speaks ironically, as though saying: Until now I have been silent; I will not remain silent any longer, but I will announce your iniquity when I hand you and your images over to the Chaldeans or the Romans. [Col. 1015B] Or, on the day of judgment, I will announce your wickedness to all the nations—how you acted against me at the time of my Passion—so that they may know that you acted wrongly.

And why will your images not profit you? Because they will be melted down, and you will be led away captive.

“When you cry out,” supply: to me in the time of your captivity and calamity, or when the Chaldeans or Romans come, or on the day of judgment, “let those whom you have gathered deliver you”—that is, let the gods you gathered from various nations release you from the evil of captivity and the punishments of hell. Hence Jeremiah says: “Where are your gods that you made for yourself?” (Jeremiah XXXVII). Let them arise and save you on the day of calamity.

“And all of them”—supply: the gods—“the wind shall carry away,” that is, they will not be able to free you, because the storm of captivity and the arrival of your enemies will carry away all your gods. [Col. 1015C] “And the breeze shall take them away,” which has the same meaning.

“But the one who trusts in me shall inherit the land,” and so forth. He is speaking of those who did not worship idols, or of those who repented after being led into captivity and returned under Zerubbabel and Jeshua from captivity, in order to worship their God in his place and serve him with all their heart.

“**And I shall say**”—understand this as addressed to Cyrus and his princes—“**Make a way for my people**,” that is, grant them permission to return to their land. “**Turn aside from their path**,” so that you do not obstruct their journey out. “**Remove the obstacles**,” that is, all impediments that could [Col. 1015D] hinder their journey, so that they may return freely to their land.

Spiritually, however, he speaks concerning all the elect who truly believe in him and adorn the faith they possess with works: they will inherit the land of the living, of which the Psalmist says, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord (Psalm XXVI),” and so forth. They will also possess the holy mountain, that is, the sacred Scripture of the Old and New Testaments, both of which were given on a mountain. It invites those who observe it to the height of rewards. Concerning it the Lord says to the Jews, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you (Matthew XXI),” that is, the sacred Scripture.

Or certainly, the holy mountain—that is, Christ—the saints will possess, concerning whom the same prophet says, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of [Col. 1016A] the Lord (Isaiah II),” that is, let us believe in Christ the Son of God. Thus Christ says to the apostles and apostolic men: “Make a way for my people who believe in me,” by preaching right faith and pure conduct, “and provide a path,” that is, a good example of what they ought to do. Remove the obstacles as well, that is, cleanse their sins through baptism; or remove them from the worship of idols by your preaching, since God is offended especially by this and they are prevented from coming to Christ through faith.

“**Thus says the One who is Exalted, who inhabits eternity**,” and so forth. This is the Exalted and Sublime One concerning whom the Psalmist says, “The Lord is exalted above all nations (Psalm CXII).” He inhabits eternity because he remains unchangeable in his divinity, having neither beginning nor end. “**And [Col. 1016B] holy is his name in the height, and he dwells in the holy place.**” By “the height” we understand heaven, where God’s throne is, according to the saying, “Heaven is my throne.” And, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne.” Or by “the height where God dwells” we may understand the angelic spirits, in whom the Almighty sits and rests as upon a throne. Thus God dwells in the height—that is, in heaven or among the angels—and in the holy place, understood as his Son, or in each of the elect through faith and love. As he himself says, “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and we shall come to him (John XIV),” and so forth. [Col. 1016C]

“And he dwells with the contrite and the humble”—understand, “he dwells with them”—“to revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite.” Concerning them he himself says, “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble (Isaiah LXVI)?” and so forth. The Psalmist likewise says of them, “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm L).” He dwells, he says, with the contrite and humble in spirit for this purpose: to revive the spirit of the humble, that is, to grant forgiveness of sins and eternal life to those who are dead to sin and live by virtues; and to revive the heart of the contrite, that is, to restore it through divine consolation, so that they may pass from the sorrow of this age, which produces death, to everlasting joy, and from the grief of the present life to joy that will remain without end.

“**For I shall not contend forever, nor [Col. 1016D] shall I be angry to the end, because the Spirit will go forth from my presence, and I shall make breath.**” This is the voice of God the Father. “I shall not contend forever,” that is, I shall not preserve my anger eternally, nor shall I bring a charge against my creature; rather, I shall strike in the present so that I may save in the future. Nor shall I be angry to the end, that is, I shall not always pour out my anger and vengeance upon them, because the Holy Spirit will go forth from my presence—he who sustains all things and gives life to all—and I shall make breath, that is, souls.

Concerning this breath it is said in Genesis: “The Lord breathed into Adam, and the man became a living soul (Genesis II).” The sense is therefore this: Since the Spirit will go forth from my presence—he who gives life to all things and governs them, who gives both sensation and understanding—and since I create a soul in everyone (Wisdom XV), it is not fitting that they should perish eternally. Rather, I shall strike and chastise them here, so that they may feel my anger and be corrected, and in the future I shall have mercy on them.

These things that we have said apply generally to all the faithful who are chastised by the Lord, but [Col. 1017A] specifically to the Jews, concerning whom it is next added:

“**Because of the iniquity of his greed I was angry, and I struck him**,” that is, the Jewish people: first by handing them over to the Assyrians, then to the Chaldeans, and finally to the Romans. A greedy person is called *avarus*, as though he were “eager for gold.” The Jews were greedy and without mercy, and therefore they were handed over to their enemies.

“**I hid my face from him**,” that is, from the Jewish people, “my presence and my help,” so that you might desire me all the more. “**And I was angry**”—understand, “against you,” either because of your idolatry or because of the killing of my Son. “**He went away wandering**,” that is, senseless and without understanding, like Cain, “**in the way of his heart**,” that is, in his wicked conduct.

[Col. 1017B] “**I saw his ways, and I let him go, and I led him back. And I restored consolations to him and to his mourners**,” that is, to those mourning for Zion. “His ways,” that is, the good actions of the Jewish people, I saw when they lamented their sins in captivity; and I restored consolations, that is, I restored consolations—that is, their own inheritance—to that people, in its princes and mourners of Zion, that is, its subjects.

Alternatively: I saw the good actions of the people who believe, and I restored consolations, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is called *Paraclete*, meaning “Comforter.” The first parent lost him through disobedience, but I restored him to those mourning for the Church.

“**I created the fruit of my lips**,” that is, what I promised through the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah XXV and XXIX): [Col. 1017C] that after seventy years I would release them from captivity. I swiftly fulfilled this promise in deed. And I created “**peace for him who was far away**,” from his own land, in Jerusalem, “**and I healed him**,” that is, the one who repented in captivity, from his sins.

Alternatively: “I created the fruit of my lips, peace for him who is far away and peace for him who is near.” This means that I fulfilled in deed what I promised through the prophets concerning my Son, that he would redeem the human race, establishing peace for the Jews who believed, who were near, and for the Gentiles, who were far away. “And I healed him,” that is, I healed both peoples who believed in him from sin: the Jews from unbelief, and the Gentiles from idolatry. Concerning them the Apostle says, “You who were once far away have been brought near (Ephesians II).” And likewise: “Coming, he preached peace to those who were far away,” that is, to the Gentiles, “and peace to those who were near,” that is, to the Jews. [Col. 1017D]

“**But the impious are like a raging sea that cannot rest, and its waves overflow into trampling and mud.**” Above he spoke of the Jews who, placed in captivity, repented, and whom he healed from their sins by bringing them back to Jerusalem; and also of those who believed after the Lord’s Passion. Now he speaks specifically of those who remained in their unbelief after the Lord’s Ascension. To them blessed Paul said: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts XIII).”

The impious—or unrighteous—Jews, he says, who during the Lord’s Passion cried out, “He is guilty of death; [Col. 1018A] crucify such a man (Matthew XXVII),” were “raging in anger toward evil,” like a raging sea that cannot rest but is always in motion. Their wickedness, or persecution, overflowed as the waves of the sea overflow. When the Romans came, they would be in trampling and mud—understand, “they would be”—and they would be trampled by enemies or by demons, like mud that is trampled by passers-by after the water has receded.

Just as the sea is always in motion, sometimes advancing and sometimes retreating, and on its return forms mud that is trampled, so they advanced into iniquity and retreated into destruction; their wickedness surged like the waves of the sea. Therefore they were trampled down or reduced to nothing.

“**There is no peace for the impious, says my God**,” [Col. 1018B] that is, the Son of God, who gave peace to the world, does not rest among the impious Jews, nor among all who act perversely.

## CHAPTER LVIII

“**Cry out; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce their crimes to my people, and their sins to the house of Jacob.**” This is the voice of God addressed to the prophet, or to the choir of apostles: O prophet, or choir of apostles, cry out without fear; do not fear their madness, and do not cease from preaching. Raise your voice like a trumpet, that is, utter a loud voice so that you may be heard by everyone, announcing to them the captivity that threatens them from the Romans and the great slaughter.

“Announce their crimes to my people,” that is, their monstrous sins—namely, idolatry, murder, [Col. 1018C] and detestable deeds that they perpetrate beyond all human measure. And announce their sins to the house of Jacob, in which they sin against God and neighbor. He still calls them his people in order to summon them to repentance.

“**For day after day they seek me, and they wish to know my ways, like a nation that has done justice and has not abandoned the judgment of its God.**” These words properly concern the Jews, who gathered daily at the Temple and in the synagogues, meditating on God’s laws, yet did not [Col. 1018D] fulfill justice and righteous judgment, because they worshiped idols in place of God.

“They seek me,” he says, “day after day,” but only with their voice and by coming to the Temple and synagogues; and they wish to know my ways, that is, my actions and intentions, asking why I do not hear them. They are “like a nation that has done justice,” that is, like the faithful now living rightly and justly in the Church and confessing Christ as God and man.

Or “a nation that has done justice” means one that has not worshiped idols in place of God but has always rightly fulfilled my commandments, and that has not abandoned the judgment—that is, the law—of its God, or has held the true faith by which the righteous person lives.

Spiritually, however, we ought to understand justice and judgment as Christ, who is justice because he justifies his elect, and who is judgment because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John V).”

[Col. 1019A] “**They ask me for judgments of justice**,” that is, they ask me to judge them rightly and to render a just judgment, by showing why I do not accept their works. “**They desire to draw near to God**”—understand, with their voice, not by their conduct.

“**Why have we fasted, and you did not look upon us**”—understand, by hearing us? “**We humbled our soul**,” that is, our life, by fasting, “**and you did not know? Behold, on the day of your fast your will is found**”—understand, your carnal will—“**and you demand all your debtors back.**”

The Jews asked the Lord why he did not hear them when they humbled themselves with fasts. But the Lord does not reject fasting; he rejects the works they performed during their fast, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your will is found,” understood as carnal. It is as though he said: I do not hear you because your fasting lacks mercy, and, moreover, you undertake it for the praise and flattery of human beings.

The Jews devote themselves to fasting, but in vain, [Col. 1019B] because it is not universal. For a universal fast is abstinence from all unlawful things, and it must not be undertaken for temporal praise. Some manuscripts, however, have: “Your will will be found on the day of your fast,” that is, your delight, namely, in taking more numerous and more sumptuous foods after the fast.

“You demand back all your debtors,” he says, that is, you contentiously demand payment from those to whom you have lent something. They sometimes fasted for this very reason: so that they could demand their debts more freely, something that cannot be done without contention.

“**Behold, you fast for quarrels and contentions, and you strike with the fist wickedly.**” The sense is: You fast in order to engage in quarrels and contentions; and, what is worse, you strike the poor and innocent with your fist, without mercy, [Col. 1019C] demanding from them things that you have not lent them, and you want me to hear you?

It follows: “**Do not fast as you have done up to this day, so that your cry may be heard on high.**” The Jews were accustomed on fast days to pray at the corners of the streets, with their hands extended toward heaven, and likewise in the middle of the Temple, with shouting and lamentation, so that those who heard and saw them might praise them (Matthew XXIII). So too did that Pharisee whom the Lord censures in the Gospel; therefore it is said to them (Luke XVIII): “Do not fast as you have done up to this day”—understand, without mercy, and so that you may demand your debts back with quarrels and contention, so that your cry may be heard on high, that is, in the Temple or in the streets, while you pray with shouting.

“**Is [Col. 1019D] this the kind of fast that I chose**”—understand, the kind that you practice—“**for a person to afflict his soul throughout the day**,” and afterward commit many unlawful acts, or be excessively filled with food? What benefit is there in restraining the body from food unless it is also restrained from vices? God does not approve such a fast, but the fast that is universal and fulfilled in humility and mercy.

“**Is it this that I chose**”—understand, “that I chose”—“**for him to bend his head like a circle**,” that is, to incline his head and feet, “**to put on sackcloth and spread ashes? Is this what you will call a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord?**” Understand: Such a fast will not be acceptable to him, because outwardly you display humility while inwardly you are swollen with the pride of arrogance, seeking human praise from it. [Col. 1020A]

The Almighty God loves the practices mentioned above—namely, bowing the head, putting on sackcloth, and spreading ashes—if they are performed with a pure heart, especially in a time of necessity and tribulation, as among the Ninevites, David, and Ahaz (Jonah III; II Kings XIII; III Kings XXI). But if they are performed with a double heart, he neither chooses nor approves them.

“**Is this not rather the fast that I chose**”—understand, “that I command you to observe?”—“**Undo the bonds of impiety; release the bundles that oppress.**” The Septuagint translated this more explicitly, saying: “Tear up every unjust document.”

It was the custom of that people that, if someone lent something to another, he would write a *chirographum*, that is, a document and written instrument by which he could later demand it from him. They also bound those to whom they provided something by an oath, [Col. 1020B] and sometimes wrote false documents against the poor, violently demanding from those who possessed nothing what they had not entrusted to them.

He calls documents and writings of this sort “bonds” and “bundles that oppress,” because through them they bound—that is, constrained—the poor and oppressed them. He commanded that such documents be undone. For if it is impious, as blessed Jerome says, to demand a debt from those who cannot repay it because they have nothing with which to do so, how much greater is the impiety of demanding something falsely?

Spiritually and morally, however, we ought to understand the bonds and bundles as sins, which we are commanded to forgive our neighbor on the day of fasting, [Col. 1020C] when the Lord says: “Undo the bonds of impiety,” and so forth. It is as though he said: Forgive your neighbor who has sinned against you whatever he has done against you, so that you may be forgiven what you have done against God, and may say with a free heart, “Forgive us, as we also forgive our brother (Matthew VI).”

“**Release those who are broken free, and tear apart every burden.**” Often, in a time of famine, some poor Jews handed themselves over into slavery to princes and wealthy men: some to serve them for seven years, some for more, some for less, and others even until the Jubilee year. Therefore they were commanded to release such people from servitude into freedom, because sometimes they detained them longer than the period that the person who had entrusted himself to them had stipulated.

“Release those who are broken free,” he says, that is, those who, when famine and necessity were pressing, had surrendered themselves to you in servitude instead of freedom; and tear apart every burden of servitude or sin. [Col. 1020D]

“**Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house.**” It should be noted that he says “your bread,” not another’s, lest anyone attempt to give alms from robbery. For whoever offers God sacrifice and mercy from robbery is like one who sacrifices a son before his father (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV).

Spiritually, we can understand by bread the faith of Christ, who said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven (John VI).” We break bread for the hungry when we make known to simpler brothers the faith of Christ that we possess. Likewise, by bread we can understand sacred Scripture, by which the soul is refreshed just as the body is refreshed by various foods. We break this bread when [Col. 1021A] we teach the ignorant, imparting to them the doctrine and wisdom of life.

“Bring the poor and homeless into your house,” he says, providing a roof for those who have none, so that you may receive a heavenly dwelling. Spiritually, we bring the homeless into the house when we gather those who are discordant and divided into the unity of charity.

“**When you see the naked, cover him**”—understand, with your garments—fulfilling the saying: “Whoever has two tunics should give to the one who has none.” “**And do not despise your flesh**,” that is, your neighbor, when you see him wasting away through illness, or naked, or placed in any misery; recognize that you are like him, carnal and mortal.

Morally: When you see someone naked, that is, alien to faith and virtues, cover him through your admonition and example; and do not despise your [Col. 1021B] flesh, that is, a sinner like yourself.

“**Then your light will break forth**”—that is, when you have done the things mentioned above—“**like the morning, and your healing will quickly arise.**” The sense is: Just as the sun drives away the darkness in the morning and illuminates the world, so you will be illuminated by your virtues, because the true Sun, Christ, will rest in your heart. Concerning him it is said: “For you who fear my name, the sun of justice will rise (Malachi IV).”

“**And your justice will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you.**” This is to be understood in two ways. Your justice and right conduct will go before your face—that is, will precede you and your presence to eternal blessedness [Col. 1021C] before Christ the Judge—and the glory of the Lord, namely the Son of God, to whom the Father says, “Rise up, my glory (Psalm LVI),” will gather you, that is, clothe you or surround you with the covering of his mercy.

Alternatively, here we ought to understand justice as Christ, from whom all the elect are justified. Your justice—Christ—will go before or precede your face to eternal glory, since he said, “I am going to prepare a kingdom for you (John IV).” And the glory of the Lord, that is, eternal brightness—namely, the Son of God himself—will gather you, that is, receive you to himself, according to the saying: “Where I am, there also will my servant be (John XII).”

“**Then you will call**”—with mouth and conduct, like Moses and the other saints—“**and the Lord will hear you,**” whose will you have fulfilled. “**You will cry out, and he will say: Here I am**” [Col. 1021D]—understand, “for recompense”—the one who was your help so that you could perform good works.

“**If you remove the chain from among you and cease extending the finger**,” that is, cease slandering your neighbor and saying what is not beneficial, because slander does not benefit good works.

“**When you pour out your soul for the hungry**,” that is, your will, “**and fill the afflicted soul**”—understand, with your good things—“**your light will rise in the darkness**,” that is, Christ, “**and your darkness will be like midday.**”

What he earlier called the bonds of impiety and the bundles that oppress, he now calls a chain, that is, the obligation of sins. You must cease meditating on the evils of your neighbors, pointing at this person and that with your finger, and cease saying what is not beneficial. Slander does not benefit [Col. 1022A] either good works or evil ones; for it would be more useful for you to recall your own deeds.

When you pour out your soul for the hungry—that is, when you show a willing and cheerful spirit toward the hungry, sympathizing with his weakness and nakedness as with your own—and when you fill the afflicted soul with fasts and other hardships, not merely breaking bread but satisfying it with every good thing, then your light, Christ, will rise in the darkness of sins.

That is, when you have done such things, darkness—your sins—will be changed into justice, so that you may say with the Apostle, “There was once darkness in me, but now I am light in the Lord (Ephesians V).” [Col. 1022B] And your darkness, that is, your sins, will be like midday, that is, they will be changed into the brightness of justice. For your iniquity will be removed, so that you may say with the bride, “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday (Song of Songs I)?”

“**And the Lord will always give you rest**,” that is, he will cause you to rest in heavenly blessedness from enemies and from vices, because the one who ceases from vices here will rest in eternal blessedness from every adversity. “**And he will fill your soul with splendors**,” that is, with virtues, or with eternal brightness from the vision of his divinity, “**and he will deliver your bones**”—understand, from hell, so that they may not be handed over to the fire.

Or, “he will deliver your bones” means that he will raise your body on the day of judgment. Let us also explain it in a third way, understanding the bones as virtues. “He will deliver your bones,” that is, he himself will preserve your virtues, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “The Lord guards all their bones (Psalm XXXIII).” Virtues [Col. 1022C] are compared to bones because just as the body is sustained by bones, so the soul is sustained by virtues.

“**And you will be like a watered garden, and like a spring of waters whose waters will not fail.**” We read in the book of Genesis that the Lord planted paradise, in the midst of which there was a spring that watered the whole of paradise (Genesis II). That garden, containing various kinds of fruit trees and many kinds of herbs, signifies the holy Church, which has diverse orders and is adorned with various flowers of virtue.

That spring watering paradise signifies Christ, to whom the Psalmist says, “For with you is the fountain of life (Psalm XXXV).” From this fountain, the living one, the Church is watered with spiritual doctrine and wisdom. The waters of this fountain—that is, its doctrine—will not fail, because heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of the Almighty God will not pass away [Col. 1022D] (Matthew XXIV).

The Church, therefore, is likened to Christ, and every elect person is his body. Hence the saying: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew XIII).” Thus it is said specifically to each elect person and generally to the Church: “You will be like a garden,” he says, that is, like paradise, “and like a spring of waters whose waters will not fail,” that is, you will be like Christ, who is your head, whose teachings will not fail.

“**And the ancient ruins will be built in you, and you will raise up the foundations of generation and generation.**” The Jews refer this to the restoration accomplished by Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest, or even to the restoration that they suppose will occur at the end of time: [Col. 1023A] But it is better to refer these words to the Church.

By “the ancient ruins,” that is, those of many ages, he means the assemblies of the Jews, which have become desolate through unbelief and have been restored in the Church through faith. “You will raise up the foundations of generation and generation,” O Church, by believing and confessing that Christ is true God and true man.

“Foundation,” expressed in the singular, signifies Christ, according to what Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians II).” But “foundations,” expressed in the plural, signifies the apostles, prophets, and preachers of the Church, as in the saying: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

By the two expressions “generation and generation,” [Col. 1023B] he wishes both peoples to be understood: Jews and Gentiles. Thus it is said to the Church: “They will build in you,” O Church, through faith, the assemblies that have become desolate among the Jews through unbelief; and “you will raise up the foundations” of both peoples, namely, the apostles and preachers who founded the Church through their teaching and examples.

“**And you will be called, O Christian people, the builder of hedges**,” that is, through the preaching of doctrine, “**turning aside the paths of iniquity**,” that is, of errors, where there is neither rest nor the peace of Christ.

The builders of the Church are the preachers. Their hedges are their teachings, which prick their hearers and defend the Lord’s vineyard and harvest from thieves—that is, the Church from the devil—because in the preaching of teachers they consider how they ought to avoid the scandals [Col. 1023C] and snares of demons. They also turn aside the paths of iniquity, that is, of error and impiety, toward the tranquility of faith, virtues, and charity.

If we say “turning aside the paths into rest,” that is, into peace, a necessary ellipsis is understood: “turning aside the paths,” understood as “of error,” into true peace.

“**If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath, from doing your will on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight**,” that is, dedicated and consecrated to the Lord, “**and the holy day of the Lord glorious**,” that is, pure and celebrated, not yours but the Lord’s; and if you glorify him—or the Lord, or the Sabbath—according to the saying, “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matthew V)” [Col. 1023D]—

“**while you do not do your own will**,” that is, carnal and private actions, imitating Christ, who said, “I did not come to do my own will (John V, VI).” When you do these things, “**your will will not be found in order to speak a word**”—understand, an idle word, or a word of blasphemy, or one suitable to idols.

All these matters can be gathered into a brief explanation, since the words are repeated there. “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath,” he says—that is, if you restrain your wicked action on the Sabbath day, so that you do not defile it with your desires, and do not kindle the fire of quarrelling, slander, and hatred—then in all these things you will glorify the Lord.

“**Then you will delight in the Lord**,” that is, you will take delight [Col. 1024A] in his grace, “**and I shall lift you above the heights of the earth**,” that is, to the height of eternal solidity, because this alone among the elements remains solid and immovable. “**And I shall feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father**,” that is, I shall give you an inheritance in heavenly blessedness, which I gave to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose children you are through faith and imitation.

Concerning this satiety the Psalmist says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed (Psalm XVI).” For all who overcome vices and demons are sons of Jacob through faith and conduct.

“**For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.**” These things—that is, the prophet through whom the Lord deigned to speak—said what has been related above.

Let us return to the beginning of this verse, where he said, “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath,” and so forth. The person who [Col. 1024B] observes the Sabbath is one who offends neither in word nor in deed, ceasing from vices and from every servile work, in accordance with what the law commands: “You shall do no servile work on it (Leviticus XXIII),” that is, no work of sin. “For whoever commits sin is a slave of sin (John VIII).”

We also keep holy days if we live well. But if we live badly, we no longer celebrate holy days, but evil ones, according to what the Apostle says concerning the reprobate: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Ephesians V).”

## CHAPTER LIX

“**Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that he cannot save**”—you, if you wish to return to him—“**nor is his ear burdened, so that he cannot hear.**”

The prophet [Col. 1024C] addresses the Jews, his fellow citizens. Behold, he says, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that is, his power has not been diminished, so that he cannot save you from enemies and from the devil, if you wish to believe in him, just as it was not once diminished when he led our fathers out of the land of Egypt. Nor is his ear burdened, so that he cannot hear, if you entreat him with a pure mind; rather, he will hear you as he heard Moses and Aaron, Samuel, David, and the other saints.

“**But your iniquities**,” that is, the worship of your idols, “**have separated between you and God, and your sins have hidden his face from you**,” that is, they have withdrawn his presence and help from you, “**so that he would not [Col. 1024D] hear**”—understand, you in the time of tribulation.

Now he shows why he permitted them to be led into captivity so many times, why he did not hear them, and why they were far from God: namely, because of idolatry.

“**For your hands are defiled with the blood**” of the righteous, “**and your fingers with iniquity.**” All Scripture testifies that the Jews were always ready to shed the blood of prophets and righteous people. Thus we read (II Kings XXI; II Chronicles XXXIII) that Manasseh, king of Judah, filled Jerusalem with the blood of the innocent, from gate to gate. They shed not only the blood of the prophets, but also that of the Lord himself, the head of all the prophets. Stephen likewise testified to this in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter VII): “Which of the prophets did your fathers [Col. 1025A] not persecute, who announced the coming of the Righteous One?” They stoned Jeremiah, cut Isaiah in pieces, and killed Ezekiel in Babylon (Jeremiah XXXIX).

“**Your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue utters iniquity**,” that is, blasphemy. They spoke falsehood when they said, “Everything that the Lord has commanded us, we shall hear and do (Exodus XXIV).” They spoke falsehood and blasphemy when they said to the Lord, “You have a demon, and you cast out demons by Beelzebub (John VIII),” along with many other innumerable things.

“**There is no one who calls upon justice**,” that is, who believes in Christ, who became redemption and justification for his elect; “**nor is there one who judges truly**,” that is, rightly. They did not judge rightly when they asked for [Col. 1025B] Barabbas and crucified Christ.

“**But they trust in nothingness**,” that is, in an idol, which is nothing, as the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing (1 Corinthians VIII).” Or they trust in Antichrist, “**and they speak vanities**,” while they blaspheme Christ daily in their synagogues, or while they say, “The Messiah has not yet come.”

“**They conceived labor**” against Christ, because they labored for his killing, “**and they gave birth to iniquity**,” in place of which it will read, “they will give birth to iniquity,” when they receive Antichrist.

“**They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs.**” The asp is an exceedingly crafty serpent. When it hears the first sound of an enchanter, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail, so that it cannot be [Col. 1025C] enchanted.

Therefore the Jews are compared to an asp, because they were poisonous, according to John the Baptist’s reproach: “Brood of vipers (Matthew III).” Just as the asp makes one ear adhere to the earth and blocks the other with its tail so that it may not be enchanted, so they, clinging to earthly things, blocked the ears of their minds so that they would not receive Christ’s preaching.

Their works and counsels are also compared to spiders’ webs, because just as spiders weave a fragile web and can catch in it only flies and gnats, and it is of no use, so their counsels and works were fragile and useless. They were unable to capture and deceive anyone except the simple and foolish.

A young creature comes forth from an egg; therefore, by the eggs we ought to understand their hearts and counsels. “They broke [Col. 1025D] the eggs of asps” when they displayed in words what they held in their hearts—blasphemy and envy—saying, “He is guilty of death,” and “Crucify such a man (Matthew XXVII).”

They also produced and wove webs, or completed them in deed, when they revealed in words what they had conceived in their hearts and completed it by crucifying him. But what happened? All their works and counsels passed away like empty air when he rose from the dead.

“**Whoever eats from their eggs**”—that is, from the eggs of asps—“**will die**,” that is, whoever assents to the counsels of the Jews, as Abel assented to Cain when Cain said, “Let us go out into the field,” will be killed by them (Genesis IV). Or whoever associates himself with their counsels, which are full of poison, and imitates their [Col. 1026A] works, will die an eternal death.

It follows: “**And what was hatched**”—that is, nourished from their eggs—“**will break forth**,” that is, will grow “**into a basilisk**”—understand, the king of other serpents, who kills birds flying through the air with his breath.

By the basilisk that is born from the eggs of asps we ought to understand Antichrist, who will be born from the Jewish people and who, by his breath—that is, by his word and teaching—will kill many of the saints flying toward their heavenly homeland.

“**Their webs**”—that is, the webs of spiders—“**will not become clothing**,” that is, any adornment, “**nor will they cover themselves with their works.**” The webs—that is, the evil teachings and works of the Jews—will not become clothing for the soul, nor will they be covered by their works; rather, they will perish naked in hell, empty of good [Col. 1026B] works.

The clothing and covering of the soul is justice, as it is said concerning the saints: “Let your priests be clothed with justice (Psalm CXIII).”

“**Their works**,” that is, the works of the Jews, “**are useless works**,” that is, wicked, because they fulfill the will of the devil, “**and the work of iniquity is in their hands.**” Behold: what he earlier called webs, he now calls works more explicitly.

“‘Their feet,’ that is, the feet of the Jews, ‘run to evil, and hasten to shed innocent blood.’ Their feet ran to evil when they came with lanterns and clubs to seize the Lord. They hastened—that is, they labored and shed innocent blood—when they persisted in asking Pilate that he should kill him. ‘Their thoughts’ against the Lord [Col. 1026C] ‘are useless thoughts,’ namely, when they said: ‘Come, let us deceive the just man,’ and so forth. ‘Desolation and destruction are in their ways,’ that is, in their actions, because they have been desolated and crushed by enemies and are now being desolated by the devil.

‘They did not know the way of peace,’ that is, Christ, who brought peace to the world, by believing in him, ‘and there is no judgment,’ namely, no discernment between good and evil, or else no uprightness, ‘in their steps. Their paths have been made crooked for them; everyone who treads upon them does not know peace.’ Their paths—that is, their actions and works—have turned from good to evil, from God to the devil, from uprightness to iniquity, and from faith to unbelief. Everyone who imitates their works does not know peace, that is, Christ.

[Col. 1026D] “‘Therefore judgment has been removed far from us.’ This is the prophet’s voice, speaking in the person of the Jewish people as they do penance. ‘Therefore,’ they say, ‘because we did not know peace, judgment has been removed far from us,’ that is, Christ, ‘and righteousness has not overtaken us’ through believing, but has gone to the Gentiles. ‘We expected light,’ that is, Christ, who had been promised to us in the Law and the Prophets, when we said: ‘Send forth your light and your truth’ (Ps. XLII); ‘and behold, darkness,’ namely, the darkness of unbelief, or of Antichrist. ‘We expected brightness,’ namely, of eternal fatherhood, ‘and we walked in darkness,’ that is, in errors and sins.

“‘We groped like the blind at a wall,’ that is, at sacred [Col. 1027A] Scripture, ‘and like those without eyes we felt our way.’ The Jews grope daily like the blind at a wall, because, although they read sacred Scripture, they do not believe that Christ lies hidden there in the mind; they touch only the leaves and the outer husks. ‘We stumbled at midday,’ that is, we immersed ourselves by reading in the Scripture of divine utterances, ‘as though in darkness,’ although it is light and open to the saints. ‘Among dark places,’ that is, in obscure mysteries, ‘we stumbled as though dead.’ For as long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.

“‘We shall all roar like bears, and, meditating like doves, we shall moan.’ The meditation that the Jews have in Scripture is compared to the roar of a lion and the moaning of a dove: just as the bear gains no benefit from its roaring, nor the dove from its moaning, so their meditation and teaching have no benefit, since they do not see that Christ lies hidden within in the mind. Or otherwise: toward those subject to them they roar savagely like bears, but toward their superiors and those equal to themselves they moan like doves. The dove is sometimes understood in a good sense, as in the Gospel, where it is said to believers: ‘Be simple as doves’ (Matt. X). At other times it is understood in the contrary sense, as in: ‘Ephraim has become like a dove without a heart’ (Gen. XLIX). ‘We expected judgment,’ that is, Christ, who had already come, concerning whom it is said: ‘O God, give your judgment to the king’ (Ps. LXXI), ‘and it is not,’ namely, among us. ‘We expected salvation,’ and ‘it has been removed far from us,’ passing over to the Gentiles, just as he himself said: ‘Your house shall be left to you desolate’ (Matt. XXIII).

[Col. 1027C] “‘For our iniquities have multiplied before you,’ namely, because we have not only despised sacred Scripture but also you, its author. ‘And our sins,’ they say, ‘have answered us,’ that is, because we deserved such things, we received such things, ‘because our crimes,’ that is, all our sins, ‘are with us,’ namely, still. This accords with what we called down upon ourselves when we said: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children’ (Matt. XXVII). ‘And we have acknowledged our iniquities,’ doing penance: namely, they sinned when they handed him over to Pilate and said: ‘He is deserving of death’ (Matt. XXVI).

“‘To lie’ in many ways ‘against the Lord.’ They acknowledged their sins and iniquity when, pierced in heart, they said to Peter and the other [Col. 1027D] apostles: ‘What shall we do, men and brothers?’ (Acts II). It follows: ‘And we have turned away,’ that is, we have declined, ‘so as not to walk behind the Lord our God,’ that is, so as not to imitate him, in accordance with what is commanded in the Law: ‘You shall walk after the Lord your God’ (Deut. VI), and in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: ‘Whoever serves me, let him follow me’ (John XII). ‘So that we might speak calumny,’ that is, blasphemy, ‘and transgression,’ of the Law, or denial of Christ. ‘We conceived,’ namely, wickedness, ‘and we spoke words of falsehood from the heart.’

“‘And judgment has turned backward,’ that is, Christ has withdrawn from us and passed over to the Gentiles, in accordance with what he himself foretold, saying: ‘The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you’ [Col. 1028A] (Matt. XXI). Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. ‘And righteousness,’ namely Christ himself, ‘stood far away,’ because, withdrawing from us, he remained among the Gentiles, who were far from God. And why this happened they make clear in what follows, when they add: ‘Because truth has fallen in the street, and equity could not enter.’ Truth, Christ, fell—that is, did not stand or remain—in the street, that is, among those who followed their own desires; and equity could not enter the hearts of the Jews because of unbelief, since through faith it dwells in the hearts of the elect, in accordance with what Paul says: ‘That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts’ (Eph. III). Hence the Lord also says: ‘My word does not find room in you’ (John VIII). *Plateia* in Greek is called *platea* in Latin from its breadth. And the meaning is this: in those who walked through the breadth of this life—that is, in the scribes and Pharisees—truth fell, the truth that says: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life’ (John XIV). It follows.

“‘And truth became,’ namely to the Jews, ‘a matter of forgetfulness. And the one who withdrew from evil,’ namely from the evil of the Jews, or from the evil of unbelief by believing in Christ, ‘became prey,’ namely to the Jews, ‘was exposed,’ that is, became their prey, because he was plundered by them, as we read in the revelation of Saint Stephen concerning Nicodemus. Hence the distinguished preacher also says to believing Jews, whose goods the unbelievers seized: ‘You joyfully accepted the seizure of your goods’ (Heb. X).

“‘And he saw, and evil appeared in his eyes, because there is no judgment.’ Up to this point the Prophet has spoken in the person of those who seemed to do penance after the Lord’s ascension. Now, however, he says that their penance did not please the Lord, because they were not sincere in heart. ‘And he saw,’ he says, ‘the penance of the Jews,’ that is, he knew that they were not doing this from a pure heart but only in words. ‘And evil appeared in his eyes,’ because it did not proceed from pure intention: they thought that by their voice they could draw near to God and deceive the Almighty with words, although he desires not lips but hearts. ‘Because there is no judgment’ of discernment between good and evil; or there was no judgment among the Jews between purity and pretense, either in their penance, and there was no judgment of uprightness. ‘And God saw,’ namely the Father, ‘that there was no man, and he was perplexed,’ [Col. 1028D] ‘because there was no one to intervene.’

“God the Father saw that there was no holy man among the Jews, such as Moses and David and many others, and he was perplexed—that is, he was grieved either by the unbelief of the Jews or on their account, because there was no one to intervene and pour forth prayers for them, as Moses once did in the wilderness, and Samuel and David. There were some in that people who, with respect to sex, were called men; but they were effeminate, as he already said above elsewhere: ‘I came, and there was no man to hear.’ ‘And his arm shall save for him, and his righteousness itself shall establish him.’ As we have said in many other places, by the arm of God the Father we must understand the Son, through whom he made all things and whom he himself saved from death by raising him from the dead. The meaning is this: while the Jews remained in unbelief, God the Father saved his Son from their persecution, and he will also save him in the future; and his righteousness, that is, his Son, who justifies all the elect, will himself establish him, that is, gladden him over the salvation of the Gentiles. Let us also interpret it otherwise: since they were unwilling to turn to true penance, God the Father saved for himself the believers from among the Gentiles through his Son; and his righteousness, or mercy—as the Septuagint translated it—will itself establish the one who wishes to turn back from error, so that he may be saved not by his own merits but by his mercy. For it is righteousness that the Creator should spare his creature, which could not be saved by its own merits.

“‘He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and he had a helmet on his head’ [Col. 1029B] when he freed his elect who believed in him from the persecution of the wicked, fighting on their behalf and pouring out his mercy upon them. Alternatively: in accordance with the vengeance that he poured out upon the Jews through the Romans, he is called helmet and breastplate, because he himself came in them, exercising his vengeance upon the Jews through the hands of the Romans. ‘He put on garments of vengeance,’ namely, like a king, and upon his Roman soldiers, ‘and he was covered as with a cloak of zeal,’ that is, of vengeance.

“‘As for vengeance,’ namely, just as any king prepares himself, ‘so he is clothed in his weapons,’ ‘and as if for repayment of indignation upon his enemies,’ namely the Jews, so that they might receive what they had done, ‘and to repay his enemies in kind,’ namely, he came to render it. [Col. 1029C] They killed the prophets who foretold his coming, and the Head himself with his apostles; they too were killed by the Romans. ‘To the islands,’ that is, the cities of the Jews, ‘he will repay their due’ by wiping them out and destroying them through the coming of the Romans.

“‘And those from the west shall fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his glory, when he comes like a violent river driven by the Spirit, and the Redeemer comes to Zion and to those who turn back from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord.’ Above, the prophetic utterance spoke of the killing of the Jews, which was carried out by the Romans, among whom the Lord came prepared for vengeance against his enemies, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation. Now, however, it speaks of the faith of the Gentiles, who flowed together from the four quarters of the world [Col. 1029D] to the faith after hearing the apostles’ preaching. ‘And those from the west,’ he says, shall fear with holy and filial fear. Those who are from the west shall fear the name of the Lord, that is, the name of the Father, concerning whom the Son says: ‘Father, I have manifested your name to men’ (John XVII). And those who are from the rising of the sun shall fear his glory, namely the Son of God the Father, who came in the name of the one to whom the Father himself says: ‘Arise, my glory.’ There are two kinds of fear. There is servile fear, by which a servant fears his master lest he be flogged by him. There is also the fear of love, by which a son fears his father lest he be disinherited. Of this it is said: ‘The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever’; and: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’; and: ‘Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,’ with holy fear, of which it is also said here.

“Of those who are from the west and the rising of the sun and who will fear the name of the Lord the Father, or his glory—that is, his Son—the Lord says in the Gospel:

“‘Many shall come from the east and from the west,’ and so forth. And when will they fear the name of the Lord? When the Son of God himself comes into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation, or when he comes to the Gentiles through the preaching and prayer of the apostles: like a violent river, that is, flowing swiftly and with force, which the Spirit of the Lord compels to come in order to redeem the human race. ‘And the Redeemer shall come to Zion,’ that is, to the Jewish people believing in him, or to the Church; and he shall also come to those who turn back from the iniquity of unbelief and denial to Jacob, that is, to those who overcome vices. The Son [Col. 1030B] of God is compared to a river because he has given us the streams of his teaching and satisfies the hearts of his elect with saving water, that is, fills them with the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning whom he himself says: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’ (John VII), and so forth. He is called violent because, within the span of three and a half years, having completed his Passion, he subjected the whole world to himself by redeeming it, just as, rising from the dead, he said: ‘All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me’ (Matt. XXVIII). The Spirit of the Lord, which compelled him to redeem the human race, must be understood as the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the same prophet said above: ‘The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him’ (Isa. XI). But lest anyone think that all who appear to have faith, yet do not have good works, will be saved, he therefore said: ‘And the Redeemer shall come to those who turn back from iniquity to Jacob, says the Lord.’ It follows:

“‘This is my covenant,’ that is, my pact or testament, ‘with them, says the Lord,’ namely with those who have turned away from iniquity, so that I might redeem them with my blood and so that they might fulfill in action the evangelical commandments that I shall give them and that these commandments might always be present in their hearts. Hence it follows: ‘My Spirit,’ that is, the Holy Spirit, ‘which is in you,’ O Prophet, through whom you proclaim future things, ‘and my words that I have placed in your mouth shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, says the Lord, from this time forth and forever.’

“By his seed we must understand all his successors who were filled with the same Holy Spirit: Jeremiah and the others before the captivity; Ezekiel and Daniel during the captivity; Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi after the captivity; and thereafter the apostles, martyrs, and all the teachers of the holy Church, from whose mouths proceeded the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. For the Holy Spirit who taught Isaiah passed through his successors to the apostles. He therefore says ‘from this time forth and forever,’ namely, my words shall not depart from your mouth or from the mouth of your seed, because no other law will succeed the Gospel. Hence John the Evangelist says that he saw an angel holding an eternal Gospel (Rev. XIV). That angel prefigured the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave us believers evangelical teaching, concerning which he himself said: ‘Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away’ [Col. 1031A] (Matt. XXIV).

## CHAPTER LX

“‘Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you.’ The Jews, deceived by false error and inventing certain empty dreams for themselves, refer all these things to the period of a thousand years, during which they say that they will reign with their Christ, whom we call Antichrist. By this Jerusalem they wish to understand that golden and adorned city which they suppose will descend from heaven, of which John the Evangelist speaks in the Apocalypse (chap. XXI). By it we understand the holy Church, which is adorned with various orders and different virtues.

“These lying speakers, burdened by the discourse of error, also say that at that time all the nations will serve them, and that camels and dromedaries from Midian and Ephah, coming from Sheba, will bring gold and frankincense; that all the flocks of Kedar will be gathered, and the rams of Nebaioth will offer sacrifice to God upon the altar of the temple that they built; and that all the other things narrated here will come to them. But judging all these things to be utterly false and vain, we refer them to the primitive Church, which was gathered from the Jews—namely, in the apostles who believed before the Lord’s Passion, and in those who, after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, received the faith of the Lord through the preaching of the apostles. Of these Luke says that three thousand believed in one day (Acts II), along with the other events that follow.

“But this also must be considered: Jerusalem is understood in sacred Scripture in four ways. First, in the literal sense, Jerusalem is the great city which was once called Jebus and thereafter Salem, situated on Mount Zion or Moriah, where Abraham offered his son (Gen. XII). Concerning it the Lord says: ‘When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army’ (Matt. XXIV), and so forth.

“Second, heavenly blessedness is called Jerusalem, where the multitude of angels and ranks of heavenly powers dwell, and where the souls of the saints have been joined and united with them. Concerning it the distinguished preacher says: ‘But that Jerusalem which is above is free’ (Gal. IV).
