“Third, the present Church is called Jerusalem, that is, the congregation of the faithful and elect established in the peace of the Lord and raised upward in vision and contemplation of him. Concerning it it is said: ‘Jerusalem, which is built as a city’ (Ps. CXXI), and: ‘Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion’ (Ps. LXXXVI).

“Fourth, each faithful soul is also called Jerusalem, since it stands upon Mount Zion, that is, in contemplation of the mind.

“Thus it is said to the primitive Church, consisting of the apostles from the Jews and of the other believers: ‘Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.’ This is said to one who has fallen or is lying down, so that she may rise. She had fallen in the unbelievers and lay in vices; therefore it is said to her: Rise through faith to perform good works, O primitive Church. You who fell through unbelief in the synagogues, rise in the Churches. You who fell among the Jews, rise among the Gentiles. You who fell through denial, [Col. 1032A] rise through true confession. You who fell in vices, rise in virtues.

“And after you have risen, be enlightened, that is, receive the faith of Christ, because your light has come—the light whose coming all the prophets promised to you for your redemption. That light, I say, has come to you which ‘enlightens every person coming into this world’ (John I): Christ, namely, who said: ‘I am the light of the world’ (John VIII). Christ has now come through the mystery of the Incarnation; you will be enlightened by him if you receive his faith.

“‘And the glory of the Lord has risen over you,’ O Church, just as the sun rises and enlightens the world. This was once shown in figure to Moses when he dedicated the tabernacle and to Solomon when he dedicated the Temple. We read that when Moses built the tabernacle [Col. 1032B] and Solomon the Temple, the glory of the Lord was revealed to them; it prefigured the Son of God, who is the glory of the Father, just as the same Father said to him: ‘Arise, my glory.’ And his glory replied to him: ‘I shall rise at dawn.’

“Or by the fact that the glory of the Lord is whatever marvelous thing takes place in heaven and on earth, we can also refer this to the glory of his miracles. The glory of the Lord was present when water was changed into wine, the dead were raised, lepers cleansed, paralytics healed, and the other signs and miracles that he performed. ‘The glory,’ he says, ‘of the Lord has risen over you’ (John II), that is, the Son of God has now been born for your redemption, and the glory of his miracles has risen over you so that you may be glorified. It follows:

“‘For behold, darkness,’ namely the darkness of unbelief, [Col. 1032C] ‘shall cover the earth,’ that is, the Jews, who seek and understand only earthly things, interpreting the matter carnally: ‘If you are willing to listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the earth’ (Isa. I). ‘And darkness,’ that is, the blindness of sins, ‘shall cover the peoples,’ namely, shall cover them. When the Lord appeared in the world and shone through faith in the hearts of the apostles and the other believers, the darkness of unbelief covered the Jews, who desired only earthly advantages, because they refused to believe even when they saw his miracles. Hence the Lord himself says: ‘For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind’ (John IX).

“‘But over you,’ O primitive Church, ‘the Lord shall rise,’ as the sun rises, so that he may enlighten you, ‘and his glory,’ that is, the splendor of his miracles, ‘shall be seen in you’ by the eyes [Col. 1032D] of the body and the eyes of the mind. Concerning this glory it is said: ‘We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father’ (John I). Indeed, glory was seen in the apostles, because he performed miracles before their eyes.

“‘And the nations shall walk in your light,’ O primitive Church—that is, in your faith, or in your Christ, by whom you are enlightened—although previously they walked in the darkness of sins. ‘And kings in the splendor of your rising,’ when you were born in the faith of Christ and from water and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with: ‘Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit’ (John III), and so forth. And: ‘To all who received him he gave power to become children of God’ (John I).

“Kings are understood here in two ways: either the kings of this world, such as Constantine, Heraclius, Theodosius, and very many others who possessed the faith of Christ; or the saints are also kings, since, being sons of the King, they ruled themselves well. Of them it is said: ‘The heart of the king is in the hand of God; he will turn it wherever he wishes’ (Prov. XXI). We all—both kings and nations—walk in the light of the apostles and in the splendor of his rising, because we have the same faith and are reborn in the same baptism.

“‘Lift up your eyes all around and see; all these have been gathered together; they have come to you.’ It is said to the primitive Church: O primitive Church, lift up the eyes of your mind all around and see, that is, consider. ‘All these have been gathered together; they have come to you,’ that is, they have come for this purpose, to join themselves to you in the unity of faith or to be your children. He is speaking of those about whom Luke wrote in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1033B] (chap. II): ‘There were dwelling in Jerusalem devout Jewish men from every nation under heaven,’ when the Holy Spirit rested upon the apostles in tongues of fire.

“Or otherwise: ‘Lift up,’ he says, O primitive Church, ‘your eyes and consider from the east and the west and from all the regions of the world. All these Gentiles dwelling around you shall be gathered to your faith and shall come to you, to be your children.’ Concerning this it is said elsewhere: ‘Rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and shall dwell in your midst, and many nations shall come to you’ (Ezek. XLIII).

“‘Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall suck milk.’ Some manuscripts read: ‘Your daughters shall rise from the side,’ which is found neither in the Hebrew truth nor among the translators of the Septuagint, nor does the sense of blessed Jerome’s exposition incline toward it. The sons and daughters of the primitive Church who come from afar are the Gentiles who had withdrawn far from God through idolatry—not in place but in merit. Concerning them the Apostle says: ‘You who were once far off have been brought near.’ For the more anyone sins, the farther he withdraws from God.

“Therefore the sons of the primitive Church are all believers who are stronger in faith and understanding, who themselves come from afar and are gathered to the faith. Concerning them the Apostle says: ‘Even if you have many fathers according to the flesh, yet through the Gospel I begot you’ (I Cor. IV). The daughters who suck milk are the souls of the faithful of either sex who are nursing, that is, seeking simple nourishment. To them the apostle Paul says: ‘As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able’ [Col. 1033D] (I Cor. III). And Peter says: ‘Like newborn infants, desire milk’ (I Pet. II). For the tender food is knowledge of God’s humanity; solid food is knowledge of his divinity.

“Thus it is said to the primitive Church: Your sons, the Gentiles, shall come from afar to you through faith, withdrawing from idolatry; and your daughters, the souls of the simple faithful, shall suck milk, that is, simple teaching. But if we say, ‘Your daughters shall rise from the side,’ as some manuscripts have it, it must be understood in this way: We read in John’s Gospel (chap. XIX) that ‘one of the soldiers opened Christ’s side with a lance,’ and immediately blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed forth from it; from these the Church was built, just as Eve, the mother of all, was formed from the rib of Adam’s side [Col. 1034A] (Gen. III). These are so joined together that we cannot be saved either without water and blood or without blood and water. For unless we believe Christ’s Passion and resurrection and recognize that he suffered all these things for our redemption, we shall not be saved, even if we are baptized. But if we believe in his Passion and resurrection and that our redemption will come to us through them, we shall not be worthy to be saved unless we have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity.

“‘Then you shall see and overflow, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has turned toward you and the strength of the nations has come to you.’ ‘Then,’ he says, when you have lifted up your eyes, your sons have come from afar, and your daughters have sucked milk, you shall see sons coming to you from all the regions of the world, and you shall overflow with the faithful like a river with waters. Your heart shall wonder at the multitude of peoples; indeed, your heart shall be enlarged, or expanded, in the breadth of joy because of the greatness of your gladness. For just as one who is placed in sadness is somehow constricted, so one who remains in joy is somehow enlarged.

“Of this enlargement and joy the Apostle says: ‘For what is our crown and joy? Are you not so in the Lord?’ (I Thess. II). And: ‘Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged in you. Be enlarged also yourselves’ (II Cor. VI). At what time these things would come to the primitive Church he makes clear when he says: ‘Then,’ you will say, ‘your heart shall wonder and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has turned toward you through faith,’ that is, all the nations of this world, which is understood by the sea; ‘the strength of the nations shall come to you,’ namely the kings, princes, and powers of this age.

“‘An inundation,’ that is, an abundance, ‘of camels shall cover you,’ or adorn you, ‘the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.’

“The camel is a humpbacked animal accustomed to carrying burdens. Therefore camels may appropriately be understood as the rich of this world, who bear the burdens of riches and sins, so that they can say with the Psalmist: ‘For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me’ (Ps. XXXVII). Among these camels was Matthew, who was changed from a tax collector into a preacher and writer of the Gospel, and Joseph of Arimathea, and those of whom the Lord said: ‘It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God’ (Matt. XIX).

“A dromedary, or *dromas, dromadis*—both forms are used—is smaller than a camel but faster. Therefore by dromedaries we must understand the Gentiles, who hastened swiftly to the Lord’s faith. Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, rich in camels and dromedaries; the whole province is called Sheba, from which the queen of Sheba also came to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Through these regions it was signified that all nations and regions would come to the Lord’s faith.

“It is not without a mystery that they are said to offer gold and frankincense. By gold is understood the understanding of faith; by frankincense, pure prayers, as the Psalmist declares: ‘Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.’ Midian is interpreted as ‘iniquity’; Ephah as ‘dissolved’ or ‘pouring out’; Sheba as ‘captivity’ or ‘conversion.’

“Thus the herds of camels and dromedaries—that is, the rich and powerful of this world and all the Gentiles who came swiftly to Christ’s faith—having loosed the bonds of iniquity, poured out their souls to the Lord. All those returning from captivity to the devil and from their former way of life, offering a gift to the Lord—that is, through the pure faith signified by gold and the pure prayers signified by frankincense—came into the fellowship of the primitive Church and adorned it with their prayers and virtues. [Col. 1035B] Nor are they content with their own salvation alone; they preached the Lord’s praise to others. That is, they declared that the Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of God the Father, who is his praise and glory, and they made known to others the majesty of Christ—that is, the miracles and virtues that he performed—and how God the Father made all things through him.

“‘Every flock of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall serve you.’ In the literal sense, he calls sheep and goats a flock; through these we must understand all the simple. Kedar was a son of Ishmael, and that region took its name from him, so that it was called Kedar, where the Saracens now dwell, descended from his lineage.

“‘The rams of Nebaioth,’ he says, ‘shall serve you.’ By rams, which provide leadership to flocks, are understood the princes and leaders of the nations. Nebaioth was one of Ishmael’s sons. Kedar is interpreted as ‘darkness’ or ‘sorrow’; Nebaioth as ‘prophecy.’

“The very ones who above were called camels and dromedaries were the flock of Kedar, that is, sons of darkness and sorrow, to whom the Apostle says: ‘You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Eph. V); and: ‘What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?’ (Rom. VI). They also became the rams of Nebaioth, that is, preachers and sons of the prophets, because they taught what the Law and the prophets had foretold concerning Christ. They served the Church, because from them bishops, presbyters, other ministers of the Church, and teachers were ordained. They served the Lord either when they handed his body and blood to the faithful, or when they supplied his word of teaching.

“‘They shall be offered upon my propitiatory altar, and I shall glorify the house of my majesty.’ We can understand ‘altar’ in this passage in two ways: either as faith, upon which good works are offered to God; or, by one altar, all the altars throughout the world upon which his body and blood are offered. For just as there is one faith in the holy Church, so there is one altar. As Isaiah demonstrates when he says: ‘In those days there shall be an altar of the Lord in the land of Egypt,’ that is, in the world, which is understood by Egypt, a name interpreted as ‘darkness’ or ‘sorrow.’

“‘The rams,’ he says—that is, teachers and the sons of the prophets [Col. 1036A] by imitation—‘shall be offered upon my propitiatory altar,’ that is, in the right faith that pleases God; or so that they may serve the altar, like those who were bishops, just as Titus and Timothy were offered by Paul, Mark by Peter, and the other martyrs and teachers, their successors. ‘And I shall glorify the house of my majesty,’ he says, that is, I shall honor my Church in such people. Just as by one altar all altars are understood, so by one house we must understand all the churches.

“‘Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?’ This is the prophet’s voice, expressing wonder at the Gentiles who believe and run swiftly to God’s faith. Who are these Gentiles who fly like clouds, raining words, flashing miracles, and lifting themselves toward heavenly things through contemplation of the mind? It follows: ‘And like doves to their windows.’ Just as doves stand at their windows so that they may enter their chambers, so these, coming through faith, entered the holy Church.

“Or, just as doves stand at their windows, so do the saints, because, rejoicing in simplicity, they guard the five bodily senses for themselves, so that death cannot enter through them, attending to the saying: ‘Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matt. X).

“‘For the islands await me,’ that is, the various nations, in accordance with what Jacob says (Gen. XLIX): ‘The prince shall not fail from Judah,’ and so forth, up to: ‘He himself shall be the expectation of the nations.’ ‘And the ships of the sea,’ that is, the Churches of this world, ‘at the beginning,’ namely of their faith, ‘await me, so that I may bring your sons’ [Col. 1036C]—the Gentiles—‘from afar,’ O primitive Church, that is, from idolatry. ‘Their silver,’ that is, confession of faith, or wisdom or understanding, ‘and their gold with them,’ that is, the understanding of faith; hence it is said: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Rom. X).

“‘To the name of your God and to the Holy One of Israel,’ namely, he shall come, because he will glorify you through them. ‘And the sons of strangers shall build your walls, and their kings shall serve you.’ This can be understood both historically and spiritually. In the literal sense, by ‘sons of strangers’ he calls the sons of the nations, namely kings, princes, and powerful men, who built Christ’s churches throughout the world. Thus Constantine constructed twelve churches at Rome in honor of the twelve apostles, and many others founded very many churches and supplied them with what was necessary.

“Spiritually, however, he calls the sons of strangers and their kings the martyrs and preachers of the nations, by whose faith and virtues the holy Church was founded. ‘For in my indignation I struck you, but in my reconciliation I had mercy on you.’ He speaks to the Church. Almighty God often strikes his elect in order to correct them. He struck the Jews when he led them into captivity; he struck the Church through the tyrants of this age in order to test and amend her. But afterward he had mercy on her through the reconciliation accomplished by the blood of his Son.”

“Your gates shall be opened [Col. 1037A]”—that is, they shall stand open—“continually; by day and by night they shall not be shut, so that the strength of the nations may be brought to you, and their kings may be led in,” namely, to you through faith. What are the gates of the Church that always stand open? The bishops and priests, through whose ministry we are brought within the holy Church. They are therefore said always to stand open because they are ready to receive believers into the Church. “By day and by night” means both in prosperity and in adversity. And why is this? So that the strength of the nations may be brought to the Church—namely, princes, the powerful, or martyrs strong in faith—and that their kings, as Constantine was, or the saints who rightly govern themselves, may be led to its faith.

“For the nation”—understand, that of the Jews—“and the kingdom,” that is, royal power, “which will not have served you” [Col. 1037B] with holy service through faith and action, O primitive Church, “will perish” on the day of judgment together with those to whom it will be said: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). “And the nations”—understand, those that will not have served you—“will be laid waste in solitude,” that is, the pagans who remain in unbelief will be abandoned by God and, handed over to the devil, will be devastated by the torments of Gehenna.

“The glory of Lebanon shall come to you, the fir tree, the boxwood, and the pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctuary; and I will glorify the place of my feet.” Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia and Palestine, on the border of the Promised Land. From it Hiram once supplied David for his palace, and Solomon for the construction of the Lord’s temple, with beautiful and incorruptible timber. Its glory lies in the height of its trees and the diversity and multitude [Col. 1037C] of its beasts. Lebanon, therefore, is understood in this passage as the world, and the glory of that mountain as the height and sublimity of this world—qualities found especially in kings and princes, who came to the Church through the confession of faith.

By the fir tree, which is a tree of marvelous size and height, are understood the rich or philosophers who were lofty in worldly wisdom, such as Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine—once towering trees existing in the world, but, when they came to the Church, adorning it with their teachings and virtues. By the pine and the boxwood, which rejoice in their greenness, are understood those who, after being joined to the Church, remained green in faith. The diversity of the trees signifies the various orders from which the holy Church has been adorned.

[Col. 1037D] People came to it from kings and princes, from the rich, from philosophers, and from every other order, through whom its holy place was adorned—that is, the Church which he himself sanctified by the blood of redemption and the washing of baptism. Thus it is said to the primitive Church: “The glory of Lebanon”—that is, the kings and princes of this world—“will come to you” through faith; likewise the fir tree, namely, the rich and philosophers; and the pine and boxwood, that is, those who possess the greenness of faith; and they will adorn you with their teachings and virtues.

What follows—“and I will glorify the place of my feet”—designates the same people by the feet and again by the fir and boxwood: namely, the apostles, preachers, and their followers, whose place is the Church, [Col. 1038A] which was founded by them. The apostles and preachers are called the Lord’s feet because he was carried by them throughout the whole world, in accordance with what he had once said through the prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI). Hence another prophet also says: “Blessed are the feet that bear peace,” that is, that bear Christ (Isa. LII). Or alternatively: preachers are called the Lord’s feet because, just as the feet carry the whole body, so they sustain the Church by their teachings, miracles, and examples. “I will glorify the place of my feet,” he says—that is, I will adorn the Church, which the apostles and their successors founded, with a multitude of believers.

“And they shall come to you”—understand, through faith, O Church—“bent down,” that is, bowed and humble, “the sons of those who humiliated you,” namely, persecutors who killed [Col. 1038B] your holy preachers, “and all those who slandered you shall worship the traces of your feet”—that is, they shall revere the signs and works of your apostles, who, as we said above, were the feet of the Church.

The Jews greatly humiliated the Church when they beheaded James, the brother of the Lord, who had been appointed bishop for them by the apostles, and when they stoned Stephen. But afterward, coming to his faith through the Lord’s grace, they were humbled and revered the signs and miracles of the apostles, as blessed Paul did. He had greatly humiliated the Church by consenting with his fellow citizens, as did those about whom Luke wrote that a great multitude of priests was obedient to the faith.

Similarly, the gentiles greatly humiliated the Church when they cut down Peter, the lofty cedar; but afterward, [Col. 1038C] having been humbled, they glorified the Lord in the works of his apostles. It follows: “And they shall call you the city of the Lord, Zion, the Holy One of Israel.” He is speaking to the Church. A city derives its name from the fellowship of its citizens, and the holy Church is called a city because all who dwell in it share one faith, one baptism, one charity, and one concord. Hence Luke also says in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

This is the city of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V)—that is, the Church founded upon Christ. Thus it is said to the Church: Those who, as I have said, slandered you, afterward coming bent down and humble, will call you the city of the Lord, Zion—that is, the watchtower of the Holy One of Israel. All who have been reborn [Col. 1038D] of water and the Holy Spirit ought to stand in Zion, that is, in contemplation and the watchfulness of the mind.

“Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was no one who passed through you, I will make you the pride of the ages and a joy from generation to generation.” The Church was forsaken or deserted among unbelieving Jews and idolatrous gentiles, and hated by both peoples. The Jews hated it because it held and preached the faith of Christ, whom they themselves had contemptuously crucified. The gentiles hated it because it said that the idols they worshiped were nothing and regarded their most vain errors as worthless.

And when the Lord came through the [Col. 1039A] mystery of the Incarnation, there was neither among the Jews nor among the gentiles any prophet or apostle who passed through them and offered assistance. But when he says, “I will make you the pride of the ages,” pride is understood here in a good sense, namely, as glory and exaltedness. For the word is ambiguous: sometimes it is used in a bad sense, as when it is said of the devil that he is king over all the sons of pride; and sometimes in a good sense, as here.

“Because,” he says, “you were forsaken among unbelieving Jews and idolatrous gentiles, and there was no apostle or prophet who passed through, offering assistance, I will make you the pride of the ages”—that is, I will place you at the summit of the virtues of all ages and in eternal glory. “And I will make you a joy,” that is, so that you may rejoice forever, “in the generation” of the Jews “and the generation” of the gentiles, or throughout all future ages.

What he also says—“there was no one who passed through you”—can be understood in this way: There was no apostle or prophet who passed through you and blessed you. Of such people it is said in the psalm: “Those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. CXXVIII). It was indeed the custom of that people for passers-by to bless those working beside the road, just as we read that Boaz did when he said to the reapers: “The Lord be with you” (Ruth II).

“And you shall suck the milk of the nations, and you shall be nursed at the breast of kings.” “You shall suck,” he says, O Church—that is, you shall receive the milk of the nations, meaning the simple teaching and simple faith of teachers from the nations; and “you shall be nursed at the breast of kings,” that is, you shall feast upon the teachings of the apostles and other teachers. Of these kings and princes it is said: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV).

Those who suck here signify people who came from paganism, filled with wisdom, to the faith, and taught many, giving some simple instruction and others solid food. It follows: And you shall know, O Church, when you have been instructed by the teachings of teachers, “that I am the Lord who saves you” from eternal death, “and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob”—that is, the one who once made Jacob strong so that he could wrestle with the angel, and who redeemed you by my blood.

Or again, you shall know that I am your Redeemer, who grant strength to those who overcome vices, so that they may always be able to resist the snares of demons.

“For bronze I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, [Col. 1039D] and for wood, bronze, and for stones, iron.” By wood and stones are understood those hard of heart, foolish, and senseless, who worship idols in place of God. When they believed, they were converted into some usefulness for the Church, which is signified by iron and bronze. The same thing is shown again in gold and silver, by which they advance toward a perfect understanding of faith and a pure confession.

Or else by bronze and iron we should understand those who possessed some usefulness among the gentiles. But when these were changed, their gifts became diverse: some became resonant in preaching like bronze, while others became teachers, signified by gold and silver, as that desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise. Others became strong in faith and were made martyrs, such as Cyprian and many others.

[Col. 1040A] “And I will make your visitation peace, and your overseers righteousness.” This is God’s voice to the Church. Here he has used “visitation” for “visitor,” just as we read in the Apostle Paul’s Epistle concerning the Jews: “God gave them the working of iniquity in place of the worker” (Rom. I). The Septuagint, however, says: “I will make your princes peace, and your bishops righteousness.”

We should understand the visitor of peace either as the Lord himself, who is our peace, or as his apostles and the shepherds of his Church. They are called peace and righteousness because, preaching peace and teaching righteousness, they justify their subjects and reconcile them to God (Eph. V). “I will make your visitation peace,” that is, I will make your bishops and shepherds peaceful, and your overseers righteous, so that they may teach you rightly to worship your Creator and judge justly, without considering persons in judgment.

“Wrongdoing”—or sin—“shall no longer be heard in your land,” that is, in the land of the living. “Desolation and destruction”—understand, shall no longer exist—“within your borders.” After you have passed into eternal blessedness, wrongdoing or sin shall no longer be heard in the land of the living, concerning which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI). Desolation—that is, affliction and destruction, or misery—shall not be within your borders, that is, in the land of the living, because you shall reign with me in everlasting blessedness.

“And salvation”—or the Savior—“shall occupy,” that is, cover or fill, “your walls, and praise your gates.” In Hebrew the Savior is read as *Jesus*. The walls of the Church are the holy apostles, preachers, and teachers, who fortify it by their writings and teachings [Col. 1040C] against heretics and pagans and against the attacks of demons. They are the gates because through their ministry we are brought into the Church, and through reception of the Lord’s body we are brought from it again into our heavenly homeland.

“The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you. But the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory.” These words refer to the day of judgment. “After you have passed,” he says, O Church, “into eternal blessedness, this visible sun shall not shine upon you, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you,” because you shall shine like the true sun, Christ, in accordance with the saying: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII).

“But the Lord shall be your everlasting light”—that is, the holy Trinity and undivided Unity shall illuminate you, and your God shall be your glory.

“Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not diminish, because the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed.” Here we should understand the sun spiritually as Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, and the moon as the Church, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.” The Church is compared to the moon because, just as the moon receives borrowed light from the sun and derives all its brightness from it, so the Church is illuminated by Christ, the true sun, and receives from him whatever good it possesses.

Therefore he says, “Your moon shall not diminish,” because in the present world the Church is sometimes diminished and sometimes increased. It is diminished when someone falls into heretical depravity or dies in sins after baptism. It is increased when the number of the elect is completed day by day—namely, when a pagan is converted to the faith or a child is baptized. But when the final judgment has ended and the reprobate have been condemned, only the righteous will then remain; none of them will afterward be diminished, nor will their number be increased.

As for the literal sense, blessed Isidore says in the *Book of Creatures* that, once the day of judgment has passed, the sun will receive the reward of its labor, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “The sun,” he says, “will shine sevenfold” (Isa. XXX). Neither the sun nor the moon will afterward come to setting; rather, they will remain in the order in which they were created, so that the impious, placed beneath the earth in torment, may not enjoy their light. [Col. 1041B] In accordance with Habakkuk’s statement (chap. III): “The sun and moon stood still,” meaning that they will stand in their proper order.

It follows: “The Lord,” he says—understand, for you—“shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed,” that is, shall be ended or shall reach their conclusion. The holy Church, which in the present mourns and laments its own sins and those of others, or because it is delayed from entering the kingdom, will receive consolation on the day of judgment. As the Lord himself said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

“But your people,” O Church, “shall all inherit the land forever”—understand, the land of the living, of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land.” This should not be understood generally of all human beings, but of the elect angels and righteous human beings [Col. 1041C], who, when the day of judgment has been completed, will remain together with God to possess the heavenly kingdom eternally, while the impious are handed over to the punishment of eternal condemnation together with their father, the devil. And when the saints continually behold their Creator, they will no longer be able to sin.

“The shoot of my planting, the work of my hands, for glorification”—understand, they themselves will be. The good angels, the apostles, and the other believers, who adorn the faith they possess with good works, are the shoot of the Lord’s planting and the work of his hands, because they were created by him and planted in the Church through faith for the glorification of their Creator. As he himself says through Jeremiah: “Those whom I created for the glory and praise of my name” (Jer. XIII).

There is also a planting that is not good, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. XV).

“The least shall become a thousand, and the little one a most powerful nation.” The least—that is, any humble person who has humbled himself for Christ’s name, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your servant” (Matt. XX), saying with the Apostle: “To the least of all the saints grace has been given” (Eph. III)—and whoever has been little, that is, humble in his own eyes, in the present Church or even on the day of judgment, will be set over a thousand or over the most powerful nation of the elect, hearing from the Lord: “Well done, good servant; be over ten or five cities” (Luke XIX).

[Col. 1042A] And in him will be fulfilled what the Lord promised him: “Whoever therefore humbles himself like this little one will be greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII), above all those whom he taught or to whom he offered an example of humility.

“I, the Lord, will suddenly do this in its time.” “In its time” means in the time of Christ’s coming, or at the opportune or appointed time, when the Son of Man sends his angels to gather from his kingdom all scandals. Suddenly or unexpectedly this will happen: the one who has been humble and little in his own eyes will be established over the many good things of the heavenly homeland, in which he will rejoice forever (Matt. XIII).

He says “suddenly” because the day of judgment will come quickly and when it is not expected, according to the prophet’s saying: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V).

## CHAPTER LXI

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, and to proclaim release to captives and opening to those who are shut in.”

The Lord Jesus, who is God and man, sometimes speaks in the person of his divinity, as in: “I and the Father are one.” At other times he speaks in the person of his humanity, as in: “The Father is greater than I,” and here in the present passage, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (John X, XIV)—that is, he is in me or greater than I—“because the Lord has anointed me,” meaning that he has filled me with the grace of that Holy Spirit.

This anointing was completed at the time of his baptism, when the Holy Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove [Col. 1042C] (Luke III). Concerning this anointing the same prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him,” and so forth up to: “He shall fill him with the fear of the Lord” (Isa. II). The Psalmist likewise says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

“Above your companions” means that he was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit more than all the saints, because the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him: for he alone, God and man, remained without sin. “For he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.”

“It was the Spirit,” he says, “the Holy Spirit who is in me, or greater than I, who anointed me, who sent me to announce good news to the meek,” that is, to the humble and poor, the joy of eternal life. Concerning them it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. V), and, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

“To heal the brokenhearted”—that is, to heal those who have a contrite heart and grieve over their sins, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L).

“He sent me to proclaim release to captives,” that is, to proclaim forgiveness of sins to all gentiles and to all human beings who were held captive by the devil and by various errors, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matt. IV).

“And to those who are shut in”—understand, in the prison of unbelief and ignorance—“opening,” that is, release from sins. Or, as Symmachus translated more explicitly: “Release to the bound.” It follows.

[Col. 1043A] “To proclaim a year acceptable to the Lord and a day of vengeance for our God; to comfort all who mourn, to place upon the mourners of Zion, and to give them a crown instead of ashes; the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.”

The “year acceptable to the Lord” should specifically be understood as the time of Christ’s preaching, which was acceptable to God the Father because it saved many. In general, however, it means the whole period from the Lord’s birth until the day of judgment, which likewise is acceptable to God the Father because a multitude of believers has been saved through the preaching of the apostles and their followers, and will be saved. Concerning this time the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

And he not only proclaimed a year acceptable to the Lord [Col. 1043B] the Father on behalf of those who believed, but also a day of vengeance or condemnation against the Jews, which came through the Romans after his ascension. He proclaimed it by saying: “Days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” And: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, know that its desolation is near” (Luke XIX, XXI).

This must also be understood: just as above he spoke in the person of his humanity, saying, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” so here, when he says, “to proclaim a day of vengeance acceptable to our God,” the Lord God is his God according to his humanity. The day of vengeance against the Jews was acceptable to God the Father—not because he rejoiced in their wickedness or desolation, but because he speaks according to our manner of speaking, since we rejoice when we take vengeance on our enemies.

For this also he sent me: “to comfort”—understand, in the present or also in the future—all who mourn their own sins and those of others. Of them it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

“And to place,” he says, “upon the mourners of Zion”—understand, a crown upon their head, or to pour the joy of eternal happiness into their hearts. He calls the mourners of Zion the apostles, who mourned for the salvation of Zion, that is, of the Jews, as blessed Paul did when he said: “I have great sorrow and continual pain for my brothers” (Rom. IX), and, “I could wish that I myself were accursed for my brothers” (ibid.).

For this also he sent me: “to give them”—understand, those who mourned for the Jews—a crown instead of ashes, that is, a heavenly reward instead of the repentance and labor [Col. 1043D] they undertook for their brothers. And to give them the oil of gladness instead of mourning, that is, joy and rejoicing instead of sadness and sorrow. And to give them the garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow, that is, a garment of happiness instead of mourning attire.

The apostles received a crown instead of ashes, and a garment of praise instead of mourning attire, when they saw multitudes of Jews and multitudes of gentiles come to the faith, girded with joy and exultation.

“And they shall be called strong ones of righteousness,” that is, strong for the practice of righteousness: “the planting of the Lord for glorification.” The prophetic speech addresses the Church. “After,” he says, “you have received joy instead of sorrow, the apostles, martyrs, and other perfect believers will be called within you strong for practicing righteousness; and they will also be called the planting of the Lord, because they were founded by him in faith within the Church for the glorification of their Creator.”

“And they shall build the wastes from ancient times, and raise up the ancient ruins, and restore the deserted cities, the places laid waste from generation to generation.” The discourse now concerns the apostles. Therefore, after the apostles have been planted by the Lord in faith within the Church and have glorified him by their resources, they will build, through their preaching and baptism, the hearts of the gentiles, which have been deserted by God from ancient times, that is, from the beginning.

“And they shall raise up the ancient ruins”—that is, what fell in the synagogues through unbelief they will restore in those Jews who believed. And what fell among the gentiles from the beginning of the world through idolatry, they themselves will restore and raise up [Col. 1044B] through the worship of almighty God. And they will restore the cities deserted by God—that is, the churches of the various nations—or the five senses of the body, which are understood as cities that had been laid waste, in the generation of the Jews and the generation of the gentiles, by unbelief and idolatry.

“And strangers shall stand and pasture your flocks, and the sons of foreigners shall be your farmers and vinedressers.” Strangers and foreigners are called gentiles because they were alienated from the knowledge of God, having withdrawn far from him through idolatry. But after they believed, they stood upright in faith and good works, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “Stand firm in the faith” (I Cor. XVI), and, “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X).

The apostles’ flocks are the simple and gentle, concerning whom the Lord says to Peter, and through him to all the apostles: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI), or “my lambs.” The preachers of the gentiles and the martyrs—such as Gregory, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, Cyprian, and many others—fed them with simple speech and spiritual teaching.

These martyrs and preachers, the sons of foreigners—that is, the sons of the gentiles—were farmers and cultivators of the Church, builders, vinedressers, and guardians, because they built the Church and cultivated the hearts of believers. Those whom the apostles, their predecessors, had brought into the Lord’s vineyard—of which the prophet says, “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel”—they themselves guarded.

Conversely, the scribes and Pharisees were bad builders, bad vinedressers, and bad cultivators. Concerning them, while they were listening, the Lord says at the end of the parable: “He will put those wicked men to a miserable death,” and, “Therefore the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

“But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be named ministers of our God.” This can be understood in two ways, as blessed Jerome says: either as referring to the preachers from the gentiles, who were the sons of foreigners, or to the apostles, concerning whom it is said, “A remnant shall be saved” (Rom. IX), so that they themselves may be called priests of the Lord, who possessed greater dignity, just as it is said of the sons of David that “they were priests in the house of the Lord” (II Sam. VIII).

The sense, or order, is this: When the sons of foreigners have become vinedressers, builders, and farmers, you apostles will be called their priests and teachers, because you will be ministers of the Lord.

“You shall eat the strength of the nations, and in their glory you shall boast.” The strength of the nations was the martyrs, who endured the torments of their persecutors bravely for Christ’s name. The apostles, feasting upon their victory and triumph—that is, rejoicing greatly—saw them pass into their fellowship, and in their glory they boasted, that is, exulted or gloried.

“Pride” is used here for glory, just as somewhat earlier, where it was said: “I will make you the pride,” or glory, “of the ages.”

“For your twofold shame and disgrace, they shall praise your portion.” The apostles were ashamed and blushed in two respects: namely, over the unbelief of the Jews and the idolatry of the gentiles. But from what caused them shame and brought them disgrace, the Jews and gentiles who were converted to the faith will praise their portion—that is, the Lord—saying with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my portion.” No one can truly say this unless he has no other portion.

“Therefore”—understand, because you had a double share of shame and disgrace over them, and because they were converted to the Lord, who is the portion of the elect—“they shall praise in their land,” that is, in the land of the living and the meek; “they shall possess double” rewards, that is, in body and soul, when they receive immortality and incorruption in the body and unchangeableness in the soul; “and everlasting joy shall be theirs.”

[Col. 1045C] “For I am the Lord, who love judgment”—understand, the judgment of truth—“and hate robbery in a burnt offering.” The rich are accustomed to offer God a gift taken from the poor, but their offering pleases him no more than the price of a prostitute or the sacrifice of a dog, or as a father would be pleased by one who sacrifices his son in his presence.

The meaning is this: “The Lord,” he says, “will grant this, because he loves the poverty of the righteous and the truth of judgment more than the gifts of the rich, which arise from robbery and injustice.”

“And I will give their work”—understand, the work of those who believed—“in truth,” so that they may eat the lamb in truth, receive circumcision of the heart, desire the eternal land, and possess in reality all that was said to the Jews in figure. “And I will make an everlasting covenant with them,” that is, I will give them the Gospel, [Col. 1045D] which no other law will follow, as one followed the law of Moses. Concerning this Gospel the Lord says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV).

“And their seed shall be known among the nations,” that is, the seed of the apostles, “and their offspring in the midst of the peoples.” Just as the apostles were good and true seed, sown by Christ and hearing from him, “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII), so the seed and offspring of the apostles are the faithful, who received from them the seed of the word of God.

“All who see them”—namely, the apostles and the successors and imitators of the apostles—“will recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed.” How will they know and recognize that they were sown by the Lord? By their teaching, chastity, contempt for the world, and power of miracles.

“I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God.” The prophet speaks in the person of the Church. “Rejoicing,” he says, “I will rejoice in the Lord,” not in riches and earthly profits, nor in nobility of lineage, as the Jews did, who gloried that they were descended from the patriarchs, nor will I rejoice in the honors of this world, but in the Lord, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “Rejoice in the Lord always.”

And I will not merely rejoice, but “my soul shall exult,” not in resounding laughter, but in my God.

“For he has clothed me with garments of salvation and covered me with the robe of righteousness.” He gives the reasons why she ought to rejoice and exult in the Lord. “Therefore,” he says, “I will rejoice in the Lord,” because he has clothed me with garments of salvation—that is, with virtues, or with Christ himself, as the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III), and, “Put on the new man” (Eph. IV).

Concerning the words “and he has covered me with the robe of righteousness,” the Psalmist sings: “May your priests, O Lord, be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI). The clothing or garment of the elect is their virtues, or Christ himself; and likewise all the elect are Christ’s garment.

“Like a bridegroom adorned with a crown”—understand, he adorned me—“and like a bride adorned with her jewels.” Here two groups of believers in the holy Church are displayed. The group of the perfect is represented by the bridegroom, concerning whom the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II). The group of the imperfect is represented by the bride, concerning whom the Apostle says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. III), and, “As to infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

[Col. 1046D] Christ the bridegroom therefore makes both bridegrooms and brides; nevertheless, there is one bride, the Church, which is adorned with a crown—that is, with the multitude of believers coming into her fellowship from every part of the world. She is adorned with jewels, that is, with the ornaments of every virtue, signified by the jewels: chastity, humility, and other virtues, as well as the various orders.

“For just as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden makes its seed sprout, so the Lord God will make righteousness and praise sprout before all the nations.” The first of these comparisons should be referred to the bridegroom, the second to the bride.

“Just as,” he says, “the earth, watered by heavenly rains, brings forth its shoot, and just as a garden, watered by the waters of springs, makes its seed”—that is, vegetables of various kinds—“sprout, so the Lord God will make righteousness sprout,” that is, will cause it to germinate or grow: “righteousness,” meaning Christ, who justifies those who believe in him, or the justification of faith, by which the righteous person lives. And he himself will cause his praise to grow before all the nations.

This justification will not exist only among the Jews, nor will the Jews alone render him praise; rather, faith will exist among all believers. And after they have been justified, they will render praise and thanksgiving to their Creator for all the benefits given to them by him. Thus, just as watered earth brings forth its shoot from heaven, so all the perfect, watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit, bring forth daily the fruit of good works.

## CHAPTER LXII

“For the sake of Zion I will not be silent, and for the sake of Jerusalem I will not rest until her righteous one goes forth like brightness”—that is, Christ, the righteous one of the Church—“and her savior is kindled like a lamp.” Until now the Church has been speaking; now the prophet speaks in his own person.

By Zion and Jerusalem we may generally understand the kings and princes of the Jewish people, who forbade the prophets to speak in the Lord’s name; or, more distinctly, by Zion the kings and princes, and by Jerusalem the priests and their subjects. The prophet therefore says: “For the sake of Zion and for the sake of Jerusalem”—that is, for the sake of the kings, princes, and priests—even if they order me to be silent, I will not cease praying. Rather, night and day I will join prayers to prayers until Christ, promised to us in the Law, comes and illuminates the whole world.

Elsewhere the same prophet makes a similar plea: “If only you would tear open the heavens, O Lord, and come” (Isa. LXIV). “I will not be silent,” he says, in my prayers, until the righteous one of the Church goes forth from the Virgin’s womb like brightness—the one who justifies his elect “and enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). He is the brightness of eternal light and the sun of righteousness, who said in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world.”

“And her savior,” that is, the Church’s savior, “is kindled like a lamp”—understand, in the hearts of believers. *Lampas* is Greek; in Latin it is called a flame of fire. Concerning this flame of fire the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). The apostles were kindled by this flame on the day of Pentecost, when they began to speak in all languages.

«And the nations shall see your righteous one,» that is, through faith, O primitive Church—namely, your Christ, who committed no sin. «And all kings,» that is, those who shall have believed, or those who have ruled themselves well. «They shall see your illustrious,» or noble, «one,» through faith. Of these the Lord says: “Blessed are those who have not seen with the eyes of the body but have believed with the mind” (John XX). «And you shall be called by a new name,» O primitive Church, [Col. 1047D] «which the mouth of the Lord has named.» It is customary in the Hebrew language for names to be assigned on the basis of new circumstances, as we can learn from Abraham. At first he was called Ram, as is found in the book of blessed Job (chapter XXXII), in the passage where it says: “And Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, was angry and indignant.” From this he was called Abram, that is, “exalted father,” and afterward Abraham. The same may be understood of blessed Peter, who was first called Simon, and then Peter, from *petra*, that is, from Christ. Thus it is said to the primitive Church: “Your name shall be called”—namely, that which the word of God the Father has decreed—so that you shall be called Christians from Christ, and you shall be named the Church through Jerusalem and Zion.

[Col. 1048A] «And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of kingship in the hand of your God,» that is, in the power of God, or in Christ himself, who is the hand and right hand of the Father. “When,” he says, “the multitude of believers coming to your faith from every part of the world has crowned you, you shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of God, and like a diadem of kingship in his power.”

«You shall no longer be called Forsaken,» by God, «and your land,» that is, your dwelling, «shall no longer be called Desolate,» implicitly because Christ shall dwell in your midst. «But you shall be called, ‘My will is in her,’» that is, the Church of Christ shall be called this, and it shall be said: “This is the Church that does the Lord’s will.” And why is this so? «Because the Lord has been pleased with you, and your land shall be inhabited.» The prophetic utterance addresses the Church gathered from both peoples [Col. 1048B] and promises that she shall no longer be forsaken by God as she once was when she faltered after idols. Just as the Jews remaining in unbelief displeased the Lord, and the nations walking after idolatry displeased him, so he was pleased with those who believed from both peoples and came to his faith.

«For a young man shall dwell with a virgin,» in bodily chastity, as Mary and Joseph, Chrysanthus and Daria.

«And your sons shall dwell in you.» The sons of the Church are those who are instructed in spiritual teaching. «And the bridegroom,» Christ, «shall rejoice over the bride,» the Church, «and your God shall rejoice over you,» that is, over your good works. This is the bridegroom of whom it is said in the psalm: «And he himself shall go forth like a bridegroom» (Psalm XVIII). And this is the bride of whom John the Baptist says: «He who has the bride is the bridegroom» (John III).

«Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not be silent.» This is the voice of almighty God to Jerusalem, that is, to the Church, which is the vision of peace. Walls are so called from *munire*, “to fortify.” Here we may understand walls and watchmen in two ways. The walls of the Church were the apostles and preachers, who fortified the Church through teaching and miracles. Their watchmen, however, are the angels who guard the walls of the Church, lest our adversary the devil, «like a roaring lion,» be able to snatch away anyone from the rams. Hence the Apostle says: «Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?» (Hebrews I).

Or alternatively: The wall of the Church was Titus and Timothy, and Mark and the other disciples of the apostles; their watchmen were Peter, Paul, and the other apostles. Therefore the divine utterance says to the Church: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen”—angels or prelates of the Churches, namely the apostles and their followers. “All day and all night they shall not be silent,” that is, neither in prosperity nor in adversity shall they cease from prayers, entreating my clemency and mercy for the walls, so that they may be fortified by my help. «You who remember the Lord, do not be silent,» implicitly, in prayers, joining vows to vows.

«And do not grant him silence,» implicitly, to the Lord, but always, at a suitable and unsuitable time, ask for his mercy «until he establishes,» that is, makes firmly stand, [Col. 1049A] «Jerusalem,» that is, his Church, and «sets her as a praise in the earth,» either so that she, spread throughout the whole world, may praise her Creator, or so that she herself may be praised by all nations. The divine utterance addresses the watchmen of the walls, so that those who know the Lord’s will and ought to guard the walls may not be silent from prayers and praises, either in prosperity or in adversity. It continues:

«The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength.» Every utterance of almighty God must be received as an oath, because he is always truthful and never deceives. His right hand and the arm of his strength are the Son, through whom he made all things, according to the saying: “All things were made through him.” «I shall no longer give your grain as food to your enemies, nor shall foreign sons drink your wine, for which you have labored.» He addresses the Church. Often, insofar as the literal sense is concerned, almighty God gave the produce of the Jews to their enemies—that is, grain and wine—as we read in the book of Judges (chapter VII), that «the Midianites, coming at harvest time, gathered their produce and expended it both for their own use and for the use of their enemies.» So also when they were led into captivity, when foreign Samaritans were settled there and ate their produce.

But in this passage we may understand the Church’s food in two ways: as virtues and good works, or also as his body and blood, which the faithful receive daily in the holy Church and by which the soul is nourished. At a certain time, before the coming of the Son of God, demons ate the produce of the Jews—that is, the praises and works they offered to idols. But after the Lord’s coming, demons did not eat the virtues and praises of the Church; rather, the Lord feasted upon them, that is, rejoiced and took delight in them.

The food of the Jews was also grain and wine, which signified the Lord’s body and blood, just as he himself said: «For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink» (John VI), because they are not received by heretics and pagans, the enemies of the holy Church. «If I give,» that is, if I shall not give, or shall no longer give, «your grain or wine, for which you have labored, as food to your enemies,» that is, I shall not give your praises and works to demons, but I myself shall receive them. Or: “I shall not give my body and blood, over which you labor in consecration, to heretics and pagans, your enemies,” who are alien to me and to your faith. Why he does not give the food of the faithful to their enemies, he makes clear when he says:

«For those who gather it,» implicitly, the grain, «shall eat it and shall praise the Lord their Creator; and those who carry it away,» implicitly, the wine, «shall drink it in my holy courts.» This is fulfilled partly in the holy Church every day, and partly in eternal blessedness. Who are these who gather and carry away the grain, and who drink in the courts of the Lord—that is, in the dwellings of the Church? Bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all the ministers of the altar, who gather and carry—that is, prepare and consecrate—the body and blood of the Lord, and eat [Col. 1050A] and drink in the Church, praising their Creator and Redeemer.

Or they are also those who now, in the present, gather virtues and carry them away—that is, bring them together. When they have passed from the present Church, they shall eat and drink, that is, exult and rejoice, in the courts of the Lord, or in the heavenly dwellings. Of these the Lord says: «In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.»

«Pass through, pass through the gates; prepare the way for the Lord; make the path level for the people; choose the stones and raise a standard for the people.» To the watchmen of the walls—the angels or prelates of the Church—to whom he had earlier said that they should not be silent from prayers and praises, he again commands that they pass through the gates, that is, through the various ministers of the Church: priests, deacons, and subdeacons, [Col. 1050B] through whose ministry believers are brought into the Church; or that they pass through virtues, walking from virtue to virtue.

They are therefore commanded to pass through the ministers of the Church so that they may guard them, lest any of them fall into the perversity of heretics, and so that they may increase still further in faith. The watchmen of the walls are also commanded to prepare the way for the people wishing to enter the Church—that is, to show them the way of righteousness through teaching and example, and to make the path level, that is, to remove all stumbling blocks by remitting sins through baptism. They are also to choose the stones, or to throw them away, as the Seventy translated it: that is, to remove from human hearts the hardness of unbelief, or to separate from the fellowship of believers the rejected and hard-hearted who refuse to believe. [Col. 1050C] They are also commanded to raise the sign of the cross for the peoples of the nations, that is, to announce to them the Passion and the Resurrection. It continues:

«Behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard to the ends of the earth.» Implicitly, through the apostles, the faith in his Passion and the mysteries of his Resurrection. «Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him.» The watchmen of the walls—angels, prophets, or apostles—are commanded to address the daughter of Zion, that is, the primitive Church, which is called the daughter of Zion either because she was first gathered from the Jews. Of her he says in the Song of Songs: «The sons of my mother fought against me» (Song of Songs I). Or she is called daughter because she received the name of adoption from the Lord, according to what John says: «As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God» (John I).

“Say,” he says, “to Zion,” that is, to the primitive Church. What is said here pertains to the second coming of the Lord. «Behold, your Savior comes,» in place of “he shall come on the day of judgment with angels and archangels and all the powers of heaven.” «Behold, his reward is with him,» so that he may reward the elect and condemn the reprobate. «And his work is before him,» that is, the power of judging in his presence.

«And they shall call them,» implicitly, those who have believed, «a holy people, redeemed by the Lord.» The angels, apostles, and other teachers, rejoicing together with those who believed through their preaching, shall call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord. Blessed Jerome [Col. 1051A] says that in Hebrew it reads “his people, redeemed,” as we have already stated; but some books have “a holy people and redeemed by the Lord.” According to this, the sense here will be: The apostles and other teachers shall call those who have believed, saying: “You are a holy people, and you are redeemed by the Lord.” But the Hebrew truth is clearer and easier in this passage.

«But you,» O Church, «shall be called a sought-out city,» implicitly, by God, «and not forsaken.» “By no means,” he says, “shall you be called a city forsaken by God, as once you were; rather, you shall be called a city sought out by Christ and redeemed by his blood.” Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: «The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished» (Luke I). And this is the sheep, or the city, which the good shepherd came to seek.

## CHAPTER LXIII

«Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength.» Certain angelic powers dwelling in heaven, ignorant of the mystery of the Lord’s birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, saw the Lord ascending to the heights with a multitude of angels and holy men. He did not need the help of any angel, but by his own power ascended above all the heavenly hosts. Struck with wonder at how the one who was worshiped as God in heaven, having become human and having died, rose again and opened the gates of heavenly heaven not only for himself as God but also for all who were then ascending and for those who would afterward believe, they said to the other angels accompanying the Lord: «Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?» The Psalmist likewise says something similar in the person of these same angels: «Who is this King of glory?» (Psalm XXIII).

But here the differing statements of the teachers must be considered. Blessed Augustine, in his exposition of the book of Genesis, says that all the angels, immediately after they were created, knew in contemplation of their Creator whatever that Creator was going to do. Nevertheless, blessed Jerome clearly declares that there were angelic ranks which, until the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation and Passion was completed, did not know it fully, as we have already said above. For example, we too know only in part what will take place on the day of judgment, through the revelation of the holy fathers, and in part we do not know. But whether it was unknown to them or not is no longer for us to investigate, except insofar as the Lord himself has deigned to reveal it. His judgments, after all, are hidden.

Nevertheless, we hold firmly that the prophet uttered this in wonder in the person of those angels who dwelt in heaven, saying: «Who is this who comes from Edom?» Edom is Esau; Esau is Seir. He was called Edom from the lentil stew, because of which he sold his birthright. Edom is interpreted as “earthly,” or “bloody,” or “bloodstained,” and signifies this world. Esau, however, is interpreted as “oaken” or “strong as an oak”; Seir means “bristly,” that is, hairy.

This must also be noted: in this passage Edom is used not for the person himself but for the interpretation of the name, just as Bozrah is used not for the place but for the interpretation of the name. Bozrah is interpreted as “fortified” or “firm,” and signifies either hell, where the souls of the dead are shut up and where the strongest guards have been stationed. Of this city the Psalmist says: «Who will lead me into a fortified city?» (Psalm LIX). Or it also signifies earthly Jerusalem, which was once surrounded by very strong walls and in which the Lord suffered. Homer, the outstanding poet of the Greeks, explains the etymology of this name, as Josephus reports, and says that *ierom*, from which “Jerusalem” derives, means “fortified” or “firm.”

As far as the literal meaning is concerned, Bozrah was situated neither in the promised land nor in Edom, [Col. 1052B] but in Moab. Therefore certain angelic ranks ask the choirs of angels who were accompanying the Lord: «Who is this who comes with so great an army from Edom,» that is, from the earthly and bloodstained world? «And with garments dyed,» that is, with bodily limbs, «comes from Bozrah,» that is, from the fortified city of Jerusalem, where he suffered, or from hell, from which he emerged victorious.

This does not mean that his limbs were dyed or sprinkled with the blood that flowed from his side and the places of the nails, but rather that they were marked by the scars that still appeared on his body. The angels persist in their wonder and ask, saying: “This one beautiful in his robe, or handsome—who is he, advancing in the multitude of his strength?” As though they were saying in other words: “Who is this, beautiful and so splendid in his robe,” that is, in the form of his humanity, “advancing, or ascending, above all the heavens in the multitude of his power,” or in the fullness of his divinity, “ascending above all the heavenly hosts without the help of any angel?”

This is the beautiful one to whom the Psalmist said: «You are beautiful beyond the sons of men» (Psalm XLIV). The ancients called a handsome person *calidus*, “warm,” so that *formosus* is as though derived from *calidus*, because one becomes ruddy from heat, like roses.

«I am he who speaks righteousness and am mighty to save.» While the angels who had been asked who he was—he who was ascending from the earthly and bloodstained world above all the heavens by his own strength—remained silent, and while those accompanying the Lord gave no answer, the Lord himself replied, saying: [Col. 1052D] “Do you wish to know who I am? «I am he to whom the Father has given all judgment» (John V).” As the Psalmist says: «O God, give your judgment to the king» (Psalm LXXI), and so forth.

“I am he who speaks righteousness,” giving good things to the good, rewards to the just, but evil and eternal punishments to the wicked and impious, according to what they deserve. He fulfills this daily, but generally on the day of judgment, when he shall say to the impious: «Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire»; and to the just: «Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom» (Matthew XXV), and so forth. And I not only speak righteousness, but am also a champion—that is, a conqueror—against demons and a defender for the salvation of the human race.

«Why then is your garment red,» that is, your body, «and your clothing,» implicitly, why «are they red,» «like those of one treading in a winepress?» When the Lord therefore said, «I am he who speaks righteousness,» and who conquers the opposing powers, the angels again questioned him and said: “If you are he who speaks righteousness, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John V), and who is the conqueror of demons for the salvation of the human race, we wish to learn from you what cause there has been for your garment—that is, your body—to be bloodstained, and why your clothing, that is, your limbs, are red, as though with dark and reddish wine.

“These things do not suit you, who are radiant from virginity and beautiful beyond the sons of men, but rather murderers, adulterers, and robbers. Tell us, therefore,” they say, “what you have deserved, so that you, who are the defender of the human race, should have bloody and dyed limbs, like any man who treads black and reddish grapes in a winepress or press?” To them the Lord replies—not with only one verse, as before, but with many words, showing them the order of events so that there would be no need to ask again—and says:

«I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.» The Lord calls the cross and all the torments of the Passion—the spitting, blows, piercing with spear and nails—in which he suffered as in a winepress, so that his blood was poured out, a “winepress.” It must be known, however, that “winepress” is sometimes used in a negative sense, for the punishments and penalties of sinners, as in Jeremiah: «The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah» (Lamentations I), that is, he brought upon her the evil of captivity and the burden of affliction; therefore I weep.

At other times “winepress” is used in a positive sense, as in Psalm LXXXIII, whose title is “For the winepresses,” that is, for the martyrs. «I have trodden the winepress alone,» says the Lord. It is as though he were saying: “I have red garments because I alone endured the pressure of the cross, and no man from the human race was with me to help.” He says “alone” because he had no helper—neither angel, archangel, nor any power of the heavenly virtues, neither Jew nor Gentile. They all abandoned him at the time of his Passion, to such an extent that the strongest apostle, Peter, denied him three times, while the others fled.

Although he was abandoned by all, he alone conquered the opposing powers and [Col. 1053D] overcame their strength. This must also be considered: why does he say that the winepress was trodden by him, that is, that the pressure of the Passion was overcome, when he himself was trodden and died? The answer is that he was trodden by the pressure of the Passion in dying, and he trod down the Passion itself by rising on the third day through his own power.

«I trod them down,» that is, I conquered and humbled «them in my fury, and trampled them in my anger.» It must not be thought that almighty God, who is unchangeable, can possess fury or anger. Scripture speaks in our manner, because he appears to rage and be angry to those to whom he renders vengeance. Thus any king, although he may be calm in spirit, appears angry to those whom he orders to be beheaded or killed.

There is this difference between fury and anger: fury is a sudden disturbance of the mind, while anger endures for a long time. But none of these things exists in God. The Lord therefore says: “Although I was trodden down by them, nevertheless I trod them down and conquered them”—that is, the demons or the Jews—in my fury and vengeance. “And I conquered them in my anger,” taking from the demons the power and dominion that they exercised in this world, and taking from the Jews their place, kingdom, nation, priesthood, temple, and every dignity, handing them over to the Romans.

«And their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my clothing.» We must not understand this to mean that demons, who are spirits, have blood. Rather, the blood of Christ, which they caused the Jews to shed by persuading them to kill him, is called their blood, because they received vengeance on account of it. [Col. 1054B] For we read in the Gospel that «the devil put it into the heart of Judas to betray him» (John XIII). He who persuaded him to be betrayed was finally the one who betrayed and killed him.

In this passage there is a figurative transfer from victorious and defeated human beings, who are sustained by blood, to the Lord who conquered the demons and to those who were defeated. For whenever a combatant kills his enemy, the blood of the slain man usually flies out and stains the garments of the killer. Thus David says, speaking of Joab (3 Kings II), that «he placed the blood of battle upon his belt.» Insofar as this sense is concerned, when he pierced the sides of Amasa or Abner, blood flew onto his girdle or belt around his loins.

If, however, we refer these words to the Jews, similarly the blood of Christ that they shed is called their blood, because they received vengeance on account of it. «Their blood was sprinkled,» he says—that is, my blood—«upon my garments,» or through my limbs, for which they shall receive vengeance; «and I stained all my clothing,» that is, my limbs. This does not mean that they were stained, but that he allowed them to be stained.

«For the day of vengeance,» implicitly, against demons and Jews, «was in my heart,» implicitly, while I hung upon the cross enduring such things. «The year of my redemption has come,» that is, the year or time of the redemption of the human race. This is the year that above he called “the acceptable year of the Lord,” and “the day of retribution” for the Jews.

The Passion of the Lord contained within itself, a second time, the punishment of demons and of the reprobate Jews and all unbelievers, as well as the rewards of the just. These two aspects are also divided in this passage into good and evil. On the evil side is “the day of vengeance in my heart”; on the good side, “the year of the redemption of the human race has come.” While the Lord hung upon the cross, enduring the Passion for us, it was in his heart that he would condemn the demons in hell and hand the Jews over to the Romans.

«I looked around,» implicitly, while hanging on the cross, «and there was no helper,» implicitly, for me—neither angel, archangel, patriarch, prophet, apostle, nor any just person, neither Jew nor Gentile. «And I sought one who would help me, and there was none,» implicitly, no helper. This is like what he says in the Psalms: «I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; for one who would console me, and I found none» (Psalm LXVIII). And again: «All my friends have abandoned me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me as strangers» (Job XIX).

«And my arm saved me, and my indignation itself helped me.» This may be understood in two ways: as spoken in the person of his humanity, or in the person of his divinity. “My arm saved me,” he says—that is, the Word, from whom I was assumed, procured resurrection for me; or, “my strength, or my arm, saved for me all those predestined to life, and my indignation”—that is, my retribution and vengeance—“itself helped me when it avenged me upon my enemies, the Jews or the evil spirits.” He speaks here in human fashion. It continues:

[Col. 1055B] «And I trampled,» that is, humbled, conquered, or defeated, «the peoples,» that is, the Jews, «in my fury, and I made them drunk,» that is, I filled them with misery and affliction, «in my anger,» or in my vengeance, «and I brought their strength down to the earth,» that is, I reduced the strength of the demons and the Jews to nothing.

He trampled and conquered the Jews in his fury, and made them drunk or filled them with misery when, in the forty-second year after his Ascension, with the Roman army arriving, he killed them by famine, sword, and pestilence, scattering them throughout every part of the world and among all nations.
