He took away from them all glory and dignity, to such an extent that those who had formerly been called the only people of the Lord are now servants of other nations, and those who were once the head are now the tail.

He brought the strength of the demons down to nothing—those who had been lifted up in pride, whose prince said: «I shall set my throne above the stars of heaven» (Isaiah XIV). Or he also reduced the strength of the Jews to nothing, for they thought themselves alone to be strong, as though they alone were fortified by God’s help and alone among all nations possessed a king.

For now the Jews are not strong, because they do not have within them the God of strength, who is the strength and victory of the elect. They are not fortified by God’s help, because on account of their impiety and unbelief the protection of the angels has departed from them. This was heard in the temple when the destruction of desolation arrived, as they said: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” They do not have the Law, because they do not receive the Gospel, nor the prophets, in whom all those things are contained as fulfilled. «For the Law and the prophets lasted until John.» With the arrival of the grace of truth, the shadow of the Law and the prophets ceased.

«I shall remember the mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord,» implicitly, I shall proclaim it, «for all that the Lord has repaid us, and for the multitude of good things bestowed upon the house of Israel according to his kindness and according to the multitude of his mercies,» implicitly, the Lord has repaid us. The Prophet speaks in the person of the Jewish people doing penance, recognizing the Lord’s great mercy toward them and recalling his benefits, which he bestowed upon them from the day when he led them out of the prison-house of Egypt. He says: «I shall remember the mercies of the Lord, and I shall proclaim his praise for all that the Lord has repaid us.»

When he says “for all that he has repaid us,” he wishes both prosperous and adverse things to be understood. It is as though he were saying: “He delivered us from Egypt and led us through the wilderness into a land better than all others because of his ineffable mercy, and he led us into Babylon because of our sins. Again, in his mercy he brought us back to the land. In all these things I shall proclaim him righteous and declare his praise to all, for according to his kindness—that is, according to the abundance of his mercy—he has repaid us with many good things.”

«And the Lord said: ‘Yet they are my people, children who do not deny,’ and he became their Savior.» The Prophet speaks: “When,” he says, “the Lord saw their repentance, he said: ‘Yet you are my people,’ O Jewish people, of whom I once said: «Israel is my inheritance» (Isaiah XIX). ‘And children who do not deny’: they shall be my children if they cease to spurn me and do not deny me. ‘And he became their Savior,’ implicitly, because by believing in him they performed true repentance.”

But if we say “children of one who does not deny,” as some books have it, the sense will be: Those who repent and believe in me are children—implicitly, children of a people that does not deny; that is, they are children of the patriarchs and prophets who truly believed in me.

«In all their tribulation he was not afflicted,» implicitly, their Savior. «And the angel of his presence saved them.» As blessed Jerome says, the Hebrew word *Io* is ambiguous: it means either “not” or “and he himself.” In the passage where he translated “he was not afflicted,” the Hebrew has this word. Therefore we can understand it in two ways.

First: “In all the tribulation that they endured in Egypt or in the wilderness, he was not afflicted,” that is, their Savior did not suffer with them in order to free them from every distress. Rather, he abandoned them for a time, withdrawing his help from them, so that, placed in tribulation, they might be compelled to ask him.

Alternatively: “In all their tribulation he himself was afflicted,” because he had compassion on their injuries and miseries and sent them his angel to save them, according to the saying: «Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall go before you» (Malachi III). This angel is to be understood as Michael, who was appointed by God over that people, according to what is said to Daniel: «There is no one who helps me in all these matters except Michael, your prince, who stands for the children of your people» (Daniel X).

He is called the angel of his presence because the angels always see the face of God, since they are in God’s presence. «In his love,» implicitly, with which I loved them, «and in his mercy,» that is, in the abundance of his mercies, «he himself redeemed them» from Egypt and Babylon, or also by the blood of his Son, «and he carried them,» implicitly, from Egypt into the promised land, according to the saying: «He spread out his wings, took them up, and carried them upon his shoulders» (Deuteronomy XXXII). «And he lifted them up,» implicitly, from misery to glory, «all the days of the age,» that is, from the beginning when he chose them as his people.

«But they provoked him to anger and afflicted his holy Spirit, and he turned against them as an enemy, and he himself fought against them»—before his coming through various nations, and afterward through Rome. What he says, “they afflicted his Holy Spirit,” while some books have “the spirit of his holy one,” may be understood in two ways.

If we say “his Holy Spirit,” it must be understood of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord says: «I shall ask my Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever» (John XIV). Or by “his holy Spirit” we can understand the angelic spirit, who was saddened when he saw them depart from God through idolatry.

But if we say “the spirit of his holy one,” we must understand in one way the spirit of Moses, whom they saddened, according to the saying: [Col. 1057B] «And they embittered Moses in the wilderness» (Psalm CV). For whoever saddens a righteous man certainly saddens the Spirit of God who is in him, according to what is said through the Prophet: «He who touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye» (Zechariah II).

In a fourth way, we can refer this to the Spirit of Christ and say that when Christ came and preached, they afflicted the spirit of his holy one by refusing to believe in him—that is, the Spirit of Christ, who is the holy and righteous Son of the Father. For the Son of God, who redeemed us at the time of his Passion, certainly also delivered the Hebrews from the Red Sea.

It continues: «And he turned against them as an enemy, and he himself fought against them.» When they departed from his ways and walked against his will, he turned against them as an enemy, changing from merciful to unmerciful, and often fought against them through their enemies, as is abundantly demonstrated in the book of Judges and in the other histories and prophetic books. This can also be referred to the time of his Incarnation, when, because they refused to believe in him, he who had healed their sick and raised their dead turned against them as an enemy and fought against them through the Romans in the forty-second year after his Ascension.

«And he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people.» Almighty God, who had changed from protector into an adversary against the Jewish people who provoked and angered him, remembered, after he had fought against them through the Romans, “the days of old,” that is, the days of ancient times, when he led them out of Egypt.

He also remembered Moses his servant, who interceded for them in the wilderness, saying: «Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from your book» (Exodus XXXII). He also remembered his people, who were saved through Moses’ prayer when he wished to strike them to complete destruction. He remembered these things because there was no one to raise up a prayer for them and free them from the sin of unbelief, as once through Moses’ prayer and intercession they had been delivered from the scourge and the error of idolatry.

It continues: «Where is he who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of his flock?» Foreseeing the rejection of his people, and the misery and affliction that threatened them because of their denial of the Son of God, the prophet Isaiah cried out in compassion, saying: “Where is the clemency of almighty God, who brought them out of the Red Sea with the shepherds of his flock—namely Moses, Aaron, Miriam, and Hur, and the other elders?”

It continues: «Where is,» implicitly, the great and ineffable mercy of almighty God, «who placed in his midst,» that is, in the midst of his people, «the Spirit of his holy one,» that is, his Son, namely the holy Paraclete Spirit, when he led them out of Egypt? We read that, when Moses prayed, the Lord took from his spirit and gave it to seventy men (Numbers XI); this event is mentioned in the present passage.

The Prophet therefore remains in the same state of wonder and, in compassion, says: “Where is he also:

«Who led Moses by the right hand with the arm of his majesty,» that is, where is the Lord’s mercy, who led Moses out of Egypt by the right hand—that is, in prosperity—through the arm of his majesty, or through the protection of his Son? For by the right hand prosperity is understood, and by the arm the Word of God the Father, or the Son of God as his protection.

“Where is”—understand, his power—“he who cleft the waters before them,” understand, into twelve parts, and in other passages according to that verse: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions”—“so as to make for himself an everlasting name,” that is, so that his name might be praised eternally? For when Moses struck the sea, it was divided into twelve parts; and while the other tribes hesitated and feared to enter, the tribe of Judah entered first (Ps. 135). For this reason it was called the royal tribe, because kings were chosen from it. “Where is he who led them through the abysses,” that is, through the depths of the sea, “like a horse not stumbling in the desert” [Col. 1058C], that is, proceeding without impediment?

“Like an animal descending in the plain,” understand, without stumbling: so they descended and entered the land promised to them. Why they walked so peacefully, he makes clear by adding: “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “was its guide.” In this passage we must understand “Spirit” as an angel, who was the guide of that people, in accordance with what the Lord promised them, saying: “My angel will go before you” (Exod. 32). For from many passages we can gather that angels are called spirits, among them: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “snatched Philip away” (Acts 8). Again, in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Col. 1058D]: “These are ministering spirits, sent for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1). It follows:

“Thus you led your people,” understand, from the land of Egypt, “so that you might make for yourself a name of your glory,” that is, so that your name might be glorified and praised eternally. For this reason the Lord struck the Egyptians with many plagues and delivered his people, leading them through the sea and through an impassable land into a land better than all others.

“Look down from heaven, and see from your holy dwelling-place and from your glory.” Now the prophet speaks in the person of the Jewish people, doing penance and acknowledging their sin, and says to God: Look down [Col. 1059A] from heaven and have mercy. We must not understand the almighty God locally, as though he were only in heaven; although the prophet says, “Look down from heaven and from your holy dwelling-place,” we must believe that he is in heaven and on earth. As he himself said: “I fill heaven and earth,” and that he is also within all things and outside all things. As blessed Gregory says: “By filling all things, he surrounds them, and by surrounding all things, he fills them; by presiding, he sustains them, and by sustaining, he presides.” And although he is wholly everywhere through the fullness of his divinity, nevertheless his dwelling-place and location are said to be in those things that are holier, according to what he himself says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66). And the Psalmist says: “He who dwells in heaven will mock them” (Ps. 2). For wherever his will is done, there is the dwelling-place and house of God: [Col. 1059B] especially in the angels, whose manner of life is in the heavenly places, and in holy people who, while remaining bodily on earth, contemplate heavenly things in their minds. What the prophet therefore says, speaking in the person of the people—“Look down from heaven and see from your holy dwelling-place”—means: “Look down from heaven and from your holy dwelling-place and from your glory, and see,” that is, have mercy. For God’s seeing means his having mercy, according to that verse: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people,” that is, I saw and had mercy.

“Where is your zeal,” that is, your love with which you loved us and our fathers? “And your strength”—understand, where is it?—with which you led our fathers out of Egypt? “The abundance of your inward affections and your mercies”—understand, where is it? “They have restrained themselves over me”—namely, your zeal, strength, and mercy. [Col. 1059C] “Zeal” has a twofold meaning, as has very often been said in many passages. There is an evil zeal, namely envy and the fervor of wickedness. And there is a good zeal, the fervor of love for God and neighbor, which is meant here: the zeal of love. The viscera are the inner parts of the belly. Therefore, not improperly, “viscera” here signifies the affections of love. “Where is,” he says, “the affection of that excessive love with which you loved us?” It follows:

“For you are our Father,” that is, our Creator; “and Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us,” that is, he did not acknowledge us as his sons, whom they understand not to be loved by their God. Righteous and holy fathers are said after death not to know their wicked sons, whom they see departing from God and not following in their footsteps, because they do not intercede with God for them; nor would they be heard, nor could they deliver them from the vengeance of the almighty God, just as God says to Jeremiah: “Do not pray,” he says, “for this people, for I will not hear you” (Jer. 7). For it is clear that perverse children who depart from God cannot be saved by the prayer and intercession of their fathers, even if those fathers were righteous. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “As I live, says the Lord, even if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in the midst of Jerusalem, they would not deliver son or daughter; by their righteousness they would deliver only their own souls” (Ezek. 14). Because these people were sinners and were known to have departed from God’s way, they say: “Abraham and Israel,” that is, Jacob, “do not know us as their sons,” so that they might pour out prayer on our behalf. But a question arises here: Why did he name Abraham and Israel, that is, Jacob, and omit Isaac in between? To this it must be said that by the first and the last we also understand what lies in the middle. When he said “Abraham and Israel,” he included Isaac as well between these two—and not only him, but also the other holy fathers who came before. “You, Lord, are our Father,” that is, Creator; “Redeemer”—understand, our Redeemer—who redeemed us from Egypt; “your name is from eternity”—understand, your holy name remains.

“Why have you made us err, Lord, from your ways, and hardened our heart so that we would not fear you?” Although the almighty God causes no one to err or depart from the way of righteousness, and hardens no human heart, he is nevertheless said to make a person err and to harden his heart when he does not recall him from error and does not soften his heart from its hardness. Thus it is said of Pharaoh (Exod. 4, 10, and 11) that the Lord hardened his heart, that is, did not soften it. In the same way these people speak when they say: Why did you permit us to err, Lord, from your ways, that is, from your commandments and judgments? And why did you permit our heart to become hardened, withholding the scourges, so that we would not fear you? (Prov. 3.) We would certainly know that your zeal, that is, your love, was with us, according to the verse: “The Lord chastises the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.” But toward those with whom he is exceedingly angry, he suspends his hand from striking in the present, so that in the future they may receive the recompense for their iniquity. Hence he says to some: “I will not visit,” he says, “upon your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor upon your sons when they have committed adultery” (Hos. 4). “Return for the sake of your servants,” understand, our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who now do not know us, seeing that we are not loved by you, “and for the sake of the tribes of your inheritance.” “Return,” he says, that is, return to us with your mercy—and not because our merits deserve it, but because of your overflowing mercy and for the sake of your servants, our fathers, who pleased you. We are their sons according to the flesh, although they do not acknowledge us because of the anger provoked by our sin.

“As though they possessed your holy people as nothing, our enemies have trampled your sanctuary; we have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us, and your name was not invoked over us.” “As nothing,” he says, that is, without our resistance and without their exertion, our enemies—namely, the Chaldeans and the Romans—possessed us. “They have trampled your sanctuary,” that is, your holy temple, both the Babylonians and the Romans. And we have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us, that is, before we were called in Abraham, since Terah once worshiped idols; or when we were in Egypt worshiping idols, without a king, princes, or prophets, but without God, without the Law, and without a priest. Although these things were fulfilled in part before the Lord’s coming, they were all fulfilled after the Lord’s Passion, and they continue to be fulfilled daily while that curse remains upon them which they called down upon themselves, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). For as long as they remain in the antiquity of the Law and do not receive the truth of the Gospel, they will in no way be called the people of God, so as to be named Christians by Christ.

## CHAPTER LXIV

“Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend. At your presence the mountains would flow down; as tinder before the fire they would melt and burn with fire.” Or, according to Symmachus, “the waters of the sea would burn with fire,” “so that your name might become known to your enemies. At your presence the nations would be disturbed”—understand, if you descended.

The prophet Isaiah, foreseeing through the revelation of the Holy Spirit the future coming of the Lord—namely, the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, the rejection of his people, and the calling of the nations—speaks in his own person and in that of all the holy patriarchs and prophets who desired his coming: Would that you would tear open the heavens, Lord, and descend, that is, would that you would open the heavens and descend from the bosom of the Father’s majesty, in which you are inaccessible and invisible to our eyes, and would show yourself incarnate and visible to human sight. The Psalmist burned with this same love when he said: “Stir up your power, Lord, and come” (Ps. 79). The patriarch Abraham was aflame with this desire, concerning whom the Lord said to the Jews: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day” [Col. 1061C] (John 8). Likewise, all the holy people from the beginning of the world, who, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, knew that the Lord would come in the flesh, desired that he should come and that they should see him, just as the Lord himself said to the apostles: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I say to you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. 13), and so forth.

Nevertheless, when the prophet says, “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend,” we must not suppose that God dwelled locally, but must believe—as the authorities say—that he is everywhere and that, where he was, there he assumed flesh, because he was wholly everywhere. He called “heaven” the fullness of the Father’s majesty, in which he himself is equal to the Father. And he is said to have descended when he humbled himself by taking flesh. [Col. 1061D] Let us see what the prophet adds. “If,” he says, “you would open the heavens and descend, at your presence,” that is, at your coming, “the mountains would flow down”—that is, demons and Jews and all who, puffed up with the swelling of pride, rise up against the knowledge of God and are called mountains because of their pride—“would fail” at your presence. And they would melt, that is, be consumed, “like tinder before the fire,” that is, as wood and straw are consumed by fire. And those mountains themselves would burn with fire, that is, they would be consumed by your judgment, which will be fulfilled on the day of judgment, when all the reprobate hear: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 26). And why this? “So that your name might become known to your enemies” through your power—namely, to demons, Jews [Col. 1062A], and all adversaries—that Jesus is your name.

But if we read according to Symmachus, “and the waters of the sea would burn with fire,” we must understand by the waters the peoples of this world, who are signified by the sea. In them unbelief was consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12), and they were inflamed with love of God and neighbor. His name became known to his enemies, the Jews, as the name Jesus, that is, Savior, who saved the people that believed in him. What follows, “At your presence the nations would be disturbed,” and in another translation, “would be moved,” pertains to the faith of the nations, whose hearts were moved to repentance and from error to faith, whereas previously they remained unmoved in unbelief.

“When you do wondrous things, we shall not endure.” Considering the stony heart of the Jews and foreseeing their hardness and blasphemy, the prophet spoke in the person of the unbelievers: When you perform many miracles on earth at the time of your incarnation, he says, we shall not endure patiently. This can be confirmed from many passages in the holy Gospel, in which the Jews are said always to have opposed the Lord’s miracles and to have been ready to blaspheme.

And as though the prophet had already been heard because of what he had cried out somewhat earlier, saying, “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend,” he added: “You descended,” that is, “the Word became flesh,” “and at your presence,” that is, at your coming, “the mountains flowed down,” that is, the demons [Col. 1062C] and the Jews believed, losing the power and glory that they had in this world. Hence the Lord says concerning the devil: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12). And concerning the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you” (Matt. 21), that is, sacred Scripture and every glory or dignity.

It follows: “From eternity they have not heard,” that is, from the beginning or origin of the world, “nor have they perceived with their ears”—understand, bodily ears—“the things that you prepared for your holy ones.” “The eye”—understand, the human eye—“has not seen, O God, apart from you, the things that you prepared for those who await you.” The ear has not heard, because there is no sound there. The eye has not seen, because there is neither body nor color there. It has not entered the human heart, because our heart must be directed there. What, then, are those good things that God prepared for his elect? Certainly, it is himself: that is, knowledge of the whole Trinity, as the Son himself said: “This,” he says, “is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). These certainly are the rewards and joys of eternal life, which none of the elect sees while remaining in the body, as the same Son said: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4), understand, as he is. Who, then, will see him? “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5).

“You met the one who rejoices and practices righteousness; in your ways they will remember.” This can be understood in two ways. You met the one who rejoiced and practiced righteousness because of your coming, as Simeon did on the fortieth day after your birth [Col. 1063A]. “In your ways,” that is, in your commandments, your elect will remember, as did that same Simeon, the widow Anna, and the other faithful (Luke 2). Alternatively: You met, that is, you helped and gave assistance, the one who rejoiced in you and trusted in you and practiced righteousness, as David and Judas Maccabaeus did.

“Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; we were always in them, and we shall be saved. And we have all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses like a woman’s menstrual cloth.” He speaks in the person of the Jewish people, who, while the Lord was preaching, refused to pass over to the truth of the Gospel. Placed in tribulation, they displayed repentance in words, which they did not possess in deeds. The order is inverted when he says, “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned.” For we sinned first, and by sinning provoked him to vengeance. It is not because he was angry that we sinned; rather, we sinned and were always in sins, and we shall be saved by your grace, not by our merits. And we have all become as an unclean thing, that is, like a leper or one polluted by something else. And all our righteousnesses—namely, circumcision, the offering of the lamb, and the observance of the Sabbath—after the grace of the Gospel came, became unclean, like a woman’s menstrual cloth, than which nothing is more unclean.

Menstruating women are so called from the moon, which in Hebrew is called *mene*; each month they customarily suffer a flow of blood. During those days every man ought to abstain from his wife. For from intercourse at that time, with God permitting it, children are often born weak and with contracted limbs, so that, because the father and mother were not ashamed to come together in intercourse in a chamber during the menstrual period, they may themselves see their shame publicly displayed in the child. Therefore, just as a menstruating woman’s cloth is considered unclean by everyone, so now the observance of the Law, which the Jews fulfilled carnally, after the grace of the Gospel was given, is considered unclean. It follows:

“And we have fallen”—under the sword of the Romans—“all of us like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind.” In sacred Scripture the wind has various meanings. Sometimes it signifies the movement of the air, as in: “He commanded the winds and the sea” (Luke 8). Sometimes it signifies the Holy Spirit, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “Suddenly there came a sound as of a rushing mighty spirit” (Acts 2). There “spirit” is used for “wind.” In the signification of the Holy Spirit it sometimes signifies the temptation of demons and wicked people, as in the Gospel: “The rivers came, the winds blew” (Matt. 7), that is, the temptation of demons or human beings. It is in this sense that it is also used in the present passage: “We have all fallen,” they say, “under the sword of the Romans, like a leaf.” And our iniquities, that is, our sins and denial of you, have carried us away like the wind, that is, the temptation of demons and the persecution of the Romans have carried us away from your presence and from our land, as the wind carries leaves from the trees.

“There is no one who invokes your name, who rises up and takes hold of you.” There is no one—understand, now among us—who invokes your name with heart, mouth, and deed [Col. 1064A], who rises for true prayer and takes hold of you, lest you pour out your fury upon us, as Moses once rose and took hold of you by his prayers (Exod. 32). “You have hidden your face,” that is, your presence and your help, “from us. And you have crushed us,” that is, struck and afflicted us, “in the hand,” that is, in the activity of our iniquity and faithlessness. Iniquity and every sin have hands, that is, an operation by which they desire to keep us bound. Hence it says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 8).

“And now, Lord, you are our Father, but we are clay, and you are our maker,” who once deigned to say: “Let my son Israel go” (Exod. 5), and: “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isa. 1). But we are clay, that is, earth, and descendants from the same stock. You are our maker, that is, our creator, and we are all the work of your hands [Col. 1064B]; therefore we cannot resist your power. The sense is: We do not say these things presuming upon our merits, which are nothing, but presuming upon your clemency and mercy, we dare to pour out our prayers.

“Do not be angry, Lord, exceedingly, and do not remember our iniquity any longer. Behold, look upon us: we are all your people.” Do not be angry, Lord, exceedingly, that is, excessively, or beyond what our weakness can bear; and do not remember our iniquity any longer. Behold, look upon us and attend to your mercy: once we were all your people.

“The city of your holy one has become desolate, Zion; Jerusalem has become desolate; the house of our sanctification and of our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become desolate; it has been made a burning fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruins.” The city of your holy one, that is, your sanctuary or temple, Zion, has been made desolate by you. Although Zion and Jerusalem are two names, in this passage they have one meaning: they signify the temple and the city, where once there was a mirror and vision of peace. But after the Jewish people denied the Lord, Jerusalem was made desolate by God, according to what the Savior said to them. In ecclesiastical history it is said that voices were heard in the temple saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

The house of our sanctification, which sanctified us, where we sacrificed and offered sacrifice, has been made desolate by you, as has the house of our glory, in which we gloried. The house where our fathers praised you has become a burning fire; it was set alight by Rome. And all our desirable things, that is, the holy of holies and so forth, whatever pertained to honor, have been turned into ruins. In general, the house of God is the holy Church; in particular, it is each believer, who is then handed over to fire and burning when he serves the heats of lust and avarice.

“Will you restrain yourself over these things, Lord? Will you keep silent and afflict us exceedingly?” Will you restrain yourself over these, our miseries, Lord, so as not to extend mercy to us? Will you keep silent, that is, will you remain in this hardness so as to afflict us exceedingly?

## CHAPTER LXV

“Those who previously did not ask about me sought me; those who did not seek me found me.” The voice of the Son of God responds to what they had said above: “Why have you made us err in your ways? Why have you hardened our heart so that we would not fear you?” He answered and said: The Gentiles sought me through faith, although previously they did not ask about me, that is, before I came in the flesh they did not pray or invoke me. They found me merciful and ready to receive them, although previously they had not sought me. Concerning them it is written: “Those to whom he was not announced will see him, and those who have not heard will understand me” (Isa. 52). The sense is: If those who previously did not seek me found me merciful and gracious—that is, the Gentiles—why did you find me so harsh and unmerciful? Understand: because, although you meditate on the Law day and night, you provoked me to anger by departing from me, and because of vain glory you display repentance in words whose deeds you do not perform.

How, then, did the Gentiles find him? Consider the centurion, concerning whom the Lord said: “Truly I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. 8). “Consider the Canaanite woman and believe” (Matt. 15). Therefore, because the Gentiles came to the faith of the Lord with a willing heart, they deserved that he himself should say of them: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17), and so forth.

“I said: Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not invoke my name.” This is the voice of the Son of God. “Behold me, behold me”—understand, I who once spoke to Moses, saying, “I am who I am”—to a nation that did not know me and that did not invoke my name.

“I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people who walk in a way that is not good, following their thoughts. A people who continually provoke me to anger before my face; who sacrifice in gardens and offer sacrifice upon bricks; who dwell in tombs and sleep in shrines of idols.” What he says—“I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people,” with the Septuagint adding “and contradicting”—can be understood in three ways.

First: I stretched out my hands all day, hanging on the cross, toward an unbelieving people who, when I prayed for them, saying to the Father, “Father, forgive them” (Matt. 27), did not wish to believe in me but contradicted me, saying: “Aha, you who destroy the temple of God!” [Col. 1065D]

Alternatively: I stretched out my hands so that I might receive them and place them in my bosom, but they themselves remained always unbelieving and contradictory.

Let us give a third interpretation: I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people, that is, I willingly bestowed upon them the gifts of all my benefits from the time when I led them out of Egypt for the sake of their ancestors’ merits until I came in the flesh. And after I came, I did not delay in fulfilling what they needed: healing their sick, feeding them with my loaves, opening to them the hidden things of the Law and the prophets that had been concealed from them, and calling them to the heavenly homeland (John 6). But they remained always unbelieving and contradictory, saying: “By Beelzebul you cast out demons” (Matt. 12), and: “You have a demon” (John 8), and other things of this kind. They walked in a way that was not good, abandoning me, who said to them: “I am the way” (John 14), and walking along the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matt. 7), following their perverse thoughts rather than the worship of the Lord.

This, I say, was done by the people who provoke me to anger, that is, to vengeance, continually before my face, that is, in my presence and before my sight, because all the works of thought, speech, and action are not hidden from my eyes. Or “in my face,” that is, in my temple, where I often manifested my presence, they placed their idols, as is set forth at length in Ezekiel.

And they did not worship idols only in the temple; they also sacrificed to foreign gods upon hills and mountains and in gardens. And, in place of the one altar in the Lord’s temple, built of polished stones according to the command of the Law, they built many altars of fired bricks and field sods; and upon them they sacrificed to demons. And, so that no evil might be lacking that they would not practice, they dwelt in tombs, that is, in little dwellings of the dead, because they slept upon Jewish tombs, lying upon the skins of sacrificial victims so that they might obtain omens through dreams.

Shrines properly were temples in which there were springs or streams where the sacrificial victims were washed and the priests cleansed. They were called *delubra* from washing the victims, or because they thought that there they obtained purification of the soul, or from becoming drunk, since they often used to become drunk there and engage in all sorts of idle behavior, which led them far from the straight path.

It follows: “Who eat the flesh of swine,” that is, pork, contrary to the precept of the Law, “and profane broth,” that is, unclean broth, “in their vessels.” Hence both they and their vessels were unclean. A *fanum* is a temple where religious worship is performed; hence *profanus* is so called, as if “far from the temple,” that is, from religion.

“Who say: ‘Withdraw from me; do not come near me, because you are unclean.’” They were filled with such great pride, although utterly unclean, that they said to one who neither worshiped idols nor ate pork: “Withdraw from us, because you are unclean.” “These”—understand, those who do such things, who sacrifice in gardens and eat pork, although they are utterly unclean and full of every impurity—“will be smoke,” that is, nothing, “in my anger,” or in my vengeance. “A burning fire”—understand, they will be such in hell—“all day,” that is, always.

“Behold, it is written before me,” that is, in my sight—understand, what they do: “I will not be silent, but I will repay and requite into their bosom your iniquities and the iniquities of your fathers together, says the Lord, who sacrificed upon the mountains and upon the hills, and reproached me; and I will measure out their former deed into their bosom.”

The one who above had said, “I was silent, I was always quiet, I was patient,” now says, “I will not be silent,” that is, I will no longer spare or tolerate their iniquities, and I will repay and return their iniquities into their bosom, along with the iniquities of their idolatrous fathers. By “bosom” we must understand the ruling faculty of the mind, as it is said in Hosea (chap. 4): “This is their reproach in their bosom,” that is, in their mind. This bosom is called by another name because it is the ruling faculty of the soul, as in: “I will repay their ways upon their head.”

Their iniquities, he says, and the iniquities of those idolatrous fathers who sacrificed their sons upon the mountains and reproached me upon the hills—that is, who insulted me by abandoning me and rendering my honor to idols—I will repay and requite into their bosom, that is, into the ruling faculty of their mind, so that their own conscience may torment them. And I will measure out, that is, repay, their former deed into their bosom, that is, they will receive things corresponding to what they did: first in the soul or in the innermost heart, as in the human being; then, after the day of judgment, in body and soul, so that outwardly they may be burned by everlasting fire and inwardly tormented by their own conscience, according to what the same prophet says elsewhere: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66).

But a question may be raised here: Since the almighty God said, “The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor shall the son bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18), why does he now say, “I will repay the iniquities of their fathers into their bosom”? The answer is that “fathers” here does not mean only those from whose seed they received their bodies, but those whose deeds they imitated. For whoever performs another’s deeds and imitates him is undoubtedly his son—not by nature, but by imitation. It is therefore as though he said: I will repay the iniquities of their fathers to them, that is, the deeds whose consequences those people endured and which these have imitated; these people too will endure the same consequences. It follows:

“Thus says the Lord: As when a grain is found in a cluster and someone says, ‘Do not destroy it, for it is a blessing,’ so I will act for the sake of my servants, so as not to destroy everything.” The Lord had threatened the Jewish people that he would repay their iniquities and the iniquities of their fathers. Then he added, by way of likeness or comparison, that the good must not be destroyed because of the wicked. For example, Abraham was delivered from Ur of the Chaldeans; Noah and his sons were saved through the flood from the whole world; and Lot was saved from Sodom.

Thus, if one sound and unspoiled grain is found in a cluster, or in a bunch of grapes after a storm, and someone says to the person who wishes to touch it, “Do not touch it, but allow it to grow, because it is the Lord’s blessing,” that is, because the Lord willed that this one grain should remain from the multitude of grapes, so I will act from the innumerable multitude of Jews. “Those who will inherit it,” he says—that is, Jerusalem or the Church—will be my elect, namely the apostles, and my servants, their successors, will dwell there. If I find a few righteous people, I will deliver them. And I will do this for the sake of my servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the other holy people, or for the sake of those who imitate them.

“And I will bring forth a seed from Jacob, and from Judah one who will possess my mountains.” We can understand the seed of Jacob and Judah in two ways: namely, Christ, who descended from the seed and stock of Jacob, from the tribe of Judah. Concerning him Jacob said: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until the one who is to be sent comes.” He possessed the mountains (Gen. 49), that is, the apostles, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains. And the mountains are around him” (Ps. 120), and other passages of this kind.

Alternatively: “I will bring forth a seed from Jacob,” that is, the company of the apostles, concerning which the same prophet says: “Unless the Lord had left us a seed, and the remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 1). “And from Judah one who will possess my mountains,” that is, the other believers whom those apostles acquired for the Lord.

Or, as it is found in the Septuagint, “one who will possess my mountain,” that is, Christ, who is the mountain of mountains [Col. 1068B], concerning whom it is said: “This is the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67). From Judah the apostles went forth, that is, from the Jewish people, and they possessed Christ because they were founded upon him. And they possessed other mountains, that is, the martyrs and their successors.

“And my elect will inherit it, and my servants will dwell there.” The Church is Christ’s inheritance, and all her children, namely believers, inherit her. Concerning this inheritance the Psalmist says: “You will inherit,” he says, “among all the nations” (Ps. 85). And the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

“And the open plains shall become sheepfolds, and the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for my people who have sought me.”

Where we have here, “the open plains shall become sheepfolds” [Col. 1068C], another translation has “Sharon,” which is the region between Joppa, Lydda, and Jamnia. It contains extremely fertile plains, suitable for pasturing flocks; but it abounds in robbers. Hence it is also interpreted as “a valley pouring out blood,” because much blood of travelers and passersby was shed there by robbers.

The Valley of Achor is the place where Achan, son of Carmi, who had stolen from the devoted things and from the spoils of Jericho, perished with his entire household. Because he had troubled the people there, Joshua said to him: “May the Lord trouble you, because you have troubled us; and he perished there” (Joshua 7). That place itself is called the Valley of Achor, that is, “the valley of disturbance” or “tumult.”

By these two names, then—Sharon or Saron, which is interpreted as “the valley pouring out blood,” and Achor, which [Col. 1068D] is interpreted as “the valley of disturbance” or “tumult”—the Gentile world is signified. It was full of the shedding of blood and remained in the tumult and disturbance of vices. But it has been changed into sheepfolds or sheep pens and into a resting place for herds—that is, into churches and the repose of preachers and other faithful people, who are represented by herds and flocks of sheep—as he makes clear shortly afterward, saying: “For the people who believed in me and sought me.”

“And you”—the Jews are understood—“who have abandoned the Lord, who have forgotten my holy mountain,” that is, the temple constructed on the mountain, or the heavenly Jerusalem; or, “who were unwilling to believe in Christ,” who is the mountain of mountains; “who set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it, [Col. 1069A] I shall number you for the sword,” that is, for punishments, “and all of you shall fall in slaughter,” with “of the Chaldeans, Romans, or demons” understood.

By “the sword” and “slaughter” here we should understand the punishment and penalties to which they were handed over. For not the entire people of Israel was killed by the sword of the Chaldeans or Romans; rather, it was afflicted by hunger, captivity, and the harsh yoke of servitude, under which it is still held. Whatever torments, whatever afflicts, whatever punishes is called the sword of God.

When he says, “who set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it,” another translation has, “who prepare a table for Fortune.” Fortune was a goddess among the Egyptians, also called the goddess of prosperity. They celebrated her festival at the end of the year, offering her a table furnished and filled with foods of various kinds, as well as cups mixed with mead, either because she had made the past year fruitful and prosperous for them, or so that she might act similarly in the coming year. The Israelites also did this, venerating the monstrous forms of nearly every idol. When they ought to have sacrificed to the Lord, they sacrificed to idols.

“Because I called, and you did not answer; I spoke, and you did not hear; and you did evil in my sight, and you chose what I did not will.”

“I called you,” he says, “through the prophets, saying: ‘Turn to me and you shall be saved’ (Isaiah 45). I called you through my own person, saying: ‘Repent, and come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 4; 11).” And you did not answer by following and obeying. I spoke through the prophets, promising good things and threatening evils; and I spoke through my own person in parables and openly, and you did not hear with the ears of the mind, or you did not obey. “And you did evil in my sight,” that is, in my presence, worshiping idols in my temple; “and you chose what I did not will,” that is, idolatry.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst.”

This eating and drinking must be understood spiritually, not of food that perishes or drink that passes away. This food and drink can be understood in three ways. In the present, the servants and elect of God eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord; without receiving them, no one can come to eternal life, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

They are also refreshed in the present by the teaching and spiritual mysteries of sacred Scripture, which in some passages is food and in others drink. In a third way, however, they will be refreshed in the future by the vision of almighty God. Concerning this refreshment the Lord said to the apostles: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one for me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

And elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me shall not hunger, and whoever comes to me shall never thirst” (John 6). The Psalmist also spoke of this fullness: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” [Col. 1070A] (Psalm 16).

But if we take this literally, as referring to ordinary bread, we cannot fully establish it, since many saints died during persecution, while hunger and poverty pressed upon them. For how many righteous people hunger while the impious are swollen with cruelties?

The meaning in this passage, therefore, is: “Not only will you, Jews who abandoned the Lord, did evil in his sight, and were unwilling to hear him when present, fall by the sword; I will also make a great distinction between you and the multitude of the Gentiles, so that they will be satisfied in the present age with my body and blood and spiritual teaching, and in the future with the vision of the whole Trinity.”

“Behold, my servants shall rejoice,” with “in eternal blessedness” understood, according to this saying: “I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” [Col. 1070B] (John 16).

“And you shall be ashamed,” that is, you shall blush for your sins when you see others succeeding to your place.

“Behold, my servants shall praise because of the exultation of their heart,” in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 8).

“But you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl,” with “in the punishments of hell” understood. As it is written: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13). Then the saints will rejoice, and sinners will howl because of the contrition of their spirit—that is, because of the sorrow of heart they will have inwardly—when the lambs of the Gentiles and of the righteous sit at the right hand, and the goats of the Jews and of other ungodly people at the left (Matthew 25).

“And you shall leave your name as a curse to my elect; and the Lord God will kill you, and he will call his servants by another name.”

“When others,” he says, “succeed to your place, you will leave your name, now condemned, as a curse to my elect.” For example, because of your wickedness, those who detest you, when they wish to swear to something, will say: “If this does not happen to me as it did to the condemned Jews, who were killed by the Romans, I did not do this or that.”

Or otherwise: the holy speech of Christians and of those who worship God ought to be so firm that it may be accepted as an oath. They will swear—that is, they will confess that they believe in God—in order not to suffer similar things, saying: “I swear,” that is, “I believe in almighty God,” just as certain Jews in former times believed in the Prophet, namely, and other righteous people.

Or because God was their oath, we now, compelled by necessity, swear by him, as they once did when they said: “The Lord lives, if I did this.” Or you will leave your name to my elect, so that just as you were once called sons of Abraham and Jacob, so they also may be called sons of Abraham, in accordance with what John the Forerunner said: “God is able from these stones”—that is, from the Gentiles—“to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3).

“And the Lord your God will kill you,” I say—not with a material sword, but he will condemn you eternally by his sentence and judgment. “And he will call his Gentile servants by another name,” so that they may be called Christians from Christ.

“In which”—the name is understood, or “in Christ” [Col. 1071A]—“who is blessed upon the earth”: that is, whoever has been blessed so as to be called a Christian and has carefully preserved that name in this earth “shall be blessed in God. Amen.”

“Whoever,” he says, “has been blessed here shall be blessed in the future with all the elect, hearing from the Lord: ‘Come, you blessed of my Father’” (Matthew 25). The Apostle also speaks of this blessing: “You were called for this purpose, children, that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance” (1 Peter 3).

“Amen” in this passage signifies “faithfully” and “truly,” because those who will be blessed by the Lord will be blessed faithfully and truly.

“And whoever swears upon the earth shall swear in God. Amen.” Amen is the Lord’s oath, that is, confirmation of the statement for which we now say: “Truly, truly.”

“Whoever,” he says, “swears upon the earth”—that is, whoever speaks the truth in the present—“shall swear,” that is, shall speak in God faithfully and truly on the day of judgment, in manifest revelation, because they will always bless the Lord. “And they shall resound with his praise,” according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83).

“Because the former troubles have been forgotten, and because they have been hidden from our eyes.”

This pertains to the day of judgment. For when the saints have received the fullness of their rewards on the day of judgment and have seen the Lord as he is, they will count as nothing all the torments and scourges they endured in this age for Christ’s name, in comparison with his glory. They will have them as though forgotten—not through the forgetting of memory, but through the cessation of their former sufferings. For they will neither see nor feel any labor there, in accordance with what is said in the Apocalypse: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21), and so forth.

Thus it is also said in this passage that the former troubles will be forgotten—that is, the tribulations by which the saints may be afflicted here—and that they will be hidden from our presence. The prophet joins himself to the number of the saints, because he himself endured many unjust adversities, so much so that he was cut with a wooden saw.

“For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, and they shall not rise upon the heart; but you shall rejoice and exult forever in the things that I create.”

We have already said many times above, in many passages, that heaven and earth do not pass away according to nature or essence, but through change, renewal, and improvement. As it is said in the Apocalypse: “There shall be a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21); and the Apostle says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7). When he says “the form is passing away,” he shows that the substance remains.

For example, when an infant grows into a boy, a boy into a young man, a young man into an adult, and an adult into an old man, he does not pass away in substance through each age. He is always the same person he was before, but he is gradually changed, and is said to have passed beyond his former age.

Similarly, although heaven and earth pass away through change, they will nevertheless remain in their own substance. In this sense also it is said, “Behold, I create,” in place of “I shall create” or “I shall renew,” new heavens and a new earth; and “the former things,” whether evils or torments, “shall not be remembered.” “They shall not rise upon the heart,” that is, they shall not be recalled.

“But you shall rejoice and exult forever,” that is, without end you shall praise me in all the things made by me, as the angels once did when they saw the world made by me.

“For behold, I create Jerusalem as exultation, and its people as joy; and I shall exult in Jerusalem and rejoice in my people.”

This should be understood of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, of the congregation of the holy angels and of all who will pass into the number of the angels, concerning whom it is said: “They shall be like the angels of God in heaven.”

“Behold,” he says, “I, almighty God, will make one heavenly Church, or Jerusalem, from angels and human beings” [Col. 1072B]; “and they will exult and rejoice” to such an extent that I, who am their creator and maker, will rejoice and exult in them. And not only will they themselves rejoice, but they themselves will be exultation and joy.

“And in it,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, “the voice of weeping and the voice of crying shall no longer be heard,” because, as John said: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying,” and the rest that follows.

For it is not fitting that in the city of the heavenly Jerusalem its people, who are destined to receive the eternal glory of exultation and joy, should have a voice of weeping or a voice of sadness. Where, then, will there be a voice of weeping and a voice of crying? In the assembly of the reprobate.

“There shall no longer be an infant of days there, nor an old man who does not fulfill his days; for the child of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.”

These things pertain to the general resurrection, after which there will be neither an infant nor an old man in the assembly of the faithful, nor in the assembly of the wicked. Rather, all will rise in perfect age, “some to life, others to destruction.” They will rise in the age at which Christ rose, that is, at the age of thirty-three and a half years. And all will fulfill their days, because afterward no one will die; the death of the body will no longer exist.

What he adds—“for the child of a hundred years shall die”—means this: if any sinner lives for a hundred years in the present age and spends all that time childishly, serving lust and other desires, as soon as he passes from this life, he will die in his sin [Col. 1072D].

And what follows—“because the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed”—means that, because he lived for a hundred years and always acted childishly by sinning, he will also be fully accursed.

“And they shall build houses and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat.”

The houses in which the saints will dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, and those who will build them, should be understood either as the virtues that they build in the present and whose reward and recompense they will possess, according to the saying: “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labor” [Col. 1073A] (1 Corinthians 3); or as the dwellings that they prepare there, concerning which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwellings” (John 14).

And in the Psalmist’s sixty-eighth psalm he promises, saying: “For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there” (Psalm 68).

In these dwellings, then—that is, in their virtues and in the heavenly Jerusalem that they prepare for themselves—they will drink and eat the fruit of the vineyards that they planted here. That is, they will be made drunk with exultation through the grace of the Holy Spirit and will be filled with every sweetness from the vineyards that they planted, namely, from the reward of good works.

They will therefore build virtues and heavenly dwellings, and they will plant vineyards, about which we have already spoken. And another—that is, the devil—will not dwell among them, nor will he devour their virtues any longer.

“For according to the days of a tree shall be the days of my people; and the works of their hands shall grow old, my elect”—or, as certain manuscripts have it, “the works of their hands shall grow old for my elect.”

“According to the days of a tree,” with “of its life” understood, “shall be the days of believers and of all the elect in eternal blessedness,” because, in accordance with the eternity of Christ, all the elect will be eternal (Romans 6).

And just as “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him,” so all the elect will rise from the dead, and death shall no longer have dominion over them. They will remain eternally with Christ when they see God as he is.

This is the tree of life that was in the middle of paradise, that is, Christ in the midst of the Church. Concerning it Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her” (Proverbs 3), that is, wisdom, which is the word and power of God the Father; and those who hold fast to her will be blessed.

What follows—“and the works of their hands shall grow old, my elect,” or “for my elect”—has a twofold meaning.

“The works of their hands,” he says, that is, the faith, teaching, and activity of the apostles, “shall grow old”: believers who follow them will become old in these works, because, having become their imitators, they will hold to what the apostles taught and did until the end of the age. And while they always hold to these things, they will be said, as it were, then to grow old.

Alternatively: “The works of their hands shall grow old for my elect,” that is, the works of the apostles themselves will grow old for the elect, because they will remain eternally for their benefit and salvation. Hence the Gospel is also said to be eternal, because it will make its followers elect forever [Col. 1073D].

“They shall not labor in vain, nor bear children in disturbance; for they are the seed of the blessed of the Lord, and their descendants are with them.”

The apostles and other teachers will not labor in preaching or in good works in vain, as the Jews once labored uselessly, because they will receive an eternal reward from this, and they will exult in the labors of their hands.

They will not bear spiritual children in disturbance, that is, in sorrow, as Rachel once bore a physical son; rather, they will be in joy and gladness, rejoicing in the number of believers, just as the Apostle Paul rejoiced when he said: “For what is our joy or crown of glory? Is it not you?” [Col. 1074A] (1 Thessalonians 2).

And why will they rejoice over them? Because they are “the seed of the blessed,” that is, the seed of the apostles of the Lord is understood; and their descendants, that is, all believers, will rejoice with the apostles in heavenly blessedness without end.

“And it shall be: before they call, I shall answer”—their will, not by replying with a voice, but by following with the greatness of signs and miracles; “and while they are still speaking, I shall hear.”

For when the apostles said to some sick or dead person, “In the name of Jesus, rise” (Acts 3), he immediately rose healthy and restored, without delay. Nor could all the Gentiles have believed in Christ within so short a time unless their faith had first arisen through miraculous signs [Col. 1074B]. While the apostles and apostolic men were speaking and crying out, the Lord answered with the greatness of miracles.

“The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion and the ox shall eat straw; and dust shall be the serpent’s bread.”

The wolf and the lamb shall feed together because Paul the persecutor and Ananias, the gentle disciple, lived together, and their food was evangelical teaching and the faith of believers (Acts 9).

This is the wolf of whom the patriarch Jacob said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Genesis 49).

Or by the wolf and the lamb we may understand any savage robber who, after coming to the faith, remained in the Church with some innocent person.

The lion and the ox also ate straw at the Lord’s coming—that is, any king or ruler of this age together with any preacher, who is represented by the ox because he plows the hearts of his hearers. In the Church they feed on straw together, that is, on simple teaching together with the profundity of the divine utterances.

But if we say, “The lion, like the ox, shall eat straw,” the meaning will be as follows: the lion will eat straw like an ox when a highly eloquent man, once powerful in the world, gives himself over to the plainness of the Scriptures, so that he is no longer nourished by worldly and philosophical eloquence, which drips like honey from the lips of the adulterous woman, but follows the lowliness and straw of the historical sense until, through much labor and diligence, he merits reaching the grain—that is, the profundity of the mysteries.

Among such people were Augustine and Cyprian, and the philosophers of the Gentiles, who, abandoning the human philosophy polished by the refinement of eloquence, turned themselves to sacred Scripture, which is arranged in a modest style while inwardly retaining ineffable mysteries.

But when such people pass into the fellowship of the Church, unstable and shallow-minded people are left as food for the serpent, or devil. These are represented by dust, because just as dust is easily carried away by the wind, so they, when temptation comes, easily slip into sin.

“They shall not harm, nor kill, on all my holy mountain, says the Lord.”

Who are those who shall not harm, and whom shall they not harm? The wolf and the lion—that is, any robber and savage tyrant—after laying aside their former corruption, once they have come to the faith, will not harm the lambs and oxen, that is, the gentle and humble.

Or they will not harm one another, nor will they kill others in the present Church or in the heavenly Jerusalem.

The Jews understand all these things carnally, referring them to a period of a thousand years and to the coming of their Christ. They say that there will be such great peace and security for them that wolves and lambs, lions and oxen, serpents and human beings will eat together and dwell together, all ferocity having been removed; and that those who dwell in the temple or on the holy mountain will be harmless. From this they infer that all who are outside the mountain will be killed.

But all these things have been devised through a false error. And lest we, deceived by that Jewish error, understand them carnally as destined to be fulfilled, the following statement makes this clear.

## CHAPTER LXVI

“Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.”

The Jews also understand this carnally. But why almighty God, who is wholly everywhere, should say that he sits in heaven, we have treated fully a little above, with the Lord’s help. Therefore it must now be touched upon briefly and concisely, and what is said through Jeremiah must be set forth: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 33); and elsewhere: “He holds heaven in his span and the earth in his fist” (Isaiah 40).

By this he shows that God is both outside and within, infused and surrounding—not only the creator of heaven and earth, but also of the invisible angels and of all the heavenly powers. “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” And: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1).

He is therefore said to sit in heaven because heaven is more beautiful and nobler than all the elements and all places. Or by heaven we should understand the angelic nature, which dwells in heavenly places, and holy human beings who lead a heavenly and angelic life, in whom he himself dwells.

By the earth, however, which is said to be his footstool, we should understand earthly people who live in an earthly manner and are lovers of the world, as well as the angels who fell from the heavenly places to earth and into the darkness of this air. He tramples them by his judgment and power. Therefore he says: “Heaven,” that is, the angels and righteous human beings, “is my throne; but earth,” that is, earthly people, “is the footstool of my feet,” because by my power and righteous judgment I restrain and trample them.

“What is this house that you will build for me? And what is this place of my rest?”

“All these things”—the things that have been made are understood—“my hand,” or “my power,” “has made, and all these things were made,” with “by me” understood, “says the Lord.”

The Jews thought and said that almighty God was nowhere upon the earth except in the temple built at Jerusalem by Solomon, judging that he was confined to a place. They did not remember what Solomon had said on the day of the dedication of that same temple: “For if the heavens, even the heavens of heavens, cannot contain you” (2 Chronicles 2) [Col. 1076A].

Therefore almighty God says to those who thought such things: “What is this house, so great and beautiful, that you will build for me, so that I may be enclosed there in one place? Did not my hand make all these things?” Certainly, all things that have been made were made by me.

But to show where his dwelling place was, he added, saying: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor, the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?”

Behold his dwelling place: he calls “poor and contrite in spirit, and trembling at his words” any humble person who has a contrite spirit by grieving over the weakness of others and mourning his own sins; and who, fearing that he will go into the punishment of eternal condemnation, ceases from evil works. This is the poor and humble person of whom the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

And elsewhere: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor.”

In these poor people, therefore, and in those who fear the words of God, God dwells through faith and good will; and they themselves are the temple of God, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3).

“He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man; he who slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog.”

All the sacrifices of the Jews—which had been permitted either so that they would not sacrifice to idols, or because of the representation of the true sacrifice—are regarded as abolished after the Lord’s preaching and after the sacrifice of his true offering and the consecration of his body and blood. Thus whoever sacrifices an ox pleases him no more than one who kills a man; and whoever slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog. Concerning the dog it is written through Moses: “You shall not offer in the house of the Lord your God the wages of a prostitute, nor the price of a dog” (Deuteronomy 23).

The dog and the prostitute are aptly joined together, because each creature is inclined toward lust.

“He who offers an offering”—a legal offering is understood—“is as one who offers swine’s blood,” contrary to the commandment of the law.

“He who remembers incense”—with “in order to offer it” understood—“is as one who blesses an idol,” that is, praises it by venerating it.

Such are the ceremonies of the Jews. And their sacrifices are regarded as acceptable in this way after the truth of the Gospel was given through Christ.

“All these things”—the things mentioned above concerning sacrifice are understood—“they chose in their own ways, and their soul delighted in their abominations” [Col. 1076D].

“They chose,” he says, by their own judgment and not by my will, to offer figurative sacrifices even after the true sacrifice; and “in their abominations,” that is, in the things they ought to have abhorred, their soul delighted.

“Therefore I also will choose their mockeries, and I will bring upon them the things they feared.”

He uses “mockeries” in place of “mockers.” The Apostle says something similar: “He will give them over to the operation of wickedness” (Romans 1), that is, to the devil and Antichrist.

We can understand the mockers in two ways: either as the worst rulers and teachers, such as the scribes and Pharisees, and evil priests, such as the sons of Eli, who were chosen by the Lord because they were permitted by him to rule that people [Col. 1077A]; or, as others say, he calls the demons and Romans, to whom they were handed over, “mockers” here.

The meaning is this: because they chose all these things in their wicked actions, I too will permit them to have, and to be ruled by, many rulers and priests who are not upright, such as they deserve. And the evils they feared—whether hunger, mortality, or captivity—I will bring upon them; or I will hand them over to demons and Romans.

They said: “But let us leave him alone; everyone will believe in him, and perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). I will bring upon them what they feared, and they will lose the place of the temple and the name of the kingdom.

He gives the reason why he inflicted such things upon them: “Because I called,” saying, “Repent” (Matthew 4); and, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11), “and there was no one who answered,” by following and obeying.

“I spoke, and they did not hear,” that is, they were not obedient. “And they did evil in my sight,” that is, in my presence; “and they chose what I did not will,” that is, false error.

“Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers who hate you and cast you out because of my name have said: ‘May the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy’; but they themselves shall be ashamed.”

This is the voice of the prophet exhorting the apostles: “Hear, people, the word of the Lord, you who tremble,” that is, who show reverence toward his word.

Your brothers, the Jews, who hate you and cast you out because you believe in me, and because of my name [Col. 1077C], which you bear, since you are called Christians from me, Christ (John 9), have said this. For the Jews had already conspired that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he would be expelled from the synagogue.

They are called “brothers” according to the flesh, not according to faith or conduct, so that the apostles might regard their persecutors and those who detested them as brothers. Hence Peter said: “Men, brothers, hear” (Acts 2), and Paul: “I have great sorrow for my brothers, who are Israelites” (Romans 9).

The Jews therefore said to the apostles: “May the Lord be glorified,” that is, may he appear exalted and glorious in the majesty and appearance of one who reigns. “And we shall see him in our joy,” that is, it will be our joy and gladness when we see him glorified. “But now do not preach to us one who is humble and despised.”

But let us hear what follows. These Jewish brothers of yours who say such things will be ashamed and will blush for their unbelief when Christ appears exalted and glorious to all human beings on the day of judgment. Or they will be ashamed and perish in the present because they said such things, as the following makes clear. For it continues:

“A voice of the people from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies.”

When the Roman army arrived and surrounded the city, as the historian Josephus writes, those who were within the city turned to sedition in three factions, each contending for supremacy: one faction choosing this leader, another another, and the third a third.

Thus it happened that one faction of the people and priests held the temple; a faction of the rulers and people held the citadel and the royal palace; and the third faction held the remaining part of the city, especially the common people.

They fought outside against the enemies and inside against their fellow citizens. But when the Romans captured the city, the voice of the people lamenting was heard amid the rejoicing Romans, who had come by the Lord’s will to render recompense to his enemies, the Jews.

And why was the voice of the priests from the temple and of the rulers and common people from the city heard? Because all were either killed by the sword, burned by fire, sold for a price to other nations, sold into slavery, or led into captivity—apart from those who, afflicted by various miseries, died inside the city at that time.

Then the Lord’s threat was fulfilled: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” [Col. 1078B] (Matthew 23).

“Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her labor came, she gave birth to a male.”

This can be understood in two ways. Before the Virgin Mary was in labor, and before her labor came, God the Father begot a male, namely his Word and his most powerful Son, through whom he made and governs all things.

Alternatively: before Zion, that is, the primitive Church, was in labor, and before her labor came—that is, with great speed—she gave birth to a strong male, namely the people. On one day four thousand believed, on another day five thousand, and afterward many thousands. Among their number was the most blessed Stephen and very many other sons of the apostles, who could be killed before they could be separated from the faith of Christ [Col. 1078C].

This is not said of physical labor and procreation, but of spiritual birth, because they begot them spiritually by pouring the faith of Christ into their hearts. For all physical generations undergo labor and give birth, whereas spiritual generations are free from pain and the experience of labor.

“Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it?”

The following is understood: that a male should be born before a woman was in labor; or, who has seen so many thousands of human beings spiritually generated in so short a time?

“Will the earth give birth in one day?” That is, will it bring forth all seeds in one day? “Or will a nation be brought forth all at once, because Zion was in labor and gave birth to her children?”

This means the apostles and apostolic men, who brought forth the multitude of believers. That people which is now called a nation was created and brought forth all at once in one day, because they were spiritually created all together in Christ, who is light and day, in the unity of faith.

The apostles were mothers, because by generating faith in the hearts of their hearers they gave them birth.

“Shall I, who cause others to give birth”—carnally is understood—“myself not give birth?”—spiritually is understood—“says the Lord?”

God the Father, who causes others to give birth physically, is not without the Son, because before all ages he begot his Word, coequal with himself. He also has many sons whom he himself begot by his grace, concerning whom John says in the Gospel: “As many as believed in him, to them he gave power to become children of God” (John 1).

“If I, who grant generation to others, shall be barren, says the Lord your God?” [Col. 1079A]—“I shall not be,” is understood.

He says this to Zion, that is, to the primitive Church. The meaning is: “I, who created all human beings from nothing, will make for myself from all the nations one Church united in believing in me.”

“Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourned over her, so that you may suck and be filled from the breasts of her consolations, so that you may milk and overflow with delights from all her glory.”

Just as the angels now rejoice over our progress, so once they grieved over our decline and over the servitude in which we served the devil. The apostles too, seeing the Jewish people remain in unbelief and foreseeing the city of Jerusalem to be destroyed by the Romans [Col. 1079B] (as the Lord had foretold), and the people to be overthrown, grieved and mourned with them. But all their consolation lay in this: they saw the nations ready to believe, from whom Jerusalem was to be built—that is, the present Church, or the heavenly one. Therefore it is said both to the angels and to the apostles, who mourned over Jerusalem—that is, over its people—that they should rejoice and exult with the heavenly Jerusalem, or with the present Jerusalem gathered from all the nations, and in her, that is, in their faith.
