By the milk which the apostles themselves are commanded to suck and milk, we should understand the simple faith of believers and their good works, in which the apostles delighted. By the two breasts, however, the two Testaments are understood, from which milk is drawn—that is, the simple and sweet teaching of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1079C], which can suit the simple. “Rejoice,” he says, “with her, so that you may be satisfied with their faith and good works; and be filled from the breasts of her consolation,” that is, of the two Testaments; and be filled in them with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, “so that you may milk and overflow with delights,” that is, so that you may take up their simple faith and abound in their perfection. And this comes “from all her glory,” that is, from knowledge of Christ’s divinity and humanity.

For although the holy Church is one, it nevertheless contains those who have milk—that is, simple faith and understanding—and those who abound in spiritual riches and in knowledge of humanity and divinity. From all these things teachers take what each one possesses, delighting in them.

[Col. 1079D] “For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn toward her,” that is, I will pour upon the Church “as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent”—“I will pour,” understood—“the glory of the nations, which you shall suck.”

This is the river of peace which he pours upon the Church, of which it is said: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God (Psalm LXXXVI),” and: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John VII),” namely, the gifts of the Holy Spirit which we receive in baptism and in the laying-on of the bishop’s hand, and through which we are reconciled to God the Father; or also the teaching of the Gospel.

By “the glory of the nations as an overflowing torrent” he calls their faith, which the Holy Spirit glorified and which is called overflowing because of [Col. 1080A] its speed. For they came swiftly to the faith.

“You shall be carried to the breasts”—“by the apostle and preacher” is understood—that is, to the gifts of the Holy Spirit; or also, you shall be carried to the teaching of the Old and New Testament, because whatever they preach they will first fulfill in their works, so that you may receive guidance from their examples.

“And upon the knees they shall caress you”—“the apostles” is understood—that is, in secret dealings, support, and tender encouragement they will cherish you, so that you may be more easily strengthened in the faith. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a holy sacrifice (Romans XII),” and: “I beseech you as strangers and sojourners (1 Peter II).”

This was said to those who were to believe from the nations through the preaching of the Apostle. It continues:

[Col. 1080B] “As a mother comforts, so I also will comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted.”

The compassionate and merciful Lord compares himself to an eagle, a hen, and a mother, wishing to draw us to his will by his tender affection, as a mother draws her son. He also shows us greater mercy than a mother shows her child: for even if she forgets him, he nevertheless does not forget us, as is said above through the Prophet to Jerusalem: “And if,” he says, “a mother can forget her son, yet I will not forget you.”

And just as eagles guard their young—whose nature, as natural philosophers say, is to place their nests in lofty and inaccessible places lest the serpent injure their offspring, and for this reason they place among them a stone called aëtites, by which all poisons are driven away—so almighty God guards us with every care, lest the ancient serpent, the devil, stain us with the poison of his envy [Col. 1080C]. And he places a stone among us, that is, his faith in our hearts; he is the true stone cut from the mountain without hands.

“Therefore, just as a mother caresses her son, so I will comfort you in the present Church (Daniel II),” in accordance with what I promised you: “Behold,” he says, “I am with you (Matthew XXVIII)”; and in the heavenly Jerusalem you shall be comforted by my presence.

“You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like grass.”

This can be understood in two ways. “You shall see,” O apostles and preachers, the multitude of believers coming to the faith; and your heart shall rejoice over their salvation; and your bones—that is, your virtues—shall cause the fruits of good will and good works to sprout in the hearts of others [Col. 1080D]. For virtues are rightly understood by “bones,” since just as the body stands and is supported by bones, so the soul subsists through virtues.

Alternatively: “You shall see,” O all the faithful, God as he is in the eternal blessedness, in accordance with the saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew V)”; and “your heart shall rejoice without end, because no one shall take your joy from you (John XVI).” And when the day of judgment comes, your bones—that is, your bodies—having received immortality, shall flourish, or shall rise again.

Therefore, just as grasses that had been dried up sprout in springtime after receiving their greenness, so the body on the day of judgment, having received its strength again, shall become green, so that just as body and soul served God in the present age, so in body and soul they may exult [Col. 1081A] in eternal blessedness.

“And the hand of the Lord shall be known over his servants, and he shall be indignant against his enemies.”

These words seem properly to belong to the day of judgment. For the hand of the Lord is the Son, because through him God the Father made all things. He shall be recognized on the day of judgment by his faithful as kind and gracious, but to the ungodly he shall be harsh and their punisher.

Or we may understand the hand of the Lord as his work and power, in accordance with what is said through Moses to Pharaoh: “Behold, the hand of the Lord,” that is, the power of the Lord, “is upon you and upon your people (Exodus V).”

The Lord, then, shall be recognized on the day of judgment over his servants, to whom he shall say: “Come, blessed of my Father (Matthew XXV).” And he shall be indignant against his enemies, the demons and the reprobate, to whom he shall say [Col. 1081B]: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire.”

“For behold, the Lord shall come in fire, and his chariot shall be like a whirlwind, to repay his fury in indignation and his rebuke in a flame of fire.”

These things concern the day of judgment. Of this fire the Psalmist says: “Fire shall go before him (Psalm XLV).” This fire shall be temporary for the elect who have hay and straw, because they shall be purified there and pass into the kingdom of life; but it shall be eternal for the reprobate, whom it shall envelop and lead to eternal punishments.

“And his chariot shall be like a whirlwind,” or storm. By his chariot we should understand the angelic powers that will accompany the Lord to judgment. This does not mean that God is carried in a chariot. Rather, just as he is said to sit upon a throne when he assumes the appearance of a judge, so [Col. 1081C], when he comes to take vengeance and defeat his adversaries, he will be shown in the appearance of a victor and triumphant conqueror.

He will repay the reprobate with his fury in indignation, saying: “Go into the eternal fire (Matthew XXV),” and with his rebuke in a flame of fire, when he says reproachfully: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth. For the terrifying sentence, like fire, will devour them.

“For the Lord shall be judged in fire, and by his sword against all flesh.”

“In fire,” that is, in judgment, he shall be distinguished by the elders of his people, condemning the reprobate by his just judgment, not by force. The sword of God is his word and sentence, concerning which the prophet Amos speaks: “By the sword,” that is, by the sentence of God, all sinners shall perish (Amos IX). Whatever punishes, whatever afflicts, whatever strikes, whatever torments, may be called a sword.

By his sword he shall be judged in relation to all human beings, because when he gives each person what he deserves, all will recognize that he is a just judge and will praise his judgment.

“And those slain by the Lord shall be multiplied.”

Jews, heretics, pagans, and all the condemned reprobate will be found in great number. For here “slaying” means nothing other than the condemnation and destruction of the reprobate.

“Those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in the gardens behind the door within.”

Among the other errors they practiced, the Jews had fountains and baths in their gardens, in which they frequently washed themselves, thinking that they were cleansed even from sins. And there [Col. 1082A] they worshiped idols and indulged in sexual excess before idols and the altars of the gods, with males and females, in the manner of dogs—which is more shameful to say.

And this is what he says: “behind one within,” that is, behind, in their very bodies.

“Those who ate swine’s flesh”—“against the law” is understood—“and abomination,” that is, sacrificial meat, as some nations still do.

“They shall all be consumed together, says the Lord. But I am coming to gather all their works and their thoughts, together with all the nations.”

The voice of the almighty Lord concerning the day of judgment. “Therefore,” he says, “I come to judgment with all nations and languages, to gather all their works and thoughts and repay them according to what they deserve.”

That all nations will come to judgment the Lord makes clear, saying: “When the Son of Man has sat upon the seat of his majesty and begun to judge, then all nations shall be gathered before him [Col. 1082B] (Matthew XXIII).”

For all nations and languages, together with their thoughts, will be brought equally into the midst and judged. The same thing is understood by “languages” as by “nations.”

“And they shall come and see my glory.”

In prophetic books the tenses, as well as the persons, suddenly change. Thus, in the present passage the things stated earlier concern the day of judgment; but the things that now follow concern the Lord’s first coming and the faith of the nations.

“They shall come,” he says, “the faithful from all nations into the Church, and they shall see”—that is, they shall understand with their minds—the glory of my divinity and the glory of my humanity: how, although I am human, I have been exalted above [Col. 1082C] all orders of angels, because I am both human and God.

“And I will place among them a sign, and I will send from them those who have been saved to the nations.”

“I will place,” he says, “in those who have believed the sign of the cross, the sign of Christianity and salvation. From them”—from the Jews, understood—“who have been saved, I will send to the nations,” namely, the apostles, of whom Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom (Isaiah L).”

To which nations he sends them he reveals by adding: “to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, whose people draw the arrow, to Italy and Greece, and to the distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory.”

By “the sea” we should understand this world in general, because just as the sea is always in motion—[Col. 1082D] now its storms rising, now falling—so the world consists now in peace, now in wars, now in famine, now in abundance; now people are born, now they die.

By Africa, he means the whole southern region in which Africa is situated. When he says, “I will send to Lydia those who stretch out the bow,” it is as though he were saying: “I will send them to the Lydians, who are highly skilled archers.”

“To Italy,” that is, to the West; “to all the islands,” and to those who have not heard me, neither through an angel nor through a prophet. Concerning these the prophet says: “Those to whom he has not been announced shall see.” And “they shall announce my glory to the nations”—“those who have been saved from the Jews” is understood.

“And they shall bring,” the apostles, “all your brothers,” O believing Jews, “from all the nations, as a gift to the Lord, on horses and chariots, and on litters, and on mules and carts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord” [Col. 1083A]—that is, to the present Church, and from the present Church to the heavenly one.

Just as the place-names which the Prophet mentioned above signify all the nations and all the places to which the report of apostolic preaching spread, so these animals signify the diversity of nations and peoples coming to the faith.

Those who believed most swiftly came to the Church carried on horses. Those who shone in philosophical learning and moral uprightness came in chariots; among them was Augustine, for example. Through that worldly wisdom they reached the true teaching, raised in mind to heavenly things by the four principal virtues [Col. 1083B].

Those who came carried and helped by the assistance of others came on litters. A litter is a bed covered above; it is also a bier.

In the sacred writings we understand mules in two ways, either positively or negatively. Negatively, because they are inclined toward lust, concerning which it is said: “Do not become like the horse and the mule (Psalm XXXI).”

Positively, as natural philosophers say, because they are sterile in offspring, although devoted to lust. Such was David and Solomon: one of whom is interpreted as “strong of hand,” the other as “peaceful.”

Therefore those who were sterile in wickedness came on mules. Yet David and Solomon had a rider seated in their hearts, one who by his own strength defeated Goliath—that is, the devil—and reconciled us to God the Father through the blood of his Passion [Col. 1083C] (1 Samuel XVII).

Those who came in carts, helped by the assistance of others, came into the Church through the preaching of the apostles and became a gift to the Lord Christ, as the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance (Psalm II).” And the Son himself says: “I have been established king by him over Zion,” that is, over the Church.

It continues:

“And if the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.”

Almighty God had commanded in the Law that everyone should come three times a year to the temple of the Lord, namely at the festivals of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles, and that everyone should offer a gift in the house of the Lord. For the Law commanded as follows: “Take care,” it says, “that you do not appear empty before the Lord (Exodus XII, XXIV).”

[Col. 1083D] And the meaning is this: “Just as,” he says, “the children of Israel, while their religion and temple still stood, used to come with great holiness, joy, and psalms to Jerusalem, offering sacrificial gifts to the Lord, so the apostles will bring your brothers from all nations with joy, on horses and mules and various vehicles, and they will offer a gift to the Lord in a clean vessel.”

This gift which the children of Israel offer daily to the Lord—that is, those who see God with the mind—consists of spiritual sacrifices: namely, faith, charity, chastity, pure prayer, and the other virtues. The clean vessels are holy and undefiled bodies, violated by no contamination.

“And I will take some of them as priests and Levites, says the Lord” [Col. 1084A].

This can be understood in two ways, so that it refers both to Jews and to Gentiles.

“I will take,” he says, “some of them,” that is, from believing Jews, “and they shall be priests and Levites to me.” One of them spoke in this way: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ (1 Corinthians IV).”

For they were priests because they gave sacred responses to the peoples, offered themselves to God, and acquired for him through their preaching others whom they could win, as Paul did Timothy. They were Levites—that is, taken up—because they were chosen by the Lord and taken up for the ministry of preaching.

Alternatively: “I will take some of them”—from the nations who will believe, understood—“and they shall be priests and Levites to me,” with the Jewish priesthood rejected. Hence the Apostle says: “When the priesthood is transferred, the transfer of the Law must [Col. 1084B] also take place (Hebrews VII).”

This can be proved by the fact that now in the holy Church either scarcely any priest or minister, or none at all, is found from among the Jews, while in every Church we see priests and ministers of the mysteries of Christ from the nations, who daily offer the body and blood of Christ for the redemption of the human race, in remembrance of his Passion.

And just as the apostles offered themselves to God, and all others whom they could, so do the priests of the nations. For example, this is what the blessed Hilary did when he offered the blessed Martin to God. They are Levites because they are taken up for this ministry.

“For just as the new heavens and the new earth which I make stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand.”

The things that follow [Col. 1084C] to the end of the book concern the final day of judgment.

In this passage we should understand neither the ethereal heaven through which the seven planets move, nor the sidereal heaven where the remaining stars are, which is also called the firmament; rather, we should understand this aerial heaven, where the clouds and the gathering of clouds are.

This aerial heaven and the earth will be renewed from the form they now have through improvement: for they will be deprived of their coarseness and pass into the subtlety of the ether. And, as John says, “afterward there will always be a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation XXI).”

The meaning is this: just as these two elements, heaven and earth, after they have been renewed, will remain eternally in their newness, so that afterward it will never be said that heaven and earth will pass away [Col. 1084D], so your seed, O apostles, shall stand and remain eternally before me, renewed from all corruption of mortality and sin.

And not only your seed, but also your name—that is, the name of Christianity and of adoption as God’s children—so that another nation may no longer succeed them, as happened to the Jews, but they may remain eternally in eternal blessedness.

By the seed of the apostles we should understand all those who are saved daily through their example and preaching, possessing their faith and imitating their works.

It continues:

“And there shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath.”

In Greek, *mēnē* means “moon,” from which [Col. 1085A] the word *neomenia* is formed, that is, “the beginning of the new moon.” And from *mēnē*, which means “moon,” the word “month” is used among those who begin and end the calendar not according to the course of the sun and the varying lengths of the months, but according to the moon’s circuit, as the Hebrews do.

By “month,” therefore, he wishes the moon to be understood. And this moon is the holy Church, of which it is said in the Psalms: “You shall remain with the sun and before the moon, throughout generations and generations (Psalm LXXI).” And in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun (Song of Songs VI)?”

What he says, “There shall be month after month,” is as though he were saying: “There shall be a future Church from the present Church,” because the future Church will be built from the present Church; and that Church which now reigns with Christ [Col. 1085B] and which will come with him to judgment will be completed.

Natural philosophers, whose concern is to discuss heavenly matters, say that the moon does not possess its own light but is illuminated by the sun’s rays. For it is always filled and shines on that side of its orb on which it is nearer to the sun.

Therefore the Church is rightly compared to the moon: just as the moon receives whatever splendor it has from the sun, so the Church receives whatever good it has from Christ, who is the true sun, concerning whom the prophet says: “For those who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise.”

And just as the moon now increases in light and now decreases, so the holy Church now grows in peace and now diminishes in persecutions.

What follows—“and there shall be sabbath after sabbath”—likewise concerns the rest of the elect. For “sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” There shall therefore be sabbath after sabbath [Col. 1085C], that is, whoever has rested here from evil work shall rest there in eternal blessedness.

“All flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord.”

This may specifically refer to the elect and generally to the whole human race. “All flesh shall come,” he says—that is, every elect person on the day of judgment—“to worship before my face,” that is, always in my presence; or, in that very judgment, both the good and the evil, terrified by indescribable fear, shall worship the power of almighty God, in accordance with the saying: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God,” that is, every human being (Isaiah LX).

“And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me.”

Those who go out are understood to be the elect alone. [Col. 1085D] “They shall go out,” he says—not spatially, but in understanding, or in clear vision—so that they may be inflamed still more to praise God. And they shall see the corpses of men, not only of the Jews [Col. 1086A], concerning whom it is said: “I begot and exalted children, but they themselves despised me (Isaiah I),” but the corpses of all the reprobate who transgressed against God, violating the commandments of the natural or written law.

Nor is it surprising if the elect, now immortal, will see the reprobate condemned, since the prophets, while still mortal, deserved to see all these things through understanding.

“Because woman was taken from man, she is the body of man (Genesis II)”: therefore women too are included under the name “men.” They are called corpses because they will fall into eternal condemnation. Hence the demons themselves may also be called corpses, since they likewise will fall into the punishments of Gehenna. They too are called “men” by the Lord: “An enemy,” he says, “has done this (Matthew XIII).”

“Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall remain until the satisfaction of sight for all flesh.”

[Col. 1086B] The worm and fire in this passage may be understood as the conscience of sinners, which torments all who have been placed in punishments because, having served vices in the present age, they lacked the good for which they might have been rewarded.

Hence it is said in one place: “The moth consumes the garment, and the worm gnaws the wood, and fire devours the logs; so grief and sorrow torture the heart of a man.”

This fire shall not be extinguished, and the worm shall not die, because they will remain eternally in punishments and will always be tormented by their own conscience.

It may also be understood in this way: one may believe that in hell there is material fire, and likewise a worm, which eat and devour their bodies—although some have falsely said that after the general resurrection the body will be aerial and will dissolve into thin air [Col. 1086C].

Their worm will therefore not die and their fire will not be extinguished because all the reprobate will be their food, and the reprobate themselves will be the material of the fire and the worm; these live as long as they have material on which to feed.

What follows—“all the reprobate shall be until the satisfaction of sight for all flesh,” that is, for every elect person—can be understood in three ways:

Either because the vision of the elect will be satisfied by seeing them separated from themselves through the just judgment of God and deprived of the power which they had exercised over the innocent;

or because they will be condemned in such a way that the righteous will no longer wish for or ask for vengeance, as they do now, saying: “How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood (Revelation VI)?”

[Col. 1086D] Or their satisfaction will consist in this: they will not rejoice over the condemnation of the reprobate, but over their own liberation. Amen.
